en: Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle One.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
1. The *Maulī Bhūmi* (Basic Section). Within the *Maulī Bhūmi*, the first is the *Pañcavijñānakāyasamprayuktā Bhūmi*. What is the *Yogācārabhūmi*?
It refers to the seventeen *bhūmis*.
What are the seventeen?
The summary verse says:
The mind associated with the five consciousnesses, The three types of samādhi such as with vitarka and vicāra,
And both the state with mind and the state without mind.
Established through hearing, reflection, and cultivation— thus possessing the three vehicles,
both with support and without support— this is called the seventeen stages.
The first is the stage associated with the five bodies of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya-saṃprayukta-bhūmi*).
Second is the stage of the mental faculty;
third is the stage with both vitarka and vicāra;
fourth is the stage with no vitarka and only vicāra.
Fifth, the stage without vitarka and vicāra;
sixth, the stage of meditative equipoise (samāhita-bhūmi);
seventh, the stage not of meditative equipoise (asamāhita-bhūmi).
Eighth is the stage with mind;
ninth is the stage without mind;
tenth is the stage consisting of what is heard.
Eleventh is the stage consisting of reflection;
twelfth is the stage consisting of cultivation;
thirteenth is the stage of the śrāvaka.
Fourteenth is the stage of the Pratyekabuddha.
Fifteenth is the stage of the Bodhisattva.
Sixteenth is the stage with remainder (sopadhiśeṣa-bhūmi).
Seventeenth is the stage of the nirvana without remainder.
Thus, these seventeen stages have been briefly explained;
they are called the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
What is the stage associated with the five groups of consciousness?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of the five groups of consciousness,
as well as their bases and their objects.
Those are their associates and those are their activities;
thus, they are collectively termed the "Stage Associated with the Five Collections of Consciousness.
What are the five collections of consciousness?
That is to say: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness,
nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness,
and visible forms.
Regarding its supports:
the simultaneous support is the eye;
the immediately preceding support is the mind.
The support of the seeds refers to this very ālayavijñāna, which comprises all seeds,
is the appropriated basis,
and is subsumed under maturation.
Thus, two kinds of bases have been briefly explained:
namely, the material and the non-material.
The eye is material; the others are non-material.
The eye is that which is derived from the four great elements;
it is the translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) that serves as the basis for visual consciousness;
it is invisible and possesses resistance.
This refers to the consciousness that has passed away immediately prior to the visual consciousness—
the all-seed consciousness (sarvabījaka-vijñāna)—
which, since beginningless time, has delighted in and clung to conceptual proliferation (prapañca).
With habitual tendencies as its cause,
the resultant maturation consciousness (vipākavijñāna) that arises possesses all seeds;
as for its object of perception (ālambana):
That is to say, form is visible and possesses resistance;
this, moreover, is of many kinds.
Briefly stated, there are three types:
namely, color (varṇa-rūpa), shape (saṃsthāna-rūpa), and informative form (vijñapti-rūpa). As for color:
That is to say: blue, yellow, red, and white;
light and shadow, brightness and darkness;
clouds, smoke, dust, and mist.
And there is the single manifest color of space.
As for shape, it refers to long, short, square, and round.
Coarse and subtle, correct and incorrect, high and low, and color.
As for manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*),
it refers to taking up, discarding, contracting, and extending.
The colors of such things as walking, standing, sitting, and reclining;
furthermore, there are manifest colors (varṇa).
That is to say, "color" refers to that which is manifested as the objective domain of visual consciousness;
"shape" refers to that which is an accumulated color characterized by distinctions such as long, short, and so forth.
Manifest form refers to this very accumulation of matter that arises and ceases in a continuous succession;
due to causes of transformation, it does not arise again in its original location but instead shifts to a different place.
They arise either immediately or with an interval;
they arise with distinctions of proximity or distance;
or they arise as transformations right in this very place.
This is called informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*).
Furthermore, visible color (*varṇa-rūpa*) refers to distinctions such as light and so forth.
"Shape-color" (saṃsthāna-rūpa) refers to the distinctions in the accumulation [of atoms] such as long, short, and so forth.
"Informative color" (vijñapti-rūpa) refers to...
That is to say, it refers to the specific movements that arise based on karmic activity;
all such manifest colors and shapes of form are the objects of the eye.
The objective domain of the eye;
the range of activity of visual consciousness;
the objective domain of visual consciousness.
The object of visual consciousness,
the range of mental consciousness,
and the domain of mental consciousness.
These are the distinctions among the names for the objects of mental consciousness.
Furthermore, this very form is of three kinds.
That is to say: whether it be a beautiful visible form,
an ugly visible form,
or a visible form that is different from both.
It appears as form.
Its companions are the various mental factors (caitta-dharma) that are co-existent and associated with it.
That is to say:
attention, contact, feeling, perception, volition,
and all other mental factors associated with and co-arising with visual consciousness.
Furthermore, those various dharmas have the same object of focus but not the same mode of apprehension;
they arise together, are associated, and function individually.
Furthermore, all those [phenomena] arise individually from their own respective seeds.
Regarding those who perform actions,
it should be known that there are six types.
That which merely discerns its own object of perception is called the first stage;
it merely discerns its own specific characteristic.
It cognizes only the present;
it cognizes for only a single moment.
Furthermore, there are two types of karma.
That is to say: it evolves in accordance with the mental consciousness;
it evolves in accordance with the wholesome or the defiled;
and it evolves in accordance with the initiation of karma.
Furthermore, that which can take up agreeable and disagreeable fruits is the sixth karma. Section 2:
The Five Characteristics of Ear-Consciousness. What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of ear-consciousness?
This refers to the discernment of sound based on the ear;
its "coexistent support" (sahabhū-āśraya) is the ear itself.
The immediate antecedent support is the mind (manas).
The seed support is...
This refers to the ālayavijñāna containing all seeds.
"Ear" refers to the translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) that serves as the basis for ear-consciousness and is derived from the four great elements.
It is without vision and possesses resistance.
The mind and its seeds are to be analyzed as previously explained.
Its object of perception is sound.
There is that which is non-visible and resistant;
this is further of many kinds,
such as the sound of a conch shell, or the sound of large and small drums.
The sounds of dance, song, and various musical instruments;
the sounds of theatrical performances and shouting; the voices of women and men;
and the sounds of wind and forests.
Clear sounds and indistinct sounds;
meaningful sounds and meaningless sounds;
inferior, middling, and superior sounds.
The sounds of rivers and such;
the clamorous sounds of strife and contention;
and the sounds of receiving, upholding, and expounding [the Dharma].
The sound of the determination of doctrinal arguments;
there are many such types of sounds as these,
which are here summarized into three categories.
That is to say: sound caused by appropriated primary elements;
sound caused by non-appropriated primary elements;
and sound caused by both appropriated and non-appropriated primary elements.
First, there is sound conditioned solely by internal factors;
next, sound conditioned solely by external factors;
and finally, sound conditioned by both internal and external factors.
This, moreover, is of three kinds:
namely, agreeable sounds and disagreeable sounds.
The term "contrary to both.
Furthermore, "sound" refers to resonance, phonemes, and roars.
Designations such as the distinctions of praise and so forth are the domain of the ear and the objective sphere of the ear.
The range of auditory consciousness,
the objective field of auditory consciousness,
and the focal object of auditory consciousness.
The range of mental consciousness,
the object-sphere of mental consciousness,
and the focal object of mental consciousness.
Its companions and its functions should be understood as being like those of visual consciousness.
Section 3: The Five Characteristics of Olfactory Consciousness. What is the intrinsic nature of olfactory consciousness?
It is the discernment of odors based upon the nose.
That which serves as its basis is the coexistent support,
namely the nose.
The immediate antecedent support is the mind;
the seed support is... [the ālayavijñāna].
This refers to the ālayavijñāna containing all seeds.
The nose is that which is derived from the four great elements;
it is the translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) that serves as the support for olfactory consciousness.
It is non-visible and resistant.
The mind and its seeds are to be analyzed as previously explained.
Its object of perception is fragrance.
There is no seeing, yet there is resistance.
This, moreover, is of many kinds:
namely, pleasant fragrances, unpleasant fragrances, and neutral fragrances.
The nose perceives the scents of roots, stalks, flowers, leaves, and fruits.
There are many such types of scents.
Furthermore, as for "scent":
This refers to the various designations such as "that which is heard by the nose," "that which is apprehended by the nose," and "that which is smelled by the nose."
This is the range of the nose, the objective sphere of the nose,
and the range of nose-consciousness.
The objective sphere of olfactory consciousness;
that which is the focal object of olfactory consciousness;
that which is the domain of mental consciousness.
The objective sphere of the mental consciousness, its focal object,
its accompanying factors, and its function should be understood as previously explained.
What is the intrinsic nature of tongue-consciousness?
It is the discernment of tastes based upon the tongue.
As for its basis:
The simultaneous support (sahabhū-āśraya) is the tongue;
the immediately preceding support (samanantara-āśraya) is...
This refers to the mind as the seed-support; that is,
the ālayavijñāna containing all seeds.
The tongue is that which is derived from the four great elements;
it is the translucent matter (rūpa-prasāda) that serves as the basis for tongue-consciousness (jihvā-vijñāna).
It is invisible and possesses resistance (sapratigha).
The mind and its seeds are analyzed as previously stated.
Their object of perception is taste,
which is invisible and possesses resistance.
This, moreover, is of many kinds:
namely, bitter, sour, pungent, sweet, salty, and bland;
agreeable and disagreeable.
If one abandons the location where it is tasted by the tongue,
furthermore, "taste" refers to that which should be tasted, swallowed, or chewed.
"Should be drunk, should be licked, should be sucked,
should be enjoyed"— such various designations as these are the domain of the tongue.
The domain of the tongue;
that which is traversed by tongue-consciousness;
the objective sphere of tongue-consciousness.
The object-conditioned by tongue-consciousness;
the range of mental consciousness;
the sphere of mental consciousness.
The objects of consciousness,
its associates, and its functions should be understood as previously explained.
What is the intrinsic nature of body-consciousness?
This means that the discernment of contact is based on the body;
its support is the co-existent support (sahabhū-āśraya).
That is to say, the body is the immediate antecedent support;
that is to say, the mind.
The basis of the seeds refers to the ālayavijñāna containing all seeds.
"Body" refers to that which is produced from the four great elements.
The pure matter that serves as the basis for body-consciousness is invisible and possesses resistance.
The mind and the seeds are to be analyzed as previously explained.
That which is its object is contact;
it is invisible and possesses resistance.
This, moreover, is of many kinds:
namely, earth, water, fire, and wind;
lightness, heaviness, smoothness, and roughness.
Cold, hunger, thirst, satiety;
weakness, slowness, urgency; illness, old age, death, itching;
distress, stickiness, fatigue, respiration; softness, timidity, courage.
There are many such types of contact.
Furthermore, these are of three kinds:
namely, pleasant contact, unpleasant contact, and neutral contact.
The object of touch abandoned;
the object of touch experienced by the body.
Furthermore, as for "touch":
This refers to the various specific names for that which is rubbed or touched, such as hard or soft,
moving or warm, and so forth.
This is the range of activity of the body,
the objective sphere of the body,
and the range of activity of body-consciousness.
The objective sphere of body-consciousness,
the focal object of body-consciousness,
and the range of mental consciousness.
The sphere of the mental consciousness,
the object-condition of the mental consciousness,
its accompaniments, and its functions should be understood as previously described.
If it arises improperly,
the eye-consciousness that would be produced will necessarily not arise;
it requires that the eye be unimpaired.
When a visible form appears before one,
it is capable of producing mental attention (manasikāra),
which then arises in full presence.
Only then can the visual consciousness that is produced arise; as it is with the arising of visual consciousness, so it is for the others.
It should be understood that the same applies up to body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).
Furthermore, by means of the arising of eye-consciousness,
three types of mind are obtainable.
In their respective order,
these are: the mind of sudden encounter and the mind of seeking.
The mind of determination:
the first occurs in visual consciousness;
the second occurs in mental consciousness.
Only after the mind has reached a state of determination do defilement and purity arise;
it is only thereafter that the eye-consciousness as a resultative flow (niṣyanda) occurs.
It revolves as wholesome or unwholesome,
yet it does so not by the power of its own conceptualization,
until this mind moves toward another object.
During that period of time,
the two consciousnesses of the eye and the mind continue to evolve in succession, whether they are wholesome or defiled.
Just as it is with the arising of visual consciousness,
so it should be understood for all others, up to tactile consciousness.
Furthermore, one should contemplate the supports of the five consciousnesses as being like the vehicle of one traveling to another region;
their objects of perception are like the destination for which one acts.
The companions are like fellow travelers;
karma is like one's own functional capacity.
Furthermore, there are distinctions.
One should contemplate the five consciousnesses as being like a householder’s home,
and their objects of perception as being like the household goods one enjoys.
The companions are like servants and attendants;
karma is like their activity.

2. Within the *Manobhūmi* (The Section on the Mind), the second part of the *Manobhūmi*: the first [section] has already explained the *Pañcavijñānakāyasamprayuktā Bhūmiḥ* (The Stage Associated with the Five Groups of Consciousness).
What is the mental stage?
This also should be understood as having five aspects, namely:
by way of its intrinsic nature.
Because it is their basis,
because it is their object,
and because it is their accompaniment.
Because of those karmic actions,
it is the nature of the basis that is followed by all seeds,
and the nature of the basis that is adhered to and clung to.
The entity that is capable of appropriation is the ālayavijñāna,
which is comprised of maturation (vipāka).
"Mind" (manas) refers to the ever-active mind (kliṣṭamanas) and the mind that has immediately ceased following the six groups of consciousness.
Consciousness (vijñāna) refers to the present discernment of an objective sphere (ālambana-viṣaya).
Regarding the two items [concerning] the support (āśraya) and its support:
the immediate antecedent support (samanantara-āśraya).
This refers to the mind (*manas*),
the seed-support (*bījāśraya*).
That is to say, it is the ālayavijñāna containing all seeds, as previously described.
Section Three: Objects of Perception.
Regarding those objects of perception, it refers to all phenomena as they correspond;
specifically, those that are the objects of perception for what is not shared [with others].
Namely, the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations; the unconditioned;
invisible and non-obstructive matter;
the six internal bases; and all seeds.

Section 4: The Retinue. As for that retinue, it consists of attention (*manasikāra*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Faith, shame, embarrassment, non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion;
diligence, pliancy, heedfulness, equanimity, and non-harming;
as well as attachment, aversion, ignorance, pride, views, and doubt.
Anger, enmity, concealment, vexation, envy, parsimony, deceit, guile, pride, and harmfulness;
lack of shame and lack of dread;
lethargy and restlessness.
Lack of faith, laziness, heedlessness;
wrong desire, wrong resolve, forgetfulness, distraction, lack of correct awareness;
regret, sleep, vitarka, and vicāra.
Such categories as these,
which possess associated mental factors (caitta),
are called "associates" (sahāya).
They have the same object of focus but not the same mode of activity;
they exist simultaneously,
yet each functions individually.
Each arises from its own seed and is mutually associated,
possessing specific modes of activity (ākāra).
It has an object of perception,
it has a basis,
and it performs an action.
That which is able to discern its own object of focus is called the initial stage;
furthermore, it is able to discern both specific characteristics and general characteristics.
Furthermore, one is able to discern the past, future, and present worlds;
moreover, one discerns them moment by moment,
or discerns them as a continuous succession.
Furthermore, it acts as the primary cause (pravṛtti) and the concomitant cause (anuvṛtti) for the karma of all phenomena, whether pure or impure;
it further appropriates desirable and undesirable fruits;
and it further induces other groups of consciousness.
Furthermore, it can also act as a cause to give rise to the body of resultant consciousness (*niṣyanda-vijñāna*) and other bodies of consciousness that possess superior functional activity.
That is to say: the object of conceptualization,
the object of deliberation,
and those who are intoxicated or insane.
Whether dreaming or awake,
whether in a state of fainting or alertness,
it is that which can initiate bodily and vocal actions.
Whether one is able to become free from desire, or falls away from freedom from desire;
whether one severs the roots of goodness or reconnects them;
or whether one dies or is born, and so forth.
How is the object of focus (ālambana) differentiated?
It is by way of seven kinds of differentiation, namely:
differentiation by signs (nimitta-vikalpa).
Non-conceptual discrimination,
spontaneous discrimination,
and investigative discrimination.
Investigative discrimination,
afflicted discrimination,
and non-afflicted discrimination.

Discrimination of signs refers to the discrimination arising in those who have mastered linguistic conventions regarding objects previously experienced through the accomplishment of the sense faculties.
Discrimination of the signless refers to all discrimination that follows what was previously induced,
as well as the discrimination of infants and others who are unskilled in linguistic conventions.
Spontaneous conceptualization refers to all conceptualization that functions spontaneously in accordance with the power of an object present before one.
Investigative conceptualization refers to the conceptualization that arises from the investigation and seeking of all phenomena.
Discerning conceptualization refers to...
This refers to the conceptualization that arises from the investigation, analysis, and formal establishment of what has already been sought and what has already been examined;
it is defiled conceptualization.
That is to say: accompanied by longing for the past,
accompanied by desire for the future,
and accompanied by attachment to the present.
All conceptual constructions:
whether they are conceptual constructions of desire or conceptual constructions of hatred.
If it is a harmful discrimination,
or a discrimination that arises in association with any one of the afflictions or secondary afflictions.
Non-defiled discrimination refers to that which is either wholesome or indeterminate;
it is called the discrimination of renunciation.
It is the discrimination of non-ill will and the discrimination of non-harming,
or it is associated with any one of the wholesome factors such as faith.
Or the various types of discrimination pertaining to the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*), the fields of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and all transformations (*nairmāṇika*);
such categories as these are called objects of discrimination (*vikalpa-ālambana*).
What is the object of deliberation?
It refers to that which is induced by correct reasoning and that which is induced by incorrect reasoning.
It is neither induced by what is irrational nor by what is rational.
That which is induced by what is rational means not superimposing that which does not truly exist.
It is like the four perversions:
namely, the perversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent,
and the perversion of perceiving suffering as pleasure.
Regarding the inversion of perceiving the impure as pure and the inversion of perceiving the non-self as self,
these do not diminish that which truly exists.
As with various wrong views—
namely, the practice of wrong views such as the denial of giving and so forth—
or the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna).
One understands all objects of knowledge as they truly are;
or, through thoroughly purified supramundane wisdom,
one realizes all phenomena that are objects of knowledge as they truly are.
This is called that which is induced by correct reasoning (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
One should know that what is contrary to this is induced by incorrect reasoning (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
As for that which is neither induced by correct reasoning nor induced by incorrect reasoning:
This refers to the thorough investigation of all phenomena by means of indeterminate wisdom (*avyākṛta-prajñā*).
This is called the object of deliberation (*pravicaya-ālambana*).
What is intoxication (*mada*)?
That is to say, it is due to the weakness of one's physical constitution,
or due to not being accustomed to drinking,
or due to drinking excessively.
Or, because of drinking in excess,
one becomes intoxicated and deranged.
What is meant by "madness"?
That is to say, it is induced by prior karma,
or by the derangement of the elements,
or by the loss of mental composure due to terror.
Either through the striking of the vital points (marmans) or by being possessed by malevolent spirits,
one may fall into madness.
What is a dream?
It refers to that which occurs due to a constitution that is weak and inferior,
or due to the fault of exhaustion.
Either due to being weighed down by food,
or due to mental attention directed toward the sign of darkness,
or due to resting from all activities.
Either due to habitual practice of sleep,
or induced by another,
such as by the fanning of a fan.
Either by means of vidyā-mantras,
or by means of medicinal herbs,
or by means of majestic spiritual power.
And one gives rise to torpor and dreams.
What is awakening?
It refers to when one who has increased sleep cannot overcome extreme exhaustion.
Because one who has performed an action intends to sleep;
or because one is led by another from a dream to wakefulness.
What is fainting?
That is to say, due to disturbances caused by wind or heat,
or due to being beaten,
or due to purging.
For example, when diarrhea and hemorrhaging occur in excess,
or when one faints due to extreme exertion,
how does one regain consciousness?
This refers to emerging again after having been overcome by despondency.
How does one initiate bodily and vocal actions?
It is because the knowledge that precedes the initiation of bodily and vocal actions acts as the forerunner.
Next, because of the desire to arise;
next, because of the arising of effort;
and next, preceded by that which accords with effort.
Because the winds of bodily and vocal karma revolve,
from these arise bodily and vocal karma.
How does one become free from desire?
That is to say: because of the accomplishment of the faculties that accord with the departure from desire;
because of obtaining the conforming instructions from others;
and because of being far removed from those obstacles.
Through skillful means and correct cultivation,
by means of non-erroneous reflection,
one is finally able to become free from desire.
What is falling away from detachment?
It refers to one who, by virtue of having dull faculties,
newly cultivates the categories of wholesome qualities.
Because they repeatedly contemplate those signs of form;
because they practice in accordance with the factors leading to decline;
and because they are obstructed by afflictions.
Because they are influenced by evil friends,
they fall away from the state of detachment from desire.
How, then, do they sever their roots of goodness?
This refers to those of sharp faculties who,
because they have accomplished the practice of superiorly unwholesome intentions and dharmas,
and because they have come to associate with such evil friends, [fall into error].
Because his fetter of wrong view is extremely heavy, perfected, and brought to its ultimate limit;
because he has attained fearlessness regarding the manifestation of all evils;
and because he lacks compassion.
It is capable of severing the roots of goodness.
In this context, the seeds are also called "roots of goodness," and non-attachment,
non-hatred, and so forth are likewise called "roots of goodness."

It is merely by establishing a continuity that is contrary to the manifest operation of wholesome roots that one is said to have "severed the wholesome roots," not because their seeds have been permanently uprooted.
What is the restoration of the roots of virtue?
It refers to [restoring them] by virtue of having naturally sharp faculties,
and by seeing one's close friends practicing meritorious deeds.
Because they approach virtuous persons and hear the true Dharma,
and because they give rise to doubt that leads to the realization of certainty,
they restore their roots of goodness.
What is death?
It refers to dying due to the exhaustion of the life-span.
This, moreover, is of three kinds.
That is to say: because of the exhaustion of the life-span;
because of the exhaustion of merit;
and because of not avoiding unevenness.
One should know that this is also death at the proper time or at an improper time.
It may occur through a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, or a neutral mind.
What is death due to the exhaustion of the life-span?
It is like a person who dies because the full extent of their lifespan has been exhausted;
this is called death at the proper time (*kāla-mṛtyu*).
What is death due to the exhaustion of merit?
Just as there is one who dies due to a deficiency of life-sustaining requisites,
how is it that one dies by not avoiding what is uneven?
As the Blessed One has said, there are nine causes and nine conditions.
One dies before the full span of one's life.
What are the nine?
They are, namely, eating without moderation.
Consuming what is unsuitable for one's constitution;
eating again before previous food has been digested;
and giving rise to illness without vomiting it up.
Having become accustomed to it, they maintain it;
they do not resort to medicine,
nor do they know whether it is detrimental or beneficial to themselves.
Engaging in unchaste conduct at improper times or in excessive measure is called untimely death.
What is death with a virtuous mind?
It is just as when someone, at the time of death,
personally recollects the wholesome dharmas they previously practiced,
or is reminded of them by another.
Due to these causes and conditions,
at that time, wholesome factors such as faith and so forth manifest in the mind,
continuing until coarse perception manifests.
When subtle mental formations proceed,
the wholesome mind immediately relinquishes them and abides solely in a neutral state of mind. Why is this so?
At that time, he is unable to recollect the wholesome deeds he previously practiced,
nor can others cause him to remember them.
What is death with an unwholesome mind?
It is as when someone whose life is about to end recollects the unwholesome dharmas they were habituated to in the past.
Alternatively, they may be reminded by another;
at that time, unwholesome states such as greed and hatred,
along with various perceptions ranging from coarse to subtle, manifest within their minds.
As previously well explained,
furthermore, when one dies with a virtuous mind, one passes away in peace;
as death approaches, one's body is not oppressed by extreme painful sensations.
One who dies with a malevolent mind passes away in suffering and distress;
at the moment of death, their body is oppressed by extremely intense painful sensations.
Furthermore, one who dies with a virtuous mind perceives unconfused visual forms.
One who dies with an unwholesome mind perceives disordered forms and signs.
What is death with a neutral mind?
It refers to one who has practiced wholesome or unwholesome deeds, or one who has practiced neither.
At the time of death, one cannot remember [the object] oneself,
nor is there anyone else to cause one to remember;
at that moment, one dies with a mind that is neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
Neither dying in peace nor dying in distress, when a person who has practiced both wholesome and unwholesome deeds is about to pass away,
they may spontaneously recollect the wholesome and unwholesome deeds previously committed.
Or, when prompted by another to recall,
at that time his mind focuses exclusively on that which was most strongly reinforced through repeated practice,
while he forgets everything else.
If both have been equally cultivated through repeated practice,
then at that time,
he either recalls it himself as first occurred or is reminded by another.
Only this [thought] is not abandoned, and no other thought arises.
At that time, he passes away due to the predominant power of two causes:
namely, the predominant power of the cause consisting in attachment to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
