and by means of the fire element, it is matured.
Hardness arises from the absence of moisture.
By means of the wind element, the limbs and joints are differentiated and each is established in its proper place.
Furthermore, there is the consciousness containing all seeds.
Although there are causes for the purity or impurity of one's own body within the process of birth,
attachment to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) alone is the predominant cause;
this applies to the results such as lineage, physical appearance, strength, lifespan, and material resources.
Thus, pure and impure karma is the supreme cause.
Furthermore, ordinary worldlings, with respect to their own bodies,
conceive of them as "I" and "mine," and give rise to the conceit of self.
All noble ones perceive that [existence] is nothing but suffering.
Furthermore, during the stage of dwelling in the womb,
there is a feeling of its own nature that is neither painful nor pleasant, which increases in dependence upon consciousness.
Only this nature of sensation is comprised within maturation;
all other sensations are either produced by maturation or are themselves maturation.
Alternatively, they arise from objective conditions;
furthermore, painful and pleasant sensations may manifest from conditions at a single moment.
At times it does not arise.
Furthermore, the substance of the seed has continued in an uninterrupted succession from beginningless time;
although its nature exists from the beginningless past, [it may still cease].
Nevertheless, because they are perfumed by the distinctions of pure and impure karma,
and are directed toward the repeated appropriation of heterogeneous ripened fruits,
they are described as "new."
If a fruit has already arisen,
this seed is said to have already yielded its fruit;
by this principle, the continuity of the cycle of birth and death flows on without interruption.
This continues until they have attained parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, those seeds that have not yet yielded their fruit may be destined to be experienced in the next life (upapadyavedanīya).
Or it may be experienced in a subsequent life;
even after passing through hundreds of thousands of kalpas,
it arises from its own seed.
The entire self-body is further produced in its full completion;
although other fruits arise necessarily from their own seeds,
this occurs until the limit of the lifespan is reached.
At that time, this particular type is said to have already yielded its fruit;
however, because the seeds of the remaining self-bodies have not yet yielded their fruit,
they are not called "having already yielded their fruit."
Furthermore, there are seeds within this very body that ought to undergo maturation,
yet they do not do so due to the deficiency of conditions.
Because it is subsumed under the category of indeterminate experience according to its circumstances,
yet these seeds likewise abide only in this state; therefore,
within each individual self-entity, [they remain so].
All possess the seeds of their own respective natures;
if there is attachment to one place,
it is said that there is attachment to all places.
If one attains detachment with respect to one place,
it is said that one attains detachment with respect to all places.
Furthermore, regarding all the seeds within the various personal aggregates (ātmabhāva):
If it is comprised within the category of afflictions (*kleśapakṣa*),
it is called "heavy dysfunction" (*dausthulya*) and also called "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*);
if it is comprised within the category of maturation (*vipākapaṅkta*), [it is not so called].
Furthermore, those seeds subsumed under other categories of the indeterminate (avyākṛta) are called only "dysfunctions" (dausthulya) and not "latent dispositions" (anuśaya). However,
seeds subsumed under the categories of wholesome factors such as faith (śraddhā) and so forth [are both].
It is not termed "gross heaviness" (*dausthulya*), nor is it a "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*). Why is this?
Because when these phenomena arise, the basis—the personal continuum—is characterized solely by functional capacity, not by incapacity.
Therefore, the entire basis of the self-substance is accompanied by coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) and is produced from coarse heaviness.
Because its intrinsic nature is coarse and heavy (*dauṣṭhulya*),
the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, establish it as suffering;
that is to say, by virtue of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Furthermore, these various seeds have many different names; that is to say,
they are called "elements" (*dhātu*).
It is called lineage,
it is called intrinsic nature,
and it is called cause.
It is called the transitory collection (satkāya),
it is called conceptual proliferation (prapañca),
and it is called the storehouse consciousness (ālaya).
Name-and-form is called suffering;
it is the basis for the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
and it is the basis for the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*).
Such distinctions of this kind should be understood.
Furthermore, at the time of parinirvāṇa, those who practice purity have already attained the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*);
they abandon the basis for all seeds of defiled phenomena and [retain] the basis for all seeds of wholesome and neutral phenomena.
It causes conditions to become deficient and further attains mastery over internal conditions;
furthermore, within the womb, it passes thirty-eight weeks.
This embryo is fully endowed with all its limbs;
from this point onward,
it passes another four days before finally being born.
As the Bhagavān has explained at length in the Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra,
this refers to one who is fully developed,
remaining for either nine months or even longer than that.
If it lasts for only eight months,
this is called "complete," but not "perfectly complete."
If it lasts for seven months or six months,
it is not called "complete," or it is deficient.
Furthermore, during the stage of the six sense bases within this embryonic development,
it grows and is nourished by the coarse nutritional essences produced from what the mother eats.
It should be understood that during the subtle stages such as the kalala and so forth,
growth occurs through the nourishment of subtle nutritive essence (*rasa*).
Furthermore, there are eight distinct stages of this embryonic development.
What are the eight?
They are the stage of kalala,
the stage of arbuda, and so forth.
The stage of the closed corpse (peśī),
the stage of the solid mass (ghana),
and the stage of the fleshy protuberance (praśākhā).
Regarding the positions of hair, body hair, and nails;
the position of the sense organs; and the position of the physical form:
if they have already coagulated and solidified within the embryo, yet remain fluid internally.
It is called *kalala*.
If it is like curd on both the surface and inside, but has not yet reached the stage of flesh, it is called *arbuda*.
If it has already become flesh yet remains extremely soft, [it is called *peśī*].
When it is named peśī,
and has become firm and thick enough to be slightly touched,
it is named ghana.
This very mass of flesh grows until the characteristics of the limbs appear;
this stage is called *praśākhā*.
From this point onward...
The stage at which hair, body hair, and nails first appear is called this stage.
From this point onward,
the development of the sense faculties such as the eye is called the stage of the faculties (*indriya-avasthā*).
From this point onward,
the locus upon which that [consciousness] relies becomes clearly manifest;
this is termed the "position of form" (*ākṛti-sthāna*).
Furthermore, within the womb,
either due to the power of prior karma or because the mother does not avoid the influence of uneven forces, winds that arise accordingly are produced.
It causes this embryo to undergo transformation and arise with respect to its hair,
complexion, skin, or other limbs and members.
Regarding the transformation of the hair:
This refers to karma created in previous lives that can induce such evil and unwholesome results,
as well as the mother’s frequent consumption of substances with tastes such as ash and salt, whether by drinking or eating.
As for the cause by which the hair and body hair of this embryo become sparse and its complexion undergoes transformation,
it is due to the causes of prior karma as previously described.
Furthermore, due to the mother’s present condition of associating with warmth and heat,
the fetus within the womb develops a dark, murky color; moreover,
if the mother associates with extremely cold rooms and the like, [the same occurs].
It causes that fetal mass to become extremely white;
furthermore, because the mother consumes much hot food,
it causes that fetal mass to become extremely red.
Regarding the transformation of the skin:
this occurs due to the causes of past karma as previously described,
and by reason of the present condition of the mother’s excessive indulgence in sexual desire.
It causes that fetal development to emerge with skin afflictions such as scabs, ringworm, or leprosy;
as for those born with deformed limbs,
this occurs due to the causes of prior karma, as previously explained.
Furthermore, due to the mother’s habitual practice of running, leaping, and jumping, and her failure to maintain proper deportment or avoid uneven ground during the present conditions,
the various sense faculties and limbs of that fetus are born deficient.
Furthermore, if that embryo is to become a female,
it dwells on the mother's left side, leaning against her spine and facing her abdomen;
if it is to become a male, [it dwells on the right side].
It remains leaning against the mother’s right flank, with its belly toward her abdomen and its back toward her spine.
Furthermore, when this embryo has reached full development,
the mother is unable to bear the weight of this heavy fetus.
Internal winds then give rise to great suffering and distress.
Furthermore, the "parting wind" (vibhajana-vāyu), produced by the retribution of karma, arises within this embryonic sac,
causing the head to turn downward and the feet to turn upward.
Wrapped in the fetal membrane, it moves toward the birth canal;
at the moment of actual emergence, the membrane then tears,
splitting apart between the two armpits.
The moment of emerging from the birth canal is called the stage of actual birth.
Following birth, one gradually encounters the sense-contact of the birth-moment,
namely, visual contact through to mental contact.
Next, they further fall into the conventional designation of affairs,
namely, by following and learning worldly speech and discourse;
thereafter, they become attached to family life.
That is to say, because they have reached full growth and their faculties are perfected,
they subsequently perform various karmas.
That is to say, one engages in worldly crafts and occupations,
and subsequently experiences objects,
namely form and so forth.
Whether it be pleasant or unpleasant,
one experiences this suffering or happiness,
which is said to be caused by prior karma.
Or, by means of present conditions,
they are led according to those conditions either toward the five destinies or toward nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, all sentient beings...
When the self-body arises within such a class of sentient beings,
that class of sentient beings acts as four kinds of conditions for this sentient being;
that is to say, by way of being drawn forth by the seed.
Because it is that which nourishes and sustains;
because it follows and guards [the person];
and because one learns to perform the bodily and vocal actions accordingly.
First, it is drawn forth by the semen and blood of the parents;
subsequently, once that birth is known,
one seeks food and drink to provide nourishment and growth.
Next, he should constantly follow him and protect him with single-minded devotion,
ensuring that he does not engage in untimely conduct or improper behavior.
Subsequently, he should cause him to practice and learn worldly speech and other such matters.
Due to the growth of their lineage and the maturation of their faculties,
this leads further to that, and that further to yet another.
In this manner, as sentient beings pass from one state to another,
they have experienced suffering and pleasure since beginningless time,
yet they have never attained the dharma that transcends both suffering and pleasure.
Until all Buddhas have realized enlightenment,
whether through hearing sounds from others or through internal right reflection.
It is by means of this that one attains the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
The meaning of these words is extremely difficult to realize:
namely, that "I" does not exist, whether as a part, as a person, or as a thing.
I, too, am entirely not that portion, nor anyone, nor any thing.
Thus has the internal division of death and birth been briefly explained.
What, then, is the destruction and formation of the external division?
This refers to the karma performed by sentient beings that brings about formation and destruction.
When the karma capable of inducing destruction becomes manifest,
at that time external conditions for destruction arise.
Because those external parts are all completely dispersed and destroyed,
unlike the internal parts which perish through the exhaustion of their life-span. Why is this?
All external portions consist of coarse matter derived from the four great elements;
they exist as a constant continuity,
unlike internal portions.
Furthermore, there is karma that brings about the receptacle world;
this karma is determinate and is able to project the duration of a kalpa as neither increasing nor decreasing.
However, for those included within the category of sentient beings, time is not determinate.
Why is this? Because of the various karmas they have created, [the duration] may exceed one kalpa,
or it may be reduced.
This continues for up to one year.
Furthermore, that kalpa of destruction occurs through three types of calamities;
the first is the calamity of fire, which is capable of destroying the world.
From the Avīci Hell up to the Brahma-world,
there are two types of calamities that can destroy everything,
extending even to the Second Dhyāna.
Third, the disaster of wind can destroy everything up to the third dhyāna;
the fourth dhyāna cannot be destroyed by any such disaster.
Because the bodies of those devas and their palaces arise and perish simultaneously,
and because there is no further causal condition capable of destroying them,
they constitute the upper limit of the three calamities.
This refers to the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
Furthermore, this world-system is destroyed during twenty intermediate kalpas,
and having been destroyed, it remains empty for twenty intermediate kalpas.
It forms during twenty intermediate kalpas;
having formed, it remains for twenty intermediate kalpas.
Thus, there are eighty intermediate kalpas.
This is conventionally designated as the duration of one great kalpa.
Furthermore, the lifespan in the Brahma-world is one kalpa;
this is both its final destruction and its initial formation.
It should be understood that this kalpa is established through distinct characteristics;
namely, for the Brahmakāyika devas,
twenty intermediate kalpas (antarakalpa) are combined to constitute one kalpa.
Based on this *kalpa*, the lifespan of the gods who benefit before Brahmā (*Brahmapurohita*) is established:
forty intermediate *kalpas* (*antarakalpa*) combined constitute one [great] *kalpa*.
The lifespan is established based on this kalpa:
for the Great Brahmā Heaven,
sixty intermediate kalpas constitute one kalpa.
The lifespan is established based on this kalpa.
How does the calamity of fire destroy the world?
It is said that there comes a time such as this.
The lifespan of sentient beings in the world was infinite;
from that point on, it gradually decreased until their lifespan reached eighty thousand years.
Because they further practiced unwholesome dharmas,
their lifespan decreased until it reached ten years.
They then attained a mind of weary detachment and began to practice wholesome dharmas.
Due to these causes and conditions, the lifespan gradually increases until it reaches eighty thousand years.
Thus, one decrease and one increase of such a lifespan constitute one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
Furthermore, within this intermediate kalpa, three types of minor calamities appear.
These are the calamities of famine, disease, and the sword.
Regarding the calamity of famine:
it occurs when the human lifespan is thirty years.
Only then did it begin to be established; at that time,
exquisite food and drink could no longer be obtained.
They do nothing but boil rotten bones together for their feasts;
yet if they should encounter even a single grain of rice, wheat, millet, or barnyard grass,
it feels as heavy as a mani jewel.
They place it in a chest or casket and guard it;
those sentient beings, for the most part lacking physical strength,
fall prostrate upon the ground and are unable to rise again.
Due to this famine, the class of sentient beings perishes almost entirely.
This calamity of scarcity lasts for seven years,
seven months, seven days, and seven nights before it finally passes.
Those sentient beings again gather together and give rise to a mild sense of weary detachment;
by this cause and condition, their lifespan does not decline further and the calamity of famine subsides.
Furthermore, when the human lifespan is twenty years—
Having previously developed revulsion [toward saṃsāra], they now regress and abandon it.
At that time, there will be much pestilence and contagious diseases;
calamities and afflictions will arise in continuous succession.
Those sentient beings who encounter these various diseases mostly perish.
Such a calamity of disease lasts for seven months,
seven days, and seven nights before it finally passes away.
Those sentient beings again gather together and give rise to a moderate sense of weary detachment.
By this cause and condition, their lifespan ceases to diminish and the calamity of disease subsides.
Furthermore, when the human lifespan is ten years, [the following occurs].
Having previously developed a sense of revulsion, they now regress and abandon it.
At that time, sentient beings, seeing one another,
each give rise to a fierce and violent intent to kill.
Due to these causes and conditions, whatever grass, wood, tiles,
or stones they grasped all became extremely sharp swords and blades;
they slaughtered one another until they were nearly extinct.
Thus, this calamity of swords lasts for a full seven days before it finally passes.
At that time, sentient beings further undergo three kinds of extreme decline.
That is to say: the decline of lifespan,
the decline of the physical basis,
and the decline of the necessities of life.
Regarding the decline of lifespan:
it refers to the lifespan reaching its minimum limit of ten years.
Regarding the decline of the physical basis:
This means that their physical stature reaches its minimum at the size of one span or even one fist.
As for the deterioration of their requisites:
at that time, sentient beings take only millet and barnyard grass as the foremost of foods.
Woolen garments are foremost among clothes;
iron ornaments are foremost among adornments;
and all five kinds of superior flavors have completely vanished.
These refer to the flavors of ghee, honey, oil, salt, and so forth, as well as the refined flavors derived from sugarcane.

At that time, sentient beings gather together in succession, giving rise to a supreme sense of weary detachment that never again diminishes, and they are further able to abandon those evil and unwholesome dharmas that cause the reduction of their lifespan.
They practice and increase wholesome dharmas that augment the lifespan;
by virtue of these causes and conditions, their lifespan, physical form, strength, wealth, happiness, and mastery all gradually increase,
until their lifespan reaches eighty thousand years.
Thus, twenty decreases and twenty increases—
these forty cycles of increase and decrease together constitute the emergence from the abiding kalpa.
At the conclusion of the final increase, [the world perishes].
At that time, sentient beings in the hells only pass away and are not reborn there.
In this manner, they gradually diminish until none remain;
one should know that this is called the destruction of the hell realm.
As it is with the destruction of the hells,
so too is the destruction of the animals and hungry ghosts.
At that time, among human beings, a certain sentient being naturally and spontaneously attains the second dhyāna.
The other sentient beings, following one another in succession, do likewise;
having all passed away from here, they are reborn within the homogeneous class of the gods of Utmost Pure Radiance (*Sudarśana*).
It should be understood that at that time, it is said that the human world has been destroyed.
Just as it is with the realm of humans,
so it is with the realm of devas.
At that time, such was the state of the abodes within the five realms of the world.
Not a single sentient being can be apprehended;
all requisite provisions likewise cannot be apprehended.
It is not only that requisite provisions can no longer be obtained.
At that time, even rain could not be obtained.
Because there was no rain, all the medicinal herbs, shrubs, and forests upon the great earth became completely withered and parched;
furthermore, this was due to the absence of the sustaining influence of rain.
It causes the thermal power of this solar disc to increase;
furthermore, it is due to the predominant force of the karma of sentient beings that brings about the kalpa of destruction,
as well as based upon six kinds of combustible objects.
Furthermore, six more sun-discs appear in succession;
compared to the original sun-discs,
the heat and power of these sun-discs exceed the former by four times.
Once seven have formed, the heat subsequently increases sevenfold.
What are the six things that are burned?
First, small and large ditches and pits.
By the second sun, the two small rivers and the great river are dried up;
by the third sun, they are completely parched.
Third is the Great Lake Anavatapta,
which is dried up by the fourth sun;
fourth is the great ocean.
It is dried up by the fifth sun and a portion of the sixth;
because the substance of the five Sumeru mountains and the great earth is solid,
they are scorched by a portion of the sixth and the seventh sun.
Then these very flames, fanned by the wind,
spread and blaze ever more intensely until they reach the Brahma-world.
Furthermore, such things as these may be summarized into three matters.
The first is things produced by water,
such as medicinal herbs and the like,
which are withered by the former [fire].
The second is the matter of water,
which is dried up by the five [fires].
The third is the matter of that which constantly abides in a continuous succession and possesses a solid essence.
Burned by these two,
this world is entirely consumed until not even soot or a trace remains to be found.
As explained at length in the sūtra,
from this point it is said that the receptacle world has been destroyed for a full twenty intermediate kalpas.
Having been thus destroyed, it remains for another twenty intermediate kalpas.
What is the calamity of water?
It occurs after seven calamities of fire have passed.
In the second dhyāna, a water element arises simultaneously,
destroying the receptacle world as water dissolves salt;
this water element and the receptacle world both perish at the same time.
Having thus dissolved,
it remains for another twenty intermediate kalpas.
What is the calamity of wind?
This means that after seven destructions by water have passed,
there are again seven destructions by fire.
Immediately following this, a wind element arises simultaneously within the third dhyāna.
It destroys the receptacle world,
just as the wind dries up the limbs and joints and can further cause them to perish;
this wind element and the receptacle world both vanish simultaneously.

Why is this? It is observed that there are some who, due to the arising of the wind element, cause their bones to be completely consumed; once destroyed by this, they remain for another twenty intermediate kalpas.
Thus has the destruction of the world been briefly explained.
How does the world form?
It is said that after twenty such intermediate kalpas have passed, [the formation begins].
Due to the predominant power of the karma of all sentient beings, the world is formed once again.
At that time, first of all, the vessel-world of the third dhyāna is established in the midst of space.
As it is with the third dhyāna,
so it is with the second and the first as well. At that time,
there are sentient beings at the summit of the third [dhyāna], which is the highest point of the calamities.
Due to the exhaustion of lifespan, the exhaustion of karma, and the exhaustion of merit,
they pass away from there and are reborn in the third dhyāna;
the same applies in succession for all other places.
Furthermore, from the upper limit of the second calamity,
beings are reborn in the second dhyāna;
it should be understood that the same applies to all other locations.
Furthermore, from the summit of the first [level of] destruction,
there was a sentient being who, due to the exhaustion of his lifespan and other factors, passed away from there and was reborn in the first dhyāna,
becoming the Great Brahmā within the Brahma-world.
Because of being alone, he feels displeasure and thus conceives a hope:
"How now may other sentient beings also come to be born here?
At that moment, he generates the thought of enlightenment (bodhicitta).
Other sentient beings, due to the exhaustion of their lifespan and so forth,
pass away from the second dhyāna and are reborn within the homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*) of the first dhyāna.
In this manner, once the three lower dhyānas—
the world of the environment and the world of sentient beings— have been formed,
the palaces of the four heavens of the desire realm gradually come into being within the void of space.
One should know that all those palaces in the void are like magical emanations.
Furthermore, sentient beings pass away from the homogeneous class of the Heaven of Utmost Pure Radiance and are reborn within these various palaces.
The rest is as previously described.
From this point onward, there is a great wind-circle (vāyu-maṇḍala) equal in measure to a trichiliocosm (trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu).
Arising from below,
it serves as the support for that world,
intended to establish therein those sentient beings who lack palaces.
This great wind-wheel has two characteristics:
namely, spreading upward and spreading laterally.
By means of this, the water is held so that it does not scatter or fall away.
Subsequently, through the predominant power of those karmas,
clouds containing gold arise within the realm of space.
From this point, rain falls and pours down upon the wind-circle (vāyu-maṇḍala).
Next, wind arises again, churning the water and causing it to solidify;
this is what is called the "earth-circle of golden nature" (kāñcana-gotra-pṛthivī-maṇḍala).
Above, it withstands the dashing torrents of rain and water;
below, it endures the buffeting force of wind and storms.
Once this earth has been formed, it exists through the sovereign power of that very karma.
Furthermore, clouds containing the treasuries of the elements arose in the sky,
and from those clouds, various kinds of rain fell;
yet as for that rainwater—
It then rests upon the golden earth and the wheel of the earth-element.
Next, wind arises again, churning the water and causing it to solidify;
this occurs precisely because of the power of that wind which draws it forth.
That which possesses the nature of purity, supreme, most excellent,
and sublime becomes Mount Sumeru;
once this mountain is formed, it has the four jewels as its substance.
That which consists of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli—
if it is of middling quality—
forms the seven golden mountains.
Namely, Mount Yugandhara,
Mount Vinataka, and Mount Aśvakarṇa.
Mount Sudarśana, Mount Khadiraka,
and Mount Yugandhara.
Mount Nimindhara and these other mountains have their peaks arranged in such a way that each is named according to its distinct shape.
They are situated in succession, encircling Mount Sumeru.
Mount Sumeru is eighty thousand yojanas in height,
and its breadth is likewise the same.
The depth below the water's edge is likewise the same.
Furthermore, Mount Yugandhara is half the height of that [Sumeru].
Following this, there are six other golden mountains in succession.
Their dimensions gradually decrease, each being half the size of the preceding one.
As for those of inferior disposition,
they reside on the four sides of Mount Sumeru, outside the seven golden mountains.
It forms the four great continents and the eight intermediate continents,
as well as the Cakravāḍa mountain range. This mountain range encircles the four continents and stands with a measurement equal to half that of Mount Nimindhara.
Furthermore, it forms the palaces of the asuras.
These palaces are situated below Mount Sumeru and dwell upon the waters.
Furthermore, it forms the Great Snow Mountains and the surrounding cliffs and shores of Lake Anavatapta;
next, it forms the eight lowest great hells, the individual hells, the cold hells, and the neighboring hells.
Furthermore, they constitute a portion of the realms of hungry ghosts and animals.
As for the four great continents, they are: Jambudvīpa in the south; [Pūrvavideha in the east; Aparagoyānīya in the west; and Uttarakuru in the north].
Pūrvavideha Island in the east,
Aparagoyānī Island in the west,
and Uttarakuru Island in the north.
The shape of Jambudvīpa is like a carriage box;
the shape of Videhadvīpa is like a half-moon;
and the shape of Aparagoyānīdvīpa is perfectly circular.
The northern continent of Uttarakuru is square in shape;
its measurement is six thousand five hundred yojanas, equal to that of Jambudvīpa.
The measure of Videha is seven thousand yojanas;
the measure of Godānīya is [the same].
The size of Kuru is seven thousand five hundred yojanas;
Uttarakuru is eight thousand yojanas.
Furthermore, between the seven golden mountains there is water possessing the eight qualities,
called the Inner Sea;
it also forms the various palaces of the nāgas.
There are eight great nāgas who each abide for an entire kalpa:
namely, the Nāga King Dharaṇīdhara,
the Nāga King Nanda, and the Nāga King Upananda.
The Nāga King Aśvataranemi,
the Nāga King Mukhilinda,
and the Nāga King Manasvin.
The Naga King Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
the Naga King Mahākāla,
and the Naga King Elāpattra.
These nāga kings, by the power of Śakra, frequently engage in battle and conflict with the asuras.
There are four types of these nāga populations:
namely, those born from eggs, those born from wombs, those born from moisture, and those born through transformation.
The four classes among the garuḍas are likewise so.
Furthermore, there is another body of water within the outer sea, which is therefore called the "outer sea.
Moreover, at the base of Mount Sumeru, there are four tiers.
From the first terrace of Mount Sumeru, it extends outward by sixteen thousand yojanas;
from this measurement, it gradually decreases by half at each successive level.
One should know that the remaining terraces follow this sequence, with the Yakṣa Dṛḍhapāṇi residing on the first terrace.
The Blood-Handed Deities dwell on the second tier;
the Ever-Intoxicated Deities dwell on the third tier;
and the Garland-Holding Deities dwell on the fourth tier.
At the four corners of the summit of Mount Sumeru are four great peaks,
each five hundred yojanas in height,
where various yakṣas reside.
That is to say, Vajrapāṇi resides therein.
Furthermore, on the four sides of the Yugandhara Mountains are the four royal capitals of the [Four] Kings,
situated respectively in the southeast, the south, the west, and the north.
These are the abodes of the four Great Heavenly Kings— Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, and Vaiśravaṇa;
all other golden mountains are their villages, towns, and settlements.
Furthermore, near the Snowy Mountains, there is a great golden cliff named Asura-pārśva.
It measures fifty yojanas in length and breadth,
and is the constant dwelling place of the Dragon King Sūpratiṣṭhita.
Furthermore, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, occasionally comes to visit and enjoy this place.
Within it stands a tree named Supratiṣṭhita,
surrounded by seven rows of tāla trees.
Furthermore, there is a great lake named Mandākinī,
which has five hundred small ponds as its retinue.
The Great Naga Sūparikṣita, surrounded before and behind by five hundred female elephants, sports in that lake.
Manifesting according to his desire,
he would enter this pond to gather lotus roots for his food.
Beside it was the great Anavatapta Pond.
Its dimensions are fifty yojanas in both depth and breadth;
fine golden sand is spread across its floor,
and it is filled with water possessing the eight qualities.
Its form and color were exceptionally sublime, dignified, and pleasing to behold.
From this, it branched out into four great rivers;
the first was named Gaṅgā.
The second is named Sindhu;
the third is named Sītā;
and the fourth is named Vakṣu.
Furthermore, at the center of the summit of Mount Sumeru is established the celestial palace of Śakra,
measuring ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
the remaining areas consist of the villages, towns, and settlements of those various devas.
That mountain faces the four great continents on its four sides and is composed of four jewels;
that is to say, it has a face of lapis lazuli facing Jambudvīpa.
Facing Videha, its surface is made of white silver;
facing Aparagoyānī, its surface is made of gold;
and facing Uttarakuru, its surface is made of crystal.
Furthermore, along the perimeter of Jambudvīpa, there is a royal road for universal monarchs made of pure gold;
it stands submerged in the great ocean at the depth of the knees of sentient beings, just like [the palaces] of the Cāturmahārājakāyika devas.
When a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world,
the waters of the ocean recede by the measure of his knees.
Furthermore, to the south of Lake Anavatapta, there is a great tree.
It is named Jambū;
therefore, this continent derives its name from that tree.
Next, to the north of this [continent].
There is a great forest of Śālmali trees where various species of garuḍas born from the four modes of birth gather and dwell.
Each of these four great continents has two intermediate continents as its satellites.
Furthermore, there is another continent inhabited by rākṣasas.
Thus, once this receptacle world has been formed,
there are sentient beings.
They pass away from the homogeneous class of beings in the Heaven of Utmost Pure Light (*Śubhakṛtsna*) and are reborn here.
The rest is as previously explained.
All of this is due to the karma they performed at the beginning of the kalpa.
This karma is foremost, most excellent,
and subtle; it is comprised within the desire realm and brings about its fruit only at this specific time.
It is not at any other time;
at that moment, sentient beings are called "those of the beginning of the eon" (kalpādya).
Furthermore, they possess form produced from the mind.
All of this is as explained at length in the sutra.
At that time, there were no houses or villages;
the entire surface of the earth was level and even.
From that time forward, through the power of the meritorious karma of sentient beings, the essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa) appeared;
likewise, in gradual succession, the earth-cake (pṛthivī-parpaṭaka), forest creepers (vanalatā),
and non-planted rice (śāli) spontaneously emerged.
There were rice grains without husks or bran;
next there was non-glutinous rice,
which had both bran and husks.
Next, non-glutinous rice grew spontaneously in various places;
at that time, sentient beings began to manifest the act of appropriation.
Subsequently, they came to rely upon the conditions of the taste and other such resources for their sustenance.
Among these classes of sentient beings, an unwholesome complexion arose and the light subsequently vanished.
Those who ate much saw their unwholesome complexions increase even further and their bodies become extremely heavy.
These sentient beings then began to disparage one another, and unwholesome dharmas came into practice.
Due to these causes and conditions, all flavors and so forth gradually vanished into the earth,
as explained at length in the sūtras.
Furthermore, because of this circumstance, sentient beings began to look at one another and subsequently gave rise to craving and attachment.
Next, due to karma that brings about male or female characteristics,
some sentient beings develop the male faculty,
while others develop the female faculty.
They mutually encroach upon one another and give rise to various forms of misconduct; consequently,
they are censured by others and only then build houses to hide themselves away.
Furthermore, because they took possession of the non-glutinous rice,
they subsequently began to take possession of the land itself;
due to these conditions, they began to contend with one another over it.
The practice of taking what is not given arose from this;
it was on account of this very condition that the office of the covenant-maker was established.
That first king was named Mahāsaṃmata.
In this way, there appeared in the world the assemblies of kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras;
the gradual sequence of causes and conditions is as explained at length in the sūtra.
Furthermore, once that reliance upon light has ceased,
great darkness arises in the world;
then the sun, moon, and stars gradually emerge.
The diameter of the solar disk is fifty-one yojanas;
it should be known that the lunar disk is one less than that.
The solar disk is composed of fire-crystal (tejas-sphatika).
The lunar disk is composed of crystal (sphaṭika).
Between these two disks,
the lunar disk moves more rapidly and its course is irregular.
Furthermore, that solar disc constantly produces light simultaneously for two continents,
and likewise produces darkness simultaneously for those same two continents;
that is to say, within a single day.
One day [the sun] rises, one night it sets, and at mid-night it disappears.
Furthermore, all the suns, moons,
and stars traverse half of Mount Sumeru.
It moves at a height equal to the elevation of Mount Yugandhara.
Furthermore, as the sun travels, its distance varies.
If one stands far from Mount Sumeru, it is designated as the cold region;
if one stands near Mount Sumeru, it is designated as the hot region.
It is precisely for this reason that there is variation in the speed of death.
Furthermore, when this lunar disk is slightly tilted upward, one perceives it as a half-moon;
because its remaining portion obstructs its adjacent part, that part becomes invisible.
As it tilts further and further, [the same occurs].
In this way, it gradually appears to become full;
just as it gradually lowers during the dark fortnight,
so too does it gradually appear to diminish.
Because the reflections of fish, turtles, and other creatures appear within the lunar disk from the great ocean, a dark mark manifests therein.
Among the constellations, those that are largest measure eighteen *krośas* in extent.
The medium-sized is ten krośas in measure;
the smallest is four krośas in measure.
Furthermore, having been born into the four castes of the world:
Only then does one initiate the karma for experiencing the five destinies, whether pleasant or unpleasant.
From this point onward, each sentient being,
by virtue of the predominant karma that brings about defilement, [proceeds].
Having been born in the hell realms as the King of Quiescence,
immediately thereafter there appear hell-wardens who arise through miraculous birth (*upapāduka*).
As well as various instruments of torment, such as copper, iron, and so forth;
only after the fires of the *naraka* hell have arisen do sentient beings, according to their karma,
take birth therein or in other realms of existence.
In this manner, there are one hundred koṭis of four great continents,
one hundred koṭis of Sumeru mountains,
and one hundred koṭis of the six heavens of the desire realm.
A hundred koṭis of Brahma-worlds and a trichiliocosm are formed together and perish together.
Furthermore, this world-system consists of three types.
A small chiliocosm refers to the total aggregation of one thousand suns and moons, up to the Brahma-world, as a single unit.
A medium dichiliocosm [is formed by aggregating a thousand such small chiliocosms].
That is to say, a thousand small chiliocosms constitute a great trichiliocosm;
that is to say, a thousand medium chiliocosms.
The aggregation of these is called a trichiliocosm (a great trichiliocosm).
In this manner, throughout the four directions, above, and below, the boundless and limitless trichiliocosms are simultaneously undergoing destruction and formation.
Just as when rain falls from the heavens like the axle of a chariot, without interval or interruption,
its waters flow continuously, falling upon all directions;
so too does this world pervade all directions.
Boundless and limitless, it is in the process of being destroyed and in the process of being formed;
this very trichiliocosm is called a single buddha-field,
wherein the Tathāgata manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
They perform buddha-activities throughout boundless worlds,
establishing them in this manner.
Once the worlds have thus been formed, the five destinies are found within them.
This refers to the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas, which are obtainable through the four modes of birth—
namely, birth from an egg, birth from a womb, birth from moisture,
and miraculous birth. Furthermore, there are six kinds of bases of support.
Furthermore, there are ten divisions of time, namely:
seasons, years, months, fortnights, days and nights, kṣaṇas, tatkṣaṇas, lava-s, and muhūrta-s.
Additionally, there are seven matters of appropriation.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of bodily requisites and ten kinds of enjoyers of sensual pleasures;
these are as explained in the Madhyama Āgama.
Furthermore, there are eight modes of conduct that follow along,
and there are eight worldly dharmas:
namely, gain and loss, fame and insignificance, praise and blame, and pleasure and pain.
Furthermore, there are three categories:
namely, enemies, friends, and neutral parties.
Moreover, there are three kinds of worldly affairs.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of speech;
furthermore, there are twenty-two kinds of outbursts of indignation;
furthermore, there are sixty-two kinds of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are eight stages;
again, there are four types of entry into the womb;
and again, there are four types of deportment.
Furthermore, there are six kinds of livelihood, six kinds of protection,
and seven kinds of suffering.
Furthermore, there are seven types of pride, seven types of arrogance,
and four types of discourse.
Furthermore, there are many other verbal expressions.
What is the destiny of hell?
It is that which is comprised of seeds and fruits.
The aggregates of the hell-beings,
as well as the karma conducive to the experience of hell,
are like the destiny of hell.
In this manner, one should understand all that applies accordingly for animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas.
What is birth from an egg?
This refers to those sentient beings who emerge by breaking out of their shells.
Who, then, are they? They are such as the swan, the goose, the peacock, the parrot, the śārika bird, and so forth.
What is birth from a womb?
It refers to those sentient beings who are enveloped by a womb and emerge after the womb has been split open.
What, then, are they? They are like elephants, horses, oxen, donkeys, and so forth.
What is birth from moisture?
This refers to those sentient beings who are born from a single type of moisture according to their respective causes.
What are they like? They are such as insects, scorpions, moths, and the like.
What is birth by transformation?
It refers to sentient beings who, through the predominance of their karma,
are born fully endowed with the six sense bases.
Or again, they may be incomplete.
What is that like? It is as in the case of the heavens and the hells in their entirety.
And a portion of humans, ghosts, and animals.
What are the six kinds of supports?
First, the support of establishment.
This refers to the lowest wind-circle, water-circle, and earth-circle,
which arise so as not to let sentient beings fall downward;
this is called the "support."
Second is the basis for concealment and support,
namely houses and the like;
these arise so that sentient beings may be protected from damage caused by such things as leaking fluids.
This is called the support.
Those dwellings and so forth are briefly of three kinds:
either produced through construction, or...
Some arise not through volitional construction,
while others manifest as transformed palaces;
these three serve as the support for abundant harvests.
It arises for the sake of the edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) of all sentient beings;
this is called the support of sustenance (*niśraya*).
Fourth is the support of security (*yogakṣema-niśraya*).
It arises for the sake of sentient beings so that they may be free from harm by weapons and the like;
this is called the support of the five days and nights. The support of the moon and sun.
It arises for the sake of sentient beings seeing forms;
this is called the support of the basis.
The sixth is the support of the sustenance of food.
That is to say, there are four nutriments:
first, edible food;
second, contact as nutriment.
Third is the nutriment of mental volition;
fourth is the nutriment of consciousness.
These arise to sustain the bodies of all sentient beings.
This is called the basis of support.
What are the seven kinds of objects of acquisition?
First, the matter of one's own parents.
Second, matters concerning wife and children;
third, matters concerning slaves, servants, and laborers;
fourth, matters concerning friends, officials, brothers, and kinsmen.
Fifth, matters concerning fields, houses, and shops;
sixth, matters concerning meritorious deeds and the performance of activities through skillful means.
The seventh is the matter of the storehouses.
What are the ten kinds of bodily requisites?
First, food; second, drink.
Third, the three vehicles; fourth, the four types of robes;
fifth, the five ornaments;
sixth, singing, laughter, dancing, and music.
Seventh, fragrant garlands and powdered incense;
eighth, household utensils;
ninth, illumination.
Ten are the practices undertaken by men and women.
What are the eight modes of conduct?
They refer to those various worldly activities that people repeatedly engage in.
First, the matter of being shrouded;
second, the matter of adorning the body;
third, the matter of deportment being easily subverted.
Fourth, the matter of food and drink;
fifth, the matter of sleep;
sixth, the matter of sexual intercourse.
Seven pertain to the matter of diligent exertion;
eight pertain to the matter of verbal expression.
What are the three kinds of worldly matters?
First, the matter of conversing and discussing with one another to offer mutual greetings and consolation;
second, the matter of marriage and hosting guests where they partake of food and drink together;
third, the matter of providing mutual assistance in various types of undertakings and activities.
What are the three kinds of speech?
They are speech concerning what exists, speech concerning what does not exist, and [speech concerning] neither existence nor non-existence.
And as for other forms of speech:
that which is speech concerning phenomena refers to the proclamation of weariness with and relinquishment of all entanglements and hindrances, and the pursuit of what is delightful and agreeable.
The detailed explanation is as stated in the sūtra.
Regarding "speech that is not the Dharma," this refers to speaking of food, drink, and so forth with a defiled mind.
As for "other speech," it refers to verbal expression arising from an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) state of mind.
What are the twenty-two kinds of provocation?
First, counterfeit measures;
second, counterfeit weights;
third, counterfeit containers.
Fourth, the employment of improper means;
fifth, quarreling;
sixth, frivolousness.
Seventh, transgressions;
eighth, disputes;
ninth, verbal abuse.
10. Anger; 11. Rebuke; 12. Coercion.
Thirteen, beating;
fourteen, killing;
fifteen, binding.
Sixteen: confinement.
Seventeen: mutilation.
Eighteen: banishment.
19. Deceitful crookedness;
20. False pretension and deception;
21. Enticement and entrapment.
Twenty-second is false speech.
What are the sixty-two kinds of sentient beings?
First, hell-beings (*naraka*).
2. Animals; 3. hungry ghosts; 4. devas.
Five [castes]:
six are Kṣatriyas, seven are Brāhmaṇas,
and eight are Vaiśyas.
Ninth, the kṣudraka;
tenth, the female;
eleventh, the male.
12. Neither male nor female;
13. Inferior; 14. Middling.
Fifteen: the sublime.
Sixteen: the householder.
Seventeen: the renunciant.
18. Ascetic practices (duṣkaracaryā).
19. Non-ascetic practices (aduṣkaracaryā).
20. Discipline (saṃvara).
Twenty-one: non-restraint;
twenty-two: neither restraint nor non-restraint;
twenty-three: freedom from desire.
24. Not yet free from desire;
25. Determination of the category of wrong nature;
26. Determination of the category of right nature.
27. Determination of the indeterminate group; 28. Bhikṣu; 29. Bhikṣuṇī.
30. Female trainees (śikṣamāṇā);
31. Male novices (śrāmaṇera);
32. Female novices (śrāmaṇerī).
33. Upāsakas; 34. Upāsikās; 35. Those who practice abandonment.
36. The reciter; 37. The person who has performed the pure gift;
38. The senior resident.
Thirty-nine is middle age;
forty is youth;
forty-one is the age of a preceptor.
Forty-two: preceptors; forty-three:
co-resident disciples and resident disciples;
forty-four: guests.
Forty-five: one who manages the affairs of the Saṃgha;
forty-six: one who craves gain, offerings, and honor;
forty-seven: one who grows weary and abandons [the practice].
Forty-eight were those of great learning;
forty-nine were those of great wisdom;
fifty were those who practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
Fifty-one: those who uphold the sūtras;
fifty-two: those who uphold the vinaya;
fifty-three: those who uphold the śāstras.
Fifty-four: ordinary beings (pṛthagjana).
Fifty-five: those who have seen the truth (dṛṣṭasatya).
Fifty-six: those in training (śaikṣa).
Fifty-seven: those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Fifty-eight: śrāvakas.
Fifty-nine: pratyekabuddhas.
Sixty bodhisattvas,
sixty-one tathāgatas,
and sixty-two wheel-turning kings.
Furthermore, there are four types of these wheel-turning kings:
some rule over one continent,
while others rule over two, three, or four.
A king who rules over one continent possesses the mark of a wheel made of iron;
a king who rules over two continents possesses the mark of a wheel made of copper;
a king who rules over three continents possesses the mark of a wheel made of silver.
For one who rules over the four continents, there is a golden wheel as a sign of his destiny.
What are the eight stages? They are:
the stage of being in the womb.
The stage of birth,
the stage of infancy,
and the stage of childhood.
The stage of youth;
the stage of middle age;
the stage of old age.
The stage of senility and maturity;
the stage of dwelling in the womb refers to the *kalala* and so forth.
The stage of birth refers to the period from that point onward until reaching senility.
The stage of infancy refers to...
This refers to the stage of childhood, which lasts until one is still unable to roam and play;
the stage of youth refers to the ability to perform those activities.
The stage of youth refers to being able to enjoy sensory objects up to the age of thirty;
the stage of middle age refers to...
The stage from this point up to age fifty is called the stage of middle age;
the stage from this point up to age seventy is called the stage of old age.
From this point upward is called the stage of senility.
What are the four ways of entering the womb?
First, entering with full awareness.
One dwells and emerges with non-reflective awareness;
one enters and dwells with reflective awareness,
but emerges with non-reflective awareness.
Three possess correct awareness;
four lack correct awareness.
The first refers to the wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin).
The second refers to pratyekabuddhas;
the third refers to bodhisattvas;
and the fourth refers to all other sentient beings.
What are the six means of livelihood?
First, agriculture;
second, commerce.
Third, tending cattle;
fourth, serving the king;
fifth, training in writing, arithmetic, calculation, and seals.
Sixth, the training in the remaining fields of craftsmanship (*śilpa-sthāna*).
What are the six kinds of protection?
They are the elephant force, the cavalry, the chariot force, the infantry, the power of the treasury, and the power of allies.
What are the seven kinds of suffering?
They are the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging,
the suffering of illness, and the suffering of death.
The suffering of association with the disliked,
the suffering of separation from the beloved,
and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
What are the seven types of pride?
They are: pride, excessive pride, pride beyond pride, and the pride of "I am."
Excessive pride (*adhimāna*), inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*), and false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
What are the seven kinds of intoxication (*mada*)? They are:
intoxication by health (*ārogyamada*).
Pride in youth;
pride in long life;
pride in noble lineage.
Pride in physical strength and beauty;
pride in wealth and status;
pride in extensive learning.
What are the four kinds of discourse?
They are discourse based on what has been seen, heard, sensed, and known.
Regarding discourse based on what has been seen: this refers to the direct perception of external forms by means of the eye.
To proclaim [the Dharma] to others on account of these causes and conditions is called discourse based on what has been seen.
As for discourse based on what has been heard:
That is to say, hearing from others and,
by virtue of this cause and condition, proclaiming it for others;
this is called discourse based on what has been heard.
Regarding discourse based on awakening:
this refers to that which is neither seen nor heard,
but is instead personally reflected upon, weighed, and examined.
To proclaim [the Dharma] for others on account of these causes and conditions is called discourse based on awakening.
As for discourse based on knowledge:
That is to say, each individually regarding what is internally experienced, realized, touched,
and attained, one proclaims it to others on that basis;
this is called discourse based on knowledge.
What are the numerous phrases of verbal expression?
They are precisely these, which are also called phrases of etymological explanation and phrases of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
It is also called "the phrase that encompasses meaning.
There are many such distinctions of this kind.
Furthermore, the various syllables (mātṛkā) are able to encompass all meanings.
It should be known that these are also called "numerous phrases of discourse. What, then, are they?
Namely: earth, faculties, objects, and phenomena.
The distinctions in the intrinsic natures of persons;
the presence or absence of activity in oneself and others;
and questions, answers, taking, and giving.
The phrases concerning right nature and wrong nature;

furthermore, the phrases concerning hearing, restraint, merit and fault, attainment and non-attainment, praise and blame, suffering and pleasure, renown and insignificance, firmness and subtlety, wisdom and decline, sinking and measure, as well as the manifestations of companionship, instruction, exhortation, and consolation.
Furthermore, there are seven types of verbal expressions;
these are the seven grammatical cases, namely:
the nominative (puruṣa).
Puluśam. Puluśaṇa. Puluśaye.
Pulūṣa, pulukasa, puluśa.

Such as these. Furthermore, there are the provisional designations, instructions, signs, tranquility, expressions, rules, establishments, accumulations, determinations, assignments, alarms, and the initial, middle, and final phrases.
Lineage and so forth;
the establishment of tenets, verbal expression, accomplishment, enjoyment, seeking, protection, shame, compassion, endurance, fear, and the analysis of phrases.
Furthermore, there are all the requisites comprised by parents, wives, children, and so on.
This should be explained in detail, including birth, aging, and so forth, up to the failure to obtain what one seeks;
sorrow and lamentation; youth, health, and long life; association with the beloved and separation from the hated; and the attainment or non-attainment of one's desires as they correspondingly arise.
Moving back and forth, looking around, bending and stretching;
walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; being alert and awake, speaking and remaining silent, awakening from sleep and dispelling fatigue;
furthermore, there is drinking, eating, chewing, and savoring.
Repeated practice and lack of repeated practice;
heedlessness and heedfulness;
expansion and contraction; increase and decrease.
Investigation and analysis; primary afflictions and secondary afflictions;
conceptual proliferation and the cessation of proliferation;
the weak and that which is accomplished, and the means of accomplishment.
Flow, determination, difference, association,
rapidity, succession, time, direction,
number, conjunction, and disjunction.
There are phrases concerning the similar and the dissimilar.
Furthermore, there are phrases concerning the intermingled and the shared, the perceptible and the imperceptible, and the manifest and the hidden.

Moreover, there are phrases concerning the agent and the acted-upon, the principles of law, worldly affairs, assets, the real and the false, benefit and non-benefit, the essential nature, doubt, and wonder.
Furthermore, there are phrases concerning cowardice, fearlessness, the manifest and unmanifest, killing, binding, confinement, mutilation, and banishment;
as well as phrases concerning verbal abuse, anger, beating, intimidation, reprimand, burning, scorching, and parching heat.
Subduing the turbid [opponents] who follow after the scriptures and pursue inferential statements.
