Maitreya Bodhisattva spoke;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.
The Second Part of the Second Section on the Mind-Basis within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Part Three. Furthermore, regarding the very nature previously described:
It should be understood that even the five matters beginning with karma are all subsumed under three bases, namely,
by way of the aggregation of matter (*rūpa-kalāpa*).
Because they consist of mind and mental factors,
and because they are unconditioned; thus,
all other phenomena that exist as designations are excluded.
Now, first we shall explain the various phenomena of the material aggregate (*rūpa-kalāpa*).
Question: Do all phenomena arise solely from their own seeds?
How is it said that the primary elements (mahābhūta) can produce derived matter (upādāyarūpa)?
In what way does derived matter depend upon them and by what means is it established?
Is it sustained by them and nourished by them?
Answer: Because the seeds of all internal and external primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) are entirely dependent upon the internal continuum of mind.
Until the primary elements (mahābhūta) have arisen from their seeds,
the seeds of derived matter (upādāyarūpa) can never arise;
derived matter must necessarily arise from them.
Derived matter arises from its own seeds; therefore,
it is said that those [great elements] can produce derived matter,
because their arising serves as the precursor.
By this principle,
it is said that the primary elements (mahābhūtas) are the cause of their arising.
How, then, do derived forms (upādāyarūpa) depend upon them?
Because derived matter, once produced, continues to function without departing from the location of the primary elements,
how is it established? It is established by way of the benefit or harm caused by the primary elements.
Because they share the same security and peril.
How is it that they are sustained by those [great elements]?
Because they do not perish, conforming to the dimensions of the great elements and so forth.
What is that which is nurtured by them?

It is the derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) that increases further and becomes more extensive by depending upon food, sleep, the cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya), meditative concentration (samādhi), and so forth.
Therefore, it is said that the primary elements (mahābhūta) act as the nourishing cause for those [derived forms].
In this way, one should understand that there are five types of functions of the primary elements in relation to derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
Furthermore, within a collection of matter (rūpa-kalāpa),
atoms (paramāṇu) have never arisen individually;
when they arise from their own seeds, they arise only as an aggregate.
Whether subtle, medium, or large,
it is not a mass of matter formed by the aggregation of atoms; rather,
it is merely the ultimate limit of matter analyzed by the discerning intellect.
They are conceptually designated as atoms (paramāṇu).
Furthermore, material aggregates possess spatial dimensions,
and atoms likewise possess spatial dimensions.
However, a collection of matter possesses parts and is not an atom. Why?
Because the atom itself is a part.
This is all that constitutes aggregated matter, and it does not consist of atoms.
Furthermore, there are other atoms;
therefore, the atom is not something possessing parts.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of non-separation:
first, non-separation by way of occupying the same location,
which refers to the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) being inseparable from [the derived qualities] such as visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
Where there is no faculty, there is that which is devoid of a faculty;
where there is a faculty, there is that which possesses a faculty.
This is called "being in the same location without being separated."
Second is "conjoined and inseparable," which means that these very atoms of the primary elements (mahābhūta) coexist with other aggregates of both primary and derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
This is called being conjoined and inseparable.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this pervasive aggregate of matter is like various substances ground into powder and mixed with water so that they are inseparable from one another;
it is not like an aggregate of sesame, mung beans, millet, or barnyard grass.
Furthermore, all derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) is entirely dependent upon the primary elements (mahābhūta);
it does not exceed the spatial extent of the primary elements, nor does it go beyond the location occupied by them.
All derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) likewise relies upon these [great elements].
For this reason, it is said that derived matter depends on the great elements (mahābhūta).
It is precisely in this sense that the great elements are called "great elements."
Because these primary elements (mahābhūta) are great by nature and because they serve as the seeds from which [derived matter] arises;
furthermore, within the various aggregates of form (rūpa-kalāpa),
there are briefly fourteen types of entities.
That is to say: earth, water, fire, and wind;
visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects;
and the five faculties, beginning with the eye.
Excluding only those forms that are the domain of the mind,
all aggregates of form that are comprised by the physical sense faculties.
There is everything,
just as the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) has been described;
it is like a collection comprised of the various material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*).
In this way, the collection comprised of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as the basis for the material sense-faculties is also like this;
as for the remaining collections of matter, they consist solely of the other elements, excluding the material sense-faculties.
Furthermore, there are fourteen matters concerning inclusion by characteristic (*lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*).
That is to say, it is by way of inclusion by characteristic that the entity of the atom (*paramāṇu*) is established.
If one considers inclusion by element (*dhātusaṃgraha*):
According to how many elements (dhātu) exist within this aggregate,
that aggregate is said to be comprised of that many things;
this is according to the inclusion by way of non-separation.
Regarding all aggregates, whether internal or external:
within whichever aggregate there may be,
as many characteristics of phenomena as can be apprehended therein.
One should know that this collection is comprised of such things as these.
Why is this? Because within some collections, only a single primary element (*mahābhūta*) can be perceived.
For example, within stone, mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, and so forth;
or within ponds, marshes, ditches, canals, rivers, and streams;
or within flames, lamps, candles, and the like.
Or, within the winds of the four directions— whether they contain dust or are free of dust—
and within certain aggregations, two of the great elements may be perceived,
such as in snow, moist tree leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth.
Alternatively, within hot mani-jewels and the like,
or within certain aggregates, the three primary elements may be perceived,
as is the case, for example, within a heated tree or similar object.
Or within movement,
or within a collection, the four great elements may be found;
that is to say, within an internal collection of matter.
As the Bhagavān has said:
"Within each individual internal body,
from the hair of the head and body down to excrement and filth, these constitute the internal earth element."
If urine and so forth are the internal water element;
if all that is warmth and so forth within the body is the internal fire element;
and if the upward-moving winds and so forth are the internal wind element.
Thus, if within this collection that characteristic can be apprehended,
one may say that the characteristic exists;
if it cannot be apprehended, one may say that the characteristic does not exist.
Furthermore, sound is said to exist because it is an element (*dhātu*) within all aggregates of matter (*rūpa-skandha*).
Its characteristics, however, are not fixed,
as they arise through present conditions (*upāya*).
Wind is of two kinds:
that which is constantly continuous and that which is not constantly continuous.
As for that which is constantly continuous:
This refers to the winds that constantly circulate within various aggregates;
those that do not continue in a constant succession are the whirlwinds and the winds that move through space.
Furthermore, dark color and bright color are designated as the space element (*ākāśadhātu*) and the interstices (*chidra*).
Moreover, those dark colors that are constantly continuous—
This refers to the intermediate spaces between worlds,
where there is no constant continuity;
it is the same in other locations as well.
"Light and form are constantly continuous" means that in the naturally luminous heavens, they are constantly continuous;
"not constantly continuous" refers to [other realms].
This refers to other locations.
Furthermore, regarding light and darkness as colors,
it should be understood that they are to be known as an accumulation of an increase in manifest color (*varṇa*).
Furthermore, due to the functional capacity of the seeds within the material aggregate (*rūpa-kalāpa*), when encountering corresponding conditions,
either a large aggregate arises immediately after a small one,
or a small aggregate arises immediately after a large one.
For this reason, it is designated that the various aggregates have increase and decrease.
As the Sūtra says:
"If there is solidity, solidity is included, whether closely included or not closely included, and appropriated," and so forth, as explained at length.
What is solidity? It is called earth.
What is the inclusion of solidity? It is those seeds.
Furthermore, solidity is the solidity of that very element (*dhātu*).
"Appropriated" refers to things such as hair and body hair, or clods of earth.
What is meant by "appropriated in proximity"? It means that which is possessed of sensation (upātta).
What is meant by "possessed of sensation"? It means that which is comprised within the internal [body].
What is meant by "not included in the near"? It refers to that which is without appropriation (*anupātta*).
What is meant by "without appropriation"? It refers to that which is included among external things.
Furthermore, this applies to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
The seeds that are grasped are termed "appropriated" (*upātta*) and "appropriated by inclusion" (*upagṛhīta*).
Those contrary to these are termed "non-appropriated" (*anupātta*) and "non-appropriated by inclusion.
Furthermore, they are termed "appropriated by inclusion" because they follow along with one's own body.
Appropriation (*upādāna*) is as previously explained.
In this same manner, the elements (*dhātu*) such as water and so forth should be understood according to reason.
Furthermore, within all aggregates of form (*rūpa-kalāpa*), [the following applies].
At all times, all great elements (mahābhūta) are present within every realm (dhātu).
This is as we observe in the world: when dry firewood or similar substances are drilled, fire immediately arises;
the same is true when striking stones and so forth.
Furthermore, when copper, iron, gold, silver, and so forth are scorched by an extreme fire, they immediately melt into water;
likewise, water flows forth from the moonstone (*candrakānta-maṇi*).
Moreover, those who have attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) [can do the same].
Through the power of mental resolve,
one transforms the great earth and so forth into gold, silver, and the like.
Furthermore, there are three modes of transformation for material aggregates.
First, that which is nurtured;
second, that which is of similar outflow;
third, that which is born of maturation.
There are two kinds of nourishment:
first, nourishment through pervasive filling of the location;
second, nourishment through the intensification of characteristics.
There are four kinds of outflow (niṣyanda):
first, outflow of nurturance;
second, outflow of maturation (vipāka).
Third, those that are outflows of transformation;
fourth, those that are outflows of self-nature.
Those born of maturation are of two kinds.
First, that which arises as the very substance of maturation is called "born of maturation.
Second, that which arises from maturation is called "born of maturation.
Furthermore, all aggregates of matter, briefly stated, function in dependence upon the six sense bases.
That is to say: the basis for establishment,
the basis for concealment,
and the basis for requisites.
The locus of the faculties,
the locus of the faculties,
and the range of activity of samādhi.
Furthermore, within the category of mind and mental factors,
there is the mind that can be apprehended, as well as fifty-three mental factors that can be apprehended,
namely: attention and so forth.
This continues up to the final stage of vitarka and vicāra, as previously explained.
Question: Among these mental factors (caitta), how many depend upon all stages?
Do they arise in all stages, at all times, and in all cases?
Answer: Five, namely attention (*manasikāra*) and so forth, with volition (*cetanā*) as the last.
How many [mental factors] depend on all bases (*sarvatra*)?
How many arise in all stages (*sarvabhūmi*) but not at all times and not in all cases?
Answer: Also five.
That is to say, beginning with desire and ending with wisdom.
How many rely solely on the wholesome and not on all [objects]?
Question: Is it the case that the mind gives rise to all stages, yet not at all times and not in all instances?
Answer: It refers to those beginning with faith and ending with non-harming.
Are there some [mental factors] that depend solely on defilement, rather than on all bases;
that arise from the mind, rather than in all stages, at all times, or in all cases?
Answer: These refer to craving and so forth.
With non-apprehension (*asamprajanya*) as the final [factor], how many rely on all bases?
Do they arise in all stages, at all times, and in all [situations]? Or not?
Answer: It refers to [mental factors] beginning with regret (kaukṛtya) and ending with investigation (vicāra).
Furthermore, it means that the faculties are unimpaired.
When the object-field appears before one and the attention capable of producing it arises,
at that time consciousness is able to arise from it.
What is meant by "the faculties being unimpaired"?
It is said that there are two kinds of causes:
first, because it is not subject to destruction;
second, because it is not weak or inferior.
How does the object appear before one?
It is either by way of its basis or by way of its intrinsic nature.
Either by way of direction,
or by way of time,
or by way of being manifest or unmanifest.
Alternatively, it is due to being either complete or partial.
If one is not obstructed by the four kinds of hindrances and is also not extremely distant—
namely, the hindrance of obscuration (*āvaraṇa-āvaraṇa*).
The obscuration of concealment,
the obscuration of eclipsing,
and the obscuration of delusive bewilderment.
Extreme distance is of two kinds:
namely, extreme distance in terms of location and extreme distance in terms of diminution.
How is it that the mental engagement capable of producing [the result] arises?
It does so by virtue of four causes.
First, by the power of aspiration.
Second, by the power of mindfulness;
third, by the power of the object;
fourth, by the power of repeated practice.
What is meant by "by the power of desire"?
It refers to the fact that when the mind has attachment toward a certain object,
the mind then frequently directs its attention toward that very object.
What is it by the power of mindfulness?
It means that if one has already well-grasped the signs (*nimitta*) of those [objects] and has formed an intense mental image (*saṃjñā*) of them,
the mind will frequently produce attention (*manasikāra*) toward them.
What is meant by "by the power of the object"?
It refers to when that object is either extremely vast or extremely agreeable,
and it is directly present before one.
The mind then frequently gives rise to mental attention toward that [object].
How is this due to the power of repeated practice?
If, with respect to that object...
Having become thoroughly habituated and fully conversant with it,
the mind then frequently directs its attention toward that object;
were it otherwise, [it would not do so].
A single mental attention (*manasikāra*) should arise at all times with respect to a single object of focus.
Furthermore, two moments of the fivefold body of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*) do not arise together in succession,
nor do they arise alternately in immediate proximity to one another.
Furthermore, once the five groups of sensory consciousness have arisen in a single moment,
immediately thereafter the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) necessarily arises.
Immediately after that, it may at times be distracted, or auditory consciousness (śrotravijñāna) may arise.
Alternatively, when any one of the five groups of consciousness arises,
if there is no distraction,
a second determinative mind (*niścaya-citta*) will necessarily arise within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Because of this, by means of the two types of mental consciousness that ascertain through seeking,
one discriminates objects;
furthermore, it is due to two kinds of causes.
Either defiled or wholesome phenomena arise,
namely, due to conceptualization and due to what was previously projected.
All [mental factors] within the mental consciousness arise from two types of causes;
those in the five sensory consciousnesses arise solely from what was previously projected. Why is this so?
Because they are induced by the power of afflicted and wholesome mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
afflicted and wholesome phenomena arise immediately thereafter within the visual and other sensory consciousnesses.
They do not arise through conceptual discrimination,
because they are themselves non-conceptual.
By this principle, it is said that the visual and other consciousnesses follow the mental consciousness in their operation.
As the Sūtra says:
"Whether one mind or many minds arise,
how is this 'one mind' established?"
This refers to a single moment of conventional discourse, not a moment of arising.
What is meant by a single moment of conventional discourse?
It means that which has a single location as its basis.
Regarding a single objective entity,
there arise as many cognitions as there are;
the aggregate of these for such a duration is termed a single mental moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, a similar continuum is also said to be "one" because it is extremely similar to the second moment of consciousness.
Moreover, when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) spontaneously becomes distracted and takes as its object a sphere that has not been previously cultivated through habituation.
When it arises without desire and so forth,
the mental consciousness at that time is called the "sudden falling mind" (*ābhoga-citta*),
which takes only past objects as its cognitive support.
The mental consciousness that arises immediately after the five sensory consciousnesses—
whether it be investigative or determinative—
should be said to take only a present object as its cognitive support.
If this [consciousness] arises precisely by taking that object as its condition,
and if consciousness is able to discern the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of an entity,
then it would follow that the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the object— which have not yet been discerned— would already have been discerned.
That which is capable of discerning is called attention (*manasikāra*).
It is precisely this [attention] that discerns the agreeable, the disagreeable, and the neutral characteristics by means of contact (*sparśa*).
This very characteristic of being conducive to, detrimental to, or neutral toward appropriation is [the object] by which it is cognized through perception;
this very characteristic of being the cause for verbal expression [is the object].
It is through the discernment of perception (*saṃjñā*) that this characteristic of the cause for conduct that is either erroneous, correct, or both inconsistent [is known];
it is through the discernment of volition (*cetanā*) that [it is known].

Therefore, it is said that those mental factors beginning with attention (manasikāra) and ending with volition (cetanā) are called the mental concomitants (caitasika-dharma) that are omnipresent across all locations, all stages, all times, and all births.
What is attention (*manasikāra*)? It is the turning of the mind.
What is contact (*sparśa*)? It is the coming together of the three.
What is feeling (*vedanā*)? It is experiencing.
What is perception (*saṃjñā*)? It is the discernment of images.
What is volition (*cetanā*)? It is the mental formation.
What is desire (*chanda*)? It is [the inclination] toward things that are pleasing.

What is mindfulness? It is the nature of clear recollection that follows various activities regarding familiar objects.
What is samādhi? It is [the state] regarding the object under investigation.
What is the one-pointedness of mind that serves as the basis for investigation according to each respective mode of activity?
And what is wisdom? It is the discernment of the nature of phenomena with respect to the very object under investigation, according to each respective mode of activity.
Either induced by what is reasoned,
or induced by what is unreasoned,
or induced by what is neither reasoned nor unreasoned.
Furthermore, what is the function of attention?
It has the function of directing the mind.
What is the function of contact?
That is to say, its function is to serve as the basis for feeling, perception, and volition.
What is the function of feeling?
Its function is to serve as the basis for the arising of craving.
What is the function of perception (saṃjñā)?
Its function is to cause the mind to give rise to various verbal expressions regarding its objects.
What is the function of volition (cetanā)?
It has the function of initiating mental investigation (vitarka) and analysis (vicāra), as well as bodily and vocal actions.
What kind of action does it intend to perform?
It has the function of instigating diligence (vīrya).
What is the function of resolve (*adhimokṣa*)?
It has the function of maintaining the qualities and defects within its object.
What is the function of mindfulness (*smṛti*)?
Its function is the recollection of what was long ago thought, done, or spoken.
What is the function of samādhi?
Its function is to serve as the basis for wisdom.
What is the function of wisdom (*prajñā*)?
Its function is to investigate, in accordance with reality, the defilement and purification that occur within the sphere of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
How are the three periods of time established?
This means that because the various seeds are not separate from phenomena,
they are established in accordance with those phenomena;
furthermore, it is due to the fact that they have either already yielded their fruit or have not yet yielded their fruit.
Regarding resultant phenomena (*phala-dharma*):
those whose characteristics have already ceased are past;
those that possess causes but whose characteristics have not yet arisen are future.
That which has already arisen but not yet ceased is the present.
How are birth, aging, duration, and impermanence established? They are established as co-occurring with the continuity of all seeds within the continuity of consciousness in every instance.
Due to the power of conditions,
phenomena that previously had not yet arisen in a continuous stream now arise for the very first time.
This is called the conditioned characteristic of arising.
This very nature of transformation is called the conditioned characteristic of aging.
This, moreover, is of two kinds:
first, transformation as difference in nature;
second, transformation as change in nature.
The nature of difference and the nature of transformation are established because there is arising that is similar;
they are established because there is arising that is dissimilar.
The establishment of the characteristics of change and transformation refers to the fact that at the very moment of arising, there is only birth;
because it persists through each successive moment, it is called the conditioned characteristic of duration (*sthiti*).
After the moment of arising,
because it does not abide for even a single moment, it is called the characteristic of impermanence and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
Thus, this is explained in terms of the distinct stages (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of all phenomena.
The four characteristics are established.
Furthermore, there are four conditions:
first, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Second, the immediately preceding condition;
third, the object condition;
fourth, the dominant condition.
The causal condition refers to the seed;
the immediately preceding condition refers to...
That is to say, if various consciousnesses necessarily arise immediately after this consciousness,
then this [preceding] consciousness is the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for them.
As for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
The objective referent (ālambana) refers to the objects of all minds and mental factors.
The dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya) refers to the remaining bases (āśraya), excluding the seeds.
Just as the eye and its auxiliary factors are in relation to visual consciousness,
so it is for the remaining consciousnesses.
Furthermore, this applies to their nature as wholesome or unwholesome.
That which can grasp agreeable or disagreeable fruits—
such categories as these are called the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
Furthermore, the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*) is established by virtue of the seed (*bīja*).
The equal-and-immediate condition is established by way of its intrinsic nature;
the object-condition is established by way of the objective sphere;
and the dominant condition is established by way of the basis, the associates, and so forth.
As the Sūtra says:
"Those causes and conditions that are able to produce consciousness are precisely these four causal conditions."
One type is both cause and condition;
the others are only conditions. How so?
That is to say, all wholesome phenomena may be established as one kind by virtue of their meaning of being blameless;
or they may be established as two kinds.
This refers to innate virtue and acquired virtue; alternatively,
three types may be established.
That is to say: intrinsic virtue,
associated virtue,
and originating virtue.
Alternatively, four types are established:
namely, merit-accruing virtue and liberation-accruing virtue.

Such spirits as these are said to have internal obstructions regarding food and drink.
What is meant by having no obstructions regarding food and drink?
There is a class of hungry ghosts known as the "Fierce Flame Garlands" (Tīvrārcirmālā).
Whatever they drink or consume is entirely consumed by flames.
For this reason:
The great suffering of hunger and thirst never ceases for even a moment.
Furthermore, there are hungry ghosts named "Excrement-Eaters," some of whom eat excrement and drink urine.
Some individuals can only consume food that is utterly loathsome, raw or cooked, foul-smelling and putrid;
even if they obtain something fragrant and delicious, they are unable to eat it.
Others, however, cut off the flesh from their own bodies and eat it.
Even if they obtain other food, they are ultimately unable to eat it.
Ghosts such as these are said to have no obstacles regarding food and drink.
Furthermore, sentient beings born within the human realm mostly experience such suffering of deprivation,
namely, the innate suffering of deprivation from hunger and thirst.
The suffering of lack when one's desires are not fulfilled;
the suffering of lack regarding coarse food and drink;
and the suffering of lack regarding the intense pursuit and grasping [of objects].
The suffering of deprivation caused by the changing of seasons, whether cold or heat;
the suffering of deprivation caused by the lack of shelter or protection against rain and leaks;
and the suffering of deprivation caused by the total suspension of all activities due to obstructions such as darkness.
Furthermore, they undergo the sufferings of change, decay, old age, sickness,
and death; however, because they perceive death as a pleasure within the hells (*naraka*),
that realm is not established as suffering [in their own experience].
Furthermore, within the heavenly realms, there is no suffering of having one's limbs and joints severed;
however, there is the suffering of death and falling [to lower realms],
as stated in the sūtras.
When certain sons of the gods are about to pass away,
five signs appear beforehand: first,
their garments, which were free from stains, appear to have stains.
Second, his two flower garlands, which previously did not wither, now become faded and shriveled.
Third, sweat flows from both armpits.
Fourth, his body becomes foul-smelling and filthy.
The gods of the five heavens and the celestial sons found no pleasure in their own seats.
At that time, those celestial sons lay prostrate among the groves, sporting together with their consorts and other celestial beings.
Having seen this, he gives rise to great sorrow and suffering due to these causes and conditions;
furthermore, he undergoes the suffering of being insulted and trembling with fear. Why is this so?
Because of his accomplishment of a vast mass of merit and his possession of the five great sensual pleasures,
when the devaputra was born, the other former devaputras of meager merit became terrified upon seeing him.
Due to these causes and conditions, they undergo great sorrow and suffering;
furthermore, they undergo the sufferings of being cut, severed, destroyed, banished, and harmed. Why is this so?
When the devas and asuras were engaged in mutual combat and conflict, the devas and asuras opposed one another,
each taking up four types of weapons:
namely, gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli.
They fought together in battle;
at that time, the devas and asuras had their limbs severed,
their bodies shattered, or were even brought to death.
If their bodies are wounded or their limbs severed, they are restored to their former state;
yet if their heads are severed, they immediately perish.
Among devas and asuras, each may achieve victory over the other.
However, because the gods generally possess superior power and great might,
when those two are defeated by others, they retreat to their own palaces;
even their own kind does not go to comfort them.
Due to these causes and conditions, they harbor grief and distress;
if the gods prevail, they enter the palace of the asuras.
It is for the sake of pleasing their daughters that this conflict arises.
If the asuras do not achieve victory, they enter the celestial palaces;
thus they engage in mutual combat and strife for the sake of the four kinds of *sudhā* nectar.
Furthermore, it should be known that all asuras are included within the realm of the gods (*devagati*).
However, because their volitions are largely filled with deceit, illusion, flattery, and deception,
they are not as suitable vessels for the pure Dharma as the various devas;
for this reason, [they do not attain it].
Sometimes the sūtras speak of them as a separate realm.
In reality, they are a class of devas; however, because they do not practice the dharmas of the devas, they are called "non-devas" (asura).
Furthermore, there are powerful sons of the gods who, upon merely manifesting a single impulse of indignation, [overcome others].
The inferior devas are then driven out from their own palaces;
for this reason, the devas undergo three kinds of suffering,
namely, the suffering of death and falling.
The suffering of contemptuous disdain;
the suffering of being cut, severed, destroyed, harmed, and banished.
Furthermore, sentient beings in the realms of form and formlessness do not possess such sufferings as these.
Because those sentient beings are not vessels for the sensation of suffering;
nevertheless, they are said to possess suffering due to the suffering of *dausthulya* (coarseness) and because they possess afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because it is subject to obstruction,
and because one lacks mastery over death and abiding,
this is the ultimate happiness.
One should know that all else is suffering.
Furthermore, among the four kinds of *naraka* hells, there is no pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*).
As it is in the hells, so it is elsewhere.
The same applies to the three kinds of hungry ghosts.
Among the powerful spirits, animals, and humans,
there can be found the pleasure of external objects and resources produced through outward gates.
Nevertheless, it is interspersed with manifold sufferings.
Furthermore, among the human realm, the bliss of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) is the most supreme and subtle;
for when such a monarch appears in the world, the seven precious jewels manifest spontaneously.
It is said that the king was endowed with the seven treasures.
What are these seven?
They are the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the mani-jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder-treasure, and the military-commander treasure.
At that time, the wheel-treasure and the others appeared.
What were their characteristics?
The appearance of the seven treasures is as described at length in the sutra.
If that Wheel-Turning King rules over the four continents,
all the minor kings will submit to his influence and transformation,
each addressing him personally, saying:
"This city and its surrounding villages belong to the gods.
We pray only that Your Majesty will deign to grant us your command;
we shall all serve as the gods' attendants."
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King immediately issued a decree:
"You kings, each within your own realm, shall encourage and transform [your subjects] through principle.
You must act according to the Dharma and not contrary to the Dharma."
Furthermore, you must not practice unrighteous conduct within the kingdom or the household,
nor practice acts of partiality.
This applies whether that wheel-turning monarch rules over three continents.
First, an envoy is dispatched, and only then do they submit to his transformation.
If that Wheel-Turning King rules over two continents,
he must raise an army and manifest his majesty before they finally submit to his transformation.
If that wheel-turning monarch rules over a single continent,
he goes there himself, brandishing his spear and wielding his blade, and they subsequently submit to his transformation.
Furthermore, the various devas enjoy vast celestial wealth and pleasure under his rule.
His physical form is exceptionally sublime and brings much delight;
he dwells for a long time within his own palace,
and both the interior and exterior of his body are entirely pure and free from any foul odor.
Furthermore, within the human body there are many impurities, namely:
dust, filth, sinews, bones, the spleen, the kidneys, the heart, and the liver;
yet none of these possess [intrinsic] existence.
Furthermore, those devas have four kinds of palaces,
made of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli.
They are adorned with various colorful patterns and ornaments, featuring diverse pavilions and multi-storied towers.
With their various tiers, various windows, and various lattices, all were delightful;
they were inlaid with various mani-jewels that emitted light from all sides,
mutually illuminating one another.
Furthermore, there are food-trees;
from within these trees emerge four kinds of edible flavors called *sūda*.
These are blue, yellow, red, and white.
Furthermore, there are trees of drink from which flows sweet and delicious liquid.
Furthermore, there are vehicle-trees from which various kinds of exquisite vehicles emerge,
namely chariots, litters, palanquins, and so forth.
Furthermore, there are clothing trees from which various kinds of exquisite garments emerge;
these garments are fine and soft, with wonderful colors that are fresh and pure, and are adorned with an intermingling of diverse hues.
Furthermore, there are trees of ornaments from which various exquisite articles of adornment emerge,
namely: mani-jewel armlets, earrings, pendants, and bracelets.
As well as ornaments for the hands and feet—
such various kinds of decorative articles—
all fashioned from diverse and exquisite maṇi jewels.
And it is interspersed with decorations. Furthermore,
there are trees of incense and garlands from which emerge various kinds of unguents, various kinds of incenses, and various kinds of flower garlands.
Furthermore, there is a great assembly tree,
most excellent and subtle;
its roots are firm and deep, extending fifty yojanas.
Its trunk rises straight to a height of one hundred yojanas;
its branches and leaves completely cover an area of eighty yojanas,
with various flowers in full bloom.
Its fragrance perfumes a hundred yojanas with the wind and fifty yojanas against the wind;
beneath this tree dwell the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens.
During the four months of the rainy season, they enjoy themselves together with the five sublime celestial sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, there are trees of song, laughter, and dance;
from these emerge various musical instruments such as singing, laughing, and dancing.
Furthermore, there are trees of requisites from which various articles of utility arise,
namely, utensils for food and drink.
Reclining and sitting implements,
as well as various other such articles of utility;
furthermore, when those devas wish to enjoy them, [they appear].
In accordance with their desires and karma, whatever they require appears in their hands.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the various asuras likewise enjoy all manner of palaces and riches according to their respective needs.
Furthermore, in the northern continent of Uttarakuru, there is a tree of such appearance called "Yathā-kāma" (As One Wishes).
Whatever requisites those people desire, [it provides].
They take from the trees without the need for thought;
whatever they require appears naturally in their hands.
Furthermore, there is non-glutinous rice that is harvested without sowing, free from the sense of "mine-ness."
Furthermore, those sentient beings ultimately have no fixed attachment and certainly advance toward excellence.
Moreover, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, possesses the Vaijayanta Palace,
which is the most preeminent among all palaces.
In that place there were furthermore a hundred multi-storied pavilions;
each pavilion had a hundred terraces and galleries;
each terrace and gallery had seven chambers; and in each chamber there were seven celestial maidens.
Each celestial maiden has seven attendants.
Furthermore, the entire terrestrial realm of those gods is as level and smooth as the palm of a hand,
entirely without any elevations or depressions.
At the moment of contact with the foot, it produces bliss;
when the foot is set down, it sinks until it reaches the knee;
when the foot is lifted, it rises back up following the foot.
At all times, mandārava flowers naturally appear, spread covering its surface.
Occasionally, a gentle breeze blows away the withered flowers and brings forth new ones.
Furthermore, on each of the four sides of those celestial palaces there are great streets;
their forms are exquisite and their layout is worthy of observation.
They are pure, dignified, and perfectly symmetrical in measurement.
Furthermore, on its four sides there are four great gates;
their scale is magnificent and their appearance is extraordinary.
One never tires of beholding them, for they are truly sublime.
It is constantly guarded by many yakṣas of various kinds and exquisite appearance;
furthermore, on its four sides, there are four gardens.
The first is named Hui-che (Variegated);
the second is named Ts'u-shih (Rough and Astringent);
the third is named Ho-tsa (Mixed).
The four are named Nandana Grove.
Outside these four gardens are four excellent sites,
whose colors and features are exquisite and whose forms are worthy of contemplation.
It is of incomparable majesty and beauty.
In the northeast corner of that palace is a place where devas assemble,
named Sudharmā.
The devas enter therein to contemplate, weigh, and examine its sublime meaning.
Beside this garden is a wish-fulfilling stone;
it is yellowish-white in color, and its substance and form are exceptionally wondrous.
Their appearance is magnificent and beyond compare;
moreover, the bodies of those devas naturally radiate light.
When the signs of darkness appear, one knows that day has passed and the portion of night is now approaching.
While sporting amidst the exquisite fivefold sensual pleasures of the heavens, he became indolent and fell asleep;
the birds of various species no longer sang in harmony.
By such signs as these, day and night were made manifest.
Furthermore, those hosts of devas find the exquisite fivefold sensual pleasures exceedingly delightful;
they experience nothing but joy and pleasure.
These hosts of devas are constantly governed by their conduct of heedlessness.
They constantly hear various sounds of singing, dancing, music, and clamor;
they hear sounds of playful banter, laughter, and jesting;
and they constantly see various forms that are pleasing to the mind.
They constantly smell various subtle and wondrous fragrances;
they perpetually taste various exquisite flavors;
and they constantly experience the most supreme tactile sensations of the various celestial maidens.
They constantly experience such pleasure,
which draws their minds toward it as they pass the time.
Furthermore, those devas enjoy many such various and wondrous sensual pleasures.
They are always free from disease and likewise free from aging.
They lack the suffering born of the deficiency of food, drink, and so forth;
nor do they experience any other deficiencies as previously described that exist within the human realm.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Four;
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Five;
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.

From the *Maulī Bhūmi* (The Main Stages), within the section on the "Three Stages with Vitarka and Vicāra," Part Two. Furthermore, regarding the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*):
The gods born in the stage of the first dhyāna experience the joy and bliss born of seclusion belonging to that stage;
so too do the gods of the second dhyāna stage.
The gods of the third dhyāna stage experience the joy and bliss born of concentration;
they experience sublime bliss free from joy.
The gods of the fourth dhyāna stage experience the bliss of equanimity,
mindfulness, purity, tranquility, and immovability; the gods of the formless realm experience the bliss of supreme, tranquil liberation.
Furthermore, it should be understood that there is a distinction between suffering and pleasure due to six kinds of excellence. First,
the excellence of physical dimensions.
Second, excellence of flexibility;
third, excellence of conditions;
fourth, excellence of time.
Fifth, the excellence of the mind;
sixth, the excellence of the basis. Why is this?
To the extent that the dimensions of the body gradually increase and expand,
to that same extent the suffering becomes increasingly intense;
to the extent that the physical basis gradually becomes more supple, [the suffering likewise increases].
In this way and that way, suffering becomes increasingly intense;
as the conditions for suffering gradually become more violent, numerous, and diverse,
so too does suffering become increasingly intense.
To the extent that the temporal interval gradually becomes shorter and more immediate,
to that same extent the suffering becomes increasingly intense; likewise,
to the extent that the power of internal discernment gradually expands and widens.
In this way and that way, suffering becomes increasingly intense;
as the basis, the vessel of suffering, gradually increases,
in this way and that way, suffering becomes increasingly intense.
Just as with the excellence of suffering,
so too should the meaning of the excellence of pleasure be understood through a detailed exposition according to what is appropriate.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of happiness:
first, happiness born of non-noble wealth;
second, happiness born of noble wealth.
Regarding the pleasure not born of noble wealth:
it arises conditioned by four kinds of requisites.
First, the requisite of gratification.
Second, the requisites for growth;
third, the requisites for purification;
fourth, the requisites for maintenance.
Objects of pleasure and utility refer to vehicles,
clothing, various ornaments, singing, laughter,
dancing, music, scented unguents, flower garlands, and all kinds of exquisite, rare, and delightful articles of enjoyment.
Regarding "the radiance shines forth, with male and female attendants, various treasuries,
and the growth of requisites," this refers to the wheel-stone that is free from discursive thought.
Striking, pounding, trampling,
massaging, and so forth—
these are the requisites for purification.
That is to say: auspicious grass (śakrābhilagna),
bilva fruits, conch shells,
jars filled [with water], and so forth.
The requisites for maintaining one's life consist of food and drink;
these are the pleasures born of the noble wealth.
It means that it arises conditioned by the seven noble riches.
What are these seven? First, faith;
second, ethical discipline; third, shame; fourth, remorse; fifth, learning; sixth, equanimity; and seventh, wisdom.
Furthermore, there is a distinction in the happiness arising from the noble and non-noble riches by way of fifteen aspects.
What are these fifteen?
That is to say, the pleasure born of non-noble wealth can give rise to unwholesome conduct,
whereas the pleasure born of noble wealth can give rise to sublime conduct.
Furthermore, the pleasure born of non-noble wealth is associated with blameworthy joy and delight.
The bliss born of the noble wealth is associated with faultless joy and happiness;
furthermore, the bliss born of non-noble wealth is minute and does not pervade the basis [of the body],
whereas the bliss born of the noble wealth is vast and completely fills the basis.
Furthermore, the happiness born of non-noble wealth does not exist at all times,
because it depends upon external conditions;
the happiness born of noble wealth exists at all times.
Because it depends on internal conditions;
furthermore, the pleasure born of non-noble wealth does not exist in all stages,
as it exists only in the desire realm.
The happiness born of the noble wealth exists in all stages,
as it pertains both to that which is bound to the three realms and that which is unbound.
Furthermore, the happiness born of non-noble wealth cannot bring about the attainment of future noble or non-noble wealth.
The happiness born from the noble wealth can bring forth both noble and non-noble wealth in future lives;
furthermore, the happiness born from non-noble wealth is finite and limited when it is experienced.
The happiness born of the noble wealth becomes even more abundant, increases, and expands when it is experienced;
furthermore, the happiness born of non-noble wealth can be plundered by others.
Neither kings, nor thieves, nor enemies, nor water,
nor fire can seize the happiness born of noble wealth;
furthermore, the happiness born of non-noble wealth cannot be carried from this life into future lives.
The happiness born of the noble wealth can be carried from this life into future lives;
furthermore, the happiness born of non-noble wealth cannot satisfy one even at the time it is being enjoyed.
When one experiences the bliss arising from the noble wealth, it is ultimately fulfilling;
whereas the bliss arising from non-noble wealth is accompanied by fear and has adversaries.
There are calamities and misfortunes;
there is burning affliction;
one cannot sever the great suffering of future lives.
Those who have fear are so called because they dread the basis for the suffering of future rebirth.
Those who have adversaries...
This means it is the basis for quarrels, disputes, and contention;
it is that which possesses calamities and misfortunes,
meaning it is the basis for old age, sickness, and death.
There is that which is characterized by burning affliction;
this means that because the nature of this pleasure is unreal,
it serves as the basis for false and inverted perceptions, such as those associated with the disease of scabies.
Because it is the basis for various forms of distress, lamentation, sorrow, suffering,
and feverish affliction; and because it is the basis for the primary and secondary delusions, such as greed and hatred, which prevent one from severing the great suffering of future lives.
The happiness born of the noble wealth is free from fear,
free from enmity,
and free from calamities.
There is no burning affliction;
one is able to sever the great suffering of future lives.
In accordance with what is appropriate, this is the opposite of the aforementioned.
This should be understood in detail as previously explained.
Furthermore, those with external desires enjoy the objects of desire,
whereas those whose life is sustained by noble wisdom enjoy the True Dharma.
There are distinctions based on five aspects.
For this reason,
it is said that those who live by the noble life sustain themselves through the purity of unsurpassed wisdom-life.
What are the five?
First, because those who enjoy the true Dharma are undefiled;
second, because those who enjoy the true Dharma reach ultimate consummation.
Third, because those who enjoy the true Dharma are exclusively and invariably fixed [in it].
Fourth, because those who enjoy the true Dharma are not shared with other seekers of the life of wisdom (*prajñājīvika*).
Fifth, because those who enjoy the true Dharma possess the bliss of reality.
Because it subdues the enmity of Māra,
herein, whatever sensual pleasures belong to those who indulge in desires are accompanied by craving that conforms to the state of joy.
This is because it conforms to the basis of sorrow and is accompanied by ill-will;
it is because it conforms to the basis of equanimity and is accompanied by an equanimity that lacks discernment.
For one who lives by noble wisdom and partakes of the True Dharma, it is not like this.
Furthermore, those who possess desire and enjoy the objects of desire,
from an unknowable beginningless limit, because of impermanence,
have abandoned one set of desire-objects and obtained another set of desire-objects.
At times, there may be nothing at all to be obtained;
however, for those whose life is the noble wisdom, the enjoyment of the True Dharma is not like this.
Furthermore, when those who indulge in desires enjoy those desires, [it is not so].
Regarding this very matter, one simultaneously gives rise to both delight and resentment;
furthermore, toward that same object, one may at times experience joy and at other times experience sorrow.
It is not so for those who live by noble wisdom and partake of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, those who have abandoned desire but whose life is sustained by external wisdom,
regarding the various views and inclinations arising from their own conceptual constructions as objects of false conviction,
their minds intensely and diversely cling to them.
They are constantly pursued by the defilement of desire;
even after having abandoned desire, they fall back and give rise to it again.
It is not so for those whose life is the noble wisdom, who partake of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, all sensual pleasures experienced by those who indulge in desire,
as well as the pleasure of renunciation experienced by those in the world who have already abandoned desire,
are not ultimately real.
All are pursued by the enmity of Māra;
they are like an illusion, an echo, a shadow, a flame, or what is seen in a dream,
just like various ornaments produced by magic.
Furthermore, for foolish people attached to pleasure who indulge in desires,
as well as for those in the world who have already abandoned desire,
whatever they enjoy is like that of one who is insane, intoxicated, or deranged.
Because they enjoy [pleasures] without having subdued the armies of Māra,
that happiness is not genuine;
nor can it subdue any of the works of Māra.
The noble ones who possess the life-force of wisdom do not partake of the True Dharma in such a manner.
Furthermore, how should one contemplate the body that serves as the support for sentient beings within the three realms?
It should be viewed as being accompanied by the heavy burdens of poisonous heat and abscesses.
When a pleasant sensation arises in this very body, how should one contemplate it?
One should contemplate it as being like a feverish, poisoned abscess that momentarily encounters a cold touch.
When a painful sensation arises in this very body, how should one contemplate it?
It is as follows: when a painful, feverish abscess is touched by hot ashes, and a sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant arises within this very body, how should one contemplate it?
One should contemplate it as being like a painful, feverish abscess that is free from the touch of cold or heat.
Because its nature is inherently poisonous and hot by its very abiding,
the Bhagavat said:
"One should know that pleasant feeling is suffering because it is subject to the suffering of change."
Painful feeling is suffering because it is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is suffering because it is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Furthermore, it is said that there is the joy of craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā-rasa*).
There is joy that is free from the savoring of craving,
and there is a superior joy that is free from the savoring of craving;
such categories as these are explained at length in the Sūtra.
It should be understood that this is subsumed within the two realms (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, the Blessed One established the bliss of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*) as the foremost among all forms of bliss;
this refers to the bliss of abiding (*vihāra-sukha*), not the bliss of sensation (*vedanā-sukha*).
Furthermore, it is said that there are three kinds of bliss:
namely, the bliss of being free from greed, the bliss of being free from hatred, and the bliss of being free from delusion.
These three kinds of bliss can be found only within the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*).
Therefore, this bliss is called "eternal bliss.
It is subsumed within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
This realm sustains the life-span of sentient beings, both those yet to be born and those already born.
In this regard, it should be understood that by means of the three kinds of nutriment— contact, mental volition,
and consciousness— the life-force of all sentient beings in the three realms is sustained.
Only the single kind of physical nutriment (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) sustains the life-force of sentient beings in the desire realm alone.
Furthermore, for sentient beings born in the hells,
there is a subtle material food;
that is to say, within their internal organs, there is a subtle moving wind.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, they are able to endure for a long time.
Among hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods, there is coarse physical food;
that is to say, it is taken by dividing it into portions and then eating it.
Furthermore, there is subtle nutriment;
namely, that of sentient beings dwelling in stages such as the kalala, as well as those of the various devas of the desire realm.
Having consumed this, they [sustain themselves].
All solid food that enters flows into all the limbs and joints of the body,
where it is immediately digested without producing excrement or urine.
Furthermore, as for the enjoyment of sexual desire:
Among all the sentient beings in the various hells, there is no sexual activity whatsoever. Why is this?
Because those sentient beings have for a long time, without interruption, experienced many kinds of extremely intense suffering.
Due to these causes and conditions,
those sentient beings do not give rise to desire for a woman in a man,
nor do they give rise to desire for a man in a woman.
How much more so when they engage in mutual union with one another?
Whether among ghosts, animals, or humans,
all embodied beings possess sexual desire because pleasure and pain are intermingled.
When men and women engage in mutual sexual union, impurity flows out;
although the various devas of the desire realm also practice sexual desire, they lack this impurity.
Nevertheless, a wind-gas issues from the sense organ, and through this, their afflictions are pacified.
In the Heaven of the Four Great Kings,
the feverish distress of sexual union subsides only after two moments;
as it is for the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, so it is for [the others].
It is the same for the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
For the gods of the Heaven of the Hours,
their feverish distress is quelled merely by embracing one another.
For the gods of the Heaven of Contentment (Tuṣita),
their feverish distress ceases merely by holding hands.
For the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanation (Nirmāṇarati).
When they look at one another and smile, their feverish affliction is immediately stilled.
In the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations,
when they look into each other's eyes, their feverish affliction is immediately stilled.
Furthermore, among the inhabitants of the three continents,
people take wives and concubines and establish the practice of marriage;
however, in Uttarakuru, because there is no sense of "mine" and no grasping, such things do not exist.
All sentient beings there have no wives or concubines to maintain, nor do they engage in marriage;
this is as it is for the inhabitants of the three continents,
and so it is likewise for the powerful spirits (*mahābala*) and the various devas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
With the sole exception of the Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas,
none of the celestial hosts in the entire desire realm possess the womb of a maiden.
However, among the Cāturmahārājika devas, [conception occurs] either upon the shoulders of the parents or within their laps.
They appear suddenly like five-year-old children;
those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are like six-year-olds,
and those of the Yāma Heaven are like seven-year-olds.
The gods of the Heaven of Contentment appear like eight-year-olds;
those of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations like nine-year-olds;
and those of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations like ten-year-olds.
Furthermore, regarding the establishment of birth, there are three kinds of births in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
There are sentient beings who currently dwell amidst the objects of desire;
because they currently dwell amidst these objects of desire, they possess wealth, honor, and sovereignty.
What, then, are they? They are all humans and the gods from the Four Great Kings up to the Sudṛśa gods.
These are called the first desire-realm births.
There are some sentient beings who transform sensual objects through their supernormal powers.
By means of these transformed sensual objects, they attain wealth, nobility, and mastery.
What, then, are they like?
This refers to the Nirmāṇarati devas.
These gods create objects of desire for their own sake,
not for the sake of others.
Because they themselves transform all objects of desire, they possess wealth, nobility, and mastery;
this is called the second birth from desire.
Or there are sentient beings who have objects of desire transformed by others.
They possess wealth, nobility, and sovereignty by means of the various sensual objects manifested by others.
Furthermore, what is meant by the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*)?
It is because those devas are able to manifest emanations for their own sake and are also able to manifest emanations for the sake of others.
Therefore, since they do not regard their own emanations as marvelous, but instead exercise sovereignty over the sensory objects emanated by others as their wealth and luxury,
this heaven is called Paranirmita-vaśavartin (Mastery over Others' Emanations).
It is not that those devas only enjoy objects of desire emanated by others;
there are also those who enjoy objects of desire emanated by themselves.
This is called the third birth of desire.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of the arising of bliss.
There are sentient beings who moisten their bodies with the joy born of seclusion;
these are the gods of the first dhyāna stage.
This is called the first birth through joy (*sukhopapatti*).
Alternatively, there are sentient beings whose bodies are moistened by the joy and bliss born of meditative concentration;
these are the gods of the second dhyāna stage.
This is called the second birth through pleasure.
Or there are sentient beings who have their bodies sprinkled with the joy born of detachment from rapture;
these are the devas of the third dhyāna stage.
This is called the third type of birth through pleasure.
Question: For what reason are three types of birth through desire and three types of birth through pleasure established?
Answer: Because there are three kinds of seeking.
First, the quest for sensual pleasures;
second, the quest for existence;
third, the quest for the holy life.
That is to say, whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas fall into the pursuit of desire,
all do so for the sake of the three types of birth from desire;
there is no further excess beyond this.
If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas fall into seeking existence,
they mostly seek pleasure;
it is because of their craving for pleasure.
All [beings] arise for the sake of the three kinds of happiness;
this is because those among worldly beings who undertake the pursuit of birth in the state of tranquility, which is neither painful nor pleasant, are extremely rare.
Beyond this, one does not establish [a further state] as "birth.
If there are any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who have fallen into the pursuit of the holy life (brahmacarya),
they all do so for the sake of seeking the untainted realm (anāsravadhātu).
Furthermore, there may be one who has fallen into a mistaken pursuit of the holy life (*brahmacarya*),
seeking the immovable states of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
One gives rise to false discrimination,
taking it to be liberation;
one should know that this is the pursuit of a superior brahmacarya.
"Seeking the unsurpassed holy life" refers to seeking the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
Furthermore, regarding "establishment by way of intrinsic nature":
That is to say, among all sentient beings within the three realms, there are four types of distinctions regarding the acquisition of their own physical existence (*ātmabhāva*).
There are those who acquire a physical existence that is destroyed by themselves, rather than being destroyed by another.
There are gods of the desire realm named "Forgetfulness Amidst Play.
As for those hosts of gods:
At times, one may become addicted to various forms of amusement and pleasure,
remaining engaged in them for a long duration;
due to this prolonged engagement, one loses mindfulness.
Due to a lapse of mindfulness, they pass away from that place;
or again, there are gods named Manovyāpādins (Mind-Anger),
and those hosts of gods...
At times they gaze at one another with sidelong glances;
because of this mutual gazing, their mental resentment increases,
and as their mental resentment increases, they pass away from that place.
There are some who possess a self-substance that is destroyed by another and not by themselves;
namely, those situated in the stages of the kalala, arbuda, peśī, and ghana.
Furthermore, all sentient beings within the mother’s womb,
or those who have already attained a physical body,
are harmed both by themselves and by others.
This refers to those very sentient beings who, having already entered the state of birth,
possess fully developed and perfected sense faculties,
or have acquired a physical body.
Nor is it through self-harm nor through harm by others;
namely, the various devas of the form and formless realms,
and all those in the hells (nāraka).
Resembling a hell-being or a hungry ghost,
he is a messenger of the Tathāgata dwelling in his final body.
Regarding the meditative absorption of loving-kindness, the meditative absorption of cessation, the meditative absorption of non-contention, or those situated in the intermediate state—
how are such categories established in terms of causes, conditions, and fruits?
Briefly stated, there are four kinds:
first, by way of characteristics;
second, by way of basis.
Third, by way of differentiation;
fourth, by way of establishment;
through their conjunction, those phenomena arise.
Is it the case that when something is acquired, accomplished, prepared, or employed,
it is described as the cause for that [result],
and thus the phenomenon arises?
Answer: It is preceded by its own seeds.

With the exception of the seed-support, it is established by means of all other supports—whether material or immaterial—as well as karma, for the sake of the conjunction of the accompanying factors and the objective referent.
In accordance with what is appropriate, there arise dharmas bound to the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, or those that are unbound.
What are these dharmas?
The answer is: they are preceded by the lineages of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and tathāgatas.
The internal factor serves as the foundation,
while the external factor serves as the condition for conjunction; thus,
one realizes nirvana, which is the dissociation from afflictions.
Internal factors refer to such internal wholesome dharmas as appropriate attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), fewness of desires, and contentment,
as well as obtaining a human body and being born in a noble land.
Having no deficiency in the sense faculties and no obstruction to one's livelihood,
and generating deep pure faith toward wholesome states—
such qualities as these are called internal power.
The power of external factors refers to the appearance of Buddhas in the world who proclaim the sublime Dharma, the continued existence of their teachings,
and those who abide in the True Dharma acting in accordance with it.
Those endowed with compassion and faith serve as the donors.
Such dharmas as these are called the power of external factors.
Who established them first?
Through the conjunction of what factors is what dharma established?
Answer: It is preceded by the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), and delight (*ruci*);
it is established by means of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Because it is not contradicted by the multitude of wholesome qualities and serves to reconcile those who hold opposing views, the established thesis is proven.
Fourth, regarding the resolution of questions: who is primary, and by whom is it established?
Through the conjunction of what is which dharma accomplished?
Answer: With skillful knowledge as the precursor, it is established according to one's diligent application.
The accomplishment of the bases of craftsmanship occurs through the conjunction of the various implements required for those crafts;
furthermore, it is preceded by craving.
That which sustains by means of nutriment is established as its support;
because the four nutriments act as a harmonious integration,
sentient beings who have taken birth abide and are fully sustained.
What is the function of this dharma?
The answer is: it takes its own seeds as primary;
that is, this very arising serves as its establishment.
It is precisely because these factors arise through conditions and are brought together that the functional activity of phenomena as one's own karma can be known.
What is called the functional activity of one's own karma?
That is to say, the eye has seeing as its function;
in this way, one should understand that each of the remaining faculties has its own respective function.
Furthermore, earth is able to support, water is able to moisten, fire is able to burn, and wind is able to dry.
One should understand that such categories as these constitute the differentiation of the external elements according to their own karma:
first, speech;
second, experience.
1. The three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
2. Seeds with moisture (*sārdrabīja*).
3. Immediate cessation (*anantaraniruddha*).
Six objects,
seven faculties,
and eight functions.
Nine: the activity of the person;
ten: the vision of reality;
eleven: conformity.
12. Differentiation of function;
13. Conjunction; 14. Obstruction.
Fifteen are unobstructed.
Regarding the distinctions among causes and so forth:
this refers to the ten causes, the four conditions, and the five fruits. As for the ten causes: [text continues].
First, the cause of conventional designation;
second, the cause of dependence;
third, the cause of projection.
1. The cause of origination; 2. The cause of arising; 3.
The cause of manifestation; 4. The cause of production; 5.
The cause of appropriation; 6. The cause of induction.
7. The cause of specific determination;
8. The cause of common activity;
9. The cause of contradiction.
The ten non-contradictory causes and the four conditions: first,
the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Second, the immediately preceding condition;
third, the object condition;
fourth, the dominant condition.
The five fruits are:
first, the fruit of maturation;
second, the fruit of outflow.
Third, the fruit of disjunction;
fourth, the fruit of human effort;
fifth, the dominant fruit.
Regarding "establishment by way of equality":
this refers to the designation of the cause of conventional expression based upon the causal basis of speech.
Why is this? Because the designation of phenomena associated with the desire realm, those associated with the form and formless realms, and those not so associated, is established first;
it is on the basis of this that perception functions.
Speech proceeds with conceptualization as its precursor;
by means of speech, various verbal expressions arise in accordance with what is seen, heard, sensed, and known.
Therefore, based upon speech and its locus, the "cause of subsequent expression" is designated.
Based on the basis of the cause of experiencing,
the expectant cause is designated. Why is this so?
Because of sentient beings,
those who seek the pleasure bound to desire depend upon this.
Regarding the various requisites for sensual pleasures, whether for the sake of seeking them, accumulating them,
or enjoying them, those who desire the happiness bound to the realms of form and formlessness rely upon these.
Regarding those various conditions, they may seek them for the sake of acquisition or for the sake of enjoyment.
Those who desire to seek the bliss of non-attachment depend upon these.
Regarding those various conditions, whether for the sake of seeking them or for the sake of enjoying them,
those beings who do not desire suffering depend upon these.
Regarding those conditions for arising and those conditions for cessation,
whether for the sake of avoidance, for the sake of attainment, or for the sake of enjoyment;
therefore, it is based on the basis of experience.
The contributory cause is established based on the basis of the cause of habitual tendencies;
the projecting cause is established based on that same basis.
Why is this so? Because the formations (*saṃskāra*) of the three realms, perfumed by pure and impure karma,
draw forth a desirable or undesirable personal existence within desirable or undesirable destinies.
Furthermore, it is precisely through this predominant power that external objects flourish or decline;
therefore, based upon the locus of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of pure and impure karma within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
one designates the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
Based on the causal basis of the moistened seed,
the cause of arising is established. Why is this so?
Because the phenomena bound to the desire, form, and formless realms each arise from their own respective seeds;
"craving" (tṛṣṇā) is called that which moistens the seeds, being the object of moistening.
It is by virtue of these seeds being moistened by this [craving] that they [arise].
The distinct individual existences previously projected shall arise;
as the Sūtra says:
"Karma is the cause that brings about birth."
Craving is the cause of arising.
Therefore, based on the locus of the moistened seed,
the cause of arising is established.
The cause of appropriation is established based on the causal basis of immediate cessation,
as well as the causal bases of the object, the sense faculty, activity,
and the reality of the fruit of human effort.
Why is this? Because it is due to the grasping of the dharmas bound by desire as they cease without interval.
Because of the appropriation of the objective sphere,
because of the appropriation of the faculties,
and because of the appropriation of activity.
Conditioned phenomena proceed because they are sustained by human effort;
as it is with phenomena bound to the desire realm,
so it is with those bound to the form and formless realms.
Alternatively, because they are embraced by the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*),
other non-bound phenomena (*apratisaṃyuktadharma*) arise.
Therefore, based upon the basis of the vision of reality— the causal efficiency (*puruṣakāra*) of the sense faculties (*indriya*) acting upon an object that has just ceased (*anantaranirodha*).
The cause of appropriation is established based on the locus of the concordant cause;
the cause of production is established [based on that].
Why is this? Because the wholesome dharmas bound to the desire realm can induce all superior wholesome dharmas bound to the desire realm.
In this way, wholesome dharmas bound to the desire realm can induce wholesome dharmas bound to the form and formless realms, as well as those that are unbound,
because they are in conformity with them.
Just as with wholesome phenomena bound to the desire realm,
so it is with wholesome phenomena bound to the form realm:
they can induce all superior wholesome phenomena bound to the form realm, as well as wholesome phenomena bound to the formless realm and those that are unbound.
Just as with wholesome phenomena bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*),
so too are wholesome phenomena bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
they can induce all superior wholesome phenomena bound to the formless realm as well as those not bound to any realm (*apratisaṃyukta*).
Just as with wholesome dharmas bound to the formless realm,
so too are the wholesome dharmas that are unbound;
they are able to induce all superior wholesome dharmas that are unbound.
Furthermore, it can induce the realization of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Moreover, unwholesome dharmas can induce various superior unwholesome dharmas;
that is to say, sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) can induce hatred, delusion, pride, views, doubt, misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.
As it is with sensual desire,
so it should be understood for all others— such as hatred, delusion, conceit, views, and doubt— as appropriate to each case.
In this way, indeterminate dharmas can induce wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas,
just as the ālayavijñāna contains the seeds of the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
Furthermore, neutral phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*) can induce superior neutral phenomena;
just as edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) can induce sentient beings who have taken birth to remain, to dwell in peace, and for their vital power to increase.
Because it conforms to that,
the inducing cause is established based on the basis of conformity.
Based on the locus of causes characterized by differentiated functional capacities,
the cause of distinctness (*viniyata-hetu*) is established. Why is this so?
Because the dharmas bound by desire possess distinctions in their own functional capacities, they are able to produce various kinds of their own functional capacities.
As it is with the dharmas bound by desire,
so it is with those bound by form, those bound by the formless, and those that are unbound.
Therefore, based on the locus of differentiated functional capacities, the cause of distinctness (*visadṛśa-hetu*) is established;
and based on the locus of the cause of combination (*saṃyoga-hetu*), [the cause of similarity is established].
The cause of commonality through designation (*prajñapti-sahabhū-hetu*) is as follows:
it is because one must obtain the concordant arising of that which is self-produced;
for example, the arising of phenomena bound by desire (*kāma-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*) is like [the arising of] phenomena bound by desire.
The same applies to phenomena associated with the form realm, the formless realm, and those that are unconditioned (unbound).
Just as there is the conjunction of birth,
so too is there the conjunction of the accomplishment of function.
Therefore, based on the locus of conjunction,
the cause of common activity is established;
and based on the locus of the cause of obstruction.
This is the cause of the contradiction in designation. Why is this so?
Because the dharmas bound to the desire realm are about to arise.
If obstacles manifest, [the dharma] cannot arise.
As it is with dharmas bound to the desire realm,
so it is with those bound to the form realm, the formless realm, and those that are unbound.
Just as it is with arising, so too is it with the accomplishment of its function.
Therefore, based on the locus of obstruction,
the contradictory cause is designated.
Based on the basis of the cause of non-obstruction,
the cause of non-contradiction is established. Why is this so?
When dharmas bound by desire are about to arise,
they do so immediately provided that no obstacles are present;
as it is with dharmas bound by desire, so it is with others.
The same applies to phenomena associated with the form realm, the formless realm, and those that are unconditioned.
As it is with birth,
so it is with the attainment and the accomplishment of function.
Therefore, based on the basis of non-obstruction,
the cause of non-contradiction is established.
Furthermore, based on the basis of the condition of the seed.
The condition of cause (hetu-pratyaya) is established based on the locus of the immediately preceding cessation;
the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya) is established based on that same locus.
The object-condition is established based on the basis of the objective field;
the remaining conditions are established based on the remaining bases.
The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is established.
Furthermore, based on the locus of the causal conditions that accord with habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*),
the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) and the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) are established.
The fruit of dissociation is established based on the causal basis of the seeing of reality;
it is established based on the causal basis of the efficient cause (*puruṣakāra-hetu*).
