The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) is designated based on the remaining causes and conditions as their basis; the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*) is designated based on the remaining causes and conditions as their basis.
The meaning of "establishment" (sthiti) is the meaning of "condition" (pratyaya).
The meaning of "accomplishment" (siddhi) is the meaning of "result" (phala).
These are the characteristics of the seeds.
First, the productive cause;
second, the instrumental cause;
third, the coexistent cause.
Fourth is the cause of immediate cessation;
fifth is the cause of long-term cessation.
As for the productive cause:
This refers to the cause of origination.
As for the instrumental cause,
it refers to all remaining causes.
The co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) refers to one portion of the supporting cause (parigraha-hetu).
Just as the eye is [the cause] for visual consciousness,
so too are the ear and the other [senses] for their respective remaining consciousnesses.
As for the "cause that has ceased immediately prior":
The cause of arising refers to the producing cause;
the cause of cessation over a long period refers to the projecting cause.
Furthermore, there are five characteristics of establishing causes:
first, the cause of the desirable;
second, the cause of the undesirable.
Third, the cause of increase;
fourth, the cause of transmigration;
fifth, the cause of cessation.
Furthermore, there are seven characteristics of establishing causes:
namely, impermanent phenomena are causes;
no permanent phenomenon can serve as a cause for another phenomenon.
That is to say, it serves either as a cause of production, a cause of attainment,
or a cause of establishment.
Either as a cause for accomplishment or as a cause for activity;
furthermore, although impermanent phenomena serve as causes for impermanent phenomena.
However, it acts as a cause for other-natures and also acts as a cause for its own subsequent nature;
it does not do so within that very same moment.
Furthermore, although it serves as a cause for the nature of another and as a cause for its own subsequent nature,
it can function as a cause only when it has already arisen and has not yet ceased.
It is not that which has not yet arisen or has already ceased.
Furthermore, although it has already arisen and not yet ceased,
it can only function as a cause when it encounters other conditions.
It is not that other conditions are not obtained;
yet, even when other conditions are obtained,
it must undergo transformation before it can function as a cause.
It is not that which has not undergone transformation;
furthermore, even though it has undergone transformation,
it must necessarily be associated with a functional capacity (*śakti*) in order to be able to serve as a cause.
It is not that their functional capacity is lost.
Furthermore, although they are associated with such capacity,
they can only function as causes when they are mutually commensurate and concordant.
It is not that they are discordant;
rather, it should be understood that the various causes are established according to their respective applications by means of these seven kinds of characteristics.
How are the designations and establishments of characteristics formulated?
The summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
Essence, object, aspect, origination, and differentiation.
One should know that the characteristics of both determination and the process of transmigration are briefly explained as being of seven types.
First is their essential nature (*tattva*).
Second, the object;
third, the mental aspect;
fourth, the motivation.
Five: differentiation;
six: discernment;
seven: transmigration.
As for the essential nature of vitarka and vicāra:
it is the lack of deep investigation into the object of focus;
volition (cetanā) constitutes its essential nature.
It should be understood that if one deeply investigates and evaluates the object of focus,
its essential nature is wisdom (*prajñā*).
As for the objects of vitarka and vicāra:
This means that taking the meaning of the sets of names, phrases, and syllables as the object of focus (*ālambana*),
the mode of activity (*ākāra*) consisting of seeking and examining is *vitarka* (initial inquiry). Specifically, the mode of activity that seeks out this very object is *vitarka*.
The mode of examination regarding this very object is vicāra (sustained thought).
That which gives rise to vitarka and vicāra is the initiation of speech.
Regarding the distinctions between vitarka and vicāra,
there are seven types of distinctions,
namely: from those with signs and those without signs, up to those that are non-defiled.
As previously stated.
Regarding the discernment of vitarka and vicāra:
if vitarka and vicāra are themselves conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*)?
Is it the case that what is conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is necessarily vitarka and vicāra?
That is to say, while all vitarka and vicāra are necessarily conceptualization,
there may be conceptualization that is not vitarka and vicāra.
That is to say, in comparison with supramundane wisdom,
all other minds and mental factors of the three realms are conceptualization (*vikalpa*),
yet they are neither vitarka nor vicāra.
Regarding the flow of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*): what are the applied and sustained thoughts of those in the hells (*naraka*),
what are their mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and what do they experience through contact (*sparśa*)?
What is it that induces?
What is it associated with?
What is it sought after?
By what karma do they arise?
Just as in the hells,
so too are the vitarka and vicāra of animals, hungry ghosts, humans, the gods of the desire realm, and the gods of the first dhyāna stage.
What is the practice?
What is the contact?
What is the induction?
With what is it associated?
What is sought?
By what karma does it proceed?
That is to say, the vitarka and vicāra of the hell-beings (naraka) are exclusively of a dejected nature;
they encounter undesirable objects,
which give rise to suffering associated with mental distress (daurmanasya).
Constantly seeking liberation from the karma that afflicts the mind, they revolve [in saṃsāra].
Just as those in the hells (naraka) exclusively experience suffering through their discursive thoughts and investigations (vitarka-vicāra),
so it is for hungry ghosts (preta).
The vitarka and vicāra of beings in the animal realm, humans,
and powerful hungry ghosts are for the most part characterized by dejection and only slightly by joy;
they mostly contact unpleasant objects.
It contacts a small portion of pleasant objects;
for the most part, it induces suffering and only a small portion of pleasure;
and for the most part, it is associated with mental distress.
A small portion is associated with joy;
for the most part, they seek liberation from suffering,
while a small portion seeks the encounter with pleasure.
The karma that agitates the mind operates as follows:
the vitarka and vicāra of the various devas in the desire realm are for the most part characterized by joyous activity and only slightly by sorrowful activity.
For the most part, one encounters pleasant objects;
for a small portion, one encounters unpleasant objects.
For the most part, it induces pleasure; for a small portion, it induces suffering.
For the most part it is associated with joy,
and for a small part with sorrow;
for the most part it seeks the attainment of pleasure, and for a small part it seeks liberation from suffering.
The karma that agitates the mind operates;
the vitarka and vicāra belonging to the gods of the first dhyāna stage are exclusively of a joyous nature.
It invariably contacts internally desirable objects;
it invariably induces pleasure;
and it is invariably associated with joy.
Seeking only not to be separated from happiness,
and with mental activity that does not afflict the mind,
how is the application of attention established according to principle?
The summary verse says:
The basis and the object, seeking and enjoyment, correct practice and the two accumulations for enlightenment,
and the skillful means for reaching the perfections.
It should be understood that the establishment [of these categories] is briefly based on eight aspects:
namely, by way of basis, by way of object,
and by way of seeking.
Because of enjoyment,
because of correct practice,
and because of the skillful means of the provisions for the Śrāvaka vehicle.

It is associated with appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) by way of the means of the provisions for the vehicle of the solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddhayāna*) and the means of bringing forth the perfections (*pāramitā*).
Regarding the bases for vitarka and vicāra,
there are six kinds of bases:
first, the time of determination.
Second, the time of cessation;
third, the time of performing activity;
fourth, the time of worldly detachment from desire.
Fifth, at the time of transcending the world and abandoning desire;
sixth, at the time of gathering and benefiting sentient beings—
these are associated with correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
Regarding the objects of vitarka and vicāra,
there are eight kinds of objects:
first, the object of the meritorious activity accomplished through giving.
Second, the activity of merit accomplished through ethical discipline;
third, the activity of merit accomplished through cultivation;
fourth, the activity accomplished through hearing.
Fifth, matters accomplished through reflection;
sixth, matters accomplished through other forms of cultivation;
seventh, matters accomplished through discernment.
Eighth, the accomplishment of the welfare of sentient beings through appropriate mental attention,
characterized by seeking with vitarka and vicāra.
That is to say, there is one who does not seek wealth through unrighteous means or through violent and dangerous methods;
rather, they employ it with appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*),
accompanied by investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*).
That is to say, having pursued wealth, one is not defiled by it,
does not dwell upon it, does not crave it, is not bound by it,
is not distressed by it, does not cling to it, nor does one grasp at it with stubborn persistence.
One who perceives deeply the defects, understands renunciation, and partakes [of sense objects] with application of appropriate mental attention (yoniśo-manasikāra),
and who practices correctly through investigation and analysis (vitarka-vicāra).
That is to say, there is someone who understands how to show respect, make offerings, benefit, and serve their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and household elders;
and who perceives great dread regarding the misdeeds committed in this life and future lives.
Regarding the practice of giving, the accumulation of merit, the observance of fasts, and the maintenance of precepts—
the expedient means for the provisions of the Śrāvaka vehicle—
I shall explain them in detail within the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
Regarding the means for the equipment of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle,
I shall explain them extensively in the *Pratyekabuddhabhūmi*.
Regarding the means for the realization of the *pāramitās*:
I shall explain this extensively in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Furthermore, there are four characteristics of a donor:
first, having the aspiration [to give].
Second, being without partiality;
third, removing poverty and deprivation;
fourth, possessing correct wisdom.
One who possesses ethical discipline (śīla) likewise has four characteristics:
first, having the aspiration;
second, constructing a bridge.
Third, non-manifestation;
fourth, possessing correct knowledge.
Those who have accomplished cultivation likewise possess four characteristics.
First, purity of aspiration;
second, purity of attraction;
third, purity of resolute concentration.
The purification of the four wisdoms has six aspects: first,
receiving and learning the gift.
Second, receiving offerings for the sake of sustaining one's life;
third, receiving offerings out of poverty and destitution;
fourth, receiving offerings through renunciation.
Fifth, receiving gifts while traveling abroad;
sixth, receiving gifts while being addicted to sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds of afflictions and harms.
First, the affliction of hunger;
second, the affliction of thirst;
third, the affliction of coarse food.
Fourth, the affliction of fatigue;
fifth, the affliction of cold;
sixth, the affliction of heat.
Seventh is the affliction of unobscured hindrances;
eighth is the affliction of obscured hindrances.
Furthermore, there are six kinds of afflictions.
First, co-arising;
second, the deficiency of what is desired;
third, oppression.
Fourth, the transformation of the seasons;
fifth, the outflows;
sixth, the cessation and abandonment of activities.
1. Beneficial assistance;
2. Beneficial assistance through courageous and undaunted protection;
3. Beneficial assistance through sheltering and safeguarding.
Fourth, benefit through the application of fragrant ointments;
fifth, benefit through clothing;
sixth, benefit through communal residence.
Furthermore, there are four characteristics of those who are not virtuous friends:
first, not relinquishing a heart of enmity;
second, inducing what is unloved in others.
Third, they restrain others from what they cherish;
fourth, they lead them toward what is unsuitable.
One should know that the opposites of these are the four characteristics of a virtuous friend.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of attraction:
first, the attraction of the requisites for life;
second, the attraction of joy and bliss.
Third, the inclusion of those who have abandoned joy and pleasure.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of attendant services:
first, the attendant service for one who is not an acquaintance.
Second, attending upon and serving one's relatives and friends;
third, attending upon and serving those who are respected;
fourth, attending upon and serving those endowed with merit and wisdom.
It should be understood that by means of these four kinds of conforming service,
five fruits are obtained based on four bases.
What are the four bases?
First, the state of being without grasping;
second, the state of being without affliction;
third, the state of being worthy of offerings.
Fourth, the sphere of conformity with the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Based on these four spheres, one is able to bring about five fruits:
first, the attainment of great wealth.
Second, their fame is heard everywhere;
third, they are free from all afflictions;
fourth, they realize nirvana.
Fifth, they may go to a happy destination.
Furthermore, there are three characteristics of wisdom for one who is wise:
first, the undertaking and practice of what is wholesome.
Second, regarding being well-determined;
third, regarding being well-firm.
Furthermore, there are three other characteristics.
First, training in higher ethical discipline;
second, training in higher mental cultivation;
third, training in higher wisdom.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Five;
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Six;
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

From the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, within the section on the Three Grounds beginning with "With Vitarka and Vicāra," Part Three. Furthermore, how are improper mental attentions (ayoniśomanasikāra) designated and established?
The summary verse says:
Adhering to the existence of the effect within the cause, Manifesting [the view that] the past and future exist, the self is eternal, and past actions are the cause;
[Belief in] Īśvara and so forth as the destroyers of the Dharma.
The sophistry of the finite and the infinite; the theories of non-causality,
nihilism, emptiness, supremacy, purity, and auspiciousness—
these are distinguished by sixteen heterodox doctrines through sixteen varieties of such divergent views.
This reveals improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
One should know that there are sixteen types;
the first is the theory that the effect exists within the cause (*satkāryavāda*).
2. Those who propound that [dharmas] are manifested through conditions;
3. Those who propound the real existence of the past and future;
4. Those who maintain the doctrine of a self (*ātman*).
5. The doctrine of eternalism;
6. The doctrine that past actions are the cause;
7. The doctrine that [a creator such as] Īśvara and others is the agent.
8. The discourse on the eight types of harmful views regarding the true Dharma;
9. The discourse on whether the world has an end or is infinite;
10. The discourse on the evasion of the question of immortality.
11. The doctrine of causelessness;
12. The doctrine of annihilationism;
13. The doctrine of nihilism.
14. The doctrine of false conceptualization regarding supremacy;
15. The doctrine of false conceptualization regarding purity;
16. The doctrine of false conceptualization regarding auspiciousness.
Those who maintain the theory that the effect exists within the cause are,
for example, certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine.
"At all times and at every moment,
the nature of the effect is fully present within all causes";
this is the view held by the Vārṣagaṇya non-Buddhists.
Question: For what reasons and conditions do those non-Buddhists give rise to such views and establish such doctrines, asserting that the nature of the effect exists within the cause?
Answer: It is by means of both scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*).
"Teaching" refers to the scriptural collections (śāsanapiṭaka) composed by those former masters,
which have been transmitted to the present day through successive hearing and recitation.
The principle that demonstrates the existence of the nature of the effect within the cause is as follows:
it is just like those śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
He is of a nature to investigate and of a nature to examine;
he dwells on the stage of investigation and dwells on the stage of self-attainment.
Abiding in the stage of ordinary beings,
and abiding in the stage of observing and examining through reflection,
he thinks as follows:
If this nature were to arise from that nature,
it would be universally known and established by all the world.
He takes this as the cause and not another;
furthermore, one who seeks a result takes only this cause and not another;
moreover, it is precisely upon this that he exerts effort and applies his labor for the sake of whatever is sought, and not upon anything else.
Furthermore, if that fruit arises from that very cause and not from anything else,
then that fruit must already exist within its cause.
Otherwise, one would have to establish that everything is the cause of everything.
In seeking a single fruit, one should take up all [causes];
one should apply effort and exertion toward all;
and from all [causes], every fruit should arise.
Thus, it is by way of designation, by way of seeking and grasping,
by way of the determination of what is done,
and by way of birth.
He perceives that within the cause there is always the nature of the effect,
the characteristic of the effect, and both characteristics of cause and effect.
Are they different or not different?
If there were no characteristic of difference,
then there would be no two-fold determination of cause and effect.
Because cause and effect are non-dual and without distinction,
the effect exists within the cause.
This is not logical.
If there were distinct characteristics,
what would you think?
Regarding the nature of the effect within the cause:
is it characterized as unarisen,
or is it characterized as already arisen?
If it has not yet arisen as a characteristic,
then while still within the cause,
the effect has not yet arisen.
To say that it exists is not logical,
if it is a characteristic that has already arisen.
It is not logical that the very essence of the fruit,
having already arisen, should arise again from a cause.
Therefore, the effect does not pre-exist within the cause;
nevertheless, the effect arises by depending upon causes and conditions.
Furthermore, there is the dharma of having signs.
Within the dharma of having signs,
by means of five kinds of characteristics:
Only then can it be fully understood:
first, that it is obtainable in a location,
such as water within a jar.
Second, it is obtainable in its basis,
such as eye-consciousness in the eye;
third, it is obtainable by way of its own characteristic.
For example, [the self] does not exist because it cannot be apprehended through inference based on its own essence;
fourth, because it can be apprehended through its own performed actions;
and fifth, because of the transformation of its causes.
The fruit becomes altered; or,
due to the alteration of conditions,
the fruit becomes altered.
Therefore, they assert that the effect exists within the cause at all times and for all eternity.
This is not logical; for this reason,
the thesis he has established is untenable.
This is not a correct statement,
because [the self] is neither non-different from nor different from [the aggregates].
Because it would entail the characteristics of being both unarisen and already arisen,
this is not tenable.
If any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa gives rise to such a view and establishes such a doctrine:
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is fundamentally existent;
it is manifested through various conditions,
but it is not produced by those conditions.
That is to say, those who maintain the theory that the effect exists within the cause,
as well as those who maintain the theory of the characteristic of sound, hold such a view.

Question: For what reason do those who maintain the theory that the effect exists within the cause perceive that the nature of the effect already exists within all causes and is merely manifested through conditions?
Answer: It is by means of both scripture and reasoning.
As for scripture, it is as previously explained.
As for reasoning, it refers to the case where there is someone whose nature is that of a seeker through reflection.
He practices investigation by nature.
As explained extensively before,
he reflects in this way:
If the effect already exists beforehand,
it would be illogical for it to arise again from a cause.
Nevertheless, it is not that effort is not required for the accomplishment of the fruit.
For what reason, then, would one exert effort?
Is it not solely for the purpose of manifesting the fruit?
Having formed such false conceptualizations,
he establishes the Abhidharma (the treatise of clear exposition) according to his own desires.
If there is an obstruction despite the absence of obstructing conditions,
does it mean that obstructing conditions actually exist?
If there are no obstructing conditions, [how can there be an obstruction]?
It is not reasonable that there should be an obstruction when the conditions for non-obstruction are present.
If there are obstructing conditions,
why do they not obstruct the cause that belongs to the fruit?
Because they are equally existent,
this is not logical; for example,
just as darkness obstructs the water within a jar, it can also obstruct the jar itself.
If it is argued that the obscuring conditions also obscure the cause,
then it should also manifest the cause, since both are equally obscured;
yet you claim that it only manifests the pre-existent nature of the fruit within the cause and does not manifest the cause itself.
This is not logical.
Furthermore, one should ask him:
"Is there a nature that serves as a condition for obstruction?"
Is it of the nature of a fruit?
If there were such a nature that acts as an obstructing condition,
then that would indeed be a nature.
That it is not always manifest is unreasonable;
for the cause also exists.
Why would it not constitute an obstruction?
If you say that the nature of the fruit is the condition for obstruction,
then a single dharma would be both cause and fruit.
Just as a sprout is the fruit of a seed and a stalk is the cause of [the sprout],
these are indeed a single dharma;
it is both manifest and unmanifest.
This is not reasonable.
Furthermore, I now ask you;
answer as you see fit.
This dharma and its manifestation are neither different nor non-different.
If they were not different,
the dharma would be constantly manifest.
To manifest what has already been manifested is not logical.
If you say they are different, [it is likewise not logical].
Is that manifested as being without cause,
or is it with cause?
If you say it is without cause...
To manifest without a cause is not reasonable.
If there were a cause, [then...]
The nature of the fruit can be manifested, whereas the nature of the cause cannot;
for it is not by manifesting the cause that one can manifest the fruit.
This is not logical;
for such [a case] would involve the absence of obstructing conditions,
whereas here there are obstructing conditions.
Because it possesses characteristics; because it possesses the characteristics of a result;
and because it is revealed as non-different [from them].
Because it would manifest a distinction,
this is not logical. Therefore,
your statement that "if the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) does not exist, then it is without characteristics (animitta)" is incorrect.
If the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) exists, it would possess characteristics;
if that nature were non-existent, it could not be manifested.
If the nature can be manifested, then it must exist.
This is not logical.
I shall now explain:
although it exists, its characteristics cannot be grasped.
That is to say, there may be cases where something exists but cannot be apprehended because it is too distant.
Furthermore, due to four kinds of obstructions,
it cannot be apprehended on account of causal obstructions.
Furthermore, it cannot be apprehended because it is extremely subtle;
or because the mind is distracted;
or because the sense faculties are impaired.
Alternatively, it may be that they cannot be apprehended because the corresponding knowledge has not yet been attained;
however, this is unreasonable according to the *Prakaraṇapāda* (Treatise on the Manifestation of Cause and Effect).
It should be understood that the theory of the characteristics of sound is likewise unreasonable.
The distinction here is as follows:
the external proponents of the theory of sound give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine.
The characteristic of sound is eternally abiding, without arising or ceasing;
yet it is only through its utterance that it becomes manifest.
Therefore, this treatise’s claim that it is like a "manifesting discourse" (vyakti-vāda) is not a tenable explanation.
Those who maintain that the past and future truly exist refer to certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who belong to this teaching.
Due to improper reflection, they give rise to such views and establish such doctrines:
"The past exists; the future exists."
Its characteristics are established as being truly existent in the present, rather than being merely nominal.
Question: For what reasons and conditions do they give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine?
Answer: It is due to both scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*).
The teaching is as previously explained.
Furthermore, those who abide in this dharma engage in improper conceptualization regarding the Tathāgata’s sūtras.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"All that exists consists of the twelve bases (āyatana).
The true nature of these twelve bases is existence."
Furthermore, the Blessed One has stated that there is past karma;
he has also stated that there is past form and future form,
and so on, in detail, up to consciousness, which is likewise.
"Principle" (nyāya) refers to one who is by nature prone to discursive investigation and by nature prone to analytical observation.
As explained at length previously,
he thinks thus:
"If a phenomenon abides by its own characteristic, that phenomenon truly exists."
If this were non-existent in the future,
then at that time it would not yet have received its characteristics;
if this were non-existent in the past, [then...]
At that time, they would lose their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). If this were the case,
the specific characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma*) would not be established.
Because this principle is likewise not ultimate,
it is unreasonable;
through such reflection, one gives rise to this view.
They establish this thesis:
that the nature and characteristics of the past and future exist substantially,
and whether they are identical to or different from the characteristics of the present.
If one says that their characteristics are identical,
then it is not logical to establish the characteristics of the three time periods;
if their characteristics are different, [it is likewise not logical].
It is not logical that their intrinsic nature and characteristics exist substantially.
Furthermore, you should state your own intended position:
do phenomena belonging to the three periods of time possess the characteristic of permanence or the characteristic of impermanence?
If it were a permanent characteristic,
it would be illogical for it to fall within the three periods of time;
if it were an impermanent characteristic...
It is not logical that it should exist as a real entity throughout the three periods of time.
Furthermore, I now ask you;
answer according to your own conviction.
Is it that future dharmas are calculated to come into the present world?
Or is it that after those [dharmas] have died, they arise in this life?
Or is it that while remaining in the future, they serve as conditions to produce the present?
Is it that what was originally without karma now possesses karma?
Is it that what was originally incomplete in its characteristics is now complete in its characteristics?
Is it that what was originally of a different characteristic is now of a different characteristic?
Is there a present part within the future?
If it were the case that a future dharma itself comes into the present,
then it would possess spatial location.
Furthermore, it would be no different from the present;
moreover, it would follow that it is eternal, which is contrary to reason.
If one were to say that what has died in the future is born in the present, then that [present] would simply be the future.
It is not produced in the present world, for dharmas fundamentally do not arise now;
furthermore, to speak of death and disappearance regarding that which has not yet arisen in the future is illogical.
If it is said that the dharma abides in the future and arises as the present by taking that [future dharma] as its condition,
then that [dharma] must be eternal.
Furthermore, it would follow that what is produced now was originally non-existent, and thus it would not be a future dharma arising.
This is not logical.

If there were originally no karmic activity and now there is karmic activity, then this would mean that what was originally non-existent has now come into existence; thus, one incurs the aforementioned fault, which is illogical.
Furthermore, what is your position?
Is this functional activity distinct in character from that fundamental dharma, or is it not distinct in character?
If there were a distinct characteristic,
it would be illogical because this characteristic of karmic activity does not exist in the future.
If there were no distinct characteristic,
it would be unreasonable for that which was originally without functional activity to now possess functional activity.
Just as there is this fault regarding the absence of functional activity,
so it is with the perfection of characteristics and distinct characteristics.
The future portion should be understood in the same way.
The distinction here is that there would also be the fault of confusion regarding their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
This is not logical.
Just as the future moves toward the present,
so too does the present proceed to the past.
The faults should be understood according to what is appropriate;
that is to say, they are just as previously considered regarding the various causes and conditions and the logical arguments for refutation,
whether by way of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Because of coming and because of death;
because of being conditioned by birth and because of karma;
because of the perfection of characteristics and because of the difference of characteristics.
Because there is a future constituent part,
it is unreasonable to maintain the theory that the past and future exist as substantial entities.
Having spoken thus, there is further objection:
"If the past and future are non-existent,
how can cognition arise taking the non-existent as its object?"
If one says that cognition arises even when its object is non-existent, how is there no fault of contradicting the teachings?
As it is said: "All exists."
That is to say, the twelve bases.
I now ask you;
answer according to your own understanding.
Does the worldly cognition that grasps at non-existence arise or does it not?
If it does not arise, [then...]
One can realize the selflessness of the grasper, as well as [the non-existence of] rabbit horns,
the son of a barren woman, and so forth.
All of these must be non-existent; this is not reasonable.
Furthermore, the Bhagavān said:
When my śrāvakas, free from deceit,
practice correctly according to what I have taught,
they know existence as existence and non-existence as non-existence.
This is not logical.
If you say that it arises,
what do you think?
This grasping is without conceptualization.
Is it performed with volitional activity, or is it performed without volitional activity?
If it were performed with volitional activity...
It is not reasonable to perceive non-existence and yet engage in activity as if it were existence;
for if one were to engage in activity as if it were non-existent, [it would be irrational].
What do you intend?
Does this perception of non-action proceed by having an objective basis as its condition?
If it were to proceed by taking non-existent things as its object, or if it were to proceed by taking existent things as its object,
then it would be unreasonable for an awareness of non-action to proceed by taking existent things as its object.
If it were to function by taking a non-existent thing as its object,
it would follow that there is no object and no cognition, which is unreasonable.
Furthermore, although those who assert that "all exists" refer to the twelve bases (āyatana), [the Sautrāntikas argue that]...
However, regarding existent phenomena (*bhāva*), it is taught with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*) that they possess the characteristic of existence;
regarding non-existent phenomena (*abhāva*), it is taught with intentional meaning that they possess the characteristic of non-existence. Why is this so?
If there is a dharma with characteristics that can maintain that which has characteristics,
or a dharma without characteristics that can maintain that which is without characteristics,
for this reason both are called dharmas and both are called existent.
If it were otherwise,
practitioners would only know existence and not know non-existence, and thus their contemplation of the objects of knowledge would not be uninterrupted;
this would be illogical.
Furthermore, although it is said that past karma exists,
and that by virtue of this karma sentient beings experience either harmful or non-harmful sensations,
this too is based upon those latencies (*vāsanā*).
It is spoken of as existing through intentional metaphor,
meaning that within the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
there have previously existed pure and impure karmas.
Whether arising or ceasing, it is by virtue of these causes and conditions that those formations proceed as a distinguished continuity; this is called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*).
It is because of this habitual tendency, which is comprised within this continuity.
Since the fruits of the agreeable and the disagreeable arise, there is no fault on my part.

Furthermore, your position is not logical; moreover, when you say that past form exists, future form exists, and present form exists—and so on up to consciousness—it is likewise based upon three modes of activity.
It is spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*).
That is to say, based on the characteristic of cause (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of self-nature (*sva-lakṣaṇa*),
and the characteristic of fruit (*phala-lakṣaṇa*), it is with reference to that characteristic of cause that it is intentionally said that the future exists.

Based on the intentionality regarding its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is said that the present exists; based on the intentionality regarding its fruit-characteristic (*phalalakṣaṇa*), it is said that the past exists.
Therefore, there is no fault.
Furthermore, one should not say that the past and future possess the characteristic of real existence (*dravyasat*).
Why is this? It should be understood that the future possesses twelve kinds of characteristics.
The first is the characteristic manifested by causes.
2. The characteristic of the entity not yet having arisen;
3. The characteristic of depending on various conditions;
4. The characteristic of the category of that which has already arisen.
5. The characteristic of phenomena that are subject to arising;
6. The characteristic of phenomena that are not subject to arising;
7. The characteristic of the defilements that have not yet arisen.
Eight, the characteristic of purity that has not yet arisen;
nine, the characteristic of what should be sought;
ten, the characteristic of what should not be sought.
Eleventh, the signs that should be examined;
twelfth, the signs that should not be examined.
It should be known that there are likewise twelve kinds of signs in the present.
1. The characteristic manifested by a single fruit;
2. The characteristic of the essence having already arisen;
3. The characteristic of the convergence of various conditions.
4. The characteristic of having already arisen;
5. The characteristic of a single moment;
6. The characteristic of a dharma that will not arise again.
7. The appearance of manifest defilement;
8. The appearance of manifest purity;
9. The appearance that is delightful.
10. The ten signs that are not to be delighted in;
11. The sign that should be examined;
12. The sign that should not be examined.
It should be known that the past also possesses twelve kinds of characteristics:
first, the characteristic of having already transcended causes;
second, the characteristic of having already transcended conditions.
3. The characteristic of having already transcended the fruit;
4. The characteristic of the substance having already disintegrated;
5. The characteristic of the category having already ceased.
Sixth, the characteristic of the state of non-arising;
seventh, the characteristic of the cessation of affliction;
eighth, the characteristic of the cessation of purification.
9. The characteristic of that which should be cherished;
10. The characteristic of that which should not be cherished;
11. The characteristic of that which should be examined.
Twelve characteristics that should not be scrutinized:
First, if any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa gives rise to such a view and establishes such a doctrine:
There is a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a living being,
a nourisher, and a person;
such things are real, true, and eternally abiding.
This refers to the way non-Buddhists and others formulate such views.
Question: For what reason do those non-Buddhists give rise to such views and establish such doctrines?
Answer: It is due to both scripture and reasoning.
The teaching is as previously explained.
As for the principle:
it refers to a certain person who, by nature, is prone to discursive investigation and by nature is prone to analytical examination.
The detailed explanation is as before.
It is due to two causes:
first, because there arises a cognition of a sentient being (*sattva*) through a sudden, unpremeditated occurrence.
Second, because they have already previously reflected and perceived that there is an agent;
they reflect in this way:
"If there were no self, one would perceive five things."
One should not give rise to the five types of perception of a self;
rather, having seen a form and shape,
one should give rise only to the perception of that form and shape.
One should not give rise to the perception of a sentient being (*sattva*).
Having observed that the two views accord with formations of suffering and pleasure,
one should give rise only to the perception of feeling (*vedanā*).
One should not give rise to the perception of sentient beings as superior or inferior.
Once the names have been established for the three views, they are termed "associated formations";
one should then give rise only to the perception and cognition thereof.
One should not give rise to [the notions of] kṣatriya, brāhmaṇa,
or vaiśya.
Śūdra, Buddhadatta,
and Guṇamitra.
Having perceived that the four [elements] are associated with the formation of the pure and the impure,
one should give rise only to the awareness of formations (saṃskāra).
One should not give rise to the perception of beings as either fools or wise; rather,
once the five views have ceased to follow after consciousness regarding its objects,
one should give rise only to the awakening of the mind.
One should not give rise to the notion of a self,
nor the perception of a sentient being (sattva), and so forth.
Because of such prior lack of conceptualization,
regarding these five things, one gives rise only to the five kinds of sentient-being-perceptions,
and not to the perception of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, because one first perceives through non-conceptual awareness and then immediately gives rise to the cognition of a "sentient being" (sattva), one thus determines that a real self exists.
Furthermore, they think in this way: "If there were no self..."
One should not, amidst conditioned phenomena, first give rise to volitional thought that there is something to be done,
such as thinking, "I shall see forms with my eye," or "I am seeing forms."
Having already seen various forms,
one might again give rise to the thought:
"I shall not see them."
All such functions are preceded by the activity of my own awareness,
just as it is with seeing through the eye.
One should know that it is likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Furthermore, regarding wholesome karma, there is the performance of wholesome karma and the cessation of [unwholesome] karma;
regarding unwholesome karma, there is the performance of unwholesome karma and the cessation of [wholesome] karma.
Such matters as these all have volition and discernment as their precursor before they can function.
Such functions as these should not be obtainable;
it is unreasonable [to claim they exist] only with respect to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Answer as you see fit:
does the perception of a sentient being arise with respect to the very object that is seen,
or does the perception of a sentient being arise as something distinct from the object that is seen?
If one were to give rise to the cognition of a sentient being (*sattva*) with respect to the very object seen,
you should not say that one imputes a sentient being to form (*rūpa*) and so forth;
for the imputation of a self (*ātman*) is a perverted cognition.
If the cognition of a sentient being were to arise as something distinct from the perceived object,
it would follow that I possess a physical dimension, which is not tenable.
Some may be superior or inferior;
some may be kṣatriyas and so forth;
some may be foolish or wise.
It would not be logical for it to be able to apprehend those objects such as form;
furthermore, what is your position on this?
Does this cognition arise solely from the intrinsic nature of this phenomenon,
or does it also arise from other natures?
If it arises solely from the intrinsic nature of this phenomenon, [then...]
If one gives rise to the cognition of "that" and "self" regarding what is seen,
it should not be called a perverted cognition.
If this cognition were also to arise with respect to another entity, [it would likewise not be perverted].
To claim that all objects of cognition are individually the causes for the awakening to all objects of cognition is unreasonable.
Furthermore, what is your position regarding the cognition of a sentient being in what is reckoned as insentient,
and the cognition of an insentient thing in what is reckoned as sentient?
Regarding other sentient beings, does the cognition of them as "other sentient beings" arise or not?
If it does arise, [then...]
In that case, the insentient would be the sentient;
the sentient would be the insentient;
and one sentient being would be another sentient being.
This is not reasonable.
If [the object] does not arise,
then it would not be a denial of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This is not logical.
Furthermore, what is your position regarding this awakening of a sentient being?
Is it for the sake of apprehending the object of direct perception (pratyakṣa),
or for the sake of apprehending the object of inference (anumāna)?
If it is for the sake of apprehending the object of direct perception, [then...]
Only the aggregates such as form are objects of direct perception;
the self is not an object of direct perception.
Therefore, [the claim that the self exists] is unreasonable.
If one takes the meaning of inference (anumāna),
it is like that of the ignorant or the young,
who are not yet capable of reflection and deliberation.
One should not rashly give rise to the notion of a self.
Furthermore, I now ask you;
answer according to your own understanding.
Regarding what is produced in the world:
is it caused by consciousness (*vijñāna*),
or is it caused by a self (*ātman*)?
If awakening were the cause,
it would be unreasonable to cling to what one has created as "mine."
If the self were the cause,
it would first have to conceive and intend that something is to be done;
this is not tenable.
Furthermore, what is your position:
is the cause of the action produced eternal or non-eternal?
If it were impermanent,
the nature of this causal agent would be subject to change; therefore,
to maintain that the self is an agent is unreasonable.
If it were permanent,
there would be no change;
for it is illogical that there should be activity in that which is unchanging.
Furthermore, what is your position:
does an active self perform actions,
or does a non-active self perform actions?
If there were a self that performs actions capable of doing something,
it would be performing eternally and should not need to act again.
If there were an inactive self that performs actions,
it would be illogical for that which is inactive by nature to perform actions.
Furthermore, what is your position:
do you hold that the self acts because there is a cause,
or that it acts without a cause?
If there were a cause,
this self would have to be impelled by another cause before it could perform an action;
this is not logical.
If there were no cause,
then everything would arise at all times;
this is not logical.
Furthermore, what is your position:
does this "self" perform its actions by depending on itself,
or does it perform its actions by depending on something else?
If it were based on a self,
it would be unreasonable for this self to perform such defiled acts as aging,
sickness, death, and so forth.
If it were dependent on another,
the notion that "I am the agent" would be illogical.
Furthermore, I shall now question you.
Answer as you see fit:
Is the self designated in relation to the aggregates themselves,
or is it [designated] within the aggregates?
Is it in a location other than the aggregates?
Or does it not belong to the aggregates at all?
If the self were designated as being identical to the aggregates themselves, [it would follow that the self is subject to arising and ceasing].
It would not be logical to conceive of a self as truly existent and permanent, given that there is no distinction between this self and the aggregates.
If [the self] were among the aggregates,
would this self be permanent or impermanent?
If it were permanent...
It is not logical that a permanent self should be subject to the benefit or harm caused by various pleasures and pains;
for if there were no such benefit or harm, neither dharma nor adharma would arise.
This is not logical. If neither dharmas nor non-dharmas were to arise,
then the aggregates and the body would never arise at all.
Furthermore, it would follow that the self is eternally liberated without depending on effort.
If it were impermanent,
it would undergo arising and ceasing apart from the nature of the aggregates.
Because a dharma that flows on in a continuous succession cannot be apprehended,
it is not reasonable;
furthermore, regarding this disintegration:
Furthermore, to obtain results in another place without having performed the corresponding action would entail a great fault;
therefore, it is not reasonable.
If it were located elsewhere outside the aggregates,
the self as you conceive it would have to be unconditioned (asaṃskṛta),
which is not tenable.
If it were not associated with the aggregates,
the self would never be subject to defilement;
furthermore, the self and the body would not be related to one another.
This is not reasonable.
Furthermore, what do you maintain regarding the self that you postulate?
Is it identical to the characteristics of the seer and so forth?
Or is it distinct from the characteristics of the seer and so forth?
If it were identical to the characteristics of the seer and so forth...
Is it that the characteristics of a "seer" and so forth are merely designated upon seeing and so forth?
Or is it that the characteristics of a seer and so forth are established separately from seeing and so forth?
If the characteristics of a seer and so forth are merely designated upon seeing and so forth...
In that case, seeing and so forth would have to be the seer and so forth;
yet, your postulation of a self as the seer and so forth is not tenable.
Because the seer and so forth are indistinguishable from the act of seeing and so forth.
If one were to establish the characteristics of the seer and so forth as distinct from the act of seeing and so forth, [it would be untenable].
Are those phenomena such as seeing and so forth the karma accomplished by me,
or are they the instruments appropriated by me?
If it were something produced by me, then,
like a seed, it would necessarily be impermanent;
this is not reasonable.
If it is said that this self is like a "person" (pudgala) conventionally established,
such as a potter and so forth, then this self must be impermanent and must be a conventional designation.
Furthermore, your assertion that this is permanent and real is not logical.
If you say it is like a "person" (pudgala) conventionally designated upon one who possesses supernormal powers, [that too is untenable].
This self would also have to be impermanent;
that it is conventionally established as having sovereign control over all its activities is likewise untenable, as explained previously.
If you say it is like earth,
then it should be impermanent;
furthermore, the self as you conceive it does not possess the qualities of the great element of earth.
It is not logical [to claim] that it manifests through its activity. Why?
Because in the world, the activity performed by the earth element is perceived as something clearly manifest.
That is to say, it upholds all things so that they do not fall downward;
yet no such activity of mine can be clearly perceived.
If it were like space, it would not be substantially existent.
It is not logical [to claim] that emptiness is merely a conceptual designation applied to form;
for although space is a conceptual existence, [it is not so in this case].
Yet its functional activity is clearly perceivable;
since it is not the self as you conceive it,
[your position] is unreasonable.
Regarding the fact that the functional activities produced within the world's space are clearly perceivable—
namely, that it is by means of space that activities such as coming and going, bending and stretching, and so forth, arise—
it follows that seeing and other such functions are the activities accomplished by the self.
This is not logical.
If it were an instrument of appropriation belonging to a self,
then it would be like a sickle.
Just as there is a function of cutting even by means of objects other than a sickle,
so too [is there a function] apart from seeing and the rest.
It is not logical,
because the functional activity of seeing and so forth cannot be found in external objects other than [the self].
If one says it is like fire,
then one is merely speculating about a self;
this is not logical.
Why is this? Because,
just as fire in the world is able to burn by itself even apart from that which is being burned.
If one claims that there is a self distinct from the characteristics of the seer and so forth,
then the imagined characteristic of the self contradicts all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is therefore unreasonable.
Furthermore, I now ask you;
answer as you see fit.
Regarding the "self" that you postulate:
Is it because of being associated with defilement and purity that there is defilement and purity?
Or is it without being associated with defilement and purity that there is defilement and purity?
If it is because of being associated with defilement and purity that there is defilement and purity, then...
Within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), there are calamities such as epidemics and their cessation, as well as favorable conditions that can be obtained;
thus, although these conditioned phenomena are devoid of a self (*ātman*),
they are said to correspond with defilement and purification.
As it is with external objects,
so it is with the internal body;
although there is no self, [it functions].
The meanings of defilement and purification are thus established;
therefore, your conception of a self is not logical.
If there were defilement and purification without being associated with them, [it would be untenable].
It is not logical that the self possesses defilement and purity while being free from the characteristics of defilement and purity.
Furthermore, I now ask you this:
Answer as you see fit:
Do you conceive that this "self" undergoes transmigration because it is associated with the characteristics of transmigration,
or is it not associated with the characteristics of transmigration?
Is there, then, both cyclic existence and its cessation?
If there were both cyclic existence and its cessation while being associated with the characteristics of cyclic existence, [how could that be?]
Within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), five characteristics of flux (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*) are observable:
first, having a cause;
second, being subject to arising; and third, being subject to cessation.
Fourth, there is the arising through continuous succession;
fifth, there is transformation.
If these characteristics of fluxion are observable within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), [they constitute the nature of saṃsāra].
Just as in the case of the body, a sprout, a river, a lamp,
a vehicle, and so forth— despite the absence of a self within their processes of flux—
their conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) nonetheless undergo both progression and cessation; why, then, must one postulate a self?
If there were transmigration and cessation without being associated with those characteristics,
then the imagined self would possess the characteristic of non-transmigration yet undergo transmigration and cessation.
This is not logical.
Furthermore, I now ask you;
answer as you see fit.
The "self" that you conceive—
does it arise from objects,
or from pleasure and pain, or from volitional karma?
It is said to be the experiencer, the agent, and the liberator because it is transformed by afflictions, secondary afflictions, and so forth;
it is not [so called] because it is not transformed by them.
Is it said that they are the experiencer and so forth?
If [the self] were to undergo transformation by means of them,
then these very conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) would be the experiencer, the agent, and the one who attains liberation.
Why must one calculate "self"?
Even if it were the self,
the self would have to be impermanent.
This is not logical. If [the self] does not undergo transformation by virtue of those [factors],
then the self would be immutable, yet it would still be the experiencer, the agent, and the one who attains liberation.
This is not reasonable.
Furthermore, you should now state your own position:
do you assert that the agent exists only in relation to me?
Or is it that [the agent] is also designated as such with respect to other phenomena?
If it were only with respect to the self,
then the world would not speak of fire as the burner or light as the illuminator.
If [the self] were also [the agent] with respect to other phenomena—
that is, with respect to the faculties such as vision—
it would be a mere vain conceptualization to designate it as a "self."
This is not logical.
Furthermore, you should state your own intended position:
do you establish the notion of "self" solely with respect to the self?
Or is the self established in relation to other phenomena as well?
If it were established in the self alone,
the world would not metaphorically designate that person’s body with names such as "Guṇamitra" or "Buddhadatta."
If it were also [designated] with respect to other phenomena,
then the designation "self" would apply merely to conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*);
why, then, must one further cling to a separate self?

Why is this? Because worldly people conceive the notion of a "sentient being" and establish the designation "sentient being" only with respect to the body of a conventionally designated person, and they speak of "self" and "other."
Because there is a distinction.
Furthermore, what is your position:
do you consider the view that conceives of a self to be wholesome or unwholesome?
If it were wholesome,
why would such extremely foolish people give rise to the view of a self so deeply,
doing so impulsively without employing skillful means?
It would be unreasonable for it to cause sentient beings to fear liberation,
or to increase their various evils and faults.
If it were unwholesome,
one could not say that it is correct and non-perverted; furthermore,
if this self-entity conceived through false perversion were substantially existent, [it would follow that it is wholesome].
This is not logical.
Furthermore, what do you maintain?
Is it that there is a view of no-self?
Is it wholesome or unwholesome? If one says it is wholesome,
then regarding that permanent, truly existent self,
one perceives the non-existence of a self.
However, it is not logical that this wholesome nature is a non-perverted conception.
If one were to say it is unwholesome...
This has been proclaimed by the Omniscient One;
it arises through diligent application of skillful means,
causing all sentient beings to have no fear of liberation and enabling them to swiftly realize the fruit of purity.
It is not logical that various faults and evils are countered as they truly are.
Furthermore, what do you think?
Is it that the nature of the self itself conceives of a self,
or is it by means of the view of self?
If it were that the nature of the self itself conceives of a self:
At all times, there should be no cognition of selflessness;
if it were by way of the view of a self,
then even though a real self does not exist, [the cognition would still arise].
Due to the power of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), one falsely asserts that there is a self among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, your reckoning that a self definitely and substantially exists is not logical;
for such a cognition arises preceded by a lack of awakening [to reality].
Because it is preceded by thought and discernment and is seen as something performed;
because it is a conventional designation among the aggregates;
and because it is established as existing based on those characteristics.
Because it establishes defilement and purification;
because it establishes the process of transmigration and its cessation;
and because it provisionally designates the experiencer, the agent, and the liberator.
Because an agent is conceptually established;
because verbal expression is conceptually established;
and because views are conceptually established.
Any conception of a real self is entirely unreasonable.
To explain the characteristics of the self from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*):
that which is called "self" [is as follows].
It is only by way of conventional designation that phenomena are established as existing;
there is no real self.
Nevertheless, this conventionally designated self—
It cannot be said that this has a nature either different from or non-different from those phenomena,
lest one claim that this self is a substantially existent entity,
or that those phenomena are themselves the nature and characteristics of the self.
Furthermore, this conventional self is characterized by impermanence;
it is not characterized by constancy.
It is not the characteristic of security;
it is the characteristic of transformation and decay,
and the characteristic of the arising of phenomena.
The marks of old age, sickness,
and death are merely the marks of all phenomena (dharmas),
for they are merely the marks of suffering and affliction.
The Bhagavān said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that within all phenomena, the designation 'self' is conventionally established."
"This self is impermanent, unstable, and cannot be relied upon;
it is a phenomenon subject to transformation and decay.
Thus it is explained at length.
For four reasons,
a self is conventionally designated within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
First, it is for the sake of making worldly discourse easy.
Second, it is because he wishes to conform to the ways of the world;
third, it is because he wishes to eliminate the fears associated with the notion that there is no self in meditative concentration;
and fourth, it is because he wishes to proclaim the virtues and faults achieved by himself and others.
This is for the purpose of causing the arising of a mind of resolute faith and understanding;
therefore, the doctrine that clings to a self is not a teaching in accordance with reality.
As for those who maintain the doctrine of eternalism:
That is to say, there is a certain śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who gives rise to such a view and establishes such a doctrine:
"Both myself and the world are truly eternal."
It is neither an agent nor an object of action;
it is neither a creator nor a creation;
it abides as an indestructible accumulation.
It is like the *iṣika* [reed],
namely those who speculate regarding the past and assert that all things are eternal,
or those who assert that some things are eternal.
Furthermore, regarding those who calculate the future limit, there are those who speak of having marks,
those who speak of being markless,
and those who speak of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, there are those who reckon that the various atoms (*paramāṇu*) are eternal, making such a reckoning.
[The Buddha] asks: for what reason do those non-Buddhists hold such a view?
They give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine:
"Are the self and the world eternal?
The answer is that their reckoning of causes and conditions is as explained at length in the Sūtra.
One should understand all [categories] according to what is appropriate.
Among these, those who speculate about the past do so by relying on either the lower, middle, or superior dhyānas.
He gives rise to the recollection of past lives;
because it has unwholesome origination as its object,
[it applies] to past conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
However, they merely recollect without knowing things as they truly are;
they reckon the past as the prior limit and give rise to the view of eternalism.
Alternatively, relying on the divine eye, one reckons the present life as the prior limit;
yet one does not know, as it truly is, the momentary arising, ceasing, and flux of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, one perceives the continuous succession of consciousnesses as they flow from this world to that world.
Because there is no interruption,
they give rise to the view of permanence;
or they see the Brahmā King established according to his will.
Some perceive the transformation of the four great elements;
some perceive the transformation of the various consciousnesses;
these are those who speculate regarding the future limit.
Although one perceives a distinction between perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*),
one does not perceive a distinction in their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*);
therefore, the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) arises.
This refers to the view that both the self and the world are entirely eternal,
as well as the reckoning that atoms are eternal;
these views arise based on worldly meditative concentration.
Because of not knowing dependent origination as it truly is,
one conceives that the arising of the accumulation of results is preceded by existence,
and the destruction of results is preceded by disintegration.
For this reason, they claim that gross objects arise as effects from the nature of the multitude of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*).
By gradually analyzing gross objects down to the point where only the subtle atom remains,
they conclude that gross objects are impermanent while the subtle atom is eternal.
The doctrine that the past limit and the future limit are eternally abiding is a doctrine of self-grasping,
because it is subsumed under the characteristic of differentiation.
My own thesis has already been refuted;
you should know that the thesis concerning the specific characteristics of the self has likewise been completely refuted.
Furthermore, I now ask you;
answer as you see fit regarding the recollection of past lives.
Is it by grasping the aggregates that one grasps a self?
If one grasps the aggregates,
one clings to the self and the world as being eternal.
This is not logical.
If one were to grasp at a self,
one would recollect such sentient beings as those with such-and-such names in the past.
"It is not reasonable to say: 'I existed in such a name and such a clan at that time,' and so forth, as explained in detail."
Furthermore, what do you think?
When visual consciousness arises in dependence upon a visible form that is present and in conjunction,
regarding other objects that are not present and not in conjunction, what of the remaining consciousnesses?
Is it for cessation or for transformation?
If you say it is for cessation,
then you are reckoning that which is destroyed and disintegrated as being permanent.
This is not logical.
If you say that it transforms,
it must be by means of a single object.
It is not logical that all consciousnesses should arise at all times.
Furthermore, what is your position regarding the self you maintain:
is it produced by perception (saṃjñā) or produced by sensation (vedanā)?
Is it subject to change or is it unchanging?
If one says it is subject to change,
then one reckons that both the world and the self are permanent.
This is not logical.
If one says it does not exist,
then having already possessed the notion of unity, there would subsequently arise various notions.
Furthermore, it would be illogical for there to be both limited perceptions and immeasurable perceptions.
Moreover, after there has been exclusively pleasure, there would again be exclusively suffering.
Furthermore, it would be unreasonable for there to be suffering, pleasure,
and that which is neither suffering nor pleasure.
Moreover, if one were to reckon that the life-principle is identical to the body...
He conceives that the self is form;
if he conceives that the life-principle is different from the body,
he conceives that the self is not form.
If one calculates that the self is both pervasive and non-dual, without deficiency,
then that person calculates the self to be both material and non-material.
If, for the sake of counteracting this,
one employs different phrases and different expressions regarding this very same meaning.
As for those who give rise to such grasping,
they conceive of a self that is neither form nor non-form;
furthermore, they perceive a limited amount of form and a limited amount of non-form.
They conceive of it as finite;
if they see it as immeasurable,
they conceive of it as infinite.
Furthermore, if one perceives them universally, yet the portion consisting of form is small while the portion not consisting of form is immeasurable,
or the portion consisting of form is immeasurable while the portion not consisting of form is small.
Their calculation is that it is both finite and infinite; in order to counteract this,
[the sūtra] merely employs different phrasing, not a different meaning,
for those who give rise to such attachments.
They reckon that it is neither finite nor infinite;
or they reckon that the liberated self is free from these two extremes.
Furthermore, there are those who maintain the doctrine of the eternal atom (paramāṇu).
I now ask you;
answer as you see fit.
Do you regard the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) as permanent?
Is it because of a failure to investigate that one conceives of them as permanent?
If it is through a failure to investigate,
then one conceives of them as permanent despite being devoid of the investigation of wisdom.
This is not logical.
If one claims that it has already been examined,
this contradicts the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and is therefore not logical.
Furthermore, what is your position?
Do you maintain that the nature of atoms is eternal because they are subtle?
Is it because its characteristics differ from those of coarse fruits that you consider it to be permanent?
If it were by virtue of being subtle,
then as it becomes dispersed, diminished, and further weakened, [it would not be permanent].
To claim that it is permanent is unreasonable.
If you say it is because their characteristics differ,
then [it follows that] the atom...
It transcends the characteristics of earth, water, fire, and wind;
yet, because its characteristics are of a different kind,
it is said to be able to produce fruits of that same kind.
This is not logical;
furthermore, no distinct characteristic can be found in those atoms.
This is illogical.
Furthermore, what is your position regarding the coarse objects that arise from the various atoms?
Is it of a non-differentiated nature or of a differentiated nature?
If one says it is of a non-differentiated nature,
it is because there would be no distinction from its cause.
It would also have to be permanent;
in that case, there would be no certainty regarding cause and effect,
which is not logical.
If they were of different characteristics,
what do you think:
would a coarse object arise from dispersed atoms?
Or does it arise from their aggregation?
If you say it arises from their separation,
then all effects should arise at all times.
In that case, there would be no certainty regarding cause and effect,
which is unreasonable. If [the result] were to arise from a collection, [it would likewise be untenable].
What do you think?
When those coarse material objects arise from atoms,
do they not exceed the dimensions of their constituent forms?
Is it because it exceeds the dimensions and substance of that form?
If you say it does not exceed the dimensions and substance of that form,
then it must be a distinct entity from the form.
It is not logical that a living being possesses a material form with parts.
If you say there is a fault [in this], [then consider the following:]
Since the essence of atoms has no parts, they cannot be analyzed;
therefore, the coarse objects produced from them would also have to be eternal.
This, too, is not reasonable.
Furthermore, if it is asserted that there are atoms which previously did not exist but now arise,
this would imply that atoms are eternal,
which is unreasonable.
Furthermore, what is your position?
Do those atoms produce coarse objects in the manner of seeds and so forth?
Is it like a potter and so forth?
If you say it is like a seed and so forth,
then it should be like a seed, whose substance is impermanent.
If it is argued that they are like potters and the like,
then those atoms must possess volition,
just like potters and the like.
This is not logical.
For if it were not like the seed and so forth, or like the potter and so forth,
then a concordant example could not be found.
This is not reasonable.
Furthermore, what do you think:
do external objects arise by means of sentient beings, or not?
If it is argued that [the world] arises from sentient beings,
then while those external coarse objects arise from sentient beings,
their underlying subtle objects do not.
This is not logical.
Who, moreover, could restrict its functional capacity therein?
If you say it is not by means of sentient beings, [then...]
This would mean that external objects arise without purpose,
which is not logical.
Thus, it is because one recollects sentient beings by way of the aggregates.
Because the stream of all consciousnesses continues uninterrupted from a single object,
and because perception and feeling undergo change and non-change,
those who speculate regarding the past and the future maintain the doctrine of eternalism.
This is not logical;
furthermore, it is because of the distinction between observation and non-observation,
and because of the universal characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa).
By way of their own characteristics,
by way of their production and formation,
and by way of the fundamental application.
The doctrine that atoms are eternal is not reasonable;
therefore, those who maintain the doctrine of permanence do not speak in accordance with reality.
I shall now explain the characteristic of permanence:
that which, at all times,
possesses no characteristic of change.
Whether it be the characteristic of non-alteration in every respect,
the characteristic of non-alteration by its own nature,
or the characteristic of non-alteration due to another.
Furthermore, one should know that the characteristic of non-arising is the characteristic of permanence.
