From the *Mūlavastu*, the section on the "Three Stages of With-Application and With-Analysis," Part Four: The Discourse on Causality through Previous Actions. It is as if there were a certain śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa.
They give rise to such views and establish such doctrines,
as explained at length in the Sūtra:
"Whatever is experienced by any person or individual (pudgala) in the world..."
This means that whatever suffering is currently experienced all has past karma as its cause;
that is to say, it is caused by past evil deeds.
Regarding "by means of exerting diligence to expel past karma," this refers to present new karma produced through extreme ascetic practices in the present life.
Regarding "by being harmed by the absence of the cause [for its production]," this refers to...
This refers to all unwholesome karmas.
As for the statement "thus, subsequently there are no further outflows," this means that they are exclusively of a wholesome nature.
It speaks of the subsequent state of being untainted (*anāsrava*).
"By means of being untainted, karma is exhausted" refers to all unwholesome karma.
"By means of the exhaustion of karma, suffering is exhausted" refers to the afflictions of suffering produced by past causes as well as those summoned by the expedients of the present life.
Regarding the statement, "By the exhaustion of suffering, one realizes the limit of suffering":
this refers to the realization that the continuity of suffering in future births has been exhausted.
This is the view held by the Nirgrantha outsiders.
Question: For what reasons and conditions do those non-Buddhists give rise to such views and establish such doctrines?
Answer: It is due to both scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*). As for scripture, it is as previously explained.
As for reasoning, it is like someone whose nature is that of an investigator (*vitarkin*).
It is by nature investigative,
as explained in detail previously;
because one perceives that the activities of a person in the present life are not determinate.
Why is this? Because he sees that in the world, although one may possess correct means, they bring about suffering;
and although one may possess erroneous means, they lead to happiness.
He thinks thus:
"If the causal factor for that were the human effort of the present life,
then that [effort] would be erroneous."
Because what they perceive is not erroneous,
they all take past actions as their cause.
For this reason, [it is said]:
They give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine:
that suffering has past actions as its cause.
This takes the skillful means of the present life as its cause.
If it were to take past actions as its cause,
then what you previously stated— that by means of diligent effort one expels old karma and that new karma in the present is destroyed by the absence of the cause of non-action— would be undermined.
Thus, it would not be logical for there to be no further outflows thereafter,
and so on, as explained at length.
If the cause were the application of skillful means in the present life,
then what you previously stated—
that all that is experienced by any person or individual in the world is caused by past actions— would be unreasonable.
Thus, it is unreasonable that the suffering of the present life has past actions as its cause and the human effort of the present life as its cause.
Therefore, this treatise does not speak in accordance with reason.
I shall now explain the characteristics of causes as they truly are:
there are some forms of suffering that have only past actions (*pūrvakṛta*) as their cause.
It is just as there is someone who, due to the predominant power of their own karma, is born in the various evil destinies or in a poor household;
or again, there is suffering produced by a combination of causes,
such as when someone, because of improper conduct toward a king, fails to obtain the fruit of happiness and instead encounters suffering.
Just as one serves a king,
so too does one engage in various occupations such as trade and commerce,
or by practicing agriculture.
Due to the karma of theft,
one may cause harm to other sentient beings; yet,
if they possess merit, they will obtain wealth and happiness.
If one lacks merit, although one exerts effort, there will be no successful result.
Alternatively, there are phenomena that are obtained solely through the causal power of present effort,
such as the karma that projects a future existence when newly created, or the discernment of the Dharma through hearing the true teaching.
Or again, they may initiate the paths of action consisting of deportment,
or they may train in the fields of arts and crafts;
such are the various categories [of activities].
Regarding those who maintain that the self-existent creator and so forth are the cause, and who argue that it is solely due to the present human effort of a person—
just as there might be a certain śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa.
They give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine:
that whatever is experienced by all persons and individuals in the world has its cause solely in the transformations of Īśvara.
Or else, other beings may transform themselves as the cause.
Such views as these are held by proponents of the theory of an unequal cause, such as Īśvara and others. One asks:
for what reason and by what causal conditions do they give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine?
Answer: It is by means of scripture and reasoning.
Scripture is as previously explained.
As for reasoning:
It is just as if there were someone who is by nature prone to discursive thought and by nature prone to investigation,
as explained in detail previously.
He forms this conception because he observes that, within the realm of cause and effect, worldly sentient beings do not act according to their own desires.
Why is this so? Because one observes worldly sentient beings directly.
At that time of the cause, although they wished to cultivate pure karma,
they did not achieve their original intent;
instead, they committed evil once again.
At the time of that fruition, although they wish to be born in a happy world within the good realms,
their original desire is not fulfilled,
and they instead fall into the evil destinies and so forth.
This means that although one intends to experience pleasure, it does not accord with one's desires,
and instead one undergoes various sufferings;
it is because of seeing this that [one acts].
He thinks thus:
"The various things in the world must necessarily have a distinct creator, progenitor, and transformer as their father—
namely, Īśvara or someone else."
The *Tattvasaṃgraha* says:
"Function has no intrinsic nature; Whether it is inclusive or exclusive, it contradicts itself;
Whether it is functional or non-functional, It results in logical fallacies when used as a reason."
Is the transformative power of Īśvara and others caused by the application of karma as its condition,
or is it without cause?
If one takes the application of karmic skillful means as the cause,
then only this functional capacity takes the application of karmic skillful means as its cause,
and not anything else in the world.
This is not logical. If there were no cause,
then this capacity alone would exist without a cause.
It is not a worldly object; this is unreasonable.
Furthermore, what is your position?
Is this Maheśvara included within the worldly realm, or is he not?
If you say he is included, [then...]
If this Maheśvara were identical to worldly phenomena,
yet could universally produce the world,
it would not be logical.
If it were not comprised [within the world],
it would be liberation;
yet you say it can give rise to the world.
This is not logical.
Furthermore, what is your position:
does the world arise through transformation for the sake of utility?
Is it useless? If it were useful,
then there would be no sovereignty over that utility.
Furthermore, it is not logical for there to be one who possesses sovereignty over the world;
if such a being were of no purpose, [then their existence would be untenable].
It is not logical that one should be born into this world without having anything required.
Furthermore, what is your position on this?
Is that which is produced caused solely by Maheśvara,
or does it also take other things as its cause?
If Maheśvara alone were the cause,
then whenever Maheśvara exists,
at that time there would be production.
If there is a time of origination, then Maheśvara exists;
therefore, to say that origination has Maheśvara as its cause is not reasonable.
If it is said that other factors are also taken as causes,
this refers only to taking desire (*chanda*) as the cause;
it does not mean that, in order to exclude desire, one takes yet other factors as causes.
If desire alone is taken as the cause,
does this desire take Maheśvara alone as its cause,
or does it also take other things as its cause?
If Maheśvara alone were taken as the cause,
then whenever Maheśvara exists, there would be desire;
and whenever there is desire, Maheśvara would exist.
It would follow that there must always be production from time immemorial;
this, too, is not logical.
If it is argued that other things are also taken as causes, [the same fault follows].
Because such a cause cannot be found,
it is not logical.
Furthermore, there is no mastery over that desire.
To claim that there is one who possesses mastery over worldly things is not reasonable;
for it is due to the exertion of effort [that things arise].
Because of being included or not included;
because of having utility or lacking utility;
and because of being the nature of a cause.
All of these are unreasonable;
therefore, this treatise does not represent a reasoned exposition.
It is like the case of certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
They give rise to such views and establish such doctrines:
"If, within those sacrificial rites,
one takes incantations as the primary means to take the lives of various sentient beings..."
Whether it be those who perform the sacrifice,
those who are harmed,
or their various associates.
In this way, all of them attain rebirth in the heavens.
Question: By what causes and conditions do those non-Buddhists give rise to such views and establish such doctrines?
Answer: This contradicts reason;
it arises from flattery and deception, and is not established through the investigation of principles.
However, when the evil age of strife and contention arises,
various Brahmins transgress the ancient Brahmin laws and falsely devise this scheme out of a desire to eat meat.
Is this the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon,
or is it the intrinsic nature of a non-phenomenon?
If it is the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon, [then...]
By abstaining from taking life,
one cannot merely obtain the fruits one desires,
but can transform that which is unrighteous into the true Dharma.
This is not logical.
If it were an entity that is non-dharma by its very nature,
it would inherently be a dharma that produces undesirable results.
Furthermore, it would be illogical for one to be able to subsequently abandon other dharmas that result in undesirable fruits;
having thus explained this:
Furthermore, there is a rescue argument which says:
"Just as poisons in the world cannot cause harm when subsumed by incantations and arts,
one should know that this method of incantation and art is likewise."
Now one should question them:
"What is your position?
Is it that just as a mantra is able to neutralize external poison?"
It can also pacify the internal poisons of greed,
hatred, and delusion— is it not so?
If it can indeed pacify them, [then...]
It is illogical because there is no place or time where greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth can be found to have been stilled in even a single person.
If they cannot be stilled,
then that which you previously stated [is contradicted].
It is unreasonable that just as a mantra is able to pacify external poisons,
it should also be able to pacify and eliminate those who engage in unrighteous actions.
Furthermore, what is your position on this?
Is this incantation and ritual method universal,
or is it not universal?
If [the self] were omnipresent,
it would be unreasonable for one not to first offer sacrifices to those whom one loves and holds dear.
If it were not universal,
the efficacy of this mantra would not be definitive,
which is unreasonable.
Furthermore, what is your position?
Does the power of this mantra only transform the cause, or does it also transform the fruit?
If it only transforms the cause, [then...]
It would be illogical for it to lack the capacity to produce a result;
if it were also to transform the result, [it would likewise lack such capacity].
One should cause the sheep and other such beings to assume lovely and wondrous forms through transformation;
however, it is only after discarding the bodies of the sheep and others that one subsequently takes on a celestial body.
This is not reasonable.
Furthermore, what is your position regarding those who compose incantations?
"Do you have the power and the compassion [to do so]?
If you say that you do,
then spare his life."
It would be unreasonable [to claim] that they cannot be led to rebirth in the heavens.
If one were to say that such a thing does not exist, [it would likewise be unreasonable].
It would not be logical for the spells he has created to be capable of accomplishing anything;
thus it is by way of the cause.
Because it is merely a metaphor;
because it is not determinate;
and because it lacks efficacy toward the result.
Because it is a matter of incantations,
it is not reasonable. Therefore,
this treatise is not a discourse in accordance with reality.
I shall now explain the characteristics of what is non-Dharma (*adharma*).
If an action harms others and its manifest fault is not remedied, this is called non-Dharma.
Furthermore, if an action is known by those who practice the path to result in an undesirable fruit, it is also non-Dharma.
Furthermore, any karma that the Omniscient One definitively declares to be unwholesome;
any karma that one does not desire for oneself;
and any karma that arises from a defiled mind.
Furthermore, if an action requires the aid of heterodox incantations and arts to achieve its efficacy,
or if the nature of the action is neutral (avyākṛta),
such things as these are all contrary to the Dharma.
Regarding those who propound the views of finitude and infinitude:
it refers to certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who,
by relying upon the various worldly dhyānas, [hold such views].
Regarding that world, they dwell with the perception of finitude, the perception of infinitude,
the perception of both, or the perception of neither;
as explained at length in the Sūtra.
From this, one gives rise to such views and establishes such doctrines:
"The world is finite," or "The world is infinite."
The world is both finite and infinite;
the world is neither finite nor infinite.
It should be understood that herein the causes and conditions, as well as the one who speculates, have already been explained.
In this context, when one seeks the limit of the world by relying on the boundary of cessation:
if one recollects the kalpa of destruction, one gives rise to the perception that the world has an end;
if one recollects the kalpa of formation, one gives rise to the perception that the world is infinite.
If one seeks the limit of the world by measuring its spatial extent,
one finds nothing further below the Avīci Hell,
nor does one find anything further above the Fourth Dhyāna.
When one cannot find a limit in the horizontal directions,
at that time, one conceives the notion of finitude regarding the zenith and nadir,
while conceiving the notion of infinitude regarding the horizontal locations.
If, in order to remedy this attachment,
one relies merely on the fact that there is no difference in meaning despite the different phrasing,
then one will give rise to the notion that the world is neither finite nor infinite.
What is your position?
Since the previous kalpa of destruction, has there been a further arising of the world,
or has there been no such arising?
If one says it exists,
it is not logical that the world has a limit. If one says it does not exist, [it is not logical that the world has a limit].
It is not reasonable to maintain that one who does not abide in the world should dwell on the limits of the world;
for such a person would still exist as a coming being.
Since their coming has no cause,
all [of these views] are unreasonable;
therefore, this treatise is not a reasoned exposition.
Regarding the death of the heterodox teachers who resort to evasive equivocation,
as explained at length in the sutra,
one should know that if anyone comes to those various heterodox teachers...
Based on the path of supreme birth,
one inquires into the wholesome and the unwholesome;
based on the path of definitive excellence.
When asked about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, he would claim for himself:
"I am one who is not subject to death or confusion; wherever I abide, I rely upon the gods of the Deathless and the Unconfused."
When interrogated, he immediately evades the question with deceptive speech;
or he resorts to other matters as a means to avoid it;
or he merely shifts his discourse to follow the words of the questioner.
Among these, the first "undying confusion" is when awakening has not yet been realized;
the second concerns the dharma that has been realized.
They give rise to overweening pride.
Upon the third awakening, they have attained enlightenment,
yet it is not yet definitive.
Fourth, they are weak, inferior, and dull-witted.
Furthermore, first, they fear speaking falsely,
and they also fear that others will recognize their lack of wisdom.
He does not answer clearly, saying, "I know nothing.
Second, regarding what he has personally realized, he has not attained fearlessness and thus fears the interrogation of others.
Out of fear of false speech and fear of wrong views,
I do not speak clearly of anything I have realized.
Third is the fear of wrong views and the fear of false speech,
because one dreads being interrogated by others.
By not speaking clearly, one does not provide a definitive answer;
thus, in these three ways,
one employs evasive speech by resorting to other matters.
The fourth [type of person] fears only being questioned by others;
they lack thorough understanding of both the path for birth in the most excellent [realms] and the path to definitive excellence.
Regarding worldly scripts and literature,
he likewise does not understand them well;
yet he does not clearly declare, "I am dull-witted and have no understanding at all."
But one should instead question them,
and by employing their own terminology,
turn it back upon them to confound them with equivocation.
Fourth, the exposition of the causes and conditions for the arising [of these views],
as well as those who hold such calculations,
together with the refutation of their attachments.
All this is as explained in the sutras.
When people come to question him on certain matters,
he immediately employs flattery and crookedness to act with deceit and confusion.
It should be understood that this view is subsumed under wrong views;
therefore, this treatise is not a reasoned exposition.
[This concludes] the doctrine of the view of no cause.
It should be understood that there are two kinds: those based on meditative concentration (dhyāna) and those based on discursive thought (vitarka).
As explained at length in the sutra.
Question: For what reason and by what causes do those non-Buddhists rely upon discursive investigation?
They give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine:
"Both the self and the world arise without cause."
Answer: To speak briefly, it is because the non-continuity of views is primary;
thus, there are immeasurable distinctions among all internal and external phenomena.
Various things arise;
or again, at times,
one sees that all causes and conditions are empty and devoid of karmic fruit.
That is to say, one perceives that the world has no causes or conditions;
for instance, at times a great wind may suddenly arise,
yet in an instant it becomes perfectly still and ceases.
At times, a torrential river may suddenly overflow,
yet in an instant it becomes completely empty; at other times,
fruit-bearing trees may suddenly burst forth in full bloom.
At one time, they suddenly became haggard and decrepit.
Because of this, they gave rise to the view that there is no cause and established the doctrine of non-causality. They—
Regarding your recollection of past lives, do you recollect the absence of self-nature,
or do you recollect a self? If it is the absence of self-nature that you recollect, [then...]
A phenomenon that lacks intrinsic nature has never been familiarized through practice,
nor has it ever been previously cognized.
It would not be logical for one to be able to recollect [them] while recollecting a self.
If one recollects a self, [it is not logical].
To calculate that I previously did not exist and then suddenly came into being is not reasonable.
Furthermore, what is your position?
All things, internal and external, within the world arise in various ways,
or they arise suddenly.
Is it without cause?
Or is it with cause?
If it were without cause, [then...]
Various things arise;
they arise suddenly,
and at times they do not arise.
This is not logical.
If there were a cause, then both the self and the world [would have arisen from it].
To arise without a cause is not reasonable,
because such a recollection lacks substantiality.
Because of mindfulness of the self,
one thinks that internal and external things do not arise from various distinct causes and conditions; rather,
it is because of those various distinct causes and conditions [that they arise].
This is not logical;
therefore, this treatise does not speak in accordance with reason. This refers to the proponents of the doctrine of nihilism (ucchedavāda).
That is to say, there is a certain śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who gives rise to such a view and establishes such a doctrine,
[claiming] that he possesses even coarse form.
When the body, composed of the four great elements,
remains sustained and has not yet perished,
at that time there is illness.
There is the abscess and there is the arrow;
if, after my death, they are severed,
destroyed, and no longer exist.
At that time, I have completely severed and extinguished [craving] regarding the various devas of the desire realm and the various devas of the form realm.
If it is comprised within the formless realm,
from the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The detailed exposition is as set forth in the sūtra;
that is to say, it describes seven types of proponents of the view of annihilationism who maintain such a position.
Question: For what causes and conditions do those various non-Buddhists give rise to such views and establish such doctrines?
Answer: It is by way of both scripture and reasoning.
Scripture is as previously explained.
As for reasoning, it refers to the case where there is someone whose nature is that of a seeker through investigation.
...and so on, as explained at length.
He thinks thus: "If, after my death, there were another body, then one would obtain the ripening of the fruit without having performed the action."
If my essential nature were eternally non-existent in every respect,
then there would be no experiencing of the maturation of karmic fruits; thus,
one should contemplate these two aspects.
Both [positions] are logically untenable.
Therefore, one gives rise to such a view and establishes such a doctrine:
"After my body has died, it is annihilated and ceases to exist."
Just as a piece of pottery or a stone, once broken, cannot be joined back together,
so too is it with that;
this should be understood through reasoning.
Is it the aggregates that are annihilated,
or is it the self that is annihilated?
If you say it is the aggregates that are annihilated, [then...]
The nature of the aggregates is impermanent;
as cause and effect arise in succession without interruption,
to say that they are annihilated is incorrect.
This is not logical.
If you say that the self is annihilated,
then what you previously stated [is contradicted].
The coarse physical body, composed of the four great elements,
is subject to illness, boils, and arrows;
so too are the various devas of the desire realm.
The devas of the form realm,
or those included within the sphere of infinite space of the formless realm,
and so forth...
It is not reasonable that it be subsumed under the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
likewise, because the aggregates would be severed and extinguished.
If [the self] were to undergo annihilation,
all [of this] would be irrational;
therefore, this treatise does not represent a reasoned exposition.
Regarding those who hold the view of nihilism (uccheda-dṛṣṭi):
it refers to certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine.
There is no giving, no offering of sustenance, and no sacrificial rites;
as explained at length, up to... [and so forth].
"There is no true arhat in the world," and further giving rise to such a view and establishing such a doctrine:
"There is no essential nature or characteristic in any phenomena whatsoever."
Thus it is argued.
The answer is: by means of both scripture and reasoning.
As for scripture, it is as previously stated.
"Principle" refers to, for example, one who is by nature prone to discursive investigation,
and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, it is based upon the various worldly meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
He saw that although a lay donor had constantly practiced giving throughout his entire life without interruption,
upon passing away from there, he was reborn into a low-born family, impoverished and destitute.
He thinks to himself:
"There certainly is no such thing as giving, nourishing, or sacrificial offerings.
Yet he further observes that there are people who, throughout the duration of their single lifetime, constantly practice sublime conduct.
Or, having committed unwholesome deeds,
one sees them at the end of life falling into the evil destinies and being born in various hells,
or else going to the happy destinies.
Born into a world of heavenly bliss,
he thinks to himself:
"There certainly are no such things as wholesome deeds or unwholesome deeds."
Furthermore, there is no differentiation in the ripening of the fruits of the two types of karma— wholesome and unwholesome conduct—
and yet one sees a member of the kṣatriya caste who,
after the end of his life, [attains such a state].
Born among the various castes of Brahmins, Vaiśyas,
or Śūdras, or as a Brahmin,
after the end of his life—
He is born among the various castes of kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras;
the vaiśyas and śūdras, and so forth, are likewise.
He thinks thus:
It is certain that the kṣatriyas and others of this world do not come from the lineages of kṣatriyas and others of that world,
nor do the kṣatriyas and others of that world go to the lineages of kṣatriyas and others of this world.
Furthermore, he observed those who were free from desire being born in lower realms;
he also saw a mother, after her life had ended, being born as her daughter,
and the daughter, after her life had ended, returning to become her mother.
A father becomes a son;
a son, in turn, becomes a father.
Having seen that fatherhood and motherhood are not fixed, he reflects in this way:
In this world, it is certain that there are no fathers and no mothers;
or else, one sees that when a person’s body perishes and life ends,
they are reborn in the realm of non-perception.
Some are born in the formless realm,
while others enter nirvana;
though one seeks their place of birth, it cannot be seen.
He forms this thought:
"There are certainly no beings born by transformation,
because their location cannot be known."
Or, having conceived the overweening pride of being an Arhat regarding oneself, one sees at the time of death the signs of rebirth.
That person then thinks:
"There can certainly be no true Arhats in this world."
Thus it is explained at length.
Question: For what further reasons do some give rise to such views and establish such doctrines?
There is no intrinsic nature or characteristic in any phenomena whatsoever.

The answer is that this is because they are unable to correctly and truly awaken to the profound teachings spoken by the Tathāgata— teachings that are profound in their resemblance yet free from verbal expression.
Furthermore, because one contemplates the established characteristics of phenomena in a manner that does not accord with correct principle,
the view of nihilism arises.
He thinks thus:
"There is certainly no intrinsic nature or characteristic in any phenomena.
Now, one should question him.
What do you intend?
Is there karma to be experienced in this life and karma to be experienced in a future life,
or is everything experienced only in this life?
If they were coexistent,
then what you previously stated—
that there is no giving— would be false.
There is no cherishing and nurturing;
there is no sacrificial offering;
there is no sublime conduct.
There is no misconduct;
there is no excellence of conduct, nor is there any ripening of the fruit of the karma of misconduct;
there is no this world.
It is not reasonable that there is no future world.
If one says that there is nothing to be experienced hereafter, [it is unreasonable].
Whosoever performs various karmic actions, whether pure or impure,
at the time of their death and subsequent rebirth,
[they experience the results].
It would not be logical for one to experience all the ripening fruits of both pure and impure karmas simultaneously.
Furthermore, what is your position?
All those who are born from that womb and from those seeds are, for them, their parents.
Are they not your parents?
If you say they are your parents,
yet you claim there is neither father nor mother.
This is not logical.
If one were to say that they are not one's parents,
yet they are born from that womb and those seeds.
To say that they are neither father nor mother is unreasonable,
for at times they have indeed been one's father and mother.
At that time, they were neither male nor female;
when they became male or female,
at that time they were no longer their parents.
There is no fallacy of uncertainty.
Furthermore, what is your position?
Is it that there are beings born in those places whom the divine eye does not see?
Or is it that they do not exist?
If you say they do exist,
then your statement that there are no spontaneously born beings is contradicted.
This is not reasonable.
If one says they do not exist,
then one is negating those who are free from conceptual desire.
To claim that one who is free from desire for form is also free from desire for the three realms is not reasonable.
Furthermore, what is your position:
does an arhat-nature exist such that one gives rise to overweening pride regarding it,
or does it not exist?
If you say that they exist,
then your statement that there are certainly no true arhats in the world is unreasonable.
If one were to say that there is none,
yet someone were to give rise to improper reflection and perversion,
claiming for themselves the status of an Arhat.
To say that this person must truly be an Arhat is also unreasonable;
furthermore, one should question him as follows.
What do you intend?
Is it the dharmas of the perfected nature,
or the dharmas of the dependent nature?
Regarding the phenomena characterized by the nature of imagined construction (parikalpita-svabhāva): do they exist or not?
If one says they exist, [then...]
Your statement that there is no intrinsic nature or characteristic in any phenomena is not reasonable;
if you say they do not exist, [it follows that...]
It would follow that there is neither inversion nor defilement and purification,
which is illogical.
This is because [the self] would be something experienced after having been born.
It is not because they are indeterminate;
it is because there are places of birth and because there is overweening pride.
Because there are three kinds of characteristics,
it is not logical; therefore,
this treatise is not a reasoned exposition.
Regarding those who propound the theory of false conceptualization as supreme:
this refers to certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who give rise to such views and establish such doctrines.
The brahmins are of the most excellent lineage;
the kṣatriyas and others are of inferior lineages.
The brahmins are of the pure white caste.
The other castes are of a dark and defiled nature;
it is possible for the Brahmin caste to attain purity,
but not the other castes.
All these brahmins are sons of Brahmā;
they were born from the mouth and belly of the Great King Brahmā,
having issued forth from Brahmā.
Those who are emanations of Brahmā,
the kinsmen of the body of the Brahma King— namely, the Brahmins of the kalpa of strife—
form such a conception.
Question: For what reasons and by what causes do the brahmins give rise to such views and establish such doctrines?
Answer: It is by virtue of both scripture and reasoning.
As for scripture, it is as previously stated.
As for reasoning, it refers to the case where, for example, there is a certain person.
He is of a nature that engages in discursive investigation,
and so forth, as explained at length;
for he perceives that the true Brahmins of the world possess the nature of complete ethical discipline.
Because of their craving for fame, profit, and honor,
they form such a conception.
[Section 2] To refute this attachment, one should now question them as follows:
What is your position?
Do you maintain that only other castes are produced from parents,
while the same is not true for Brahmins?
If there were only the remaining types,
one would observe in the world that all brahmins are born from mothers.
It is unreasonable for you to slander what is manifest.
If it were the same for the Brahmins as well, [then...]
As you previously stated:
"The Brahmins are of the most superior lineage;
the Kṣatriyas and others are of inferior lineages."
This is illogical.
Just as one is produced from a mother,
so too does one create unwholesome karma.
One performs wholesome karmas;
one performs unwholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind;
and one performs sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind.
In this present life, one experiences pleasant and unpleasant fruits;
consequently, in future lives, one is born into the various evil realms or into the happy realms.
If these three conditions are present— this being that,
this being by means of that—
one enters the mother's womb and is born from it; or [one enters] into the various worldly crafts and skills.
Whether it be a place of action,
whether wholesome or unwholesome,
whether a king or a minister.
Whether they are quick-witted,
or have attained full development,
or are taken into the service of a king as attendants.
If one does not take account of it,
whether it be subject to old age, sickness, and death,
or not subject to old age, sickness, and death.
If one has cultivated the Brahma-abodes, one will be reborn in the Brahma-world;
otherwise, if one cultivates the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas), [the same result follows].
Whether one cultivates or realizes the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha,
or unsurpassed enlightenment—
or even if it is otherwise.
Furthermore, what is your position: is this person called "superior" because they are born from a superior lineage, or is it due to their ethical discipline, learning, and so forth?
If it were by virtue of being born from a superior lineage, [then...]
In your treatise, you state that within sacrificial rites,
if one’s ethical discipline, learning, and so forth are superior, these are taken as the standard of authority.
Such a statement would not be consistent with reason;
for if [the distinction] were based on ethical discipline, learning, and so forth, [then...]
As you previously stated:
"The Brahmins are the most excellent class;
all others are inferior classes."
This is not logical,
because it would entail such production and the performance of action.
Because of birth,
because of the spheres of arts and crafts,
and because of predominance.
Because they are recorded by him;
because they are the Brahma-abodes;
and because they are the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment.
Because they have realized awakening and because their morality and learning are superior,
[that it would be otherwise] is not reasonable.
Therefore, this treatise is not a teaching in accordance with reality.
Whether they be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas,
they give rise to such views and establish such doctrines.
If my liberated mind has attained mastery and my contemplation has attained mastery,
such that regarding the subtle fivefold sensual desires of the devas—
They cling firmly to them, take possession of them,
play and enjoy themselves with them,
and experience them according to their desires.
This is called attaining the foremost purity of nirvāṇa in the present life.
Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who give rise to such views and establish such doctrines.
If there is one who, being detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states,
attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, and so on,
up to attaining and dwelling in the fourth dhyāna.
This is also called attaining the first purity of nirvāṇa in the present life.
Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who give rise to such views and establish such doctrines.
If there are sentient beings who bathe their limbs in the Sundaḷikā River,
all their evils will be entirely eradicated.
Just as at the Sundaṛikā River,
so too did he bathe his limbs in the Bahudā, Gayā, Sarvatī, Gaṅgā, and other rivers.
It should be understood that it is likewise so.
Regarding the first purity,
there are furthermore non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
They observe the dog-vow as a means of purification;
or they observe the cow-vow;
or they observe the ink-brush vow.
Some observe the vow of nakedness;
some observe the vow of smearing ashes;
some observe the vow of self-mortification.
Or they observe precepts such as those regarding filth and impurity,
reckoning them to be purification;
these are called the non-Buddhists who claim there is nirvana in the present life.
Furthermore, regarding the non-Buddhists who propound the purity of water and so forth, they hold such views;
one asks them: what is the cause and condition for this?
They give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine.
The answer is: on account of both scripture and reasoning.
As for scripture, it is as previously stated.
"Principle" (*nyāya*) refers to one who, for instance, is by nature prone to discursive investigation,
and so forth, as explained at length.
He claims that attaining mastery over all relaxations and masteries— namely, mastery over desire and mastery over contemplative practice— is called "supreme purification."
Yet they do not know, as it truly is, the characteristics of such things as self-indulgence and mastery.
Furthermore, there are some who reckon that by means of their own bodily suffering,
they will achieve liberation from their own evil.
Or having committed transgressions and evils,
one seeks liberation from those transgressions and evils,
desiring to sport and experience pleasure.
Is it for the sake of being free from desire and greed,
or for the sake of not yet being free?
If one has already become free, [what of] the five worldly desires?
It is not reasonable that one who has not yet abandoned [defilements] should experience pleasure through play.
To reckon this as liberation and purity is not reasonable.
Furthermore, what is your position on this?
Those who have attained the first dhyāna,
up to those who dwell fully in the fourth dhyāna—
they have already become free from all sensual desire.
Or has he not yet abandoned them?
If one says that he has abandoned them all,
then he would merely be abiding fully in [the stages] up to the fourth dhyāna.
This is not logical.
If one claims that those who have not yet abandoned all desires are reckoned to have attained ultimate liberation and purity, [it is unreasonable].
This is not logical.
Furthermore, what is your position:
is ultimate purity attained through internal purity?
It is through external purification that ultimate purification is achieved;
if it were by means of the internal,
one would reckon that bathing in a river results in purification.
This is not logical.
If it were due to external factors,
then one would still possess all internal defilements such as greed, hatred, and delusion.
To consider something as pure merely because its external impurities have been removed is not logical.
Furthermore, what is your position on this?
Is one purified by receiving pure things,
or is one purified by receiving impure things?
If one attains purification through receiving pure things, [then...]
It is commonly seen in the world that dogs and such are impure;
therefore, your assertion that one can attain purity by accepting dogs and such is unreasonable.
If it were by means of grasping impure things,
it would be unreasonable for that which is itself impure to make another pure.
Furthermore, what is your position:
do those who undertake the precepts of dogs and other such animals attain purification by engaging in evil conduct of body and so forth?
Is it by practicing right and sublime conduct of body and so forth that one attains purification?
Or, if one practices wrong and evil conduct,
does one consider oneself purified by practicing such wrong and evil conduct?
This is not logical;
for if one were to observe the precepts of dogs and so forth by means of correct and sublime conduct, [it would be untenable].
That would be a futile waste;
therefore, to calculate that one can thereby attain purity is not reasonable.
Thus, it is because of being free from desire or not free from desire;
because of being internal or external;
and because of experiencing the pure or the impure.
Because it treats wrong conduct as right conduct,
it is not logical; therefore,
this treatise is not a teaching in accordance with reason.
Regarding those who propound theories of false auspiciousness:
this refers to certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who give rise to such views and establish such doctrines.
If in the world there are eclipses of the sun and moon,
or the stars lose their proper courses.
Whatever they wish to accomplish will not succeed; however,
if they act in accordance with it, [they will succeed].
Whatever one desires shall be accomplished.
For this reason, one should diligently make offerings to the sun, the moon, the stars, and so forth.
Perform fire worship and recite mantras;
arrange bundles of *kuśa* grass and fill a basin with *bīla* fruits.
And Śaṅku and others—
namely, those who calculate the calendar—
make such a reckoning.
Question: By what causes and conditions does he give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine?
Answer: It is by means of scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*).
As for the scripture, it is as previously stated.
"Principle" refers to one who is by nature prone to discursive investigation,
and so forth, as explained at length;
such a person, through the attainment of mundane dhyāna.
The world all regarded him as an Arhat.
If anyone desired to attain personal wealth and happiness, or wished for their prayers to be fulfilled,
they would go to him to seek counsel.

However, they do not know, as it truly is, the principle of dependent origination associated with the fruits of karma; they merely observe the eclipses of the sun and moon in the world and the movements of the stars and constellations,
[thinking that] at those times the pure and impure karmic fruits of sentient beings reach maturation.
They then calculate that [the world] is created by the sun, moon, and so forth;
furthermore, for those who have faith and delight in this matter,
they establish and proclaim it.
Section 2: Refuting Adherence. One should now question them:
What is your position regarding such matters as the rise and decline of the world?
Are these caused by the eclipses of the sun and moon,
the movements of the stars and constellations,
and so forth, or are they produced by pure and impure karma?
If one were to claim that the sun and other celestial bodies are the agents [of experience],

we observe that throughout one's entire life, one follows the performance of meritorious or non-meritorious karma and thereby experiences the resulting fruits of prosperity and decline, suffering and pleasure, and so forth.
This is not logical.
If it were produced by pure or impure karma,
it would be reckoned as being produced over the course of days and so forth.
This is not logical,
because [the world] is produced by such things as the sun,
and because it is produced by pure and impure karma.
This is not logical;
therefore, this treatise is not a reasoned exposition.
Such are the sixteen kinds of heterodox views.
One initiates investigation by means of two doors,
through correct reasoning.
When subjected to critical investigation,
[this position] is in every respect untenable.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle seven.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Eight.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

In the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the three stages beginning with "With Vitarka and Vicāra," the fifth section asks: How is the establishment of the designation of defilement (*saṃkleśa-prajñapti-vyavasthāna*) to be understood?
It should be known by way of three kinds of defilements. What are these three?
First, the defilement of afflictions;
second, the defilement of karma;
third, the defilement of birth.
Section 1: Defilement of Afflictions (kleśa-saṃkleśa) What is the defilement of afflictions?
The summary verse (uddāna) states:
Its intrinsic nature, its classification, Its causes, its stages, and its gates.
The superior grades of perversion encompass the various distinctions of faults and afflictions;
one should know that these constitute the defilement of afflictions by way of their intrinsic nature.
By way of discrimination,
by way of cause,
and by way of stage.
Because it is a gateway;
because it is of the highest grade;
and because it is comprised within perversion.
It should be understood through its distinctions and its defects;
thus is the explanation.
The intrinsic nature of afflictions refers to those phenomena which,
at the moment they arise, manifest naturally as non-quiescent;
it is by virtue of their arising that [they are so designated].
It proceeds as a continuous stream of non-quiescent activity;
this is called, in brief, the intrinsic nature of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
As for the classification of the afflictions:
Some establish a single category,
namely by way of the meaning of afflictive defilement (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*).
Others divide it into two categories.
That is to say, those abandoned through the path of seeing,
those abandoned through the path of cultivation,
or alternatively, divided into three types.
That is to say, they are bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm;
or alternatively, they are divided into four kinds:
those bound to the desire realm, and those that are determinate or indeterminate.
It is indeterminate with respect to the realm of form (rūpāvacara) and indeterminate with respect to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara);
alternatively, it is divided into five types.
That is to say: those abandoned through the vision of suffering,
those abandoned through the vision of origin,
and those abandoned through the vision of cessation.
They are abandoned through the path of seeing,
abandoned through the path of cultivation,
or are divided into six types.
That is to say: greed, hatred, pride, ignorance, views, and doubt;
or alternatively, they are divided into seven kinds, namely the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
1. The latent tendency of sensual desire;
2. the latent tendency of ill will;
3. the latent tendency of attachment to existence.
1. The underlying tendency of pride; 2. The underlying tendency of envy; 3. The underlying tendency of miserliness; 4. The underlying tendency of pride; 5. The underlying tendency of ignorance;
6. The underlying tendency of views.
The seventh is the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*).
Alternatively, it is divided into eight types:
namely, attachment (*rāga*), hostility (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and the two kinds of grasping (*parāmarśa*).
Alternatively, they are divided into nine kinds,
namely the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*):
first, the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*).
2. The fetter of ill will;
3. the fetter of pride;
4. the fetter of ignorance.
5. The fetter of views;
6. The fetter of grasping;
7. The fetter of doubt.
The eighth is the fetter of envy;
the ninth is the fetter of avarice.
Alternatively, they may be divided into ten types.
First, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi);
second, the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi);
third, false view (mithyādṛṣṭi).
Fourth, adherence to views;
fifth, adherence to precepts and observances;
sixth, craving.
7. Hatred; 8. Pride;
9. Ignorance.
The ten doubts.
Alternatively, they may be divided into one hundred and twenty-eight afflictions,
namely, the aforementioned ten afflictions.
It should be understood that [this] is established through the deluded adherence to twelve kinds of truths.
What are these twelve kinds of truths?
That is to say: the truth of suffering and the truth of origination in the desire realm;
the truth of suffering and the truth of origination in the form realm;
and the truth of suffering and the truth of origination in the formless realm.
The Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path that have the desire realm as their predominance, which are the fruit of that universal knowledge and are manifested by that universal knowledge;
and the Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path that have the form realm as their predominance, which are the fruit of that universal knowledge and are manifested by that universal knowledge.
The Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path, which are predominant in the formless realm, are the fruit of that universal knowledge and are manifested by that universal knowledge.
Herein, [one contemplates] the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of Origination in the desire realm,
as well as the Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path predominant in the desire realm.
There are ten afflictions of deluded clinging directed toward the truths of suffering and its origin in the form realm,
as well as toward the truths of cessation and the path that prevail therein.
Aside from hatred, there are other afflictions and deluded attachments;
as it is in the realm of form,
so it is also in the formless realm.
Within the cultivation of the antidotes for the desire realm,
there are six afflictions that constitute deluded attachments;
namely, with the exception of wrong view, the view of grasping at views, the view of grasping at precepts and observances, and doubt.
Within the cultivation of the antidotes for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
there are five afflictions of deluded attachment;
that is to say, among the aforementioned six, anger (*pratigha*) is excluded.
As it is with the cultivation of the antidote regarding the form realm,
so it is also with the cultivation of the antidote regarding the formless realm;
as with the deluded attachment.
The hindrances are likewise.
As for the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
it arises from associating with unwholesome persons, hearing what is not the true Dharma, and engaging in improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
Furthermore, due to spontaneous loss of mindfulness,
one regards the five aggregates of clinging as a self through either conceptual or non-conceptual defiled wisdom, which constitutes its essence.
The view of extremes refers to that which arises due to associating with unwholesome persons, hearing non-Dharmic teachings, improper mental attention,
and through the spontaneous loss of mindfulness.
Having grasped the five aggregates of clinging as having the nature of a self, one subsequently views them as either annihilated or eternal.
Its essence consists of afflicted wisdom, whether it is conceptualized or non-conceptualized.
Wrong view refers to the denial of cause,
the denial of effect, or the denial of functional activity, resulting from associating with unwholesome persons, hearing what is not the true Dharma, and engaging in improper mental attention.
It destroys true reality;
its essence consists solely of afflicted discernment (*vikalpa*).
As for the "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*):
That is to say, by virtue of associating with unwholesome persons, hearing what is not the true Dharma, and engaging in improper mental attention,

one [possesses] the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), along with their bases, objects, causes, co-existent factors, and associated phenomena.
For example, when one perceives [such things] as being supreme, superior, excellent, and foremost through equal contemplation,
this has as its essence only a defiled wisdom consisting of discrimination.
This is the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
That is to say, due to associating with unwholesome persons, hearing what is not the true Dharma, and engaging in improper mental attention,
one adheres to those views and follows along with them.
Whether it be precepts or prohibitions,
as well as their basis, their object,
and their cause.
One regards co-existent, associated,
and other such phenomena as pure,
as liberation, and as deliverance.
It has as its essence only the defiled wisdom of conceptual discrimination.
"One who is greedy" refers to one who,
due to associating with unwholesome persons, hearing non-Dharmic teachings, and improper mental attention, [becomes so].
And due to the spontaneous loss of mindfulness,
regarding external and internal attractive objects,
whether they are conceptually differentiated or not.
Its essence is attachment.
As for "hatred," it refers to that which arises from associating with unwholesome persons, hearing what is not the true Dharma, and engaging in improper mental attention.
And due to the spontaneous loss of mindfulness,
one regards external and internal unpleasant objects,
whether through conceptualization or non-conceptualization.
Its essence is hatred and malice.
As for pride (*māna*), it arises from associating with unvirtuous persons, hearing what is not the true Dharma, and improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*),
as well as from the spontaneous loss of mindfulness (*smṛti-pramoṣa*).
Whether with respect to external or internal objects, whether they are high or low, superior or inferior,
and whether through conceptual differentiation or non-differentiation,
its essential nature is haughtiness.
Ignorance refers to that which arises from associating with unwholesome persons, hearing what is not the true Dharma, and improper mental attention;
as well as from the spontaneous loss of mindfulness.
Regarding objects of knowledge, whether they are conceptually differentiated or not,
its essence is defiled ignorance.
As for doubt:
That is to say, due to associating with unwholesome persons, hearing what is not the true Dharma,
and engaging in improper mental attention,
one takes as the very essence of the objects of knowledge nothing but conceptualizations and discursive cognitions.
Regarding the causes of afflictions,
there are six kinds of causes.
The first is by way of the basis.
Second, by way of the object of focus; third, by way of intimacy;
fourth, by way of false teaching;
and fifth, by way of repeated practice.
Sixth, by way of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Through these six causes,
various afflictions arise.
Regarding "by way of being the basis":
this means that various afflictions arise by means of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Regarding "by way of being the object": this means...
"Because objects conducive to afflictions manifest and one associates with them" means that it is due to following and learning from unvirtuous persons.
"Due to false teachings" means by hearing what is not the true Dharma;
"due to repeated practice" means...
Regarding the phrase "by means of the power of the force of repeated cultivation planted previously through mental attention":
this means that various afflictions arise by virtue of initiating improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
Regarding the state of affliction,
there are briefly seven types:
first, the state of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Second, the stage of the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*);
third, the stage of arising through discrimination;
fourth, the stage of innate arising.
Five: the stage of weakness;
six: the stage of medium strength;
seven: the stage of superiority.
Due to two conditions,
the latent dispositions of the afflictions remain latent:
first, because they persist as seeds.
Second, by way of their predominance.

Regarding the gateway of the afflictions (*kleśa*), briefly, one is afflicted by the afflictions through two gateways: namely, the gateway of the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) and the gateway of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
There are five types of the gates of entanglement (*paryavasthāna*):
first, because they cause one to dwell in a state of non-quiescence;
second, because they obstruct the wholesome.
Third, because it gives rise to misconduct leading to the miserable realms;
fourth, because it entails contemptibility in the present life;
and fifth, because it can induce the suffering of birth and so forth.
In what sense are they afflicted by way of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)?
It means that they serve as the basis for the various outbursts (*paryavasthāna*),
and that they are capable of inducing the suffering of birth and so forth.
Furthermore, it should be understood that all afflictions act as obstacles to both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation by virtue of seven doors;
that is to say, because they constitute a false comprehension.
Because of a lack of clear understanding;
because of understanding what is not understood;
and because of deluded attachment to false understanding.
Because it has that as its causal basis, because that fear arises from it,
and because it manifests spontaneously— this is its characteristic.
This refers to the characteristic of intensity and the characteristic of extreme gravity.
Briefly stated, these characteristics are of six kinds.
First, by way of transgression;
second, by way of birth;
and third, by way of continuity.
Fourth, by way of the object;
fifth, by way of the commission of evil karma;
sixth, by way of the completion [of the act].
"By way of transgression" means that due to being bound by these afflictions (*kleśa*),
one violates all the training rules (*śikṣāpada*).
Regarding "by way of birth":
this means that by virtue of this,
one is born into the suffering of the evil destinies within the desire realm.
Regarding "by way of continuity":
this refers to those whose faculties have matured through the practice of craving and so forth,
who are in the prime of youth, yet lack the nature for nirvāṇa.
"By way of the object" means:
taking either a field of respect as the object,
or taking a field of merit as the object.
If it arises by taking as its object a field that should not be cultivated,
and does so because of the commission of unwholesome karma— meaning that due to being bound by these afflictions—
one initiates bodily and vocal actions with a mind of predominant delight.
Regarding "by way of being ultimate":
this refers to the fact that this intrinsic nature is comprised within the superior grade and is abandoned by the initial path of weak antidotes.
Regarding that which is subsumed under the afflictions of perversion,
it refers to the seven perversions:
first, the perversion of perception.
Second, inversion of view;
third, inversion of mind;
fourth, inversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent.
5. The perversion regarding suffering and pleasure;
6. The perversion regarding the impure and the pure;
7. The perversion regarding the non-self and the self.
Perverted perception refers to [the perception] regarding that which is impermanent,
suffering, impure, and non-self.
The inversion of view that gives rise to the conceptual discrimination of permanence, bliss, purity,
and self refers to that which occurs precisely within those objects discriminated by such conceptualization.
"Acceptance, desire, inclination, establishment, and attachment" refer to the mental distortions,
which are the afflictions such as craving and so forth, directed toward those very objects of attachment.
It should be known that afflictions, in brief, are of three kinds.
There are some afflictions that are the root of inversion.
Some afflictions are the very essence of perversion;
some afflictions are the outflow of perversion.
The root of perversion is ignorance;
the essence of perversion is as follows:
That is to say: the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi),
a portion of the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi),
the grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), the grasping at precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), and craving (rāga).
Regarding those that are outflows of perversion:
these refer to false view, a portion of the view of extremes,
anger, pride, and doubt.
Among these, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the inversion of taking what is non-self to be a self;
it is also a portion of the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
This is the inversion of taking the impermanent as permanent.
The adherence to views is the inversion of taking the impure as pure.
The adherence to precepts and observances is the inversion of taking suffering as pleasure.
Greed extends to two types:
namely, the inversion of the impure into the pure,
and the inversion of suffering into pleasure.
Regarding the distinctions among the afflictions (*kleśa*),
one should know that there are many types of distinctions;
namely, the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Fetters,
latent tendencies,
and secondary afflictions.
The fetters,
the floods,
and the yokes.
Grasping,
fetters,
and hindrances.
A stump, filth,
and constant harm.
The arrow. All. The faculties.
Misconduct,
outflows,
and deprivations.
Burning,
vexing,
and contentious.
Fire; blazing;
dense forest.
Constriction.
One should understand that afflictions such as these are differentiated in this way because they are capable of bringing about the conjunction with suffering.
They are called "fetters" (saṃyojana) because they cause one to be unable to act according to one's will regarding wholesome conduct; they are called "bonds" (bandhana) for that same reason;
and they are called "latent tendencies" (anuśaya) because they are pursued by the seeds that increase all worldly existence.
They are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) because they arise from a perverted and defiled mind;
they are called envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) because they frequently manifest in active operation;
and they are so named because they are deep and difficult to cross.
They are called floods (*ogha*) because they drift along with the current;
they are called yokes (*yoga*) because they are the means for engaging in misconduct;
and they are called grasping (*upādāna*) because they are able to take up the continuity of one's own personal existence so that it remains unbroken.
They are called "bonds" (saṃyojana) because they are difficult to liberate from;
they are called "hindrances" (nīvaraṇa) because they conceal the true meaning;
and they are called "stumps" (khila) because they destroy the field for the cultivation of wholesome crops.
Because its intrinsic nature is defiled, it is called "stain" (*mala*).
Because it is constantly capable of causing harm, it is called "constant harm" (*nitya-hiṃsā*).
Because its characteristic is lack of tranquility and because it persists as a remote accompaniment, [it is so designated].
Therefore, it is called an "arrow.
It is called "possessions" because it can grasp at the basis of things.
It is called a "root" because it serves as the basis for unwholesome states.
They are called "misconduct" because their intrinsic nature is that of deviant conduct.
They are called "outflows" because they cause the mind to fluctuate.
They are called "deprivations" because they cause one to experience insatiable craving for sensory enjoyments.
They are called "burning" (*paridāha*) because they cause one's desires to be perpetually deficient;
they are called "afflictions" (*upāyāsa*) because they lead to decline and loss;
and they are called "contentious" (*saraṇa*) because they serve as the causes for strife, litigation, dispute, and competition.
It is called "fire" because it burns the fuel of all accumulated roots of goodness;
it is called "blazing" because it is like a severe fever;
and it is called a "dense forest" because it is a gathering of various great trees that are one's own bodies.
Because they cause sentient beings to take pleasure in and become attached to various kinds of wonderful sensory objects (*viṣaya*),
and because they can obstruct the realization of supramundane dharmas, they are called "obstructions" (*saṃyojana*).
Such are the various distinctions among these afflictions (*kleśa*).
The Buddha, the Bhagavān, establishes distinctions according to whichever [afflictions] are predominant among those various gateways of affliction.
The fetters (*saṃyojana*) are the nine fetters,
namely the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) and so forth,
as explained in detail previously.
The fetters are the three fetters:
namely, greed, hatred, and delusion.
The latent dispositions are the seven kinds of latent dispositions.
This refers to the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) such as sensual desire (*kāmarāga*),
as explained in detail previously.
As for the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*):
There are three secondary afflictions, namely:
greed, hatred, and delusion.
As for the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), there are eight envelopments.
That is to say: lack of shame and lack of dread,
lethargy and drowsiness,
