In the form realm, there are eight [bases] along with the matter subsumed under the sphere of mental objects;
however, this does not include all [types of matter].
This is also of two kinds:
namely, the seed-name-and-form (nāmarūpa) comprised by the seeds of consciousness,
and the resultant name-and-form produced from those seeds.
What is the eye-base?
It is the translucent matter that serves as the support for visual consciousness,
by means of which one has seen, sees, or will see visible forms.
As it is with the sense base of the eye,
so it is for all others up to the sense base of the mind, as appropriate.
One should know that,
in all cases, the distinctions in the functional activity of karma across the three time periods must be explained.
This also has two kinds:
namely, the six sense bases as seeds, which are comprised within the seeds of name-and-form;
and the six sense bases as the fruit produced from them.
Five belong to the desire and form realms;
the sixth pertains to all three realms.
What is eye-contact?
This refers to that which arises from the conjunction of the three,
capable of apprehending objects such as the pure, the sublime, and so forth.
In this manner, it should be understood that the remaining types of contact are each explained according to their respective objects.
This, moreover, is of two kinds:
the seed-contact comprised within the seeds of the six sense bases,
and the resultant contact produced from them.
The desire realm possesses all six;
the form realm possesses four;
the formless realm possesses one.
What is pleasant feeling?
It refers to the agreeable feeling produced with conditions consisting of the sense faculties and their objects that are conducive to pleasure.
Included within feeling.
What is painful feeling?
It refers to that which arises conditioned by the two [types of contact] conducive to suffering.
It is not a feeling of pleasure;
it is comprised within feeling.
What is the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant?
This refers to that which is produced with the two [factors] conducive to neither-pain-nor-pleasure as conditions:
a feeling that is neither pleasant nor unpleasant,
and is comprised within feeling (*vedanā*).
Three in the desire realm,
two in the form realm,
and above the fourth dhyāna.
Up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
there is only the third [feeling], which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
this also has two kinds.
This refers to the seed-feeling (vedanā) comprised within the seeds of contact,
as well as the resultant feeling produced therefrom.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle Nine.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Ten.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Regarding the seven [topics] in the "Three Lands with Vitarka and Vicāra" within the *Maulī Bhūmi*: what is sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*)?
It is the defiled longing for the formations of the desire realm, produced with those very formations of the desire realm as its condition.
By means of this, the fruit of suffering in the desire realm is produced.
What is craving for the form realm?
It refers to that which is produced with the various formations of the form realm as its condition.
It is the defiled longing for conduct within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*);
by means of this, the fruit of suffering in the realm of form is produced.
What is craving for the formless (*ārūpyatṛṣṇā*)?
It refers to that which is produced with the formations of the formless realm as its condition;
it is the defiled longing for the formations of the formless realm,
by means of which the fruit of suffering in the formless realm is produced.
What is the grasping for sensual pleasures?
It refers to all desire and lust regarding sensual pleasures.
What is the grasping for views?
That is to say, excluding the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi),
it refers to all desire and greed regarding the remaining views.
What is the grasping at precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa)?
This refers to the desire and greed regarding the precepts and observances arising from wrong aspirations.
What is the grasping at a self-identity?
This refers to the desire and greed regarding the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The first [existence] can only produce the fruit of suffering in the desire realm;
the remaining three can produce the fruits of suffering in all three realms.
What is meant by "desire-existence" (kāma-bhava)?
That is to say, in the desire realm, there are the existence of the prior period,
the existence of karma,
and the existence of death.
Therein are the existence of intermediate state, the existence of birth,
and the existences of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas.
Taken collectively, these are called the existence of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, this is perfumed and activated by the appropriation of the afflictions (*kleśa*) from previously performed formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
What is the existence of form (*rūpadhātu*)?
That is to say, with the exception of those in the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, and humans,
the remainder should be known as the existence of form (*rūpabhava*).
What is the formless existence (*ārūpyabhava*)?
That is to say, with the exception of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the remainder should be understood as the formless existence (*ārūpyabhava*).
Question: On what basis are the seven existences established?
The so-called existences of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and gods; the existence of karma (*karmabhava*);
and the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
Answer: Because they depend upon three kinds of activities.
First, that which can induce existence;
this refers to one [type].
Second, that which leads to the existence of rebirth.
That is to say, one;
there is the existence of the fruit of enjoyment,
which is fivefold.
What is birth?
It refers to the initial moment of taking rebirth within the two modes of birth from a womb or an egg.
What is "arising" (*upapatti*)?
It refers to the state when that very body is fully formed,
yet one has not yet emerged [from the womb].
What is "going"?
It refers to emerging from that.
What is "arising"?
This refers to that which has emerged and increased.
What is meant by "emergence"?
It refers to birth from moisture and miraculous birth.
The physical constituents arise all at once.
How, then, are the aggregates acquired?
It is said that it occurs precisely within those various states of birth.
The five aggregates of clinging undergo transformation.
What is the acquisition of the realms?
It refers to the nature of those very aggregates being encompassed by causes and conditions.
What is the state of abiding?
It refers to the nature of those very aggregates being sustained by other conditions.
What is the arising of the aggregates?
This refers to how those very aggregates are sustained and nourished day by day by food and drink, whereby the life-faculty arises.
How does it appear?
It appears through the remaining power of the lifespan of those very aggregates.
It abides in continuous succession.
Regarding the brief meaning of these factors of birth (*jāti-aṅga*):
it refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of birth itself.
Whether it be the state of birth,
that which is born,
or that which is comprised by causes and conditions.
Whether it be that which sustains what has been induced,
or that which is the co-emergent support—
this is the summary of the meaning.
What is decline?
It refers to that which causes agitation due to reliance upon what is inferior.
What is old age?
It refers to the fading and changing of the color of the hair.
What is wrinkling?
It refers to the slackening and wrinkling of the skin.
What is meant by "matured"?
It refers to the decline of the vital heat (*tejas*).
They no longer possess the power to enjoy sensory objects;
how is their physical strength impaired?
It is because they are by nature prone to many illnesses.
There is no power capable of performing any activity.
As for "the body interspersed with dark moles," it refers to the appearance of dark splotches that mar one's complexion.
What is meant by "the spine is hunched and the breathing is labored"?
It refers to the physical manifestation of one's bodily posture while walking.
From this, extremely heavy labored breathing and coughing are initiated.
As for the hunched posture of the body,
it refers to the physical position of sitting.
With body and head bowed low,
leaning upon a staff— how is this?
It refers to abiding in the posture of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).
One dwells supported by the power of a staff.
What is "obscuration"?
It refers to the posture of lying down.
Repeated sleep. What is debility?
It refers to the lack of power to awaken quickly while in this very state.
What is decline? It refers to the deterioration of mindfulness and wisdom.
What is deterioration?
This means that because mindfulness and wisdom are deficient,
one is unable to bring wholesome dharmas into actual practice.
What is meant by "the faculties being worn out by old age"?
This refers to the body being weak and emaciated, and its functional capacity being impaired. How so?
It means that one no longer possesses clarity or sharpness regarding objects.
In what way are all conditioned phenomena subject to decay?
This means that when they are about to reach their end in the future,
how does their physical form become putrid and corrupt?
That is to say, when the span of life is about to end and the physical form is on the verge of perishing,
regarding all activities.
It no longer possesses functional capacity.
This is the brief meaning of "aging":
it refers to the deterioration of the physical basis and the deterioration of the hair and beard.
The transformation of satiation and gratification;
the transformation by the power of fire;
and the transformation of freedom from illness.
The physical form undergoes transformation and decay;
the deportment undergoes transformation and decay;
and the formless sense faculties undergo transformation and decay.
The material sense faculties undergo transformation and decay;
the time has passed,
and the lifespan is nearing its end.
The summarized meaning should be understood as follows:
"those various sentient beings" refers to those in the hells and so forth.
What are the categories of sentient beings?
They are all those very [beings] mentioned above.
How does it end?
What is death by dismemberment? It refers to those sentient beings who die after their limbs and joints have been severed.
What is death by exhaustion?
It refers to those sentient beings who die because their limbs and joints have been severed.
What is "dissolution"?
It refers to consciousness departing from the body.
What is "passing away"?
This refers to the cessation of the physical sense faculties.
What is the relinquishing of life?
It refers to the stage when the vital breath is about to be exhausted.
What is the relinquishing of warmth?
It refers to the abandonment of the aggregates at the stage of immovability.
What is the cessation of the life-faculty?
This refers to timely death.
What is untimely death?
It refers to dying at an improper time due to encountering adverse conditions.
What is the exhaustion of the life-force (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*)?
It refers to the stage shortly after death has occurred.
Furthermore, the activity of the Māra of Death is termed the exhaustion of the life-force.
The brief meaning of this death is as follows:
namely, death itself, the nature of death,
and the distinctions of death.
The state after death is called the summarized meaning.
Thus should the distinctions of dependent origination be understood.
Question: For what reason are the various links of existence, beginning with ignorance,
explained in such a sequential order?
Answer: For all those who are deluded, one must first be deluded regarding the objects that ought to be known;
subsequently, one then initiates wrong conduct toward those very objects.
Due to wrong conduct,
the mind becomes inverted;
because the mind is inverted...
Through the linking of rebirth,
because of the continuity of birth,
the sense faculties become complete.
Because the faculties are complete;
secondly, because of the enjoyment of objects;
and because of the enjoyment of objects.
Whether it be through attachment or through longing;
by reason of that longing,
at the time of searching for it in various directions.
The afflictions increase.
Because the afflictions increase,
one initiates karma that leads to future existence, whether pleasant or unpleasant.
Due to the power of the growth of the karma that has been initiated,
the fruit of suffering arises within the cycle of birth and death in the five destinies;
once the fruit of suffering has arisen, [it continues].
There are sufferings such as old age and death;
that is to say, the suffering of old age and death induced by the transformation of the internal body,
and the suffering of grief and lamentation induced by the transformation of external objects.
It is the suffering of feverish affliction.
For this reason, World-Honored One,
you have thus explained the twelve links in their proper sequence.
Furthermore, there is a sequential distinction:
namely, the sequence of dependent origination is established based on two kinds of conditions.
First, the condition of the internal body;
second, the condition of the enjoyment of objects.
The condition of the internal body.
The first six factors comprise the condition for the enjoyment of objects;
the latter six factors comprise [the condition for the arising of suffering].
First, one gives rise to delusions such as the grasping at a self within the internal body;
because of this, one fails to understand that the ripening of the fruits of suffering is induced by various karmas,
and thus initiates those karmas.
Once it has been initiated,
one immediately gives rise to many discursive thoughts in accordance with that karma.
Because karma and consciousness act as mutual auxiliaries,
they are able to bring about three kinds of resultant suffering in the future;
that is to say, the resultant suffering comprised by the initial arising of the sense faculties.
The fruit of suffering comprised by the perfection of the sense faculties,
and the fruit of suffering comprised by the enjoyment of objects,
have name-and-form as their precursor.
Contact is the final one.
Furthermore, within this present life,
feeling arises conditioned by contact.
It is initiated by craving;
through the condition of experiencing sense objects,
it gives rise extensively to seeking.
Either by way of ritual action,
or by way of gain and honor,
or by way of ascetic observances and prohibitions.
Or, by way of the gates of liberation,
one initiates the seeking of desire, the seeking within the internal body,
and the seeking of false liberation.
When seeking in this manner,
the fruits of birth within the five destinies of saṃsāra— drawn forth by previously arisen afflictions and karma— are brought to manifestation.
Once they have been manifested, [the process continues].
Old age and death follow in pursuit.
Furthermore, there is a sequential distinction,
namely, by way of three types of aggregates of sentient beings.
First, delighting in supramundane purity;
second, delighting in mundane purity;
third, delighting in attachment to sensory objects.
By means of the first accumulation,
one extinguishes all dependent origination and increases the pure factors.
Due to the second group of sentient beings,
they do not know the principles of the truths as they truly are,
even if they abide in right mindfulness.
Whether performing meritorious karma,
or performing immovable karma induced by contaminated cultivation,
if one does not abide in right mindfulness.
One then gives rise to non-meritorious karma,
whether it is induced by remorse or induced by a mind of joy free from remorse.
It continues to persist.
Furthermore, as before, it sequentially brings about three kinds of future results of suffering according to the lower, middle, and superior birthplaces.
That is to say, with name-and-form as the beginning and contact as the end,
by virtue of the third group of sentient beings.
Based on the feeling produced by the objects currently being experienced,
the subsequent six branches arise in this present life according to the sequence previously described.
That is to say: with birth as the beginning and old age and death as the end, [the intermediate states] are in between.
With old age and death as the starting point,
the various links of dependent origination are taught.
This is because they are explained by relying upon the principle of the Truths.
Birth and old age and death can manifest the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
As the Blessed One said:
"The dharma headed by the cessation of new name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)."
Question: Why is it not stated that the cessation of all ignorance is the primary factor?
Answer: Because it is established in dependence upon the liberation of the mind.
Because of that, there is suffering as a seed in the present life,
as well as the fruit of suffering in the future.
They cease without arising; therefore,
it is said that name-and-form come first,
and feeling comes last.
One attains ultimate cessation.
Furthermore, while experiencing various sensations within this present life, one...
When craving and its underlying tendencies are forever uprooted so that they no longer arise,
this is called cessation.
Due to the cessation of that [ignorance],
with it as the precursor,
the remaining links also cease.
One should understand that the sequence of dependent origination is taught in such categories as these; for,
bound by afflictions, one repeatedly arises within the various realms of existence.
It is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda). This is an etymological explanation based on its characters.
Furthermore, it relies upon and depends on various conditions.
Having swiftly ceased and dissolved,
it continues to arise through conjunction; therefore,
it is called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
This is explained according to the meaning of "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*).
Furthermore, although the various conditions have passed away, they do not abandon [their influence];
because [the result] arises based upon one's own continuum (*svasaṃtāna*), it comes into being.
This is called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). As it is said: "Because this exists, that exists;
because this arises, that arises."
It is not otherwise.
Based on this meaning,
one should understand the explanation of its name.
Furthermore, because it repeatedly ceases moment by moment and arises again in continuous succession,
it is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda).
This is explained according to the sense of being destroyed and extinguished by number.
Furthermore, having awakened to the nature of conditions in the past,
they arise in a continuous succession.
It is called dependent origination.
As the Blessed One said:
"I have awakened to it."
It is correctly proclaimed and taught;
because it is transmitted from one to another by means of this very name,
it is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda).
How many kinds of conditions are there?
Answer: With respect to all form-conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), it serves as the predominant condition (adhipatipratyaya).
The formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) serve as three conditions; namely,
the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya).
Regarding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya):
how many such remaining factors serve as conditions?
It should be understood in this way:
that is to say, a material factor (rūpa-aṅga), in relation to another material factor, serves as one predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya);
in relation to a non-material factor (arūpa-aṅga), it serves as two conditions.
That is to say, the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
If an immaterial factor is considered in relation to a material factor, it serves as only one such condition.
The formless factors are regarded as three conditions:
namely, the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya) and the object condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
The predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Question: Why is it that the various factors (*aṅga*) do not stand in a causal relationship (*hetu-pratyaya*) with respect to one another?
Answer: As for the causal condition...
Because it is manifested through the conditions of its own essential seeds.

Question: If the various members [of dependent origination] lack the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) when viewed in relation to one another, why is it said that dependent origination is established based on the nature of cause and effect?
Answer: It is based on the projecting cause (ākṣepahetu) and the drawing-in cause (āvāhakahetu), which are subsumed under the dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya).
Because it is the cause for the arising [of existence], it is called a "cause" (*hetu*).
Question: How many members (*aṅga*) are subsumed under the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepahetu*)?
Answer: From ignorance up to feeling.
Question: How many links are subsumed under the cause of birth?
Answer: From craving up to existence.
Question: How many members are subsumed under the two types of causal results—the projecting cause and the produced result?
Answer: Within both the present life and the subsequent life, from consciousness up to feeling.
The causes comprised within the various links during the stages of birth, aging, and death.
For what reason is it not taught first within the doctrine of dependent origination?
The answer is: because it is solely a cause for non-interruption, and not a cause for affliction. Why is this so?
It is not that one who is not ignorant gives rise to this mental attention.
The teaching on dependent origination is expounded based on the cause of affliction;
the intrinsic nature of ignorance is defiled.
Because the nature of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) is non-defiled,
it cannot defile ignorance (*avidyā*).
However, being defiled by the power of ignorance,
and further impelled by the power of karma and afflictions which constitute the defilement of birth, there arises the primary cause of karma,
namely the first link of dependent origination.
Therefore, improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) is not mentioned.
Question: Why is its own essence (*svabhāva*) not mentioned as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?
Answer: Because that very entity, if it does not encounter other conditions,
can neither increase its own defilement nor undergo diminution.
Therefore, it is not mentioned.
Question: For what reason are meritorious formations (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*) and immovable formations (*āniñjyābhisaṃskāra*) [not mentioned]?
If it arises through the power of correct discernment (*samyak-pravicaya*), why is it still said that ignorance (*avidyā*) serves as its condition?
Answer: It is because it takes the failure to comprehend the causes of conventional suffering as its condition.
One initiates non-meritorious formations.
Due to the failure to comprehend the ultimate cause of suffering as a condition,
one gives rise to meritorious and immovable formations.
Therefore, it is also said that those [formative forces] have ignorance as their condition.
Question: As it is stated in the sūtras that all karmas have greed, hatred, and delusion as their conditions, why is it that here only delusion is said to be the condition?
Answer: This section explains the conditions for meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable karma in general;
however, since the conditions of greed, hatred, and delusion give rise exclusively to non-meritorious karma, [the text] now asks concerning bodily and vocal karma.
Since it is volition that initiates [karmic formations], then formations would also have formations as their condition. Why, then,
is it said only that ignorance conditions formations?

Answer: Because it is taught in reliance upon the conditions that initiate all formations (*saṃskāra*), and because it is taught in reliance upon the conditions for the arising of wholesome and defiled volitions (*cetanā*).
Question: Consciousness (*vijñāna*) also has name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as its condition.
Why is it that, in this context, only volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are said to be the condition?

The answer is: volitional formations are the condition for the defilement of consciousness (*vijñāna*), because they are capable of projecting and producing the fruit of future existence (*punarbhava*).
It is not like name-and-form (nāmarūpa), which serves merely as the basis and object-condition for its arising.
Question: Name-and-form is also produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) and arises from contact (sparśa).
Why is it said that consciousness alone is the condition?
The answer is: because consciousness can serve as the cause for their new arising;
once they have already arisen, [it is no longer required].
Or at the very moment of arising,
the primary elements and contact can only serve as the supporting cause for that [mind].
Question: As it is said in the sūtras, one enters the mother’s womb with the six elements as conditions.
Why, then, is only the consciousness element mentioned here?
Answer: If there is a consciousness-element,
it will certainly [enter] the great elements of semen and blood within the mother’s womb.
Because the element of the abdomen is never absent;
because the element of consciousness is preeminent;
and because it is taught in reference to all instances of birth and the arising of all that is born.
Question: Since the six sense bases also have food and drink as their condition, why is it stated here that name-and-form alone is the condition?
Answer: Because in this context, name-and-form is taught as the cause of their arising.
Once it has arisen, it likewise takes food and drink as its sustaining cause.
Question: Contact has the coming together of the three as its condition.
Why, in this context, is it stated that only the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) serve as conditions?
Answer: Because if the six sense bases exist, the other two [conditions] necessarily exist without deficiency.
Furthermore, because the six sense bases are preeminent, and because the two types [of suffering] are subsumed within the six sense bases.
Question: If one is oppressed by what belongs to oneself...
Whether due to being oppressed by others,
a change in the seasons,
or the influence of past karma.
All of them obtain feeling upon arising.
Why, then, is it shown here that contact alone is their condition?
Answer: Because contact is their proximate cause.
Because it is induced by contact,
the feeling produced by other conditions also arises from contact.
It is necessarily not separate from contact;
therefore, it is specifically mentioned.
Question: The Sūtra also states that ignorance, as a condition, gives rise to craving.
Objects that are agreeable to one's desires can also serve as conditions. Why,
then, is it said here that feeling alone is the condition?
The answer is: because it is influenced by sensation,
it either seeks union with a similar object.
Or they seek separation;
through the power of delusion,
they attend only to the characteristics of arising and ceasing within all feelings.
One does not know it as it truly is;
consequently, one is unable to control the mind.
Question: Is this because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have not been abandoned?
Since grasping arises in accordance with all those various phenomena,
why is it that in this context craving alone is said to be the condition for grasping?
Answer: Because they arise from aspiration,
they are able to manifest latent tendencies (anuśaya) at the time of seeking.
And because it can induce those dharmas that are concordant with them.
Question: It was previously stated that ignorance (*avidyā*) serves as the condition for initiating karmic existence (*karmabhava*);
why is it now said that grasping (*upādāna*) is the condition for existence (*bhava*)?

Answer: It is by the power of grasping (*upādāna*) that those very karmas are able to project the fruits of consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and so forth, within their respective places of birth.
Question: Birth also takes semen, blood, and other factors as its conditions.
Why is it that only "existence" (bhava) is mentioned here as the condition for arising?
Answer: Because when existence exists, there is necessarily no deficiency in the remaining conditions.
Furthermore, because it is superior, only that is stated to be the condition.
Question: Is it also due to traveling a great distance?
Not avoiding inequality and being constrained by others serve as conditions through which aging and death come to be.
Why is it that, in this context, only birth is said to be the condition for aging and death?
The answer is: although these various conditions exist, birth is necessarily their fundamental basis.
Even if those conditions are absent,
birth alone serves as the condition,
for old age and death necessarily exist [when there is birth].
Question: Among these twelve links, how many constitute the path of afflictions,
how many constitute the path of karma,
and how many constitute the path of suffering?
Answer: Three are the path of afflictions,
two are the path of karma,
and the remainder are the path of suffering.
Question: How many are exclusively causes?
How many are exclusively effects?
How many function as both cause and effect?
Answer: The first is exclusively cause;
the last is exclusively effect;
the remaining ones pertain to both cause and effect.
Furthermore, regarding this very question,
another answer is given:
three are exclusively causes.
Two are exclusively results.
It should be understood that the remainder are both causes and results.
Question: How many are unique characteristics?
Question: How many are of mixed characteristics?
Answer: Three are of individual characteristics;
the formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth are of mixed characteristics.
Question: For what reason do formations (saṃskāra) have this characteristic of being mixed?
Answer: Because they are explained in two ways;
that is to say, because they can induce desirable and undesirable fruits.
And because they can produce the distinctions among the realms of existence (*gati*).
Question: For what reason do consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and one portion of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) possess mixed characteristics?
Answer: Because they are explained in three ways.
That is to say: by way of the time of defilement,
by way of the time of moistening,
and by way of the time of transformation.
Question: For what reason do consciousness through feeling share the same characteristics as old age and death?
Answer: Because they are explained in two ways;
that is to say, because their specific characteristics of suffering are manifested separately.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of manifesting the distinction between projecting and actualizing [causes].
Next, within the context of dependent origination,
what is the meaning of "successive progression"?
This refers to the meaning of not remaining once having arisen.
What is the meaning of conjunction?
It refers to the meaning of the gathering together of various conditions.
What is the meaning of "arising"?
It refers to the sense of being newly and repeatedly produced, as induced and encompassed by the conjunction of various conditions.
What is "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*)?
What is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)?
It is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) whereby conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) arise;
once they have arisen, that very same process is called "dependently originated" (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
Question: How many members are subsumed under the truth of suffering and constitute suffering in the present life?
Answer: Two;
namely, birth and old age and death.
Question: How many factors are subsumed under the truth of suffering that will become suffering in the future?
Answer: From consciousness up to feeling, in their nature as seeds.
Question: How many members are subsumed within the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*)?
Answer: The remaining members.
Question: Does ignorance (*avidyā*) act as a co-existent condition (*sahabhū-pratyaya*) for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)?
Does it act as a condition for that which has ceased immediately, or as a condition for that which has ceased long ago?
Answer: It should be understood that it acts as all three conditions.
That is to say, due to ignorance,
it serves as a simultaneous obscuring condition for those phenomena that accord with the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
For the sake of various specific matters,
one initiates various formations;
furthermore, this occurs through ignorance conjoined with wrong views and negligence.
It acts as the condition for the arising of [phenomena] immediately after their cessation,
giving rise to all conditioned formations (saṃskāra) through ignorance.
Because it serves as the projecting condition (*ākṣepaka-pratyaya*) for that which has long since ceased, it establishes a continuity (*saṃtati*) that is conducive to its future arising.
Question: How should one understand how the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) act as three kinds of conditions with respect to consciousness?
Answer: Because it is able to perfuse and generate those seeds, it acts as a simultaneous condition (*sahabhū-pratyaya*);
subsequently, [the result] arises through the force of that [perfuming].
It serves as the condition for arising through immediate cessation,
because by means of that [cessation], the future fruit is able to arise;
it serves as the condition of projection through long-term cessation.
As it is with volitional formations in relation to consciousness,
so it is with consciousness in relation to name-and-form,
and name-and-form in relation to the six sense bases.
The same applies to the six sense bases in relation to contact, and to contact in relation to feeling.
Question: How should one understand that feeling serves as three kinds of conditions for craving?
Answer: It should be known that because they give rise to attachment and delight, they serve as simultaneous conditions (*sahabhū-pratyaya*).
Immediately thereafter, by their power, [the subsequent state arises].
Because it functions as the activity of seeking and so forth,
it serves as the condition for arising immediately after its own cessation;
thus, it establishes what is to come.
Because it is difficult to liberate that continuum, it serves as the projecting condition for cessation over a long period.
Question: In what way does craving (tṛṣṇā) serve as three kinds of conditions for grasping (upādāna)?
Answer: Because, accompanied by sensual desire,
one establishes a longing for those phenomena conducive to grasping,
it serves as a co-existent condition.
Because it functions through the power of immediate cessation,
it serves as the condition for arising and establishes what is to come.
Because it is difficult to liberate that continuum, [ignorance] serves as the projecting condition for cessation over a long period.
Question: In what way does grasping act as three kinds of conditions for becoming?
Answer: Because they act together with it to enable karma to attract the fruits of the various realms of existence, they serve as simultaneous conditions (*sahabhū-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, it is by their power that [karma produces its fruit].
Because it can induce consciousness and so forth within this place of birth,
it serves as the condition for their arising immediately upon cessation;
furthermore, it can also trigger the functional capacity of those elements.
It serves as the projecting condition (*ākṣepaka-pratyaya*) for that which has long since ceased.
Question: How do the [past] existence (*bhava*) and birth (*jāti*) function as three kinds of conditions?
Answer: Because they perfume and project those seeds (*bīja*).
It serves as the co-existent condition (*sahabhū-pratyaya*),
because it functions continuously in immediate succession through the power of that [condition].
It serves as the productive condition (*janman-pratyaya*).
Although it has long since ceased,
because the fruit continues to evolve,
it serves as the projecting condition (*ākṣepa-pratyaya*).
Just as birth is the condition for aging and death,
one should know that the relationship between birth and aging and death as conditions is likewise.
Furthermore, there are two ways of establishing the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
First is establishment by way of the predominant factor:
namely, karma that is grasped by clinging (*upādāna*).
As previously stated,
there is a complete establishment of two factors:
namely, karma and consciousness.
It should be understood that even up to the point of receiving all seeds and being grasped by appropriation,
they are established as existence.
Question: Regarding these links of existence (*bhavāṅga*),
do they only function in succession as conditions for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth,
up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), or do they have other functional activities?
The answer is: one should understand that these very functional activities, as well as all other functional activities within their respective individual spheres of operation,
are to be known according to what is appropriate for each.
This is called the second function of karma.
Question: Does ignorance serve as a condition only for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), or does it also serve as a condition for the other links?
Answer: Ignorance serves as a condition for everything up to and including old age and death.
As for the previous statement that it serves as a condition only for formations (*saṃskāra*), this merely refers to the sense of being an immediate condition.
In this manner, all remaining cases should be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, a subsequent member is not a condition for a preceding member. Why is this?
Just as, for the sake of abandoning the subsequent member,
one exerts effort to abandon the preceding member;
because the preceding is abandoned, the subsequent is also abandoned accordingly.
It is not for the sake of severing the former that one exerts effort to sever the subsequent member;
therefore, it should be known that only this serves as the condition for that.
Question: Why is it said that "because this exists, that exists"?
Answer: Because, as long as the conditions have not been severed, there is the sense that other [phenomena] can arise.
Question: What is meant by "because this arises, that arises"?
Answer: It is because, through the condition of impermanence, other things acquire the sense of arising.
Question: Why is it said that because birth exists, there is old age and death;
that old age and death necessarily exist by reason of the condition of birth;
and so on, up to ignorance in relation to volitional formations?
Answer: This is because, through this principle of scriptural teaching, it is revealed that the meaning of "other" arises from conditions that lack real activity.
Question: For what reason is it said that "because there is birth, there is aging and death"?
There is no aging and death apart from the conditions for birth;
and so on, up to ignorance in relation to volitional formations.
This is answered by this scriptural principle.
This clarifies that [the acquisition] arises from conditions within its own continuum, because it signifies the meaning that another acquisition arises from within its own continuum.
Question: If a phenomenon has ignorance as its condition...
Is that dharma conditioned by volitional formations?
If it is conditioned by volitional formations,
is it conditioned by ignorance?
It can be answered with four propositions.
There are formations that have volitional activity but do not have ignorance as their condition;
namely, untainted (anāsrava) and non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) bodily, vocal, and mental formations.
Or there are cases where ignorance is the condition but it is not volitional formations;
that is to say, with the exception of those links of existence subsumed under volitional formations,
the remaining links of existence.
Or there may be that which has ignorance as its condition and is also volitional formations (*saṃskāra*);
namely, meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable bodily, vocal, and mental volitional formations.
Excluding such characteristics constitutes the fourth alternative.
Question: If volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) serve as conditions for that, is it also consciousness (*vijñāna*)?
And if it is consciousness, do volitional formations serve as its conditions?
Answer: One should provide a fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Either formations serve as conditions for consciousness—
meaning all other members of dependent origination except for consciousness—
or consciousness does not have formations as its condition.
This refers to untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) and non-obscured neutral consciousness (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-vijñāna*),
excluding that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Alternatively, it may also mean having both consciousness and formations as conditions.
This refers to the consciousness that is the seed of future existence and the consciousness that is its fruit;
excluding these characteristics constitutes the fourth alternative.
By this principle,
up to "conditioned by contact,
feeling arises," it should be applied accordingly.
These four propositions should be understood.
Question: Is everything that has feeling as its condition necessarily craving?
And is everything that is craving necessarily conditioned by feeling?
It can be answered in four propositions.
There may be cases where there is craving that does not have grasping as its condition;
this refers to the aspiration for supreme liberation.
Furthermore, based on wholesome craving, one abandons other cravings;
or there may be feeling that serves as a condition for craving, yet is not itself craving— namely,
with the exception of feeling produced by contact associated with ignorance serving as its condition.
The remaining factors of the dependent origination arise;
some have feeling as their condition and are also craving,
namely, those conditioned by feeling produced from contact associated with ignorance.
Defiled craving arises.
Excluding such characteristics constitutes the fourth alternative.
Question: If craving is a condition, is it always grasping?
If it is asked whether all forms of grasping (*upādāna*) have craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as their condition, the answer is:
one should know that in this context it follows the "subsequent clause" (*paścātpada*).
That is to say, whatever constitutes grasping has craving as its condition.
There are cases where craving is the condition but it is not grasping;
that is to say, excluding grasping, the remaining links of existence,
as well as the arising of various wholesome dharmas such as wholesome craving, diligence, and vigor, which are conditioned by [craving].
Question: If all that has grasping as its condition is existence, and conversely, if all existence has grasping as its condition?
Answer: This should also be treated according to the "subsequent clause" (paścātpādaka) formula.
That is to say, all that exists (bhava) has grasping (upādāna) as its condition;
however, there are cases where grasping is a condition but is not itself existence—
namely, all other members of existence (bhavāṅga) excluding existence itself.
Question: Are all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) that have conditions necessarily births?
And are all things that are births necessarily conditioned phenomena with conditions?
Answer: All things that are births are conditioned phenomena with conditions.
There are factors that have birth as their condition but are not themselves birth;
namely, all other links of dependent origination from old age and death onwards, excluding birth itself.
Question: Is it the case that whenever there is birth as a condition, there is necessarily old age and death?
Is it the case that all instances of old age and death have birth as their condition?
Answer: All instances of old age and death have birth as their condition;
however, there may be cases where something has birth as its condition but is not old age and death.
What are called illness,
encountering those one hates,
and separation from those one loves.
The failure to attain what is sought,
as well as the grief, lamentation, sorrow, suffering,
and various kinds of burning afflictions that arise therefrom.
Question: Among these members of existence (*bhavāṅga*), how many constitute the primary obstacles to right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) as it is subsumed within the members of the path (*mārgāṅga*)?
Answer: Ignorance (*avidyā*) and the mental formations (*manasaḥ saṃskārāḥ*) arising from it constitute the primary obstacles, at least in part.
As it is with right view,
so it is with right intention and right effort as well.
If there is right speech, right action, and right livelihood,
they consist of bodily conduct, verbal conduct,
and one portion thereof.
They constitute superior obstacles.
If right livelihood and right concentration [are impaired],
it is by means of the remaining factors of existence.
It should be understood as a supreme obstacle.

Question: Among these links of existence (*bhavāṅga*), how many belong exclusively to the category of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), and how many pertain to both the categories of affliction and purification (*vyavadāna*)?
Answer: Four [links] belong exclusively to the category of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), while the remaining ones pertain to both the categories of affliction and purification (*vyavadāna*).
Question: Why does the link of birth (*jāti*) pertain to both categories?
Answer: If one is born in the evil destinies or in places of difficulty, it is exclusively of the defiled category;
if one is born among humans or devas in places free from difficulties, [it is otherwise].
This applies to both the defiled and purified categories;
it should be understood that the remaining factors follow accordingly as appropriate.
Both apply to the two categories.
Question: By the non-existence of what kind of ignorance does volitional formation (*saṃskāra*) not exist?
And by the cessation of what kind of ignorance does volitional formation cease?
Answer: There are three kinds of origins: the outbursts (paryavasthāna), the latent tendencies (anuśaya), and ignorance (avidyā).
Due to the cessation of this ignorance,
that ignorance ceases; due to its cessation,
[the subsequent factors cease].
Volitional formations also cease accordingly.
Question: Due to the non-existence of which volitional formations does consciousness not exist?
Through the cessation of which volitional formations does consciousness cease?
Answer: It refers to those conditioned phenomena within one's own continuum that have already been performed and have already ceased,
and for which an antidote has not yet arisen.
Furthermore, because mental formations exist,
bodily and vocal formations arise;
because these exist, [the subsequent states] come to be.
Because that exists,
and because that is absent, consciousness conditioned by that is also absent.
If this were to be completely extinguished, [it would be so].
When consciousness also ceases accordingly, it is asked:
by the non-existence of which consciousness do name-and-form not exist?
And by the cessation of which consciousness does name-and-form cease?
Answer: Because the seed-consciousness does not exist, the resultant consciousness does not exist;
for these two perish together.
Both are called the cessation of name-and-form.
Just as the principle applies to consciousness in relation to name-and-form,
so it is for the remaining links up to feeling.
It should be understood that it is likewise according to what is appropriate;
just as is the principle of ignorance being the condition for volitional formations, so too is craving the condition for clinging.
The principle regarding the condition of grasping for existence should be understood to be likewise,
just as is the principle regarding the condition of volitional formations for consciousness.
In this way, one should know that "with birth as condition" is likewise;
it is just like the principle of consciousness being the condition for name-and-form.
It should be understood that birth as a condition for aging and death is likewise so.
Question: Due to the non-existence of which feeling does craving not exist?

What is the cessation of craving due to the cessation of feeling? Answer: It should be understood that it is just like the principle of consciousness being conditioned by volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Question: Regarding the eight gates of dependent origination as previously explained...
How many categories are revealed by the twelvefold dependent origination, and how many are not?
Answer: Three categories are revealed by it.
That is to say, it is manifested by one part of two [factors] and manifested by the entirety of one;
other categories are not so.
What are the two aspects manifested by a single part?
They are the gateway of the arising of internal consciousness and the gateway of the performance of one's own karma.
What is that which is manifested by a single complete portion?
It is the gateway of the transformation of the world of sentient beings.
Question: For one who does not know the principle of dependent origination as it truly is—
How many kinds of faults are there?
The answer is five:
namely, the arising of the view of a self.
And one is able to give rise to views associated with the past;
as with views associated with the past,
so too are there views associated with the future.
The same applies to the views that operate regarding both the past and the future limits.
Furthermore, one possesses intense and firm attachment toward those views,
characterized by grasping and fear.
Not attaining parinirvāṇa in this present life is called the fifth fault.
Question: How many kinds of benefits are there for one who knows things as they truly are?
Answer: One should know that, by reversing the five aforementioned faults, there are likewise five kinds of benefits.
Furthermore, regarding these twelve links of dependent origination:
How many members are substantially existent?
They are nine.
How many members are not substantially existent?
That is to say, the remainder.
How many have a single thing as their intrinsic nature?
That is to say, five.
How many have multiple things as their intrinsic nature?
It is the remainder.
How many are the causes of the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)?
That is to say, one [factor] can produce suffering;
that is to say, five [factors].
How many are the wombs of suffering?
They are five.
How many are exclusively suffering?
That is to say, there are two.
How many are said to be the causal factors?
That is to say, the first six.
From ignorance up to contact,
as well as craving and grasping— these three are taught as the causal portion.
How many are taught as the resultant portion?
That is to say, the latter two [links] are said to constitute the fruit-portion;
how many are said to constitute the mixed cause-and-effect portion?
That is to say, the remaining links are said to constitute the mixed portion.
Why is this? There are two kinds of feeling called "mixed portions."
The first refers to feeling in a future life, which has contact as its causal condition;
the second refers to feeling in the present life, which is the resultant feeling that serves as the condition for craving.
These two are explained together as "feeling conditioned by contact."
Furthermore, how many members can produce the fruit of desirable and undesirable objects,
and how many members can produce the fruit of the personal existence?
It is said that the first six members can produce the former fruit.
The final three members can produce subsequent fruits;
one member produces two fruits simultaneously.
Furthermore, how many members are accompanied by pleasant feeling?
That is to say, excluding the two [remaining] factors,
how many factors are accompanied by painful feeling?
It is those very same factors and one among those excluded.
How many members are associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
This should be understood according to the principle applied to pleasant feeling.
How many members are not associated with feeling?
That is to say, one among those [factors] to be excluded.
Furthermore, how many factors are subsumed under the suffering of change?
They are the factors associated with pleasant feeling.
And a portion of the factors that do not coexist with feeling.
How many factors are subsumed under the suffering of suffering?
They are the factors that coexist with painful feeling.
And a portion of the factors that do not accompany sensation.
How many factors are subsumed under suffering?
That is to say, all forms of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
The branch of suffering-as-suffering is also the branch of suffering-as-conditioning; or,
it may be subsumed under the category of suffering-as-conditioning.
It is not the other two types of suffering;
namely, the factors associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,
as well as a portion of those factors not associated with feeling.
Question: Is it the case that in all places of birth and within all meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the manifestation of all factors (*aṅga*) can be found?
Answer: It cannot be found.
That is to say, within the Heaven of Non-conception,
as well as within the meditative attainment of cessation and the meditative attainment of non-conception.
The members of the form realm can be obtained,
but not the members of the formless realm,
if one is born in the formless realm.
The factors of the formless realm can be attained, but not the factors of the realm of form.
Question: Is it possible to attain the factors of liberation by relying on the factors of existence?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, based on the factors of a higher stage and dissociated from the factors of a lower stage.
This is only a partial [cause], not the whole;
it is merely temporary, not ultimate.
Question: How many factors (*aṅga*) are defiled (*kliṣṭa*)?
How many factors are non-defiled?
Answer: Three are defiled;
the remainder are of both kinds.
If it is non-defiled,
it should be understood as being divided into two types, namely the wholesome and the unobscured-neutral, because they are distinct.
Question: How many factors are bound to the desire realm?
Answer: All factors, because they arise in conjunction.
Question: How many factors are bound to the realm of form?
Answer: A portion of all [factors].
Question: How should this be understood?
Does that [conditioned entity] possess aging?
Answer: Because those conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) possess the nature of decay and corruption, just as in the case of those bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
It should be understood that the same applies to those factors associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Question: How many members (*aṅga*) are those of training (*śaikṣa*)?
Answer: None.
Question: How many factors are those of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
Answer: None. Question:
How many factors are neither of one in training nor of one beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa)?
[The interlocutor] answers:
"All [of them]. [The questioner asks: "Why are all those wholesome, outflow-tainted factors not considered 'in training' (*śaikṣa*)?"
Answer: Because they fall into the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
As for all those wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) dharmas of one in training (*śaikṣa*), they are contrary to the nature of that cycle.
Furthermore, because it takes clear knowledge (*vidyā*) as its condition, it is not a constituent (*aṅga*).
Question: Regarding the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), how many constituents should be said to have been abandoned?
Answer: A portion of all [constituents] has been abandoned; none have been abandoned in their entirety.
As it is with the fruit of stream-entry, so it is with the fruit of once-returning.
Question: Regarding the fruit of non-returning, how many factors should be said to have been abandoned?
Answer: All [factors] of the desire realm;
those of the form and formless realms are indeterminate.
As for the question, "How many factors have been abandoned? [the answer follows].
Answer: All three realms.
Furthermore, in various sūtras, by means of how many modes of verbal expression is dependent origination taught?
Briefly stated, this refers to six modes of discourse:
first, by way of direct order;
second, by way of reverse order.
Third, by way of explaining through a single branch;
fourth, by way of explaining through all branches;
fifth, by way of explaining through the dark side (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
Sixth, by way of the white category (*śuklapakṣa*).
Question: As the Blessed One has said that dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is profound, what is the meaning of this profundity?
How should it be understood?
Answer: It should be understood that the profound meaning of dependent origination is to be known by way of ten aspects.
That is to say, based on the meaning of impermanence,
the meaning of suffering,
and the meaning of emptiness.
Regarding the explanation of the meaning of selflessness:
as for the meaning of impermanence,
it refers to arising from its own seeds.
It also depends on other conditions;
furthermore, it arises from other conditions while also depending on its own seeds.
Furthermore, it arises from its own seeds and from other conditions;
yet, regarding this produced phenomenon, both the seeds and the conditions are without agency and without purposeful activity.
Nor is there any movement;
furthermore, the causal functional capacity of these two is not non-existent.
Furthermore, although the characteristics of the various links of existence have been established since beginningless time,
they undergo a continuous transformation, becoming ever new from moment to moment.
Furthermore, although the members of dependent origination perish instantaneously,
they nevertheless appear to exhibit the characteristics of stability and motion;
this is according to the sense of "suffering."
This refers to the links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda),
which have the single flavor of the characteristic of suffering yet appear as if they possess three distinct characteristics.
This is according to the meaning of emptiness (śūnyatā).
That is to say, although the factors of dependent origination are devoid of a sentient being, an agent, or an experiencer,
they nevertheless appear as if they were not so devoid.
It is explained by way of manifestation.
Regarding the meaning of selflessness,
this refers to the factors of dependent origination.
Although there is no real characteristic of a self because it lacks autonomy,
it nevertheless appears as if it were a self;
this is according to the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
Although the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena (*dharma*) is inexpressible, it is said that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is expressible.
Question: By how many types of knowledge (*jñāna*) should one understand dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)?
Answer: There are two,
namely, the knowledge of the abiding of phenomena (dharmasthiti-jñāna) and the knowledge of reality (tattva-jñāna).
What is the knowledge of abiding by means of the Dharma?
It refers to knowing without error, just as the Buddha has established and revealed it.
How is it by means of knowledge of reality?
It refers to the way one who has attained the vision of the path observes the profound meaning.
Question: As the Blessed One said:
This dependent origination was not created by me,
nor was it created by another. Why is that?
Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear,
the nature of phenomena remains established, and the realm of phenomena remains fixed.
What is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)?
What is the stability of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā)?
What is the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)?
Answer: These various dependent originations, having existed since beginningless time, are established by principle as their very nature; this is called *dharmatā*.
Just as with the nature of accomplishment,
that which is established through non-erroneous phrases and syllables is called the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthiti*).
Because this dharma abides by taking that dharmatā as its cause, it is therefore called the "dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu).
Question: As the Sūtra says:
If arising were non-existent,
there would be no place or occasion where arising could be said to exist.
If birth were non-existent in every respect,
then the condition for aging and death—
namely, birth— would be unobtainable.
Why is it said here that their own nature conditions their own nature?
The answer is: because it is taught that the fruit arises from its own seeds.
This refers to the factors from consciousness up to feeling.
Because it is the seed of birth,
it is figuratively described as "birth.
It exists by virtue of this [condition].
At a later time, this very link of the fruit is called "existence-conditioned-arising.
The same applies to the remaining links.
As stated in the sūtra,
all should be understood according to their respective applications.
Question: It has already been stated that not all factors serve as mutual conditions for one another.
Why, then, is it established that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are mutual conditions?
Answer: Because in the present life, consciousness...
Because name-and-form (nāmarūpa) serves as the condition,
and because name-and-form, in turn, serves as the condition for consciousness (vijñāna) within subsequent states of existence.
Why is this? Because there is a moment of continuity within the mother’s womb.
Because it is taught that they are mutually conditions;
by means of consciousness as a condition,
[it arises] within the mother's womb.
The various colors of the semen and blood are termed "appropriated," and through their combination,
they collectively form the nature of the *kalala*.
With this very name-and-form as a condition, it further causes that consciousness to abide therein.
Question: For what reason does the Bodhisattva, when contemplating the dark side (kṛṣṇapakṣa), [do so]?
Does the mind turn back only upon reaching the link of consciousness,
and not upon reaching any other link?
Answer: Because these two factors serve as mutual conditions for one another;
just as consciousness is conditioned by name-and-form, so too is name-and-form conditioned by consciousness.
Therefore, when observing the mind up to the point where consciousness turns back,
there is no such principle of turning back among the remaining members [of dependent origination].
In this one section,
the principle of mutual conditionality is demonstrated; therefore,
it is called "revolving and returning."
In the section on cessation,
name-and-form is not the cause for the cessation of the consciousness of future existence;
for this reason, one further examines it.
Question: For what reason and by what causal conditions is it said that the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are not self-made,
not made by another,
and not made by both?
Nor is it produced without a cause?
Answer: Because that which arises does not exist [independently], and because conditions have no functional activity.
Because it is produced by the power of conditions.
Question: Within dependent origination, what is the sprout of suffering?
Who nurtures the sprout of suffering?
What constitutes the tree of suffering?
Answer: From consciousness conditioned by ignorance and formations, up to feeling, these are the sprout of suffering.
Craving, which is induced by sensation,
and so forth up to becoming, are the guardians and nourishers of the sprout of suffering;
[from these arise] birth, along with aging and death.
One should know this to be the tree of suffering.
Question: How many links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) should be known as being like the wick?
Answer: From consciousness (vijñāna) up to feeling (vedanā).
Question: How many factors are like grease?
Answer: Ignorance, formations, craving, clinging, and existence.
Question: How many factors are like a flame?
Answer: One should know that they are birth, old age, and death.
Question: For what reason?
In the teaching on the dark side of dependent origination,
this is called "superimposition" (samāropa).
The answer is that it is because all the factors of existence (bhavāṅga) result ultimately in a mass of pure great suffering.
Furthermore, because each preceding member of the links of existence serves as a condition for each subsequent one that follows it.
Question: For what reason?
In the teaching on the side of purity (*śuklapakṣa*), it is called "diminution.
The answer is: because each preceding factor is permanently abandoned, each subsequent factor is diminished.
Furthermore, because it is the cause for the diminution of this entire mass of suffering.
Question: How many members of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) are called "dharmas with causes" (sahetuka-dharma)?
Answer: They are the first seven.
Question: How many links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) are termed "suffering with cause" (sa-hetuka-duḥkha)?
Answer: The remaining five.
Question: Through the cessation of how many links is the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya) manifested?
Answer: Three.
Question: How many members are manifested by the exhaustion of conditions?
Answer: These same three, because they are the conditions for the remaining members.
Question: How many factors, when extinguished, are manifested by the exhaustion of feeling?
Answer: One;
namely, because the afflictions have already been abandoned.
When the basis ceases,
all these feelings are forever stilled and extinguished.
Question: For what reason and by what causal conditions are the seventy-seven knowledges established based upon dependent origination?
The answer is: it is in order to reveal the knowledge that affliction (*saṃkleśa*) has causes;
furthermore, it is to reveal the knowledge that within one's own continuum, affliction is produced by oneself;
and furthermore, it is to reveal that the various links (*aṅga*) of the past limit are beginningless.
Furthermore, it is to demonstrate that the factors belonging to the future limit can possess the sense of being defiled or subject to cessation;
and furthermore, it is to demonstrate the sense of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) regarding all contaminated wisdom not subsumed under those [twelve] factors.
Since seven types of knowledge are applied to each individual limb,
one should know that there are seventy-seven types of knowledge in total.
Question: For what reason are forty-four types of knowledge established within the context of dependent origination?
Answer: It is to reveal that for each individual limb, one observes according to the principles of the Four Noble Truths;
therefore, there are forty-four cognitions in total.
Furthermore, if one is born in the desire realm...
Based on a body belonging to the desire realm,
one brings forth the eyes or ears of the higher realms; by means of these,
one sees and hears the forms and sounds belonging to lower realms as well as those of one's own level.
Furthermore, based on this body,
the minds of the three realms as well as the unconditioned mind arise and manifest before one.
If one is born in the realm of form or the formless realm,
all [defilements] except those belonging to the lower stages manifest.
As it is in the desire realm,
furthermore, these three types of defilement are as follows:
namely, the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*).
In order to sever the defilement of karma and the defilement of birth.
One cultivates the six kinds of clear realization.
One should know what these six are:
namely, the clear realization through reflection.
The clear realization of faith,
the clear realization of ethical discipline,
and the clear realization of the truths through the knowledge of clear realization.
The Culminating Insight of Knowledge at the Edge of Clear Realization and the Ultimate Clear Realization.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle Ten.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Eleven.
