The sixth [section], the *Samāhitā-bhūmi*, within the *Maulī Bhūmi*, part one: Having already explained the three states beginning with "with vitarka and vicāra," what is the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhitā-bhūmi*)?
The summary verse says:
The general headings and the formal establishment, The distinctions of mental engagement and characteristics,
And the inclusion of the essential points of all sūtras— These constitute the final section on various miscellaneous topics.
If one were to explain the stage of meditative equipoise (samāhita-bhūmi) briefly,
it should be understood by way of its general designation and its formal establishment.
Because of the distinctions in mental attention (*manasikāra*),
because of the distinctions in characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*),
and because of the concise summary of the essential tenets of the various sūtras.
First, meditative concentration (dhyāna);
second, liberation (vimokṣa);
third, meditative equipoise (samādhi).
Fourth is meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
Regarding "meditative absorption" (*dhyāna*), it refers to the four meditative absorptions (*catur-dhyāna*).
First, the dhyāna with vitarka and vicāra arising from detachment;
second, the dhyāna without vitarka and vicāra arising from concentration;
third, the dhyāna free from joy.
The fourth is the meditative absorption of purity through equanimity and mindfulness.
As for "liberations," this refers to the eight liberations.
1. The liberation of one possessing form who perceives external forms;
2. The liberation of one who, having no internal perception of form, perceives external forms;
3. The liberation of the pure, which is realized by bodily witness and dwelt in fully.
The fourth is the liberation of the sphere of infinite space;
the fifth is the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness;
the sixth is the liberation of the sphere of nothingness.
The seventh is the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The eighth is the liberation consisting in the bodily realization and full attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
As for meditative concentration (*samādhi*):
That is to say, the three samādhis:
first, emptiness;
second, wishlessness.
Third is the signless.
Furthermore, there are three types, namely:
with vitarka and vicāra.
There are those with no vitarka and only vicāra, and those with neither vitarka nor vicāra.
Furthermore, there are three types:
namely, the small, the great, and the immeasurable.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
namely, partial cultivation and complete cultivation.
Furthermore, there are three kinds:
namely, that accompanied by joy, that accompanied by pleasure, and [that accompanied by equanimity].
They are associated with equanimity.
Furthermore, there are four kinds,
namely the four meditative attainments through cultivation.
Furthermore, there are five kinds,
namely the five noble wisdom samādhis.
Furthermore, there are five kinds.
That is to say, the noble five-factored samādhi;
furthermore, there is the noble right samādhi with its cause and its equipment;
and furthermore, there is the vajra-like samādhi.
Furthermore, there are the samādhis and attainments (*samāpatti*) of those in training (*śaikṣa*),
those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
As for "attainments":
That is to say: the five samāpattis of direct perception,
the eight bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) samāpattis,
and the ten totalities (kṛtsnāyatana) samāpattis.
The four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*),
the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*),
the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and so forth.
How is it established?
It means that these alone— namely, name and so forth— constitute the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*),
and not the one-pointedness of mind within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Because these concentrations and so forth are induced by the absence of regret, joy, and bliss,
whereas the desire realm is not so.
It is not that there is no thorough and correct investigation of phenomena at all within the desire realm;
furthermore, in the first dhyāna,
it is said that joy born of seclusion arises.
By realizing and abiding in this, one abandons five things:
namely, joy induced by desire and sorrow induced by desire.
Joy induced by the unwholesome,
sorrow induced by the unwholesome,
and equanimity induced by the unwholesome.
Furthermore, one brings five factors to perfection through cultivation:
namely, joy, bliss, and samādhi.
Regarding the joy induced by desire:
when one first obtains the five exquisite sensual pleasures.
If one has already realized it,
then at the time of its correct enjoyment,
whether seeing or hearing it, [one experiences it].
Or having previously experienced them,
one recollects them with joy due to these various conditions.
Regarding "sorrow induced by desire":
it refers to when one seeks the five excellent sensual pleasures but does not attain them.
If what has already been enjoyed can no longer be obtained,
or if it is lost immediately after being acquired,
one gives rise to much grief and distress due to these various conditions.
Joy induced by the unwholesome refers,
for example, to when someone engages in the act of killing up to wrong view while accompanied by joy and pleasure.
Sorrow induced by the unwholesome refers to...
This refers, for example, to someone who, accompanied by sorrow and suffering, commits acts of killing up to and including wrong views.
Regarding "equanimity induced by the unwholesome":

this refers, for example, to someone—whether a king, a royal official, another high-ranking administrator, or a person of high status—who personally does not take pleasure in committing evil deeds such as killing.
Yet, when his servants commit evil deeds,
he endures them without restraint and does not establish them within the Vinaya.
Due to negligence and indifference,
they consequently commit evil karma;
regarding this karma, they...
It is a direct realization, not one that is not manifest;
furthermore, while abiding in equanimity,
one seeks and investigates.
Employing skillful means for evil,
they furthermore remain attached to various evils without ceasing.
It induces equanimity;
furthermore, when unwholesome states manifest,
it gives rise to a neutral feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant.

Joy (*prāmodya*) refers to the nature of mental exhilaration and gladness, preceded by freedom from regret, which arises when a practitioner who has been pure from the very beginning contemplates the pure conduct cultivated on the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-bhūmi*).
Joy (*prīti*) refers to the nature of profound celebration, satisfaction, and mental exultation that arises preceded by the correct cultivation of skillful means; it is the state of being at ease.
It refers to the state of physical and mental pliancy resulting from the departure from coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
"Bliss" refers to that which arises because of such mental pliancy.
One then attains the bliss of the body and mind being free from harm, as well as the bliss of liberation;
because one has abandoned the coarse and heavy nature (*dausthulya*) belonging to that category,
one attains liberation from all afflictions.
Samādhi refers to the careful and correct observation of the object of focus.
"One-pointedness of mind":
in the context of the untainted means,
the Blessed One first taught samādhi.
Next, liberation is explained:
by the power of the perfect accomplishment of samādhi,
with respect to all afflictions.
Because the mind is eternally liberated,
liberation is mentioned first among the skillful means regarding the outflows (*sāsrava*).
The samādhi is explained later,
because one only attains the fundamental samādhi after the afflictions have been abandoned as the fruit of the attention that culminates in skillful means.
Alternatively, some explain both samādhi and liberation simultaneously.
This refers to the attention that culminates in the application of skillful means (*upāya-paryavasāna-manasikāra*),
as well as within the other samādhis of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*);
for it is because the samādhi and its liberation (*vimukti*) exist simultaneously.
Briefly, there are five hindrances that act as obstacles when one is about to realize that [state].
What are these five?
First, the hindrance of sensual desire;
second, the hindrance of ill will; third, the hindrance of lethargy and drowsiness;
fourth, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse.
The five hindrances of doubt.
Regarding "sensual desire":
this refers to [craving] for the five exquisite objects of desire.
Following after pure signs,
they desire to see,
desire to hear, and so on, up to desiring to touch.
Or, following upon recollection,
one seeks out and pines for what was previously experienced through initial application and sustained investigation.
Regarding ill will (*vyāpāda*):
it refers to the manifestation of ill will either when one's transgressions are pointed out by fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*),
or when one recollects past experiences of harm that were not beneficial.
The mind gives rise to anger;
or one desires to perform harmful acts;
these are the characteristics of hatred regarding what is about to be done.
For one who frequently follows discursive thought and investigation,
anger arises in the mind;
as for one who is dull and lethargic:
That is to say, it may be due to the destruction of any one of the virtuous practices, such as pure ethical discipline (*śīla*),
failing to guard the doors of the sensory faculties,
not knowing moderation in eating, lacking diligence in energetic effort, or not reducing sleep.
Abiding in lack of clear comprehension,
one performs actions that do not accord with diligent application toward what is to be cultivated and abandoned.
It gives rise to all afflictions;
body and mind become dull and obscured,
lacking the capacity for functional adaptability.
Sleep refers to the extreme dullness and contraction of the mind;
furthermore, it conduces to the arising of afflictions and the destruction of the application of effort toward abandonment.
This is the nature of lethargy;
it is the extreme dullness and contraction of the mind.
This is the nature of sleep.
Therefore, these two are combined and designated as a single hindrance.
Furthermore, that state of mental dullness and lack of functional fitness is called *styāna* (sloth).
Sleep is defined as a state of mental dullness and extreme contraction.
When *styāna* (sloth) gives rise to the primary and secondary afflictions,
there is no other proximate condition like sleep.
Other afflictions and secondary afflictions may either arise or not arise.
If torpor and mental dullness arise,
sleep will certainly and inevitably occur.
As for restlessness:
That is to say: seeking out thoughts concerning relatives,
seeking out thoughts concerning one's country,
and seeking out thoughts concerning immortality.
Or, by recollecting past experiences of play, laughter, and amorous pleasures,
the mind becomes agitated and develops a restless, leaping nature;
this is what is meant by "evil action."
This means that due to reflecting upon one's relatives and so forth,
remorse arises in the mind,
thinking: "For what reason have I been separated from my relatives?"
For what reason did you not go to such lands?
For what reason did you abandon such lands to come here and eat such food?
One drinks such drinks;
one obtains only such clothing, bedding,
and medicinal requisites for the treatment of illness.
Regarding these various requisites for sustaining the body:
by what cause did I originally leave home at such a young age?
Why not wait until my years have grown old and worn?
Or, due to recollecting past instances such as those involving laughter and play,
one gives rise to regret, thinking:
"For what reason did I [neglect] the time when I ought to have enjoyed amusements, ornaments, and the company of friends?"
He acted contrary to the wishes of his kinsmen, friends, and others,
causing them to grieve and long for him with tears filling their eyes,
as he forcibly entered the monastic life.
Due to various causes and conditions such as these,
a mind of sorrowful attachment arises,
accompanied by remorse and regret.
Because the aforementioned restlessness (*auddhatya*) and this remorse (*kaukṛtya*) share the same basis,
they are combined and taught as a single hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, regarding matters that ought to be done and those that ought not to be done:
According to what is appropriate,
it may have been performed previously,
or it may not have been performed.
A sense of regret arose in his mind:
"Why did I in the past fail to do what should have been done,
and instead do what should not have been done?"
Apart from the remorse already arisen from prior regret,
this obsession with remorse has still not been abandoned;
subsequently, a continuous stream of sorrowful longing arises once more, without interruption.
Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and regret (*vipratisāra*).
This is another variety of remorse,
specifically the remorse that arose previously regarding what was done in an improper place.
Furthermore, although subsequent remorse (*kaukṛtya*) does not share the same locus as restlessness (*auddhatya*),
it nevertheless shares with its counterpart the characteristic of leaping up and agitated movement;
this present [remorse] is likewise a characteristic of sorrowful attachment.
Therefore, it is spoken of together with that [doubt] as a single "cover.
Doubt refers to uncertainty regarding the Teacher, the Dharma, the training, the instruction, and the realization.
They give rise to delusion and doubt;
because their minds harbor such uncertainty,
they are unable to enter into the courageous application of right effort for the sake of tranquility.
Furthermore, regarding the past, future, and present, as well as the truths such as suffering and so forth,
one gives rise to delusion and doubt,
harboring a state of dualistic mind.
Deluded and failing to understand,
they waver and speculate;
what is their sustenance?
Answer: There are pure and sublime signs,
as well as improper mental attention toward those signs.
Having extensively practiced this,
one takes it as one's sustenance;
such is the mark of purity and excellence.
That is to say, regarding the characteristics of the foremost, most excellent, and sublime desires,
if one can remain free from a defiled mind toward these,
one will also become free from defilement toward other inferior things.
Just as one who possesses great strength subdues others who are weak,
how is this further explained?
It refers to the eight parts of a woman’s body that comprise desirable and pure characteristics.
By means of these eight points,
women bind men: namely,
song, dance, laughter, and the sidelong glance.
Regarding the progression of her beauty,
she approached with a wondrous touch and paid her respects;
by virtue of these causes and conditions.
All forms of sensual desire that have not yet arisen cause to arise,
and those already arisen cause to increase.
Therefore, it is called "nutriment.
Question: What serves as the non-nutriment for this hindrance of sensual desire?
Answer: The sign of impurity.
And one should cultivate, through correct mental attention, the perception of those signs extensively,
taking them as non-nutriments.
What, then, is this? It refers to the livid discoloration and so forth;
that is, contemplating how this body is filled with various kinds of impurities and filth.
It is called the contemplation of the impure characteristics of the internal body.

Furthermore, contemplating various impure characteristics such as the bluish discoloration and so forth of the external [body] is called the contemplation of the impure characteristics of the external body.
By contemplating these two aspects of impurity,
one prevents unarisen sensual desire from arising and is able to sever it once it has arisen.
It is called "non-nutriments" because,
through appropriate mental attention toward those signs,
their arising is prevented.
Because of extensive cultivation,
one is able to sever [the afflictions] once they have arisen.
This was previously explained in the section on the black category (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
Because of improper reflection upon those signs,
they cause what has not yet arisen to arise;
this is due to extensive cultivation.
It increases and expands even further.
Question: What is the nutriment of the hindrance of ill-will?
Answer: It is the nature of ill-will.
There is the sign of ill will,
as well as improper mental attention toward that sign.
Having extensively practiced this,
they take it as their sustenance;
based on various harmful matters, their minds give rise to affliction and malice.
That which is termed the nature of anger is harmful action;
this is termed the characteristic of anger.
Improper attention toward the nine grounds for resentment is called improper reflection.
Such matters as these are all termed "nutriments.
Question: What serves as the non-nutriment for this hindrance of ill-will?
Answer: Benevolence, compassion, and virtuous goodness.
And regarding those signs,
one applies appropriate attention and practices them extensively.
It is regarded as non-food.
Furthermore, this loving-kindness has the characteristic of constantly wishing to bestow peace and happiness upon others,
and it is encompassed by the power of cultivation.
By means of attention encompassed by the power of discernment,
one subdues the nine afflictions,
because it is able to eliminate the hindrance of ill-will.
In the Sūtra, it is stated only that this is not nutriment.
Question: What is the nutriment for the hindrance of torpor and drowsiness?
Answer: It is the sign of darkness.
Furthermore, one engages in improper mental attention regarding those signs,
practicing it extensively.
Taking this as food.
Question: Who is it that does not take this as food?
Answer: There is the sign of radiance.
And regarding those signs,
one applies correct mental attention and practices them extensively.
Considering that it is not food,
there are three kinds of light:
first, the light that dispels darkness.
Second is the light of the Dharma;
third is the light of the supporting body;
and fourth is the light that remedies darkness.
Furthermore, there are three kinds.
The first occurs during the night,
namely the stars, the moon, and so forth.
The second is during the daytime,
namely, the light of the sun.
The third is during both [day and night].
This refers to fire-pearls and the like.
As for "the light of the Dharma," it is as when someone, according to what they receive, contemplate, or touch, [experiences illumination].
One observes all phenomena,
or else practices by recollecting the Buddha and so forth accordingly.
Regarding "relying on the radiance of the body":
this refers to the natural bodily radiance of sentient beings;
it should be understood as the first light.
It remedies three kinds of darkness:
first, the darkness of night;
second, the darkness of clouds.
Third is the darkness of obstruction,
which refers to such things as caves and dwellings.
The light of the Dharma can remedy these three kinds of darkness.

Because of not knowing all phenomena as they truly are, one gives rise to much doubt regarding the past, future, and present; it is likewise so with respect to the Buddha’s teachings and other matters.
In this context, both ignorance (*avidyā*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are termed "darkness."
Furthermore, it is proven that observation can counteract lethargy, drowsiness, and darkness,
because it is capable of clearly discerning the nature of all phenomena.
Question: What is the nutriment for the hindrance of restlessness and remorse?
Answer: Discursive thoughts concerning relatives and so forth.
Improper mental attention toward memories of past laughter and play,
as well as toward their signs.
Having extensively practiced this,
one takes it as sustenance.
As for the reflection on relatives:
That is to say, due to the prosperity or decline of one's relatives,
or their separation or reunion,
one gives rise to states of elation or dejection.
Regarding "the mind gives rise to deliberation" and so forth:
"reflection on the realm" refers to [deliberation] based on the signs of the prosperity and decline of a country.
This is explained in detail as previously stated.
Regarding the reflection on immortality:
it refers to all activities performed during the stages of youth and old age, whether for one's own benefit or for the sake of others.
It gives rise to feelings of joy and sorrow;
the mind conceives deliberations and so forth.
As for "laughing": [it refers to...]
That is to say, there may be someone who, either by discussing things separately or by discussing them in combination,
reveals their teeth and smiles, gathering together with joyful and cheerful chatter.
"Games" refers to games such as *śāri* (backgammon), *akṣa* (dice), and *maṇi* (bead-rolling),
or any other similar forms of amusement.
That is to say, they mutually enjoy one another and enjoy their respective objects,
experiencing various pleasures,
whether by virtue of being in the same place.
Or perhaps, due to frivolous discourse,
they dwell in pleasure;
such is their conduct.
This refers to grasping or holding by means of the hands, arms, hair,
or other such features, or touching any part of the body.
Some embrace or coo;
some gaze at one another;
others engage in various other activities.
Question: What serves as the non-nutriment for this hindrance?
Answer: There is śamatha and its respective signs.
One should cultivate appropriate mental attention extensively and regard it as non-nutriments.
Śamatha refers to the nine stages of mental abiding and all phenomena subsumed under the category of śamatha.
That is to say, regarding the phenomena of decline or prosperity in oneself or others that are to be reviled,
one gives rise to a mind of weary detachment, alarm, and contempt,
and abides in tranquility.
Question: What is the nutriment of the hindrance of doubt?
Answer: It consists of the past, future, and present, as well as their respective signs.
One frequently cultivates improper reflection and takes it as one's sustenance.
That is to say: "Did I exist in the past, or did I not exist?
as explained in detail above.
Improper reflection refers to reflection subsumed under the category of the inconceivable.
As for the inconceivable:
That is to say: the contemplation of self,
the contemplation of sentient beings,
and the contemplation of the world.
If, within one's own sphere,
one contemplates the characteristic of a self according to worldly distinctions.
It is called "contemplation of self.
If it occurs in relation to others,
it is called "contemplation of sentient beings."
If one contemplates the world of sentient beings and the world of the physical environment,
it is called "contemplation of the world."
That is to say: the world is eternal; or it is non-eternal;
or it is both eternal and non-eternal; or it is neither eternal nor non-eternal, and so forth.
Question: What serves as the non-nutriment for this hindrance?
Answer: It is the object-conditioned arising and its characteristic mark.
One should cultivate appropriate mental attention extensively and regard it as non-nutriments.
Because he perceives that there is only phenomena and only the causes of phenomena,
and only suffering and only the causes of suffering.
With all improper mental attention as the condition,
ignorance regarding objects of the three times does not arise for that which has not yet arisen.
That which has already arisen can be abandoned.
If one applies attention forcefully in an improper manner,
that which is proper will not occur.
These two, taken together, are collectively termed improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
If, within this context, it accords with reason,
one should know that such a case is called "in accordance with principle" (*yoniśas*);
that is to say, conceiving of light within darkness.
By means of this skillful method,
one applies attention in accordance with reality,
not in an improper manner.
In other locations as well,
there are further modes of appropriate attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*).
Furthermore, regarding the first dhyāna:
It is endowed with five factors:
first, vitarka;
second, vicāra.
Third, joy;
fourth, bliss;
fifth, one-pointedness of mind.
The second dhyāna has four factors:
first, internal serenity;
second, joy.
The third dhyāna has five factors:
three kinds of bliss, one-pointedness of mind, and equanimity.
The third dhyāna possesses these five branches.
First, equanimity;
second, mindfulness;
third, clear comprehension.
The fourth dhyāna has four factors:
equanimity, mindfulness, alertness, and one-pointedness of mind.
The fourth dhyāna has four factors.
First, purity through equanimity;
second, purity through mindfulness;
third, the sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
Regarding the one-pointedness of mind within the first dhyāna,
vitarka and vicāra serve as the apprehension of the object.
Samādhi serves as its basis;
joy is the object of experience;
and bliss serves to eliminate the heavy burden of coarse afflictions.
In the second dhyāna,
internal serenity (adhyātmasaṃprasāda) serves as the apprehension of the object,
and samādhi serves as its basis.
The rest is as previously explained.
Within the third dhyāna, equanimity,
mindfulness, and clear comprehension take the object of focus.
Samādhi is its basis;
the rest is as previously explained.
Within the fourth dhyāna:
The purity of equanimity and the purity of mindfulness serve as the objects of apprehension;
concentration is their basis.
The rest is as previously explained.
Although there are other factors within the various meditative absorptions (dhyāna),
these [factors] are preeminent.
Because it is of great benefit to one who cultivates meditative concentration, it is established specifically as a limb.
Question: For what reason?
Is there vitarka and vicāra in the first dhyāna?
Answer: Because one enters the first dhyāna by means of being weary of the desire realm, within that first dhyāna...
However, because one has not yet been able to observe the faults of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*),
the second dhyāna is able to observe those faults.
Therefore, it is said that vitarka and vicāra are stilled.
Just as one sees the faults of those [states] in the second dhyāna and thus calls them "stilling of vitarka and vicāra," so it is with the third dhyāna.
It is called "tranquility of joy" because one perceives the faults of joy;
it is called "tranquility of pleasure" because one perceives the faults of pleasure in the fourth dhyāna.
One should understand that there is a distinction in the purity of equanimity and mindfulness.
Furthermore, regarding the distinctions in the names of these meditative absorptions (dhyāna):
they are sometimes called "higher mind" (adhicitta),
meaning that they arise through the predominant power of mental purity.
Because it is correct contemplation,
it is called "abiding in bliss," meaning that within this state one experiences supreme happiness.
Why is this? Because, by relying on the various meditative concentrations (dhyāna),
one experiences the joy and bliss of the first dhyāna, the bliss of tranquility, the bliss of equanimity, and the physical and mental bliss of the higher stages.
Furthermore, one who has attained meditative concentration repeatedly enters and emerges from the various dhyānas.
Because one experiences the dwelling in happiness in the present life;
by means of this, one directly experiences the dwelling in happiness in the present life while in meditative concentration,
and having arisen from it.

furthermore, it is by means of this that—
They attain the path of non-retrogression.

Should they pass away while still possessing further grasping (*upādāna*), [they proceed accordingly].
By reason of these causes and conditions,

One becomes a Great Brahmā through the soft,
medium, and superior grades; specifically, through the superior,

By the power of cultivation through perfuming,
one is born in the five Pure Abodes;

Having been born in the dhyāna stages,

once born there, [one remains].
If one gives rise to attachment for its flavor,
one immediately falls away;
if one cultivates purity, one progresses.
They are reborn there,
or they are born into a lower meditative absorption,
or they advance to a higher meditative absorption.
Having first cultivated and attained meditative concentration in this world,

Why is this? Because one who has not yet abandoned desire cannot be reborn there;

As explained at length in the Sūtra:

Because one forms such a resolute conviction.

Whether good or bad, inferior or superior—
in this way, regarding the many,

For what purpose does one cultivate such contemplative practice?
It is for the sake of purifying and refining the skillful means that lead to the most excellent qualities.
What are these so-called most excellent qualities?
That is to say: the bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana),
the bases of totality (kṛtsnāyatana),

Although one has previously attained detachment from the various forms of the desire realm regarding the knowledge of non-contention, the vow-knowledge, the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and so forth.

therefore, in order to attain it,
one repeatedly contemplates them with resolute conviction.
What is the internal non-perception of form while observing external forms?
It refers to one born in the desire realm who has already become detached from the desires of the form realm.
The formless attainments do not manifest before him,
nor does he contemplate the signs of those perceptions;
rather, he forms a resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) solely toward external forms.
If one has already attained detachment from this form,
it is designated as "external" due to two causes and conditions.
This is called "internal non-perception of form," meaning that one has already realized the formless attainments and also personally knows that one has attained this meditative concentration.
Because one does not contemplate the internal mark of luminosity;

What is the purification liberation, which one realizes with the body and dwells in, having fully attained?
That is to say, there is one who has already attained the perfection of equanimity and mindfulness that is pure and bright;
taking this as a basis,
they cultivate the perfection of the pure noble conduct, which is called the liberation of purity.
Why is this? Because of three causes and conditions;
that is to say, because one has already transcended all suffering and pleasure.
Because all agitation has been stilled and because it is well-polished,
one realizes it through bodily witness.
Since many noble and holy ones dwell within this abode,
what is the liberation of the sphere of infinite space?
That is to say, there is someone who has already attained detachment from that state of emptiness;
they then contemplate and resolve upon space in this way:
"This is the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness."
Having attained detachment from that sphere of consciousness,
one contemplates and resolves upon that very consciousness;
this is the liberation of the sphere of nothingness.
This refers to one who, having already attained the sphere of nothingness,
contemplates and resolves upon the sphere of infinite consciousness;
this is the liberation of the Peak of Existence.
One should not form a resolute conviction toward anything else; rather,
one should form a resolute conviction precisely within that very place where a perception can arise, extending even to all such locations.
Furthermore,

because one is only able to give rise to superior knowledge and superior vision after having previously cultivated the mental attention of resolute conviction, they are called "bases of mastery" (abhibhvāyatana).
This excellence should be understood to have five further types.
First, it is called excellence because it displaces others by means of one’s own inferiority;
that is to say, for example, when someone uses their own superior skill in crafts or other matters to displace another and place them in an inferior position.
Second, it is called "victorious" because it subdues those who are weak and inferior;
that is to say, as when someone uses their own great strength to crush those who are inferior.
Third, it is called "victorious" because it is able to obscure others.
This means that objects such as jars and basins can provide concealment and obstruction,
or that various medicinal herbs, incantations, and supernormal powers can effect hiding and obscuration.
It is called "victory" because it overcomes and destroys the focal object through these four ways.
It is called "supreme" because it involves the rejection of all afflictions through the revulsion toward sense objects and because of mastery over the five powers of turning.
This refers to a worldly king who issues commands to his ministers and servants according to his will;
within this context,
the meaning intends to clarify concealment and sovereignty.
While previously one possessed mastery over resolve within the liberations (*vimokṣa*),
now one possesses mastery in subduing [the object] within the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
One contemplates the smallness of form.
This refers to the forms of the requisites and so forth belonging to sentient beings.
Regarding the observation of "abundant forms," this refers to the forms of palaces, houses, and the like.
"Beautiful color" refers to exquisite manifest color (*varṇa*),
because it is exclusively pure and sublime.
That which is contrary to this is called "unpleasant color.
As for what is called "inferior color":
That is to say, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles,
and forms that are disagreeable; the opposite of these should be understood as superior forms.
These four primary colors comprise the sustenance,
requisites, palaces, and so forth of sentient beings;
as for the term "superior cognition," it refers to this.
This refers to the repeated concealment of the object through resolve.
To have such a perception means to have a perception of suppression.
Furthermore,
they are called "totalities" (*kṛtsnāyatana*) because one generates a pervasive resolve regarding the object through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
As for the statement that they are "without duality":
This means that all noble ones (ārya) are without the two distinctions of "self" and "what belongs to self.
It is called "immeasurable" because it pervades all things.
For what reason are the *kṛtsnāyatanas* (totalities) established solely with respect to the two bases of visible form and tangibility?
It is because these two types [of objects] are constantly and continuously present throughout the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) within both one's own body and the bodies of others.
The sense organs, such as the eye,
belong exclusively to one's own body;
as do the two objects, fragrance and flavor.
It does not pervade everything;
there are intervals between sounds.
Therefore, it is not so described.
Thus, these material universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) constitute the final stage of the meditative concentrations of the form realm;
within the formless realm, they do not exist.
Because space pervades all things, it is established as a *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality).
Because the objective sphere traversed by consciousness pervades all things,
it is also established as a *kṛtsnāyatana*.
Furthermore, the practitioner of meditation first contemplates and resolves upon the object of focus,
and subsequently becomes able to subdue [the afflictions].
Once one has attained mastery over this subduing,
thereafter one forms a resolute conviction (adhimukti) regarding it as pervading all places, exactly as one desires.
Therefore, these three follow this sequence;
because the eight spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) are thoroughly purified.
It can induce the supernormal power of resolute conviction (adhimukti-abhijñā) of the noble ones and the supernormal power of transformation regarding all things,
according to one's resolute conviction.
According to whatever they transform,
they are able to accomplish it all;
furthermore, they can also transform them into objects such as gold and silver.
It is capable of being employed;
because the *vijñānakṛtsnāyatana* (sphere of totality of consciousness) is thoroughly purified,

one is able to induce various supreme qualities such as the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇājñāna*), the knowledge resulting from resolution (*praṇidhijñāna*), and the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Because of the complete purification of the sphere of infinite space,
everything transforms into space according to one's wish, just as,
for example, an ordinary blacksmith or goldsmith in the world [transforms their materials].
Just as when clay and other materials have not yet been properly refined through kneading and so forth,
so too is it at the stage of liberation;
whereas when they have been well-refined, it is like that [final state].
The same applies to the stage of the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*);
just as [the mind] has been trained and can transform things at will,
so too is it with the stage of the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Furthermore,
regarding the three samādhis:
what is the emptiness samādhi (śūnyatā-samādhi)?
That is to say, with the mind abiding on a single object while remaining detached from [notions of] a sentient being, a life-principle, a nourisher, or a person;
one should know that emptiness, in brief, is of four kinds.
First, the observation of emptiness:
that is, observing that all phenomena are empty, impermanent, and without bliss,
and so forth, up to...
Emptiness refers to the absence of self and what belongs to a self, and so forth.
Second is the emptiness of their fruit,
namely, the unshakable liberation of mind.
It is empty of all afflictions such as greed and so forth.
Third is internal emptiness,
which means that one's own body is empty.
It is devoid of all perverse attachments, such as the conception of "I" and "mine," as well as the pride of "I am.
Fourth is external emptiness,
which means being empty of the five desires and free from craving for them.
As it is said: "Because I have transcended all perceptions of form,
I have realized and dwell in the external emptiness of the body," and so forth,
as extensively explained.
In this context, the perception of excellent sensual desires is called the "perception of form" (rūpa-saṃjñā).
Because the craving and desire arising from this perception have been severed, [it is called the cessation of the perception of form].
This is called external emptiness.
Furthermore, for the practitioner,
it is empty of that fruit.
At times he directs his attention to contemplate external emptiness;
at times he directs his attention to contemplate internal emptiness;
and by means of observing emptiness, at times he contemplates the emptiness of both the internal and external.
By the power of this,
the mind realizes and attains [this] simultaneously;
even regarding this internal and external emptiness.
One who has not yet realized this assembly should apply their attention to the immovable;
as for what is called "the immovable":
That is to say, the perception of impermanence,
or alternatively, the perception of suffering;
one contemplates in this manner.
He is then no longer moved by that conceit of self (*asmimāna*) and so forth;
because his mind is not moved by that calculation of a self, by conceit of self, and so on, as explained at length,
he realizes and attains the two emptinesses simultaneously.
What is the wishless concentration of mind?
It refers to contemplating the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent.
Or, by contemplating suffering,
the mind abides in a single object.
What is the signless mental concentration (animitta-cetosamādhi)?
That is to say, regarding the cessation of those very aggregates of clinging,
one contemplates their tranquility,
and the mind abides in a single object of focus.
As the Sūtra says:
"The signless mental samādhi is neither depressed nor exalted."
...and so forth, as explained at length.
What is meant by "neither low nor high"?
It is because it is not associated with the two characteristics of opposition and compliance.
Furthermore, there are two causes and conditions for entering the concentration of signlessness:
first, not conceptualizing any signs;
second, correctly contemplating the realm of signlessness.
Because they do not contemplate any signs,
they neither feel aversion toward nor destroy those signs;
they simply engage in mental attention through non-application of effort.
Therefore it is called "not low," because one correctly contemplates the signless realm; thus,
one does not stubbornly cling to that signlessness.
Therefore, it is called "Not Arrogant.
This samādhi is briefly of two kinds:
first, the preparatory means (upāya).
Second is the fruit of the means (*upāya*).
As for "means," it refers to repeated exertion and self-urging.
While investigating and establishing [the teachings],
one has not yet attained liberation from those various signs.
Because the consciousness that apprehends secondary characteristics disturbs the mind from time to time.
Furthermore, by repeatedly exhorting and encouraging himself,
and through careful reflection and stabilization,
he is finally able to grasp the fruit.
Regarding the liberation that conforms to its characteristics: because one is liberated even from this liberation,
one dwells without needing to exert oneself through deliberate reflection and discernment.
Therefore, it is called "thoroughly well-liberated.
If one repeatedly exerts oneself, applies discernment,
and establishes [the mind] in stability.
Those who merely abide [in this state],
though it is called liberation,
is not a well-liberated state.
Furthermore, it is the clear understanding of the fruit and the clear understanding of merit;
the latter refers to the ultimate severance of the afflictions.
Because it is the ultimate state of dwelling in happiness in the present life;
furthermore, both cessation and the path should be thoroughly understood—
namely, these two kinds.
In accordance with their sequence,
these are called the "clearly understood fruit" and the "clearly understood qualities.
Furthermore, there is the "clear realization of the truth" (satyābhisamaya) and the "fruit of arhatship" (arhattvaphala).
Both should be clearly understood;
within the stage of the path of seeing (darśanamārga),
it is termed the "clearly understood fruit" (abhisamaya-phala).
Regarding the fruit of arhatship,
it is called the "merit of thorough understanding.
If that thing does not exist in this place, [then it is so].
Viewing it as empty by means of this principle,
it is therefore called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*); that is,
the emptiness which is the object of observation.
Because there is nothing to be hoped for or desired,
it is called "wishless" (apraṇihita).
Because one contemplates this as being free from all mental formations (saṃskāra-nimitta), it is called "signless" (animitta).
Why is emptiness taught here first,
whereas elsewhere impermanence is taught as suffering,
and suffering as non-self?
It is subsequently explained that emptiness is taught [for this purpose]:
namely, if there were no selflessness,
the contemplations on impermanence and suffering would never become pure.
One must first abide in the perception of non-self;
immediately following this, one attains wishlessness.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
All perceptions of impermanence rely upon the perception of non-self to achieve stable abiding.
...and so on, as extensively explained.
Having contemplated selflessness within that which is impermanent, he...
They do not give rise to aspirations;
they wish only for the signless and seek exclusively liberation.
Therefore, immediately following this, the signless is proclaimed.
Furthermore, what is the concentration with directed thought and sustained examination?
It refers to a concentration that is associated with directed thought and sustained examination.
What is the concentration with no applied thought and only sustained thought?
It refers to a concentration associated exclusively with sustained thought.
Having cultivated this, Mahābrahmā became the Great Brahmā King.
What is the concentration without applied thought and sustained thought?
It refers to a concentration in which both applied thought and sustained thought are absent.
In both cases, they are not associated;
by cultivating this,
one is born in the successive higher stages up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Excluding the untainted (*anāsrava*) samādhis,
what is the characteristic of the samādhi without applied thought and sustained thought?
It refers to [the state] regarding applied and sustained thought.
The mind gives rise to relinquishment;
by means of a single flavor alone,
it [abides] upon the internal object of focus.
And one forms this resolute conviction.
Furthermore, it appears as a single flavor and as equal.
Next, what is the small samādhi?
That is to say, it is "small" either by way of its object (*ālambana*),
because it contemplates a limited amount of form,
or by way of its mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Because of small faith, small desire, and small resolve.
What is great samādhi? It is that which is great either by way of its object (*ālambana*)...
Because one contemplates many forms,
yet it is not because one contemplates forms as being infinite or boundless; or because of the application of attention (*manasikāra*),
it is "great" due to superior faith, superior aspiration, and superior resolve.
It is not because of an infinite or boundless faith, aspiration, or resolute conviction.
What is immeasurable samādhi?
It refers to that which arises either by way of its object of focus (ālambana).
Because one contemplates all forms as immeasurable, boundless, and limitless;
or because of mental attention;
or because of immeasurable, boundless, and limitless faith, aspiration, and resolute conviction.
Among these, the samādhi of the great mind refers to forming the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that the light of all devas is present beneath a single tree,
and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding the "immeasurable samādhis," this refers to the four immeasurables.
How is it that one generates resolute conviction by visualizing the light of the devas beneath a single tree?
This means that having become thoroughly weary of and having overcome the desire realm, one attains the first dhyāna;
then, for the sake of making this concentration perfectly pure,
one further cultivates the means.
Furthermore, hearing that the bodies of the various devas are adorned with radiance,
he then contemplates the characteristics of that bodily radiance, extending from beneath a single tree all the way to the great earth and the limits of the great ocean.
One generates resolute conviction,
which increases further and further through meditative concentration.
Because there are distinctions [among objects],
that which arises is made to have distinctions.
How is it that attention (manasikāra) can be established as being only of two kinds?
This means that because mental attention (*manasikāra*) is designated according to the extent of one's resolute conviction (*adhimukti*),
how is it that mental attention has only two as its conditions and is cultivated to consist of only those two?
That is to say, it is precisely by the power of this mental attention (*manasikāra*) that one designates the distinctions among the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) practiced;
for they become perfected, purified, and increasingly superior.
How is it that by taking the cultivation of the two alone as a condition, practice becomes the two alone?
It means that to the extent that one skillfully cultivates meditative concentration so that it becomes increasingly superior,
to that same extent there is the differentiation of the rebirths brought about through such designation.
How is it that, based on the two types of conduct as conditions, persons are established as being of only two kinds?
That is to say, based on these causes and conditions,
sentient beings are designated with the distinctions of high and low, superior and inferior.
Question: What is the difference between the radiance of the devas of the first two dhyānas?
Answer: Just as a mani-jewel has radiance on its exterior but no radiance within, so too is it with the bodies of those in the first dhyāna.
While it emits light externally, internally it is not so.
For example, just as a bright lamp emits light externally while illuminating itself internally,
the body in the second dhyāna is likewise.
Whether internal or external, there is light in both cases;
therefore, the Sūtra states that from that stage upward there is only one kind of body,
but not in the lower stages.
Furthermore, how are the four immeasurable concentrations established?
It is because sentient beings are of three categories:
first, those who experience neither suffering nor pleasure.
Second is the existence of suffering;
third is the existence of pleasure,
according to their respective order.
I desire to grant them happiness;
I desire to cause them to be free from suffering;
I desire to ensure that their happiness never departs from them.
Regarding that mental attention (*manasikāra*),
because there are four types, they correspond respectively to the sequence [of the four foundations of mindfulness].
Four types are established:
namely, by means of the mental attention of bestowing happiness and the mental attention of extracting from suffering.
The first three are established by means of the mental attention of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā-manasikāra*) that does not involve separation from happiness;
it is precisely regarding these three that one desires to bestow happiness and so forth.
It is for the purpose of causing them not to dwell with longing or attachment,
so that their mental attention is undefiled by ill-will,
undefiled by malice, and undefiled by sensual desire.
One establishes oneself in equanimity.
As the Sūtra says: "With a mind accompanied by loving-kindness," and so forth, as explained at length.
It is called "conjoined with loving-kindness" because it provides immediate benefit;
it is called a "virtuous friend" because its characteristic is to provide benefit.
There are, in brief, two kinds of this characteristic of providing benefit.
First, the desire to benefit;
second, the desire for peace and happiness.
These are the two types of characteristics.
It is manifested by all that is immeasurable.
It is without enmity,
because it is free from malicious intent.
One who is invincible,
because they are free from manifest conflict and contention;
one who is without affliction or harm.
Because it is free from things that are unbeneficial.
As for "extensive," it is because its objective referent (*ālambana*) is vast.
"Great" means that the contemplation of benefit and happiness is supreme.
"Immeasurable" means...
Because the fruits are immeasurable;
it is like the confluence of the many streams of the four great rivers for one who practices well.
Because it is utterly refined,
even if someone were to ask:
"What are the characteristics of the mind that is associated with loving-kindness?"
Therefore, the next response says:
"He dwells having fully attained and suffused with resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
As for "suffused with resolute conviction":
Regarding the phrase "the superior intention and resolute conviction are universal,
and the meaning is complete":
this is because they are perfectly pure and white.
"Abiding" means that the meditative practice one cultivates is focused day and night, being concentrated at all times.
Question: As the Sūtra says:
"Having well cultivated loving-kindness, it reaches its limit in the Sphere of Total Purity," and so on,
as explained at length.
What is the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) of this?
Answer: Among all forms of pleasure, the pleasure of the third dhyāna is supreme;
one recollects this pleasure.
One cultivates a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Because loving-kindness is supreme,
it is said that the cultivation of loving-kindness reaches its limit in the Sphere of Total Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*).
To recollect the sphere of empty space and cultivate compassion is likewise the most supreme.
Because one who cultivates compassion desires to extract others from suffering,
and within the formless realm,
there is an absence of manifold sufferings such as those involving disintegration and destruction.
Because that [perception] is entirely absent,
one therefore recollects the sphere of infinite space and cultivates the meditative attainment of compassion.
One should form this thought:
"I shall cause all sentient beings who suffer to reach the state where there is no suffering and its basis."
One who cultivates the meditative concentration of sympathetic joy also constantly recollects the sphere of infinite consciousness,
rejoicing in the peace and happiness attained by all sentient beings.
He forms this thought:
"I shall cause all classes of sentient beings to experience immeasurable bliss,
just as in the sphere of infinite consciousness."
Consciousness is immeasurable;
therefore, one recollects the sphere of infinite consciousness and cultivates the meditative concentration of joy.
It is the foremost.
One who cultivates the meditative concentration of equanimity also constantly recollects the sphere of nothingness.
He forms this thought:
"The untainted mind-ground of the sphere of nothingness is the very limit;
it is the most supreme relinquishment."
Just as an arhat bhikṣu is entirely free from affliction during the state in which all suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure manifest,
may all classes of sentient beings likewise attain such equanimity.
Therefore, recollecting the sphere of nothingness and cultivating the meditative concentration of equanimity is the most supreme.
All such practices as these constitute the noble conduct.
Only the noble ones are able to cultivate it;
therefore, the Sūtra proclaims that it is practiced in conjunction with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
Furthermore:
What is the cultivation of samādhi in one part?
It refers to that in which one attends exclusively to the sign of light.
Or one may enter meditative absorption by attending solely to the mental image of form;
these two types follow their respective order.
Either perceiving light or beholding various forms:
what is the cultivation of samādhi with all its parts?
It refers to entering meditative concentration while contemplating both simultaneously.
One both perceives light and sees various forms.
Such are the specific difficulties encountered by one who cultivates the concentration on light.
There are eleven kinds,
namely doubt and so forth,
as explained at length in the Sūtra.
Question: Who raises this objection?
Answer: It is the characteristic of samādhi.
There are two kinds of characteristics.
That is to say, the characteristic of the object of focus and the characteristic of the causal condition;
relying upon these as a basis, one abides in samādhi.
If one regresses from that sign, one is unable to remain [in it].
This is because, at the very beginning, one has not skillfully understood the characteristics of the luminous forms that appear.
One then becomes aware of doubt;
because one has relaxed one's efforts,
there is a lack of mental attention.
Just as one who does not wish to see various forms either closes their eyes or turns their back.
It is likewise for this practitioner of meditation who does not intend to attend to any forms.
Due to not properly guarding the sense faculties and so forth,
there is physical heaviness and a tendency toward excessive sleep.
Alternatively, if there is excessive wakefulness,

Because one exerts extreme effort for these two matters and applies forceful,
strenuous reflection,
there arises an excessive degree of courageous and vigorous diligence (*vīrya*).
Because of the faults of excessive exertion and over-exertion,
one falls back into extreme inferiority,
like someone who tries to catch a quail by grasping it too tightly.
He merely intends to seek the appearance of light;
yet when this [intention] and the seeing of form arise simultaneously,

He immediately felt a surge of joy,
like a person who has discovered two hidden treasures.
Yet, as he suddenly beheld inauspicious colors appearing everywhere in all directions, he was seized by great terror.
It is just as if a person were spinning rapidly on both sides and then suddenly stops;
whether walking or standing still,
they would give rise to various perceptions regarding the diverse beings of the world.
Such external perceptions pose a hindrance to meditative concentration;
alternatively, they may arise because of the very concentration one is practicing.
Thinking oneself superior and viewing others as inferior,
one then becomes self-exalting.
In this way, it may also be called "various perceptions," or "much discursive speech," or "prolonged investigation."
This causes the body to become weary and the mind to fail to attain concentration;
