consciousness is compared to the mind.
Just as one perceives the presence of earth by seeing obstruction in water, so too is it known through inference.
If one sees that the vegetation in a place is lush and the stems and leaves are verdant, one infers from this that there is water.
If one sees hot ashes, one infers from this that there is fire.
If one sees a grove of trees swaying, one infers from this that there is wind.
With eyes closed and staff in hand, he asks others where to go or stop;
stumbling and falling, he loses his way.
From such matters as these, one knows by comparison that he is blind.
Listening intently at a loud voice, one knows by comparison that the person is deaf;
yet those with right faith and wisdom,
whether they have abandoned desire or not, [discern this].
Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas,
through such categories as these,
infer by means of karma.
This should be understood as previously explained.
Regarding inference based on dharma (*dharmānumāna*):
it refers to [inference] by means of a phenomenon that is spatially contiguous or logically connected.
By means of inference based on other phenomena that are adjacent and interconnected—
for instance, inferring suffering because [phenomena] are subject to impermanence—
one infers emptiness and non-self because they are subject to suffering.
Because it belongs to birth, one infers that it possesses the nature of aging;
because it belongs to aging, one infers that it possesses the nature of death;
because it belongs to that which has form, is visible, and is resistant, one infers that it possesses spatial location and physical substance.
Because it belongs to the outflowing (sāsrava), one infers that it possesses suffering;
because it belongs to the outflow-free (anāsrava), one infers that it is without suffering;
and because it belongs to the conditioned (saṃskṛta), one infers that it is subject to the dharmas of arising, abiding, change, and cessation.
Because it belongs to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one infers by analogy that it lacks the dharmas of arising, abiding, change, and cessation.
Such categories as these are called "inference based on dharmas" (*dharmānumāna*).
As for "inference based on cause and effect" (*kāryakāraṇānumāna*):
This means inferring one thing by means of its cause and effect through successive comparison.
For example, seeing that there was movement, one infers [the person's] arrival at another location;
seeing their arrival at another location, one infers that there was prior movement.
If one sees someone serving a king in accordance with the Dharma, one infers that they shall obtain vast rank and emolument;
seeing them possess great rank and emolument, one infers that they have previously served the king in accordance with the Dharma.
If one sees someone who has prepared well for their work, one infers that they will certainly obtain great wealth;
if one sees someone with great wealth, one infers that they have previously prepared well for their work.
Observing that good and evil deeds practiced in the past correspond to subsequent prosperity and decline,
one sees prosperity and decline and infers that they were preceded by the performance of good and evil deeds.
One infers satiety by seeing an abundance of food and drink;
one infers an abundance of food and drink by seeing satiety.
Or, if one sees someone whose eating is uneven, [one infers their state of satiety].
When there is illness,
one infers that this person has consumed food in an uneven manner;
when one observes meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one infers that they have attained freedom from desire (*vairāgya*).
Seeing one who is free from desire, one infers that they possess meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
If one sees someone on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one infers that they shall attain the realization of the fruits of śramaṇaship (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
If one sees someone who has attained the fruits of śramaṇaship...
Inferring the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) from such categories as these,
one should know that these are collectively termed "inference by cause and effect" (kāryakāraṇānumāna).
This is called inference (anumāna).
As for authoritative scripture (āptāgama),
it refers to the verbal teachings spoken by the Omniscient One.
Either one hears it from them,
or follows their Dharma; this,
moreover, is of three kinds.
First, it does not contradict the words of the Sage;
second, it is able to remedy afflictive obscurations;
third, it does not contravene the characteristics of phenomena.
"Not contradicting the words of the Noble Ones" refers to what is spoken by the noble disciples or what is spoken by the Buddha himself in the sūtras and teachings.
It has been transmitted and disseminated from one to another until the present day,
without contradicting the True Dharma or the True Meaning.
That which can remedy affliction refers to the fact that when these dharmas are properly cultivated,
one is able to forever subdue all afflictions and secondary afflictions, such as greed, hatred, and delusion.
"Not contradicting the characteristics of phenomena" means that by reversing what contradicts the characteristics of phenomena,
one should know that this is precisely "not contradicting the characteristics of phenomena."
What is meant by "characteristics contrary to reality"?
It refers to superimposing the characteristic of existence upon that which is without characteristics,
such as the grasping at a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a nourisher, and so forth.
Whether eternal or annihilated,
with form or formless—
such categories as these.
Or one may reduce that which possesses characteristics to being characteristicless,
or establish as indeterminate that which is determinate;
for example, [reducing] "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" [to something else].
All that is with outflows is by nature suffering;
all phenomena are empty and without self.
Yet, they falsely establish that one portion is permanent and another portion is impermanent.
One part is suffering and one part is not suffering;
one part has a self and one part is without a self—
regarding these indeterminate matters established by the Buddha.
Seeking a formal prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
That is to say, it is something that can be predicted,
or it is established as a prediction.
Or, one may establish what is indeterminate as being determinate,
such as when one maintains that all pleasant sensations are invariably underlain by latent attachment (*rāga-anuśaya*),
and all painful sensations are invariably underlain by latent aversion (*dveṣa-anuśaya*).
All feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant are underlain by delusion (*moha*).
All pleasant feelings are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
All volitional karma created in conjunction with pleasant feeling is likewise with outflows.
They are invariably destined to experience the ripening of suffering as their maturation;
such categories [of phenomena] may also exist within the realm of conditioned phenomena (*sa-nimitta-dharma*).
Establishing distinctions within the characteristic of non-distinction;
establishing non-distinction within the characteristic of distinction—
just as with the characteristic of non-distinction regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, he establishes [them] within the unconditioned; yet,
regarding the unconditioned dharmas, there is no characteristic of differentiation,
whereas such characteristics do exist for conditioned dharmas.
It is likewise established;
as it is with the conditioned and the unconditioned,
so it is with the material and the immaterial.
With vision and without vision;
with resistance and without resistance;
outflowing and non-outflowing.
One should understand all these matters according to their respective requirements.
Furthermore, regarding the presence of characteristics, one should not establish the characteristics of cause and effect in a manner that deviates from correct principle.
Just as it is established that sublime conduct brings about unlovely results,
it is likewise established that various forms of evil conduct bring about lovely results;
such is the reckoning within the poorly taught Dharma and Vinaya.
To practice various wrong conducts and yet claim to attain purification,
while regarding the practice of right conduct within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya as defilement— this is [the case].
Within the characteristic of unreality, one establishes the characteristic of reality through conventional verbal expression;
within the characteristic of reality, one variously posits it through conventional verbal expression.
This is like establishing verbal expressions regarding all ineffable phenomena and speaking of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Categories such as these are called characteristics contrary to the Dharma.
One should know that those which are the opposite of these are characteristics not contrary to the Dharma;
this is termed the "Right Teaching."
Question: If all phenomena are established by their own specific characteristics and each abides within its own intrinsic nature,
for what further reason and condition are two types of accomplished objects established?
Answer: It is for the purpose of causing others to give rise to faith and understanding;
it is not for the purpose of producing the intrinsic nature and characteristics of phenomena.
Question: Is it for the purpose of establishing the meaning that is to be proven?
Why is the thesis (pakṣa) established first?
Answer: It is in order to first demonstrate the meaning of the thesis that one personally favors.
Question: Why is the reason (hetu) explained next?
Answer: It is for the purpose of clarifying the definitive principles based on perceptible phenomena, so that others may accept the established thesis.
Question: Why is an analogy cited immediately thereafter?
Answer: It is in order to demonstrate the empirical facts upon which the principles for establishing [the proof] depend.
Why, then, are "homogeneous" and "heterogeneous" cases, as well as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), explained later?
Is it the same as the correct teaching?
Answer: It is for the purpose of revealing the knowledge of the two types of contradiction and non-contradiction regarding causes and examples.
Furthermore, as for contradiction:
It is due to two causes and conditions:
first, because it is indeterminate;
second, because it is of the same nature as that which is to be established.
Regarding non-contradiction,
there are likewise two causes and conditions:
first, because of its definitiveness.
Second, because they are established through different means.
As for their contradiction:
regarding the establishment of the thesis (*pratijñā*) to be proven.
Because it cannot serve as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
it is not called a means of valid cognition.
As for "not being contradictory":
Because it serves as the valid authority (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the thesis (*pakṣa*) one intends to prove, it is called "authority";
this is what is meant by the "basis of the treatise" (*śāstrāśraya*).
Regarding the adornment of treatises,
there are briefly five kinds: first,
being skilled in one's own and others' tenets.
Second, his speech is perfectly complete;
third, he is fearless;
fourth, he is dignified and solemn.
The fifth is the "Worthy of Offerings.
One who is skilled in their own and others' doctrines refers to someone who, regarding this Dharma...
Having developed a profound affection for the Vinaya,
one should read, recite, and uphold the essential tenets of this very treatise.
Having heard, reflected upon, and contemplated it,
one has matured in practice;
it is well-mastered, well-expounded, and clearly elucidated.
If one has no affection for and no delight in that Dharma and Vinaya,
yet reads, recites, and upholds the tenets of its treatises;
Though one’s hearing and reflection have become mature,
one does not engage in practice; yet,
it has already been well-mastered, well-expounded, and clearly elucidated.
This is called being skilled in one's own and others' tenets.
Regarding what is called "possessing perfection," it refers to someone who, whenever they speak, [speaks correctly].
All [these] are by means of sound, not by what is not sound.
What constitutes sound?
It refers to that which is endowed with five virtues.
This is what is called sound.
First, it is not base or vulgar;
second, it is easy to understand.
Third, it is clear and resonant;
fourth, it is appropriate;
fifth, its meaning is excellent.
"Not vulgar" means being free from the coarse and rustic speech of remote regions and borderlands.
"Not contemptuous" refers to [the manner of speaking].
This means that whatever is spoken is entirely by means of terminology commonly used in the world.
As for "magnificent," it refers to establishing speech based on meaning such that it skillfully and powerfully accomplishes that meaning.
"Correspondence" means that the preceding and succeeding meanings of the dharma accord with one another without distraction.
"Excellence of meaning" means...
This means it is capable of inducing superior rebirths, meditative concentration, and excellence, and is free from error.
Furthermore, this science of grammar (śabdavidyā) possesses the perfection of expression through nine characteristics:
first, it is not confused or disordered.
Second, not being coarse or harsh;
third, being clear and distinct;
fourth, being measured.
Fifth, it is consistent with the meaning;
sixth, it is timely;
seventh, it is definitive.
Eighth, manifestation;
ninth, continuity.
All such characteristics taken together are termed "endowment with perfection."
"Fearlessness" means that there is someone who,
when situated among a single person, a small group, a mixed group, a large assembly, a group of followers, a group of truth-seekers, or a virtuous assembly,
their mind is never inferior or constantly apprehensive.
His body was free from perspiration;
his face showed no sign of fear;
and his voice was not stammering.
Speech that is free from timidity—
speaking in such a manner is called fearlessness.
"Solemnity" refers to when someone speaks only after waiting for the proper time and does not speak hastily;
this is called solemnity.
Regarding the "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat):
it refers to one who is by nature disciplined and virtuous, who does not afflict others,
and who never transgresses the ground of discipline and virtue maintained by those who are disciplined and virtuous.
He speaks in accordance with the minds of others;
at the proper time, he is able to lead them toward meaningful benefit with words that are gentle,
as if addressing a virtuous friend.
This is called "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).
If there are those who rely on these five treatises as adornments to engage in discourse,
it should be known that:
Furthermore, there are twenty-seven kinds of praised merits.
What are these twenty-seven? First, being respected and honored by the multitude.
Second, his words are invariably trusted and accepted.
Third, he is entirely without fear when in the midst of a great assembly.
Fourth, he deeply understands the flaws in the tenets of other schools as being as fleeting as a crack in a window.
Fifth, knowing the superior excellence of one's own school;
sixth, being free from biased attachment and having no partiality toward the treatises one has received;
seventh, being incapable of having one's own True Dharma and Vinaya led astray or wrested away.
Eighth, one is able to quickly comprehend what others say;
ninth, one is able to quickly receive what others say;
tenth, one is able to quickly respond to what others say.
Eleventh, possessing the excellence of speech so as to cause the assembly to feel affection and joy;
twelfth, delighting those who can believe and understand this vidyā-śāstra;
thirteenth, being able to skillfully explain and expound the meanings, phrases, and syllables.
Fourteenth, it causes the body to be free from weariness.
Fifteenth, it causes the mind to be free from weariness.
Sixteenth, one's speech is not stammering or obstructed.
Seventeenth, his eloquence is inexhaustible.
Eighteenth, his body does not suddenly wither.
Nineteenth, his mindfulness is never lost.
Twenty: his mind is free from affliction or harm.
Twenty-one: his throat is free from impairment.
Twenty-two: whatever he utters is clear and easy to understand.
Twenty-three: skillfully guarding one’s own mind so that it is free from anger.
Twenty-four: skillfully conforming to the minds of others so that they are free from resentment.
Twenty-five: causing those with whom one debates to give rise to pure faith in their hearts.
Twenty-sixth, whatever he does does not provoke enmity or opposition.
Twenty-seventh, his vast reputation flows throughout the ten directions;
the world everywhere proclaims that this great Dharma master ranks among the number of Great Masters.
Just as those who enjoy sensual pleasures adorn themselves with precious ornaments such as bracelets and bangles set with jewels like mani-gems, pearls, and lapis lazuli,
their majestic power blazes forth and their radiance shines everywhere.
Thus, this proponent, adorned with these twenty-seven qualities of praise as the five ornaments of discourse,
is resplendent with majestic power and illuminates all with his radiance.
For this reason, it is called the "ornament of debate.
This is what is meant by the "ornament of debate.
As for "defeat in debate":
There are three kinds:
first, relinquishing the argument;
second, being defeated in the argument.
The third is called "transgression," which means abandoning the discourse one has undertaken.
What are the thirteen types of speech? They are as follows:
The proponent addresses the opponent, saying:
"My argument is unskillful, while yours is skillful;
it was I who failed to examine it properly."
"You have observed well.
My argument is without reason while yours possesses reason;
my argument is powerless while yours possesses power."
My argument has been refuted and your argument established.
My eloquence extends only this far;
beyond this, you should reflect further, and I shall explain it to you.
Let this matter rest; I shall say no more.
By means of these thirteen kinds of statements, one expresses an apology to the opponent and relinquishes the discourse under discussion.
Because one has abandoned what was being discussed,
it should be known that one is defeated and overcome by the other.
Falling behind the other and being defeated by them; therefore,
abandoning one's argument is called the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
"Defeat" refers to when a proponent is overcome and subdued by an opponent.
Or they may withdraw under the pretext of some other matter as a skillful means;
or they may cite external sayings;
or they may manifest indignation.
Sometimes he manifests anger;
sometimes he manifests pride;
sometimes he manifests being obscured by afflictions.
They may manifest affliction and harm;
they may manifest intolerance;
or they may manifest lack of faith.
Or again, they remained silent;
or again, they were filled with sorrow and distress;
or they hunched their shoulders and bowed their faces.
"Or, when one’s thoughts are exhausted and words fail,
they resort to expedients by feigning other matters to withdraw.
This refers to abandoning what was previously established and instead resorting to another school of thought.
Having set aside the previous reasons— namely, the evidence of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and valid scripture (*āptāgama*) based on similar and dissimilar classes—
and further relying on other causes up to and including valid scripture,
he cites the words of an outsider.
This refers to abandoning the subject matter under discussion—
such as discourse on food, drink, kings, ministers, thieves, roads, or lewdness—
and resorting to external pretexts to relinquish one's original position.
Regarding "manifesting indignation in order to refute the challenges of others":
this refers to using coarse, vulgar, and insolent speech.
To rebuke the opponent and manifest anger means to respond with words of resentment.
To those who engage in contentious debate and manifest arrogance,
one should address them with words concerning their lowly lineage and so forth.
"Destroying the opponent" means using words that expose the evil conduct concealed by another.
Regarding the interlocutor:
"manifesting affliction and harm" refers to using cruel and resentful speech to cause injury.
To revile the opponent while manifesting intolerance means to voice grievances out of fear of the opponent.
Those who manifest lack of faith do so by slandering their interlocutors through speech that destroys [virtuous] conduct.
"Those who remain silent" refers to those whose verbal karma has suddenly ceased;
"those who are sorrowful" refers to those who are grieving.
This refers to the mental karma of being scorched by affliction;
"shrugging one's shoulders and bowing one's face" refers to the physical demeanor of majesty suddenly withering away.
"One whose thoughts are stilled and words exhausted" refers to one whose eloquence and intellectual resources are both depleted.
It is by means of these thirteen kinds of matters that [this state occurs].
One should know that the term "defeat" refers to the first two types of false conduct, which are deceptive and confused;
the middle seven give rise to perverse conduct.
When the latter four lines of reasoning are exhausted,
this is called "defeat" (nigrahasthāna), falling into a position of loss.
As for the term "transgression":
This refers to the proponent defiling their speech with nine kinds of faults;
therefore, it is called "faults of speech. What are these nine?
First, confusion;
second, coarseness;
third, lack of clarity.
Fourth, they are not immeasurable;
fifth, they are not associated with what is meaningful;
sixth, they are not delivered at the proper time.
Seventh, it is indeterminate;
eighth, it is not manifest;
ninth, it is non-continuous.
"Confused" means to abandon the subject under discussion and speak of irrelevant matters.
"Harsh" means...
This refers to agitation arising from resentment and agitation arising from restlessness.
"Lacking discernment" means that neither the phenomena (*dharma*) nor their meaning (*artha*) are understood by the assembly or the interlocutor.
"Immeasurable" means that the words used to express the meaning are either redundant or deficient.
"Inconsistent with the meaning" refers to [the same].
It should be known that there are ten kinds:
first, that which is meaningless;
second, that which contradicts the meaning.
Third, the impairment of the principle;
fourth, being equivalent to the probandum;
fifth, the incurrence of fallacies and difficulties.
Sixth, one does not obtain meaningful benefit;
seventh, meanings lack proper order;
eighth, meanings are indeterminate.
Ninth, establishing what is capable of establishing;
tenth, conforming to irrational and false evil treatises.
Regarding "at an improper time":
This refers to that which ought to be explained being presented out of order,
and that which is indeterminate,
meaning that having established a position, one subsequently subverts it.
They are destroyed and then re-established;
their rapid transformation is difficult to comprehend.
That which is not clearly manifest—
This refers to responding without understanding when one is being ridiculed or mocked;
for instance, beginning with formal, canonical language and subsequently using vernacular speech, or conversely,
beginning with vernacular speech and subsequently returning to formal, canonical language.
"Non-continuity" refers to the interruption of the discourse in the interim.
Any discussion that commits these nine faults is considered defective.
This is called a verbal fault that results in defeat.
Regarding the "departure from the debate," this refers to the proponent.
First, one should examine the opening of the discourse by means of those three types of investigation before engaging in the discussion.
Alternatively, not engaging in debate is called "withdrawal from debate.
As for the three types of investigation:
First, observing gain and loss;
second, observing the assembly;
third, observing skillfulness and lack of skillfulness.
Regarding the observation of gain and loss:
this refers to the proponent who is just beginning to initiate the discourse.
First, one should examine:
"In establishing this thesis,
will it not result in harm to myself, harm to others, or harm to both?"
Will it not give rise to offenses in the present life, the future life, or both?
Will it not cause various forms of mental and physical distress?
And will you not, because of this, take up swords or staves to engage in fighting or quarreling?
Is it initiated by strife, litigation, flattery, deception, and false speech?
Will various evil and unwholesome states not thereby grow and increase?
Will it not fail to bring benefit and happiness to oneself, others, or the great multitude?
Is it not that he lacks compassion for all the world?
Is it not because of this that gods and humans find no purpose, no benefit, and no peace and happiness?
When that proponent of the thesis observes in this way:
If one realizes for oneself that the thesis one has established will cause harm to oneself,
and even brings no benefit, profit, or peace and happiness to gods or humans,
one should then reflect and exert oneself to refrain from establishing such a thesis.
If one understands in this way that the treatise I have established does not bring harm to oneself,
but can even lead to the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans,
then one should personally reflect and strive to establish the correct treatise.
This is called the first characteristic of renunciation regarding the debate on "whether it was done or not done.
As for the observation of the assembly:
it refers to the proponent of the thesis just beginning to introduce the subject of the debate.
One should skillfully observe the assembly present before one:
is there anyone with biased attachments, or is there none?
Is there anyone who is noble and upright, or is there none?
"Is there skillful means, or is there none?
When observing in this way,
if one knows that the assembly possesses only perverse attachments and is not devoid of perverse attachments, [one understands accordingly].
Thinking, "There is only the unvirtuous and the improper, and no one who is virtuous and proper;
there is only the unskillful, and no one who is skillful," he then exerts himself through his own reflection.
In such a gathering, one should not establish a formal thesis.
If one knows that the assembly is free from biased attachments and lacks any such bias,
consisting solely of the virtuous and upright rather than the unvirtuous and perverse.
Being skillful and not unskillful,
one should then reflect and exert oneself, thinking:
"I shall establish a formal argument within this assembly."
This is called the second characteristic of renunciation regarding the discourse on "whether one acts or does not act.
One should personally investigate what is wholesome and what is unwholesome.
Regarding the essence of debate, the locus of debate, the basis of debate,
the adornments of debate,
the defeat in debate, and the departure from debate, I [have explained them].
"Am I skillful or unskillful?
Do I possess the power to establish my own doctrine and refute the doctrines of others?"
When one considers whether it is possible to be liberated from points of defeat in debate, if one understands for oneself: "I am not skillful; I do not possess skill."
"Thinking, 'I lack the power and do not possess the power,' one should reflect for oneself and not establish a formal argument against an opponent."
If one knows for oneself: "I possess skill, not a lack of skill;
I possess power, not a lack of power," one then reflects and exerts oneself.
One should establish a formal debate together with the opponent;
this is called the third characteristic of the departure from the "either-doing-or-not-doing" argument.
Regarding the factors that are frequently employed in debate:
There are three types of qualities that are of great utility for establishing a formal argument: first,
being skilled in one's own and others' tenets.
Second is courageous fearlessness;
third is inexhaustible eloquence.
Question: Why are these three qualities said to be of great utility for the treatise one has established?
Answer: Because they are able to thoroughly understand their own and others' tenets,
they are capable of engaging in discourse regarding all phenomena with courage and fearlessness.
He is able to initiate discourse among all assemblies because his eloquence is inexhaustible;
he skillfully provides answers to whatever questions or challenges are posed.
Therefore, these three perform many functions regarding the treatise being established.
The section on the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*) has been explained,
along with its six characteristics.

1. The characteristic of the establishment of the designation of phenomena (dharma-prajñapti-vyavasthāna-lakṣaṇa). 2. The characteristic of the establishment of the designation of meanings (artha-prajñapti-vyavasthāna-lakṣaṇa).
3. The characteristic of the establishment of the designation of persons (pudgala-prajñapti-vyavasthāna-lakṣaṇa).
The characteristic of the establishment of the designation of the four seasons;
the characteristic of the establishment of the designation of number;
and the characteristic of the establishment of the designation of location and root-source.
The summary verse says:
Phenomena, meaning, persons, Time, number, and location;
If [there are] roots, bases, and so forth— This is the brief definition of grammar.
What is the establishment of the designation of phenomena?
It refers to the group of names, the group of phrases, the group of syllables,
and sounds endowed with the five qualities.
First, not vulgar or base;
second, easy and light;
third, powerful and resonant.
Fourth, the association;
fifth, the excellence of meaning.
What is the establishment of the designation of meaning?
It should be known that there are briefly ten kinds:
first, establishment by way of the faculties;
second, establishment by way of the primary elements.
1. Establishment through the three types of action;
2. Establishment through seeking;
3. Establishment through what is not the Dharma.
Sixth is the establishment of dharmas;
seventh is the establishment of prosperity;
eighth is the establishment of decline.
Ninth, the establishment of enjoyment;
tenth, the establishment of protection.
The summary verse says:
The eye and so forth, the earth and so forth, the body and so forth, as well as seeking,
the flourishing of what is non-dharmic and what is dharmic, decline, enjoyment,
guarding the faculties, and establishment.
That is to say: seeing the object, hearing the object,
smelling the object, tasting the object,
touching the object, and cognizing the object.
The establishment of the great elements refers to their meanings as support and so forth,
and as moistening and so forth.
The establishment of karma regarding the meanings of illumination and equality,
and the meanings of movement and agitation.
That is to say, it refers to the sense of coming and going;
the sense of proclaiming and so forth;
and the sense of recollecting and discerning, and so forth.
"Seeking to establish" means to pursue and investigate such matters;
"establishing what is not Dharma" refers to the same.
This refers to the meaning of killing, stealing,
and so forth. The establishment of phenomena refers to the meaning of giving, ethical discipline, and so forth.
Establishment of prosperity refers to the attainment of meanings such as joy and so forth;
establishment of decline refers to...
This refers to the meanings of destruction, fear, sorrow, distress, and so forth.
Regarding the establishment of enjoyment,
it refers to the meanings of food and drink, clothing and shelter, embracing, and the practice of receiving and utilizing [objects].
"Guarding and establishing" refers to the meanings of guarding, nurturing, and bringing to full maturity.
Furthermore, to state it briefly, there are six kinds of meanings.
First, the meaning of intrinsic nature;
second, the meaning of cause;
third, the meaning of fruit.
4. The meaning of function;
5. The meaning of differentiation and association;
6. The meaning of transformation.
The summary verse says:
Regarding intrinsic nature, cause, result, function, and their corresponding activities,
how are persons (pudgala) conventionally designated and established?
This refers to the establishment of the distinctions between the vocal characteristics of males, females, and those who are neither male nor female;
or alternatively, the establishment of the distinctions between the vocal characteristics of inferior, middling, and superior persons.
When, then, are these designations established?
This refers to three temporal distinctions in the characteristics of sound:
first, the excellence of the past past;
second, the excellence of the future future.
Third is the excellence of the present.
How is it designated, established, and formulated through enumeration?
It refers to the threefold numerical distinction of vocal characteristics.
First, the number one;

The Eleventh [Chapter], the Stage of that Accomplished through Reflection (*cintāmayī-bhūmi*), within the *Maulī Bhūmi*, Part One. The Stage of that Accomplished through Hearing has already been explained.
What is the stage consisting of cultivation through reflection?
It should be known that,
briefly stated, it is characterized by three aspects.
First, by virtue of natural purity;
second, by virtue of the discernment of the objects of knowledge;
and third, by virtue of the discernment of all phenomena.
What is natural purity?
It should be understood through nine aspects.

The first is as follows: there is someone who, dwelling alone in a secluded place, reflects with careful discernment upon the principles of all phenomena as they were heard and as they were investigated.
Second, they remain far removed from all inconceivable matters and reflect with precise discernment upon that which is to be contemplated.
Third, they are able to thoroughly understand both the "black" teachings and the "great" teachings.
Fourth, whatever one contemplates, one relies solely on the meaning and not on the literal expression.
Fifth, regarding a small portion of the Dharma, one gives rise to faith and understanding;
regarding another small portion of the Dharma, one examines it with wisdom.
Sixth is firm contemplation;
seventh is stable contemplation;
eighth is continuous contemplation.
Ninth, one is able to thoroughly complete what is being contemplated, never becoming weary, terrified, or disheartened along the way.
By virtue of these nine characteristics, it is called "pure and perfectly pure contemplation."
What is the discernment of the objects of knowledge?
It refers to the thorough discernment of the meanings that are investigated.
What are called the meanings that are investigated?
That is to say, to understand the characteristic of existence regarding existent phenomena,
and to understand the characteristic of non-existence regarding non-existent phenomena;
this is called the object of investigation.
What are the phenomena that are to be examined?
It should be known that these phenomena are, in brief, of five kinds.
1. phenomena existing by way of their own-characteristic (svalakṣaṇasat);
2. phenomena existing by way of a common-characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇasat);
3. phenomena existing by way of a conceptual-characteristic (prajñaptisat).
There are four types of phenomena existing as causal characteristics and five types of phenomena existing as resultant characteristics.
What are called phenomena existing by way of their own-characteristic?
It should be known that this phenomenon is briefly of three kinds:
first, existence as ultimate characteristic;
second, existence as phenomenal characteristic.
Regarding the three types of existence:
as for existence by way of ultimate characteristics,
it refers to the ineffable meaning within all phenomena, which is the objective domain of supramundane wisdom and possesses non-conceptualized characteristics.
Regarding the existence of characteristics (*nimitta*):
it refers to the four kinds of observed characteristics.
First, the name is obtainable in this location.
Second, the object is obtainable in this location;
third, this designation is not non-definitive with respect to this object,
meaning that it might otherwise be confused or indeterminate.
Alternatively, because it is impermanent and indeterminate,
this designation proceeds unimpededly with respect to this object;

Or, in this context, "receding" refers to that which possesses present characteristics;

Fifth, the common characteristic of all phenomena (*dharma*).
