because, respectively, neither a master nor an agent exists.
There is no functioning that can follow along with it;
third, there is no function of producing others,
meaning a dharma cannot produce another.
Fourth, it lacks the function of self-arising;
that is, it cannot arise by itself.
Fifth, it lacks the function of transmigration.
That is to say, because various conditions exist, there is arising;
it is not that something new arises anew.
The six [factors] lack the function of causing cessation.
This means that a phenomenon cannot destroy another.
Seventh, it lacks the function of self-destruction;
that is, it also cannot destroy itself. Question: Just as things arise because various conditions exist, [so too do they cease].
"Is it also because of the presence of various conditions that they cease?
He replied: "Because of the presence of various conditions they arise;
having arisen, they cease spontaneously."
As previously stated,
regarding the existence of phenomena that have causes:
this is intended to reveal the existence of phenomena with causes that constitute the nature of the defilements of both householders and those who have gone forth.
Therefore, the subsequent statement says: "By relying on these two categories, this birth can be obtained," and so forth.
Through these two verses, it is shown that ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) exist as phenomena that have causes.
The subsequent five verses clarify the basis,
causes, and temporal periods for the differentiation of the category of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
Among these, regarding "all phenomena that have causes":
That which has ignorance as its cause up to feeling is called "suffering with a cause.
That which consists of craving up to old age and death is called "the mass of suffering."
These words demonstrate the three types of defilements: those of affliction (*kleśa*), karma, and birth.
Regarding the phrase "because of the two fundamental delusions," this indicates that the defilement of affliction refers exclusively to the most predominant forms of the defilement of affliction.
From the words "itself lacks capacity for action" and so forth,
the meaning of the defilement of karma is further specifically elucidated,
because there are distinctions among its effects.
Because that fruit of maturation is inconceivable,
it possesses no inherent agency of its own; rather,
it is induced by others, depending upon virtuous or non-virtuous friends.
Nor is it produced by another agent,
because it is accomplished through its own functional activity;
no other has the capacity to act as its creator.
It is only by depending on the distinctions of causes from previous lives that there can be what is produced;
this is as stated in the verse beginning with "Neither internal nor external."
This demonstrates that while depending on future non-arising, one relies on present and past formations (*saṃskāra*) which can produce affliction (*saṃkleśa*);
even if formations have already arisen,
by this very characteristic, there is no conceptual differentiation.
Because the future is signless,
there is no such conceptual differentiation;
thus, that which is yet to come is definitively unknowable.
If it were not thus, one might occasionally find that different categories could be distinguished.
If it pertains to the past, then it can indeed be distinguished in this way,
because such a previously existing characteristic can be distinguished.
It is not only that which has been previously experienced that can be discerned;
even that which has never been experienced,
although its characteristics are not clearly grasped, [is discernible].
Nevertheless, they may also be distinguished according to their categories.
This demonstrates that, based on present formations (*saṃskāra*), one discriminates them as causes that give rise to various forms of affliction (*saṃkleśa*);
although these formations are beginningless.
"However, it is only then that it can be obtained" indicates the distinction of the periods of affliction (*saṃkleśa*),
for it has constantly followed [the mind] since beginningless time.
Because it arises anew moment by moment;
from this point onward, the category of purity (*viśuddhi-pakṣa*) is revealed,
for one attains purity when viewing things as they truly are.
Either by way of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*),
meaning contemplating form and so forth as being like a mass of foam and so on;
or by way of common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
This refers to contemplating the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*)— namely, their simultaneous arising, abiding, and ceasing—
either by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) or ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
That is to say, although there is no deluded agent, it is not that the state of being deluded does not arise from a multitude of conditions.
According to conventional truth, it is said that delusion can cause one to be deluded.
Furthermore, this demonstrates that it is not the case that one who is not ignorant engages in improper reflection;
therefore, such a person is deluded by ignorance.
Furthermore, from the perspective of conventional truth,
it is taught that the various consciousnesses follow along with formations such as merit; however,
from the perspective of ultimate truth, there is nothing that follows along.
Furthermore, the three that should be known are the three types of karma: those of the past, future, and present.
This refers to bodily and other types of karma.
"All are non-concordant" means that they are mutually non-concordant with one another.
Why is this? Because the present quickly perishes,
and the past dwells nowhere.
Not yet arisen,
it depends upon various conditions,
and furthermore, the mind evolves accordingly.
If that and this were to correspond with one another,
there would be no conjunction, just as in the case of meritorious actions and the like;
the principle of the correspondence of those minds is likewise.
How could there be a real nature of concomitance?
For what reason?
Because if the mind were associated with those various formations, [it would follow that they are identical].
Or they may be dissociated;
it is not that this is dissociated from that,
but rather that at certain times they are dissociated.
At times they are not dissociated;
furthermore, they are not associated with all minds,
but may be either associated or dissociated.
Thus, from the perspective of ultimate truth,
the nature of the mind’s conformity [to the body] cannot be established;
this shall now be demonstrated.
From the perspective of conventional truth,
it is said that there are causes and conditions by which the mind functions in accordance [with its objects];
in this stream, there is no interruption.
In this verse, it is shown that conventional truth is not devoid of functional activity or causal succession.

Furthermore, because from the perspective of ultimate truth there is no agent or experiencer, it is nevertheless taught through the lens of conventional truth that one performs actions oneself and experiences their results oneself.
Furthermore, whether the agent and the experiencer are identical or distinct,
neither can be asserted.
To clarify this meaning,
the subsequent verses beginning with "the distinction between prior and posterior" are spoken.
Thus, from the perspective of ultimate truth, there is no controller, no agent, and no experiencer.
There is only cause and effect.
Regarding the characteristics of cause and effect,
the resolution of doubts and difficulties is briefly demonstrated by five verses concerning the arising of the inversion of self.
The first verse demonstrates that although there is no self (*ātman*), there is nevertheless a future existence (*punarbhava*) that is not subject to annihilation;
furthermore, causes and effects do not exist simultaneously all at once,
nor does everything arise from everything.
Furthermore, this causal path is without interruption.
The four lines of the verse correspond to these in their respective order.
These four objections are explained by means of the second verse,
which clarifies the characteristics of cause and effect.
By means of the final three verses,
it is shown that the inversion of self arises with respect to the causes and effects that are devoid of self;
herein, the objective referent (*ālambana*) of that inversion is revealed.
Regarding its basis,
its cause, and its fruit:
the first verse reveals its objective referent (*ālambana*).
Realized within oneself,
it is formless, difficult to see, and difficult to investigate;
therefore, it is called "formless."
Because the Sūtra states that the characteristic of form is an object of discursive investigation (*vitarka*),
and because it is difficult to demonstrate to others, it is invisible;
this is established by the second verse.
This reveals the fruit of dependence:
ordinary beings are the basis of dependence,
and the various views are the fruit.
The third verse demonstrates its cause:
the co-emergent view of self.
The speculative views of self held by non-Buddhists arise from the grasping at a general unity and from the latent dispositions (anuśaya) inherent in their own seeds;
they arise from such factors as past habitual tendencies.
Furthermore, these non-Buddhist views arise because of repeated habituation and because of improper reflection.
Furthermore, it grows by way of following and hearing non-Dharma from others. Herein,
it is shown that this occurs due to the faults of the basis, the attention, and the object of focus.
The view of a self arises only through conceptual discrimination.
The subsequent five verses demonstrate how that view of a self gives rise to suffering through the sequence of its accumulation.
Furthermore, this very suffering, together with the view of self, constitutes two causes and conditions for suffering.
Moreover, they act as obstacles to liberation.
Herein, the first verse reveals [the truth] regarding the origin of suffering (*samudaya*).

The second and third [verses] demonstrate that, once the ālayavijñāna— which is subsumed under the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā)— has been cherished as a storehouse, one then proceeds toward conceptual proliferation (prapañca),
such as thinking, "I shall exist" or "I shall not exist," and so forth.
As for "cherished and concealed," it means that [suffering] is grasped as one's own self.
Furthermore, this suffering constantly pursues one at all times.
There is not a single moment in which it ceases even temporarily.
By means of the fourth verse,
it is shown that this suffering is the basis for the conceptualization of a self and the conditions for pleasure and pain.
By the fifth verse,
it is shown that the conception of a self,
through the obstacle of delusion, hinders liberation.
It is called "predominant" because it is compared to the other two types of suffering.
It is called "pervasive" because...
Because it follows after all feelings;
"pervasive in its operation" means it pervades the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
Now, the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) subsumed within the *ālayavijñāna* shall be demonstrated as being similar to that of others,
and its distinctions shall also be revealed,
for it can only be exhausted through the practice of the True Dharma.
Among the various currents of the world, it is the most violent and evil.
As for what are called "the various currents," they are,
for example, the six sense bases such as the eye, the five destinies, and the three realms.
Furthermore, the practitioner of the Dharma demonstrates the thorough understanding of liberation and the thorough understanding of bondage.
Regarding the thorough understanding of bondage:
One then understands suffering;
that is, one understands that my experiences of pain and pleasure all depend upon suffering.
Furthermore, this discrimination can give rise to various views.
That which arises from it can also give rise to it.
Having thus demonstrated the thorough knowledge of bondage through understanding,
there are six further verses.
This demonstrates the thorough knowledge of liberation through understanding; that is,
the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*),
which at all times arises and ceases simultaneously with all afflictions.
Regarding the statement that liberation from all afflictions occurs neither before nor after,
"not before" means:
Because it arises simultaneously with all afflictions;
nor is it the latter, because it ceases at the same time as those delusions.
Furthermore, this reveals the characteristic of the liberation being described.
This means that it is not the case that [the mind] becomes pure only after having already arisen;
rather, there is a distinct, further "mind-born" (manomaya) purity.
Because that very [mind] was originally free from defilement, it is said to be "liberated."
To establish this meaning,
it is further stated in verse that "that which is defiled is ultimately pure by nature," and so forth;
furthermore, this demonstrates two kinds of liberation.
This refers to liberation from afflictions and liberation from objects.

Regarding the phrase "because all seeds are extinguished and all afflictions are exhausted": it means that because the seeds of all phenomena have been extinguished and all afflictions have been brought to an end.
This demonstrates liberation from afflictions;
that is, within this very state of being unstained,
it demonstrates liberation from phenomena.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that if desire for the eye is forever severed..."
"In this way, this eye, too, shall be permanently severed," and so forth,
as explained at length.
Thus, the liberation with remainder has been demonstrated.
Next, the liberation without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa-vimukti) shall be demonstrated;
that which is realized within oneself is shown because it is inconceivable.
The phrase "only the exhaustion of all suffering" is intended to dispel the false conceptualization that clings to the notion of mere non-existence,
namely, the belief that there remains a residual basis for existence.
Because it is eternally quiescent,
it is called "quiescence"; it is not,
however, a state of total non-existence.
That which is free from conceptual proliferation is this nature of liberation,
realized solely within.
Whether [the self] is different or not different from the aggregates,
it will exist after death,
or it will not exist, and so forth.
Because all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are unable to express it;
and in order to demonstrate that neither the person (*pudgala*) nor phenomena (*dharma*) transmigrate through birth and death or attain parinirvāṇa, the verse further states:
"Sentient beings are a continuity of names."
Furthermore, within the characteristics of the perception of dharmas,
there is neither the cycle of birth and death nor is there nirvāṇa.
The verses on the ultimate meaning of the noble teachings have already been explained.
Next, the verses on the intended meaning shall be established,
as spoken by the Blessed One.
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side,
and praised him with a sublime verse, making this request:
"O You who have reached the ultimate in training, who have thoroughly severed the web of all doubts."
Now I request to learn what is to be learned;
O Great Sage, please listen well as I explain the training. There are briefly three kinds of training:
higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom; one should practice and train in these.
One should fulfill the six branches;
having achieved the four abodes of bliss, one practices the fourfold conduct for each. Wisdom is ever pure;
first, one establishes the foundation of the initial abiding, and next, the mind attains tranquil joy.
Later, the Sage perceives wrong views— both those associated and those unassociated—
with prior purity and delight in meditative concentration, as well as skillfulness regarding the truths;
thus, within the various truths, he should give rise to and further increase [right view].
Among all the points of training, there are four courses and three things to be avoided;
regarding two courses, there is the attainment of two [results] and two types of abiding; one is that which leads to nirvāṇa.
Gradually acting as causes and conditions, one practices both purely and mixedly;
first, one abandons misconduct, and finally, one delights in the fulfillment of all trainings—this is the beginning.
In these trainings, the wise are discerning.
Through this wisdom one cultivates purity; from purity arises joy, and the trainings are brought to fulfillment.
This is the middle way. One who is wise in these trainings attains liberation of mind from this state, whereby all conceptual proliferations are forever extinguished.
These trainings are supreme; for one who is wise in these trainings, even if they proceed toward the impure, they will proceed toward a happy destination.
This practice is said to be the beginning; know that this is not shared [with others].
If one practices the path leading to purification, this practice—which is not the ultimate end of the various realms—is called the Middle Way; know that it is also not shared [with ordinary beings].
If one practices the path leading to purification, it reaches the ultimate end of all realms.
This practice is said to be supreme; one should know that it is necessarily shared by both those in training and those beyond training. One should know that [those in training] are all wise;
one should know that [those beyond training] are all fools.
If one abandons what is to be grasped and also cuts off the heavy burdens as well as the objects of direct knowledge, this is the upholding of the three trainings—
whether with or without an object— and whether subtle, coarse, or manifest.
By undertaking and maintaining the abstentions, the beginner has only one [training] induced by verbal awakening;
the second training has two kinds;
the third training possesses all three. The wise transcend them all.
Not violating the śīla, one is able to follow the rules of training;
being beyond reproach, one remains far removed from the five bases [of transgression].
If there is no transgression, there is liberation; there is neither remorse nor the state of being remorseful.
In that regard, one should train in seeking [the Dharma] and diligently practice those deeds without ever abandoning them;
even at the cost of one's life, one should never let them decline,
remaining constantly within right conduct and acting in accordance with the Vinaya.
Cultivation is preceded by vows, and one also cultivates a pure livelihood,
remaining far removed from both extremes. Furthermore, having abandoned improper aspirations,
one never indulges in attachment toward any obstructing phenomena.
As soon as a thought that disturbs the mind arises, one should swiftly distance oneself from it;
neither too sluggish nor too flighty, always dwelling well in right mindfulness,
with the root and its retinue purified, one should practice the holy life.
One should arouse diligent effort, always remaining firm and courageous;
constantly practicing without negligence, one should remain well-established in the five factors.
One should conceal one's own virtues and openly confess all evils.
Obtaining various robes and such, whether coarse or fine, he is joyful in all;
with few worldly affairs, he follows along even with what is rough and worn-out.
He accepts the virtues of the dhūta practices in order to become tranquil and free from afflictions.
One should be fully endowed with dignified deportment and accept things only in appropriate measure;
never acting for ulterior motives, one should not falsely manifest the appearance of dignified deportment,
nor speak of one's own true virtues, nor cause others to do so.
Although one may seek [the Dharma] through various means, one does not manifest strange signs nor beg from others;
ultimately, one obtains it through the Dharma without using forceful intimidation,
and having obtained it, one does not disparage it.
Not being attached to gain and offerings, nor to any form of respect;
not clinging to various views, such as those of superimposition or denial;
not adhering to worldly conventions, nor to meaningless words or incantations.
Nor should one delight in hoarding; for robes and bowls beyond what is necessary may increase various afflictions.
Without being stained by the ways of householders, cultivate wisdom through pure practice, and draw near to the noble and holy ones.
He does not dwell in the homes of friends, for he fears they will give rise to the turmoil of sorrow and grief,
which can produce painful afflictions; as soon as such thoughts arise, he departs immediately,
refusing to accept offerings of faith, for he fears they might cause him harm like an ulcer or a pustule.
Never abandoning the True Dharma of the Tathāgata,
one remains effortless and at ease regarding the transgressions of others,
while constantly examining one’s own faults; having recognized them, one swiftly confesses them.
If one has committed an offense, one should emerge from it according to the Dharma;
regarding the tasks that ought to be performed, one should be able to exert oneself with vigor.
Toward the Buddha and his disciples, one should attend to their majestic power and their verbal instructions.
All believe and accept [it]; contemplating its great significance, they do not slander the most profound Dharma;
able to abandon the tenets of former teachers in that which is beyond conceptual measurement, they do not stubbornly cling to their own views.
Always delighting in dwelling in seclusion and in remote lodgings,
constantly practicing wholesome dharmas, firm in vigor and courageous,
free from desire for rebirth and free from aversion toward that which is loathsome.
Free from drowsiness and sleep, one does not dwell in stillness at the improper time;
free from remorse and regret, one is without anxious anticipation.
At all times and in every way, one accomplishes right effort.
That which incites and awakens, And that which is bound by conjunction with signs;
If it is intimate, Or if it is assailed by many kinds of joy and pleasure—
This extreme intimacy is called false conceptualization.
It gives rise to sensual desire; the wise should keep far from it.
Desires can never bring satisfaction; they are shared by many and are a cause for unrighteousness, increasing craving.
That which the noble ones should abandon, which swiftly leads to destruction,
and which relies upon a multitude of conditions— the basis for danger and heedlessness—
is like a dry bone, and also like a piece of soft flesh.
Like a grass torch, like a great pit of fire,
Like a venomous serpent, and like what is seen in a dream,
Like borrowed ornaments, and like ripe fruit atop a tree.
Knowing all desires to be thus, one should never indulge in them with delight;
one should listen to the True Dharma and constantly contemplate and practice it.
First, one observes the coarse and the tranquil; next, one becomes single-minded in cultivation.
Having abandoned the heavy burden of afflictions, one gives rise to joy in their abandonment;
by observing all signs, one attains the culmination of application and is able to become free from the desires of the desire realm as well as the desires of the form realm.
Entering the clear realization of the ultimate truth, one is able to abandon all desire and realize nirvāṇa in the present life;
furthermore, with the permanent exhaustion of the basis [of existence],
one reaches the culmination of training.
"Having well severed the net of all doubts,
I now request to learn what is to be learned; please explain to me that which is to be practiced"—
in this verse:
The Great Brahma King first praised the World-Honored One and subsequently raised a question.
Regarding his praise of the World-Honored One:
This means that among all trainings, one has already attained the foremost ultimate perfection;
this is spoken in reference to the uncommon virtue of the fulfillment of practice for one's own benefit.
Furthermore, one is able to thoroughly sever all webs of doubt that arise in succession.
This is spoken in reference to the uncommon virtue of the perfection of conduct for the benefit of others.
One who raises the inquiry asks:
"What constitutes training?"
How many kinds of training are there?
How should one train therein?
Such is the intention of the Blessed One.
In order to encourage those sentient beings who are fearful of extensive practice and are indolent,
all [the teachings] are subsumed and briefly explained as the three trainings.
Therefore, he next said: "Great Seer, you should listen well.
There are three types of training:
higher virtue, mind, and wisdom."
One should train therein;
this demonstrates that one relies upon ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom.
If they are distracted,
he employs skillful means to speak to them of the training in higher ethical discipline so as to bring about non-distraction.
For those whose minds are not yet concentrated,
he teaches the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*) as a skillful means to enable them to attain concentration.
For those whose minds have already attained concentration but are not yet liberated...
In order to bring about liberation, he teaches the training in higher wisdom as a skillful means;
by virtue of this cause and condition, practitioners—
All that is to be done is brought to ultimate completion.
This reveals the Blessed One’s intentional teaching that there are no trainings whatsoever that are not subsumed within these three trainings.
Furthermore, in order to demonstrate that among all the trainings, one accomplishes what is to be trained through these very means, it is subsequently stated:
"One should fulfill the six branches and the four abodes of bliss."
Regarding each of the four, there are four modes of practice,
and wisdom is ever pure.
Now, within this verse:
These demonstrate, in their respective order, the means for accomplishing the three trainings.
Regarding the phrase "one should fulfill the six branches," one should train by relying on the means of the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*).
What are the six branches?
First, abiding in pure ethical discipline;
second, guarding the vows of the Prātimokṣa.
Third, the perfection of the three modes of conduct.
Fourth, the perfection of the sphere of activity.
Fifth, perceiving great fear even in minor transgressions.
There are six trainings in the precepts.
These six branches demonstrate the fourfold purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
One who abides in pure ethical discipline...
This is the fundamental basis.
For one who guards the prātimokṣa vows,
it demonstrates renunciation.
Their ethical discipline (*śīla*) is pure for the sake of seeking liberation and renunciation;
their conduct and observances are both perfected.
These two demonstrate the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*) that is beyond reproach;
"seeing great dread in even minor transgressions" demonstrates the purity of ethical discipline that is without breach or flaw.
"Training in the points of training" (śikṣāpada) reveals the purity of ethical discipline (śīla) free from error,
because these six branches are thus perfectly fulfilled.
The training in higher ethics serves as the basis for the other skillful means.
As for the accomplishment of the four abodes of happiness:
This demonstrates the skillful means for the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*).
The four types of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) are called the "four abodes of mind.
They are termed "bliss" because they constitute dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha-vihāra*).
Regarding the phrase "the wisdom that is constantly pure through four sets of four practices," this is explained in reference to the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*); that is,
with respect to the Four Noble Truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
Each of these consists of four aspects,
namely impermanence and so forth;
for the training in higher wisdom is manifested by means of this purified knowledge.
First, one is well-established in the root;
next, one delights in mental tranquility;
finally, there is noble vision and false vision.
Regarding "concordant" and "non-concordant":
this verse demonstrates the sequential arising of the three higher trainings.
As for the "root":
This refers to higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*),
because the latter two [types of training] are the natural outflow of this initial stage.
Having been endowed with ethical discipline (*śīla*), one is free from remorse and so forth.
By practicing in successive stages, one can attain the second [dhyāna], the meditative concentration of mental joy and tranquility.
Because one whose mind has attained concentration perceives reality as it truly is,
one can attain the third [dhyāna], the accomplishment of noble vision and the distancing from unwholesome views.
First, one purifies the dhyānas of joy and becomes skilled in the truths; that is,
within the various truths themselves.
Regarding "one should give rise to that which increases through distance," this verse demonstrates the distinctions in the sequential purification of the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*).
That which is purified first is the initial training.
Delighting in meditative concentration is the second training;
skillfulness regarding the truths is the third training.
Furthermore, within such skillfulness regarding the truths:
That which should be produced refers to the Truth of the Path,
because it is that which should be brought into being.
That which should be distanced refers to the truths of suffering and its origin,
because they are to be abandoned.
That which should be increased refers to the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya),
[attained] through the successive stages of weak, medium, and superior afflictions (kleśa).
They are gradually severed again and again because of the increase of their cessation; thus,
among the various points of training (śikṣāpada).
There are four destinies and three bases;
one remains far removed from two destinies,
while attaining realization within two destinies.
This verse demonstrates the training in higher ethics, mind,
and wisdom, according to the respective success or failure of what is practiced therein.
The distinctions among the four destinies as the resulting retribution are as follows:
all the auspicious destinies comprised within the human and celestial realms of the desire realm are the fruits obtained through the perfection of superior ethical discipline.
That is to say, all the evil destinies included within the other destinies of the desire realm are the fruits obtained from the failure of superior ethical discipline;
whereas all the higher destinies included within the celestial realms of the form and formless realms are [the fruits of its fulfillment].
This is the fruit of higher mind (*adhicitta*);
it is the path to nirvāṇa, which is not subsumed within the three realms.
This is the fruit of higher wisdom (*adhijñāna*).
Within these various destinies,
having distanced oneself from the first two— the good and evil destinies—
one should realize the latter two superior destinies as well as the destiny of nirvāṇa.
These words indicate that which is attained through both the mundane and supramundane paths;
they consist of two types of abiding:
first, that which leads toward nirvāṇa.
Regarding the phrase "gradually acting as causes and conditions" and "practicing both purely and mixedly," within this verse:
This demonstrates that the initial training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*) and the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*) serve,
in successive order, as the causal conditions for abiding in the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).

It demonstrates that the training in higher ethical discipline, which is subsumed under the intermediate meditative concentration of higher wisdom, serves as the causal condition for two types of abiding;
it demonstrates that the supreme single type serves as the causal condition for abiding in nirvāṇa.
It should be understood that herein the cultivation of [the factors] is shown, whether individually or collectively as appropriate;
first of all, one must abandon remorse.
The finality is the fulfillment of bliss;
these trainings are the beginning.
In these trainings, the wise one excels.
This verse demonstrates that through the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*), one gradually cultivates non-regret and so forth as the successive causes for subsequent transformation.
By means of this wisdom, purification is cultivated;
from purification, joy arises; and through the perfection of joy, fulfillment is attained.
All trainings are the middle;
herein, the wise train.

This verse demonstrates that because the wisdom born of cultivation arising from the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*) is the most excellent root of virtue, it serves as the cause for the supreme training.
From this, the mind is liberated;
all conceptual proliferations are forever extinguished.
Among all trainings, this is the most venerable.
Regarding this training, the wise person is one who,
through the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*), is able to bring about the supreme fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
If one proceeds toward impurity...
They also proceed toward the happy realms.
This practice is said to be the first;
one should know that this is not shared [with others].
This verse demonstrates that if the training in higher ethics is impaired, it becomes a cause for the miserable realms;
if it is successfully established, it becomes a cause for the happy realms.
This is because it is unique in that it can also be established even when separated from the latter two trainings.
If one practices for the sake of purification,
yet does not reach the ultimate end of all realms of existence,
such practice is said to be "middling."
It should be understood that this is also not shared [with others].
This verse shows that because one practices the intermediate training to abandon desire for the desire realm and thereby attains purity, it is called "tending toward purity" (*śuddhiprasthāna*);
however, one has not yet been able to completely abandon desire for the higher realms.
Furthermore, because the latent tendencies of desire have not yet been permanently uprooted,
one cannot be said to have attained ultimate purity within the various realms of existence;
this [state] is merely the highest degree of detachment.
It is also called "unshared" because it can accomplish [the goal];
it is not separate from the initial [stage].
If one practices toward purification, [it is so called].
That which reaches the ultimate limit among all realms of existence is called the supreme practice;
one should know that this must necessarily be shared.
This verse demonstrates that because the practices of the supreme training distance one from all desires of the three realms and are able to forever uproot all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*),
they are the ultimate among all destinies.
Because it cannot function independently apart from the former two,
it is necessarily shared;
this applies whether one is a trainee (śaikṣa) or beyond training (aśaikṣa).
"One should know that they are wise" refers to the first half-verse;
it demonstrates the characteristics of one who is wise regarding the three trainings.
Because there is right training and no false training,
those who possess either training or have completed their training should be known as being identical to fools.
The latter half of this verse reveals the characteristics of the foolish among the three trainings;
for they possess false training and lack authentic training.
If one abandons what is to be grasped,
one also eliminates the coarse heaviness and directly perceives that which is to be known.
This refers to those who uphold the three trainings.
This verse demonstrates that they are able to renounce what is grasped by householders, kin, and relatives,
and are able to eliminate the coarse and heavy obscurations to samādhi.
If one can directly perceive the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths through the principles of what is to be known,
then the three trainings will be brought to fulfillment in their respective order,
whether there are conditions or no conditions.
Regarding the phrase "appearing as both subtle and coarse," this first half-verse clarifies the latter two trainings as well as the initial training.
There are, respectively, distinctions of having an object and being without an object, as well as subtle and coarse;
these arise from undertaking the practice of abstinence,
which is induced by verbal expression and awakening.
The latter half of this verse reveals the causes and conditions for the initial, middle, and final stages respectively;
that is to say, because they are induced by the formal vow.
Because it is induced by physical and mental seclusion,
and because it is induced by internal right reflection upon the sounds of others' speech,
there is only one [type] for the beginner.
In the second [dhyāna], one trains in two kinds;
in the third, one trains in all three.
The wise transcend them all.
This verse demonstrates that the first is unique;
the middle is not separate from the first,
and the last is not separate from the [first] two.
Surpassing all those,
one should know that the one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is an Arhat who does not violate the ethical discipline (śīla).
One who is able to comply with the training vows,
whose conduct is beyond reproach by the preceptors,
and who remains far removed from the five points— such a person is one who dwells in the forest.
Hereafter, the characteristics of upholding the precepts are revealed.
For the practitioner who does not violate the *śīla*,
this means abiding in pure ethical discipline.
"One who vows to act in accordance" refers to one who guards the discipline of the prātimokṣa and whose conduct is beyond reproach.
This refers to being free from transgressions regarding the rules of conduct (*ācāra*).
Regarding "being distant from the five points," this refers to being free from transgressions regarding one's sphere of activity (*gocara*).
Briefly, there are five places where bhikṣus and others should not go.
That is to say: royal families,
families that issue proclamations,
and taverns that sell liquor.
Those who frequent impure households, those who are *caṇḍālas* or *kaṭhina*, and those who make proclamations. Regarding "those who make proclamations":
[this refers to] those who announce public edicts.
This refers to those such as sheep-slaughterers;
by means of a general proclamation,
it is said that these sheep-slaughterers and others [are to be excluded].
They have committed extremely grave offenses and have accumulated much evil karma because they slaughtered sheep and other animals.
If there is no transgression and no emergence [from one],
and no misdeed or non-misdeed,
this demonstrates that one perceives great terror even in minor offenses.
If there is renunciation, there is no remorse;
if there is remorse, there is no transgression.
One should seek training therein.
Furthermore, it demonstrates that those who diligently practice that training will never abandon the precepts they have undertaken to study,
even at the cost of their lives.
"Abiding constantly in right practice,
one turns according to the Vinaya"—
these are the four lines of the verse.
These respectively demonstrate the nature of constant ethical discipline,
the nature of firm ethical discipline,
and the nature of constant practice.
The nature of constant accompaniment;
preceded by the cultivation of vows,
it is also the cultivation of a pure livelihood.
This first half-verse displays the purity of conduct and livelihood;
for it is through the preceptors that one first generates the vow.
Only then does one engage in practice;
therefore, it is called a vow.
One remains far removed from both extremes.
"Furthermore, one abandons wrong aspirations.
This latter half-verse demonstrates the avoidance of the two extremes of indulgence in sensual pleasures and self-mortification.
Furthermore, because they have abandoned aspirations such as rebirth in the heavens, their ethical discipline (*śīla*) is pure;
they never indulge in or become attached to any obstructive phenomena.
"The moment a dharma that disturbs the mind arises,
one should immediately and swiftly abandon it.
This verse demonstrates the obstacles to purity, such as failing to guard the doors of the sense faculties.
Within the dharmas being studied, one does not perceive any merit,
because there is no attachment or defilement; thus,
regarding all unwholesome states such as sensual desire, ill will, and discursive thought that disturb the mind, [one remains detached].
Because one eliminates [distractions] immediately after they briefly arise, one attains purity through training;
neither too sunken nor too floating,
one always dwells well in right mindfulness.
"Fundamental and retinue-purified;
thus one practices the holy life"—
this verse demonstrates the avoidance of inferior and base remorse.
Because of being far removed from remorse regarding improper objects,
and because of being far removed from loss of mindfulness,
both at the time of the ultimate goal and at the time of the preparatory means.
Practicing the holy life, all attain purity.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle Sixteen;
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle Seventeen.
Maitreya Bodhisattva spoke;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.
Section Eleven, Part Two: The Stage of that Accomplished through Reflection. One should exert diligent effort.
Always firm and courageous,
constantly practicing heedfulness,
one who is well-established in the five factors.
This verse demonstrates that through the application of donning the armor,
one cultivates the five branches because of non-retrogressive diligence.
Because of heedfulness,
that which is practiced and studied becomes pure and sublime.
As for the five factors of heedfulness:
That is to say, one should conceal all past, future, and present good deeds previously performed as well as those currently being practiced,
and likewise confess all evil deeds.
Obtaining various garments and such,
they rejoice in both the coarse and the fine;
they engage little in worldly affairs.
Coarse and inferior things also follow along;
one undertakes the dhūta qualities for the sake of becoming tranquil and detached from afflictions.
Within these two verses, it is shown that one distances oneself from the causes of craving for kin, excessive desire, and lack of contentment,
as well as distancing oneself from the obstacles of excessive desire and lack of contentment.
Because one trains for the sake of purity,
one attains purity through training; therefore,
one should be fully endowed with dignified deportment.
One should accept things in accordance with the proper measure;
there is never anyone who feigns the appearance of dignified deportment for some ulterior motive.
This verse demonstrates that he is fully endowed with dignified deportment.
Because he does not feign deceptive appearances before others;
because he knows the proper measure in all that he accepts;
and because it serves as the sustenance for his life in order to cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Because there is that which is received, one attains purity through training;
yet one does not speak of one's own true virtues.
Nor does he cause others to speak [of it].
Although there are methods and pursuits,
he does not manifest extraordinary signs.
One should beg from others and never use force or intimidation;
one should obtain [what is needed] through the Dharma.
"Having attained [it], one does not disparage it"—
this is shown in these two verses by way of avoiding frivolous speech and by way of not feigning deceptive appearances.
Because of being coerced by force,
one turns the gains already obtained into further profit;
this causes the training one cultivates to become pure and sublime.
They do not crave gain or offerings,
nor do they cling to any forms of respect,
nor do they adhere to any views.
Regarding "increase and decrease":
this verse demonstrates that because one does not crave gain and honor,
and because one does not cling to the five types of wrong views.
He causes his practice and study to be pure and sublime,
remaining unattached to worldly conventions,
meaningless words, or incantations.
Nor does one delight in hoarding;
that which is an unrighteous surplus of robes and bowls—
this verse demonstrates non-attachment to the causes of various evil views.
The heterodox and erroneous treatises of non-Buddhists obstruct the liberation from the appropriated aggregates;
those composed by them are called "worldly" (loka-anuvartin).
Furthermore, they are produced for the sake of distancing oneself from attachment to gain and honor.
Because the causes such as extra robes and alms bowls are pure,
one attains purity through training;
for fear that various afflictions might increase.
One should not become habituated to the household life;
for the pure cultivation of wisdom,
one should draw near to the noble and holy ones.
This verse demonstrates that by distancing oneself from the causes of what is to be abandoned and by drawing near to the causes of the remedy,
one attains purity through training.
One should not keep friends at home, for fear that they may give rise to the confusion of sorrow and grief;
since they can produce the afflictions of suffering,
one should distance oneself from them as soon as they arise.
This verse demonstrates that if one associates with householders,
sorrow, lamentation, and distraction arise,
and all afflictions increase.
It can serve as the cause of manifold sufferings;
by associating with it,
one is able to give rise to manifold sufferings.
As soon as afflictions arise,
they are immediately dispelled;
in this way, the cause of the antidote is demonstrated.
I do not accept offerings of faith,
fearing that they might inflict further harm upon my sores and blisters regarding the True Dharma of the Tathāgata.
There has never been anyone who abandons this.
This verse demonstrates non-attachment to gain and honor,
and the lack of stubborn adherence to various evil and false views.
They do not consume the offerings of the faithful in vain;
they do not slander the true Dharma;
and they are also able to remain far removed from attachment to the desires of future lives.
Furthermore, it gives rise to the causes of various wrong views;
such training is pure and sublime regarding the transgressions of others.
Abiding in effortless bliss,
one should constantly examine one's own faults;
having recognized them, one should swiftly confess them.
This verse demonstrates the cultivation of mental attention that remains free from seeking out the faults of others;
it shows how one never becomes distracted from one’s own virtuous qualities and constantly gives rise to joy.
One understands one's own faults as they truly are,
confesses and eliminates them, and abandons overweening pride;
by these causes and conditions, one trains until purity is attained.
If one commits an offense,
one should emerge from it in accordance with the Dharma;
regarding the tasks that ought to be performed:

"One who is able to exert oneself with vigor" is a verse that demonstrates renunciation of transgressions and the ability to remain far removed from greed for receiving the honors and service of others.
By means of these causes and conditions, one trains to attain purity regarding the Buddha and his disciples,
their majestic power, and their verbal teachings.
"All accept it with faith;
those who contemplate its great faults do not slander it.
This verse demonstrates that because one's faith is perfected, one perceives the great fault in slandering [the teaching], and thus attains purity through training.
Regarding the most profound Dharma, which is beyond the reach of thought and measurement,
those who are able to relinquish the tenets of their former teachers and do not stubbornly cling to their own views—
This verse demonstrates the excellence of purity through dwelling in seclusion, having distanced oneself from attachment to one's own views;
it also shows the constant delight in living in solitude and using remote lodgings.
"Constantly practicing wholesome dharmas with firm diligence and valor"—
this verse demonstrates that one is detached from both body and mind.
Because he habitually resorts to bedding and seating conducive to meditative concentration,
he remains far removed from all unwholesome discursive thoughts and exclusively cultivates pure and wholesome dharmas.
Because it is not overwhelmed or obscured by secondary afflictions such as lethargy or agitation,
and because it is able to perfectly fulfill correct application,
the skillful means of the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*) are preeminent.
One who has no desire gives rise to desire;
one who does not feel aversion gives rise to aversion;
one who is free from sloth gives rise to sloth.
At that time, one does not dwell in quietude;
one is free from remorse and from the state of being remorseful,
and free from anxiety and from the state of being anxious.
"In all aspects and at all times,
one who has accomplished the correct means"—
this refers to these two verses.
It demonstrates the distancing from sensual desire,
ill will, lethargy and drowsiness,
restlessness and remorse.
Furthermore, because of the hindrance of doubt,
because of the arising of desire for all wholesome dharmas,
and because of extreme loathing and revulsion toward all sensual desires.
It serves as the application of skillful means for cultivating the category of wholesome qualities,
providing both functional capability and mental tranquility.
Because one practices sleep from time to time,
if the mind becomes sunken,
or if one apprehends signs of purity and excellence.
Because when one attends to mental reflection and wanders about,
one does not abide in tranquility.
One gives rise to anxiety and regret regarding what was previously transgressed;
because there is no anxiety or regret regarding what was not transgressed;
and because one conceives a sense of wonder and apprehension regarding subsequent, increasingly superior states.
Through earnestness, continuity, and correct application,
the training in higher mind becomes purified,
giving rise to both meditative attainment and awakening.
And those bound by association,
as well as those with shared characteristics who are intimate,
likewise possess many kinds of joy and pleasure.
That which assails and excessively clings to intimacy is called false conceptualization;
it is capable of generating sensual desire.
Regarding the phrase "the wise should remain far removed from it," these two verses demonstrate eight kinds of false conceptualization.
It is capable of generating sexual desire;
all forms of craving and attachment arise sequentially from the initial application of means.
Up to the ultimate point,
because of this distancing,
all that is cultivated and studied becomes pure and sublime.

Discrimination that incites [the mind] refers to all discrimination belonging to a mind associated with improper mental attention toward attractive objects that is capable of inciting [such attachment].
Discrimination that awakens refers to...
That is to say, regarding those very objects of desire,
it refers to the conceptualization associated with the awakening of the fetters of greed,
which is the conceptualization that binds through conjunction.
That is to say, it refers to all conceptualizations regarding those very desirable objects.
Conceptualization with signs refers to [conceptualization] regarding those very same desirable objects.
The discrimination that grasps at various pure and exquisite characteristics refers to the discrimination of intimacy regarding objects already obtained that are cherished.
As for the discrimination of intimacy,
it means [the attachment] toward beloved things that have already been acquired.
Regarding the discrimination associated with courageous exertion and the discrimination of joy and delight:
these refer to the very objects that have been attained therein.
The conceptualization that consists of various forms of enjoyment, longing, and delight, which operates through various gateways,
refers to the conceptualization that occurs at the time of the union of the two organs. This is what is meant by "assaulting conceptualization."
The most intimate discrimination refers to the discrimination that occurs at the time of impure emission;
it is that which all desire, which is insatiable and shared by many.
These are unwholesome conditions that can increase craving;
they are what the noble ones should abandon.
"Swiftly tending toward destruction;
relying upon various conditions as a basis for instability and negligence"—
these two verses demonstrate the eight kinds of faults associated with sensual desires, both in the present life and in future lives, as they correspondingly apply.
If one can contemplate and see them as such, this is the skillful means for severing sensual craving;
all desires are like dry bones,
and also like pieces of soft flesh.
It is like a grass torch;
it is like a great pit of fire;
it is like a venomous serpent.
It is also like what is seen in a dream,
like borrowed ornaments,
or like ripe fruit at the tip of a tree.
Thus, one who knows that all desires should never be indulged in or enjoyed—
herein, as extensively cited as previously stated, [one reflects on] how they lead to no satiety and so forth regarding those desires.
These eight kinds of faults and calamities are universally established as metaphors throughout the world,
demonstrating that the faults and calamities of sensual desires are profound and grave.
Furthermore, this is to demonstrate that within all sensual desires there exist such numerous faults and afflictions,
clearly evident to be understood;
how could any wise person find delight in them?
Furthermore, those various desires are like dry bones,
for they bring no satisfaction;
they are like a piece of meat.
It is shared by many,
like a grass torch,
because it arises and manifests as an extreme torment.
Unlawful conditions are like a great pit of fire, for they give rise to craving and thirst,
thereby increasing greedy attachment.
Because they are like the venom of a python,
the noble ones keep far away from them;
because they are like things seen in a dream.
It swiftly moves toward disintegration and destruction,
for it is like borrowed ornaments that depend upon and rely upon various conditions.
Just like a ripe fruit at the tip of a tree,
it is a ground for peril, ruin, and heedlessness;
therefore, one should listen to the True Dharma.
One constantly contemplates and practices this:
first, one observes and perceives the coarseness and the tranquility;
subsequently, during cultivation, one exclusively abandons the coarse heaviness of the afflictions.
One feels joy in the abandonment [of defilements],
observes all signs,
and attains the culmination of the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
One is able to abandon desire for the realm of desire and abandon desire for the realm of form,
thereby entering the clear realization of the true truths.
One who is able to leave behind all desires,
realize nirvana in the present life,
and bring about the eternal exhaustion of the remaining substratum.

In this context, it is shown that through the seven types of mental attention, beginning with "attention to discernment" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-manaskāra*), both the mundane and supramundane paths are purified, thereby realizing the two fruits of nirvāṇa:
that with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and that without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).
The training in higher wisdom is ultimately purified.
One who constantly reflects upon the sublime Dharma they have heard demonstrates the mental engagement that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*).
The phrase "constantly practicing" indicates the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*),
because one practices by means of generating resolute conviction.
The phrase "first observing the coarse and the calm" indicates the mental attention of withdrawal (*prāvivekya-manasikāra*).
The expression "exclusively in the cultivation" [indicates] the mental attention of joy in solitude (*ratisaṃgrāhaka-manasikāra*).
The phrase "observing all signs" indicates the mental attention of relishing (*āsvādana-manasikāra*),
while the phrase "observing" indicates the mental attention of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*).
The phrase "culmination of the preparatory stage" (*prayoga-niṣṭha*) indicates the mental attention that culminates the preparatory stage (*prayoga-niṣṭha-manasikāra*).

The phrases "able to abandon the desires of the desire realm," "able to abandon the desires of the form realm," "entering the clear realization of the true truths" (*satyābhisamaya*), and "able to abandon all desires" and so forth [indicate this].

Having already explained the verses of the sacred teaching regarding the intended meaning (*abhiprāya*)— which manifest the mental engagement with the fruit of the culmination of mundane and supramundane application—
I shall now establish the verses concerning the essential meaning (*tattvārtha*).
As it is said in verse:
"Commit no evil with body, speech, or mind in any way throughout the world;
Through mindfulness and clear comprehension, remain free from all desires, And do not associate with that which leads to meaningless suffering."
What is referred to here as "evil" in this verse refers to all types of unwholesome conduct.
Under all circumstances and in all places,
one must not commit any unwholesome actions whatsoever.
What is meant by not committing evil in every respect?
It means not creating any evil through body, speech, or mind.
What is meant by not committing evil under any causal conditions?
This means that because one never commits any evil arising from greed, hatred, or delusion,
how is it that one does not commit evil in any situation?
This means that one does not commit various evils with respect to the bases of sentient beings or the bases of non-sentient things.
How, by means of mindfulness and clear comprehension, does one distance oneself from all desires?
It means that one abandons the desire for objects and abandons the desire for afflictions.
What is the abandonment of desire for things?
It is when someone attains pure faith in the True Dharma and Vinaya realized by the Tathāgata.
Understanding that living at home is as confining as a prison, one seeks liberation from it;
as explained at length, up to:
through right faith, one abandons the household life.
One enters the homeless life,
yet has not yet permanently abandoned sensual desire;
this is called the abandonment of the objects of desire.
How does one abandon the desire for defilements?
It means that once he has gone forth,
it is for the sake of abandoning sensual craving without remainder.
He went toward the wilderness and mountain forests,
dwelling in lodgings at the borders of the rainy-season retreat,
or residing in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka).
Or even when in a secluded and quiet chamber,
for the purpose of counteracting all afflictions arising from various sensory desires— specifically the grasping at false conceptualizations and craving— he [practices].
He cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness;
or alternatively, he returns to dwell near a village or town,
well-guarding his body.
He well guards the sense faculties and,
dwelling securely in right mindfulness,
enters villages or wanders through towns and hamlets.
Turning back;
departing and arriving;
advancing and halting.
He dwells constantly in clear comprehension.
In order to dispel drowsiness and all forms of fatigue,
he relies upon the well-established right mindfulness within these four foundations of mindfulness.
In order to permanently sever the underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) of sensual desire,
one cultivates its antidote and dwells with that very same clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*).
For the sake of providing a basis,
one distances oneself from the hindrances;
body and mind become harmonious and supple, becoming capable and fit for practice.
He ardently cultivates the tranquility of abandonment through skillful means;
by relying upon such mindfulness and clear comprehension,
he is able to realize the abandonment of the desires of the afflictions.
Having distanced himself from all desires,
he dwells having fully attained the first dhyāna;
in this way, he is able to [avoid] the extreme of indulging in sensual pleasures.
Regarding the base, contemptible, and defiled natures of all ordinary beings' dharmas—
whether they are abandoned or known—
what is it that is called "drawing forth meaningless suffering"?
That is to say, there are certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who practice self-mortification,
afflicting and tormenting themselves with various forms of suffering in this present life.
Being thoroughly scorched and tormented,
he thinks to himself:
"I am now oppressed by the suffering of the present life."
They seek liberation from suffering,
yet though they pursue this goal, they only torment themselves;
in the end, they will not attain it.
However, it further invites great harm and affliction;
this is what is called inducing meaningless suffering.
The noble disciples are able [to recognize] such extremes of self-mortifying asceticism.
Having thoroughly understood that which leads to non-noble, meaningless, and painful states,
one keeps far away from it, avoids it, neither associates with nor draws near to it,
and does not serve it.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what has been stated above.
How is it explained in brief?
It is said that sentient beings possess two kinds of fulfillment.
First, the fulfillment of higher rebirth;
second, the fulfillment of the definitive excellence.
Regarding the fulfillment of higher rebirth:
This refers to proceeding toward the happy realms.
As for the definitive fulfillment of excellence,
it refers to the exhaustion of craving, dispassion, cessation, and nirvāṇa.
To be able to sever and realize these two fulfillments as well as their obstacles—
this is the summarized meaning.
This applies to all aspects.
Under all causes and conditions,
and in all places,
one shall not commit unwholesome deeds.
He is then able to sever all obstacles to the fulfillment of higher rebirth and is also able to realize the fulfillment of higher rebirth,
even while engaged in the extreme of indulging in sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, by resolutely distancing oneself from the extremes of indulgence and self-mortification,
one is able to sever all obstacles to the definitive,
supreme fulfillment and can likewise realize that definitive, supreme fulfillment.
One should know that this is the summarized meaning herein.
It should be explained that sentient beings are conceptualized; it should be explained that they abide based on what should be explained;
and it should be explained that through non-comprehension, they gather together birth and death.
If one understands what should be said, there is no anxiety regarding the speaker;
because such [anxiety] does not exist, others should not criticize the discourse.
If one reckons [others as] equal, superior, or inferior, one will consequently give rise to contentious debate.
Immovable in the three states, equal toward the superior and inferior without interruption;
free from craving for name-and-form and pride, unattached, smokeless, tranquil, and without affliction or expectation;
he is not seen by gods, humans, or those of the world.
Within these four verses,
the first statement,
"should be explained," refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Why is this so? Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are subsumed under three types of verbal objects (*vāgvastu*).
In this context, the five excellent sensual pleasures (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) are taught as the appropriate subject matter.
Furthermore, because other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas seek out and solicit the five excellent sensual pleasures from donors through speech,
they are called "those who should be addressed."
Furthermore, when various rulers summon their servants and attendants by word of mouth to enjoy the five excellent sensual pleasures,
for this reason they are also called "those who should be addressed."
Furthermore, those who indulge in sensual pleasures are unable to naturally recognize the faults and dangers of the five exquisite sensual desires,
with the sole exception of the Buddhas and their disciples.
Having proclaimed those faults for their sake, they are then able to understand them;
for this reason, those who indulge in sensual pleasures are also said to be "those for whom it should be taught."
Regarding various sensual desires, one engages in improper mental attention and grasps their signs; furthermore,
grasping their secondary characteristics, one immediately gives rise to attachment and craving toward those desires,
indulging in them with relish.
They even become firmly attached to them.
Furthermore, they do not know the various faults and afflictions of sensual desires as they truly are;
that is to say, they do not realize that all sensual desires are impermanent and deceptive.
Emptiness is devoid of reality and is of a nature subject to decay;
it is like a magical illusion that deceives the foolish,
possessing very little flavor and many faults.
Nor does one truly understand, as it really is, that such sensual pleasures have little flavor and many dangers,
nor the renunciation of those sensual desires,
namely, the subduing of craving for them.
Up to the point of transcending it—
this is his deliverance.
Having thus perceived the danger in this way, he...
Not knowing how to transcend them, they indulge in various desires;
by reason of this,
they give rise to all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) that take the desire realm as their root.
Having deeply conceived a sense of attachment,
and having further performed those karmas that have birth as their fundamental cause,
one undergoes birth in the desire realm.
Having been born, they die and perish;
having been born, they pass away.
For this reason, it is said that one should speak of "sentient beings possessed of perception."
One should explain that [the practitioner] abides accordingly;
yet, because they do not understand what should be explained, they gather in saṃsāra.
If they encounter a virtuous friend and hear the true Dharma...
Through proper mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*),
one understands, as they truly are, the faults and the escape regarding all sensual desires;
that is to say, all sensual desires are impermanent and deceptive.
To speak at length, up until:
having transcended sensual desire,
they [apply themselves] to the True Dharma and Vinaya realized by the Tathāgata.
Having attained pure faith,
they perceive the faults and perils of all sensual desires even more deeply and with increasing intensity;
they are thus able to relinquish wealth and treasures, whether small or great.
Having renounced his treasury,
retinue, and associates,

Relatives and elders—

With this as a condition, the various types of grasping (*upādāna*) are able to arise.
All those factors, such as greed and hatred, take this as their common condition (*sādhāraṇa-pratyaya*). As for "its own":
That is to say, with greed and hatred as the precursor and discursive thought as the subsequent,
there are the distinct natures of the seed-elements.
How is it that greed, hatred, and even discursive thought separately bind one to various desires?
It is just as the *māluka* creeper entwines the trees of a forest.
Briefly stated, there are six distinct types of sensual desire (*kāma*).
There is the sensual desire for present objects brought about by the power of one's own body and hands.
This refers to the various desires belonging to those living at home, which arise with these objects as their sphere and with these as their conditions, giving rise to greed and anger;
or it refers to the various present objects of desire obtained from others.
This refers to all desires belonging to one who has gone forth for the sake of a livelihood;
it is the joy that arises with respect to these objects, taking them as a condition,
or it consists of desires for matters of the past or the future.

That is to say, when one who has suddenly exerted themselves and gone forth [into homelessness] encounters various desires within this sphere of experience, using these as a condition, sorrow and distress arise;
or else, other various afflictions and desires arise.
Briefly, there are two kinds:
namely, regarding the physical body and its life-sustaining requisites within the desire realm,
there may still be unsevered false conceptualization and craving.
That is to say, for one who has gone forth out of right faith,
when dwelling in tranquility and seclusion, they encounter various circumstances during the dusty night;
with these as their objective sphere and taking them as conditions, fear and terror arise, and the hair on their body stands on end.
There may be those who have not yet abandoned false conceptualization and craving;
that is to say, such a person, during the daytime,
[encounters] external objects of form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible phenomena.
Taking this as a condition, there arise discursive thoughts belonging to the level of mental consciousness.
Furthermore, there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who,
as previously described, understand with perfect clarity greed, hatred, and so forth, along with their causes and conditions.
Furthermore, having understood the impermanent nature of phenomena arising from various conditions,
one does not give rise to craving or attachment toward whatever arises;
instead, one immediately relinquishes, vomits out, and brings it to cessation.
Because one is free from craving for the two realms of form and formlessness,
one crosses over the flood of existence;
because one is free from sensual craving, one crosses over.
He has crossed over the flood of sensual desire.
Such a flood as this, which he had not crossed before,
having now crossed it, he shall never again fall back.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what has been stated above.
That is to say, in this verse, the Bhagavat briefly reveals three stages:
first, the stage of the householder.
Second, the stage of going forth;
third, the stage of seclusion.
Furthermore, this briefly demonstrates both the common and the uncommon [aspects].
Arising from causes and conditions,
whether it be craving or aversion,
these two types of distinct fetters exist among all sensual desires.
Furthermore, one should know that the brief meaning herein consists of the methods for abandonment and the benefits of abandonment.
Moreover, within this context, there are all discursive thoughts (vitarka) characterized by attachment, exultation, or dependence on sensual indulgence.
One should know that within the category of craving, there are anger,
dejection, and terror.
One should know that regarding the category of aversion,
one ought to act as a brahmin: namely, by severing [aversion], being without negligence,
seeking to abandon all desires, and having no longing for this existence.
If there is still something further to be done, one is not a true brāhmaṇa.
Know that a brāhmaṇa is one for whom what was to be done has been accomplished;
though his body may still labor, he has not yet reached the ultimate depth nor crossed over.
Having already attained crossing over and dwelling on dry land, O Deva, you who have reached the further shore without effort,
you should now know this: one who has forever exhausted all outflows and attained constant, diligent meditative concentration is called a true brahmin.
Having forever severed all sorrow, anxiety, and burning fever,
he dwells constantly in right mindfulness and his mind is always liberated.
Regarding this verse:
This demonstrates that those devas rely on the conventional [perspective] of various brahmins when speaking to the World-Honored One;
that is to say, there are brahmins of noble lineage who claim for themselves, "I am a true brahmin."
Considering the Brahma-world to be the ultimate goal,
they aspire for the Brahma-world and dwell in the realm of form with constant diligence,
their minds free from weariness or indolence.
He constantly delights in seclusion and dwelling in tranquility;
he diminishes sleep and cultivates meditative concentration in order to sever the desire for worldly affairs and the desire for afflictions.
Because those Brahmins of that lineage regard the Brahma-world as the ultimate goal,
they aspire to the Brahma-world and do not seek existence within the realm of desire;
furthermore, this reveals how the Tathāgata, relying on the ultimate truth, responds to those Brahmins regarding that celestial realm.
If a brahmin, having performed what was to be done,
must perform it again and again because there remains further superior work to be accomplished,
one should know that he is not a true brahmin.
If a brahmin realizes that which a brahmin ought to accomplish,
he transcends and ascends beyond the entire shore of *satkāya*,
and dwells securely upon dry land.
One should know that this is the true brāhmaṇa.
By this it is shown that both those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are brāhmaṇas.
There are two kinds of those in training.
This refers to those in the desire realm who have not yet abandoned desire, or those who have already abandoned it.
Regarding those who have not yet abandoned desire:
they have not reached the source or bottom, nor have they arrived at the further shore.
Regarding two kinds of dharmas, they are as yet not fully perfected:
first, the superior śamatha of the internal mind has not been attained;
second, although the vipaśyanā of the dharma of superior wisdom has been attained, it is not yet thoroughly purified.
Because they lack internal śamatha,
they rely on the life-preserving float of the noble path as it has been attained;
this is for the purpose of realizing internal śamatha.
One exerts oneself with vigor like a foot for the sake of superior wisdom;
furthermore, one exerts oneself with vigor like a hand for the sake of thoroughly purifying the dharma of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
As he thus exerts himself with diligence,
he leaves behind the desires of the desire realm as if reaching its very source and bottom;
he realizes arhatship as if arriving at the further shore.
One who has already abandoned desire realizes the superior śamatha of the internal mind and also attains the thoroughly pure vipaśyanā.
He exerts diligent effort solely for the purpose of further severing the fetters of the higher realms,
not for the sake of the various parts of the body;
once he has transcended them, he becomes an Arhat.
Having accomplished what was to be done and being free from the exertion of effort,
they are said to dwell on dry land and have reached the further shore.
This demonstrates that, according to the ultimate truth, there are briefly three kinds of brāhmaṇas.
Two are those in training (śaikṣa),
and one is those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
These are the brāhmaṇas who have already reached the ultimate further shore.
One who has eternally exhausted all outflows is called "one whose taints are forever ended.
If one who has not yet abandoned desire applies diligent effort with every part of their being,
they are called "one who attains constant and deliberate application."
If one has already become free from desire and has reached the source and bottom [of the mind],
this is called attaining meditative concentration (dhyāna).
One who has attained meditative concentration...
Because they have forever severed all lower fetters,
they have already abandoned all the burning of grief and sorrow belonging to the categories of sensual desire and ill will;
they have eternally exhausted the outflows.
Because they have permanently severed all afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation,
they have already well cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness and constantly abide in right mindfulness and the liberation of the mind.
He does not repeatedly perform what has already been done,
nor is there any further superior task for him to accomplish;
therefore, he is called a true brāhmaṇa in the ultimate sense.
"O Bhikṣu, has the Bhikṣu already crossed over the flood?
He replied,
"It is so, O Deva."
"Without grasping and without dwelling,
have you already crossed over the torrent?
He replied:
"O Deva, bhikṣu, how are you now?"
Without grasping and without dwelling,
having already crossed the torrential flood;
as I have exerted myself in such a manner, so too has it become diminished.
To the extent that my inferiority has ceased, to that same extent I abide in suchness;
having abided in suchness, to that same extent I am carried away by the gods.
To the extent that I relinquish my exertion, to that same extent there is no further decline or inferiority.
Thus the "Chapter on the Pure and White" is explained in detail. Herein, one should know the *Gāthā* of Jyotiṣka:
"Without grasping, without dwelling. Regarding this verse, "without grasping" means:
This refers to nirvāṇa and the meditative attainment of cessation,
as previously explained.

It concerns the Blessed One’s reliance on those most extreme ascetic practices and difficult austerities— performed while he was manifesting the cultivation of bodhisattva conduct— which were not subsumed under skillful means, but rather characterized by fierce and heroic diligence.

Furthermore, because he demonstrates sitting upon the seat of enlightenment through the abandonment and thorough knowledge [of afflictions] by means of vigor and diligence that are not subsumed under skillful means,
he spoke these words:
"O Deva, you should know that in whatever measure I formerly exerted myself in vain,
in that same measure I became diminished;
and in whatever measure I became diminished, in that same measure I came to a standstill."
In this way and that, one is again swept away and drowned;
the opposite of this should be understood as the white category (*śuklapakṣa*).
In this context, it is shown that when practicing asceticism, a form of courageous diligence not subsumed under skillful means is called "exhaustion.
Through such wrong means, one falls away from wholesome qualities.
This is called "diminution and inferiority.
Once one has recognized the loss of various wholesome dharmas and ceased improper means,
it is called "abiding."
Abandoning all ascetic practices, he sought out other teachers;
he subsequently visited the heterodox strongholds of Udraka Rāmaputra and others.
Because he observes in accordance [with reality], he is said to be "drifting and drowning.
Furthermore, at a later time, while seated upon the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*),
he abandons all forms of unskillful exertion and applies himself with courageous diligence.
All wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*) subsequently increase.
As each wholesome quality increases,
one does not give rise to contentment regarding those wholesome qualities.
Having no leisure to remain stationary,
one successively seeks that which is superior, more excellent, and subtle within the practices of abandonment;
thus, by means of such lack of contentment, [one proceeds].
