Thereupon, he no longer sought out other non-Buddhist teachers;
without a teacher, he spontaneously cultivated the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
He is named the Great Awakened One (*mahābuddha*).

Within this context, one should understand that the four meanings—such as "abandoning toil" and so forth—are to be explained by correlating them respectively with the four phrases of the sutra. Furthermore, how is the distinction revealed by relying on *nirvāṇa* as being without support and without abiding?
This means that one is unable to cross over the floods of the entanglements and latent tendencies of the various afflictions;
briefly, this is due to four causes. What are these four?
This means that first there is a thought based on attachment to worldly enjoyment;
because one relies upon such thoughts of attachment to enjoyment,
there arises indolence.
Furthermore, by relying on indolence, one remains in the state of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana);
and by relying on remaining in the state of an ordinary person, [one continues in that condition].
Driven by the power of craving that follows the stream of birth and death,
one is carried away and submerged with the current in the river of saṃsāra within the five destinies;
this is due to four causes that are contrary to this.
One should understand that it is capable of crossing the violent torrents as appropriate.
Furthermore, how does one manifest the distinction by relying on the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling?

That is to say, there is someone who has previously attained the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*), yet subsequently dwells in negligence;
they dwell frequently in perception and feeling,
rather than dwelling frequently in the cessation of all perceptions and feelings.
Due to these causes and conditions,
one falls away from the meditative absorption of cessation;
because of this falling away, [the attainment is lost].
It returns once more to abide in the causes for birth in the lower stages;
because it abides in those causes, the mind then definitely tends toward the fruit obtained therein.
This is the opposite of the former case.
One should understand the fourfold distinctions of the white category (*śuklapakṣa*):
To dwell alone in a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*), to practice meditation while renouncing precious wealth,
and to seek elsewhere for a different method, or to covet a fief and territory.
Why not associate with others? By having no companions at all, one attains a mind of meaning that is tranquil;
having crushed the army of the Māra of exquisite form, I dwell alone in reflection, experiencing the most supreme peace and happiness.
Therefore, he does not associate with others and remains entirely without companions;
this is because of the verses asked by the goddess,
which speak of attaining the meaning.
Briefly, there are two kinds:
first, the meaning of realizing the fruits of śrāmaṇya;
second, the meaning of realizing the noble supernormal powers.
By attaining the first meaning,
one transcends all the great suffering of birth and death;
by attaining the second meaning, one realizes the eight liberations and dwells in the bliss of the present life through tranquil contemplation.

Furthermore, the first attainment of the goal consists in subduing the demonic hosts of lovely and exquisite forms; the second attainment of the goal consists in dwelling alone in reflection and experiencing supreme peace and bliss.
Herein, the meaning intended is that of the noble supernormal powers (*ārya-abhijñā*); why is this so?

That is to say, there is someone who, desiring to accomplish the meaning of noble supernormal powers and to bring about liberation that is pure and perfect, practices by means of the ten universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
By reason of this cause and condition:
It causes the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) to become pure and perfected;
it also causes liberation to further attain purity, perfection, and brilliant whiteness;
and it is able to accomplish the purpose of the noble supernormal powers (*āryābhijñā*).
Once he has understood that this has been accomplished,
he realizes for himself that his own purpose is fulfilled and that the goal of the fruit of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) is also achieved.
Such a person is a true śramaṇa;
he deeply cultivates revulsion and disdain for those who seek wealth,
and avoids places such as cities, towns, and social gatherings.
He understands its origin;
he understands its danger;
he understands the escape from it.
One is also able to understand the practice leading to renunciation;
the arising of its causes and conditions is called the first [stage].
It is the nature of impermanence, suffering, and transformation.
This is called a fault;
the subduing, abandoning, and transcending of sensual desire is called renunciation.
The Noble Eightfold Path is called the practice leading to deliverance.
If one does not perceive its beginning therein,
up to and including not perceiving the practice leading to deliverance, [one does not see it].
Due to these causes and conditions,
one is unable to feel revulsion toward or disparage sentient beings who possess abundant wealth and resources.
While constantly engaging in social interactions and wandering through towns and cities,
one might claim that the mind has attained tranquility;
yet, it is only for those who have renounced the household life and realized the eight liberations through meditative concentration that the inner mind is truly tranquil.
On the contrary, they give rise to slander. Consequently,
regarding the tranquility of their inner minds,
they are unable to see well, know well, discern well, or penetrate well.
If, in the ultimate sense, the internal mind is tranquil and contrary to this [state of agitation],
then one will be able to see well, up to and including attaining thorough penetration.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what was stated above.
This means that the Bhagavān has briefly indicated here that for those who indulge in sensory desires and delight in socializing,
there is no ultimate inner tranquility, even if they have attained the eight liberations of meditative concentration.
Being free from all relish for sensory flavors is called the inner tranquility of the ultimate truth;
one should know that this is the summarized meaning herein.
"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; they are of the nature to arise and cease.
Because they arise and cease, their stillness is bliss.
In this verse, both the aggregates (*skandha*) and the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) are termed "conditioned phenomena."
The meaning here intends the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*).
These five aggregates of clinging are, in brief, of three kinds:
namely, those of the past, the future, and the present.
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent" means that those conditioned phenomena originally do not exist but arise, and having arisen, they immediately perish;
this refers to their past arising.
All the aggregates (skandhas) contained within all the personal existences (ātmabhāva) obtained in the past are past,
for they have already ceased and passed away.
Because it perishes after having arisen,
its nature is impermanent.
If it were to arise in the future...
Because all the aggregates (skandhas) within all future bodies that will be obtained have not yet arisen,
have not already originated, and have not yet ceased or passed away.
Because it can arise, it is a phenomenon subject to arising.
If it arises in the present, [it is so].
Within all the various physical bases currently acquired, that which constitutes their temporary abiding, support, and survival—
all the aggregates (*skandha*) of sentient beings— are subject to death, for they are liable to be extinguished by the process of passing away.
These are phenomena subject to cessation.
If those aggregates,
while yet in the future, were to obtain their own substantiality, they would be phenomena subject to arising.
Within this, there is absolutely no obtainable self-essence that is permanent or eternal;
one should thus abide correctly in this very way.
Except for those that perish immediately upon arising,
if sentient beings were to permanently exhaust the causes for future aggregates within the present life,
then all future personal aggregates would never arise.
This is called "quiescence.
Furthermore, this quiescence is described as "bliss" for two reasons:
first, because all causes of suffering have been extinguished.
Because all coarse and heavy states have been permanently stilled,
one dwells in happiness within this present life;
therefore, it is called "bliss."
Second, because one is forever liberated from all the various sufferings of future birth, old age, sickness, and so forth,
it is called "happiness.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what was stated above.
That is to say, the Blessed One here briefly explains the basis of right view and the fruit of right view.
Furthermore, there is another distinction:
namely, he briefly demonstrates the basis of thorough knowledge and its subsequent abandonment.
Furthermore, it briefly demonstrates the phenomena to be fully known (*parijñeya*) and full knowledge (*parijñā*).
It also briefly demonstrates all the afflictions (*saṃkleśa*) of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the three times, as well as their purification (*vyavadāna*) through their pacification.
Furthermore, it briefly demonstrates all phenomena of dependent origination and the cessation of dependent origination;
it briefly demonstrates the truth of suffering and the truth of cessation;
and it briefly demonstrates the basis for the two doors of liberation: emptiness and wishlessness.
Furthermore, it reveals the basis for the single liberation door of signlessness (*animitta*),
and briefly demonstrates the basis for abandoning the two factors that are contrary to the realization of the noble truths (*āryasatyābhisamaya*).
Regarding the two dharmas:
first, conforming to conceptual proliferation;
second, fearing the absence of conceptual proliferation.
Furthermore, this briefly demonstrates two unique remedial methods that distinguish [this teaching] from non-Buddhists. What are these two?
First, the non-erroneous nature of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
Second is the nature of non-perversion in that which is realized:
"The track of the heedless is death; the track of the heedful is immortality.
For those who are negligent, there is constant death."
In this verse, how is it that heedfulness is the path to the deathless?
It refers to a certain person who, relying on four bases, establishes four kinds of protection.
That is to say: protection of life,
protection of body,
and protection against the defilements of the mind.
Guarding through right effort is called heedfulness.
This heedfulness serves as the basis and the support.
For those whose provisions for nirvāṇa are not yet fulfilled,
may they quickly reach fulfillment;
for those who have already fulfilled them, [may they abide therein].
It causes one to attain parinirvāṇa in this very life.
How is it that negligence is the path to death?
It is as follows: there is a certain householder, a white-robed layperson, who, being attached to and indulging in various sensual objects, commits unwholesome deeds.
Or there may be those who have gone forth and manifest the four kinds of non-restraint—
namely, non-restraint regarding life, and so on, up to non-restraint regarding right effort.
Such negligence pertains to both categories.
That is to say, the class of householders and the class of those who have gone forth;
with this very negligence as their basis and support,
they delight in the primary formations that give rise to birth and perform the primary karmas that bring about birth.
For this reason, there is birth;
having been born, one reaches the end of life;
having been born, one dies prematurely.
How is it that those who are not heedless do not die,
while those who are heedless are as if always dead?
It is said that there are five kinds of death.
First, death with a well-disciplined mind;
second, death with an undisciplined mind;
third, past death.
Fourth is death in the present;
fifth is death in the future.
If a person (pudgala) practices these well and without negligence...
In the present life, at the time of dying properly through a well-disciplined death,
one has already died through a past [death];
likewise, in the past, one also died through an undisciplined death.
In the present life, one does not die through death that is not preceded by lack of discipline;
in future lives, one does not die through death that is not preceded by discipline,
nor does one die through death that is not preceded by lack of discipline.
Therefore, it is called "immortal.
If there is a person who is heedless,
at the time of their actual death in the present life, due to being undisciplined and unrefined;
In the past, they died because of lack of self-discipline;
in the present, they die because of lack of self-discipline;
and in the future, they will die because of lack of self-discipline.
Therefore, they are called "constantly dead.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what was stated above:
that is to say, herein the Bhagavān has concisely indicated the Truth of the Path and the Truth of Cessation for those who are not heedless.
Those who are heedless [experience] the truth of origination and the truth of suffering.
Furthermore, this briefly demonstrates the nature of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna*) and the nature of the performance of one's own karma (*svakarmakṛtatva*).
The former half demonstrates the nature of the possible and the impossible.
The latter half demonstrates the nature of one's own karma as the agent;
furthermore, the former half demonstrates what the teacher must do for the disciples,
while the latter half demonstrates the purpose of what the disciples themselves must accomplish.
Sentient beings are pierced and shaken by discursive thoughts;
as they contemplate intense sensual desire, their attachment increases manifold and they wander in saṃsāra, thereby binding themselves with firm fetters.
In this verse, what is meant by being "pierced and shaken by discursive thoughts"?
That is to say, there is someone who, with improper mental attention toward various objects of sensual desire previously obtained and previously enjoyed,
gives rise to unwholesome and evil discursive thoughts based on craving and attachment.
What is intense craving?
It refers to a certain person who, in previous lives,
cultivated craving and cultivated it extensively.
Due to these causes and conditions,
although one correctly attends to the various objects of desire previously obtained and previously enjoyed during this life,
one's mind is nonetheless distracted and destroyed by craving.
What is the contemplation of impurity?
It is as follows: there is someone who does not properly guard the body and does not restrain the sense faculties.
Lacking established mindfulness,
he wandered through the villages;
having seen women of very young age with lovely and beautiful forms, he [was affected].
One then improperly grasps at signs of purity and excellence;
by reason of this,
body and mind are consumed with affliction.
How does defiled attachment increase?
It should be understood that defiled attachment grows by means of five aspects.
What are the five?
They are as follows: there is someone who, even toward inferior objects of sensual desire, gives rise to intense fetters of craving.
They are attached to them and do not relinquish them,
let alone superior and exquisite things;
furthermore, they accumulate precious wealth through largely unlawful and violent means.
They do not employ the true Dharma,
yet they constantly acquire superior requisites;
furthermore, they are unwilling to relinquish even those things that are of little value or no practical use.
How much more so for those things that are precious?
Even for the sake of pursuing meager and inferior wealth,
they still commit numerous misdeeds of body, speech, and mind.
How much more so regarding many superior practices?
Furthermore, even toward the few minor sublime practices they uphold,
their minds lack any inclination or delight.
How much less so the vast [teachings]?
Furthermore, they do not even take pleasure in hearing about nirvāṇa,
let alone desiring to attain it.
What is the firm bond?
It is known as a firm bond by way of three characteristics:
first, because it is solid.
Second, because it is touched by suffering;
third, because it persists for a long duration;
and within the present life, because of the roots of misconduct—namely, greed, hatred, and delusion.
He knows that the bonds are firm and secure;
he knows that in future lives, by being born in the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts,
he will be touched by suffering and pursued by it for a long time.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what has been stated above.
That is to say, it is briefly shown that there are two kinds of ruin based on two causes of ruin.
What are these two causes of ruin?
This refers to the power of improper reflection and the power of causes.
What are the two kinds of ruin?
They are the ruin of seeking and the ruin of enjoyment.
What is the power of improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*)?
It refers to improper mental attention arising from the causal conditions of recollecting previously experienced objects,
or improper mental attention arising from the causal conditions of erroneously conceptualizing present objects.
Either through erroneously grasping signs and improper mental attention,
or through improper mental attention while dwelling or acting upon those very objects—
what is the power of the cause?
This refers to how one seeks out and encounters the ruin of desire and greed previously cultivated toward attractive objects.
That is to say, there is a certain person who, due to having accomplished two kinds of causes for ruin, [encounters such loss].
By means of what is not the true Dharma or through violence, one seeks and accumulates all manner of illicit wealth.
What is the loss of its enjoyment?
It refers, for example, to someone who, regarding the objects previously obtained that are conducive to pleasure, conducive to pain, or conducive to neither-pain-nor-pleasure:
Or there may be those who, throughout a single lifetime, become stained by and attached to [sensual pleasures], and so on at length,
until they enjoy them without knowing how to transcend them.
Some may give rise to hatred toward one person and be obscured by that hatred;
some may give rise to delusion toward one person and be obscured by that delusion.
Thus, they are obscured by such defilements of craving.
Even unto being obscured by ignorance,
they engage in various unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind,
and are entangled by the three firm fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion.
They are likewise bound by the various fetters of the hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts;
furthermore, there is a distinction,
namely that they are bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*).
Briefly stated, there are seven types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) pertaining to the person (*pudgala*),
all of which should be understood as being produced by craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Namely, the affliction of recollecting (*anusmaraṇa*).
The affliction of lack of mastery,
the affliction of the objective sphere,
and the affliction of burning distress.
The afflictions associated with the happy realms,
the afflictions associated with the miserable realms,
and the afflictions of various views.
What is defilement through recollection?
It refers to when someone improperly recollects previously experienced attractive objects,
thereby longing for and pursuing them so as to cause the mind to become distracted and disintegrated.
What is the defilement of lack of mastery?
It refers to a certain person who, due to having habituated themselves to the phenomena of sensual desire in previous lives,
possesses a nature of intense and sharp sensual desire in the present life.
Even though he attends to and recollects desirable objects in accordance with reality,
his mind is scattered and destroyed by the greed of longing and pursuit;
this is because his greed is extremely intense.
The mind lacks self-mastery.
What is the defilement of the objective sphere?
It refers, for example, to someone who wanders through cities and towns and so forth.
When one encounters a present object that is beautiful and lovely in appearance,
because that object is so exceedingly sublime,
the mind-consciousness becomes entangled with its exquisite features.
Consequently, there arises the longing and pursuit of various forms of craving.
What is the defilement of feverish distress?
It refers to how, due to these three kinds of defilements that can increase craving, a certain person [experiences such distress].
This causes craving to increase further and further,
such that one laments over objects already enjoyed in the past and hankers after objects yet to be enjoyed in the future.
Being attached to objects currently being experienced causes the body and mind to be pervaded by burning affliction; what, then,
is the defilement associated with the happy realms?
That is to say, by the predominant power of that very craving which is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*),
one performs various sublime deeds of body, speech, and mind,
thereby attaining birth in the happy realms, whether as a deva or a human.
He remains attached to pleasant feelings, refusing to let them go;
intoxicated and bewildered, he dwells solely in heedlessness.
What is the defilement associated with the miserable realms?
That is to say, due to the predominant power of that very craving— the truth of origination—
one engages in various unwholesome actions of body,
speech, and mind; at the dissolution of the body after death, one falls into the various miserable realms.
They are born in the hells and other such realms;
having been born there, they are immediately afflicted by various kinds of extremely heavy sorrow, suffering, evil thoughts, and agitated minds.
What is the defilement of views?

This means that precisely due to the predominant power of that craving—the truth of origination—and because one encounters evil friends who preach perverted doctrines for the sake of attaining liberation from what is actually defilement; [one falls into error].
Although they aspire for liberation from affliction,
because they encounter such erroneous teachings,
they do not realize liberation.
Among the sixty-two types of speculative views,
one or another form of false view will increase,
due to the predominance of delusion regarding the nature of dependent origination.
Bound by such fetters of views,
they fail to attain liberation from the great ocean of birth and death within the five destinies and so forth.
Abiding in the Dharma and possessing ethical discipline (*śīla*), they are conscientious and speak with truth.
One who is able to protect and cherish oneself will also cause others to cherish them.
Regarding this verse,
what is meant by "abiding in the Dharma"?
That is to say, within the well-expounded True Dharma and Vinaya realized by the Tathāgata,
one leaves the household life with pure faith and delights in practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
How does one possess ethical discipline (*śīla*)?
That is to say, because he has thus gone forth and thus delights [in the training],
his ethical discipline is without deficiency;
it proceeds as a continuous stream, even unto its being free from any admixture.
One is able to receive and train in all the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
What is meant by having a sense of shame (*hrī*)? It is being ashamed of that which is shameful;
it is being ashamed of that which gives rise to evil and unwholesome states (*akuśala-dharma*).
This refers to that which conduces to unwholesome conduct and serves as a causal condition for the breach of precepts;
namely, improper signs and improper discursive thoughts.
If these are all afflictions and secondary afflictions,
how can they be said to be true and real?
This means to disclose all evils and not conceal them;
if one has committed an offense, one immediately confesses it truthfully before a wise fellow-practitioner.
One should apply the appropriate remedies in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what was stated above:
that is to say, in this verse, the Bhagavat concisely reveals the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*) as being subsumed under four causes.
That is to say: because one is able to correctly receive [the precepts];
because, having received them, one does not perforate them;
and because one remains far removed from the causes of perforation.
Although one has already entered the hole of ignorance and negligence,
because one immediately applies the appropriate antidote in accordance with the Dharma,
you should know that this is the summarized meaning herein.
If one sees the evil karma of others, one should reflect with careful discernment and never perform such deeds oneself; for that karma is capable of binding one—
this is the meaning of the present verse.

What is the observation of the evil karma of others through careful reflection? It is as follows: there is a certain son of good family or daughter of good family who is by nature intelligent and has accomplished the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) that consists in the correct contemplation of phenomena according to reality.
Because others perceive him as the cause for their own current engagement in unwholesome conduct,
he suffers various forms of humiliation and physical punishment;
furthermore, he is seized by the king’s officers and brought before the king.
The detailed exposition is as in the sutra,
up to the point of taking life.
Having seen this, one then reflects in this way:
Observing this person, one sees that having performed such evil and unwholesome karma in the present life,
they immediately experience such bitter retribution in this very same life.
"Stop, stop! Such evil and unwholesome karma should never be undertaken,
should never be performed,
should never be practiced, and should never be transgressed."
Furthermore, he sees those who engage in the various forms of non-restraint, such as sheep-butchers, poultry-keepers, pig-butchers, and so forth, including all such groups;
they do not live by means of such crafts, skills, or livelihoods.
Yet he rides upon elephants, horses, chariots, and palanquins;
moreover, he is unable to ensure that his vast treasuries of wealth and jewels remain intact and do not dissipate.
Consequently, he is censured and reviled by the world.
Even among ordinary worldly people, one does not temporarily allow oneself to be touched or receive contact from another,
but rather avoids it from afar;
how much more so for other sages and philosophers?
Having seen this, he then reflects as previously described;
furthermore, he sees others who are immensely wealthy and possess vast treasures.
However, due to laziness and frequent indulgence in negligence,
as days and nights pass and years accumulate,
all one's precious wealth, servants, estates, and various wholesome qualities gradually decline.
Having seen this, he then reflects as previously described.
Furthermore, he perceives the various distinctions in the physical forms of sentient beings.
Some are born blind, deaf, or mute;
some are sightless, lame, scabby, or lepers;
others have short lifespans or ugly physical forms.
Or they may have many illnesses; or they may be from poor or lowly families;
or they may have few kinsmen; or they may possess inferior or wicked wisdom;
or they may be *śandha*, *pandaka*, or those of ugly appearance.
The others are not like this; having seen it, they immediately reflect:
"I observe that this person previously committed various kinds of evil and unwholesome deeds, and now undergoes such bitter and evil retribution."
"Stop, stop! Such evil and unwholesome karma [must cease].
The rest is as previously stated.
Then he further sees others who are wise, free from indolence, and endowed with alertness and vigor.
That is to say, they are capable of engaging in such activities as farming, commerce, and seafaring,
as well as correctly undertaking the business of discourse;
yet, although they possess such vigor and diligence, [they do not attain the goal].
The undertakings he performs gradually decline and fail to reach completion.
Having observed this, he reflects as follows:
[the rest is as previously stated].
Furthermore, he saw two others who had gone forth from the home life into homelessness and were practicing the holy life together;
yet one of them was destitute of necessities such as robes and food.
In one case it is not so;
having seen [it], he immediately reflects in this way,
as previously described.
Furthermore, he sees that there may be kings or those like them who have completely conquered the vast territories of the great earth, yet they remain stubbornly attached to it and refuse to let go—
merely for the sake of a single body, a single set of skeletal remains.
Merely for the sake of a small amount of present peace and happiness,
they engage in immeasurable and vast unwholesome conduct through the doors of body, speech, and mind,
thereby destroying the peace and happiness of many future lives and many bodies.
One will undergo the great suffering of many births and many bodies.
Having seen this, one should then reflect thus:
"Observe, observe whether this is a king or someone equal to a king."
They are exceedingly foolish and debased;
they know only to cherish and protect this single life and this single body,
yet they do not know how to cherish and protect their many future lives and many future bodies.
They cherish only the brief and minor pleasure of the present,
yet do not cherish the great pleasure of the future;
nor do they fail to cherish the profound suffering of many future births.
"Stop, stop! Such evil and unwholesome karma should never be undertaken,
should never be performed,
should never be practiced, and should never be transgressed."
Furthermore, there may be a son of good family or a daughter of good family who,
being naturally intelligent and having attained the divine eye,
uses this divine eye to see sentient beings at the time of death and at the time of birth.
As explained at length in the sutra,
up until the point where one is born in the great hells;
having seen this, one then reflects as follows:
He observes that this person, in the present life, has performed such evil and unwholesome karma as will cause them to experience bitter retribution in future lives;
he thinks: "Stop, stop! Such evil and unwholesome karma!"
The rest is as previously explained.
Thus, whether it be a son of good family or a daughter of good family,
having seen the various evil karmas committed by others, [they...]
One thoroughly reflects upon and carefully examines the truths through four modes of practice. What are these four?
First, one examines whether there has been transgression, or wrong livelihood, or negligence and indolence.
First, having performed various kinds of evil and unwholesome deeds in the present life,
one experiences their disagreeable karmic results in that very same life.
Second, there are sentient beings who, based on the distinctions of their physical bodies, engage in such observation.
There may be actions that do not reach fruition,
or there may be requests that do not reach fulfillment;
all of these are due to having previously committed evil and unwholesome karma.
In this present life, each experiences such undesirable karmic results.
Third, one observes that there may be certain kings or those equal to kings who,
due to having committed various evil deeds in their present lives, [experience such consequences].
Fourth, he observes that when various classes of sentient beings die and are reborn,
they will certainly experience various undesirable karmic results in the future due to having committed various evil and unwholesome deeds during their present lives.
In future lives, one will experience unpleasant karmic results.
Because he knows this as it truly is,
he ultimately does not act [on such impulses] himself.
What is the bondage of karma?
It refers to delighting in various karmas and because of the gravity of those karmas.
Because they lack mastery over the retribution of karmic actions,
those who delight in various types of karma are,
for example, some individuals who have habitually practiced evil.
One takes delight in various evils;
due to these causes and conditions,
the mind cannot enter into any wholesome dharmas.
This is the bondage of initial karma.
Regarding "due to the gravity of karma," this refers,
for example, to someone who has committed an *ānantarya* (immediate) offense.
There may be those who have fully practiced or those who have not fully practiced.
Due to these causes and conditions,
although they may take delight in the well-spoken True Dharma and Vinaya realized by the Buddha, [they do not attain realization].
If one cannot even achieve temporary renunciation,
how much less could one possibly attain the realization of the fruits of the śramaṇa?
This is called the second bond of karma.
Regarding "lack of mastery over the retribution of karmic results," it refers,
for example, to someone who, by reason of misconduct of body, speech, and mind, [experiences such consequences].
They are born into the various evil realms; having been born there,
they lack autonomy and are unable to control themselves as they endure suffering throughout the long night.
Or they may be born in a border region where the fourfold assembly of the noble and virtuous—
namely, the bhikṣus, and so forth, up to the upāsikās— is entirely absent.
This is called the third bond of karma.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what was stated above:
that is to say, the Bhagavān has here concisely demonstrated the karmas and the karmic fruits of sentient beings.

One should understand that the brief meaning here is as follows: it consists of correct reflection, as well as the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma preceded by such correct reflection.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Volume 18.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Volume 19.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree:
The Noble Ones always speak words that are most excellent; Second, they do not speak words that are unloving;
Third, they do not speak words that are untrue; Fourth, they do not speak words that are contrary to the Dharma.
In this verse, the term "virtuous speech" refers to well-spoken words,
virtuous utterances, and excellent discourse.
It should be understood that well-spoken words possess three characteristics:
they are pleasing, untainted, and exclusively virtuous.
By means of the first [characteristic], one causes others to rejoice.
By the second statement, one's own ethical discipline (*śīla*) remains forever without breach;
by the third statement, one is able to lead others out of unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states.
Therefore, it attracts benefit and happiness.
There may be pleasant speech that is neither true nor in accordance with the Dharma;
for example, there is someone who uses beautiful and charming words.
To praise others for qualities they do not truly possess;
or to speak words that are true but unpleasant and contrary to the Dharma—
such as when someone, with a defiled mind, utters harsh and abusive speech.
One rebukes others for their actual faults and evils.
Or there may be speech that is both affectionate and truthful;
that is to say, there is someone who well understands how to praise and how to rebuke.
Having understood what is worthy of praise and what is worthy of censure,
he neither praises nor censures; rather,
through skillful means, he teaches the True Dharma.
It enables those persons to emerge from unwholesome states and abide in wholesome states.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what was stated above;
that is to say, the Blessed One has here concisely indicated all well-spoken words, whether they be headings or explanations.
One should know that this is the summarized meaning herein:
Faith, shame, virtue, and generosity—these qualities praised by the virtuous are called the path leading to heaven;
they enable one to go to the celestial world.
This is what is clarified by the verse:
namely, there is someone who has attained right faith in the Dharma and Vinaya realized by the Buddha.
He feels shame regarding his domestic life;
having received and maintained the pure precepts, he attains robes, food and drink, and bedding,
and thus gives rise to contentment.
He reduced his utensils and lived frugally regarding his requisites;
whatever righteous offerings he obtained, he never kept private.
One must share and enjoy [the teachings] together with wise companions in the holy life (*brahmacārin*).
All the true Dharma is good in the beginning, middle, and end, and it extols the holy life;
that is to say, from the discourses (*sūtra*) up to the treatises (*upadeśa*).
They are all able to receive, uphold, investigate, and master [the teachings],
transmitting them to others and expounding them extensively.
Having accomplished these various wholesome dharmas, they...
One should know that one will certainly obtain three kinds of benefits:
first, being praised by all Buddhas and their disciples, as well as by true and virtuous persons;
second, being drawn toward and sustained by the wealth of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and material generosity (*dāna*).
One who has fully perfected the accumulation of wisdom through the gathering of the accumulation of merit by means of the gift of Dharma,
shall attain entry into the pure state of the assembly of devas who have realized liberation.
Third, if those two kinds of accumulations are not yet perfected,
he can cause them to be swiftly perfected;
after the dissolution of the body, he will certainly be reborn in a happy destination.
They frequently go to the heavenly realms and worlds of bliss;
furthermore, there is a distinction:
namely, there is someone who, regarding the Dharma and Vinaya realized by the Buddha, [proceeds accordingly].
He attains right faith.
He believes that unwholesome ethical conduct leads to rebirth in the miserable realms, and he believes that those who are stingy and greedy will receive the retribution of poverty.
Having thus gained faith, he reflects as follows.
In this present life, they feel deep shame regarding immoral conduct and stinginess;
because of this shame,
they abandon unwholesome discipline (*duḥśīla*) and undertake pure ethical precepts (*viśuddha-śīla*).
Having abandoned stinginess and greed, they dwell at home with a stainless mind.
As explained in detail, up to:
they practice giving well.
By reason of this cause and condition,
one is praised by the noble ones in the present life,
and after the dissolution of the body, one will be reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world of bliss, up to that point.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what has been stated above.

That is to say, herein the Bhagavān has concisely demonstrated the benefits of both the correct practice and the fruit of correct practice for the two classes of practitioners: the householders and those who have gone forth.
One should know that this is the summarized meaning herein:
The learned can know the Dharma; The learned can distance themselves from evil;
The learned abandon what is meaningless; The learned attain Nirvana.
This is what is clarified by the following verse:

namely, there is someone who, regarding the unerring teachings concerning the discourse on giving, the discourse on ethical discipline, and the discourse on rebirth in heaven—teachings that were previously and correctly intended to be practiced—[becomes discouraged].
They listen with reverence; having heard it,
they are then able to understand its meaning—
namely, that various types of unwholesome conduct in the present life, as well as [actions] leading to the suffering of the miserable realms in the future, are causes of what is meaningless.
One should swiftly abandon all unwholesome conduct,
as well as the causes of birth in evil destinies and the suffering of those destinies, which are devoid of purpose;
this is because one understands the meaning of such dharmas.
Practice in accordance with the Dharma can distance one from the causes of suffering and draw forth the causes of happiness;
for this reason, [one should practice].
One attains happiness and abandons suffering by respectfully listening to the teachings associated with the four noble truths and other such exalted doctrines.
Having heard this, he was then able to understand its meaning:
namely, that all existence is the great suffering of birth and death, and that nirvāṇa is peace.
By understanding the meaning of these dharmas in this way, he...
If one's faculties have already matured and the provisions have been fulfilled, one is able to attain such meaning because the consciousness and mind are purified; thus,
as soon as the Dharma is heard, even those who have not yet realized the Noble Truths [attain it].
One is able to enter into clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Having realized it, one then attains the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
However, if the faculties are not yet mature and the provisions (*sambhāra*) are not yet complete, [one does not attain it].
Thus, by means of such distancing from all evils,
one gives rise to higher training in mind based on higher training in ethical discipline,
and brings forth higher training in wisdom based on higher training in mind.
By means of this, one is able to abandon all afflictions— the root of suffering— which are devoid of purpose,
and thereby realizes nirvana. Furthermore,
I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what has been stated above.
This means that the Blessed One has here briefly shown that one first hears the true Dharma and reflects upon it correctly;
having first reflected correctly, one practices in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānudharmapratipatti).
Because this practice in accordance with the Dharma serves as the primary cause, one attains the fruit of superior benefit.
One should know that this is the summarized meaning herein:
The wise one is unstained like space, Unshakable like the banner of Śakra, Like floating upon a clear,
cool, and overflowing pool, They take no delight in the mire of the ocean of birth and death.
In this present verse,
it is explained that the mind of an Arhat Bhikṣu is well-liberated and transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), being like space. Why is this so?
Just as space is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and cannot be defiled by either purity or impurity,
so too it is with all Arhats.
All worldly phenomena, whether favorable or adverse—
namely gain and loss, up to suffering and pleasure—
are unable to defile him. Furthermore, those in training who have already abandoned sensual desire [are likewise unaffected].
When one is directed toward arhatship and,
being well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness,
cultivates the signless mental concentration (animitta-cittasamādhi).
Like the banner of the Lord of Devas,
it cannot be shaken by any craving that arises in conjunction with the movement of pride, arrogance, conceptual proliferation, and worldly activity,
nor by the formation of aspirations.
Furthermore, those in training who have already abandoned sensual desire and attained the fruit of non-returning conceive a longing for the higher liberations,
just as one might wish to play in a clear, cool spring pool.
One never takes delight in the mire of the feverish defilements of the higher fetters within the meditative absorption of relishing;
because one does not take delight therein,
one likewise does not take delight in the great ocean of birth and death.
Furthermore, there is another distinction:
that which pertains to an Arhat— namely, their food, drink, speech, movement, and dwelling in the signless—
is still pursued by the suffering of the remaining substrate (sopadhiśeṣa-duḥkha).
These three locations should be understood according to their respective order.
Furthermore, there is another distinction:
namely, those Arhats who are liberated through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*).
The śaikṣas who have attained realization through the body (kāyasākṣins) and the arhats liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimuktas)—
these three categories should be understood according to their respective order.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what was stated above.

That is to say, the Bhagavān here briefly demonstrates that although one has abandoned desire for the three realms, there still remains a residual basis (sopadhiśeṣa) within the Buddha’s noble intent.
There is another distinction regarding the path of advancement that subsumes the abandonment of desire for the realm of desire and the fruit of non-returning;
namely, it briefly demonstrates the excellence of liberation, the excellence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and the excellence of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, there is another distinction:
namely, it briefly demonstrates the fruits obtained from the trainings in higher mind and higher wisdom,
as well as the two trainings in higher mind and higher wisdom themselves.
If one seeks to measure me by my form, or seeks me by my voice,
being gripped by desire and greed, they will not know me.
If one understands me within, they will not see me without.
By observing internal results, one who lacks knowledge regarding what is drawn forth by those sounds may nevertheless perceive it externally;
likewise, by observing external results, one may also perceive what is drawn forth by those sounds.
If one lacks knowledge within, one cannot see without;
such a person is universally obstructed by ignorance and is led astray by sounds.
But if one realizes what is within, one can also see what is without.
This verse clarifies that the hero’s wisdom of transcendence is not induced by sound.
That is to say, there is one whose nature is that of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Not yet having severed false conceptualization and sensual desire,
he beheld the Blessed One endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and immediately made this assessment:
"This Bhagavān is certainly a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha."
The Dharma he teaches is certain and subtle;
the conduct of his assembly of disciples is necessarily virtuous.
Yet, at a later time, he draws near to unwholesome people and hears the incorrect Dharma.
Following the arguments of others and their voices,
one places trust in and complies with others, being led by them;
because of being thus led by others, one gives rise once again to slander toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
All this has come about because they do not know the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body as it truly is.
Furthermore, there are other worldlings.
Through the supernormal power of the divine eye, which is the fruit of internal meditative concentration,
he saw the Blessed One from afar and formed this understanding:
"This Blessed One is certainly a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha."
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, there are those who, having seen with their physical eyes the karmic retribution associated with the external desire realm, make estimations;
it should be known that they too follow after the treatises and the voices of others.
They follow others and are led by others;
furthermore, there are ordinary persons for whom such views do not exist at all,
as they are universally obstructed.
For a long time, one has been led by the sounds of others;
now, if the noble ones sever, subdue,
and transcend sensual desire, they attain the noble eye of wisdom.
By means of such a noble eye of wisdom,
he realizes the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body within; yet,
although he perceives the Tathāgata’s form-body externally, [he does not perceive it as such].
Or, seeing a *caitya* or a painting and being able to understand that it is not,
in the ultimate sense, the Truly Perfectly Awakened One—
by means of such right knowledge internally and right contemplation externally.
They do not follow the treatises or the voices of others;
they do not place their trust in others nor are they led by others;
they possess resolute faith and acceptance in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
All this results from the thorough and accurate understanding of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body;
it is for this reason that such [results] are brought about.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what has been stated above.
It means that the Blessed One briefly indicates herein that if one views the Tathāgata solely from the perspective of conventional truth, it is not definitive; however,
if one views the Tathāgata from the perspective of ultimate truth, it is definitive.
One should know that this is the summarized meaning herein.
When the sixth sovereign king—the defiled—is defiled, it takes on defilement for itself;
yet in the absence of defilement, it is undefiled. That which is defiled is called a fool.
In this verse, the sixth sovereign ruler refers to the mind, intellect,
and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*).

If one has already crossed the five floods but has not yet crossed the sixth flood of the mind, at that time the mind follows after the relish for all meditative absorptions; therefore, it is called "the time of defilement."
Furthermore, there is a person who,
throughout the long night, becomes defiled by grasping and takes [phenomena] as his own;
he clings to and stores up agreeable dharmas, refusing to let them go.
Therefore, it is said that they are defiled by their own grasping.
Greed is called "defilement," and the suffering of future lives produced by greed is also called "defilement."
If, when defilement arises, one does not follow the functioning of the defiled mind by means of cultivating the mental application of restraint and the mental application of remedial counteraction,
then that mind will remain undefiled in the present life.
Within an undefiled mind, this defilement is grasped by itself;
yet in future lives, even due to those various sufferings, there is no defilement.
If one exerts effort toward them accordingly, [there is no defilement].
Neither embracing nor restraining [the mind],
one does not cultivate the mental attention that serves as an antidote to the mind;
therefore, by relying on this cause of suffering, one undergoes suffering for a long night.
Because they are unable to distance themselves from this cause of suffering, they are called "fools.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what was stated above;
that is to say, the Blessed One here concisely indicates the benefits of distancing oneself from the cause of suffering.
Furthermore, it is revealed that the nature of the fool is to perceive the cause of suffering as something that brings about their own suffering.
This should be understood as the summary meaning of this passage:
"There is a city with bones for its walls, plastered over with flesh and sinews."
Within it, greed, anger, pride, and concealment are maintained;
in this verse, that which is called a "city" refers to these.
That is to say, it consists of mind, intellect, and consciousness.
This city has only bones serving as its bricks and stones;
sinews take the place of its cords and threads, and flesh serves as its plastered surface.
It is surrounded on all sides by the walls of the physical body.
Within this city, there are four types of evil dharmas that sustain and obstruct all wholesome dharmas of the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
Second, those householders who indulge in sensual desires,
namely greed and hatred;
and second, those who have gone forth within a poorly taught Dharma and Vinaya.
This refers to pride (*māna*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*).
Due to attachment to various desires and the seeking after them,
these are not in contradiction with base and defiled conduct.
They do not even have faith in or accept the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
let alone practice what is wholesome;
instead, they rely on poorly expounded teachings to give rise to arrogance.
They are unable to proceed spontaneously to the presence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
or his disciples; even if the Buddha, the World-Honored One, or a disciple of the Buddha should go to their location out of compassion, [they still cannot approach].
However, because their minds are defiled by the entanglement of the secondary affliction of concealment (*mrakṣa*),
they are still unable to disclose their own faults as they truly are;
how much less could they believe, understand, and cultivate various wholesome dharmas?
In this way, one should know that they cannot enter either of these two kinds of mental citadels associated with the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya;
how much less could they possibly take them as their own?
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what has been stated above.

That is to say, the Bhagavān here briefly demonstrates that both householders and renunciants, by means of four kinds of causes and conditions for defilement, bring about the ruin of the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
One should know that this is the summary of the meaning herein:
Just as a tortoise withdraws its limbs within its own shell, So should a bhikṣu well restrain his mental discursive thoughts.
Without dependence on anything and without harming others, He realizes parinirvāṇa, free from all slander.
This is what is clarified by the verse:
namely, there is someone who, relying on the first dhyāna, abandons the three types of unwholesome vitarka,
namely, the vitarka of sensual desire (*kāma-vitarka*).
He is able to abandon ill-will thoughts, harmful thoughts,
and all wholesome thoughts belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna.
Abiding in the meditative concentration free from applied and sustained thought,
one briefly withdraws all discursive thinking,
just as a tortoise withdraws its limbs into its own shell.
Regarding the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra:
it should be understood that this extends upward to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
When one is correctly established in this concentration, one does not give rise to relish for it.
Having emerged, he accomplishes qualities that are lovely and delightful;
he becomes disciplined, gentle, and easy to dwell with,
not troubling his wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life.
Furthermore, he is one with whom wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin) delight to dwell together;
moreover, he has accomplished the qualities that prevent conflict.
It is by means of such correct application (samyak-prayoga) that he attains these.
They are able to enter into the clear realization of the noble truths and attain the destruction of the outflows; for,
regarding all phenomena, they do not rely on faith in others,
having attained a thoroughly pure and superior knowledge and vision.
One understands phenomena as they truly are:
that what is the Dharma is truly the Dharma, and that what is the Vinaya is truly the Vinaya.
It is by knowing them in this way that...
They will never, relying on various views and perversions, slander the Dharma regarding the Dharma,
nor slander what is not the Dharma regarding what is not the Dharma;
they will never present what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma.
They treat what is Dharma as non-Dharma;
they treat what is not Vinaya as Vinaya, or what is Vinaya as non-Vinaya.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what has been stated above.
That is to say, herein the Blessed One concisely demonstrates the fourfold path of remediation for abandoning the disturbances of one who speaks the Dharma well.
What are the four kinds of disturbances?
First, the disturbance of tainted and untainted discursive thought;
second, the disturbance of attachment to the savoring of superior meditative concentration.
Third, the disturbance of mutual conflict and litigation;
fourth, the disturbance of slandering the true path.
One should know that this is the summarized meaning herein.
Born from both equality and inequality, the Muni abandons conditioned existence and enters the distinctions of internal bliss and meditative concentration;
as explained in this verse in the *Abhidharmakośa* regarding egg-birth.
This refers to when the Buddha manifests his dwelling in the state of a bodhisattva in his final existence; at that time,
the wondrous physical body— previously obtained and adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics— is born in its full perfection.
Later, when he realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
his physical body that arises will be exactly equal to the former one.
The arising of its name-body is unequal to the preceding [state] because it is superior and dissimilar to the untainted (anāsrava).
Furthermore, it is because the Buddha manifests the bliss of internal tranquility and the bliss of the sublime gateway as his basis.
Having attained mastery over meditative concentration,
by the power of that concentration, they relinquish the formations of life-span and the formations of existence;
from the limit of that relinquishment, a body of exquisite form arises.
It arises with a name-body identical to the preceding one, yet because it is not identical to the preceding one, there is a distinction between them.
This is like a chicken born from an egg; it depends upon the egg for its birth.
Once born, it gradually grows;
its offspring, being of a similar kind, emerge from their shells.
One should understand that the principle regarding the distinction between the Tathāgata’s form-body (rūpakāya) and name-body (nāmakāya) is likewise.
The distinction here is this:
if the Buddha, the World-Honored One, does not relinquish his life-force,
he will enter parinirvāṇa only after completing his full lifespan.
Because they maintain their life-force through the power of meditative concentration,
they enter parinirvāṇa before the full completion of their lifespan.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what has been stated above.

This means that herein the Bhagavat briefly demonstrates the two distinctions between the relinquishing of the life-force (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) and the physical body (*rūpakāya*) and the name-body (*nāmakāya*),
as well as revealing the causes and conditions for abandoning the basis [of existence].
One should know that this is the summarized meaning herein:
there is no desire such as mud; there is no hatred such as demons;
there is no delusion such as nets; and there is no craving such as rivers.
This verse clarifies that there are four kinds [of things] that constitute conventional phenomena lacking self-mastery.
In the world, we clearly observe two things that cause sentient beings to lose their autonomy:
first, being mired in the mud;
second, being possessed by malevolent spirits.
Third, they enter a net;
fourth, they fall into a swift-flowing river and are swept away and drowned by the current.
Furthermore, there are four other kinds.
It can act as a truly non-autonomous phenomenon;
one should know that it likewise causes sentient beings to function without autonomy. What are these four? They are as follows:
suppose there is someone born and raised in the desire realm.
They are mired in the mire of impure, putrid, and foul-smelling sensual desires,
unable to freely initiate, protect, or increase wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, it is as if there were someone who has abandoned all sensual desires.
Having gone forth within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
one harbors anger in the heart and is prone to harsh speech;
being possessed by anger, one lacks self-mastery.
He does not attend to the rules of training and frequently commits transgressions before wise companions in the holy life.
He repeatedly struck, prodded, rebuked, expelled, harassed, and insulted him with coarse words.
Furthermore, there was another who, having renounced all sensual desires,
went forth as a monk within a poorly taught Dharma and Vinaya.
They enter the great net of deluded views of the wicked Māras;
having entered it, they wander through birth and death without autonomy.
It is like someone born in the higher realms of the stages free from desire.
Having not yet permanently severed the fetters of craving,
nor having fully understood them or attained mastery over them,
one returns to dwell in the lower realms, flowing with the current.
It is difficult to escape from.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what was stated above:
that is to say, the Blessed One here briefly demonstrates how fools are bound by various elements (dhātu) and various categories.
Furthermore, there is another distinction:
namely, there is one who, having fallen into the mire of desire and being unable to attain mastery,
goes forth into the pure life within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
Furthermore, suppose there is someone whose nature is prone to anger;
so overwhelmed by anger that his mind is entangled in resentment,
he might even harm or injure himself.
How much more so toward others?
Furthermore, suppose there is one who has accomplished the various evil and false views belonging to the category of delusion,
such that they claim there are no parents and revile their own parents.
If one expects respect and support from one's parents,
how much more so should one provide it oneself?
Furthermore, it is like someone who extensively gathers all manner of sensual desires.
Swept away by craving and lacking self-mastery,
one does not even wish to eat for oneself,
much less bestow anything upon others.
These four dharmas should be known as those that can obstruct the wise.
There are four dharmas that should be understood.
That is to say, within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, one has gone forth in purity,
remains free from malice and harm,
and reverently serves one's parents.
They delight in practicing the gift of wisdom.
Just as there are no bird tracks in the sky, there are no true śramaṇas among the outsiders;
fools delight in frivolous debate, but the Tathāgata has none.
This is what is clarified by the verse:
namely, there are sentient beings who aspire to and delight in superior sensual desires, which are subsumed under the pursuit of desire;
and there are also sentient beings who aspire to and delight in a superior body, which are subsumed under the pursuit of existence.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who desire and delight in the liberation and holy life (brahmacarya) possessed by śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas;
among these, there are those who seek through sensual desire and those who seek through existence.
That is to say: "Because I have practiced giving to a small extent and maintained the precepts to a small extent,
I shall be reborn in a happy destination, in a world of heavenly bliss,
where I may enjoy myself, take pleasure, and sport with the five exquisite sensual desires."
Having cultivated such aspirations,
he attains supreme desire and a supreme body;
it is like various birds soaring through the void of space.
Throughout the entirety of space there is no place to set foot;
likewise, sentient beings find no stable footing whatsoever within the impermanent desires they have obtained, nor within their own physical bodies.
It should be understood that it is likewise so.
Furthermore, for those who delight in the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas and seek the liberation of the holy life (brahmacarya),
there are two further types.
Either by relying on the well-expounded Dharma or by relying on the ill-expounded Dharma—
among those who rely on the ill-expounded Dharma, such as the various non-Buddhist sectarians, there are no true śramaṇas.
Among those who are embraced by the pursuit of a false holy life through reliance on poorly taught Dharma, there are no true śramaṇas;
however, among those who are embraced by the pursuit of the correct holy life, there are indeed śramaṇas.
Furthermore, all of this is subsumed under three doors:
either the door of seeking through desire,
or the door of seeking through existence.
Or there is the gate of seeking the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
All such as these are called attachment to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
One should know that because the Tathāgata has relinquished all seeking, he is free from conceptual proliferation.

By means of this same principle, one should know that the community of the Tathāgata’s disciples, who are embraced by the pursuit of the true brahmacarya, is likewise free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Furthermore, I shall now briefly elucidate the meaning of what has been stated above.
This means that the Blessed One has here briefly shown that for those who exert themselves in what is not well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, all such efforts are empty and useless.
This should be understood as the summarized meaning of this section.
Abiding in the absence of all conceptual proliferation, having leaped over the walls and moats and departed from craving,
the Muni wanders through the world; gods and humans cannot comprehend what this verse elucidates.
That is to say, an Arhat bhikṣu is forever free from craving and attachment.
By means of four aspects,
he is no longer bound to Māra, the enemy, who is the master over all foolish worldlings.
Liberated and possessing mastery, they wander at will through empty dwellings and villages.
Yet there are foolish people who, upon encountering such true arhats wandering in ultimate sovereignty, [fail to recognize them].
Not knowing things as they truly are,
he falsely conceives contempt and disparagement toward these two positions,
saying: "How can this son of good family..."
Having abandoned the precious wealth belonging to oneself that sustains one's life,
why does one instead seek the various requisites for livelihood belonging to others?
Why abandon the means for being reborn in heaven?
They exert themselves with painful diligence seeking the cessation of existence.
These foolish people perceive superior merit in being born in the heavens,
and they perceive great wealth and property in remaining at home.
They give rise to false contempt for the Muni;
even the deity they serve cannot comprehend the vast merit of this Muni.
How much less could those who perform tasks recognize it?
How then can Arhats, who are free from craving, [recognize it]?
It is by means of four aspects.
He is liberated and sovereign over the Evil Māra, the Enemy, and all the masters to whom foolish worldlings are bound;
that is to say, he is liberated from those foolish worldlings who, by means of the four stations of consciousness, remain subject to them.
They are driven and enslaved by the lord of Māra and his host,
causing them to wander back and forth among the five destinies within birth and death rather than becoming Arhats;
furthermore, these foolish worldlings are as if burdened by heavy transgressions.
Driven and enslaved by the lord of Māra and his enemies, they increase or diminish various evil views;
thus, they give rise to all manner of unwholesome and evil dharmas, such as grasping for swords and staves.
Falling into various conceptual proliferations and giving rise to the various evil destinies,
they cause the creation of manifold conditions for unwholesome karma;
such persons are not arhats.
Furthermore, just as fools are driven and enslaved by the Lord of Māra through their own internal transgressions,
they are made to dwell within the walls of the bonds of sensual craving,
unable to escape the suffering of birth in the desire realm.
They are not arhats.
Furthermore, like fools who, due to their slight transgressions,
are driven into service by the Lord of Māra, the Enemy.
They cause one to be born in the realm of form and the formless realm;
surrounded on all sides by the deep moat of ignorance and confined within the prison of the manifold sufferings of birth and death,
they are unable to escape from the suffering of birth and so forth, and are not Arhats.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what was stated above.
That is to say, herein the Blessed One has concisely demonstrated how all foolish worldlings feel shame for what they should not feel ashamed of,
and fail to feel shame for what they ought to feel ashamed of.
One should know that the brief meaning here is this: perceiving fear where there is no reason for fear, and perceiving an absence of fear where there is reason for fear.
If one has perfumed away all discursive thoughts, Is internally free from all remainder of conceptualization,
And has transcended perceptions of form along with attachment, Having eliminated the four yokes, one will not be reborn here;
this is what is clarified by this verse.
That is to say, there is one who has already entered the stage of training (śaikṣa) but has not yet abandoned the desires of the desire realm,
and who relies upon the first dhyāna.
Having perfumed and eliminated all evil discursive thoughts of the desire realm,
one relies upon the internal purity and one-pointedness of mind of the second dhyāna to [eliminate] all conceptualization belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna.
Being without remainder, eternally detached, and no longer subject to conceptual discrimination,
one relies upon the third dhyāna and transcends all joy,
obstacles, and attachments belonging to the stage of the second dhyāna.
Relying on the fourth dhyāna,
one transcends all attachment to the pleasure of the level of the third dhyāna; relying on the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti), [one transcends the fourth dhyāna].
Transcending all perceptions of form,
he proceeds in this gradual manner through various meditative absorptions up to the Peak of Existence;
whether by way of concentration or rebirth, he eliminates the four yokes.
What are the four?
First, the removal of the yoke of defiled discursive thoughts;
second, the removal of the yoke of non-defiled discursive thoughts.
Third, one eliminates the yoke of attachment to joy and pleasure;
fourth, one eliminates the yoke of all perceptions of form.
For these reasons:
One will no longer be reborn in any of the lower stages.
It should be understood that although ordinary beings may reach the Peak of Existence—whether by meditative concentration or by birth—they remain bound by the four yokes.
They return once more to be reborn in the various lower realms.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what has been stated above:

namely, that herein the Bhagavān has concisely demonstrated the two distinctions between those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) regarding the limit of existence (*bhavāgra*).
One should know that this is the summary of the meaning herein:
Generosity increases merit; Avoiding what is wrong extinguishes enmity and harm;
Cultivating the wholesome and abandoning all evil, When delusions are exhausted, one attains nirvāṇa.
This is what is elucidated by the verse:
namely, there is someone who has attained right faith in the Dharma and Vinaya realized by the Buddha.
Although dwelling in the household life,
his mind remains far removed from the fetters of the stain of stinginess,
as he upholds the seven types of meritorious actions based on material gifts.
For this reason,
whether walking or standing— as explained at length in the sūtra—
one generates such merit as this.
If there should be one who is further able to go forth in the pure manner within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
and having gone forth, is fully endowed with the power of patience.
In order to protect their ethical discipline (*śīla*),
even when they encounter others who revile, harass, or rebuke them,
or who strike and injure them with hands, bodies, tiles, stones, swords, or staves.
Fearing that the violation of ethical discipline (*śīla*) would become an obstacle,
one should harbor no evil thoughts in the mind and utter no harsh words; rather,
one should focus solely upon that object with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
It abides pervading all directions.
By this cause and condition,
all enmity and harm within the continuums of oneself and others are entirely stilled in this present life.
One shall be born in the world-system of Untroubled Bliss,
where there are few enemies and one is held in high esteem by the world.
He becomes one whom the multitude delights to behold.
Having thus correctly cultivated skillful means,
he relies upon superior morality to give rise to the superior mind.
Based on the higher mind, one develops the higher wisdom.
When entering into the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Noble Truths,
one is then able to permanently relinquish the karma that leads to the miserable destinies as well as those miserable destinies themselves.
Furthermore, by cultivating the path as previously attained,
one gradually and permanently eliminates all fetters and attains parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder.
In this way, at a later time, they further enter parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what was stated above;
that is to say, the Bhagavān here briefly demonstrates the four kinds of right practice for those who have attained pure faith.
First, the practice that brings about wealth;
second, the practice that brings about rebirth in the happy realms;
and third, the pure practice that brings about liberation from the suffering of the miserable realms.
Fourth is the pure practice that is free from all suffering.
One should know that this is the summarized meaning herein:
"Commit no evil; perform all that is good."
"To discipline one's own mind—this is the noble teaching of all Buddhas.
This verse elucidates the following:
namely, there is someone who, regarding the Dharma and Vinaya realized by the Buddha, [proceeds accordingly].
Having attained right faith,
one is able to completely eradicate all unwholesome conduct in every respect, through every cause and condition, and in every location.
Within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
one is able to properly undertake and train in the ethical discipline of the precepts;
by means of three characteristics, such a person practices all that is wholesome.
That is to say, being well-established in ethical discipline (*śīla*),
guarding the pure restraint of the Prātimokṣa,
and even training in all the precepts (*śikṣāpada*) that have been received.
Based on the training in higher ethics, one develops the training in higher mind;
based on the training in higher mind, one develops the training in higher wisdom.
By means of this, one comes to know and see the objects of knowledge as they truly are.
Having thus become fully endowed with all wholesome dharmas,
one further tames one's own mind by means of three characteristics;
that is to say, through knowing things as they truly are, one is able to give rise to wearying revulsion.
Through weariness [with conditioned existence], one is able to attain freedom from passion;
through freedom from passion, one is able to attain liberation.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what has been stated above.
This means that the Blessed One has here briefly indicated the three trainings and the fruits of those trainings,
demonstrating that his own holy teaching is not shared with others;
this should be understood as the summarized meaning herein.
Difficult to subdue and fickle, one falls into the various desires;
by well-subduing the mind, a subdued mind brings about peace and happiness—
this is what this verse clarifies.
This refers to the teaching that if the mind, the intellect, or consciousness has for a long night delighted in and frequented crowded and tumultuous places,
it will be difficult to find solitude in such tumultuous places and difficult to subdue.
Although one dwells securely and practices diligently among all wholesome dharmas,
one is nonetheless unable to remain consistently free from greed, hatred, and delusion;
nor is one able to remain consistently uplifted, yet without agitation, and tranquil.
Nevertheless, there quickly arises again greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as inferior restlessness and lack of tranquility,
even though one has forcefully established oneself within internal calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Because they have long cherished and delighted in forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles,
they rush toward and sink into the objects of the five desires.
Noble disciples regard such attachment to defiled pleasures as a source of suffering that gives rise to mental anguish.
He never allows [the mind] to function independently; rather,
by repeatedly reflecting and discerning in accordance with [reality], he accomplishes seclusion,
constantly cultivating wholesome dharmas and one-pointedness of mind.
By means of such a mind of right concentration, he is able to know things as they truly are.
Because he knows them as they truly are, he is able to give rise to revulsion.
Through revulsion, he is able to attain detachment from passion.
Through the abandonment of defilements, one is able to attain liberation.
Since he has thus well-subdued his mind and exhausted the causes of suffering,
he attains a dwelling in happiness within this very life.
Furthermore, all future sufferings shall also be eternally exhausted.
Next, I shall briefly explain the meaning of what was stated above:
that is to say, the Bhagavān here briefly demonstrates the mind capable of not following the left-hand path that flows through the long night.
And the benefits that do not follow from non-conformity—
these should be known as the summarized meaning herein.
One who well understands the characteristics of the mind is able to savor the flavor of seclusion.

This verse elucidates the following: there is a certain trainee (śaikṣa) who has seen the tracks [of the path], who is concentrated, constant, and mindful, and who experiences untainted joy and bliss.
One is able to skillfully discern the signs of tranquility (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
By virtue of these causes and conditions, one attains four merits:
namely, the mind abides upon a single object and becomes free from heaviness and rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Being able to skillfully enjoy the peace and happiness of body and mind is the first merit.
Furthermore, it is because the purified concentrated mind has brought its cultivation to completion.
Because he has practiced accordingly,
he is able to correctly and thoroughly examine the principles of all phenomena,
thereby attaining internal *vipaśyanā*.
This is the second merit.
Because he relies upon such purified śamatha and vipaśyanā,
regarding the factors of enlightenment that he practices:
To be able to practice constantly with vigor and without interruption;
to be able to practice thoroughly without laziness or dread—
this is the third merit.
By means of such a mind free from indolence and weariness,
he attains supreme right mindfulness and right situational awareness,
and his mind is well-liberated.
