Furthermore, one is able to enjoy the joy and bliss of liberation as well as the bliss of non-attachment,
attaining a state of abiding in peace and happiness within this very life;
this is the fourth merit.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what has been stated above.
That is to say, herein the Bhagavat briefly demonstrates four kinds of qualities regarding skill in signs (*lakṣaṇa-kauśalya*),
which consist of the functions of śamatha.
That which is performed through vipaśyanā;
that which is performed without indolence or weariness;
and that which is performed to reach the ultimate consummation.
One should know that this is the summary of the meaning herein:
Without a craft for livelihood and not disparaging oneself, Delighting in the excellence of the faculties,
fully liberated, Homeless, without possessions, and free from longing, Having severed desire and wandering alone— such a one is a true bhikṣu.
This verse clarifies that one who has accomplished the five factors and permanently abandoned the five factors should be known as a true bhikṣu.
What are the five? They are:
not relying on the practice of deceitful expedients for a wrong livelihood, nor depending upon families of power and influence.
Nor do they cultivate a reputation for noble lineage;
nor do they falsely claim to have received the teachings spoken by the Buddhas or the noble disciples.
Rather, like those who rely on a craft, they unrighteously seek after clothing and food.
This is called the first limb. Furthermore,
one reduces the number of utensils and implements, skillfully discards precious wealth,
wears clothing that merely covers the body, and takes food only to satisfy the belly, remaining content and joyful.
Whenever he travels, he must always carry his robes and alms bowl;
this is the second limb.
Furthermore, he aspires to be a śramaṇa and delights in being a śramaṇa.
Out of aspiration for the precepts and a joyful devotion to them, one would not transgress the prohibitions of the training even for the sake of a life-threatening circumstance,
let alone for the sake of minor gains and offerings.
This is the third limb.
Furthermore, he thus correctly cultivates the means [of practice],
being pure in livelihood, content, and delighting in the training precepts.
For those who have not yet realized the noble truths,
this enables them to enter realization and attain pure vision; or,
at times when mindfulness is lost, it may arise momentarily.
When evil and unwholesome thoughts arise, giving rise to greed, hatred, and delusion,
one swiftly dispels them with sluggishness and forgetfulness;
this is the fourth factor.
Furthermore, by practicing as he previously attained the Path,
his mind becomes liberated from all fetters, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, and entanglements.
This is the fifth limb.
Thus, one is said to have accomplished the five limbs.
What, then, is called the permanent abandonment of the five limbs?
This refers to an Arhat bhikṣu who is no longer capable of transgressing in five respects; that is to say,
he is incapable of abandoning the precepts he has undertaken and falling back into them.
Furthermore, he is unable to amass stores and take possession of them as his own for personal enjoyment;
nor does he enjoy the objects of sensual desire.
Moreover, he is unable to knowingly speak falsehoods for the sake of wealth or for the sake of his life.
Furthermore, being unable to renounce sensual desires, they commit taking what is not given;
nor can they ever remain aloof from greed, dwelling and traveling alone,
but instead associate with those who practice unchaste conduct, engaging in sexual union two by two.
Some reckon that suffering and pleasure are brought about by one's own actions;
some reckon them to be caused by another, or by both oneself and another;
others reckon them to be neither caused by oneself nor by another.
Without arising from causes, one does not encounter suffering or pleasure;
this is called the eternal severance of the five branches.
The mind travels afar and wanders alone, bodiless, it slumbers within the cave.
"One who can subdue that which is difficult to subdue— I call him a brāhmaṇa.
In this verse, what is referred to as "mind" (citta) is also called "intellect" (manas) and "consciousness" (vijñāna).
Regarding all these infinite and diverse individualities of foolish beings throughout the past,
which have arisen through mutual succession and causal succession, although there is no creator,
they flow through birth and death such that their prior limit is unknowable.
Therefore it is called "Far-Reaching" (*dūramgamā*).
This [stage] proceeds one by one in the present,
because the second accompanying mind has been left far behind.
Because the mind does not transform all at once in every respect,
it is called "solitary.
Furthermore, this present [mind] arises and manifests in accordance with its own nature from the very beginning.
Whether by way of the nature of greed, the nature of hatred, or the nature of delusion;
or by way of any one of the remaining afflictions or secondary afflictions—
their very substance does not function ultimately, just as the five material sense-faculties do not.
Whether identical or different, inferior or superior,
as soon as its own essence first arises and manifests,
that very essence continues to evolve until the end.
The mind is not like this.
Why? Because the mind passes through various stages such as days, nights, kṣaṇas, and lava-s.
They are not a single entity but are manifold and of various kinds;
they arise at different times of arising and perish at different times of perishing,
because their nature as defiled by the mind is not established as real.
It is called "bodiless.
In this future world, it dwells within the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) and possesses latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
thus, it possesses the sense of coming and going within subsequent births.
This is called "sleeping in a cave.
If one who is wise, by means of these four characteristics,
[examines] the mind across the past, present, and future lives...
Knowing as it truly is the cultivation of disenchantment, cessation, and the liberation of the mind,
they are able to transcend all views of a personal identity (satkāya),
reach the further shore, and dwell securely on dry land.
He is called a Brahmin.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what was stated above:
that is to say, the Blessed One here briefly demonstrates that the mind, throughout the long duration of the past, is defiled and lacks the nature of an agent.
In the present world, its nature is momentary and intrinsically pure;
in the future world, it becomes defiled or purified depending on whether there is negligence or non-negligence.
One should know that this is the summarized meaning herein:
Who can obscure the world? Who can cause it not to appear?
Who, moreover, can defile it? And who is the great terror?
Ignorance shrouds the world; heedlessness prevents it from shining forth.
Proliferation (prapañca) defiles it, and suffering is the great terror.
The floods leak everywhere; who can stop these outflows?
I shall explain who guards: by what are the world’s flowing streams dammed?
These outflows are stilled by mindfulness;
I say that one guards by means of this, for through wisdom they are dammed.
Regarding mindfulness, wisdom, name-and-form—now I ask:
when shall all these be utterly extinguished? I pray that you explain to me how mindfulness, wisdom, and name-and-form are so; I shall explain them all to you.
If all consciousnesses are eternally extinguished, and within this they are forever brought to an end,
how can one recollect their objects? Since all consciousnesses shall be eternally extinguished,
I now entreat you to grant us skillful means, explaining this so that we may be free from doubt.
Regarding all internal and external sensations, one does not give rise to delight at all;
such is the practice of mindfulness, wherein all consciousnesses shall be eternally extinguished.
This applies to those who have well expounded the Dharma, as well as to those of various types who are still in training.
He who is constant and diligent can proceed; he should request the Great Sage to explain how one does not indulge in desires.
With a mind free from turbid defilement and skillful mindfulness regarding all phenomena, such a bhikṣu can proceed.
This is from the *Pārāyaṇa*,
a verse concerning the questions posed by Aśvajit.
As for the term "the world" (*loka*):
Briefly, there are three kinds:
first, the world of desire;
second, the world of form.
Regarding the three formless worlds (*ārūpyadhātu*), in this context the intention is to distinguish between the two types of worlds:
the monastic and the lay. Furthermore, the monastic world is itself of two kinds.
First, the teaching of the evil Dharma;
second, the teaching of the sublime Dharma.
Regarding the teaching of the evil Dharma:
Enveloped by ignorance,
that which is well-expounded by the teacher should be made manifest through the presence of knowledge.
Due to negligence, they fail to manifest [the truth].
As for householders of various kinds who wear white robes,
they are defiled by manifold conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
It should be understood that there are, in brief, three kinds of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
That is to say, the three types of objects of speech are called conceptual proliferation;
furthermore, whatever is proclaimed or discussed within the four modes of discourse is also called conceptual proliferation.
The vitarka and vicāra that give rise to speech are also called conceptual proliferation (prapañca). If,
with respect to the three types of verbal objects— past, future, and present—
one initiates heterogeneous conceptualizations and reflections based on the four modes of discourse.
Whether it be contrariety or conformity, this is called "defilement.
Such prior conceptual proliferation and subsequent defilement are mostly found among householders.
Therefore, it is said that they are defiled by all manner of conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
Among these, those who teach the Dharma poorly are shrouded by ignorance;
those who teach the Dharma well remain unmanifest due to negligence.
Those householders are defiled by conceptual proliferation;
when the causes of suffering manifest in this present life,
they are unable to know these causes of suffering as they truly are, as causes of suffering.
One dwells with craving and delight for this cause of suffering;
by reason of this,
future suffering arises.
This suffering is precisely what is called "great terror.
Furthermore, those who practice wrongly-spoken teachings, through the gateway of ignorance,
leak forth manifold sufferings from the six sense bases.
Householders, through the gateway of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*),
leak out manifold sufferings from the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*);
those who preach the Dharma well, through the gateway of negligence (*pramāda*).
From the six sense bases, the various sufferings flow and leak forth.
In this way, the gates of ignorance, heedlessness, and conceptual proliferation leak and flow forth.
Through hearing the voice of another and through correct internal attention, [these are stilled].
By thoroughly understanding the defects within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
mindfulness associated with this [understanding] proceeds against the current;
thus, it is able to restrain them.
Such skillful means are called the antidote of suppression.
If the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) subsumed under supramundane right view (*lokottara-samyag-dṛṣṭi*) is applied,
it can completely block all three streams.
Such skillful means are called the "antidote of abandonment," because both types of antidotes—
those that suppress and those that eradicate— are capable of abandoning these outflows.
Both are termed "protection.
Furthermore, those who propound false teachings and those who are householders are invariably included within the category of the defiled.
In the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, two categories are found:
those who are heedless fall into the class of affliction and are not included in what is manifest;
those who are heedful fall into the class of purification and are included in what is manifest.
Furthermore, whether it has already been manifested or is yet to be manifested,
one should know that in both cases, Arhats are free from negligence.
Since they have already manifested non-negligence, there is no further need for them to perform acts of non-negligence.
Because mindfulness and wisdom regarding the four foundations of mindfulness have been well-cultivated,
and because pure consciousness has been well-realized, there remains only certainty;
for within the realm of nirvana without remainder, that well-purified consciousness shall be eternally extinguished.
If mindfulness and wisdom are also permanently extinguished accordingly,
then all name-and-form (nāmarūpa) induced by prior karma, which is comprised within the remainder of the basis (upadhi), will also be extinguished and exhausted accordingly;
this continues until those phenomena have been permanently extinguished.
He is constantly and well-established in the six constant abidings;
regarding all internal sensations belonging to the stage of detachment from desire,
as well as external sensations associated with the various desires.
They do not give rise to delight.
This is called the manifestation of right mindfulness by all Arhats until the end of their lives, when consciousness finally and eternally ceases.
This should also be clearly understood to apply to those in training (śaikṣas).
Regarding heedfulness, one must further apply oneself to the tasks of heedfulness.
These are of two kinds:
heedfulness itself and the tasks of heedfulness.
This refers to those who act constantly,
those who act with thoroughness,
and those of the class of trainees (*śaikṣa*), such as the various trainees who are "at most seven times reborn" (*saptakṛtvah-parama*).
Or again, there are those who are householders, once-returners, and so forth,
as well as those capable of attaining parinirvāṇa in the present life;
their minds are undefiled by the lower fetters and the higher fetters.
In order to sever them, one cultivates their antidotes;
furthermore, because one does not become attached to sensual desires,
the lower fetters are unable to defile one.
Because the mind is free from turbidity, the higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) cannot defile it.
Furthermore, regarding all phenomena characterized by suffering,
one knows their origin, up to their transcendence, exactly as they are.
With his mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness,
he cultivates the noble path as previously attained,
which leads to the ultimate goal.
By thus cultivating the path of antidotes,
he attains the ultimate perfection of all those acts of heedfulness that ought to be performed among all forms of heedfulness.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what was stated above.
That is to say, the Blessed One has here concisely demonstrated that for all householders and for those who have gone forth from the external teachings, defilement is inevitable.
And it reveals that among those who have gone forth within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
those who act with negligence fall into the category of defilement,
while those who do not act with negligence fall into the category of purity.
One should know that this is the summarized meaning herein:
In the pursuit of various desires, or upon attaining the expected result, the mind becomes fixed in joy;
this cherished attachment persists until death.
For those beings who delight in sensual desires, if they fall away from those desires,
their physical forms will undergo transformation and decay, like one struck by a poisoned arrow;
yet if they remain far removed from all desires, they are like the head of a venomous serpent.
Those who delight in this world of craving—
be it fields, gold, and silver, or cattle, horses, pearls, bracelets, and female slaves—
find their pleasure increased by such desires. Yet, through right mindfulness, one is able to transcend them all.
When the mind clings to and sinks into inferior objects, it undergoes transformation and gives rise to various outflows;
from this, all manner of suffering accumulates, like water flooding a broken ship.
If one were to forever sever all desires, it would be like cutting off the crown of a tāla tree.
"Abandoning all sorrows and anxieties, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf"—
this is a verse from the *Arthavargīya* concerning sensual desires (*kāma*).
It refers to a certain person who yearns for all the various sensual pleasures of the future.
One exerts effort and employs skillful means for the sake of acquisition;
having acquired them, one becomes attached to and indulges in their immediate enjoyment.
Thus, one both longs for and correctly enjoys the various sensual desires that have been obtained.
From these causes and conditions, joy arises and pleasure arises;
this is collectively termed the "taste of sensual desires.
Furthermore, it refers to all those sensual desires that one longs for and actually enjoys.
When one falls away from those things acquired or enjoyed,
the longing for and attachment to the savor of those desires enters the heart like a poisoned arrow.
One experiences great sorrow and suffering, or even meets with death.
Such are called the faults and perils of sensual desires.
Furthermore, poisonous snakes are used as a metaphor for the objects of sensual desire.
The head of a venomous serpent is a metaphor for all the flavors of craving found within the various sensual desires.
If foolish people crave the flavors of these desires, becoming greedily attached to them and indulging in their enjoyment.
Just as one who has been bitten by a snake,
so too a learned noble disciple remains far removed from all the relish of sensual desires.
Like the head of a venomous snake, one never indulges in it with attachment or craving;
as explained at length, even unto... [end].
He does not give rise to attachment.
He [abandons] all craving for forms,
up to and including all craving for tangibles.
One is able to subdue, eradicate, and transcend them all;
this is what is called renunciation from all desires.
Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of all desires briefly consists of two kinds.
First is the desire for objects;
second is the desire for afflictions.
There are two types of desire for objects.
First is grain, which refers to its basis,
namely the field;
second is wealth, which refers to its basis.
This refers to matters such as gold and silver. Why is this?
Because those who seek grain must necessarily seek land.
Those who seek wealth must necessarily seek such things as gold and silver.
Furthermore, there are two ways to seek gold and silver:
the first is to serve a king.
Second are merchants.
Those seeking grain and fields require oxen as a means;
those seeking wealth and serving the king require horses as a means.
Regarding the skillful means employed by merchants seeking wealth:
if [the items] are associated with gold, silver, and so forth,
this refers to various precious gems.
Regarding the statement that gold and silver are of different categories and thus do not correspond:
this refers to items such as bracelets and armlets;
these are cited as the most prominent examples.
One should know that the same applies to matters of buying, selling, and speech.
Having accumulated such wealth and grain,
one then enjoys amusements together with all their attendants.
This refers to the various forms of women,
as well as their attendants, who have not yet been accumulated, gathered, or protected,
and who exist within the context of profits and interests.
That is to say, there are many servants,
and such wealth and grain have been accumulated to such a vast extent that one becomes attached to this place, finding pleasure therein and refusing to leave.
All such [desires] are called desires for objects (*vastukāma*).
As for the desire for afflictions (*kleśakāma*),
it refers to the pursuit of the relishable flavor (*āsvāda*) within those desires for objects.
Based on the consciousness of attachment, various false discriminations and cravings arise;
furthermore, through the craving for sensory objects, one becomes submerged by afflictive desires,
causing the mind to sink into a state of inferiority.
If those objects undergo change, decay, or loss, then various outflows arise;
grief, lamentation, distress, sorrow, and manifold afflictions ensnare his mind.
Because of this, in the present life, he is obscured and overwhelmed by these outflows, lacking any remedy.
It is like a ship that has been wrecked and gradually fills with water,
which brings about various sufferings such as birth, old age, and sickness in the future;
yet, one may achieve liberation from all such desires.
One is then able to forever sever those defiled consciousnesses that arise from attachment to the savoring of sensual desires,
just as when the crown of a tāla tree is cut off, it no longer grows.
Furthermore, regarding those objects of desire that are lovely, delightful, and even agreeable to the mind,
when they undergo transformation and decay, no sorrows, lamentations, or any other forms of suffering can take hold within the pure consciousness.
Just as water droplets do not adhere to the petals of a lotus flower, so it is here.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what was stated above:
namely, that in this passage the Bhagavān has concisely demonstrated the threefold nature of sensual desires—their gratification, their peril, and the renunciation thereof.
Furthermore, it reveals the defects inherent in the relish of craving, as well as the virtues of its transcendence;
this should be known as the summarized meaning herein:
"Without attachment to the past, one does not long for the future."
"Among all phenomena of the present, the wise who observe everywhere and in every way cause [wisdom] to increase; this is unassailable and immovable—
this is the verse composed by the Virtuous One."
That is to say, there is someone who, having attained pure faith in the Dharma and Vinaya realized by the Buddha,
abandons the life of a householder out of that right faith and goes forth into the homeless state.
The holy life is practiced and rendered thoroughly pure by means of five aspects:
namely, being able to relinquish all activities of the household life without any lingering attachment.
Furthermore, one does not give rise to longing for them, nor does one again develop defiled attachment;
this is called the first sign.
Moreover, regarding the various formations belonging to future categories, such as gains and honor in this present life, [one does not give rise to longing].
He does not give rise to expectations,
nor does he aspire for or seek any conditioned phenomena pertaining to humans or devas in the future while practicing the holy life;
this is the second characteristic.
Furthermore, one correctly observes the various phenomena such as form, which are subsumed within the five aggregates of clinging in the present,
as well as their conventional designations;
and one likewise observes the bodily misconducts and their evil retributions in both the present life and future lives.
That is to say: "I should not initiate any unwholesome conduct regarding the body," as explained at length in the sūtra, up to:
"One should abandon all unwholesome conduct of the body and cultivate wholesome conduct of the body."
One should know that the same applies to the wholesome conduct of speech.
Furthermore, one is able to observe the aggregates, such as form and so forth,
[and realize] that those of the past, future, and present are all impermanent.
Because it is impermanent, it is suffering;
because it is suffering, it is non-self.
Due to its being non-self, one does not grasp at any of those things as "mine."
Even unto that, one does not grasp it as a self;
thus observing with correct wisdom according to reality—
this is the third characteristic.
Furthermore, by relying on the first dharma, vipaśyanā brings the faculties to maturity,
and the two types of provisions— merit and wisdom— are thoroughly realized and increased in future lives.
It cannot be plundered by kings and the like;
this is the fourth characteristic.
Furthermore, it relies upon the second dharma, vipaśyanā.
In this present life, the qualities of nirvāṇa are able to increase well,
and they cannot be shaken by any afflictions or secondary afflictions;
this is the fifth characteristic.
By means of these five characteristics,
one practices the holy life so as to make it thoroughly pure.
If one relies upon such [practice] for even a single day and night, [it is sufficient].
Furthermore, they are the most excellent among the virtuous and the foremost of the most excellent;
one should know that they transcend all other forms of holy life (brahmacarya) whatsoever.
Next, I shall now briefly explain the meaning of what has been stated above.
This refers to the Blessed One’s concise demonstration herein of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) practiced within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya;
it is entirely pure in all its aspects and is not shared with others.
One should know that this is the summarized meaning herein.
The summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
Bad speech, craving, flow, fear, Categories, ponds, flows, and craving.

The Twelfth Stage: That Accomplished through Cultivation, within the *Mūlabhūmi*, spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva and translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
The stage accomplished through reflection has already been explained.
What is the stage consisting of cultivation?
Briefly, it should be understood that the stage consisting of cultivation is fully subsumed by four points.
What are the four bases?
First, the basis of cultivation;
second, the causal conditions for cultivation.
Third is the cultivation of yoga;
fourth is the cultivation of the fruit.
These four points are subsumed within the seven branches.
What are the seven?
First, the perfection of birth;
second, the perfection of hearing the true Dharma.
Third, taking nirvana as the foremost.
Fourth, the ripening of the wisdom that brings about liberation.
Fifth, the cultivation of remedies.
Sixth, all-aspect purity of the mundane;
seventh, all-aspect purity of the supramundane.
These four points are subsumed within the seven branches.
It should be understood that the meaning of the universal holy teaching is explained extensively;
by relying upon the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya,
all training precepts are brought to fulfillment.
What is the perfection of birth?
It should be known that there are briefly ten kinds;
namely, five based on the internal.
There are five based on the external.
Taken together, there are ten types based on both the internal and external.
What are the five based on the internal within the perfection of birth?
That is to say: the perfection of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*),
the perfection of the location (*sthāna*),
and the perfection of the physical basis (*āśraya*).
The perfection of being free from karmic obstructions,
the perfection of being free from obstacles to faith and understanding,
and the perfection of the homogeneous class of beings.
That is to say, there is someone born among human beings who has obtained a male body with fully developed male organs and whose physical location is complete.
That is to say, there is someone born among human beings,
and moreover, dwelling in a central land rather than a border region—
that is, in a place where the fourfold assembly practices.
This refers to bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas,
and upāsikās who are not born among the Daradas or the Mlecchas—
that is, in places where the fourfold assembly does not practice.
Furthermore, there are no noble ones, those who have attained the right path, those who practice correctly,
or virtuous persons who rely upon the perfections.
This refers, for example, to someone born in a central land.
He is not deficient in eyes or ears, nor in any other limb or faculty;
by nature he is neither dull-witted nor stupid, nor is he mute or speech-impaired;
he is capable of understanding and discerning the meaning of all teachings, whether well-spoken or ill-spoken.
One who is perfected in the absence of karmic obstructions is,
for example, someone who relies upon a perfected basis.
Regarding any one of the five immediate karmic obstructions (*ānantarya-karma*),
one should neither commit them oneself nor incite others to do so;
for if one commits such acts, one will certainly not become a vessel for realizing the noble state (*ārya-dharma*) within this very lifetime.
Regarding the perfection of the absence of obstacles to faith and understanding:
it refers to a certain individual who will certainly not commit the five deeds of immediate retribution and does not give rise to faith and understanding toward evil states.
One does not give rise to a pure mind toward evil places;
that is to say, toward various abodes of false deities and various abodes of non-Buddhist paths.
Because in their previous lives they cultivated pure faith within the well-expounded teachings of the Buddha’s holy doctrine, and because this continued over a long period of time,
by virtue of these causes and conditions,
in this present life they [find themselves] only in a holy place.
Regarding how one generates faith and understanding and gives rise to a pure mind within the perfection of arising, there are five external factors:
namely, the perfection of the Teacher,
and the perfection of the conventional designation of the True Dharma.
The perfection of the conformity to the ultimate true Dharma;
the perfection of the non-extinction of correct practice;
and the perfection of the conducive material conditions.
Regarding the perfection of the Great Master:
it means that once such a person has already attained the five internal perfections of birth,
they further encounter the appearance of a Great Master in the world.
That which is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat,
the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the All-Knowing One,
and the All-Seeing One.
Regarding the phrase "attaining unimpededness toward all objects and the perfection of the conventional designation of the true Dharma":
this refers to that very same person encountering the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
Furthermore, it extensively reveals and elucidates wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, those with fault and those without fault;
it provides detailed explanations up to the various dependently originated dharmas and their extensive analysis—
namely, the Sūtras.
Geya, Vyākaraṇa, and Gāthā.
Discourses spoken by the Buddha himself (Udāna), Discourses on dependent origination (Nidāna),
and Discourses with parables (Avadāna).
Itivṛttaka, Jātaka,
and Vaipulya.
The marvelous Dharma,
as well as the discourses and treatises,
which perfectly accord with the ultimate true Dharma.
That is to say, once the Great Teacher has skillfully revealed the sublime Dharma of the mundane world,
the assembly of disciples relies upon this sublime Dharma and further receives from others instructions and exhortations that are in accordance with it.
He cultivated the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment,
attained the fruits of the śramaṇa,
and reached perfection in the realization of those fruits.
Furthermore, it is the realization of all virtues that successively increase and expand in excellence;
it is the perfection of right practice such that it does not cease even after the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, has entered parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the conventional true Dharma still remains without having been extinguished,
the ultimate true Dharma has not yet vanished or been severed,
and the conducive conditions and resources are complete.
This refers to the four ways of enjoying the true Dharma through the presence of the necessary conditions for such enjoyment: namely,
those who possess right faith, such as elders, householders, and brahmins.
Knowing that they might fear a lack of material resources while practicing the true Dharma, and thus lose what they have received,
one should therefore diligently offer various robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, medicinal requisites for illness, and personal articles for their use.
These ten kinds are called the perfection of birth based on the internal and external.

By means of these five aspects, [he practices].

Furthermore, regarding the ethical discipline (śīla) undertaken by those who have gone forth within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya:
It is manifested by the brief relinquishing of two things:
first, the abandonment of parents, wife and children,
slaves, and servants.
It is manifested by friends,
kinsmen, wealth, grain, precious jewels, and so forth; second,
it is the renunciation of singing, dancing, and theatrical performances.
Laughing, playing, and enjoying pleasures;
wandering about with negligence and dissipation;
and gathering with those one holds dear.
Various worldly affairs manifest therein;
furthermore, he abides in the restraint of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*),
never privately reproaching himself for transgressing the precepts.
Nor does he rebuke or expel fellow practitioners of the holy life for their faults according to the Dharma;
yet, if there is a transgression of the śīla, he does not fail to censure it lightly.
If there is any deficiency or violation regarding the śīla...
For this reason,
he reproached himself, thinking:
"If my fellow practitioners of the holy life were to censure and expel me according to the Dharma..."
Even if one has repented and removed [the fault] in accordance with the Dharma,
one should cultivate oneself toward fellow practitioners of the holy life who have pointed out one’s transgression,
remaining free from resentment, malice, injury, or affliction.
By means of these five aspects,
this is called the observation regarding the second point.
Thus, having brought ethical discipline (*śīla*) to perfect completion, [one proceeds].
One should diligently apply skillful means through five aspects to cultivate all categories of wholesome qualities.

That is to say: from time to time, one should consult and receive instruction, recite and chant, deliberate and investigate, and resolutely determine the meaning, while persevering in the cultivation of wholesome qualities.
In this way, one should indeed accept the offerings of faith from others.
Furthermore, delighting in seclusion, one cultivates various mental attentions through correct means.
Moreover, throughout day and night, regarding the two factors of the regressive portion and the progressive portion:
One knows what is to be abandoned and what is to be cultivated;
furthermore, one perceives the great faults of saṃsāra and perceives the supreme virtues of nirvāṇa.
By means of these five aspects,
this is called the third station of observation.
Thus does one who exerts themselves diligently cultivate the category of wholesome qualities.
Briefly stated, one is pursued by four types of suffering,
because one has not yet attained any of the realizations corresponding to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
They are still pursued by the sufferings of the miserable realms,
for their very nature consists of the phenomena of birth, aging, sickness,
and death; thus, they are pursued by the suffering of internal change.
Because all that is beloved is subject to separation,
it is pursued by the suffering of change resulting from attachment;
because it is produced by one's own karma, it is pursued by the causes of all suffering.
He is pursued by these four kinds of suffering and should examine them correctly through seven aspects.
Because of these seven aspects, this is called the examination of the fourth station.
When he correctly observes these four bases by means of twenty-two aspects,
there arises in him such appropriate mental attention (yoniśo-manasikāra).
That is to say: "For the sake of seeking such matters as these, I vow to accept inferior physical appearance, deportment, and requisites for sustaining the body;
I vow to accept the prohibitive precepts."
"I vow to embrace diligent effort and constantly cultivate wholesome dharmas.
As for me now, from which of the four kinds of suffering shall I seek liberation?"
"If, despite thus exhorting and encouraging myself and vowing to undergo these three states,
I am still pursued by the four sufferings and have not attained liberation,
I must now ensure that I am no longer pursued by suffering."
Without yet having attained mastery over superior meditative concentration,
one might cease midway or even regress;
thus one should apply oneself with diligence and correct mental attention.
Thus, one obtains what are called the perception of renunciation and the perception of being a śramaṇa.
By relying on the cultivation of various skillful means for their perfection,
one realizes the perfection of samādhi through the mundane path.
While they have not yet realized the abandonment of the afflictions,
they continue to rely on the abandonment of pleasure and diligently practice with constant effort;
furthermore, they have already attained the wholesome mundane path.
In order to repeatedly attain mastery over samādhi,
he proceeds by relying on the uninterrupted practice of joyful cultivation;
furthermore, [he does so] toward those with right faith, such as householders, lay devotees, and brahmins.
Having obtained various gains and honors,
one does not give rise to craving or attachment based on those gains and honors,
nor does one [crave] the gains and honors of others.
Furthermore, regarding various disagreeable physical and verbal actions and manifest deeds— whether performed in their presence or behind their backs— by other faithless brahmins and others,
he gives rise to resentment in his mind.
Furthermore, he harbors no harmful intent toward others;
nor do various secondary afflictions—such as attachment, pride, views, ignorance, and doubt—arise within his various states of meditative concentration.
He is well-guarded in the foundations of mindfulness;
furthermore, it is not by means of having attained superior śamatha that he [proceeds],
but rather by means of this very śamatha.
Thinking, "I have completed all that was to be done," he does not proclaim to others what he has realized;
thus, through such delight in abandonment and delight in cultivation, he proceeds.
With a mind free from greed and anger,
maintaining present mindfulness and free from overweening pride,
one feels joy and contentment upon obtaining whatever robes are suitable.
Just as it is with clothing,
one should know that it is likewise with regard to other things such as food, drink, and bedding.
Furthermore, one partakes of them with correct comprehension,
thinking: "These various requisites for life serve only to maintain the body so that it does not perish."
To temporarily cease hunger and thirst and to uphold the holy life;
as explained at length, up to:
knowing moderation in food.
Because he practices correctly in this way,
he attains mastery over samādhi;
by relying upon that, his mind becomes pure and bright.
Free from blemish and free from secondary afflictions;
as explained at length, up to:
attaining immovability.
That which can induce all supreme supernormal powers and wisdom is called mastery over samādhi.
This is the extensive meaning of mastery over samādhi.
One should know that there are only the characteristics as they have been described;
beyond these, there is nothing further, neither exceeding nor adding to them.
Furthermore, regarding the attainment of samādhi previously mentioned:
The perfection of samādhi described in the middle [section],
together with the mastery over samādhi described here,
is collectively termed the unsurpassed, all-aspect purity of the mundane.
It should be known that this purity exists only in the True Dharma and not among the various non-Buddhist paths.
What is the supramundane purity in all its aspects?
It should be known that, briefly stated, there are five kinds.
What are the five?
First, entering the clear realization of the noble truths;
second, having entered the clear realization of the noble truths, being free from all obstacles.
Third, having already entered the clear realization of the noble truths,
one attends to joyful matters with the intention of attaining swift supernormal knowledge.
Fourth, one cultivates the path as it has been attained.
Fifth, the merit of attaining the path and its fruit of supreme purity.
How does one enter the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the noble truths?
It refers to the community of disciples of the Tathāgata.
Having well cultivated worldly purity,
he knows that throughout the long night his mind has been accumulated by means of the five sublime sensual pleasures,
and that his mind has been nourished by being sustained by food.
Because they give rise to attachment and delight toward those various desires,
they perceive the faults of those desires deeply,
and perceive the quality of tranquility in the superior, sublime states.
He is easily able to abide in the realm free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca-dhātu*),
that is, in the complete purity of all aspects within the world,
within the realm free from conceptual proliferation.
It is difficult to abide [therein],
namely, in the complete purity of the supramundane; therefore,
one dwells there with a sense of revulsion toward it.
It is not that they lack revulsion.
Furthermore, those who abide in the True Dharma [do so] within the realm of nirvāṇa,
which is free from conceptual proliferation.
The mind delights in abiding in happiness and desires to realize it;
yet, due to the lack of the predominant power of realizing the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*),
it remains associated with its own defilements (*saṃkleśa*).
A sense of wearying revulsion arises;
it is incompatible with one's own purity,
and a sense of wearying revulsion arises.
One gives rise to a sense of wearying revulsion toward the faults associated with one's own defilements,
and toward the faults of not being associated with one's own purification.
A sense of weary aversion arises in the mind;
one perceives that one's own purification is difficult to accomplish,
and a sense of weary aversion arises in the mind.
In this regard, there are briefly three types of association with affliction (*saṃkleśa*):
first, the association with the affliction of dying while undisciplined and unpliant;
second, the association with the affliction of falling into the great pit of defilements after death.
Third, by the power of mastery over those afflictions,
one performs various evil and unwholesome karmas,
proceeding toward states of fear and remaining associated with defilement.
He observes that his own person lacks the realization of the fruits of śrāmaṇya;
because of that lack, he finds himself associated with the three kinds of defilement.
Having observed this, a sense of weary revulsion arises in his mind.
It should be understood that there are also three aspects of purity that are not associated [with the mind].
First, the ultimate nirvana resulting from the severance of all afflictions is called the state free from fear.
Second, that which is able to realize this.
That is to say, based on the concentration of a virtuous mind belonging to the training in higher mind,
three [factors] can realize this;
and regarding the sublime noble path subsumed under right view belonging to the training in higher wisdom.
Because he observes that his own body is not in accord with these three kinds of purity,
weariness and aversion arise in his mind.
It should be understood that there are likewise three kinds of faults associated with the correspondence to defilement.
First, birth as the root of the suffering of old age, sickness, and death;
second, birth in an unfavorable state (akṣaṇa) by the nature of things;
third, the impermanent nature of birth in all places.
Observing that his own body possesses these three kinds of faults associated with defilement,
he gives rise to a sense of weary detachment.
It should be known that there are five kinds of faults associated with non-correspondence to purity.
First, birth in the borderlands has not yet been brought to rest;
second, birth in the evil realms has not yet been brought to rest;
third, the various deeds of immediate retribution among the householders have not yet been suppressed.
Fourth, they are not inconsistent with the immeasurable views and inclinations of the monastic community;
fifth, although they may reach even the Peak of Existence through the mundane path— whether by meditative concentration or rebirth—
they [remain aware] of the beginningless and endless cyclic flow of birth and death.
Not having reached the ultimate limit,
he observes that his own person possesses these five kinds of faults incompatible with purity,
and a sense of weary aversion arises in his mind.
Regarding the difficulty of accomplishing one's own purification,
it should be known that there are also five kinds.
First, if one abandons [the practice], one cannot accomplish it by oneself.
Second, because regarding other matters one cannot rely on others to accomplish them;

third, because it must be performed with determination—for if one does not purify one’s own mind, one will certainly fail to attain liberation from all suffering and achieve the nature of auspiciousness.
Fourth, it is not the case that one who does not currently engage in unwholesome karma is thereby said to have already accomplished purification; rather,
this is called having already attained, within the present life, the permanent departure from the blazing fire of afflictions through a path of non-antidote.
Because the evil and unwholesome karma previously created cannot possibly be destroyed;
and fifth, because it is manifested through the attainment of the paths of training and no-more-training (*śaikṣa* and *aśaikṣa*) which purify them—
this is the observation of purity.
Because these five aspects are difficult to accomplish,
weariness arises in the mind; yet,
one further initiates firm and steadfast diligence.
Desiring to realize that [state],
he gives rise to a sense of weary detachment through observing the association and dissociation of affliction and purification.
Furthermore, because one perceives the faults associated with the conjunction and disjunction of affliction and purification,
fear arises in the mind.
Moreover, regarding the realization of purification and the cessation of affliction:
Because of the presence of indolence and laziness,
the mind is obstructed;
furthermore, by means of mental attention and contemplation upon those signs, the mind gives rise to weariness and aversion.
Because one has extensively practiced with respect to these very signs,
the mind becomes utterly weary of them—
just as one who is weary and utterly weary [of them].
One should know that it is likewise for fear, extreme fear, restraint, and extreme restraint.
Thus, by means of the perception accompanied by revulsion, he [proceeds].
Because one attends to and contemplates these with twenty aspects across five locations,
it is called "thoroughly cultivated and purified."
Furthermore, there are five causes,
comprised of twenty aspects,
which cause one to dwell swiftly and frequently in the extinction of craving, the peace of *nirvāṇa*.
The mind neither regresses nor feels anxiety,
thinking, "Where am I now?
What are the five causes?
First, by means of the mental application of thorough penetration (*prativedha-manasikāra*);
that is to say, through such a mental application of thorough penetration,
one will immediately and inevitably enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-nyāma*).
One enters the clear realization of the truths and realizes the vision of noble wisdom.
Second, it is by way of the basis;
that is to say, by relying on this basis, one is immediately able to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth.
The rest is as previously explained.
Third, it is by way of entering the gateway of the objective field;
that is, by means of taking this as the gateway for entering the objective field.
One will certainly be able to enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth.
The rest is as previously explained.
Fourth, by means of gathering the accumulations.
That is to say, by means of this gathering of the provisions,
one will certainly be able to enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
The rest is as previously explained.
Fifth, by way of embracing the skillful means;
that is to say, by embracing such skillful means,
one will certainly be able to enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth.
...and so on, as explained at length.
These five causes should be understood as being taught according to the reverse order of the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*),
and not according to their direct order.
Based on the most excellent cause,
it is explained in reverse order according to the matters previously mentioned.
It refers to the mental state associated with the subtle manifestation of the conceit "I am" (asmimāna),
which operates intermittently or continuously during the application of attention that enters into the practices of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness.
Because it obstructs the correct thorough penetration of mental attention (*manasikāra*) regarding clear realization (*abhisamaya*);
once that has been thoroughly penetrated, within the spontaneous engagement of the mind accompanied by mental attention,
one is able to skillfully relinquish it so that it ceases without interval.
Based on the mind that has just ceased, one reflects upon it as it truly is through the modes of impermanence and so forth by means of a newly arisen attention;
because of the cultivation and repeated practice of this attention, [the path is realized].
The wisdom of the equality of the object and the subject arises;
at that time, the conceit of "I" which obstructs clear realization and disturbs the mind is forever severed and extinguished,
and one realizes one-pointedness of mind.
He then reflected to himself:
"I have realized one-pointedness of mind;
I know it as it truly is."
One should know that this is called entering the clear realization of the truths by means of the mental application of thorough penetration.
Furthermore, if one has previously attained samādhi through the mundane path, it shall also be brought to fulfillment.
He also attains mastery. He may,
with respect to the signs of entering samādhi— that is,
by means of which he enters samādhi— [exercise this mastery].
Either on the sign of abiding in samādhi—
meaning that by means of which one abides in samādhi—
or on the sign of emerging from samādhi.
That is to say, by means of this, one emerges from samādhi;
one directs the mind toward these various signs, stabilizes the mind therein,
and enters the clear realization of the truths (satyābhisamaya).
If one has attained samādhi but it is not yet perfected,
nor mastered, that person may contemplate the sign of calm abiding (śamatha-nimitta).
Either contemplating the sign of exertion or contemplating the sign of equanimity,
they settle the mind and enter the clear realization of the truths.
Thus, one should know that the mind abides by virtue of its basis.
Furthermore, there are two factors that constitute extreme obstacles to the cultivation of clear realization.
What are these two?
First, the mind is disturbed and lacks tranquility due to improper reflection;
second, the mind is inverted regarding the objects of knowledge.
To counteract such obstacles,
one should know that there are two ways of stabilizing the mind upon the object of focus; specifically,
this is for the purpose of counteracting the first obstacle.
One cultivates mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) as an antidote to the second hindrance,
and cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Thus it should be understood that by way of entering the gateway of the objective sphere, the mind becomes settled.
Furthermore, those who habitually indulge in the pleasures of the five sublime sensual desires do not range within the domain of the Noble Dharma and Vinaya.
If one gives rise to contentment with whatever robes, food and drink, and bedding and seating one happens to obtain as appropriate,
and with whatever gains and honors one may receive;
To subdue the mind by relying on the five sublime sensual pleasures,
rather than through the gains and honors one has obtained.
The mind then becomes firmly established.
By this cause and condition,
one remains far removed from all improper spheres of activity.
Having thus distanced himself [from distractions], relying upon the foundations of mindfulness, he delights in abandonment and delights in cultivation;
throughout the divisions of day and night, he repeatedly observes all matters concerning the decline and prosperity of both himself and others.
He gives rise to a sense of weary detachment.
Furthermore, he cultivates the recollection of the Buddha and other practices to purify his mind.
Moreover, he dwells securely within the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
Thus, one should understand that the mind abides through the provisions;
this is explained with reference to the supreme path of provisions.
Furthermore, once he has thus established himself in the accumulations,
there are two types of preparatory application for the sake of practicing the application of attention (*manasikāra*).
What are these two? First,
one personally studies, recites, receives, and upholds the sūtras and abhidharma,
and correctly practices mental attention (*manasikāra*).
One becomes highly skilled in the phenomena of the aggregates and so forth;
second, one relies on the teacher’s instruction,
namely, the Great Teacher.
The upādhyāya and ācārya shall,
from time to time, provide instruction, admonition, support, and formal reliance.
Furthermore, one should know that the mental attention of correct application is called the third skillful means;
this refers to the mental attention of correct application.
This is called "correct application.
The meaning herein refers to the mental engagement (*manasikāra*) associated with the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
This is called "correct preparatory application of mental attention," because he himself reflects upon the purity of his ethical discipline (*śīla*).
There is no regret or distress.
Because there is no regret or distress, joy arises.
To speak at length, up until:
the mind enters right meditative concentration.
For this reason, he proclaims this right preparatory application of mental attention.
This is called the skillful means for the mind to abide.
By means of such skillful means, the mind quickly becomes settled.
At that time, through these five causes and twenty aspects, he [attains stability].
He restrains his mind and causes it to dwell securely within the realm of nirvana, which is the extinction of craving and utter tranquility.
Without further regression and with a mind free from alarm or fear—
thinking, "Where am I now?"— one should cause the mind to abide in such a state.
One should know that this is already called "entry into the clear observation of the truths" (*satyābhisamaya*).
Thus is what is meant by "entry into the clear observation of the noble truths.
Furthermore, the meaning of this clear observation of the noble truths should be understood as explained at length.
That is to say, there are twenty aspects of the mind’s weariness with [conditioned] phenomena,
and twenty aspects of the mind’s stable abiding;
beyond these, there are neither more nor fewer.
How does one enter the clear realization of the noble truths and become free from all obstacles?
It should be known that these obstacles are, in brief, of two kinds:
first, the obstacle to the sphere of practice (*gocara*).
Second is the obstacle to the dwelling place.
Regarding the obstacle to the sphere of practice:
it refers, for example, to when a noble disciple dwells together with a community.
Whenever monastic duties arise,
he abandons the cultivation of wholesome qualities and frequently joins the assemblies;
or else, while maintaining the practice of constant alms-seeking, he becomes attached to and values fine food and drink.
Or they may engage in both places simultaneously,
delighting in activities such as preparing robes and alms bowls,
or for the sake of reciting the scriptures, delighting in idle conversation.
Some, dwelling during the night, delight in attachment to sleep;
some, dwelling during the day, delight in defiled discourse concerning kings, thieves, and the like;
or they dwell in places where there is the presence of relatives, friends, and idle chatter.
Yet, in this situation, one does not delight in seclusion;
that is to say, due to the predominant power of having repeatedly practiced dwelling together with them throughout the long night,
or because one instead delights in dwelling together with a second person.
These and others like them are called obstacles to the sphere of practice (*caryā-vibandha*).
As for obstacles to the place of residence (*sthāna-vibandha*),
this refers to practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* in a secluded location.
This is collectively termed "abiding.
Based on śamatha and vipaśyanā,
one should know that there are furthermore four kinds of obstacles.
First, the state of non-conformity with the factors of vipaśyanā;
second, the state of non-conformity with the factors of śamatha;
third, the state of non-conformity with the mindfulness associated with both.
Fourth is the nature of non-conformity with the proper locus.
This refers to one who, considering themselves clever,
gives rise to arrogance and does not hear the true Dharma from others nor contemplate it accordingly.
This is called the non-conformity of the factors of vipaśyanā.
It refers to when one’s conduct of body, speech, and mind is not tranquil;
being restless, fickle, and frequently violating the śīla, one gives rise to worry, regret, and so forth.
Up to the point where the mind cannot attain a state of wholesome stability,
one should know that this is called the non-conformity with the factors of śamatha.
This occurs when there is the predominant force of forgetfulness.
One should know that failing to guard the mind against secondary afflictions such as lethargy and agitation is termed the non-conformity of mindfulness with its associated factors. Furthermore,
if one habitually resorts to seats and bedding that are associated with the five faults, [this is also non-conformity].
One should know that this is called a location that does not accord with one's nature.
Alternatively, it may be that during the day there is much clamor and distraction,
and during the night one is afflicted by many sufferings such as contact with mosquitoes and gadflies.
Furthermore, it is full of terrors and many calamities;
resources are scarce and lack all that is delightful;
one is held fast by evil friends and lacks virtuous friends.
All such factors as these are called obstacles to the dwelling place.
Furthermore, it should be understood that there are two kinds of causes and conditions by which these two obstacles can be removed:
first, having much meditative bliss.

Second, regarding the abundance of analytical investigation (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) and the abundance of the bliss of meditative concentration (*samādhi-sukha*), it should be known that there are briefly six types.
That is to say, when one has already attained *samādhi* but it is not yet perfected and mastery has not been attained.
He should cultivate the three types of skillfulness— quiescence (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*),
and equanimity (*upekṣā*)— by means of which many forms of meditative bliss are produced.
If he has already attained perfection and mastery in samādhi, [he should apply these].
He should cultivate the three types of skillfulness regarding entering, abiding in, and emerging from meditative absorption.
From this, many forms of meditative bliss arise.
What is meant by "many forms of analytical discernment"?
That which is called superior, wholesome wisdom is termed "discernment" (pratisaṃkhyā). By means of this wisdom,
one understands as it truly is the increase of one's own wholesome qualities throughout the divisions of day and night.
He understands as it truly is the increase of unwholesome states;
he understands as it truly is the decline of wholesome states;
and he understands as it truly is the decline of unwholesome states.
Furthermore, just as with day and night,
whether walking or standing,
he cultivates familiarity with clothing, food and drink, and the requisites for life.
Due to such association,
unwholesome qualities increase and wholesome qualities decline;
or, wholesome qualities increase and unwholesome qualities decline.
He understands all these as they truly are.
Relying precisely upon this analytical discernment,
regarding those unwholesome states that have arisen:
By means of the principle of non-attachment to skillful means,
one expels and distances oneself from [unwholesome states] and is able to diligently cultivate all wholesome dharmas; such are the ten types of skillfulness regarding these two bases.
In these two locations, one is able to sever the eleven kinds of hindrances;
as soon as they arise, one immediately distances oneself from them.
This is what is called "distancing oneself from obstacles."
Furthermore, this meaning of being far removed from hindrances should be understood in detail according to the characteristics as they have been described;
beyond this, there is nothing further, neither exceeding nor adding to it.
How is it that, having entered the clear observation of the noble truths,
one attends to and contemplates joyful matters in order to realize swift super-knowledge?
This refers to a noble disciple who has already seen the Noble Truths and attained verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*).
Relying precisely upon that verified confidence,
they direct their attention toward the field of supreme merit consisting of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, thereby generating joy.
Furthermore, based on matters of one's own higher rebirth and matters of definitive excellence—
that is, the prosperity realized through one's own body and wealth—
one attends to them with mental attention, thereby generating joy.
Furthermore, based on being free from envy,
one treats others exactly as one treats oneself;
furthermore, based on recognizing kindness.
That is to say, regarding those who have been kind,
one recollects the kindness of the Great Master, attends to it with mental attention,
and thereby gives rise to joy.
By relying upon that,
one distances oneself from all suffering and its causes,
and brings forth all happiness and its causes.
Because such reflection accords with the joyful matters of the path of cultivation,
one is able to realize swift superknowledge (*abhijñā*).
Furthermore, this reflection accords with the meaning of the joyful matters of the path of cultivation.
The detailed exposition should be understood according to the characteristics as described;
beyond this, there is nothing further, neither exceeding nor adding to it.
How does one cultivate the path as it has been attained?
That is to say, his mind is irrigated by such vast and blameless joy as has arisen;
and for the sake of reaching the ultimate, his heart yearns intensely within this present life.
Through such a mind of longing and yearning,
he repeatedly manifests the desire for renunciation,
thinking: "When shall I be able to dwell fully perfected in such a noble state?"
Just as an arhat dwells in full possession [of his qualities],
so too, having given rise to such a desire and aspiration,
he exerts diligent effort that is uninterrupted, constant, and resolute.
He applies himself with skillful means to the diligent cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Furthermore, because he exerts such diligence,
he does not dwell in association with either householders or those who have gone forth.
He frequents remote lodgings for sitting and reclining,
delighting his mind in seclusion;
furthermore, he thus generates a longing and aspiration for it.
Having aroused diligent effort and taken delight in seclusion,
one does not give rise to complacency regarding a small measure of superior realization.
The mind is never content;
it dwells in the aspiration for all wholesome dharmas that are increasingly superior, increasingly excellent, and increasingly subtle.
By means of these four factors, one embraces the cultivation of the path.
It is thoroughly and skillfully embraced;
that is, based upon these four kinds of cultivation of the path,
there arises joy from the various joyful matters previously described.
At that time, he has cultivated and perfected the principle of the most extreme attenuation of afflictions;
because his afflictions have been severed,
he has attained the distinguished state of realized Dharma.
Furthermore, it causes joy to be cultivated to perfection.
Moreover, because the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) associated with the categories of afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation has been removed,
one attains pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
Due to pliancy,
there arises a refreshing coolness of body and mind,
which is intensely embraced.
In this way, these two types of cultivation reach fulfillment.
Furthermore, because this learner’s diamond-like concentration has reached its ultimate limit,
its cultivation reaches fulfillment.
This is called the cultivation of the path as it has been attained.
Furthermore, the meaning of this cultivation of the path as it has been attained should be understood through its detailed exposition.
This means that by relying upon four kinds of dharmas,
one is able to bring five dharmas to the perfection of cultivation;
beyond these, there is nothing further, neither exceeding nor adding to them.
How does one realize the merit of the extremely pure path and its fruition?
It is said: within the three states—the state of pleasure, the state of suffering, and the state of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
There are two types of persons (*pudgala*) who are predominantly characterized by being under the influence of latent afflictions (*anuśaya*):
the first is the ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjana*).
The second is those in training (*śaikṣa*).
Furthermore, there are two types that can give rise to the category of affliction (*saṃkleśapakṣa*):
first, grasping at the category of affliction; [and second, ...].
Second is the category of affliction regarding conduct;
it is for the sake of severing these two categories of affliction that one enters the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
All those afflictions capable of acting as obstacles function as latent tendencies (*anuśaya*),
penetrating deeply into the mind.
Furthermore, it can give rise to various kinds of suffering;
if one can permanently sever this without remainder,
it is called attaining the fruit of the utterly pure path.
Furthermore, there are the five aggregates of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-skandha) subsumed within the ten branches of one beyond training,
namely: the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīla-skandha) and the aggregate of meditative concentration (samādhi-skandha).
The aggregate of wisdom,
the aggregate of liberation,
and liberation.
The aggregate of knowledge and vision is called the path of supreme purity.
Furthermore, it is by virtue of realizing this path of supreme purity that [one attains liberation].
Abiding free from the ten faults, one dwells in the abode of the noble ones.
What are called the ten kinds of faults?
They are as follows: all lamentation and grief based upon external sensual desires.
Sorrow and suffering;
various forms of affliction and disturbance;
and the faults associated with the suffering of suffering.
Furthermore, there is the fault of failing to guard the internal sense faculties;
because one does not guard the sense faculties,
sorrow, lamentation, and so forth arise.
Furthermore, there is the fault of dwelling in attachment to the savor of pleasure;
furthermore, there is the fault of negligence in conduct;
furthermore, there are the verbal expressions arising from the distinct and individual false views that are unique to non-Buddhists.
One investigates and pursues three kinds of faults;
furthermore, there are faults based on the limits of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Furthermore, there is the fault of initiating the category of affliction consisting of grasping (*upādāna*) as subsumed under dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*);
and there is the fault of initiating the category of affliction consisting of formative activities (*saṃskāra*).
If one is forever dissociated from these ten kinds of faults:
It is sustained only by the final body;
no other subsequent body will ever arise again within the most tranquil realm of nirvana.
Abiding ultimately,
among all sentient beings— even those who have ascended as far as the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra)— he becomes the most supreme among them all.

Therefore, it is called "dwelling in the dwelling of the noble ones," because one is able to remain far removed from the ten kinds of faults and can securely abide in the dwelling place of the noble ones.
It is called "merit.
Furthermore, whether it be that fruit, that path of extreme purity, or those merits—
all such things taken together are briefly termed the "attainment of the merit of the extremely pure path and its fruit."
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of this realization of the extremely pure path and its resultant qualities,
it should be understood in detail according to the characteristics as they have been described;
beyond this, there is nothing further, neither exceeding nor surpassing them.
If one attains such supreme dharmas of those beyond training (aśaikṣa),
the mind associated with such noble dharmas will feel extreme revulsion toward the five exquisite sensual pleasures.
Because it lacks maturation (*vipāka*), it does not continue further thereafter.
Even if a worldly mind has already been severed, it may still manifest;
however, at a later time, it ceases spontaneously.
Furthermore, the path of karma that leads to future existence, which follows the path of afflictions,
has already been permanently severed within this present life.
Because it has been severed, the path of suffering in the future will no longer recur.
Because this cause and effect are forever extinguished,
it is called the "end of suffering.
There is nothing further beyond it— nothing higher or more supreme.
In this context, it refers to entering the clear realization of the noble truths,
being free from hindrances,
and for the sake of attaining swift super-knowledge.
One attends to and contemplates various joyful matters:
whether it be the cultivation of the path as attained,
or the realization of the extremely pure path and its resultant qualities.
This is called the supramundane purity in all its aspects.
Furthermore, the meaning of this supramundane purity in all its aspects should be understood as it has been explained at length according to the characteristics described.
Beyond this, there is nothing further, neither superior nor additional.
Thus, whether it be the aforementioned mundane purification in all its aspects,
or this aforementioned supramundane purification in all its aspects.
That which has been explained:
namely, the cultivation of the basis, the cultivation of the causal conditions,
the cultivation of yoga, and the cultivation of the fruit.
All these are collectively termed the Stage Accomplished through Cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-bhūmi*).
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 20.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 21.

The Stage of the Lineage, the First Part of the Initial Yoga Station within the Stage of the Śrāvakas, the Thirteenth [Stage] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva and translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Thus has been explained the stage consisting of that which is cultivated through meditation (*bhāvanā-mayī-bhūmi*).
What is the Śrāvaka-bhūmi?
The summary verse (uddāna) for the entire Śrāvaka-bhūmi states:
To speak briefly of this stage, it concerns the lineage (gotra) and so forth of the person (pudgala).
Established according to their respective natures, these stages—mundane and supramundane—are briefly of three kinds:
namely, the stage of lineage, the stage of entry, and the stage of departure from conceptualization;
these are called the levels of the śrāvakas.
What is the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhūmi*)?
To state it in brief, the summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
"In brief, one should know that all [stages] are the stage of the lineage."
That is to say: the intrinsic nature of the establishment [of the lineage], and the various characteristics of the person (pudgala)—
namely, the intrinsic nature of the lineage and the establishment of the lineage.
All the characteristics belonging to one who abides in the lineage,
as well as the person (pudgala) who abides in the lineage—
all such things are collectively and briefly designated by the single name "the stage of the lineage" (gotrabhūmi).
Because there exists a seed-dharma by virtue of its actual presence,
a person (pudgala) abides in their spiritual lineage (gotra).
If one encounters superior conditions, there is then capability and there is then power;
thus, one is able to attain and realize nirvāṇa.
Question: What are the distinctions between these types of lineages?
Answer: It is called "seed" (bīja), or it is called "element" (dhātu), or it is called "nature" (gotra);
these are its distinctions.
Question: Now, what constitutes the essence (svabhāva) of this lineage?
Answer: It is attached to its basis and possesses such characteristics;
it is comprised within the six sense bases, transmitted successively from beginningless time, and obtained through the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
In this regard, distinct designations are established;
namely, lineage (*gotra*), seed (*bīja*), element (*dhātu*), and nature (*prakṛti*).
These are called "lineage."
How is the lineage established?
One should ask:
"Is this lineage to be described as subtle, or is it to be described as coarse?"
One should answer that it is subtle. Why?
Because this seed has not yet been able to yield its fruit and has not yet habituated the fruit; therefore, it is called subtle.
If the fruit has already been bestowed and the cultivation of the fruit has already been accomplished,
then at that time, both the lineage, whether as seed or as fruit, are said to be coarse.
This is the continuity.
Answer: It should be said that they fall within a single continuum. Why is this?
Because if dharmas possess distinct characteristics yet arise and function simultaneously.
One observes their respective and various continuities and various modes of evolution.
Thus, these seeds do not possess distinct characteristics within the six sense bases;
rather, they exist as a specific excellence of the six sense bases within such a particular state.
Transmitted through successive generations from beginningless time, it is acquired by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*).
There exist such conceptions and verbal expressions as "lineage," "seed," "element" (*dhātu*), and "nature."
Therefore, it should be said that they fall into a single continuum.
A person (pudgala) of such a lineage possesses the dharma of nirvāṇa;
this person who abides in the lineage possesses the dharma of nirvāṇa.
For what reason is there the dharma of nirvāṇa, yet [beings] have been wandering for a long time since the beginningless past without entering parinirvāṇa?
Answer: For four reasons they do not enter parinirvāṇa.
What are the four?
First, being born in an unfavorable state;
second, the fault of negligence.
Third, because of wrong practice;
fourth, because of the fault of obstacles.
How does one give rise to the states of no leisure?
That is to say, there are those born in border regions or among the *ḍomba* and *mleccha*,
where the fourfold assembly of the virtuous, the noble, and the true persons do not travel.
This is called being born in an unfavorable state.
What is the fault of negligence?
It refers to someone who, although born in a central land, is neither a Dasyu nor a Mleccha.
The fourfold assembly of the virtuous, noble, upright, and excellent persons all frequent it;
having been born into a noble family with abundant wealth and treasures,
they become deeply attached to and indulge in various exquisite sensual pleasures.
Not seeing faults and not knowing the way of escape—
this is called the fault of negligence.
What is wrong practice?
That is to say, for example, there is one who, although born in a central land—
and so forth, as extensively described— possesses various evil views of non-Buddhists;
that is, they give rise to such views and establish such doctrines.
There is no giving; [this is] explained at length up until: "I myself know that there are no further states of existence.
Furthermore, due to such views of these non-Buddhists, they do not encounter the appearance of Buddhas in the world.
To lack virtuous friends who preach the true Dharma is called "wrong practice.
What is the fault of having obstacles?
That is to say, there is someone who, though born in a central land—
as described in detail previously— also encounters the appearance of Buddhas in the world and meets virtuous friends who proclaim the true Dharma.
Furthermore, his nature was dull, stubborn, and ignorant;
moreover, he was mute and communicated by means of gestures with his hands,
lacking the power to comprehend the meaning of the teachings, whether they were well-spoken or ill-spoken.
Furthermore, to have committed various deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*),
or to have given rise to various afflictions (*kleśa*) for a long period of time—
this is called the fault of having obstructions.
These are called the four kinds of causes and conditions.
Due to these causes and conditions, although they possess the nature for parinirvāṇa, they do not attain parinirvāṇa.
However, if they should encounter the appearance of Buddhas in the world and hear the true Dharma, [they will attain it].
Having obtained instructions and admonitions that are conducive [to liberation],
and lacking no causal conditions for them, one's roots of virtue can then reach maturity,
gradually leading even to the attainment of parinirvāṇa.
The person who lacks the nature for parinirvāṇa abides in the fixed group;
whether they encounter favorable conditions or do not encounter them,
they are ultimately incapable of attaining parinirvāṇa in every respect.
Regarding the condition of the dharma of nirvāṇa, it is said that because of its absence, its non-existence, or the failure to encounter it, one does not attain parinirvāṇa.
The answer is: there are two kinds of conditions.
What are the two? First, the superior; second, the inferior.
What is the superior condition?
It refers to the voice of another concerning the sublime Dharma as a predominant condition,
and internal appropriate attention.
What are the inferior conditions?
That is to say, these inferior conditions are of many kinds:
namely, the perfection of oneself, the perfection of others,
and the desire for wholesome qualities.
Whether it be the formal going forth,
the restraint of the precepts,
or the restraint of the sense faculties.
