If one knows moderation in eating;
if one constantly and diligently practices the yoga of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night;
and if one dwells in clear comprehension.
If one delights in seclusion,
if one purifies the hindrances, or if one relies upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
[one attains] a human body.
Born in a noble place,
with unimpaired faculties,
and possessing supreme faith in the sublime realm.
Free from all karmic obstructions.
What is meant by "having successfully obtained a human body"?
It refers, for example, to someone who has been born with the common lot of humanity.
To obtain a male body with the male organ fully developed,
or to obtain a female body—
this is called having successfully attained a human body.
What is meant by being born in a noble land?
It refers to someone who is born in a central region, as explained in detail previously,
such that even virtuous persons all frequent and travel there.
This is called being born in a noble place.
What is meant by having no deficiency in the faculties?
It refers to one who, by nature, is not dull-witted.
Nor is he dull-witted or mute;
and so on, as explained at length, his limbs and joints are not deficient.
It is by virtue of such completeness of limbs and joints, and the absence of defects in his ears and so forth, that [he attains this].
Being able to diligently cultivate and accumulate virtuous qualities—
this is called having no deficiency in the faculties.
What is meant by "supreme confidence in the bases of mastery"?
That is to say, there is someone who attains pure faith in the Dharma and Vinaya rightly awakened to by the Tathāgatas;
this is called "pure faith in the superior bases."
Regarding the term "superior bases" (abhibhvāyatana):
it refers to the Dharma-Vinaya taught by the Tathāgatas who have attained perfect enlightenment,
for it is capable of generating all pure and white dharmas of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
The pure faith that arises herein, preceded and dominated by these preliminary practices,
is called "supreme confidence" (*adhimukti*),
because it is capable of removing all stains, impurities, and turbidity of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
What is meant by being free from all karmic obstructions?
It refers to being able to remain far removed from the five deeds of immediate retribution:
namely, harming one's mother, harming one's father, harming an arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and with a malicious mind drawing blood from the body of a Tathāgata.
Not committing or performing any of the various immediate karmic obstructions (*ānantarya-karma-āvaraṇa*) in this present life—
this is called being free from all karmic obstructions.
If one has committed and accumulated these five deeds of immediate retribution,
one will ultimately be unable to turn back from them in this present life, nor attain parinirvāṇa by giving rise to the noble path.
Therefore, summarizing that teaching, one is said to be free from all karmic obstructions;
because one’s own being is perfected solely through these five factors,
this is called "perfection of self."
What is the perfection of others?
It refers to the appearance of Buddhas in the world and their teaching of the true Dharma.
The teaching of the Dharma shall endure for a long time;
the Dharma will remain and continue to evolve,
being cherished by others.
What is meant by "the appearance of the Buddhas in the world"?
It refers to when there is one who, toward all classes of sentient beings,
gives rise to a superior intention for their universal benefit and welfare.
Having practiced thousands of difficult and painful asceticisms over three great incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*),
he accumulated the vast twofold provisions of merit and wisdom.
Having attained the final and most sublime body,
he sat upon the unsurpassed and supreme seat of enlightenment and severed the five hindrances.
With his mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness,
he cultivated the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.
This is what is called the appearance of the Buddhas in the world.
All Buddhas of the past, future,
and present appear in the world by means of this very [method].
What is called the teaching of the True Dharma?
It refers to the appearance in the world of these Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, out of compassion for all śrāvakas.
Based on the Four Noble Truths, he proclaimed the immeasurable teachings of the Dharma regarding the reality of suffering, its origin, its cessation,
and the path. These are known as the sūtras and the geyas.
Prophecies, verses, spontaneous utterances,
accounts of causes and conditions,
parables, and past events.
Jātaka, Vaipulya, Adbhutadharma, and Upadeśa—
these are called the teachings of the True Dharma.
All the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones,
as well as their noble disciples and all true persons, have attained liberation by riding upon this Dharma;
thereafter, they proclaim and praise it for the sake of others.
Therefore, this is called the proclamation of the True Dharma;
for this reason, it is called the teaching of the True Dharma.
What is meant by the long endurance of the teaching of the Dharma?
That is to say, from the time he had taught the true Dharma and turned the wheel of Dharma,
until the Blessed One’s lifespan had long endured,
and for such a period of time following his parinirvāṇa.
When right practice has not yet declined and the true Dharma has not yet vanished,
this is called the long endurance of the true Dharma.
One should understand that such long endurance refers to the principle of realizing the ultimate true Dharma.
What is meant by "the persistence and conformity of the Dharma"?
It refers to one who has thus realized the True Dharma,
and who understands that there are sentient beings capable of realizing such a True Dharma.
That is to say, it is the instruction and admonition that accords with and conforms to what has been realized;
this is called "conforming to the stability of the Dharma" (*dharmasthitinisyanda*). What is meant by "being pitied by others"?
He says to the donor:
"Out of compassion for me, the practitioner,
you have bestowed these requisites for a pure livelihood that are conducive [to my practice]."
That which consists of robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicinal requisites for the treatment of illness in accordance with the Dharma—
this is called being "compassionately cared for by others.
What is the "desire for wholesome qualities" (kuśala-dharma-chanda)?
That is to say, there is someone who, having heard the true Dharma from either the Buddha or his disciples, attains pure faith;
having attained pure faith, they should train themselves in this way.
Living at home is as vexing and turbulent as dwelling within a dusty world;
leaving the home life is as spacious and serene as abiding in empty space.
Therefore, I should now renounce all wives, children, kinsmen, wealth, grain, and precious treasures.
Within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
he rightly renounces the household life to go forth into homelessness;
having gone forth, he diligently practices the correct conduct until it is brought to perfection.
The arising of such a desire for wholesome qualities is called "desire for wholesome qualities" (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*).
What is "right renunciation"?
It refers to that which occurs precisely through the predominant power of this superior desire for wholesome qualities.
Receiving the full ordination through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, or receiving the training in the morality (*śīla*) of the ascetic life—this is called "rightly going forth.
What is the restraint of morality? It refers to that which follows once one has thus rightly gone forth.
Abiding securely in the full precepts with firm protection,
he brings to perfection the rules of conduct and the observances of the Prātimokṣa discipline;
regarding even the slightest transgression, he perceives great fear.
To train in all the precepts that exist is called the restraint of morality (*śīla-saṃvara*).
What is the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*)?
That is to say, based precisely upon this ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*),
one guards right mindfulness and cultivates constant and diligent mindfulness;
using mindfulness to protect the mind, one abides in a state of equanimity.
Having seen forms with the eye, one does not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics,
fearing that by dwelling without having cultivated the restraint of the eye faculty, the mind would become unprotected in reliance upon such a basis.
Because they would leak out all covetousness, grief, and evil, unwholesome states,
one therefore practices restraint regarding those very objects and guards the faculty of the eye;
one practices restraint regarding the faculty of the eye by relying upon it.
In this way, when a practitioner has heard sounds with the ear, smelled odors with the nose, tasted flavors with the tongue, felt tangibles with the body, or cognized mental phenomena with the mind,
they do not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics.
I fear that by not dwelling with the mind protected through the cultivation of restraint over the mental faculty (*manaindriya-saṃvara*),
all covetousness, grief, and evil unwholesome states will leak forth from it.
Therefore, one cultivates the practice of restraint regarding that very [object], guarding the faculty of the mind;
by relying upon the faculty of the mind, one cultivates the practice of restraint—
this is called "restraint of the faculties" (*indriya-saṃvara*).
What is moderation in food?
It means that having thus guarded the sense faculties,
one eats what is consumed with right discernment.
He does not eat for the sake of indulgence or for the sake of pride and negligence;
he does not eat for the sake of beautification or for the sake of physical splendor.
He eats what is to be eaten, eating that which is to be eaten only for the sake of the body’s maintenance and for its temporary support.
It is for the removal of hunger and thirst; for the undertaking of the holy life; for the cessation of existing sensations; so that new sensations may not arise;
and for the sake of maintaining strength, happiness, blamelessness, and dwelling in peace.
This is called moderation in eating.
What is the constant and diligent practice of the yoga of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night?
It means that, having thus practiced moderation in eating, [he applies himself].
During the daytime, he purifies his mind from obstructive states through the two modes of conduct: walking meditation and sitting meditation.
During the first watch of the night, he likewise practices walking meditation and sitting meditation.
Having purified his mind by means of the factors conducive to the removal of obstacles,
and having passed beyond this stage, he goes outside his dwelling and washes his feet.
He then lies down on his right side with one foot upon the other, maintaining the perception of light.
With right mindfulness and clear comprehension, one should attend to the thought of rising;
in the latter part of the night, one should quickly awaken and practice the two modes of deportment: walking meditation and sitting in seclusion.
He purifies his mind by means of those factors that are conducive to the removal of hindrances.
This is called constantly and diligently practicing the yoga of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night.
What is dwelling with clear comprehension?
That is to say, having thus constantly and diligently practiced the yoga of wakefulness,
he dwells with clear comprehension whether going or coming,
and dwells with clear comprehension whether looking ahead or looking aside.
Whether bending or stretching, he dwells with clear comprehension.
Whether wearing the saṃghāṭī robe or carrying the bowl and robes, he dwells with clear comprehension.
Whether eating, drinking, chewing, or tasting, he dwells with clear comprehension.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he dwells with clear comprehension;
while awake, he dwells with clear comprehension;
whether speaking or remaining silent, he dwells with clear comprehension.
Just as when one is dispelling fatigue and sleep, one dwells with clear comprehension;
this is called dwelling with clear comprehension.
What is delighting in seclusion?
That is to say, having correctly cultivated and refined the stage of a beginner through such well-practiced wholesome dharmas,
one becomes free from all attachment to bedding and requisites.
Dwelling in forest hermitages,
at the foot of trees, in empty rooms,
in mountain valleys, on mountain peaks, or in caves.
Grass-thatched huts stand exposed in the distance;
among burial mounds lie forests and thickets;
vast and desolate are the level plains.
Using bedding at the edge [of the monastery] is called delighting in seclusion.
How does one purify the hindrances?
That is to say, dwelling thus in an araṇya, or at the foot of a tree, or in an empty dwelling,
he purifies his mind of the five hindrances:
namely, the hindrance of sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
Having purified the mind from those hindrances,
the mind dwells free from all hindrances in a noble and excellent samādhi;
this is called the purification of the hindrances.
What is reliance upon samādhi?
It means that having thus abandoned the five hindrances,
one is then able to distance oneself from the secondary afflictions that follow the mind.
Distant from all desires and unwholesome states,
with directed thought and sustained evaluation,
he enters and dwells, having attained, in the first dhyāna born of seclusion, accompanied by joy and bliss.
With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is characterized by internal clarity and mental unification,
free from applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and bliss born of concentration.
Dwelling detached from joy and greed, one abides in equanimity and mindfulness,
experiencing happiness with clear comprehension;
this is what the Noble Ones describe as dwelling in bliss, endowed with equanimity and mindfulness.
He fully attains and dwells in the third dhyāna,
having utterly abandoned pleasure and previously abandoned pain.
With the fading away of both joy and sorrow, and with the disappearance of previous pleasure and pain,
he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
This is called the basis for the samādhi that transforms and further cultivates all conditions.
Beginning with the fulfillment of one's own [qualities] and culminating in samādhi,
one attains such purity and clarity of mind,
free from all blemishes and impurities.
Free from secondary afflictions,
being upright, capable, and abiding immovably; furthermore,
having attained that which relies upon the four noble truths for the sake of full comprehension, permanent abandonment, and realization.
By cultivating the instructions and admonitions received from others,
one gains such capacity and power as to give rise to attention that is properly induced.
And with that right view as its precursor,
one is thereby able to enter into the true direct realization of the Four Noble Truths and achieve perfect liberation.
He attains parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder;
he is liberated,
attaining parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
This is called the true cultivation and accumulation of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
From the perfection of one's own [resources] up to the final reliance upon *samādhi*,
it should be known that this is called the cultivation and accumulation of inferior conditions.
If one relies upon the external voice of instruction and admonition regarding the Dharma-teachings of the Four Noble Truths as a dominant influence,
or if one engages in mental attention (manasikāra) induced by correct reasoning,
it should be known that these are called the cultivation of superior conditions; this is what is termed the "establishment of the spiritual lineage" (gotra-vyavasthāna).
One should know that the characteristics of a person destined for nirvāṇa (parinirvāṇadharman-pudgala),
which are the opposites of [the characteristics of one not destined for it], are precisely the characteristics possessed by a person who abides in the lineage (gotrastha-pudgala).
These are the characteristics possessed by a person destined for nirvāṇa.
Because these [characteristics] are established, one should know that such a person is designated as an individual lacking the nature for parinirvāṇa.
Answer: There are many characteristics of an individual lacking the nature for parinirvāṇa.
I shall now briefly explain their characteristics:

namely, that from the very beginning, those individuals (pudgala) who do not abide in the spiritual lineage and lack the nature for parinirvāṇa possess a craving for the ālayavijñāna in all its aspects.
All are bound and attached to their respective bases;
they constitute immeasurable phenomena that cannot be overturned or uprooted.
Following them for a long duration, they are ultimately firm, adhering in a continuous succession.
They cannot be saved by any of the Buddhas;
this is called the first non-abiding lineage,
the characteristic of a person (pudgala) who lacks the spiritual lineage (agotra).
Furthermore, there are other signs of the lack of lineage in a person who does not abide in the lineage:
namely, when they hear the many faults of saṃsāra being censured through immeasurable methods.
Furthermore, although they hear the praises of the manifold virtues of nirvāṇa through immeasurable gateways,
they do not perceive even the slightest fault of conceptual proliferation within saṃsāra.
One does not perceive even the slightest portion of its faults and perils,
nor is one able to feel even the slightest degree of weary detachment.
Thus, having seen and become weary of it, one was unable to bring about its cessation in the past.
It cannot arise in the future;
it cannot arise correctly in the present;
furthermore, it [does not lead] to the extinction of craving, which is the peace of nirvāṇa.
One does not perceive even a slight portion of inferior merit;
one does not perceive even a slight portion of any benefit;
nor is one able to feel even a slight degree of joyful interest.
Thus, one who views [existence] as pleasant cannot have already produced [craving] in the past,
cannot produce it in the future,
and cannot correctly produce it in the present.
This is called the second characteristic of the lack of lineage in a person who does not abide in the lineage.
Furthermore, there are other characteristics of the lack of lineage in a person who does not abide in the lineage.
That is to say, they are by nature endowed with a superior degree of lack of shame and lack of dread;
for this reason, they feel no sense of revulsion and have no fear or timidity,
but proceed to commit various evils with a joyful mind.
Due to these causes and conditions, they never feel regret and contemplate only the present life.
Because of these causes and conditions, there is the fault of the decline of their own person and wealth.
This is called the third mark of a person lacking the lineage who does not abide in the lineage.
Furthermore, there are other signs of the lack of lineage (agotra) in persons who do not abide in a spiritual lineage,
which are complete in every respect, distinct, and consistent with reason.
It is exquisite, sublime, and easy to understand;
it may be based on the truth of suffering or based on the truth of the origin [of suffering].
When he proclaims and reveals the teaching of the True Dharma based either on the Truth of Cessation or the Truth of the Path.
They are unable to attain even a slight resolve or a slight conviction;
how much less could they attain such a state that their body hairs stand on end and they weep with falling tears?
This is likewise distinguished according to the past, future, and present times.
This is called the fourth characteristic of the lack of lineage in a person who does not abide in a spiritual lineage.
Furthermore, there are other characteristics of the lack of lineage in a person who does not abide in a spiritual lineage.
That is to say, they may at some time temporarily go forth into homelessness within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
either because they are oppressed by a king or because they are oppressed by mad bandits.
Either because they are oppressed by creditors,
or because they are oppressed by fear,
or because they are oppressed by the fear of being unable to survive.
It is not for the sake of self-subduing,
not for the sake of self-pacifying,
and not for the sake of one's own nirvana.
It is not for the sake of the nature of a śramaṇa,
nor for the sake of the nature of a brāhmaṇa,
that one seeks to go forth into homelessness.
Having gone forth, he delights in dwelling in close association with both householders and those who have gone forth;
or he practices the holy life with perverse aspirations,
namely, seeking rebirth in the heavens or other celestial realms.
Some take pleasure in abandoning the precepts they have undertaken or violate the *śīla*;
inwardly rotten yet outwardly appearing genuine,
they are like water-born creatures, foul-smelling snails, those with the voice of a conch, or those who act like dogs.
In truth, they are not śramaṇas,
yet they call themselves śramaṇas;
they do not practice the holy life, yet they claim to practice the holy life.

In this way, one should understand that such individuals who do not abide in the spiritual lineage (agotra) go forth under a mere semblance of ordination, distinguished according to the past, future, and present times.
A person who does not delight in training is not called one who has truly gone forth;
they have not received full ordination and do not possess the nature of a bhikṣu.
It is by this alternative formulation and this underlying intention that the meaning is revealed regarding them.
This person is not truly a renunciant;
they merely possess the outward appearance of a renunciant and are thus counted among the ranks of renunciants.
This is called the fifth characteristic of a person lacking the lineage (*agotraka*), namely, one who does not abide in the lineage.
Furthermore, there are other signs of the lack of lineage (agotra) in a person who does not abide in a spiritual lineage:
namely, that they perform only a small amount of wholesome action,
whether by way of body, speech, or mind.
All of these are sought for the sake of existence:
either seeking a superior future existence,
or seeking wealth and treasures.
Or they seek all manner of extraordinary wealth and treasures;
this is called the sixth mark of a person lacking the lineage who does not abide in a lineage.
There are many such marks of this kind.
Because they have accomplished that, they fall into the category of those whose nature is not to attain parinirvāṇa.
What is a person who abides in the lineage?
It refers to a person who dwells in the lineage.
There are those who abide solely in the lineage (gotra) without having entered it or yet having emerged from it;
and there are those who, while abiding in the lineage, have already entered it but have not yet emerged from it.
Some abide in the spiritual lineage and have both entered and emerged from it;
some possess dull faculties, some middling faculties, or some sharp faculties;
some are of a greedy temperament, some of a hateful temperament, or some of a deluded temperament.
Some are born in states of no leisure, while others are born in states of leisure;
some are heedless, while others are not heedless;
some engage in wrong conduct, while others do not engage in wrong conduct.
There may be obstructions or no obstructions;
they may be distant or near; they may be unripened or already ripened;
they may be unpurified or already purified.
Rāva abides solely within the spiritual lineage (gotra) but has neither entered nor emerged from it;
that is to say, there is a certain person (pudgala) who possesses the seeds of supramundane noble dharmas (lokottara-āryadharma).
Yet they have not yet encountered a virtuous friend to hear the true Dharma,
nor have they attained right faith in the Tathāgata’s perfectly awakened and correctly taught Dharma and Vinaya.
They have not yet undertaken the pure precepts;
they have not yet embraced extensive learning;
and they have not yet increased their wisdom and renunciation.
When the various views have not yet been made pliant,
such a person is called one who abides solely in the lineage (*gotra*) but has neither entered nor emerged [from it].
What is meant by a person who abides in the lineage, has already entered, but has not yet emerged?
It should be understood that the aforementioned white factors, which are the opposites of all black factors,
constitute what is called a person who both abides in the lineage and has already entered [the path].
As for the distinction:
it refers to those who have not yet attained any noble path or the fruit of the noble path that consists in the dissociation from afflictions.
What is meant by a person who both abides in the lineage and has already entered and already emerged?
It is as previously stated;
however, the distinction is that there is already the attainment of the noble path and its fruit, which is the dissociation from afflictions.
What is a person of dull faculties?
It refers to a person who, regarding the objects of knowledge as their focal domain, [is characterized by such qualities].
All the faculties that function extremely slowly or function weakly—
whether consisting of what is heard or what is reflected upon.
Or it is produced by cultivation and associated with mental attention;
that is to say, either the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, or the faculty of wisdom.
One who lacks the capacity and lacks the power to penetrate the meaning of the Dharma and swiftly realize the truth is called a person of dull faculties (mṛdv-indriya-pudgala).
What is a person of middling faculties (madhya-indriya-pudgala)?
This refers to a person whose faculties function slowly and with difficulty in relation to the objects of knowledge and their respective spheres of perception.
All should be explained in detail as before;
this is called the person of medium faculties.
What is the person of sharp faculties?
This refers to a person whose faculties,
with respect to the objects of knowledge and the spheres of perception, function neither sluggishly nor weakly.
Either accomplished through hearing,
or accomplished through reflection,
or accomplished through cultivation.
It is associated with mental attention (*manasikāra*),
meaning that through either the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, or the faculty of wisdom,
one becomes capable and possesses great power, thereby penetrating the meaning of the Dharma and swiftly realizing the truth.
This is called a person of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya-pudgala*).
What is a person of greedy temperament (*rāga-carita-pudgala*)?
It refers to a person such as this: [who possesses the following characteristics].

One who possesses intense greed and long-lasting greed for objects of perception that are attractive and capable of provoking attachment is called a person of greedy temperament (*rāgacarita-pudgala*).
What is a person of a hateful temperament?
It refers to such a person who,
with respect to an object of focus that is loathsome or provocative to anger, [acts accordingly].
One who possesses intense hatred and long-lasting hatred is called a person of hateful temperament (*dveṣacarita-pudgala*).
What is a person of deluded temperament?
It refers to a person who, with respect to the objects of knowledge and the spheres of perception, [is characterized by such a nature].
One who possesses intense delusion and long-lasting delusion is called a person of delusional temperament (*mohacarita*).
Such a person may be born in an unfavorable state (*akṣaṇa*).
Whether they are those who are heedless,
those who engage in misconduct,
or those who are obstructed individuals (pudgala).
All such cases should be understood as previously explained.
Conversely, one should know that the opposite constitutes being born in a state of leisure (*kṣaṇa*).
There is no indolence;
there is no misconduct;
there is no obstructed person (pudgala).
What is meant by a "distant person" (pudgala)?
It refers to such a person who,
because of the distance of time, is far from nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, there are those who are said to be "distant" because of the distance of their preparatory application (*prayoga*).
How is it that one is distant from nirvāṇa due to the distance of time?
It refers to such a person (*pudgala*) as follows:
After passing through many hundreds of births, many thousands of births, or many hundreds of thousands of births, one is finally able to encounter superior conditions and attain parinirvāṇa.
Why is it called "distant" because the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is distant? It is so named because the application of effort required to reach that goal is remote.
This refers to a person who merely abides in the spiritual lineage (gotra) but has not yet entered [the path],
and is unable to quickly encounter superior conditions to attain parinirvāṇa.
Because they have not yet been able to initiate superior application toward nirvāṇa,
they are said to be "distant" by virtue of the distance of their application,
not by virtue of the distance of time.
These two types, taken together as one,
are called the "distant" *pudgala*.
What is meant by the "near" *pudgala*?
This refers to a person (pudgala) who,
because their time [of death] is near, is close to nirvāṇa;
or alternatively, one who is said to be "near" because they are close in terms of their application (prayoga).
What is meant by "being near to nirvāṇa due to the proximity of time"?
It refers to a person (pudgala) who dwells in their final birth,
dwells in their final existence, and dwells in their final body.
One shall attain nirvāṇa by means of this very body,
or else, immediately following this very moment,
one shall realize the abandonment of the afflictions.
This is called being near to nirvāṇa by virtue of the proximity of time.
What is meant by being called "near" by virtue of the proximity of application?
It refers to a person (pudgala) such as this:
One who both abides in the spiritual lineage and has already entered [the path]—
these two types, taken together as one,
are called a "near" (*āsanna*) person.
What is an immature person?
It refers to a person who has not yet attained the body of their final existence.
That is to say, one who, by abiding in this state,
is able to attain parinirvāṇa or is able to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma)—
this is called an immature person (apari-pakva-pudgala).
What is a person who has already reached maturity?
It refers to a person who has already attained the final body of existence, meaning that by abiding in this state, they are able to attain parinirvāṇa.
Or one who is able to enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma)—
this is called a person who has already reached maturity.
What is a person who is not yet purified?
That is to say, there is such a person who has not yet produced the noble path and has not yet realized the dissociation from afflictions that constitutes the fruit of the noble path.
This is called an impure person (pudgala). What is a purified person?
It should be understood that their characteristics are the opposite of those described above.
This is called the distinction among individuals who abide in the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
When a World-Honored One appears in the world,
he causes those who have not yet entered [the path] to enter it.
He brings those who are not yet matured to maturity,
and those who are not yet purified to purification;
he turns the wheel of the true Dharma and establishes the precepts.
In the *Maulī Bhūmi*, the thirteenth chapter, the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*, within the second section, the *Praveśa-bhūmi*, of the first *Yogasthāna*: thus has the *Gotra-bhūmi* been explained.
Regarding the summary verse (*udāna*) on entering the stages (*bhūmi*):
In brief, one should know that all entries into the stages consist of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
their formal establishment (*vyavasthāna*), their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and the person (*pudgala*).
That is to say: the entry into intrinsic nature,
the entry into formal establishment,
and all the characteristics belonging to one who enters.
If a person has already entered [the path],
all such cases taken together as one are called the stage of entry (avatāra-bhūmi).
What is the entry into the nature?
It refers to a person who abides in the spiritual lineage (gotra) and by nature possesses the seeds of nirvāṇa.
If at that time a Buddha appears in the world,
one is born in a central land and not among the Dasyus or Mlecchas;
and so forth, as explained at length.
Having first seen the Buddha and his disciples,
one approaches them to serve them, hears the Dharma from them, attains initial right faith,
upholds the pure precepts, and embraces extensive learning.
They increase their generosity and soften their views.
Thereafter, through these teachings and by this cause,
once their bodies have perished and they have passed beyond this life, they will attain liberation.
Having obtained the distinguished faculties comprised within the maturation of the six sense bases,
they are able to produce and sustain superior right faith over a long period;
furthermore, they are able to rely upon these as a basis for upholding the pure precepts and embracing extensive learning.
Increasing generosity and relinquishment, and harmonizing all views,
they serve as a basis that becomes increasingly superior, increasingly excellent, and increasingly subtle. Furthermore,
by means of such dharmas as faith and the rest, which become increasingly superior, increasingly excellent, and increasingly subtle...
Furthermore, one attains other extraordinary maturations (*vipāka*).
By means of these maturations, one further attains other increasingly superior wholesome dharmas conducive to the supramundane.
In this way, they successively serve as mutual bases and causes, mutually providing their respective power.
In successive future births, one progresses ever further toward excellence,
until finally attaining the body of the final existence—
that is, abiding therein, one attains parinirvāṇa.
Or one may enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth;
this is called "entering. Why is that?
Whether it be a path, a road,
or a right track that can attain nirvana and lead toward nirvana,
at that time one is able to ascend it, enter it, and correctly traverse it.
Gradually progressing toward the ultimate consummation,
it is therefore said that this is called "having entered.
This is what is meant by entering one's own lineage (*gotra*).
How is the entry established?
It is said that there may be a lineage,
or there may be an entry.
Some are about to reach maturity; some have already reached maturity.
Some merely enter [the path] but are neither about to mature nor have matured.
Some both enter and are about to mature, but have not yet matured.
There are those who have both entered and already matured, but are not currently maturing;
there are those who have neither entered, nor are currently maturing, nor have already matured. This refers to their lineage (*gotra*).
This is as previously explained.
What is the process of entry?
It refers to an individual who abides in the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
For the first time, he attains a correct faith in the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgatas’ perfectly awakened and perfectly taught [teachings], which he has never before attained;
he undertakes the pure precepts and embraces extensive learning.
Increasing generosity and relinquishment, and harmonizing all views—
this is called "entering.
What is "being on the verge of maturation"?
This refers to a person who has already attained entry [into the path],
excluding the final body they have acquired— that is,
one who, abiding in this [body], attains parinirvāṇa.
Or they may enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth;
after entering that state,
in each subsequent life, they cultivate and accumulate the faculties so that they become increasingly superior, increasingly excellent, and increasingly subtle.
This is called "about to mature.
What is "already matured"?
It refers to having obtained the final body of existence (*antya-bhava*).
If, by abiding in this, one attains parinirvāṇa or is able to enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth,
this is called "already matured."
What is meant by "merely entering" rather than being "ripening" or "already ripened"?
It refers to the initial attainment of right faith in the perfectly awakened and correctly taught Dharma and Vinaya of all Tathāgatas.
To speak extensively, this continues until they have become pliant regarding all views.
Without undergoing even one more birth after this point,
this is called "merely having entered" [the path], rather than being "about to mature" or "already matured."
What is it that both enters [the path] and brings about maturation, yet has not already matured?
It refers to the initial attainment of right faith in the Dharma and Vinaya correctly awakened and correctly taught by all Tathāgatas.
To speak at length, this continues until they have rendered all views pliant.
From that point onward, they may pass through one, two,
or more further births before finally attaining their last existence.
This means that by abiding in this, one attains parinirvāṇa;
the rest is as previously explained.
This is called both entering and being on the verge of maturation, but not yet matured.
What is one who has both entered and already matured, but is not about to mature?
It refers to a person (*pudgala*) who has thus already attained entry and has further obtained their final existence (*antya-bhava*).
If one abides in this, one attains parinirvāṇa;
the rest is as previously explained.
This is called "having both entered and matured, but not being about to mature."
What is it that has neither entered, nor is about to mature, nor has already matured?
It refers to a person (*pudgala*) who possesses the nature for *nirvāṇa* and abides solely within the lineage (*gotra*), but has not yet entered [the path].
This is called a person who has neither already entered [the path], nor is currently maturing, nor has already matured;
yet they possess the capacity and will certainly enter and attain maturity.
Furthermore, there is a class of persons who definitely lack the capacity to enter [the path] or to reach maturity;
that is to say, those persons who lack the spiritual lineage and are devoid of the nature for nirvāṇa.
It should be understood that because such a person lacks the spiritual lineage (*gotra*),
they are certainly incapable of entering [the path] or reaching maturation;
how much less could they possibly attain parinirvāṇa?
All these individuals (pudgala) are subsumed within six stages.
What are these six?
First, individuals who possess the capacity;
second, individuals who have accomplished roots of goodness of the inferior grade;
third, individuals who have accomplished roots of goodness of the middling grade.
4. the person who has accomplished superior roots of virtue;
5. the person whose skillful means are consummate;
6. the person who has reached the ultimate consummation.
A person who abides in the spiritual lineage (gotrastha-pudgala),
yet has not yet attained the initial right faith in the Buddha’s perfectly awakened and correctly taught Dharma and Vinaya—
extending through the detailed explanation up to the thorough taming of all views.
This is called a capable person (pudgala).
What is a person who has accomplished inferior roots of virtue?
It refers to a person who abides in the spiritual lineage (gotra).
Having already attained, for the first time, right faith in the Buddha’s perfectly awakened and perfectly taught Dharma and Vinaya—
extending in detail up to the thorough taming of all views.
This is called a person who has accomplished the inferior grade of roots of goodness.
What is a person who has accomplished the middling grade of roots of goodness?
It refers to a person who abides in the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Having already attained, for the first time, right faith in the Buddha’s perfectly awakened and perfectly taught Dharma and Vinaya—
extending in detail up to the thorough taming of all views.
From this point onward, after one, two, or more lifetimes,
they progress through successive stages of excellence until they have not yet attained the final existence—
that is, the state in which one abides and is able to attain parinirvāṇa.
Or they may enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth;
such a person is called one who has accomplished middling roots of virtue.
What is a person who has accomplished superior roots of virtue?
This refers to a person who, having thus progressively advanced,
has already attained the body of their final existence;
if they abide in this state, they are able to attain parinirvāṇa.
Or one who is able to enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth—
this is called a person who has accomplished superior roots of virtue.
What is meant by a person who possesses the ultimate skillful means?
This refers to a person who has already attained their final existence,
who, for the sake of exhausting all outflows,
listens to the true Dharma or receives unerring instruction and admonition.
One who practices the preparatory application correctly but has not yet attained the permanent exhaustion of all outflows in every respect,
and has not reached the ultimate goal—
such a person is called an individual at the stage of the means to the ultimate.
What is meant by a person who has reached the ultimate goal?
It refers to such a person who,
for the sake of exhausting all outflows (*āsrava*), listens to the true Dharma.
Having obtained unerring instructions and admonitions,
one practices the application of effort in such and such a manner;
having thus attained the permanent exhaustion of all outflows in every respect, one has accomplished what was to be done.
Having attained ultimate, supreme coolness,
such a person is called an individual who has reached the final goal (*pudgala*).
Taking that very lineage as one's support and basis,
one is then able to obtain inferior-grade roots of goodness and is able to enter [the path].
Having thus entered, relying upon and dwelling in the inferior roots of goodness,
one is further able to attain the middling roots of goodness,
and by means of these roots of goodness, one brings oneself to maturity.
When he thus brings himself to maturity,
relying upon and abiding in medium-grade roots of goodness,
he is further able to attain superior-grade roots of goodness.
Having already attained maturity,
he has acquired this physical basis as a result of having cultivated and accumulated such superior roots of virtue.
Furthermore, one is able to cultivate and accumulate increasingly superior provisions;
by means of this, one realizes one-pointedness of mind and is able to enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth.
One who has realized the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning,
yet has not yet realized the supreme, foremost fruit of arhatship—
such a person is called an individual whose means are ultimate.
If one has already realized the fruit of arhatship, wherein all afflictions are forever severed,
at that time one is called a person who has reached the ultimate goal.
This demonstrates the correct practice cultivated by all śrāvakas throughout the beginning, middle,
and end; it establishes six types of individuals based on the correct practice of those śrāvakas who possess the spiritual lineage (gotra).
This demonstrates the first type of person;
by means of reaching the ultimate goal of the śrāvaka's correct practice,
it demonstrates the last type of person.
By means of the correct practice cultivated by other śrāvakas,
the intermediate *pudgala* is revealed.
Is there a fixed measure such that all attain parinirvāṇa equally at all times?
Or is there no fixed measure, such that they do not attain parinirvāṇa equally across all time periods?
Answer: There is no fixed measure, nor do all attain parinirvāṇa at the same time or with identical limits;
rather, they attain parinirvāṇa according to what is appropriate and through the distinctions of the conditions they encounter.
It should be understood that herein, some individuals take an extremely long time,
some do not take an extremely long time,
and some attain parinirvāṇa most swiftly.
This refers to a person abiding in the spiritual lineage who attains parinirvāṇa at the very fastest;
such a person requires three lifetimes,
entering the path for the first time during the first lifetime.
In the second birth, one cultivates it until it reaches maturity.
Having cultivated it to maturity in the third birth,
one may attain parinirvāṇa in that very body.
Alternatively, if one does not attain parinirvāṇa, one will necessarily enter the stage of training (śaikṣa),
whereupon one may pass away prematurely after at most seven existences before attaining parinirvāṇa.
This is called "entering and being established."
What are the characteristics of one who has already entered?
They refer to a person established in the spiritual lineage (gotra) who, having merely entered [the path], even if they were to undergo another birth.
Even though one may harbor false conceptions regarding one's own Great Teacher and his well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
should one encounter in the world both a poorly expounded Dharma and Vinaya as well as a well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, [one should examine them].
Although they have long heard the Dharma-vinaya of the evil teachings praised through immeasurable doors as possessing supreme merit,
they do not believe, understand, or joyfully practice it.
Nor do they seek to go forth from the household life therein;
even if they should temporarily go forth and just manage to enter,
they soon and swiftly abandon it and retreat.
By nature, they find no pleasure in abiding therein;
it is like placing maggots born in honey into strong vinegar,
or like placing one who delights in and craves exquisite sensual pleasures into a mire.
Because he is sustained by the power of the roots of virtue from his past lives,
if he hears even a small portion of the praise for the merits of the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, [he will be inspired].
Or they have not heard it at all; yet,
even having heard it only briefly or not at all,
they are able to swiftly believe, understand, enter into, and take delight in its practice, or seek to go forth into homelessness.
Having gone forth, they ultimately enter [the path] and never regress;
by nature, they find delight in and abide securely therein,
like insects born from honey.
He places it upon honey;
or, like one who delights in and enjoys sublime sensual pleasures, he places it amidst superior desires.
This is because he is sustained by the power of the roots of goodness from his past lives.
This is called the first characteristic of a person who has already attained entry and has already entered.
Furthermore, there are other characteristics of a person who has already attained entry and has already entered.
This refers to those who, although they have not yet attained the dissociation from afflictions that prevents rebirth in any of the evil destinies or states of lack of leisure,
are nevertheless able to avoid being born in such evil destinies or states of lack of leisure;
it is with reference to these individuals who have already entered [the path] that the Blessed One spoke.
It is taught with intentional meaning that if one possesses the highest degree of mundane right view,
even after passing through a thousand lifetimes, one will not fall into the evil destinies.
If they have already entered into superior roots of virtue and are gradually approaching maturity,
at that time they will be able to avoid being born in the states of no leisure or other evil destinies.
This is called the second characteristic of a person who has already attained entry and has entered [the path].
Furthermore, there are other characteristics of a person who has already attained entry and has already entered [the path], namely:
having briefly heard of the supreme qualities of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha.
He then attains a pure faith that accords with mindfulness,
which gives rise to the vast and wholesome dharmas of renunciation;
he repeatedly takes these as objects of contemplation to refine and purify his mind.
The hairs on his body stand on end and he weeps with tears falling like rain.
This is called the third sign of a person who has already attained entry and has already entered.
Furthermore, there are other signs of a person who has already attained entry and has already entered.
That is to say, being naturally endowed with sharp and intense shame and dread of blame,
one feels profound embarrassment regarding all instances of unwholesome conduct that manifest.
This is called the fourth characteristic of a person who has already attained entry and has already entered.
Furthermore, there are other characteristics of a person who has already attained entry and has already entered.
That is to say, within the practice of upholding, reciting, inquiring about, reflecting upon, and contemplating the observance of wholesome dharmas,
there exists a profound aspiration and an intense aspiration;
this is called the fifth characteristic of a person who has already attained entry and has already entered.
Furthermore, there are other characteristics of a person who has already attained entry and has already entered [the path],
namely: the cultivation and accumulation of all types of wholesome applications regarding every blameless activity.
Within right effort, one is able to skillfully cultivate and accumulate it,
initiating it with firmness, initiating it for a long duration, and initiating it with certainty.
This is called the sixth characteristic of a person who has already attained entry and has already entered [the path].
Furthermore, there are other characteristics of a person who has already attained entry and has already entered [the path], namely:
that by nature their defilements are subtle and thin, and their afflictions are weak and feeble.
Although he may give rise to various fetters, they do not continue in succession for a long time or persist for a long duration.
Being free from guile and deceit, he is able to restrain pride and the grasping at "I" and "mine.
He delights in taking up virtues and detests and turns away from faults.
This is called the seventh characteristic of a person who has already attained entry and has already entered.
Furthermore, there are other characteristics of a person who has already attained entry and has already entered.
That is to say, one is skillful in concealing and guarding the mind;
regarding the vast states that ought to be realized, one does not disparage oneself,
nor does one settle complacently therein.
He possesses no power to be overcome by them;
his faith and understanding increase and become intensely vigorous.
This is called the eighth characteristic of a person who has already attained entry and has already entered.

Section 2: Those Who Have Already Entered. It should be understood that the signs of individuals who have already attained entry and those who have already entered—such as these three categories and others of this kind—are immeasurable.
I have already explained a small portion of this herein.
Thus, regarding these various characteristics, if there are those who enter by abiding in inferior roots of goodness,
one should know that "inferior" is termed "having gaps."
They have not yet attained uninterruptedness;
they have not yet become thoroughly purified.
If there are those who enter by abiding in middling roots of goodness, [they are as follows].
One should know that it is of medium grade.
If one enters while abiding in superior roots of goodness,
one should know that it is of superior grade.
Being without intervals, having already become uninterrupted, and being thoroughly purified—
this is the characteristic of a person who has entered [the path].
One who has accomplished such a characteristic of entry is [so described].
One should know that such a person has fallen into the category of those who have already entered [the path].
It should be understood that for a person who thus abides in the lineage (*gotra*) and has attained entry, there are many auspicious marks of a noble being (*śiṣṭa*).
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and his disciples who have reached the ultimate consummation,
perceive this through their excellently pure, sublime wisdom and vision; they realize it directly and provide salvation accordingly,
in accordance with each being's spiritual lineage and the path they have entered.
What is meant by a person who has already attained entry?
It refers to a person who has indeed attained entry,
yet has only entered [the path] without having reached maturation, without being matured, and without having attained liberation.
There are some who have both entered and are about to reach maturity, yet have not reached maturity and have not attained liberation;
there are some who have both entered and reached maturity, yet have not attained liberation.
They act according to their desires.
Such distinctions should be understood as having already been explained previously regarding the characteristics of all the various types of *pudgalas*.
Now, within this context, one should likewise understand all the distinctions as they appropriately apply.
Thus, what has been explained concerns both the entry into intrinsic nature and the entry into formal establishment.
All the characteristics of one who has already entered,
as well as the person (pudgala) who has already entered,
are collectively designated as the "stage of entry" (avatāra-bhūmi).
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Twenty-one;
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Twenty-two;
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

In the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, the Thirteenth [Section] of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the First Yoga Station, this is the first part of the Third Stage: the Stage of Renunciation (*Nairyāṇika-bhūmi*). Thus has been explained the Stage of Entry (*Praveśa-bhūmi*).
What is the stage of renunciation?
The summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
Whether it be worldly renunciation of desire, or likewise the supramundane.
And these two provisions are called the stage of renunciation;
that is to say, whether one proceeds toward freedom from desire by means of the mundane path or by means of the supramundane path.
If all the provisions for these two paths are condensed into a single category,
it is called the "ground of renunciation" (*nairyāṇika-bhūmi*).
For example, there is one who contemplates the lower desire realm as having the characteristic of coarseness (*audārikatva*).
Regarding the joy and bliss born of seclusion in the first dhyāna,
whether in meditative concentration or at birth, one contemplates it as having the characteristic of tranquility.
When one dwells frequently in such contemplation, one attains detachment from the desire realm.
One is also able to realize and enter the first dhyāna.
Likewise, regarding the first dhyāna and all lower stages above it,
one gradually contemplates them as having coarse characteristics (audārikatva) as appropriate.
One regards all higher stages as having the characteristic of tranquility.
When one dwells frequently in such contemplation, one becomes free from desire for everything up to and including the sphere of nothingness.
One is also able to realize and enter up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is called proceeding toward detachment by means of the mundane path;
beyond this, there is nothing superior or more extensive.
What is meant by "proceeding toward the abandonment of desire by means of the supramundane path"?
It refers to someone who associates with virtuous persons and has already become wise within the noble Dharma.
Having attained discipline within the noble Dharma,
one knows the noble truth of suffering as it truly is as suffering,
and knows the noble truth of the origin as it truly is as the origin.
One knows the noble truth of cessation as it truly is: cessation;
one knows the noble truth of the path as it truly is: the path.
Having thus attained the accomplishment of the knowledge and vision of one in training (śaikṣa), [one is said to have entered the stream].
From this point onward, they gradually cultivate the noble path;
throughout all phenomena within the three realms that are to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation,
they are able to sever their fetters by themselves and attain liberation by themselves.
In this way, one is able to transcend the three realms.
This is called proceeding toward the freedom from desire by means of the supramundane path.
What is meant by the provisions for these two paths?
The summary verse says:

The desire for the wholesome dharma that fulfills oneself and others, Virtuous conduct, the faculties, restraint, moderation in food, Awakening, dwelling in right mindfulness, and reliance on virtuous friends;
Adorned with hearing, reflection, freedom from obstacles, and equanimity.
That is to say: whether it be one's own fulfillment,
another's fulfillment,
or the desire for wholesome qualities.
Whether it be the restraint of the precepts,
the restraint of the sense faculties,
or moderation in eating.
If one constantly and diligently practices the yoga of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night;
if one dwells with clear comprehension;
and if one possesses the nature of a virtuous friend.
Whether hearing the true Dharma, reflecting on the true Dharma,
being free from obstacles,
or practicing wise relinquishment.
If these factors constitute the adornment of a śramaṇa,
they are called the mundane and supramundane paths of detachment and the provisions for proceeding toward them.
It should be understood that herein, there is the perfection of oneself, the perfection of others, and the desire for wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*).
These three have already had their characteristics explained among the inferior conditions for cultivating and accumulating seeds as previously described. What, then,
is the restraint of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*)?
The summary verse says:
One should know that the ethical discipline of restraint Is distinguished by three aspects, sixteen modes of deficiency and fulfillment,
Three types of purity, and ten kinds of supreme qualities.
Regarding the restraint of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*):
it refers to a certain person who dwells in the possession of ethical discipline,
as described at length up to the point of undertaking and training in the precepts (*śikṣāpada*).
Regarding all the precepts of training,
he does not fail in his physical actions,
nor does he fail in his verbal actions.
Without deficiency and without breach—
this is called abiding in the possession of ethical discipline.
What is meant by being well able to guard the prātimokṣa restraint?
This refers to being able to guard the prātimokṣa vows received by the seven classes of practitioners;
that is, because of the distinctions among these classes, these vows constitute many types of discipline.
In the present context, however, it refers exclusively to the bhikṣu discipline.
It is said that one is well able to guard the Prātimokṣa vows.
What is meant by "perfection of conduct" (*īryāpatha-sampad*)?
It refers, for example, to someone who, in their daily activities (*iryāpatha*), [acts accordingly].
Whether in regard to the tasks to be performed,
or in regard to the application of effort toward virtuous qualities,
one achieves proficiency in proper conduct.
He conforms to the world without transgressing the world;
he conforms to the Vinaya without transgressing the Vinaya.
What is meant by "achieving proper conduct in the modes of deportment,
conforming to the world and not transgressing the world"?
Conforming to the Vinaya and not transgressing the Vinaya;
that is to say, there is someone who acts as they ought to act and acts in accordance with how one should act.
One practices in this very way; by practicing thus,
one is not censured or reviled by the world,
nor by the virtuous, the upright, and the noble persons.
All those who follow the same Dharma,
all those who uphold the Vinaya,
and all those who study the Vinaya.
Just as he is censured regarding his conduct,
it should be understood that the same applies to his dwelling, his standing, and his reclining.
This is called being accomplished in the rules of conduct regarding the modes of deportment;
it is to be in accordance with the world without transgressing the world, and in accordance with the Vinaya without transgressing the Vinaya.
What is called the rule for accomplishing tasks?
It is that which accords with the world without transgressing the world,
and accords with the Vinaya without transgressing the Vinaya.
That is to say, there is someone who,
regarding their various activities— whether matters of clothing,
matters of excretion, matters of using water, or matters of tooth-sticks— [proceeds accordingly].
Whether entering a village to go on almsround for food,
or engaging in the matter of using [requisites], or the matter of rinsing the bowl,
or the matter of setting it down, or the matter of washing the feet.
If one performs tasks such as preparing bedding and so forth,
these are briefly described here.
Matters concerning robes, matters concerning the alms-bowl, and other similar categories of duties that ought to be performed are called "tasks to be done" (*karaṇīya-kriyā*).
In accordance with what is appropriate, regarding what ought to be done,
and in the manner in which it should be done, one acts precisely within this context in such a way.
Because of acting in this manner, one does not become subject to the censure or reproach of the world.
He is not esteemed as a virtuous, upright,
and excellent person by his fellow practitioners of the Dharma or by those who uphold the Vinaya.
That which is censured by those who study the Vinaya is what is called the failure of the rules regarding the accomplishment of tasks.
He conforms to the world without transgressing the world;
he conforms to the Vinaya without transgressing the Vinaya.
What is meant by "achieving the rules of conduct (*ācāra*) in the sphere of application for all categories of wholesome qualities"?
He conforms to the world without transgressing the world;
he conforms to the Vinaya without transgressing the Vinaya;
that is to say, he applies himself to various categories of wholesome qualities.
Whether it be receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the True Dharma;
or practicing acts of harmony and respect toward elders, visiting them, and serving them;
or giving rise to a heart of compassion for the sick and attending to them with earnest devotion.
If, regarding the preparatory application for a formal declaration in accordance with the Dharma,
one abides in a mind of loving-kindness and compassion and successively grants consent;
and if, regarding the inquiry and reception of the True Dharma, one is diligent and free from negligence.
He exerts all his physical strength to practice respectful service toward wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life,
and he constantly and diligently encourages others in their virtuous qualities.
He constantly delights in proclaiming the true Dharma for the sake of others;
he enters a quiet room, sits in the full lotus posture, and fixes his mindfulness in contemplation.
Such are the various other immeasurable wholesome dharmas he cultivates.

All these are called the preparatory applications (*prayoga*) for the category of wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*). Regarding such preparatory applications for the category of wholesome qualities as they have been taught,
he acts accordingly toward what ought to be done and in the manner in which it ought to be done.
One acts in this very manner within this context;
by acting thus, one is not censured or reviled by the world,
nor by those who are virtuous, upright, and excellent persons.
All those who follow the same Dharma,
all those who uphold the Vinaya,
and all those who study the Vinaya.
This is what is censured;
thus, it is called the accomplishment of proper conduct (*ācāra*) regarding the application (*prayoga*) to all categories of wholesome qualities.
He conforms to the world without transgressing the world;
he conforms to the Vinaya without transgressing the Vinaya.
Thus, he is fully endowed with all the various aspects, modes, and rules of conduct as thus described.
One should know that this is called the perfection of conduct (*ācāra-saṃpanna*).
What is meant by the perfection of resort (*gocara-saṃpanna*)? It refers to the five types of improper resorts for bhikṣus.
What are the five?
First, the family of a professional crier;
second, the family of a courtesan.
Third, the house of a liquor-seller;
fourth, the house of a king;
fifth, the house of a caṇḍāla or kaṭhina.
If one is able to skillfully avoid such places of non-conduct as prescribed by the Tathāgata,
and acts at the proper time within other blameless spheres of conduct that one knows, [this is right conduct].
This is called the perfection of conduct.
What is meant by "seeing great fear in even minor transgressions"?
It refers to [the observance of] all the minor and secondary rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
If there is an offense committed that can be restored to purity,
it is called a minor offense (*sūkṣmāpatti*);
this refers to the actual transgression of the various rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
It is designated as a transgression;
yet, once it has been committed, it can be restored to purity with little effort,
and is thus called "minor."
For this reason, it is called a minor offense.
How can one perceive great fear within it?
It is by making this observation:
May I not, due to the cause and condition of this transgression,
become incapable of attaining what has not yet been attained, touching what has not yet been touched, or realizing what has not yet been realized;
may I not, because of this, draw near to the evil destinies or go to the evil destinies.
One should either reproach oneself,
or be rebuked by the Teacher, the devas, or wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life in accordance with the Dharma,
thinking: "May no evil reputation, ill repute, bad name, or foul report concerning me spread far and wide throughout all directions and intermediate points because of this."
Seeing great terror in the undesirable fruits that arise from such transgressions in this present life and in the future,
for this reason, regarding even the smallest and most minor training rules—
Even when there are circumstances involving life-threatening danger, one does not intentionally commit an offense;
yet, at times or in certain places, one may commit an offense through loss of mindfulness.
Immediately thereafter, one swiftly confesses according to the Dharma so as to restore purity.
This is called perceiving great dread in even minor offenses.
What is meant by "training in the precepts"?
It refers to having previously received the Prātimokṣa vows through the formal ritual of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
At the time of receiving full ordination, one hears a portion of the essential nature of the training rules from the preceptor;
furthermore, one hears the remainder of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra from the personal preceptor or the instructor.
In brief, he proclaims more than two hundred and fifty rules of training (*śikṣāpada*),
all of which he vows to train in himself. Furthermore,
from others who engage in constant discourse, those who share his discourse, those with whom he constantly associates, and those for whom he has affection, he hears the rules of training.
Furthermore, during each half-month, they regularly proclaim the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
Upon hearing the precepts, they all vow to train themselves in them;
for they have undertaken to train in every single point of training that ought to be practiced.
This is called "attaining the prātimokṣa restraint.
From this point forward, regarding the various training rules (śikṣāpada),
if one has become proficient, one will be able to remain free from transgressions.
Should one commit an offense, one immediately repents according to the Dharma.
If, regarding the various rules of training (śikṣāpada), one has not yet attained skillfulness or full comprehension,
it is because of one's prior vow to undertake and maintain them.
Now, at this time, desiring to seek out skillfulness and seeking to achieve clear understanding,
one should inquire as previously described regarding the various points of training from either a preceptor (upādhyāya) or a teacher (ācārya).
Having attained skillfulness and achieved awakening,
they are able to receive and study the instructions exactly as taught, without addition or subtraction.
Furthermore, when one is able to correctly receive the training precepts— both in letter and in meaning— as taught by those who are respected or equally respected,
this is called "receiving and training in the training precepts."
Having thus extensively analyzed the restraint of morality,
how should one understand its summarized meaning? In this regard,
the Blessed One has revealed that the summarized meaning of the aggregate of morality consists of three aspects.
First is the characteristic of non-destruction;
second is the characteristic of intrinsic nature;
third is the characteristic of the qualities of intrinsic nature.
What does this mean? It means that if one says,
"abiding in the possession of ethical discipline," this demonstrates that the restraint of śīla is characterized by being free from impairment.
Furthermore, if it is said that one is able to skillfully guard the prātimokṣa vows,
this reveals the essential characteristic of the śīla-vinaya.
Moreover, if it is said that one's conduct and observances are entirely perfected, [this reveals its secondary characteristics].
This demonstrates that the prātimokṣa restraint, in accordance with how it is undertaken, has as its essential characteristic the quality of being governed by others. Why is this so?
Because others perceive such a person as one whose conduct and observances are perfected.
Those who have not yet developed faith will come to believe, and those who already believe will find it further increased.
Through this, a basis for pure faith arises;
the mind feels no aversion, and one refrains from speaking with derision or disparagement.
If one were otherwise, being fully endowed with ethical discipline (*śīla*), proper conduct (*ācāra*), and ritual practice (*pratipatti*),
there would be no superior qualities or benefits to be observed in others.
The opposite faults would otherwise necessarily follow.
Furthermore, if it is said that one perceives great dread even toward minor offenses and undertakes the training in the precepts (*śikṣāpada*),

this demonstrates that the Prātimokṣa restraint (*saṃvara*) possesses the characteristic of its own essential nature (*svabhāva-guṇa-lakṣaṇa*), which is characterized by self-mastery (*adhipatya*) according to how it was received.
Why is this? Although one attains all-round perfection in conduct through such rules and thereby gains the aforementioned superior benefits of observing others, [the former is still more excellent].
Nevertheless, due to the cause and condition of violating the pure precepts, one will be reborn in the evil destinies,
or will lack the capacity to attain what has not yet been attained,
as explained at length previously.
If one can perceive great fear even in minor transgressions and correctly train in the superior precepts previously received,
by reason of these causes and conditions, after the dissolution of the body, one shall be reborn in a happy destination.
Furthermore, there is the capacity to attain what has not yet been attained,
as explained extensively before.
For these reasons, this is called the prātimokṣa restraint.
Regarding the observation of the superior merits and benefits of what has been received,
there is another method:
namely, that herein the Buddha, the World-Honored One, briefly reveals three types of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
First, the nature of undertaking the precepts;
second, the nature of renunciation;
third, the nature of cultivation.
That is to say, if it is said that one "dwells established in the complete precepts," this demonstrates the nature of upholding the precepts;
and if it is further said that one "is able to well guard the prātimokṣa vows."
By this, the nature of the precepts of renunciation is revealed. Why is this?
Because the pure morality comprised within the prātimokṣa vows—
One should know that this is called the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*).
Based upon this very training in higher ethical discipline,
one cultivates the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*) and the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).
By means of this, one is able to attain the ultimate liberation that brings an end to all suffering.
Such liberation takes superior ethical discipline as its preliminary practice and its foundational support.
Therefore, this Pratimokṣa restraint is called the nature of the morality of renunciation.
Furthermore, it is said that its rules of conduct and behavior are entirely perfect,
and that one perceives great dread even in minor transgressions while training in the precepts.
This demonstrates the cultivation of the nature of ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Why is this so? Because if one cultivates pure ethical discipline by means of the distinct types of restraint (*saṃvara*) through the characteristics thus described, [it is called the cultivation of the nature of ethical discipline].
It is called "well-cultivated" and "thoroughly well-cultivated.
Just as this one kind of ethical discipline (*śīla-vinaya*) is thus proclaimed,
it should be understood that the six kinds are likewise exactly so.
One should know that there is deficiency due to ten causes and conditions;
conversely, one should know that there is fulfillment due to these same ten causes and conditions.
What are the ten kinds of causes and conditions for deficiency?
First, the initial improper undertaking of the ethical discipline of the śīla-vinaya;
second, excessive sinking;
third, excessive floating and distraction.
Fourth, it is comprised by negligence and indolence;
fifth, by the arousal of wrong aspirations;
and sixth, by the impairment of proper conduct.
Seventh, it is comprised of the impairment of pure livelihood;
eighth, falling into the two extremes;
ninth, being unable to achieve transcendence.
Tenth is the loss and ruin of what has been received.
What is meant by "the initial faulty reception of the ethical discipline (*śīla*) and restraint (*vinaya*)"?
It refers, for example, to someone who, being oppressed by a king, seeks to go forth into homelessness.
Or they may be oppressed by madmen or bandits;
or they may be oppressed by creditors;
or they may be oppressed by fears.
Or, being oppressed by the fear of not being able to make a living, they seek to go forth into homelessness;
yet they do not possess the nature of a śramaṇa,
nor do they possess the nature of a brāhmaṇa.
Not for the sake of self-discipline,
not for the sake of self-peace,
and not for the sake of self-nirvana.
And thus he seeks to go forth into homelessness.
This is called the first instance of improperly undertaking the ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*).
What is meant by being "excessively depressed"?
That is to say, there is someone whose nature is devoid of shame and remorse, who is weak and inferior, and whose nature is lax;
such that regarding the various training rules (*śikṣāpada*), their practice is likewise lax.
This is what is called being excessively sunken.
What is meant by "excessive floating and scattering"?
It refers to a certain person who stubbornly clings to and wrongly grasps what is improper,
engaging in unwholesome mental activity regarding matters that should not be done, and thus acting with misplaced and excessive remorse.
To give rise to a mind of contempt or malice toward others,
or to forcefully attempt to awaken them in an inappropriate manner—
this is called excessive floating and distraction.
In what way is it subsumed under negligence and laziness?
It refers to a certain person who, due to transgressions committed in the past,
fails to maintain mindfulness regarding those very transgressions.
A certain class of people is unable to restore purity in accordance with the Dharma;
as it was by way of the past,
so it should be understood to be by way of the future and the present as well.
This refers to the transgression of what has been committed as an offense;
because of a lapse of mindfulness regarding this transgression,
a certain class of individuals is unable to restore themselves to purity in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, it is not that at the outset one has generated a fierce and intense desire for non-transgression regarding what has been violated, thinking:
"I shall certainly act exactly as I have acted and abide exactly as I have abided."
In such a manner one acts in what is to be done;
in such a manner one abides in what is to be abided in.
One never transgresses that which has been prohibited.
Due to these causes and conditions, wherever one goes or stays,
one repeatedly commits transgressions; thereby,
one accomplishes all forms of heedlessness associated with the past, the future, and the present, as well as those performed previously and those that follow along simultaneously.
Furthermore, one personally clings to sleep as pleasure, reclining as pleasure, and lying on one's side as pleasure;
by nature, one lacks exertion, being lazy and devoid of initiative.
To be unable to visit, inquire after, and serve wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life from time to time is called being encompassed by negligence and indolence.
What is called "arousing wrong aspirations"?
It refers to someone who, relying on wrong aspirations, practices the holy life, saying:
"Whatever precepts or prohibitions I possess..."
If one is constantly diligent or practices the holy life (brahmacarya),
one shall be reborn in heaven or another celestial realm;
or else, one may practice the holy life out of a fondness for gain and honor.
That is to say, because of this, one seeks gain and honor from others,
and consequently develops a deep attachment to such gain and honor;
this is called initiating wrong aspirations.
What is meant by being subsumed under the impairment of rules of conduct?
