It refers to when someone, regarding the rules of conduct pertaining to the modes of deportment, to their various activities, or to the application of the various categories of wholesome qualities.
They do not conform to the world and transgress the world;
they do not conform to the Vinaya and transgress the Vinaya,
as explained in detail previously.
This is called being subsumed under the impairment of proper conduct.
What is meant by being subsumed under the impairment of pure livelihood?
It refers to someone who, by nature, has great desire, does not know contentment, and is difficult to support and difficult to satisfy.
They constantly seek clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites for illness through unrighteous means rather than through the True Dharma.
Furthermore, they do so for the sake of greedily seeking various kinds of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and other such necessities.
Using skillful means to manifest his own superior virtues,
he hypocritically assumes an artificial and unnatural demeanor.
For the sake of deceiving others, he constantly feigns that his faculties are free from agitation, free from movement, and perfectly tranquil.
By this means, one causes others to perceive that one possesses virtue,
such that they feel there is something to be given and something to be done—
namely, to provide service and offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and various other articles of necessity.
Furthermore, many are violent, perverse, and boastful, assuming airs of arrogance;
they cultivate their reputations and rely upon their noble lineage,
whether seeking extensive learning or maintaining the Dharma.
For the sake of gain and honor, they also proclaim the true Dharma to others—
whether spoken by the Buddha, spoken by his disciples,
or speaking for themselves of their own actual virtues.
Or they may slightly exaggerate;
or, in the presence of others, they may employ artful gestures to seek clothing or any other requisite for a śramaṇa.
Whether seeking abundance or seeking excellence,
although they lack nothing, they manifest themselves wearing tattered and worn garments so that pure-faithed elders,
householders, and brahmins may perceive that their clothing is in a state of deficiency.
He reverently served him and provided him with a great many excellent and superior garments;
as he did for the garments,
so too did he provide for each and every other requisite for the livelihood of a śramaṇa.
Or, among pure-faithed elders, householders, and brahmins,
they may not obtain what they desire as they wish;
or their wealth and possessions may be deficient.
When they cannot obtain what they seek, they immediately resort to coercion,
using harsh words and grinding insults to demand it with bitterness; yet,
that person's wealth and possessions may be entirely without deficiency.
When they obtain something inferior, they immediately confront the donor and disparage the acquired wealth before them,
speaking as follows:
"Alas, O man! Such-and-such a son of good family,
such-and-such a daughter of good family!"
Given that your lineage and your wealth are extremely lowly and you are utterly destitute,
yet you are able to bestow such various, exquisite, and pleasing assets and provisions as these.
"Given that you expect [to receive from] those of noble lineage, high status, and abundant wealth,
why do you give such meager, inferior, and unpleasant things?
He does so either out of such hypocrisy or through false speech."
Whether by feigning appearances, or by harsh interrogation and coercion,
or through various other means of seeking profit from profit,
they improperly solicit from others all manner of requisites for life, such as clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal supplies for the treatment of illness.
One does not seek anything by means of the True Dharma;
because it is contrary to the Dharma, it is called wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
This is what is meant by being subsumed under the impairment of pure livelihood (*śīla-brahmacarya-vyasana*).
What is meant by "falling into the two extremes"?
It refers, for example, to someone who is attached to the extreme of indulging in the enjoyment of pleasures obtained from others—
namely, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine for the treatment of illness, and various requisites, whether they be lawful or unlawful.
To indulge in play and enjoyment while failing to contemplate their faults and disadvantages, and remaining ignorant of the way to transcendence—
this is called one extreme.
Furthermore, there is another class who delight in seeking enjoyments while adhering to the extreme of self-mortification.
By means of immeasurable methods, they torment themselves and undergo extreme suffering;
that is to say, by relying on thorns, or ash and dust, or a wooden pestle, or a wooden board.
Some practice the yoga of cultivation and abandonment by squatting like a fox or sitting like a fox;
others serve fire,
meaning they attend to the fire for as many as three [periods].
Or again, he may ascend the water,
meaning he ascends above the water up to three times;
or he may stand on one foot, turning with the movement of the sun.
Or again, those who practice such other forms of self-mortification as these constitute the second extreme.
Thus, one is said to have fallen into the two extremes.
What is meant by "incapable of renunciation"?
It refers to someone who, out of dogmatic adherence to views, clings to either a precept or a vow, thinking:
"By means of this precept or this vow, I shall attain purification, liberation, and renunciation."
All the prohibitions and precepts of the various non-Buddhist paths,
though well-guarded and well-purified,
are not called "renunciation" despite their purity.
This is called being unable to transcend.
What is meant by the ruin of what has been received?
It refers to someone who is entirely devoid of shame and disregards the status of a śramaṇa.
Violating the pure precepts and practicing various evil dharmas,
they are rotten within while appearing honest and sincere without;
they are like snails born in clear water, possessing the whorled sound of a conch yet the behavior of a dog.
In truth, he is not a śramaṇa though he claims to be a śramaṇa;
in truth, he does not lead the holy life (brahmacarya) though he claims to lead the holy life.
This is called the ruin of what has been undertaken.
Briefly, it is by means of these ten causes and conditions that morality is said to be impaired.
The Blessed One has sometimes spoken of the impairment of *śīla*,
and at other times he has spoken of the difficulty of *śīla*.
It should be understood that among those various causes and conditions, there are two primary factors:
namely, the inability to attain liberation and the loss and ruin of what has been received.
One should understand that by other causes and conditions, it is only the impairment of ethical discipline (*śīla*) that is being described;
conversely, one should understand that what is called the "perfection" and "purity" of ethical discipline refers to these [other] causes and conditions.
The Venerable One has proclaimed that ethical discipline (śīla) is called the root.
As a gāthā says:
"If one is well-established in the root, the mind becomes tranquil."
The Blessed One has taught that there are instances where right view and wrong view are either associated or dissociated with ethical discipline (*śīla*),
which he described as an ornament. As a verse says:
For bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, the adornment of the precepts is complete;
they are able to abandon what is unwholesome and are able to cultivate what is wholesome.
In this regard, the World-Honored One has declared that ethical discipline (śīla) is called "scented ointment."
As a verse says:
"O bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, with the ointment of the precepts complete,
you are able to abandon what is unwholesome and cultivate what is wholesome."
In some places, the Blessed One has declared that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is called "incense.
As a verse (*gāthā*) says:
"Ānanda, there is a kind of fragrance That is able to perfume well with the wind."
It can also perfume against the wind; it perfumes both with and against the wind in this same way.
In some places, the World-Honored One has proclaimed that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is called "wonderful conduct" (*sucarita*).
As a verse says:
Wholesome conduct of body can bring about desirable maturations in both the present life and the future; wholesome conduct of speech is likewise.
In some instances, the Blessed One has declared that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is called restraint (*saṃvara*).
As it is said in a gāthā:
"Those who are donors, endowed with ethical discipline, abiding in restraint,
possessing the vision of the Āgamas, and possessing the right view regarding the fruits [of action]."
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"Abiding securely in the complete precepts,
one is well able to guard the prātimokṣa discipline."
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what reason does the Blessed One declare that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is called the "root"?
Answer: Because it has the sense of being able to establish and the sense of being able to sustain.
This is the fundamental meaning.
By means of this ethical discipline (*śīla*), one establishes and sustains all mundane and supramundane states,
and is able to bring forth the merit of blameless, most excellent, and foremost happiness.
It causes [virtues] to arise and to be realized;
therefore, ethical discipline (śīla) is called the "root.
It is, for example, like the great earth, which establishes and sustains all medicinal herbs, grasses, trees, and forests, causing them to grow and flourish.
Such is ethical discipline (*śīla*), as explained extensively above.
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One declare that ethical discipline is called an "ornament"?
Answer: Because it is superior to all other worldly ornaments, such as earrings, rings, bracelets, armlets, jeweled seals, and garlands of gold and silver.
If one who possesses the youthful vigor of black-haired adolescence and a beautiful, excellent physical form were to adorn themselves with fine garments, they would appear exceptionally handsome;

whereas one who possesses the decrepitude of old age—whose teeth have fallen out, whose hair is white, and who is over eighty or ninety years of age—even if they were to adorn themselves with such garments, they would not appear handsome.
Except when used for theatrical performance to bring laughter to the assembly,
if one encounters the suffering of illness, the depletion of wealth, or the death of relatives,
taking it at such times will yield no excellent benefit.
The ornament of ethical discipline (śīla) is excellent for all types of beings at all times whenever it is worn;
therefore, śīla is called an "ornament."
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One declare that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is called "scented ointment"?

Answer: Because this pure, blameless, and sublime ethical discipline, once undertaken, is able to correctly eliminate all physical and mental afflictions caused by the undertaking of unwholesome discipline.
For example, when it is most intensely hot and scorching, the application of sandalwood, camphor, and other such perfumes causes all that oppressive heat to be extinguished;
therefore, ethical discipline (śīla) is called "scented unguent."
Question: For what reason does the Blessed One declare that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is called "incense"?
Answer: A person who possesses the precepts is renowned throughout all regions;
his excellent reputation and verses of praise are heard everywhere.
For example, just as various fragrances from roots, stalks, and so forth waft with the wind to all directions, their pleasing scent spreading far and wide,
ethical discipline (śīla) is therefore called "incense."
Question: For what reason does the Blessed One declare that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is called "wonderful conduct" (*sucarita*)?
Answer: Because this pure and virtuous practice of ethical discipline leads toward sublime happiness and causes one to proceed to the sublime celestial realms.
It is called "sublime conduct" because it leads toward sublime peace and security.
Question: For what reason does the Blessed One declare that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*)?
Answer: Because by means of this ethical discipline, wholesome qualities are purified.
It is called discipline (*saṃvara*) because it has the nature of protection, the characteristic of pacification,
and the essence of distancing oneself [from unwholesome states].
There are three kinds of observance (*saṃvara*) that contemplate the characteristics of the causes of purity. What are these three?
First, contemplating bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
Second, observing verbal action;
third, observing mental action.
How does one observe these various types of action?
One causes the restraint of the precepts to become entirely pure;
that is, when about to perform an action or while actually performing it with the body, one observes in this manner.
"Is this bodily action of mine capable of harming myself and others, such that it is of an unwholesome nature, able to produce manifold suffering and bring about the maturation of suffering?
Or is it incapable of harming either myself or others, such that it is of a wholesome nature, able to produce all forms of happiness and bring about the maturation of happiness?"
Having observed in this way, if one understands for oneself: "This bodily action of mine harms both myself and others;
it is of an unwholesome nature, capable of producing manifold suffering and inviting the maturation of suffering."
One immediately restrains oneself from performing such actions and does not provide them an opportunity;
if one understands for oneself that this bodily action of mine does no harm to self or others, it is of a virtuous nature.
The rest is as previously explained.
That is, regarding this very karma, one does not exercise restraint in its performance and execution;
furthermore, concerning physical karma already performed in the past.
Furthermore, he repeatedly examines whether this bodily action of his is capable of harming himself,
as previously described.
Having observed in this way:
If one understands for oneself that this bodily action of mine harms both myself and others—
the rest being as previously described—
one should then, in the presence of wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life...
One should disclose it as it truly is and repent according to the Dharma.
If one knows for oneself that this bodily action of mine does not harm oneself or others,
the rest is as previously stated.
He then gives rise to joy and dwells in peace day and night, extensively practicing and training accordingly.
In this way, he is able to skillfully examine and skillfully purify the bodily actions he has performed in the past, future, and present lives.
As it is with bodily action,
so it should be understood for verbal action as well:
mental action arises conditioned by past actions.
Based on future volitional formations as condition, there arises volition;
based on present volitional formations as condition, there arises volition.
One repeatedly observes this very volition, thinking: "This is my volitional action."
This leads to self-harm;
the rest is as previously explained.
Having contemplated thus:
If one understands for oneself that this mental action of mine belongs to the dark category, then one restrains oneself from that action, does not initiate it, and does not provide it an opportunity.
If one understands for oneself that this mental action of mine belongs to the white category...
One does not harbor or give rise to the impulse toward such karma;
thus, regarding the mental actions performed in the past, future, and present,
one is able to examine them well and purify them well.
Why is this? Because among all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the past, future, and present worlds,
regarding the three types of action— of body, speech, and mind— ...
Either has been observed, will be observed, or is being observed;
either has been purified, will be purified, or is being purified;
or has already been frequently dwelt upon, will be frequently dwelt upon, or is currently being frequently dwelt upon.
All this is purified through such observation and such purification.
As the Blessed One once said to the Elder Rāhula:
"Now, Rāhula, regarding the actions of body, speech, and mind..."
One should repeatedly and correctly observe, And keep in mind the holy teachings of all Buddhas.
Rāhula, you should Train in this work of a śramaṇa;
If one can train in this, there will be only supreme goodness and no evil.
If one carefully and correctly examines such actions of body, speech, and mind, [one considers]:
"Do these various actions of mine cause harm to myself?
and so forth, as explained in detail previously.
This is called "investigation.
If one restrains oneself in part, neither acting nor granting permission, and so forth,
as explained at length, until finally confessing and purifying [the offense].
Furthermore, regarding one portion [of the teaching], he does not withdraw or withhold his application and practice;
as explained at length, he even gives rise to joy.
Day and night, he dwells securely, extensively following and training in it.
This is called purity.
One should know that such pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) possesses ten meritorious benefits.
What are the ten? They are as follows:
whenever a person, a male individual, who possesses ethical discipline observes the purity of his own precepts, he then becomes free from regret.
Because there is no regret, there is joy; because of joy, gladness arises.
Through gladness of mind, the body attains pliancy;
through pliancy of body, one experiences supreme bliss.
Because of joy, the mind becomes concentrated.
Because the mind attains concentration, one is able to know things as they truly are and see them as they truly are.
Through such true knowledge and vision, one is then able to give rise to disenchantment.
Because one is able to give rise to revulsion, one attains freedom from passion (*vairāgya*).
By virtue of being free from passion, one realizes liberation (*vimukti*).
Having attained liberation, one knows and sees for oneself: "I am liberated," up to: "I shall attain parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*)."
In this way, all such individuals who are persons possessing ethical discipline (śīlavat-pudgala) obtain freedom from regret through the predominant power of their pure morality (śīla-viśuddhi),
gradually proceeding even unto the attainment of nirvāṇa.
This is called the first merit and benefit of the ethical discipline of restraint (*śīla-saṃvara*).
Furthermore, there is another person, a virtuous individual (*pudgala*),
who at the time of death gives rise to this thought:
"I have well performed actions of body, speech, and mind;
it is not that I have poorly performed actions of body, speech,
and mind," and so forth, as explained at length.
If there is a destination for those who perform meritorious deeds, those who practice wholesome actions, and those who are able to rescue others from all fears—
a destination to which they ought to go— then I shall certainly go to that destination.
Thus one attains rebirth in the happy realms.
Second, regarding freedom from regret: a man or individual who is without remorse is said to have a noble death, a noble passing away, and a noble departure.
This is called the second merit and excellence of the ethical discipline of restraint (*śīla-saṃvara*).
Furthermore, there is another virtuous person (*puruṣa-pudgala*) who possesses the precepts,
whose excellent reputation and verses of praise are widely heard throughout all regions.
This is called the third merit and excellence of the ethical discipline of restraint.
Furthermore, any other person or individual endowed with ethical discipline sleeps in peace and awakens in peace,
remaining far removed from all physical and mental afflictions.
This is called the fourth merit and benefit of the ethical discipline of restraint (*śīla-saṃvara*).

Furthermore, there is another merit: any person or individual (*pudgala*) who possesses ethical discipline will be protected by the devas whether they are asleep or awake; this is called the fifth merit and benefit of the ethical discipline of restraint.
Furthermore, there is another person, a man endowed with ethical discipline,
who does not consider the wickedness of others as evil;
he is free from all fear and his mind is devoid of alarm or terror.
This is called the sixth merit and benefit of the ethical discipline of restraint (*śīla-saṃvara*).
Furthermore, there are other persons (*pudgala*) who possess the precepts;
even if those who delight in killing—enemies or evil associates—should find an opportunity against them, [they will not succeed].
Furthermore, they always protect and recognize this person as a virtuous individual (*pudgala*) who possesses ethical discipline,
whether as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) or one who remains neutral.
This is called the seventh merit and benefit of the ethical discipline of restraint.
Furthermore, there may be other virtuous persons, individuals endowed with ethical discipline,
whom all classes of non-human beings— such as malevolent spirits, yakṣas, household deities, and the like—
may find an opportunity or a vulnerability to exploit.
And they are constantly protected,
because they possess the superior power of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
This is called the eighth merit and benefit of the ethical discipline of restraint (*śīla-saṃvara*).
Furthermore, there is another person, a man endowed with ethical discipline,
who obtains from others various forms of gain without difficulty—
namely, robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for the treatment of illness, and other such necessities.
By virtue of the dominant causal power of relying upon ethical discipline (śīla),
kings, ministers, commoners, wealthy elders, and merchant leaders will all honor and respect him.
This is called the ninth merit and excellence of the ethical discipline of restraint (*śīla-saṃvara*).
Furthermore, any other person or individual (*pudgala*) who possesses such ethical discipline will have all their aspirations fulfilled according to their wishes.

If, within the desire realm, one aspires to be born among the great kṣatriya clans, the great brāhmaṇa clans, the great householder clans, or the great merchant clans; or among the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three Gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, or the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods—within such a commonality of rebirth.
Because of the purity of their ethical discipline, they shall be reborn in accordance with their aspirations.

Furthermore, if they aspire to enter the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) for dwelling in happiness in the present life, or to abide in or be born among the classes of sentient beings in the form realms, they shall attain these states.
Because of the purity of ethical discipline, one becomes free from desire and all one's aspirations are fulfilled.
Furthermore, if one aspires to and delights in tranquility with resolute conviction,
one transcends the meditative absorptions of the form realm and enters the meditative absorptions of the formless realm, abiding therein in full perfection.
Or they shall attain rebirth within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the formless realm deities;
the rest is as previously described.
Furthermore, if they aspire and delight in realizing the most ultimate *nirvāṇa*, [they shall do so].
Because of the purity of ethical discipline, one realizes the ultimate transcendence of all desire.
This is called the tenth excellence and benefit of the śīla-vinaya.
Thus has the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīla-skandha) been explained.
An extensive analysis of the impairment of the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*),
the perfection of the aggregate of ethical discipline,
and the various classifications of the aggregate of ethical discipline.
The examination of the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) and the merits and benefits of that pure aggregate of ethical discipline;
herein, the restraint of morality (*śīlasaṃvara*) comprised within the most perfect provisions in all their aspects is clearly proclaimed and revealed.
If there are sons of good family who cherish themselves and delight in the state of a śramaṇa or the state of a brāhmaṇa,
they should diligently practice and study this.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 22.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Twenty-three.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

In the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, the thirteenth part of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the first *Yogasthāna*, the third section, "The Stage of Renunciation" (*Naiṣkramyabhūmi*), part two: What is the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasamvara*)?
It refers to a certain person who is well-established in the thorough protection of the doors of the sense faculties.
He guards right mindfulness and maintains constant, diligent mindfulness;
this is explained at length.
What is meant by "closely guarding the doors of the sense faculties"?
This refers to guarding right mindfulness and constant, diligent right mindfulness;
as explained at length, up to the protection of the faculty of the mind,
and the correct practice of the restraint of the mental faculty.
This is called "thoroughly guarding the doors of the sense faculties.
What is meant by "maintaining watch over right mindfulness"?
It refers to a certain person who, through the predominant power of thoroughly guarding the doors of the sense faculties, [proceeds as follows].
One embraces extensive learning,
reflects upon it, and practices it;
through the predominant power of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one attains right mindfulness.
This is for the purpose of ensuring that this attained right mindfulness is not forgotten,
is able to lead toward realization,
and is not lost or destroyed.
From time to time, he correctly applies himself to yoga regarding what has been heard, reflected upon, or cultivated;
he practices with right diligence, without ceasing his application and without abandoning his application.
In this way, by means of the mindfulness accumulated through hearing, reflection, and cultivation,
one is well able from time to time to guard the yogic activity of correct hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
This is called guarding right mindfulness.
What is meant by constant and thorough right mindfulness?
It refers to that mindfulness which is practiced continuously and performed with meticulous care.
It should be understood that herein, what is performed constantly is called "uninterrupted practice," and what is performed with meticulous care is called "reverent practice.
It is precisely regarding such uninterrupted and reverent practice [that this is said].
Taken collectively, this is called "constant and thorough mindfulness.
Just as one possesses guarded mindfulness,
so too is one able to avoid forgetting that mindfulness.
In accordance with his constant and thorough mindfulness,
he thereby attains the power of sustained retention regarding non-forgetfulness;
it is precisely through such functional efficacy that this occurs.
Having subdued forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects,
what is meant by "guarding the mind through mindfulness"?
It refers to the arising of visual consciousness conditioned by the eye and visible forms.
Immediately after visual consciousness, a conceptual mental consciousness arises.
By means of this conceptual mental consciousness,
one becomes attached to pleasant forms as they are about to arise.
When an unattractive form is about to give rise to hatred and resentment,
one is able to guard the mind against the arising of such afflictions through improper conceptualization by means of the predominant power of this very mindfulness.
This causes all afflictions not to arise.
One should know that the detailed explanation for the ear, nose, tongue, and body is likewise.
With the mind and mental objects as conditions, mind-consciousness arises.
This very mental consciousness is accompanied by irrational discrimination capable of giving rise to afflictions;
by means of this mental consciousness, one is about to give rise to defiled attachment toward attractive forms.
When unattractive forms are about to give rise to aversion and anger,
one is likewise able to guard the mind against the afflictions arising from such irrational conceptualization through the predominant power of this very mindfulness.
Causing all afflictions not to arise—
this is called "mindfulness guarding the mind.
What is meant by "practicing the state of equanimity"?
The state of equanimity refers to either wholesome equanimity or neutral equanimity;
it arises because one has properly guarded the mind against the afflictions produced by irrational conceptualization regarding this [object].
Within the midst of wholesome equanimity and neutral equanimity, one practices correctly;
for this reason, it is called "practicing the state of equality.
Thus is it called "practicing the state of equality."
How does one effectively guard the mind so that it does not give rise to afflictions through irrational conceptualization regarding these?
It means that with respect to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena,
one does not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics.
He never relies on those [thoughts] to give rise to various evil and unwholesome reflections that cause the mind to leak away.
Even if, at some time, he should lose mindfulness,
or because his afflictions are extremely intense, [he does not allow them to persist].
Although he is free from grasping at signs and secondary characteristics,
unwholesome and evil states nevertheless arise and cause his mind to leak;
he then cultivates restraint.
By means of these two characteristics,
one is able to effectively guard the mind that gives rise to afflictions through irrational conceptualization.
How does this mind become well-guarded by means of these two characteristics?
It is either wholesome equanimity or neutral equanimity;
that is, it is due to these two characteristics.
What are the two characteristics?
That is to say, as it has been taught regarding the guarding of the eye faculty and the correct practice of the restraint of the eye faculty,
so too has the guarding and restraint of the eye faculty been explained.
One should know that the guarding of the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue,
body, and mind, as well as the correct practice of the restraint of the mental faculty,
are likewise to be understood through these two characteristics.
Within that wholesome equanimity and neutral equanimity,
one causes the mind to proceed correctly.
How does one not grasp at the signs within the forms cognized by the eye?
Regarding the phrase "grasping at signs":
this refers to grasping the signs of the objects within the range of visual consciousness by means of that visual consciousness itself.
This is called grasping at the signs within the forms cognized by the eye.
If one can remain far removed from such signs that constitute the objective domain of visual consciousness,
this is called not grasping at the signs within the forms cognized by the eye.
Just as it is with respect to forms cognizable by the eye,
so it should be understood to be likewise with respect to phenomena cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
How does one not grasp at secondary characteristics among the forms cognized by the eye?
Grasping at secondary characteristics refers to [grasping] within those very forms cognized by the eye.
Immediately following visual consciousness, there arises a simultaneous conceptualizing mental consciousness that grasps the characteristics of its objective sphere;
it may give rise to attachment, aversion, or delusion.
This is called grasping at the secondary characteristics within forms cognized by the eye.
If one can distance oneself from these modes of activity,
no mental consciousness will arise with respect to this object of focus.
This is called not grasping at secondary characteristics among the forms cognized by the eye.
Just as it is with the forms cognized by the eye, so it is [with the others].
One should know that it is likewise with respect to the phenomena cognized by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Furthermore, there are other types who grasp at their general characteristics (*nimitta*) and grasp at their secondary details (*anuvyañjana*).
Regarding the phrase "grasping at characteristics":
That is to say, when the objective field of form is within range of visibility and capable of giving rise to mental attention,
the eye sees various forms as they are directly present before it.
This is called grasping its general characteristics (*nimitta*).
As for grasping its secondary details (*anuvyañjana*),
it refers to when the objective field of visible form is within range of sight and can give rise to mental attention (*manasikāra*).
When the eye is correctly present and has seen a form,
one then recalls that previously one had heard from another about such-and-such forms cognizable by the eye,
according to the names, phrases, and syllables as they were heard.
Taking that as the dominant influence, the basis,
and the support, such a person or individual,
according to what they have heard, engages in various conceptualizations regarding forms cognizable by the eye.
This is called grasping at secondary characteristics.
As it is with regard to forms cognized by the eye, so it is with regard to others.
One should know that it is likewise with respect to the phenomena cognized by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Furthermore, regarding this grasping of signs and grasping of secondary characteristics,
there may be certain causes and conditions for this.
Based on this basis and with this as the predominant condition,
various evil and unwholesome states arise, causing the mind to leak out.
Or there may be, by reason of this cause,
by means of this basis,
and through this predominance.
One does not give rise to various evil and unwholesome states that cause the mind to leak away.
If, within this, one grasps at their signs or grasps at their secondary characteristics, [the mind will flow out].
It is not in accordance with correct principle.
For these reasons and on this basis.
With this as the dominant condition,
various evil and unwholesome states arise, causing them to flow and leak into the mind.
Regarding such objects of that kind, he—
One remains far removed from grasping at signs and grasping at secondary characteristics.
What are called evil and unwholesome dharmas?
They refer to all forms of sensual desire and the various bodily misconducts arising from such desire.
All forms of verbal misconduct,
all forms of mental misconduct,
as well as all forms of ill will and all forms of delusion, along with the various bodily misconducts arising from those two.
All verbal misconduct and all mental misconduct—
these are called various kinds of evil and unwholesome dharmas.
How does it cause the mind to flow and leak?
It means that when the mind, intellect, and consciousness arise and wander, flowing and dispersing toward various objects of perception.
Regarding each respective object of focus,
it associates with the mind, intellect, and consciousness in various ways,
thereby giving rise to all unwholesome conduct of body and speech.
Greed, hatred, and delusion arise, wander, and disperse;
this is called "causing the mind to flow and leak" by means of them.
Thus it is with respect to forms cognized by the eye.
Even regarding phenomena cognized by the mind,
one grasps their general characteristics and their specific details;
from this, various forms of affliction arise.
Because he is able to distance himself from grasping at signs and grasping at secondary characteristics,
various defilements do not arise. However,
should they arise through forgetfulness or because the afflictions are extremely intense, [he recognizes them].
Although dwelling alone in seclusion, it occurs through the predominant influence of forms previously perceived by the eye,
or through the predominant influence of dharmas previously experienced by the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
When various unwholesome and unvirtuous states arise,
one does not cling to them as they arise; rather,
one immediately abandons, eliminates, discards, and spits them out.
This is called practicing restraint with regard to those [objects].
If one should exert control over the eye faculty regarding forms cognized by the eye,
and likewise exert control over the mind faculty regarding phenomena cognized by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Even when applying attention to that object and exerting effort,
one exerts oneself in such a way as to remain undefiled;
by this means, one guards the eye faculty against such defilement.
To speak at length, up to the guarding of the faculty of mind;
this is called guarding the faculty of eye,
and so on, up to guarding the faculty of mind.
If, regarding the forms cognized by the eye,
one should not exert the faculty of the eye;
and likewise regarding the phenomena cognized by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
One should not exert the faculty of mind;
thus, one does not exert it in any respect whatsoever.
Because one does not exert it, one remains undefiled.
For this reason, one practices restraint over the sense faculties regarding these defilements;
this is called practicing the restraint of the eye faculty correctly,
and so on, up to practicing the restraint of the mental faculty correctly.
Thus, it should be understood that the characteristics of the restraint of the sense faculties have been extensively analyzed.
Herein is the summary of the meaning.
This summary of the meaning is as follows:
That is to say: that which is able to guard,
that which is to be guarded, and that from which one guards.
Whether it be guarding or correctly guarding— in short,
all such instances are collectively termed "restraint of the sense faculties" (indriya-saṃvara).
In this context, who is able to guard?
It is the guarding of right mindfulness and the constant, diligent cultivation of right mindfulness that is able to guard.
What is it that is guarded?
It refers to guarding the faculty of the eye,
and guarding the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
This is that which is to be guarded against. From what is it guarded?
That is to say, from pleasant and unpleasant forms.
To speak at length, this extends even to correctly guarding against both agreeable and disagreeable phenomena.
How does one guard?

not for the sake of adornment;

...and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, one should understand the summarized meaning herein:
namely, for the purpose of embracing the remedies.
It is for the sake of avoiding the extreme of indulgence in sensual pleasures,
for the sake of avoiding the extreme of self-mortification,
and for the sake of embracing the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Regarding the consumption of food and drink:
what is the antidote for the grasping involved in consuming food and drink?
It is as it has been said: "One consumes food with right discernment."
What is meant by avoiding the extreme of indulgence in sensual pleasures while partaking of food and drink?
It refers to that which is described as not for the sake of dissipation,
nor for the sake of arrogance and negligence.
Not for the sake of adornment,
nor for the sake of physical beauty;
one eats what is eaten.
What is meant by avoiding the extreme of self-mortifying asceticism while partaking of food and drink?
It refers to what is said: for the sake of removing hunger and thirst, and for the sake of terminating past sensations.
In order that what has been newly received may not arise again, and so that it may be maintained through strength or ease,
one partakes of food.
How is it that one partakes of various foods for the sake of sustaining the holy life (*brahmacarya*)?
That is to say, as it is said: "One eats what is eaten for the sake of sustaining the holy life (brahmacarya) and for the sake of attaining dwelling in blamelessness and security."
Furthermore, one should know that the summarized meaning herein is twofold:
first, there is nothing to be eaten.
Second, there is that which has something to eat and that which has nothing to eat;
"that which has nothing to eat" means that in every respect, it has absolutely nothing to eat.
Because they have nothing to eat, they die prematurely.
Those who do have food to eat are of two kinds.
First, equal food;
second, unequal food.
As for equal food:
That is to say: eating neither too little, nor too much,
nor unsuitable food.
It is not that food is not digested;
it is not that food is defiled;
it is not that food is consumed unequally.
That is to say: either eating too little, or eating too much,
or eating unsuitable food.
Or food that is not digested,
or food that is defiled;
one should know that in this context, it refers to moderate eating and not to eating too little.
He causes his body to be free from hunger and emaciation, ensuring that what has not yet arisen does not arise and what has already arisen is brought to cessation.
By eating with moderation rather than excessive food,
his body is neither heavy nor sluggish, but becomes capable and fit for the practice of abandonment.
As explained in detail previously,
it is because he eats with equanimity, not unsuitable food,
and not undigested food.
Because one is able to sever [craving], new feelings do not arise.
By this cause and condition, one shall obtain sustenance, whether it be strength or pleasure,
through balanced food rather than defiled food.
One will dwell in peace and security, free from transgression.
Because of eating so little,
although one’s life is sustained, one remains emaciated by hunger and survives only with great difficulty.
Due to eating excessively,
it is as if his body is weighed down by an extremely heavy burden;
he is unable to digest and transform the food he has eaten in a timely manner.
Due to undigested food remaining within the body,
it causes the disease of indigestion,
or gives rise to various physical ailments and sufferings.
Just as with undigested food,
one should know that it is the same in the case of unsuitable food.
As for the specific distinctions regarding this unsuitable food:
This refers to the accumulation of various afflictions within the body,
by which one further encounters the suffering of extremely grave illness,
due to defiled food.
Having sought various foods and drinks through unrighteous means,
they consume them with defilement, craving, indulgence,
and gluttony, as previously explained in detail.
Because one partakes of food with equanimity and avoids food that is unequitable,
it is said that one performs the practice of equanimity regarding food.
This very practice of equanimity regarding food is extensively proclaimed,
revealed, and elucidated through various phrases;
that is to say, it is taught that one eats what is consumed through correct discernment.
Not for dissipation;
not for arrogance or indulgence;
not for the sake of ornamentation.
It is not for the sake of physical beauty,
as explained extensively before.
In this context, it is said:
One partakes of food with correct discernment,
neither for the sake of indulgence nor for the sake of arrogance and negligence.
It is not for the sake of adornment,
nor for the sake of beauty;
it is for the sake of the body’s stability and for temporary support.
By this, it is refuted that there is nothing at all to be eaten.
Furthermore, if it is said [that eating is for] the purpose of removing hunger and thirst,
or for the sake of upholding the holy life (brahmacarya), [it is still not tenable].
To speak at length, up until dwelling in peace and security;
by this, one prevents unequal eating.
How does one prevent unequal eating?
That is to say, if it is said that [eating] is for the purpose of removing hunger and thirst,
this precludes eating an excessively small amount;
and if it is further said that it is for the purpose of supporting the holy life (brahmacarya).
By this, eating in excessive amounts is prohibited; furthermore, it is said that this is for the purpose of severing existing sensations and ensuring that new sensations do not arise again.
By this, one also prohibits eating before what has been consumed has been digested, as well as eating what is unsuitable.
Furthermore, if it is said "for the sake of maintaining life" or "for the sake of gaining strength," this demonstrates that one does not eat too little nor eat too much.
Furthermore, if it is said "for the sake of attaining happiness," [it means for the sake of a balanced state].
By this, it is shown that one eats after having digested and that one eats what is appropriate.
Furthermore, when it is said, "so that one may dwell blamelessly and in security," by this it is shown that the food is free from defilement.
Why is this? If one seeks food and drink through improper means,
and having obtained them, partakes of them with attachment and craving as extensively described before.
It is called defiled sustenance and is also termed blameworthy.
For one who diligently cultivates the side of virtue,
regarding the meditative application of yoga while dwelling in seclusion:
While upholding, reciting, and contemplating the meaning [of the teachings],
those various evil and unwholesome discursive thoughts cause the mind to leak away and cause the mind to continue in succession.
It proceeds by conforming to, inclining toward,
and entering [the state], and by reason of this,
one does not dwell in peace. Furthermore, this dwelling in peace is of two kinds.
First, one avoids eating in excess;
by reason of this, the body is not heavy,
and one possesses the capacity and fitness to practice for abandonment.
As explained extensively above,
second, one does not give rise to attachment to the flavors of food.
By reason of this, one remains far removed from all evil discursive thoughts and dwells in peace, free from agitation and unrest.
Regarding food, such equal application as this is called the detailed and abbreviated exposition on knowing the proper measure in eating.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 23; *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 24.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

In the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, the Thirteenth [Section] of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the First Yoga Station, the Third Part of the *Nairyāṇikabhūmi*: Furthermore, regarding those who constantly and diligently practice the yoga of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night:
What is the first watch of the night? What is the last watch of the night?
What is the yoga of wakefulness?
What is the constant and diligent cultivation of the yoga of wakefulness?
One part constitutes the first watch of the night.
As for "the latter part of the night," it refers to that which follows the first part among the four divisions of the night; this is the final portion of the night.
The yoga of wakefulness refers to what is said as follows: during the daytime, one purifies the mind of obstructive factors through walking meditation and sitting meditation.
During the first watch of the night, he practiced walking meditation and seated meditation,
purifying his mind of obstructive states.
Having purified his mind, he went outside his dwelling and washed his feet.
Returning to his dwelling, he lies down on his right side with one foot resting upon the other;
maintaining the perception of light, with mindfulness and clear comprehension, and mindful of the thought of rising, he lies down skillfully.
In the latter part of the night, he quickly awakens and practices walking meditation and seated meditation.
He purifies his mind from factors that obstruct [practice],
constantly and diligently cultivating the yoga of wakefulness.
That is to say, there is a disciple of the Blessed One who,
having heard the yoga of awakening,
desires to train in it with joyful diligence.
Then, relying upon such yoga of wakefulness,
he forms this thought:
"I shall accomplish the yoga of wakefulness permitted by the Buddha."
He gives rise to aspiration, diligence, and tireless exertion;
he transcends through courageous power and initiative;
he is valiant, resolute, and invincible.
One should exert the mind so that it continues uninterruptedly.
In this regard, how does one, during the daytime, purify the mind from obstructive factors through walking meditation and sitting meditation?
"Daytime" refers to the period from sunrise until sunset.
"Walking" refers to...
This refers to the bodily action of moving back and forth within a space that is broad and long according to its measured dimensions;
as for the term "sitting in quietude":
That is to say, there is someone who, whether on a large couch, a small rope-seat,
or a seat of grass and leaves, sits cross-legged,
with body erect and mindfulness directed toward the front, dwelling in right resolve.
What is called "obstruction" refers to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).
"Factors conducive to obstruction" refers to—
This refers to those factors that induce the hindrances and are conducive to the hindrances.
What are the five hindrances?
They are the hindrance of sensual desire and the hindrance of ill will.
Regarding the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse,
and the hindrance of doubt:
what are the factors conducive to these hindrances?
That is to say: the sign of purity and excellence, the sign of ill-will, the sign of darkness, and the reflections on relatives, one’s country, and immortality;
as well as the recollection of past laughter, play, joy, pleasure, and service, and the contemplation of the three periods of time.
Or one contemplates dharmas that are unreasonable with respect to the three times.
Question: During the time of walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), from how many obstructive dharmas does one purify the mind?
How does one purify the mind from them?
Answer: One purifies the mind with respect to the hindrance of sloth and torpor, as well as those factors conducive to sloth and torpor,
in order to eliminate them.
Being skillful and earnest regarding the perception of light,
one correctly grasps, correctly contemplates, correctly understands, and correctly penetrates it; thus,
with a mind accompanied by clarity and a mind accompanied by radiance.
Whether in a secluded place or an open space, he walks back and forth in meditation.
While walking, he focuses on a certain kind of pure and sublime object,
skillfully manifesting it to instruct, encourage, inspire, and comfort his mind.
That is to say, one either recollects the Buddha, or the Dharma, or the Saṅgha;
or one recollects ethical discipline, or renunciation, or the devas;
or one attends to the true Dharma that explains the faults associated with lethargy and drowsiness.
Within this teaching, in order to eliminate those [faults],
he censures and reviles the faults of sloth and torpor through immeasurable methods,
and he extols and praises the merit of the permanent abandonment of sloth and torpor through immeasurable methods.
That is to say:
the sūtras, the verses (geya),
the prophecies (vyākaraṇa), and the chants (gāthā).
Discourses on causes and conditions,
parables, past events,
birth stories, and vaipulya teachings.
In order to eliminate those [obstacles], such as attachment to mere rules and rituals and to speculative debate,
one listens to and upholds this True Dharma.
With a great voice, one should read or recite it,
explain it to others, contemplate its meaning,
weigh it, and examine it.
Alternatively, one may observe the cardinal directions;
or gaze upon the stars, the moon, and the various lunar mansions and celestial paths;
or wash and sprinkle the face and eyes with cold water.
By this means, the hindrances of torpor and drowsiness that have not yet arisen do not arise, and those already arisen are eliminated.
In this way, through such skillful means, one purifies the mind of factors that are obstructive.
Question: When sitting in meditative seclusion, from how many obstructive factors does one purify the mind?
How does one purify the mind from them?
Answer: One purifies the mind from four obstructive factors.
That is to say: the hindrance of sensual desire,
ill will, restlessness and remorse,
doubt, and those factors that lead toward them.
He purifies his mind so that the already arisen fetters and hindrances of sensual desire may be swiftly dispelled,
and so that those not yet arisen may be utterly prevented from arising.
Sitting cross-legged with the body upright and the mind set in right intention,
one dwells in mindfulness directed toward the back [of the body],
or contemplates it as livid, or as festering, or as decomposing, or as bloated.
Or one contemplates them as being devoured, or contemplates them as smeared with blood;
or one contemplates their bones, or contemplates their skeletons,
or contemplates the chain of bones.
Alternatively, one attends to and contemplates any one of the signs of a virtuous meditative concentration,
or the sublime Dharma that explains the faults and disadvantages associated with sensual desire.
Within this Dharma, in order to sever craving,
he censures and reviles sensual desire and sensual attachment through immeasurable methods.
They desire to conceal it, they desire to protect it,
and they desire to cling to its faults through immeasurable means.
One extols and praises the merit of the eternal severance of all craving,
as set forth in the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, and so forth, in detail;
this is for the purpose of severing craving.
Regarding this True Dharma, they listen to it and receive and uphold it;
they master it thoroughly through speech and investigate it skillfully with the mind.
Seeing this clearly and penetratingly,
one sits in meditative composure within these very dharmas and reflects upon them according to reality.
By means of this cause and condition, the fetters and hindrances of sensual desire that have not yet arisen do not arise, and those already arisen are eliminated.
In this way, by means of such skillful methods, he purifies his mind of those factors that are obstructive.
Regarding the specific distinction concerning the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*), it is as follows:
he sits in meditative seclusion with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Without enmity and without adversaries;
without harm and without affliction;
vast, immeasurable, and perfectly cultivated.
One develops resolute conviction toward all directions and dwells fully established therein;
likewise for the second, the third, and the fourth,
extending upward, downward, and across.
He universally pervades all boundless worlds,
giving rise to resolute conviction and dwelling therein fully;
the rest is as previously explained.
Regarding the distinction between the hindrances of restlessness and remorse:
it refers to sitting in such a manner that one causes the mind to abide within, achieves one-pointedness, and attains samādhi.
The rest is as previously explained; however, regarding the distinction concerning the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*), it is as follows:
while thus seated in meditative composure, one does not engage in improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) directed toward the past.
In the future world and in the present world, one does not engage in improper mental attention by thinking:
"Did I exist in the past? Or did I not exist?"
What was I in the past? How was I in the past?
What shall I be in the future?
How will it come to be? What do I have in the present? And how does it exist?
One should correctly distance oneself from such improper mental attention as: "From where have these sentient beings come?
Having perished here, where will they go? and so forth.
Reflecting in accordance with reality,
one perceives in the past, future,
and present worlds only phenomena and only events.
Knowing the conditioned as conditioned and the unconditioned as unconditioned;
observing only causes and observing only effects;
neither adding to nor augmenting that which is substantially non-existent.
One does not disparage or slander that which truly exists;
one understands that which truly exists as being truly existent—
namely, within all phenomena that are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
One thoroughly understands impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
By being able to reflect in this manner according to the truth,
one becomes free from confusion and doubt regarding the Buddha.
The rest is as previously stated.
Regarding the Dharma and the Sangha;
regarding suffering and its origin.
Regarding cessation and the path,
as well as causes and the phenomena produced by causes,
he is without confusion and without doubt.
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, regarding the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*), it should be stated as follows:
for the sake of abandoning ill-will and the signs of ill-will.
Regarding this True Dharma, one should listen to it, receive and uphold it, and so forth, as explained at length.
Concerning the hindrance of restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*), one should speak in this way:
for the sake of abandoning restlessness and remorse, as well as those factors conducive to them.
Regarding this True Dharma, one listens to it, receives and upholds it, and so forth, as explained at length.
Concerning the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*), one should speak thus:
for the sake of severing the hindrance of doubt and for the sake of conforming to that Dharma.
Regarding this true Dharma, one listens to it, receives and upholds it, and so forth, as explained at length.
By such means, one [is freed] from sensual desire,
ill will, sloth and torpor.
He thoroughly purifies his mind of the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, as well as the hindrance of doubt,
and those factors conducive to them.
Therefore it is said: "Whether walking or sitting, one purifies the mind by means of the factors conducive to the hindrances.
Thus has been explained, with reference to the Dharma, how [one proceeds] from the factors conducive to the hindrances.
He purifies his mind. Furthermore,
there are those who, through the influence of themselves and the influence of the world,
[turn away] from factors that are conducive to hindrances.
He purifies his mind.
What is meant by "by means of self-mastery"?
It refers to a case where someone gives rise to any one of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
He then understands for himself that this is not a wholesome dharma;
he does not cling firmly to the hindrance that has arisen,
but quickly abandons, casts out, and spits it away.
Furthermore, one is able to observe for oneself that these arisen hindrances are deeply shameful;
they defile and afflict the mind and weaken wisdom, constituting a category of harm.
This is what is meant by "predominance through oneself."
One purifies the mind by means of the factors that are conducive to the obstacles.
What is meant by "predominance through the mundane"?
One purifies the mind by means of the factors that counteract obstacles;
that is to say, there is someone for whom one or another of the hindrances has already arisen, or is about to arise.
He then thought: "If I were to give rise to an unarisen hindrance,
I would be censured by the Great Teacher."
Furthermore, they disparage the various devas and their wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life by means of the Dharma;
because of such worldly preeminence, they [suffer].
It causes unarisen hindrances not to arise and causes already arisen hindrances to be swiftly abandoned;
this is what is meant by "predominance through the worldly."
He purifies his mind by means of the factors conducive to overcoming obstacles,
and furthermore, for the sake of protecting and maintaining his bedding and requisites.
In accordance with worldly etiquette,
during the first watch of the night, he practices walking meditation and sits in quietude,
thereby distancing himself from factors that obstruct [the path].
He purifies his mind.
Having purified his mind from factors that obstruct [the path], he proceeds.
Having gone outside the dwelling, he washes his feet.
Having washed his feet, he returns to the dwelling and lies down to sleep according to the Dharma,
in order to nourish and sustain the great elements through rest.
Once they have increased, they further benefit the body;
their power becomes greater and they become increasingly able to accord with the continuous and constant application of wholesome qualities.
Question: For what reason does he lie on his right side?
Answer: Because it is similar to the manner of the lion king.
Question: In what way is it similar?
The answer is: Just as the lion king is the foremost among all beasts for its courage, ferocity,
and steadfastness, so too is the bhikṣu regarding the constant cultivation of the yoga of wakefulness.
He exerts diligent effort that is courageous, steadfast, and fierce,
which is preeminent; for this reason, his manner of lying down resembles that of the lion king,
unlike the way other spirits, devas, or those who indulge in sensual desires lie down.
Because they are all indolent, lazy, and inferior,
their power of diligence is weak;
moreover, such is the nature of things.
Just as the lion king lies on his right side,
when he sleeps in this manner, his body is free from agitation,
his mindfulness does not fail, his sleep is not excessive, and he sees no evil dreams.
Those who lie down in a manner contrary to this possess all faults; therefore,
it is said that one should lie on the right side with the feet placed one upon the other.
What is meant by lying down with skillful means while dwelling upon the perception of light?
It refers to being skillful and earnest regarding the perception of light,
properly grasping it, properly reflecting upon it, properly understanding it, and properly penetrating it.
He reflects with a mind focused on the radiance of the devas and lies down with skillful means;
by reason of this, although he is sleeping, his mind does not become clouded or darkened.
This is called lying down with skillful means by dwelling upon the perception of light.
What is lying down with skillful means through right mindfulness?
It refers to those phenomena that have been heard, reflected upon, and repeatedly cultivated.
Its essential nature is wholesome and capable of leading to meaningful benefit.
By means of right mindfulness, it continues to function even during sleep and dreams.
Through right mindfulness, one maintains constant recollection within sleep and dreams, causing the characteristics of those phenomena to appear clearly before the mind.
He then frequently observes that very state of mind with mental attention;
through right mindfulness, he remains aware of whatever the mind is inclined toward,
whether it falls asleep in a wholesome state or in a neutral state.
This is called lying down with skillful means through right mindfulness.
What is lying down with skillful means through right awareness?
It refers to the time when one lies down while possessing right mindfulness.
If any single affliction should manifest and defile the mind,
at the very moment that affliction arises,
one is able to correctly discern it and ensure that one does not become firmly attached to it.
One should swiftly abandon them;
having mastered this, one causes the mind to turn back.
This is called lying down with correct awareness and skillful means.
What is meant by lying down with skillful means while maintaining the perception of being aroused by reflection?
It refers to lying down after having first exerted and roused the mind through diligence.
When lying down to sleep, one should wake up at frequent intervals;
like a deer in the forest, one should not allow the mind to run wild,
nor should one follow its inclinations as it drifts toward falling asleep.
Again, he thinks:
"I should now fully accomplish and complete all the yogas of awakening permitted by the Buddhas."
In order to accomplish this,
one should abide in a state of diligent application characterized by an extremely intense desire for practice,
and further reflect as follows:
Now, for the sake of cultivating the yoga of wakefulness,
I should dwell having rightly aroused diligent effort,
desiring to practice all wholesome dharmas.
One should be correctly ardent and diligent, free from all sloth and indolence, and endowed with the arousal of energy.
Having passed this night, when the clear dawn arrives,
one should redouble the arousal of effort and diligence, abiding fully endowed with the arousal of energy.
It should be understood that herein, by means of the first reflection, one forms the perception [of time],
does not fall into deep sleep,
and is able to arise quickly at the time for arising, never missing the appointed hour.
Only then does one awaken;
by means of the second reflection,
one gives rise to the perception that allows for the lion’s posture, which is permitted by all the Buddhas.
Lying down in accordance with the Dharma, neither increasing nor decreasing,
one should, through the third reflection,
form the perception of arising so that wholesome aspiration and delight remain ever free from laxity or negligence.
Even if one experiences lapses in mindfulness, one is able to receive and study [the teachings] successively and continuously so that they are never interrupted.
This is called lying down with skillful means through the cultivation of the perception of rising.
How does one, during the latter part of the night, quickly awaken and engage in walking meditation and sitting meditation,
purifying the mind from obstructive states?
Regarding "the latter part of the night":
That is to say, among the four parts of the night, the period after the final quarter is called the latter part of the night.
By means of such a practice, he dwells with the perception of light,
and with right mindfulness and clear comprehension, he lies down while reflecting on the thought of rising through skillful means.
During the middle watch of the night— having passed one-quarter of the four watches—
one practices sleep so that,
upon waking, the body possesses the necessary capability for activity.
One should arise at the proper time,
not being overcome by the fetters of intense torpor and drowsiness,
which would cause one to be dull-witted, weak, indolent, and lazy when it is time to rise.
Because one is free from such dullness, feebleness, indolence, and laziness,
there is no difficulty when directing the mind for even a moment,
and one is able to arouse it with great speed.
Regarding the purification of the mind from obstructive states,
it should be understood as previously explained. Thus,
having extensively analyzed the constant and diligent practice of the yoga of wakefulness during both the first and last watches of the night, [the text continues].
For any person or individual who practices the yoga of awakening,
there are briefly four kinds of correct tasks to be performed. What are these four?
First, until one awakens, one never abandons the categories of wholesome qualities being cultivated;
one practices with uninterrupted, constant, and diligent vigor within the cultivation of wholesome dharmas.
Second, one sleeps at the proper time and not at an improper time.
Third, one practices sleep with an undefiled mind, not with a defiled mind.
Fourth, one awakens at the proper time and does not rise past the appointed hour.
These are called the four kinds of constant and diligent cultivation of the yoga of wakefulness.
Whatever right activities are performed by any person or individual,
it is based upon these four kinds of right activities that the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, have taught the practice of the yoga of wakefulness for the assembly of śrāvakas.
How is this taught?
It is said: "During the daytime, one should purify the mind by means of walking meditation and sitting meditation, [thereby] cleansing it of factors that are obstructive."
During the first watch of the night, one practices walking meditation and sits in seclusion,
purifying the mind of obstructive states;
by these words, the first task to be correctly performed is proclaimed.
This means that until one awakens, one never abandons the cultivation of wholesome qualities;
with uninterrupted and constant diligence, one applies heroic effort in the practice of wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, it is said that one goes outside the dwelling to wash one's feet.
Returning to his dwelling, he lies down on his right side with one foot overlapping the other.
By this statement, the second proper practice is proclaimed:
namely, that one should sleep at the proper time and not at an improper time.
Furthermore, if it is said that one dwells with the perception of light,
being mindful and clearly comprehending, and lies down with the thought of rising in mind through skillful means—
by this statement, the third right practice is proclaimed.
This means that one practices sleep with an undefiled mind, not with a defiled mind;
furthermore, it is said that during the latter part of the night, one quickly awakens to practice walking meditation or sitting meditation.
One purifies the mind by means of the factors that are conducive to the removal of hindrances.
By this statement, the fourth right task is proclaimed:
namely, awakening at the proper time and not letting the time for rising pass by.
In this context, the description of one who lies down with skillful means— dwelling in the perception of light,
with right mindfulness and clear comprehension, and attending to the thought of rising—
demonstrates that one practices sleep with an undefiled mind through two conditions, rather than with a defiled mind.
That is to say, by means of right mindfulness and right situational awareness,
and further through two conditions, one awakens at the proper time and does not let the time pass.
That is to say, by means of dwelling upon the perception of light and by means of reflecting upon the perception of arising;
furthermore, how is this accomplished through right mindfulness?
He lies down having withdrawn his mind into a virtuous object of focus.
By means of clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*), if his mind should lapse from that virtuous object and afflictions arise,
he is able to immediately and correctly recognize it.
Thus, it is said that for two reasons the mind is undefiled:
one practices sleep with an undefiled mind by dwelling in the perception of light and by reflecting on the thought of rising.
There is no heavy sleep nor the obsession of sleep that can persistently follow him from afar.
This is called awakening at the proper time and not missing the appointed hour due to two conditions.
The summary meaning of the yoga of awakening,
as well as the detailed explanations and interpretations previously set forth.
Taken together, this is called "constantly and diligently practicing the yoga of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night" for the sake of dwelling in clear comprehension.
That is to say, there is someone who...
Whether going out or returning, he dwells with clear comprehension;
whether looking ahead or looking aside, he dwells with clear comprehension;
whether bending or stretching, he dwells with clear comprehension.
He dwells with clear comprehension while wearing the saṃghāṭī robe and carrying the bowl and robes;
he dwells with clear comprehension whether eating, drinking, chewing, or tasting;
he dwells with clear comprehension whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
He dwells with clear comprehension while awake;
he dwells with clear comprehension whether speaking or remaining silent;
he dwells with clear comprehension when dispelling fatigue and drowsiness.
Regarding "dwelling with clear comprehension whether going out or returning":
what is going out? What is returning?
What is dwelling with clear comprehension regarding going and returning?
As for "going," it refers to a certain person who goes to a village or travels between villages.
He goes to family members and among family members;
he goes to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and among those at the site of enlightenment.
As for what is meant by "returning":
That is to say, there is someone who returns from one village to another village,
from one family to another family,
or from one place of practice to another place of practice.
Regarding what is called "dwelling with clear comprehension in going and returning":
it means being clearly aware when going out that "I am going," and being clearly aware when returning that "I am returning."
He correctly understands what should be gone toward and what should not be gone toward;
he correctly understands what should be returned from and what should not be returned from;
and he correctly understands the proper time to go and the improper time to go.
He correctly understands the proper time for returning and the improper time for returning;
he correctly understands exactly where one should go and where one should not go.
To correctly understand, as they truly are, what should be pursued and what should not be pursued in such and such a manner is called clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*).
By virtue of accomplishing this clear comprehension, he...
Knowing for oneself, one goes; knowing for oneself, one returns.
One goes where one ought to go, not where one ought not to go;
one returns where one ought to return, not where one ought not to return.
One should go and return at the proper time, not at an improper time.
According to one's social class, one should proceed and return with the correct rules of conduct, ritual propriety, and dignified demeanor;
thus one goes, and thus one returns.
This is called dwelling with clear comprehension whether going out or returning.
Regarding dwelling with clear comprehension when looking or gazing:
what is meant by "looking"?
What is looking?
What is looking while dwelling in clear comprehension?
As for "looking":
That is to say, regarding the various matters previously enumerated,
whether going or returning, there was previously no discerning wisdom and no deliberate effort.
First there is no desire or pleasure;
in the interval between these, seeing various forms with the eye is called "beholding.
As for what is called "gazing":
That is to say, regarding the various matters previously enumerated,
whether going or returning,
one is preceded by awakened wisdom.
With effort as the precursor and desire as the precursor,
one sees various forms with the eye.
That is to say, whether they be kings or those like kings,
or ministers and officials, or commoners,
or brahmins, or householders.
Or wealthy elders and merchant leaders with abundant treasures;
or other external objects such as houses, dwellings, palaces, halls, and courtyards;
or other various and wonderful worldly things.
To observe and see these things is called "looking" (prekṣaṇa).
Furthermore, if one can correctly understand the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of what is being seen and looked at,
one can correctly understand that which should be seen and that which should be looked at.
When it is time to look and when it is time to gaze, one is able to understand correctly;
understanding correctly what should be looked at and what should be gazed upon is called "clear comprehension" (saṃprajanya).
By virtue of accomplishing this clear comprehension,
he sees with self-awareness and looks with self-awareness;
he sees what ought to be seen and looks at what ought to be looked at.
When it is time to look and when it is time to gaze,
one looks and gazes correctly; one looks and gazes in the manner that one should look and gaze.
This is called dwelling with clear comprehension whether looking or gazing.
Regarding dwelling with clear comprehension when bending or stretching:
what is meant by "bending"?
What is stretching?
What is meant by dwelling with clear comprehension whether bending or stretching?
It refers to when one looks or gazes in such a manner.
Whether going forward first or returning first,
whether bending or extending the feet, or bending or extending the arms,
or bending or extending the hands.
Alternatively, the bending and extending of any single limb or joint is called "bending and extending.
If one can correctly understand the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) inherent in this bending and extending, [that is the practice].
If one can correctly understand what is being bent or extended;
if one can correctly understand at the time of bending or extending;
if it is bent in such a manner.
And when one thus applies oneself and is able to understand correctly,
this is called "clear comprehension.
Because he has accomplished this clear comprehension, [he acts with full awareness].
He knows when to bend and knows when to extend;
he bends where it is appropriate to bend and extends where it is appropriate to extend;
he bends at the time it is appropriate to bend and extends at the time it is appropriate to extend.
Bending as it should be bent and stretching as it should be stretched, one bends in such a manner and stretches in such a manner.
This is called dwelling with clear comprehension whether bending or stretching.
Regarding "dwelling with right mindfulness while carrying the saṃghāṭī, as well as the robes and the bowl":
how does one carry the saṃghāṭī?
How does one carry the robes?
How does one carry the alms-bowl?
How does one dwell with clear comprehension while carrying the saṃghāṭī, as well as the robes and the bowl?
This refers to possessing a great robe, such as one consisting of sixty strips or nine strips, and so forth.
Alternatively, that which is double-layered is called a *saṃghāṭī*.
To wear it and use it so as to properly protect [the body] is termed "wearing" (*dhāraṇa*).
Whether there be an intermediate robe or a lower robe,
whether it has been held as a robe, or there be an extra robe,
or one that ought to be purified, or one already purified.
All such things are called "clothing";
that which is worn and used for the purpose of properly protecting [the body] is called "possessing."
If one is able to accept and maintain an alms-bowl made either of iron or clay for the purpose of begging food,
it is called a *pātra*;
it is currently used for consumption and should be properly protected.
This is called "retention. If,
regarding such a *saṃghāṭī*, robe, or bowl,
one is able to correctly cognize their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding what should be maintained— whether it be the saṃghāṭī, the robes, or the bowl—
he correctly understands them as pure or impure.
At such a time, whether it be the saṃghāṭī, the robes, or the bowl...
Having taken up what should be taken up, he is able to correctly understand it.
Whether it be a saṃghāṭī, a robe, or an alms bowl,
he is able to correctly understand that it should be carried in such a manner.
This is called right knowledge (*saṃprajanya*).
Because he has accomplished this right knowledge,
regarding that which he should carry— whether it be his outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*), or his [upper] robe, or his bowl—
