Knowing for oneself, one maintains it;
regarding that which should be maintained and the time when it should be maintained, one is able to maintain it correctly.
To hold [the robes] in the manner they should be held—
this is called dwelling with clear comprehension while holding the saṃghāṭī, as well as the robes and bowl.
To dwell with clear comprehension whether eating, drinking, chewing, or tasting [is likewise].
What is food? What is drink?
What is that which is chewed?
What is tasting?
How does one dwell in clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, or tasting?
All that is consumed as food and drink is collectively termed "nutriment" (āhāra).
This, moreover, is of two kinds:
first, chewing; second, tasting.
What is meant by "chewing"?
It refers to chewing cakes, parched grain flour, or boiled rice, or gruel, or soup, or broth;
or whatever else has been prepared or transformed that may be chewed or eaten.
That which can sustain life—
such categories as these are all termed "chewing" (khādanīya) and are also termed "eating" (bhojanīya).
What is meant by "tasting"?
It refers to tasting milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, oil, honey, sugar,
fish, meat, vinegar, and pickled fish.
Whether it be fresh fruits or various kinds of chewable substances—
all such things are collectively termed "tasting" and also termed "eating."
What constitutes a drink?
It refers to sugarcane juice,
or honey-juice, or rice-gruel, or buttermilk.
Whether it be sour gruel as a drink, or the churning of curdled milk as a drink,
even down to water— all such things are collectively termed "drinks.
Whether it be food, drink, chewing, or tasting, if one [partakes] in such things...
One correctly understands all specific characteristics.
Furthermore, regarding everything that is eaten,
drunk, chewed, or tasted, one correctly understands them.
If at that time there is something to be eaten, drunk,
chewed, or tasted, one is able to correctly discern it;
if there is such as this to be eaten or drunk...
To be able to correctly discern what should be eaten and what should be tasted is called "clear comprehension.
Because he has accomplished this clear comprehension, [he acts with full awareness].
Regarding whatever food, drink, chewing, or tasting one possesses,
one eats with self-awareness, drinks with self-awareness,
chews with self-awareness, and tastes with self-awareness.
Regarding what should be eaten, what should be drunk,
what should be chewed, and what should be tasted,
he eats, drinks, chews, and tastes with proper moderation.
One should eat at the proper time and drink at the proper time;
one should chew at the proper time and taste at the proper time—
eating as is appropriate, and so on, up to tasting as is appropriate.
Thus one eats, and so on, up to thus tasting.
This is called dwelling with clear comprehension whether eating, drinking, chewing, or tasting.
Whether walking or standing, and so forth, up to being established in clear comprehension when dispelling fatigue and sleep—
what is meant by "walking" and what is meant by "standing"?
What is sitting?
What is lying down?
What is being awake?
What is speech? What is silence?
What is called "understanding fatigue and sleep"?
And what is "dwelling in clear comprehension" regarding walking, and so forth, up to understanding fatigue and sleep?
This refers to, for example, when someone walks back and forth on a path for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*),
or goes to visit those of like dharma, or travels along a road;
such categories as these are called "walking" (*caryā*).
Furthermore, it is as if there were someone staying at a place for walking meditation,
or staying in the presence of fellow practitioners of the Dharma, ācāryas, upādhyāyas, and other elders and venerable ones.
Such categories as these are called "abiding.
Furthermore, it is like someone who, on either a large couch or a small rope-couch,
or on a seat of grass and leaves, or upon various other bedding materials, [remains].
Alternatively, one may sit cross-legged upon a *niṣīdana*,
with body upright and mindfulness established before oneself;
such categories as these are called "sitting."
Furthermore, it is as if there is someone who goes outside the dwelling to wash his feet,
then returns to the dwelling and sits upon either a large bed or a small rope-couch.
Whether on a seat of grass and leaves, in a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka),
at the foot of a tree, or in an empty, quiet room,
he lies down on his right side with one foot overlapping the other.
Such categories as these are called lying down.
Furthermore, there is one who, during the daytime, practices walking meditation and sits in quietude,
purifying his mind of obstructive states.
During the first watch of the night and the last watch of the night,
one practices walking meditation and sits in seclusion, purifying the mind of obstructive states;
this is called wakefulness.
Furthermore, there is another who constantly and diligently practices such wakefulness,
whereby he brings to ultimate perfection the teachings not yet received, as well as those already correctly received and practiced—
namely, the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, and so forth, as explained at length previously.
Regarding these very teachings already received,
one says they have been well-mastered;
that is, one reads or recites them with a loud voice.
Or again, he extensively explains and reveals it to others from time to time,
together with wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life.
Or other virtuous and noble householders may speak with him,
engaging in conversation and mutual greetings,
desiring to encourage him and seek the requisites for his needs.
Such categories as these are called speech.
Furthermore, there is one who, according to what was previously heard and according to what was previously practiced,
speaks with complete mastery and thorough penetration regarding all phenomena.
Dwelling alone in seclusion,
he contemplated its meaning,
deliberating and examining it.
Or, staying in a quiet room, one causes the mind to abide internally, to abide equally, to abide securely, and to abide closely;
it is tamed, stilled, thoroughly stilled, and brought to one-pointed concentration.
Or again, one may practice the yoga of *vipaśyanā* (insight) therein;
such categories as these are called "silence.
Furthermore, it is like someone during the hot season, at a time of extreme scorching heat.
Whether oppressed by heat or exhausted by toil, one gives rise to weariness;
to become drowsy at an improper time and to take pleasure in attachment to sleep is called "fatigue-induced sleep.
Furthermore, regarding walking, and so forth in detail up to the resolution of fatigue-induced sleep, one correctly understands their respective specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
He correctly discerns that which should be practiced, up to and including the removal of fatigue and drowsiness;
he correctly discerns the time for practice, up to and including the time for removing fatigue and drowsiness.
To correctly understand, as it truly is, what should be done up to the point of dispelling drowsiness and fatigue—
this is called *saṃprajanya*.
Because he is endowed with this *saṃprajanya*, [he acts accordingly].
Regarding his own conduct, up to his own awakening from drowsiness and fatigue, he acts with clear comprehension;
up to his awakening from drowsiness and fatigue, he does so with clear comprehension.
Whether it be that which should be done, up to that which should be done for awakening from drowsiness and fatigue.
He walks when it is time to walk, and so on, until he dispels fatigue and sleep when it is time to dispel them; at whatever time it is appropriate to walk,
and so on, at that very time he walks, and so on, until at that very time he dispels fatigue and sleep.
Just as one should act, up to just as one should dispel drowsiness and fatigue,
so one acts, up to so one dispels drowsiness and fatigue.
This is called [the practice] regarding walking and standing.
Whether sitting or lying down,
whether awake or speaking,
whether silent or dispelling drowsiness and fatigue.
He dwells with clear comprehension.
Furthermore, regarding this dwelling with clear comprehension:
what is the sequence, and what matter does it reveal?
That is to say, there is someone who dwells depending upon such a village,
town, market, or watch-station, and reflects:
"I should now go to such a village, town, market, or watch-station."
He wanders for alms;
having thus begged, he returns to his original place.
Furthermore, within such villages, towns, and so forth...
There are households to which I should not go.
What kind of households?
Namely, those that are professional bards.
Or at a tavern, or at the house of a courtesan,
or at the palace of a king.
Or there are families of caṇḍālas or kaṭhinakas;
or again, there are families that are entirely given to slander and cannot be turned back.
There may be households to which I ought to go,
namely, the great clans of the kṣatriyas or the great clans of the brāhmaṇas.
Or [there may be] lay devotees from great aristocratic families,
or from the families of officials and assistants,
or from families of great wealth.
Either in the house of a householder,
or in the house of a merchant leader,
or again in a lay residence.
Although I should go,
I should not go too early or too late;
nor should I go when the donor’s household is preoccupied with urgent affairs.
One should not go when there is amusement and play, nor when there are matters of construction or decoration,
nor when one is engaged in the base and defiled dharmas of the world,
nor during times of anger and contention.
Furthermore, one should proceed exactly as one intends to go;
one should not travel together with violent and unruly elephants, nor should one travel together with violent chariots, or with wicked horses, wicked oxen, or wicked dogs.
One does not enter amidst the noisy thicket, nor tread upon thorns;
one does not scale walls,
nor leap over moats and trenches.
One should not fall from a mountain precipice, nor drown in deep water,
nor tread upon filth; rather,
one should visit the household of a donor following the analogy of the moon.
Fully endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame, they remain far removed from arrogance and thoroughly cleanse their bodies and minds.
They do not seek material gain nor do they hope for honor;
rather, they feel joy in their hearts as if they themselves had obtained all such gains.
In this way, one should also feel joy in the mind upon seeing others receive offerings;
one should not be self-exalting nor disparage others, but maintain a heart of compassion.
Furthermore, one should maintain the mind in this manner when going to the homes of donors.
How could one who has gone forth go to another's place with the expectation that the other will give?
It is not that they do not bestow gifts; rather, as explained at length, they should act with promptness and not with delay.
Furthermore, one should form this thought:
"Now, when I go to the house of a donor on a pretext,
I must know the proper measure of the alms I receive."
Furthermore, I should not practice hypocrisy for the sake of gain and offerings,
nor should I seek profit through profit by manifesting deceptive and delusive appearances;
having obtained gain and offerings, I shall remain free from defilement and craving.
Nor does he indulge in gluttony or voraciousness;
nor does he consume [objects] with delusion, stubborn attachment, or infatuation.
Furthermore, whether in the past or at the present moment, he observes various forms.
Among these various forms, one should contemplate some parts,
while there may be some parts that should not be contemplated.
Regarding those forms that should not be contemplated:
One should restrain the eye and well-guard the sense faculties;
regarding all forms that ought to be observed,
one should dwell securely in mindfulness and correctly examine what kind of form it is.
One should not contemplate those things that are improper to observe, namely:
various performances of music, laughter, and amusements;
or other activities of play, such as dancing, singing, and instrumental music.
Furthermore, there may be women who are exceptionally youthful, in the prime of their youth, and possessed of exquisite form and color;
or there may be other various sights that are capable of destroying one's holy life.
They can obstruct the holy life and cause various kinds of evil and unwholesome discursive thoughts to manifest.
One should not look upon any forms of such a nature.
What kind of form is that which should be contemplated?
It refers to all those forms of bodies that are aged, decrepit, and senile;
bodies that are hunched, leaning on staffs, and trembling.
Or those suffering from various ailments and severe illnesses,
whose bodies have swollen feet, swollen hands, swollen bellies, and swollen faces;
whose complexions are withered and yellow, and who suffer from sores, scabs, eczema, and leprosy.
Oppressed by manifold sufferings, their physical forms are exhausted and weary;
their bodies swell and rot, and their faculties become dull and darkened.
Some meet with untimely death, having passed away for as long as a single day.
After two days or seven days have passed,
they are devoured by crows, magpies, hungry dogs,
kites, vultures, foxes, and wolves.
They are devoured by various fierce beasts of prey, such as jackals and other wild animals; or,
after their lives have ended, they are placed upon high couches and draped with canopies and curtains,
while the great assembly before and behind them either laments or wails.
Because the ashes, soil, and dust covered his body and hair,
he experienced sorrow, suffering, grief, resentment, distress, and vexation.
Regarding all such forms as these,
I should observe them, contemplating that these forms are conducive to the holy life and encompass the holy life.
One should enable wholesome discursive thoughts to manifest;
one should not swing the body, swing the arms,
shake the head, or leap about.
With hands joined and one hand resting on the hip, and with shoulders held high, one enters the house of a donor.
One should not sit abruptly on a seat that is not permitted;
nor should one sit without carefully examining the seat.
One should not let any part of the body become lax;
one should not lift the feet up, nor cross the feet;
the feet should be neither too close together nor too far apart.
One should sit with dignified composure;
one should not loosen the fastenings, nor should one spread them out or let them hang loose,
nor should one lift them up or billow them out while wearing the dharma-robes.
The Dharma robes he wears are all perfectly adjusted;
they are neither too high nor too low, unlike the trunk of an elephant,
nor like the clusters of buds on a *tāla* tree.
One should not have a head like that of a dragon nor a body like a bean-bundle.
When wearing the Dharma robes, one should not take up the alms bowl and go ahead to receive food;
one should not hold the alms bowl over the food and drink.
One should not place the bowl in a place that is defiled or impure, nor in a pit, a stream, or on a precipice.
Furthermore, one should consume food and drink in the proper sequence;
one should not cover the soup or stew with rice.
One should not cover one's rice with soup or gravy.
One should not greedily consume various foods and drinks.
One should not receive various foods and drinks with feelings of resentment or dissatisfaction.
One should not eat food that is too coarse nor too fine.
One should not form the food into round balls.
One should not lick the hands, nor should one lick the bowl.
One should not eat by shaking the hands;
one should not eat by shaking the feet;
one should not bite off pieces of food and eat them.
Returning from the donor’s house to his residence,
he walks back and forth in his own private place for walking meditation during both day and night;
he does not do so in another location, nor in a place where he is not familiar.
One does not practice walking meditation when it is not a place free from disturbances nor when it is not a place where one has been granted permission;
nor does one practice walking meditation when the body is overexerted or fatigued, nor when the mind is overcome by restlessness.
For the sake of cultivating wholesome qualities and for right reflection,
one should practice walking meditation with the sense faculties withdrawn within and the mind undistracted externally,
neither moving too fast nor being overly restless.
Nor does he exclusively devote himself to coming and going while practicing walking meditation;
rather, he practices walking meditation by advancing at times and stopping at other times.
Thus, he does so in his own dwelling place, in his own courtyard, in his own room, in his own private quarters, or in a place assigned to him by the Saṃgha.
Having practiced walking meditation neither in an unsuitable place nor in a place where he is not at ease, nor in a place where he is not permitted to act as he pleases,
he then sits upon a large couch, a small rope-couch, or a seat of grass and leaves.
Whether on a *niṣīdana*, or in an *āraṇya*, at the foot of a tree, among graves,
or in an empty and quiet room, one sits cross-legged,
with body upright and mindfulness directed before oneself, dwelling securely in the practice of meditative seclusion (*pratisaṃlayanā*).
One should rest according to the Dharma during the middle watch of the night;
during the daytime and the first watch of the night,
one should cultivate various wholesome qualities without being overly hurried.
When lying down to sleep, one should maintain the perception of light as previously described;
with right mindfulness and clear comprehension, one should attend to the thought of rising,
so as to awaken quickly during the latter part of the night.
Whether engaged in debate or in the diligent practice of recitation and study,
or when dwelling in solitude and silence to contemplate the Dharma for the sake of cultivation and abandonment,
one should remain far removed from worldly treatises that consist of flowery syllables, flowery phrases, and flowery embellishments which lead to what is meaningless.
They are unable to realize the superknowledges, perfect enlightenment, or ultimate nirvāṇa; furthermore,
regarding the True Dharma taught by the Tathāgata—
which is most exceedingly profound, which appears to be profound, and which accords with and conforms to emptiness and dependent origination— [they are unable to realize it].
And regarding all dependent originations,
he earnestly and continuously gathers them well and receives them well,
causing them to become firm, stable, and free from loss or destruction.
One practices for the sake of accomplishing right conduct, not for the sake of gain, honor, or reputation;
furthermore, one is well-versed and proficient in these teachings,
and observes them with wisdom.
He does not delight in associating with noisy crowds;
he does not delight in much activity nor in much speech;
from time to time, he dwells in right mindfulness.
He engages in conversation and discussion with wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life,
mutually offering greetings and comfort, and joyfully inquiring after one another.
They joyfully seek all that is wholesome with a mind free from conflict;
their speech is measured and their words are reasonable;
their speech is upright and their discourse is tranquil.
One should delight in diligently proclaiming the sublime Dharma for others;
furthermore, one should remain in silent seclusion, taking no pleasure in unwholesome or evil discursive thoughts,
nor taking pleasure in contemplating any phenomena that are irrational.
He is free from overweening pride regarding what he has realized for himself;
he does not give rise to complacency with a slight or inferior degree of realization;
and he does not become discouraged regarding the higher realizations yet to be attained.
He is well able to remain far removed from improper objects of thought;
from time to time he cultivates the yoga of śamatha and vipaśyanā;
he delights in abandoning and delights in cultivation, practicing continuously and practicing with earnest devotion.
Furthermore, during the hot season when it is extremely scorching,
he rouses himself with courage and exerts diligent effort,
performing whatever task is to be done.
Due to the causes and conditions of fatigue, one may consequently give rise to drowsiness at an improper time;
for this reason, one should rest for a short while in order to quickly dispel that drowsiness.
Do not allow a long period of time to pass in which wholesome qualities are diminished or obstructed. When sleeping,
either close the door or have a bhikṣu stand guard nearby.
Alternatively, according to the concealed rules of the Vinaya,
one may cover the body with robes in a secluded place and rest for a short while to dispel all weariness and drowsiness.
This is called dwelling with clear comprehension.
The sequence of before and after refers to the time of walking and the time of standing.
Furthermore, when one has not yet previously entered into the category of wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*),
the sublime wisdom (*prajñā*) that arises together with mental application (*manasikāra*) and the exertion of the mind is called "clear comprehension" (*saṃprajanya*).
This very clear comprehension, at the time of acting and at the time of abiding, accomplishes everything without any deficiency.
This is called dwelling with clear comprehension.
One should know that herein, whether going or returning,
or looking straight ahead or looking aside;
Whether bending or stretching,
whether carrying the saṃghāṭī robe, the bowl, or the robes;
whether eating, drinking, chewing, or tasting— he dwells with clear comprehension.
For this reason, it is called dwelling in clear comprehension while acting in accordance with the Dharma in villages, towns, and so forth;
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down;
whether practicing wakefulness, speaking, or remaining silent; or when dispelling drowsiness and fatigue, one dwells in clear comprehension.
For this reason, it is called "dwelling with clear comprehension" when one dwells according to the Dharma in one's place of residence.
Thus, one should understand that the detailed analysis of dwelling with clear comprehension has been fully explained.
There are five kinds of activity while walking;
there are five kinds of activity while standing;
and there are four kinds of activity when dwelling in clear comprehension while both walking and standing.
This is called dwelling with clear comprehension.
What is the summarized meaning?
When walking, there are five kinds of activity.
First is the action of the body;
second is the action of the eyes;
third is the action of all the limbs and joints.
Fourth is the activity of robes and alms-bowl;
fifth is the activity of food and drink.
These are called the five activities while walking.
That is to say, if it is said "whether going or returning," these words indicate the bodily action (kāyakarman) at the time of movement;
and if it is further said "whether looking or gazing," [these indicate the same].
These words indicate the activity of the eyes while walking.
Furthermore, the statement "whether bending or stretching" indicates the activity of all the limbs and joints while walking.
Furthermore, if it is said that one "carries the saṃghāṭī,
as well as the robes and the bowl," these words indicate the activity regarding the robes and bowl while traveling.
Furthermore, if it is said "whether eating, drinking, chewing, or tasting," [these indicate the activity regarding food].
These words indicate the activities of eating and working while moving about.
What are the five activities while staying?
The first is bodily activity.
Second is vocal action;
third is mental action;
fourth is daytime action.
Fifth is the activity at night.
This refers to the statement, "whether walking, standing,
or sitting," which indicates the bodily action (*kāyakarman*) during the time of staying.
If it is further stated, "whether speaking," this expression indicates vocal action during the time of remaining [awake].
If it is further stated, "whether lying down, whether silent, or whether relieving fatigue through sleep."
These words indicate the mental action during the period of abiding.
Furthermore, if it is said, "if one practices wakefulness," these words indicate the bodily and vocal actions during both the daytime and nighttime periods of abiding.
Furthermore, as for "if one lies down," these words indicate the activity during the period of staying;
it should be understood that this is called the five activities during the period of staying.
What are the four types of action that constitute dwelling in full awareness while walking or standing? They are:
first, the action based on that [state] which consists of the action of walking, the action of standing, and the arising of such actions.
One should immediately abide in that very action with established right mindfulness and without negligence;
it should be understood that such an action is encompassed by right mindfulness and encompassed by non-negligence.
Regarding this matter, at this place and at this time:
Whatever is to be done according to its measure, its principle, and its specific category—
regarding that very matter, at that very place, and at that very time—
one acts with correct knowledge in accordance with its measure, its principle, and its specific category.
Because he acts with such correct awareness,
in this present life he is without fault or transgression;
he is without remorse, without agitation, and without regret.
In future lives as well, they shall be free from fault;
after the dissolution of the body at death,
they shall not fall into the evil destinies nor be born among any of the hell-beings (nāraka).
It is distinct in that it involves the accumulation of the provisions for what has not yet been attained;
in brief, this entire meaning is collectively termed "dwelling with clear comprehension."
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Twenty-four and Fascicle Twenty-five,
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

In the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, the Thirteenth [Section] of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the First Yoga Station, the Third [Sub-section], the *Nairyāṇika-bhūmi*, Part Four: What is meant by "the nature of a virtuous friend" (*kalyāṇamitratā*)?
It should be understood that the nature of a spiritual friend is perfected in every respect by virtue of eight causes and conditions.
What are these eight?
That is to say, there is one who abides in the precepts,
is endowed with extensive learning,
and is capable of realization.
He is naturally compassionate and free from weariness;
he is well-able to endure and possesses no fear; his speech is perfect.
How is it that he is said to abide in the observance of the precepts?
That is to say, he dwells established in the complete precepts, being well able to guard the prātimokṣa restraint as extensively explained before;
he delights in the nature of a śramaṇa and delights in the nature of a brāhmaṇa.
To discipline oneself, to pacify oneself,
and to practice the right path for one's own nirvana—
this is called abiding in the precepts.
What is meant by being "endowed with extensive learning"?
It refers to those teachings that are proclaimed and revealed,
which are virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end, and are skillful in both their phrasing and meaning.
He alone has fully perfected the pure and holy life;
he is well able to receive and uphold such numerous sublime dharmas,
and he has thoroughly mastered them.
One who reflects well with the mind and penetrates well through insight is said to be "endowed with extensive learning."
What is meant by "being able to realize"?
It refers to being able to realize the superior perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence,
the perception of non-self in suffering, and the perception of revulsion toward food.
The perception of the lack of delight in all worlds, the perception of its defects,
the perception of abandonment, the perception of detachment, the perception of cessation, and the perception of death.
The perception of impurity, the perception of bluish discoloration,
the perception of festering, the perception of disintegration,
the perception of bloating, and the perception of being devoured.
One contemplates the visualization of blood-smeared corpses,
the visualization of disintegration, the visualization of the skeleton, and the contemplation of emptiness;
furthermore, one is able to realize the first dhyāna.
The second dhyāna, the third dhyāna,
the fourth dhyāna, and the sphere of infinite space.
The sphere of infinite consciousness,
the sphere of nothingness,
and finally, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, they are able to realize loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy,
and equanimity; or the fruit of stream-entry,
or the fruit of once-returning.
Either the fruit of non-returning,
or the supernormal power of the divine realm,
or the supernormal power of recollecting past lives.
Either the supernormal power of the divine ear,
or the supernormal power of knowledge of death and rebirth,
or the supernormal power of discerning the minds of others.
Or there may be an Arhat who possesses the eight liberations, meditative absorptions, and so forth,
and who has great capability and great power.
He is able to skillfully manifest for others the three types of miraculous transformations (*prātihārya*) through instruction and admonition.
As for the three miraculous transformations:
the first is the miraculous transformation of supernormal power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*).
Second is the miraculous power of discourse;
third is the miraculous power of instruction.
These are called the capacities for realization.
What is meant by being compassionate by nature?
It means that one constantly gives rise to compassion and pity for others,
and delights in providing them with what is beneficial.
One delights in its benefit;
one delights in its pleasure;
one delights in its easeful contact.
To bring joy and security—
this is called having a nature of compassion.
What is meant by "a mind free from weariness"?
That is to say, they are skilled at manifesting [the Dharma], skilled at instructing,
skilled at exhorting and inspiring, and skilled at providing consolation;
they proclaim the True Dharma to the fourfold assembly without weariness or fatigue.
Being uplifted and diligent without falling into indolence,
one brings forth a perfect exertion; being by nature inclined toward and delighting in the arousal of diligence and vigor—
this is called having no weariness of mind.
What is meant by being well-able to endure?
It means not returning abuse for abuse, not returning anger for anger,
not returning blows for blows, and not returning mockery for mockery.
They are able to endure the blows of hammers and pestles;
amidst all the various sufferings of oppression, binding, confinement, flogging, humiliation, intimidation, and being hacked or cut,
they reflect upon their own faults and take the ripening of karma as their ultimate refuge.
They never give rise to anger toward others,
nor do they harbor resentment or latent tendencies that they fail to relinquish.
Thus, even when encountering contempt, humiliation, or disgrace, they remain steadfast.
Yet their fundamental nature remains entirely unchanged;
they constantly contemplate the welfare of others and are further able to endure cold and heat,
hunger and thirst, and the bites of mosquitoes and gadflies.
The harsh touch of wind, sun, snakes, and scorpions;
the offensive and cruel speech of others;
and the fierce, sharp, and rigid sensations arising within the body.
Painful sensations that are piercing to the heart and life-threatening;
to have the nature of being able to endure and to be capable of accepting them—
this is called being well-able to endure.
What is meant by being "without fear"?
It refers to when one teaches the True Dharma in the midst of a great assembly:
the mind is free from timidity or inferiority, the voice does not tremble, and the eloquence is without error.
Ultimately, they are never oppressed by various fears due to the causes and conditions of cowardice or dread;
their armpits do not sweat and the hairs on their bodies do not stand on end.
This is what is called being without fear.
What is called the perfection of the instruments of speech?
It refers to his accomplishment of speech that is preeminent, speech that is exceedingly beautiful,
speech that is highly distinct, and speech that is easy to understand.
He delights in hearing speech that is free from contradiction,
free from dependence, and boundless;
such is called the perfection of the equipment of speech.
With skillful speech,
they accomplish these eight kinds of causes and conditions,
being well able to offer admonitions and reminders.
They are well able to instruct and well able to admonish;
they skillfully expound the True Dharma.
What is meant by being "well able to reprove and exhort"?
That is to say, if there are others who have violated the śīla of higher ethical discipline or violated the rules of higher conduct,
one may properly admonish them based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
Speak what is true and not what is false;
speak at the proper time and not at an improper time;
speak for the benefit of others and not for their detriment.
Being gentle rather than harsh,
and being a virtuous friend rather than one characterized by malice and envy—
this is what is meant by being well-able to offer admonition and censure.
What is meant by "skillfully inducing recollection"?
It refers to causing one to recollect a previously committed offense, or a [specific] dharma, or a meaning.
What is meant by "causing one to recollect a previously committed offense"?
That is to say, if there is another who has previously committed an offense but does not remember it,
one should employ skillful means to cause him to recall it,
saying: "Venerable sir!"
"At such a place, regarding such a matter, at such a time,
one committed such and such an offense of this kind.
This is called causing them to recollect their previously committed offenses.
What is called the method for causing recollection?
It refers to when another person, dwelling alone, reflects upon the true Dharma previously heard and received—
namely, the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, and so forth, as explained in detail above.
If they do not remember, he causes them to remember;
or he recites and transmits it to them so that they may remember;
or he poses questions and raises challenges to cause them to remember.
This is called causing one to recollect the Dharma.
What is called causing one to recollect the meaning?
It refers to when another person [reminds one] of the correct meaning previously heard and received.
He provides recollection for whatever has been forgotten;
he proclaims and reveals it so that it may become fresh and manifest.
Furthermore, regarding whatever is conducive to meaningful benefit and conducive to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), whether performed long ago or spoken long ago—
If they should forget anything, he causes them to remember it;
this is called being skillful in providing reminders.
What is meant by being skillful in instruction?
That is to say, regarding seclusion, tranquility, yoga, attention, calm abiding, and insight,
one proceeds in accordance with the instructions from time to time,
and from time to time proclaims unerring discourse that is consistent with them.
That which is able to lead the mind toward freedom from hindrances and obscurations, being exceedingly delightful:
discourse on ethical discipline (*śīla*), discourse on meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
discourse on noble wisdom (*prajñā*), and discourse on liberation (*vimukti*).
Discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation; discourse on fewness of desires;
discourse on contentment; discourse on perpetual cessation;
discourse on dispassion; and discourse on peace.
Discourse on non-diminution, discourse free from confusion,
and discourse that accords with dependent origination through conditions—
this is called being well-able to provide instruction.
What is meant by being "well-able to instruct"?
It means that regarding the noble teaching spoken by the Great Master,
one is able to provide impartial instruction through the True Dharma and the Vinaya.
Whether it be a preceptor, a teacher, a fellow practitioner of the Dharma,
or any other person worthy of respect or highly esteemed,
they know according to reality that such a person has transgressed or violated [the precepts] in one particular instance.
From time to time, they should reprimand them in accordance with the Dharma,
subjecting them to disciplinary measures or banishment to bring them to submissiveness.
Once they have been subdued, they should accept all offerings and requisites in a manner that is lawful and impartial.
With harmonious and clear realization,
one gathers and takes hold [of the mind] so that what should be practiced and what should not be practiced may respectively manifest or not manifest.
Regarding what has been accumulated through habituation and what has not,
he instructs and exhorts;
this is called being well-able to provide instruction and admonition.
What is called "skillfully teaching the true Dharma"?
It refers to being able to skillfully proclaim at the appropriate times the unerring discourse concerning what should be practiced at the outset— namely,
the discourse on generosity, the discourse on ethical discipline, and the discourse on rebirth in heaven.
He extensively reveals the teachings on the defects of sensual desires, as well as the factors pertaining to renunciation and purification;
furthermore, from time to time, he proclaims discourses associated with the four noble truths that are transcendent and supreme.
These are the discourse on suffering, the discourse on its origin, the discourse on its cessation,
and the discourse on the path. They are for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity and for the sake of bringing sentient beings to purification.
In order that the True Dharma may endure for a long time,
he proclaims the corresponding associates that are in accordance with it and are clear and bright.
It is purposeful and appropriate;
it consists of discourse corresponding to the sets of names, phrases, and syllables,
and this discourse is uttered at the proper time with earnestness.
Through gradual succession and simultaneous presence,
they cause him to rejoice, to find delight, and to experience gladness.
Causing them to be courageous and bold,
without being censured or expelled,
and possessing corresponding companions.
Without confusion, he accords with the Dharma and is in harmony with the assembly;
he possesses a heart of compassion and a heart of benefit.
Possessing a mind of compassion,
he does not rely on gain, honor, or praise,
nor does he exalt himself.
One does not treat others with contempt.
This is called the well-expounded True Dharma.
By accomplishing these eight factors, one is so designated.
From time to time, they are well able to admonish and censure, well able to cause one to remember,
well able to instruct,
and well able to exhort.
They skillfully expound the true Dharma;
for this reason, they are called "virtuous friends.
Having thus extensively analyzed the nature of a virtuous friend, [the text proceeds].
Being by nature compassionate in secret,
he first desires to bring them benefit and desires to bring them peace and happiness.
Furthermore, regarding this very benefit and happiness,
one understands them as they truly are,
without error and free from inverted views.
Furthermore, regarding this very benefit and happiness,
there is great power and skillful means capable of causing them to be accumulated and brought forth.
Furthermore, regarding this very benefit and happiness,
he is diligent and unwearied, bringing about fulfillment through exertion;
by nature, he delights in initiating energetic diligence.
One should know that by means of these four causes and conditions,
all aspects of the nature of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) are subsumed, summarized,
and perfected. This is called the concise meaning of the nature of such a virtuous friend.
The essential meaning of all this is summarized as follows:
the nature of a virtuous friend and the contemplation of the true Dharma.
That which is called the True Dharma refers to the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, or his disciples—
the true persons, those who have reached the goal, and sublime beings.
It is proclaimed, revealed, analyzed, and clearly elucidated.
What, then, is this? It refers to the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, and so forth, as explained in detail previously.
The twelvefold division of the teaching is called the True Dharma.
What is a sūtra?
It refers to that which the Bhagavān [taught] in various places and circumstances.
For the sake of those various sentient beings to be trained,
and in accordance with the various distinctions of the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) of those respective beings to be trained,
he proclaims immeasurable discourses associated with the aggregates (skandha) and discourses associated with the bases (āyatana).
Discourse associated with dependent origination; discourse associated with nutriment;
discourse associated with the truths; discourse associated with the elements;
discourse associated with the vehicle of the śrāvakas; and discourse associated with the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.

Discourse associated with the vehicle of the Tathāgata, such as discourse associated with the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the factors of the path;
and discourse associated with foulness, mindfulness of breathing, the trainings, and the verified faiths.
Those who compiled the Tathāgata’s treasury of the true Dharma collected such various noble utterances in order to ensure that the holy teaching would endure long in the world.
By means of various excellent bodies of names, phrases, and syllables,
they are arranged and compiled in their proper sequence;
that is to say, they are able to thread together and stitch into a whole the various things that lead to meaningful benefit.
That which can lead to the holy life and possesses true, wholesome,
and sublime meaning is called a Sūtra.
What is the *geya*?
It refers to verses (*gāthā*) spoken either in the middle or at the end [of a discourse],
or alternatively, discourses of unexpounded meaning (*neyārtha-sūtra*).
This is called *geya* (verses).
What is *vyākaraṇa* (prophetic declarations)?
It refers to those instances in which the future rebirths and other matters concerning disciples after their passing away are prophesied.
Furthermore, when one expounds sūtras of definitive meaning,
this is called vyākaraṇa (elucidation).
What is geya (versified teaching)?
That is to say, it is not spoken in prose, but is spoken in verse;
it may consist of two lines, three lines, four lines, five lines, six lines, and so forth.
This is called *geya* (verses).
What is *udāna* (inspired utterance)?
It refers to that in which the name and lineage of the person who requested [the teaching] are not disclosed.
To cause the True Dharma to endure for a long time and the Noble Teaching to endure for a long time in the future,
he speaks without being requested;
this is called "Spontaneous Utterance" (Udāna).
What is the causal condition?
It refers to that wherein the name and lineage of the person who makes the request are revealed,
and [the teaching] is spoken because of that request.
Furthermore, all those *vinaya*-related *pratimokṣa-sūtras* that possess causes and conditions are called "causes and conditions" (*nidāna*).
What is a "simile" (*avadāna*)?
This refers to that which contains an illustrative simile;
because of the simile, the original meaning becomes clear and lucid.
This is called an illustration (nidarśana).
What is the *itivṛttaka* (past events)?
It refers to all teachings concerning matters and meanings associated with previous lives;
this is called the *itivṛttaka*.
What is a *jātaka*?
It refers to those discourses in which it is proclaimed that in various regions of the past, the Blessed One—
whether dying or being born— practiced the conduct of a bodhisattva and performed difficult deeds.
This is called Jātaka.
What is Vaipulya?
It refers to that in which all the paths of the bodhisattvas are explained in detail.
It is called Vaipulya because it causes one to cultivate and realize all merits, such as the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and unobstructed wisdom, pertaining to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
What is the Dharma of Aspiration?
It refers to that in which the Buddhas, the disciples of the Buddhas— namely bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs,
and śikṣamāṇās— are proclaimed.
Whether they be male or female laborers,
laymen or laywomen, and so forth— if they are superior,
whether collectively or individually, they are superior to all others and to the entire world.
The agreement upon what has been permitted— wondrous, marvelous, and of supreme merit—
is called "Marvelous Dharma" (adbhutadharma).
What is "Exegesis" (upadeśa)?
That is to say, all the *mātṛkā-abhidharma*,
which investigates the profound meaning of the *sūtras* and elucidates the essential tenets of all the *sūtras*.
This is called "discourse" (upadeśa).
Thus, the twelvefold division of the teaching as explained here is subsumed within the Three Piṭakas.
That is to say, some are included within the Sūtra Piṭaka,
some are included within the Vinaya Piṭaka,
and some are included within the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
It should be understood that herein, when the sūtras, geyas,
vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas,
and avadānas are spoken;
The Itivṛttakas, Jātakas,
Vaipulyas, and Adbhutadharmas—
these are called the Sūtra Piṭaka.
If it speaks of causes and conditions, it is called the Vinaya Piṭaka;
if it speaks of exegesis and discussion, it is called the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
Therefore, such are the twelve divisions of the teaching.
It is comprised within the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*).
Because it has been proclaimed by all such true persons, those who have attained the goal, and sublime beings,
it is called the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
Hearing this is called "hearing the true Dharma.
What, then, does this mean?
It refers to someone who, for instance, receives and upholds the Sūtras.
Some uphold the Vinaya; some uphold the Abhidharma;
and some uphold both the Sūtras and the Vinaya.
Some uphold the Sūtras and the Abhidharma;
some uphold the Vinaya and the Abhidharma;
and some fully uphold the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma.
All this is called hearing the sublime Dharma.
This hearing of the sublime Dharma is further of two kinds:
first, hearing its words.
Second, having heard its meaning,
one dwells alone in a secluded place, far removed from the six types of improper objects of thought, in accordance with the true Dharma as it was heard and believed.
That is to say: one conceives of a self, conceives of sentient beings, conceives of the world;
one conceives of the karma of sentient beings and the ripening of its results.
The sphere of meditative concentration consists of the objects of meditative concentration that are subject to conceptualization;
the sphere of the Buddhas consists of the Buddhas themselves and their objects,
characterized by both specific and general characteristics.
Such reflection is further of two kinds:
first, by means of the mode of calculation,
one skillfully employs expedient means to calculate all phenomena.
Second, by means of the mode of weighing,
one examines the virtues and faults of all phenomena based on correct reasoning;
that is, when reflecting upon the teachings associated with the aggregates.
Furthermore, if one contemplates any other teaching whatsoever as previously described,
all are contemplated through the skillful means of these two modes of practice.
What, then, is this? It refers to what is called "form," namely the ten bases of form and the various forms subsumed under the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
This is called the aggregate of form.
As for what is called "feeling," it refers to the three types of feeling.
This is called the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
As for what is called perception (*saṃjñā*),
it refers to the six groups of perception (*ṣaṭ-saṃjñā-kāya*).
This is called the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
As for what is called "volition," it refers to the six groups of volitional formations (*ṣaṭ-saṃskāra-kāya*) and so forth.
This is called the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
As for what is called consciousness (vijñāna),
it refers to the six groups of consciousness and so forth.
This is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
In this way, one contemplates the corresponding teachings on the aggregates by means of the mode of calculation;
or alternatively, by means of this mode of calculation.
One should know that through distinct contemplations, there are successive differences, which in turn involve immeasurable variations.
How so? By means of the mode of weighing, one contemplates the teachings concerning the aggregates (*skandha*) in accordance with correct reasoning.
This refers to investigating without error by means of the four principles.
What are these four?
First, the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*).
2. The principle of efficacy;
3. The principle of logical proof; 4.
The principle of natural law.
What is called the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*)?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of dependence:
first, dependence regarding origination (*utpatty-apekṣā*).
Second is the dependence of designation (*prajñapti-upaniṣad*).
Regarding the dependence of origination (*utpatti-upaniṣad*),
it refers to the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*) through the power of various causes and conditions.
The arising of these aggregates must depend upon various causes and conditions.
As for the designation of dependence,
it refers to [dependence] by means of the sets of names (nāmakāya), phrases (padakāya), and phonemes (vyañjanakāya).
The designation of the aggregates must depend upon the sets of names, phrases, and syllables;
this is called the dependence regarding origination and the dependence regarding designation with respect to the aggregates.
That is to say, there is the dependence upon arising and the dependence upon designation;
the arising of the aggregates and the designation of the aggregates are called the principle, the yoga, and the expedient means.
Therefore, this is called the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*).
What is called the principle of efficacy (*kāryakāraṇa-yukti*)?
It refers to the fact that once the aggregates (*skandha*) have arisen, they do so by virtue of their own conditions.
There are distinct individual functions,
namely: the eye can see forms, the ear can hear sounds,
the nose can smell odors, and the tongue can taste flavors.
The body can perceive tangibles, and the mind can cognize phenomena (*dharma*).
Form is the object of the eye and the sphere of activity of the eye;
likewise, up to and including phenomena, which are the objects of the mind and the sphere of activity of the mind.
Furthermore, it should be understood that for other such categories as these,
the distinct functions of their respective phenomena are likewise so; that is,
each of these phenomena possesses its own specific function.
All principles of yoga and skillful means are collectively termed the principle of efficacy (*kāryakāraṇayukti*).
What is termed the principle of proof (*upapattisādhanayukti*)?
That is to say, one observes all aggregates as being impermanent,
produced by various conditions, suffering, empty, and non-self,
through the three means of valid cognition in accordance with reality.
That is to say, by means of the authority of scripture (*āptāgama*), by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
and by means of inference (*anumāna*);
it is through these three measures that the principle is established and verified.
All those who possess wisdom correctly grasp, maintain, and establish this:
that all aggregates are impermanent by nature, dependently originated by nature,
suffering by nature, and empty by nature.
And the nature of selflessness.
Such as these are called the principle of logical proof (*upapattisādhanayukti*).
What is meant by the principle of natural law (*dharmatāyukti*)?
That is to say, by what causes and conditions do those very aggregates and such types of the receptacle world come to be?
They are thus arranged.
For what reason is solidity the characteristic of earth, moisture the characteristic of water,
warmth the characteristic of fire, and light movement the characteristic of wind?
For what reason are the aggregates impermanent, all phenomena selfless, and nirvana tranquil?
For what reason does form have the characteristic of transformation and decay, and sensation have the characteristic of experiencing?
Perception has the characteristic of conceptualizing; formations have the characteristic of volitional activity;
consciousness has the characteristic of discernment.
This is because such is the inherent nature of those phenomena.
Such is its intrinsic nature;
such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
This very *dharmatā* is designated as "reasoning," "yoga," and "skillful means."
Whether it be thus, or otherwise, or not thus,
everything relies upon the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
and everything returns to the principle of the nature of phenomena.
Causing the mind to abide securely and causing the mind to understand clearly—
this is called the principle of natural law (*dharmatā-yukti*).
This is what is meant by relying upon the four principles.
By means of the mode of calculation and the mode of weighing,
one examines the teachings associated with the aggregates;
thus, it is by these two modes that [one investigates].
To examine all other verbal teachings in this manner is collectively termed "thorough and correct examination.
It consists of contemplating all the sublime Dharma that has been taught.
This is what is called hearing and reflecting upon the sublime Dharma.
What is meant by "absence of obstacles"?
Briefly stated, this absence of obstacles is of two kinds.
The first is based on the internal;
the second is based on the external.
I shall first explain the obstacles based on both the internal and the external.
One should know that what is contrary to those [obstacles] constitutes the two kinds of non-obstruction.
What is meant by "internal obstacles"?
It refers, for example, to someone who has not cultivated merit in previous lives.
Because they do not cultivate merit,
they are unable from time to time to obtain the various requisites for livelihood that are conducive to well-being—
namely, clothing, food, bedding and seating, medicinal requisites for illness, and other such utensils.
There is intense greed as well as long-lasting greed;
there is intense hatred as well as long-lasting hatred;
there is intense delusion as well as long-lasting delusion.
Either due to having accumulated and performed karma that results in many diseases in previous lives,
for which those acts serve as the cause of numerous ailments; or else,
it is due to practicing an imbalance in the present life.
Due to these causes and conditions, wind, heat, and phlegm are repeatedly provoked;
or there may be undigested food remaining within the body,
or one may consume coarse and heavy food while engaging in many activities and many labors.
They have many activities and frequent large assemblies;
they delight in worldly affairs, delight in idle talk,
delight in sleep, and delight in noisy crowds.
Delighting in living in company, delighting in attachment to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*),
delighting in self-exaltation, being agitated and negligent, and dwelling in improper places—
all such categories should be understood as internal obstacles (*antarāya*).
What is meant by "relying on external obstacles"?
It refers to a certain person who relies upon an unvirtuous person;
due to those causes and conditions, they are unable to obtain from time to time the appropriate instructions and admonitions.
Or one may dwell in an unfavorable location;
in such a residence, during the daytime, there may be much bustle, various gatherings of people,
and many disturbances, while at night, there may be much loud noise, great clamor, and the commotion of large crowds.
Furthermore, there are various kinds of fierce, sharp, and painful afflictions from wind and sun;
or there may be various fears and terrors caused by humans and non-humans.
All such categories should be understood as being based on external obstacles.
Having thus extensively analyzed the internal and external obstacles,
how then is the summarized meaning herein to be understood?
It is said that, in brief, there are three obstacles within this context.
First, the obstacle to application;
second, the obstacle to withdrawal;
third, the obstacle to tranquility.
What is the hindrance to application?
It refers to when this hindrance encounters and manifests itself,
[thereby obstructing] all application toward the categories of wholesome qualities.
They are entirely incapable and lack all power.
What does this mean?
It refers to being constantly afflicted by chronic illness, suffering, and grave disease.
Wind, heat, phlegm, and mucus frequently flare up;
or there may be undigested food remaining within the body;
or one may be bitten by snakes, scorpions, centipedes, or millipedes.
Whether one is harassed by humans or non-humans,
or is unable to obtain clothing, food, bedding, medicine for the treatment of illness, or other requisites—
such categories as these should all be understood as obstacles to preparatory application (*prayoga-āvaraṇa*).
What is the distancing from hindrances?
It refers to coarse physicality, many affairs, many activities, many tasks to be performed, or a fondness for worldly undertakings;
due to these causes and conditions, one takes pleasure in various kinds of active pursuits.
Because his mind wanders among various objects or delights in speech,
for these reasons, although he may possess the capacity and great power for seclusion, abandonment, and the cultivation of tranquility, [he fails to achieve them].
However, they become complacent merely by reciting and chanting, or take pleasure in sleep;
due to these causes and conditions, they are constantly entangled by lethargy and drowsiness,
being lazy by nature and regarding sleep as a pleasure.
They take pleasure in reclining and take pleasure in lying down;
or they delight in noisy crowds.
By reason of these causes and conditions, they take pleasure in associating with both householders and those who have gone forth.
They engaged in various kinds of talk concerning kings,
thieves, food, drink,
fine garments, and the streets of courtesans.
Discourses on various kingdoms, discourses on the biographies of great men,
discourses on worldly legends, and discourses on the great ocean—
such categories as these lead to what is meaningless.
In frivolous and ornate discourses, they delight in idle conversation to pass the time;
furthermore, they frequently take pleasure in frequenting assemblies,
allowing their minds to become distracted by various matters.
This causes the mind to become agitated or leads one to delight in dwelling amidst distractions;
for this reason, among both the householders and those who have gone forth,
if they have not yet met [the teacher], they long for him and desire to see him.
If one has already encountered [others] and does not wish to part from them, or delights in frivolous discourse (*prapañca*),

then by reason of these causes and conditions, one becomes attached to the various frivolous discourses of the world and proceeds with a longing for those things toward which one should instead be heading.
One takes delight in abandoning the yoke of virtue within seclusion;
such categories of numerous obstructive dharmas should all be known as "obstructions to seclusion."
If these obstacles should arise and manifest before one,
it will be difficult to abandon attachment to lodgings in forest hermitages, mountain ranges, wildernesses, or remote borderlands.
Furthermore, one is unable to dwell in forest hermitages (*āraṇya*), among cemeteries, at the foot of trees, or in secluded and quiet rooms.
What is the obstacle to tranquility?
Regarding "tranquility": it refers to...
That is, śamatha and vipaśyanā.
There are obstacles to śamatha;
there are obstacles to vipaśyanā.
What are the obstacles to śamatha?
They are negligence and dwelling in improper places.
Due to negligence, one's mind may be entangled by lethargy and sleep.
Either one develops a craving for the taste of śamatha alone;
or the mind inclines toward entering into a state of inferiority;
or the mind takes delight in and becomes attached to a state of obscurity.
Because he dwells in such an improper place,
he is distracted and disturbed by the clamor of humans and non-humans;
he is oppressed by others, and his mind wanders outwardly.
This is called the hindrance to śamatha.
It should be understood that this hindrance obstructs tranquility.
What is the hindrance to vipaśyanā?
This refers to self-conceit and agitation.
Regarding self-conceit:
it is when someone thinks as follows:
"I was born into a noble family and have left the household life out of pure faith;
I am not inferior. Other bhikṣus are not like this.
For this reason, he exalts himself, puffs himself up, and treats others with contempt.
Thus, having been born into a wealthy family, I have left the household life out of pure faith and not out of poverty.
I possess exquisite form, am pleasing to behold and dignified, and am learned, retaining what I have heard.
My learning is accumulated, my speech is skillful, and my expression is perfect.
Other bhikṣus, however, are not like this.
For this reason, they exalt themselves and hold themselves in high esteem while looking down upon others.
Because they thus exalt themselves and hold themselves in high esteem, [they fall into ruin].
If there are bhikṣus who are elder, possessed of great wisdom, and long-established in the holy life,
yet they do not from time to time respectfully inquire [of their teachers],
those teachers will likewise not from time to time reveal to them those points that have not yet been revealed.
For the sake of clarifying what has not yet been clarified, he does not,
for their sake, employ intense diligence and earnest application to penetrate the meaning of profound phrases with wisdom,
nor does he skillfully reveal them even to the point of purifying their knowledge and vision.
This is called the hindrance to vipaśyanā consisting in delighting in self-exaltation.
Furthermore, there is another who, having attained only a small portion of inferior knowledge and vision, dwells in a state of complacency.
By abiding in such a limited and inferior wisdom and vision,
he becomes conceited; because of this self-exaltation, [he falls].
One then gives rise to contentment and no longer seeks higher progress;
this is called the obstacle to the vipaśyanā abiding in self-conceit.
As for "restlessness":
That is to say, there is one whose faculties are not tranquil,
whose faculties are restless and agitated,
and who at all times thinks what is evil, speaks what is evil, and performs what is evil.
One is unable to dwell securely in the contemplation of all phenomena,
nor is one able to contemplate all phenomena with firm stability;
by reason of these causes and conditions, vipaśyanā cannot be brought to fulfillment.
One cannot attain purity;
this is called the agitation that obstructs vipaśyanā.
Thus, these two factors obstruct śamatha.
That is to say, excessive negligence and dwelling in inappropriate places—
these two factors can obstruct vipaśyanā. Furthermore,
delighting in self-conceit and agitation— these two factors can obstruct vipaśyanā.
Thus, both the obstacles to śamatha and the obstacles to vipaśyanā are collectively termed the obstacles to tranquility (praśrabdhi).
This is the concise meaning of the obstacles.
It acts as an obstruction.
One should know that the absence of this obstruction—which is the opposite of this obstruction—is the state of being free from it;
that is, the very non-existence and distancing of this obstruction.
That which is neither conjoined nor associated is called "unobstructed.
Giving, by its very nature, being free from fault, serves as an adornment for the mind,
an associate for the mind, a support for yoga, and is practiced in order to attain the supreme goal.
This is called wise relinquishment.
Who is able to give?
To whom is it given?
With what does one give, with what characteristics does one give,
how does one give, and for what reason does one give?
Through these causes and conditions, the nature of giving is free from fault.
Answer: Who is it that can give?
It is the giver, the donor; this is called "one who can give.
What is the giver? What is the donor?
That is to say, if one gives with one's own hand, it is called "giving";
if one gives from one's own property and gives with joy rather than without joy,
it is called a "donor."
Regarding "to whom one gives":
this refers to four kinds of recipients.
First, those who are suffering.
Second, those who have been kind;
third, those who are beloved;
fourth, those who are venerable and superior.
Who are those who possess suffering?
They are the impoverished, or beggars,
or travelers, or those seeking [something].
Some were blind or deaf;
some were destitute or without a refuge; some had no destination;
and some were lacking various necessities of life.
Furthermore, there are others of this same class who are called "those who suffer.
What are "those who have been kind"?
This refers to either one's parents or those who nursed one with milk.
Some are those who nurture and raise, some are those who bring to maturity;
some are those who can deliver [beings] from wildernesses, sandy deserts, and the like;
some are those who can provide relief during times of famine.
Or those who rescue others when they are terrified by enemies;
or those who can release others when they have been captured and bound;
or those who provide medical treatment when others encounter illness.
One who teaches for the sake of benefit and teaches for the sake of happiness;
one who leads toward benefit and leads toward happiness;
amidst whatever affairs may arise.
As for being a companion:
one who shares in joy, one who shares in sorrow,
and one who does not abandon another when encountering calamity or hardship.
Furthermore, those of this and similar categories are called "benefactors.
What are "loved ones"?
They refer to various kinsmen and friends, or those toward whom one has affection and respect.
Some follow his words with faith;
some converse and engage in discourse with him frequently;
and some are intimate with him.
Furthermore, there are others of a similar class who are called "beloved.
What is meant by "venerable and eminent"?
It refers to those who are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
Those whom the world collectively acknowledges as virtuous and good—
those who are free from harm, utterly free from injury,
and free from sensual desire.
Those who practice for the sake of subduing greed;
those who are free from hatred;
and those who practice for the sake of subduing hatred.
Those who are free from delusion;
those who practice for the sake of subduing delusion;
and furthermore, others of such a kind are called "Venerable and Exalted Ones."
As for what is used as the gift:
to speak briefly,
it refers to practicing generosity by means of things that belong to the category of sentient beings.
Or one may practice giving by means of things that are insentient.
What are the sentient things used for giving?
They are, namely, wives, children, slaves, and laborers.
Or elephants, horses, pigs, cattle, sheep, chickens, ducks, camels, mules, and the like;
or various other great men, great women, small boys, and small girls;
or whatever other such things may be used as objects of giving.
Alternatively, one may give away the internal parts of the body— head, eyes, hands, feet, blood, flesh, marrow, and bones—
in accordance with one's vows;
this is also called giving material things belonging to the category of sentient beings.
These are the deeds manifested by these bodhisattvas;
they are not the kind of giving intended here.
This would apply if one were to have mastery over those sentient beings.
Whether one possesses power or is able to subdue others,
if one should give that which ought to be held to another,
there is no fault for oneself at the time of giving.
If, by reason of that act of giving, the minds of others do not become resentful,
and if one knows that the sentient being to whom the gift is given will not be harmed or afflicted; [then one should give].
This is called giving away things that belong to the category of sentient beings as a blameless gift.
What are the things belonging to the category of non-sentient beings that are given as gifts?
Briefly stated, there are three kinds of such things.
First, material wealth;
second, grain; third, land.
Regarding "wealth and goods," this refers to mani-jewels,
pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, agate, variegated stones, naturally colored dyes, red pearls, and right-spiraling shells.
Furthermore, there are other such things as these:
various precious gems, or gold, or silver,
or various garments, or various household articles.
Either incense or garlands are called material wealth. What are grains?
They refer to all things that can be eaten or drunk.
Barley and wheat;
rice and millet; foxtail millet, panicled millet, and sesame.
Various types of beans, both large and small;
sugarcane, grapes, milk, curd, fruit juices,
and diverse kinds of fermented drinks.
Furthermore, whatever else is of this same category is called "grain.
What are "places"? These refer to fields, houses, dwellings, shops, and market stalls.
The establishment of houses of merit, monasteries, guesthouses,
and so forth— furthermore, whatever else belongs to this same category— is called "place and object.
This refers to giving as a gift those things that are blameless and classified as insentient.
One should know that herein there are sentient things and insentient things;
all of these taken together are called "the gift of what is used.
What are the characteristics of such a giver?
It refers to the mental karma consisting of volition (cetanā) accompanied by non-attachment,
as well as the bodily and vocal karma arising therefrom, and the relinquishing of gifts—
whether belonging to one's own continuum or that of another. This is called the characteristic of giving.
What is the giver?
It refers to one who practices giving out of pure faith,
and who practices giving out of right teaching and vision.
One practices giving out of the view that there is a result;
one practices giving with extreme earnestness;
and one practices giving with one's own hands out of a mind of reverence.
One should not treat others with contempt, but give at the appropriate time;
one should practice giving by providing what others need without causing them harm or distress,
acting with impartiality in accordance with the Dharma.
One does not practice giving by accumulating wealth through violence and cruelty;
one practices giving with fresh and clean items;
one practices giving with exquisite and refined items.
One practices giving with pure things;
by this, both oneself and others are free from fault.
One practices giving repeatedly, having subdued the defilement of stinginess and the power of its accumulation.
One first gives gifts with a joyful heart;
at the time of giving, the mind is pure; and after having given, one has no regret.
Thus does one give.
For what reason does a donor practice giving?
It is because of compassion toward those who are suffering.
Or one practices giving out of gratitude for kindness received;
that is, one practices giving toward those who have been kind, whether out of affection, respect, or faithful compliance.
That is to say, one practices giving out of affection for loved ones, or with the hope of attaining superior mundane or supramundane merit.
That is to say, one who is noble and eminent,
or one who has gone forth from the household life,
practices giving as an adornment of the mind and as an aid to the mind.
One practices giving for the sake of supporting yoga and for the sake of attaining the supreme goal.
By reason of these causes and conditions, the nature of giving is blameless;
this is called "generous relinquishment.
What is meant by "the adornment of a śramaṇa"?
The summary verse says:
Possessing right faith and free from deceit, Having little illness, being diligent, endowed with wisdom,
Having few desires and being content, Easy to support and easy to satisfy.
Dhutaguṇa-possessing, dignified, knowing the proper measure, endowed with the qualities of a noble person,
and possessing the marks of one who is wise— patient, gentle, virtuous, and excellent; that is to say,
there is someone who is fully possessed of right faith and free from deceit.
He has few illnesses, is by nature diligent and energetic, and has achieved sublime wisdom.
He has few desires and is easily contented; he is easy to support and easy to satisfy, being fully endowed with the ascetic practices (dhūta-guṇa).
He is majestic and dignified in his merit;
he knows the proper measure and is fully accomplished in the qualities of a noble person;
he is fully accomplished in the marks of one who is wise.
Patient and gentle by nature, virtuous and upright,
respectful and compliant,
they possess abundant resolute conviction and a great desire for what is wholesome.
He develops deep, pure faith toward all wholesome dharmas and the Great Teacher,
remaining free from confusion and doubt;
he regards the Great Teacher with reverence, respect, service, and offerings.
Having thus practiced such reverence, respect, service, and offerings,
he dwells with single-minded devotion, relying upon and drawing close to [the teacher] as if to a Great Master.
In this way, regarding the Dharma, toward fellow practitioners of the holy life,
toward all that is to be learned, toward instruction and admonition,
toward cultivation and making offerings, and toward heedfulness.
One should know that it is likewise with respect to samādhi.
This is called being endowed with right faith.
What is meant by being free from guile and crookedness?
That is to say, one who is pure by nature and upright reveals himself as he truly is to the Great Teacher and to those wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life.
This is called being free from guile and crookedness.
What is meant by having few illnesses?
It means that one is naturally free from disease and that one’s digestion proceeds smoothly in accordance with the seasons.
It is evenly sustained, being neither excessively hot nor excessively cold;
it is free from harm and provides comfort at all times.
For these reasons, [it is so].
Whatever is eaten, drunk,
chewed, or tasted is easily transformed and digested.
This is called having few illnesses.
What is meant by being naturally diligent and energetic?
It refers to being able to abide in vigor.
Possessing diligence and valor, firm and resolute,
one is able not to cast off the yoke regarding wholesome qualities;
being alert and untiring, one’s exertion is perfect.
Being capable of performing tasks,
he personally serves and attends upon his wise fellow practitioners of the holy life;
this is called being naturally diligent and energetic.
What is meant by "accomplishing sublime wisdom"?
It refers to having the faculties of intelligence, mindfulness, and awakening all fully perfected,
such that one's sensory faculties are neither dull nor obtuse.
Their faculties are neither dull nor foolish;
they are neither mute nor speech-impaired,
and they do not communicate by means of their hands.
He possesses the power to discern the meaning of all teachings, whether well-spoken or ill-spoken;
he is fully endowed with innate intelligence and fully endowed with acquired intelligence.
This is called being accomplished in sublime wisdom.
What is fewness of desires?
It refers to one who, although already accomplished in all such virtues as fewness of desires and so forth, [remains content].
Yet one does not seek for others to know this— that is,
one does not desire others to know that one possesses few desires and has accomplished meritorious qualities;
this is called having few desires.
What is contentment?
It refers to the arising of joy and the cultivation of right satisfaction with respect to any one thing, such as clothing, food and drink, or bedding.
Regarding any robes, whether coarse or fine, that have not yet been obtained,
he has no further longing or expectation;
regarding those already obtained, he is neither stained by nor attached to them.
One should utilize them as extensively explained previously;
one should know that this applies equally to clothing, food and drink, bedding, and other such matters.
This is called contentment.
What is meant by being "easy to support"?
It means being able to sustain oneself alone and find contentment without depending on others—
whether they be servants, attendants, or other groups of people.
Furthermore, one does not pursue excessive wealth or treasures,
so as not to cause those who give, such as donors and the like,
to feel that one is difficult to support.
This is called being easy to support.
What is meant by being easy to satisfy?
It means that one sustains oneself with even the slightest amount.
If one obtains coarse and inferior [food] and yet sustains oneself with it,
this is called being "easy to satisfy.
What is the accomplishment of the dhūta qualities?
That is to say: always maintaining the practice of begging for alms, begging in successive order from house to house;
eating in a single sitting and abstaining from food after rising;
wearing only the three robes; wearing only woolen garments; and wearing only rag-robes discarded in refuse heaps.
He dwells in forest hermitages, constantly residing under trees,
constantly residing in the open air, constantly residing among burial mounds,
and always intending to sit upright in the posture of one who sits perpetually.
Such are the supports:
whether food, clothing, or bedding, these are the ascetic virtues (*dhūtaguṇa*),
numbering either twelve or thirteen kinds.
Within the practice of alms-gathering, there are two types:
first, gathering alms as they are obtained;
second, gathering alms by sequential order.
"Taking alms as they are obtained" means that one accepts food immediately upon obtaining it as one proceeds from house to house.
"Alms in regular order" means...
This means that when entering villages or alleys, one should go from house to house to beg;
as soon as food is obtained, one should manifest it and accept it immediately,
without raising the hand high to leap over to other houses.
"May I obtain exquisite food and drink," up to "may I have much to gain"—
one should know that herein, these are based on the undifferentiated nature of alms-seeking.
There are only twelve; however,
if one includes the distinct category of those who subsist on alms-food,
there are thirteen.
