What is meant by "eating in a single sitting"?
It means that once seated, one accepts all food that is to be eaten;
having risen from that seat, one shall certainly not eat again.
This is called eating in a single sitting.
What is meant by "stopping first and then eating"?
It means sitting upon the appropriate seat for the purpose of eating.
Before eating, one should first fully receive all that is to be eaten and correctly understand:
"I shall now receive only this much food and drink, which will suffice to sustain myself."
Furthermore, one correctly understands: "Beyond this point, I shall not eat.
Having made such a commitment, one then eats.
This is called "eating after having first ceased."
What is meant by "wearing only the three robes"?
It means sustaining oneself with only the three robes.
What are these three robes?
1. The saṃghāṭī; 2. the uttarāsaṅga;
3. the antarvāsaka.
Apart from these three robes, he never stores or accumulates anything;
any robe exceeding these is considered "extra.
This is what is meant by "wearing only the three robes."
What is meant by "wearing only garments of wool"?
It refers to the robes one wears, whether they belong to the set of three robes (*tricīvara*) or are extra robes (*atirekacīvara*),
all of which are made entirely of wool.
He never stores up any other robes he has made;
this is called "wearing only felt robes.
What is meant by "wearing refuse-rag robes"?
That is to say, whatever robes have been abandoned or discarded by others on a street,
an alleyway, a marketplace, or a shop.
Some are paths or non-paths;
some are mixed with excrement and filth;
some are smeared and defiled by excrement, urine, pus, blood, mucus, and saliva.
Having taken up such impure garments,
he removes gross filth and, with firm resolve, washes, sews, dyes,
and wears them; this is called wearing rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*).
What is meant by "dwelling in an araṇya"?
It refers to dwelling in empty, secluded places such as mountain forests and remote wildernesses,
making use of all bedding and furniture found at the periphery.
To remain far removed from all villages, towns,
and settlements— this is called dwelling in an araṇya.
What is meant by "constantly residing under trees"?
This means always vowing to dwell beneath trees, relying upon the roots of trees;
this is called "always dwelling under trees.
What is meant by "always dwelling in the open air"?
This means that one constantly vows to dwell in an open, unsheltered place free from obstructions;
this is called "constantly residing in the open air.
What is meant by "constantly dwelling among tombs"?
This refers to one who constantly makes a vow to dwell among cemeteries,
in those places where the corpses of the deceased are conveyed;
such a person is said to be one who "constantly dwells in a cemetery."
What is meant by "always intending to sit upright"?
It refers to sitting with the body erect upon a large couch, a small rope-seat,
or a seat of grass and leaves, calculating the passage of time and days.
One never leans against a large bed, a small rope seat, a wall, a tree, or a seat of grass and leaves, whether with one's back or one's side.
This is called "always remaining in the upright sitting posture."
What is meant by "dwelling as one who sits upon his usual seat"?
It refers to sitting or reclining upon a seat of grass or a seat of leaves,
just as those grass or leaf seats were previously arranged.
One always sits or lies down;
after having spread out the bedding once, one never repeatedly turns it over, lifts it up, or repairs it.
This is called "dwelling in a seat as usual."
Question: Why is it called the "merit of ascetic purification" (*dhūtaguṇa*)?
Answer: It is, for example, like wool or cotton in the world that has not yet been beaten, nor carded, nor teased, nor split apart.
At that time, they remain adhered to one another,
being neither soft nor light; they are unfit for making thread,
cord, felt, or bedding, whether by whipping, stretching, twisting, or carding.
At that time, it becomes dispersed, soft, supple, and exquisite,
fit for being made into thread, yarn, felt, or rugs;
such is the practitioner.
Through craving for food and drink, one causes the mind to become stained and attached to various foods and drinks;
through craving for clothing, one causes the mind to become stained and attached to various garments;
through craving for bedding and seats, one causes the mind to become stained and attached to various bedding and seats.
By means of such dhūta qualities,
he is able to purify and cultivate himself, making him upright,
supple, light, and subtle, and rendering him capable of bearing his burden.
Because one can practice the holy life by relying upon and conforming to these [practices],
they are called the dhūta-guṇas (ascetic virtues).
Regarding food and drink, there is the craving for fine food and the craving for eating much.
Because it obstructs the cultivation of wholesome qualities,
and desiring to eliminate craving for fine food,
one always intends to beg for alms and practices begging from house to house in regular order.
In order to sever the craving for eating excessively,
one should eat only in a single sitting and first cease from eating before rising;
regarding clothing:
There are three kinds of craving that can obstruct the cultivation of wholesome qualities:
first, craving for many garments;
second, craving for soft textures.
Third, there is attachment to superior and exquisite [robes].
In order to sever this greed for many robes,
one maintains only the three robes.
In order to eliminate craving for the soft touch of various garments,
he wears only robes of wool;
in order to eliminate craving for the excellence of various garments, [he wears only coarse ones].
Wearing rag-robes,
there are four types of craving regarding bedding and seating that can obstruct the cultivation of virtue.
First, greed for clamor and social bustle;
second, greed for dwellings;
third, greed for the pleasure of reclining and the pleasure of lying down.
Fourth is greed for bedding and seating.
In order to eliminate greed for the clamor and bustle of society,
one dwells in an araṇya (forest hermitage).
In order to sever craving for dwellings,
he constantly dwells beneath trees, in the open air, or among burial mounds; furthermore,
in order to sever craving for sensual pleasure, he practices celibacy.
He dwells constantly among burial mounds in order to sever attachment to the pleasure of reclining and the pleasure of lying down;
he always intends to remain in a seated posture.
In order to eliminate attachment to bedding and seats,
one dwells in a place such as a regular seat;
this is called accomplishing the dhūta qualities.
What is meant by being dignified?
It refers to being accomplished in going and returning, looking ahead and looking aside,
bending and stretching, and in carrying the saṃghāṭī, the robes, and the alms bowl.
A dignified physical appearance is what is called "dignity.
What is meant by "knowing the proper measure"?
That is to say, with regard to pure-minded brahmins, householders, and lay devotees,
one excessively indulges them with clothing, food and drink, bedding,
and various requisites such as medicine for the sick and other articles.
To gather with moderation is called "knowing the measure.
What is meant by "accomplishing the qualities of a virtuous person"?
That is to say, one is born into a noble family and leaves the household life out of pure faith,
or is born into a wealthy family and leaves the household life out of pure faith;
his countenance is exceptionally beautiful, pleasing to behold, and dignified.
Possessing extensive learning and perfected speech,
or having attained even a small degree of wisdom, insight, or peaceful abiding,
one does not, by reason of these causes and conditions, exalt oneself or disparage others.
One is able to know that only the practice in accordance with the Dharma is the truth;
having understood this, one practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma with diligent effort.
This is called accomplishing the qualities of a virtuous person.
What is meant by accomplishing the characteristics of a wise person?
It means that one recognizes a fool by the signs of their actions.
One knows wisdom through the manifestation of its activity.
What is this activity?
It refers to [the conduct of] the foolish.
Those who have thought what should not be thought, spoken what should not be spoken,
and done what should not be done are the unwise;
whereas those who have thought what should be thought, spoken what should be spoken, and done what should be done are the wise.
This is called the mark of one who has achieved wisdom.
What is forbearance?

It refers to a case where someone, when reviled, does not revile in return; when provoked to anger, does not respond with anger; when struck, does not strike back; and when mocked, does not mock in return.
Furthermore, that venerable one is capable of enduring cold and heat, hunger and thirst,
mosquitoes, gadflies, wind, sun,
and the touch of venomous snakes and scorpions.
Furthermore, one is able to endure the coarse and malicious speech uttered by others;
and one is also able to endure all the intense, piercing, harsh, and agonizing sensations within the body that cut to the heart and deprive one of life.
To be of a nature that is patient and capable of acceptance is called "endurance.
What is "gentleness"?
That is to say, there is someone who, toward the Great Teacher and others,
fully accomplishes compassionate bodily action and fully accomplishes compassionate verbal action.
Fully accomplishing a mental action characterized by loving-kindness and compassion,
he shares and enjoys with wise fellow-practitioners whatever is appropriate for their use.
Whatever food or drink one consumes is done without secrecy;
whatever is obtained and acquired in accordance with the Dharma,
having fallen into the alms bowl and being contained therein, is then utilized for sustenance.
Possessing such six qualities as identical precepts and identical views,
they are delightful, lovely, and worthy of esteem;
they possess no qualities of contention or dispute, are easy to dwell with, and by nature do not afflict others.
To dwell together in one place with wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life and always cause them to rejoice—
this is called gentleness.
What is meant by being "virtuous and excellent"?
It refers to one who, for instance, avoids frowning, maintains a relaxed countenance and level gaze,
smiles, speaks first, and always utters words of affection.
One whose nature frequently embraces virtuous companions,
and whose body and mind are serene and pure,
is called "noble and good."
Dharma:
delighting in the true Dharma and delighting in merit;
not delighting in gain, honor, or praise.
Furthermore, they do not establish the two types of false views— namely, superimposition and denial.
They never superimpose existence upon phenomena that do not exist,
nor do they ever deny existence upon phenomena that truly exist.
Regarding those worldly matters that are elegant in composition,
he is able to correctly understand the various poetic treatises composed in accordance with the world, which employ diverse phonetic characters and are adorned with refined phrasing.
That which is meaningless and without benefit, one should avoid from afar and abandon;
one should not practice it, nor cherish it, nor propagate it.
One should take no pleasure in hoarding surplus robes or alms bowls.
He stays far removed from living in common with householders,
as that increases afflictions;
he delights in dwelling in harmony with the noble assembly.
Because they have purified their wisdom,
they take no pleasure in gathering in kinsmen or friends,
lest they be led astray by the causes and conditions of such relatives and associates.
One will encounter immeasurable disturbances and affairs;
when these deteriorate, one will give rise to various forms of sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and distress,
as well as the primary and secondary afflictions that arise accordingly.
Without clinging firmly to them, one should immediately abandon, dispel, and cast them out,
thinking: "May no manifold suffering arise for me in this life or in future lives on account of these two afflictions."
They shall never waste or squander any offerings made out of faith;
they shall never violate their pure precepts;
and while enjoying offerings made out of faith, they shall never disparage the offerings of others.
He never abandons the precepts he has undertaken;
he constantly delights in examining his own faults and takes no pleasure in seeking out the transgressions of others.
They conceal their own virtues and disclose their own faults;
even for reasons involving life-threatening danger, they do not intentionally commit any transgressions against the multitude of precepts.
Should they happen to commit a minor offense through forgetfulness, [they immediately acknowledge it].
Even if one swiftly repents and eliminates [faults] according to the Dharma,
one remains diligent and untiring in what ought to be done;
whatever one undertakes, one is able to accomplish by oneself.
They never seek others to serve as their attendants;
and regarding the inconceivable majestic power and spiritual efficacy of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, as well as his disciples, and the profound teachings of the Dharma.
They will develop deep faith and understanding, never disparaging or slandering [the teachings].
They will correctly understand that these are known and seen only by the Tathāgata and are not within their own sphere of experience;
they will never take pleasure in dwelling in their own deluded views.
If one adopts discourses and incantations produced by irrational, perverse attachments and evil views,
yet these are associated with such meritorious qualities as these.
Abiding thus and training thus,
he adorns himself with the various ornaments of a true śramaṇa,
which are exceedingly subtle and refined.
It is, for example, like a person who is robust, handsome, and well-adorned;
delighting in the enjoyment of various desires, he bathes his body and head,
anoints them with exquisite perfumes, and puts on fresh white garments.
It was adorned with various kinds of exquisite ornaments,
namely: necklaces, earrings,
signet rings, and bracelets.
Bracelets of various exquisite jewels and seals,
along with flower garlands made of gold, silver, and other materials—
such adornments were exceedingly wonderful and marvelous.
Thus, the practitioner adorns himself with the various excellent ornaments of the virtues of a true śramaṇa;
his merit blazes forth, its majestic radiance shining everywhere.
Therefore, these are called the adornments of a śramaṇa.
This is the meaning of the "adornment implements of a śramaṇa.

Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Twenty-Six.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

In the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, the thirteenth [section] of the *Maulī Bhūmiḥ*, within the first part of the second yoga station, it is asked: regarding the stage of renunciation (*naiṣkramyabhūmi*) as previously cited and explained, [how is it so?]
How many types of persons (pudgala) are there who are able to realize liberation?
How are these persons established?
What is the object of focus?
What is the instruction?
What is the training?
What are the dharmas conducive to training?
What is the failure of yoga? What is yoga?
What is mental attention?
What is the practice of a yoga practitioner? How many types of yoga practitioners are there?
And what is the cultivation of yoga?
What is the fruit of cultivation?
How many types of designations for persons (pudgala) are there?
And how many types of persons are there?
How many kinds of causes and conditions are established for the *pudgala*?
How many kinds of Māras are there, and how many kinds of deeds of Māra?
In what way does one set out toward emptiness and yet find no fruit?
The summary verse says: Regarding all individuals,
the establishment of objects of focus, the teaching of the trainings,
the dharmas that accord with training, and the destruction of yoga and mental attention.
The practitioner of yoga performs cultivation; regarding the gates of the fruit, the person (pudgala), causes, demonic activities, and the absence of fruit—all these shall be explained extensively.
There are twenty-eight varieties of distinctions among persons (pudgalas).
What are the twenty-eight?
They are those of dull faculties and those of sharp faculties.
Those for whom greed predominates,
those for whom hatred predominates,
and those for whom delusion predominates.
One for whom pride is predominant,
one for whom discursive thought is predominant,
and one who has attained equanimity.
Those of slight defilement,
those who are practicing toward the goal,
and those who abide in the fruit.
The follower by faith,
the follower by dharma,
and the one resolved through faith.
Those who have attained through vision,
those who have realized through the body,
and those who will be reborn no more than seven times at most.
Those who go from family to family,
those who attain parinirvāṇa with one interval,
and those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
Those who attain parinirvāṇa upon birth,
those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion,
and those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion.
The upward-streamer,
the one liberated by occasion,
and the one of immovable dharma.
Regarding those liberated through wisdom and those liberated through both parts:
what is a person of dull faculties?
This refers to a person who possesses dull faculties,
whose engagement with objects of knowledge is sluggish and feeble,
as has been explained previously.
This, moreover, is of two kinds;
their characteristics should be understood as follows:
first, those of a lineage with naturally dull faculties.
Second, those who have not yet well cultivated the faculties.
What is a person of sharp faculties?
It refers to a person who possesses sharp faculties.
Regarding the objects of knowledge, it functions without sluggishness and functions without weakness,
as previously explained;
this also has two aspects.
One should know its characteristics:
first, the lineage of naturally sharp faculties;
second, having already well cultivated all the faculties.
What is a person for whom greed is predominant?
It refers to a person who,
in previous lives, [was characterized] by the affliction of greed.
Having cultivated, practiced, and repeatedly developed it,
by reason of these causes and conditions, there now arises in this life an intense craving and a long-lasting craving for beloved objects.
This is called a person dominated by greed.
What is a person dominated by hatred?
It refers to a person who...
Because in previous lives one has already cultivated, practiced, and frequently cultivated the affliction of anger,
by reason of those causes and conditions, in this present life, toward objects of aversion...
One who possesses intense hatred and long-lasting hatred is called a person dominated by hatred.
What is a person dominated by delusion?
This refers to a person who,
in previous lives, has already cultivated, practiced, and repeatedly habituated themselves to the affliction of delusion.
Due to these causes and conditions, in this present life, one possesses both intense delusion and long-lasting delusion regarding the objects of ignorance;
such a person is called an individual dominated by delusion (*moha-adhipateya-pudgala*).
What is a person for whom pride is predominant?
It refers to a person who,
in previous lives, [has cultivated] the affliction of pride.
Having cultivated, practiced, and repeatedly developed this,
by reason of these causes and conditions, one now possesses intense pride and long-lasting pride regarding the objects of pride within this present life.
This is called a person for whom pride is predominant.
What is a person for whom discursive thought is predominant?
It refers to a person who...
In previous lives, one has already cultivated, practiced, and repeatedly mastered those very thoughts;
by virtue of this cause and condition, in this present life, regarding the objects of thought...
There is the person who possesses intense discursive thought and long-lasting discursive thought;
this is called a person for whom discursive thought is predominant.
What is a person who has attained equanimity?
That is to say, there is a person who,
in previous lives, although they did not cultivate, practice, or frequently practice [the antidotes to] greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and discursive thought.
Yet, regarding those phenomena, one has not yet perceived their faults,
has not yet become weary of them or destroyed them, and has not yet skillfully investigated them.
Due to these causes and conditions, with respect to objects that are beloved, hated, deluded about, arrogant toward, or objects of discursive thought, [one remains bound].
There is no intense greed nor long-lasting greed;
however, greed manifests with respect to those objects.
As it is with greed, so it is with hatred, delusion, pride, and discursive thought.
This is called the person who has attained equanimity.
What is the person whose nature is of attenuated defilements?
It refers to a person who...
In previous lives, he did not cultivate, practice, or frequently habituate himself to the affliction of greed;
he was already able to perceive many faults and disadvantages therein.
Having already been able to cultivate weariness and having thoroughly investigated [the nature of things],
by virtue of these causes and conditions, one now gives rise to only slight and inferior attachment toward beloved objects when encountering numerous,
exquisite, and superior sensory domains present before one in this life.
Within those objects of medium and inferior grades, desire does not arise at all.
It should be understood that this is likewise true for hatred, delusion, pride, and discursive thought.
Such a person is called an individual of "thin-defilement" nature (*tanu-rajas*).
What is a person who is practicing toward [the fruits]?
It refers to a person who is practicing toward the four fruits. What are the four?
1. One who is a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry;
2. one who is a candidate for the fruit of once-returning;
3. one who is a candidate for the fruit of non-returning.
The fourth is the candidate for the fruit of arhatship;
these are called persons who are candidates for practice.
What is a person who abides in the fruit?
This refers to individuals abiding in the four fruits.
What are the four?
First, the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).
2. The fruit of once-returning;
3. the fruit of non-returning;
4. the fruit of arhatship.
This is called a person who abides in the fruit.
What is a person who follows by faith?
It refers to a person who...
One seeks instructions and admonitions from others;
by the power of these, one practices and realizes the path to the fruit.
This is not merely as it was heard, received, or mastered.
Regarding those phenomena that are contemplated, measured, and investigated,
one possesses inherent capacity and inherent power to practice in accordance with the Dharma;
yet, one practices solely by means of faith in another person.
This is called the person who follows by faith (śraddhānusārin).
What is the person who follows by dharma (dharmānusārin)?
It refers to a person who...
According to those dharmas as they have been heard, received, and mastered;
as they have been reflected upon, weighed, and investigated—
one possesses the inherent capacity and inherent power to practice in accordance with those dharmas.
One who does not seek from others instructions or admonitions regarding the practice for realizing the fruit is called a person of "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (dharmānusārin).
What is a person of "resolute conviction through faith" (śraddhādhimukta)?
This refers to the person who follows by faith (śraddhānusārin), who,
through the instructions and admonitions of others,
attains direct realization of the fruits of śramaṇaship.
Such a person is called an individual resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*).
What is an individual who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*)?
It refers to the very same individual who was practicing in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
When one attains direct realization of the fruits of asceticism,
one is called a person who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta-pudgala).
What is a person who has attained realization through the body (kāyasākṣin-pudgala)?
It refers to a person who enters into and emerges from the eight liberations in both forward and reverse order,
personally realizes them with the body, and dwells therein extensively.
Yet they have not yet attained the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
This is called a person who is a bodily witness (*kāyasākṣin-pudgala*).
What is meant by a person who is "one who returns at most seven times" (*saptakṛtvobhava-parama-pudgala*)?
It refers to a person who,
having permanently severed the three fetters— namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—
has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), is established in the state of non-falling, and is destined for enlightenment.
One who returns as a deva or a human for at most seven more existences,
and having returned for at most seven times, realizes the end of suffering—
such a person is called a *saptakṛtparama* (one who returns seven times at most).
What is a *pudgala* who goes from family to family (*kulaṃkula*)?
There are two kinds of *kulaṃkula*:
first, one who goes from heaven to heaven (*deva-kulaṃkula*).
The two types of *kulaṃkula* (family-to-family).
Regarding the *devakulaṃkula* (family-to-family among the gods):
this refers to one who goes from family to family within the heavenly realms.
Whether going or coming, one realizes the end of suffering.
"From family to family" means moving from household to household among human beings.
Whether going or returning, they realize the end of suffering;
it should be known that both of these are *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) individuals.
What is a *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner) individual?
That is to say, a person who is a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin),
having already set out toward the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala),
is able to permanently abandon the superior and medium grades of afflictions of the desire realm.
Only the inferior grade remains;
he will experience only one more existence as a deva in the desire realm,
and will attain parinirvāṇa right there.
They will no longer return to be born in this world;
such a person is called an *ekavīcika* (one-interval) *pudgala*.
What is a *pudgala* who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyī*)?
There are three types of individuals who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*).
First, there is one type of individual who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state:
having passed away from this life, they continue their existence through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Among them, there is one who attains parinirvāṇa immediately after being born,
like a small spark of fire that vanishes as soon as it is raised.
Second, there is a type of person (pudgala) who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
Having passed away from here, one is reborn through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Having been born in the intermediate state, one remains for a short time;
before proceeding to the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*), one attains parinirvāṇa.
It is like a glowing, fiercely burning iron ball or ingot from which sparks fly when struck by a hammer; they vanish before they have even fallen.
Third, there is the person who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
Having passed away from here, one is reborn through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Once the intermediate state has arisen, one proceeds toward the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*).
Before attaining that existence of birth, one enters parinirvāṇa.
Just as sparks flying from the hammering of heated iron vanish immediately upon falling before they reach the ground,
so too are those individuals who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state among these three types.
Taken collectively, these are called individuals who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
What is an individual who attains parinirvāṇa upon being born?
It refers to one who, as soon as they have been born there, immediately attains parinirvāṇa.
This is called the person who attains parinirvāṇa upon birth.
What is the person who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion?
It refers to one who, having been born there, does not initiate preparatory application nor perform effortful activity.
One who attains parinirvāṇa through the manifestation of the path without relying on strenuous effort is called a person who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin).
What is a person who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (sābhisamskāra-parinirvāyin)?
That is to say, having been born there, they initiate application and exert great effort;
through extreme exhaustion, the path manifests before them and they attain parinirvāṇa.
This is called the person who attains parinirvāṇa with application (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin).
What is the person who goes upstream?
It refers to a non-returner who,
having been reborn from here in the first dhyāna, ascends further.
Abiding in that place, they do not enter parinirvāṇa;
having passed away from there, they are reborn successively in higher realms of existence,
until they eventually reach the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Or one who reaches the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
this is called an "upstream-bound" (ūrdhva-srotas) person.
What is a "liberated-in-time" (samaya-vimukta) person?
This refers to a person of dull faculties who,
belonging to a lineage [capable of liberation], may experience a decline from the pleasant dwellings in the present life within the world;
such a person might either contemplate self-harm or guard their liberation.
One should exert effort and diligently cultivate the practice of heedfulness;
that is to say, because it possesses the predominant power to prevent decline and loss,
or because one simply abides in one's own portion of wholesome qualities.
Or, through exerting effort for various days, nights, moments (kṣaṇa), instants (tatkṣaṇa), breaths (śvāsa), and brief intervals (muhūrta),
until one has realized the most intense [attainment],
such a person is called a *samayavimukta* pudgala.
What is a person of immovable nature?
It refers to a person who is the opposite of the aforementioned [type].
One should know that such a person is called an *akopyadharman* (one of immovable nature).
What is a person liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*)?
It refers to a person who...
One who has already been able to realize the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*),
yet has not yet personally realized and fully dwelt in the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*),
is called a person liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta-pudgala*).
What is a person who is liberated through both parts?
It refers to a person who has already been able to realize the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
Having personally realized the eight liberations and dwelling fully therein,
his mind is liberated from both the portion of the afflictive obscurations and the portion of the obscurations to liberation.
This is called the person liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta-pudgala*).
How are persons established?
It is by means of eleven modes of differentiation.
One should know that the establishment of the *pudgala* (person) is based on eleven modes of differentiation. What are these eleven?
First, the differentiation of the faculties (*indriya*).
Second, because of the distinction between the two assemblies;
third, because of the distinction between the three types of conduct;
fourth, because of the distinction between their vows.
1. Due to the distinctions among the five traces of the elements;
2. due to the distinctions among the fruits of the six destinies; 3.
due to the distinctions among the seven preparatory practices.
8. Because of the distinction of the eight meditative concentrations;
9. because of the distinction of births;
10. because of the distinction between falling away and not falling away.
Eleventh, due to the distinction of obstacles:
regarding *pudgalas*, two types of *pudgalas* are established based on the distinction of their faculties (*indriya*).
First, those of dull faculties;
second, those of sharp faculties.
How are persons established based on the distinctions among groups?
This means that seven types of *pudgalas* are established based on distinctions among the assembly:
namely, the bhikṣu, the bhikṣuṇī, the śikṣamāṇā,
the śrāmaṇera, and the śrāmaṇerī.
Laymen and laywomen.
How are individuals (pudgala) established by way of the distinction of their conduct?
It means that seven types of individuals are established on account of the distinction of their conduct.
That is to say, a person for whom greed is predominant is called one who acts out of greed;
a person for whom hatred is predominant is called one who acts out of hatred;
and a person for whom delusion is predominant is called one who acts out of delusion.
A person for whom pride is predominant is called one who acts out of pride;
a person for whom discursive thought is predominant is called one who acts out of discursive thought;
and a person who has attained equanimity is called one of equal temperament.
If a person of dull defilements is called one who practices with dull defilements, one should ask:
what are the characteristics of a person who practices with greed?
The answer is: a person who practices with greed...
Even toward objects of affection that are subtle and inferior,
one is still able to give rise to an extremely dense and superior-grade entanglement of greed;
how much more so toward objects of the middling or superior grades?
Furthermore, this entanglement of greed dwells within the body,
persisting through a long succession and binding one for a great length of time;
because of this entanglement of greed, one is brought under the sway of attractive phenomena.
He is unable to subdue those attractive phenomena;
his faculties are delighted, his faculties are not firm,
and his faculties are not coarse.
His faculties are not coarse;
by nature he does not delight in harming others through evil deeds of body or speech;
he is difficult to lead away from [unwholesome states] and difficult to cause to feel revulsion toward them.
Having inferior resolve,
yet firm in their undertakings and long-established in their activities.
Their precepts are firm and stable;
their observance of the precepts is long-enduring and solid;
they are able to endure and accept [all hardships].
Regarding the requisites for life,
he is by nature prone to attachment and deeply cherishes them;
he is full of joy and gladness, and is free from frowning.
With a relaxed countenance, looking straight ahead and smiling, they are the first to speak.
One should know that such characteristics as these are the signs of one who acts out of greed (*rāga-carita*).
Question: What are the signs by which a person who acts out of hatred (*dveṣa-carita-pudgala*) should be known?
Answer: A person of irascible temperament can give rise to an extremely heavy,
superior-grade obsession of anger even toward objects of aversion that are slight and inferior.
How much more so for middling and superior objects!
Furthermore, this entanglement of hatred dwells within the body,
persisting for a long duration and binding one continuously over an extended period of time.
Being thus constrained by the fetter of hatred,
one is overpowered by that which is loathsome and cannot overpower it;
the faculties become withered and the faculties become rigid.
Their faculties are coarse and rough; their faculties are harsh and parched.
By nature they delight in harming others through evil deeds of body and speech;
they are easily led away from such conduct and easily made to feel weary of it.
Fierce and violent, with harsh speech and a rugged appearance, they lack much resolute conviction;
their undertakings are neither firm nor stable,
and their observance of precepts is neither firm nor stable.
He is unable to endure or accept [adversity], being full of much anxiety and much distress.
By nature he is inclined toward contrariness and disobedience regarding what is taken up;
by nature he is full of sorrow and dejection, and by nature he is fond of coarse speech.
They harbor much resentment and their disposition is cruel;
they are perverse, malicious, and venomous, delighting in confrontation.
Upon receiving even a few words, they become full of hatred and indignation.
Remaining haggard, he gives rise to anger with ease;
his brows and face are knit in a frown, and he never displays a relaxed countenance.
With a sidelong gaze and downward look, he harbors much hatred and much envy toward the prosperity and gains of others.
One should know that such categories as these are called the characteristics of those whose temperament is dominated by hatred (*dveṣacarita*).
Question: What characteristics should be known for a person (*pudgala*) whose temperament is dominated by delusion (*mohacarita*)?
Answer: A person whose temperament is dominated by delusion...
If they are still able to give rise to extremely dense, superior-grade fetters of delusion even regarding objects that are subtle and inferior,
how much more so in the case of middling or superior-grade objects?
Furthermore, this entanglement of delusion dwells within the body,
persisting for a long duration and binding one continuously over a great length of time;
by means of this entanglement of delusion, one is overcome by those phenomena that are subject to delusion.
They are unable to subdue those dharmas that lead to delusion;
their faculties are dull, their faculties are ignorant, and their faculties are weak.
Their physical actions are slack, and their verbal actions are slack.
One thinks evil thoughts, speaks evil words, and performs evil deeds;
one is overcome by indolence and laziness, failing to achieve fulfillment;
one’s eloquence is weak, one’s nature is dull-witted, and one frequently forgets what has been learned.
Dwelling in lack of clear comprehension, they grasp at what is deviant and perverse;
they are difficult to lead away from it and difficult to cause to feel revulsion toward it,
possessing inferior resolve.
Stupid, dull-witted, mute, and speech-impaired, they communicate by means of hand gestures.
They lack the power or capacity to comprehend the meaning of well-spoken or ill-spoken teachings.
Bound and entangled by external conditions, they are led astray by others and coerced into service by others.
One should know that such categories as these are called the characteristics of one who acts out of delusion (*moha-carita*).
Question: What characteristics should be known for a person (*pudgala*) who acts out of pride (*māna-carita*)?
Answer: A person who acts out of pride...
If one can give rise to an extremely dense and intense,
superior-grade obsession of pride even regarding objects that are slight and inferior,
how much more so in the case of middling or superior-grade objects?
Furthermore, this entanglement of pride dwells within the body,
persisting in a continuous succession for a long duration and binding one over time.
Due to this entanglement of pride, one is overcome and subdued by those things that give rise to pride.
He is unable to subdue those qualities that give rise to conceit;
his faculties are restless, his faculties are haughty,
and his faculties are distracted as he zealously delights in adorning his body.
Their speech is arrogant and they take no pleasure in humility;
toward their parents, kinsmen, and teachers,
they are unable to serve them properly and at the appropriate times.
Abounding in arrogance, they are unable to show physical reverence, inquire after their well-being, join their palms in greeting,
or perform acts of harmony and respect; instead,
they are self-exalting and self-aggrandizing, looking down upon and despising others.
They are attached to gain and offerings, attached to honor and respect,
and attached to worldly fame, reputation, and praise.
Their conduct is frivolous, and they delight in making sarcastic remarks.
It is difficult to cause them to distance themselves from [suffering] and difficult to cause them to feel weary of it;
their resolute conviction is vast, yet their compassion is feeble;
they hold views such as the self, a sentient being, a life-force, a nourisher, a person, and a being.
For the most part, they have many enemies and harbor much resentment;
such types as these should be known as the characteristics of one whose temperament is dominated by pride (*mānacarita*).
Question: What should be known as the characteristics of a person whose temperament is dominated by discursive thought (*vitarkacarita*)?
Answer: A person whose conduct consists of discursive thought can still give rise to extremely dense,
heavy, and superior fetters of discursive thought even regarding objects that are subtle and inferior.
How much more so for middling and superior objects;
these fetters of discursive thought abide within the body,
persisting in a continuous succession and binding one for a long duration.
Due to these envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), one is overpowered by things that are subject to discursive thought (*vitarka*) and is unable to overpower those things subject to discursive thought.
The faculties do not abide; the faculties are agitated and tossed about.
The faculties are restless and the faculties are distracted;
there is error in bodily action and error in verbal action;
it is difficult to cause them to distance themselves from unwholesome states and difficult to cause them to feel revulsion toward them.
They delight in frivolous discourse and are attached to frivolous discourse;
they are full of delusion and doubt, harboring many desires;
their observance of precepts is neither firm nor stable.
Their undertakings are not steadfast and their undertakings are unstable;
they harbor much fear and anxiety, and their mindfulness is frequently lost;
they take no delight in seclusion and greatly enjoy distraction.
Regarding the various wonderful things in the world, their craving flows along with them;
they are diligent and untiring, initiating and perfecting [their efforts].
Such types as these should be known as the characteristics of one who practices through investigation (*vitarkacarita*).
This is called the establishment of individuals by way of the distinction of their conduct.
How is the establishment of individuals by way of the distinction of their aspirations?
It refers to those individuals who...
There may be a person who has already made a correct vow for the Śrāvaka Vehicle,
or one who has already made a correct vow for the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
There may be a person who has already made a correct aspiration for the Mahāyāna;
it should be understood that among these, there is also the person who has already made a correct aspiration for the Śrāvakayāna.
They may belong to the lineage of the śrāvakas,
or the lineage of the pratyekabuddhas,
or the lineage of the Mahāyāna.
If a person has already made a correct aspiration for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha,
they may belong either to the lineage of a pratyekabuddha or to the lineage of a śrāvaka.
Or one of the Mahāyāna lineage:
if a person has already formed the correct aspiration for that Mahāyāna,
they are either of the Mahāyāna lineage.
Either the lineage of a pratyekabuddha or the lineage of a śrāvaka;
if it is a person (pudgala) of the śrāvaka lineage.
They have already made the correct aspiration for either the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha or for unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment.
Because he belongs to the lineage of the śrāvakas,
at a later time he will certainly renounce that vow and will necessarily abide only in the vow of the Śrāvaka-yāna.
It should be understood that the same applies to individuals belonging to the lineage of the Pratyekabuddhayāna and the Mahāyāna.
Among these, there are individuals whose aspirations may be redirected or whose aspirations may be relinquished.
It is certain that one cannot shift or abandon the lineage;
in this context, it should be understood that only the aspiration for the Śrāvaka vehicle is being discussed.
This refers to an individual belonging to the śrāvaka lineage.
This is called the establishment of persons by way of the distinction of their aspirations.
How is the establishment of persons by way of the distinction of their paths?
It refers to the persons as they have been cited and as they have been explained.
One attains liberation by means of four modes of practice. What are these four? They are as follows:
there may be a mode of practice that is painful with slow super-knowledge.
There may be a path of practice that is painful with quick penetration;
there may be a path of practice that is pleasant with slow penetration;
and there may be a path of practice that is pleasant with quick penetration.
It should be understood that herein, for a person of dull faculties who has not yet attained the fundamental dhyānas,
there is a certain course of practice.
This is called "slow penetration with suffering.
If a person of sharp faculties has not yet attained the fundamental dhyānas, [their progress is likewise slow].
All modes of practice are called "swift penetration with difficulty.
If a person of dull faculties has already attained the fundamental dhyānas, their modes of practice are called "slow penetration with ease."
If a person of sharp faculties has already attained the fundamental dhyānas,
their path of practice is called "pleasant and swift penetration."
This is called the establishment of individuals (pudgala) by way of the distinction of their paths of practice.
How, then, are individuals established by way of the distinction of the paths and fruits?
This refers to those practicing the four paths and those abiding in the four fruits.
Regarding those practicing the four paths:
first, the person (pudgala) who is a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna-phala-pratipannaka).
2. the person proceeding toward the fruit of once-returner;
3. the person proceeding toward the fruit of non-returner;
4. the person proceeding toward the fruit of arhatship.
Those who abide in the four fruits are:
first, the fruit of stream-entry;
second, the fruit of once-returning.
Third, the fruit of non-returning;
fourth, the fruit of arhatship.
If one turns toward the path leading to these, they are called those who are practicing toward them (pratipannaka).
Based on the path, four types of persons (*pudgala*) are established;
if one has attained the fruit of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), they are called "one who abides in the fruit.
Based on the path and its fruit, four types of persons are established.
This is called the establishment of persons (pudgala) by way of the distinction between the paths and their fruits.
How is the establishment of persons made by way of the distinction of application (prayoga)?
This refers to the individuals known as those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who follow by dharma (dharmānusārin).
If one diligently cultivates correct practice based on faith in another individual,
they are called an individual who follows by faith.
If one does not depend on others regarding all phenomena,
but diligently practices the correct conduct in accordance with the Vinaya,
such a person is called an individual who practices in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānusārī-pudgala).
This is called the establishment of persons (pudgala) by way of the distinction of application.
How is the establishment of persons by way of the distinction of meditative attainment?
It refers to the person who is a bodily witness (kāyasākṣin).
One who has personally realized and fully dwells in the eight liberations,
yet has not attained the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*),
should be known as a person (*pudgala*) who, while possessing form, perceives forms within the liberation.
The liberation consisting of perceiving external forms while having no internal perception of form;
the pure liberation, which is realized bodily and dwelt in fully;
and the liberation of the sphere of infinite space.
The liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness,
the liberation of the sphere of nothingness,
and the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Having attained mastery in entering and emerging from the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling in both forward and reverse order,
such a person is designated as an individual established by the distinctions of meditative concentration.
How are persons established by way of the distinction of birth?
They are: those who have at most seven more existences (saptakṛtvah-parama), and those who go from family to family (kulaṃkula).
The ekabījī, the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyī),
and the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyī).
The one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion,
the one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion,
and the person who is a "stream-winner to the higher realms" (ūrdhvasrotas).
This is called establishing the *pudgala* by way of the distinction of birth.
How is the *pudgala* established by way of the distinction between falling away and not falling away?
That is to say, by virtue of falling away, one establishes the arhat of occasional liberation (*samayavimukta*);
such a person may still experience falling away from the blissful dwelling in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
By virtue of not falling away, one establishes the arhat of immovable dharma (*akopyadharman*).
He will certainly not fall away from the dwelling in happiness in this very life.
This is called the establishment of individuals by way of the distinction between falling away and not falling away.
What is the establishment of individuals by way of the distinction of hindrances?
This refers to the Arhat liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta) and the Arhat liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta).

An Arhat liberated by wisdom is one who has already been liberated from the obstacle of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa) but has not yet been liberated from the obstacle to meditative concentration (samāpattyāvaraṇa).
An Arhat liberated through both parts is one who has already been liberated from the hindrance of afflictions and has already been liberated from the hindrance to meditative concentration; therefore,
they are called "liberated through both parts."
Thus, the establishment of individuals (pudgala) by way of the distinctions of their hindrances has been explained.
One should now understand the sequential establishment of individuals.
What is the objective referent (ālambana)?
It refers to four kinds of objective referents. What are the four?
First, the pervasive objective referent.
Second, the objective referent for purifying conduct;
third, the objective referent for skillfulness;
fourth, the objective referent for purifying afflictions.
The objects of focus that are pervasive consist of four types:
first, the conceptual image.
Second, the image free from conceptual differentiation;
third, the limit of phenomena;
and fourth, the accomplishment of what is to be done.
What is the conceptual image?
It refers to someone who, relying either on hearing the true Dharma or on instructions and admonitions, [engages in meditation].
Due to seeing, hearing, or conceptualizing,
one engages in the practice of vipaśyanā within the stage of meditative equipoise (samāhita-bhūmi) regarding a concordant image of the object of knowledge.
Observing, discerning, thoroughly discerning, fully investigating,
and fully examining the objects of knowledge refers,
for instance, to the impure.
Either through compassion,
or by taking dependent origination as an object,
or through the analysis of the elements.
Either mindfulness of breathing,
or skillfulness regarding the aggregates,
or skillfulness regarding the elements.
Skillfulness regarding the bases (*sthāna*),
skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*),
or skillfulness regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*).
Either the coarseness of the lower stages and the tranquility of the higher stages;
or the truth of suffering and the truth of origination,
and the truth of cessation and the truth of the path.
This is called the object of knowledge.
This object of knowledge is based either upon instruction and admonition,
or upon hearing the true Dharma as its support.
He brings to presence the mental engagement of the stage of meditative equipoise;
he then gives rise to resolute conviction toward those very phenomena,
and he gives rise to resolute conviction toward those very objects of knowledge.
At that time, with respect to the object of knowledge,
he proceeds by means of a resolute conviction that accords with how it is currently being experienced.
Although that object of knowledge is not directly experienced as present and manifest,
nor is it another object of that same kind,

it is nevertheless experienced through the resolve (*adhimokṣa*) and the experience of a corresponding mental attention (*manasikāra*) belonging to the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*).
That object of knowledge appears as a resemblance [to itself].
By this principle, it is called the "concordant image" (sabhāga-pratibimba) of the object of knowledge.
For the practitioner of meditation:
In order to investigate this,
one examines and definitively ascertains the virtues and faults within those objects of knowledge that constitute their fundamental nature.
This is called the image with conceptual differentiation.
What is the image without conceptual differentiation?
It refers to the practitioner of meditation.
Having thus grasped the characteristics of this mental image,
one no longer examines, investigates, thoroughly investigates, extensively searches, or thoroughly scrutinizes it; rather,
one remains focused precisely upon this objective image.
One quiets the mind through the practice of śamatha;
that is, one causes the mind to abide by means of nine modes of mental abiding, namely:
causing the mind to abide internally, causing it to abide continuously, and so forth.
Abiding and closely abiding;
subduing and pacifying;
and most thoroughly pacifying.
There is a single-pointed concentration;
at that time, he achieves an object of focus consisting of a non-conceptual image,
and it is precisely upon such an objective image that [he meditates].
Abiding with mindfulness directed toward a single point and a single course,
one no longer observes, discerns, thoroughly discerns, universally investigates, or universally examines;
this is called the non-conceptual image.
This very image is also called an "image," it is also called the "sign of samādhi," and it is also called the "object of engagement of samādhi."
It is also called the mouth of samādhi,
it is also called the gate of samādhi,
and it is also called the locus of mental attention (manasikāra).
It is also called the "internal essence of discrimination" and "light and shadow.
Such categories as these should be understood as various synonymous designations for the "image that is a counterpart to the object of knowledge."
What is the nature of the limit of phenomena?
It refers to the objective referent’s *yāvadbhāvikatā* (the extent of its existence) and *yathāvadbhāvikatā* (its mode of existence). What is meant by *yāvadbhāvikatā*?
This means that apart from the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), there is no further form;

apart from the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (vedanā-, saṃjñā-, saṃskāra-, and vijñāna-skandhas), there are no further feelings, perceptions, mental formations, or consciousnesses.
All conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) are subsumed within these five factors.
All phenomena are subsumed within the realms and locations;
all knowable objects are subsumed within the four noble truths.
This is called the nature of the full extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*).
What is called "the nature of things as they are" (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*)?
It refers to that which is an object of focus (*ālambana*) that is of the nature of reality (*tattvabhāva*) and of the nature of suchness (*tathatābhāva*),
possessing the quality of being logical by virtue of the four principles of reasoning.
That is to say: the principle of dependence,
the principle of function,
and the principle of proof.
By the principle of natural law (*dharmatā-yukti*),
the totality of objects of focus, both in their full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and in their mode of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*),
is collectively termed the "limit of things" (*vastuparyantatā*).
What is the accomplishment of what is to be done?
It refers to the practitioner of meditation regarding śamatha and vipaśyanā.
By virtue of cultivating, practicing, and repeatedly practicing these as causes and conditions,
all mental attentions (manasikāra) directed toward the images of objects become perfected. Through this perfection,
one attains the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti).
All heavy burdens (*dauṣṭhulya*) are completely extinguished.
Because one has attained the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), one transcends mental images;
that is, regarding the objects of knowledge, there is no longer any conceptualization of existence or non-existence.
Direct perceptual knowledge and vision arise.
When one who has entered the first dhyāna attains the first dhyāna,
regarding the objective sphere traversed within that first dhyāna:
Regarding those who enter the second, third, and fourth dhyānas:
at the time they attain the second, third, and fourth dhyānas,
[they dwell] upon the objective spheres traversed by the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
They enter the sphere of infinite space,
the sphere of infinite consciousness,
and the sphere of nothingness.
Regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception:
when one attains that meditative concentration,
it concerns the objective domain traversed within that very concentration.
This is called the accomplishment of what is to be done.
These four kinds of objective referents pervade all [meditative objects].
It enters into all objects of focus,
being that which has been proclaimed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the past, future,
and present; therefore, it is called the "pervasive object of focus."
Furthermore, this object of focus pervades the category of vipaśyanā,
the category of śamatha, and all matters.
Because it pervades all truly real things and pervades all things characterized by the causal relationship between cause and effect,
it is called "pervasive" (vyāpya).
That is to say, if one speaks of the conceptual image,
it refers to the category of vipaśyanā herein;
if one speaks of the non-conceptual image, [it refers to the category of śamatha].
This refers here to the category of śamatha.
If one speaks of the nature of the limit of phenomena (vastuparyantatā),
this refers here to the true reality of all phenomena.
If one speaks of the accomplishment of what is to be done,
this refers precisely to the matter of the mutual connection between cause and effect herein,
just as the Blessed Buddha once spoke this meaning for the Elder Revata.
I have heard that the Elder Kṣemaka once asked the World-Honored One:
"Venerable Sir,
there are bhikṣus who diligently cultivate contemplative practice and are practitioners of yoga."
One is able to settle the mind upon an object of observation.
Why does one settle the mind upon an object?
How does one settle the mind upon an object?
"What is meant by the mind being well-settled?
The Buddha said to the Elder Kātyāyanīputra,
"Excellent, excellent!"
You have now skillfully asked about such a meaning.
Listen attentively and reflect deeply;
I shall proclaim and reveal it for you.
Kṣemadatta: Any bhikṣu who diligently cultivates contemplative practice is a yogācāra;
such a person is able to settle the mind upon the object of focus.
Whether delighting in pure conduct, or delighting in skillfulness,
or delighting in the liberation of the mind from all outflows,
they establish their minds upon corresponding objects.
He establishes his mind upon similar objects;
he establishes his mind correctly upon those objects;
and he is able to remain undistracted from meditative concentration therein.
How is it that a bhikṣu who diligently cultivates contemplative practice is a yogācāra?
It is when he establishes his mind upon a corresponding object;
that is to say, if that bhikṣu is one whose temperament is characterized solely by greed.
One should settle the mind upon the object of impurity.
This is called settling the mind upon a suitable object.
This applies if one possesses only a temperament prone to aversion.
One should dwell the mind in loving-kindness;
if there is only conduct characterized by delusion,
one should dwell the mind in dependent origination through conditions.
If there is only the tendency toward pride,

one should settle the mind upon the differentiation of the elements (*dhātu-prabheda*). If there is only the tendency toward discursive thought (*vitarka*), [one should settle the mind upon the mindfulness of breathing].
One should establish the mind in mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
This is called establishing the mind upon a suitable object.
*Nakṣatra-vardhana*.
Furthermore, if that bhikṣu is deluded regarding the specific characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
or is deluded regarding the entities of a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a living being, a nourisher, or a person (*pudgala*),
he should dwell with his mind well-established in skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha*).
If one is ignorant of its cause,
one should skillfully settle the mind upon the elements (*dhātu*).
If one is ignorant of its conditions (*pratyaya*), [one should do the same].
One should skillfully establish the mind in the [four] foundations;
if one is deluded regarding impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self,
one should skillfully establish the mind in the foundations of dependent origination, the possible, and the impossible.
If one desires to be free from the desires of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),

one should settle the mind upon the coarseness of all sensual desires and the tranquility of all forms (*rūpa*). If one desires to be free from the desires of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), [one should settle the mind upon the coarseness of all forms and the tranquility of the formless].
One should settle the mind upon the coarse nature of all forms and the tranquil nature of the formless.
If one desires to penetrate thoroughly and desires liberation from the basis of the view of a personal identity (*satkāya*) throughout all places.
One should settle the mind upon the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path.
This is called a bhikṣu who diligently practices contemplation—a yogācāra who settles the mind upon a corresponding object.
Kṣemadatta said:
"How does a bhikṣu who diligently cultivates contemplative practice—a practitioner of yoga—abide his mind upon a concordant object?
That is to say, that bhikṣu, regarding each and every object of knowledge..."
For the purpose of discerning, thoroughly discerning, universally searching, and universally examining,
one relies on the predominant power of what was previously seen, heard, sensed, and known, with respect to those objects that were seen, heard, sensed, and known.
By means of mental attention and conceptualization based on the stage of meditative equipoise (samāhita-bhūmi),
one gives rise to resolute conviction (adhimukti).
Although [the practitioner] does so regarding the fundamental object of knowledge (jñeya-vastu),...
It cannot be observed as being present through synthesis;
rather, it arises resembling its original basis (*pūrvavastu*).
Within that object of focus, there exists a resemblance to that [original basis].
There is only wisdom, only vision, and only right mindfulness.
Furthermore, from time to time that bhikṣu causes the mind to become tranquil;
from time to time, relying on the dharma of higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*), he diligently cultivates the practice of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
This is called a bhikṣu who diligently cultivates contemplative practice, a yoga practitioner who establishes the mind upon a concordant object. Kṣemaka,
how does a bhikṣu who diligently cultivates contemplative practice, a yoga practitioner, establish the mind upon an object without error?

That is to say, when a bhikṣu who is a yogācāra diligently cultivates contemplative practice, he establishes his mind upon the object of focus and understands the objects of knowledge as they correspond to their nature.
To understand things as they truly are, without error,
is called a bhikṣu who diligently cultivates contemplative practice— a yogācāra who dwells with his mind unerringly upon its object.
Kṣemadatta said:
"How does a bhikṣu who diligently cultivates the practice of contemplation, being a practitioner of yoga (*yogācāra*), remain without abandoning meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) therein?
It is when a bhikṣu who diligently cultivates the practice of contemplation, being a practitioner of yoga, correctly practices with respect to the object of focus."
Through uninterrupted application and earnest application,
one cultivates the signs of tranquility (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) from time to time;
by reason of this cultivation, practice, and frequent cultivation, these become the causes and conditions [for progress].
All heavy burdens are completely stilled and extinguished;
accordingly, one attains and realizes the purification of the basis,
because of the direct perception of objects of knowledge.
One successively attains contact with and realizes the purity of the object;
by being free from greed, one successively attains contact with and realizes the complete purity of the mind;
and by being free from ignorance.
Attaining the wisdom that realizes contact with universal purity—
this is called a bhikṣu who diligently practices contemplation, a yogācāra who is able to not relinquish meditative concentration therein.
Kṣemadatta: This bhikṣu establishes his mind upon the object of focus;
in this manner, he establishes his mind upon the focal object.
When the mind has thus been established upon the object, it is said to be "well-established.
Regarding this, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"The practitioner practices with various signs, yet knows the true meaning of all things."
"Always meditating on the reflection, one attains the realization of universal purity.
Herein, it is said that "the practitioner practices the various signs";
by this, it is explained that the practitioner of insight cultivation [practices] the signs of tranquility (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
It is uninterrupted practice and reverent practice.
Furthermore, if it is said that one "knows all true meanings," this proclaims the nature of the ultimate limit of phenomena (*vastuparyantatā*).
Furthermore, if it is said that one constantly meditates on the reflection,
this proclaims the conceptual image and the non-conceptual image.
Furthermore, if it is said that one attains and realizes universal purity, [this refers to the purification of the basis].
By this, the accomplishment of what was to be done is proclaimed.
Regarding this, the Blessed One further spoke these verses:
"Thoroughly knowing the characteristics of the mind, One is able to experience the flavor of seclusion."
Through meditative concentration, constant mindfulness, and the experience of joy and bliss free from passion,
it is said herein that "thoroughly knowing the characteristics of the mind" refers to the conceptualized image (*savikalpa-pratibimba*).

The non-conceptual image is designated by the name "mental aspect" (*cittanimitta*); the limit of phenomena (*vastuparyantatā*) is designated by the name "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*). Furthermore, that which is said to be able to experience the flavor of seclusion (*vivekarasa*)— [is designated by the name] "meditative cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
