By this, it is taught that one who practices correctly with respect to the object of focus delights in abandonment and delights in cultivation.
Furthermore, by the statement "one who is composed in meditative concentration and possesses constant mindfulness," it is taught [to practice] śamatha and vipaśyanā.
One constantly and diligently practices with thorough mastery.
Furthermore, if it is said that one experiences joy and bliss while free from defilement,
this proclaims the accomplishment of what was to be done.
One should know that such an all-pervasive object of focus accords with the pure teachings and conforms to correct reasoning;
this is what is called the all-pervasive object of focus.
The differentiation of the realms of dependent origination;
the differentiation of objects such as mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*);
and what is the object of impurity (*aśubhālambana*)?
Briefly stated, there are six kinds of impurity:
first, the impurity of decay and filth;
second, the impurity of suffering and affliction.
Third, inferior impurity;
fourth, relative impurity;
fifth, afflictive impurity.
Sixth is the impurity of rapid decay.
What is called the impurity of putridity?
Briefly stated, this impurity relies upon two types.
The first is based on the internal; the second is based on the external.
What is meant by "internal decay and impurity"?
It refers to the hair, body hair, nails, and teeth within the internal body.
Dust, filth, skin, and flesh;
bones, marrow, sinews, and veins;
heart, gallbladder, liver, and lungs.
The large intestine and small intestine;
the raw receptacle and the cooked receptacle;
the abdomen, stomach, spleen, and kidneys.
Pus and blood, hot phlegm;
fat, grease, muscle, and marrow;
brain membrane, nasal mucus, and saliva.
Tears, sweat, feces, and urine—
such categories as these are called internal, decaying, and impure.
What is external, decaying, and impure?
That is to say: either bluish-black discoloration, or putrefaction;
or decomposition, or swelling;
or being devoured, or turning crimson.
Or again, it may be scattered and decayed,
or bone, or a chain, or a skeleton,
or made of excrement, or made of urine.
Or it is smeared with saliva, or smeared with nasal mucus;
or it is smeared with blood, or smeared with pus;
or it is a place of excrement and filth.
These and other such categories are called the impurity of external decay and corruption.
Likewise, there is the impurity of internal decay and corruption,
as well as the impurity of both internal and external decay and corruption.
Taken collectively, these are described as the single impurity of decay and filth.
What is meant by the impurity of suffering and affliction?
It refers to that which arises conditioned by contact associated with painful feeling.
Whether physical or mental, any unequal feeling included within the category of feeling is called the impurity of suffering and affliction.
What is called the impurity of inferiority?
This refers to the most inferior matter and the most inferior realm,
namely the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Beyond this, no other realm can be found that is more extremely low, more inferior, or more utterly base and defiled.
This is called inferior impurity.
What is called relative impurity?
It refers to when there is some inferior pure thing.
In relation to other more excellent and pure things, they appear as impure;
for example, in relation to the more excellent and pure things of the formless realm,
the phenomena of the form realm appear as impure.
Waiting for the nirvana that is the cessation of the transitory collection (*satkāya*),
everything up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) appears as impure.
All such categories are termed "impurity by comparison" (*apekṣā-aśubhā*).
What is called the impurity of afflictions?
It refers to all fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, and entanglements within the three realms;
all these are termed the impurity of afflictions.
What is called "impurity of rapid disintegration"?
It refers to the five aggregates of clinging as being impermanent, unstable, unreliable, and subject to the nature of transformation and decay.
This is what is called the impurity of rapid disintegration.
In this way, impurity is the object of focus for purifying conduct characterized by desire.
There are five types of desire:
first, sensual desire and lustful craving directed toward one's own internal body.
Second, sensual desire and sensual greed for external bodies;
third, desire for objects and greed for objects;
fourth, desire for forms and greed for forms.
The five types of desire for the transitory collection (*satkāya*) and the craving for the transitory collection (*satkāyarāga*);
these are called the five desires.
It is for the purpose of bringing about the cessation, elimination, and non-occurrence of these five kinds of desire and craving that [this is taught].
One establishes six kinds of impure objects of focus;
that is to say, by relying on the internal impurity of putridity as an object of focus,
one brings about purification of the mind regarding sensual desire and lust for the internal body.
By relying on the external objects of meditation consisting of decay and impurity,
one brings about purification of the mind regarding lust and sensual desire for the external body.
Furthermore, there are four types of greed associated with lust.
First, greed for color;
second, greed for shape;
third, greed for exquisite touch.
Fourth is the craving for service.
Based on the four external objects of impurity as its focal point,
it consists of sexual craving corresponding to these four types.
The mind attains purity.
Whether it be regarding the livid, or the festering,
or the disintegrating, or the bloated.
Alternatively, one may contemplate the act of eating;
by doing so, one purifies the mind of attachment to visible forms.
Or, one may contemplate the process of turning red [during digestion].
One purifies the mind of craving for form and color by attending to the bones,
or the skeleton, or the chain of bones.
One purifies the mind of craving for exquisite tactile sensations by reflecting upon their disintegration;
one purifies the mind of craving for service by reflecting upon their dissolution.
These four types are called the purification of the mind regarding sensual desire.
Therefore, the Blessed One [taught] all the various distinctions of external putridity and impurity.
All are correctly established based on four kinds of charnel grounds (*śmaśāna*).
That is to say, if one speaks of seeing various corpses in those charnel grounds after they have been dead for one day, two days, or seven days;
They are devoured by crows,
magpies, hungry dogs, owls, vultures,
foxes, wolves, jackals, and various birds and beasts.
One then takes those characteristics as a metaphor for that body:
it is of such a nature and of such a kind;
it cannot transcend such a dharma-nature.
This demonstrates the stages beginning from the bluish discoloration up to the state of being devoured.
Furthermore, it speaks of seeing various corpses along a desolate road,
stripped of skin, flesh, and blood, and merely bound together by sinews.
This demonstrates all that has turned red.
Furthermore, if it is said that one sees various bones, or bones, or skeletons along a desolate road,
this demonstrates either bones, or skeletons, or both bones and skeletons.
Furthermore, it is said that by means of a desolate path, one sees various bones here and there:
the hand-bones in one place,
the foot-bones in another.
The hip bones are in one place, the knee bones in another;
the arm bones are in one place, the elbow bones in another;
the vertebrae are in one place, the shoulder blades in another.
The ribs are scattered in different places;
the jaw, the circle of teeth, the crest of hair, and the skull are each dispersed.
This may occur after one year, or two, or three, or even up to seven years.
Its color is a fresh white like that of a conch shell or like the color of a pigeon;
or one sees those bones mixed with dust and soil.
This demonstrates all that is disintegrated and decayed.
In this way, by relying on external objects that are decayed, putrid, and impure,
one brings about purification of the mind regarding the four types of greed associated with sexual desire;
this is achieved through the object of suffering and impurity (*duḥkha-aśubhatā*) and the object of inferior impurity (*parīttāśubhatā*).
Through the application of mindfulness to objects, one purifies the mind of desire and lust associated with those objects;
by relying on the contemplation of impure objects,
one purifies the mind of desire and lust associated with forms.
By means of the impurity of afflictions as an object of focus and the impurity of rapid decay as an object of focus,
one brings about purification of the mind regarding desire and craving for the *satkāya* (the transitory collection) from the desire realm up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
This is called the object of focus for purifying the conduct of greed.
Thus far, this has been a general exposition of all [objects] with respect to that which can purify the conduct of greed.
While this is included among the objects of meditation on impurity that treat all [aspects] universally,
the primary intention within this specific context refers exclusively to the impurity of decay and putrefaction.
The remaining impure objects are also objects of other pure practices.
What is the object of loving-kindness (*maitrī*)?
It refers either to the category of friends or to the category of enemies.
Alternatively, within the medium degree,
one abides in equanimity with the intention to benefit,
capable of inducing the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) of the meditative states that bring forth happiness of low, medium, and high degrees.
It should be understood that herein, the categories of friends, enemies, and neutral persons constitute the object of focus (*ālambana*).
The resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the meditative state (*samāhitabhūmi*) that brings about happiness through the intention to benefit [others] is what is intended.
This constitutes the subjective cognition.
When the objective referent and the subjective cognition are condensed together into one,
it is called the "object of loving-kindness."
If a sutra states,
"one whose mind is accompanied by loving-kindness," this indicates the intention to benefit those within the three categories of objects— namely, friends, enemies, and neutral persons.
Furthermore, if it is said that there is no enmity, no hostility, and no harm,
this demonstrates that the intention to benefit has three aspects.
Because there is no enmity, it is called the superior intention to benefit.
This nature of being without enmity is revealed by two phrases:
namely, because there is no adversary and because there is no harm or affliction.
The meaning of "no adversary" is the absence of a desire for opposition or contention.
The meaning of not wishing for what is non-beneficial is "non-harmful.
Furthermore, if it is said to be "vast and immeasurable," this demonstrates its capacity to induce inferior, middling, and superior levels of happiness.
The pleasure of the desire realm is called "vast";
the pleasure of the first and second dhyāna stages is called "great";
and the pleasure of the third dhyāna stage is called "immeasurable."

Furthermore, if it is further stated that one "dwells pervaded by and fully endowed with resolute conviction," this demonstrates the resolute conviction pertaining to the meditative states (*samāpatti-bhūmi*) that can induce bliss.
Moreover, as for this resolute conviction:
That is to say, it is accompanied by an attention consisting of resolute conviction,
which is subsumed under the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) that leads to happiness and benefit;
[it is directed] toward the three classes of sentient beings— those who are neither suffering nor happy, as well as friends and enemies.
One should know that loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the desire to bestow happiness equally upon all sentient beings—
whether they are suffering, whether they are happy, or whether they belong to the three categories of friends, enemies, or neutral persons.
To impartially desire to uproot their suffering and to desire to celebrate their happiness—
know that these are compassion and sympathetic joy.
Sentient beings who possess suffering are the objects of focus for compassion.
Sentient beings who possess happiness are the objects of joy;
this is called the object of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
If there is a person (*pudgala*) whose temperament is characterized by hatred, [the following applies].
Cultivating loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings so that anger becomes attenuated is called "purifying the mind of hatred.

Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.
In the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, the thirteenth part of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the second yoga station, it is asked: What is the object of focus regarding the nature of dependent origination?

It refers to that which, throughout the three times, consists solely of formations, solely of phenomena, solely of entities, solely of causes, and solely of results, and thus falls within the sphere of correct reasoning.
That is to say: the principle of dependence,
the principle of function,
and the principle of logical proof.
By the principle of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā-yukti), it is only dharmas that can induce other dharmas;
there is no agent and no experiencer.
This is called the object of focus consisting of dependent origination by way of conditions.
By attending to and reflecting upon this object of focus,
all tendencies toward delusion in a person whose behavior is dominated by delusion become attenuated.
The mind attains purification regarding all deluded activities;
this is called the object of focus consisting of dependent origination by way of conditions.
What is the object of focus consisting of the differentiation of elements?
That is to say, the differentiation of the six elements:
first, the earth element; second, the water element; third, the fire element; fourth, the wind element;
fifth, the space element; and sixth, the consciousness element.
What is the earth element?
The earth element is twofold:
first, internal; second, external.
The internal earth element refers to that which,
within this body, is of an internal, distinct solid nature;
it is comprised of what is firm and rigid, and is categorized as the earth element.
The external earth element that is clung to and appropriated refers to external solidity.
That which is comprised of solidity and hardness, and which is comprised of earth,
is neither adherent nor appropriated.
Furthermore, what is the nature of the internal earth element?
That is to say: hair of the head,
body hair, nails, teeth, filth, skin,
flesh, bones, and sinews.
The liver, gallbladder, heart, and lungs;
the spleen, kidneys, stomach, and intestines;
the large intestine and small intestine.
The raw digestive organs,
the cooked digestive organs, and excrement and filth are called the internal earth element.
Furthermore, what are the characteristics of the external earth element?
They are such things as tiles, wood, clods of earth, pebbles, trees, stones, mountains, and cliffs;
these and similar categories are called the external earth element.
What is the water element?
The water element is twofold:
first, internal; second, external.
The internal water element refers to the distinct moist nature within this body,
comprised of moisture and comprised of water.
What are the things that adhere to and are grasped?
They are tears, sweat, mucus, and saliva.
Fat, grease, marrow,
heat-phlegm, pus, blood,
brain-membranes, urine, and so forth.
That which is called the internal water element refers to the external moist nature. The external water element refers to that which is external and has the nature of moisture.
What is the nature of that which is comprised by moisture and comprised by water,
yet is neither adherent nor appropriated? How is this so?
That is to say: wells, springs, ponds, pools, marshes, lakes, rivers, and oceans—categories such as these are called the external water element.
What is the fire element?
The fire element is twofold:
first, internal; second, external.
As for the internal fire element:
It refers to the internal, specific quality of warmth within this body,
which is comprised of heat and comprised of warmth,
and which is closely attached to and appropriated by [consciousness].
What is that phenomenon?
It refers to all the warmth within the body,
which causes the body to become hot, thoroughly heated, and completely inflamed.
By reason of these causes and conditions, what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is easily and properly digested and transformed.
Because that [fire element] is predominant, it is classified as "internal heat.
Such categories as these are called the internal fire element (*tejodhātu*).
The external fire element refers to that which is external and possesses the nature of heat;
it is comprised of warmth and comprised of intense heat.
It is neither attached nor grasped.
What is its nature?
It refers to seeking fire among humans by means of fire-drills and the like, or cow-dung powder and the like.
Once the fire has arisen, it is able to burn cow dung,
or grass, or firewood, or shrubs, or wild lands, or mountains, or islands;
or the villages and their districts, or the cities and their districts, or the kingdoms and their districts.
Furthermore, whatever else is of this same category is called the external fire element.
What is the wind element?
The wind element is twofold.
There are two types: internal and external.
The internal wind element refers to the distinct nature of wind within this body.
What is the nature of being light and mobile, which is comprised within the category of being carried by the wind,
and how does it adhere to and cling to the appropriated [body]?
That is to say, within the internal body there are upward-moving winds, downward-moving winds,
winds that move along the sides,
and winds that move along the spine.
There is the wind in the waist, there is the wind in the hips,
there is the "small-knife" wind,
and there is the "great-knife" wind.
There is the needle-pricking wind, the pippala wind,
the inhalation and exhalation wind, and the wind that follows the limbs and joints;
such categories as these are called the internal wind element.
The external wind element refers to the external nature of wind;
it is characterized by lightness and mobility, comprised of that which is wafted by the wind.
It is neither attached nor grasped.
What is its nature?
It refers to the wind coming from the east and the wind coming from the west that exist outside the body.
There are winds coming from the south and winds coming from the north.
There are winds with dust and winds without dust.
There are narrow winds and vast winds.
There is the Viśvaka wind and the Vairambha wind;
there are winds of the wind-circles and occasional great winds that suddenly arise and accumulate,
breaking trees, collapsing walls, shattering mountains, and churning the oceans.
Once it has been stirred up, having no further basis for support,
it naturally subsides. If sentient beings desire wind,
they move their garments, shake fans, or clap their hands like palm trees.
Such categories as these are called the external wind element.
What is the space element?
It refers to all the cavities, such as those of the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, throat, and so forth.
By means of this swallowing;
once it has been swallowed,
it then flows down and leaks out through this orifice.
Such categories as these are called the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
What is the consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*)?
It refers to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousnesses.
Furthermore, the threefold distinction of mind, mentation, and consciousness is called the element of consciousness (vijñānadhātu).
If a person of predominantly discursive temperament (carita) attends to and contemplates the distinctions among these elements, [he attains liberation].
Thereupon, within his own body, he abandons the perception of a composite whole and attains the perception of impurity;
his arrogance and pride no longer arise, becoming thin and faint,
and his mind becomes purified regarding all tendencies toward conceit.
This is called the person of proud temperament (*pudgala*).
Regarding the distinction of elements (*dhātu*), what is the object of focus for the purification of conduct?
What is the object of focus for mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*)?
That is to say, mindfulness that takes inhalation and exhalation as its object is called *ānāpānasmṛti*.
The objects of this mindfulness are the inhalations, exhalations, and so forth.
This is called the object of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti).
It should be understood that within this, there are two types of inhalation. What are these two?
The first is inhalation; the second is intermediate inhalation.
Exhalation also has two [types]. What are these two?
The first is the exhalation;
the second is the intermediate exhalation.
As for inhalation:
The "internal wind turning" immediately following exhalation refers to its movement down to the navel region.
The "intermediate inhalation" refers to the period from the cessation of inhalation until exhalation has not yet arisen.
In the interval between those pauses,
a subtle wind arises for a brief moment that resembles [the breath];
this is called the intermediate inhalation.
As it is with the intermediate inhalation within the inhalation,
so too should one know it to be with the intermediate exhalation within the exhalation.
The distinction here is as follows:
This refers to the outward movement of wind immediately following the inhalation,
beginning from the region of the navel up to the opening of the mouth,
or reaching the tip of the nose, or even exiting externally.
There are two causes and conditions for inhalation and exhalation. What are the two?
First, the karma of牵引 (projecting karma).
The two apertures at the navel region,
or whatever apertures exist in the upper part of the body,
are the two bases for inhalation and exhalation.
What are these two? First, the body;
second, the mind. Why is this so?
It must depend on both body and mind for the inhalation and exhalation to proceed as appropriate.
If the breath were to proceed depending on the body alone,
then it would continue even when one has entered the meditative attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) or the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
The breaths of those sentient beings born in the Heaven of Non-conception should still function;
if the breaths functioned solely in dependence upon the mind,
then for those who have entered the formless attainments and are born in the formless realm, [the breaths would likewise function].
That breath should cease.
If it were to proceed based solely on the body and mind, rather than as it ought to be,
then for those sentient beings who have entered the fourth dhyāna or are born there, [it would not exist].
Furthermore, the breaths of sentient beings in the stages of the kalala, arbuda, peśī,
and so forth, ought to circulate;
yet they do not circulate.
Therefore, one should know that the inhalation and exhalation proceed in accordance with what is appropriate based on the body and mind.
There are two modes of activity for inhalation and exhalation.
What are these two?
First, the inhalation proceeds downward;
second, the exhalation proceeds upward.
Inhalation and exhalation have two types of bases. What are these two?
First, coarse apertures.
Second are the subtle apertures.
What are the coarse apertures?
They refer to the apertures from the region of the navel up to the mouth and the nostrils.
Furthermore, from the openings of the mouth and the nose down to the opening at the navel:
what are the subtle apertures?
They refer to all the pores within the body.
Inhalation and exhalation have four alternative names. What are these four?
The first is called "wind" (vāyu).
The second is called *ānāpāna*;
the third is called inhalation and exhalation;
the fourth is called bodily formations (*kāyasaṃskāra*).
The first type of wind is a shared name;
the remaining three types are unique names.
There are two defects for one who practices the inhalation and exhalation of breath.
What are these two?
First, an overly lax application of means;
second, an overly urgent application of means.
Due to overly lax means, laziness arises;
or the mind becomes entangled by lethargy and sleep,
or it causes the mind to be distracted toward external objects.
Due to excessively forceful means,
it may cause his body to become unbalanced,
or it may cause his mind to become unbalanced.
How does it cause the body to become unbalanced?
It is by exerting force to hold the inhalation and exhalation;
because the inhalation and exhalation are thus forcibly restrained.
This causes the uneven winds within the body to circulate;
consequently, trembling first arises in all the limbs and joints,
which is called "capable of trembling."
When this trembling wind increases, it can produce diseases;
by reason of this, various ailments arise in the limbs and joints.
This is called causing the body to become unbalanced.
How does it cause the mind to become unbalanced?
It means either causing the mind to give rise to various forms of distraction,
or being oppressed by extremely heavy grief and affliction.
This is called causing the mind to become unbalanced.
Furthermore, it should be understood that there are, in brief, five ways to cultivate this mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti).
What are the five?
First, the cultivation of counting;
second, the cultivation of penetrating the aggregates.
Third, the cultivation of penetrating dependent origination;
fourth, the cultivation of penetrating the noble truths;
fifth, the cultivation of the sixteen superior practices.
What is called the cultivation of counting?
Briefly, there are four kinds of cultivation of counting.
What are these four?
First is counting by taking one as one;
second is counting by taking two as one;
third is sequential counting.
Fourth is counting in reverse order.
How does one count by taking one as a single unit?
It refers to when, upon the inhalation of the breath, one takes that entry as the object of focus.
One counts the exhalation as one while maintaining mindfulness.
When the inhalation ceases and the exhalation arises,
counting it as it moves outward is the second.
In this manner, they proceed sequentially until reaching ten.
Because this calculation is neither too brief nor too extensive, it stops at ten.
This is called "counting by ones."
How does one perform the calculation by taking two as one?
It means that when the inhalation has entered and already ceased,
and the exhalation has arisen and already issued forth.
At that time, they are combined and counted as one;
by means of this principle of calculation,
they are counted up to ten.
This is called counting by taking two as one.
Inhalation and exhalation are designated as "two," and these two types are combined and counted as "one."
Therefore, this is called the calculation of two as one.
What is sequential counting?
It refers to counting by means of one as one, or alternatively, by means of one as one.
Alternatively, by calculating two as one and proceeding sequentially through successive stages until reaching ten,
it is called "ascending calculation" (anuloma-gaṇanā).
What is reverse counting?
It refers to the process of counting in reverse order by means of the two aforementioned methods of calculation, proceeding from the tenth number.
Next nine, next eight, next seven, next six, next five, next four, next three, next two;
counting them in this manner is called counting in reverse order (*pratilomagaṇanā*).
When, at that time, the practitioner...
Either taking one as one as the basis for calculation,
or taking two as one as the basis for calculation,
they have thoroughly practiced both forward and reverse counting.
During that interval, the mind should remain undistracted.
Once the mind has been well-trained in counting through this lack of distraction,
one should further explain the superior progression of counting.
What is called "superior calculation"?
It refers to either calculating by taking one as one,
or calculating by taking two as one.
One combines the two into one and calculates them as such.
If one were to calculate by taking each as a single unit,
then the inhalation and exhalation would be combined into one.
If one calculates by combining two into one,
then four inhalations and exhalations are taken as a single unit;
in this manner, one proceeds sequentially until reaching ten.
In this manner, they gradually increase, even counting by making one hundred equal to one.
By means of this calculation where one hundred is treated as one,
they continue to count in succession until reaching ten such units.
Thus, for one who diligently cultivates the mindfulness of counting the breaths,
they count ten by ten as one,
gradually increasing the count until it reaches ten.
By means of this, one performs the calculation of ten as one;
during this process, the mind remains undistracted.
Up to this point, it is called "thoroughly cultivated."
Furthermore, for one who diligently practices this mindfulness of counting the breaths,
if the mind becomes distracted in the interim,
they should again revert to the beginning and start counting anew, either in forward or reverse order.
When, through extreme familiarity with counting,
the mind spontaneously enters the path of effortless flow and abides in the object of focus— the inhalation and exhalation.
It proceeds as an uninterrupted and continuous succession.
First, there is the activity of the grasper with respect to inhalation;
once inhalation has ceased, there is the activity of the grasper with respect to the state of the breath’s absence.
Next, there is the activity of the grasper with respect to the exhalation;
once the exhalation has ceased, there is the activity of the grasper in the state of the empty space of the breath.
In this manner, they proceed in succession, flowing in a continuous stream.
It is unmoving and unshaking;
it is free from distracted activity and proceeds with joyful delight.
Reaching this point is called "transcending the stage of counting," where one should no longer count;
rather, one should cause the mind to abide in the object of the inhalation and exhalation,
correctly following the inhalations and exhalations.
One should thoroughly comprehend and clearly discern the distinctions between the phases of inhalation, exhalation, and the two intervals between them— both their progression and their return.
One should achieve full and skillful awareness of all these states.
This is called the cultivation of counting.
Furthermore, for those of dull faculties, one should explain this cultivation of counting through mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
By means of this, they [are able to remain] in the face of distraction.
He causes the mind to abide peacefully and brings joy to the mind;
for if it were otherwise than through the mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation involving counting, that mind would be ensnared and disturbed by lethargy and drowsiness.
Alternatively, that mind might wander outwardly;
however, through the correct and diligent cultivation of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), none of these occur.
This is especially so for one of sharp faculties whose awakening and wisdom are keen and brilliant.
He does not take pleasure in this practice of calculation; yet, if it were to be taught to him,
he would also be able to swiftly and unerringly comprehend it, though he would not find delight in it.
Furthermore, having established mindfulness upon this object of inhalation and exhalation,
he dwells therein, whether it proceeds in that manner or even up to that extent.
Whether it turns in such a manner or at such a time,
in all these instances, by means of established mindfulness,
one is able to correctly follow along.
One is able to correctly understand that such preparatory application has such characteristics;
by taking as causes and conditions the cultivation, practice, and frequent cultivation of this preparatory application,
one gives rise to physical pliancy and mental pliancy.
He realizes one-pointedness of mind and enters into that object of focus with delight.
Thus, he practices the mindfulness of breathing through counting.
Having cultivated this well,
one further applies attention to the two factors of the grasped and the grasper,
thereby gaining insight into the aggregates.
How does one enter into realization?
It means that by attending to and reflecting upon the inhalation and exhalation, as well as the body which is the basis for the breath,
one enters into realization of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
One enters into the aggregate of feeling by reflecting upon and attending to the experience associated with mindfulness that apprehends those inhalations and exhalations; that is,
one equally discerns that which is associated with that very mindfulness.
By attending with mental attention, one enters into the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Then, by attending with mental attention to those very thoughts, as well as the volition (*cetanā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with those thoughts,
one enters into the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
If one contemplates and penetrates the aggregate of consciousness through the mental engagement with all those minds,
mentals, and consciousnesses associated with that mindfulness,
such a practitioner—
When one dwells extensively within the aggregates until reaching full mastery, this is called "having entered" them;
this is known as the cultivation of entry into the aggregates.
It occurs at the time when one is able to see and know them without error.
There are only the aggregates, only conditioned formations;
there are only phenomena and only dharmas.
At that time, he is able to penetrate into dependent origination regarding those conditioned formations.
How does one enter into realization?
It means that the practitioner thus investigates these inhalations and exhalations.
What is its basis and what is its condition?
Having thus investigated, one realizes it as it truly is:
these inhalations and exhalations depend on the body and are conditioned by the body; they depend on the mind and are conditioned by the mind.
Furthermore, he further investigates what this body and this mind depend upon and what they take as their conditions.
Having investigated, he realizes them as they truly are:
this body and this mind depend upon and are conditioned by the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Furthermore, he further investigates what this life-faculty (jīvitendriya) depends upon and what its conditions are.
Having investigated, he realizes it as it truly is:
that this life-faculty depends upon and is conditioned by prior formations (pūrvakṛta-saṃskāra).
Furthermore, he further investigates what the basis and what the condition were for such prior formations.
Having investigated, he penetrates to reality as it is:
that such prior formations are based upon and conditioned by ignorance.
Thus one understands that ignorance has prior formations as its condition;
prior formations have the life-faculty as their condition;
and the life-faculty has the body and mind as its condition.
The body and mind depend on conditions for inhalation and exhalation.
Furthermore, one can understand that because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease;
because volitional formations cease, the life-faculty ceases.
Because the life-faculty ceases, body and mind cease;
because body and mind cease, inhalation and exhalation cease.
This is called entering into the dependent origination.
His entry into dependent origination and his frequent abiding therein are called "well-practiced cultivation";
this is termed the cultivation of the entry into dependent origination.
In this way, having thoroughly cultivated the entry into dependent origination,
he further understands all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as they truly are— arising from a multitude of conditions—
and thus enters into their impermanence.
That is to say, one realizes that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent; they exist having been originally non-existent, and having existed, they disperse and perish.
If they were originally non-existent and yet come to exist...
That which has already perished is precisely the nature of birth, the nature of aging, the nature of sickness, and the nature of death.
If it is the nature of birth, aging, sickness, and death, [it is subject to cessation].
This is precisely suffering.
If it is suffering, then it is non-self, lacking autonomy, and devoid of a sovereign master.
This is what is meant by the practice of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
One penetrates the truth of suffering.
Furthermore, one is thus able to correctly penetrate that all conditioned phenomena arise from various causes and conditions.
Its nature is suffering, like a disease and like an abscess;
all are conditioned by craving.
Furthermore, one correctly realizes that this very craving is what gives rise to manifold sufferings.
If there is no remainder to be abandoned, that is ultimate tranquility and subtlety.
If I understand this thus, perceive this thus, and dwell frequently in this state, [I shall attain liberation].
When one is able to abandon craving without remainder,
this is called being able to penetrate the truth of origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path.
Having dwelt extensively in this penetration, [one attains realization].
To realize clear observation (*abhisamaya*) regarding the various truths is called "entering into the cultivation of the noble truths.
Having thus cultivated the noble truths well, [one proceeds further].
All afflictions to be abandoned through the path of seeing are forever severed;
only those afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation remain.
To abandon them, one further advances to practice the sixteen sublime modes of activity.
What are called the sixteen superior practices? They are as follows:
while mindful of the inhalation, one thinks, "I am now training myself to be mindful of the inhalation";
while mindful of the exhalation, one thinks, "I am now training myself to be mindful of the exhalation."
Whether long or short, regarding the inhalation that is fully aware of the whole body, I am now able to train myself: "I am fully aware of the whole body while inhaling.
Regarding the exhalation that is fully aware of the whole body, I am now able to train myself: "I am fully aware of the whole body while exhaling."
"I am now able to train myself in inhaling while calming the bodily formations;
I am now able to train myself in exhaling while calming the bodily formations."
Experiencing joy while breathing in, I am now able to train myself: "Experiencing joy while breathing in.
Experiencing joy while breathing out, I am now able to train myself: "Experiencing joy while breathing out."
Experiencing pleasure while breathing in, I am now able to train myself: "Experiencing pleasure while breathing in.
Experiencing pleasure while breathing out, I am now able to train myself: "Experiencing pleasure while breathing out."
Experiencing mental formations while breathing in, I am now able to train myself in experiencing mental formations while breathing in;
experiencing mental formations while breathing out, I am now able to train myself in experiencing mental formations while breathing out.
"I am now able to train myself in inhaling while calming mental formations;
I am now able to train myself in exhaling while calming mental formations."
"Experiencing the mind while inhaling, I am now able to train myself in experiencing the mind while inhaling;
experiencing the mind while exhaling, I am now able to train myself in experiencing the mind while exhaling."

"Experiencing joy in the mind, I shall now train myself in breathing in experiencing joy in the mind; experiencing joy in the mind, I shall now train myself in breathing out experiencing joy in the mind."
When concentrating the mind while inhaling, I am now able to train in concentrating the mind while inhaling;
when concentrating the mind while exhaling, I am now able to train in concentrating the mind while exhaling.
"Experiencing the mind of liberation, I shall now train in breathing in while experiencing the mind of liberation;

experiencing the mind of liberation, I shall now train in breathing out while experiencing the mind of liberation. Contemplating impermanence, I shall now train in breathing in while contemplating impermanence."
Contemplating impermanence while breathing out, I am now able to train in contemplating impermanence while breathing out.
Contemplating cessation while breathing in, I am now able to train in contemplating cessation while breathing in.
"I am now able to train in breathing out while contemplating cessation;
I am now able to train in breathing in while contemplating dispassion."
Contemplating renunciation while breathing out, I am now able to train in breathing out while contemplating renunciation.
Contemplating cessation while breathing in, I am now able to train in breathing in while contemplating cessation.
"Contemplating cessation while breathing out, I am now able to train in contemplating cessation while breathing out.
Question: What are these sixteen distinctions?
Answer: There is the learner who has seen the path and has already attained the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth.
Regarding the object of mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation,
one further cultivates mental attention in order to sever the remaining fetters.
Therefore, one reflects:
"In mindfulness of the inhalation, I am now able to train in mindfulness of the inhalation;
in mindfulness of the exhalation, I am now able to train in mindfulness of the exhalation."
When taking the long inhalation and exhalation as the object of focus, one forms this thought:
"I am now able to train in mindfulness of a long inhalation and mindfulness of a long exhalation.

When taking the intermediate inhalation and intermediate exhalation as the object of focus, one likewise forms this thought: [I am now able to train in mindfulness of a short inhalation and mindfulness of a short exhalation].
I am now able to train in mindfulness of short inhalation and mindfulness of short exhalation,
just as the long turning of inhalation and exhalation, and the short turning of the intermediate inhalation and intermediate exhalation.
One understands it in this way.
This is called being "long" or "short.
When the inhalation and exhalation enter the subtle apertures within the body, they pervade and follow along into all the pores.
When one takes this as an object and gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), one forms this thought:
"I am clearly aware of the inhalation and exhalation pervading the entire body;
I am now able to train in being clearly aware of the inhalation and exhalation pervading the entire body."
If at this time, while the inhalation has already ceased during the interval between inhalations,
and the exhalation has not yet arisen during the interval between exhalations,
there is a state of emptiness regarding the inhalation and exhalation.
The object is the state of being free from both inhalation and exhalation;
that is, when the exhalation has ceased during the interval between exhalations,
and the inhalation has not yet arisen during the interval between inhalations.
Taking the emptiness and absence of location of the out-breath and in-breath as the condition,
and taking the state of the out-breath and in-breath being far removed as the object,
one then forms this thought at that very moment:
While breathing in while calming bodily formations, I am now able to train myself: "I shall breathe in while calming bodily formations.
While breathing out while calming bodily formations...
I am now able to train in breathing out while calming the bodily formations.
Furthermore, by reason of cultivating, practicing, and repeatedly practicing this very [training],
when one has not previously become habituated to the inhalation and exhalation—
All harsh and painful tactile sensations that previously occurred have now been pacified through the cultivation of mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation; furthermore,
other soft and pleasant tactile sensations arise.
He then forms this thought:
"While breathing in while calming bodily formations,
I am now able to train myself in breathing in while calming bodily formations."
Regarding the exhalation that calms bodily formations:
"I am now able to train in the exhalation that calms bodily formations.
Furthermore, for one who diligently practices this mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*):
When one attains the first dhyāna or the second dhyāna,
one then forms this thought:
"I am breathing in and out while clearly perceiving joy."
"I am now able to train in clearly perceiving joy while breathing in and out.
When one attains the third dhyāna, which is free from joy,
one then reflects:
Regarding the inhalation and exhalation while experiencing pleasure:
"I am now able to train in experiencing pleasure while inhaling and exhaling.
This refers to the third dhyāna and above.
Regarding mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti),
there is no further principle for the cultivation of preparatory application;
therefore, mindfulness of breathing is taught up to the third dhyāna.
Included within the preparatory application (*prayoga*),
furthermore, for one who thus clearly realizes joy and clearly realizes bliss,
there may at times arise a lapse of mindfulness.
Some may conceive of a self and what belongs to a self;
some may give rise to the conceit "I am";
some may think "I shall exist," or they may think "I shall not exist."
Some say, "I shall have form"; some say, "I shall be formless.
Some say, "I shall have perception"; some say, "I shall be without perception.
Some say, "I shall be neither with perception nor without perception."
Such delusion arises;
accompanied by perception and volition, various fluctuations and conceits emerge,
and as soon as the fabrications of conceptual proliferation and the formations of craving arise, [they persist].
He is then able to swiftly penetrate [reality] with wisdom without becoming deeply attached;
through skillful means, he brings about its cessation, eliminates it, and expels it.
By means of this application, he then forms this thought:
While breathing in and out while clearly comprehending mental formations,
I am now able to train in breathing in and out while clearly comprehending mental formations.
While breathing in and out while calming mental formations...
I am now able to train in the inhalation and exhalation that pacifies mental activity.
Furthermore, if one attains the fundamental first, second, or third dhyānas,
one has already attained the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) of the first dhyāna, which relies upon the concentration of "not-yet-arrived" (anāgamya).
Based on this, one observes the mind that has arisen,
knowing it as it truly is and awakening to it as it truly is—
whether it is a mind possessed of greed or a mind free from greed.
There may be a mind of anger or a mind free from anger;
there may be a mind of delusion or a mind free from delusion;
there may be a contracted mind, a distracted mind, a sunken mind, or an uplifted mind.
There is a restless mind and a non-restless mind;
there is a tranquil mind and a non-tranquil mind;
there is a concentrated mind and a non-concentrated mind.
He knows as they truly are and realizes as they truly are the well-cultivated mind and the uncultivated mind, and the well-liberated mind and the unliberated mind.
Therefore, one reflects:
"While breathing in and out with clear comprehension of the mind,
I am now able to train in breathing in and out with clear comprehension of the mind."
If at times he perceives that his mind is shrouded and obstructed by the hindrance of lethargy and drowsiness due to dwelling excessively in internal tranquility,
then at that time he should attend to some kind of pure and sublime external object.
Manifesting instruction, encouragement, inspiration, and gladdening to stimulate the mind,
he thus reflects: "I shall breathe in and breathe out with a joyful mind."
"I am now able to train in breathing in and out with a mind of joy.
Should he at any time see his mind covered and obstructed by the hindrance of restlessness and remorse,
it is because he dwells excessively in external agitation.
At that time, dwelling in inner tranquility, one restrains and controls the mind.
Therefore, one maintains mindfulness, thinking:
"While restraining and controlling the mind, I am inhaling and exhaling."
I am now able to train in the restraint of the mind while inhaling and exhaling.
When the mind has been well-cultivated and well-practiced,
and because of the causes and conditions of having extensively cultivated it, [it becomes stable].
This causes all currently active hindrances to be abandoned,
so that the mind attains purity regarding those hindrances;
therefore, one reflects as follows:
Breathing in and breathing out with a liberated mind, he trains himself:
"I shall now train in breathing in and breathing out with a liberated mind.
His mind is already liberated from those hindrances that obstruct the path of cultivation.
There remain other underlying tendencies that must still be abandoned;
in order to abandon them, one brings forth the path,
namely, [the realization] of the impermanent nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
With extreme skill, earnestness, and correct observation,
he thus reflects:
"I am attending to the inhalation and exhalation while contemplating impermanence."
"I am now able to train in the mindfulness of impermanence while inhaling and exhaling.
Furthermore, previously, he may have relied upon one of the lower three dhyānas,
or relied upon the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-samādhi).
Having already practiced the yoga of śamatha,
one now practices the yoga of vipaśyanā by relying on the contemplation of impermanence.
Having thus cultivated the mind through śamatha and vipaśyanā,
one seeks liberation from those latent tendencies (anuśaya) within the various elements (dhātu).
What are these elements?
What are called the three realms:
first, the realm of abandonment;
second, the realm of detachment from desire.
Third is the realm of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*).
The abandonment of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is called the realm of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*);
the abandonment of all conditioned phenomena to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is called the realm of detachment (*virāgadhātu*).
The cessation of all dependence is called the element of cessation.
Contemplating these three elements as tranquil,
secure, and free from affliction, one cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Because he has cultivated and practiced this repeatedly,
his mind attains liberation from the remaining afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation;
therefore, he reflects:
While breathing in and out, he contemplates cessation, contemplates dispassion, and contemplates relinquishment;
he trains himself thus: "I shall now learn to breathe in and out while contemplating cessation, contemplating dispassion, and contemplating relinquishment."
Thus, because he has eternally severed all afflictions to be abandoned through both seeing and cultivation,
he becomes an Arhat;
all outflows are eternally exhausted.
Thereafter, there is nothing further to be done;
having reached the ultimate consummation regarding what has been resolved,
this is called the sixteen superior practices.
Cultivating these five kinds of practice is called the cultivation of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
A person whose mental conduct is characterized by excessive discursive thought (*vitarka*) should,
with right effort, train in this very practice and take delight in mastering it.
If one has urgent mental preoccupations regarding the object of focus or experiences distraction,
one should personally cultivate such contemplative practice within oneself individually.
If one applies oneself diligently to this, [the mind will become settled].
Investigative thoughts and mental agitation are both entirely absent;
the mind swiftly becomes settled upon its object and develops deep affection for it.
This is called the fifth object of purification for a person whose conduct is dominated by discursive thought.
These are collectively termed the objects of focus for purifying conduct (*caritaviśodhana*).
Briefly stated, these objects of focus are of five kinds;
the first is skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*).
2. Skillfulness regarding the two realms;
3. skillfulness regarding the three bases;
4. skillfulness regarding dependent origination.
Skillfulness regarding the five points of what is possible and what is impossible.
Regarding skillfulness regarding the aggregates:
what are the aggregates?
What is skillfulness regarding the aggregates?
It refers to the five aggregates,
namely, the aggregate of form.
The aggregate of feeling,
the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations.
The aggregate of consciousness.
What is the aggregate of form?
It refers to all that is form.
All these are the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements.
Furthermore, whether past, future, or present;
internal or external; coarse or subtle.
Whether inferior or superior, distant or near,
these are collectively termed the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
What is the aggregate of feeling (vedanāskandha)?
That is to say: feelings conditioned by contact conducive to pleasure;
feelings conditioned by contact conducive to suffering;
or feelings conditioned by contact conducive to neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Furthermore, there are six classes of feeling:
namely, feeling born of eye-contact,
and feelings born of contact with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
These are collectively termed the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*). What is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*)?
It refers to the perception of signs (*nimitta-saṃjñā*) and the perception of signlessness (*animitta-saṃjñā*).
The perception of narrowness, the perception of vastness,
the perception of the immeasurable, the perception of nothingness, and the perception of the sphere of nothingness.
Furthermore, there are six groups of perceptions.
Thus, the perceptions born of eye-contact,
and those born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact,
are collectively termed the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha).
What is the aggregate of formations?
It refers to the six groups of volition:
namely, volition born of eye-contact.
Volition produced by contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
furthermore, all other mental factors (caitasika-dharma) excluding feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā)—
these collectively are called the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
What is the aggregate of consciousness?
It refers to mind (citta), mentation (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna);
furthermore, there are the six groups of consciousness.
Thus, eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness are collectively termed the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). These,
together with the previously mentioned aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, [constitute the five aggregates].
Each of these possesses distinctions such as past, future, and present, as well as internal and external,
as explained extensively before;
this is what is called an "aggregate" (skandha).
What is skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*)?
It refers to thoroughly understanding the various differentiated natures of the aggregates as they have been described— their manifold and plural nature—
and realizing that apart from these phenomena, nothing further can be apprehended or conceptually constructed.
This is called the brief explanation of the meaning of skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*).
What is meant by the various distinctions among the aggregates? It refers to the fact that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is distinct [from the others].
The aggregate of sensation is distinct,
up to and including the aggregate of consciousness;
this is called the nature of manifold differentiation.
What is meant by the "non-oneness and multiplicity" of the aggregates?

It refers to the fact that the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) consists of many and numerous categories due to the distinctions between the primary elements (mahābhūta) and their derivatives (upādāyarūpa).
Because of the distinctions among the categories of past, future, and present,
this form aggregate is characterized by a multiplicity rather than unity.
In the same way, the remaining aggregates should be understood accordingly as appropriate.
How is it that, apart from these phenomena, nothing further can be found or differentiated?
It means that only the aggregates (*skandha*) can be found and only the entities (*vastu*) can be found;
apart from the aggregates, no self (*ātman*) can be found that is permanent or eternally abiding.
That which is an immutable dharma is not to be apprehended;
nor is there even the slightest dharma that belongs to a self.
Therefore, apart from this, nothing further is to be apprehended and nothing further is to be conceptualized.
What are the elements?
What is skillfulness regarding the elements?
It is said that there are eighteen elements.
That is to say: the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element;
the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element;
the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element.
The tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element;
the body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element;
the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
This is called the "elements" (dhātu).
Furthermore, regarding those eighteen kinds of phenomena,
they arise from their respective elements, respective seeds, and respective lineages.
To understand, accept, and examine thoroughly the arising and manifestation [of phenomena] as they truly are is called skillfulness regarding the elements (*dhātu-kauśalya*).
To understand, as they truly are, that eighteen kinds of phenomena proceed from their respective and distinct elements,
and thereby to attain skillfulness regarding causes and conditions—
this is why it is called "skillfulness in the elements" (*dhātu-kauśalya*).
What are the bases?
What is skillfulness regarding the bases?
It is said that there are twelve bases.
That is to say: the sense base of the eye and the sense base of forms;
the sense base of the ear and the sense base of sounds; the sense base of the nose and the sense base of odors.
The sense base of the tongue and the sense base of tastes; the sense base of the body and the sense base of tangibles;
the sense base of the mind and the sense base of mental phenomena.
This is called the "basis.
Skill in the basis refers to the eye serving as the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
Visible form serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*);
the mind that has just ceased serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
The arising of visual consciousness and its associated mental factors:
the ear serves as the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*),
and sound serves as the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
The mind that has ceased in immediate succession serves as the equal-and-immediate condition for the arising of ear-consciousness and its associated mental factors.
In this manner, up to the point where the mind serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
the mental attention produced thereby serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*),
and the phenomena serve as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The arising of the mental consciousness and its associated mental factors—
thus, all six groups of consciousness and their associated factors flow on by means of three conditions.
That is to say: the dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya),
the object condition (ālambanapratyaya),
and the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya).
If one attains skillfulness regarding these internal and external bases (āyatana),
it is called "skillfulness in the bases.
What is dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda)?
What is skillfulness regarding dependent origination?
It is as follows: conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness.
Consciousness conditions name-and-form;
name-and-form conditions the six sense bases;
the six sense bases condition contact.
Contact conditions feeling;
feeling conditions craving;
craving conditions clinging.
With grasping as condition, existence arises;
with existence as condition, birth arises;
with birth as condition, aging and death arise.
Thus, up to the point of bringing about this entire mass of pure suffering,
it is called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Furthermore, if one thoroughly understands that only phenomena moisten phenomena, [it is called dependent origination].
Only dharmas moisten dharmas;
only conditioned formations (saṃskāra) give rise to conditioned formations.
Yet those formations, being produced from causes and produced from conditions, exist having previously been non-existent.
That which has already perished and ceased is impermanent.
Because it is impermanent, it is subject to the nature of birth, the nature of aging, the nature of illness, and the nature of death;
it is subject to the natures of sorrow, dejection, lamentation, grief, pain, and affliction.
Because these are phenomena subject to arising, up to and including being phenomena subject to affliction, they are called suffering.
Because they are suffering, one lacks mastery; their power is weak and inferior.
For this reason, it is certain that there is no self.
If, within such dependently originated phenomena,
one is skillful through these various modes of analysis, [one realizes the absence of self].
To thoroughly comprehend either the knowledge of impermanence, the knowledge of suffering,
or the knowledge of non-self is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination.
Furthermore, there is skillfulness regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).
One should know that this is precisely the differentiation of skill in dependent origination.
In this context, the differentiation refers to skill in what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).
One who can correctly understand that the principle of cause and effect is not unequal will know that wholesome and unwholesome phenomena have ripened fruits;
if various wholesome phenomena are capable of producing desirable ripened fruits, [they are so by virtue of their specific nature].
All unwholesome phenomena are those that bring about undesirable results as their maturation;
if one can understand this thus according to reality,
it is called skillfulness regarding the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).
These five types of skillfulness are, in brief, twofold:
first, skillfulness regarding specific characteristics;
second, skillfulness regarding common characteristics.
Skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*) reveals skillfulness regarding specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-kauśalya*);
skillfulness regarding the remaining [categories] reveals skillfulness regarding general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-kauśalya*).
These are collectively termed the objects of skillfulness (*kauśalyālambana*).
The object of delusion refers to contemplating the coarseness of the lower stage and the tranquility of the higher stage,
such as the desire realm in relation to the first dhyāna, up to the sphere of nothingness in relation to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What is the nature of coarseness?
It is said that there are two kinds of coarseness:
first, the coarseness of substance.
Second is the coarseness of enumeration.
Regarding the coarseness of essence:
this refers to the desire realm in comparison to the first dhyāna.
Although all [realms] possess the five aggregates,
within the desire realm the afflictions are profound and heavy, and the dwelling in suffering is predominant;
it is most base and utterly loathsome.
It is not like that;
it is utterly tranquil and utterly sublime.
Therefore, it is said that its essence is the nature of tranquility.
Regarding the coarseness of number:
this refers to the fact that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) in the desire realm consists of many varieties,
which should be understood and abandoned.
In this manner, it is the same up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Therefore, these are said to be coarse by way of enumeration.
Thus, it is the same when the higher stages are compared with one another in succession.
Whether it be grossness by way of substance or grossness by way of number,
it should be understood accordingly as appropriate.
Such is grossness.
As one looks upward through the successive higher stages,
up to the Peak of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana),
in all the lower stages, suffering and affliction increase while the lifespan decreases.
In all higher stages, suffering and affliction decrease while the lifespan increases.
The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is exclusively tranquil and sublime,
for there is no higher stage superior to it.
In brief, the sense of having faults and afflictions is the sense of being coarse; that is,
when the faults and afflictions increase in various respective stages.
It is precisely because of this increase in defects that it is termed "coarseness. If, however,
those various stages possess a reduction in defects, [they are termed "subtle"].
Precisely because of this quality of diminished faults,
it is called "the state of tranquility.
This is the object for purifying afflictions through the mundane path of conventional truth.
Why is this? Because he contemplates the lower stages as being full of many faults and afflictions,
like a disease, like an ulcer, and like a poisoned arrow.
One regards the state of insecurity as coarseness,
and contemplates the higher stages as tranquility because they are the opposite of that; thereby,
one abandons all afflictions belonging to the lower stage.
From the desire realm up to the highest limit of the sphere of nothingness,
this is a temporary cessation, not a final cessation,
because it continues again at a later time.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of objects for purifying afflictions through the supramundane path:
first, the noble truth of suffering;
second, the noble truth of the origin [of suffering].
The noble truth of cessation.
The noble truth of the path.
What is the noble truth of suffering?
That is to say: the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death,
the suffering of association with the disliked,
and the suffering of separation from the beloved.
The suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
briefly stated, the suffering of all five aggregates of clinging is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
What is the noble truth of origination?
It refers to craving, craving for renewed existence,
and craving accompanied by delight and lust.
Whatever constitutes that craving for various forms of pleasure and delight is called the Noble Truth of Origination.
What is the Noble Truth of Cessation?
That is to say, the complete and remainderless abandonment of this very craving and so forth is called the Noble Truth of Cessation.
What is the Noble Truth of the Path?
That is to say, the Noble Eightfold Path and so forth are called the Noble Truth of the Path.
It should be understood that herein, [the truths] are established based on the causes and fruits of the dark side and the bright side.
Therefore, the Four Noble Truths are established.
That is to say, the truth of suffering is the fruit of the dark category,
and the truth of origination is the cause of the dark category.
The truth of cessation is the fruit of the white category;
the truth of the path is the cause of the white category,
because it is that which can attain and realize [the fruit].
Furthermore, the truth of suffering is like a disease and should first be fully understood;
the truth of origination is like the causes and conditions of a disease and should next be abandoned;
the truth of cessation is like the state of being free from disease and should next be realized.
The Truth of the Path is like an excellent medicine; it should be cultivated and practiced extensively.
Furthermore, this applies from the meaning of suffering in the Truth of Suffering, up to the meaning of the path in the Truth of the Path.
This is thus real and not unreal;
it is non-erroneous and not erroneous.
Therefore, it is called a truth (*satya*).
Furthermore, because its own-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is devoid of deception and false views,
non-erroneous cognition arises with respect to it;
therefore, it is called a truth (satya).
Question: For what reason are the truths called only "Noble Truths" (āryasatya)?
Answer: It is because only the Noble Ones (ārya) unanimously designate these truths as truths;
they understand them as they truly are and perceive them as they truly are.
All foolish commoners do not know things as they truly are and do not see them as they truly are;
therefore, these truths are called only "Noble Truths" (āryasatya).
Furthermore, for foolish commoners, these are called "truths" merely by the nature of things (dharmatā), not by virtue of their awakening.
For all noble ones, it is by means of both types.
Furthermore, regarding the suffering of birth:
at the time of birth, various physical and mental feelings of suffering arise.
Birth itself is not suffering; rather,
it is called suffering because it serves as the cause and condition for suffering.
To speak at length, this extends even to the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
that is to say, by reason of the failure to obtain what is sought,
various physical and mental feelings of suffering arise.
That which one seeks but does not obtain is itself suffering;
because it serves as a causal condition for suffering, it is called suffering.
In this way, one should understand that, in brief, all five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
That is to say, through various aspects such as birth and so forth, it is only the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) that is made manifest;
by means of this suffering of the five aggregates of clinging, [the other two types of suffering are also implied].
This also clearly reveals the remaining types of suffering: the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*) and the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*). Why is this?
Because the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandhāḥ*) fully encompass the three kinds of sensation (*trivedanā*).
In this way, it serves as a vessel for the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) as previously described;
one should know that herein are also fully present the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), which were not mentioned before.

Question: For what reason does the Blessed One describe the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) using its own specific term, while describing the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) by means of alternative formulations?
Answer: Regarding the suffering of suffering, the cognition of suffering arises equally for all—both ordinary worldlings and noble ones.
Furthermore, the nature of suffering-as-suffering is extremely loathsome;
moreover, for those who have not previously practiced wisdom,
it is easy to enter [the path] as soon as it is explained.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of enabling those beings to be tamed and transformed to easily enter into the truths.
How are the three types of suffering established?
They are as previously described: first, the suffering of birth.
Up to the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks,
this reveals that painful feelings and their bases constitute the nature of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
This is called the establishment of the nature of the suffering of suffering.
Whatever exists that is the counteragent to those [states]—
that is to say, youth is the counteragent to old age,
and health is the counteragent to illness.
Life is countered by death;
the meeting with those one holds dear is countered by the meeting with those one hates;
separation from what is not loved is countered by separation from what is loved.
The non-attainment of what one seeks is that which is to be remedied by the attainment of one's desires.
Furthermore, there are afflictions arising from painful sensations and their bases;
additionally, there are conditions such as health and so forth, which are conducive to pleasant sensations.
And the feelings produced therein, as well as the afflictions that arise from them— these, taken together,
are collectively termed the nature of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
In this context, because pleasant feeling and its basis are impermanent, they undergo transformation and alteration.
One experiences the various sufferings arising from their predominance.

When afflictions arise correctly in all circumstances, they bind the mind and cause it to deteriorate, thereby giving rise to suffering; thus, it is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*).
As the Blessed One said: "One enters with a mind of transformation and grasps the hand of a woman," and so forth at length;
and as it is further said: "One experiences while abiding in the entanglement of sensual desire."
The physical and mental distress arising from the conditions of the fetter of sensual desire;
likewise, abiding in ill will, lethargy,
torpor, and restlessness.
One experiences the entanglements of regret and doubt;
from those entanglements arise mental and physical distress and suffering.
This is the foremost authoritative teaching.
Within all afflictions, the sense of suffering can be found,
and the sense of disintegration can be found;
therefore, afflictions are said to have the nature of the suffering of change.
This is called establishing the nature of suffering due to change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*).
As for the nature of suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*), it pervades all five aggregates of clinging;
to state it briefly:
Excluding the nature of suffering as suffering;
excluding the nature of the suffering of change subsumed under the afflictions;
and excluding the nature of the suffering of change pertaining to pleasant feelings and their bases.
All other aggregates that are associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,
whether they are produced by it, or are the conditions for its production,
or serve as the basis for its arising and persistence.
This is called the nature of suffering inherent in conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Because those aggregates are by nature impermanent and are associated with arising and ceasing,
they are accompanied by all forms of grasping (*upādāna*).
The three feelings are pursued by coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*),
are comprised within lack of peace,
and are not liberated from the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*).
Because it does not turn according to one's will due to the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), it is called "suffering.
This is what is meant by establishing the nature of the suffering of conditioned formations.
Furthermore, that very craving is also termed "seeking" (*prārthanā*).
It is also called longing and also called delight.
This very seeking proceeds by way of three doors,
namely, the seeking for future existence.
And there is the craving for objects of experience.
Craving for future existence is that which seeks after future becoming.
Furthermore, craving for objects of experience is of two kinds.
This refers to craving that accompanies joy and attachment toward objects already obtained; or,
if toward objects not yet obtained—
There is craving that accompanies the longing for union;
it should be understood that herein, regarding objects already acquired,
there is craving that accompanies attachment with delight.
Craving accompanied by joy and greed is called craving for what has already been obtained.
Craving that proceeds with the longing for union with objects not yet obtained is called craving for various delights.
Cessation is of two kinds:
first, the cessation of afflictions;
second, the cessation of the basis.
The Path is of two kinds:
first, the path of those in training (śaikṣa);
second, the path of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
In this way, one should know that this is the object of focus for purifying the afflictions on the supramundane path.
Thus, the four kinds of objects of focus have been explained:
first, the pervasive object of focus.
Second, the object of focus for purifying conduct;
third, the object of focus for skillfulness;
fourth, the object of focus for purifying afflictions.
First, the unerring instruction;
second, the gradual instruction;
third, the instructional instruction.
The fourfold instruction on realization.
What is the unerring instruction?
It refers to the teaching of the meaning of the Dharma without inversion.
Causing them to receive, uphold, recite, and study [the teachings],
so that they may emerge from reality as it is and correctly exhaust all suffering, bringing an end to suffering—
this is called unerring instruction.
What is gradual instruction?
It means proclaiming the meaning of the Dharma according to the appropriate time and occasion;
first causing [the student] to receive, uphold, read, and recite what is shallow and proximate, and only afterwards causing them to study what is profound and remote.

Furthermore, in order to lead them into the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the first truth, one first teaches the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), followed by the truths of origin, cessation, and the path. Moreover,
in order to enable them to attain the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna-samāpatti*),
one first teaches the initial meditative absorption.
Subsequently, he teaches the remaining dhyānas and samāpattis.
Such categories as these should be known as "gradual instruction.
What is "instruction through teaching"?
That is to say, one hears the authentic teaching from a respected person or one who resembles a respected person—
a preceptor or instructor proficient in the rules of yoga— or from the Tathāgatas or their disciples.
To instruct others exactly according to that teaching, neither adding nor subtracting anything, is called "instruction through teaching.
What is "instruction through realization"?
