It refers to when one dwells alone in a secluded place.
The various dharmas that have been attained, touched,
and realized are taught through skillful means so that others may likewise attain, touch,
and realize them; this is called "instruction on realization" (adhigama-avavāda).
This refers to instruction by means of the three types of miraculous transformations (*prātihārya*).
As for the three miraculous transformations:
the first is the miraculous transformation of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).
Second is the miraculous power of mind-reading;
third is the miraculous power of instruction.
By means of the miraculous power of supernatural movement, [one performs these].
One is able to manifest various supernormal powers and spheres of experience,
causing others to conceive extreme respect for oneself;
because they have conceived such respect for oneself, [they become receptive].
Regarding the yoga of listening with focused attention,
one generates extreme reverence through the supernormal power of mind-reading.
One is able to seek out the distinctions in the mental activities of others through the miraculous power of instruction (*anuśāsanī-prātihārya*),
according to their faculties, their conduct, and their mode of realization.
By expounding the true Dharma, one is able to provide correct instruction regarding the practices to be cultivated;
thus, the three miraculous transformations (ṛddhiprātihārya) can encompass all aspects of the perfect instructions.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 27.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Twenty-Eight.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
In the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, the thirteenth [section] of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the third part of the second *yogasthāna*, it is asked: "What is training?
It refers to the three superior trainings (*adhiśikṣā*):
first, the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*)."
Second, the training in higher mind;
third, the training in higher wisdom.
What is the training in higher ethical discipline?
This refers to abiding in the possession of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and so forth,
as explained extensively above;
this is called the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*).
What is the training in higher mind?
It is the state of having departed from sensual desires and unwholesome states,
accompanied by directed thought and evaluation, and characterized by the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
Entering the first dhyāna and fully abiding therein, up to entering the fourth dhyāna and fully abiding therein—
this is called the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*).
Furthermore, it includes all formless attainments (*ārūpya*) and other meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*).
These are also all termed the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*).
However, it is by relying on dhyāna that one is first able to enter the correct nature free from outflows (*samyaktva-nyāma*) through the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Noble Truths;
it is not by completely abandoning all dhyāna that this can be accomplished.
Therefore, meditative concentration (dhyāna) is the most excellent;
for this reason, it is specifically designated as the training in higher mind (adhicittam śikṣā).
What is the training in higher wisdom (adhiprajñām śikṣā)?
That is to say, the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are regarding the Four Noble Truths and so forth is called the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).
Question: For what reason are there exactly three trainings, neither fewer nor more?
Answer: Because it establishes definitions;
because it is the referent upon which knowledge relies;
and because it clarifies the meaning of its functions.
That which establishes the definition is the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*). Why is this so?
Through ethical discipline, one establishes one-pointedness of mind,
which enables the mind to touch samādhi;
this is the meaning of being the basis for wisdom.
This refers to the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*). Why is this?
Because through right concentration, the mind maintains one-pointedness.
The turning toward knowledge of objects of cognition as they truly are, through such knowledge and such vision,
which accomplishes the intended purpose,
refers to the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).
Why is this? Because through wisdom and vision that are thoroughly purified,
one is able to realize the ultimate abandonment of all afflictions.
Because the afflictions have been abandoned,
this is one's own true benefit and the supreme task to be accomplished;
for beyond this, there is no further superior task to be performed.
For this reason, there are only three trainings.
Question: For what reason are the three trainings arranged in this order?
Answer: Because one first becomes thoroughly pure in ethical discipline (*śīla*), one is then free from remorse.
Because one is free from remorse, there is joy and ease;
because there is ease, the mind attains right concentration;
because the mind is concentrated, one is able to know as it truly is and see as it truly is.
By knowing and seeing things as they truly are, one is able to give rise to revulsion;
through revulsion, one becomes free from passion;
and by being free from passion, one attains liberation.
Because one attains liberation, one realizes the ultimate nirvana of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
In this way, by first practicing pure ethical discipline (*śīla*),
one gradually advances until finally realizing the ultimate nirvana of non-action.
Therefore, the three trainings follow this sequence.
Question: For what reason are the three trainings called "higher training in ethics, mind, and wisdom" (*adhiśīla-adhicitta-adhiprajñā*)?
Answer: They are called "higher" (*adhi*) in the sense of being the goal to be reached and in the sense of being preeminent.
What is the meaning of "the goal to be reached"?
It refers to practicing pure ethical discipline for the sake of reaching higher mental states;
this is called the training in higher ethics.
Cultivating the concentrated mind for the sake of attaining higher wisdom is called the training in higher mind;
cultivating knowledge and vision for the sake of abandoning the afflictions is [the training in higher wisdom].
This is called the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).
In this way, it is called "higher" (*adhi*) because it is the sense of that which is to be approached.
What is the sense of "most excellent" (*pra*)?
That is to say: the training in higher ethics,
the training in higher mind,
and the training in higher wisdom.
Only within the Noble Teaching do these three exist exclusively and not in common with non-Buddhists;
thus, because they are of the most supreme meaning,
they are called "superior" (adhipati).
Furthermore, there may be the training in higher mind that can induce the training in higher wisdom,
or the training in higher wisdom that can induce the training in higher mind;
this refers to a noble disciple who has not yet attained fundamental dhyāna.
Having first trained in the realization of the tracks already seen,

one subsequently applies oneself with right effort to the practice of cultivating the awakening factor of mindfulness in order to further sever all afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation.
Up to the cultivation of the awakening factor of equanimity;
this is called the training in higher wisdom that brings forth the training in higher mind.
As for the training in higher mind bringing forth the training in higher wisdom:
As previously stated,
there may be one who possesses the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*) but lacks the training in higher mind (*adhicitta*) and the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*);
or there may be one who possesses the training in higher ethical discipline as well as the training in higher mind, yet lacks only the training in higher wisdom.
It is not the case that there is training in higher wisdom without training in higher ethical discipline and training in higher mind.
Therefore, if there is training in higher wisdom,
it should be known that it is necessarily complete with all three trainings.
Within these three established trainings,
all practitioners of yoga should apply themselves with diligence.
Furthermore, there are three types of individuals regarding these trainings.
Based on these three trainings, one enters the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*).
What are the three?
First, those who have not yet abandoned desire.
Twice removed from desire;
three, already removed from desire.
It should be understood that among these, one who has not yet completely abandoned any desire at all—
Through diligent cultivation of the preparatory application, one enters the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*).
Having attained clear observation regarding the truths, one realizes the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).
As for one who is further detached from desire:
At that time, one realizes the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala).
There are three faculties:
first, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya).
Second, the faculty of one who has known;
third, the faculty of one who has fully known.
How are these three faculties established?
This refers to one who has not yet realized the truths (*satya*) and who,
through diligent application of effort, cultivates the realization of those truths;
based on this, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is established.
If one has already attained direct realization (abhisamaya) regarding the truths and remains in the stage of training (śaikṣa),
the faculty of "I have known" (ājñātendriya) is established on this basis.
If one is an Arhat who has accomplished what was to be done and dwells in the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Based on this, the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātendriya) is established,
as well as the two doors of liberation: the door of emptiness and the door of wishlessness.
The three doors of liberation characterized by signlessness.
How are these three doors of liberation established?
It is because the objects of knowledge are, in brief, of two kinds.
There is existence and non-existence.
Existence is of two kinds:
first, the conditioned.
The second is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Regarding the conditioned, we shall here speak of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) bound to the three realms;
regarding the unconditioned, we shall here speak of *nirvāṇa*.
These two types— the conditioned and the unconditioned— taken together are called "existence.
If one speaks of a self, or a sentient being, a living soul, a creature, and so forth,
these are called "non-existence."
Because one perceives faults within the conditioned and perceives its perilous defects,
one has no aspiration for it; because there is no aspiration,
based upon this, the door of liberation of wishlessness (apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha) is established.
Because there is no aspiration for the conditioned,
one consequently develops a profound aspiration for nirvāṇa;
one perceives it as ultimate tranquility, perceives it as most subtle, and perceives it as eternal transcendence.
Because one attains permanent transcendence through the middle way,
the liberation door of signlessness (animitta-vimokṣamukha) is established based upon this;
it pertains to that which is non-existent and utterly devoid of anything.
It is neither with aspiration nor without aspiration.
As it is not existent, it returns to being thus;
one knows it to be non-existent.
Seeing that [the self] does not exist,
one establishes the door of liberation of emptiness based upon this;
this is called the establishment of the three doors of liberation.
What are the dharmas conducive to training?
There are ten types of dharmas that oppose training;
as their antidotes, one should know the ten types of dharmas conducive to training.
What are the ten kinds of factors that oppose the training?
First, the youthfulness, vigor, and lovely form of women constitutes a superior obstacle for sons of good family who are correctly practicing the training.
Second, the arising of craving and attachment toward the conditioned phenomena comprised within the view of a personal identity (*satkāya*).
Third, indolence and laziness.
Fourth, the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Fifth, one relies on physical food and becomes greedily attached to its delicious flavors.
Sixth, amidst the various discursive proliferations heard from the world—many, numerous, and of distinct categories—one gives rise to desire, greed, and craving within such mental preoccupations.
Seventh is the contemplation of the faults associated with the mental engagement of yoga regarding all phenomena.
Furthermore, how many are there?
They are eleven kinds.
First, doubt and hesitation regarding the truths, the jewels, the aggregates, and the results of karma;
second, the physical heaviness and rigidity of those who delight in the cultivation of abandonment;
and third, the laxity of those who possess pride regarding the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
The mental attention to faults [regarding] lethargy and drowsiness obscures the mind, causing it to become extremely withdrawn.
Fourth, one who exerts excessive diligence experiences physical fatigue and mental distress.
Fifth, those whose diligence is too feeble fail to achieve superior progress and suffer the decline of wholesome qualities.
Sixth, they become deeply elated by even a single instance of minor gain, reputation, or praise.
Seventh, restlessness, which is a lack of tranquility characterized by leaping up and agitation;
eighth, the arising of fear and dread toward *nirvāṇa*, the eternal cessation of the transitory collection (*satkāya*);
ninth, excessive engagement in verbal discourse that exceeds the bounds of valid cognition.
Although he expounds the Dharma and its treatises, he delights in employing skillful means to suppress others and incite disputes.
Tenth, regarding the various objects of experience—seen, heard, and perceived—which are manifold, numerous, and of distinct categories:
The mind races and the mind scatters.
Eleventh, one forcibly contemplates that which is not a proper object for reflection;
one should know that this is called the fault associated with the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of yoga when contemplating all phenomena.
Eighth, they develop a deep relish for the bliss of the various meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and attainments (samāpatti).
Ninth, those who desire to enter the signless concentration (animitta-samādhi) find themselves distracted and dispersed among conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra).
Tenth, when experiencing painful sensations of the body, even up to the sensation of pain that threatens one's life,
one craves for life and hopes for survival;
following this hope, one laments, sighs, and becomes bewildered and distressed.
These are called the ten kinds of dharmas that oppose the training.
What are the ten kinds of dharmas that accord with the training which serve as the remedies for these ten kinds of dharmas that oppose the training? They are as follows.
First, the perception of impurity;
second, the perception of impermanence;
third, the perception of suffering in impermanence.
Fourth, the perception of selflessness within suffering;
fifth, the perception of revulsion toward food;
sixth, the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in.
7. The perception of light;
8. The perception of detachment from desire;
9. The perception of cessation.
The ten perceptions of death.
When these ten perceptions are well-cultivated, well-practiced, and frequently developed,
they are able to sever the ten kinds of obstructive dharmas and dharmas that oppose training.
It should be known that within this there are four kinds of illumination:
first, the illumination of the Dharma;
second, the illumination of the meaning.
Third, the light of śamatha;
fourth, the light of vipaśyanā.
Based on these four kinds of light, one establishes the perception of light as predominant.

In this context, the intended meaning is that those factors which obstruct the yoga of mental attention (*manasikāra*) consisting of the contemplation of all phenomena for the purpose of severing [afflictions]— namely, the factors conducive to training (*śaikṣa-dharma*)— are what are being taken up.
What are the ten? First, past causes;
second, conformity with the teaching.
Third, application in accordance with reality;
fourth, practice that is uninterrupted and earnest;
fifth, intense aspiration.
Sixth, maintaining the power of yoga;
seventh, pacifying the coarse heaviness of body and mind;
eighth, repeated investigation.
Ninth, they are free from timidity;
tenth, they are devoid of overweening pride.
What is the causal condition from former lives?
This refers to the maturation of the faculties and the accumulation of the faculties through what was previously practiced.
What is the teaching that accords with reality?
It is the teaching that is explained without error and in a gradual sequence.
What is practice in accordance with reality?
It refers to practicing without error according to the teachings.
Such practice is able to give rise to right view.
What is practice that is uninterrupted and earnest?
It refers to the fact that, by means of such correct application,
one does not spend one's life in vain regarding the categories of wholesome qualities.
One is able to swiftly accumulate all categories of wholesome qualities.
What is meant by "intense aspiration"?
It refers to a certain person who generates a longing for the supreme liberation.
That is to say: "When shall I be able to dwell fully established in this state, just as the noble ones dwell fully established in this state?
How does one maintain the power of yoga?
That is to say, there are two causes and conditions by which one is able to attain the power of maintaining yoga:
first, because one's innate nature is that of a sharp faculty;
second, because of long-term cultivation through repeated practice.
How does one pacify the coarseness and heaviness of body and mind?
It is as when someone, perhaps due to physical exertion or physical fatigue,
gives rise to coarseness of body and gives rise to coarseness of mind.
This cause ceases once one easily shifts from that posture; or,
it may arise from excessive vitarka and vicāra,
giving rise to heaviness of body and heaviness of mind.
This [distraction] ceases through the application of mental tranquility (*śamatha*). Alternatively,
it may arise from being enveloped by mental contraction, mental inferiority, lethargy (*styāna*), or sleep (*middha*),
which gives rise to physical rigidity (*dausthulya*) and mental rigidity.
This cause ceases through the cultivation of the dharma of superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) and *vipaśyanā* accompanied by attention conducive to purification;
or, due to its inherent nature, it belongs to the category of afflictions that have not yet been abandoned.
The heaviness and rigidity of body and mind have not yet been abandoned;
this [heaviness] ceases through the continuous application of effort in cultivating the Noble Path.
How does one repeatedly observe?
That is to say, based on ethical discipline (*śīla*), one repeatedly examines what was poorly done and what was not done,
and repeatedly examines what was well done and what was done;
thus, one does not persist in that which was poorly done or left undone.
He does not regress from what is well-done that has been performed;
he abandons what is ill-done that has been performed;
and he performs what is well-done without abandoning it.
Furthermore, through the dominant influence of the mental application that examines whether afflictions have been abandoned or not yet abandoned,
one repeatedly investigates them;
if one knows they have been abandoned, one gives rise to joy.
If one knows that [defilements] have not yet been abandoned, one then repeatedly and diligently cultivates the right path.
How is it that there is no timidity?
This refers to that which is to be known, seen, and realized at a later time.
Because they have not yet known, seen, or realized it, a sense of timidity arises;
their minds become weary and their spirits are depleted.
Once this has arisen, they do not cling to it firmly, but are able to quickly sever and extinguish it.
What is freedom from overweening pride?
It refers to being free from overweening pride regarding what has been attained, touched, and realized,
and thus being free from inverted attachments.
Regarding that which is truly attained, one gives rise to the perception of attainment;
regarding that which is truly touched, one gives rise to the perception of contact;
regarding that which is truly realized, one gives rise to the perception of realization.
These ten dharmas are to be practiced by those yogins who delight in training; they should be cultivated at all times—
beginning, middle, and end— in constant conformity and without contradiction.
Therefore, these are called the dharmas of training in accordance [with the goal].
There are, in brief, four types of impairment of yoga. What are the four?
First, the failure of ultimate yoga;
second, the failure of temporary yoga;
third, the failure through the loss of what has been attained in yoga.
Fourth is the impairment of yoga caused by misconduct;
this refers to individuals who lack the spiritual lineage (*agotra*). Why is this?
Because within that body there is no capacity for the factors conducive to nirvāṇa,
one ultimately loses the supramundane yoga;
as for the temporary loss of yoga:
This refers to a person (pudgala) who possesses the spiritual lineage (gotra). Why is this?
Because within that person's continuum exists the dharma capable of leading toward nirvana.
Although external conditions may be lacking and a long period of time may elapse,
they will certainly encounter the necessary conditions to practice yoga and cause [the realization] to manifest.
Having practiced well, they shall attain parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is said that his yoga is temporarily impaired.
Regarding the one whose attained yoga has been lost and destroyed:
this refers to someone who has fallen away from what was attained, touched, and realized.
Whether it be wisdom, vision, or abiding in peace,
that which is impaired by yoga practiced through wrong conduct refers,
for example, to someone who practices with diligence but not in accordance with correct principle.
Although much effort is expended, nothing is accomplished;
one is unable to achieve any yoga,
nor is this a wholesome dharma.
Furthermore, suppose there is someone who, despite having many afflictions and a nature full of much dust and defilement,
possesses sharp faculties and keen wisdom, such that innate awareness is perfected;
they skillfully retain what they have heard and reach the ultimate in learning.
Whether few or many, whether dwelling in seclusion,
there are those who are householders and those who have gone forth;
being upright by nature, they come to where he is.
Because they preach the Dharma to gladden the mind,
they further practice deceit,
falsely manifesting various forms of conduct that appear to be disciplined and harmonious in both body and speech.
By reason of these causes and conditions, one gathers gain, honor, praise, and the notion of great merit;
and one obtains various kinds of clothing, food, bedding, medicine for the treatment of illness, and personal requisites.
He was venerated and respected by kings, ministers, householders, and even merchant leaders,
all of whom collectively regarded him as an arhat;
or [he was so regarded] by his disciples who followed him.
Whether they be members of the monastic community or the householders,
if they remain attached to their loved ones and follow after them, it will lead to much entanglement;
furthermore, they will give rise to this thought:
These disciples, both ordained and lay, have faith and compliance with me;
they all collectively declare that I am an arhat.
If they were to approach me to inquire about matters such as yoga, mental attention, calm abiding, and insight, based upon those [teachings], [I would explain them].
If I am unable to answer those questions, they will,
on that account, abandon their faith and confidence in me,
no longer regarding me as an Arhat.
Consequently, he has fallen away from gain and honor;
therefore, I should now personally reflect upon, deliberate, and examine the establishment of yoga.
By means of the predominant power of these matters, [he shall proceed].
Attached to gain, honor, and reputation, he dwells alone in a secluded place,
engaging in analytical reflection, deliberation, and observation to establish himself in yoga;
yet this yoga does not accord with the sūtras, does not appear in the vinaya, and contradicts the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
If there are bhikṣus who have mastered the Tripiṭaka,
yet they conceal their own yoga regarding it and are unwilling to reveal it to their lay and ordained disciples.
This yoga should be taught privately and not made public. Why is this?
For fear that there may be those who uphold the teachings of the Tripiṭaka well.
Having heard such a locus of yoga,
one examines it with the Sūtras and finds it does not accord with the Sūtras;
one illuminates it with the Vinaya and finds it does not appear in the Vinaya.
They examine phenomena with a mind that opposes the nature of reality;
for this reason, they do not believe or accept it.
Out of this lack of faith, they interrogate me with words of doubt, contending and challenging me.
Consequently, kings, ministers, householders, and even wealthy elders and merchant leaders no longer revere or honor me;
furthermore, I no longer obtain clothing, food, bedding, medicines for the occasion of illness, or any other requisites for sustaining the body.
Driven by the predominant power of their attachment to gain and honor,
they conceive the notion of "Dharma" regarding what is not Dharma,
and they conceive the notion of concealment.
Giving rise to evil desires, they manifest and proclaim what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma;
and those who tolerate and accept their views likewise conceive the notion that what is not the Dharma is the Dharma.
Because they are ignorant and dull-witted, giving rise to the perception of Dharma within what is not Dharma,
one should know that even if they practice with diligence according to the teachings,
it is all entirely wrong conduct.
This is called the ruin of yoga caused by wrong practice.
It is a counterfeit of the true Dharma, not the true Dharma itself,
and it acts as an obstacle to the true Dharma for those bhikṣus who diligently cultivate meditative concentration.
The yogācāra should thoroughly understand these four factors that corrupt yoga and should distance himself from them. What is yoga?
It refers to the four yogas. What are the four?
First, faith.
Second, aspiration;
third, diligence;
fourth, skillful means.
Regarding the two aspects of the mode of activity:
first, the aspect of faithful compliance.
The two aspects of pure conduct.
Regarding the two bases:
first, the basis of investigating the principles of all phenomena.
Regarding the second, the basis for the supernormal power of the *pudgala* who is resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*),
there are four kinds of desire (*chanda*). What are these four?
First is the desire for realization;
second is the desire for inquiry;
third is the desire for the accumulation of provisions.
The fourth is the desire for conformity with yoga.
Regarding the desire for realization:
it refers, for example, to someone who gives rise to a longing for higher liberation.
As explained extensively before,
regarding those who desire to inquire:
it is as when someone, having conceived a longing, goes to a monastery.
One approaches those who possess discernment, who practice the holy life together, and who have accomplished the sublime wisdom of yoga,
in order to hear what has not yet been heard, to reach the ultimate understanding of what has been heard,
and for the desire to cultivate and accumulate the provisions for realization.
That is to say, there is someone who, for the sake of the purity of restraint through the precepts and for the sake of the purity of restraint through the sense faculties,
practices moderation in eating and reduces sleep.
While dwelling in correct awareness, one successively develops superior excellence and gives rise to a yearning for it,
in order to conform to the desire for yoga;
that is to say, through uninterrupted application and earnest application.
While practicing the path, one gives rise to longing and gives rise to joy.
There are four kinds of diligence regarding what one wishes to accomplish. What are these four?
First is diligence in hearing;
second is diligence in reflection;
third is diligence in cultivation.
The fourth is diligence for the purification of obstacles.
Regarding diligence for the sake of hearing:
this refers to listening to what has not yet been heard, and bringing to completion what has already been heard.
The application of diligent, courageous, and resolute effort is for the purpose of contemplating with vigor; that is,
dwelling alone in a secluded place regarding the Dharma as it has been heard.
Reflecting upon its meaning and weighing it through observation,
one who cultivates diligence is said to enter into tranquility and diligently practice calm abiding and insight from time to time.
Regarding the purification of diligence that serves as an obstacle:
this refers to exerting oneself with vigor day and night through walking meditation and seated meditation,
purifying the mind from all obstructive phenomena.
With a diligent mind, courageous and resolute,
there are four skillful means of exertion:
namely, by the predominant power of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), one properly guards mindfulness.
Because one maintains mindfulness well, one is able to be free from negligence;
guarding the mind, one cultivates all wholesome dharmas.
Being free from negligence, the mind is correctly directed inward to cultivate *śamatha*, the dharma of higher wisdom, and *vipaśyanā*.
These four yogas consist of sixteen types.
One should develop profound faith and understanding regarding the goal to be attained.
Having gained such faith, one should give rise to a yearning for all wholesome dharmas.
Out of a desire for [attainment], one exerts oneself day and night, abiding in diligent application;
having aroused firm and courageous vigor,
one employs skillful means to acquire what has not yet been acquired.
Because they are able to contact what has not yet been contacted and to realize what has not yet been realized,
these four dharmas are called yoga.
What is attention?
It refers to the four types of attention. What are the four?
1. The attention of forceful application;
2. The attention of interrupted application;
3. The attention of uninterrupted application.
Regarding the four types of mental engagement,
what is the mental engagement that operates with effort?
It refers to the beginner causing the mind to abide and abide evenly within.
Alternatively, one may engage in unerring discernment regarding all phenomena;
until the attention that has been cultivated is attained,
at that time the power of attention functions with strenuous exertion.
Because one forcefully exerts effort to subdue the mind and cause it to abide in a single object,
it is called the mental application of forceful exertion (*balavāhana-manaskāra*).
What is the mental application of interrupted engagement (*sachidravāhana-manaskāra*)?
This means that after having attained the cultivated *manasikāra*,
one gradually advances through the mundane and supramundane paths;
the *lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-manasikāra* is interspersed with intervals of *samādhi* and reflection (*cintā*).
Because one has not yet been able to engage in practice that is consistently and purely directed toward transformation,
it is called "intermittent engagement of attention" (*sāntarā-vāhana-manasikāra*).
What is "uninterrupted engagement of attention" (*nirantarā-vāhana-manasikāra*)?
This refers to the mental attention from the stage of "attention that discerns characteristics" onwards,
up until the "attention that culminates in application";
this is called the mental attention of uninterrupted progression.
What is the mental engagement that operates without effort?
It refers to the mental engagement that is the fruit of the culmination of application;
this is called the mental engagement that operates without effort.
Furthermore, there are four other types of mental attention (*manasikāra*):
first, conforming mental attention;
second, remedial mental attention.
Third, the attention that accords with purification;
fourth, the attention that accords with investigation.
What is the attention that accords [with reality]?
This refers to generating a profound sense of revulsion toward the object of focus and initiating correct application,
yet not having yet abandoned the afflictions.
What is the mental attention of counteractive application?
This refers to the ability to sever the afflictions.
What is the attention conducive to purification?
It refers to the mind being drawn inward to grasp signs of purity and excellence, thereby exhorting it toward joy.
What is the attention of conformable observation?
It refers to the attention of observation;
it is by the predominant power of this attention that [the process occurs].
One contemplates in accordance with whether the afflictions have been abandoned or not yet abandoned.
Question: When one is correctly attending to the object of focus, how many aspects does one contemplate?
Answer: Four.
What are the four? First, the characteristic of the object of focus (ālambana-nimitta).
Second, the characteristic of causes and conditions;
third, the characteristic of what should be abandoned;
fourth, the characteristic of what should be cultivated.
The characteristic of the object-condition (*ālambana-nimitta*) refers to the clear manifestation of an image that is concordant with the object to be known.
The characteristic of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya-nimitta*) refers to...
It refers to the accumulation of the requisites for samādhi;
the intense aspiration that accords with the instructions and accompanies their cultivation;
and the profound sense of revulsion toward phenomena that are to be loathed.
One is able to discern and fully understand what is distracted and what is undistracted,
and is not disturbed or provoked by others,
whether their actions are performed by humans or non-humans.
It may be produced through sound or produced through effort.
If vipaśyanā is predominant, one internally withdraws the mind and subsequently contemplates the signs of causal conditions with extreme intensity.
If śamatha is the precursor,
then the signs of the causal conditions for the subsequent arising of vipaśyanā and extremely intense calm abiding (śamatha) should be avoided;
furthermore, there are four such signs.
First is the mark of sinking;
second is the mark of agitation;
third is the mark of attachment.
The fourth is the sign of distraction.
Regarding the sign of sinking:
it refers to that which causes the mind to become inferior due to the causal conditions of the signs of the focal object.
The characteristic of restlessness (*auddhatya*) refers to that which causes the mind to become uplifted due to the causal conditions of the characteristics of the object (*ālambana-nimitta*).
The characteristic of attachment (*saṅga-nimitta*) refers to...
That is to say, by means of the characteristic of the object of focus and the characteristic of causal conditions,
the mind gives rise to defilement and attachment toward its objects, resulting in various disturbances.
As for the characteristic of disturbance:

That is to say, by means of the characteristics of the object of focus (*ālambana-nimitta*) and the characteristics of causal conditions (*pratyaya-nimitta*), the mind is caused to scatter outwardly and become agitated.
These various characteristics have already been explained above in the section on the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*).
When there is resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), how many types of resolute conviction are there?
Answer: Nine. What are these nine?
First, the resolute conviction of luminous purity;
second, the resolute conviction of non-luminous purity;
third, dull resolute conviction.
Fourth, swift resolute conviction;
fifth, narrow resolute conviction;
sixth, vast resolute conviction.
Seventh, the resolute belief in the immeasurables;
eighth, pure resolute belief;
ninth, impure resolute belief.
There is the resolute conviction of luminous purity;
this refers to the resolute conviction associated with light that arises when one has clarified the mind and properly apprehended the sign of light.
There is also the resolute conviction of non-luminous purity.
That is to say, it refers to the resolve associated with darkness when one is unable to properly apprehend the sign of light.
"Dull resolve" refers to the resolve present within a body of dull faculties.
"Swift resolute conviction" refers to all resolute convictions present within the continuum of those with sharp faculties.
"Narrow resolute conviction" refers to...
This refers to the resolve that accompanies limited faith and desire,
as well as the resolve of mental engagement with a limited object;
thus, because such mental attention is limited.
And because its object of focus is narrow and limited,
it is called "narrow and limited resolve.
As for "vast resolve":
This refers to the resolute confidence (adhimokṣa) that accompanies vast faith and aspiration,
as well as the resolute confidence of mental engagement with a vast object;
such is the case because the mental attention is vast.
Furthermore, because its object of focus is vast,
it is called "vast resolute conviction.
As for "immeasurable resolute conviction":
This refers to the resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) accompanied by faith and aspiration that is boundless and limitless,
as well as the resolute conviction of mental engagement with an object that is boundless and limitless.
Thus, it is because the mental engagement is immeasurable and the object is immeasurable.
It is called "immeasurable resolve.
Regarding "pure resolve," it refers to the resolve that is well-cultivated, perfected, and brought to ultimate completion, accompanied by all [virtuous qualities].
Regarding those with impure resolute conviction (*adhimukti*):
this refers to resolute conviction that is not well-cultivated, not fully perfected, and not brought to ultimate completion, yet which functions in conjunction [with other factors].
How many types of yogic practice (*yoga-kṛtya*) are there?
Answer: Four.
What are the four?
First, the cessation of the basis.
Second, the transformation of the basis;
third, thorough knowledge of the object;
fourth, delighting in the object.
Regarding the extinction of the basis and the transformation of the basis:
this means that through the diligent cultivation of yogic mental attention (*manasikāra*),
the basis accompanied by all coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) is gradually extinguished.
The gradual transformation of the basis accompanied by all-pervasive pliancy is called the yoga-practice of the cessation of the basis and the transformation of the basis.
This refers to the thorough knowledge of the object of focus and the cultivation of delight in the object of focus.
That is to say, there may be a thorough knowledge of the object of focus and a delight in the object of focus, which, with the cessation and transformation of their basis as their primary factor,
arise through the predominant power of this thorough knowledge of the object of focus and delight in the object of focus.
It causes the cessation of the basis and the transformation of the basis;
alternatively, there is the thorough knowledge of the object and the delight in the object,
taking the purification of the basis as its primary focus.
By the dominant power of this purification of the basis,
one attains thorough purity regarding the object of thorough knowledge,
as well as thorough purity regarding the object of delight.
It operates at the time when what was to be accomplished has been completed;
this is called the fourfold yoga-activity of the practitioner of yoga.
Question: How many kinds of practitioners of yoga are there?
Answer: Three.
What are the three?
First, the yoga practitioner who is a beginner in training.
2. The yoga practitioner who has already practiced;
3. The yoga practitioner who has already transcended mental attention (*manasikāra*).
What is the yoga practitioner who is a beginner?
There are two kinds of beginners:
first, those who are beginners in mental attention;
second, those who are beginners in the purification of afflictions.
What is the beginner’s practice regarding attention?
It refers to an individual who is a beginner abiding in a single object and diligently cultivating attention until they have attained the attention that is the object of their cultivation.
Having not yet attained one-pointedness of mind,
how does a beginner purify the afflictions?
It refers to one who has already attained the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that is to be cultivated.
One who, amidst various afflictions,

desires to purify the mind and initiates the cultivation of the "attention that discerns characteristics" (lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra) with right effort and application is called a beginner in the purification of afflictions.
What is a practitioner who has already practiced yoga?
It refers to one who, having set aside the mental application of removing signs (*nimittāpagata-manasikāra*),
has already well cultivated the remaining five mental applications up to the culmination of the preparatory stage (*prayoganiṣṭha*).
What is the yoga practitioner who has already transcended mental attention (*manasikāra*)?
It refers to one who dwells in the stage of mental attention that is the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala-manasikāra*).
By means of this, they have transcended the mental attention cultivated through the methods of application and abide in the fruit of cultivation.
Therefore, it is called "the attention that has already transcended.
Furthermore, this refers to the period beginning from the cultivation of the desire for wholesome dharmas up until the roots of goodness conducive to penetration have not yet arisen.
During that period, one is said to be "initially engaged in practice.
If one has already generated the roots of goodness conducive to penetration—

namely, heat (*uṣmagata*), summits (*mūrdhan*), patience in accordance with the truths (*satyānulomikī kṣānti*), and the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*)— one is said to be "already practiced."
If one has already entered the state of rightness and separation from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) and attained the clear observation of the truths (satya-abhisamaya),
then regarding the Buddha’s holy teaching,
one does not rely on others and cannot be led astray or diverted by other conditions.
At that time, it is called the "attention of transcendence," because by means of it one transcends attention dependent on others and abides in attention that is not dependent on others.
Therefore, it is called "the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment through the attention that has already crossed over.
What is the cultivation of perception?
That is to say, either when cultivating the mundane path,
one cultivates the perception of defects regarding the lower stages;
or when cultivating the path to nirvāṇa.
Regarding the realm of abandonment, the realm of dispassion, and the realm of cessation,
one perceives their supreme qualities of tranquility and cultivates the perception of abandonment,
the perception of dispassion, and the perception of cessation.
Either when practicing śamatha, one cultivates the perception of the upper and lower [realms] belonging to the category of tranquility;
or when practicing vipaśyanā.
Regarding the cultivation of the perceptions of the preceding and succeeding parts of the body,
and the perceptions of above and below:
this refers to observing this body exactly as it is situated and exactly as it is disposed.
From the crown of the head down to the soles of the feet,
it is filled with various kinds of impurities;
that is to say, all the various hairs of the head, body hair, nails, and teeth within this body.
As explained extensively before.
Regarding the "perception of before and after":
it refers to a certain person who applies themselves with diligent and earnest effort toward the object of observation.
He skillfully grasps, skillfully reflects upon, skillfully understands,
and skillfully penetrates; that is to say, while standing he observes while sitting, while sitting he observes while lying down,
or while walking behind he observes those walking ahead.
This demonstrates the practice of vipaśyanā:
observing all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) arising through dependent origination across the three periods of time.
That is to say, it refers to the statement: "While standing, one contemplates while sitting."
This demonstrates that one observes all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to be known in the future by means of mental attention (*manasikāra*) in the present. Why is this so?
Because the state of mental attention in the present has already arisen, it is designated as "abiding" (*sthiti*).
Because the state of the knowable in the future has not yet arisen and is about to emerge, it is called "sitting.
Furthermore, it is said that while sitting, one contemplates what is lying down.
This demonstrates that one observes all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) known in the past by means of present mental attention (*manasikāra*). Why is this so?
Because the stage of present mental attention is called "sitting" since it is on the verge of ceasing.
Because the state of what was previously known has already passed away and ceased, it is called "lying down. Furthermore,
if it is said that one may observe the preceding [mental state] while in the subsequent course,
this indicates that one observes the mental state currently manifesting— which has just ceased without interval— by means of present attention (*manasikāra*).
Why is this? If the attention that has already arisen and ceased in immediate succession is called the "preceding" [attention],
then the attention that newly arises in immediate succession to it is the "apprehending" [attention].
That which has previously ceased immediately prior [to the present] is called the "subsequent practice.
It should be understood that herein,
for the sake of cultivating śamatha and vipaśyanā, [this is established].
To cultivate that twofold superior perception of light is called cultivation through perception and cultivation through the factors of enlightenment.
It refers to approaching, accumulating, cultivating, practicing, and frequently training in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
this is called the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment.
What are called the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment?
They are the four foundations of mindfulness and the four right endeavors.
The four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties and five powers,
and the seven factors of enlightenment.
The Eightfold Noble Path.
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness:
first, the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
Second, the application of mindfulness to feelings;
third, the application of mindfulness to the mind;
fourth, the application of mindfulness to phenomena.
Regarding the four right endeavors:
first, for the purpose of abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen,
one generates desire, exerts effort, and arouses diligent energy.
The right effort of exerting the mind and maintaining the mind consists of two parts:

first, for the sake of abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen; second, for the sake of preventing evil and unwholesome states that have not yet arisen from arising, one generates desire, exerts oneself, and arouses diligent vigor.
The right effort of exertion regarding the mind consists of three aspects:
first, for the sake of generating unarisen wholesome dharmas,
one generates desire, exerts oneself, and arouses diligent vigor.
The right exertion of applying the mind and maintaining the mind;
fourth, for the sake of causing already arisen wholesome dharmas to endure, not to be lost,
to reach full cultivation, and to be practiced further.
He causes them to increase and causes them to expand;
he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses diligence and vigor,
and applies right effort to restrain and sustain the mind.
The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are:
first, the basis of psychic power consisting of the accomplishment of the cultivation of concentration through desire;
second, the basis of psychic power consisting of the accomplishment of the cultivation of concentration through exertion.
The basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind accompanied by the formations of abandonment;
the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of investigation accompanied by the formations of abandonment.
As for the five faculties:
1. The faculty of faith;
2. the faculty of diligence;
3. the faculty of mindfulness.
The four faculties of concentration and the five faculties of wisdom.
As for the five powers:
First, the power of faith;
second, the power of diligence;
third, the power of mindfulness.
The four powers of concentration and the five powers of wisdom.
As for the seven factors of enlightenment:
First, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness;
second, the factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena;
third, the factor of enlightenment of energy.
4. The enlightenment factor of joy;
5. The enlightenment factor of tranquility;
6. The enlightenment factor of concentration.
The seventh is the enlightenment factor of equanimity.
The eightfold noble path consists of:
first, right view.
Second, right intention;
third, right speech;
fourth, right action.
5. Right livelihood.
6. Right effort.
7. Right mindfulness.
Regarding the eight right concentrations:
herein, what is the body? And how does one dwell in the contemplation of the body with regard to the body?
What is mindfulness? What is the application of mindfulness?
Briefly stated, there are thirty-five aspects of the body.
That is to say: the internal body and the external body;
the body comprised of sense faculties and the body not comprised of sense faculties;
the body belonging to the category of sentient beings and the body not belonging to the category of sentient beings.
The body accompanied by coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and the body accompanied by pliancy (*praśrabdhi*),
as well as the primary body (*bhūtakāya*) and the derived body (*bhautikakāya*),
are called the "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) and the "form-body" (*rūpakāya*).
The bodies of hell-beings, the bodies of animals,
the bodies of hungry ghosts, the bodies of humans, and the bodies of devas;
conscious bodies and unconscious bodies.
The intermediate body and the manifest body;
the transformed body and the untransformed body;
the female body, the male body, and the neuter body (*paṇḍaka*).
The body of a kinsman and the body of one who is not a kinsman;
the mediocre body and the inferior body;
the middling body and the sublime body.
The body of youth, the body of middle age, and the body of old age—
these are called the distinctions of bodily characteristics.
There are, in brief, three kinds of abiding in the contemplation of the body.
This refers to the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation based on the predominance of the body;
by means of this wisdom, one correctly observes and correctly investigates all aspects of the entire body.
It is the mindfulness that follows and awakens to observation;
that is to say, based on the body as the primary condition, one upholds the true Dharma,
contemplates its meaning, practices it, and realizes it.
Regarding both the words and the meaning, while practicing and realizing them, one’s mind does not forget them.
If one reflects carefully:
"Have I correctly received and upheld the True Dharma, or have I not?"
"Is it not so that one has thoroughly understood those various meanings with wisdom?
Is it not so that one has effectively touched and realized those various liberations?
Thus, one dwells with mindfulness established in such careful scrutiny.
It is called the foundations of mindfulness;
furthermore, it serves to guard mindfulness and to remain unstained by objects.
That which serves as the basis for abiding securely is called a foundation of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna);
it is that which guards mindfulness.
That is to say, as it has been taught: "First, one guards mindfulness;
if one possesses constant and diligent mindfulness, one will remain unstained by objects."
That is to say, as it is said: "One maintains mindfulness to guard the mind, abiding in a state of equanimity;
one does not grasp at signs nor grasp at secondary characteristics.
This is explained in detail up until: "guarding the faculty of the mind and cultivating the restraint of the mental faculty."
Regarding "abiding securely in the objects of focus," this refers to what is said: one establishes mindfulness upon four objects of focus—
namely, the pervasive object of focus, the object of focus for purifying conduct, the object of focus for skillfulness, and the object of focus for purifying afflictions.
Because mindfulness is well-established through these three characteristics, it is called "application of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna).
What is feeling? It refers to pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neutral feeling.
Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
pleasant bodily feeling, painful bodily feeling,
and neither-painful-nor-pleasant bodily feeling.
As it is said regarding bodily feeling, so it is with mental feeling as well.
There is pleasant feeling that has a relishable flavor,
and there is painful feeling that has a relishable flavor.
There is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling accompanied by attachment,
feeling unaccompanied by attachment,
and feeling based on worldly indulgence.
It should be known that it is likewise:
pleasant feeling based on renunciation,
and painful feeling based on renunciation.
The sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure based on renunciation—
thus, there are twenty-one sensations in total,
or nine kinds of sensations.
What is the mind? It refers to the mind with attachment and the mind free from attachment;
the mind with aversion and the mind free from aversion.
There is a mind with delusion and a mind free from delusion;
a contracted mind and a distracted mind;
a depressed mind and an uplifted mind.
A restless mind and an un-restless mind;
a tranquil mind and an un-tranquil mind;
a concentrated mind and an unconcentrated mind.
The well-cultivated mind and the poorly cultivated mind;
the well-liberated mind and the poorly liberated mind.
Thus, there are twenty types of mind in total.
What is the Dharma?
It refers to the Dharma of discipline for greed regarding greed,
and the Dharma of discipline for hatred regarding hatred.
Whether it be the Dharma of delusion or the Vinaya for delusion;
whether it be the Dharma of contraction or the Dharma of expansion;
whether it be the Dharma of depression or the Dharma of upliftment.
Whether it be states of agitation or non-agitation,
states of tranquility or non-tranquility,
or states of concentration or non-concentration.
Whether it be the well-cultivated and the uncultivated dharmas,
or the well-liberated and the unliberated dharmas—
one should understand that in this way twenty kinds of dharmas are established: those of the dark category and the bright category, and those of the defiled category and the pure category.
Furthermore, pleasant feeling refers to that which is comprised within the category of feeling as an even sensation produced with contact conducive to pleasant feeling as its condition;
this is called pleasant feeling.
If this is associated with the five consciousnesses, it is called bodily sensation;
if associated with the mental consciousness, it is called mental sensation.
This is as in the case of contact conducive to pleasant sensation.
In this way, conditioned by contact conducive to painful feeling and contact conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,
there arises an uneven feeling comprised within the category of feeling.
That which is neither equal nor unequal, and is comprised within feeling,
is called painful feeling and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
If this is associated with the five consciousnesses, it is called bodily feeling.
If those associated with the mental consciousness are called mental feelings (*cittavedanā*),
then such feelings as conform to *nirvāṇa*,
conform to discernment (*viniścaya*), and lead to ultimate deliverance, ultimate purification, and the ultimate [state].
That which enables the perfection of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is called "reception without craving" (*anāsvādita-vedanā*).
If it falls within the realms (*dhātu*), it is called "reception with craving" (*sāsvādita-vedanā*).
This applies to that which is bound to the realms of form and formlessness, or that which accords with the departure from desire.
That which is called "feeling based on renunciation" refers to that which is connected to the desire realm or does not accord with the departure from desire;
that which is called "feeling based on worldly attachment" refers to the same.
Furthermore, there is one who possesses a mind of greed,
meaning one who is entangled by the fetters of greed regarding an object of perception that is desirable.
There is also one whose mind is free from greed.
That is to say, one who is free from such entanglements of greed,
yet possesses a mind of hatred—
that is, one who is bound by the entanglement of hatred toward an object of perception that is loathsome.
"Free from a mind of hatred" means that one is indeed far removed from such entanglements of hatred.
"Possessing a deluded mind" means...
This refers to being bound by the fetter of delusion (*moha-paryavasthāna*) regarding an object that is subject to delusion.
One whose mind is free from delusion is one who has distanced themselves from such a fetter of delusion.
It should be understood that these six states of mind all arise during the course of activity as belonging to the three categories of afflictions.
Regarding the distinctions among these three types of remedies:
"concentrating the mind" means binding the mind internally upon the object of focus through correct practice.
"Distracted mind" refers to that which flows out and scatters in accordance with the five external sensory pleasures.
"Depressed mind" refers to...
This refers to that which proceeds together with lethargy and drowsiness.
"Lifting the mind" means that it becomes clearly manifest upon a pure and sublime object of focus.
A restless mind refers to that which is agitated by the fetter of restlessness due to excessive exaltation.
A non-restless mind is its opposite.
This means that one attains equanimity at the time of uplifting and at the time of withdrawing.
A "calmed mind" refers to having attained liberation from the hindrances.
"One whose mind is not tranquil" refers to one who has not yet attained liberation from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
"A concentrated mind" refers to...
That is to say, having attained liberation from the hindrances,
one is further able to realize and enter the fundamental dhyānas;
this refers to one whose mind is not yet fixed.
This means one has not yet entered it.
One who has well-cultivated the mind refers to one who has practiced this concentration for a long period of time.
One attains [the goal] according to one's desire, without difficulty and without obstruction,
and is able to swiftly realize entry.
This is not the case for one who has not cultivated the mind well.
The characteristics of the opposite should be understood accordingly.
One whose mind is well-liberated means one who is ultimately liberated from everything.
Regarding the mind that is not well-liberated:
this refers to that which is not liberated from all things in an ultimate sense.
It should be understood that these fourteen types of mind all arise during the state of abiding.
When abiding in the stage of the pure covering (*viśuddhāvaraṇa-bhūmi*), eight kinds of mind arise;
that is, from the contracted mind and the distracted mind, up to the tranquil and non-tranquil minds.
When abiding in the stage of the pure afflictions (*viśuddhakleśa-bhūmi*), six kinds of mind arise.

That is to say, he knows a concentrated mind as concentrated, an unconcentrated mind as unconcentrated, and so on, up to a well-liberated mind as well-liberated and an unliberated mind as unliberated.
Furthermore, when there are hindrances within, he is able to know for himself: "I have hindrances."
When there are no hindrances within, one is able to know for oneself: "I am free from all hindrances.
One is likewise able to know when those hindrances that have not yet arisen do arise, and one is also able to know when those hindrances that have already arisen are dispersed and extinguished.

When there is a fetter regarding the eye, up to and including a fetter regarding the mind, one is able to know for oneself: "I have a fetter regarding the eye, up to and including a fetter regarding the mind.
When there is no fetter regarding the eye, up to and including no fetter regarding the mind...
He is able to know for himself that his eye is free from fetters, up to and including his mind being free from fetters;
likewise, he is also able to know when those fetters of the eye, up to and including the fetters of the mind, have arisen that had not previously arisen.

Just as he can discern that those various fetters have already arisen and then dispersed and ceased, so too, when the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness is present within him, he is able to know for himself: "I possess the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness."
Internally, regarding the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, one is able to know for oneself: "I possess the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness.
Likewise, one is also able to know when the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness has not yet arisen that it has now arisen.
Just as one knows that once arisen, it remains, is not forgotten, is cultivated to fulfillment, and is further practiced,
increased, and expanded; likewise, one is able to understand the awakening factor of mindfulness.
In the same way, it should be understood that the factors of enlightenment—discrimination of phenomena, diligence, joy, serenity, concentration, and equanimity—are likewise so.
If one can thus thoroughly and accurately know the intrinsic nature, causes and conditions, disadvantages, and remedies of all defiled phenomena.
This is the essence of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). As it is said that one dwells in the contemplation of the body with regard to the body,
so too should it be understood accordingly for feelings, the mind, and phenomena.
How does one dwell contemplating the body in the internal body?
How does one dwell contemplating the body in the external body?
How does one dwell contemplating the body in both the internal and external body?
That is to say, if one dwells in the contemplation of the body by taking as an object the internal physical form belonging to the category of sentient beings,
this is called dwelling in the contemplation of the body with respect to the internal body.

If one dwells in the contemplation of the body by taking as an object external physical form not belonging to the category of sentient beings, [this is called dwelling in the contemplation of the body with respect to the external body].
This is called dwelling in the contemplation of the body with respect to the external body.
If one dwells in the contemplation of the body taking as the object the physical form of another sentient being categorized as external,
this is called dwelling in the contemplation of the body with respect to both the internal and external body.

If one dwells observing the three [categories] in accordance with the objects— namely, the feelings, mind, and phenomena that arise based on the internal physical form belonging to the category of sentient beings—
this is called dwelling in the observation of feelings, mind, and phenomena in relation to the internal.

If one dwells contemplating the three [categories] in accordance with the objects— namely, the feelings, mind, and phenomena produced by taking as object external forms that do not belong to the category of sentient beings—
this is called dwelling in the contemplation of feelings, mind, and phenomena with respect to the external feelings, mind, and phenomena.

If one dwells observing the three [aggregates] in accordance with their nature, taking as objects the feelings, mind, and phenomena that arise based on the physical form of other sentient beings external to oneself,
this is called dwelling in the observation of feelings, mind, and phenomena regarding internal and external feelings, mind, and phenomena.
Furthermore, there is another distinction:
if one takes as an object the form that is comprised by the sense faculties and is characterized by grasping and sensation,
this is called "dwelling in the contemplation of the body within the internal body."
If one takes as an object matter that is not comprised within the sense faculties, which is without grasping and without sensation,
this is called dwelling in the contemplation of the body with regard to the external body.
If one takes as an object matter that is not comprised within the sense faculties, which is with grasping and with sensation...
This is called dwelling in the contemplation of the body with respect to the internal and external body.
Likewise, if one takes as objects the feelings, mind, and phenomena that arise based on the three types of form mentioned above,
it should be understood accordingly that this is dwelling in the contemplation of those three.
Furthermore, there is another distinction:
if one takes as an object the form associated with pliancy that belongs to one's own internal meditative stage,
this is called "dwelling in the contemplation of the body within the internal body."
If one takes as an object the form associated with the heaviness (dausthulya) of one's own internal state that is not in meditative equipoise,
this is called dwelling in the contemplation of the body with regard to the external body.
If one takes as an object the form associated with both pliancy (praśrabdhi) and heaviness belonging to another...
This is called dwelling in the contemplation of the body with regard to the internal and external body.
Likewise, if one takes as objects the feelings, mind, and phenomena that arise dependent upon the three aforementioned types of form, this is likewise so.
It should be understood that, according to the circumstances, this is precisely abiding in the contemplation of the three [objects].
Furthermore, there is a distinction:
namely, when one takes as an object the internal primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which constitute form.
This is called dwelling in the contemplation of the body with respect to the internal body.
If one takes as an object the external primary elements (mahābhūta) that constitute form,
this is called dwelling in the contemplation of the body with respect to the external body.
If one takes as an object the derived matter comprised of the sense bases and objects that arise based on the primary elements which serve as their support,
this is called "dwelling in the contemplation of the body with regard to the internal and external body."
In this way, if one takes as objects the feelings, mind, and mental factors arising in dependence upon the three preceding types of form,
one should know that, according to the circumstances, this constitutes dwelling in the contemplation of the three [feelings,
mind, and phenomena]. Furthermore, there is a distinction.
That is to say: if one takes as an object the internal physical form of the conscious body, this is called "dwelling in the contemplation of the body with respect to the internal body.

If one takes as an object the physical forms of a sentient being—such as those in the state of bluish discoloration and so forth—that belong to the unconscious body, [this is called dwelling in the contemplation of the body with respect to the external body].
This is called dwelling in the contemplation of the body with regard to the external body.
If one takes as an object the form of a non-conscious body which had the nature of being conscious at a past time,
or the form of a conscious body which will have the nature of being non-conscious at a future time.
Taking the similar nature of phenomena (*sabhāga-dharmatā*) and the equal nature of phenomena (*sama-dharmatā*) as the object,
this is called "dwelling in the contemplation of the body with regard to the internal and external body.
Likewise, if one takes as the object the feelings, mind, and phenomena that arise based on the three aforementioned types of form, [this is the same].
It should be understood that, according to what is appropriate, this is precisely abiding in the contemplation of the three [bodies].
Furthermore, there is a distinction:
namely, when one takes as an object the signs of one's own internal body, such as hair, body hair, nails, and teeth.
This is called dwelling in the contemplation of the body with regard to one's own internal body.
If one takes the characteristics of another’s internal body, such as hair, body hair, nails, and teeth, as the object,
this is called dwelling in the contemplation of the body with regard to the external body.
If one takes as an object the internal physical body, whether it has undergone transformation or not, such as the signs of bluish discoloration and so forth,

and likewise takes as an object the external physical body, whether it has undergone transformation or not, such as the signs of bluish discoloration and so forth— namely, their similar dharma-nature and equal dharma-nature.
This is called dwelling in the contemplation of the body with regard to the internal and external body.
Likewise, if one takes as objects the feelings, mind, and phenomena that arise dependent upon the three types of form mentioned above,
it should be understood accordingly that this is dwelling in the contemplation of the three [feelings, mind, and phenomena].
One should know that there are many such various categories of distinctions regarding body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
Herein, for the time being, only a few of these various categories of distinctions shall be revealed.
Furthermore, in order to counteract the four inversions,
the Blessed One established the four foundations of mindfulness;
that is to say, as a counteragent.
The application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is established to counteract the perversion of perceiving the impure as pure,
because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, taught the characteristic of impurity within the application of mindfulness to the body.
One should attend to the four foundations of mindfulness;
if one can frequently contemplate these,
one will then eliminate the inversion of perceiving purity within the impure.
The foundation of mindfulness of feeling is established as an antidote to the perversion of perceiving pleasure within what is actually suffering,
by means of abiding in the contemplation of feelings regarding all feelings.
By understanding as it truly is that all sensations whatsoever are suffering,
one abandons the inversion of perceiving pleasure within suffering;
this serves as the remedy for the inversion of perceiving permanence within the impermanent.
He establishes the application of mindfulness to the mind,
being able to discern the various distinctions such as the mind possessed of greed,
and observing the nature of the arising and ceasing of many, numerous, and diverse types of mental states throughout various days, nights, moments, instants, and brief intervals.
Thus, one abandons the inversion of permanence regarding impermanence;
and in order to counteract the inversion of conceiving a self within what is non-self,
the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) is established.
Because they have long possessed afflictions such as the view of a self,
and because they lack wholesome dharmas such as the view of non-self,
they give rise to the view of a self with respect to the aggregates.
By dwelling in the contemplation of phenomena regarding all phenomena,
one understands, as they truly are, the specific and general characteristics of the aggregates that are conceptually imputed;
thus, one abandons the inversion of self with respect to what is non-self.
Furthermore, there is another distinction:
namely, that most people in the world, regarding the aggregates, do not know as they truly are that there is only the nature of aggregates and only the nature of phenomena;
instead, they erroneously conceive of a self that relies upon the body.
Because one experiences pleasure and pain based on the body,
and because those who experience pleasure and pain possess defilement and purification through dharma and non-dharma,
[this analysis] is intended to eliminate the delusion regarding the objective basis of what is "mine."

The application of mindfulness to the body is established for the purpose of eliminating delusion regarding the objects experienced as "mine. The application of mindfulness to feelings is established for the purpose of eliminating delusion regarding those very objects of experience.

The application of mindfulness to the mind is established in order to eliminate the delusion regarding the self in relation to the mind, intellect, and consciousness, as well as the delusion regarding the objective basis of that self;
and it is established in order to eliminate the delusion regarding the objective basis of the self that is clung to as being capable of defilement and purification.
There is another distinction regarding the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*):
namely, that which serves as the basis for the performance of various karmas.
If one performs various karmas for this reason,
or if one who performs such karma does so because of this,
all such cases are collectively indicated by the establishment of the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
It should be understood that herein, one performs various karmas based upon the body;
one performs various karmas for the sake of seeking experience;
and the mind is able to perform karma through wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, there is another distinction:
namely, that which, depending upon it, is subject to defilement or purification;
and that for the sake of which defilement or purification arises.
Whether it be defilement or purification, or that by which one becomes defiled or purified—
in order to demonstrate all such cases collectively, the four foundations of mindfulness are established.
It should be understood that herein, based upon the body, there is both defilement and purification.
For the sake of seeking sensation, one gives rise to defilement and purity.
That the mind becomes defiled or pure is due to various phenomena (dharmas).
Question: What is the meaning of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna)?
Answer: If one dwells in mindfulness upon this, or if by means of this one dwells in mindfulness, all such cases are called foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Regarding "dwelling in mindfulness upon this": [it refers to the objects].
This refers to the foundation of mindfulness as the object of focus.
By means of this, one abides in mindfulness;
that is to say, whether it be wisdom or mindfulness, they maintain concentration.
This is the foundation of mindfulness as intrinsic nature;
the remaining associated minds and mental factors are the foundation of mindfulness as conjoined.

Furthermore, the wholesome, contaminated, and uncontaminated paths arising through the predominance of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena are all called foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
These are again of three types:
first, those produced by hearing (*śrutamaya*).
The second is that produced by reflection;
the third is that produced by cultivation.
Those produced by hearing and reflection are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).
That which is produced through cultivation (bhāvanā-maya) is both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava).
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle twenty-eight; *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle twenty-nine.
Thus, by virtue of having practiced and cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness, as spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree,
in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, the thirteenth part of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the fourth section of the second *Yogasthāna*.
Having already been able to dispel the coarsest inversions and having already attained thorough understanding of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena,
immediately thereafter, for the sake of preventing the arising of various unarisen evil and unwholesome phenomena, [he applies himself].
For the sake of abandoning all evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen;
for the sake of giving rise to all wholesome states that have not yet arisen;
and for the sake of maintaining all wholesome states that have already arisen so that they are not forgotten or lost.
The detailed explanation is as before,
up to the point of collecting the mind and maintaining the mind.
What are called evil and unwholesome dharmas?
This refers to the defiled bodily, vocal, and mental actions bound by desire;
these are subsumed under the misdeeds of body, speech, and mind,
as well as all the afflictions that give rise to them.
If they have not yet come together and have not yet manifested before one,
they are said to be "unborn."
If they have already been brought together and have already manifested, they are said to be "already arisen.
What are called all wholesome dharmas?
They are those which are the antidotes to those [unwholesome states], the antidotes to the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and the antidotes to the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The unarisen and the already arisen should be understood as previously explained.
When evil, unwholesome states have not yet arisen, and when evil,
unwholesome states have not previously come into combination;
In order to prevent them from arising, one generates the aspiration:
"I shall cause all of these, each and every one, never to arise again.
This is called generating desire for the sake of the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states.
When unwholesome and unvirtuous states have already arisen and previously coalesced, one generates a longing aspiration for their abandonment, thinking:
"I shall not tolerate any of them whatsoever; I shall sever, eliminate, and dispel them."
This is called generating the desire for the purpose of abandoning all evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen.
