Furthermore, all those evil and unwholesome states arise either with past objects as their condition.
Or it arises conditioned by future phenomena;
or it arises conditioned by present phenomena.
Such is that dharma.
It may take as its object an unmanifest realm or it may take as its object a manifest realm.
If it takes as its object a past or future phenomenon, this is called taking an unmanifest realm as its object.
If one takes a present object as the focal point,
this is called "focusing on a directly perceived object.
It should be understood that herein, regarding the focusing on an imperceptible object:
Regarding unwholesome and unvirtuous states that have not yet arisen, one desires that they not arise;
regarding those that have already arisen, one desires that they be permanently abandoned. To thus exert oneself and encourage oneself is called "exertion" (*pragraha*).
Regarding objects currently appearing before one,
one applies courageous and correct effort (*vīrya-samyak-pradhāna*) with the desire that unwholesome and evil states not yet arisen do not arise,
and that those already arisen are permanently abandoned.
This is called the arousal of diligent effort.
Why is this? Because one must be firm and exert oneself through self-urging and self-stimulation.
Only through courageous and right effort can one cause those [defilements] either not to arise again or to be permanently severed. Furthermore,
regarding the minor and medium grades of the various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*):
He exerts himself with self-urgency because he desires that what has not yet arisen should not arise,
and that what has already arisen should be permanently severed.
Regarding the most intense fetters (*paryavasthāna*), he desires that those which have not yet arisen should not arise.
Regarding those [afflictions] that have already arisen, he exerts diligent effort with the desire to bring them to permanent cessation.
Furthermore, if he engages with past objects,
while so engaging, he does not allow afflictions to arise in dependence upon them.
Even if, through a lapse of mindfulness, [unwholesome thoughts] should arise for a moment, he does not tolerate them;
he is able to quickly sever, eliminate, dispel, and cast them out,
just as he did when taking the past as his object.
One should know that it is the same for future practice.
In this way, one can prevent unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising,
and can eliminate those that have already arisen.
This is called exertion.
When one practices with a present object of focus,
one ensures that afflictions do not arise by taking that object as their condition during such practice.
Even if, through a lapse of mindfulness, unwholesome states should momentarily arise, he does not tolerate them;
rather, he swiftly abandons, dispels, and eliminates them.
In this way, he ensures that unarisen evil and unwholesome states do not arise.
Having arisen, one is able to abandon them;
this is called the exertion of diligence.
Furthermore, there may be evil and unwholesome states.
Some unwholesome and evil dharmas arise solely through the power of conceptualization, not through the power of the object;
others arise both through the power of conceptualization and the power of the object.
"Arising solely through the power of conceptual construction and not through the power of objects" means that while remaining [in the present],
one generates those [cognitions] by reflecting upon past and future objects.
That which arises through the power of reflection and also through the power of the object refers to when,
while walking, one gives rise to that [thought] by taking a present object as its condition.
At that time, it should be understood that there will certainly also be irrational conceptualization (*ayoniśovikalpa*).
Among these, one should know that unwholesome and evil dharmas arise solely through the power of conceptualization,
and not through the power of the objective sphere (*viṣaya*).
If those [defilements] have not yet arisen, he causes them not to arise;
if they have already arisen, he is able to sever them.
This is called "exertion" (*pragraha*).
If [a thought] arises through the power of conceptualization as well as the power of its object,
then that which has not yet arisen can be prevented from arising,
and that which has already arisen can be severed.
This is called the arousal of diligent effort.
Regarding all wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen,
one generates the desire for their arising.
That is to say, regarding all wholesome dharmas that have not yet been attained and have not yet appeared before one,
one generates a mind of aspiration and a fervent resolve with the desire to attain them and cause them to appear.
The desire for attainment and the desire for manifestation arise;
this is called generating the desire for the sake of causing all unarisen wholesome dharmas to arise.
Regarding the desire to cause all already arisen wholesome dharmas to remain,
to prevent them from being forgotten or lost, and to bring them to full cultivation and perfection:
this refers to all wholesome dharmas that have already been acquired and are currently present.
These are called the wholesome dharmas that have already arisen.
Regarding these wholesome dharmas, having attained them and not lost them, and having attained them and not regressed from them, it is with reference to this that it is said:
"for the purpose of causing them to abide."
Regarding these wholesome dharmas, they are clearly manifest before one and free from dullness;
based on this, it is said that they are not forgotten.
These wholesome dharmas have already been brought into manifestation.
Through repeated cultivation, it reaches fulfillment and ultimate perfection;
based on this, it is said that one causes cultivation to be perfected,
giving rise to a fervent aspiration for these wholesome dharmas.
The desire for firm abiding, the desire for non-forgetfulness, and the desire for cultivation and fulfillment arise;
this is called generating the desire so that all already arisen wholesome dharmas may remain, not be forgotten, and be brought to full completion through cultivation.
"Exerting oneself" means causing that which has already been attained to manifest;
"arousing diligent effort" refers to this.
It is for the purpose of causing that which has not yet been attained to be attained.
Furthermore, "exertion" (vīrya) refers to the desire to cause wholesome states that have already arisen to endure and not be forgotten.
One who exerts diligent effort does so in order to bring them to full cultivation;
furthermore, regarding even inferior and middling wholesome dharmas.
To cause that which has not yet arisen to arise, and to cause that which has already arisen to remain and not be lost—
this is called exertion regarding superior wholesome qualities.
To cause that which has not yet arisen to arise, and once it has arisen, to bring it to full cultivation and perfection—
this is called exerting diligent effort (*vīrya*).
As for "striving to uplift the mind":
That is to say, when the mind applies itself with right effort and skillful means toward one-pointedness in the cultivation of śamatha,
so that various unarisen evil and unwholesome states do not arise.
To speak at length, even regarding all wholesome states that have already arisen,
because he desires to cause them to remain, to prevent their loss, and to bring them to full cultivation,
his mind may become excessively withdrawn within, becoming inferior or fearing inferiority due to these causes and conditions.
Having observed this, one then selects any one of the various signs of uplifting that are pure and sublime;
by diligently exerting oneself and gladdening the mind,
this is called "exerting the mind."
How does one hold the mind?
It means that when practicing uplifting, if the mind becomes agitated or if one fears it will become agitated,
having observed this, one then withdraws and collects the mind within once more.
Cultivating śamatha is called "holding the mind.
These four types are also called the "right efforts" (samyakpradhāna).
That is to say, regarding the phenomena of the dark side (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), one generates desire, exerts effort, arouses diligence,
and applies oneself with vigor to ensure that those not yet arisen do not arise,
and to ensure that those already arisen are abandoned; and one rouses the mind and sustains the mind.
These are the two right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*).
Regarding the dharmas of the white category (*śuklapakṣa*) that have not yet arisen, one desires their arising,
as was explained at length previously regarding the black category (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
One should know that these two right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*)— these four types— are also called right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*).
The first is called abandonment through restraint (*saṃvara-prahāṇa*),
which refers to [the effort] regarding evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen.
In order to bring about their abandonment, one generates desire and exerts effort;
this is explained at length.
This second is called "abandoning through abandonment" (*prahāṇaprahāṇa*).
That is to say, for the sake of not giving rise to unwholesome and unvirtuous states that have not yet arisen,
one generates desire and exerts effort;
and so forth, as explained at length.
Since unwholesome and unvirtuous states have already arisen,
one should cultivate restraint to bring them to cessation;
they must not be tolerated.
For this reason, it is called "restraint-abandonment.
Regarding those evil and unwholesome states that have not yet arisen,
it is the abandonment intended to prevent them from manifesting.
Because one desires to cause those [defilements] not to manifest and cuts them off for the sake of their abandonment,
it is called "abandonment through cutting off" (*prahāṇaprahāṇa*).
The third is called "abandonment through cultivation" (*bhāvanāprahāṇa*).
That is to say, for the sake of causing all unarisen wholesome dharmas to arise,
and so forth, up to rousing the mind and sustaining the mind;
this is because one repeatedly cultivates and repeatedly practices these wholesome dharmas.
That which was previously unattained is now brought into manifestation;
because it is capable of abandoning [defilements], it is called "abandonment through cultivation.
Fourth is "abandonment through protection."

That is to say, regarding all wholesome dharmas that have already arisen, for the purpose of causing them to endure— and so forth, as extensively explained, up to "exerting the mind" and "sustaining the mind"—
it refers to those wholesome dharmas that have already been attained and are currently manifest.
Distant from negligence, one cultivates heedfulness;
this enables wholesome qualities to remain without being lost and brings their cultivation to fulfillment,
thereby protecting all wholesome qualities already arisen.
Because it is capable of effecting abandonment,
it is called "abandonment through protection.
Having thus extensively analyzed the four right endeavors, [the text continues].
Furthermore, how is the summarized meaning herein to be understood?

It is for the purpose of demonstrating the perfection of the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) and the perfection of the application (*prayoga*) regarding the acts of abandoning and adopting within the categories of the black and white sides.
Therefore, the four right endeavors are proclaimed.
It should be understood that herein, through the arising of desire, the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) is perfected;
and through self-exertion, the arousal of diligence, the uplifting of the mind, and the sustaining of the mind, the application (*prayoga*) is perfected.
For a practitioner of yoga, there are only these two tasks that ought to be performed:
namely, the task of abandoning what is to be abandoned and the task of attaining what is to be attained.
First, one should give rise to aspiration and desire.
In order to sever the various fetters,
one should further, from time to time, diligently cultivate the signs of tranquility (śamatha), exertion (pragraha), and equanimity (upekṣā).
In order to sever all fetters and latent tendencies,
one should further cultivate and accumulate the wholesome dharmas that serve as their antidotes;
for the sake of manifesting all such activities, this is what must be done.
The four right efforts and the four right abandonments are called the summary meaning.
Following this, one further cultivates the four samādhis.
Namely, the samādhi of desire,
the samādhi of diligence,
and the samādhi of the mind.

If at this time one purely generates a desire for delight;
having generated that desire, [one contemplates] the intrinsic nature, causes and conditions, disadvantages, and remedies regarding all evil and unwholesome phenomena.
He correctly examines and investigates with one-pointed mindfulness the intrinsic nature,
causes and conditions, merits, and renunciation of all wholesome phenomena;
he dwells with one-pointed mindfulness, correctly examining and investigating them.
By means of such repeated cultivation,
one touches upon one-pointedness of mind and is able to distance oneself from all active obsessions (*paryavasthāna*) regarding all evil and unwholesome phenomena.
Yet, because the latent tendencies of the afflictions have not been permanently destroyed,
this is called the samādhi obtained through the predominant power of desire. If,
with respect to objects of focus in the past, future, or present...
It is able to conform to all evil and unwholesome dharmas,
and to conform to all afflictive entanglements of inferior, middling, and superior grades;
regarding those that have not yet arisen, it causes them not to arise.
Regarding those [defilements] that have already arisen,
in order to bring them to cessation, one exerts oneself, rouses oneself, and initiates diligent application toward that object;
one contemplates the intrinsic nature, causes and conditions, disadvantages, and remedies regarding that objective sphere.
Abiding in one-pointed mindfulness through correct investigation and examination,
by means of such frequent stabilization,
one is able to correctly give rise to one-pointedness of mind.
That which enables one to distance oneself from the active entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) of all existing evil and unwholesome phenomena,
yet does not yet permanently destroy the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions—
this is called the samādhi obtained through the predominant power of diligence.
Furthermore, if one rouses inferior states of mind,
or restrains and sustains agitated states of mind,
or at times cultivates superior equanimity;
By means of these causes and conditions, regarding all evil and unwholesome dharmas,
as well as those things that conform to evil and unwholesome dharmas and those that conform to wholesome dharmas—
namely, their intrinsic nature, causes and conditions, disadvantages, benefits, antidotes, and renunciation— [he understands them].
Abiding in one-pointed mindfulness through correct investigation and examination,
by means of such frequent stabilization,
one is able to correctly give rise to one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
To speak at length, this is called the concentration attained through the dominant power of the mind.
If one attends to and contemplates those factors conducive to evil and unwholesome states as being improper,
[this is known as improper attention].
Furthermore, one attends to all wholesome dharmas that are conducive [to liberation] with correct mental attention;
thus, one becomes detached from those various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).

Furthermore, because it can give rise to all wholesome dharmas— of which the meditative concentration that serves as the primary antidote to the various entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) is the foremost—
it causes all evil and unwholesome dharmas to never manifest again.
He then reflected to himself:
"Is it that there currently exist, and I am currently experiencing, evil and unwholesome states which I do not perceive?
Or is it that there currently do not exist, and I am not currently experiencing, evil and unwholesome states which I do not perceive?"
I should thoroughly examine this;
by the predominant power of that examination-attention (*manasikāra*),
he correctly examines for himself what has been abandoned and what has not yet been abandoned.
By correctly examining with one-pointed mindfulness,
and through dwelling extensively in this manner,
one is able to correctly touch and realize one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*).
By reason of this, one is free from overweening pride;
one knows for oneself as it truly is: "I am liberated from the mind's entanglements (paryavasthāna), but I am not yet liberated from the mind's all-encompassing latent tendencies (anuśaya)."
I have only attained and cultivated those wholesome dharmas— headed by meditative concentration— that serve as the antidotes to the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*),
but I have not yet attained or cultivated the antidotes to the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
This is called the samādhi obtained through the predominant power of contemplation.
By means of the predominant power of these four types of samādhi,
he has already distanced himself from all envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).
Furthermore, it is for the sake of permanently eliminating all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of every kind of evil and unwholesome phenomena,
and for the sake of cultivating and accumulating those wholesome phenomena that serve as their antidotes.
He then further generates desire and exerts effort;
the detailed explanation of the method for practicing the four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*) is as previously described.
While he is thus correctly practicing, there are eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*).
They proceed with differentiation for the sake of permanently destroying all latent tendencies (anuśaya) and for the sake of attaining the perfection of samādhi.
What are the eight kinds of abandonments?
First is desire (*chanda*),
which refers to the arising of such aspiration and longing.
"When shall I cultivate samādhi so that it becomes perfected?
When shall I be able to eradicate all latent tendencies (anuśaya) of evil and unwholesome dharmas?"
Second is exertion,
which means not relinquishing application until all remedies have been cultivated.
Third is faith.
This means that because one does not abandon application and remains correctly established,
one develops deep faith and understanding toward what has been realized above.
Fourth is tranquility.
That is to say, with pure faith as the foremost, a state of joy arises in the mind;
because the mind is joyful, the heavy burdens of all categories of evil and unwholesome dharmas are gradually pacified and eliminated.
Fifth is mindfulness,
which refers to nine aspects;
[it consists of] these nine aspects.
Sixth is correct awareness (*saṃprajanya*), which refers to the wisdom belonging to the category of *vipaśyanā*, because it is able to sustain the mind as it abides in the category of *śamatha*.
Seventh is volition (*cetanā*).
It refers to mental formation;
it is the formation of the mind at the time of correctly examining what has been abandoned and what has not yet been abandoned.
It initiates bodily and vocal actions that accord with the two categories of calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā).
Eighth is equanimity (upekṣā),
which refers to the practice regarding the past, future, and present.
While conforming to various evil and unwholesome states, there is no defilement in the mind;
this mental equanimity allows for the discerning knowledge of the abandonment of latent tendencies through two causes and conditions.
That is to say, it is by means of volition regarding objects that are not directly perceived,
and by means of equanimity regarding objects that are directly perceived;
these are called the eight types of formative acts of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*).
They are also called "superior practices" (*viśeṣa-caryā*).
These eight kinds of abandonment-practices (*prahāṇa-saṃskāra*) and superior practices constitute the yoga for overcoming the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
In this context, "desire" (chanda) is that very desire;
in this context, "exertion" (pragraha) is that very vigor (vīrya).
In this context, faith is precisely that same faith;
herein, there are also serenity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, volition, and equanimity.
That very means is as follows:
herein, there are first the four samādhis, such as desire and so forth,
and then the eight kinds of exertions (prahāṇasaṃskāra) now described.
When one fully accomplishes the samādhi for the permanent abandonment of all latent tendencies (anuśaya),

this is collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through the cultivation of the exertions for abandoning desire" (chanda-samādhi-prahāṇa-saṃskāra-samanvāgata-ṛddhipāda).
The basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of energy and the accomplishment of the formations of abandonment;
the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind and the accomplishment of the formations of abandonment;
and the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of investigation and the accomplishment of the formations of abandonment.
Question: For what reason and by what causal conditions is it called "supernormal power" (ṛddhipāda)?
Answer: Just as one who possesses feet is able to go and return, to leap and bound with vigor and strength, and is able to attain and realize all the extraordinary and sublime dharmas of the world.
The sublime qualities of the world are called "divine" (*ṛddhi*);
because one can reach these through them, they are called "bases of divine power" (*ṛddhipāda*).
Thus, when such dharmas as these are fully perfected and accomplished through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), [they constitute the bases of divine power].
That mind is thus pure, bright white, and free from all defilements;
being detached from secondary afflictions,
it abides in uprightness, possesses capability, and attains immovability, such that it can go and return, leap and bound with vigor and strength.
One is able to attain and realize supramundane dharmas;
because of the supreme mastery over these supramundane dharmas, this is the supreme *ṛddhi*.
Since one is able to realize this, it is called a "basis of supernormal power" (*ṛddhipāda*).
Relying upon and taking as his support such superior samādhi,
he is able to further cultivate the yoga pertaining to the training in higher mind and the training in higher wisdom.
By virtue of practicing this yoga through diligent cultivation,
one develops profound resolve and deep pure faith toward the realizations attained by the disciples of other great teachers.
This pure faith is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) because it has the sense of being predominant.
Question: In what respect is it predominant?
Answer: It is predominant as the forerunner in the ability to give rise to supramundane phenomena (*lokottaradharma*).
Furthermore, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom serve as the predominant conditions for their own arising; likewise,
the remaining factors such as diligence serve as the predominant conditions for the arising of supramundane dharmas.
And regarding that which can arise, there is a successive progression up to wisdom being its predominant condition;
even that wisdom has as its predominant condition only the ability to give rise to supramundane dharmas.
Therefore, faith and the others are called the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
Furthermore, if one understands that there is a distinction between what has been realized previously and what is realized subsequently,
one will accordingly be able [to progress] toward each subsequent realization of supramundane dharmas (*lokottara-dharma*).
One generates profound resolute conviction and profound pure faith.
Because this pure faith has the sense of being difficult to overcome, it is called the "power of faith.
Question: Who is unable to overcome it?
Answer: This pure faith—
whether by devas, māras, śramaṇas,
brāhmaṇas, or anyone else in the world.
There is nothing conforming to the Dharma that can lead it astray or seize it;
even the fetters of the various afflictions cannot subdue it.
Therefore, it is called "difficult to overcome."
This is the foremost and this is the precursor; the other factors such as diligence are also called "powers.
By means of these powers, one possesses great majesty and subdues all the forces of the māra armies.
Because it is able to realize the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava),
it is called a power (bala).
One should contemplate the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya) and the power of faith (śraddhābala) within this context.
It is the pure faith contained within the four types of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*).
Why is this? Because it is the verified confidence belonging to one who has entered into the state of rightness and transcendence of birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
All of these arise from this cause, this condition, and this sequence;
that [result] is precisely the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala) of this.
Therefore, the Blessed One, with respect to the principle of the mutual connection between cause and effect, [taught as follows].
It is said that one should contemplate those very purities of realization (avetyaprasāda),
yet they are neither identical to its substance nor identical to its characteristics;
rather, one should contemplate within this the faculty and power of diligence (vīryendriya-bala).
This refers to the diligence found within the four right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Which abandonment is this?
It is that which can permanently sever all afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Regarding "skillful right exertion" (*samyakprahāṇa*),
the intended meaning here is this very right exertion,
because by means of this right exertion one is ultimately able to abandon all evil and unwholesome dharmas.
One should contemplate herein the faculty of mindfulness and the power of mindfulness;
these are precisely the right mindfulness contained within the four foundations of mindfulness,
meaning that the four foundations of mindfulness are able to sever all inversions without exception.
One should contemplate herein the faculty of concentration and the power of concentration;
that is, all right concentration found within the four dhyānas— namely,
those dhyānas which serve as the means for realizing the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
One should contemplate herein the faculty of wisdom and the power of wisdom,
which constitute all correct knowledge regarding the Four Noble Truths; that is,
the knowledge of the Noble Truths which is able to realize clear comprehension (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Noble Truths and attain the fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
Precisely by means of these faculties and powers,
through the causal conditions of gradual cultivation, gradual practice, and repeated intensive cultivation,
one is able to give rise to the four kinds of wholesome roots conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), categorized as inferior, intermediate, and superior.
What are the four? First, heat;
second, the summit; third, receptivity to the truths; and fourth, the supreme mundane dharmas.
It is, for example, like a person who wishes to perform the functions of fire by means of fire.
For the sake of seeking fire, he places dry wood below and applies a fire-drill above;
with diligent exertion and courageous effort, he drills for it.
While he is thus diligently exerting himself and courageously drilling,
Upon the lower wood, heat first arises;
next, as the heat increases, the hot vapor surges upward;
then, as it intensifies further, smoke is produced.
Next, flameless fire suddenly flows forth;
as soon as the fire emerges, fierce flames arise,
and once these fierce flames have arisen, they are able to perform the functions of fire.
Just as a person drilling for fire exerts themselves with diligence, vigor, and perseverance in their drilling,
so too should it be understood that the gradual cultivation, gradual practice, and repeated cultivation of the five faculties and the five powers proceed in the same manner.
Just as the initial warmth produced upon wood,
so too should the root of goodness that is warmth be understood;
for it is the precursor to the arising of the fire of untainted dharmas that burns away all afflictions.
Just as when warmth increases, the hot vapor surges upward,
one should know that the roots of goodness at the crown of the head are likewise;
it is like smoke subsequently arising.
One should know that the patience in accordance with the truths (*anulomikī kṣānti*) is likewise.
Just as a flameless fire suddenly bursts forth,
one should know that the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) are likewise.
Just as a fierce flame arises immediately after fire,

one should know that the supramundane, untainted noble dharmas arising immediately after the five faculties and five powers subsumed within the "highest mundane dharma" (laukikāgra-dharma) are likewise so.
What, moreover, is this?
It refers to the seven factors of enlightenment for those individuals who have already entered into the state of rightness and transcendence from birth.
Because the wisdom of realization as it truly is takes these as its factors, they are called "factors of enlightenment" (bodhyaṅga).
These seven factors of realization as it truly is are subsumed within three categories.
That is to say, three factors of enlightenment are subsumed under the category of śamatha;
three factors of enlightenment are subsumed under the category of vipaśyanā;
and one factor of enlightenment is subsumed under both categories.
Therefore, they are called the seven factors of enlightenment:
namely, the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (dharma-vicaya-sambodhyanga) and the factor of enlightenment of diligence (vīrya-sambodhyanga).
The factor of enlightenment of joy is subsumed under this category of insight;
the factor of enlightenment of tranquility...
The factor of enlightenment of concentration and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity—
these three are subsumed under the category of tranquility (śamatha).
The single factor of the awakening factor of mindfulness is subsumed under both categories and is called "universal" (sarvatraga). Because he has,
at that time, first attained the seven awakening factors, he is called a "first-stage learner" (ādikarmika-śaikṣa).
Having seen the path to the noble truths, one has forever severed all afflictions to be abandoned by the path of seeing;
only the afflictions to be abandoned by the path of cultivation remain.
To abandon those, one cultivates the Noble Eightfold Path comprised within the three aggregates.
Among these, right view, right thought, and right effort are subsumed under the aggregate of wisdom;
right speech, right action, and right livelihood [are subsumed under the aggregate of morality].
Right mindfulness and right concentration are subsumed under the aggregate of morality;
concentration is subsumed under the aggregate of concentration.
Question: For what reason is it called the Noble Eightfold Path?

Answer: Because for all noble learners who have already seen the tracks, the path of practice and the right path are subsumed within these eight factors, enabling them to completely and without remainder abandon all afflictions.
One is able to realize liberation in its ultimate perfection;
therefore, it is called the Noble Eightfold Path.
It should be understood that herein, the true awakening attained at the time of the factors of enlightenment—
Having attained that, one establishes it through wisdom and realizes it as it was realized;
the synthesis of these two is collectively termed right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
By the predominant power of this right view, [the path proceeds].
The arising of the conceptualization of renunciation, non-ill will, and non-harming is called right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
When the mind enters into various objects of thought,
it engages only in such modes of searching as those characterized by these [qualities].
If the mind enters into various discourses,
then by the predominant power of right view, one gives rise to wholesome reflection and initiates various forms of discourse in accordance with the Dharma.
This is called right speech.
If one seeks clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, medicinal requisites for illness, and personal belongings in accordance with the Dharma,
one dwells with clear comprehension whether going out or returning during that pursuit.
Whether looking ahead or looking aside, whether bending or stretching,
whether carrying the robes and bowl or the saṃghāṭī,
whether eating, drinking, chewing, or tasting, one dwells with clear comprehension.
Or, while dwelling, regarding matters such as the pursuit of clothing and so forth—
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—
and so on in detail until: whether dispelling weariness and sleep, he dwells with clear comprehension.
This is called right action (samyak-karmānta).
It consists of seeking clothing, food and drink, and even household utensils in accordance with the Dharma,
while remaining far removed from all things that give rise to wrong livelihood (mithyājīva).
This is called right livelihood.
If one is far removed from [wrong] speech, action, and livelihood,
then at the time of realizing the attention that is free from outflows (*anāsrava-manasikāra*) and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), these have already been previously attained.
Question: Why is this called the "precepts beloved by the noble ones" (*āryakānta-śīla*)?
Answer: Because all noble ones—those who are virtuous, excellent, and rightly attained—have long cherished, delighted in, yearned for, and found pleasure in them.
"When shall I truly attain the restraint of non-engagement in all verbal misconduct, physical misconduct, and wrong livelihood? For by means of that,
throughout the long night, my heart will deeply love, yearn for, and take delight in this ethical discipline."
Therefore, when it is attained, it is called "the morality beloved by the noble ones.
Having thus attained this morality beloved by the noble ones,
one never speaks a deliberate falsehood without clear comprehension.
He never intentionally takes the life of a living being;
he never intentionally takes what is not given;
and he never intentionally engages in sexual misconduct.
He never seeks clothing or other requisites through unrighteous means.
Precisely by the predominant power of such virtue cherished by the noble ones,
all his verbal, physical, and livelihood-related activities proceed during the cultivation of the path.
These are also termed right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
For one who relies upon right view and right intention and diligently practices right speech, right action, and right livelihood,
there arises a desire, exertion, diligence, renunciation, heroism, power, and arousal of effort that inspires and rouses the mind.
Uninterrupted continuity is called right effort.
One who accomplishes such right effort does so through the predominant power of the four foundations of mindfulness.
Attaining right mindfulness, which is comprised of nine types of non-erroneous mental aspects, one is able to encompass the mental abiding that consists of those same nine types of aspects;
this is called right mindfulness and right concentration.
Thus, this entire Noble Eightfold Path is established as two types:
namely, that which is to be practiced while not remaining [in meditative equipoise] and that which is to be practiced while remaining [in meditative equipoise].
That which is without action refers to right speech, right action, and right livelihood;
that which abides in action refers to...
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
namely, śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Right view, right thought, and right effort constitute vipaśyanā.
Right mindfulness and right concentration constitute śamatha.
Taking such purified right speech, right action, and right livelihood as a basis,
one practices śamatha and vipaśyanā from time to time.
It is able to sever all fetters without remainder, achieving their permanent eradication,
and is able to attain the supreme fruit of arhatship;
this continuous succession over a long period is called the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
Because one has long practiced the severance of afflictions,
the sudden arising of wisdom is called the Path of Seeing;
for the momentary arising of this wisdom is capable of permanently severing all afflictions.
For this reason, right speech, action,
and livelihood are only established during the stage of cultivating the path.
Through such gradual cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) by means of preparatory applications and skillful methods, [the path is realized].
This is called the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment.
What is the fruit of cultivation?
It refers to the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
First, the fruit of stream-entry;
second, the fruit of once-returning;
third, the fruit of non-returning.
The four supreme fruits of arhatship,
O śramaṇa—
what is meant by "fruit"?
That is to say, the noble path is called the śramaṇa,
and the abandonment of afflictions is called the fruit.
Furthermore, the subsequent path may be either middling or superior.
This is the fruit produced by the path cultivated in previous lives.
Question: For what reason are these four fruits established?
Answer: Because they serve as remedies for the four types of afflictions.
This refers to those non-existent things that are capable of inducing rebirth in the miserable destinies and serve as the causes for going to those miserable destinies;
because the afflictions have been abandoned and because their antidotes have arisen.
Regarding the establishment of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*),
the Blessed One stated that this fruit is established through the permanent abandonment of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
This means that there are three grades [of practitioners], and because these three types of fetters obstruct the Noble Path and prevent it from arising.
1. The Chapter on Householders;
2. The Chapter on the Ill-spoken Dharma and Vinaya;
3. The Chapter on the Well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya.
Based on the category of householders, there exists the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Due to this view, fear arises first,
such that one initially has no desire to set out upon the Noble Path.
Based on the category of the poorly taught Dharma and Vinaya, there arises the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Due to this grasping, although one has already set out [on the path], one proceeds in a deviant manner;
because of this, one is unable to give rise to the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
There may be doubt regarding the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya;
because of this doubt, although one has already set out on the path and does not practice perversely,
one has not yet become habituated to the right path.
Regarding the objects of knowledge as they truly are,
hesitation and doubt act as obstacles that prevent the Noble Path from arising;
for this reason, it is taught that the fruit of Stream-entry is established solely through the abandonment of these.
This fruit of stream-entry has at most seven remaining existences;
by reason of this, although many births may continue in succession,
once the afflictions that cause rebirth have been severed, birth no longer continues in succession.

The establishment of the fruit of Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) means that if one has permanently abandoned all afflictions pertaining to the continuity of rebirth included within the realms of gods and humans,
such that one will experience at most one more birth as a god and one more birth as a human.
Therefore, at that time, the fruit of Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) is established.
If one has already permanently abandoned those afflictions that cause rebirth in this [realm],
one shall only undergo birth within the celestial realms.
At that very moment, the fruit of non-returning is established;
if one has already permanently severed all afflictions capable of inducing rebirth in existence,
the supreme fruit of arhatship is established.
The Bhagavat taught that by permanently severing the three fetters (saṃyojana) and binding greed,
hatred, and delusion, one establishes the fruit of a Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin).
By permanently severing those [fetters] conducive to the five lower-tier fetters (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana), one establishes the fruit of a Non-returner (anāgāmin).
The permanent severance of all afflictions and the ultimate establishment of the supreme fruit of arhatship is called the fruit of cultivation.
Furthermore, among these, for those who practice through desire, hatred, delusion, pride, or discursive thought:
He should first purify his practice by means of the object of pure conduct;
only then will he realize the mind’s perfect composure.
He [should apply this] to each respective object of focus.
It is certainly through the power of the distinction of the object of focus that one diligently cultivates the preparatory application;
this applies to a person of balanced temperament (*samabhāga-pudgala*).
One diligently applies effort by taking as an object whatever is pleasing; thus, through such diligent application,
one merely causes the mind to abide, rather than purifying one's conduct,
as is the case with a person of equal temperament (*sama-bhāga-carita*).
One who practices with attenuated defilements should know that it is likewise so;
yet there is a distinction among those various practices.
That is to say, when one whose temperament is dominated by greed and so forth exerts themselves in practice:
It requires a long duration before one realizes abiding of the mind; however,
for those whose afflictions are equally distributed,
they are able to realize abiding of the mind without much time when they apply themselves diligently to practice.
When one who is of the "thin-dust" temperament practices diligently, they are able to realize mental abiding with the utmost swiftness.
Question: Previously, the distinctions in the characteristics of the conduct of individuals (pudgala) characterized by desire and so forth were explained in detail.
What are the characteristics of the individuals who are of equal temperament (*sama-bhāga-carita*) and those who are of slight defilement (*tanu-rajas-carita*)?
Answer: As for those of equal temperament:
Just as a person characterized by greed and so forth possesses all the modes of conduct,
yet those modes of conduct are neither superior nor preeminent,
being merely like that of one characterized by greed and so forth.
There are various designations established according to the conditions encountered;
this practice is similar to that.
As for the specific characteristics of the person (pudgala) of attenuated defilements:
That is to say: being free from heavy obstacles,
being pure from the very beginning,
and having already perfected the provisions.
Possessing abundant pure faith,
they have achieved wisdom and are endowed with all merits.
"Endowed with all merits and free from heavy obstructions" means being without the three obstructions.
What are the three?
First, the obstacle of karma;
second, the obstacle of afflictions.
Third is the obstacle of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the "obstacle of karma" (*karmāvaraṇa*),
it refers to the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantaryakarma*) and all other intentionally committed karmas that are particularly grave.
When that matured fruit (*vipākaphala*) is actualized,
it can obstruct the right path and prevent its arising;
this is called the obstruction of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*).
The afflictive hindrance refers to intense afflictions and long-lasting afflictions;
by means of these afflictions, within this present life...
Because various objects of pure conduct cannot bring about purification,
this is called the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
As for the obstacle of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*):
This means that in certain places of birth, the Noble Path does not arise or grow;
yet, in those very places of birth, the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) arises.
Or, there may be places of birth where the Noble Path, depending upon them, does indeed attain growth.
Within that state, the fruit of maturation arises:
they are deaf, mentally deficient, dull-witted, blind, and mute, communicating by means of hand gestures;
they lack the power or capacity to understand the meaning of well-spoken or ill-spoken teachings.
This is called the obstacle of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
"Initial purity" refers to perfectly pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) and upright view (*dṛṣṭi*).
The precepts are well-purified through ten causes and conditions,
as should be understood from what was stated previously.
Regarding "one with upright views":
That is to say, because it is associated with pure faith,
associated with resolute conviction,
and free from deceit and guile.
Because one reflects well upon the meaning of the Dharma, being without confusion or doubt, and because of the application of effort toward liberation,
it is called "uprightness.
Such is upright view.
Because it is associated with pure faith,
one cannot be led astray from the Buddha’s true Dharma and Vinaya;
because it is associated with resolute conviction.

Regarding the inconceivable majestic power and spiritual might of the Tathāgatas and their noble disciples, the inconceivable distinctions of their places of birth, the profound teachings on the unconditioned, and matters that cannot be predicted.
They give rise to profound conviction, being without alarm, without fear, and without dread;
because they are far removed from deceit and flattery,
their view is upright.
These upright individuals practice correctly according to the holy teaching;
they manifest themselves in accordance with reality because they apply themselves to renunciation through the correct contemplation of the meaning of the Dharma, free from confusion and doubt.
Regarding the meanings of all phenomena as impermanent, suffering, empty, selfless, and so forth,
one correctly contemplates, correctly deliberates, and correctly examines them.
With this as the cause, one becomes free from confusion and doubt.
Having distanced oneself from the two paths and attained advancement,
the aforementioned view characterized by these four aspects is called "straightforward view" for one who has already fulfilled the provisions.
The detailed explanation of the accumulations should be understood as previously stated;
briefly, there are four kinds.
First, the accumulation of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*).
Second, the accumulation of wisdom;
third, the accumulation from previous lives;
fourth, the accumulation in the present life.
The equipment of merit refers to that by which one now obtains abundant wealth and resources conducive to practice,
and encounters true fields of merit as spiritual friends.
Being free from all obstacles, one is able to practice with diligence.
As for the accumulation of wisdom,
it means that by means of this, one achieves intelligence, strength, and capability.
Having understood the meaning of well-spoken and ill-spoken teachings,
one obtains the instructions, exhortations, and admonitions that accord with the Dharma and its meaning;
this is the equipment from previous lives.
This means that by virtue of having accumulated roots of goodness in past lives,
one now attains the perfection of the faculties;
as for the provisions for the present life:
This means that in this present life, there is a desire for wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*), the faculties are matured,
and one is endowed with the restraint of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*) and the restraint of the faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*),
as explained in detail previously.
One who possesses abundant pure faith is one who,
regarding the Great Teacher, is without confusion or doubt,
and gives rise to deep pure faith as well as resolute conviction.
As it is toward the Great Teacher,
so it is toward the Dharma and the training;
the rest should be understood as previously explained in detail.
The accomplishment of wisdom means that by means of this,
one is able to quickly comprehend both the phenomena and their meanings, and even after a long period of time,
one is able to retain them without forgetting either the phenomena or their meanings.
One is able to swiftly penetrate both the Dharma and its meaning.
Regarding "possessing all merits," this means that by virtue of these merits,
one's physical form is upright and majestic, such that all people delight in beholding it.
They shall give rise to pure faith, be free from illness and long-lived;
their speech shall be earnest and dignified, and they shall possess great noble lineage.
They shall be well-known to all and achieve great merit.
They will obtain many requisites for life, such as robes and other necessities,
and will be honored, revered, respected, and praised by kings, ministers, and others.
"One endowed with all virtues" refers to the natural accomplishment of various virtues,
such as having extremely few desires and so forth.
The characteristics of the adornments of a śramaṇa as previously described should be understood;
such categories as these should be known as the distinctions in the characteristics of the conduct of individuals whose defilements are thin.
What are the different designations for a person (pudgala)?
There are six kinds. What are these six?
First, the śramaṇa;
second, the brāhmaṇa;
third, the brahmacarya.
Fourth, the bhikṣu;
fifth, the diligent practitioner;
sixth, the renunciant.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of first śramaṇas:
the śramaṇa who excels in the path,
and the śramaṇa who speaks of the path.
Third, the śramaṇa who lives by the path;
fourth, the śramaṇa who ruins the path.
It should be known that those called Sugatas are the śramaṇas who have attained the supreme path.
Those who correctly expound the True Dharma are called śramaṇas who proclaim the Path.
Those who practice virtuous conduct are called śramaṇas who live by the Path.
Those who engage in deviant conduct are called śramaṇas who destroy the Path.
The "Sugatas" refers to those who have realized the complete and permanent exhaustion of greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth;
they are the "Proclaimers of the True Dharma."
This refers to proclaiming the true Dharma for the sake of subduing greed, hatred, and delusion;
and practicing wholesome conduct,
which means diligently cultivating right practice for the sake of subduing greed, hatred, and delusion.
One who practices deviant conduct refers to one who violates the śīla and engages in various unwholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are called śramaṇas of the supreme path.
Because the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) destroys all afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation;
if there were no Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas who diligently cultivate correct practice for the sake of enlightenment (bodhi).
Those among the assembly of śrāvakas who uphold the Tripiṭaka are called "śramaṇas who speak the Path";
they maintain the mundane Dharma and Vinaya.
In order to turn the eye of the true Dharma so that it shall not be interrupted:
if there are ordinary individuals (*pṛthagjana-pudgala*) whose natures are well-disciplined,
who diligently cultivate correct practice for their own benefit.
Possessing a sense of shame and remorse, one delights in right training in order to attain what has not yet been attained and to realize what has not yet been realized.
In order to realize what has not yet been realized,
they diligently cultivate the preparatory applications;
possessing power and capability, they are fit to attain what has not yet been attained.
One who is capable of touching what has not yet been touched and capable of realizing what has not yet been realized is called a śramaṇa on the path of life.
Because they currently possess the various wholesome dharmas of "warmth," which are capable of generating the life-faculty of noble wisdom,
they are said to be "living" and not "dead."
Therefore, they are called "shamans who live by the path.
As for those individuals who violate the precepts and frequently practice unwholesome dharmas—
extensively described up to those who, while not actually practicing the holy life, claim to practice the holy life— [they are shamans who live by the path].
He is called a śramaṇa who ruins the path;
because he destroys the very root of the original right path,
he is powerless and incapable, lacking the capacity to generate the path.
Although there are currently those who preach the path of the True Dharma and there are currently those who realize the path of the True Dharma,
he does not obtain [the fruit thereof].
For this reason, he is called a monk who destroys the path.
The Blessed One, based on this, spoke thus:
"This is the first śramaṇa," and so on at length, up to "the fourth śramaṇa.
[These] are empty and non-existent among the teachings of the external śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
Wherever the Noble Eightfold Path can be established,
there exist the first śramaṇa, and so forth, up to the fourth śramaṇa.
The second type of brāhmaṇa is further divided into three kinds:
first, the brāhmaṇa by birth;
second, the brāhmaṇa by name and designation.
Third, the brahmin by right conduct.
Regarding the brahmin by birth:
this refers to one who is born into a brahmin family.
Born from the mother’s birth canal,
one who is fully endowed with both parents is called a brāhmaṇa;
this is what is meant by the designation "brāhmaṇa."
That is to say, it is by virtue of their perceptions and conventional designations that people in the world employ the verbal expression "brāhmaṇa.
As for those who are true practitioners of the brāhmaṇa way:
This means that the task to be accomplished has been definitively finalized;
one has already been able to expel evil and unwholesome states.
This should be understood as it was taught.
The Brahmin has nothing further to do;
his task is already accomplished.
This is what is called a Brahmin.
The third holy life (brahmacarya) further has three types:
first, the holy life of undertaking seclusion;
second, the holy life of temporary cessation.
Third, the ultimate abandonment of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
One who undertakes the seclusion of the holy life is one who is able to undertake training in the seclusion from all forms of non-holy conduct and the practice of sexual desire.
The temporary abandonment of the holy life refers to ordinary beings who,
by means of the mundane path, become free from desire for the desire realm.
The ultimate abandonment of the holy life refers to...
This refers to those noble ones who have attained the fruit of non-returning and further attained the supreme fruit of arhatship.
Furthermore, there are five types of fourth bhikṣus.
First, the mendicant bhikṣu;
second, the self-proclaimed bhikṣu;
third, the nominal bhikṣu.
Fourth, the bhikṣu who has destroyed the afflictions;
fifth, the bhikṣu who has received full ordination through the white fourfold *karmavācanā*.
Regarding the fifth, diligent practice, there are again three kinds.
First, the diligence of ceasing transgressions of the precepts,
which means being able to distance oneself from all unwholesome physical and verbal actions.
Second, the diligence of ceasing [attachment to] sense objects.
This refers to closely guarding the doors of the sense faculties, cultivating protective mindfulness and constant mindfulness,
as explained in detail previously;
and third, the diligent application of effort to pacify the afflictions.
That is to say, it is that which can forever sever all afflictions abandoned through seeing and cultivation,
as well as all previously arisen thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, or thoughts of harm.
Whether it be greed, hatred, or various wrong views;
or anger, resentment, concealment, vexation, deceit, and flattery—
these can lead one to evil places such as the hells and other perilous, miserable realms.
These are not the dharmas of a śramaṇa;
as they arise, he does not tolerate them,
but immediately cuts them off, eliminates them, and casts them out.
It should be understood that, in this context, there are briefly two kinds of cessation of afflictions:
first, the cessation of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
second, the cessation of active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
The sixth, renunciation, is further of two kinds:
first, those who go forth within a well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya;
second, those who go forth within a poorly expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
Those who have gone forth within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya—
namely, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs—
and who are themselves able to transcend all evil and unwholesome states within their own bodies.
One should know that this is called true renunciation.
As for those who renounce within a poorly taught Dharma and Vinaya—
namely, the various non-Buddhist practitioners who are either entirely naked or wear discolored robes.
There are also those such as the ash-smearing ascetics and other superior non-Buddhists (tīrthika), as well as many other similar types of non-Buddhists;
therefore, it is said: "If there are any śramaṇas..."
Whether they be brahmins,
those practicing the holy life, bhikṣus,
those who are diligent, or those who have gone forth.
All these are synonyms for the *saṃskṛta-pudgala* (the person who undergoes repeated existence).
Briefly stated, there are eight kinds of causes and conditions for the establishment of the *pudgala*.
Briefly, there are four kinds.
What are the eight types of persons (*pudgala*)?
First, those who possess capability.
Second, those who lack capability;
third, those who skillfully understand the means;
fourth, those who do not skillfully understand the means.
Fifth, those who practice without interruption;
sixth, those who do not practice without interruption;
seventh, those who have already cultivated the practice repeatedly.
Regarding the eight who have not yet practiced cultivation:
what are the causal conditions for establishing the four types of *pudgalas*?
They are established by means of four kinds of differentiated causal conditions.
Eight types of individuals (pudgala) are established:
first, by way of the distinction of faculties (indriya),
there are those whose faculties are already matured and those whose faculties are not yet matured.
Second, by way of the distinction of yoga,
there are those who are skilled in yoga and those who are unskilled in yoga.
Third, by way of the distinction of application (*prayoga*).
There is cultivation that is both uninterrupted and ardent, as well as cultivation that is neither uninterrupted nor ardent;
these four distinctions arise from differences in time.
There is also cultivation that has been practiced for a long duration and cultivation that has not yet been practiced for a long duration.
How do these four kinds of distinctions serve as the causal conditions for establishing the preceding eight types of persons?
It is said that one whose faculties are already perfected is "one who possesses capability."
One whose faculties are not yet perfected lacks the capacity;
one who well understands yoga is one who well understands skillful means,
while one who does not well understand yoga is one who does not well understand skillful means.
One who possesses uninterrupted and ardent cultivation is one who possesses uninterrupted cultivation;
this is also called possessing constant and deliberate cultivation.
One who lacks uninterrupted and ardent cultivation is one who lacks uninterrupted cultivation.
This is also called "cultivation that is neither constant nor diligent.
For one who has practiced the path for a long time, it is already familiarized;
for one who has not practiced the path for a long time, it is not yet familiarized.
Thus, it is called [the classification] by way of differences in faculties,
differences in yoga,
differences in application, and differences in time.
Eight types of persons are established.
If there are any persons whose faculties are not yet perfected,
they possess skillful means regarding all that is wholesome, and they have practiced it without interruption and have already cultivated it repeatedly.
They are unable to discern anything according to principle, according to the Dharma,
or with skillful means. Even if certain individuals have mature faculties,
they may not yet be well-versed in skillful means.
Furthermore, they are unable to discern any of those things that exist.
If there are individuals whose faculties have already matured,
who well understand skillful means, and who practice without interruption;
They will not be able to attain swift superknowledge.
As for those individuals whose faculties are already matured,
who are well-versed in skillful means, and who have practiced without interruption yet have not yet become thoroughly habituated through repeated cultivation—
That is, while all that one has personally undertaken to do has not yet been accomplished,
there are certain individuals whose faculties are already matured,
who well understand skillful means, and who have practiced without interruption and have become thoroughly habituated through repeated cultivation.
He is able to accomplish everything that exists,
and he is also able to attain swift super-knowledge;
thus, all his own tasks have already been accomplished.
One should know that there are, in brief, four kinds of māras.
The activities of the māras are of immeasurable variety;
yogins who diligently cultivate contemplative practice should thoroughly understand them and correctly distance themselves from them.
What are the four māras?
First, the māra of the aggregates (skandhamāra);
second, the māra of afflictions (kleśamāra).
Third is the māra of death;
fourth is the māra of the devas;
and the māra of the aggregates.
This refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
As for the māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*),
it refers to all afflictions within the three realms.
The Māra of Death refers to the premature loss,
passing away, and demise of various sentient beings from their respective communities of sentient beings.
The Māra of the Deva King (Māra-devaputra) refers to...
This refers to when one who is diligently cultivating the supreme categories of virtue seeks to transcend the three māras— the aggregates, the afflictions, and death—
at which time there arises a most exalted son of the gods in the desire realm who has attained great sovereignty.
That which creates obstacles and initiates various disruptive activities is called the celestial Māra.
It should be understood that herein, that upon which death depends is [the basis].
Whether it is that which causes death,
whether it is death itself,
or whether it constitutes an obstacle to death such that one does not transcend it.
Based on these four types, the four māras are established.
That is to say, death exists only because of the five aggregates of clinging that have already arisen and entered the present;
and through afflictions, one brings about future birth.
Once born, there is inevitably death, passing away, and perishing.
For all classes of sentient beings, the exhaustion and cessation of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), their passing away and perishing,
is the very nature of death.
When one who diligently cultivates virtue applies themselves correctly to the practice in order to transcend death,
that Devaputra Māra attains great mastery and is able to create obstacles.
Due to these obstacles, they may be unable to emerge from the phenomena of death.
Or, it may take a very long time and extreme hardship before one can transcend them.
Furthermore, Māra may temporarily lack mastery over certain individuals,
namely, ordinary worldlings who have attained detachment through the mundane path.
Either remaining in this world or being born there,
Māra gains great mastery over them;
that is to say, they have not yet abandoned desire.
If one has not yet abandoned desire, one remains in the hands of Māra, subject to whatever he does;
if one abandons desire by means of the worldly path,
one is still bound by the fetters of Māra and has not escaped from Māra’s snare.
Because one must inevitably return to be born in this realm,
what constitutes the work of Māra?
It refers to all those wholesome desires for renunciation that lead [one away], yet which arise through the predominant power of attachment to sensual pleasures.
If one subsequently regresses and abandons it,
you should know that this is indeed the work of Māra. If, however,
one dwells correctly and guards the doors of the sense faculties with secrecy, [there is no such regression].
Regarding all desirable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena,
the mind enters into them by grasping at their signs and grasping at their secondary characteristics.
One should know that this is precisely the work of Māra.
If one dwells correctly in moderation regarding food,
yet partakes unequally of various delicious flavors, [this too is the work of Māra].
One should know that when the mind enters into the pursuit of sensual desire through craving, this is the work of Māra; however,
if one dwells correctly and practices with diligent effort, [this is not so].
Regarding the yoga of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night:
when the mind tends toward falling into sleep due to the power of indolence— finding pleasure in sleep, pleasure in reclining, and pleasure in lying on one's side.
One should know that this is indeed the work of Māra.
If one dwells correctly established in clear comprehension while engaged in various activities such as coming and going, [one is not subject to such interference].
If one sees young women in the prime of their youth with beautiful complexions and,
through improper mental apprehension of signs, the mind enters into delight;
or if one sees various excellent and wonderful things in the world and the mind enters into delight.
Or, one’s mind may take pleasure in entering into many affairs and many activities;
or one may see householders and those who have gone forth living together in merriment;
or one may see them dwelling together with evil companions.
If one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and enters into it with delight,
know that all such instances are the work of Māra. Furthermore,

if one conceives doubt or uncertainty regarding the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, or regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, or concerning this world and the next, [these too are the work of Māra].
One should know that all such things are the deeds of Māra.
While dwelling in an araṇya, at the foot of a tree, in a cemetery, or in a secluded and quiet chamber,
if one sees vast and terrifying sights that cause alarm and make the hair stand on end—
Or one may see figures resembling śramaṇas or brahmins— neither human nor non-human— who suddenly appear and,
contrary to correct principle, urge the abandonment of wholesome qualities (*śukla-pakṣa*) and urge the adoption of unwholesome qualities (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa*).
One should know that all such things are the works of Māra.
Whether it be the mind’s inclination toward gain, honor, and praise,
or stinginess, vast desires, and a lack of contentment— these are all such works.
One should know that when the mind inclines toward and enters into states such as anger, resentment, concealment, vexation,
and hypocrisy— states which are the opposites of the adornments of a śramaṇa—
all of these are the deeds of Māra.
Such categories of immeasurable and boundless demonic activities as these are all produced by the four māras;
one should correctly understand them according to their respective natures.
Emptiness has no fruit.
What are the three?
First, because the faculties have not yet been fully accumulated.
Second, because the instructions are not concordant;
third, because the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is weak and inferior.
This applies when the faculties (*indriya*) have not yet been fully accumulated.
Even though one has attained a powerful meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that accords with the instructions,
diligent application toward emptiness will be fruitless. This is because,
although the various faculties have been cultivated and the power of that meditative concentration is likewise strong, [the result does not follow].
Yet they do not obtain the corresponding instructions;
their diligent application toward emptiness is fruitless.
Even if their faculties have already been fully developed, [they remain so].
Furthermore, even if one obtains instructions that are conducive [to practice],
if the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is not strong,
diligent exertion will be fruitless.
If one possesses faculties that have already attained the accumulation of instructions, are compliant with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and are powerful;
and if one applies oneself with diligence toward a goal that is certain to bear fruit—
such a case is called "empty and without fruit" by virtue of three causes and conditions.
The fruit is determined by three causes and conditions.
