In the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, the thirteenth part of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the first section of the third *Yogasthāna*: Thus has been explained the establishment of the categories of *pudgala*.
I shall now explain how the objects of focus (*ālambana*) and so forth, up to the cultivation that leads to results or lacks results,
should be established as appropriate.
The summary verse (*uddāna*) states:

When a person who cherishes themselves is a beginner first practicing, they should attend to the mental application (*manasikāra*) that seeks out joy and inquiry, and which establishes, protects, nourishes,
and leads to renunciation within one-pointedness, thereby purifying obstacles.
When first beginning the practice, for the sake of attaining one's own welfare through realization,
one should first establish right mindfulness in four places,
and thereafter approach those who are well-versed in yoga.
Whether it be a preceptor, a teacher,
or others who are respected or worthy of respect—
what are the four bases?
First, the state of seeking realization exclusively without a mind that seeks to find fault;
second, the state of generating deep reverence without a mind of arrogance;
third, the state of seeking only supreme goodness rather than displaying one's own capabilities.
With a mind solely intent on establishing the roots of virtue for oneself and others, and not seeking gain, honor,
or fame, one who possesses such right mindfulness approaches the teacher and first requests permission for the time of questioning.
Thereafter, with a composed and reverent demeanor, he personally requested an audience for his inquiry.
As he was about to ask his question, he bared his left shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground,
or sat in a lower position with his body slightly bowed.
With palms joined in reverence, deeply feeling shame and trepidation,
he lowered his gaze and spoke with gentle words, inquiring about yoga:
"I wish to seek instruction and training in such a practice of yoga."
“Please, out of compassion, explain this for me.
Having been thus requested,
the yogis who were thoroughly proficient in yoga [responded].
In order to establish the beginner in the mental engagement of yoga,
one should encourage, inspire, and comfort them with words that are compassionate and gentle;
furthermore, one should extol the virtues of cultivation and abandonment.
He exclaimed, "Excellent, excellent!
O Worthy One,
you are now indeed able [to do so] while others have fallen into negligence and are attached to the pleasures of negligence."
Amidst beings who are submerged in the realm of existence and delightfully attached to its objects,
he alone is not negligent and joyfully cultivates the practice of renunciation.
Now you are indeed able, amidst the various sentient beings who have long fallen into the perilous and evil prison of manifold sorrows and sufferings,
to seek liberation alone from such a prison.
Now you are able, amidst the classes of sentient beings who are constantly and firmly bound by the shackles, manacles, and collars of various forms of greed, hatred, and delusion,
to seek alone the severing and breaking of such firm bonds.
Now you are able, amidst the classes of sentient beings who have entered the wilderness and perilous paths of birth and death,
to seek alone to transcend and cross over that wilderness and perilous path.
Now you are able, amidst the classes of sentient beings who have encountered poverty and lack of various roots of goodness...
Seeking only to obtain abundant roots of goodness,
you are now able [to act] among the classes of sentient beings who have fallen into the vast terrors of the various enemies and thieves of affliction.
Seeking alone to realize the ultimate peace and eternal bliss of nirvāṇa,
you are now able [to act] amidst the masses of sentient beings who are being devoured by the grave illness of the afflictions.
Seeking solely to realize the supreme, illness-free, and eternal bliss of nirvāṇa,
you are now able [to do so] amidst the masses of sentient beings who are adrift and submerged in the four torrents.
Seeking alone to cross over such a torrential flood,
you are now able to seek alone to obtain the light of great wisdom among the masses of sentient beings who have entered the vast darkness of ignorance.
Venerable sir, you should know that if you are indeed able to thus diligently cultivate the practice of yoga,
you may be called one who does not receive in vain the offerings of faith from the people of the country.
Truly practicing the noble teachings of the Tathāgata without forsaking them,
they achieve meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), increase their insight (*vipaśyanā*), and delight in dwelling in solitude.
As spiritual companions, they apply themselves with diligence to the yoga of their own ultimate purpose.
You do not bring shame upon your wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life.
You now desire to diligently cultivate the right practice for your own benefit and the benefit of others.
You now desire to bring benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.
Out of compassion for the world, including the devas, humans, asuras, and others,
I have come to question you so that they may attain benefit, welfare, and happiness.
With such gentle words, I offer praise, encouragement, celebration, and consolation.
Having extolled the various merits of cultivation and abandonment, one should further interrogate him regarding the four points of formal inquiry.
One should address him, saying: "Venerable sir."
"Have you already taken exclusive refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha?
Are you not a follower of non-Buddhist teachers or their assemblies of disciples in false teachings?
Have you already, for the first time, purely cultivated the holy life, being well-purified in ethical discipline and possessing upright views?"
"Have you already heard, received, and upheld— whether in small measure or in great measure— the teachings on the various Noble Truths as they were summarized and analyzed? Have you,
with a deep-seated mind of faith and understanding, gone forth into homelessness for the sake of realizing nirvana and attaining cessation?"
Having asked thus,
if he should say so,
one should subsequently [examine him] regarding four further points.
One should seek correctly by means of four causes and conditions.
What are the four points that should be sought? First, one should seek their aspiration;
second, one should seek their spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Third, one should seek its root;
fourth, one should seek its conduct.
What are called the four kinds of causal conditions?
First, one should seek correctly through interrogation;
second, one should seek correctly through discourse;
third, one should seek correctly through what has been done.
Fourth, one should seek correctly by means of the knowledge that discerns the minds of others.
What is meant by "seeking its aspiration through careful interrogation"?
It refers to asking as follows:
"Elder, for what purpose have you made this right vow?
Is it for the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas,
or the vehicle of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?"
When he receives this question,
he should answer according to his own aspiration.
This is what is meant by seeking out one's aspiration through careful inquiry.
How is it that one should seek the lineage, the faculties, and the conduct through careful interrogation?
It means asking as follows:
"Venerable sir," [and so forth].
Does one examine one’s own lineage, faculties, and conduct?
That is to say: "What was my original lineage?
Is it that of the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle?"
Is it the Mahāyāna and so forth?
What are their faculties?
Are they dull, middling, or sharp?
Yes. What kind of temperament does he have?
Is it a temperament of greed, or a temperament of hatred?
To speak at length, up to:
"Does he investigate his conduct?
If he is wise, he is able to discern for himself the distinctions between his prior and subsequent lineages, faculties, and modes of conduct.
He correctly grasps their characteristics and answers according to what is asked.
However, if his nature is dull and he is unable to discern the differences between preceding and succeeding moments,
he will not even be able to correctly grasp their characteristics.
Because of this, one is unable to answer as asked.
From this point forward, one should seek those three through discourse;
that is to say, before them, one should employ words that are clear, consistent with correct reasoning, diverse, elegant, and easy to understand.
He speaks discourse associated with the Śrāvaka-yāna;
when they hear this discourse being proclaimed,
if there is the śrāvaka-gotra within their bodies, [they will understand it].
Upon hearing this discourse, they give rise to the utmost exuberance, joy, and profound faith and understanding;
and if within their continuum there exists the lineage of a pratyekabuddha or the lineage of the Mahāyāna.
If they do not give rise to the utmost exultation and joy, nor produce faith and understanding regarding this discourse,
he next explains for them the discourse associated with the Pratyekabuddhayāna.
When they hear this discourse being proclaimed,
if there is within them the lineage of a pratyekabuddha,
they will immediately experience the utmost exultation and joy, and will give rise to profound faith and understanding toward this discourse.
If there are within that person the lineage of a śrāvaka or the lineage of the Mahāyāna, it is not like that;
subsequently, one further proclaims for them discourse corresponding to the Mahāyāna.
When they hear this discourse being proclaimed,
if there is the lineage of the Mahāyāna within their continuum,
they will then give rise to the utmost exultation and joy, and develop profound faith and understanding toward this discourse.
If one possesses the lineage of a śrāvaka or the lineage of a pratyekabuddha within one's continuum, it is not like this;
even if such a person hears the proclamation of coarse and shallow discourses, [they do not attain realization].
Yet, regarding the meaning of the Dharma, one must apply diligent effort and careful reflection before being able to receive, comprehend, and penetrate it. If, however,
one possesses sharp faculties,
although one hears the exposition of profound and subtle discourse, [one understands it immediately].
They are able to quickly receive, comprehend, and master the meaning of the Dharma;
those of middling faculties, however, do not do so.
If there is one whose temperament is characterized by craving,
upon hearing discourses on purity and excellence spoken for their sake,
they will immediately give rise to the most supreme pure faith and joyful affection, thereby gaining entry into that path.
The hairs on his body all stood on end as he wept with sorrowful tears;
his physical form externally manifested a state of moist luster,
while his mind internally harbored gentleness and joy.
If there is a temperament of hatred,
one should know that all [characteristics] are the opposite of those mentioned above.
If there is a temperament of delusion, [the same applies].
Upon hearing discourse that definitively penetrates nirvāṇa and corresponds to the state free from defilement,
he gives rise to the utmost alarm and dread,
as was said regarding those of dull faculties.
One should know that the same applies to those who act out of delusion.
Furthermore, if there are those who act out of pride,
they will not show great respect when hearing discourses on the true Dharma being explained.
Though he lends an ear and delights in hearing, does not abide in ultimate tranquility, and seeks to understand by following the teachings with a compliant mind,
[the teacher] employs skillful means to inspire his heart so that he may receive correct transformation.
Yet they do not speak clearly, saying "well done.
If they engage in discursive reflection,
they hear him preach discourses on the True Dharma.
Although he listens with his ears attentive, his mind is distracted and he experiences what is received as unpleasant;
whatever he perceives is neither firm nor stable,
and he loses it immediately upon receiving it, requiring repeated questioning.
This is called seeking the lineage (*gotra*) and the faculties and conduct (*indriya-carita*) by means of speech.
What is called seeking them by means of what is done?
Those three are as previously described.
The characteristics of individuals belonging to the śrāvaka lineage and those whose conduct is dominated by craving and so forth are called "the performed.
By means of these performed [characteristics], they are categorized as appropriate.
When one is correctly seeking the lineage (*gotra*), faculties (*indriya*),
and conduct (*carita*), how is it that one should seek the lineage and conduct by means of the knowledge of the diversity of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)?
That is to say, there is a certain practitioner of yoga who has thoroughly mastered yoga and,
by means of the knowledge of discerning the distinctions of others' minds, possesses such knowledge of others' minds.
By virtue of this knowledge of others' minds, he...
Having understood the lineages, faculties, and conducts as they truly are,
and having correctly sought them out through four causes and conditions within four bases,
one further establishes them appropriately within five bases.
What are the five bases?
First, the basis of protecting and nourishing the requisites for concentration;
second, the basis of seclusion.
1) The state of one-pointedness of mind;
2) the state of purification from the four hindrances;
3) the state of cultivating mental attention (*manasikāra*).
What is the cultivation of the requisites for concentration?
It refers to one who has accomplished the restraint of ethical discipline,
and who, in that very state, acts with heedfulness so as not to fall away from it.
In accordance with what the Buddha has admonished and what the Buddha has permitted,
one should practice with diligence and never slacken in the various distinctions of the training rules (śikṣāpada) that perfect the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha).
In this way, one is able to avoid regression from the path of training associated with the ethical discipline (śīla) already realized,
and is also able to realize the superior path of training associated with ethical discipline that was previously unrealized.
Just as it is said that one accomplishes the restraint of the moral precepts,
so too does one accomplish the restraint of the sense faculties and practice moderation in eating.
During the first and last watches of the night, he remains awake and engaged in yoga, dwelling with clear comprehension.
In this way, he accomplishes all the adornments of a śramaṇa,
according to the various distinctions of wholesome dharmas comprised within the provisions he has acquired.
They are all able to guard [the practitioner] so that they do not fall away or lose [these qualities].
Regarding the subsequent distinctions of superior and progressive wholesome dharmas,
they act to swiftly bring them to fulfillment, exactly as described, without increase or decrease.
They practice with equanimity,
giving rise to a superior longing and admiration,
and constantly abide in courageous diligence.
This is called protecting and nurturing the provisions for meditative concentration (*samādhi-sambhāra*).
Thus, having distanced oneself from factors conducive to decline,
when one cultivates factors conducive to excellence, one dwells happily in seclusion.
What is seclusion?
It refers to the perfection of the location and the perfection of the deportment.
Seclusion is perfected;
this is called seclusion.
What is the perfection of the location?
That is to say: either in an araṇya, or at the foot of trees in a forest, or in an empty, secluded dwelling.
A mountain valley, a rock cave, a heap of rice straw, and so forth, are called an empty, secluded dwelling.
A grove of great trees is called "at the foot of trees in a forest."
Dwelling or sitting in open spaces, remote areas, cemeteries, or at the boundaries is called *araṇya*.
One should know that this includes such places as mountain valleys,
caves, and stacks of straw.
In a great forest,
in an open space, or at the edge of a cemetery;
or in an araṇya, or beneath a tree, or in an empty, quiet room.
These are collectively termed "locations.
There are five ways in which a location is perfected:
namely, if a location has from the very beginning possessed a beautiful form that is pleasing for all to behold, and is pure and free from defilement.
Gardens, groves, ponds, and pools are all fully present;
it is pure, serene, and delightful.
The ground is level without elevations or depressions, and there are no thorns or brambles anywhere.
Furthermore, it is free from numerous bricks, stones, tiles,
and debris, such that those who see it develop a mind of purity and take delight in dwelling therein to cultivate the preparatory practices for abandonment.
With a joyful and delighted mind, one maintains the state of abandonment;
this is called the first perfection of the location.
Furthermore, if the location is free from bustle by day and has little noise at night.
Furthermore, there is little contact with mosquitoes, gadflies, wind, sun, snakes, scorpions, or other harmful poisons;
this is called the second perfection of the location.
Moreover, if the location is free from wicked lions, tigers, leopards, jackals, and wolves.
Regarding enemies,
thieves, humans, non-humans, and all such terrifying matters,
they will dwell in that place with body and mind at ease, entirely free from doubt or anxiety, and in a state of peace and happiness.
This is called the third perfection of the location.
Furthermore, if the location is conducive to obtaining the requisites for sustaining life and body,
such that seeking clothing and other necessities is not particularly difficult;
Food and drink are provided without any lack;
this is called the fourth perfection of the location.
Furthermore, it is a place where one is sustained by virtuous spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
Furthermore, he dwells together with wise fellow practitioners of the holy life;
in matters not yet understood, he is able to correctly bring them to understanding,
and in matters already understood, he causes them to become even more clear and pure.
One thoroughly penetrates the meaning of these profound phrases with wisdom and skillfully, diligently reveals them,
thereby enabling one's insight and vision to swiftly attain purity.
This is called the fifth perfection of the place.
What is the perfection of deportment?
It refers to walking and sitting meditation during the daytime.
During the first watch of the night, he likewise does so;
during the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side;
and during the last watch of the night, he quickly rises again to practice walking meditation and seated meditation.
Then, upon such a fully prepared bedding—
whether it be a large or small rope-cot or a seat of grass and leaves permitted by the Buddhas— he sits cross-legged,
and so forth, as described at length.
For what reason does one sit in the full lotus posture?
It is because of correctly contemplating five causes and conditions:
first, by withdrawing the body, one quickly gives rise to pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
Such postures are most excellent for giving rise to pliancy in accordance with the practice;
secondly, by means of this seated meditation, one can endure for a long duration,
as such a posture does not cause the body to become excessively fatigued quickly.
Third, this meditative seclusion is an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*),
for such deportment is entirely absent among non-Buddhists and other proponents of heterodox doctrines.
Fourth, by means of this meditative seclusion, one’s physical appearance becomes dignified and majestic.
Because others, having seen such deportment, develop extreme faith and respect;
and fifth, because this meditative seclusion is authorized by all Buddhas and their disciples,
as such deportment is praised alike by all noble ones and sages.
One should correctly contemplate these five kinds of causes and conditions;
therefore, one ought to sit in the full lotus posture,
straightening the body and setting the right aspiration.
What is the straightening of the body?
It means exerting and uplifting the body so that it becomes upright.
What is right aspiration?
That is to say, it causes the mind to be free from flattery and deceit,
becoming supple and upright; because the body is raised and held straight,
the mind is not entangled or disturbed by lethargy and drowsiness.
Because he is free from flattery and deceit, his mind is not entangled or disturbed by the agitation of external objects.
Regarding "abiding in the mindfulness of turning away":
what is meant by "abiding in the mindfulness of turning away"?
That is to say, mindfulness associated with appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) is called "mindfulness turned away," because it turns its back upon,
abandons, and opposes all dark factors (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
Furthermore, mindfulness that takes the signs of meditative concentration (*samādhi-nimitta*) as its object is called "mindfulness turned away."
Because one abandons, turns away from, and eliminates all objects of focus belonging to the non-concentrated states (*asamāhita-bhūmi*),
this is called the perfection of deportment (*īryāpatha-sampad*).
What is the perfection of seclusion (*viveka-sampad*)?
There are two kinds:
first, physical seclusion;
second, mental seclusion.
Physical seclusion means not dwelling in association with either householders or those who have gone forth;
to be alone and without companion is called physical seclusion.
"Mental seclusion" refers to being secluded from all defiled and neutral modes of attention (*manasikāra*),

and cultivating all modes of attention that are by nature wholesome, which lead to meaningful goals, pertain to the stages of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bhūmi*), and constitute the preparatory applications for the requisites of concentration.
This is called physical and mental seclusion.
Thus, herein, there is both the perfection of the location and the perfection of the deportment.
Whether it be physical seclusion or mental seclusion,
taken together as one, they are called "seclusion."
What is one-pointedness of mind?
It refers to the continuous flow of the mind, associated with faultless joy, which repeatedly recollects a homogeneous object;
this is called samādhi.
It is also called one-pointedness of virtuous mind.
What is meant by "repeated recollection"?
It refers to hearing and upholding the True Dharma.
By the superior power of the instructions and teachings obtained from the master,
the various signs of the meditative states are made to appear before him;
he then takes these as his objects of focus.
The flow is faultless and associated with mental pliancy;
all right mindfulness follows along and remains settled.
What is meant by "having a similar objective referent" (*sabhāga-ālambana*)?
This refers to the objects of focus belonging to the various stages of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*),
which are not singular but manifold and of diverse categories;
taking these as objects, one causes the mind to proceed correctly.
This is called "concentration" (samādhi).
This is precisely what is termed the "homogeneous object" (sabhāga-ālambana).
Question: To whom does this objective sphere belong such that it is described as "homogeneous"?
Answer: It is called "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) because it is a category similar to the objects of knowledge.
Furthermore, by means of that mindfulness, there is non-distraction regarding the focal object, as well as continuity and lack of interruption.
It proceeds with uninterrupted and earnest application, in association with pliancy;
therefore, it is called "a continuous flow associated with pliancy.
Furthermore, because that mindfulness is free from defilement regarding its object of focus.
Abiding in supreme tranquility, the path has reached maturity;
it proceeds in association with well-being,
and is therefore called "blameless association with well-being."
Therefore, it is said that the continuous flow of the mind,
which repeatedly recollects its homogeneous object and is associated with faultless joy, is called samādhi.
It is also called "one-pointedness of virtuous mind.
Furthermore, such one-pointedness of mind may belong to the category of śamatha.
Or it belongs to the category of vipaśyanā. If,
among the nine stages of mental abiding, there is one-pointedness of mind,
this is called the category of śamatha.
If there is one-pointedness of mind within the four modes of wisdom-practice,
this is called the category of vipaśyanā.
What are the nine stages of mental abiding?
That is to say, there is a bhikṣu who causes the mind to abide internally,
to abide evenly, to abide securely, and to abide closely;
he makes it compliant, tranquil, and most thoroughly tranquil.
Focusing on a single object and through meditative equipoise—
these are called the nine stages of mental abiding.
What is internal abiding?
It means withdrawing the mind from all external objects of focus and binding it within so that it does not become distracted.
This is the initial binding of the mind,
causing it to abide within and not be distracted externally; therefore,
it is called "internal abiding" (sthāpanā).
What is "even abiding" (*samasthāpana*)?
It refers to that very mind which was initially bound;
because its nature is coarse and restless, it has not yet been made to abide evenly or abide pervasively.
Next, with respect to this very object of focus,
one should use the method of continuity and the method of purification to subdue it so that it becomes subtle,
and then fully collect and settle it.
Therefore, it is called "even abiding" (*samasthiti*). What is "settled abiding"?
It refers to when this mind, although it has thus been inwardly settled and evenly settled, [continues in that state].
However, because one has become distracted outwardly due to a lapse of mindfulness,
one again gathers and restrains the mind to settle it within the internal object;
therefore, this is called "abiding."
What is "dwelling closely"?
It means that one should first approach the foundations of mindfulness in such and such a manner;
by means of this mindfulness, one repeatedly applies attention to cause the mind to dwell within.
Because it does not allow this mind to dwell far away in external objects,
it is called "near-dwelling" (*upasthāpana*).
What is "taming" (*damana*)?
This refers to various signs that cause the mind to become distracted, namely:
the signs of form, sound, odor, taste, and touch;
as well as the signs of greed, hatred, delusion, male, female, and so forth.
He should first apprehend those various signs as being defects.
By the predominant power of such a perception,
he subdues his mind with respect to those signs and prevents it from wandering.
Therefore, it is called "well-tamed.
What is "tranquility"?
It refers to the various evil discursive thoughts such as desire, ill-will, and harmfulness, as well as the secondary afflictions such as the hindrance of sensual desire.
Because it causes the mind to become agitated,
one should first conceive of those phenomena as being defects;
by the predominant power of such a conception, [the agitation is stilled].
Because one causes the mind to cease its discursive thoughts and secondary afflictions,
preventing them from wandering and scattering,
it is called "tranquility" (śamatha).
What is meant by "supreme tranquility"?
It refers to the fact that when those two types [of mental states] momentarily manifest due to a lapse of mindfulness,
one does not tolerate the various unwholesome discursive thoughts and secondary afflictions that arise in accordance with them.
One immediately cuts it off, eliminates it, and casts it out;
therefore, it is called "supreme tranquility.
What is meant by "focusing the mind on a single object"?
This refers to abiding in a continuous flow of samādhi that is accompanied by application and effort, and which is without deficiency or interruption;
therefore, it is called "one-pointed concentration."
What is meditative concentration (*samādhi*)?

It refers to the path that proceeds spontaneously, without applied effort or exertion, by virtue of the causes and conditions of repeated cultivation, repeated practice, and frequent intensive cultivation.
By reason of these causes and conditions, through neither application nor effort,
the mind’s samādhi proceeds spontaneously in a continuous stream without distraction; therefore,
it is called "equipoise" (samāhita).
It should be understood that herein, it is only through six kinds of power that the nine stages of mental abiding can be accomplished.
First is the power of hearing.
Second, the power of reflection;
third, the power of mindfulness;
fourth, the power of clear comprehension.
The five powers of diligence and the sixth power of habitual practice;
the former arises from the two powers of hearing and reflection.
By the superior power of repeated hearing and reflection,
one first causes the mind to abide upon internal objects,
and then establishes it thoroughly through the application of continuity and the application of purification.
Having thus bound the mind internally,
one repeatedly applies attention through the power of mindfulness,
gathering and restraining the mind so that it does not become distracted, but remains settled and closely established.
From this point onward, by the power of correct awareness (*samprajanya*),
one regulates the mind so that it does not disperse toward various signs, evil discursive thoughts, or secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), but remains disciplined, compliant, and tranquil.
By the power of diligence, when those two types [of afflictions] momentarily manifest, one is able not to tolerate them;
they are immediately severed, eliminated, cast out, and thoroughly pacified,
as one focuses the mind on a single point.
Through the power of repeated practice, meditative concentration (samādhi) is brought to fulfillment.
Within these nine stages of mental abiding,
it should be understood that there are further four types of mental attention (manasikāra).
1. The attention that operates with strenuous effort;
2. The attention that operates with interruptions;
3. The attention that operates without interruptions.
The mental engagement of effortless operation occurs during internal abiding and thorough abiding, whereas during [the stages of] forceful operation,
there is the mental engagement of exertion.
Regarding stability, close placement,
taming, pacification,
and thorough pacification.
There is attention that operates with interruptions;
within the state of one-pointed concentration,
there is attention that operates without interruptions.
Within meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
there is the mental application (*manasikāra*) that operates without effort;
it should be understood that these constitute the four kinds of mental application.
Among the nine stages of mental abiding, this belongs to the category of śamatha.
Furthermore, for one who has thus attained internal śamatha,
when diligently practicing vipaśyanā:
Furthermore, it is precisely by means of these four types of mental attention that one is able to cultivate vipaśyanā;
therefore, this too belongs to the category of vipaśyanā.
What are the four kinds of vipaśyanā?
They are as follows: there is a bhikṣu who, relying upon internal śamatha, is able to correctly investigate and thoroughly examine all phenomena.
Thoroughly investigating and thoroughly examining—
these are called the four kinds of vipaśyanā.
What is meant by "correctly discerning"?
That is to say, regarding the objects of focus for pure conduct,
or the objects of focus for skillfulness,
or the objects of focus for the purification of afflictions.
One is able to correctly discern the nature of all that exists.
What is meant by "thoroughly discerning"?
It refers to precisely those very objects of focus.
Regarding the thorough investigation of the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāva*):
what is meant by "thoroughly searching" (*parivitarka*)?
It refers to that very same objective referent (*ālambana-viṣaya*).
By means of a discerning mental attention (manasikāra) accompanied by wisdom,
one grasps those characteristics and conducts a thorough investigation.
What is meant by "thorough examination"?
That is to say, it is the thorough investigation and pervasive examination of that very same object of focus;
furthermore, it is precisely this *vipaśyanā*.
One should know that there are many further varieties based on the distinctions of the three doors and six objects.
What are the three doors of vipaśyanā?
1. Insight (vipaśyanā) that proceeds by way of following mere characteristics;
2. Insight that proceeds by way of following investigation;
3. Insight that proceeds by way of following analysis.
What is called vipaśyanā that proceeds solely by way of signs?
It refers to [the practice] regarding the teachings one has heard and upheld,
or regarding the various dharmas of instruction and admonition.
Through appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) belonging to the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*),
one briefly contemplates [the object] without yet having reflected, measured, inferred, or investigated it;
this is called *vipaśyanā* that proceeds merely by way of signs (*nimitta-anuvartana*).
If one further reflects upon and investigates those [objects],
at that time it is called vipaśyanā that proceeds in accordance with investigation (vitarka).
Furthermore, once one has finished investigating them...
One further examines with careful scrutiny that which has been thus established;
this is called vipaśyanā consisting of investigative analysis.
This is known as the three-gated vipaśyanā.
What is insight (*vipaśyanā*) with respect to the objects of focus distinguished by six aspects?
It refers to the time of investigation when one investigates six aspects:
first, the meaning (*artha*).
Two matters,
three characteristics,
and four categories.
Having already investigated the five periods and the six principles,
one further examines them with careful scrutiny.
What is called "investigating the meaning"?
It refers to correctly investigating that such-and-such words have such-and-such meanings;
this is called investigating the meaning.
What is called the investigation of things?
It refers to correctly investigating the two types of things: internal and external.
This is what is called the investigation of things.
What is called "investigating characteristics"?
It refers to correctly investigating the two characteristics of all phenomena:
first, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The second is the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
This is called the investigation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-paryeṣaṇā*).
What is called the investigation of categories (*pakṣa-paryeṣaṇā*)?
That is to say, one correctly investigates the two categories of all phenomena:
first, the dark category;
second, the bright category.
One investigates the faults and disadvantages of the dark side,
and one investigates the virtues and benefits of the bright side;
this is called investigating by way of the categories.
What is called "investigating time"?
It refers to correctly investigating the three times— past, future, and present—
and investigating that such-and-such a thing previously existed in the past.
To investigate that such matters will exist in the future,
and to investigate that such matters exist now in the present—
this is called investigating with respect to time.
What is meant by "investigating the principles"?
It refers to correctly investigating four kinds of principles:
first, the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*).
2) the principle of efficacy;
3) the principle of logical proof;
and 4) the principle of natural law.
It should be understood that herein, by means of the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*),
one investigates the conventional as the conventional, the ultimate as the ultimate,
and causal conditions as causal conditions.
One investigates the functions of all phenomena by means of the principle of efficacy,
considering that such-and-such phenomena possess such-and-such functions;
one investigates the three types of valid cognition by means of the principle of proof.
First, the authority of scripture;
second, the authority of inference;
third, the authority of direct perception.
That is to say, one correctly investigates whether there exists authoritative scripture regarding such and such a meaning,
and whether it can be attained through direct realization.
Is it not by means of inference?
It is through the principle of the nature of things (*dharmatā-yukti*) that the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as they truly are is established.

The inconceivable nature of phenomena (dharmatā) abides as the nature of phenomena; one should give rise to faith and understanding toward it, but should not contemplate it nor engage in conceptual discrimination.
This is called investigating the principle.
Thus, the vipaśyanā that takes these six types of differentiated objects as its focus,
along with the vipaśyanā of the three doors,
briefly encompasses all forms of vipaśyanā.
Question: For what reason are these six distinct categories of vipaśyanā established?
Answer: They are established based on three types of realization (*avabodha*).
What are the three types of realization?
First, the realization of the meaning of words;
second, the realization of the limits of phenomena;
third, the realization of reality as it is.
By investigating the meaning, one gives rise to the awareness of the meaning of words;
by investigating the particulars and their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), one gives rise to the awareness of the limits of things;
and by investigating common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), categories, time, and principles, one gives rise to the awareness of reality as it is (*yathābhūta*).
For the practitioner of yoga, the objects of knowledge are limited to these: namely, the meaning of words and the entities that are known;
that is to say, the nature of exhaustiveness and the nature of suchness.
What is the vipaśyanā that investigates the distinctions of the six objects of focus for one who diligently cultivates the meditation on impurity?
It refers to [the investigation] based upon the sublime Dharma that has impurity as its predominant theme.
By the superior power of hearing and upholding [the teaching],
one understands its meaning through correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) in the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*).
One knows that this impurity is truly impure and is profoundly loathsome.
Its nature is decayed, filthy, foul-smelling, and putrid;
by means of such various characteristics,
one reflects upon the sublime Dharma previously heard, which was taught based on the various aspects of impurity.
Having understood its meaning in this way,
it is called "investigating the meaning of the various impurities.
What is meant by "investigating those objects"?
That is to say, having thus understood the meaning,
one contemplates impure objects by establishing two categories:
namely, the internal and the external.
This is called the investigation of that object.
What is called the investigation of specific characteristics?
It refers, for instance, to generating resolute conviction regarding all the foul, decayed, and impure things within one's own internal body.
One understands that within the body there are hair, body hair, and so forth, extensively described up to the brain membrane and urine;
furthermore, one recognizes all the many impure substances contained within such a body.
One gathers these into two elements and gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*),
namely, the earth element and the water element.
Beginning with the hair of the head and ending with excrement, one gives rise to the resolute conviction that they are earth.
Beginning with the contemplation of tears and filth, up to the resolution regarding water arising from urine—
this is called reflecting on the specific characteristics of internal impurity.
Furthermore, one [reflects] upon various external impure things.
One gives rise to resolute conviction through various aspects such as the livid-blue and so forth; that is,
one first gives rise to resolute conviction regarding the livid-blue,
either having seen it for oneself or having heard of it from another.
Or, by means of conceptualizing all corpses—
such as corpses that are male,
female, or neither male nor female.
Whether they be friends, enemies, or neutral parties;
whether they be inferior, middling, or superior;
or whether they be young, middle-aged, or old.
Having grasped that sign, if this corpse has been dead for one day,
with the flow of blood having already ceased and not yet reaching the stage of putrefaction,
one then gives rise to the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) of the bluish-black discoloration (*vinīlaka*).
If this corpse has been dead for two days,
having reached the stage of putrefaction but not yet produced maggots,
one then develops the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding that putrefaction.
If this corpse has been dead for seven days,
such that maggots have already emerged and the body is decomposed,
one then develops the resolve of putrefaction and the resolve of bloating.
If this corpse is being devoured by foxes, wolves, owls, crows, vultures, eagles, ravens, magpies, and hungry dogs,
one then generates the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that it is being devoured.
Once this corpse has been devoured until the skin,
flesh, and blood are exhausted, leaving only sinews binding the bones,
one then generates a distinct and superior resolve regarding its redness.
If this corpse has been devoured so that its limbs and joints are separated and scattered in various places,
whether there is flesh remaining or no flesh at all, or only a small amount of flesh left;
Thereupon, one generates the resolve for dispersal:
"If these bones and joints of the corpse were to disperse,
such that the hand-bones were in one place," and so forth.
The bones of the feet were scattered in different places;
the bones of the knees were scattered in different places;
the bones of the thighs were scattered in different places.
The hip bones are in different places;
the shoulder blades are in different places;
the arm bones are in different places.
The vertebrae were scattered in different places;
the jawbones were scattered in different places;
the rows of teeth were scattered in different places.
The skulls are in different places.
Having seen this, one develops the resolve regarding the bones.
Furthermore, one contemplates how these skeletal remains are interconnected and not dispersed.
One grasps only the coarse features and does not grasp the details of the joints and articulations;
in this way, at that time, one gives rise to the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) of the chain.
If one were to grasp the details of the joints and articulations...
At that time, one initiates the contemplation of the supreme chain of bones.
Furthermore, there are two types of chains:
first, the chain of the physical frame.
Second is the chain of joints.
Regarding the chain of the physical frame:
it refers to that which resides from the blood-filled cauldron of the spine up to the skull.
The "chain of limbs and joints" refers to the skeletal chains of the arms, shoulders, and so forth, as well as the skeletal chains of the thighs, calves, and so forth.
Among these, the skeletal chain of the physical body is what is designated as the "chain."
If the chain of limbs and joints is called a "skeleton," there are two ways of apprehending the sign of the skeleton: first,
one apprehends the sign of a skeleton made of conventional designations, such as those fashioned from painting, wood, stone, clay, and so forth.
Second, one takes up the sign of the skeleton as a reality.
When one contemplates the sign of the skeleton as a mere conventional designation,
at that time, only the name gives rise to the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) of the skeleton.
It is not called the "skeleton chain.
When one contemplates the true characteristics of the skeleton chain,
at that time it is called the arising of the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the skeleton chain.
Furthermore, there are three types of transformation and disintegration regarding the characteristics of external derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*):
first, natural transformation and disintegration;
second, transformation and disintegration caused by others.
The transformation and decay of the three together begins from the stage of bluish discoloration up to that of bloating;
this is natural transformation and decay.
From the initial consumption until its final dispersal,
it is transformed and corrupted by others—
whether as bones, or skeletons, or even as a skeleton-chain.
This is the transformation and decay common to both.
If one can thus understand the external signs of impurity as they truly are,
this is called the thorough investigation of the specific characteristics of all external impurities.
What is the investigation of the common characteristic of impurity?
It refers to the fact that while the internal body has not yet undergone transformation and decay regarding its external appearance of purity,
the external body already possesses an appearance of impurity that has undergone transformation and decay.
By means of generating resolute conviction through the similarity of the dharma-nature and the concordance of the dharma-nature with the impure physical forms within one's own body,
one is able to personally realize that one’s own pure physical forms likewise possess this same shared dharma-nature.
If sentient beings possess such pure physical forms,
those pure physical forms likewise share the same dharmatā as those [impure forms],
just like the impure physical forms found externally.
This is called the investigation of the common characteristic of impurity.
What is meant by "investigating its category"?
It refers to reflecting as follows:
If I were not to know, as it truly is, the impure nature of those various pure-colored forms,
and were instead to give rise to lustful desire for internal and external pure-colored forms, that would be a perversion.
Subsumed under the dark category,
these are phenomena subject to contention, accompanied by suffering and harm,
fraught with calamities and afflictions that burn all-pervasively.
By reason of these causes and conditions, there arise in the future the various afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, and suffering.
If I [regard] those pure physical forms as being of the nature of impurity...
When one contemplates according to reality, there is no inversion;
this is comprised within the white category (śuklapakṣa),
and is a dharma free from contention, without suffering, and without harm.
To speak at length, it continues until: "By means of these causes and conditions, one is able to extinguish future birth, old age, sickness, death, and even all forms of affliction.
As for all things of the dark class (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), I should not tolerate them now; I should sever them and dispel them."
Regarding all wholesome qualities (*śuklapakṣa*),
those that have not yet arisen, I shall now cause them to arise;
those that have already arisen, I shall cause them to remain, increase, and expand.
This is called the investigation of that category.
What is called the investigation of that time?
It refers to forming this thought:
Whatever pure material forms exist internally in the present,
whatever impure material forms exist externally in the present,
and whatever pure material forms existed in the past;
Although they possessed pure characteristics in the past,
they are now, in the present, variously impure in such a sequence; likewise,
all those things belonging to me that appear as pure-colored forms in the present world—
Although this pure form possesses a pure appearance in the present life,
it shall not become impure in the future as external impure forms do in the present.
This is impossible. Throughout the past,
future, and present, this physical body of mine has never had such characteristics,
nor will it ever have such characteristics, nor does it manifest such characteristics.
Such is the nature of this impurity;
this is called the investigation of that time.
What is called the investigation of that principle?
That is to say, one reflects thus:
whether internally or externally, no self or sentient being can be found that might be described as pure or impure.
There is only the appearance of form and only the physical body;
within these, one employs conceptual designations and verbal expressions,
calling them either "pure" or "impure."
Furthermore, as it is said: "Vitality, warmth, and consciousness—when these abandon the body, it lies cast aside, devoid of its sustaining support and without thought, like a piece of wood.
Once dead and passed away, its stages of gradual transformation and decay can be observed."
That is to say, from the stage of bluish discoloration up to the skeleton:
this body of mine is produced by the impetus of past karma and afflictions,
and is born from the union of the impurities of my parents.
Due to this cause, this condition, and by depending upon this, although there may temporarily appear something resembling pure matter (*rūpa*), it is merely increased by food such as gruel and rice.
One can clearly understand that within the internal body, whether internally or externally,
it is at all times completely filled with various kinds of impurities.
This is called the principle of dependence based on the conventional, the ultimate, and causal conditions.
Investigating that principle,
he further reflects:
"If one can thus properly cultivate, properly practice, and repeatedly cultivate this meditation on impurity, it will be able to sever sensual desire."
In this way, sensual desire must certainly be abandoned.
This is called investigating that principle by means of the reasoning of function.
Furthermore, one reflects as follows:
As the Blessed One has said:
"If one thoroughly cultivates, practices, and frequently develops the meditation on the foul, it can sever sensual desire"—
this is the authoritative teaching.
I too am able to personally perceive within myself all manner of impurities.
In whatever way I direct my attention and cultivate such contemplation,
to that same extent I cause the fetters of sensual desire that have not yet arisen not to arise, and those already arisen to be dispelled.
This is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The method of inference (*anumāna*) may also be obtained;
that is to say, one should reflect as follows:
"How is it that when one now directs the mind toward the remedial factors,
afflictions might still arise with respect to the objects of those very remedies?
This is called investigating that principle by means of the reasoning of logical proof."
Again, he reflects thus:
"Such dharmas establish the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
This inconceivable nature of phenomena abides as the nature of phenomena."
This means that the cultivation of the meditation on impurity serves as the antidote for the abandonment of sensual desire;
it should not be conceptualized nor should it be analytically discriminated, but should be accepted through faith and understanding alone.
This is called investigating that principle by means of the principle of the nature of things (*dharmatā-yukti*).
This is called the cultivation of the meditation on impurity by one who investigates the six types of objects through the discernment (*vipaśyanā*) of their distinctions.
What is the cultivation of the meditation on loving-kindness (*maitrī*)?
One investigates vipaśyanā through the objects of focus distinguished by the six matters;
that is to say, by the predominant power of having heard and upheld the sublime Dharma based upon loving-kindness and compassion.

The characteristic of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the cultivation of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) toward the bestowal of happiness upon all sentient beings, arising from the intention to bring them benefit and well-being.
If one can understand its meaning in this way,
this is called investigating the meaning of all forms of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Having thus understood the meaning, one is further able to exercise discernment (*pravicaya*).
"This is the category of kin, this is the category of enemies, and this is the category of neutrals"—
since all these categories are comprised within the continuums of others,
one generates a resolute conviction regarding external objects therein.

Furthermore, if one takes the category of friends as "internal matters" and the categories of enemies and neutral persons as "external matters," this is called investigating the objects of loving-kindness.
Furthermore, one is able to discern these three categories:
if there is no suffering or pleasure, and one desires happiness for them, wishing that they may obtain it—
this present state, characterized by benefit, is called the category of kin.
The characteristic of non-benefit is called the category of the enemy;
the characteristic of being contrary to both is called the category of the neutral.
If these three categories are devoid of suffering and pleasure, yet one desires happiness—
Briefly, three types of distinctions in the mind that seeks pleasure can be found:
first, the desire to seek the various pleasures of the desire realm;
second, the desire to seek the various pleasures of the form realm characterized by joy and rapture.
Third, desiring to seek the various pleasures that are free from joy:
thus, if there is a lack of sensual pleasure,
may they all obtain blameless sensual pleasure.
If there is any deficiency regarding the various pleasures associated with joy or free from joy,
one should know that it is likewise so.
This is called the investigation into the specific characteristics of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Furthermore, one should carefully examine and discern whether they belong to the category of friends, the category of enemies, or the category of neutral persons;
toward all of them, one should give rise to a mind of similarity and a mind of equanimity.
Why is this? If I were to direct my attention toward giving happiness to those who are my kin, this would not be difficult;
nor would it be particularly difficult to direct my attention toward giving happiness to those who are neutral.
If it is extremely difficult to direct one's thoughts toward those who are hostile and wish them happiness,
I should nevertheless resolve to wish for their happiness;
how much more so, then, should I do so for those who are friends or neutral parties?
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no one who reviles nor anyone who is reviled;
no one who is angry nor anyone who is the object of anger.
The manipulator and the manipulated,
the striker and the struck—
these exist only as sounds and only as names.
Furthermore, this body of mine, wherever it arises,
is composed of the coarse and heavy four great elements;
wherever it dwells, it is thus oppressed by such contact.
Briefly, there are two kinds of contact:
namely, the contact of sound,
and the contact of hands, feet, clods of earth, swords, staves, and so forth.
This body and its contact are both impermanent;
that which can cause such lack of benefit is also impermanent.
Furthermore, all classes of sentient beings possess the phenomena of birth, aging, sickness, and death.
Their nature is suffering; therefore,
I should not inflict further suffering upon sentient beings whose nature is already suffering,
nor fail to grant them happiness.
Furthermore, one should not fail to act as a spiritual friend to one's enemies, nor should one fail to embrace all categories of sentient beings as one’s own self.
Moreover, the Blessed One said:
I do not perceive any such sentient beings who,
having undergone the long process of birth and death and wandered through beginningless time,
have not at some point served one another as father, mother, brother, or sister.
Whether it be one's preceptor, one's teacher,
or others who are respected or worthy of respect,
by virtue of these causes and conditions, all those who are objects of enmity are none other than my own kin.
Furthermore, there is no fixed or real nature to be found in the categories of enemies and kin.
Why is this? Because those who belong to the category of kin may at another time turn into the category of enemies.
Those who belong to the category of enemies may at other times transform into those of the category of kin;
therefore, nothing whatsoever is fixed.
Thus, I should now [regard] all classes of sentient beings as such.
All should give rise to a mind of equanimity and a view of equanimity,
as well as the intention for similar benefit, the intention for happiness, and the resolute conviction in bestowing joy.
This is called the investigation of the common characteristics of loving-kindness and compassion.
Furthermore, one should carefully examine and discern: "If I were not to benefit them..."
The arising of ill-will is a perversion;
it is comprised within the dark category and is a dharma associated with contention.
As explained at length previously:
if I do not give rise to anger toward them, I am free from perversion and am comprised within the category of the white side.
This is the dharma free from contention.
A detailed exposition is as previously described.
This is called the thorough investigation of the dark and bright categories of loving-kindness and compassion.
Furthermore, he reflects and discerns:
"All those classes of sentient beings who, in past lives, sought and desired to obtain happiness have all passed away."
"How shall I be able to grant happiness to all classes of sentient beings existing in the present world?
I now vow that they shall, throughout the future, at all times, constantly experience happiness."
This is called the thorough investigation of the occasion for loving-kindness.
Furthermore, one carefully examines and discerns that within this [state], there is absolutely no self, nor sentient beings, nor anyone who seeks happiness, nor anyone who bestows happiness.
There are only the aggregates and only conditioned formations;
within these, one conceptually designates and employs verbal discourse.
This is for the sake of one who seeks happiness.
Regarding this bestowing of happiness:
furthermore, those various karmas, afflictions, and so forth serve as its causes and conditions.
This is called investigating loving-kindness by means of the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*).
If, through the thorough cultivation, thorough practice, and frequent cultivation of loving-kindness, one is able to sever ill will—
this is called investigating loving-kindness by way of the principle of function.
This meaning is established by the authority of the ultimate teaching;
it can be realized through the manifestation of my own internal wisdom and vision,
and it can also be apprehended through the method of inference.
This is called investigating loving-kindness by means of the principle of logical proof.
Furthermore, this very dharma establishes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā):
the inconceivable nature of phenomena and the abiding nature of phenomena.
That is to say, one should cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*) as it is able to sever ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
One should not engage in discursive thought nor conceptual discrimination, but should instead give rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
This is called investigating loving-kindness by means of the principle of the nature of things (*dharmatā-yukti*).
This is called the cultivation of loving-kindness and compassion by one who investigates the six types of differentiated objects through vipaśyanā.

Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
