In the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*, the thirteenth part of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the second section of the third yoga station, it is asked:
"How does one who diligently cultivates the contemplation of dependent origination investigate the vipaśyanā that takes the six categories of distinctions as its object?"
That is to say, by the predominant power of hearing and upholding the sublime Dharma of dependent origination based on conditions,
one is able to correctly understand that such and such phenomena arise because this or that phenomenon arises.
In this way, through the cessation of various phenomena, those respective phenomena cease.
Within this, there is absolutely no sovereign, agent, creator, or transformer capable of producing these phenomena.
Nor does it possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
There is no person (*pudgala*) in between who could transform all phenomena.
If one can thoroughly understand these and other such meanings, [one attains realization].
This is called the thorough investigation of the meaning of dependent origination.
Furthermore, when one carefully examines and discriminates the twelve links of existence, whether internal or external, and gives rise to resolute conviction,
this is called the thorough investigation of the phenomena of dependent origination.
Furthermore, one carefully examines and discriminates the ignorance regarding the past and the ignorance regarding the future within the link of ignorance (*avidyā*),
as explained at length in the previous analysis of the links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
This is called the thorough investigation of the specific characteristics of dependent origination.

Furthermore, one carefully examines and discriminates that all such conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) produced by conditions are entirely such that they did not exist before but now exist, and having existed, they perish.
Therefore, both the preceding and the succeeding are impermanent; because they all possess the nature of birth, old age, sickness, and death, their essence is suffering and lacks self-mastery;
and because an intermediate person cannot be found.
Its nature is empty and without self;
this is called the investigation of the common characteristic of dependent origination.

Furthermore, one carefully examines and discriminates whether a self exists within those conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) that are, according to the principle of reality, impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self.
The arising of delusion constitutes perversion;
it is comprised within the "black category" (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*),
as explained in detail previously.
If one is not deluded, there will be no inversion;
this is comprised within the category of the white side,
as explained in detail previously.
This is called the thorough investigation of the categories of dependent origination.
Furthermore, one carefully examines and discriminates that the self-identity obtained in past lives lacks any permanent nature; thus it has remained.
The self-identity obtained in the present world lacks any permanent nature and thus abides as such;
the self-identity that will be obtained in future worlds likewise lacks any permanent nature and will abide as such.
This is called the thorough investigation of the time of dependent origination.
Furthermore, one carefully examines and discerns that there are only various karmas and their ripened fruits,
and that within them, no sovereign agent can be found at all.
That which is called the "agent" and the "experiencer" is merely a provisional designation established among phenomena;
that is to say, within the sequence from ignorance conditioned by formations, up to birth conditioned by aging and death.
Based on the conventional designation of conceptual signs,
one speaks of an agent and an experiencer, saying:
"There is such a name and such a lineage."
Such is his clan; such is his food and drink;
such is his experience of suffering or pleasure.
Thus long-lived, thus enduring for a long time,
thus reaching the very limit of the lifespan.
Furthermore, within this there are two kinds of fruits and two kinds of causes.
As for the two kinds of fruits:
the first is the fruit of self-nature (*svabhāva-phala*).
Second, the fruit of the enjoyment of objects.
Regarding the two kinds of causes:
first, the projecting cause.
Second, the cause of arising.
Regarding the fruit that is its own nature:
this refers to the dharmas such as the six sense bases that arise from maturation in the present life.

The fruit of the enjoyment of objects refers to the various feelings produced by the six types of contact, which arise through the predominant influence of karma that is either desirable or undesirable.
The projecting cause refers to the arising of delusion regarding these two fruits.
Ignorance acts as the precursor to meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formations (*saṃskāra*).
These formations are able to appropriate the consciousness (*vijñāna*) that leads to future existence, causing the sprout of birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) to arise;
this is because they are able to appropriate the seed of consciousness.
It causes these to successively encompass the seeds of future name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the seeds of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and the seeds of contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*),

so that the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*)— consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling— may arise in succession in the future, being subsumed under the category of perception (*saṃjñā*).
Now, first of all, one grasps the seeds of those dharmas;
all such [factors] are called the projecting cause (*ākṣepahetu*).
As for the productive cause (*abhinirvṛttihetu*):
That is to say, when one experiences the feelings produced by contact associated with ignorance,
through craving for objects, there arises craving for future existence as well as all forms of grasping belonging to the category of craving and the category of delusion.
By this power and by this efficacy, it moistens the seeds of karma,
enabling them to yield various fruits of maturation (*vipāka*).
All such factors are termed the "causes of arising" (*utpatti-hetu*).
Due to the predominant power of these two causes,
one is pursued by the three types of suffering and brings about the entire mass of pure, great suffering.
In this way, one investigates the principles of dependent origination by relying on the principle of dependence.
Furthermore, one carefully examines and discriminates within this contemplation of the nature of conditions and dependent origination.
Thoroughly cultivating, practicing, and frequently training in this enables the severance of delusion.

Furthermore, one carefully examines and discriminates such principles through authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*), internal direct realization (*pratyātma-adhigama*), and inferential reasoning (*anumāna*).
There is also the establishment of the meaning of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
This is called the principle of functional efficacy and the principle of logical proof.
The principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-yukti*) is the investigation of the principles of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
This is called the vipaśyanā that investigates the six distinct objects of focus for one who diligently cultivates the contemplation of dependent origination.
What is the diligent cultivation of the contemplation of the differentiation of the elements (*dhātu-prabheda-vipaśyanā*)?
It is the insight (*vipaśyanā*) that investigates the objects of focus through the differentiation of six matters;
namely, by the predominant power of hearing and upholding the sublime Dharma based on the differentiation of the elements.
One is able to correctly understand the meaning of all *dhātus*.
That is to say, the meanings of lineage (*gotra*), seed (*bīja*), cause (*hetu*), and nature (*prakṛti*) constitute the meaning of *dhātu*.
This is called the investigation of the meaning of the elements (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, by correctly investigating the internal and external distinctions among the six elements, such as earth and so forth, one gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*);
this is called the investigation of the entities of the elements.
Furthermore, one correctly investigates that earth has the characteristic of solidity,
up to wind having the characteristic of lightness and motion,
and consciousness having the characteristic of discernment.
The space element has the characteristic of emptiness, being pervasive throughout the characteristics of form and characterized by non-obstruction;
this is called the thorough investigation of the specific characteristics of the elements.
Furthermore, one correctly investigates that, in brief, all these elements are impermanent, and so forth, up to being selfless.
This is called the thorough investigation of the common characteristics of the elements.
Furthermore, when one correctly investigates those who do not understand the distinct nature of the elements within what appears as a unified whole,
[one sees that] it is by means of the body composed of the differentiation of the elements [that they are sustained].
To give rise to arrogance is a perversion;
it is subsumed under the category of the dark side (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*),
as explained in detail previously.
That which is contrary to the above is free from inversion;
it is comprised within the category of the white [virtuous] factors,
as explained in detail previously.
This is called the investigation of the elements (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, correctly investigating how the six elements of the past, future, and present serve as conditions for entering the mother’s womb is called the investigation of the time of the elements.

Furthermore, one correctly reflects that just as grass, wood, and so forth, through the combination of various conditions, surround space and are conventionally designated by the name "house," so too,
because the six elements serve as the basis [for consciousness], they are likewise designated.
The various conditions of tendons, bones, flesh, and blood combine and encircle space;
through conceptualization, equalization, and conventional designation,
it is numerically termed "body."
Furthermore, by means of the various karmas and afflictions from past lives as well as one's own seeds as causes and conditions—
in this way, it is called "investigating the principle of the differentiation of the elements based on the principle of dependence."
Furthermore, one correctly reflects that if one skillfully cultivates,
practices, and repeatedly develops this contemplation of the differentiation of elements (*dhātu-prabheda*), it can sever conceit (*māna*).
One also correctly reflects that such a principle is supported by the authority of the authoritative scriptures (*āptāgama*).
There is wisdom realized within oneself;
there is the method of inference;
and there is the establishment of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
The inconceivable nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and the abiding nature of phenomena—
this is called the principle of functional efficacy (kāryakāraṇayukti).
The principle of logical proof,
the principle of the nature of phenomena,
and the principle of investigating the distinctions between the elements.

This is called the insight (vipaśyanā) that investigates the six objects of focus through the differentiation of the elements by one who diligently practices the contemplation of the differentiation of the elements.
What is the insight that investigates the six objects of focus through the differentiation [of the elements] by one who diligently practices mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti)?
This means that by the predominant power of hearing and upholding the sublime Dharma based on mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation,
one is able to correctly comprehend the objective sphere of the inhalation and exhalation.
Binding the mind to achieve clear comprehension and mindful recollection—this is the meaning of *ānāpānasmṛti*.
This is called investigating its meaning.
Furthermore, one correctly investigates that the inhalation and exhalation are perceivable within.
Because they are bound to the body and are included among the external bases, there is a distinction between internal and external.
This is called the thorough investigation of the object.
Furthermore, one correctly investigates that there are two types of inhalation and two types of exhalation.
If the wind enters within, it is called inhalation; if the wind goes outwards, it is called exhalation.
Furthermore, one correctly understands that such is long inhalation and exhalation.
In this way, one attends to short inhalations and exhalations.
In this way, the breath pervades all parts of the body.
This is called the investigation of the specific characteristics of the breaths.
Furthermore, he correctly reflects that when the inhalation has ceased, the exhalation arises;
and when the exhalation has ceased, the inhalation arises.
The movement of inhalation and exhalation is dependent upon the life-faculty and the body possessed of consciousness.
These inhalations and exhalations, as well as their basis, are all impermanent;
this is called the investigation of the common characteristic of the breaths.
Furthermore, one correctly investigates these inhalations and exhalations as follows:
Not abiding in right mindfulness,
his mind is disturbed by evil discursive thoughts and thus becomes inverted;
it is comprised within the dark category.
These are phenomena associated with contention;
the detailed explanation is as previously stated.
Contrary to the above, there is then no perversion.
It is comprised within the white category;
it is a dharma free from contention,
as explained in detail previously.
This is called investigating its category.
Furthermore, one correctly investigates that the turning of inhalation and exhalation in the past, future, and present is dependent upon the body and mind;
the body and mind are dependent upon inhalation and exhalation.
In this way, one investigates the timing.
Furthermore, one correctly investigates that within this [process], there is no one who holds the inhalation,
nor anyone who holds the exhalation.
Inhalation and exhalation are dependent upon those [formations];
they are merely conceptual designations and verbal expressions applied to formations that arise from causes and conditions.
To say that there is one who can maintain the inhalation and exhalation—
this is called investigating the principle by relying on the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*).
Furthermore, one correctly investigates this mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
Through skillful cultivation, practice, and frequent exercise, one is able to sever discursive thought.
Furthermore, one correctly investigates this principle through the authority of the sacred teachings and through the wisdom of internal realization.
There is the method of inference;
there is the establishment of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā);
there is the inconceivable nature of phenomena.
Abiding in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
one should not engage in discursive thought,
nor should one engage in conceptual discrimination.
One should simply have faith and resolve [in this].
This is called the principle of efficacy and the principle of logical proof.
To investigate the principle through the principle of natural law (dharmatā-yukti) is called one who diligently cultivates mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti).
One investigates the discerning insight (*vipaśyanā*) that takes the sixfold differentiation of objects as its focus.
Having thus investigated the observation of the sixfold differentiation based upon the objects of pure conduct (*caritaviśuddhi*), [one proceeds].
Repeatedly, one causes the mind to become tranquil within;
repeatedly, one further scrutinizes with insight exactly as it has been investigated.
Because he relies upon śamatha,
vipaśyanā quickly attains purification;
furthermore, because he relies upon vipaśyanā, [śamatha likewise attains purification].
One causes śamatha to increase and expand.
If one relies upon the objects of skillfulness and the objects for purifying afflictions,
one investigates the vipaśyanā of the six types of differentiated objects.
I shall explain its own locus later.
Furthermore, within this context, there are nine types of application subsumed under the white category (*śukla-pakṣa*);
one should know that those contrary to these are the nine types of application subsumed under the black category (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa*).
What are called the nine types of application subsumed under the white category?
First, the application of correspondence.
Second, the application of cultivation;
third, the application of non-erroneousness;
fourth, the application of non-laxity.
Fifth, application at the appropriate time;
sixth, application of thorough understanding;
seventh, application of insatiability.
Eighth, the application of not relinquishing the yoke;
ninth, the correct application.
It is by means of these nine types of applications subsumed under the category of the white side that [this is established].
It enables the mind to swiftly attain concentration and causes meditative absorption (*samādhi*) to progress further; moreover,
by means of this, one proceeds to the stage that ought to be reached.
Furthermore, according to what is appropriate to be attained,
one is able to proceed and attain it with great speed, without any delay.
These are the nine types of preparatory application subsumed under the dark category (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
One cannot cause the mind to attain concentration swiftly,
nor can one cause samādhi to progress further toward excellence.
Furthermore, because of this, regarding the stage to which one ought to proceed and that which one ought to attain—
Because it is extremely delayed, one cannot quickly attain it.
What is called "concordant application"?
It refers to one who is of a greedy temperament (*rāga-carita*).
One should settle the mind upon the foul;
if one is of a hateful temperament,
one should settle the mind upon loving-kindness.
If one is a person of deluded temperament,
they should settle the mind upon dependent origination.
If one is a person of arrogant temperament...
One should settle the mind upon the differentiation of the elements;
if one is a practitioner of discursive thought,
one should practice mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti).
He stabilizes his mind.
This applies whether he is one whose mental afflictions are in equal proportion or one whose afflictions are slight.
One should, according to one's preference, focus the mind upon a single object of observation and dwell therein,
diligently practicing the application of effort.
This is called the application of union (*yogamanasikāra*).
What is called "familiarized application"?
It refers to having already practiced śamatha and vipaśyanā repeatedly, even if only to a small degree.
Not all of them are beginners in their practice. Why is this?
Because those who are beginners...
Although one diligently applies effort toward the objects of focus associated with meditative application,
various hindrances repeatedly manifest, and there is heaviness and rigidity within body and mind;
due to these causes and conditions, one is unable to cause the mind to quickly attain concentration.
This is called the application of familiarization.
What is called the application of non-slackness?
It refers to the diligent cultivation of meditative practice through uninterrupted means and reverent means.
Whether emerging from meditative concentration, or for the purpose of begging for alms,
or for the purpose of respectfully serving one's teachers and elders,
or for the purpose of tending to the sick.
Either for the sake of practicing concordant acts of respect and harmony,
or for the sake of other such activities of this kind,
his mind remains focused upon those tasks to be performed.
He does not fully comply with them, does not fully incline toward them, and does not fully enter into them;
rather, he swiftly brings the matter to completion and returns once more to diligent practice,
sitting in quietude to cultivate various contemplative exercises.
If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas,
or kṣatriyas.
Brahmins and various other diverse groups gathered together;
though they had long lived in close association, they manifested the formal etiquette of conversation.
Without engaging in continuous discursive speech,
they take sole delight in seclusion and diligently cultivate meditative practice;
furthermore, they are able to exert themselves with such heroic vigor.
"I shall certainly realize that which is to be realized;
I must not be negligent."
Why is this? Because there are many causes and conditions for untimely death for me, namely:
the occurrence of wind, heat, or phlegm within the body.
Or, when food and drink are not properly digested,
they remain within the body and cause the ailment of indigestion;
or one may be afflicted by various venomous insects from without, such as snakes, scorpions, centipedes, millipedes, and the like.
They may be infested by maggots and insects,
or again, they may be terrified by humans, non-humans, and the like,
and thereby meet an untimely death.
Regarding such places of untimely death as these,
one should constantly contemplate and cultivate the perception of impermanence, dwelling in heedfulness.
By dwelling thus in heedfulness, [one attains liberation].
He constantly reflects to himself:
"Suppose my lifespan could be extended for seven days, six days, five days, four days, three days, two days, one day, one watch, half a watch, a brief moment, or even half a brief moment."
It may last for the duration of a meal,
or from the inhalation to the exhalation,
or from the exhalation to the inhalation.
For as long as they remain alive,
they shall diligently apply their attention to and practice yoga within the Buddha’s holy teaching;
for that duration, they shall abide within the Buddha’s holy teaching.
"I shall certainly accomplish much.
This is called non-lax application.
What is called non-erroneous application?
That is to say, as is realized by those yogis who are well-versed in the practice of yoga,
one should train accordingly and grasp the teachings and their meaning without error.
There is no conceit of self,
nor does one abide in the grasping of one's own views;
there is no perverse attachment.
One never disparages or slights the Venerable One’s instructions;
this is called non-erroneous application.
What is meant by timely application?
That is to say: from time to time one cultivates the sign of calm abiding;
from time to time one cultivates the sign of insight;
and from time to time one cultivates the sign of uplifting.
From time to time, one cultivates the sign of equanimity (*upekṣā-nimitta*).
Furthermore, one is able to know, as it truly is, when there is calm abiding (*śamatha*), the sign of calm abiding, and the time of calm abiding;
and one knows, as it truly is, when there is insight (*vipaśyanā*), the sign of insight, and the time of insight.
When one thoroughly knows the act of uplifting and the characteristic of uplifting at the time of uplifting,
and thoroughly knows the act of relinquishing and the characteristic of relinquishing at the time of relinquishing—
what is "cessation" (śamatha)?
This refers to the nine stages of mental abiding through which one is able to cause the mind to dwell in signlessness, non-conceptuality,
tranquility, and utter tranquility, thereby attaining calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Because it is pure, singular, and unmixed, it is called "calming" (śamatha).
What are the characteristics of calming?
They are of two kinds.
First, the characteristic of the object-condition;
second, the characteristic of the causal condition.
Regarding the characteristic of the object-condition:
That is to say, the image which is of the same category as the object of knowledge belonging to the class of śamatha is called the "characteristic of the object of focus" (ālambana-nimitta).
By means of this object of focus...
It causes the mind to become tranquil.
As for the characteristic of the causal condition,
it refers to the mind that has been permeated by *śamatha*.
In order to ensure that all future states of śamatha concentration are purified,
one practices the preparatory applications of yoga-vipaśyanā;
this is called the characteristic of the causal condition.
What is the time for calming?
It refers to when the mind is agitated,
or when there is apprehension that it may become agitated.
This is the time for cultivating calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Furthermore, it is when the mind, having been perfumed by insight (*vipaśyanā*),
is disturbed by discursive thoughts and distracted by various activities.
This is the time for cultivating calm abiding (*śamatha*).
What is insight (*vipaśyanā*)?
It refers to the practice of insight that takes as its object the distinctions among the four modes, the three gateways, and the six matters.
What is the observation of characteristics?
It is said that there are two kinds:
first, the characteristic of the object of focus (*ālambana-nimitta*).
Second, the characteristics of the causal conditions.
Regarding the characteristic of the object of focus (ālambana-nimitta):
it refers to the image that is concordant with the objects of knowledge belonging to the category of vipaśyanā.
By means of this object of observation, wisdom is made to investigate.
As for the characteristic of causal conditions,
it refers to the mind perfumed by vipaśyanā.
In order to ensure that vipaśyanā becomes completely purified at a later time,
one practices the preparatory application for the internal śamatha concentration.
When is it that one observes?
That is to say, when the mind has become sunken or when there is fear that it might become sunken,
this is the time for cultivating insight (vipaśyanā).
Furthermore, based on the mind perfumed by śamatha,
one should first realize the objects of knowledge exactly as they are; therefore,
at that time, it is the time for cultivating vipaśyanā.
What is "exhortation" (*pragraha*)?
It refers to taking up any one kind of pure and sublime object of focus (*ālambana*),
thereby manifesting encouragement and gladdening the mind.
What is the characteristic of uplifting?
It refers to rousing the mind by means of a pure and sublime object of focus.
And how does one apply diligent effort in accordance with that?
What is the time for uplifting?
It is when the mind has become sunken.
Or when one fears sinking,
that is the time for cultivation of uplifting.
What, then, is equanimity?
It refers to the state of mental equanimity in which the mind is undefiled with respect to its object;

it is the quality of being pliant, upright, and spontaneously directed toward the categories of serenity (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), as well as the capacity of the pliant mind for effective action.
It causes the mind to function spontaneously in accordance [with its object].
What is the characteristic of equanimity?
It refers to causing the mind to attain equanimity by means of the focal object.
Furthermore, one does not exert excessive diligence regarding the object of focus.
When is it the time for equanimity (*upekṣā*)?
It is when the mind has already been liberated from agitation (*auddhatya*) pertaining to the categories of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
This is the time for cultivating equanimity.
This is called timely application.
What is called the application of thorough understanding?
That is to say, having correctly grasped, correctly understood, and correctly comprehended these aforementioned characteristics,
one is able to enter meditative concentration immediately upon the desire to do so.
When he wishes to abide in meditative concentration, he is able to abide in it immediately;
when he wishes to emerge from meditative concentration, he is able to emerge from it immediately;
or at times, he relinquishes the mental images that are the objects of the various samādhis and attends to them with mental attention.
The natural objects of focus belonging to all the non-concentrated states are what is called the application of thorough comprehension.
What is called the application of insatiability?
That is to say, one never tires of or becomes satiated with wholesome qualities, never ceasing the cultivation of what is to be abandoned;
and regarding successively higher and more excellent stages,
one dwells frequently in a state of longing for them.
Not only does one not become discouraged midway after attaining a small degree of meditative concentration,
but one always maintains a forward-striving pursuit toward further accomplishments;
this is called the application of non-contentment.
What is called the application of not abandoning the yoke?
It refers to being without breach or flaw regarding all the precepts one has undertaken,
even upon seeing a young woman of beautiful and lovely countenance.
Without grasping at signs or secondary characteristics,
one should diligently cultivate wakefulness with equanimity toward food,
having few concerns, few activities, and little distraction.
Regarding what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago, and so forth,
being able to personally recollect them and causing others to recollect them—
such qualities as these are called the application of not relinquishing the yoke (*ayuktāparityāga-prayoga*).
By means of these dharmas, one can correctly conform to one-pointedness of mind;
not relinquishing that yoke, one prevents the mind from becoming distracted and does not allow the mind to wander toward external objects.
One does not allow the mind to become internally unpliant.
This is called the application of not relinquishing the yoke.
What is called right application?
This refers to repeatedly generating resolute conviction toward the object of focus and repeatedly and correctly eliminating [distractions];
this is called right application (*samyak-prayoga*).
It is like one who diligently cultivates the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
He correctly eliminates all impurities by attending to the signs of impurity;
he arouses attention through vipaśyanā that proceeds in accordance with those signs.
Regarding the object of focus, one repeatedly eliminates it and repeatedly brings it to presence.
There are five ways in which this correct elimination occurs:
first, by withdrawing the mind within.
Second, because of non-attention;
third, because of attention directed toward something else;
fourth, because of remedial attention.
Through the mental engagement with the five signless realms,
it should be understood that herein the nine modes of mental abiding have vipaśyanā as their primary focus.
Therefore, it is called "internally withdrawing the mind.
Because one dwells undisturbed by initially turning away from all signs,
it is called "mental attention without recollecting" (*amanasikāra*).
Because one contemplates the objects of another meditative stage by taking that other stage as a condition,
it is called "attention directed toward another.
Because one contemplates impurity as the antidote to purity, [it is called "attention directed toward the antidote"].
Up to the point of contemplating mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) as the antidote to discursive thought (*vitarka*),
and contemplating the element of space (*ākāśadhātu*) as the antidote to all forms (*rūpa*); therefore,
it is called "attention as an antidote" (*pratipakṣamanasikāra*).
Because one does not attend to any signs and attends instead to the signless realm,
it is called "attention to the signless realm."
Although there are generally five types of signs to be thoroughly eliminated when establishing all objects of focus,
this is the primary meaning intended here.
One merely takes up internal withdrawal of the mind and does not attend to mental engagement.
When a beginner first begins their practice,
at the very outset they do not at all bind the mind to the object of focus.
Whether regarding the impure or some other object, one simply forms this thought:
"How may my mind become free from distraction, signless, and non-conceptual—
tranquil and utterly serene?"
Without turning, without wavering, and without expectation,
free from all activity and inwardly at ease,
one thus exerts oneself regarding all external signs that arise.
Without conceptualizing and without forming mental attention, by means of such non-attention, one eliminates the focal object; therein, one practices yoga and experiences a sense of well-being.
Furthermore, how does one practice with signs and conceptualization regarding objects such as the impure? It is practiced by way of following signs (*nimitta*),
following discursive thought (*vitarka*),
and following analytical investigation (*vicāra*).
Regarding the practice of vipaśyanā:

although that is its object, one does not exclusively and diligently cultivate vipaśyanā; rather, having set aside the signs of observation, one again contemplates the practice of śamatha upon the focal object.
For this reason, at that time,
he neither rejects nor grasps at the object of focus.
Because it proceeds by way of stilling with respect to the object of focus,
it is not called "equanimity"; that is,
because one does not form mental signs regarding that very object of focus.
Because it is non-conceptual,
it is not called "grasping.
It is precisely by means of such inwardly withdrawing the mind that one eliminates the focal object.
Furthermore, because one does not grasp at the signs of observation therein, there is no distraction regarding the object; yet,
because one grasps the mode of activity of calm abiding (*śamatha*),
one again takes the characteristics of the objects of knowledge as one's focal point.
If one merely repeatedly applies resolute conviction toward the object of focus without repeatedly dispelling it,
one will not cause that resolute conviction to become increasingly clear, pure, and ultimate.
One is unable to proceed toward, and even to realize, the objects and phenomena that are to be known;
however, through repeated resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) and repeated elimination,
subsequent stages of resolute conviction proceed with ever-increasing clarity and purity until they reach their ultimate consummation.
Furthermore, one is able to proceed toward and even directly realize the objects of knowledge;
this is like a disciple of a worldly painter who, when first practicing the craft of painting,
first receives from his teacher the model he has been taught to study.
Contemplate and contemplate thoroughly, fashioning that form;
having fashioned it, immediately destroy it;
once destroyed, immediately fashion it again.
Just as one repeatedly removes what has been defaced and acts again,
so too do the subsequent forms become increasingly distinct and increasingly pure until they are ultimately manifested. Thus,
through such correct training over a long period of time, [the result is achieved].
He is universally recognized by the world as a master painter or a master sculptor;
if one does not count the forms he has already produced,
one would have to paint over them again and again.
Thus, regarding the form, there will be no further obscuration, and it will be ultimately and clearly manifest;
one should know that the principle here is likewise.
Once one has given rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) toward this object, [it becomes manifest].
Having become certain regarding this object, one further correctly eliminates it;
it is not that one correctly eliminates it while remaining uncertain regarding this object.
Having become certain regarding this object, one further gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
Having given rise to resolute conviction regarding a limited object,
one correctly eliminates that very limitation;
it should be understood that the same applies to vast and immeasurable objects.
Having correctly eliminated [the perception of] a narrow and limited object,
one may again form a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding it as narrow and limited,
or one may again form a resolute conviction regarding it as vast.
Or one may further give rise to resolute conviction regarding the immeasurable;
it should be understood that the same applies to the vast and the immeasurable.
Whatever characteristics, images, or manifestations appear among all material phenomena (rūpa-dharma), [one should likewise apply this].
One should know that this is a coarse transformation resembling [the original];
it is preceded by the provisional designation of all formless phenomena,
and the image manifests through the predominant power of what has been experienced.
All such [practices] are called right application.
These nine types of virtuous application should be understood as being conducive to śamatha and vipaśyanā.
One should know that the nine types of application contrary to these are in opposition to *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Thus, there are eighteen types of application established through the distinction between the dark side (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) and the white side (*śuklapakṣa*).
This is called one-pointedness of mind.
What is the purification of hindrances?
It refers to those practitioners of yoga who thus correctly cultivate the preparatory application.
By means of four causes and conditions, one is able to purify the mind and eliminate all hindrances.
What are these four?
First, by thoroughly knowing its intrinsic nature.
Second, by means of thoroughly knowing the causes and conditions;
third, by means of thoroughly knowing the disadvantages;
fourth, by means of cultivating the remedies.
What is the thorough knowledge of the intrinsic nature of the hindrances?
It refers to the thorough knowledge that there are four kinds of hindrances:
first, the hindrance of cowardice.
Second, the hindrance of concealment;
third, the hindrance of discursive searching;
fourth, the hindrance of self-exaltation.
The hindrance of timidity refers to all defiled longing, lack of joy, yearning, and distress that arise when one is striving in the practice of renunciation and seclusion.
The "obscuration of the hindrances" refers to the five hindrances, such as sensual desire and so forth.
The "obscuration of discursive thought" refers to...
This refers to defiled discursive thoughts such as sensual desire and so forth.
Regarding the obstacle of self-exaltation:
it refers to [being satisfied with] a small amount of inferior knowledge and vision.
While dwelling in a state of peace and security, one becomes self-exalting,
thinking: "I am able to attain this,
whereas others are not."
The details are as extensively explained above;
one should understand that this is called the thorough knowledge of the intrinsic nature of all obstacles.
What is the thorough knowledge of the causes and conditions of all obstacles?
This refers to thorough comprehension.
Regarding the first obstacle of timidity, there are six causes and conditions.
First, it arises through the predominant influence of prior karma.
Or, due to being afflicted by illness,
his body becomes weak and frail;
second, there is excessive application of effort.
Third, not cultivating preparatory application;
fourth, initially cultivating preparatory application;
fifth, the intensity of afflictions.
Sixth, regarding those who have not yet become habituated to seclusion,
and who possess the causes and conditions for the hindrances of thorough knowledge, concealment, discursive thought, and self-exaltation:
this refers to those factors that accord with the states of concealment, discursive thought, and the basis for self-exaltation.
The habitual practice of improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) is called the causal condition for the obscuration of the "searching-for-self-exaltation" (*vitarka-samutthāna-unnati*).
This occurs if one does not bring impurity (*aśubha*) to mind through mental attention.
To attend to and reflect upon pure signs while doing so is,
in this context, termed improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
If one does not attend to and reflect upon loving-kindness and compassion, but instead attends to and reflects upon signs of malice, [this likewise constitutes improper mental attention].
This is called improper mental attention (ayoniśo-manasikāra) in this context:
if one does not attend to the sign of light,
but instead attends to the sign of darkness.
This is called improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) in this context.
If one does not attend to the signs of śamatha,
but instead attends to relatives, one's country, immortality, or the past;
To direct one's attention toward and contemplate various unwholesome reflections, such as past instances of pleasure, amusement, laughter,
and service, is what is meant here by "inappropriate attention" (ayoniśomanasikāra).
If one does not apply attention to dependent origination based on its nature,
but instead applies attention through incorrect conceptualization, reckoning a self and what belongs to a self within the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the three times.
This is what is called improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) in this context.
How does one fully understand the faults and disadvantages of these hindrances?
It means fully understanding that because these hindrances exist, one fails to realize the four kinds [of truths] that have not yet been realized, and loses what has already been realized.
They ruin all applications of yoga;
they dwell in defilement and dwell in suffering; they destroy themselves and destroy others;
and at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in the various evil destinies.
This is called thoroughly knowing the faults and disadvantages of all obstacles.
What is meant by "cultivating the remedies"?
It refers to using mindfulness as the remedy for all forms of cowardice.
By means of mental attention through recollection, one gladdens the mind;
this causes all timidity that has already arisen to be dispelled and that which has not yet arisen not to arise,
thereby removing physical weakness and excessive application of effort.
When first practicing the preparatory application (*prayoga*), one uses diligence and impartial penetration as the antidote;
when not practicing the preparatory application,
one uses respectful listening and diligent inquiry as the antidote.
When afflictions are intense,
one employs the preparatory applications of focal objects such as the impure as an antidote; however,
this is so when one has not yet become habituated to them.
One should employ such analytical skillful means as an antidote,
thinking: "Because I was not previously habituated to solitude,
I now feel timidity and weakness regarding the practice of solitude."
If I do not practice seclusion now,
I will certainly be the same in future lives. Therefore,
I should now correctly deliberate and, abandoning lack of delight in seclusion, cultivate delight in it.
The remaining hindrances, such as concealment and so forth, consist of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*);
their antidote is proper mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*), which is their opposite.
One should understand that this is called the cultivation of the antidote.
Furthermore, one thoroughly understands that the intrinsic nature of all hindrances is that which obstructs,
that which defiles,
and that which is comprised within the dark category.
These should be abandoned;
for one can only abandon such obstacles after having fully understood the causes and conditions for their abandonment.
One should seek out the causes and conditions of the various obstacles and thoroughly understand what ought to be abandoned;
for one who does not abandon them, what faults and disadvantages arise?
Therefore, one should seek out the faults and disadvantages of the various obstacles.
Having already distanced oneself from them, one further reflects upon these obstacles:
"How may they not arise in future lives?
Therefore, one should seek to cultivate their remedies.
By means of these causes and conditions, one is able to purify the mind and eliminate all obscurations.
It should be understood that herein, because the teachings to be followed are manifold,
vipaśyanā is likewise manifold.
Because vipaśyanā is manifold,
it causes śamatha to be manifold as well;
furthermore, this very vipaśyanā is manifold because the objects of knowledge are limitless.
One should know that its measure is likewise without limit;
that is to say, by means of three gateways and six kinds of matters,
one enters into the principle through each of these infinite varieties of distinctions.
For the practitioner of correct cultivation, through the superior power of the purification resulting from the repeated practice of vipaśyanā in accordance with suchness,
there arises an ever-increasing and expansive pliancy of both body and mind.
It should be understood that as the category of śamatha increases and expands, the body and mind attain pliancy;
in this way and to this extent, the one-pointedness of mind toward its object further increases.
To the extent that one-pointedness of mind toward the object increases further and further,
to that same extent one further attains pliancy of body and mind; thus,
there is one-pointedness of mind and pliancy of body and mind.
These two dharmas are mutually dependent and mutually connected:
physical and mental lightness and tranquility, and one-pointedness of mind.
Only when these two dharmas attain the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) do they reach ultimate perfection.
Because one has attained the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), direct perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*) arises regarding the objects of knowledge.

Question: To what extent may it be said that one has ultimately attained the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), and so on, up to: to what extent may it be said that one has ultimately attained mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*)?
Answer: To state it briefly,
a practitioner of meditation who is engaged in the formal application of the contemplation of impurity should cultivate it through close proximity and repeated practice.
Due to extensive cultivation,
whether walking or standing, although various objects appear before him,
he continues to observe all their characteristics.
Abiding in its own nature without relying on application,
for the most part, impure aspects appear rather than pure aspects;
because of having well-cultivated the perception of the impure, with respect to those phenomena that are conducive to the entanglement of sensual desire, [it does not arise].
When the mind does not enter [into the object], does not find delight in it, and does not have faith or understanding in it,
but instead dwells in equanimity with a deep sense of aversion,
at that time the practitioner of meditation should recognize this for themselves.
"I have now attained the contemplation of impurity;
I have now attained the fruit of my cultivation.
To this extent, it is said that one has reached the ultimate consummation of the contemplation of impurity."
That which is contrary to this should be known as not having attained the ultimate.
As it is with the contemplation of impurity,
so it is with loving-kindness, the nature of objects, dependent origination, the differentiation of elements, and mindfulness of breathing at every moment.
It should be understood that it is likewise so.
The distinction therein is as follows:
for the most part, the aspect of loving-kindness manifests rather than the aspect of ill-will with respect to those phenomena that are conducive to the obsession of ill-will.
The mind does not enter [into them], and so forth, as explained at length.
For the most part, the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self appear;
it is not the aspect of delusion associated with the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) that conceives of permanence and bliss.
Regarding those phenomena that accord with the fetters of delusion,
the mind does not enter into them, and so forth, as explained at length;
for the most part, these consist of various natures of elements rather than a single nature of elements.
The manifestation of the perception of the distinction between the aggregates of the body is not the perception of the aggregates of the body itself.
Regarding those phenomena that accord with the entanglement of conceit,
the mind does not enter into them, and so forth, as explained at length.
For the most part, the perception of internal tranquility and the perception of *śamatha* appear, while the perception of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) does not;
thus, the mind does not enter into those phenomena that are conducive to the entanglements of discursive thought, and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: At what point should one say that śamatha and vipaśyanā are combined, proceeding in equilibrium and simultaneously, such that it is called the path of "coupled operation"?
Answer: If one attains the ninth stage of mental abiding among the nine stages of mental abiding—
namely, *samāhita* (equipoise)—
one relies upon such perfected *samādhi* as a basis.
Within the contemplation of phenomena, one cultivates superior wisdom.
At that time, by means of the contemplation of phenomena, the path proceeds spontaneously;
it turns effortlessly, not through deliberate application.
Vipaśyanā is pure and bright;
it is harmonized and integrated by śamatha,
proceeding in accordance with the integration of the path of śamatha.
When these two are thus balanced and proceed together in equal measure, this is called the path of the simultaneous operation of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
This is therefore termed the path of the dual progression of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
The summary verse (*uddāna*) states:
Investigation of characteristics, examination, and subsequent application; There are three gateways:
meaning, phenomena, characteristics, categories, and time; And the six principles regarding the distinctions of things.
First is the application of preliminary practice;
next is familiarization that is neither lax nor erroneous, performed at the proper time;
then there is comprehension characterized by lack of satiety and non-abandonment of the yoke of virtue; and finally, correct application.
These nine should be known; one should understand their two-fold distinctions, their intrinsic natures, and their causes and conditions.
By perceiving those various faults and correctly practicing the remedies, one brings the obstacles to purification.
What is the cultivation of mental attention?
It refers to when a beginner first begins their practice,
[directing it] toward such universally established characteristics as they have been established.
By means of one-pointedness of mind and the purification of all hindrances,
one abandons incorrect application and trains in correct application;
such a person should first form this thought:
Now, in order to realize one-pointedness of mind and to abandon [the attachment to] joy and pleasure,
I shall diligently cultivate the four types of mental attention (*manasikāra*). What are these four?
First, the mental attention of training the mind;
second, the mental attention of moistening the mind;
third, the mental attention of generating pliancy.
Fourth is the mental application of pure knowledge and vision.
What is the mental application of training the mind?
It refers to that mental application by which one causes the mind to become weary of and detached from phenomena that should be reviled.
This is called the mental attention of training the mind.
What is the mental attention of moistening the mind?
It refers to that mental attention by which one causes the mind to find joy and delight in those phenomena that are worthy of aspiration.
This is called the mental attention that moistens the mind.
What is the mental attention that generates pliancy?
It refers to that mental attention by which, from time to time, one brings about a sense of wearying detachment toward phenomena that are to be reviled.
From time to time, he causes the mind to find joy in things that are inspiring;
having thus settled within internal tranquility, free from signs and non-conceptualization, his mindfulness proceeds with one-pointedness.
By means of these causes and conditions, one counteracts all physical and mental heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*),
brings about pliancy and satisfaction throughout the entire body and mind,
and gives rise to all-encompassing physical and mental lightness and tranquility (*praśrabdhi*).
This is called the attention that produces pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
What is the attention that purifies knowledge and vision?
It refers to the fact that, by means of this attention, from time to time one takes such internal tranquility as the basis.
By repeatedly applying oneself through internal mental tranquility,
one cultivates superior wisdom within the contemplation of phenomena;
this is called the attention of purified knowledge and vision.
That practitioner,
from time to time, brings about a sense of weary detachment toward phenomena that should be found loathsome;
likewise, he does so toward the outflows (*āsrava*) and the phenomena that serve as the basis for the outflows.
It is able to cause the mind to produce heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, and to produce revulsion (*nirvid*) and so forth.
What is called the "object of revulsion"?
Briefly, there are four kinds of objects of revulsion.
That is to say, when one encounters and directly faces one's own decline and the decline of others,
through the repeated contemplation of appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), it becomes an object of revulsion.
When one's own prosperity or the prosperity of others has passed away, been extinguished, departed, and undergone transformation,

by means of systematic attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) and repeated reflection, it becomes an object of revulsion; at such times, that practitioner should from time to time cause the mind to find delight in things that are grounds for rejoicing.
Thus, because one generates delight toward that,
the mind becomes thoroughly moistened, supple, harmonious, and clear.
What is called "a state worthy of delight"?
Briefly, there are three kinds of objects worthy of aspiration:
first, the Three Jewels;
second, the purity of the training precepts and the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Third, one develops deep faith and understanding regarding the distinctions of what one has personally realized, such that the mind is free from timidity.
How does one recollect the Three Jewels so as to cause the mind to rejoice?
It is by reflecting as follows:
I have now well obtained such a great benefit,
namely, that I have been graced by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, as my Great Teacher.
I have now well obtained such a great benefit.
That is to say: "I have obtained ordination within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya;
I have now well attained such great benefit as this, namely, that I am together with those who are endowed with precepts and endowed with virtue."
Through patience and gentleness, one accomplishes the qualities of a noble person.
One dwells as a fellow practitioner of the holy life with companions in the Dharma.
Thus, I shall now meet a noble death and pass away in a noble manner.
One will attain a virtuous rebirth in future lives.
This is called recollecting the Three Jewels so as to gladden the mind.
What is the recollection of the purity of the training precepts?
Purity of ethical discipline brings joy to the mind;
that is to say, one reflects:

"I have now well obtained such a great benefit as being among the disciples of the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who has well expounded the Dharma and Vinaya and whose followers practice correct conduct."
May I be one who shares the same holy life with those fellow practitioners,
sharing the same precepts, the same studies, and the same cultivation of compassionate physical,
verbal, and mental actions; may I share their views and share what they enjoy.
This is called gladdening the mind by means of mindfulness of the training rules and the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*),
which gives rise to joy preceded by freedom from regret.
How does one gladden the mind by generating deep faith and understanding in the distinctions of what has been personally realized, such that the mind is free from timidity?
That is to say, one reflects:
"I now possess the power and capability; my ethical discipline (*śīla*) is pure, and I am fit to be a vessel for the Dharma.
Thus, I may share in the same pure precepts as these fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*)."
I have attained a view in common with wise, upright, and virtuous persons.
I possess the capacity to diligently cultivate such right practice,
whereby I may attain what has not yet been attained in this present life.
One is able to contact what has not yet been contacted and realize what has not yet been realized;
thereby, the mind gives rise to great joy.
This is called the distinction regarding one's own realization.
Deeply generating faith and understanding, one’s mind is free from timidity; one causes the mind to find joy in the state [of practice].
Furthermore, through courageous diligence applied before and after, one attains the specific distinctions of the realization already established in stability.
By recollecting this, one develops profound faith and understanding regarding the distinctions realized at a later time,
causing the mind to feel joy;
this is called an alternative formulation.
That practitioner disciplines his mind regarding phenomena that should be reviled;
he prevents his mind from inclining toward those things conducive to the outflows (*āsrava*), remaining instead in opposition to them,
rejecting them, turning away from them, and dwelling in phenomena that are to be delighted in.
It gladdens and moistens the mind;
because there is a sense of endearment toward all phenomena produced through renunciation and detachment,
it causes the mind to incline toward them, becoming attached to joy and bliss, and abiding in union with them.
In this way, through these two modes of activity— aversion and aspiration—
that mind turns away from all dark qualities and toward all bright qualities, becoming easily detached and shifting accordingly. Such is that mind.
Turning away from all dark qualities,
one proceeds toward all bright qualities by means of mental attention that disciplines the mind.
By means of the mental attention that moistens the mind,
from time to time one inwardly sustains the mind through *śamatha*; and by means of the mental attention that gives rise to pliancy,
from time to time one discriminates, thoroughly discriminates, extensively investigates, and extensively examines phenomena.
Through the mental engagement of pure knowledge and vision,
his mind becomes, from time to time, capable of being sustained by śamatha and vipaśyanā.
It acts as the cause for the gathering of all aspects of conduct and all merits;
throughout various days, nights, kṣaṇas, lava-s, and muhūrta-s, one attains progressive advancement.
For example, it is like a wise smith of gold and silver, or his apprentice,
who from time to time smelts and refines the gold and silver,
causing it to cast off all impurities.
From time to time, they pour clear, cold water [upon it],
making those various ornaments capable of being worked, supple, and compliant; then,
a wise goldsmith or his apprentice [proceeds].
Having thoroughly understood them through their resemblance to exquisite craftsmanship and skillful intelligence,
they employ them as instruments for action,
manifesting various transformations within the ornaments according to their inclinations.
In this way, the practitioner who diligently cultivates yoga causes the mind to turn away from all defilements such as greed,
and causes it to turn away from afflicted sorrow and distress.
One develops deep revulsion toward phenomena that are to be reviled.
To induce inclination toward all pure and wholesome qualities,
one generates delight toward phenomena that are to be delighted in.
Thereupon, as the practitioner inclines toward whichever category— whether that of śamatha or vipaśyanā— in which he wishes to establish himself,
he is able to skillfully and closely associate with that very category.
They are able to skillfully harmonize [all things] without shifting or wavering;
within the various meanings according to what they delight in,
they can accomplish everything exactly as they have resolved with faith and understanding.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 31 [continued] / Fascicle 32,
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
In the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, the thirteenth part of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the third *Yogasthāna*, section three: What is the manner in which a beginner first undertakes the practice?
When one practices mental attention as it has been appropriately established,
at the very beginning of practicing correctly according to that establishment,
one first realizes the unification of mind through the abandonment of joy.
This refers to a skilled practitioner of yoga who,
at the outset, instructs a beginner engaged in that very practice of yoga as follows:
Welcome, O noble ones.
You should now rely upon three kinds of causes and conditions for grasping signs—
whether through seeing, hearing, or mental inference.
The predominant discrimination grasps five kinds of signs:
first, the sign of revulsion;
second, the sign of joyful aspiration.
Third, the characteristic of faults;
fourth, the characteristic of light;
fifth, the characteristic of discerning objects.
Question: If, according to the practice of yoga, a beginner practitioner is of a greedy temperament and can only be tamed through the meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā),
why is he instructed to apprehend the five types of signs?
"I accept these instructions.
Welcome, noble ones!
You may each dwell in whichever villages or towns you choose as your respective places of residence."
If one hears that in various other villages or market towns,
whether men or women, first experienced peace and happiness but later encountered suffering and calamity;
or that those men or women themselves have fallen gravely ill and passed away.

Having correctly grasped the signs, one sits in the proper posture.

By means of a mental engagement belonging to the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*), which is accompanied by the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) for the welfare and happiness of others,
one first directs [the mind] toward one friend, one enemy, and one neutral person.
One generates resolute conviction;
regarding these three categories,
one employs mental attention accompanied by the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) for equal benefit and happiness.
Desiring to grant them happiness,
one reflects and says:
"May all those classes of sentient beings who seek happiness attain happiness."
That is to say: either desire for pleasure that is blameless,
or joy and pleasure that are blameless,
or pleasure that is blameless and devoid of joy.
Thereafter, one may [practice] toward two relatives,
or three, or four, or five, ten, twenty, thirty, and so on,
as previously described, until it extends throughout all directions and intermediate points.
Within that, the category of relatives fills it completely without any gaps, giving rise to resolute conviction;
therein, there is not even space sufficient to accommodate the tip of a single staff.
As it is with the category of relatives, so it is [with the others].
One should know that it is likewise with respect to enemies and neutral persons.
Furthermore, they do not abandon the application of loving-kindness and compassion;
rather, it is precisely through the cultivation of such loving-kindness and compassion [that they proceed].
One is able to correctly enter into the foundations of mindfulness. How does one enter?
It means that at the time of entering, one should give rise to such a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
Just as others regard me as a friend, an enemy, or one who is neutral,
and since I desire pleasure and wish to avoid suffering,
this is called practicing the contemplation of the body in the internal body.
Furthermore, regarding others as well— whether they be friends, enemies, or those of neutral character— one considers that just as I do,
they also desire pleasure and recoil from suffering.
This is called practicing the contemplation of the body in relation to external bodies.
Just as it is with me, so it is with all those sentient beings;
just as I myself desire to seek and attain supreme happiness.
Those sentient beings are likewise so.
Those sentient beings are equal to me and similar to me;
I shall bestow benefit and happiness upon them.
This is called the cultivation of the contemplation of the body with respect to the internal and external body.
Since these four foundations of mindfulness take the aggregates as their collective object,
they should be known as the "foundations of mindfulness with disintegrating objects."
If a practitioner grasps only the signs of form—
namely, grasping the signs of color, shape, and manifestation—
they give rise to resolute conviction toward the category of friends, the category of enemies, and the category of neutral persons.
Based on this, the application of mindfulness to the body alone is established;
furthermore, by relying upon attention through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*),
one is able to correctly enter into genuine attention (*tattva-manasikāra*).
This means that at the time of entry, one gives rise to this resolve:
"I shall direct my resolve toward as many as immeasurable sentient beings,
with the superior intention of bringing them benefit and happiness."
In this way, from the beginningless past,
all those sentient beings belonging to the categories of kin, enemies,
and neutral parties who have passed away and ceased to exist—
Their number is immeasurable, far exceeding those of the present;
such were the classes of sentient beings in the past who acted through resolute conviction.
Having been my relative, they again become my enemy;
having been my enemy, they again become my relative;
and having been both enemy and relative, they again become neutral.
Having established them as neutral, one further regards them as enemies and kin;
through this methodological approach, all sentient beings are equal.
In this equality, there is not even the slightest degree of the nature of enemy, the nature of kin, or the nature of neutrality.
Yet it is not real.
For this reason, one should give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all three categories of beings;
with such equanimity, one should bestow benefit and happiness upon them.
As it was from the prior limit,
so it will be at the subsequent limit;
one shall continue to wander through birth and death once again.
It should be understood that it is likewise so.
Furthermore, from the beginningless past,
I have never before given rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion toward any sentient beings.
Since they have all passed away,
what further benefit is there in now giving rise to loving-kindness and compassion?
It is solely for the purpose of removing the defilements of one's own mind.
In order to bring about purification, one gives rise to the thought:
"I shall cause all sentient beings of the past to attain peace and happiness;
and those of future ages who have not yet existed."
He also causes them all to attain peace and happiness.
Thus entering into authentic mental attention (*manasikāra*),
he dwells in compassion, wherein all merits and all virtues are nourished and moistened.
Compared to the mass of merit obtained while dwelling in loving-kindness (*maitrī*) through the previously cultivated mental attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*),
that [former merit] does not approach even one hundredth part of this.
That [former merit] does not approach even one-thousandth part of this;
it does not approach even a numerical part, a calculable part, a fraction, or a *upaniṣad* part of this.
The rest is as previously stated.
Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of dependent origination through conditions, a beginner,
by the predominant power of the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection,
conceptually grasps signs.
It means that because sentient beings possess various forms of ignorance and delusion,
they perceive what is impermanent as permanent and perceive what is impure as pure.
They perceive suffering directly before them yet falsely conceive it as pleasure;
they perceive selflessness directly before them yet falsely conceive it as a self.
Those sentient beings possess such various kinds of inversions.
With inversion as the cause, one gives rise to craving for the experiences of the present life and for the various self-bodies that will arise in the future.
Due to this craving, one performs the various karmas that are the root of birth.
With these afflictions and karma as causes and conditions,
one brings about a mass of pure great suffering in the future.
Having correctly grasped such signs, he—
Furthermore, one develops conviction within it as follows:
"This entire mass of suffering of mine arises in this very same way.
Moreover, my own self, being boundless and limitless, has come from a prior limit that is originally unknowable, and it likewise arises in this very same way."
All those sentient beings—whether past, future, or present—are comprised within the aggregate of suffering of their respective selves;
they have all likewise already arisen or will arise.
Thus one correctly contemplates this dependent nature and dependent origination.
All of these are attention consisting of reality;
there is no other attention consisting of resolute conviction.
If one attends to the nature of conditions and dependent origination regarding the present aggregates within oneself.
This is called dwelling in the contemplation of the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena within one's own internal body.
If one attends to and contemplates the nature of conditions and dependent origination regarding the present aggregates of another's body:
This is called dwelling in the contemplation of external body, feeling, mind, and phenomena.
If one [contemplates] all the aggregates—whether belonging to oneself or others, whether past or future—as being of the nature of conditions and dependently originated.
To attend with mental attention is called dwelling in the contemplation of the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena internally and externally.
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, regarding the beginner who practices the contemplation of the differentiation of the elements,
they first apprehend all external marks of solidity,
namely, the great earth.
The mountains, forests, grasses, trees, bricks, stones, and rubble;
mani-jewels, pearls,
lapis lazuli, conch shells, and cowries.
Having grasped the characteristics of coral, jade,
and so forth, one further develops resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding their internal solidity;
next, one grasps the characteristics of the great waters outside.
That is to say, having taken the signs of the various currents of rivers,
ponds, lakes, marshes, wells, and so forth,
one then gives rise to resolute conviction regarding internal moisture.
Next, one should take up the various external signs of great fire,
namely: the scorching midday sun during the heat of summer,
and its blazing, incandescent conflagration.
Having grasped the signs of all fires within mountain thickets, marshes, spreading conflagrations, kilns, chambers, and so forth,
one then gives rise to resolute conviction regarding internal warmth. Next,
one grasps the signs of the external great elements of wind.
Regarding what are called the winds of the east, west, south, north, and so forth, up to the wind-circles:
having grasped their characteristics, one then forms a resolute conviction regarding the internal winds.
Next, one grasps the characteristic of external great space.
That is to say, within all material aggregates that are unobstructed and unimpeded in every direction, there are interstices, cavities, and hollows that provide space for containment.
Having correctly apprehended such characteristics of the space element (*ākāśadhātu*), [one should contemplate it].
One forms a resolute conviction regarding the internal space element;
subsequently, through the predominant power of hearing and reflection,
one gives rise to subtle discrimination and grasps the characteristics of the consciousness element.
That is to say: the internal eye-base is unimpaired,
external visible-form objects are present,
yet the attention capable of producing [consciousness] does not arise.
The visual consciousness that would arise [from those conditions] cannot arise;
however, a visual consciousness contrary to these [conditions] can arise.
It should be understood that this applies likewise, up to and including the mental faculty, mental objects, and mental consciousness.
Having grasped these signs, one next gives rise to resolute conviction,
clearly understanding that within this body composed of the four great elements, there exists the element, lineage, and intrinsic nature of all seeds of consciousness.
Furthermore, regarding these four great elements,
one first gives rise to the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) of the coarse and large parts of the limbs and joints,
and subsequently gives rise to the resolute conviction of analyzing them into various subtle and minute divisions.
In this manner, one gradually analyzes [the object] down to the size of a mote of dust moving in a sunbeam;
thus, step by step, one develops resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) even regarding a single atom (*paramāṇu*).
One develops resolute conviction that each individual part is still an accumulation of immeasurable, most subtle atoms.
How much more so for all the limbs within the body.
This is called the subtle, superior resolve that analyzes the limits of the differentiation of the various elements within the contemplation of the differentiation of the elements.
Next, regarding the space element, one should first generate a resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) concerning all its coarse and gross aspects,
namely the various cavities such as the eye sockets, the ear canals, and the nostrils.
From this, one swallows;
having swallowed, impurity flows out from the lower parts.
Thereafter, one gradually gives rise to various subtle forms of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
He thoroughly understands all the subtle pores and cavities within the body;
subsequently, within the element of consciousness, he gradually gives rise to its basis and its object.

Furthermore, when one applies mental attention to the distinctions of time periods, categories, and immeasurable types of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*),
at that very moment of generating resolute conviction toward the element of consciousness,
one analyzes the element of consciousness by means of its various bases (*āśraya*) and objects (*ālambana*).
One also gives rise to resolute conviction regarding the ten kinds of derived matter;
just as the primary elements are analyzed into subtle parts, so too is this.
If one gives rise to resolute conviction regarding the various distinct elements within one's own body,
this is called abiding in the contemplation of those [elements] among the internal applications of mindfulness;
if one does so regarding other things that do not belong to the category of sentient beings, [it is called the external].
To give rise to resolute conviction regarding all elements belonging to the category of external phenomena is called dwelling in the contemplation of those [elements] externally.
If one gives rise to resolute conviction regarding all elements belonging to the category of other sentient beings, [it is likewise].
One abides in the contemplation of names internally and externally.
Furthermore, there is another method:
namely, one gives rise to resolute conviction regarding one's own body.
At the time of passing away, as described in detail previously,
when one reaches the stage of bluish discoloration or further putrefaction,
one then develops the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the various exudations arising from that putrefaction.
Gradually, the flowing pus spreads and expands until it completely fills the great oceans and reaches the very limits of the great earth.
Having thus cultivated this resolute conviction regarding the pus, [one should contemplate as follows].
Next, one further develops the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) of fire burning:
that this body, with its immeasurable and boundless varieties of parts,
becomes a great mass of fire and is consumed by those immeasurable and boundless varieties of flames.
Once the fire has been extinguished, one further gives rise to the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the remaining bones and ashes;
then, one again gives rise to immeasurable and boundless resolute convictions,
reducing these bone-ashes to fine powder.
Again, one generates the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) of immeasurable great winds,
which blow and scatter these fragments throughout all directions and intermediate points.
Once they have been scattered, one no longer perceives the ashes and bones being blown away, nor the wind that blows them.
One observes only the remaining vast and boundless empty space.
Thus, by means of attention through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*),
one enters into the differentiation of the elements based on the practice of internal and external impurity.
Abiding in the contemplation of the body regarding its physical characteristics,
one enters into authentic mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) by means of such resolute attention (*adhimukti-manasikāra*).
Abiding in the contemplation of the body with respect to the internal and external body,

through the power of resolute conviction, one perceives these immeasurable and boundless characteristics of the water element, fire element, earth element, wind element, and space element as being produced by oneself.
Since beginningless time, as I have wandered through the stream of saṃsāra,
the realms I have passed through have been immeasurable and boundless, far exceeding even this; that is to say,
by reason of the death of parents, brothers, sisters, and kinsmen.
Furthermore, due to the separation and destruction of kinsmen, friends, wealth, treasures, rank, and position,
one weeps and sheds tears like rain;
moreover, one drinks the mother’s milk.
Furthermore, due to committing robbery by means of intimidation and plunder— such as breaking through walls or picking locks—
one encounters immeasurable punishments,
including having one's hands cut off or one's feet amputated.
Their heads were severed and their noses cut off;
their various limbs and joints were dismembered and cut apart.
Because of these causes and conditions, blood flowed in immeasurable quantities.
If all the water elements and masses of water comprised by such tears, milk, and blood were collected together,
they would completely fill the waters of the four great oceans;
yet even a hundredth part of those oceans would not equal them.
The detailed explanation is as before.
Furthermore, throughout all states of existence and all realms of rebirth, they undergo death and birth,
