their corpses being cremated by immeasurable fires.
Likewise, there is no comparison for this mass of fire;
nor is there any comparison for the countless times one’s skeletal remains have been discarded and left scattered upon the ground;
nor is there any comparison for the countless times the wind element has arisen and ceased, disintegrating the corpse.
Furthermore, it passes through the eye-orifices and other apertures within countless corpses;
it passes through the incessant flow of countless consciousnesses;
and subsequently, new and ever-renewing corpses are brought forth.
Thus, even until this final corpse, the various consciousnesses continue to transmigrate.
In this way, the limits of future rebirths are established as being indefinite.
This continues in such a manner throughout the immeasurable realms of consciousness.
Furthermore, within the correct practice of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*),
the beginner first [observes] the breath at the front or back of their dwelling, at a window or door, or at a blacksmith’s forge.
Or like a smith working with gold or silver,
blowing through tubes and beating with hammers;
or like wind gathering from outside, entering and exiting, coming and going.
Having correctly grasped the signs,
by means of mindfulness of breathing directed toward internal inhalation and exhalation,
one develops resolute conviction regarding the inhalation and exhalation.
Furthermore, he first forms a resolute conviction regarding the subtle wind of the breath as it moves through the coarse openings at the region of the heart and chest;
thereafter, he gradually forms a resolute conviction regarding a multitude of winds.
That is to say, one forms the resolute conviction that even the winds within all the pores enter accordingly.
Likewise, all these bodily parts are followed by masses of wind, encompassed by masses of wind, and contain hidden stores of wind; therein, immeasurable masses of wind are accumulated.
Just as with tūla-cotton, silk floss, or similar light and floating objects,
one forms a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding these various signs.
If one then applies mental attention to the uninterrupted flow of internal inhalation and exhalation, [one attains stability].
At that time, it is called "dwelling in the contemplation of the body with regard to one's own internal body.

Furthermore, if one attends to the inhalations and exhalations as they cease to flow within the various stages of another's corpse, such as the stage of livid discoloration (*vinīlaka*), this is likewise [contemplation of the body].
At that time, it is called "dwelling in the contemplation of the body with regard to the external body.
Furthermore, one may form a resolute conviction regarding oneself at the point of death,
or form a resolute conviction regarding the cessation of the flow of inhalation and exhalation once death has occurred.
Or, one may form a resolute conviction that, even while not yet dead, there is no further circulation of inhalation and exhalation;
by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*),
at that time, this is called "dwelling in the contemplation of the body with regard to the internal and external body."
Throughout all correct applications,
one should cultivate such non-erroneous application as is comprised within the category of calm abiding (śamatha) and its auxiliary factors;
all else should be understood as previously described.
In this way, when all such beginners receive correct instruction and cultivate right practice,
they abide in ardent, clear comprehension, and full mindfulness.
He subdues all worldly greed and sorrow.
Within such correct application,
he constantly practices, practices to completion, and maintains non-erroneous mental attention.
It cannot be disturbed or agitated by clamor and the like;
this is called "blazing.
If, within such right application, [one remains thus...]
Cultivating śamatha and vipaśyanā,
one discerns and thoroughly understands the characteristics of distraction and non-distraction;
this is called being endowed with correct knowledge and mindfulness.
If one can skillfully grasp the signs of revulsion and the signs of joyful aspiration,
this is called subduing all worldly greed and anxiety.
For this reason, it is said that such a person is able to abide in fervent practice.
Even when one first initiates such correct application in order to subdue worldly greed and anxiety,
the one-pointedness of mind and the pliancy of body and mind proceed in a state so subtle that they are difficult to perceive.
Furthermore, through the cultivation of superior śamatha and vipaśyanā,
the body and mind become clear and pure, the body and mind become pliant and supple, and the body and mind attain lightness and ease— that is,
the aforementioned slight one-pointedness of mind and the lightness and ease of body and mind.
Gradually increasing further, it is able to induce a powerful and easily discernible one-pointedness of mind and physical and mental pliancy;
that is to say, by means of the principle of expedient application, it is successively induced through the power of causes.
At that time, before long, he will give rise to a powerful,
easily understood, and tranquil state of physical and mental lightness, along with one-pointedness of mind;
this continues until those aforementioned signs appear.
At the crown of the head, there arises a sensation as if something heavy were pressing down,
yet it is not of a nature that causes affliction; because this sign arises internally,
it is able to obstruct the abandonment of pleasure.
The heaviness and rigidity of the mind associated with all categories of afflictions are entirely eliminated;
that which counteracts them—
the pliancy of the mind and the flexibility of the mind— arise.
Because this arises, there is the ability to give rise to physical pliancy that accords with it;
the wind element increases excessively, and a great many primary elements enter into the body.
Because these primary elements enter into the body, [physical pliancy arises].
The heaviness of the body belonging to the category of afflictions, which is capable of obstructing the abandonment of pleasure,
is entirely eliminated.
It serves as the antidote to that [distraction]:
the pliancy of the body and the physical serenity which pervade the entire body, appearing as if overflowing it.
When it first arises, it causes the mind to leap up and causes the mind to be joyful;
accompanied by gladness, it causes the mind to be delighted,
and the nature of the object appears within the mind.
From this point onward, the force of that initial pliancy (praśrabdhi) gradually subsides, and a sublime pliancy arises, accompanying the body and circulating within it.
By reason of this, the mind's tendency toward agitation (auddhatya) progressively diminishes.
Because it is sustained by śamatha,
the mind proceeds in a state of tranquility toward its object;
from this point onward, regarding the practice of yoga:
A beginner practitioner is said to "possess mental attention" (*manasikāra*);
they first come to be included within the category of those possessing mental attention. Why is this?
Because one has thereby initially attained a small portion of subtle and correct mental attention (manasikāra) subsumed under the dhyāna stages of the form realm,
for this reason it is called "possessing mental attention."
A beginner who has attained this mental attention possesses these characteristics:
namely, they have already acquired a limited degree of meditative concentration belonging to the form realm,
as well as a limited degree of physical and mental pliancy and one-pointedness of mind.
Possessing power and capability, one skillfully cultivates the preparatory application of objects for purifying the afflictions,
causing the mental continuum to proceed with moisture; thus,
being sustained and protected by śamatha, one is able to purify all conditioned phenomena.
Although they move among various desirable objects,
intense bonds of craving do not arise; even if they arise slightly,
they do so by relying on a small degree of weak counteractive measures.
When one applies the mind for even a moment,
these can be dispelled— just as with a desirable object—
so too with an undesirable object, an object that causes delusion, an object that gives rise to pride, or an object of discursive thought.
One should know that it is likewise so:
when sitting in meditation in a quiet room and briefly holding the mind,
physical and mental pliancy (praśrabdhi) will swiftly arise.
They are not excessively afflicted by the heaviness of the body;
they do not excessively and frequently manifest the active occurrence of the hindrances;
and they do not excessively manifest longing thoughts.
He does not take pleasure in thoughts or mental attentions associated with anxiety;
although he has arisen from meditative concentration and is walking outside,
a slight remnant of pliancy continues to pervade his body and mind.
One should know that such categories as these are called the characteristics of purity for one who possesses mental attention (*manasikāra*).
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 32; *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 33.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya spoke;
translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.
In the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*, the thirteenth part of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, this is the first of the four sections of the fourth yoga station. Furthermore, the summary verse (*uddāna*) states:
Through the seven modes of mental attention, one becomes free from desire;
the two meditative attainments and the five supernormal powers are extensively explained.
By observing the various characteristics of the distinctions in rebirth, one penetrates the truths as they truly are.
Having extensively analyzed the cultivation [of the path],
for those yogins who have attained mental attention (*manasikāra*) and have entered such a state of partial delight in abandonment, this constitutes the final stage.
From this point onward, there are only two destinies and no others.
What are these two?
First, the mundane world.
Second is the supramundane. Therein,
the beginner yogācāra, by means of this mental attention,
either thinks, "I shall go to the worldly realms," or [thinks of] mindfulness.
Or one thinks, "I shall go forth into the supramundane realm," and repeatedly cultivates such mental attention.
To whatever extent one cultivates this extensively, [to that same extent...]
In this way, whatever pliancy and one-pointedness of mind there may be,
it becomes increasingly expanded as it proceeds through various stages such as days and nights;
provided that this mental attention continues in a firm, uninterrupted, and powerful manner.
Having generated resolute conviction regarding the pure object of focus,
they correctly apprehend the signs pertaining to the categories of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
At that time, they may either delight in proceeding along the mundane path and initiate the application of effort.
Some take delight in applying effort toward supramundane paths,
while others take delight in the Dharma and apply effort toward mundane paths,
not supramundane ones.
Answer: Briefly, there are four types of persons (*pudgala*).
What are the four? First, all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Second, those whose faculties are weak and inferior within the True Dharma first cultivate the practice of *śamatha*.
Third, those whose faculties are sharp but whose roots of goodness are not yet matured.
Fourth, all bodhisattvas who delight in realizing great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) in a future life rather than in the present life.
These four types of persons initiate the application of effort toward the worldly path that leads to rebirth within the present life.
Regarding this initiation of the application of effort toward the worldly path that leads to rebirth:
Furthermore, there are two types:
first, those bound by all fetters,
namely, ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Second, those who do not possess all fetters;
this refers to all those in training (śaikṣa).
Furthermore, what does this mean?
That is to say, one first contemplates the desire realm as being coarse in nature,
and contemplates the first dhyāna— whether in meditative absorption or as a rebirth state— as being peaceful in nature;
thereby initiating the preparatory application to abandon desire for the desire realm.
In this manner, it should be understood that even up to the arousal of the preparatory application for the sake of abandoning desire for the sphere of nothingness,
it is likewise so. Furthermore,
based on the dhyānas and so forth, one is able to induce the attainment of non-perception and so forth, as well as to give rise to the five supernormal powers and so forth.
Yogācāras who diligently cultivate meditative practice within the desire realm are able to attain freedom from desire for that realm only through seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
What are these seven types of mental attention?
Namely, the attention that discerns characteristics,
the attention of resolute conviction,
and the attention of seclusion.
The attention of relishing,
the attention of investigation,
and the attention of the culmination of application.
Regarding the mental application of the fruit of the culmination of the preparatory stage:
what is called the "mental application that discerns characteristics"?
It refers to the mental application by which one correctly and fully realizes the coarse characteristics of the desire realm and the tranquil characteristics of the first dhyāna.
How does one clearly comprehend the coarse characteristics of the desire realm?
It refers to correctly investigating six matters of the desire realm.
What are these six?
First, the meaning;
second, the entity;
third, the characteristic.
Fourth, the four categories;
fifth, the five periods;
sixth, the six principles.
How does one investigate the coarse nature of sensual desires?
It means correctly investigating that such sensual desires have many faults,
many afflictions, many epidemics, and many calamities.
The sense that among all desires there are many faults,
and so forth, up to the sense that there are many calamities—
this is called the meaning of coarseness.
How does one investigate the coarse nature of sensual desires?
It means correctly investigating that among sensual desires there is internal craving for them,
and among sensual desires there is external craving for them.
How does one investigate the specific characteristics of sensual desires?
It means correctly investigating that "this is the desire for affliction" and "this is the desire for objects.
Furthermore, this [desire] is of three kinds.
That is to say: the sphere conducive to pleasant feeling,
the sphere conducive to painful feeling,
and the sphere conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The sphere conducive to pleasant feeling is the basis for sensual desire;
it is the basis for the inversion of perception and mind.
The sphere conducive to painful feeling is the basis for malice.
This is the basis for anger and resentment;
it is the basis for delusion, which accords with feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant;
and it is the basis for concealment, vexation, deception, guile, lack of shame, and lack of dread of blame.
This is the basis for the inversion of view;
that is, one correctly investigates how these desires are pursued by extremely evil sensations and pursued by extremely evil afflictions.
This is called the investigation into the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all desires.
How does one investigate their common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)?
It means correctly investigating that all these desires—
They are pursued and bound by the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, and so forth, up to the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
those who indulge in sensual desires are driven and impelled by their fulfillment of those desires.
Furthermore, because one is not yet liberated from phenomena such as birth and so forth,
although those various desires may be excellent, sublime, and perfect, they exist only for a brief moment;
this is called the investigation of the common characteristics of desires.
How does one investigate the coarse nature of sensual desires?
It means correctly investigating that all such sensual desires belong to the dark category (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*),
being like a chain of bones or like congealed blood and flesh.
It is like a torch of grass, like a fragment of charcoal fire,
like a great venomous serpent, like what is seen in a dream,
and like borrowed ornaments.
Like fruits at the tip of a tree,
sentient beings who pursue various sensual desires experience the suffering produced by that pursuit amidst those very desires.
One experiences the suffering caused by the need for protection;
one experiences the suffering caused by the loss of loved ones;
and one experiences the suffering caused by lack of contentment.
One experiences the suffering caused by lack of mastery over one's feelings and the suffering caused by unwholesome conduct;
all such matters should be understood as previously explained.
As the Blessed One has said:
there are five disadvantages in indulging in sensual desires;
namely, that those sensual desires possess extremely little flavor.
They involve much suffering and affliction, as well as many faults and calamities.
Furthermore, when one indulges in those sensual desires,
they lead to no weariness, no contentment, and no fulfillment.
Furthermore, those sensual desires have been constantly censured and disparaged through immeasurable means by the Buddhas,
their disciples, and the virtuous, upright, and well-established noble beings.
Furthermore, when those various desires are cultivated and pursued,
they cause the fetters to accumulate and increase.
Moreover, when those various desires are cultivated and pursued...
I say that there is no evil or unwholesome karma that one does not create.
Such desires cause one never to find satisfaction and are shared by many;
they are the cause for the increase of unrighteous conduct, evil conduct, and sensual craving.
That which is abandoned by the wise and swiftly moves toward extinction, depending upon a multitude of conditions—
this is the ground of perilous ruin for all those who are heedless;
it is a phenomenon that is impermanent, false, deceptive, and subject to loss.
It is like a magical illusion that deceives the foolish—
whether it be desire for the present life or desire for future lives,
whether it be desire for the heavens or desire for the human realm.
All these are the activities of Māra and the abodes of Māra;
in such places, immeasurable unwholesome and evil states of mind arise from the basis of the mental faculty.
That which is called greed, hatred, and contention, and so forth,
can act as obstacles when a noble disciple is practicing correctly;
it is by means of such various causes and conditions [that these arise].
In this way, these various desires for the most part fall under the category of the dark side (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
This is called the investigation into the coarse nature of desires.
What is the investigation into the coarse timing of desires?
That is to say, one correctly investigates that these various desires,
throughout all times and at all moments in the past, future, and present,
possess many faults and afflictions and cause much harm and distress.
There are many epidemics and many calamities;
this is called reflecting on the coarseness of sensual desires in terms of time.
How does one reflect on the coarseness of sensual desires in terms of principle?
That is to say, one correctly investigates these sensual desires as requiring vast provisions, vast seeking, and great toil,
as well as various and immeasurable distinctions of fields of craft and industry.
Only then can they be summoned, generated, and increased.
Furthermore, although those desires may arise well and increase well, [they remain subject to decline].
For the most part, all these are objects of external appropriation, namely:
parents, wives and children, slaves and laborers, friends, and kinsmen;
or they serve as remedies.
Internally, there are the coarse and heavy four great elements of form,
which are nourished by rice and gruel, constantly requiring covering, bathing, and massage; they are subject to decay,
severance, dispersion, and extinction, being of the nature of the physical body.
In accordance with the various sufferings that arise,
food can counteract the suffering of hunger and thirst,
and clothing can counteract the suffering of cold and heat.
Furthermore, it can cover those parts of the body that should be concealed from shame;
bedding can remedy the suffering of fatigue and drowsiness,
as well as counteract the suffering of walking, standing, and sitting.
Just as medicine and medical treatment can cure the suffering of illness,
so too do sensual desires merely serve as remedies for the various forms of affliction that arise from time to time; therefore,
one should not indulge in them with attachment.
One should maintain only right mindfulness,
just as a person afflicted by a grave illness takes foul medicine in order to eliminate that disease.
Furthermore, those various sensual desires possess a coarse characteristic that is established by authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*).
Moreover, regarding all such coarse characteristics of those various sensual desires,
I also have direct knowledge and vision arising within myself.
Furthermore, those various desires can be known through inference to possess coarse characteristics.
Moreover, from beginningless time, those various desires have been established as coarse and defiled by their very nature;
this dharma-nature is inconceivable.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) should not be conceptualized and should not be discriminated;
this is called the coarse principle for investigating all desires.
In this way, by means of these six matters, one discerns the coarse characteristics of the desires of the desire realm and further discerns all the tranquil characteristics within the first dhyāna.
This means that all coarse qualities within the desire realm are entirely absent in the first dhyāna;
it is because one has become detached from the various coarse qualities of the desire realm.
In the first dhyāna, it is said that there is tranquility;
this is called discerning the characteristic of tranquility present within the first dhyāna.
It is precisely by means of such mental attention belonging to the stage of meditative concentration [that this occurs].
Within the desire realm, one perceives it as having coarse characteristics;
within the first dhyāna, one perceives it as having calm characteristics.
Therefore, this is called the attention that perceives characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*).
This very mental attention should be said to still be interspersed with hearing and reflection.
Having thus engaged in such thorough investigation,
he understands that all sensual desires are coarse in nature.
Knowing that the first dhyāna is its characteristic of tranquility,
from this point onward, one transcends hearing and reflection and employs only cultivation;
one then gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the characteristics of the object of focus.
One cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā; having cultivated them,
one repeatedly generates resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the signs of coarseness and the signs of tranquility, exactly as they were investigated.
This is called the mental engagement of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*).
By means of this very resolute conviction being well-cultivated, well-practiced, and frequently cultivated,
it serves as the causal condition for the initial arising of the path that abandons the afflictions.
The attention that arises together with the path for abandoning the afflictions is here called "the attention of withdrawal" (*prāvivekya-manasikāra*),
because it is by means of this that one first abandons those afflictions of the desire realm that were previously to be abandoned.
Furthermore, because they are able to eliminate the coarse and heavy nature (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to the category of those afflictions,
from that point onward they take delight in abandonment and take delight in seclusion;
they perceive the supreme merit within all forms of abandonment.
Having realized a small portion of the joy and bliss of seclusion,
from time to time he experiences profound delight through the mental application of aspiration,
and from time to time he experiences profound weariness through the mental application of renunciation.
In order to eliminate lethargy, drowsiness, restlessness, and so forth,
this is called the attention of "embracing joy.
Through such delight in abandonment and delight in cultivation, he [proceeds].
Through the sustained application of the wholesome qualities of correct cultivation,
the various afflictions and entanglements bound to the desire realm no longer manifest,
whether he is walking or staying still.
He then thought to himself:
"Do I currently possess the affliction of sensual desire among all desires, yet fail to perceive it?
Or do I not possess it?"
In order to examine such matters thoroughly, one attends to and contemplates any one of the various attractive and pure signs;
yet, because the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) have not been permanently severed,
when contemplating such pure and sublime signs, [the mind wavers].
He then further gives rise to a mind that follows after intimacy, a mind that inclines toward intimacy, and a mind that approaches intimacy;
he is unable to abide in equanimity,
nor can he feel revulsion, reject, subdue, or oppose it.
He thinks to himself:
"My mind is not yet liberated from sensual desires;
I have not yet attained true liberation."
My mind is still constrained by conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
like water held back by a dam;
it has not yet been brought under the control of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Now, furthermore, in order to permanently sever the remaining latent tendencies (*anuśaya*),
I should correctly exert myself and dwell in the joy of abandonment and the joy of cultivation.
This is called the mental attention of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*).
From this point on, he redoubles his delight in abandonment and cultivation, practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
He earnestly observes and cultivates the remedies,
and from time to time examines what has already been abandoned.
By this cause and condition, the mind becomes dissociated from all afflictions bound to the desire realm;
this is achieved through the expedient means of temporary suppression and abandonment,
rather than the ultimate and permanent destruction of their seeds.

At that time, the preparatory path (prayoga-mārga) of the first dhyāna stage has reached its culmination, and the mental attention (manasikāra) that serves as the antidote to all afflictions has already arisen.
This is called the "mental attention of the culmination of the preparatory stage" (*prayoganiṣṭha-manasikāra*).
Immediately following this, by means of these causes and conditions, one realizes and enters the fundamental first dhyāna concentration.
This is precisely the mental attention that accompanies this fundamental first dhyāna concentration.
This is called the mental application that is the fruit of the culmination of preparatory effort (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala-manasikāra*).
Furthermore, when the mental application of delight in seclusion (*viveka-praśrabdhi-manasikāra*) is currently active,
it brings about a physical pliancy and the joy and bliss born of seclusion (*vivekaja-prīti-sukha*).
At times, when the mental application of the culmination of the preparatory stage manifests in a subtle and slight manner,
that very joy and bliss manifest and further increase and expand.
From time to time, as the mental attention directed toward the fruit of the culmination of application manifests with profound intensity,
the joy and bliss born of seclusion pervade all parts of the body.
It was completely filled without any gaps.
At that time, he remained far removed from all sensual desires and far removed from all evil and unwholesome states.
Possessing vitarka and vicāra, and endowed with the joy and bliss born of seclusion,
one dwells having fully perfected the five factors of the first dhyāna;
this is called abiding in the fruit of the cultivation that serves as the antidote to the desire realm.
It is called "conforming to attainment" because one has become free from desire for the realm of desire;
furthermore, the "attention that discerns characteristics" correctly understands that which is to be abandoned.
One correctly understands that which is to be attained;
for the sake of abandoning what should be abandoned and attaining what should be attained,
one generates an aspiration, a resolute conviction, and mental attention.
One correctly initiates application for the sake of abandoning [defilements] and attaining [realization].
Through the mental attention of seclusion,
one is able to relinquish all superior-grade afflictions.
The attention of "embracing joy" (*ratisaṃgrāhaka-manasikāra*) is able to abandon all intermediate-grade afflictions;
[this is followed by] the attention of "investigation" (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*).
One is able to dwell with the mind established in what has been attained, free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
The mental attention of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭha-manasikāra*) can abandon all inferior-grade afflictions (*mṛdukleśa*).
This is the mental attention of the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala-manasikāra*).
One is able to correctly receive the fruits of the well-cultivated practice of those various forms of attention (*manasikāra*).
Furthermore, this applies to both the attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manasikāra*) and the attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika manasikāra*).
These are collectively termed the "attention that accords with [the truth]," which is accompanied by both the counteractive of revulsion and the counteractive of abandonment;
this includes both the attention of withdrawal and the attention of the culmination of application.
Collectively, these are called the attention of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-manasikāra*) and proceed together with the counteraction of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*).
If it is the attention of delighting in cultivation (*ratisaṃgrāhaka-manasikāra*),
it is called both the attention of counteraction and the attention conducive to purification (*viśuddhy-anukūla-manasikāra*).
If one observes through mental attention,
it is called "mental attention conforming to observation.
In this way, it should be understood that the remaining four types of mental attention are subsumed within these six types of mental attention.
That is to say: attention that conforms [to the object],
attention that serves as an antidote,
and attention that accords with purification.
Just as there are seven types of mental application (*manasikāra*) in the first dhyāna concentration when observing in accordance [with the truth],
so it is for the second, third, and fourth dhyāna concentrations,
as well as for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
The sphere of infinite consciousness,
the sphere of nothingness,
and the meditative absorption of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
It should be understood that there are seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) for each.
If one perceives the coarse characteristic (*audārikatva*) in the stage of the first dhyāna with applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*),
and perceives the calm characteristic (*śāntatva*) in the stage of the second dhyāna without applied or sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra*).
In order to realize and enter the second dhyāna,
one should know that this is called the "attention that discerns characteristics" (lakṣaṇapratisamvedī manaskāra);
that is to say, having already realized the meditative absorption of the first dhyāna.
One who has already attained the first dhyāna correctly understands that,
within the state of meditative concentration, all vitarka and vicāra are by nature coarse.
Regarding its object, it arises initially as a sudden encounter;
it operates upon a domain of urgent activity and possesses the nature of coarse mental verbalization.
This is called vitarka (applied thought).
It arises following that object and proceeds in accordance with it,
moving slowly through the range of its domain.
The nature of subtle mental verbalization is called *vicāra* (investigation).
Furthermore, one correctly understands that such *vitarka* and *vicāra* are the nature of mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
When the mind arises,
it arises together with [mental factors] that are associated and function upon the same object.
Furthermore, one correctly understands that such vitarka and vicāra arise internally and are subsumed under the external sense bases.
Furthermore, one correctly understands that all such things, comprised within the past, future,
and present, arise from causes and arise from conditions.
Whether increasing or decreasing, it does not abide for long but exists only momentarily, appearing abruptly;
it causes the mind to be restless and agitated, causing the mind to be distracted, and causing it to proceed in an unpeaceful manner.
When seeking a higher stage, one remains subject to painful abiding;
therefore, all these are subsumed under the dark category and follow after various desires,
[offering only] a small measure of the benefit of the joy and bliss born of seclusion.
According to the intrinsic nature of whatever location it occupies,
it can cause such characteristics to appear at all times and for all eternity.
The mental activity associated with applied and sustained thought takes an object and proceeds in a restless manner, failing to attain tranquility;
by means of such various modes of operation, [it functions].
One discerns the coarse characteristics (*audārikalakṣaṇa*) of all vitarka and vicāra;
furthermore, one correctly understands that the second dhyāna is without vitarka and without vicāra.
Thus, all such aforementioned coarse characteristics are entirely absent.
Therefore, it is taught that the second dhyāna possesses the characteristic of tranquility,
because all those coarse characteristics have been abandoned;
this is for the purpose of entering the second dhyāna.
The remaining applications of attention (*manasikāra*) should be understood as previously described according to their respective requirements.
This continues in this manner, up until the desire to realize and enter the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samāpatti*),
wherein one proceeds through each successive stage (*bhūmi*) as appropriate.
One should know that all [of these] possess seven types of mental application (*manasikāra*).
Furthermore, their coarse characteristics (*audārikalakṣaṇa*) are omnipresent throughout all lower stages,
extending from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) upward through successive levels to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
It should be understood that there are, in brief, two kinds of coarse characteristics: namely,
that the states of suffering in the lower stages are predominant,
because compared to the abodes above, they are not tranquil.
Furthermore, their lifespans and durations are brief,
as they are progressively shorter than those above;
these two coarse characteristics are established by the preceding six matters.
One should correctly investigate according to what is appropriate.
Whenever one desires to become detached from a particular stage,
one should, as is fitting, investigate the sign of tranquility regarding the immediately higher stage.
Gradually, one proceeds until attaining the attention that is the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala-manasikāra*).
Furthermore, regarding the one who is free from desire herein,
there are two kinds of desire.
The first is the desire for afflictions;
the second is the desire for objects.
There are two kinds of renunciation.
First is detachment through association;
second is detachment from objects.
These constitute the detachment from evil and unwholesome states.
The various evil and unwholesome states produced by the causes of afflictions and desire—
namely, physical misconduct, verbal misconduct, and so forth;
as well as wielding staves and swords, engaging in strife, litigation, and contention.
Flattery, deception, fraud, and hypocrisy give rise to false speech and the like;
because one abandons these, it is called "being free from evil and unwholesome states.
As for "with vitarka and vicāra":
Because one has not yet perceived the faults of vitarka and vicāra,
and because there still exist within one's own stage wholesome vitarkas and vicāras that serve as antidotes to those of the desire realm,
it is therefore called "with vitarka and with vicāra."
What is called "separation" refers to having already attained the mental attention that culminates in application (*prayoganiṣṭhamanaskāra*).
What is called "arising" refers to...
Because it arises immediately following this as its cause and condition,
it is called "born of seclusion.
As for the terms "joy" and "bliss":
This refers to having already attained the desired goal and not yet perceiving any faults within that joy,
because all forms of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) have been eliminated.
Furthermore, because one has already attained vast pliancy (*praśrabdhi*),
and body and mind are harmonious, supple, and capable,
it is called joy and bliss (*prītisukha*).
What is called "the first" refers to the very initial upward progression from the desire realm,
wherein one first attains the sequential order of the bases.
This is called the first [dhyāna].
As for "meditative absorption" (dhyāna),
it refers to the quieting of the mind by binding mindfulness to a single object of focus, and engaging in correct and thorough reflection.
Therefore, it is called "meditative absorption" (*dhyāna*).
As for the term "endowed with," it means that one has already attained the mental attention (*manasikāra*) which is the fruit of the culmination of preparatory practice.
Regarding the term "abiding securely":
it means that at a later time, because of the extensive accomplishment of what has been cultivated,
one attains [the goal] according to one's wish, without difficulty and without obstruction.
Within the meditative absorptions, his mind is able to correctly conform to,
incline toward, and enter them day and night according to his desire;
he can remain correctly established therein for as long as seven days and seven nights.
Therefore, it is called "abiding securely.
Furthermore, the mind is able to relinquish the signs of the samādhi accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
He fixes his mindfulness and dwells securely upon the sign of the concentration that is without applied thought and sustained thought,
regarding all objects of activity and busy affairs.
He is able to correctly distance himself [from distractions] and dwells in a sphere of activity free from haste;
his mind turns toward a single flavor, becoming tranquil and utterly serene.
Therefore, it is said: "Because applied thought and sustained thought have subsided, there is internal serenity.
Furthermore, that very [state] occurs within the samādhi that is without applied thought and without sustained thought.
Through repeated cultivation,
one transcends the state characterized by applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) and its interruptions,
and is able to correctly attain the state that is uninterrupted.
Therefore, it is said that because the mind is one-pointed,
there is no applied thought (*vitarka*) and no sustained thought (*vicāra*);
this is because all applied and sustained thoughts have been completely severed.
That which is called "concentration" refers to having already attained the attention that culminates in application (*prayoganiṣṭha-manasikāra*).
That which is called "arising" refers to...
Because it is produced immediately following this as its cause and condition,
it is called "born of concentration.
As for the terms "joy" and "bliss":
This means that one has already attained the sought-after goal;
furthermore, within this state of joy (*prīti*), one has not yet perceived any faults, and thus there is still delight and rejoicing.
All heaviness (*dausthulya*) belonging to the category of afflictions on the level of the first dhyāna, including all discursive thoughts (*vitarka* and *vicāra*), is completely removed.
Therefore, it is able to counteract that vast pliancy;
because the body and mind are supple, wieldy, and accompanied by bliss,
it is called "possessing joy and bliss."
Following the sequential order, this is the second.
All such cases should be understood as before.
Furthermore, he perceives deep faults in the characteristic of joy (*prīti*).
Therefore, it is said that one becomes free from desire for joy (*prīti*).
Furthermore, at that time, having distanced oneself from the two kinds of afflictions that disturb the mind,
one is able to maintain the mind within the third dhyāna, which is free from joy.
In the second dhyāna, one is already free from applied and sustained thought;
now, within this state, one is further free from joy.
Therefore, it is said that one dwells in equanimity.
These two factors can disturb the mind and obstruct equanimity of uninterrupted application (*ānimjya-upekṣā*).
Because initial meditative absorption (*prathama-dhyāna*) contains applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*),
they cause equanimity of uninterrupted application to function without mastery.
Because the second dhyāna possesses joy (*prīti*),
it causes equanimity (*upekṣā*) to function without mastery;
therefore, this equanimity is said to be absent in the first two dhyānas.
For this reason, it is only in the third dhyāna that the practitioner of meditative concentration is said to possess equanimity;
because of the presence of equanimity.
To the extent that one dwells securely in right mindfulness,
to that same extent those perceptions and mental attentions accompanied by joy no longer manifest.
Furthermore, this is because one has not yet cultivated the third dhyāna well.
At times, when mindfulness lapses and those perceptions and mental attentions associated with joy manifest again,
he immediately and swiftly penetrates them with wisdom and correctly understands them.
Whatever arises, one does not tolerate it;
through skillful means, one abandons, dispels, and ejects it,
so that the mind abides in supreme equanimity.
Therefore, it is said that there is right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
At that time, he dwells in such equanimity,
cultivating and practicing it with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
Through extensive cultivation, it causes the mind to leap with joy;
the concomitant feeling of rapture is thereby extinguished,
giving way to a state free from rapture that is tranquil and supremely serene.
A mental feeling arises that is contrary to joy;
at that time, his physical body and mental body experience the sensation of pleasure and the pleasure of pliancy.
Therefore, it is said that he experiences pleasure with the body.
In all stages below the third dhyāna,
there is neither such bliss nor uninterrupted equanimity;
in all stages above the third dhyāna, [the same applies].
Although this equanimity of the immediate [attainment] can be obtained, it is devoid of pleasure;
for in the lower stages, neither pleasure nor equanimity exists together,
and in the higher stages, while equanimity exists, pleasure does not.
Therefore, it is said that this state is called the third dhyāna;
the noble ones proclaim that by relying upon it, a person (pudgala) has attained stable abiding.
Possessing equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension,
he dwells experiencing happiness with the body;
thus he fully attains and abides in the third dhyāna.
The term "all noble ones" refers to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and his disciples.
Furthermore, it is because they are similar in their category of counteractive power (*pratipakṣa-jāti-vega*).
The antidote for the abandonment of pleasure is not explained in detail;
rather, only that which constitutes the antidote’s activity of abandoning pleasure is taught.
What, then, is called the "antidote" in this context?
That is to say, equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension.
By repeatedly cultivating these very qualities,
one is able to relinquish [the third dhyāna] so as not to emerge from the third dhyāna.
Because there is superior bliss within the stage of the third dhyāna,
it is said that "by the abandonment of pleasure," the practitioner of dhyāna at that very moment transcends all suffering and pleasure.

For this reason, that which was previously abandoned and that which is now being abandoned are collectively described as "the abandonment of pleasure and the abandonment of pain," wherein prior joy and sorrow have subsided.
This means that when entering the fourth dhyāna, pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) is abandoned;
when entering the second dhyāna, painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*) is abandoned;
and when entering the third dhyāna, joyful feeling (*saumanasya-vedanā*) subsides.
Because the feeling of mental distress (*daurmanasya*) has subsided upon entering the first dhyāna,
it is here stated— provisionally— that the two feelings of suffering and pleasure are abandoned;
however, there remains the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanā*).
Therefore, it is said that at that time he experiences neither suffering nor pleasure;
for from the first dhyāna, all calamities of the lower stages have been abandoned—
namely, vitarka, vicāra, joy, bliss, inhalation, and exhalation.
Because those [hindrances] have been abandoned, equanimity and mindfulness therein are pure and bright;
by this cause and condition, when one correctly enters the fourth dhyāna, the mind abides in immovability.
All disturbances are entirely removed;
therefore, it is said that "equanimity and mindfulness are purified.
The fourth "and so forth" refers to the first dhyāna and the others as previously described.
One should know its characteristics.
Furthermore, because one gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) toward space,
all [colors] such as blue, yellow, red, and white [appear].
It is associated with the perception of color-form;
because it does not manifest [externally] and because of the cultivation of revulsion and detachment from desire.
One is able to transcend them all.
Therefore, it is said that "the perception of form is transcended," because by means of its non-manifestation,
one takes the transcendence of that perception as the cause.
All the various and manifold categories [of objects],
through the aggregation and accumulation of diverse manifest colors,
cause all perceptions of obstruction to be completely dispelled.
Therefore, it is said that because the perception of resistance has ceased and disappeared,
and by virtue of being separated from that perception as its cause,
all the various differentiated perceptions that arise within those diverse aggregates [no longer occur].

That is to say, the perceptions of food, drink, vessels, clothing, vehicles, ornaments, cities, houses, armies, gardens, mountains, forests, and so forth—all these no longer function through mental attention.
Therefore, it is said: "Because one does not attend to various perceptions."
Having dispelled such various perceptions of form and resistance,
one gives rise to the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) of space as having the characteristic of being infinite;
therefore, it is said that one enters the "infinite space" (*ākāśānantya*).

Because one has already transcended the preparatory attention (*prayoga-manasikāra*) of the access concentration and enters the meditative absorption of the fundamental fruit of the ultimate preparatory attention (*mūla-prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala-manasikāra*),
it is therefore said that one "fully dwells" in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
It should be understood that herein, from the preparatory stages up until one has not yet entered the higher fundamental meditative absorptions,
one takes only space as the object; however,
once one has already entered the higher fundamental absorptions, [the object is different].
They also take empty space as their object,
as well as all the aggregates belonging to their own level;
furthermore, within the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), they also take all the aggregates belonging to the lower levels as their objects.
Furthermore, if by means of this consciousness one gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding infinite space,
it should be known that this consciousness is associated with the resolute conviction in the characteristic of infinite space.
If there is one who wishes to enter the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), [it should be known that]...
First, one abandons the perception of the sphere of infinite space;
then, regarding that very consciousness, one successively gives rise to a resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) characterized by infinity.
At that time, one transcends both the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) and the fundamental state (*maula*) of the sphere of infinite space.
Therefore, it is said that having transcended the sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness;

this is because one has transcended all the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) up to the mental application of the culmination of the practice (*prayoganiṣṭha-manasikāra*) belonging to the sphere of infinite consciousness.
One enters the meditative absorption of the fundamental application, the culmination of application, and the fruit of the higher stage;
therefore, it is said that one "fully dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Furthermore, when seeking further progress from the sphere of infinite consciousness:
Apart from that consciousness, one seeks no other object and finds nothing at all;
that is to say, regarding whatever objective nature there may be, whether material or non-material,
when one seeks those objects, nothing is found.
Transcending both the preparatory and fundamental stages of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness,
one gives rise to the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that there is no objective sphere whatsoever;
this is called the "resolute conviction in the mental image of nothingness" (*ākiṃcanya-saṃjñā-adhimukti*).
By extensively cultivating such imaginative resolve (*adhimukti*),

one is then able to transcend all access concentrations (*sāmantaka*) up to the attention that culminates the preparatory application (*prayoga-niṣṭha-manasikāra*) of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
He enters the meditative absorption of the fundamental application, culmination, and fruition of mental attention;
therefore, it is said that he transcends the sphere of infinite consciousness and fully dwells in the sphere of nothingness, wherein there is not even the slightest thing.
Furthermore, when seeking further advancement from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
because one perceives the ideation of the sphere of nothingness as coarse,
one is then able to relinquish that ideation of nothingness.
For this reason, when he previously entered the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness,
he transcended all perceptions of existence;
now, moreover, he transcends the perception of nothingness.
Therefore it is said that they do not possess perception.
This means that they may have the perception of "something existing," or the perception of "nothing existing," yet they are not without perception.
This means that it is not like the attainment of non-conception or the attainment of cessation, wherein all perceptions are entirely extinguished;
rather, there remains only a subtle perception that functions by taking the signless object as its condition.
Therefore, it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
At the very moment one gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding this state,
one transcends all access and fundamental stages of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),

as well as the access stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), up to and including the mental attention of the culmination of the preparatory application (*prayoganiṣṭhā-manasikāra*).
He enters the meditative absorption of the fundamental application, culmination, and fruition of attention;
therefore, it is said that he transcends the sphere of nothingness and fully dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, in this context, when entering the meditative absorptions of the form realm (*dhyāna*),
the physical appearance of the body is as if one were situated within a room;
when entering the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), it is likewise.
At that time, the appearance of his body is like being situated in empty space.
One should know that herein, by means of the characteristic of *śamatha*,
he abides in superior equanimity and diligently cultivates the application of effort.
Furthermore, based on the meditative concentrations (dhyāna) and so forth, one should know that it is possible to enter two mindless attainments:
first, the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti);
second, the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
As for the attainment of non-perception,
only ordinary worldlings can enter it through the skillful means of mental attention that turns away from perception.
As for the attainment of cessation:
Only the noble ones can enter these two meditative attainments through the application of the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of the cessation of perception and feeling; thus,
these two attainments are entered by means of two distinct mental orientations.
This refers to the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
By taking the mental application (*manasikāra*) of turning one's back on perception as its primary factor,
one diligently cultivates the preparatory practice and gradually enters it.
As for the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),

it arises from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) by taking as its primary factor the mental attention that seeks to temporarily suspend objective referents in order to progress further upward.
By diligently practicing the preparatory application, one can gradually enter [the state].
If ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) should form such a thought:
"All perceptions (*saṃjñā*) are like a disease, all perceptions are like an abscess, all perceptions are like an arrow."
There is only the subtle and wondrous grasping of the tranquility of non-perception;
thus, one attends to the mind by turning away from all perceptions that have arisen.
One diligently cultivates the mental attention of non-recollection;
by virtue of this cultivation as a causal condition,
there is a state of mind within the path of application (*prayogamārga*).
Immediately upon entering meditative absorption, the mind no longer turns [toward objects].
Thus, preceded by the mental attention of the perception of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa-saṃjñā-manasikāra*),
the various minds and mental factors cease for one who has already abandoned craving for the Subhakṛtsna realm but has not yet abandoned craving for the Bṛhatphala realm.
This is called the attainment of non-perception.
By means of this expedient, one realizes this meditative state.
If noble beings have already attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, [they may enter this state].
Furthermore, desiring to abide for a time in the abiding of tranquility,
he seeks to advance his mind from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
As his mind advances, he seeks a superior object of focus, yet ultimately finds nothing at all to be obtained.
Because there is nothing to be apprehended, it ceases and does not proceed.
Thus, a learner who has already abandoned craving for the sphere of nothingness,
or an arhat, applies attention to the perception of abiding for a time.
When the preceding mind and mental factors have ceased,
this is called the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
By means of this method, one realizes this attainment.
Furthermore, based on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one brings forth the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth.
As for "concentration," it refers to having already attained the fundamental, pure meditative absorption.
Taking such purified meditative concentration as his basis,
he hears, receives, and upholds the sublime Dharma that predominates the five supernormal powers,
bringing it to complete perfection.
That is to say: the supernormal power of the divine realm,
the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, and the supernormal power of the divine ear.
One attends to and contemplates the supernormal knowledge of the death and rebirth of beings, the supernormal knowledge of the diversity of mental dispositions, and so forth.
Furthermore, by means of the attention arising from the stage of meditative concentration,
one understands the meaning and understands the phenomena;
because of understanding the meaning and understanding the phenomena, [one attains realization].
In this way and that way, one cultivates and purifies the mind.
Through this repeated cultivation and extensive practice,
there comes a time when the fruits of cultivation, such as the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), arise within certain portions of it.
Furthermore, having thus understood the meaning and understood the phenomena (*dharma*),
one cultivates the twelve perceptions (*saṃjñā*) in order to bring forth the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth.
What are these twelve?
First, the perception of lightness;
second, the perception of flexibility;
third, the perception of the space element.
4. The perception of mental and physical conformity;
5. The perception of resolute conviction;
6. The perception of recollecting the sequence of previously experienced practices.
7. The perception of sounds gathered from various kinds and categories;
8. The perception of the characteristics of light and color;
9. The perception of the transformation of form produced by afflictions.
10. The perception of liberation;
11. The perception of the spheres of mastery;
12. The perception of the spheres of totality.
The perception of lightness refers to the generation of a resolute conviction regarding the body as being light,
such as cotton wool, or like taffeta, or resembling a wind-wheel.
Having thus generated such light resolve,
through the mental application of resolve, he causes his body to shift from place to place;
that is to say, he shifts it from the bed and places it upon a small table.
Again, he was wafted from the small table and placed upon the bed;
likewise, from the bed he was wafted and placed upon a grass mat;
and again, from the grass mat he was wafted and placed back upon the bed.
The perception of pliancy refers to the generation of a superior resolve regarding the body as being pliant by means of this perception—
either like a cotton bag, or like fine wool, or like something well-refined.
This perception of softness nurtures and sustains the preceding perception of buoyancy;
at the time of its sustenance,
it causes the perception of buoyancy to increase and expand.
Regarding the perception of the space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu-saṃjñā*):
it means that by means of this perception, one first generates two types of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*)—lightness and flexibility—with respect to one's own body;
then, as one proceeds wherever one desires, if there are any accumulations of matter (*rūpa-kalāpa*) in the intervening space that could act as obstructions, [one overcomes them].
At that time, one gives rise to the mental attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*).
Within those forms, one forms the conviction of emptiness and is able to proceed without obstruction.
This is what is meant by "the perception of bodily and mental conformity."
That is to say, by means of this perception, either the mind conforms to the body or the body conforms to the mind;
through this, the body becomes increasingly buoyant and light.
It becomes increasingly supple;
it becomes increasingly workable;
it becomes increasingly radiant and pure.
It conforms to the mind, is bound to the mind, and functions in dependence upon the mind.
As for the perception of resolve (*adhimukti-saṃjñā*),
it refers to that perception by which one resolves the distant as near and the near as distant.
One understands the coarse as subtle and the subtle as coarse;
one understands earth as water and water as earth.
In this manner, each of the distinct great elements mutually acts upon one another.
Just as in the case of the resolute conviction regarding the deeds of a transformation,
whether it be a transformation of form or a transformation of sound,
through these five perceptions, cultivation reaches fulfillment.
They receive various sublime supernormal powers (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*):
for instance, they manifest many bodies from a single body by means of the conceptualization of creative resolve (*nirmāṇādhimokṣa-saṃjñā*).
Or, from many bodies, one may manifest a single body,
by means of the conceptualization of the resolve for concealment and transformation;
or, with that body, one may pass through thick obstructions such as walls, enclosures, and city ramparts.
They pass through directly without obstruction; or they emerge from and submerge in the earth as if it were water;
or they cut through flowing water to travel back and forth, treading upon it as if it were solid ground;
or like flying birds, they sit cross-legged and soar through the void of space.
Or they may touch with their hands the orbs of the sun and moon, which possess vast majesty, power, and influence;
or they may, by means of their own bodies, move with sovereign mastery even as far as the Brahma-world.

One should know that these various kinds of miraculous transformations are all encompassed by the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) and the perception (*saṃjñā*) that accords with the thought of a light, supple, and empty realm of body and mind.
He is capable of performing all actions as appropriate.
In this regard, there are briefly two kinds of mastery and turning by means of the body within that Brahma-world.
First, mastery in coming and going and in revolving;
second, mastery in revolving at will through the power of resolute conviction regarding a portion of the four great elements and derived matter within the Brahma-world.
Regarding the mental image that sequentially recollects past practices:
this refers to the mental image by which, from the stage of childhood until the present,
one recollects and proceeds with mastery and unimpededness.
In whatever state— whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—
he recollects and clearly knows all his previous activities in detail,
according to their coarse sequence without skipping over them.
By practicing and repeatedly cultivating this, one realizes the fruit of cultivation;
one is able to recollect, in detail, all the various modes of existence in immeasurable past lives,
including all their characteristics and all that was proclaimed therein.
Regarding the perception of the sounds of various types of assemblies:
this refers to the perception by which one pervades various villages and towns,
whether it be an assembly of elders, an assembly of local leaders, or any other great multitude.
Whether in vast or narrow places, in houses or rooms,
amidst various assemblies of diverse kinds of people,
there arise various sounds of many different types.
This is called the sound of clamor.
Or, one may properly grasp the characteristics of the sounds of the surging currents and turbulent waves of a great river’s many streams.
By means of the attention belonging to the stage of concentration accomplished through cultivation,
one exerts effort to listen to and attend to all sounds— whether distant or near, whether of gods or humans,
whether noble or ignoble.
Through cultivating and repeatedly practicing this, one realizes the fruit of cultivation: the pure divine ear.
By means of this, one is able to hear all sounds—whether distant or near—in both the human and celestial realms.
Regarding the perception of the marks of light:
it means having thoroughly grasped the various marks of light as previously described.
One then attends to and contemplates those signs.
Furthermore, one correctly grasps the signs regarding the various distinctions in the karmic activities of sentient beings,
such as their wholesome and unwholesome deeds.
One then attends to and contemplates that very sign;
this is called the perception of the sign of the color-form of light.
Through cultivating and repeatedly practicing this, [one attains mastery].
He attains the supernormal power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth as the fruit of cultivation.
By means of this purified divine eye,
he sees all sentient beings, and so forth, up until their passing away from this life and their subsequent rebirth in the heavenly worlds of the happy realms.
The perception of the transformation of form produced by the afflictions refers to that perception by which one [perceives] greed,
hatred, delusion, anger, enmity, concealment, vexation, deceit, guile, stinginess, envy,
as well as pride, harmfulness, lack of shame, and lack of dread, along with all other remaining afflictions.
Furthermore, secondary afflictions entangle their minds,
and they discern and differentiate the various changes in color, state, and physical appearance among sentient beings.
In such a person who possesses desire,
there is a state of the physical form characterized by a transformation of its appearance:
namely, the sense faculties are restless and agitated, and they constantly maintain a smiling expression.
Such a person of this kind who possesses anger undergoes a transformation in the physical state and appearance of the body;
that is to say, their face is constantly furrowed, their speech is stammering and faltering, and their facial color is perpetually altered.
Such are the types of individuals who are deluded:
they possess certain physical states and transformations of physical characteristics,
such as being mostly mute, obscure regarding matters and meanings, unable to articulate speech clearly, and speaking with vulgar, low-class diction.
Through such modes of activity and their like,
and as explained at length up to those who are entangled by shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*),
there occurs a transformation of the characteristics of form within the state of having form (*rūpabhava*).
Having correctly grasped that sign,
one further attends to and contemplates that sign;
through practicing and cultivating this repeatedly, [the mind becomes concentrated].
He gives rise to the knowledge of the distinctions among minds that is the fruit of cultivation.
By means of this knowledge, regarding other sentient beings and persons,
he knows their mind, thought, and consciousness exactly as they are, in accordance with whatever he investigates and examines.
Regarding the perceptions of the liberations, the bases of mastery, and the spheres of totality,
their characteristics of cultivation should be understood as they were previously explained in the *Samāhitabhūmi*.
Because one approaches, cultivates, and practices these perceptions extensively, [they become manifest].
It can induce the most excellent supernormal powers of the noble ones—
whether the power of transformation, the power of creation, or the power of resolute conviction—
as well as the ability to bring forth the absence of contention, the knowledge resulting from prayer, and the four analytical knowledges.
That is to say, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid), the analytical knowledge of meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid), the analytical knowledge of expression (nirukti-pratisaṃvid),
the analytical knowledge of eloquence (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid), and various other such meritorious qualities.
Furthermore, regarding the distinction between the supernormal power of the miraculous (ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna) of the noble and that of the non-noble:
it means that the noble's supernormal power conforms to the objects transformed and the objects emanated.
According to their respective inclinations,
all are able to be accomplished exactly as they are;
there is no alteration or deviation, and they are fit for practical application.
The supernormal powers of those who are not noble cannot be like this;
they are like magical illusions, which can only be observed but cannot be utilized.
One should know that these twelve kinds of perceptions are likewise.
Through approaching, cultivating, and practicing extensively,
one is able to induce the five supernormal powers as appropriate,
as well as to induce the uncommon [powers].
Ordinary beings [attain] the various noble qualities as appropriate.
Furthermore, having cultivated the first dhyāna in its weak, medium, and superior degrees,

they are reborn accordingly within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the Gods of Brahmā’s Retinue (*Brahmapāriṣadya*), the Ministers of Brahmā (*Brahmapurohita*), or the Great Brahmās (*Mahābrahmā*).
Having cultivated the second dhyāna in its weak, medium, and superior degrees,
one will accordingly be reborn among the gods of the Heaven of Limited Light, the Heaven of Infinite Light, or the Heaven of Utmost Purity.
Having cultivated the third dhyāna to a low, medium, or superior degree,
one will accordingly be reborn among the fellowship of the Śuddhāvāsa, Apramāṇaśubha, or Śubhakṛtsna devas, as appropriate.
Having thoroughly cultivated the fourth dhyāna in its lower, middle, and superior degrees,
one will accordingly be reborn within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, or Bṛhatphala devas, as appropriate.
If one is a non-returner,
by means of the untainted fourth dhyāna,
one intersperses and cultivates the tainted fourth dhyāna.
Having thoroughly cultivated these [states] in their lower, middle, upper, superior, and supreme degrees,
one will accordingly be reborn within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
That is to say: the heavens of Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha;
as well as the lower, middle, and superior grades of the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Having practiced well,

one will be born among the classes of devas who frequent the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
for those devas possess no form or color.
Therefore, there is also no distinction in terms of location;
however, there is a distinction in the activity performed while abiding therein.
Having well cultivated the attainment of non-ideation (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), [one enters it].
When one is born into the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñi-sattva*).
Furthermore, how should the characteristics of one who is free from desire (*vītarāga*) be understood therein?
That is to say, one who is free from desire...
His bodily actions are stable and his sense faculties are unmoving;
his deportment and movements are free from agitation.
He is able to remain for a long time in a single posture without becoming easily startled or fearful.
He never repeatedly changes his dignified deportment;
his speech is gentle and his speech is tranquil;
he does not delight in clamor or in large assemblies.
His speech is composed.
Having seen forms with the eye, he perceives only the forms;
he does not give rise to craving for forms because of that perception.
In this way, having heard sounds with the ear,
smelled odors with the nose, tasted flavors with the tongue, and felt tangibles with the body,
one perceives only the sounds and so forth, up to those tangibles.
Not because of awakening does one give rise to craving for sounds, nor even craving for tangibles;
thus one is able to be fearless.
One’s awakened wisdom is profound and subtle, one’s pliancy is vast and great, and body and mind are hidden in secrecy.
He is free from greed and free from malice;
he is capable of endurance,
and his mind is not disturbed by various evil thoughts, such as the pursuit of sensual desires.
Characteristics such as these should be known as the marks of one who has become free from desire.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 33; *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 34.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.
In the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, the thirteenth [section] of the *Maulībhūmi*, within the second part of the fourth *Yogasthāna*: Thus has the progression toward the worldly path been explained.

If one delights in proceeding toward the supramundane path, one should rely upon the objects of the Four Noble Truths to gradually give rise to the seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*). These are:
first, the mental attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manasikāra*).
Finally, there is the attention to the ultimate fruit of the final application,
which extends to the realization of the fruit of arhatship;
this briefly indicates and extensively explains the superior teachings.
Having heard and received [the teaching],
or having well cultivated mental attention (*manasikāra*), or having attained the fundamental dhyānas or formless attainments (*ārūpya*),
one perceives the characteristics of the truth of suffering through four modes of activity (*ākāra*).
That is to say, by means of the contemplation of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
One understands the characteristics of the truth of origination through four modes of contemplation:
namely, the mode of cause, the mode of origination, the mode of arising, and the mode of condition.
One understands the characteristics of the truth of cessation through four aspects:
namely, as cessation, as tranquility, as excellence, and as detachment.
One understands the characteristics of the truth of the path through four aspects.
That is to say, the path is practiced as it is practiced, practiced as it is practiced,
and practiced as it is practiced in its emergence. This is called the attention that characterizes the truths.
One is able to follow and penetrate the four aspects of the Truth of Suffering.
What are these ten?
First, the aspect of transformation.
Second, the practice of destruction;
third, the practice of separation;
fourth, the practice of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
5. The practice of association;
6. The practice of bondage;
7. The practice of the unlovely.
Eighth, the practice of non-peace;
ninth, the practice of non-attainment;
tenth, the practice of lack of mastery.
In this way, one correctly examines these ten modes of practice by means of the principle of logical proof (*upapattisādhanayukti*).
Herein, first, according to the principle of authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*), as the Blessed One has said: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
Furthermore, these conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are briefly of two kinds:
first, the world of sentient beings (sattvaloka);
second, the receptacle world (bhājanaloka).
The Blessed One, with reference to that world of sentient beings, spoke these words:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that with my supramundane, purified divine eye..."

He observes all sentient beings at the time of death and at the time of birth, and so forth, up to their rebirth in a happy destination within the world of the devas after the dissolution of the body.
By this Dharma-gate, it is shown that the Blessed One perceives with his purified divine eye.
The entire world of sentient beings is impermanent in nature.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know this."
This receptacle world remains stable for a long period;
after this time has passed, it gradually proceeds until seven suns appear,
as explained in detail in the *Saptasūryodaya-sūtra*.
Even all the great earth, its mountains, and its great oceans,
as well as Sumeru, the king of great jewel-mountains,
and even the various vessel-worlds up to the Brahma realm, are all consumed by fire.
After the calamitous fire has been extinguished, not even ashes or embers remain;
even the slightest trace cannot be found.
By means of this dharma-gate, the Blessed One demonstrates that the receptacle world is impermanent in nature.
Thus, based on the principle of authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*),
through the power of the mental application (*manasikāra*) of purified faith,
the practitioner of meditation attains certainty regarding the impermanent nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Having attained certainty, by the power of such attention dominated by pure faith,
he repeatedly investigates and examines that which is directly perceived,
which is non-contradictory, and which does not depend on others.
Regarding the nature of impermanence:
how does one repeatedly investigate and examine it?
It is by first establishing two categories: internal and external phenomena.
What is called "internal phenomena" refers to the six sense bases and so forth.
What is called "external phenomena" refers to...
There are sixteen kinds.
The first is the matter of the earth (*bhūmi-vastu*),
which refers to cities, towns, villages, houses, markets, and bazaars.
The second is matters concerning gardens,
namely medicinal herbs, groves, forests, and so forth.
The third is matters concerning mountains.
This refers to the various arrangements and distinctions of mountains.
Fourth is the matter of water,
which refers to rivers, streams, marshes, lakes, all flowing currents, and ponds.
Fifth, the matter of labor;
sixth, the matter of storehouses;
seventh, the matter of food.
Eighth, matters concerning drinking;
ninth, matters concerning vehicles;
tenth, matters concerning clothing.
Eleventh, matters concerning ornaments;
twelfth, matters concerning dance, song, and music;
thirteenth, matters concerning perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Fourteenth, the matter of the requisites for life;
fifteenth, the matter of various radiances;
sixteenth, the matter of men and women attending upon one.
These are called the sixteen types of objects.
Having thus established these internal and external objects,
one then, through the power of attention characterized by direct perception regarding those objects, [proceeds].
One investigates and examines the nature of impermanence through the mode of seeking by way of transformation.
In this regard, there are fifteen kinds of functional transformations of internal phenomena,
as well as eight kinds of causal conditions for transformation.
What are the fifteen kinds of transformation through internal activity?
First, transformation through the state;
second, transformation through color.
Third, transformation caused by changes in shape and form;
fourth, transformation caused by rise and decline;
fifth, transformation caused by the presence or absence of limbs and joints.
Sixth, the transformation caused by the exertions of labor;
