seventh, the transformation caused by injury inflicted by others;
eighth, the transformation caused by cold and heat.
Nine, transformation caused by postures;
ten, transformation caused by contact;
eleven, transformation caused by defilement.
12. The transformation caused by diseases;
13. The transformation caused by death; 14.
The transformation caused by the bluish discoloration [of the corpse] and so forth.
Fifteenth, the transformation of total non-appearance through the complete cessation of all that has been produced.
What are the eight kinds of causes and conditions for transformation?
First, long-term storage and accumulation.
Second, damage by others;
third, impairment through utilization;
fourth, alteration of the seasons.
Fifth, they are burned by fire;
sixth, they are swept away and rotted by water;
seventh, they are parched and withered by wind.
Eighth, the meeting of diverse conditions regarding that which has been accumulated and stored over time refers to those phenomena that possess form.
Even though it is placed and guarded in a favorable location,
after a long period of time, its natural decay occurs, such that its color can be seen to fade and undergo transformation;
this is what is meant by "being damaged by others."
This refers to various material phenomena (*rūpadharma*).
If one is subjected to various beatings or various harms by another,
one's various forms and appearances immediately undergo transformation.
Regarding "deprivation through enjoyment":
this refers to various material objects belonging to individual owners which undergo diminution and transformation due to the dominant influence of the enjoyer’s act of enjoyment.
Regarding the transformation of seasons:
this refers to how, during autumn and winter, the groves, medicinal herbs, flowers, leaves, and fruits wither, yellow, and fall;
whereas during spring and summer, the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are verdant and flourish in abundance.
"Those burned by fire" refers to when a great fire runs wild,
burning villages, towns, kingdoms, cities, and royal capitals until they are all reduced to ashes.
"Those swept away and rotted by water" refers to...
This refers to great floods overflowing and surging, causing villages, towns, cities, and royal capitals to be completely submerged;
"dried up by the wind" refers to being blown and fanned away by great winds.
Damp clothing, damp ground, crops, and forests that are parched and withered.
"The meeting of diverse conditions" refers to when one experiences a pleasant feeling upon encountering a contact associated with pleasant feeling.
When encountering a contact associated with painful feeling,
conditioned by a contact associated with painful feeling,
one experiences a painful feeling.
When encountering a contact associated with pleasant feeling,
or conditioned by a contact associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,
one experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Whether encountering contact associated with pleasant feeling or contact associated with painful feeling,
furthermore, one who possesses greed may encounter anger; through this,
the fetter of greed comes to cease.
One gives rise to the obsession of hatred;
it should be understood that for one who possesses such hatred and delusion,
the same applies when encountering conditions for the arising of discordant afflictions.
In this way, while visual consciousness is present before one,
it encounters objects such as sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles;
through other objects and other conditions, a consciousness of a different category arises.
All other [cases] should be understood accordingly.
These are called the eight causes and conditions for transformation;
they encompass all transformations of every conditioned phenomenon, whether possessing form or formless.
All [these] arise from these eight kinds of causes and conditions;
beyond these, there is nothing further, neither more nor less.
How does one investigate the nature of impermanence as the transformation produced by the various states of internal phenomena?

That is to say, by observing the differences between the preceding and succeeding moments of the continuity of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)— whether in oneself or in another— from the stage of youth up to the stage of old age,
one sees that they are mutually dissimilar.
Having seen this, he then reflects:
"Such conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent. Why is this?"
Since these internal states are currently observable as undergoing change and variation over time,
how does one investigate the impermanent nature of change produced by the primary colors (*varṇa*) of internal things?
That is to say, by observing that either oneself or another first possessed a beautiful complexion with skin that was fresh and lustrous,
and later saw it become an ugly complexion with skin that was withered and parched,
and then at a subsequent time saw it again possess a beautiful complexion with skin that was fresh and lustrous.
Having seen this matter, he then forms this thought:
"Such conditioned phenomena are by nature impermanent. Why is this?"
Since these internal visible colors are perceptible as undergoing change from moment to moment,
how does one investigate the nature of impermanence resulting from the transformation of the shape of internal objects?
That is to say, just as it was explained regarding visible color (*varṇa*),
so too should one understand that this applies to shape (*saṃsthāna*) by way of its being plump or emaciated.
How does one investigate the nature of impermanence as the transformation resulting from the rise and fall of internal phenomena?
It refers to observing, whether in oneself or others, the former status of one's kin, wealth, and position.
At times one sees them all flourishing;
later, one sees them all decline;
and at a subsequent time, one again sees them flourishing.
Having seen this matter, he then forms this thought:
"Such conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent. Why is that?"
Because the phenomena of arising, decaying, and changing can be observed.
How does one investigate the nature of impermanence regarding the changes occurring to the limbs and joints of internal things?
This refers to observing that, whether in oneself or another, the limbs and joints were previously without deficiency or loss.
At a later time, he observes that his limbs and joints are missing or impaired, whether caused by a king, a thief,
a human being, or a non-human being.
Having seen this, he then forms this thought:
"Such conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent," and so forth,
as previously explained.
How does one investigate the nature of impermanence as transformation resulting from the exertion of internal affairs?
It refers to observing the state of physical fatigue or physical exhaustion, whether in one's own body or that of another.
Or those performed while running,
or those performed while leaping,
or those performed while jumping.
Or it may be produced by riding a horse;
or by performing various types of rapid physical actions;
and yet, at another time, one sees that person free from fatigue and exhaustion.
Having seen this, he then forms this thought:
"Such conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent.
The rest is as previously explained.
How does one investigate the impermanent nature of internal phenomena as being subject to transformation through injury inflicted by others?
This refers to observing the transformation of the body— whether one's own or that of another— resulting from injury inflicted by others.
Or they may be destroyed by swords, staves, whips, leather thongs, ropes, spears, lances, and the like;
or they may be harmed by various contacts with mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, scorpions, and other malevolent poisons.
Furthermore, at another time, he sees that it does not change;
having seen this fact,
he then forms this thought:
In this way, these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are by nature impermanent;
the rest is as previously explained.
How does one investigate the impermanent nature of internal phenomena through the transformations caused by cold and heat?
That is to say, by observing that either oneself or another, during a time of intense cold, finds the body unrelaxed and at ease,
but remains hunched, trembling, and tormented by freezing cold, longing for the encounter with warmth.
During the height of the summer heat, though his body was relaxed and at ease,
he would rouse himself with dry gasps as sweat poured down like drizzling rain;
tormented by the feverish thirst, he longed for the encounter with coolness.
When winter arrives once again,
he sees them as before; having seen these things, [he reflects].
Then he reflects:
"In this way, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent.
The rest is as previously stated.
How does one investigate the nature of impermanence as a transformation resulting from the performance of internal postures?
This refers to observing, whether in oneself or another,
any one of the postures— walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
At times it causes harm, and at times it brings benefit.
Having observed this,
he then forms this thought:
In this way, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are by nature impermanent;
the rest is as previously explained.
How does one investigate the nature of impermanence through the transformation produced by contact with internal objects?
That is to say, by encountering a contact conducive to pleasant feeling,
when experiencing the pleasure produced conditioned by that pleasant contact, one is able to discern for oneself the state of the pleasant feeling;
just as one discerns the state of the pleasant feeling.
In this same way, one should understand that the discernment of the state of painful feeling and the state of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is likewise.
Through such discernment, he perceives the successive transformations of these various feelings.
This is a nature of constant renewal rather than a nature of enduring antiquity;
it exists momentarily, subject to increase or decrease,
appearing all at once only to undergo immediate transformation and decay.
Having understood this matter,
he then thought:
"Such conditioned phenomena are by nature impermanent."
The rest is as previously explained.
How does one observe the nature of impermanence through the transformation caused by internal defilements?
It means being able to understand that which arose previously.
There may be a mind of greed or a mind free from greed;
there may be a mind of hatred or a mind free from hatred;
there may be a mind of delusion or a mind free from delusion.
Furthermore, one can discern a mind defiled by each individual type of secondary affliction (*upakleśa*),
and one can also discern a mind undefiled by each individual type of secondary affliction.
Furthermore, one is able to discern that the continuity of that mind, through various afflictions and secondary afflictions,
undergoes a state of transformation or non-transformation across its preceding and succeeding stages.
Having seen this matter, he then forms this thought:
"Such conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent. Why is that?"
Since the transformation produced by mental afflictions (*saṃkleśa*) can be observed as it manifests,
how does one contemplate the impermanent nature of the transformation produced by physical illness within internal phenomena?
That is to say, by observing that oneself or another was previously free from illness, at ease, and robust,
one later observes that oneself or another has encountered the suffering of a grave illness.
They experience intense physical painful sensations,
as described extensively before;
yet at another time, they again see themselves free from illness, at ease, and robust.
Having seen this,
he then reflects:
"Such conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent."
The rest is as previously explained.
How does one observe the nature of impermanence through the transformation caused by the death and passing away of internal phenomena?
It means observing that which is currently alive, abiding, and sustained.
Furthermore, at another time, he observes a person who has died and passed away, seeing only a corpse, empty and devoid of mind and consciousness. Having seen this,
he then forms this thought:
In this way, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are by nature impermanent;
the rest is as previously explained.
How does one observe the nature of impermanence through the transformations produced by internal states such as bluish discoloration (*vinīlaka*)?
That is to say, by observing the corpse after death,
one may at one time see it in the stage of discoloration (vinīlaka),
or at another time see it in the stage of putrefaction (vipūyaka).
In this manner, proceeding even until the stage of the skeleton,
having seen these things,
he then forms this thought:
Thus, these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are by nature impermanent;
the rest is as previously explained.
How does one observe the nature of impermanence as the transformation resulting from the complete disappearance and total cessation of all internal things?
That is to say, by observing that at other times this state of the skeletal chain no longer appears—
having entirely decayed, disintegrated, and been obliterated in every respect— it is no longer seen by the eye.
Having seen this,
he then thought:
"Such conditioned phenomena are by nature impermanent."
Why is this? Because such physical characteristics are repeatedly subject to change,
and their transformation from former to latter states is perceptible in the present.
Thus, by means of the power of attention based on direct observation,
one examines the nature of impermanence through fifteen modes regarding the various transformations of internal phenomena.
Having observed this,
he further observes the various modes of transformation and the nature of impermanence regarding the sixteen external objects.
How does he observe the nature of transformation and impermanence regarding the element of earth?
That is to say, by observing that this place was previously without the construction of a site for a *maṇḍala*, a celestial temple, a residence, a marketplace, city walls, or the like,
and later seeing it newly constructed, well-made, and beautifully adorned.
Furthermore, at another time, he saw that it had become old and dilapidated,
fallen into ruin and decay, shattered and breached,
consumed by fire and swept away by water.
Having seen this matter,
he then formed this thought:
"Such conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent."
Why is this? Because such physical characteristics are observed to undergo transformation from one state to another.
How does one contemplate the nature of impermanence through the transformation of the park?
That is to say, he first observes that within the various gardens and groves, the medicinal herbs, thickets, forests,
flowers, fruits, branches,
and leaves are all flourishing and luxuriant.
It was lush and verdant with crimson luster, exceedingly delightful;
yet at a later time, one sees it withered and decayed, devoid of flowers and fruit,
its branches and leaves fallen away.
Having seen these things— being consumed by fire or swept away by water— he then reflects:
"Such conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent."
The rest is as previously explained.
How does one observe the nature of impermanence through the transformation of mountain phenomena?
It means that at one time, one observes a mountain with lush, verdant forests and towering, jagged crags.
Furthermore, at another time, he saw that forest with its jagged, towering crags,
dilapidated and ruined, uneven in height,
scorched by fire and swept away by water.
Having seen this, he then reflects:
"Such conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent.
The rest is as previously explained.
How does one observe the nature of impermanence through the transformation of water?
It refers to first seeing at one time various rivers, streams, ponds, springs,
and wells overflowing with surging waves and filled with sweet water, and later, at another time, seeing all of them parched, dried up, and exhausted.
Having seen this, he then reflects:
"Such conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent.
The rest is as previously explained.
How does one observe the nature of impermanence through the transformation of karmic activities?
It refers to first observing at one time how various activities—such as pursuing profit, herding cattle, farming, craftsmanship, formal debate, and seafaring—are all flourishing and prosperous.
Again, at another time, he saw that those undertakings had all declined and perished.
Having seen this, he then thought:
"Such conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent."
The rest is as previously explained.
How does one observe the nature of impermanence through the transformation of storehouses?
It refers to observing various kinds of storehouses.
At one time they are full and at another time they are utterly extinguished.
Having seen this, he then reflects:
"Such conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent."
The remainder is as previously explained.
How does one observe the nature of impermanence through the transformation of food and drink?
It refers to observing various kinds of food and drink.
At one time it is not yet prepared; at another time it is already prepared.
At one time it enters the mouth and is chewed by the teeth;
mixed with saliva, it is swallowed bit by bit.
At one time it enters the belly and is gradually digested;
at another time it transforms into excrement and urine and flows out.
Having seen this, he then forms this thought:
Thus, these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are by nature impermanent;
the rest is as previously explained.
How does one observe the nature of impermanence through the transformation of the vehicle (*yāna*)?
That is to say, at one time he sees various vehicles newly and exquisitely adorned, most delightful;
yet at another time, he sees them decayed and worn out, devoid of all ornamentation.
Having seen this, he then reflects:
"In this way, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent.
The rest is as previously explained.
How does one observe the nature of the transformation and impermanence of clothing?
It means observing that various garments are newly produced at one time and become old and ruined at another.
At one time they are fresh and clean, and at another time they are soiled and greasy.
Having seen this, he forms this thought:
"Such conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are by nature impermanent," and the rest is as previously explained. How does one observe the nature of impermanence through the transformation of ornaments?
That is to say, by observing that all ornaments are sometimes unformed and sometimes formed,
and sometimes firm and sometimes destroyed.
Having seen this, he then reflects:
"In this way, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent.
The rest is as previously explained.
How does one observe the nature of change and impermanence inherent in dancing, singing,
and musical performances? It means observing that the various melodies and distinctions of the current dance,
song, and music arise and perish in diverse ways.
Having seen this, he then reflects:
"Such conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent," and so forth,
as previously described.
How does one observe the nature of impermanence in the transformation of perfumes, garlands, and ointments?
It means first observing that various perfumes, garlands, and ointments were once fresh, flourishing, and fragrant.
At a later time, he sees that it has become withered, putrid, and rotten. Having seen this, he reflects:
"Such conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent."
The rest is as previously explained.
How does one observe the impermanent nature of the transformation of requisites?
It means observing their prior non-existence, their subsequent completion, and their final destruction—thus perceiving the transformations that occur before and after.
Having seen this, he then reflects: "In this way,
all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent," and so forth,
as previously explained.
How does one observe the nature of impermanence through the transformation of light?
It means that by observing the various transformations of the arising and ceasing of light and darkness, and having seen these phenomena, one then forms this thought:
Thus, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are by nature impermanent;
the rest is as previously explained.
How does one observe the impermanent nature of the transformations undergone by men and women who provide service?
That is to say, one observes that those [conditioned phenomena] are either declining or flourishing and do not endure for long;
having seen this fact, one then forms this thought:
"Such conditioned formations (saṃskāra) are by nature impermanent."
The rest is as previously explained.
Thus, among all external conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
the first six types are the objects that are grasped.
The latter ten types are matters pertaining to the requisites for the body; in brief,
one should understand that their nature is entirely impermanent.
Why is this? Because the transformation of form and characteristics can be perceived as manifest.
It is because of such reasons as those previously explained.
By means of the power of attention directed toward what is directly perceived through various modes of transformation,
one observes all internal and external phenomena as being impermanent according to their respective natures, by means of those very modes of transformation.
By means of these causes and conditions, regarding the nature of transformation and impermanence in all things,
one perceives it directly, does not turn away from it, does not rely on external conditions, and is not led by others; rather,
one reflects upon it with mindfulness, examines it, and reaches a definitive conclusion through careful scrutiny.
It is precisely by virtue of these aforementioned causes and conditions that it is called "attention characterized by direct perception.
And it is precisely by the power of this attention characterized by direct perception that—
Having observed the nature of impermanence through transformation,
those conditioned phenomena of form, though they appear to exist,
are momentary in their arising and ceasing, characterized by destruction and impermanence.
Because it is subtle and not obtained through direct perception,
one should correctly infer it by means of a mental attention (*manasikāra*) based on what is directly seen.
How does one infer?
That is to say, those conditioned phenomena must undergo momentary arising and ceasing;
only through such destruction can there be the attainment of prior and subsequent transformation.
It is not the case that there can be transformation while abiding in such a manner.
Therefore, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) must necessarily undergo momentary arising and ceasing.
Because they exist through the conjunction of various conditions,
such and such conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise;
once arisen, they perish spontaneously without depending on causes for their destruction.
All such causes and conditions for transformation are able to cause conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to undergo change and arise;
these are the causes and conditions for the arising of transformation.
This is not the cause and condition for the destruction of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Why is that?
Because those conditioned phenomena [are distinct] from the causes and conditions for destruction as they are perceived in the world.
After they have all been destroyed and ceased, a dissimilar arising can be observed;
it is not the case that all of them fail to arise entirely.
Alternatively, there are some conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) which, once destroyed and ceased, cannot be observed to arise at all.
Just as when boiling water and so forth,
at the end all is completely consumed; likewise,
the fires of the calamity incinerate the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
There is already no ash or ember remaining at all;
even a residual trace cannot be found.
That, too, is due to causes and conditions.
Because they gradually diminish and are exhausted through successive stages,
at the very end, everything becomes utterly non-existent;
it is not by means of that fire that such a state occurs.
Therefore, through the eight kinds of causes and conditions previously explained,
transformation arises and naturally perishes;
it is by the power of such inferential mental attention that this occurs.
By means of the mode of disintegration, one attains certainty regarding the momentary arising, ceasing, and destruction—the impermanence—of those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Having attained certainty regarding such matters, [one proceeds].
Furthermore, regarding the arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in other worlds which is not directly perceived,
one should correctly apply inference.
What is inference?
It refers to the fact that sentient beings are currently perceived to possess various distinctions,
such as having either beautiful forms or ugly forms.
Whether of high birth or low birth,
whether of wealthy lineage or poor lineage,
whether of great clan or small clan.
Some have long lifespans, while others have short lifespans;
some are majestic and dignified, while others are not;
some are by nature of sharp faculties, while others are by nature of dull faculties.
In this way, all these distinctions among sentient beings can only be established through the differences in their karmic actions;
there are no such distinctions in the physical forms of sentient beings that exist without karmic action.
It is certain that through the performance and accumulation of various types of wholesome and unwholesome karma in previous lives,
these causes and conditions give rise to the distinct differences of one's current physical existence.
It should not be held that the transformation of Īśvara is the cause. Why?
Because if one asserts that the transformation of Īśvara as the cause can produce all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), [it would follow that they arise without dependence].
Regarding these produced formations (*saṃskāra*),
do they arise solely with that sovereign as their condition,
or do they depend upon other conditions?
Only one who possesses such mastery is able to perform transformations.
If it were solely that mastery acting as the condition,
then all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) would have to exist primordially along with that mastery.
What need is there for further rebirth?
If it is claimed that the self-nature of Īśvara exists first and only then do conditioned phenomena arise,
then these phenomena would not arise solely with Īśvara as their condition.
If it is said that Īśvara creates according to his will,
yet requires effort and prayer to bring about transformation,
then desire must also be employed as a causal condition.
It is not merely a matter of sovereignty.
If that is so, does this desire have a cause,
or is it without a cause?
If it is claimed that there is a cause,
and that very Īśvara is taken as that cause,
then this is identical to the fault previously stated.
This is not logical.
If one were to say that this desire has yet another cause,
then it would follow that, like desire, effort, and aspiration, other phenomena— apart from Īśvara— are the causes.
In this way, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) should likewise take other phenomena as their causes.
Why, then, is it necessary to falsely imagine a useless *Īśvara*?
This is due to the power of such inferential and dominant mental attention (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*).
Having attained certainty regarding the arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in future lives,
one thus briefly investigates and examines the impermanence of internal and external conditioned phenomena by means of three kinds of predominant mental attention (*adhimokṣa*).
That is to say: by the power of attention dominated by pure faith;
by the power of attention dominated by direct perception;
and by the power of attention dominated by inference.
Having already explained the two modes of transformation and disintegration among the five modes of impermanence previously cited,
how does one further contemplate the nature of impermanence by means of the mode of separation?
That is to say, one should understand that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent based on two kinds of separation: internal and external.
Regarding impermanence based on internal separation:
That is to say, suppose there is someone who was previously a master over others—

not a slave nor a servant— capable of enjoying himself and capable of employing others to perform various tasks; at a later time, he falls away from that status of mastery and ceases to be a non-slave and non-servant.
One attains the nature of another's slave or servant;
this, in relation to the nature of a master, is called the nature of impermanence through separation.
This refers to external impermanence through separation.
This refers to the presence of material wealth and possessions that have not yet undergone transformation,
have not yet been separated from, and have not yet been destroyed by impermanence;
subsequently, they are plundered by kings, thieves, those who are unloved, or common creditors.
Or it may be lost due to the failure of a wrongful preparatory effort,
or sought through skillful means yet not obtained;
such categories should be understood accordingly.
This is called knowing the nature of impermanence through the practice of separation.
Furthermore, how does one contemplate the nature of impermanence by means of the practice of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)?
It refers to that which is characterized by the impermanence of transformation.
The impermanence of disintegration;
the impermanence of separation;
and that which has not yet been joined together in the present life.
There will be a nature of phenomena in future ages;
one should penetrate these conditioned formations as they truly are,
[realizing] that there will be a nature of phenomena in future ages.
Such categories as these are called "thoroughly penetrating the impermanence of the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā-anityatā*).
Furthermore, how does one contemplate the nature of impermanence by way of the process of conjunction?
It refers precisely to this impermanence of transformation (*vipariṇāma-anityatā*).
The impermanence of disintegration;
the impermanence of separation;
and that which, having come together in the present life, is now manifest before one.
To penetrate such conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as they truly are—
namely, that they manifest and assemble in the present world—
in this manner is called "penetrating the impermanence of assembly."
Regarding these five types of impermanence in internal and external conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
he practices mental attention (*manasikāra*) according to their respective applications through five modes of cultivation;
by practicing them extensively, he attains certainty.
Thus, through the reasoning of proof and the predominance of cultivation,
once one has attained certainty regarding the aspect of impermanence,
one immediately thereafter enters into the aspect of suffering.
He reflects in this way:
"All such conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent.
Because they are impermanent, they must necessarily possess the nature of arising."
Since these conditioned phenomena are subject to arising, there is the suffering of birth.
Since there is the suffering of birth,
one should know that there is likewise the suffering of aging, illness, and death.
The suffering of association with the disliked;
the suffering of separation from the beloved;
and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
Thus, for now, one enters into the contemplation of suffering by way of the aspect of the unattractive.
Furthermore, regarding all the aggregates that are with outflows, with grasping, and conducive to pleasant feeling:
One enters into the practice of suffering by means of the fetters. Why is this?
Because the fetters such as craving arise within the spheres of the fetters such as craving.
When the fetters of greed and so forth arise in relation to their respective objects,
they are able to bring about and accumulate birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and all manner of afflictions— the entire great mass of suffering.
Furthermore, regarding all contaminated and grasped aggregates that are neither painful nor pleasant,
one enters into them as being of the nature of suffering because they are unstable. Why is this so?

Because all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and grasped (*sopādāna*) aggregates, which accord with neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, are accompanied by heaviness (*dausthulya*), pursued by the seeds of suffering and pleasure, and are thus not liberated from the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
All things are impermanent and subject to cessation.
Thus, a practitioner [contemplates] those formations that are conducive to pleasant feeling, as well as the pleasant feeling itself.
One enters into the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*) through the mode of being bound;

one enters into the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*) through the mode of being undesirable with respect to those formations conducive to painful feeling as well as within painful feeling itself.
Regarding those formations that are conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,
as well as within the state of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling itself,
one enters into the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*) by way of their lack of stability.
Thus, by the predominant influence of the modes of being bound, the modes of being unlovely, and the modes of being insecure,
it is said with respect to the three types of feeling:
"Whatever feelings there are, all are suffering."
This is called entering into the contemplation of suffering preceded by the mental attention to impermanence.
Furthermore, one forms this thought:
At this time, for me there are only the sense faculties, only the objects of the senses,
and only the various sensations born from them;
there is only the mind and only the conventional designations of "self" and "what belongs to the self."
There is only this view and only this provisional designation;
these are all that can be found herein,
and beyond these there is nothing further, whether by way of excess or addition.
In this way, only the aggregates (skandhas) are to be found;
within these aggregates, there is no permanent, eternal, stable,
or sovereign entity that is called "self" (ātman) or "sentient being" (sattva).
Furthermore, it is here described as that which is born, ages, falls ill, and dies;
or again, it is described as that which can perform various karmas and can experience their diverse fruits and maturations (vipāka).
Because all these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely empty and devoid of a self (*ātman*),
this is called entering the practice of emptiness by means of the practice of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, he reflects as follows:
All conditioned phenomena, together with their specific characteristics,
are associated with the characteristic of impermanence and the characteristic of suffering;
furthermore, because they all arise from conditions, they lack autonomy.
Because they lack self-mastery, none of them are "I.
This is called entering into the practice of non-self by way of the mode of lacking self-mastery.
One who practices in this manner—
The ten modes of practice subsume the four modes of practice.
Furthermore, one comprehends the characteristics of the Truth of Suffering through these four modes.
Specifically, the mode of impermanence is subsumed by five modes of practice.
First, the aspect of transformation;
second, the aspect of disintegration;
third, the aspect of separation.
The four are the practice of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā-caryā). The fifth is the practice of convergence (saṃnipāta-caryā).
The practice of austerity (duṣkara-caryā) is subsumed within these three practices.
First, the mode of being bound by fetters;
second, the mode of being unlovely;
third, the mode of being insecure.
The practice of emptiness is subsumed within a single practice,
namely, the practice of non-apprehension.
The practice of selflessness is subsumed within a single practice.
This refers to the mode of non-mastery.
One enters into the four modes by means of ten modes;
furthermore, having correctly awakened to the characteristics of the truth of suffering by means of those four modes, [one proceeds].
Next, one further examines this truth of suffering:
what is its cause, its origin, its arising, and its condition?
By the abandonment of these, suffering is likewise abandoned.
In this way, one understands the characteristics of the truth of origination through the four aspects of the truth of origination;
that is, because one understands that craving leads to suffering,
it is designated as the cause.
Because it has already drawn forth suffering and further gathers and causes it to arise,
it is called "origination" (*samudaya*).
Because once suffering has arisen, it causes that [suffering] to continue, it is so named.
It is called "arising" because it further grasps the seeds of future sufferings,
thereby sequentially attracting and inducing the accumulation of suffering.
Therefore, it is called a "condition" (pratyaya).
Furthermore, there is another distinction:
namely, that craving is known to be the cause of grasping (upādāna).
Furthermore, it can summon and assemble [them],
because existence (bhava) exists precisely by taking that grasping as its cause;
furthermore, it can give rise to conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta), having existence as its primary factor.
Because it brings about future birth,
and because it can further give rise to various phenomena of suffering— such as old age, sickness, and death— which have birth as their condition;

one should understand that the terms "cause" (*hetu*), "origination" (*samudaya*), "arising" (*prabhava*), and "condition" (*pratyaya*) are explained with these respective distinctions according to their appropriate application.
That is to say, one correctly understands that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions, which are attached to their respective bases—
such as the latent disposition of craving (*tṛṣṇānuśaya*) and so forth— are the causes for future rebirth. Furthermore,

one correctly understands that the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) produced by them are, according to their respective natures, the conditions for the origination of the mass of suffering (*samudaya*).
This means that craving for future existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*) is able to draw [rebirth] forth;
it is itself the origin (*samudaya*).
Furthermore, this craving for future existence can also give rise to craving accompanied by joy and attachment (*nandī-rāga-sahagatā tṛṣṇā*).
This craving, which is accompanied by joy and greed, further serves as the condition for various kinds of delight and attachment toward this or that object.
Thus, it relies upon the underlying tendency of craving (*tṛṣṇā-anuśaya*) and the three types of envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).
It is able to produce future existence and to give rise to the various distinctions of craving;
therefore, it is called the cause, the accumulation, the origination, and the condition.
Thus does the practitioner [contemplate].
One discerns the characteristics of the truth of origination through four modes of conduct.
Having correctly awakened to the characteristics of the truth of origination,
one further correctly awakens to the complete cessation of such a truth of origination without remainder.
It is called "cessation" (*nirodha*).
Because all truths of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) are stilled without remainder,
it is called "tranquility" (*śānta*).
This very cessation and tranquility is primary, supreme,
and unsurpassed.
It is called "sublime" because it is eternally abiding and because it is forever transcendent.
This is called "separation.
In this way, the practitioner discerns the characteristics of the truth of cessation through these four modes of discernment.
Having correctly awakened to the characteristics of the truth of cessation,
one further correctly awakens to the true path of antidote,
because it is capable of thoroughly seeking out the meaning within the objects of knowledge.
Because it is able to seek the meaning in accordance with reality;
because its meaning accords with the four gateways;
and because its meaning leads exclusively toward nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is said that the path is "proceeding as it should proceed.
A practitioner who acts in this way discerns the characteristics of the truth of the path through four modes of practice.
This is called the attention that realizes characteristics through internal personal realization regarding the four noble truths.
Having thus personally and internally perceived the aggregates, he—
Having investigated and correctly observed by means of non-erroneous reflection upon the principles of the truths,
one further employs inference to observe the remaining aggregates that belong to dissimilar realms and are not directly perceived.
That is to say, all that is conditioned and with outflows,
in every location, in every manner, and at all times, possesses such dharmas.
All fall within this principle;
all possess this nature.
That which is their cessation is eternally quiescent, permanently abiding, and blissful.
All paths belonging to that [category] are capable of permanently severing [afflictions] and leading to ultimate liberation.
It should be understood that herein, there is the knowledge of the truths regarding the directly perceived aggregates,
as well as the inferential knowledge of the truths regarding other, non-homogeneous realms that are not directly perceived.
This is precisely the basis for the seeds of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent-knowledge that are capable of being produced.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this very attention characterized by the discernment of signs (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) is still interspersed with hearing and reflection.
If a practitioner of meditation, regarding the various truths,
has attained certainty through the sixteen aspects concerning the principles established for the four noble truths,
they further [investigate] the full extent of those truths.
The nature of things as they are transcends the mixture of hearing and reflection;
when attention is directed exclusively toward the arousal of resolute conviction in practice,
this is called "attention consisting of resolute conviction" (adhimokṣika-manasikāra).
Applying the mind in this way,
focusing exclusively on the objects of the truths while remaining one-pointedly in meditative concentration,
through the repeated cultivation and frequent practice of this, [one attains mastery].
One attains boundless wisdom regarding the objects of the two truths of suffering and its origin.
By means of this wisdom, one understands impermanence and gives rise to the superior resolve that impermanence is boundless.
Having thus understood suffering and the other [truths],
one generates the resolute conviction that suffering is boundless,
and the resolute conviction that emptiness and selflessness are boundless.
The conviction that unwholesome conduct is boundless;
the conviction that rebirth in evil destinies is boundless;
and the conviction that the cycle of rise and fall is boundless.
And the resolve regarding the boundless nature of old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering,
and all disturbances; herein, "boundless" refers to the cyclic flow of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
In this way, these dharmas are boundless and limitless;
as long as the cycle of birth and death continues without interruption,
these aforementioned dharmas will always exist.
Only birth and death can be extinguished without remainder;
there is no other means for their extinction.
It is precisely within these phenomena of death and birth across all realms of existence and destinies that [this occurs].
By means of the practice of wishlessness,
the practice of non-reliance,
and the profound practice of revulsion toward conditioned existence.
He generates resolute conviction and diligently practices the mental engagement of resolute conviction;
furthermore, he develops a superior intention and a deep-seated mind of revulsion and dread toward all such states of existence and rebirths.
Furthermore, regarding nirvāṇa, they may occasionally give rise to a single thought of deep aspiration and longing;
yet throughout the long night, their minds have remained attached to and delighted in worldly forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
Because they are nourished and accumulated by various forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles,
for this reason, although they deeply aspire to and take delight in nirvana with their whole hearts,
they are nonetheless unable to enter into it.
They are unable to realize purity,
unable to abide [therein], and unable to attain resolute conviction;
their minds regress from the realm of tranquility because they have not yet developed a deep sense of longing and admiration for it.
Because of these doubts, his mind repeatedly feels weary, detached, alarmed, and terrified;

yet, regarding both the truths of suffering and its origin, he repeatedly develops a deep-seated sense of weariness, detachment, alarm, and terror, while toward nirvāṇa, he repeatedly gives rise to a deep-seated aspiration and longing.
Nevertheless, they are still unable to enter [the path] with a profound mind.
Why is this? Because they still possess a coarse form of the conceit "I am" (asmimāna) that acts as an obstacle to clear realization (abhisamaya).
Entering into the mental engagement (*manasikāra*) and proceeding from moment to moment without interruption, he reflects thus:
"I have long wandered through saṃsāra;
I shall wander through saṃsāra once again."
"I shall be able to enter into nirvāṇa;
for the sake of nirvāṇa, I cultivate all wholesome dharmas;
I am able to contemplate suffering as truly being suffering."
I am able to contemplate that what is truly arising is arising; I am able to contemplate that what is truly ceasing is ceasing.
I am able to contemplate that what is truly the path is the path.
I am able to contemplate that what is truly empty is empty.
I contemplate wishlessness as truly wishless;
I contemplate signlessness as truly signless.
Such dharmas as these are my own possession.
Due to these causes and conditions, although they deeply aspire to and take pleasure in nirvāṇa with their whole heart,
their minds are unable to enter into it.
Having thus understood that such pride is an obstacle, [they abandon it].
He is then able to swiftly penetrate with wisdom,
spontaneously relinquishing the mental engagement that follows objects,
and subduing all external objects of knowledge.
Entering into the mental engagement of application,
he applies himself with diligence and uninterrupted observation of the Noble Truths;
as each moment of mind that arises subsequently passes away.
He observes with mental attention arising in uninterrupted succession;
his skillful means flow on without interruption.
Having thus focused the mind upon the mind with single-minded diligence and without substitution, he proceeds.
He is then able to cause that person to enter into mental engagement (*manasikāra*),
such that the coarse form of the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*), which obstructs clear realization (*abhisamaya*), has no room to arise.
Thus does the practitioner of yoga diligently cultivate.
Observe that the continuity of the mind undergoes successive transformations,
arising ever anew, sometimes increasing and sometimes decreasing.
It exists for a moment and appears abruptly;
its transformation before and after is the nature of impermanence.
One should contemplate that the continuity of the mind is subsumed within the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*).
This is the contemplation of the continuity of the mind as having the nature of suffering.
To be free from a second dharma is the contemplation of the continuity of the mind as having the nature of emptiness.
Arising from various conditions and lacking autonomy is the nature of non-self.
This is called entering into the realization of the truth of suffering.
Next, one further observes this continuity of mind,
seeing that it has craving as its cause and craving as its origin.
With craving as its origin and craving as its condition—
this is called entering into the truth of origination (samudaya-satya).
Next, one further observes this mental continuum.
All analytical cessations (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) are of the nature of eternal extinction,
the nature of eternal tranquility, the nature of eternal excellence, and the nature of eternal detachment.
This is called entering into the truth of cessation (nirodha-satya).
Next, one further observes this continuity of mind:
the ultimate path that serves as the antidote and leads toward cessation is the nature of the true path and the nature of suchness.
This is the nature of true practice; this is the nature of true emergence.
This is called entering into the Truth of the Path.
Thus, that which was previously not well-examined [is now understood].
Now, through skillful means of right attention and subtle wisdom,
one is able to correctly awaken to and enter the Four Noble Truths;
by approaching, cultivating, and practicing this wisdom extensively, one attains mastery.
When the cognition that realizes the equality of the subject and the object arises in perfect equanimity,
through its arising, one is able to sever the coarse manifestations of the conceit "I am," which obstruct the aspiration for nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, with a deep-seated aspiration for nirvāṇa,
one is swiftly able to enter it with a mind that does not regress and is free from all fear,
thereby embracing the joy of the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).
A practitioner who acts in this way is encompassed by the lower degree of patience regarding the Noble Truths.
The arising of wisdom in which the subject that perceives and the object perceived are equal and identical is called "Heat" (ūṣmagata);
it is subsumed under medium patience (madhyakṣānti).
When the subject that perceives and the object perceived are equal,
and equal wisdom arises,
this is called the "Summit" (mūrdhan).
Subsumed under the highest patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*),
it is the equality of the subject and object of cognition;
the arising of the wisdom of this equality is called the "patience in conformity with the truths" (*satyānulomikī-kṣānti*).
Having thus abandoned the coarse form of the conceit of "I am" which acts as an obstacle,
and having attained the joy of the superior aspiration that embraces nirvāṇa,
he is then able to relinquish all further application of effort associated with the successive moments of contemplative mind.
Abiding in a state of non-application and non-conceptualization,
at that time his mind appears to cease, yet it does not actually cease;
it appears to lack an object of focus, yet it is not without an object.
Furthermore, at that time, although his mind is tranquil and appears to be secluded, it is not actually secluded;
nor, at that time, is it shrouded by pleasant sleep.
There is only the practice of śamatha, which is lucid, without high or low.
Furthermore, there is a class of people who are dull-witted and ignorant;
their minds are shrouded by pleasant sleep, appearing to have ceased when in fact they have not truly ceased.
One gives rise to overweening pride,
claiming it to be clear realization; this is not so.
Having attained such a mind that has entered into clear realization (*abhisamaya*),
one will before long enter into the state of rightness and separation from birth (*samyaktva-nyāma*).
It is precisely at this stage of the tranquil mind, at the very last moment of non-conceptual cognition, that [this occurs].
When one gives rise to internal mental attention toward the principles of the Noble Truths as they are being contemplated, this is precisely termed the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
From this point onward, supramundane consciousness arises; it is no longer mundane consciousness.
This is the final boundary and limit of all worldly conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
therefore, it is called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
Immediately following this, one gives rise to internal mental attention (*manasikāra*) regarding the principles of the Noble Truths previously contemplated.
Immediately following the mental engagement, in accordance with the sequence of the truths previously contemplated—
whether those noble truths are directly perceived or not directly perceived—
there arises, respectively, a definitive knowledge free from conceptual differentiation and a knowledge of direct perception regarding those truths.
Due to its arising,

all categories of afflictions associated with the basis— which are bound to the three realms and abandoned by the path of vision— along with their entire mass of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), are forever severed.
Because this has been permanently severed,
if one has previously already become detached from the greed of the desire realm,
then at this present time, having entered such a clear observation of the truths (satyābhisamaya), one attains the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
One should know that his characteristics do not differ from those previously described for one who has abandoned desire;
however, there is a slight distinction in this case.
This means that they will undergo birth by transformation (upapāduka),
and will attain parinirvāṇa right there without returning again to be born in this world.
This applies to those who have already doubly detached from the craving of the desire realm.
Having now entered such a clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), he attains the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*).
If he had not previously abandoned the craving for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
then having now entered such a clear realization of the truths, [he attains it].
With the permanent subsiding of the coarse and heavy [defilements], one attains the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
Because the knowing wisdom and the known object are in accord and not at variance, and because they are observed as being present before one, it is called "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*).
Just as when a kṣatriya and a kṣatriya come together without discord and observe them face-to-face, it is called "clear observation" (abhisamaya);
one should know that the same applies to brahmins and others.
This also accomplishes many characteristics;
that is to say, because one realizes the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of such truths, one attains the four knowledges (*jñāna*).
This is because, within all mental engagements (*manasikāra*), whether in motion or at rest, one skillfully investigates them.
One attains the knowledge that there is only phenomena (*dharmamātra*), the knowledge that they are not subject to annihilation, and the knowledge that they are not subject to permanence.
One attains the knowledge that conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) arise dependently and are like illusory things.
If, however, one engages with these objects due to a lapse of mindfulness...
Although they may give rise to intense entanglements of the afflictions,
these are swiftly dispelled upon a momentary application of attention;
furthermore, they are ultimately never reborn in the miserable realms.
He never intentionally transgresses what he has studied;
he does not even take the life of an animal;
and he never regresses or abandons what he has studied.
He can no longer commit the five deeds of immediate retribution.
He knows with certainty that suffering and pleasure are not created by oneself, nor created by another,
nor created by both oneself and another, nor produced without cause from neither self nor other.
He never seeks to request non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) as his teachers,
nor does he conceive of them as fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
He never gazes upon the mouths or the faces of other śramaṇas, brahmins, and the like.
One sees the Dharma for oneself, attains the Dharma,
knows the Dharma, and realizes the depths of the Dharma; having transcended doubt and uncertainty,
one does so without depending on the conditions of others.
Not led by others regarding the Teacher’s instruction,
he attains fearlessness among all phenomena;
he never falsely reckons worldly omens or auspicious signs as being pure.
He will never again undergo an eighth birth;
he fully accomplishes the four kinds of verified confidence.
Such is the practitioner.
Up until the stage prior to the "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgradharma), it is called "attention consisting of resolute conviction" (adhimokṣika-manaskāra).
Following the clear realization (abhisamaya) of the noble truths,
up until the permanent abandonment of all afflictions to be abandoned by the path of seeing (darśanamārga-prahātavya-kleśa), it is called "attention consisting of detachment" (viveka-manaskāra).
Thereafter, desiring to further abandon the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
he repeatedly practices the path as previously attained;
having permanently severed the superior and medium grades of afflictions of the desire realm, he attains the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
Just as with all the characteristics of the fruit of stream-entry,
so too should they be understood here;
however, there is a slight distinction.
That is to say, when one engages with an object of experience that is conducive to the occurrence of intense and sharp afflictive entanglements (*kleśa-paryavasthāna*),
due to a lapse of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), there briefly arises a slight and weak entanglement of various afflictions.
Upon reflecting, they are able to swiftly dispel [these thoughts];
having come to be born in this world for only one more time,
they are then able to bring an ultimate end to suffering.
The attainment of the fruit of non-returning and the characteristics of non-returning are as previously explained;
it should be understood that herein, this is by means of the mental application of investigation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-manasikāra*).
Having repeatedly examined all paths of cultivation as to what has been abandoned and what remains unabandoned,
one correctly practices according to the path as it has been attained.
Furthermore, in this context, what is meant by the "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) of cultivation?
What is called the cultivation of practice?
What is called the cultivation of the distinctions among categories?
It refers to that which is performed by means of attention belonging to the stage of meditative concentration.
One cultivates and increases mundane and supramundane wholesome conditioned phenomena;
performing them without interval and with earnestness,
one causes the mental continuum to converge with their essential nature.
This is called the intrinsic nature of cultivation.
It should be known that the activities of cultivation are, in brief, of eight kinds.
First, there is a class of dharmas that are attained through cultivation.
Second, there is a class of phenomena that are cultivated through practice;
third, there is a class of phenomena that are purified through practice;
fourth, there is a class of phenomena that are eliminated through practice.
5. There is a class of phenomena that are known through cultivation;
6. there is a class of phenomena that are abandoned through cultivation;
7. there is a class of phenomena that are realized through cultivation.
Eighth, there is a class of phenomena that become distant through cultivation.
If one has not previously attained superior wholesome dharmas,
by practicing them so as to attain them, they are said to be "attained through cultivation."
If that which was previously attained is brought into manifestation,
it is called "cultivating what has been practiced";
if that which was previously attained is not yet brought into manifestation, [it is called "preserving"].
However, by practicing those types of dharmas,
one should cause them to manifest and cause them to arise in a state that is increasingly pure and bright.
It is called "purified through cultivation.
If there is the occurrence of defiled phenomena due to a lapse in mindfulness,
the power of cultivated wholesome qualities causes one not to tolerate them, but rather to sever and expel them.
It is called "cultivation" because it dispels [afflictions].
If dharmas that ought to be abandoned have not yet arisen,
one understands through the power of cultivating wholesome dharmas that they are like a disease, and with a deep mind, one brings them to ruin through weariness.
To thoroughly understand [the body] as being like an abscess, like an arrow, an obstacle, impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and to deeply loathe and destroy it with the mind—
this is called cultivation through thorough knowledge.
Having known it thus, one practices it repeatedly.
Therefore, when the path of uninterrupted activity arises and severs all afflictions,
it is called "severing through cultivation.
Once the afflictions have been severed, one realizes liberation.
It is called "realization through cultivation.
Just as one progressively advances toward the wholesome dharmas of higher stages,
so too does one cause those [dharmas] of lower stages that have already been abandoned to become further refined.
The transformation of all phenomena through the stages from the remote portion up to the ultimate is called cultivation;
thus it is "remote" by virtue of being cultivated.
One should know that these are called the eight types of cultivation-practice.
It should be understood that there are eleven varieties of this cultivation:
first, the cultivation of śamatha;
second, the cultivation of vipaśyanā.
1. Cultivation of the mundane path;
2. Cultivation of the supramundane path;
3. Cultivation of the inferior path.
Sixth, the cultivation of the medium path;
seventh, the cultivation of the superior path;
eighth, the cultivation of the preparatory path.
1. Cultivation of the nine paths of uninterrupted transition;
2. Cultivation of the ten paths of liberation;
3. Cultivation of the path of superior progress.
The cultivation of śamatha refers to causing the mind to abide through nine modes of practice,
as previously explained.
The cultivation of vipaśyanā is also as previously described.
As for the cultivation of the mundane path,
it refers to perceiving the coarse characteristics of the lower stages.
Because one perceives the signs of tranquility in the higher stages,
one is able to proceed toward the complete freedom from desire for everything up to the sphere of nothingness;
this refers to the cultivation of the supramundane path.
That is to say, right reflection that suffering is truly suffering,
the origin is truly the origin,
and cessation is truly cessation.
The Path is indeed the Path.
It consists of the untainted noble path beginning with right view,
extending even to the complete detachment from desire up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The cultivation of the inferior path refers to that by which one is able to abandon the coarsest and most superior afflictions.
The cultivation of the middling path refers to...
This means that by means of this, one is able to abandon all middling-grade afflictions.
As for the cultivation of the superior path,
it means that by means of this, one is able to abandon all last-to-be-abandoned low-grade afflictions.
The cultivation of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) refers to that by means of which one initiates application (*prayoga*) for the sake of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The cultivation of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*)...
This means that by means of this, one correctly abandons the afflictions.
As for the cultivation of the path of liberation,
it means that by means of this, one either abandons [the afflictions] immediately or realizes liberation.
Regarding the cultivation of the path of superior progress:
this refers to that by means of which one subsequently cultivates superior wholesome dharmas,
up until the point where the preparatory application (*prayoga*) that serves as the antidote to the afflictions of other stages has not yet arisen.
Alternatively, for one who has not yet arisen [into the path] but is heading toward the stage of culmination,
it should be known that these are called the eleven varieties of the categories of cultivation.
Thus, for one who exerts themselves in the practice of cultivation:
From time to time, one should correctly examine whether all afflictions have been abandoned or not;
from time to time, one should cultivate a deep sense of longing and aspiration for those qualities that are to be rejoiced in.
This is called the attention of "relishing" (*āsvādānābhoga-manasikāra*).
Through its frequent cultivation,
one is able to completely and irreversibly abandon the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*).
Finally, the stage of final training arises like the vajra-like samādhi;
through its arising, one is able to permanently sever all afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.
Question: For what reason is this samādhi named "diamond-like" (vajropama)?
Answer: It is because, for example, the diamond, when compared to all other precious gems such as mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, and coral, [is superior].
It is the most solid;
it can pierce and destroy all other precious objects,
yet it cannot be pierced or destroyed by any other precious objects.
Thus, this samādhi is the most supreme, the most excellent, and the most firm among all the samādhis of those in training;
it is capable of destroying all afflictions whatsoever.
It cannot be obscured or overcome by the higher afflictions;
therefore, this samādhi is called "diamond-like" (*vajropama*),
as it [destroys] the seeds of the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) of the [lower] stages.
His mind attains ultimate liberation from those [afflictions],
realizes the purification of the lineage of the ultimate state, and,
within the context of the ultimate exhaustion of all afflictions, gives rise to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Because the causes have been exhausted, future bitter fruits will never again arise;
within this very state, one gives rise to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
At that time, he becomes an Arhat whose outflows (*āsrava*) are completely exhausted.
Having accomplished what was to be done, there is nothing further to be done.
Having realized their own goal and exhausted all fetters of existence,
they have correctly carried out the noble teaching of the Tathāgata.
The mind is well-liberated.
He has fully accomplished the ten qualities of one beyond training (*daśāśaikṣadharma*), namely:
the right view, right intention, and so forth, up to the right liberation and right knowledge of one beyond training.
Within all the stages of dwelling and within all acts of mental attention,
one is able to function with mastery according to one's own mind;
wherever one wishes to dwell— whether in a noble dwelling, a celestial dwelling, or a Brahma dwelling— one is immediately able to abide therein.
Whatever sublime Dharma one contemplates according to one's inclination that can lead to mundane or supramundane benefit and welfare, one is able to contemplate it.
As for what is called the "noble abiding" (āryavihāra):
This refers to dwelling in emptiness, dwelling in the wishless, dwelling in the signless, and dwelling in the meditative attainment of cessation.
What is called "dwelling of the gods" refers to dwelling in the various dhyānas and the formless attainments.
What are called the "Brahma-abodes" (brahmavihāra) are the abiding in loving-kindness, the abiding in compassion, the abiding in sympathetic joy,
and the abiding in equanimity. Furthermore, at that time, they reach the ultimate limit, being ultimately stainless and ultimate.
He has realized the ultimate limit of the holy life (brahmacarya), freed from all fetters;
he has emerged from the deep pit and crossed over the deep moat;
he has been able to utterly subdue that *īṣikā*.
This is what constitutes a true noble one:
having destroyed the high banner, severed the five limbs, and accomplished the six limbs,
they resolutely guard the four bases of reliance.
Utterly secluded,
alone, and devoted to the truth, he has abandoned all longing;
his thoughts are undisturbed and his bodily activities are calmed.
With mind well-liberated and wisdom well-liberated,
he stands alone without companion, established in right practice;
he is called one who has drawn near to the Unsurpassed Man, fully accomplished in the six modes of constant abiding.
That is to say, having seen forms with the eye, one is without joy and without sorrow,
dwelling in sublime equanimity with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
Likewise, having heard sounds with the ear, smelled odors with the nose, tasted flavors with the tongue, felt tangibles with the body, and cognized mental phenomena with the mind.
Free from joy and free from sorrow, he dwells in sublime equanimity with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension;
at that time, he experiences the complete and total exhaustion of sensual desire without remainder,
and he experiences the complete and total exhaustion of ill will without remainder.
Having received [this teaching], ignorance is exhausted without remainder;
because greed, hatred, and delusion are all forever exhausted,
one refrains from committing various evils and draws near to all that is wholesome.
His mind is like the void, like pure water, and like exquisite sandalwood;
he is universally revered and made offerings to by all the celestial emperors and heavenly kings,
abiding in the realm of nirvana with remainder.
Having crossed the ocean of birth and death, they have already reached the other shore;
this is also called "sustaining the final body of existence.
The aggregates, which were drawn forth by prior karma and afflictions, cease spontaneously.
Therefore, because there is no further grasping and because there is no further continuity,
one attains parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder; yet within this,
there is absolutely no one who attains parinirvāṇa.
Just as there is no further wandering within birth and death,
there is only the eternal cessation of all suffering— tranquil, cool, extinguished,
and vanished; this alone is the most peaceful state.
That which is called the relinquishing of all attachment to a basis,
the exhaustion of desire, its perpetual cessation, and nirvāṇa—
know that within this there are such characteristics.
An Arhat bhikṣu, whose outflows are forever exhausted,
cannot resort to five types of places:
first, he cannot intentionally take the life of any living being.
Second, one cannot take what is not given without it being offered.
Third, one cannot engage in unchaste conduct or practice the dharma of sexual desire.
Fourth, one cannot speak falsely knowing the truth.
Fifth, they are unable to store up or enjoy the various requisites for sensual pleasures.
Being thus, they falsely speculate that suffering and pleasure are self-made, made by another, made by both self and another, made by neither self nor another, or produced without cause.
Furthermore, they are unable to be terrified by any matters that should not be recorded;
nor are they able to give rise to deep alarm and fear upon seeing various terrifying events such as clouds, thunder, lightning, thunderbolts, calamities, and hail.

It should be understood that the attention (manasikāra) subsumed within this diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) is called the "attention of the culmination of application" (prayoganiṣṭha-manasikāra),
and it is the attention subsumed within the supreme fruit of arhatship.
This is called the attention that is the fruit of the culmination of application.
Through these and many other types of attention,
one realizes the ultimate by means of the supramundane path.
All of this is called the Śrāvaka-bhūmi.
This is that which was taught by all the Perfectly Enlightened Ones;
it is the root of all teachings associated with the śrāvakas.
It is like all collections of names, phrases, and syllables, which serve as the basis for the composition of literary works, incantations, and heterodox treatises. 14.

Thus ends the fourteenth [chapter], the Stage of the Pratyekabuddhas, within the *Maulī Bhūmi* of the *Pratyekabuddhabhūmi*. Having thus explained the Stage of the Śrāvakas, [the Stage of the Pratyekabuddhas follows].
What is the stage of the solitary realizer?
It should be known that this stage has five characteristics.
The first is the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
The second is the path; the third is practice;
the fourth is abiding;
the fifth is conduct.
What is the lineage of the pratyekabuddhas?
It should be correctly understood through three characteristics.
First, by their very nature, those of the pratyekabuddha lineage possess a lineage of attenuated afflictions prior to having realized that awakening.
For these reasons, they do not find delight in bustling places,
but instead feel deep-seated delight for solitary, tranquil places. Second,
by their very nature, Pratyekabuddhas possess a meager lineage of compassion prior to their realization of that enlightenment.
For these reasons, his mind finds no delight in the task of teaching the true Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings;
rather, he takes deep pleasure in dwelling in tranquility with few concerns.
Third, those who are by nature solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddha*) possess a medium-faculty lineage prior to attaining that awakening;
they belong to the class of those characterized by conceit.
For this reason, with a profound aspiration in their hearts, they seek to realize awakening without a teacher and without a rival.
What is the path of the solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha*)?
It should be correctly understood by way of three characteristics.
Namely, there is a certain class of persons who abide in the lineage of the solitary realizer.
Having passed through a hundred kalpas and encountered a Buddha appearing in the world,
he drew near and served him to bring his mental continuum to maturity,
and with single-minded devotion sought to realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Skillfulness regarding the aggregates, skillfulness regarding the sense bases,
skillfulness regarding the elements, skillfulness regarding dependent origination,
skillfulness regarding what is possible and impossible, and skillfulness regarding the truths.
By diligently practicing and training,
one will be able to swiftly realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha in a future life;
this is called the first path of the pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, there is another class of persons who encounter a Buddha appearing in the world, draw near to virtuous friends,
hear the true Dharma, and apply their minds correctly.
One brings forth and gives rise to the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) that had not previously arisen—
namely, *ūṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, and *kṣānti*— yet lacks the power to realize the direct vision of the Dharma (*dharmābhisamaya*) and attain the fruits of the śramaṇa within this very life.
Furthermore, one cultivates skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*), cultivates skillfulness regarding the bases (*āyatana-kauśalya*),
cultivates skillfulness regarding the elements (*dhātu-kauśalya*), cultivates skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*),
cultivates skillfulness regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*), and cultivates skillfulness regarding the truths (*satya-kauśalya*).
In a future life, they will be able to realize the clear observation of the Dharma and attain the fruit of śrāmaṇya;
this is called the second path of the pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, there is another class [of beings].
Encountering the appearance of a Buddha in the world, they draw near to virtuous friends,
hear the true Dharma, attend to it correctly,
realize the direct vision of the Dharma, and attain the fruits of the śramaṇa.
Yet, lacking the power to reach the ultimate limit of the holy life— the Arhatship that is supreme in every respect, utterly purified, and finally realized—
he further cultivates skillfulness regarding the aggregates and skillfulness regarding the sense bases.
By cultivating skill in the elements, skill in dependent origination,
skill in the possible and the impossible, and skill in the truths,
one relies upon the supramundane path for future lives.
Having reached the ultimate, the final, and the absolute freedom from defilement, one fully realizes the limit of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and attains the fruit of arhatship.
This is called the third path of the pratyekabuddha.
What is the training of a pratyekabuddha?
This refers to a certain class of individuals who, relying on the path of the first Pratyekabuddha,
complete the accumulation of provisions over the course of a hundred kalpas;
having passed those hundred kalpas, they appear in a world where no Buddha exists.
Without a teacher, he was able to cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment on his own;
he realized the direct vision of the Dharma and attained the fruit of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.
Having forever severed all afflictions, he became an arhat.
Furthermore, there is another class [of beings] who, relying either on the second or the third path of the Pratyekabuddhas,
by virtue of those causes and conditions, appear in a world where no Buddha exists;
without a teacher, they are able to cultivate for themselves the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Some realize the clear observation of the Dharma and even attain the fruit of arhatship;
others attain the fruits of the ascetic life,
reaching the ultimate limit, becoming finally free from defilement, and ultimately attaining the culmination of the holy life.
One realizes the supreme fruit of arhatship.
It should be understood that among these, those who become pratyekabuddhas through the first stage of practice are called "rhinoceros-like" (khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa);
those who become pratyekajinas through the second and third stages of practice are called "troop-dwelling" (vargacārin).
Awakened.
He delights in dwelling in solitary groves, delights in living alone,
and delights in profound resolute conviction.
He delights in contemplating the profound principle of dependent origination;
he delights in dwelling in the mental orientations of supreme emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness;
and whether practicing in groups for a second or third time, he is like one who excels in solitude.
It is not necessary to always delight in dwelling in solitary forests or living alone;
one may also delight in living together with a community.
