As for the remaining characteristics of his dwelling, they are like those of the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha].
The Pratyekabuddha dwells in whatever village or town he may inhabit,
well-guarding his body, well-restraining his sense faculties, and abiding in right mindfulness;
he enters those various villages and towns either for the purpose of seeking alms.
Or, in order to deliver others who are inferior and ignorant,
one delivers them through physical action rather than through words. Why is this?
Manifesting only physical forms to preach the Dharma for them without speaking words,
he thus displays various supernatural powers and realms;
this is done even to cause those who harbor slanderous thoughts toward his mind to develop faith and take refuge.
Furthermore, it should be known that all those [phenomena] are from the very beginning invariably oriented toward quiescence.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle thirty-four;
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle thirty-five.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya spoke;
translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.

In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth part of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, within the first section on the "Foundations of Practice" (*yogasthāna*), this is the first chapter, "Lineage" (*gotra*). Thus has been explained the Stage of the Pratyekabuddha.
What is the Bodhisattva-bhūmi?
The summary verse (uddāna) says:
First, the foundations; next, the characteristics and divisions; and the dwelling in the superior intention (adhyāśaya).
The stages of practice for gathering [beings] and the establishment [of the goal] are the final [elements].
These ten dharmas fully encompass the Mahāyāna bodhisattva path and its fruition.
What are these ten?
First, upholding;
second, characteristics;
third, classification.
Fourth is superior intention;
fifth is abiding;
sixth is birth.
Seventh is gathering;
eighth is the stages;
ninth is the practices.
Tenth is the establishment of the arousal of the mind and all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
This is called "retention.
Why? Because it is by means of the lineage of their own vehicle that bodhisattvas [retain it].
Because it serves as a basis and as a foundation,
it possesses the capacity and great power to realize unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, it is said that their own lineage (*gotra*) serves as the basis for the capacity of bodhisattvas,
because it is from this that bodhisattvas first generate the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
For the sake of providing a basis and for the sake of establishment,
[one practices] generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—
these six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
They are able to diligently train in the accumulation of merit,
the accumulation of wisdom, and all the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Therefore, it is said that their initial generation of the mind of awakening serves as the support for the application of all bodhisattva practices,
by means of all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) practiced by bodhisattvas.
Because they serve as the basis and the foundation for the fulfillment of unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment,
all those factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) practiced therein are so described.
It serves as the support for the fulfillment of great enlightenment;
because those individuals who lack the spiritual lineage (agotra) remain in that state of lacking a lineage,
even though they may possess the arousal of the mind of enlightenment and engage in preparatory practices as their basis.
They are certainly incapable of fulfilling unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
By this reasoning, even though they have not yet generated the mind [of awakening] nor practiced the preparatory applications of a bodhisattva’s conduct, [they are nonetheless considered such].
If there is a lineage (gotra), one should know that it is designated as such in relation to that [lineage].
Furthermore, a person who abides in the lineage,

even if they do not generate the resolve [for awakening] and do not cultivate the applications of the bodhisattva's conduct, possesses the capacity [for realization], yet does not quickly realize unsurpassed awakening.
One should know that the opposite of this leads to swift realization.
Furthermore, this lineage has already been described as "support," and it is also called "aid" and "cause."
It is called a basis, and it is called a stage;
it is called a precursor, and it is called a dwelling.
As it is said regarding the lineage, it is the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).
It should be understood that the application of practice is likewise.
What is the lineage (*gotra*)?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds.
First, the lineage abiding by nature;
second, the lineage acquired through practice.
Regarding the lineage abiding by nature:
This refers to the fact that the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) of bodhisattvas possess such a distinctive excellence,
which has been transmitted successively from beginningless time and is acquired through the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
this is called the lineage existing by nature (*prakṛtistha-gotra*), as opposed to the lineage formed through cultivation (*samudānīta-gotra*).
That which is obtained through the prior cultivation of roots of goodness is called the lineage accomplished through practice (*abhyāsa-niṣpanna-gotra*).
In this context, both meanings are intended.
Furthermore, this lineage is also called the seed (*bīja*), the element (*dhātu*), and the nature (*prakṛti*).
Furthermore, this lineage when its fruit has not yet been cultivated and realized is called "subtle," because the fruit does not yet exist;
when its fruit has already been cultivated and realized, it is called "coarse," because it coexists with the fruit.
If bodhisattvas who have accomplished their spiritual lineage surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
how much more so do they surpass all other sentient beings?
One should know that the spiritual lineage (gotra) is unsurpassed and most excellent. Why is this?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of purity.
First, the purification of the afflictive obscurations;
second, the purification of the cognitive obscurations.
[This applies to] all those of the lineage of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Only [the śrāvaka lineage] is able to realize the purification of the afflictive obscurations,
but it cannot realize the purification of the cognitive obscurations.
The bodhisattva lineage, however, is also able to realize the purification of the afflictive obscurations.
It is also capable of realizing the purification of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Therefore, it is said that, in comparison to all others, it is unsurpassed and most excellent.
Furthermore, this is due to four matters.
It should be known that the bodhisattva excels all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
What are the four?
First, excellence of faculties (indriya).
Second is the excellence of practice;
third is the excellence of skillful means;
fourth is the excellence of the fruit.
Regarding "superiority of faculties":
this refers to bodhisattvas who possess sharp faculties by nature, pratyekabuddhas with middling faculties, and śrāvakas with dull faculties;
this is called superiority of faculties.
Regarding those whose conduct and speech are superior:
this refers to bodhisattvas who are able to benefit themselves and also benefit others,
bringing welfare and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.
Out of compassion for the world, they cause devas and humans to obtain ultimate benefit and happiness;
whereas śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas practice only self-benefit— therefore,
these are called the supreme victors who possess skill in the superior practice.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are able to cultivate skillfulness regarding the aggregates, elements, bases, dependent origination, and the possible and the impossible;
bodhisattvas, however, are able to cultivate skillfulness in these as well as in all other fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*).
This is called the excellence of skillfulness.
Regarding the excellence of the fruit:
the śrāvaka is able to realize the enlightenment of a śrāvaka.
Pratyekabuddhas are able to realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha,
and bodhisattvas are able to realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
this is called the excellence of the fruit.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas possess the signs of the lineage (*gotra*) for each of the six perfections (*pāramitā*).
By means of these signs, others can recognize that they are truly bodhisattvas.
These are called the signs of the lineage for the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*).
The characteristics of the lineage of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
What are the characteristics of the bodhisattva’s lineage of the perfection of generosity? They are as follows:
by their very nature, bodhisattvas delight in giving; regarding all existing things that are suitable to be given, they are capable of bestowing them.
Constant and uninterrupted, he is able to distribute [resources] equally among others;
his mind delights in giving, his intention is free from regret,
and though the objects of charity be few, he is able to share them impartially.
His giving is vast and not narrow; he is deeply ashamed of not practicing generosity.
He always delights in praising and encouraging others to give.
Seeing those who are able to give, his heart is filled with joy.
Toward those who are venerable, elders, fields of merit, and worthy recipients of offerings,
he rises from his seat and respectfully presents them with gifts;
and regarding matters that bring blameless benefit to sentient beings in this world and the next, he acts accordingly.
Whether requested or unrequested, one teaches the Dharma according to the truth.
Furthermore, to those sentient beings who fear kings, thieves, water, fire, and so forth,
one bestows the gift of fearlessness.
He was able to rescue and deliver others from various and constant states of extreme peril according to his strength;
he never failed or deviated when receiving deposits entrusted to him by others,
and if he incurred a debt to another, he never defaulted or deceived them.
He does not deceive others regarding shared property.

Nor does he cause mental confusion or delusion in those who possess various kinds of jewels and articles for livelihood, such as mani-gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, gold, and silver.
Being capable of correct awakening, he would not even allow others to deceive him,
much less do so himself;
his nature is one that delights in vast wealth and status.
They take pleasure in the enjoyment of all those vast resources;
they delight in great undertakings rather than narrow paths;
and they are addicted to various worldly diversions such as wine, women, gambling, singing, dancing, and performances.
They swiftly cultivate weary detachment and give rise to profound shame and remorse;
they do not cling even to great wealth and treasures,
let alone minor gains.
Such categories as these should be known as the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*).
What are the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*)?
This refers to those bodhisattvas who, by their very nature, possess a mild degree of unwholesomeness;
whose physical, verbal, and mental actions are not extremely violent or evil;
and who do not excessively harm or afflict sentient beings.
Although they may commit evil deeds, they are able to repent swiftly;
they constantly practice shame and remorse and do not give rise to delight;
they do not afflict or harm sentient beings with weapons, staves, hands, clods of earth, or similar means.
One should always maintain loving-kindness toward the nature of all sentient beings;
when it is time to show respect, one should rise to welcome them,
join the palms in greeting, and perform prostrations in their presence, thus cultivating the practice of harmonious reverence.
His actions are nimble and not dull or obtuse;
he skillfully accords with the minds of others,
always first smiling with a relaxed countenance and looking upon them with an even gaze.
He remains free from frowning and is the first to speak with greetings;
toward sentient beings who have been kind to him,
he recognizes their kindness and repays it.
Toward those who come seeking, one should always act with sincerity and straightforwardness;
one should not reject or decline them through flattery or deception.
When seeking wealth, one should do so according to the Dharma, neither by unlawful means nor by violence.
By nature, they always delight in cultivating various meritorious deeds;
they are even able to encourage and assist others in cultivating merit,
let alone doing so for themselves.
If one sees or hears others undergoing suffering—
namely, being killed, bound, cut, beaten, reviled, or threatened—
one regards such sufferings as more intense than those one undergoes oneself.
They value the undertaking of the precepts and value future lives;
they perceive even minor transgressions with deep fear.
How much more so for those with many transgressions,
regarding the various tasks that ought to be performed by others—
namely, commerce, agriculture, animal husbandry, service to the king, writing, sealing, and arithmetic.
Skilfully reconciling disputes,
seeking wealth and treasures,
and guarding one's accumulations.
Expediently exhaling [the breath],
as well as practicing relinquishment and charity,
and attending weddings and social gatherings.
In all such matters consistent with the Dharma,
they engage in the same activities;
and regarding the various disputes, litigations, and rivalries of others, [they remain impartial].
Furthermore, regarding all other matters that involve mutual affliction and harm,
which cause oneself and others to experience suffering and distress without meaning or benefit—
one does not participate in any such unrighteous activities.
He is well able to restrain what should not be done— namely, the ten kinds of evil and unwholesome courses of action—
and does not oppose the lives of others, but is virtuous and harmonious with others, sharing the same forbearance and the same precepts.
Regarding the affairs of others, he sets aside his own tasks as they desire them to be accomplished;
his mind is warm and moist, and his mind is pure.
A mind of malice or a mind of harm does not persist for long;
as soon as it arises, one abandons it and gives rise to a virtuous and noble mind.
One respects truthful speech and does not deceive others.
He does not alienate others' kin,
nor does he delight in speaking words that are frivolous, meaningless, unbeneficial, or inappropriate;
his speech is always gentle and never coarse or harsh.
One does not even use harsh words toward one's own servants,
much less toward others who are respected, beloved, or virtuous; rather,
one praises them according to reality.
Such categories as these should be known as the characteristics of the lineage of the bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
What are the characteristics of the lineage of the bodhisattva’s perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*)?
It refers to the nature of bodhisattvas such that,
when encountering harm from others,
they harbor no mind of anger or malice and do not retaliate.
If, when others offer counsel or apologize, one is able to accept it quickly,
never harboring resentment or maintaining a grudge for long—
such characteristics as these should be known as the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
What are the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of diligence?
It refers to the nature of bodhisattvas who are naturally alert and energetic,
rising early and retiring late, and who do not deeply indulge in the pleasures of sleep or reclining.
Regarding the tasks to be performed, one acts with courageous resolve and delight, without giving rise to indolence;
having deliberated upon the skillful means, one ensures they reach completion.
In all actions and undertakings, one remains firm and resolute.
If they have not yet all been performed or fully completed,
one shall never in the interim become lax, desist, or yield;
nor shall one’s mind feel any cowardice regarding the vast and supreme ultimate truth.
Without disparaging oneself, one should arouse a courageous mind, thinking:
"I now possess the power to realize that [truth].
Whether entering a great assembly or engaging in debate with others, one should do so with such resolve.
Furthermore, regarding various other difficult tasks that lead to meaningful benefit, he is entirely without fear or hesitation;
he does not even feel profound weariness amidst great affairs,
let alone minor ones.
Such categories as these should be known as the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
What are the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*)?
This refers to the nature of bodhisattvas who are able to reflect deeply upon the meaning of the Dharma without much distraction;
whether seeing or hearing of forest hermitages, mountain crags, groves, thickets, or remote borderlands.
Regarding bedding and requisites, he does not associate with them nor with evil beings;
conforming to silent seclusion,
he gives rise to this thought:
In this state, there is peace, happiness, renunciation, and seclusion;
one constantly develops a deep longing for renunciation and seclusion.
With a nature in which afflictions are thin and the hindrances are slight, and with all coarse heaviness weakened, one goes to a place of seclusion to contemplate one’s own welfare.
The mind is not excessively entangled or disturbed by evil discursive thoughts;
it is even able to swiftly abide in a mind of loving-kindness toward those who are hostile,
let alone toward those who are kin or neutral.
If one sees or hears that sentient beings suffering from various afflictions are being oppressed by manifold miseries,
one should give rise to great compassion and,
according to one's ability and strength, act for the sake of those beings.
By means of skillful expedients, they rescue and deliver others, causing them to be free from all suffering.
Toward all sentient beings, their very nature is one that delights in bestowing benefit and peace.
[They provide aid to those] whose relatives have perished, who have lost their wealth and treasures, or who are subjected to execution, bondage, and imprisonment.
Furthermore, they are able to endure all hardships such as being expelled or banished;
by nature they are intelligent, capable of receiving, upholding, and reflecting upon the Dharma, and they have perfected the power of mindfulness.
Regarding matters long ago performed or spoken,
one is able to remember them oneself and cause others to remember them as well.
Such categories as these should be known as the signs of the lineage for the bodhisattva’s perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
What is the characteristic of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom?
It is that bodhisattvas possess innate wisdom (*sahaja-prajñā*) and are able to enter the spheres of all fields of knowledge (*vidyā-sthāna*).
Their nature is not dull, their nature is not obscure, and their nature is not foolish.
They possess the power of analytical discernment throughout all various states free from negligence.
Such categories as these should be known as the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
One should know that this is called the coarse characteristic of the bodhisattva lineage (*gotra*) through inference.
The definitive, ultimate reality is perceived only by the World-Honored Buddha;
for the nature of the various bodhisattvas' lineages is endowed with such qualities.
Having accomplished all virtuous and pure dharmas,
one is therefore able to attain the fruit of the Tathāgata— difficult to obtain, most supreme, inconceivable, immovable, and unsurpassed.
In order to realize the objective through correct reasoning,
one may be defiled by the presence or absence of the four secondary afflictions that contradict the Dharma;
yet, such a state remains associated with these pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*).
If they are defiled in this way, all such pure dharmas (śukla-dharma) do not manifest;
or at some time, one is born in the evil destinies (durgati),
and within those evil destinies...
By virtue of the power of their spiritual lineage (*gotra*), it should be understood that they differ greatly from others who are born in the evil destinies;
for these bodhisattvas remain for a long time in saṃsāra,
and only at certain times are they born in the various evil destinies.
Although they may briefly be born there, they are quickly able to attain liberation;
though they remain in the miserable realms, they do not undergo intense painful sensations as other sentient beings who are born in those miserable realms do.
Although they encounter slight suffering, they are able to give rise to superior revulsion;
they develop deep compassion for sentient beings who undergo suffering by being born in the evil destinies.
Such matters as these all arise from their spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
It is impelled by the perfuming of the Buddha’s great compassion;
therefore, one should know that although a bodhisattva of noble lineage may be born in the evil destinies,
there is a great distinction between him and those others who are born in the evil destinies.
Affliction (*pīḍā*):
This refers to those who are heedless, whose nature has become characterized by intense and long-lasting afflictions due to their prior habituation to various defilements (*kleśa*).
This is called the first nature of secondary afflictions.
Furthermore, when one who is deluded and unskilled relies upon evil friends,
this is called the second nature of secondary afflictions.
Furthermore, for those who are constrained and oppressed by elders, husbands, kings, thieves, or enemies,
they lose their autonomy and their minds become confused;
this is called the third nature of secondary affliction.
Furthermore, those who lack the necessities of life cling to their own bodies and lives;
this is called the fourth nature of secondary affliction (*upakleśa*).
Moreover, although bodhisattvas possess the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), [they may still encounter such obstacles].
Due to four causes and conditions, one cannot quickly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
What are these four? They are:
that various bodhisattvas have not previously encountered Buddhas, bodhisattvas, or true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) who can explain the non-erroneous path to enlightenment.
This is called the first causal condition.
Furthermore, although bodhisattvas may encounter virtuous friends who explain the true path to them,
they hold inverted views and practice in a distorted manner regarding that which is the correct training for bodhisattvas.
This is called the second causal condition.
Furthermore, although bodhisattvas may encounter virtuous friends who explain the correct path to them,
they practice and train without error within that which is the proper object of study for bodhisattvas.
Yet, regarding the preparatory applications and skillful means, one is lax, indolent, and lazy,
failing to achieve courageous and fervent diligence;
this is called the third cause and condition.
Furthermore, although these bodhisattvas encounter virtuous friends who explain the correct path to them,
they practice without error within that which is the proper training for bodhisattvas,
and they apply themselves with courageous diligence in their preparatory practices.
However, their roots of virtue have not yet matured;
the provisions for enlightenment have not yet been perfected;
and they have not yet practiced all the factors conducive to enlightenment over a long period of time.
This is called the fourth causal condition. Thus,
although a bodhisattva possesses the spiritual lineage,
because of the deficiency of these conditions, they cannot quickly realize unsurpassed enlightenment.
If the causes and conditions are complete, one can swiftly realize [enlightenment].
However, it should be known that a person lacking the spiritual lineage (agotra),
even if they possess every single factor in every respect, will certainly never realize bodhi.

Chapter Two: Generating the Resolve. In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth part of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, within the first section on the Foundation (*Maulī Bhūmi*), this is the second chapter: Generating the Resolve. Furthermore, the initial generation of the resolve by a bodhisattva constitutes all the correct aspirational prayers (*samyak-praṇidhāna*) of all bodhisattvas.
This initial right vow is universally able to encompass all other right vows;
therefore, the generation of the mind takes this initial right vow as its essential nature at the time of its arising.
Generating such a mind and speaking these words:
"May I certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and be able to bring about all that is beneficial for sentient beings."
Ultimately establishing oneself in perfect nirvāṇa and within the vast wisdom of the Tathāgata—
such a generation of the mind necessarily seeks supreme enlightenment for oneself.
Furthermore, they seek to act for the benefit of sentient beings;
therefore, the arousal of the mind has the aspect of a definite aspiration as its characteristic,
taking great enlightenment as its object.
Furthermore, one generates the aspiration seeking all forms of benefit and welfare for sentient beings;
it is not without an object of focus.
Therefore, the generation of the mind takes great enlightenment and all the benefit and welfare of sentient beings as its objective sphere.
Because it takes as its foremost [factor] the preeminent roots of goodness that encompass all factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), it is good, supremely good;
it is virtuous, supremely virtuous; it is sublime, supremely sublime.
It is capable of counteracting the three types of non-virtuous conduct in all places where sentient beings dwell;
it is endowed with merit and consists of the correct vows generated by the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Among all other aspirations for worldly and supramundane goals that are sublime, virtuous, and correct,
this is the foremost and unsurpassed.
Thus, it should be understood that the initial generation of the mind has five characteristics.
First is its intrinsic nature;
second is its mode of activity;
third is its object of perception.
Fourth is merit;
fifth is supremacy.
Furthermore, from the moment a bodhisattva first generates the mind of enlightenment...
This is called "entering into unsurpassed bodhi" and being included among the ranks of the Mahāyāna bodhisattvas;
this is according to the principles of conventional discourse.
Therefore, it is subsumed under the "arousing of the mind" and "entering."
Only then can one gradually and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
it cannot be realized by those who have not yet resolved their minds toward awakening. Therefore, the generation of the resolve for awakening serves as the root of unsurpassed enlightenment.
Furthermore, because bodhisattvas feel compassion for all sentient beings who suffer and give rise to the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) with the desire to rescue and deliver them,
this arousal of the mind is the outflow of compassion.
Taking the initial resolve as the basis and foundation,
[the bodhisattva] engages universally in all factors conducive to enlightenment and in the bodhisattva training that accomplishes the welfare of all sentient beings.
They are all capable of practicing and studying them.
Therefore, the arousal of the mind is the basis upon which all bodhisattvas rely for their training.

It should be understood in this way: the initial arousal of the mind is the basis for entering and encompassing the root of awakening, the natural outflow of great compassion, and the training itself.
Furthermore, there are briefly two kinds of initial resolve among bodhisattvas:
first, that which is definitive emergence;
second, that which is non-definitive emergence.
"Permanently emerged" means that once the mind has been generated, one proceeds accordingly until the ultimate end without ever regressing.
"Not permanently emerged" refers to...
This refers to having generated the resolve [for awakening] but failing to follow through to the end and instead regressing.
There are two kinds of such regression from this resolve:
first, that which is ultimate.
Second is non-finality.
Regarding final regression:
this refers to one who, having once regressed, is unable to again resolve to seek the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
Regarding "not ultimate":
this refers to repeatedly generating the mind seeking enlightenment again after having regressed,
by means of the four powers.
What are the four conditions?

They are as follows: when a son of good family or a daughter of good family sees the inconceivable, most marvelous, and rare supernormal transformations and majestic powers of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Or, having heard such matters from a trustworthy source,
and having both seen and heard them, one then forms this thought:
"Unsurpassed enlightenment possesses great majesty and power."
It causes those who abide in peace and those who practice to achieve such inconceivable power of miraculous transformations as they have seen and heard;
by the predominant force of these sights and sounds, [they attain realization].
One generates deep faith and understanding toward great enlightenment;
based on this, one gives rise to the mind of great enlightenment.
This is called the first condition for the initial arousal of the bodhicitta.
There may be a certain class of persons who,
although they have not seen or heard of the miraculous powers as previously described,
nevertheless hear the proclamation of the subtle and sublime Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, which is based upon unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Having heard this, they develop deep faith.
Through the predominant power of hearing the true Dharma and that deep faith,
they give rise to profound faith and understanding in the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
One generates the bodhicitta for the sake of attaining the subtle and wondrous wisdom of the Tathāgata;
this is called the second causal condition for the initial generation of the mind.
Alternatively, there is a certain class [of beings].
Although they do not hear the sublime Dharma as described above,
they see that all the teachings of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka are on the verge of disappearing.
Having seen this, they then form this thought:
The *Bodhisattvapiṭaka* dharma shall long abide in the world,
capable of extinguishing the great suffering of immeasurable sentient beings.
I should uphold the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka* dharma and resolve to attain bodhicitta.
In order to extinguish the great suffering of immeasurable sentient beings,
and by the predominant power of upholding the Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka,
they develop profound faith and understanding in the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
One generates the bodhicitta for the sake of attaining the subtle and wondrous wisdom of the Tathāgata;
this is called the third condition for the initial generation of the mind.
Alternatively, there is a certain class [of beings].
Although they do not perceive the extinction of the True Dharma,
in the final eon, the final age, and the final time,
they see all sentient beings of the turbid and evil world being afflicted and disturbed by the ten secondary afflictions of body and mind.
That is to say: much delusion and much lack of shame and remorse;
much stinginess and envy; much sorrow and suffering;
much heaviness and many afflictions.
Having seen that there is much misconduct, much negligence,
much indolence, and much lack of faith,
he then forms this thought:
The great age of turbidity and evil is now arising;
at this time, when one is afflicted and distracted by various secondary afflictions,
it is already difficult to find those who can give rise to the bodhicitta of the inferior śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
How much more so for those who are able to resolve their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment!
I should now give rise to the great bodhicitta,
so that the immeasurable sentient beings of this degenerate age may follow my example and give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
Because they perceive that it is difficult to generate the resolve for awakening during the final age,
they develop a profound faith and understanding toward great enlightenment;
by means of this, they give rise to the mind of great enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
This is called the fourth condition for the initial generation of the mind of awakening.
What are the four causes?
They are as follows: bodhisattvas are endowed with the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
This is called the first cause for the initial arousal of the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, that Bodhisattvas are sustained by the guidance of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas,
and spiritual friends is called the second cause for the initial arousal of the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings;
this is called the third cause for the initial arousal of the mind of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*).
Moreover, for an extremely long period of time, bodhisattvas undergo various intense, uninterrupted, and unbroken sufferings of birth and death, as well as difficult ascetic practices.
To be free from cowardice and fear is called the fourth cause for the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment. Furthermore,
the excellence of the six sense bases of bodhisattvas, which has been transmitted successively from beginningless time and is obtained through the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
It should be understood that this is called the perfection of lineage.
It should be understood that a bodhisattva’s perfection of spiritual friends is characterized by four aspects.
This refers to the spiritual friends encountered by bodhisattvas who,
by nature, are not dull-witted but are intelligent and wise, and do not fall into wrong views;
this is called the first perfection of a spiritual friend.
Furthermore, the virtuous friends encountered by bodhisattvas never instruct others to practice heedlessness,
nor do they provide them with the requisites for heedlessness.
This is called the second fulfillment of a virtuous friend.
Furthermore, whatever virtuous friends a bodhisattva encounters will never instruct them to engage in unwholesome conduct.
Nor does he provide them with the requisites for unwholesome conduct;
this is called the third perfection of a virtuous friend.
Furthermore, regarding the virtuous friends encountered by bodhisattvas:
They never encourage the relinquishing of superior faith, aspiration, training, diligence, skillful means, and merit,
nor do they encourage the cultivation of inferior faith, aspiration, training, diligence, skillful means, and merit.
That is to say: one never encourages the abandonment of the Mahāyāna to encourage the cultivation of the two vehicles;

nor encourages the abandonment of the wisdom of cultivation to encourage the cultivation of the wisdom of reflection; nor encourages the abandonment of the wisdom of reflection to encourage the cultivation of the wisdom of hearing.
They urge the relinquishing of the wisdom derived from hearing;
they urge the cultivation of meritorious deeds;
they urge the relinquishing of ethical discipline; and they urge the cultivation of wisdom and generosity.
One never encourages the relinquishing of such superior virtues,
nor does one encourage the cultivation of such inferior virtues;
this is called the fourth perfection of a virtuous friend.
One should know that bodhisattvas give rise to great compassion toward sentient beings due to four causes and conditions.
That is to say, although there are immeasurable and boundless worlds free from suffering throughout the ten directions for the bodhisattvas;
They are born into worlds characterized by suffering,
where various forms of suffering are constantly present and not absent;
or at times they see others encountering and being oppressed by any one of those sufferings.
At times, one sees oneself encountering and being oppressed by a particular painful contact;
or one sees oneself and others encountering and being oppressed by a particular painful contact;
or one sees both encountering long-lasting, diverse, intense, and uninterrupted great suffering through contact and oppression.
However, this bodhisattva, by virtue of their own spiritual lineage and natural benevolence,
is able to give rise to inferior, middling, and superior compassion without interruption, even toward the four types of objects despite not having practiced them habitually.
One should know that by virtue of four causes and conditions, a bodhisattva first gives rise to compassion toward all sentient beings;

thus, even regarding the great sufferings of birth and death over an extremely long period—sufferings that are manifold, intense, uninterrupted, and without interval—and even regarding difficult ascetic practices, they remain entirely free from fear or cowardice.
How much more so for minor suffering?
It should be understood that the fact that bodhisattvas are by nature courageous,
resilient, and powerful is called the first cause and condition.
Furthermore, it should be known that the fact that bodhisattvas are by nature intelligent, capable of correct reflection,
and endowed with the power of discernment is the second causal condition. Moreover,
bodhisattvas are able to achieve a superior degree of pure faith and resolve regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
One should know that this is called the third causal condition.
Furthermore, one should know that when bodhisattvas achieve a superior degree of profound resolve and compassion toward all sentient beings,
this is called the fourth causal condition.
What are the four powers?
First, the power of self;
second, the power of others.
Third is the power of causes;
fourth is the power of application.
This means that by the power of their own effort, bodhisattvas are able to generate a profound aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This is called the first power of the initial resolve.
Furthermore, through the influence of others, bodhisattvas are able to develop a profound yearning for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This is called the second power of the initial resolve.
Furthermore, those bodhisattvas who have previously cultivated wholesome dharmas associated with the Mahāyāna now briefly behold the Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
If even those who merely hear their praises and eulogies are able to swiftly generate the bodhicitta,
how much more so for those who behold their supernormal powers and hear their true Dharma?
This is called the third power of the initial resolve.
Furthermore, in this present life, bodhisattvas draw near to virtuous friends, listen to the true Dharma, and engage in correct reflection, and so forth.
Having cultivated various wholesome dharmas over a long period of time,
one generates the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) through this application;
this is called the fourth power, the power of the initial generation of the mind.
If bodhisattvas, relying on the aforementioned four general and specific conditions and four causes—
whether by their own power, by the power of causes,
or by both powers combined— generate the resolve for awakening, [they do so].
One should know that this mind is firm and unshakable;
whether it is generated through the power of others,
the power of application, or both powers combined.
One should know that this mind is neither firm nor stable, yet it is not without movement.
There are four causes and conditions that can cause a bodhisattva to retreat from the bodhicitta. What are these four?
First, they lack the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Second, they are influenced by evil friends.
Third, their compassion for all sentient beings is meager.
Fourth, regarding the great suffering of saṃsāra— extremely long-lasting, diverse, intense, continuous, and uninterrupted— as well as the difficult ascetic practices,
his mind gives rise to extreme timidity, fear, and terror.
These four causes for the regression of the mind are the opposites of the four causes for the initial arousal of the mind;
their characteristics should be understood in detail as previously explained.
A bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind with firm resolve possesses, in brief, two extraordinary and most marvelous qualities not shared by the world.
What are these two?
First, they gather all sentient beings as their own retinue.
Second, one cannot be defiled by the faults of gathering a retinue.
There are two kinds of faults in gathering a retinue:
namely, being defiled by attachment to or aversion toward the benefit or harm experienced from that retinue.
A bodhisattva who has firmly resolved upon the initial aspiration is devoid of both these conditions; rather,
they give rise to two kinds of virtuous and superior intentions toward all sentient beings.
First is the intention for benefit;
second is the intention for happiness.
Regarding the intention for benefit:
This refers to the intention to rescue sentient beings from those various unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states and happiness;
that is, to be free from a defiled mind toward those sentient beings who are destitute, without support, and without refuge.
For a bodhisattva who has first generated the firm resolve to bestow various means of benefit and happiness, there are two types of application: first, the application of intention;
[second, the application of practice].
Second is the application of correct practice.
Regarding the application of intention:
it refers to the day and night growth of the intention for the benefit and happiness [of others].
Regarding the application of correct practice:
it refers to the application that can bring the Buddha-dharma to maturity within oneself throughout day and night,
as well as the application based on the previously mentioned intention toward sentient beings, according to one's capacity and strength.
Regarding the application for the sake of benefit and happiness,
there are two gateways for the increase of great wholesome dharmas for a bodhisattva who has first generated a firm resolve:
the first is the application for one's own benefit.
First, it is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; second,
through the application of benefiting others,
it is able to liberate all sentient beings from their manifold sufferings.
Just as it is with these two gateways for the increase of great wholesome dharmas,
so too should one know that the two kinds of great accumulations of wholesome dharmas and the two kinds of immeasurable treasuries of wholesome dharmas are likewise.
The wholesome dharmas encompassed by a bodhisattva who has first generated a firm resolve for awakening,
by virtue of seeking awakening through that initial generation of the mind,
surpass all other wholesome dharmas that have been encompassed.
There are two kinds of excellence:
first, excellence of cause;
second, excellence of fruit.
This means that all the wholesome dharmas embraced by bodhisattvas are the causes capable of realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; therefore,
the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that is realized is the fruit of these.
Therefore, it is already superior to all other wholesome dharmas comprised by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
let alone to all other wholesome dharmas comprised by any other sentient beings.
Therefore, the wholesome dharmas embraced by the bodhisattva surpass all other embraced wholesome dharmas in both cause and fruit.
For a bodhisattva whose initial resolve is firm, there are briefly two kinds of benefits from generating that mind.
First, once the initial aspiration for enlightenment has been generated,
one immediately becomes a field of merit respected by sentient beings.
All sentient beings should make offerings to them;
they also act as the parents of all sentient beings.
Second, once they have first resolved their minds toward bodhi, [they should be honored].
He is thus able to gather the merit of non-affliction and non-harm;
by virtue of this, the bodhisattva, having accomplished such merit of non-affliction and non-harm,
becomes doubly protected by the guardianship of a wheel-turning monarch.
Because they have obtained such protection,
whether sleeping, waking, or in a state of confusion, they cannot be harmed by any demons, yakṣas, household deities, humans, non-humans, or the like.
Furthermore, when this bodhisattva undergoes subsequent births,
because he is sustained by such merit, he has little illness and remains free from disease;
he is not afflicted by long-lasting or severe illnesses.
Regarding the welfare and benefit to be performed for all sentient beings,
he is able to act with vigor through both body and speech,
and constantly proclaims the true Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
The body knows no extreme fatigue, mindfulness is never lost, and the mind suffers no exhaustion or impairment.
When a bodhisattva naturally abides in the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*),
all states of heaviness (*dausthulya*) are inherently subtle and slight.
Once the mind has been generated, all forms of grossness and heaviness— namely,
the grossness and heaviness of the body and the grossness and heaviness of the mind—
become increasingly subtle and light. This is so that other sentient beings may extinguish epidemics, calamities, and adversities.
If even the incantations and vidyā-mantras that have no proven efficacy become effective when employed by a bodhisattva,
how much more so those that do possess efficacy?
He achieves superior gentleness and patience;
he is able to endure the provocations of others without provoking them in turn,
and seeing others causing one another harm, he gives rise to deep compassion.
All secondary afflictions, such as vexation, anger, envy, and deceit,
can be subdued so that their power becomes weak and thin;
or, should they momentarily manifest, they can be swiftly dispelled.
In whatever country or city they may dwell,
all terrors, strife, famine, faults, calamities wrought by non-human beings, and epidemics and misfortunes therein— [shall be pacified].
What has not yet arisen does not arise, and even if it should arise,
it is immediately extinguished. Furthermore, this bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening may,
at one time, be born within the most wretched destinies of the hells (*naraka*).
For the most part, they will swiftly attain liberation from this destiny of hell-beings;
experiencing slight suffering, they will give rise to great revulsion and,
toward those sentient beings undergoing such suffering, they will conceive a heart of great compassion.
All of this is due to the bodhisattva’s initial resolve being firm through the gathering of merit that is free from harm and affliction;
by means of being able to gather such merit free from harm and affliction.
One then attains many such benefits as these.

Thus ends the first part of the third chapter, "Benefit for Oneself and Others," within the fifteenth section, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, of the *Yogācārabhūmi*. Once the bodhisattva has thus generated the resolve, [he proceeds as follows].
How does one practice the various bodhisattva practices?
Briefly stated, the places where a bodhisattva trains, the manner in which they train, and the ability to train—
this entire collection is subsumed under the single term "bodhisattva practice."
In what places do these bodhisattvas train?
They train in seven places.
What are the seven places?
The summary verse says:
The true meaning of the welfare of oneself and others, power, maturing sentient beings,
and maturing one's own buddha-qualities— this is the seventh locus of awakening.
First, the sphere of self-benefit;
second, the sphere of benefiting others;
third, the sphere of ultimate reality.
Fourth, the basis of power;
fifth, the basis of maturing sentient beings;
sixth, the basis of maturing one's own buddha-qualities.
Seventh is the stage of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
What is the stage of benefiting oneself and others?
Briefly stated, there are ten kinds of ways to benefit oneself and others.
1. Pure self-benefit and benefit for others;
2. Shared self-benefit and benefit for others;
3. Self-benefit and benefit for others categorized by their types of benefit.
Fourth, the categories of peace and happiness consisting of self-benefit and benefit for others;
fifth, self-benefit and benefit for others as subsumed under causes;
sixth, self-benefit and benefit for others as subsumed under results.
7. Self-benefit and benefit for others in this world;
8. self-benefit and benefit for others in future worlds;
9. ultimate self-benefit and benefit for others.
Tenth, not ultimately benefiting oneself and others.
What is the bodhisattva’s purely common benefit for oneself and others?
It refers to those bodhisattvas who, regarding the purely self-benefiting and other-benefiting [practices],...
One should know that those things which violate and are inconsistent with the bodhisattva’s code of conduct must be abandoned;
therefore, regarding all else, one should diligently train so as not to transgress and to remain in accordance with the bodhisattva’s code of conduct.
Thus, herein, a bodhisattva should know and abandon those things that pertain solely to self-interest.
That is to say: seeking wealth and enjoyments for one's own pleasure;
or, out of stinginess regarding the Dharma, pursuing, receiving, and upholding the teachings spoken by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
or, in order to be born in heaven and experience celestial happiness, upholding the prohibitive precepts.
Exerting diligent effort, they cultivate meditative concentration and wisdom;
or, seeking worldly and defiled fruits of retribution,
they offer worldly wealth, food, and respectful offerings to the various stūpas of the Buddhas.
Or, being greedy for gain and offerings,
for the sake of gain and offerings, they themselves proclaim various kinds of unreal merits that lack any true benefit,
thereby deceiving others and attracting gain and offerings.
Or, desiring to make others his own servants for the sake of being driven about,
he gathers a following through unrighteous means rather than according to the True Dharma,
falsely contriving expedient means to rescue sentient beings.
They cause others to be spared from servitude,
while they themselves take on the role of servants;
they rescue sentient beings and cause them to be liberated from their bonds.
They return to their own narrow attachments to accomplish their own ends;
they rescue sentient beings from the various terrors of punishment by others,
yet they themselves subjugate them so that those beings stand in fear of them.
If bodhisattvas become attached to various meditative absorptions and dwellings in happiness in the present life,
thereby abandoning the contemplation of benefiting sentient beings,
it should be known that these are called "pure self-benefit."
In this regard, the bodhisattva’s purely self-benefiting conduct should be understood and abandoned; however,
if a bodhisattva takes compassion as their primary motive, [they should not do so].
Whether for the sake of dedicating [merit] toward unsurpassed enlightenment or for rebirth in the heavens,
one practices giving, patience, and so forth at all times;
know that this is called benefiting oneself and others in common.
Furthermore, setting aside the various characteristics previously described,
one should know that all other practices for one's own benefit performed by bodhisattvas— which are contrary to those [previously mentioned]—
are termed "benefiting oneself and others together."
A bodhisattva should diligently train in this.
In this context, that which a bodhisattva should know and abandon regarding purely altruistic action refers to practicing generosity and so forth with wrong views.
They violate the precepts through views of causelessness and views of non-consequence;
they distance themselves from right practice while preaching the Dharma to others.
If Bodhisattvas are skillful in the mastery of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), [they do not fall into such errors].
Having already transcended the lower stages, they further embrace the wholesome dharmas (*śukladharma*) of those lower stages;
that is to say, having been able to abide securely in meditative absorption (*dhyāna*),
they relinquish those absorptions through the power of their compassion and vows.
According to their inclinations, they are reborn in the desire realm.
Furthermore, these bodhisattvas have already attained mastery and manifest various transformations throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
They bring about various kinds of benefit for all sentient beings.
Furthermore, the Munis, having already accomplished their own tasks,
rely upon all the unique Buddha-qualities (āveṇika-buddhadharma) such as the powers (bala) and fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya) of the Tathāgata.
Being able to perform immeasurable deeds of great benefit for immeasurable sentient beings throughout the ten directions—
know that these are called "purely benefiting others."
Regarding these aforementioned practices of purely altruistic conduct,
a bodhisattva should understand that the two types previously mentioned ought to be abandoned,
while they should extensively train in the remaining practices of purely altruistic conduct that have been described.
Furthermore, setting aside the various characteristics previously described,
one should know that all other bodhisattva practices for the benefit of others that are contrary to those [characteristics] are termed "benefiting others while being common to oneself."
A bodhisattva should diligently train in this.
What is the category of benefit consisting of self-interest and the interest of others?
Briefly stated, it should be understood that there are five aspects.
First, the aspect of being faultless;
second, the aspect of inclusion;
third, the aspect of this world.
Fourth, the characteristic of future worlds;
fifth, the characteristic of cessation.
If bodhisattvas, whether to a small or great extent, personally appropriate and cultivate wholesome dharmas, these increase those wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, if one causes others— whether few or many— to embrace wholesome dharmas and increase wholesome dharmas,
exhorting, disciplining, settling, and establishing them,
this is called the bodhisattva’s type of benefit characterized by self-benefit and benefit for others that is free from fault.
If bodhisattvas are able to bring about all forms of undefiled happiness— whether for themselves or others—
be it the happiness of material requisites or the happiness of dwelling in meditative concentration,
this is called the characteristic of the bodhisattva’s benefit-oriented self-benefit and benefit-of-others that is capable of being embraced.
If bodhisattvas act for their own benefit and the benefit of others,
there may be cases where they can bring benefit in this life but not in future lives,
or cases where they can bring benefit in future lives but not in this life.
There are those that benefit both this life and the next;
there are those that benefit neither this life nor the next.
Such are the four types of self-benefit and benefit for others.
Regarding the four ways of undertaking dharmas (*dharmasamādāna*), one should understand them according to their respective order as appropriate.
What are these four ways of undertaking dharmas?
There is a way of undertaking a dharma that results in pleasure in the present life but brings about a painful ripening (*vipāka*) in future lives.
There are certain types of karmic experience that involve suffering in the present life but result in a pleasant ripening in future lives;
there are also certain types of karmic experience that involve pleasure in the present life and result in a pleasant ripening in future lives.
There are some dharmas that, when received in the present, result in suffering in the present and a ripening of suffering in future lives.
These four should be understood as explained at length in the sūtras.
This is called the bodhisattva’s type of benefit consisting of self-interest and the interest of others, characterized by its effects in future lives.
Whatever nirvāṇa belongs to bodhisattvas,
as well as the attainment of nirvāṇa and the factors conducive to nirvāṇa— both mundane and supramundane—
this is called the concise characteristic of the pacification of the self-benefit and benefit-of-others category of benefit for bodhisattvas.
It should be understood that, in comparison with all others, this is unsurpassed and most excellent.
How does a bodhisattva’s category of happiness—which benefits both self and others—arise?
Briefly stated, it should be understood as being comprised of five types of happiness.
What are the five kinds of pleasure?
First, the pleasure of cause;
second, the pleasure of sensation.
Third is the bliss of the remedy for suffering;
fourth is the bliss of the cessation of feeling;
fifth is the bliss of being free from affliction and harm.
Regarding the statement "caused by pleasure":
this refers to the faculties and their objects belonging to the category of the two types of pleasure.
If these serve as the cause for contact conducive to pleasant feeling, [it is said to be caused by pleasure].
Whatever karma exists that has desirable fruits in the present life or in the future—
all such [karma] is collectively subsumed under the single term "pleasure as cause.
Beyond this, there is nothing further, neither more nor less.
Regarding the statement "experiencing pleasure," this refers to the subsiding of suffering due to the three causes and conditions subsumed under the aforementioned cause of pleasure.
That which is capable of benefiting the body and mind through rebirth is called the experience of pleasure (*sukha*).
Briefly stated, this pleasure is further of two kinds:
first, that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The second is the untainted (*anāsrava*).
As for untainted bliss, it is the bliss of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
As for "pleasure with outflows" (sāsrava-sukha),
it is the pleasure bound to the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
Furthermore, all such pleasure bound to the three realms is [of this nature].
According to their respective distinctions among the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), there are six types:
namely, those produced by eye-contact (*cakṣu-saṃsparśaja*) up to those produced by mind-contact (*mano-saṃsparśaja*).
These six types are further subsumed into two.
First is physical pleasure;
second is mental pleasure.
That which is associated with the five consciousnesses is called physical pleasure.
That which is associated with mental consciousness is called mental pleasure (*citta-sukha*).
As for the pleasure that serves as an antidote,
it refers to the various kinds of manifold and numerous types of painful sensations (*duḥkhā vedanā*) that arise due to causes such as cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and so forth.
Because it can counteract and pacify sufferings such as cold, heat, hunger, and thirst,
a sensation of pleasure arises precisely at the time when such suffering is extinguished;
this is what is called the "pleasure that is the remedy for suffering."
The meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling is called the bliss of the severance of sensation.
It should be understood that, in brief, there are four kinds of the bliss of non-affliction:
first, the bliss of renunciation.
Second, the joy of seclusion;
third, the joy of tranquility;
fourth, the joy of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
With right faith, one leaves the home life for the homeless state,
attaining liberation from the confinement of the household and its various great sufferings;
this is called the bliss of renunciation, which consists in abandoning all desires and unwholesome, evil states.
Realizing the joy and bliss born of seclusion in the first dhyāna is called the bliss of withdrawal;
from the second dhyāna upward, all meditative concentrations are characterized by the cessation of applied and sustained thought.
It is called the bliss of tranquility;
it is the ultimate dissociation from all afflictions and the realization of the objects of knowledge exactly as they are.
This bliss is called the bliss of *sambodhi*.
In this context, it is called "bliss" because the causal bliss is the cause of bliss,
not because it is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
In this context, pleasure is so called because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the experience of pleasure,
not because it is a cause of pleasure.
Furthermore, the pleasure that is the antidote to suffering is so called because it pacifies manifold sufferings and dispels manifold sufferings.
Because it is not a cause of pleasure,
nor is it its intrinsic nature.
That experience of the bliss of cessation is neither a cause of pleasure nor its intrinsic nature.
Nor is it called "happiness" because of the cessation of various forms of suffering;
rather, it is so designated from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
All sensations whatsoever are suffering.
When one abides in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), this ultimate suffering is temporarily stilled;
therefore, it is called "bliss."
The final three types of the bliss of awakening, which are comprised within the bliss free from affliction and harm,
arise because, in future lives, this ultimate suffering is eternally extinguished,
and in the present life, all heaviness (*dausthulya*) associated with the category of afflictions attached to the basis is eternally extinguished.
It is designated as "pleasure" because all other forms of pleasure free from affliction and harm are conducive to this ultimate pleasure.
Because it is a constituent part of that [bliss] and because it can induce that,
it should be known as "the bliss of non-affliction."
In this regard, a bodhisattva contemplates only the happiness belonging to the category of benefit for sentient beings;
they never contemplate the happiness belonging to the category of non-benefit.
Regarding all such pleasures found within these categories of non-benefit,
the bodhisattva understands them as they truly are through unerring wisdom and exhorts all sentient beings to completely abandon them.
One may, according to one's capacity and through skillful means, deprive them [of such things].
Even if there is a beneficial matter that is accompanied by suffering,
sentient beings may have no desire for it.
Relying on skillful means, a bodhisattva may even grant that which is accompanied by sorrow and suffering; however,
they do not grant that which follows after pleasure but lacks benefit.
Although sentient beings may have a desire for this,
a bodhisattva, relying on skillful means (upāya-kauśalya),
should even deprive them of it if it is accompanied by attachment and delight.
Why is this? One should know that such skillful means are accompanied by both sorrow and suffering, yet they possess beneficial purpose.
He removes even pleasant things that are of no benefit,
so that those sentient beings may certainly attain peace and happiness in the future.
Therefore, if a bodhisattva desires to benefit sentient beings, [he acts in this way].
One should know that the intended meaning is the bliss of peace and happiness.
If one bestows benefit upon sentient beings,
one should know that the intended meaning is the granting of peace and happiness.
Why is this so? Because benefit is like the cause and happiness is like the fruit.
Therefore, one should know that if one bestows benefit upon sentient beings, one necessarily bestows happiness.

It should be understood that all forms of happiness included within karma that yields desirable fruits in the present life and in the future— namely, the happiness that serves as an antidote to suffering,
the happiness of the cessation of feeling, and the happiness free from affliction— are [to be understood].
A bodhisattva should not deliberate upon this;
rather, they should bestow it one-sidedly upon all sentient beings,
because it is beneficial and blameless.
Regarding the pleasure therein, as well as the causal pleasure comprised of the faculties,
objects, and contact— if these can give rise to defilement, or if their very nature is defiled,
being blameworthy, unbeneficial, and inappropriate— [they should be abandoned].
One should not bestow [these things] upon sentient beings; however,
if they do not give rise to attachment, or if their nature is not one of attachment,
and it would be blameless and beneficial, then it is appropriate to do so.
One should bestow these upon all sentient beings.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should likewise practice and train in this according to their own capacity and power.
One should know that this is called the bodhisattva’s category of self-benefit and benefit for others consisting of benefit and happiness;
beyond this, there is nothing superior or additional.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Scroll 35.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 36.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.

In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth part of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the first section on the *Yogasthāna*, the third chapter on the Benefit of Self and Others (*svaparārthavarga*), it is asked: How does a bodhisattva’s benefit of self and others consist of both cause-inclusion (*hetu-saṃgraha*) and result-inclusion (*phala-saṃgraha*)?
In brief, one should know three causes and three fruits.
What are these three?
First, the ripening cause and the ripening fruit.
Second is the cause of merit and the fruit of merit;
third is the cause of wisdom and the fruit of wisdom.
What is maturation (*vipāka*)?
Briefly stated, there are eight:
first, the perfection of lifespan;
second, the perfection of physical form.
Third, the perfection of noble lineage;
fourth, the perfection of sovereignty;
fifth, the perfection of authoritative speech.
Sixth, the perfection of great power;
seventh, the perfection of human nature;
eighth, the perfection of great strength.
If bodhisattvas live for a long time and endure for a long duration,
this is called the perfection of the bodhisattva’s lifespan.
Their physical form is upright and majestic, pleasing to all who behold it, and their countenance is exquisite and sublime.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of physical form.
Being born into a noble and wealthy family is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of lineage.
Attaining great wealth and status, possessing a vast circle of allies, and being endowed with a great retinue—
this is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of mastery.
He is one whom the multitude reveres and trusts, serving as the standard for adjudicating disputes.
He does not practice flattery, deception, or the use of false weights and measures;
he never fails to return entrusted objects;
and his speech toward all sentient beings is free from falsehood.
For this reason, whatever he says is accepted with faith by all;
this is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of trustworthy speech.
He possesses great renown that spreads throughout the world.
That is to say, he is endowed with courage, vigor, fortitude, and agility;
he thoroughly understands the precepts of good conduct;
and through various arts, crafts, and fields of activity, he possesses a refined mastery that surpasses all others.
For these reasons, he is cherished and respected by the world;
he is provided with offerings, honored, revered, and praised by the great assembly.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of great power.
Possessing the attributes of a man and being endowed with the male organ—
this is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of human nature.
Furthermore, having little illness or being entirely free from disease, he possesses great capability.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of great power.
What is the cause of maturation?
It refers to the fact that Bodhisattvas do not inflict harm upon sentient beings.
To remain far removed from all intentions to cause harm is called the cause for a bodhisattva’s perfection of lifespan.
To give gifts of bright, fresh, and pure clothing.
This is called the cause for a bodhisattva’s perfection of physical form and complexion.
To abandon pride toward all sentient beings is called the cause for a bodhisattva’s perfection of lineage.
To bestow gifts according to the desires of those sentient beings who wander about begging due to a lack of the necessities of life—
this is called the cause for the bodhisattva’s perfection of mastery.
To speak words that are truthful and sincere, and not to habitually engage in speech that is divisive, harsh, or inappropriate—
this is called the bodhisattva’s cause for being endowed with trustworthy speech,
which sustains various merits in the future.
Within one's own being, one generates great aspirational vows and makes offerings to the Three Jewels and all venerable elders;
this is called the cause for the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of great power.
Delighting in the male body and loathing the female body, and seeing its faults deeply,
one bestows a male nature upon others for two reasons:
first, for women who delight in the female body.
First, they exhort women to cultivate revulsion for their female bodies and seek liberation from them.
Second, when a man is about to lose his male organ,
they employ skillful means to protect and sustain it so that it is not lost or destroyed.
Furthermore, preaching the True Dharma so that others may attain a male body is called the cause for a bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the human nature.
Serving all sentient beings with one's own person.
He goes to assist in whatever righteous activities are being performed according to his ability,
employing the true Dharma rather than violence. He provides various kinds of food and drink,
such as cakes, rice, and gruel, thereby increasing the strength of both body and mind.
Bestowing [these] upon all sentient beings is called the cause for the Bodhisattva’s perfection of great power.
One should know that the eight types of maturation previously explained [arise from this].
With these eight kinds [of causes] thus explained as the causes,
furthermore, these various causes briefly increase by means of three conditions,
thereby being able to induce the arising of fully perfected, superior, and vast maturations (*vipāka*).
What are the three conditions?
First, purity of mind;
second, purity of application.
Third is purity of field.
If one possesses a pure intention regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
one should resolutely dedicate those roots of virtue toward it.
He practices with a sharp intention that is pure, profound, vast, and characterized by serene faith;
he feels deep joy upon seeing those who share the same Dharma;
and throughout the day and night, in every moment, he frequently engages in reflection and investigation in accordance with the Dharma.
This is called the purification of the mind.
Within this state, one practices for a long duration,
acting without interruption and with constant diligence.
Regarding these virtues, he encourages those who have not yet undertaken them to undertake them;
he praises those who have already undertaken them to bring them joy;
and he establishes and settles them all within such roots of virtue.
This is called the purity of application.
It should be understood that, in brief, this refers to being able to correctly initiate such application and to correctly abide in the fruit of this application.
This is called the purity of the field.
What is the fruit of maturation?
It refers to the bodhisattvas’ perfection of lifespan.
Being able to cultivate wholesome qualities over a long period,
and thereby accumulating and increasing immeasurable roots of goodness for the benefit of oneself and others—
this is called the bodhisattva’s fruit of the perfection of lifespan.
If bodhisattvas possess a perfect physical form,
the great assembly will love and delight in them;
because the assembly loves and delights in them, they all together turn toward them with reverence and devotion.
Because such physical forms are lovely and pleasing,
the entire assembly reveres and looks up to him; thus,
there is no word he utters that is not listened to and followed.
This is called the fruit of a bodhisattva’s perfection of physical form.
Because bodhisattvas possess a noble lineage,
they are respected, honored, and praised by the great assembly.
Because they are respected, honored, and praised by the multitude,
they exhort sentient beings toward various matters;
all diligently train themselves therein, respectfully applying themselves and swiftly practicing without transgression or violation.
This is called the fruit of a bodhisattva’s perfection of lineage.
Because bodhisattvas possess mastery,
they are able to gather sentient beings through generosity and cause them to ripen swiftly.
This is called the fruit of the bodhisattva’s perfection of mastery.
Because bodhisattvas possess the perfection of authoritative speech,
they are able to benefit others through pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.
They gather all sentient beings and cause them to ripen swiftly;
this is called the fruit of a bodhisattva’s perfection of trustworthy speech.
This is because these bodhisattvas possess great power.
Regarding the various activities of all sentient beings,
he is able to assist them in every way and bestow his benevolence and virtue upon them;
through this benevolence and virtue, he moves the hearts of sentient beings.
Because they recognize his kindness, they all come to revere and look up to him;
whatever instructions he utters are swiftly followed, respected, and trusted.
This is called the fruit of a bodhisattva’s perfection of great power.
If bodhisattvas possess the human nature, they achieve the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) and are thus capable of being vessels for all supreme merits;
they are able [to accomplish] all tasks and activities.
He investigates all objects of knowledge with total fearlessness and proceeds without obstruction;
at all times, for all sentient beings, he acts thus.
All come together to assemble in a single gathering;
whether in private or in public, their discussions, shared dwellings, and enjoyment of food and drink are entirely free from resentment or obstruction.
This is called the fruit of a bodhisattva’s fulfillment of human nature.
Because bodhisattvas are fully endowed with great power,
they never grow weary in their application toward the cultivation of wholesome dharmas or in their application toward benefiting sentient beings.
Through courageous diligence and steadfast diligence, they swiftly realize supernormal knowledge and wisdom;
this is called the fruit of a bodhisattva’s perfection of great power.
If bodhisattvas accomplish these eight kinds of maturation, [they attain this fruit].
It possesses eight kinds of fruits;
it is able to effectively benefit all sentient beings and accords with the arising of all Buddha-dharmas.
Abiding within the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*),
the bodhisattva possesses the personal power and capability to perform various and manifold deeds for the benefit of sentient beings,
and is well-established in guiding those beings to be converted.
He acts in accordance with his own task;
this is called accomplishing what is to be done according to one's desire.
If a bodhisattva possesses personal power and capability, [he likewise acts accordingly].
He does not properly establish the sentient beings he seeks to convert;
thus, they do not act in accordance with their own tasks,
nor do they act for the benefit of others.
It is not called "blazing," nor is it called "conformable.
For these reasons, it is not called "capable of performing deeds for the benefit of others.
This is the case when bodhisattvas themselves lack the power and capability.
And they skillfully establish the sentient beings they transform so that those beings act in accordance with their own tasks;
such is the benefit performed for others.
It is not called "blazing" nor is it called "conformable.
For these reasons, it is not called "capable of performing deeds for the benefit of others.
Therefore, a bodhisattva must possess both matters.

When one's activities for the benefit of sentient beings are termed "blazing" and "conducive," it is by virtue of these causes and conditions that one is said to be capable of performing deeds that benefit others.
Thus, the bodhisattva dwelling in the fruit of maturation is able to mature all Buddha-dharmas for himself,
and is also able to cause others to quickly attain maturity according to their respective needs on the paths of the three vehicles.
Furthermore, it enables oneself to swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
and also enables others who have already reached maturity to swiftly attain liberation;
this is because bodhisattvas abide within these eight types of maturation fruits.
It is able to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings;
therefore, while all sentient beings dwell in a beginningless cycle of birth and death that is empty and devoid of purpose,
the bodhisattva dwells therein and makes it not empty, possessing great significance and benefit.
What is merit? What is wisdom?
Briefly stated, merit consists of three perfections (pāramitās).
First, the perfection of generosity;
second, the perfection of ethical discipline;
third, the perfection of patience.
Wisdom is of only one kind of pāramitā,
namely the prajñāpāramitā;
it should be understood that the vīryapāramitā and dhyānapāramitā both pertain to two parts.
First is the portion of merit;
second is the portion of wisdom.
If one practices giving in reliance upon diligence, [it constitutes the portion of merit].
Receiving and guarding the pure precepts,
as well as cultivating the four immeasurables such as loving-kindness—
diligence of this kind and its like is termed the "merit portion."
If, relying on diligence, one practices the three types of wisdom— those consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation—
one cultivates skillfulness regarding the aggregates, skillfulness regarding the elements,
skillfulness regarding the sense bases, and skillfulness regarding dependent origination.
One cultivates skillfulness regarding the possible and the impossible,
practicing the ability to discern that suffering is truly suffering and its origin is truly the origin.
Cessation is true cessation and the path is the true path;
this applies to all phenomena, whether wholesome or unwholesome, blameworthy or blameless,
inferior or superior.
Whether black or white,
they are able to correctly discern and examine them all through the detailed analysis of dependently arisen phenomena.
