All such types of diligence as these are called the "wisdom portion.
If one cultivates the four immeasurables, such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), based on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
all such types of meditative concentration as these are called the "merit portion."

If, by relying on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one is able to cultivate the skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*) and so forth as previously explained in the section on diligence (*vīrya*),
then all such types of meditative concentration are called the "wisdom factor" (*jñānāṅga*).
Thus, merit and wisdom briefly comprise six types;
one should understand that each of these, when analyzed individually, is immeasurable.
What are the causes of merit?
What is the cause of wisdom?
Briefly stated, it should be understood that there are three types of causes for merit and wisdom in total.
The first is the desire to acquire, maintain, and increase both merit and wisdom.
Second, being well-able to accord with and not oppose the conditions for merit and wisdom;
third, having already familiarized oneself with merit and wisdom in the past.
Regarding these, "conditions that accord and do not oppose" refers to:
This refers to the state of inverted conditions not being present and not being encountered;
the state of non-inverted conditions being truly present and truly encountered;
and encountering evil friends who perversely explain merit and wisdom.
Alternatively, when one attends to things erroneously and apprehends them in a distorted manner,
this is called the "presence and encounter with inverted conditions.
Conversely, all wholesome factors (*śukla-pakṣa*) that are contrary to this should be known as the "presence and encounter with non-inverted conditions."
If, regarding merit and wisdom, one is able to attain them, remain in them,
and increase them, and if through diligent cultivation obstacles are distanced and do not arise,
you should know that this is called the "non-contradictory condition."
If Bodhisattvas lack any one of these three causes of merit and wisdom,
it should be known that they will be unable to produce merit or produce wisdom.
What is the fruit of merit?
What is the fruit of wisdom?
It refers to the fact that because bodhisattvas rely upon merit, even though they continue to circulate through birth and death for a long time,
they are not afflicted or harmed by extreme suffering.
Furthermore, according to their wishes, they are able to gather in sentient beings and act for their benefit.
Because they rely on wisdom, the merit they gather is correct and not perverse.
Moreover, they are able to initiate various and immeasurable skillful activities.
Up until the ultimate point of realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—
thus has the fruit of merit and the fruit of wisdom been briefly explained.
One should understand that according to their respective applications, there are four types of categories, and furthermore, they are immeasurable.
It should be understood that herein there is the essence of maturation,
the cause of maturation,
and the fruit of maturation.
All of these depend upon merit and are produced from merit;
furthermore, merit depends upon wisdom and arises from wisdom.
Therefore, although both are superior for the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, [wisdom is the more essential].
Within this, merit is the most excellent and wisdom is unsurpassed.
If bodhisattvas lack either merit or wisdom,
they will certainly be unable to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This is called the bodhisattva’s self-benefit and benefit for others through the inclusion of causes and the inclusion of results.
What is the bodhisattva’s self-benefit and benefit for others in this life and in future lives?
It refers to the bodhisattvas’ human exertion in accordance with proper methods regarding crafts, occupations, and activities.
Having accumulated wealth,
one knows the proper measure in the enjoyment of such accumulated wealth;
furthermore, the ripening of the results of previously performed actions that yield desirable fruits matures.
They experience those fruits within the present life.
Furthermore, those bodhisattvas who are skillfully adept at the meditative absorptions do so with the desire to attain a pleasant dwelling in the present life.
In this present life, one relies upon this meditative concentration;
it is not for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others that one relies upon this meditative concentration.
Furthermore, it pertains to the mundane sphere of the parinirvāṇa in the present life of all Tathāgatas.
And all supramundane conditioned phenomena that can lead to nirvana in the present life—
these are called the bodhisattva’s benefit for oneself in the present life.
Just as there are these benefits for oneself in the present life for bodhisattvas, so too...
In this way, one should understand that when the sentient beings transformed by a bodhisattva obtain benefit in the present life through this means,
it constitutes benefiting others in the present life.
If, within the desire realm, one is able to obtain the perfection of wealth and treasures in future lives as well as the perfection of the physical body,
and is able to be reborn in the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) or the formless realms;
or if one is already born within those meditative absorptions or the formless realms.
One will obtain the perfection of wealth and treasures and the perfection of one's own physical form in future lives;
furthermore, within this present life, while accompanied by sorrow and suffering, one repeatedly reflects upon and cultivates wholesome causes.
This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the subsequent dharma for the benefit of oneself and others.
If bodhisattvas, in the present life, cultivate together with joy and bliss all the wholesome causes for the future perfection of wealth and the perfection of the physical body.
And all meditative attainments (samāpatti) of the dhyānas and formless realms that are not subject to regression—
these are called the bodhisattva’s benefit for self and others in this life and in future lives.
What are ultimate and non-ultimate benefit for self and others?
This refers to the abundance of wealth and the perfection of the physical body within the desire realm—
both in terms of their causes and results—
as well as the mundane purification of ordinary worldlings, both in terms of its causes and results.
This is not the ultimate benefit for oneself and others.
Rather, it is the permanent and complete severance of all afflictions and the possession of the entire Eightfold Noble Path.
If, by relying on this, one attains all mundane wholesome dharmas,
this is called ultimate benefit for oneself and others.
One should understand the ultimate and the non-ultimate through three causes and conditions.
First, by way of intrinsic nature;
second, by way of falling away or not falling away;
third, by way of the fruit being exhausted or inexhaustible upon enjoyment.
Regarding "by way of intrinsic nature":
ultimate nirvāṇa is called "final," while all conditioned phenomena are called "non-final."
Regarding the phrase "due to falling away or not falling away, and due to the exhaustion or non-exhaustion of the enjoyment of the fruit":
this is because the Noble Eightfold Path is subject to no falling away,
and because the enjoyment of its fruit is never exhausted.
This is called "ultimate.
All other wholesome, contaminated dharmas are not so,
because they are subject to regression.
Furthermore, because the enjoyment of its fruits has an end,
it is called "not ultimate.
Such are the ten kinds of self-benefit and benefit for others of a bodhisattva.
Whether in brief or in detail,
a bodhisattva should diligently train according to their strength and capacity;
beyond this, there is nothing superior or additional.

All that has been studied and all that will be studied for the benefit of oneself and others in the past and future is likewise comprised solely within these ten kinds of self-benefit and benefit for others.
Beyond this, there is nothing superior or additional.

In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth section of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, within the "Chapter on the Meaning of Reality" (*Tattvārtha-paṭala*), the fourth chapter of the first "Station of Yoga" (*Yogasthāna*), it is asked: What is the meaning of reality?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds:
first, that which relies on the true nature of all phenomena according to their mode of being (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*);
second, that which relies on the totality of all phenomena according to their full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*).
Thus, the true nature and all natures of these phenomena should be understood collectively as the "meaning of reality.
Furthermore, there are four distinct categories of this meaning of reality.
First, the reality established by worldly consensus;
second, the reality established by reasoning;
third, the reality that is the object of knowledge purified of the afflictive obscurations.
Fourth is the reality that is the object of knowledge purified of cognitive obscurations.
What is the reality established by worldly consensus?
It refers to the conventional designations applied in accordance with various things by all worldly people.
The objects perceived by the cognitive wisdom that enters through worldly habitual practice are of a uniform nature;
that is to say, earth is only earth and not fire or other elements.
As it is with earth, so it is with the rest.
Water, fire, and wind;
form, sound, odor, taste, and touch;
food, drink, clothing, and vehicles.
Various ornaments,
assets, household goods, fragrant ointments,
flower garlands, song, dance, music, and manifold radiances.
One should know that the same applies to serving men and women, as well as matters such as fields, gardens, shops, and dwellings;
suffering is exclusively suffering and not pleasure, and so forth.
Pleasure is exclusively pleasure and not suffering, and so forth.
To state it briefly:
this is exactly thus and not otherwise.
This is precisely as it is, not otherwise;
it is an object of engagement for resolute conviction,
which has been transmitted from its very beginning through successive generations throughout all the world.
That which is established through mutual conceptualization and is apprehended without depending on reflection, deliberation,
or investigation is called the reality universally established in the world.
What is the reality established by reasoning?
It refers to those principles that are logical for the wise—
those who are sagacious and discerning.
One who is capable of vitarka (initial inquiry) and vicāra (sustained investigation);
one who dwells on the stage of vitarka and vicāra; one who possesses their own eloquence;
one who abides in the state of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana); and one who practices according to observation.
The objects of knowledge and the domain of the determinative wisdom that has been thoroughly investigated by relying on the means of valid cognition— namely, direct perception, inference,
and authoritative scripture— and which are established and designated through the principles of proof (*upapatti*).
This is called the reality established by reasoning.
What is the reality that is the object of the knowledge purified of the afflictive obscurations?
It refers to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Whether it be untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*),
that which can induce untainted knowledge,
or the objective sphere traversed by the mundane knowledge obtained subsequent to the untainted state.
This is called the reality that is the object of the wisdom purified of the afflictive obscurations.
By taking this as its objective condition,
the wisdom [of the practitioner] becomes purified from the afflictive obscurations.
In future worlds, one will abide without obstruction;
therefore, it is called the reality that is the object of the knowledge purified of the afflictive obscurations.
Furthermore, what is this?
They are the four noble truths:
first, the noble truth of suffering;
second, the noble truth of the origin [of suffering].
The third is the noble truth of cessation;
the fourth is the noble truth of the path.
It is precisely regarding the meaning of these four noble truths that—
Having thoroughly and skillfully investigated, one enters into clear realization (*abhisamaya*);
having entered into clear realization, knowledge in accordance with reality (*yathābhūtajñāna*) arises.
This is the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*).
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are able to contemplate that only the aggregates (skandhas) are apprehendable,
and that apart from the aggregates, a self cannot be found;
this is because they have repeatedly cultivated wisdom associated with the arising and ceasing of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāras) produced through dependent origination.
Because one has repeatedly practiced the view that the person (pudgala) is devoid of self-nature as distinct from the aggregates,
there arises such a direct realization (abhisamaya) of the Noble Truths.
What is the reality that is the object of the purified wisdom regarding the cognitive obscurations?
That which obstructs knowledge regarding the objects of knowledge is called the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The sphere of activity of the wisdom that has attained liberation from the cognitive obscuration—
this should be known as the reality that is the object of the wisdom purified of cognitive obscurations.
What, then, is this? It refers to how all bodhisattvas and Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, enter into the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Having entered, they thoroughly purify the ineffable intrinsic nature of all phenomena and [understand] its conventional designative nature.
It is the sphere of activity of the non-conceptual wisdom that is perfectly equal and impartial;
such a sphere is the foremost, the true thusness, and the ultimate limit of all that can be known.
All analytical investigations of these various aspects of the true Dharma will turn back and fail to transcend it.
Furthermore, one should know that the establishment of this characteristic of ultimate reality is manifested by non-duality.
What is called "the two" refers to existence and non-existence.
Herein, as for "existence":
That is to say, the imputed nature of conventional designation is that which has been grasped by the world for a long time,
and it is also the root of all worldly conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Some say it is form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
some say it is the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
others again say it is earth, water, fire, and wind.
Some say they are form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects;
some say they are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate;
some say they are arising and ceasing.
Some say it is dependent origination;
some say it is the past, future, or present;
some say it is conditioned, and some say it is unconditioned.
Some say it is this world; some say it is another world;
some say it is the sun and moon;
others say it is that which is seen, heard, sensed, and known.
Whatever is sought and obtained follows the mental investigation and analysis;
finally, it may even be termed "nirvāṇa.
Such categories as these constitute the conventional designations of intrinsic nature for all phenomena as they are commonly understood by the world.
This is called "existence.
That which is called "non-existence" refers to the imputed self-nature of all forms (*rūpa*).
Even up to nirvāṇa, there is only the conventional designation of intrinsic nature;
there is no objective basis and no characteristic for that which is conventionally designated.
Thus, all conventional designations and verbal expressions are entirely non-existent.
That which arises in dependence upon those [conditions] is entirely non-existent;
this is called "non-being.
What was previously described as "being" is now described as "non-being."
That reality which is comprised within the characteristics of phenomena and is free from both existence and non-existence is called "non-duality.
Because it is non-dual, it is termed the "Middle Way."
Being free from the two extremes is also called "unsurpassed.
The wisdom of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is perfectly purified regarding this reality;
the wisdom of the bodhisattvas is manifested through training on the path regarding this reality.
Furthermore, this very wisdom is the vast skillful means by which bodhisattvas are able to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is this?
Because bodhisattvas abide within saṃsāra.
In each successive birth, they cultivate resolute conviction in emptiness,
thereby skillfully bringing to maturity all Buddha-dharmas as well as all sentient beings,
and are further able to understand birth and death as they truly are.
One does not develop a profound sense of weary detachment toward birth and death through such practices as its impermanence.
If bodhisattvas cannot understand birth and death as it truly is,
they will be unable to profoundly renounce all afflictions, such as greed, hatred, and delusion.
Because they are unable to abandon the various afflictions,
their minds become defiled and they undergo birth and death.
Because they undergo birth and death with a defiled mind, [they continue in saṃsāra].
They would be unable to bring to maturity all the Buddha-dharmas and all sentient beings.
If bodhisattvas were to develop a profound sense of weary detachment toward saṃsāra through such modes of contemplation as impermanence and so forth, [they would fail in their task].
This would mean entering parinirvāṇa too quickly.
If one were to enter parinirvāṇa so quickly,
one would still be unable to bring to maturity all the Buddha-dharmas and all sentient beings.
How much less could they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Furthermore, because bodhisattvas cultivate such resolute conviction in emptiness,
they do not harbor deep fear toward nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, they do not aspire much toward nirvāṇa.
If bodhisattvas are deeply terrified of nirvāṇa,
they will be unable to fulfill the provisions for that nirvāṇa.
Because they harbor deep fear and dread toward nirvāṇa, they do not perceive its benefits and virtues.
Due to this lack of perception, they become entirely devoid of pure conviction regarding nirvāṇa.
If bodhisattvas dwell frequently in the aspiration for and delight in nirvāṇa,
they will swiftly enter parinirvāṇa.
If they were to swiftly enter parinirvāṇa...
Consequently, one will be unable to bring the Buddha-dharma and all sentient beings to maturity;
the mind will continue to circulate within birth and death.
If, however, one develops a profound sense of weary detachment toward birth and death, [the mind will turn away].
Even if one were to swiftly enter parinirvāṇa,
if one feels deep-seated fear toward nirvāṇa, one will be unable to fulfill the provisions necessary for its realization.
If they dwell extensively in the aspiration for nirvāṇa,
they will swiftly enter parinirvāṇa;
such bodhisattvas lack the great skillful means for realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
If one can understand birth and death as they truly are,
then the mind will not be defiled as it flows through birth and death. If,
regarding birth and death, one does not cultivate a deep sense of weary detachment through such practices as contemplating impermanence, [one will remain bound].
One does not then enter parinirvāṇa too quickly;
if one does not harbor deep fear toward nirvāṇa,
one will be able to fulfill the provisions for nirvāṇa.
Although they perceive the subtle, wondrous, and meritorious benefits of nirvana,
they do not deeply aspire to realize nirvana quickly;
these bodhisattvas possess great skillful means for realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This is the supreme resolve regarding emptiness that relies upon great skillful means;
therefore, it is the supreme resolve regarding emptiness subsumed within the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the path of training.
This is called the vast skillful means for realizing the sublime wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, by virtue of being able to deeply penetrate the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*),
bodhisattvas [realize] the ineffable intrinsic nature (*nirabhilāpyasvabhāva*) of all phenomena.
Having known it as it truly is, one reaches the state where there is not even the slightest dharma or category for which conceptualization could arise;
one grasps only the object and grasps only suchness,
and does not form such thoughts.
This is merely phenomena and merely suchness;
it functions solely in accordance with the meaning.
Thus, the bodhisattva practices because of the ultimate truth.
Regarding all phenomena as equal,
one observes them with the wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness) exactly as they are.
Possessing the view of equality and the mind of equality toward all things, one attains the most excellent equanimity (*upekṣā*).
When, relying on this equanimity, one diligently cultivates skillfulness in all fields of knowledge,
even though one encounters every kind of exertion and every kind of hardship.
Without falling back,
they are swiftly able to bring about freedom from fatigue in body and freedom from fatigue in mind.
They are able to swiftly accomplish all forms of skillfulness and attain great power of mindfulness;
yet they do not become conceited because of their skillfulness,
nor do they harbor any secretiveness or stinginess toward others.
Regarding all forms of skillfulness, his mind is free from timidity;
he possesses capability and his conduct is unimpeded,
being fully endowed with the application of firm armor.
As these bodhisattvas undergo the cycle of birth and death, flowing along as it is and encountering great hardships and difficulties,
to that same extent they become increasingly capable of increasing their progress toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
To the extent that one attains excellence in honor and status,
to that same extent one’s pride toward sentient beings gradually diminishes;
to the extent that one realizes excellence in wisdom, [to that same extent...]

In this way and that, he repeatedly observes his own excessive engagement in challenging others, disputes, clamorous discourse, root afflictions, secondary afflictions, and the transgression of prohibitions,
and with a profound mind, he abandons them.
As their virtues increase further and further,
so too do they increasingly conceal their own goodness without seeking for others to know it,
nor do they hope for gain or honor.
Such are the many benefits possessed by bodhisattvas;
these factors conducive to enlightenment that accord with awakening all depend upon that wisdom.
Therefore, all those who have attained, will attain, or are now attaining enlightenment [do so] by means of it.
All depend upon that wisdom;
apart from this, there is nothing else, whether inferior or superior.
All bodhisattvas ride upon such a principle free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
Having attained such manifold benefits,
one acts for the sake of maturing the qualities of a Buddha within oneself,
and for the sake of maturing others in the three vehicles of the Dharma.
He practices the correct conduct.
While he is thus practicing the correct conduct,
he remains free from craving and attachment toward his own person and possessions.
Regarding all sentient beings, he trains in detachment from craving and is able to relinquish both body and wealth solely for the sake of benefiting them;
furthermore, he is capable of guarding and thoroughly protecting [them].
Through training in the discipline of body, speech, and so forth,
they are by nature disinclined toward evil and are exceedingly virtuous;
furthermore, they are able to endure all injuries and afflictions inflicted by others.
Regarding those who commit evil deeds, he is able to train in the nature of forbearance, diminishing anger and resentment, and refraining from harming others;
furthermore, he is able to diligently cultivate all fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) so as to become skillful in them.
To sever all doubts and difficulties of sentient beings;
to bestow upon sentient beings all manner of beneficial matters;
and to personally gather the causes for omniscience.
Furthermore, one is able to dwell the mind within so as to bring it to excellent concentration;
one constantly and diligently trains in dwelling the mind within for the sake of purifying and cultivating the four sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
It is for the sake of being able to sport with the five supernormal powers;
it is for the sake of being able to accomplish the welfare of sentient beings;
and it is because one wishes to dispel the fatigue produced by diligently training in all forms of skillful means.
Furthermore, being naturally wise, he achieves ultimate true knowledge.
He constantly and diligently trains for the sake of that ultimate true knowledge,
and practices the Mahāyāna for the sake of his own parinirvāṇa in the future.
Furthermore, while these bodhisattvas are thus practicing correct conduct,
they always delight in manifesting offerings and paying respect to sentient beings who possess virtuous qualities.
Toward all sentient beings who possess faults,
they constantly delight in manifesting the most excellent compassion and sympathy,
causing those beings to eliminate and sever all their faults according to their ability and strength.
Toward those sentient beings who have been hostile toward oneself, one should constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness;
according to one's capacity and strength, without guile or deceit,
one should bring about their various benefits and well-being.
May all faults of intention and application, as well as feelings of resentment and hostility, naturally be severed in those enemies;
and toward all sentient beings who have been kind to oneself, [may one cultivate gratitude].
Because they are well aware of kindness, they repay it directly with an equivalent or even greater measure.
According to their ability and strength, they satisfy the other's aspirations in accordance with the Dharma;
yet even if they lack the power to do so, should the other person request it, [they will still respond].
Regarding each and every task to be performed,
he manifests earnestness and diligent application in his endeavors,
never abruptly ceasing that which is sought after.
"How may they know that I lack the power [to act], yet not the desire [to do so]?
Such categories as these should be understood as the bodhisattva’s skillful mastery of the principle of non-proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
Relying on ultimate true wisdom, one cultivates correct application.
By what reasoning should one know that all phenomena possess a nature beyond words?
It is because the self-characteristics of all phenomena are merely conventional designations.
Some speak of it as form (*rūpa*), others speak of it as sensation (*vedanā*),
as explained at length previously;
one should know that everything up to and including nirvāṇa is merely a conventional designation and lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Nor does it have a self-nature (svabhāva) that exists separately from those [conventions];
it is the domain of speech and the objective range of speech.
Thus, these phenomena do not possess a self-nature as it is expressed by words.
Nor is it the case that everything is utterly non-existent.
In this way, it is not existent,
yet it is also not the case that everything is utterly non-existent.
How can it exist? It means being free from the false attachment that superimposes reality upon what is non-existent,
and being free from the false attachment that denies reality to what actually exists.
That which exists in this manner is the ultimate intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*) of all phenomena;
one should know that it is exclusively the objective sphere of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
If, regarding various phenomena and various entities, whenever verbal expressions arise,
those phenomena and entities possessed an intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
then a single phenomenon or a single entity would consequently have a manifold intrinsic nature.
Why is this? Because numerous conventional designations are established to express a single phenomenon or a single entity;
furthermore, these numerous conventional designations do not yield any determinate object of expression.
This means that a particular conventional designation applies to a given phenomenon or entity as having substance, parts, and intrinsic nature,
whereas other conventional designations do not. Therefore, whether all conventional designations are complete or incomplete [in this regard], [the distinction remains].
Regarding all phenomena and all things, none possess an essence, parts, or an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore,
as previously stated regarding the various phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth,
if they were to possess an intrinsic nature even according to conventional designation (*prajñapti*), [it would be untenable].
One must first have a thing and only then establish a conventional designation according to one's desire.
Prior to the establishment of that conventional designation,
that phenomenon and that thing would have to lack intrinsic nature.
If there were no intrinsic nature and no objective basis for the establishment of conventional designations and expressions,
it would not be logical; yet since conventional designations and expressions do exist,
those phenomena and those objects possess an intrinsic nature in accordance with those conventional designations.
This is not logical.
Furthermore, if the nature of form existed prior to the establishment of conventional designations to express it,
[it would follow that form exists independently of such designations].
Furthermore, if one were to establish a conventional designation based on the nature of form to apprehend form,
then apart from that conventional designation expressing it,
a cognition of "form" would have to arise with respect to the conceptualization of form and the objective entity of form.
Yet, in reality, they do not arise.
By this cause and by this principle,
one should know that all phenomena possess an ineffable intrinsic nature.
As it was said regarding form (*rūpa*),
so it should be understood that feeling (*vedanā*) and the others are as previously described,
up to and including *nirvāṇa*.
There are two kinds of persons who,
regarding the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Buddha,
are both ruined and lost.
First, regarding phenomena such as form and entities such as form,
one conceives of an imputed nature and specific characteristics; thus,
one gives rise to the adherence of superimposition toward that which is actually a non-entity.
Second, regarding the basis for conventional designation and the dependently designated nature, which is the ineffable intrinsic nature and ultimate dharmatā—
namely, that in every respect it is utterly non-existent.
One gives rise to the misconception of negation regarding that which truly exists,
and the misconception of affirmation regarding that which does not truly exist;
all such faults of those who falsely establish dharmas have already been fully revealed and elucidated as previously described.
Because they give rise to the error of superimposing existence upon phenomena such as form— which in reality lack any substantial entity—
they utterly ruin the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Buddha.
Regarding phenomena such as form, one gives rise to the erroneous attachment of repudiating their actual existence as mere entities;
this constitutes the fault of one who destroys all phenomena.
By virtue of this fault...
They have utterly ruined the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Buddha;
I shall now explain this.
That is to say, if one conceives a deprecating attachment toward those phenomena such as form, asserting that they exist merely as substantial entities.
Thus, there is neither reality nor unreality;
both of these two positions are illogical.
For example, it is only when the aggregates such as form exist that a person (pudgala) can be conventionally designated.
It is not that a person (pudgala) is conventionally established in the absence of a real entity;
rather, it is because there are the real entities of the dharmas such as form that one can then obtain the conventional designations expressed by the dharmas such as form.
It is not that there is no underlying reality (vastu) upon which the conventional designations (prajñapti) of "form" and so forth are based.
If there were only the conventional designation and no real entity,
then since there would be no basis, the designation itself could not exist.
This is what is called being one who destroys all phenomena.

For example, there is a certain class of people who, upon hearing the teaching of profound sūtras associated with the Mahāyāna, associated with emptiness, and containing implicit meanings that are not yet fully explicit, [react as follows].
Unable to understand the meaning of what was taught as it truly is,
they give rise to irrational and false conceptualization through reflections induced by a lack of skillful means.
They give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine:
that all things are merely conventional designations and this alone is the ultimate reality.
To contemplate in this manner is called correct contemplation.
He negates the existence of the mere thing (*vastumātra*) that actually exists as the basis for designations;
thus, all designations would be non-existent.
When could it ever be that all things are merely conventional and yet constitute reality?
By this reasoning, they slander both the real and the conventional, asserting that neither exists at all.
Because they slander both the real and the unreal,
you should know that such persons are called the most extreme nihilists.
Such nihilists should not be spoken to nor should they be lived with by any wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life.
Such non-existence leads to one's own ruin and likewise ruins those in the world who follow that view.
With this underlying intention (*saṃdhāya*), the Blessed One said:
It would be better for one to give rise to the view of a self than for one to wrongly grasp emptiness. Why is this?
Those who give rise to the view of self are merely deluded regarding the objects of knowledge;
they do not deny any object of knowledge whatsoever.
One does not fall into the various evil destinies because of this cause;
when others seek the Dharma or seek liberation from suffering,
one does not act with deceit nor cause them delay.
They are also able to establish themselves in the dharmas and the truths,
and they do not give rise to laxity or pride regarding the various points of training.
Those who have wrongly grasped emptiness are likewise deluded regarding the objects of knowledge.
They also slander all objects of knowledge.
For this reason, they fall into the various evil destinies,
while others seek the Dharma and seek liberation from suffering.
They are capable of being deceitful and also of causing procrastination;
they are unable to establish themselves in the Dharma or the Truths,
and they become extremely lax regarding the various rules of training.
Those who thus diminish the reality of existing things are utterly ruined regarding the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Buddha. How,
then, is one called a "wrong-grasper of emptiness"?
That is to say, there are some śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who do not believe in or accept that it is empty by virtue of that [factor],
nor do they believe in or accept that it is empty with respect to this [factor].
This is what is meant by one who has wrongly grasped emptiness. Why is this?
Because that by which something is empty is actually non-existent.
In this regard, that which is empty is actually existent;
by this principle, it can be said to be "empty.
If one were to say that everything is utterly non-existent, [it would not be emptiness].
In what place, by what means, and for what reason is something called "empty"?
Nor should it be said that by this [means] and in this [place] it is therefore declared empty.
For this reason, such a person is called one who has wrongly grasped emptiness (*mithyā-śūnyatā-grāhin*).
What, furthermore, is meant by "one who correctly grasps emptiness"?
It means that because something does not exist within a given thing,
one correctly contemplates that thing as empty by virtue of that very absence.
Furthermore, because that which remains here truly exists,
one knows it as it is through that which remains;
this is called entering into emptiness as it truly is, without error.
This means that within all those things conceived as form and so forth, as previously described,
the dharmas characterized by the nature of conventional designations such as "form" and so forth do not exist at all.
Therefore, regarding these things designated as "form" and so forth,
they are said to be empty by virtue of the nature of those conventional designations such as "form."
Regarding all these objects of perception such as form and so forth, what remains?
It is precisely that upon which the conventional designations of form and so forth depend.
One should know both of these types exactly as they are.
This means that within this context, there is truly only the bare thing (*vastumātra*);
and within the bare thing itself, there is also only the provisional designation (*prajñaptimātra*).
One does not give rise to the attachment of superimposition (*samāropa*) regarding what is non-existent in reality.
One does not give rise to the misconception of deprecating what truly exists;
one neither adds to nor subtracts from it, neither grasps nor rejects it,
but understands, as it truly is, the ineffable intrinsic nature of suchness as it really is.
This is what is meant by one who correctly grasps emptiness;
such a person is able to thoroughly penetrate the nature of empty phenomena with right wisdom.
In this way, they accord with the principles of logical proof.
One should know that all phenomena have an ineffable intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, one should know that all phenomena have an ineffable intrinsic nature by means of the authoritative teaching.
As the Blessed One said in the *Bhavasamkrānti-sūtra* to clarify this meaning, he spoke in verse:
"By means of various names, various phenomena are expressed;
yet within these, those [names] do not exist. This is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena."
How does this verse clarify such a meaning?
It means that one establishes the names "form" and so forth upon the conceptualized phenomena of form and so forth.
One expresses these phenomena, such as form and so forth, by means of names;
according to how one speaks of the conceptualization of form and so forth,
one may speak of them as "form," or speak of them as "feeling," or speak of them as "perception."

To speak extensively, up to and including its being called "nirvāṇa," within all these conceptualized phenomena such as form and so forth, the intrinsic nature of form and so forth is entirely non-existent.
Furthermore, there are no other dharmas possessing the nature of form and so forth;
rather, within those very things, the nature of the referent that transcends verbal expression— the conceptualization of form and so forth—
is truly existent.
One should know that this is the ultimate intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*) and also the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, in the "Chapter on Meaning" (*Arthavargīya*), the Blessed Buddha said:
"The Muni does not cling to any worldly conventions."
"How can that which is non-existent be grasped? How can one not be attached to what is seen and heard?
This verse reveals the following meaning:
namely, regarding the various conventional designations such as "form" applied to the perceived objects of form and so forth within the world.
These are called "conventionalities.
Just as those conventional designations [impute] an intrinsic nature to these conceptual objects,
the Sage does not adhere to such conventionalities.
Why is this? Because they are free from views of exaggeration or depreciation,
and because they are free from manifest perverted views.
By this principle, it is called "non-attachment.
Since there is thus no attachment, who could possibly grasp?
Because there is no [false] view, one does not grasp at things by way of superimposition or denial.
Because it is able to correctly observe the objects of knowledge,
it is called "view" (*darśana*).
It consists of hearing the verbal expressions concerning the objects of knowledge.
Therefore, it is called "hearing.
Based on this seeing and hearing, craving does not arise nor does it increase;
rather, one brings about its ultimate cessation with respect to those conditions.
Because he abides in supreme equanimity (*upekṣā*), he is called "without affection.
Furthermore, the Blessed One spoke thus to Saṃtha Kātyāyana:
"O bhikṣu Saṃtha..."
One practices dhyāna without relying on earth;
one does not rely on water, fire, or wind;
one does not rely on the sphere of infinite space, nor the sphere of infinite consciousness.
He does not rely on the sphere of nothingness, nor on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
he does not rely on this world or another world,
nor on the orbs of the sun and moon.
It does not rely on what is seen, heard, sensed, or known;
it does not rely on what is sought or attained;
it does not rely on mental reflection or discursive investigation.
One practices meditative concentration without relying on anything.
How does a bhikṣu practicing meditative concentration do so?
He practices meditative concentration without relying on the earth element.
To speak at length, up to: "The bhikṣu Saṃtha cultivates meditative concentration without relying on anything whatsoever.
Or, there may be one who eliminates the perception of earth regarding the earth.
There may be those who eliminate the perception of water regarding water;
as explained at length, up to those who eliminate the perception of all things regarding all things.
Such is the bhikṣu who cultivates meditative concentration.
He practices meditative concentration without relying on the earth,
and so forth, up to practicing meditative concentration without relying on anything at all.
A bhikṣu who practices meditative concentration in this manner—
Acting as Indra, as Īśāna,
and as the lords of the world along with the hosts of devas,
they paid homage from afar and praised him, saying:
Homage to the Auspicious Hero! Homage to the Honored One among Heroes!
I do not now know upon what basis you practice meditative concentration, nor how this sūtra reveals such a meaning.
This refers to the designation and conventional establishment of names such as "earth" and so forth with respect to objects that are perceived as being equal across all stages;
this is called the "perception of earth and so forth."
These very perceptions, with respect to those objects of perception such as form and so forth,
either give rise to superimposition or give rise to denial. If,
with respect to those objects, they give rise to an adherence that superimposes a substantial intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The conceptualization that superimposes [attributes] is called "superimposition.
The conceptualization that gives rise to the grasping of ultimate reality as being merely the thing itself [when it is not] is called "denial."
Because he is able to correctly eliminate, sever, and relinquish these perceptions,
they are called "eliminated.
There are immeasurable such scriptural statements of this kind.
This is called the authoritative teaching (*āptāgama*).
By means of this most excellent authoritative teaching of the Tathāgata,
one should understand that all phenomena have a nature that transcends verbal expression.
Question: If this is so, for what reason does one give rise to verbal expression regarding the ineffable intrinsic nature (*nirabhilāpya-svabhāva*) of all phenomena?
Answer: If one did not give rise to verbal expression, [the teaching of the Dharma would be impossible].
Then one would be unable to explain to others that all phenomena have an ineffable intrinsic nature,
nor could others hear such a meaning.
If there were no hearing, one would be unable to know this ineffable intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Desiring to cause others to hear and know that the self-nature of all phenomena is beyond verbal expression,
one therefore employs verbal expression regarding this ineffable self-nature.
Furthermore, because foolish worldlings do not understand such *tathatā* (thusness) as it is thus revealed, [they remain in ignorance].
From these causes and conditions, the eight types of conceptualization evolve and are able to produce three things,
giving rise to the entire world of sentient beings and the receptacle world.
What are called the eight kinds of conceptualization?
First, discrimination of intrinsic nature;
second, discrimination of distinctions;
third, discrimination of grasping at a whole.
Fourth is the discrimination of "I";
fifth is the discrimination of "mine";
sixth is the discrimination of craving.
Seventh is the discrimination of the unloved;
eighth is the discrimination that is contrary to both.
How do these eight kinds of discrimination give rise to the three things?
That is to say: conceptualization of intrinsic nature,
conceptualization of distinctions,
and conceptualization of grasping as a whole.
These three types of discrimination produce the basis for the proliferation of conceptual proliferation and the objective referent of that proliferation;
that is, they take the objective referents of the perceptions of form and so forth as their basis and object.
It is comprised of names, concepts, and verbal expressions;
it is manifested by names, concepts, and verbal expressions as conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
It is precisely with regard to these things that one engages in conceptualization and deliberation.
There are manifold varieties of categories,
such as the discrimination of "I" and the discrimination of "mine.
These two discriminations give rise to the root of all other views.
Furthermore, it includes the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which is the root of pride,
as well as all forms of self-conceit (*asmimāna*) that serve as the root for the arising of all other types of pride,
and the conceptualization of craving.
If it is a discrimination of the unlovely,
or if it is a discrimination contrary to both of those,
as appropriate, it can give rise to desire, hatred, and delusion.
These are called the eight kinds of conceptualization that can produce these three things:
namely, the objective basis for the proliferation of conceptual play;
and the things of views and the conceit "I am."
Regarding the objects of greed, hatred, and delusion:
one should know that herein, based upon the objective referents of conceptual proliferation,
there arise the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the conceit "I am" (asmimāna).
The view of a self-identity and the conceit "I am" serve as the basis for the arising of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Through these three factors, all phenomena pertaining to the cycle of worldly existence are fully manifested.
What is called discrimination of intrinsic nature?
It refers to the discursive thoughts that discriminate the various intrinsic natures of all things conceived as "form" and so forth, such as form itself.
This is called discrimination of intrinsic nature.
What is called discrimination of distinction?
It refers to those very things conceived as objects, such as form and so forth.
That is to say: "this is with form" and "this is formless";
"this is visible" and "this is invisible";
"this is resistant" and "this is non-resistant"; "this is with outflows" and "this is without outflows."
That is to say: "This is conditioned," "this is unconditioned"; "this is wholesome," "this is unwholesome";
"this is indeterminate."
That is to say: "This is the past," "this is the future," and "this is the present.
By means of such immeasurable categories of distinctions, one engages in conceptualization regarding the basis of intrinsic nature itself.
To differentiate the various meanings of those distinctions is called "differentiation-discrimination" (*viśeṣa-vikalpa*).
What is called "global-grasping discrimination" (*piṇḍagrāha-vikalpa*)?
That is to say, it is the conceptualization induced by the provisional designation of "self," "sentient being," "life-force," "born one," and so forth,
with respect to those very objects of perception such as form;
it proceeds as a conceptualization based on the grasping of a totality within a plurality of dharmas.
The conceptualization induced by the provisional designation of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, and so forth within a village, an army,
or a forest is called the conceptualization of grasping at a whole.
What is called the discrimination of "I" and "mine"?
It refers to those things that are with outflows and with grasping,
which have been accumulated through the long-term and repeated practice of clinging to "I" and "mine."
Due to the habitual practice of those false attachments in previous lives,
there arises a false discrimination conditioned by the objects within one's own sphere of views;
this is what is called the discrimination of "self" and "mine."
What is called "discrimination of the agreeable"?
It refers to discrimination arising from objects that are pure, excellent, and pleasing to the mind.
What is called "discrimination of the disagreeable"?
This refers to discrimination arising from objects that are impure, excellent, or disagreeable.
What is meant by "discrimination that is contrary to both"?
It refers to discrimination arising from objects that are free from both the pure and the impure, as well as the agreeable and the disagreeable.
Regarding the discrimination that arises,
there are briefly two kinds mentioned here: first,
the discrimination of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*).
Second, there is the discrimination that relies upon [the basis] and the objective entity that is the object of discrimination.
One should know that these two kinds have functioned as causes for one another in a reciprocal manner since beginningless time;
that is to say, discrimination in the past serves as the cause.
It can produce the bases and objects of present conceptualization.
Once these bases and objects of present conceptualization have been produced,
they in turn serve as causes to produce the conceptualizations of the present world that arise from those very bases and objects.
Because one does not understand through discrimination at this present time,
there arises again the objective basis and conditions for the future.
Since that [future] will arise, the discrimination that arises depending upon and conditioned by that [basis] will certainly arise.
How is such conceptualization thoroughly understood?
It is by means of the four kinds of thorough investigation and the four kinds of knowledge of reality as it is.
What are called the four kinds of thorough investigation?
First is the investigation of names;
second is the investigation of things;
third is the investigation of the conventional designation of intrinsic nature.
Fourth is the investigation into the provisional designation of distinctions.
Regarding the investigation into names:
it means that bodhisattvas perceive names as being merely names.
This is called the investigation of names.
As for the investigation of things,
it means that bodhisattvas perceive only things as mere things.
This is called the investigation of things (*vastu-paryeṣaṇā*).
Regarding the investigation of the designation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prajñapti-paryeṣaṇā*):
it means that bodhisattvas, with respect to the designation of intrinsic nature, perceive only the designation of intrinsic nature.
This is called the investigation into the provisional designation of intrinsic nature.

As for the investigation into the provisional designation of distinctions, it means that bodhisattvas perceive only the provisional designation of distinctions within the provisional designation of distinctions.
This is called the investigation of the provisional designation of distinctions.
Regarding those names and things, these bodhisattvas may contemplate them either as having distinct characteristics or as having combined characteristics.

Because one relies on the contemplation of the characteristics of the conjunction of names and things, one penetrates the two kinds of self-nature: the provisional establishment of differentiation and the provisional establishment of designation.
What are called the four types of knowledge in accordance with reality?
First is the knowledge of reality as it is, induced by the investigation of names;
second is the knowledge of reality as it is, induced by the investigation of things;
third is the knowledge of reality as it is, induced by the investigation of the designation of intrinsic nature.
Fourth is the knowledge of reality as it is, which is induced by the investigation of the provisional designation of distinctions.
What is meant by "knowledge of reality as it is induced by the investigation of names"?
It refers to when bodhisattvas, having investigated names, realize that there is only the name.
One understands this name as it truly is:
that is to say, such a name is a conventional designation for such an object,
established for the sake of causing the world to give rise to perceptions, views, and verbal expressions.
If, regarding all things conceived as form and so forth, the designations "form" and so forth were not established by convention,
no one would be able to give rise to the conception of "form" and so forth with respect to those things conceived as form and so forth.
If there is no perception, then there can be no arising of the grasping that superimposes [existence].
If there is no grasping, then there is no verbal expression.
If one can understand this thus, according to reality, [one attains liberation].
This is called the knowledge of reality as it is, induced by the investigation of names.
What is the knowledge of reality as it is, induced by the investigation of things?
It refers to when bodhisattvas, having investigated things, realize that there are only things.
One observes that all things, such as forms and other conceptual objects,
are by nature devoid of verbal expression and are inexpressible.
If one can thus understand them as they truly are, [one realizes their ultimate nature].
This is called the knowledge of reality as it is, induced by the investigation of things.
What is the knowledge of reality as it is, induced by the investigation of the designation of intrinsic nature?
It refers to when bodhisattvas investigate the designation of intrinsic nature.
Once the provisional designation of intrinsic nature has been established,
one penetrates and understands as it truly is that all provisional designations of intrinsic nature within the referential objects of perception, such as form,
are not the actual intrinsic nature of those things, yet they appear as if they were the intrinsic nature of those things.
Furthermore, one is able to understand that the intrinsic nature of those phenomena is like a magical transformation,
a reflection, an echo, a shadow, a light,
the moon in water, a mirage, a dream, or an illusion.
It appears as similar [to its object] but does not have that as its essence.
If one can thus understand, in accordance with reality, the sphere of activity of the most profound meaning,
this is called the "knowledge of reality as it is" induced by the investigation of the provisional designation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prajñapti-paryeṣaṇā-niṣyanda-yathābhūta-jñāna*).
What is the knowledge of reality as it is, which is induced by the investigation into the conceptual designation of distinctions?
It refers to when bodhisattvas, regarding the conceptual designation of distinctions,
realize that there is only the conceptual designation of distinctions.
One penetrates and understands, as they truly are, the meaning of non-duality as it is conventionally designated within the distinctions among phenomena such as form;
that is to say, those various phenomena are neither of the nature of existence nor of the nature of non-existence.
Because its nature as expressible is not established as real, it is not of the nature of existence;
because its nature beyond expression is truly established, it is not of the nature of non-existence.
Thus, from the perspective of ultimate truth, it is not a form that possesses color.
Because there are no material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) therein, it is not formless from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*);
yet because material phenomena are said to exist therein, it possesses both existence and non-existence,
and both form and formlessness, just as with the nature of existence and the nature of non-existence.
In this way, all such conceptual designations of distinctions— such as "having views" and "being without views"—
should be understood through this principle.
If one can thus understand, in accordance with reality, the meaning of non-duality within these conceptual designations of distinction, [one realizes it].
This is called the knowledge of reality as it is, induced by the investigation into the provisional designation of distinctions.
Because fools lack these four knowledges of reality and because they do not manifest them, [they remain deluded].
Thereupon, eight kinds of false conceptualization arise,
which are able to produce three things and give rise to the entire world of sentient beings as well as the receptacle world.
That is to say, due to such false conceptualization, various defilements arise;
because defilements arise, one wanders through birth and death;
and because one constantly wanders within birth and death.
There is always an immeasurable variety of sufferings—birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth—that follow along with the cycle of birth and death, flowing on without ceasing.
The bodhisattva relies upon these four kinds of knowledge of reality as it is.
By being able to correctly understand the eight kinds of conceptualization,
one correctly understands them in the present life; consequently,
the objective bases and conditions comprised of proliferation will not arise again in future lives.
Because it does not arise, the conceptualization that would otherwise arise from those bases and conditions in future lives will no longer be produced.
This is because both such conceptualization and the objective basis for those conditions have been extinguished.
One should know that all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are extinguished.
Because the bodhisattva thus extinguishes conceptual proliferations,
they are able to realize the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Mahāyāna.
Because their wisdom regarding the sphere of the supreme true meaning within the present life is utterly purified,
they universally attain all forms of mastery;
that is to say, bodhisattvas attain mastery over the supernormal power of transformation with respect to various emanations.
He attains mastery over the supernormal power of transformation regarding various manifestations;
he attains mastery over all knowledge and objects of knowledge throughout the entire range of the knowable;
and if he wishes to remain for a long time, he is able to abide there at will according to his pleasure.
If they wish to pass away, they can do so at will without depending on external causes of death.
Because bodhisattvas have attained such immeasurable masteries,
they are supreme and unsurpassed among all sentient beings.
Because the bodhisattva thus attains universal mastery over all things,
they obtain five kinds of supreme benefits.
First, they attain the ultimate tranquility of mind.
Because he abides in supreme tranquility, rather than through the mere pacification of afflictions;
secondly, his pure, stainless, and sublime wisdom-vision proceeds without any obstruction regarding all fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*).
Third, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings,
they undergo the cycle of birth and death without weariness.
Fourth, they skillfully enter into the intentional terminology and meanings of all Tathāgatas.
Fifth, the superior resolve (adhimukti) attained in the Mahāyāna cannot be led astray nor is it dependent on other conditions.
It should be understood that these five kinds of benefits have five kinds of functions.
First, the bodhisattva achieves the most excellent dwelling in happiness in the present life,
which is able to extinguish all various physical and mental fatigues arising from the diligent application of effort directed toward awakening.
One should know that this is called the activity of the excellence of the mind’s ultimate tranquility.
Second, a bodhisattva is universally able to bring all Buddha-dharmas to maturity;
one should know that this is called the activity of the excellence of unimpeded, pure, and subtle wisdom-vision regarding all fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*).
Third, that a bodhisattva is universally able to bring all sentient beings to maturity—
this should be known as the activity of the benefit of being without weariness or fatigue while transmigrating through birth and death.
Fourth, the bodhisattva is able to correctly eliminate all doubts that arise in the sentient beings they seek to convert,
and protects and upholds the sublime eye of the Tathāgata’s true Dharma so that it may endure for a long time.
One who is able to recognize, reveal, and correctly eliminate that which obscures the Tathāgata’s holy teaching— the counterfeit Dharma—
should be known as one who has successfully entered into the activity of the benefits of the Tathāgata’s intentional terminology and meaning.
Fifth, the bodhisattva is able to crush all the heterodox arguments of external paths;
their diligence is firm and their right vows are unshakable.
It should be known that this is called the karma of the superior victory of the Mahāyāna resolute conviction, which cannot be led astray or taken away, and does not depend on other conditions.
In this way, all that is performed by a bodhisattva is encompassed by these five types of beneficial activities,
and remains free from defilement.
It is able to universally mature all Buddha-dharmas;
it is able to universally mature all sentient beings;
it protects and upholds the unsurpassed true Dharma of the Tathāgata, and subdues the arguments of others.
With diligence, valor, right aspiration, and immovability—
one should know that these four points of ultimate truth have the first two as inferior.
Within the third section,
the fourth is the most excellent.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle Thirty-six.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 37.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth part of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, within the first section on the "Foundations of Yoga," the fifth chapter, "Power" (*Prabhāva*), asks: What is the power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?
It should be known that, in brief, there are three kinds.
First is the power of the noble ones (*ārya-prabhāva*).
This refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi-vaśitā*);
by virtue of this mastery over concentration, they accomplish all things according to their wishes.
Because the mind has been made pliant and well-cultivated,
this is called the power of the noble ones (ārya-prabhāva).
Second is the power of the Dharma (dharma-prabhāva).
It refers to the fact that all sublime dharmas possess vast fruits and great benefits;
this is called the power of the Dharma.
Herein, "Dharma" means:
These are the six perfections, namely:
from generosity up to wisdom.
Such dharmas as these possess great power and majesty.
This is called the power of the Dharma.
Third is the power of co-arising,
which refers to the Buddha and Bodhisattvas having previously accumulated vast stores of merit and provisions.
The realization of the most marvelous quality of co-nascence is called the power of co-nascence.
Furthermore, there are five further categories of such powers possessed by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
First is the power of supernormal faculties;
second is the power of the Dharma;
third is innate power.
Fourth is the power shared with all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
fifth is the power not shared with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
What is the supernatural power of the buddhas and bodhisattvas?
They are the six supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).
First is the supernormal knowledge of realization through the cognition of miraculous powers (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā-abhijñā*).
Second is the supernormal knowledge of realization through the cognition of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā-abhijñā*).
Third is the supernormal power of the realization through knowledge of the divine ear;
fourth is the supernormal power of the realization through knowledge of death and rebirth;
fifth is the supernormal power of the realization through knowledge of the diversity of mental dispositions.
Sixth is the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*).
This is called the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñāprabhāva*).
What is the buddhas' and bodhisattvas' supernormal power of the knowledge of the sphere of psychic transformation (*ṛddhiviṣayajñānābhijñā*)?
The supernormal knowledge of the power of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is, in brief, of two kinds:
first, the power of transformation (*pariṇāmikī-ṛddhi*);
second, the power of creation (*nairmāṇikī-ṛddhi*). Each of these two types has many further subdivisions.
What are the categories of the supernormal power of transformation (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā*)?
They are the eighteen transformations.
The first is trembling.
Second is blazing;
third is dissemination;
fourth is manifestation.
Fifth, transformation;
sixth, coming and going;
seventh, contraction.
Eighth, extension;
ninth, the entry of all forms into one's own body;
tenth, proceeding toward those of the same class.
Eleventh is manifestation;
twelfth is concealment;
thirteenth is mastery over what is created.
Fourteenth, he restrains the supernatural powers of others.
Fifteenth, he is able to bestow eloquence.
Sixteenth, he is able to bestow mindfulness.
Seventeenth, they are able to bestow peace and happiness;
eighteenth, they emit great radiance.
Such categories as these are all termed the supernormal power of the knowledge of the transformation of the psychic realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā*).
"Vibrating" refers to the fact that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have attained mastery over meditative concentration, their minds are pliant and supple,
and they have skillfully cultivated the mind.
By the mastery of meditative concentration, they are universally able to cause the shaking of monasteries, residences, villages,
towns, hamlets, cities, kingdoms,
the worlds of hell-beings, and the worlds of animals.
The world of the grandfather, the world of humans,
the world of devas, the four great continents,
a small thousandfold world system, and a medium two-thousandfold world system.
A trichiliocosm; a hundred trichiliocosms; a thousand trichiliocosms.
He is able to cause the shaking of hundreds of thousands of trichiliocosms, even up to immeasurable and innumerable trichiliocosms;
this is called "shaking."
"Blazing" refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, through their mastery of meditative concentration,
emitting fierce, blazing flames from their bodies.
He pours clear, cold water beneath his body,
while from beneath his body fierce flames of fire erupt;
he pours clear, cold water over his body.
Entering the fire-element meditative absorption (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), his entire body blazes forth;
from every part of his body issue various flames of blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, emerald, green, and the color of crystal (*sphaṭika*).
This is called "blazing.
As for "pervading," it refers to the Buddha and Bodhisattvas relying on the mastery of meditative concentration.
The radiance spread and pervaded all temples, monasteries, and dwellings,
filling even immeasurable and innumerable worlds,
just as they had previously caused them to tremble.
This is called "pervasion.
As for "manifestation," it refers to the Buddha and Bodhisattvas relying on the mastery of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
According to their inclinations, he revealed this to all those gathered in the assembly— śramaṇas, brahmins, śrāvakas, bodhisattvas,
devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas.
He causes the asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth,
to all see him clearly; furthermore,
he causes those in the lower evil realms and those among the higher humans and devas to likewise see him clearly.
All other buddha-fields and the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas therein,
even including those buddha-fields designated by various names throughout as many buddha-lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
He causes them to see all the Tathāgatas with such-and-such names within those lands;
he also proclaims the names of those Buddha-lands and the names of those Tathāgatas, extending from that place all the way here.
Furthermore, beyond those buddha-fields and those Tathāgatas, he causes them all to appear before him—
exactly as they desire, even to the furthest extent of their wishes—
and also expounds the Dharma for them.
This is called manifestation.
As for transformation,
it refers to the mastery of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas based upon meditative concentration.
If one forms the resolute conviction that a certain place is water, it immediately becomes water,
exactly as intended and not otherwise.
The same applies to the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding fire and wind.
If one forms the resolute conviction that water is earth, it immediately becomes earth,
exactly as it is and not otherwise.
The same applies to the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding fire and wind.
If one forms the resolute conviction that fire is earth, it immediately becomes earth,
exactly as it is and nothing else.
The same applies to the resolute conviction regarding water and wind.
If one forms the resolute conviction that wind is earth, it immediately becomes earth;
it is exactly so and nothing else.
The same applies to the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding water and fire.
If one gives rise to another resolute conviction regarding anything whatsoever,
it is exactly according to that conviction and nothing else.
Just as it is with the mutual transformation of the primary elements (mahābhūta),
one should know that the same applies to visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility;
this is also the case with grass, leaves, cow dung, mud, and so forth.
One gives rise to a resolute conviction regarding food, drink, vehicles, clothing, ornaments, various utensils, ointments, flower garlands, and so forth;
then, in accordance with that resolute conviction, it is exactly as it is and not otherwise.
If one forms the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that objects such as sand,
stones, or rubble are mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, or coral,
then according to that resolute conviction, they are exactly as they appear and not otherwise.
If one forms the resolute conviction that the various mountains, such as the King of Snow Mountains (Himavat), are made of gold,
then in accordance with that conviction they become exactly so and nothing else;
likewise, if one forms a different resolute conviction regarding all things, they become exactly so.
That is to say, it follows one's resolute conviction exactly as it is and not otherwise:
if one forms a resolute conviction that a being of beautiful appearance has an ugly appearance,
or forms a resolute conviction that a being of ugly appearance has a beautiful appearance.
One forms the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding both [types of beings] as being either beautiful or ugly;
one forms the resolute conviction regarding both [types of beings] as being neither.
This is exactly according to that resolute conviction, and not otherwise.
Just as it is with beautiful and ugly forms,
one should know that it is likewise with those possessing limbs and those lacking limbs, as well as with the plump and the emaciated, and so forth.
In this same way, one should give rise to other resolute convictions regarding all other material objects whose specific characteristics are subject to change.
All transformations follow according to one's resolute conviction;
they are exactly as such and nothing else.
This is called transformation.
"Coming and going" refers to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who, by virtue of their mastery over meditative concentration,
manifest according to their own inclination through walls, mountains, rocks, and so forth.
He moves back and forth with his body without any obstruction;
as explained at length, he even goes to the Brahma world,
and ascending further up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, he returns without hindrance.
Alternatively, they may traverse immeasurable and innumerable trichiliocosms,
whether going or coming, without any obstruction;
or they may move their coarse bodies composed of the four great elements.
Alternatively, one may resolve upon a distant object as being near;
or one may travel back and forth with a speed as swift as that of the mind's power—
this is called "coming and going."
Regarding "contracting and expanding":
this refers to how Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, through their mastery of meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
are able to contract the entirety of the King of Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*) and so forth into a single atom (*paramāṇu*).
To expand a single atom so that it becomes like all the kings of mountains, the Himālayas,
is called "contracting and expanding.
As for "various forms entering the body":
This means that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, relying on the mastery of meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
are able to [manifest] various assemblies present before them,
as well as all villages, towns, and settlements.
He causes all grasses, trees, forests,
mountains, the great earth, and all forms and images to enter within his own body,
so that the entire assembly each knows for themselves that they have entered inside his body.
This is called "the entry of various forms into the body.
Regarding those who proceed by way of similarity:
this refers to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who, relying on the mastery of meditative concentration, [manifest such forms].
Or he may go among the kṣatriya assembly, matching their class,
resembling them in physical stature, and mimicking their speech and sounds;
if they use such a name for such a meaning, [he does likewise].
It is also by means of this name that such a meaning is expressed;
yet he does not express such a meaning by means of this name,
nor does he express such a meaning by means of this name.
Thereafter, he expounded the True Dharma for them,
providing instruction, exhortation, encouragement, and consolation;
once his transformative work was complete, he suddenly vanished.
After he had passed away, the assembly looked at one another and said,
"We do not know whether the deceased was a deva or a human.
If he were able to go toward the assembly of kṣatriyas...
In this manner, he approaches the assembly of brahmins,
or the assembly of śramaṇas,
or the assembly of elders, or the assembly of householders.
The Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three,
the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven,
the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
The Brahmakāyika devas, the Brahmapurohita devas,
the Mahābrahmā devas,
and the Parīttābha devas.
The Heaven of Immeasurable Light and the Heaven of Light-Sound;
the Heaven of Limited Purity and the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity;
the Heaven of Universal Purity and the Heaven Without Clouds.
The Heaven of the Birth of Merit, the Heaven of Vast Results,
the Heaven Without Affliction, the Heaven Without Heat,
the Heaven of Excellent Manifestation, and the Heaven of Excellent Vision.
It should be known that the same applies to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven;
this is called "transmigration among similar types."
Regarding "appearing and disappearing":
this refers to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who, through the mastery of meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
appear before a great assembly a hundred times, a thousand times, or even more than that.
To cause oneself to vanish and then manifest again is called "disappearance and appearance.
As for "mastery over what is done":
This means that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, relying on the mastery of meditative concentration,
exercise sovereign control over all activities— such as coming, going, and abiding— throughout the entire realm of sentient beings.
If one commands them to go, they go; if one commands them to stay, they stay;
if one commands them to come, they come; if one commands them to speak, they speak.
This is called mastery over what is done (*kṛtyavaśitā*).
Regarding "subduing the supernatural powers of others":
this refers to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who, by virtue of their mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
are able to suppress the supernatural powers manifested by others.
The Tathāgata’s supernormal powers are universally able to subdue all the supernormal manifestations displayed by others who possess such powers;
he brings their undertakings to completion exactly as he desires.
The supernormal powers possessed by a bodhisattva bound to one more birth, or those in their final existence—
excluding those of a class equal to the Tathāgatas.
He is able to completely subdue all the supernatural powers manifested by all other beings endowed with supernormal faculties,
as well as all the supernatural powers of other bodhisattvas—
with the exception of those bodhisattvas who have entered the higher stages and similar classes.
They are able to completely subdue all the supernatural powers manifested by any other beings possessed of supernatural powers;
this is called "subduing the supernatural powers of others.
They are also able to bestow eloquence.
This refers to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who,
by virtue of their mastery over meditative concentration, can bestow eloquence upon sentient beings whose eloquence has been exhausted;
this is called "the ability to bestow eloquence."
"Capable of bestowing mindfulness" means that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, relying on the mastery of meditative concentration,
can grant mindfulness to sentient beings who have lost it regarding the Dharma.
This is called being able to bestow mindfulness and being able to bestow peace and happiness;
that is to say, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas rely on the mastery of meditative concentration.
When teaching the True Dharma, one provides the listener with the benefit of physical and mental pliancy and bliss,
causing them to abandon all hindrances and listen to the Dharma with single-minded focus;
this is a temporary expedient rather than the ultimate goal.
Furthermore, it causes the various elements to no longer conflict or transform in ways that cause harm;
