it brings to cessation all calamities, pestilences, and epidemics wrought by non-human beings.
This is called "bestowing peace and happiness."
"Emitting great radiance" means that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, relying on the mastery of meditative concentration,
emit light from their bodies through the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*).
Or there may be rays of light that travel to immeasurable and innumerable worlds in the ten directions,
causing all sentient beings in the evil realms and elsewhere to cease their manifold sufferings.
Or there is a ray of light that goes to the various celestial realms,
causing the gods of great majesty and power, as well as the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas [to rejoice].
While dwelling within his own palace,
he was awakened by the light, and all [beings] gathered there.
Furthermore, some rays of light proceeded to immeasurable and innumerable worlds throughout the ten directions.
They cause the bodhisattvas dwelling in other world-systems who have been awakened by this light to all assemble. In brief,
the Tathāgatas are able to emit immeasurable and innumerable varieties of diverse rays of light.
It is able to perform immeasurable and innumerable acts of benefit for immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings across immeasurable and innumerable worlds;
this is called "emitting great light."

One should know that all such categories and distinctions within the supernormal power of the transformation of the psychic realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā*) are individually infinite and incalculable;
by means of this supernormal power, one is able to transform other entities that possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because it causes [an object] to become another thing,
it is called the supernormal power of transformation (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā*).
What are the distinctions in the categories of the supernormal power of creation (*nirmāṇa-ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā*)?
Briefly stated,
that which exists without a real basis is called a transformation.
Because one can, by means of a mind of transformation,
create various unprecedented things according to one's desire,
it is called the supernormal power of the knowledge of the basis of transformation.
This further comprises many types:
either manifesting as a body or manifesting as an object,
or manifesting as speech.
Regarding those who manifest transformations as bodies or as objects:
these manifestations may resemble one's own body or not resemble it;
they may resemble the body of another or not resemble it.
Furthermore, whether the manifested body is one's own or that of another, and whether it resembles [the original] or not,
it can only manifest as something similar to the sense faculties and their bases;
however, these are not actual sense faculties.
Furthermore, they are able to manifest illusory objects that resemble real things,
such as food and drink,
as well as mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, and other precious gems.
All external requisites of life comprised of form, odor, taste, and tangibility—
whether similar to them or different from them—
one can emanate all of these according to one's desire.
Furthermore, the manifested bodies are of the same class as himself;
they are not merely one, but many, with various distinctions—
sometimes appearing as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, or gandharvas.
The forms of asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas;
or the forms of humans, animals, pretas, and hell-beings;
or the forms of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas.
If the manifested body is extremely similar to the Bodhisattva’s own body,
it is called a manifested body that resembles oneself;
if it is not so, it is called a manifested body that does not resemble oneself.
Furthermore, there are many types of emanated bodies that are of the same class as others.
If one assumes a celestial body that is extremely similar to the body of a particular deity,
it is called an emanated body that resembles another.
If it were not so, the manifested body would not be similar to others;
for example, when manifesting as a celestial body,
and even up to a Buddha body, one should know that it is likewise.
What is meant here by "manifesting many bodies"?
It refers to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifesting various forms and types simultaneously throughout immeasurable and innumerable worlds in the ten directions.
They are able to perform deeds for the benefit of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings.
Among those various types of beings thus transformed,
there are some for whom Buddhas and Bodhisattvas continue to act accordingly through the power of their sustaining presence even after they have entered parinirvāṇa.
There are cases where, having brought about temporary benefit, the transformative activity (nirmāṇa-karma) ceases;
furthermore, there are instances where Buddhas and Bodhisattvas perform transformative activities solely to allow sentient beings to behold them.
That which is produced by illusion is unfit for practical use;
yet, one may also manifest as food, drink, clothing, mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, vehicles, and so forth, which are no different from real things.
In this way, the various requisites of wealth and food that are produced enable all sentient beings to constantly enjoy them;
this is called the transformation body and its transformed realm.
Some manifest transformed speech;
some manifest transformed speech endowed with wondrous tones;
some manifest transformed speech complete with a vast resonance.
Some emanated speech is connected to oneself;
some emanated speech is connected to another;
and some emanated speech is unconnected to anything.
Some emanated speech is comprised of words that proclaim the sublime Dharma;
some emanated speech is comprised of words that reprove negligence.
This is what is meant by "being endowed with wondrous sounds."
This refers to the transformative speech uttered by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
its sound is profound and far-reaching like the roar of thunderclouds,
and its tone is harmonious and elegant like the call of the kalaviṅka bird.
It is able to move the hearts of the multitude, being exceedingly lovely and delightful.
Furthermore, this emanated speech is perfect, sublime, subtle, and clear;
it is easy to understand, pleasant to hear, non-contradictory, independent, and inexhaustible.
"Endowed with a vast range of sounds" means that the emanated speech uttered by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is magnanimous in its resonance,
manifesting in immeasurable varieties according to the inclinations of beings.
Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas,
asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, śrāvakas, bodhisattvas,
humans, non-humans, and so forth.
An immeasurable assembly filled the entire space of one yojana; with a wondrous,
perfect voice, he proclaimed to them all according to their respective kinds.
Furthermore, according to their inclinations, they may manifest within a small chiliocosm, a dichiliocosm, a trichiliocosm,
or even throughout the infinite and incalculable worlds of the ten directions.
Whether near or far, to all the assembled multitudes,
he proclaims universally with a wondrous, perfect voice, adapting to each type of being;
from within this sound, various tones emerge.
For the sake of all sentient beings,
he expounds various teachings so that each may obtain benefit according to their respective needs.
That which belongs to oneself refers to the transformative speech uttered by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
which produces various sounds from their own transformed bodies.
The proclamation of the True Dharma and the admonition against negligence refers to the transformative speech uttered by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas for those who are dependent on others.
Regarding the proclamation of the true Dharma through a transformed body to admonish those who are heedless and lack any sense of commitment:
this refers to the transformative speech uttered by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Whether in the midst of space or upon non-sentient phenomena that have been emanated, there is that which is spoken;
this refers to the words comprised by the discourse of the True Dharma as uttered by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas through their emanated speech.
Revealing correct principles so that all who are deluded may attain understanding regarding various phenomena,
and admonishing those who are heedless—
this is what is comprised by speech.
This refers to the transformative speech uttered by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
which, for those who have attained pure faith and are not deluded,
reproaches the heedless for their negligence and causes them to feel shame and remorse.
He instructs them in heedfulness and exhorts them to diligent practice.
These numerous transformative acts thus described can be summarized into three types:
the transformation of the body, the transformation of the environment, and the transformation of speech.
It should be understood that all such categories of the supernormal power of the divine realm of transformation are individually differentiated in infinite and innumerable ways.
These two kinds of supernormal power of the knowledge of the spiritual realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can accomplish two tasks:
first, by manifesting various types of supernatural powers,
they lead all sentient beings to enter the holy teaching of the Buddha.
Second, he manifests various supernormal powers to bestow immeasurable benefit,
peace, and happiness upon the many classes of sentient beings who are suffering.
What is the buddhas’ and bodhisattvas’ supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives?
It refers to the fact that, by means of the knowledge of past lives,
buddhas and bodhisattvas are themselves able to recollect their own past lives.
"I had such a name among such a class of sentient beings," as is described at length in the sūtras; furthermore,
one is also able to recollect all the various distinctions of other sentient beings, such as their bodies and so forth.
Just as one recollects one's own affairs without distinction,
they are also able to cause others to attain the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*).
They are able to personally recollect all the various categories and distinctions of bodies— whether their own or those of others— that have occurred throughout the prior limit of time.
"Among such classes of sentient beings,
I had such a name," and so forth,
as extensively explained.
In this way, these sentient beings further enable others to obtain the knowledge of past lives,
so that they too can personally recollect all their former existences exactly as they did before, without any difference.
In this manner, they successively cause him to recollect his past lives as if they were occurring within the present life itself;
furthermore, he is able to recollect all subtle matters, whether few or many, that were previously performed and previously contemplated.
He is entirely without forgetfulness;
furthermore, he is able to recollect every successive moment,
because his sequential actions are uninterrupted.
Furthermore, one can recollect the distinctions of past lives that are limited and numerable,
because the kalpas of time known therein can be calculated;
and one can also recollect the distinctions of past lives that are immeasurable and innumerable.
Because the time periods and kalpas of what is known are incalculable;
to state it briefly,
this knowledge of past lives [extends] to such places, of such kinds, and to such an extent.
They function without obstruction according to their wishes;
this is called the power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas comprised within the recollection of past abodes.
Furthermore, by means of the knowledge that recollects past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*),

he recalls his former births and reveals to all sentient beings the various types of most marvelous and difficult-to-perform ascetic practices (*duṣkaracaryā*) undertaken by the Bodhisattva in previous existences.
It is to cause them to give rise to pure faith toward the Buddha,
to engender reverence,
and to foster a profound sense of weary detachment from birth and death.
Furthermore, by means of this knowledge,
one recollects past lives and reveals to sentient beings the various karmic fruits and maturations corresponding to their previous existences;

this is done to cause those sentient beings who falsely speculate regarding the prior limit of existence— namely, those who hold eternalist views, partial-eternalist views, or the view of permanence— to abandon their adherence to permanence.
What is the supernormal power of the divine ear-knowledge of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?
It refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who, by means of their purified divine ear,
are able [to hear] various sounds of gods and sounds of humans.
Noble sounds and non-noble sounds;
loud sounds and soft sounds;
eloquent sounds and non-eloquent sounds.
Whether it be transformed sounds or non-transformed sounds,
distant sounds or near sounds,
they hear them all completely.
Regarding those who hear celestial sounds:
if they do not apply their attention,
[the sound extends] from the Desire Realm below up to the Akaniṣṭha Palace above.
Therein, one is able to hear all the various sounds of the sentient beings born within those realms.
Furthermore, when one directs the mind toward them,
one is likewise able to hear the sounds of all worlds beyond these.
Regarding "hearing the sounds of people":
he is able to hear all the various sounds of sentient beings born throughout all the four great continents in their surroundings.
Regarding "hearing the voices of the noble ones": [he hears them].
Regarding the Tathāgatas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas,
if one hears from them and subsequently proclaims to other sentient beings various demonstrations,
instructions, exhortations, and consolations.
They exhort others to cultivate all that is wholesome and exhort them to abandon all that is unwholesome;
they are able to hear every sound,
and furthermore, their minds are entirely free from defilement toward all things.
He hears all sounds whatsoever—whether they concern receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, debating, or making definitive determinations;
whether they consist of unerring admonitions, instructions, reminders, exhortations, or counsels; or any other well-spoken, virtuous words that lead to meaningful benefit.
Such categories as these are called noble sounds.
As for hearing non-noble sounds,
they consist of falsehood, divisive speech, malice, frivolous chatter, and harshness directed toward sentient beings.
The various sounds of those born in the miserable realms, those born in the celestial realms, and those born in the human realm.
They are able to hear them all.
As for hearing loud sounds,
this refers to the voices of great assemblies of sentient beings in vast gatherings.
The sounds of being tormented by various instruments of suffering;
the sounds of great wailing and mutual calling;
the roar of great thunder and the sounds of various conch shells.
One is able to hear all various sounds, such as those of drums and horns;
one hears even the faintest sounds.
Down to the subtle sounds of whispered words, they are able to hear them all.
Regarding those who discern sounds,
they are able to hear all various vocalizations whose meanings are easily understood.
Regarding "hearing sounds that are not articulate speech":
this refers to various sounds whose meanings are difficult to discern, such as the diverse incantations of the Dravidians,
the sound of wind chimes, the rustling of trees, and the calls of parrots and mynas.
One is able to hear all the sounds produced by the hundred-tongued bird, the oriole, the yellow bird, the *jīvañjīvaka*,
and others. As for "hearing emanated sounds," this refers to those who have attained mastery over the mind and possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) regarding all things.
They are able to hear all sounds manifested through the power of supernormal knowledge;
as for those who hear sounds that are not manifested, [they do so]...
That is to say, one is able to hear all various sounds other than those [already mentioned].
Regarding "hearing distant sounds":
Except for all sounds within the villages, towns, cities, and so forth where Buddhas and Bodhisattvas dwell,
[he hears] all other sounds, even those throughout immeasurable and innumerable worlds.
They are able to hear them all.
Those who hear nearby sounds hear the sounds that have been eliminated.
What is the supernormal knowledge of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas regarding the death and rebirth of beings?
It refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas perceiving, with the pure divine eye that transcends that of humans,
all sentient beings at the time of their death and rebirth— whether they possess beautiful or ugly forms, or whether they are inferior or superior.
Furthermore, having been born in the future limit, the sense faculties grow and mature;
the body’s various activities—whether virtuous, non-virtuous, or neutral—proceed with their respective distinctions.
Moreover, one directly perceives and knows all luminous forms, subtle forms, transformed forms, and pure, exquisite forms.
From the Avīci Hell below up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven above,
they are able to see and know all without deliberate mental application.
When they do apply their attention, they are able to see the forms of immeasurable and innumerable other worlds, both above and below.
They are also able to see all forms within immeasurable and innumerable world-systems in the surrounding directions,
even unto seeing those various Tathāgatas seated in their respective Buddha-lands amidst various assemblies of different kinds, proclaiming the True Dharma.
It is clearly without confusion.
Furthermore, with their pure divine eye,
Buddhas and Bodhisattvas universally perceive the pure and impure karmic actions performed by the bodies of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
Having seen them, he performs various acts of benefit and happiness according to what is appropriate and suitable for each,
using his purified divine ear.
He universally hears the verbal activities of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings throughout the ten directions— both their pure and impure karmic actions—
and having heard them, he acts according to what is appropriate and suitable for each.
They perform various kinds of benefit and happiness.
This is a brief explanation of the activities performed by the divine eye and divine ear of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
What is the supernormal power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas that knows the distinctions between minds?
This refers to how Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, by means of their knowledge of the minds of others,
universally know all other sentient beings throughout the infinite and incalculable worlds of the ten directions,
including those whose minds are entangled with afflictions.
Whether it be a mind of affliction that is separated from active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*),
or a mind of affliction that is accompanied by latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and bound by them,
or a mind of affliction that is free from both binding tendencies and latent dispositions.
Furthermore, he thoroughly understands the defiled mind and the mind of wrong aspiration—
namely, the minds of non-Buddhists and those with craving and attachment—
and he also thoroughly understands the undefiled mind and the mind of right aspiration.
It refers to a mind that is the opposite of the aforementioned;
furthermore, it is the thorough knowledge of inferior minds,
namely those of all sentient beings born in the desire realm.
It extends downward to the minds of all birds, beasts, and so forth.
Furthermore, it thoroughly and completely knows the middle-range minds,
namely, all the minds belonging to sentient beings born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Furthermore, he thoroughly understands superior minds,
namely all the minds of sentient beings born in the formless realms.
He also thoroughly understands minds associated with pleasure, minds associated with pain, and minds associated with neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
Furthermore, he is able to know, by means of a single instance of the knowledge of others' minds,
all that exists and the very nature of a single sentient being.
In this manner, with such characteristics,
and with such limits, the mind arises and manifests before one.
In a single moment of thought, he knows them all as they truly are;
furthermore, by means of a single knowledge of others' minds,
he knows all that exists within many sentient beings.
Such is its essential nature,
such its categories,
and such its modes of manifestation.
In this manner, as these mental states arise and manifest,
he knows them all simultaneously and exactly as they are, even within a single moment of thought.
Furthermore, this is the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others possessed by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
He knows the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings;
he knows the various inclinations of all sentient beings;
and he knows the various elements and conducts of all sentient beings.

One should know that the ability to correctly establish beings, as appropriate for each, in the various right practices leading to the palace of Nirvāṇa is called the "activity performed" by this [knowledge].
What is the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna-abhijñā*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?
This means that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know, as it truly is, the exhaustion of afflictions;
they know, as it truly is, whether for themselves or others, that the destruction of all outflows has been attained or not yet attained.
One understands, as they truly are, all the means for attaining the exhaustion of outflows for both oneself and others;
just as one understands the means as they truly are,
one likewise understands what is not a means as it truly is.
He knows, as it truly is, that others possess overweening pride regarding the attainment of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*);
he knows, as it truly is, that others are free from overweening pride regarding the attainment of the destruction of the outflows.

Furthermore, although Bodhisattvas are able to know, as it truly is, all the qualities of the destruction of the outflows and the means for realizing them, [they do not give rise to overweening pride].
Yet they do not realize [nirvana].
For this reason, the bodhisattva does not swiftly abandon contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-vastu*) nor the outflows (*āsrava*).
Although they engage in various kinds of contaminated activities, they remain undefiled.
Such power is the most preeminent among all powers.
Furthermore, because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are themselves free from defilement through their knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣayajñāna),
they are also well able to extensively analyze and explain for others how to destroy overweening pride (adhimāna).
One should know that this is called "the action performed.
What is the power of phenomena (*dharma-prabhāva*)?
It refers to the power of generosity (*dāna*), up to and including the power of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding the power of these dharmas, such as generosity and the rest,
one should know that each briefly possesses four characteristics.
The first is the characteristic of abandoning what is to be counteracted.
Second is the characteristic of the maturation of the provisions;
third is the characteristic of benefiting oneself and others;
fourth is the characteristic of the fruit to be attained in the future.
Regarding the four characteristics of giving:
it means that when bodhisattvas practice the perfection of generosity, they are able to sever stinginess,
which is the specific antidate to giving.
This is called the first.

Furthermore, this very act of giving serves as one's own provision for enlightenment (bodhipariṣkāra) and also serves as the means of gathering beings through the practice of generosity (dāna-saṃgrahavastu) to bring them to maturity.
This is called the second [type of giving]:
before giving, one’s mind is joyful; while giving, the mind is pure; after having given, there is no regret.
Thus, at these three times, the mind is always filled with joy.
By means of this, one benefits oneself and is also able to remove for others various sufferings— such as hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and manifold diseases—
as well as the lack of desired things, fears, and all forms of suffering, thereby benefiting others.
This is called the third:
in future lives, wherever one is born, one will always possess constant wealth and happiness;
one will attain high rank and position, and acquire great riches and treasures.
One gains a great circle of followers and a great retinue;
this is called the fourth.
These are the four characteristics of the power of giving.
Furthermore, there is nothing beyond or superior to this.
Regarding the four characteristics of upholding the precepts:
it means that bodhisattvas, by undertaking the pure discipline of body and speech, are able to sever the violation of precepts.
That which is the antithesis of ethical discipline is called the first;
it refers to the pure śīla that one has undertaken and maintains.
It can serve as one's own provision for enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) and also functions as the means of attraction through "acting in common" (samānārthatā) to bring sentient beings to maturity;
this is called the second.
One upholds the pure precepts and abandons the violation of precepts,
[thereby avoiding] the various fears, transgressions, enemies, and other such matters born of conditions.
One sleeps and awakens in peace and happiness, thereby benefiting oneself; furthermore,
through pure ethical discipline, one is free from remorse and experiences joy,
even up to the concentration of the mind, thereby benefiting oneself.
To uphold the pure precepts without harming or vexing others,
and to universally bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings to benefit them—
this is called the third.
By reason of these causes and conditions, after the dissolution of the body,
one is reborn in a happy destination, in the world of the devas;
this is called the fourth.
These are called the four characteristics of the power of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Beyond these, there is nothing superior or additional.
As for the four characteristics of patience (*kṣānti*):
It means that when bodhisattvas practice patience, they are able to sever impatience,
which is the specific counteragent to patience;
this is called the first.
This very patience can serve as one's own provision for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*),
and it can also serve as the means of gathering through "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*) to bring sentient beings to maturity;
this is called the second.
By means of this patience, one rescues oneself and others from great terrors and benefits both self and others;
this is called the third [type].
By virtue of these causes and conditions, it enables the bodhisattva to, in future lives...
There will be few enemies,
little separation,
and little sorrow or suffering.
In this present life,
at the time of death, his mind will be free from sorrow and regret;
after the dissolution of the body, he will be reborn in a happy destination, in the world of the devas.
This is called the fourth.
These are the four characteristics of the power of patience.
Beyond these, there is nothing superior or additional.
Regarding the four characteristics of diligence:
it means that when bodhisattvas abide in diligent effort,
they are able to sever indolence.
That which is counteracted by diligence is called the first;
this very diligence can serve as one's own provision for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*) and its basis.
This is also the practice of the means of attraction through "acting in concert" (*samānārthatā*) to bring sentient beings to maturity;
this is called the second [basis].
By means of diligent application, one attains a state of abiding in peace and happiness.
They are not disturbed by any evil or unwholesome dharmas;
as they realize each successive stage, it becomes increasingly superior to the preceding one, giving rise to redoubled joy.
Thus benefiting themselves, they diligently cultivate the categories of wholesome qualities.
One does not harm or afflict others through body or speech,
but instead causes others to generate diligence and aspiration for the sake of benefiting them;
this is called the third.
By the power of this cause, one will in future lives delight in the distinguished achievements of great beings;
this is called the fourth.
These are called the four characteristics of the power of diligence;
beyond these, there are none that surpass or exceed them.
As for the four characteristics of meditative concentration:
This means that when bodhisattvas enter meditative absorption (*dhyāna*),

they are able to sever the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)— such as the afflictions, speech, discursive thought (*vitarka*), analytical investigation (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*)—
which are the objects to be abandoned by meditative absorption.
This is called the first.
This very meditative concentration serves as one's own provision for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*) and its basis;
it also serves as the means of conversion through "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*) to bring sentient beings to maturity.
This is called the second [benefit]:
dwelling in happiness in the present life for one's own benefit,
with a mind that is tranquil, supremely serene, and free from craving.
To be without harm or affliction toward any sentient beings and to benefit others—
this is called the third.
By virtue of this cause and condition, one's wisdom becomes purified and one is able to manifest supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
In future lives, one will be born in the Pure Heavens and attain the fruits of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
This is called the fourth [sign].
These are known as the four characteristics of the power of meditative concentration.
Furthermore, there is nothing beyond or superior to this.
Regarding the four characteristics of *prajñā*:
it means that bodhisattvas, being endowed with sublime wisdom (*sūkṣma-prajñā*), are able to sever ignorance (*avidyā*).
That which is the direct opposite of wisdom is called the first [obstacle].
This very prajñā serves as the provision for one's own bodhi.
To ripen sentient beings by means of the four bases of sympathy— generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct,
and collaborative action— is called the second.
It is the awakening to the objects of knowledge according to their true meaning.
It is able to induce vast, pure joy,
thereby benefiting oneself;
and for the sake of all sentient beings, it expounds the Dharma in accordance with reason.
Causing them to obtain benefit and happiness in both the present life and future lives,
thereby benefiting others—
this is called the third.
By means of these causes and conditions, one gathers all roots of virtue and is able to perform what is rightly to be done;
in future lives, one will be able to realize the dissociation from the two obstacles,
namely, dissociation from the obstacle of afflictions.
And the dissociation from the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*);
this is called the fourth.
These are the four characteristics of the power of *prajñā*.
Furthermore, there is nothing that exceeds or surpasses this;
this is called the power of the Dharma.
What is the innate power shared by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?
This refers to the natural capacity to recollect the events of various previous births,
whereby, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings,
one is able to endure all manner of extremely long-lasting, intense, and uninterrupted great sufferings without the need for deliberate reflection.
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, one joyfully accepts [suffering];
it is capable of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.
This suffering is for the purpose of benefiting all sentient beings.
He is reborn in the fourth heaven, Tuṣita,
where he dwells for the full duration of the lifespan of Tuṣita.
There, he outshines the assembly of all other devaputras born there by three superior qualities.
First, the lifespan of the devas;
second, the physical form of the devas;
third, the renown of the devas.
When he was about to descend to be born and enter his mother’s womb,
he emitted a great radiance that illuminated the entire world;
he maintained full and clear awareness throughout the stages of descending into, abiding in, and emerging from the womb.
Having emerged from the womb, he immediately walked seven paces upon the ground without waiting for support,
proclaiming his own virtuous titles.
At the time of his birth, there were great and majestic devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas.
The asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, and others scattered various kinds of celestial, exquisite flowers and incense.
They made offerings with celestial music, exquisite garments, banners, pennants, precious parasols, and other supreme articles of worship;
furthermore, they adorned their bodies with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, which are unsurpassed.
Abiding in their final existence and final birth,
they cannot be harmed by any enemies, any demonic armies, or any calamities;
seated upon the seat of enlightenment, they subdue all demons through the power of meditative concentration on loving-kindness.
Every single limb and joint was fully endowed with the strength of Nārāyaṇa;
even from the time he was a young child, without having practiced or studied,
he naturally possessed skill and could swiftly enter into all worldly arts and crafts.
Without a teacher, he spontaneously dwelt alone within the trichiliocosm and realized unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment. Then, Mahābrahmā,
the Lord of the Sahā World, spontaneously descended from above.
He earnestly exhorted him, out of compassion for the world, to proclaim the True Dharma.
His meditative absorption was so tranquil that even when great clouds and thunder arose, he had no perception of them and remained peacefully unmoved.
When he was a bodhisattva,
all birds, beasts, and even the wriggling insects looked up to him with utmost faith and constantly came to take refuge in him.
They will approach and dwell with him according to their desires;
once he has attained Buddhahood, even those as low as animals will come to make offerings,
just as that monkey offered pure honey.
The World-Honored One accepted them with compassion, leaping for joy;
the dragon-clouds constantly waited for his bathing to send down rain,
yet if he went out on a journey, they would cease their falling.
So it is with the Bodhisattva:
when he sits beneath a tree, all its branches cast their shadows together,
shading his body at all times without ever failing or withdrawing.
Having realized awakening, for six years Māra sought an opportunity [to disturb him] but was ultimately unable to find one.
Constant mindfulness accompanied him and remained ever-present before him.
By virtue of this mindfulness, he was fully aware of everything, including the arising, abiding, and ceasing of sensation, perception, and discursive thought.
Furthermore, the Buddha possesses innate power (*sahaja-prabhāva*),
which is comprised either of that which benefits beings upon being seen,
or of that which is comprised within the conduct and abiding of the noble ones (*ārya*).
Regarding the innate power comprised of benefit upon being seen:
it refers to how those in the world who see the Tathāgata recover their original state of mind if they were suffering from epilepsy or mental derangement.
Those with inverted fetuses attain a normal position;
the blind regain their sight, and the deaf are able to hear.
Those who harbor greed and desire become free from the entanglements of craving.
Those who harbor malice shall be freed from the entanglement of malice;
those who harbor delusion shall be freed from the entanglement of delusion.
Such categories as these should be understood as being comprised within the innate power that benefits others upon mere sight.
Regarding the innate power encompassed by the conduct and abiding of the noble ones:
it refers to how Buddhas and Bodhisattvas always lie on their right sides like lion kings,
even when manifesting as resting upon beds of grass, leaves, and the like.
He lies on one side without ever moving or becoming disturbed.
Although all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas may appear to sleep, they do not turn over.
Even when a great wind suddenly arises, it does not move their bodies or robes.
He walks with the gait of a lion or a bull-king;
he first lifts his right foot and then shifts his left foot.
Wherever the ground upon which he walks is high, it becomes level.
The lower ground then becomes high and level like the palm of a hand,
free from all pebbles, stones, bricks, tiles, and the like;
with a mind solely intent on seclusion, he enters the village.
Whatever gate they enter, if it is narrow or small, it naturally becomes high and wide.
When eating their food, every grain is crushed so that no morsel remains unchewed.
Such instances as these should be understood.
This is called the innate power encompassed by the conduct and abiding of the noble ones (ārya).
At the time of parinirvāṇa, the great earth quakes;
the stars flash brilliantly and fall in crisscrossing patterns.
Simultaneously in all directions, a great heat suddenly arose,
pervading the void as celestial music resounded;
such were the immeasurable and most rare occurrences.
All of these are the innate power of the Tathāgatas;
they are not produced by the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*).
This is what is called the innate power of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
What is the power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?
How is it that they share or do not share it with Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas?
Briefly, it should be understood as non-shared by way of three characteristics.
First, because of their subtlety;
second, because of their categories;
third, because of their realms.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, regarding immeasurable and innumerable classes of sentient beings,
perform all beneficial deeds as appropriate through immeasurable and innumerable powers and skillful means.
He knows all things as they truly are and is capable of performing them all;
this is called "subtlety.
He fully accomplishes all categories of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), the power of dharmas (*dharma-vaśitā*), and innate power (*sahaja-vaśitā*).
This is called the category (*vastu*).
Taking all world-systems and the entire realm of sentient beings as the sphere of its majestic power (*prabhāva*) is called the element (*dhātu*).
Śrāvakas take as the domain of their supernormal powers only the two-thousandfold world system and the realm of sentient beings;
pratyekabuddhas take as the domain of their supernormal powers only the three-thousandfold world system.
Why is this? Because they practice the correct path solely for the sake of subduing their own single body,
and not for the sake of all sentient beings.
Therefore, at the ultimate level, the range of supernatural power consists of only a single realm.
Apart from what has been described above,
this refers to the remaining powers of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
One should know that the coarse characteristics are shared with the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas,
and others; such majestic power of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas cannot even be matched by the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
How much more so for all other gods, humans, ordinary beings, and non-Buddhists!
In brief, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess three kinds of miraculous power (*ṛddhi-prabhāva*):
the first is that which is subsumed under the miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-viṣaya-ṛddhi-prātihārya*).
The second is subsumed under the supernormal power of mind-reading (*ādeśanā-prātihārya*);
the third is subsumed under the supernormal power of instruction (*anuśāsanī-prātihārya*).
It should be understood that these three are respectively included within the three types of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-bala*).
That is to say: the power of the supernormal knowledge of the miraculous display,
the power of the supernormal knowledge of the diversity of minds,
and the power of the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.
Chapter Six: Maturation, from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the Fifteenth Section of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, within the First Yogasthāna. What is maturation?
It should be known that, in brief, there are six kinds of maturation.
First, the nature of maturation;
second, the individuals to be matured;
third, the distinctions of maturation.
Fourth is the skillful means of maturation;
fifth is the person who can bring about maturation;
sixth is the characteristics of a person who has already been matured.
What is the nature of maturation?

It refers to the attainment of a predominance conducive to the abandonment of the two obstacles, by virtue of possessing the seeds of wholesome dharmas and through the repeated practice of various wholesome dharmas.
The body and mind possess pliancy and extreme adaptability;
having fulfilled the correct application, one dwells therein,
whether encountering a Great Master or not.
All possess the capacity and great power to realize the abandonment of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the abandonment of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) without interval.
It is like an abscess that has reached full maturity and can be lanced immediately.
It is called "matured" (pakva).
Furthermore, just as a clay vessel that has been matured to its ultimate limit is immediately usable,
it is called "matured."
Furthermore, just as when various fruits have reached their ultimate state of ripeness and can be eaten immediately thereafter,
they are said to be "ripe," so too it is by virtue of possessing the seeds of wholesome dharmas and through the repeated cultivation of those wholesome dharmas that [the mind becomes ripe].
Having attained that which is conducive,
and so forth, up to the fulfillment of correct application,
one is able to realize the purification of the two obstacles immediately thereafter.
This is called "maturation.
Such is what is termed the essential nature of maturation.
What are the individuals who are to be matured?
That is to say, there are briefly four types of individuals to be matured:
first, those who abide in the lineage of the śrāvakas and are individuals who should be matured in the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
Second, those who abide in the lineage of pratyekabuddhas and are persons who should be brought to maturity in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas;
third, those who abide in the lineage of buddhas.
Regarding persons who should be matured for the Unsurpassed Vehicle;
fourth, regarding persons who abide in the absence of lineage and who should be matured for abiding in the happy realms.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, regarding these four matters,
should bring these four kinds of individuals to maturity;
these are called the individuals to be matured.
What is the differentiation of maturation?
Briefly stated, there are six kinds of such differentiation:
first, the maturation of the faculties (*indriya*).
Second, the maturation of the roots of goodness;
third, the maturation of wisdom;
fourth, inferior maturation.
Fifth is middling maturation;
sixth is superior maturation.
Regarding the maturation of the faculties:
That is to say: perfection of lifespan, perfection of physical form,
perfection of lineage, perfection of sovereignty,
perfection of authoritative speech, and perfection of great power.
Human nature is endowed with great power;
because it is based upon the fulfillment of the maturation of the physical body,
one is capable of initiating courageous diligence to cultivate all wholesome dharmas.

Regarding the maturation of the roots of virtue: it refers to having a nature in which the defilements are thin as the basis for applying oneself to the cultivation of all fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) without weariness of mind.
By nature, his mind does not delight in entering into various evil and unwholesome states;
his hindrances are slight and his discursive thoughts are weak;
he is gentle and upright, and he adopts [the teachings] in accordance with them.
One whose wisdom is matured is characterized by being endowed with right mindfulness, possessing a keen intellect,
being capable of undertaking tasks, and having great power.
They are able to understand the meaning of well-spoken and ill-spoken teachings;
they are able to receive, uphold, and correctly penetrate them;
and they are endowed with fully matured, innate, sublime wisdom.
Relying on this sublime wisdom, one possesses the capacity and great power to bring about the ultimate liberation of the mind from all afflictions.
It should be understood that herein, because the faculties have matured, one is liberated from the obstacle of karmic maturation (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*).
Because the roots of goodness have matured, one is able to be liberated from the obstacle of karma;
because wisdom has matured, one is liberated from the obstacle of afflictions.
Regarding "maturity of the lower grade," this refers to maturity of the lower grade by means of two causes and conditions.
First, they have not long practiced, and the causes and conditions for the maturation of their faculties, roots of goodness,
and wisdom have not yet reached full development.
Second, they are habituated to inferior causes and conditions.
Those of middling maturity refers to those who,
regarding these two types of causes and conditions,
lack one while possessing the other.
Regarding those of superior maturity:
this refers to those for whom both causal conditions are present without deficiency;
there are twenty-seven such types.
First, the increase of the elements;
second, the gathering of present conditions;
third, the entry.
Fourth, the gathering of joy;
fifth, the initial point of departure;
sixth, that which is not the initial point of departure.
Seventh is distant purity;
eighth is proximate purity;
ninth is preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Tenth is the intention;
eleventh is the gathering through material things;
twelfth is the gathering through the Dharma.
Thirteenth is the attraction through supernormal powers;
fourteenth is the proclamation of the true Dharma;
fifteenth is the teaching of the Dharma in secret.
Sixteenth is the teaching of the Dharma through clear elucidation;
seventeenth is inferior application;
eighteenth is middling application.
Nineteenth is superior preparatory application;
twentieth is hearing;
twenty-first is reflection.
Twenty-second is cultivation;
twenty-third is gathering;
twenty-fourth is subduing.
Twenty-fifth is self-maturation;
twenty-sixth is requesting others to bring about maturation;
twenty-seventh is the realm of mutual maturation.
"Augmentation" refers to having as a basis the full possession of the seeds of naturally wholesome dharmas,
due to having previously cultivated various wholesome dharmas.
In successive stages, the seeds of wholesome dharmas increase, become more excellent, arise, and remain firm;
this is called the growth of the element (*dhātu-vṛddhi*).
As for "being sustained by present conditions":
That is to say, within this present life, one teaches the Dharma without error, upholds it without error,
practices according to the Dharma, and engages in the practice that accords with the Dharma.
It should be understood that the increase of the elements occurs through the maturation in the present of causes from previous lives.
Regarding "being embraced by present conditions," this refers to maturing through present causes.
As for "entering," it means attaining the dominant power of pure faith.
There are those who, remaining at home, distance themselves from misconduct and undertake the training rules;
or those who go forth into homelessness, distance themselves from all sensual desires, and undertake the training rules.
"One who delights in gathering" refers to one who relies on the path of practice for the renunciation of all suffering.
Furthermore, relying on the practice that avoids the two extremes of sensual pleasure and self-mortification,
they develop deep affection for the Buddha’s well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, the true holy teaching.
Regarding the "initial point of departure":
it refers to first generating a profound sense of weary detachment toward phenomena that should be loathed, and then,
having correctly understood that there is a superior merit in accomplishing the true meaning and principle, one initially enters [the path].
This is called the "initial point of departure.
That which is not the initial point of departure refers to the time when a person who has already entered [the path] is currently undergoing maturation.
Never abandoning the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one becomes increasingly clear regarding the various points of thorough understanding;
through this maturation, one progressively advances toward ultimate purity.
This means that due to indolence or adverse conditions, it may take an extremely long time—
spanning many lifetimes or many eons— before one is able to attain purification.
As for those who are close to purification:
It should be understood that everything contrary to this is [the case for] the preparatory application (*prayoga*),
which means acting for the sake of attaining one's own ultimate benefit (*paramārtha-hita*).
Because they rely upon an intense desire [for liberation],
or because they fear falling into the various evil destinies in the future,
or because they fear being reviled and disparaged by others in the present life.
Regarding the objects of training, one constantly and diligently guards and upholds them;
this refers to the intentionality of performing them without interruption and with profound earnestness.
That is to say, by relying on the patience that correctly observes all phenomena,
one cannot be led astray regarding the Buddha’s well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
and one develops profound faith and understanding in what others have realized.
Because faith possesses merit as its basis,
one who is embraced by the wealth of unwavering, profound conviction toward the Three Jewels and toward the attainment of their own welfare is a "wealth-possessor."
That is to say, to those who lack all things such as food and drink,
one gives all such things as food and drink; or,
to those who lack things that are conducive to food and drink, one gives them.
Giving consists of providing things such as food and drink that are conducive [to well-being].
Gathering through the Dharma means,
for instance, teaching the true Dharma to sentient beings.
"Or manifesting the correct meaning to bestow upon all sentient beings;
regarding 'attracting through supernormal powers,' this refers to one who possesses supernormal powers."
Out of compassion for sentient beings;
or for the sake of purifying the intention (*āśaya*) of sentient beings;
or by the predominant power of purifying the application (*prayoga*) of sentient beings.
He manifests various supernatural transformations and miraculous feats,
desiring that sentient beings, having seen and heard them,
may attain purity of intention regarding the Buddha’s holy teaching.
Alternatively, they may practice unerring application;
because those sentient beings have their minds drawn in by this miraculous power,
some may attain purity of intention.
There may be those who practice unerring application and proclaim the true Dharma;
that is to say, regarding the attainment of their own ultimate benefit.
If they lack the capacity, one should preach the True Dharma to them and provide assistance so that right practice may arise within them;
if they possess the capacity, one should preach the True Dharma to them.

To cause them to swiftly realize supernormal knowledge and wisdom in accordance with their needs is what is meant by "teaching the Dharma cryptically," which refers to [teaching] sentient beings whose wisdom is like that of infants.
He conceals the vast and profoundly deep meanings of the Dharma and teaches instead those that are coarse and shallow, easy to comprehend and enter,
and serve as skillful means for entering the path.

One who elucidates the teaching refers to one who reveals the principles of vast and profound doctrines to sentient beings of expansive wisdom who have already well entered into the reasoning of the Noble Teaching.
Inferior application refers to that which is devoid of both uninterrupted application and earnest application.
Middling application refers to...
That is to say, either one is far removed from uninterrupted application,
or one is far removed from earnest application; thus,
one lacks one or the other of these two types of application.
The superior grade of application consists of both uninterrupted application and earnest application,
which are conjoined together.
"Those who listen" refers to those who develop deep faith and understanding in the Buddha’s words,
and who diligently listen to, receive, uphold, read, and recite the Dharma of the sūtras and other teachings.
"Contemplation" refers to dwelling in seclusion and delighting in the contemplation of dharmas,
investigating their meaning, and attaining definitive understanding.
As for "cultivation," it refers to first correctly and thoroughly examining the signs of tranquility (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*),
and then cultivating tranquility, exertion, and equanimity with deep mental aspiration and joy.
"Acceptance" refers to a mind free from defilement,
[acting] through the preceptor and the instructor.
The skillful means of reasoning are free from error and serve as a basis for practice;
furthermore, one initiates various distinct acts of worship toward that very object.
That is to say, it refers to the practice of attending to the sick;
the practice of providing, according to the Dharma, clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicinal requisites for the treatment of illness;
and the practice of dispelling sorrow and remorse.
The practice of dispelling afflictions and secondary afflictions—
such categories as these should be known as the practice of distinct service.
As for "subduing":
That is to say, it refers to deeply guarding oneself against defilements;
regarding those who have committed transgressions, if they have committed a minor offense, one should admonish them with a compassionate heart;
if they have committed a middling offense, one should reprimand them with a compassionate heart.
If one commits a grave offense, they should be expelled with a mind of compassion;
it should be understood that through such admonition, instruction, and censure,
both that person and others will attain benefit and happiness.
If one expels a certain individual only to receive them back again later,
it brings benefit and happiness to both that person and others; however,
if one expels them and does not receive them back, [it does not].
It is merely to ensure the benefit and peace of others.
Why? Because if others see that person expelled due to having committed a transgression, [they will be inspired to avoid such faults].
This is because one protects oneself so as not to give rise to transgressions.
Regarding "maturing oneself," it refers to personally proclaiming that which accords with the True Dharma.
He causes all sentient beings to emerge from unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states;
as he himself has taught,
he also personally practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
He causes all sentient beings to follow along with his commonality, so that others may not say of him:
"You yourself are unable to emerge from the unwholesome state and establish yourself in the wholesome state."
How does one provide instruction, admonition, and reminder to others?
One should likewise provide instruction, admonition, and reminder to them.
This refers to requesting others to bring [the person] to maturity.
That is to say, there are other immeasurable sentient beings who conceive a superior degree of love and reverence toward him,
or there are others who are skilled in means.
Having well trained in the teaching of the True Dharma,
one should then earnestly exhort and assist them to bring immeasurable sentient beings to maturity;
those who mature together [with them].
This means possessing two types:
either maturing oneself or exhorting others to bring them to maturity, by means of these twenty-seven kinds of skillful means for maturation that have been explained.
It should be understood that this brings to completion the six kinds of distinctions in maturation,
namely: the maturation of the faculties,
the maturation of the roots of virtue, and the maturation of wisdom.
Lower-grade maturation,
middle-grade maturation,
and upper-grade maturation.
Bodhisattvas dwelling in the six bodhisattva stages are able to bring sentient beings to maturity.
First, the bodhisattva practicing through resolute belief dwells in the stage of practice through resolute belief.
Second, the bodhisattva with pure superior intention dwells in the stage of pure superior intention;
third, the bodhisattva practicing correct conduct dwells in the stage of practicing correct conduct;
fourth, the bodhisattva who has entered certainty dwells in the stage of having entered certainty.
Fifth, the bodhisattva of definitive practice and correct conduct dwells on the stage of definitive practice and correct conduct.
Sixth, the bodhisattva who has reached the ultimate dwells on the stage of reaching the ultimate.
When a person belonging to the lineage-less (agotra) matures for rebirth in a happy realm,
there is repeated regression and repeated necessity for action.
When a person of the lineage who abides therein matures for the sake of proceeding toward the three vehicles,
there are countless instances of regression and countless things that ought to be done.
The characteristic:
it refers to those śrāvakas who, because they have previously cultivated various wholesome dharmas,
abide at the stage of inferior maturation.
At that time, there is inferior desire and inferior application;
one still goes to the evil destinies and does not realize the fruits of śrāmaṇya in the present life.
One does not attain parinirvāṇa in the present life.
When one abides in middling maturation,
at that time there is middling aspiration and middling application.
One does not go to the evil destinies;
one realizes the fruits of śrāmaṇya within this very life,
yet does not attain parinirvāṇa in this very life.
When one abides in the highest degree of maturation,
at that time there arises the highest degree of aspiration and the highest degree of application,
and one does not go to the evil destinies.
In this present life, one realizes the fruit of śrāmaṇya;
that is, one attains parinirvāṇa in this very life,
just as it is said of the śrāvaka.
The Pratyekabuddha is also like this.
Why? Because his path is of the same category as that of the Śrāvaka.
The distinction between these Pratyekabuddhas and the Śrāvakas is as follows:
they dwell in their final existence and possess their final acquired body;
by the power of past habituation, they do so without a teacher.
By practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment,
they completely eradicate all afflictions and realize arhatship;
therefore, they are called pratyekabuddhas.
If bodhisattvas abide on the stage of practice through resolute belief, it is called inferior maturation;
if they abide on the stage of pure superior intention, it is called middling maturation;
and if they abide on the stage of certainty leading to the ultimate, it is called superior maturation.
When a bodhisattva dwells in the stage of inferior maturation,
at that time they possess inferior aspiration and inferior application,
and may still go to the evil destinies.
This marks the conclusion of the first incalculable eon;
it is blazing and immovable.
One should know that all the extremely pure and wholesome factors of enlightenment are as yet unassociated [with the mind].
When a bodhisattva dwells in middling maturation,
at that time they possess middling aspiration and middling application,
and do not go to the evil destinies.
This marks the conclusion of the second incalculable eon,
characterized by intense fervor and immovability.
The wholesome dharmas of the category of awakening have already attained correspondence and are utterly pure.
When the wholesome dharmas of the awakening category have not yet attained correspondence [with the mind],
and at that time the bodhisattva abides in the highest degree of maturation.
At that time, there arises superior desire for joy and superior application;
one does not go to the evil destinies.
This marks the end of the third incalculable eon.
One should know that all the factors of enlightenment and wholesome dharmas— blazing, immovable,
and utterly pure— are fully accomplished.
Now, because it is pure and profound in nature, because it is extremely intense,
because it can produce superior, vast fruits, and because it possesses great benefits,
it is called "blazing."
Because it does not turn back, because it does not fall away, and because it constantly progresses toward excellence,
it is called "immovable.
It is the most unsurpassed among the bodhisattva stages.
It should be known that this is called "thoroughly purified.
As for the maturation through the performance of attracting others by means of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), it is as follows:
Whether it be maturation through the teaching of the Dharma in secret,
maturation through inferior application,
or maturation through mere hearing.
These five types of maturation through practice,
even if cultivated for a long period of time,
are still considered inferior.
How much more so for those who have practiced that dharma for a short time;
it should be understood that all other forms of maturation produced by the causes and conditions of ripening likewise follow a threefold principle.
That is to say: if one practices at a low level, it results in low-level maturation;
if one practices at a medium level, it results in medium-level maturation;
and if one practices at a high level, it results in high-level maturation.
Regarding these three grades of maturation— low, medium, and high—
it should be understood that each one further consists of three grades.
Within the low grade:
There are three grades of maturation: the lowest-of-the-low, the middle-of-the-low, and the highest-of-the-low.
Within the middle grade, there are three further grades of maturation: the lowest-of-the-middle, the middle-of-the-middle, and the highest-of-the-middle.
Within the superior grade, there are three sub-grades:
lower-superior, middle-superior, and upper-superior maturation.
In such ways do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas bring sentient beings to maturity.
One should know that there are immeasurable categories of the principles of progressive differentiation.
Because they have matured their own Buddha-dharma,
they diligently cultivate and accumulate the maturation of the faculties.
The roots of goodness have matured;
wisdom has matured;
they are of inferior grade of maturity.
Middling maturation and superior maturation;
furthermore, [the desire] to cause other sentient beings and individuals to [attain such states].
Because they depart by means of the vehicle of the Three Vehicles and proceed to the happy realms,
they cultivate and accumulate these six kinds of maturation.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Thirty-seven;
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Thirty-eight;
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth part of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the first section on the *Yogasthāna*, the seventh chapter, "Enlightenment" (*Bodhipaṭala*): What is enlightenment?
Briefly stated, it refers to two abandonments and two knowledges;
this is called bodhi.
As for the two abandonments:
First, the abandonment of the afflictive obstructions;
second, the abandonment of the cognitive obstructions.
Regarding the two types of wisdom:
First, because the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) have been severed,
there is the wisdom that is ultimately free from defilement and is not bound by any afflictions.
Second, because the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) have been severed...
Regarding the unimpeded and unobstructed knowledge of all that is knowable,
there is another formulation:
namely, pure knowledge, omniscience, and unhindered knowledge.
The permanent destruction, without remainder, of all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies,
and the permanent severance, without remainder, of non-afflicted ignorance in all its aspects—
this is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Because all afflictions along with their residual habitual tendencies have been utterly severed,
it is called pure wisdom.
Regarding all realms, all objects, all categories, and at all times, this wisdom functions without obstruction.
It is called "omniscience.
There are two kinds of realms:
first, the world-realm.
Second is the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*).
Its phenomena are of two kinds:
first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The second is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
These two categories— the conditioned and the unconditioned— possess immeasurable varieties of classification,
which are termed "all categories" (*sarvākāra*).
That is to say: because of the distinctions among the various types of their own-characteristics;
because of the distinctions of their common characteristics;
and because of the distinctions of cause and effect.
Due to the distinctions among realms and destinies,
and due to the distinctions among the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate,
there are three kinds of time.
First, the past;
second, the future;
third, the present.
Because one knows all realms, all phenomena, all categories, and all times exactly as they are,
it is called omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
This is the wisdom that is unimpeded.
When one directs the attention for even a moment,
unimpeded, swift, and unhindered knowledge proceeds throughout all things,
without the need for repeated mental cultivation.
Based on thorough knowledge through a single mode of attention (*manasikāra*),
there is another formulation:
namely, the one hundred and forty unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
As well as the Tathāgata’s absence of strife (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*),
and so forth— this is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi*).
As for the one hundred and forty unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*):
That is to say: the thirty-two marks of a great man,
the eighty secondary characteristics,
and the four kinds of purity in every respect.
The ten powers,
the four fearlessnesses,
and the three foundations of mindfulness.
The three ways in which he needs no protection,
great compassion,
and the quality of non-forgetfulness.
The permanent eradication of habitual tendencies and the sublime wisdom of all aspects shall be analyzed in detail within the chapter on the establishment of the qualities of all Buddhas.
Thus, this awakening is called "supreme" because it is worthy of such [veneration].
For these reasons, it is the most excellent among all forms of awakening.
What are the seven kinds of supremacy?
First, the supremacy of the basis;
second, the supremacy of correct practice.
Third is the supremacy of fulfillment;
fourth is the supremacy of wisdom;
fifth is the supremacy of majestic power.
Sixth is the excellence of abandonment;
seventh is the excellence of abiding,
because all Tathāgatas adorn their bodies with the thirty-two marks of a great man.

It is called the supreme basis for the designation [of "Buddha"] because the Tathāgatas, through their practice of right conduct, bring about the welfare and happiness of immeasurable sentient beings—
both for their own benefit and for the benefit of others— and out of compassion for the world, they cause gods and humans to attain meaningful goals, benefits, and peace.
It is called the supreme right conduct because of the four kinds of unsurpassed and peerless perfections of all Tathāgatas, namely,
the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃpad*).
Perfection of view,
perfection of conduct,
and perfection of pure livelihood.
Because all [qualities] are fully accomplished,
it is called "perfectly supreme.
This is due to the unsurpassed and peerless four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of the Tathāgatas.
That is to say: the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid), the analytical knowledge of meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid),
and the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (nirukti-pratisaṃvid).
Because they have fully accomplished the analytical knowledge of unimpeded eloquence,
they are called "Supreme in Wisdom."
Because the Tathāgatas have fully accomplished the six kinds of supernormal powers as previously described— powers that are unsurpassed and unequaled—
they are said to possess the most excellent majesty.
Because the Tathāgatas have forever severed all afflictions and habitual tendencies (vāsanās) in a manner that is unsurpassed and unequaled.
Because they have fully accomplished the permanent severance of all cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
it is called the "supreme abandonment."
Because the Tathāgatas frequently abide in the three unsurpassed and peerless abidings—
namely, the noble abiding, the celestial abiding, and the Brahma abiding—
they are said to have the most excellent abiding.
It should be known that among these, dwelling in emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness, as well as dwelling in the attainment of cessation,
is called the noble dwelling (āryavihāra).
The four dhyānas and the four formless attainments [are the sublime dwellings].
These are called the celestial abodes.
The four immeasurables are called the Brahma abodes.
Among these three dwellings,
the Tathāgata dwells predominantly in four most excellent dwellings;
that is to say, among the noble dwellings, he dwells predominantly in the dwelling of emptiness and the dwelling in the meditative attainment of cessation.
Among the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), he dwells frequently in the immovable fourth dhyāna;
among the [four] sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*), he dwells frequently in the abode of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
By means of this, the Tathāgata, during the six periods of day and night—three times by day and three times by night—[attends to sentient beings].
He constantly observes the world with the Buddha-eye:
who is increasing and who is decreasing;
whom I should cause to plant roots of goodness that have not yet arisen.
The full explanation continues up to: "I should cause whom to establish the most supreme fruit of arhatship.
Furthermore, because they are the most supreme basis for all Tathāgatas, they are called "Great Beings" (mahāpuruṣa).
Because their correct practice is supreme, they are called those of great compassion;
because their perfection is supreme, they are called those of great morality and great Dharma;
because their wisdom is supreme, they are called those of great insight.
He is called "the one of great supernormal powers" because his power is most supreme;
he is called "the one of great liberation" because his abandonment is most supreme;
he is called "the one who dwells much in vast abidings" because his dwelling is most supreme.
Furthermore, there are briefly ten kinds of meritorious titles for the Tathāgatas that constitute the merit of recollection.
What are these ten? They are:
the Bhagavān is titled the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,
perfected in knowledge and conduct.
Sugata, Knower of the World,
Unsurpassed Charioteer of Men.
The Teacher of Gods and Humans,
the Buddha,
the Bhagavān.
Because his speech is free from falsehood, he is called the Tathāgata.
Having attained all that ought to be attained,
he should be regarded as the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
One should offer respectful worship to all; therefore,
they are called "worthy" (arhat),
because they have awakened to all phenomena according to their ultimate meaning (paramārtha).
He is named the Perfectly Awakened One (Samyaksaṃbuddha).
"Knowledge" refers to the three types of supernormal knowledge (vidyā).
His conduct is as described in the sūtras.
The two categories of śamatha and vipaśyanā are perfectly fulfilled;
therefore, he is said to be "perfectly endowed with knowledge and conduct.
He ascends to the ultimate height and never again falls back.
Therefore, he is called the Sugata.
Because he thoroughly knows all categories of the world and the realm of sentient beings, including their aspects of defilement and purification,
he is called the Knower of the World (Lokavid).
He is the sole Great Man in all the world,
who skillfully knows the supreme methods for taming the mind;
therefore, he is called the Unsurpassed Great Man, the Tamer of Men.
For the sake of the true eye, for the sake of true wisdom,
for the sake of the true meaning, and for the sake of the true Dharma;
it is for the purpose of providing guidance by elucidating the meaning.
Because it serves as the basis for all meanings;
because it enables the understanding of what is not yet understood;
and because it enables the severing of doubts that have arisen.
Because it serves to reveal the profound depths,
because it brings about clarity and purity,
and because it is the root of all phenomena.
For the sake of guidance and as a basis for reliance,
he is able to correctly instruct and teach devas and humans,
enabling them to transcend all forms of suffering.
Therefore, the Buddha is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
[He is so called] because he is able to lead others toward the collection of dharmas that bring about benefit and profit,
and [he is able to lead others away from] the collection of dharmas that do not bring about benefit and profit.
Because he has attained manifest, complete enlightenment in every respect regarding the collection of dharmas that lead neither to what is beneficial nor to what is not beneficial,
he is called a Buddha.
He is called Bhagavān because he is able to destroy the great armies of all Māras and is endowed with manifold virtues.
In some cases, a single Buddha appears in the world;
in others, many Buddhas appear in a single kalpa.
Throughout those various worlds in the ten directions—immeasurable and innumerable—[such occurrences take place].
One should know that there are immeasurable Buddhas appearing in the world simultaneously.
Why is this? Because in the worlds of the ten directions, there currently exist immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattvas.
At the same time, they made a vow to diligently cultivate and accumulate the provisions for enlightenment together;
thus, if one bodhisattva, on such a day and at such a time...
In such a month, in such a year,
having generated the bodhicitta and vowed to proceed toward enlightenment,
on this very day and at this very hour.
In this very month, in this very year—
all is likewise so.
Just as one bodhisattva is courageous, resolute, and ardently diligent.
It is the same for all. At present, we see in this world many hundreds of bodhisattvas simultaneously making their vows.
They practice giving together, they practice pure ethical discipline together,
they practice patience together, they practice diligence together,
they practice meditative concentration together, and they practice wisdom together.
How much more so regarding the immeasurable and boundless Buddha-worlds of the ten directions;
furthermore, there currently exist immeasurable and innumerable trichiliocosm Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions.
Two bodhisattvas simultaneously cultivate and accumulate the provisions for enlightenment;
they both reach perfection at the same time and appear together in a single buddha-field, attaining buddhahood at once.
Moreover, there are immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattvas who attain buddhahood in a single world at one and the same time;
furthermore, one should not say that a multitude of bodhisattvas simultaneously cultivate and accumulate the provisions for enlightenment.
They are perfected simultaneously;
it is not the case that they attain Buddhahood sequentially by avoiding one another,
nor should it be said that all bodhisattvas fail to attain Buddhahood.
Therefore, one should know that when many bodhisattvas simultaneously cultivate and accumulate the provisions for enlightenment and all reach full completion, there are,
throughout the ten directions, immeasurable and innumerable Buddha-lands where the Tathāgatas have passed away and which are empty.
Each attains supramundane enlightenment and becomes a Buddha simultaneously.
By this principle, it must necessarily be the case that in many worlds there are numerous Bodhisattvas who attain Buddhahood at the same time.
It is certain that there is not a single buddha-field in which two Tathāgatas appear simultaneously.
Why is this? Because for a long night, Bodhisattvas have given rise to such vows and caused them to increase accordingly.
I shall alone, in these worlds that lack a leader,
act as a guide;
I shall discipline sentient beings, liberating them from all suffering and leading them to parinirvāṇa.
In this way, the great vows arising throughout the long night are caused to increase accordingly,
so that by embracing correct practice, they reach fulfillment.
Two Tathāgatas do not appear simultaneously in a single world-system.
Furthermore, a single Tathāgata is universally capable of performing all Buddha-activities within a single trichiliocosm Buddha-field; therefore,
the appearance of a second Tathāgata would provide no further benefit.
Furthermore, when a single Tathāgata appears in a single buddha-field,
he causes all sentient beings to accomplish their own welfare with extreme vigor and great conformity.
Why is this? Because he thinks thus:
"In all the world, there is only one Tathāgata; there is no second."
If your work of transformation in this land is completed,
and you depart for other regions or enter parinirvāṇa,
from whom shall we receive instruction as we cultivate the holy life?
"From whom shall we hear the True Dharma?
Having reflected thus, they gave rise to profound desire, diligence, and vigor,
swiftly practicing the holy life and swiftly hearing the True Dharma.
If many Buddhas were to appear in a single Buddha-field,
they would be unable to perform their activities with swiftness;
therefore, only one Buddha appears in a single Buddha-field.
It causes all sentient beings to accomplish their own welfare with extreme vigor and great conformity;
all the qualities of all Tathāgatas are equal and without distinction.
Excluding four things:
first, the span of life;
second, the name and title.
Third is lineage;
fourth is physical characteristics.
All Tathāgatas possess these four dharmas, which may appear to increase or decrease.
It is not through other merits;
furthermore, it is not possible for one in a female body to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is this?
All bodhisattvas, from the time they have passed beyond the first incalculable aeon until they sit upon the seat of sublime enlightenment,
