never again assume a female body; nor do they ever belong to the class of women, which is by nature prone to many afflictions and characterized by much unwholesome wisdom.
One whose nature is characterized by many afflictions and whose body is possessed of much unwholesome wisdom cannot realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
such is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
One should know the supreme teaching as it truly is;
just as one recollects the merit of the names and titles of the ten kinds of qualities, so should one know it as it truly is;
just as it is said that he appears, so should one know it as it truly is.
As it has been taught, its distinctions should be known as they truly are:
because it transcends all paths of discursive thought,
and because it is accumulated from immeasurable and boundless merits.
Because it brings about the production of all the virtues of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas for those who have no higher [refuge],
therefore, enlightenment is realized only by the Buddha.
Supreme, most venerable, most wondrous, and most excellent.

In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth section of the *Maulībhūmi* within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in the eighth chapter on the Lineage of Powers (*Balagotrapaṭala*) under the first stage of yoga (*Ādhārayogasthāna*), the trainings to be practiced by bodhisattvas have already been explained.
One should train in this manner.
I shall now explain it.
The summary verse (uddāna) says:
Abounding in resolute conviction, seeking the Dharma, teaching the Dharma, practicing the Dharma, and providing correct instruction and admonition;
through skillful means, they gather [disciples] by means of the three types of action.
If bodhisattvas wish to diligently train in the precepts that a bodhisattva should study...
At the outset, one must certainly possess manifold resolute convictions;
one should seek the true Dharma and preach the true Dharma;
one should correctly practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
One should provide correct instruction and correct admonition;
one should abide in physical, verbal, and mental actions subsumed under the skillful means of unerring instruction and admonition.
How does a bodhisattva possess abundant resolute conviction?
This means that bodhisattvas, regarding these eight bases of resolute belief,
are fully endowed with a decisive joy and delight preceded by pure faith.
First, regarding the basis of resolute conviction in the qualities of the Three Jewels,
one is endowed with pure faith as a prerequisite and possesses certain joy and delight.
That is to say: first, possessing great resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the true merits of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha;
second, [possessing great resolute conviction] regarding the basis for resolute conviction in the majestic power (*prabhāva*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Being fully endowed with pure faith as a prerequisite,
one possesses certain joy and delight regarding the power described previously.
Third, regarding the basis for resolute conviction in the meaning of reality,
one is fully endowed with pure faith as the prerequisite.
Definitive joy and happiness:
that is, possessing great resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the true meaning as previously described.
Fourth, regarding the basis of resolute conviction in the cause:
preceded by the perfection of pure faith,
there is certain joy and delight.
That is to say, regarding the various non-erroneous causes as they are appropriately subsumed,
one possesses abundant resolute conviction;
fifth is the basis for resolute conviction regarding the result.
Being fully endowed with pure faith as the prerequisite,
one possesses certain joy and delight regarding the various, non-erroneous fruits as they are appropriately subsumed.
They possess manifold resolute convictions.
Sixth, regarding the basis for resolute conviction concerning the goals to be attained,
they are fully endowed with pure faith as their precursor.
It is the joy of certainty;
that is to say, regarding the goal to be attained— unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— one thinks,
"I am capable and shall certainly be able to attain it."
They possess manifold resolute convictions.
Seventh, regarding the basis for resolute conviction in the means of attainment,
they are fully endowed with pure faith as their precursor.
It is definitive joy and bliss;
that is to say, one is able to attain skillful means regarding the entire path of training for bodhisattvas.
By means of these skillful means, one attains the goals that ought to be attained.
They possess manifold resolute convictions.
Eighth, regarding the basis for resolute conviction in well-spoken words, well-articulated speech, and excellent expositions,
they are fully endowed with pure faith as their primary quality.
It is the definitive joy and delight;
that is to say, possessing abundant resolute confidence (*adhimukti*) in the teachings such as the discourses (*sūtra*), verses (*geya*), and prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*).
Regarding these eight bases for resolute conviction,
it should be understood that a bodhisattva possesses abundant resolute conviction due to two causes and conditions:
first, because of having extensively cultivated resolute conviction.
Second, because they have accumulated intense patience.
When those bodhisattvas seek the true Dharma,
what should they seek, how should they seek it, and for what purpose do they seek it?
In brief, it is said that bodhisattvas should seek all the teachings of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka,
the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, all external treatises, and all treatises on worldly arts and crafts.
One should know that among those twelve divisions of the teaching,
the single division of Vaipulya belongs exclusively to the Bodhisattva Piṭaka,
while the remaining divisions belong to the Śrāvaka Piṭaka.
All external treatises are, in brief, of three kinds:
first, those on logic (hetu-śāstra);
second, those on grammar (śabda-śāstra).
Third, the treatises on medicine and the treatises on all worldly crafts and occupations,
which consist of many, numerous, and diverse categories.
This refers to the fields of knowledge regarding crafts, such as those of goldsmiths, blacksmiths, and jewelers.
All such fields of knowledge are subsumed within the five branches of learning (*vidyāsthāna*).
The first is the inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*).
2. The field of logic (hetuvidyā);
3. The field of grammar (śabdavidyā);
4. The field of medicine (cikitsāvidyā).
Regarding the five fields of knowledge pertaining to the arts and crafts:
if a bodhisattva correctly and diligently seeks these five types of fields of knowledge,
they are said to be diligently seeking all fields of knowledge.
The speech of all Buddhas is called the *adhyātma-vidyā* (inner science).
Through how many aspects does it proceed?
In this manner, up to and including all worldly crafts and occupations, which are called the *śilpakarmasthāna-vidyā* (science of arts and crafts).
In how many aspects does this proceed?
Briefly stated, the inner science (adhyātma-vidyā) proceeds in two aspects:
first, the aspect that reveals the correct cause and effect.
Second, it demonstrates the characteristic that what has been done is not lost and what has not been done is not obtained.
The *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (Logic Treatise) also proceeds by way of two characteristics:
first, it demonstrates the characteristic of the excellence of subduing the arguments of others.
Second, it displays the characteristics of the excellence of being liberated from the arguments of others.
The treatise on grammar also proceeds by way of two characteristics:
first, it displays the characteristic of establishing the *dhātus* (roots/elements) and the characteristic of valid proof.
The second [section] displays the characteristics of the excellence of skill in speech.
The Treatise on Medical Science (*cikitsāvidyā*) proceeds by way of four characteristics.
The first is the characteristic of skill in discerning the nature of diseases.
Second, the characteristic of skillfulness in displaying the causes of illness;
third, the characteristic of skillfulness in displaying how to eliminate illnesses that have already arisen;
fourth, the characteristic of skillfulness in displaying that illnesses which have been eliminated shall not arise again.
The treatises on worldly arts and crafts (*śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā*) reveal the various distinct characteristics of the accomplishments achieved through individual fields of skillful activity.
How does the inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*) reveal the characteristics of correct cause and effect?
It should be understood that there are ten kinds of causes which,
when established as non-erroneous causes, encompass all causes,
whether for the sake of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) or for the sake of purification (*vyavadāna*).
Or it functions with respect to various indeterminate phenomena of the world, such as agriculture and so forth.
What are the ten causes? First, the cause of conventional designation (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*).
2. The relational cause (apekṣā-hetu).
3. The projecting cause (ākṣepa-hetu).
4. The sustaining cause (parigraha-hetu).
1. The cause of origination;
2. The cause of projection;
3. The cause of specific determination.
8. The cause of commonality;
9. The contradictory cause;
10. The non-contradictory cause.
This means that because names precede all phenomena, there is conceptualization;
because conceptualization precedes them, they are expressed.
This is called the "cause of conventional designation" for those phenomena.
Because it is in dependence upon this that this exists, and because it serves as its cause,
when one seeks or grasps at various things,
this is called their "dependence cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*).
Just as, in dependence upon the hand and with the hand as cause, there is the activity of grasping;
in dependence upon the feet and with the feet as cause, there is the activity of coming and going;
and in dependence upon the joints and with the joints as cause, there is the activity of bending and extending.
One should understand the characteristic of dependence as the cause in such ways as seeking or taking up food and drink due to the state of hunger and thirst,
and because hunger and thirst act as the cause; one should understand the characteristic of dependence through such immeasurable principles.
All seeds, in relation to their own subsequent fruits,
are called the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
This excludes all other conditions besides the seeds themselves.
It is called the "appropriating cause" (*parigrahahetu*).
That is to say, with respect to their own initial fruits,
all seeds are called the "producing cause" (*janakahetu*).
The fruit produced by the initial seed,
in relation to the fruit projected by a subsequent seed,
is called the "projecting cause" (ākṣepa-hetu).
The various distinct causes and conditions for each different category are called determinative specific causes (*pratiniyama-hetu*).
As for the causal condition of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*):
Whether it be the projecting cause,
the sustaining cause,
or the productive cause.
Whether it be the cause of production or the cause of specific determination,
all such causes are subsumed together as one.

That which is called the cause of common purpose (*samānārtha-hetu*) is so named because it acts as a cause for the production [of a result]. That which acts as an obstacle to the produced phenomenon is called the contradictory cause (*virodha-hetu*).
When these causes of obstruction are absent or relinquished,
they are called non-contradictory causes.
One should know that contradictions are, in brief, of six kinds.
First, contradiction in verbal expression;
that is to say, there is a class of people, whether śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, whose treatises contain internal contradictions between earlier and later statements.
Second, contradiction in reasoning.
That is to say, in order to establish the various objects of knowledge that are to be established,
one formulates an inference that is not consistent with the principles of proof (*sādhana-yukti*).
Third is the contradiction regarding origination,
which refers to the produced phenomena being produced when the producing conditions are absent,
obstructed, or when the conditions for production have assembled.
Fourth is contradiction by coexistence,
referring to phenomena such as light and darkness, greed and hatred, or pleasure and pain.
Fifth is contradiction by enmity.
This refers to venomous snakes, mongooses, cats, wildcats, and mice, which act as mutual enemies and evil associates;
it also refers to the six pairs of obstacles and their remedies that are mutually contradictory,
such as the cultivation of the meditation on impurity in relation to various forms of sensual desire.
Cultivating loving-kindness while harboring hatred;
cultivating compassion while harboring malice;
and cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold noble path while being bound by all the afflictions of the three realms.
In this context, the primary meaning refers exclusively to that which is contradictory to arising.
All such causes are subsumed under two types of causes:
first, the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*).
Second, the causal condition of skillful means (*upāya-hetu*).
It should be understood that herein, the seeds of attraction (*ākṣepaka-bīja*) and the seeds of production (*abhinirvartaka-bīja*) are called the "generating cause" (*janana-hetu*);
all remaining causes are called the "causal condition of skillful means."
Furthermore, there are four conditions:
first, the causal condition;
second, the immediately preceding condition.
Third is the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya);
fourth is the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
It should be understood that among these, that which is capable of producing [an effect] is called the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya).
If the causal condition of skillful means (*upāya-hetu*) is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*),

it applies to all mind and mental factors; however, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) apply only with respect to all minds and mental factors.
Because all those minds and mental factors are governed by the guidance and opening provided by their preceding moments,
and because they are governed by their objective referents,
they arise and proceed only then.
Therefore, one should know that the equal-and-immediate condition and the object-condition are subsumed within the grasping cause;
such are the ten causes.
How is it that they cause the various affairs of all worlds to proceed?
How is it that they cause defiled affairs to proceed?
How is it that they cause purified affairs to proceed?
This refers to all the various names, concepts,
and verbal expressions applied to the diverse crops of the world— those things that fall within the category of grain and serve as material resources for the world.
This refers to barley, wheat, rice, grain, sesame, large and small beans,
and so forth; these serve as the causes for conventional designation in relation to those various types of cultivated crops.
Just as one might say of barley: "take it away," "bring it here," "grind it," or "set it down"—and various other such descriptions according to circumstances;
so too is it with the case of barley.
It should be understood that the same applies to other items such as barley.
It is in dependence upon hunger and thirst,
and it is in dependence upon the maintenance of a weak and inferior body.
Regarding the craving for the flavors of physical food,
the pursuit, grasping, and enjoyment thereof—
these very factors are said to be the condition of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*).
Due to their respective individual seeds,
various types of crops arise in their distinct differences; thus,
those seeds are said to be the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepahetu*) for them.
Conditions such as the earth and rain that can produce a sprout are called "appropriating causes" (*parigrahahetu*). That is to say,
with respect to the sprout to be produced, the seed itself [is the appropriating cause].
This is called the cause of arising.
The successive continuity of sprouts, stalks, leaves, and so forth,
in relation to those crops, whether they have been harvested or have ripened, [is the cause].
It acts as the cause for production;
from a barley seed, a barley sprout and a barley crop arise,
and not anything else of a different kind.
In this way, it should be understood that the remaining [causes] are likewise.
That is to say, those very [factors] are explained as the cause of specific determination (*pratiniyamahetu*).
Thus, all of them, from the cause of dependence (*apekṣāhetu*) up to the cause of specific determination, [are included].
That they all undergo the processes of cultivation and harvesting to achieve maturity is called the cause of common purpose (*sahakāri-hetu*).
It is not that such cultivation and harvesting can reach maturity if even one of these causes is missing.
Therefore, all things that are in harmony are said to constitute this cause of common purpose (*sābhoga-hetu*).
This includes various obstructive phenomena such as frost, hail, and calamities.
The expectation of those flourishing crops is a contradictory cause;
their absence of obstruction constitutes those flourishing crops.
The non-contradictory cause.
These ten causes [apply] to various other worldly phenomena.
It should be understood according to what is appropriate,
as explained at length in the *Saṃgrahābhidharma-śāstra*.
Furthermore, regarding all defilements...
The various designations, concepts, and verbal expressions pertaining to dependent origination—
namely, ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth,
up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
This very [conditioned origination], in relation to those various defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), serves as the cause for their conventional designation (*prajñapti-hetu*).
For example, it is said: "ignorance conditions volitional formations," up to "birth conditions aging and death."
Such various descriptions as these explain the relish for objects in relation to the continuous flow and circulation of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
That [purity] is the condition of dependence for these various defiled phenomena; thus,
within the present life, factors such as ignorance and so forth [arise].
All seeds that have already arisen and grown serve as the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) for the subsequent arising of birth, aging, death, and so forth.
Associating with unwholesome persons, hearing the incorrect Dharma, improper mental attention,
and the force induced by prior habitual practice, which give rise to ignorance and so forth,
are called the "appropriating causes."
The individual seeds of phenomena such as ignorance and so forth are called the "causes of arising.
These range from the link of ignorance up to the link of existence.
Arising successively and inducing each subsequent moment in the continuum,
it serves as the productive cause for birth, aging, death, and so forth, in relation to future lives.
The remaining branches of ignorance and their own seeds, up to and including the branch of existence (*bhava*),
are able to produce [beings] in hell.
The remaining branches of ignorance and their own seeds, up to and including the branch of existence...
One should know that it is likewise for those who are born as animals, hungry ghosts, humans,
or devas. Thus, with respect to those various defiled phenomena,
this [cause] is termed the "definite and specific cause."
All those [causes] from the relational cause (*apekṣā-hetu*) up to the determinative cause (*pratiniyama-hetu*) are called the cooperating cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
This is the contrary cause for these defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*).
That is to say: being endowed with the supramundane lineage;
encountering a Buddha’s appearance in the world and his preaching of the true Dharma;
drawing near to virtuous friends; hearing the true Dharma; and applying the mind in accordance with reality.
The practice in accordance with the Dharma and all factors conducive to enlightenment—
namely, the various wholesome dharmas as they have been described— if these are lacking or abandoned,
they constitute the cause for the non-opposition of afflicted dharmas.
These ten causes should be understood as being able to give rise to all the defilements of all sentient beings,
as well as [to their opposites] regarding all factors conducive to purification and to cessation, which is nirvāṇa.
All various names, concepts, and verbal expressions serve as the causes for conventional designation with respect to those pure phenomena.

As it is said: "From the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations," and so on in detail, up to "from the cessation of birth comes the cessation of aging and death. Furthermore, from the cessation of ignorance come the cessation of the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, and so forth, up to the eightfold noble path. From the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations;
and so on in detail, up to: from the cessation of birth comes the cessation of aging and death.
Various such explanations are given accordingly,
because one observes that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have many faults and afflictions;
thus, one seeks purity and embraces purity.
The fulfillment and purification [of the former] serves as the condition of dependence for this.
A person who abides in the lineage,
being fully endowed with that lineage,
is capable of being foremost in realizing both the nirvāṇa realm with remainder and the nirvāṇa realm without remainder.
That aspiration for purity serves as the cause of attraction;
it consists in approaching virtuous persons, hearing the true Dharma, and applying correct mental attention.
Furthermore, the maturation of the faculties through previous actions is called the "appropriating cause" (parigraha-hetu).
This refers to all seeds of the untainted factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) that are subsumed within the spiritual lineage (gotra).
One regards all those factors conducive to enlightenment as the causes for their arising; that is,
all factors conducive to enlightenment produced from their own respective seeds.
The gradual ability to realize the two nirvana realms— both with remainder and without remainder—
is called the cause of production (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
Those of the śrāvaka lineage attain parinirvāṇa by means of the śrāvaka vehicle.
Those of the pratyekabuddha lineage attain parinirvāṇa by means of the pratyekabuddha vehicle;
those of the mahāyāna lineage attain parinirvāṇa by means of the unsurpassed vehicle.
In comparison to them, [the former] is pure.
Regarding the causes for purification:
from the expectant cause up to the cause of specific determination,
these are considered in relation to purification.
They act as a cause for [others] to engage in the same practice;
yet their spiritual lineage is incomplete,
and they do not encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
They are born in states of no leisure;
they do not associate with virtuous persons,
nor do they hear the true Dharma.
Through improper mental attention and the repeated practice of various wrong conducts,
they look toward purification.
It constitutes a contradictory cause.
When this contradictory cause is absent or departed from,
it is called the pure non-contradictory cause.
One should know that whatever are the discordant causes for the category of affliction (saṃkleśa) are themselves the causes for pure phenomena (vyavadāna); likewise,
whatever are the discordant causes for the category of purity are [the causes for affliction].
One should know that these are the causes of the defiled dharmas.
Thus, there currently exist ten causes of defilement and ten causes of purification;
likewise, those that were defiled or purified in the past and will be so in the future are all the same.
There are only these ten causes;
apart from these, there is neither more nor less.
Within these characteristics, what constitutes the result?
Briefly stated, there are five:
first, the fruit of maturation;
second, the fruit of outflow.
Third is the fruit of dissociation;
fourth is the fruit of human effort;
and fifth is the dominant fruit.
All unwholesome dharmas receive their maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) in the various evil destinies;
wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas receive their maturation fruit in the various good destinies.
This is called the maturation fruit.
Because one habituates to the unwholesome, one dwells with delight in the unwholesome and unwholesome dharmas increase;
because one cultivates the wholesome, one dwells with delight in the wholesome and wholesome dharmas grow.
Alternatively, it is like the subsequent result following and conforming to the prior karma.
This is called the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
The extinction of all afflictions through the Noble Eightfold Path is called the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).
Because ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) eliminate the afflictions through the mundane path (laukikamārga) without reaching ultimate completion,
it is not a fruit of dissociation (visamyogaphala).
This applies to certain individuals within the present life.
Relying on any one of the various fields of craft and industry,
one exerts human effort, namely: such activities as agriculture and commerce,
or the affairs of kingship, writing, painting, arithmetic, and divination.
The accomplishment of results such as various crops and material wealth through this [activity] is called the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
If visual consciousness and so forth arise from the eye faculty, these are its dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Up to and including consciousness and so forth, these are the dominant fruits of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
That the constituent parts of sentient beings do not disperse or perish is the dominant fruit of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Each of the twenty-two faculties can produce its own dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*);
it should be understood that all [fruits] are called dominant fruits.
This is the dominant function of the twenty-two faculties.
Its characteristics should be understood as they are presented in the *Vinayavastu-saṃgrahaṇī*.
Having understood, as they truly are, the characteristics of correct cause and effect as revealed by this inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*), the bodhisattva practices them with diligent application.
It causes the lineage of the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible to gradually become purified and gradually increase.
How does the inner science (adhyātma-vidyā) reveal the characteristics of what has been done not being lost and what has not been done not being obtained?
This means that the karma performed by sentient beings,
even though it has been committed many hundreds of kalpas ago,
never loses its capacity to yield fruit, nor does it fail to produce its result.
Or again, there may be a different action that has a different maturation, or a different fruit that ripens.
Regarding this, the Bodhisattva understands the characteristic of what has been done not being lost and what has not been done not being obtained, as revealed by the inner science (adhyātma-vidyā).
Having known this as it truly is,
one practices with diligence so that the lineage of the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma gradually becomes purified and gradually increases.
How does a bodhisattva seek to hear the true Dharma?

This means that bodhisattvas, regarding well-expounded teachings, should abide in intense affection and reverence for the seeking and hearing of the true Dharma; such is the brief explanation of the characteristics of abiding in intense affection and reverence for well-expounded teachings.
It means that if a bodhisattva wishes to hear a single well-spoken teaching,
even if the path must pass over a ground of glowing, fiercely burning, and intensely hot iron,
and there is no other means by which they can hear this well-spoken teaching, [they would endure it].
If they enter [into the teaching] even with such intense affection, respect, and joy,
how much more so when they wish to hear many virtuous words and meanings?
Furthermore, regarding their own persons, the bodhisattvas—
Furthermore, there is the cherishing of all requisites for sustaining the body, such as food and drink,
and the cherishing of hearing various well-spoken teachings.
The esteem one had previously for the [former] does not equal even a hundredth part of the esteem one has now;
it does not even equal a thousandth part.
It does not even amount to a fraction of a number;
it does not even amount to a fraction of a calculation;
and so on, up to it does not even amount to an *upaniṣad* fraction.
In this way, the bodhisattva develops profound reverence for well-spoken teachings;
they always delight in hearing all well-spoken teachings,
never experiencing weariness nor ever feeling satiated.
With pure faith that is deep and profound, a nature that is gentle and flexible, and a mind that is upright and a view that is straight;
out of love and reverence for virtue and love and reverence for the Dharma,
they approach the Dharma teacher without any intent to challenge or find fault.
Possessing a mind of reverence and free from arrogance,
one strives solely to seek what is wholesome rather than to manifest one's own virtues,
desiring to establish the roots of goodness for both oneself and others.
Not for the sake of gain, offerings, or honor,
the bodhisattva, endowed with such virtues,
approaches the Dharma teacher with a mind free from defilement and a mind free from distraction to listen to the true Dharma.
How does a bodhisattva listen to the true Dharma with a mind free from defilement?
It means that when listening to the Dharma, their mind remains far removed from the defilement of arrogance,
and their mind remains far removed from the defilement of contempt.
He is free from the defilement of cowardice.
By six aspects, his mind is free from the defilement of arrogance;
by four aspects, his mind is free from the defilement of contempt.
By means of a single characteristic, his mind becomes free from the defilement of cowardice:
namely, when listening to the Dharma,
he listens at the proper time, listens with earnestness, and listens with reverence.
He does not act to cause harm, does not act to comply [with worldly desires], and does not seek out faults.
By means of these six characteristics, his mind remains free from the defilement of arrogance.
Furthermore, when listening to the Dharma:
They revere the sublime Dharma and the persons who teach the Dharma;
they do not disparage the sublime Dharma nor the persons who teach the Dharma.
By these four characteristics, their minds remain free from the defilement of contempt.
Furthermore, when listening to the Dharma,
one does not disparage oneself;
by this single characteristic, the mind remains free from the defilement of cowardice.
In this way, a bodhisattva listens to the true Dharma with a mind free from affliction.
How does a bodhisattva listen to the true Dharma with a mind free from distraction?
It is by means of five aspects.
First, listening to the true Dharma with a mind seeking realization and understanding;
second, listening to the true Dharma with a single-minded focus;
third, listening to the true Dharma with ears attuned to the sound.
Fourth, they cleanse their minds to listen to the true Dharma.
Fifth, they collect all their mental faculties to listen to the true Dharma.
In this manner, the bodhisattva seeks to hear the true Dharma.
For what reason does a bodhisattva seek to hear the true Dharma?
It is because when bodhisattvas seek inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*),
they do so for the sake of practicing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*).
To provide extensive instruction for the benefit and awakening of others,
when bodhisattvas seek the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*),
it is because they wish to understand, as they truly are, that the treatises on logic composed by non-Buddhists are erroneous discourses.
It is for the purpose of subduing the various heterodox arguments of others,
and for the purpose of inspiring pure faith in those who have not yet attained it regarding this true and holy teaching.
For those who have already attained pure faith,
he causes it to increase and expand further.
When bodhisattvas seek the science of grammar (śabdavidyā),...
In order to inspire deep reverence and faith in the person of the Bodhisattva among sentient beings who delight in the language of the scriptures;
and desiring to lead them to penetrate the distinctions of glosses, phonemes, and phrases, he teaches through various categories and diverse sounds regarding a single meaning.
If bodhisattvas seek the science of medicine, it is for the sake of pacifying the various diseases of sentient beings and out of a desire to benefit the entire great assembly.
If bodhisattvas seek the various worldly fields of knowledge concerning crafts and occupations, [it is likewise for such purposes].
To accumulate vast wealth with little effort,
for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings,
and to inspire in sentient beings a sense of profound wonder.
It is for the sake of skillfully and impartially benefiting and gathering in immeasurable sentient beings that the bodhisattva seeks all five sciences;
it is for the sake of swiftly bringing to full completion the great accumulation of wisdom for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
It is not that one cannot attain unobstructed omniscience by training sequentially in all these fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*).
Thus has been explained that which all bodhisattvas should correctly seek.
Seeking in this manner is seeking for the sake of this meaning.
When a bodhisattva speaks the true Dharma to others,
what should he say?
How is it taught? For what purpose is it taught?
It is said that that which is rightly sought by bodhisattvas is precisely what is being taught.
Seeking for the sake of this meaning, one speaks of it to others for that very same purpose.
One should speak to others based on two kinds of application:
first, one should speak to others based on speaking in accordance with [the truth].
Second, one should speak for the sake of others based on purity.
How should one speak for the sake of others based on conformity?
It means that bodhisattvas should abide in a dignified deportment in accordance with the Dharma when speaking for the sake of others.
He does not fail to abide in the dignified deportment prescribed by the Dharma.
He does not preach the True Dharma to one who is not ill while seated on a high seat.
He does not preach the True Dharma while standing to one who is seated.
One should not preach the True Dharma while standing behind someone who is walking ahead.
One should not preach the True Dharma to those with their heads covered.
This should be understood as it is explained in detail in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas revere the Dharma;
furthermore, when they give rise to respect for the True Dharma, [they act accordingly].
He causes others to regard the Dharma with the utmost preciousness and reverence, so that they listen to it without disparaging or rejecting it.
Furthermore, he expounds all dharmas for everyone,
teaching them without interruption.
Furthermore, one does not give rise to stinginess regarding the true Dharma nor form a "teacher's fist" (withhold its meaning).
Moreover, one presents the true Dharma according to the sequence of its words and phrases.
It is explained according to the sequence of its words and phrases;
its meaning is analyzed according to that same sequence.
Furthermore, it encompasses both the benefit of the teaching and the meaning of the Dharma.
It should be indicated, it should be explained, and it should be analyzed in detail;
it is not that it fails to encompass the meaning and the principles of the Dharma.
Furthermore, it should manifest that which ought to be manifested.
Furthermore, one should instruct those who need instruction;
one should encourage those who need encouragement;
and one should console those who need consolation.
Furthermore, he teaches the True Dharma by relying on the principles of direct perception, inference, and authoritative scripture;
it is not that he fails to rely on these three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Moreover, what he proclaims is conducive to rebirth in the happy realms.
Furthermore, what he proclaims is unconfused and easy to enter, yet not obscure;
furthermore, what he proclaims accords with the Four Noble Truths;
furthermore, when he teaches the True Dharma in the midst of all assemblies.
He proclaims the teaching according to what is appropriate for each being.
Based on these fifteen aspects, the bodhisattva provides teachings that accord with the needs of others for the universal benefit of all.
It should be stated thus:
How should one speak based on purity when teaching others?
It refers to those bodhisattvas who, toward sentient beings who have committed offenses against them, [act with purity].
One should abide in a mind of loving-kindness when teaching the true Dharma.
Toward sentient beings who engage in unwholesome conduct,
one should abide in a mind of altruism when teaching the true Dharma.
Toward sentient beings who are subject to pleasure or pain, who are negligent, or who are inferior,
one should abide in a mind of benefit, happiness, and compassion, and preach the True Dharma for them.
Not through the predominant power of being fettered by envy, one does not praise oneself or disparage others;
with an undefiled mind and without seeking profit, honor, or praise, one teaches the Dharma to others.
Relying upon these five aspects,
the Bodhisattva’s various pure teachings for the universal benefit of others should be explained in this manner.
Such are the characteristics of a bodhisattva’s exposition of the true Dharma;
briefly stated, there are twenty.
The first is: being timely.
Second, the gravity of the Dharma;
third, the sequential order;
fourth, the continuity.
Fifth is compliance;
sixth is joy; seventh is delight.
Eighth, joy; ninth, exultation;
tenth, non-rejection.
Eleventh, it is logical;
twelfth, it is consistent;
thirteenth, it is free from confusion.
Fourteenth, acting in accordance with the Dharma;
fifteenth, being in harmony with the assembly;
sixteenth, possessing a compassionate mind.
Seventeenth is the mind of benefiting others.
Eighteenth is the mind of compassion.
Nineteenth is not praising oneself and disparaging others.
Twentieth: not relying on gain, honor, or praise.
In this way, a bodhisattva should constantly proclaim the true Dharma for others.
What is a bodhisattva’s practice in accordance with the Dharma?
It should be understood that this practice consists briefly of five types:
namely, the unerring engagement of the actions of body, speech, and mind in accordance with the teachings as they were sought and as they were received.
One should practice right reflection and right cultivation.

If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has prescribed certain dharmas for which he restrains the body, speech, and mind from engaging in action, and has permitted other dharmas for which he allows the body, speech, and mind to engage in action; [one should reflect upon these accordingly].
Within these two kinds of dharmas,
to correctly distance oneself from and correctly cultivate and realize the actions of body, speech,
and mind is called the bodhisattva’s practice of dharma in accordance with dharma, wherein the actions of body, speech, and mind proceed without error among all dharmas.
How does a bodhisattva correctly reflect upon the Dharma?
It means that when a bodhisattva dwells alone in seclusion,
they take delight in reflecting upon the teachings as they have heard them.
Desiring to weigh and desiring to examine,
one should first distance oneself from inconceivable matters and contemplate those phenomena.
One should constantly contemplate with uninterrupted application and earnest application, without any laxity or negligence.
When these bodhisattvas contemplate the Dharma with courageous diligence,
they penetrate it through reasoned observation regarding some small portion,
while regarding another small portion, they merely gain profound faith and understanding.
In all that one contemplates, rely only on the meaning and not on the literal expression.
One should understand, as they truly are, the "black" teachings and the "great" teachings,
and thus be able to correctly enter into the initial contemplation.
Having already attained realization, they repeatedly apply mental attention to ensure its firm stability.
These bodhisattvas are able to do so because they avoid contemplating that which should not be contemplated.
His mind does not fall into confusion, bewilderment, or distraction,
because he constantly and uninterruptedly engages in earnest application with diligence and reflects upon it; thus,
regarding meanings previously unknown, he attains correct understanding and definitive comprehension.
Having already understood the meaning, one attains non-destruction and non-forgetfulness;
because one enters into realization by investigating even a small portion through reasoning,
one does not rely on others when investigating phenomena in accordance with correct principle.

Because they possess only a limited degree of faith and understanding, regarding those extremely profound dharmas that their own meager wisdom cannot fathom, they look up to the Tathāgata and defer to him, saying:
"Such dharmas are the domain of the Buddha; they are not within my sphere."
In this way, one does not give rise to slander regarding the Dharma nor cause harm to oneself;
one remains far removed from misfortune and affliction, free from all faults and transgressions.
This is because when Bodhisattvas contemplate the Dharma, they rely solely upon its meaning and not upon the literal expression.
They are able to penetrate and realize all the intentional language spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
because these bodhisattvas have attained skillfulness regarding all the provisional teachings and the definitive teachings.
Regarding the true meaning, nothing and no phenomenon can overturn or move it,
because these bodhisattvas are able to correctly enter the first stage of contemplation; thus,
they are able to attain the patience (kṣānti) that they had not previously attained.
Because these bodhisattvas repeatedly attend to this very patience they have already attained in order to make it firm,
they are able to enter into its cultivation in accordance with that attainment.
By means of these eight aspects,
a bodhisattva is able to correctly practice the practice in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānudharmapratipatti) that is subsumed under right reflection.
How does a bodhisattva correctly cultivate the Dharma?
It should be known that this cultivation briefly consists of four aspects:
first, śamatha; second, vipaśyanā.
Third, the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā;
fourth, the delight in cultivating śamatha and vipaśyanā. What is śamatha?
This means that because bodhisattvas rely upon eight kinds of reflection as a virtuous support,
they bind their minds and cause them to abide within the objects of focus that consist of mere phenomena and mere meaning, which are beyond verbal expression.
Because one is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and free from mental agitation through the application of attention (*manasikāra*),
one forms resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the objects of focus; thus,
one causes the mind to abide internally, to remain settled, and to be thoroughly established within the characteristics of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Explained at length, up to the one-pointedness of concentration (*ekāgra-samādhi*),
this is called śamatha. What is vipaśyanā?
This means that by means of mental attention cultivated through śamatha,
the bodhisattvas contemplate the characteristics of those very dharmas as they were previously reflected upon;
they investigate them according to reason and investigate them most thoroughly.
The thorough discernment of phenomena, explained at length up to the practice of awakening,
clarity, and wisdom— this is called vipaśyanā.
How does one cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā?
It refers to when bodhisattvas constantly practice śamatha and vipaśyanā through uninterrupted application and earnest application;
this is called the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
What is the joyful cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā?
It refers to the bodhisattvas whose minds remain unmoved within these very characteristics of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
In the state where one proceeds spontaneously, free from effort and all application, and maintains non-distraction,
this is called the joyful cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
It should be understood that herein, to the extent that these bodhisattvas cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā,
to that same extent they dwell with ease in śamatha and vipaśyanā.
To the extent that one dwells happily in śamatha and vipaśyanā,
to that same extent śamatha and vipaśyanā become purified;
to the extent that śamatha becomes purified...
In this way, as the tranquility of body and mind increases and expands,
so too does insight (*vipaśyanā*) become purified;
and in this way, as insight becomes purified, so too do knowledge and vision increase and expand.
This is called that which should be cultivated:
namely, the removal of the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) within the basis,
and the cultivation of pure knowledge and vision regarding all objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
All such tasks to be accomplished through cultivation can be fulfilled by a bodhisattva by means of the four aforementioned modes of cultivation.
This is the instruction.
It should be known that there are, in brief, eight kinds of instruction.
That is to say, a bodhisattva either relies upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or dwells together with them for a long period of time.
Out of compassion for them, he desires to provide instruction;
or it may be provided by other bodhisattvas, or by the Tathāgata himself.
At the time of instruction, one should first carefully investigate the mind.
Having understood the investigation as it truly is,
and having understood the mind as it truly is, one then investigates the faculties.
He understands discursive thoughts as they truly are;
having understood the faculties as they truly are, he understands the underlying intentions of those discursive thoughts;
thus he understands discursive thoughts as they truly are.
Having known the underlying intention as it truly is, one investigates the latent dispositions;
having investigated them, one understands the latent dispositions as they truly are.
Having known the latent dispositions as they truly are...
According to what is appropriate and as is fitting for each,
they manifest various gateways of entry so that beings may enter them;
that is to say, some practice the meditation on impurity.
Alternatively, one may cultivate loving-kindness;
or cultivate the various modes of dependent origination;
or cultivate the differentiation of the elements.
Or they may practice mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti);
having thus manifested various gateways of entry according to what is appropriate and suitable for each, they cause them to enter.
For them, he teaches the practice of the Middle Way that remedies the false attachment to the extreme of eternalism;
for them, he teaches the practice of the Middle Way that remedies the false attachment to the extreme of nihilism;
thereby causing them to abandon the error of claiming to have accomplished what has not been accomplished.
To claim what has not been attained as attained;
to claim what has not been touched as touched;
to claim what has not been realized as realized.
Regarding all forms of overweening pride,
it should be understood that these eight types of instruction for bodhisattvas are,
in brief, subsumed within three points.
What are the three bases?
First, for the sake of causing one whose mind is not yet settled to become settled,
one causes them to bind their mindfulness unerringly to the object of focus.
Second, for those whose minds have already become settled,
he proclaims the path of correct means so that they may attain their own welfare.
Third, for those who have not yet completed what was to be done by themselves.
He causes them to abandon all intervening obstacles;
having understood their mental faculties, dispositions, and latent tendencies,
he acts according to what is appropriate and suitable for each.
One manifests various gateways for entry to cause them to enter;
it should be understood that this is called causing those whose minds have not yet settled to settle by having them apply their mindfulness correctly to the object of focus.
If one expounds for them the practice of the Middle Way that remedies the false attachments to the two extremes of eternalism and nihilism,
it should be known that this is called teaching the path of correct means to those whose minds are already settled, so that they may attain their own welfare.
If one causes them to abandon all forms of overweening pride— ranging from claiming to have done what has not been done to claiming to have realized what has not been realized—
one should know that this is called causing those who have not yet perfected their own practice to relinquish all intervening obstacles.
One should know that these three points encompass eight kinds of instruction. Thus,
a bodhisattva may obtain correct instruction from another.
Alternatively, by bestowing unerring instruction upon others,
one causes the lineage of the remaining eight powers to gradually become purified and gradually increase; that is,
the lineage of the power of knowledge regarding dhyānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
The lineage of the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties;
the lineage of the power of knowing various inclinations;
and the lineage of the power of knowing various elements.
The lineage of the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere;
the lineage of the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of past abodes;
and the lineage of the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth.
Regarding the lineage of the power of knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*),
the precepts are briefly of five kinds.
The first is the prohibition of the manifestation of transgressions.
Second, permitting the practice of what is without fault;
third, if there are those who temporarily commit an offense regarding the permitted dharmas that were previously prohibited,
they should be exhorted and instructed in accordance with the Dharma.
Fourth, if there are those who repeatedly show contempt for and violate that Dharma,
one should maintain a disposition of affectionate friendliness that is free from defilement and unchanging.
Fifth, if there are those who correctly practice according to the teachings regarding matters that have been prohibited or permitted,
one should show them loving-kindness and praise their genuine virtues.
Causing them to rejoice—
know that this is called a brief explanation of the five kinds of instruction for bodhisattvas,
namely: prohibition.
Granting permission;
admonishing and instructing;
and censuring and expelling.
This is the consolation.
To know that these briefly stated four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) possessed by bodhisattvas are called skillful means (*upāya*).
As the Blessed One has said:
"Only when a bodhisattva accomplishes the skillful means encompassed by the four bases of sympathy is he truly called a bodhisattva."
Furthermore, for what reason are only the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) designated as "skillful means" (*upāya*)?
It is because Bodhisattvas, in brief, employ four kinds of skillful means that are subsumed by these very means of integration.
He is universally able to embrace, discipline, and bring all sentient beings to maturity;
beyond this, there is nothing superior or more extensive.
What are the four kinds of skillful means?
First, the skillful means of following and gathering;
second, the skillful means of being able to gather;
third, the skillful means of causing entry.
Fourth is the skillful means of conformity.
If bodhisattvas first practice generosity,
it should be known that this is called the skillful means of conforming to gathering [beings].
Why is this? Because one first benefits sentient beings by giving various kinds of material wealth,
desiring to cause them to listen to and receive what is taught, and to practice according to the instructions.
If bodhisattvas subsequently practice kind speech,
they do so because, wherever there are those who are deluded,
they wish to eliminate all that delusion so that nothing remains.
Causing them to embrace and examine correct principles—
such loving speech should be known as the skillful means of gathering [beings].
If bodhisattvas, having understood those sentient beings by means of gathering them and examining the correct principles,
subsequently practice beneficial conduct to extract those sentient beings from unwholesome states.
To exhort, discipline, settle, and establish others in those wholesome states—
such beneficial conduct should be known as the skillful means for causing entry.
If bodhisattvas, through such skillful means,
have caused sentient beings to enter [the path],
they finally engage in the same correct practice as them, causing them to follow along.
For this reason, those being converted do not say:
"It is you yourself who lack perfect pure faith and perfect ethical discipline."
Having perfected generosity and perfected wisdom,
why would one rely on others for virtuous exhortation, admonition, reprimand, or being reminded?
Therefore, it should be understood that the fourth means of integration practiced by a bodhisattva—
acting in common— is called the "conforming expedient. Thus,
whether taken collectively or individually, the physical, vocal, and mental actions subsumed within these four types of expedients of a bodhisattva [are to be understood].
This is called the three types of action encompassed by skillful means (*upāya*), which are able to correctly gather in, discipline, and bring to maturity all sentient beings.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Scroll 38; *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Scroll 39.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.

In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth part of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, within the first section on "Foundations of Practice" (*yogasthāna*), the ninth chapter: "Generosity. Furthermore, once the bodhisattva has successively brought the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) to completion...
One is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment through the perfection of generosity and the perfection of ethical discipline.
The perfection of patience,
the perfection of diligence,
and the perfection of meditative concentration.
The Perfection of Wisdom.
What is the Bodhisattva’s perfection of generosity?
The summary (udāna) says:
Intrinsic nature, all-encompassing, difficult to perform,
The noble person in every respect fulfilling all requests, Purity of happiness in both worlds—
These nine characteristics are called, in brief, generosity.
That is to say, giving characterized by nine aspects is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
First, giving by its essential nature (*svabhāvadāna*);
second, all-encompassing giving (*sarvadāna*).
Third, the gift that is difficult to practice;
fourth, the gift of all doors;
fifth, the gift of a true person.
Sixth, giving in every respect;
seventh, giving that fulfills requests;
eighth, giving for the sake of happiness in this world and the next.
The nine types of pure giving.
What is the bodhisattva’s giving by its own nature?
It refers to when bodhisattvas have no regard or attachment for their own bodies or wealth.
The volition that arises together with non-greed, which is capable of bestowing all things that ought to be given,
as well as that which is produced on account of it.
He is able to bestow all blameless objects of generosity.
His two activities of body and speech abide in restraint; he possesses the vision of the Āgamas and the conviction that there is certainly a result [of actions];
and according to whatever is requested, he practices giving with those very objects.
One should know that this is called the bodhisattva’s giving by its essential nature.
What is the bodhisattva’s all-encompassing giving?
"All-encompassing" refers, in brief, to two kinds.
First, objects of giving that are internal;
second, objects of giving that are external.
If bodhisattvas relinquish only their own bodies, [this refers to the former].
This is called giving only internal objects of offering. Furthermore,
if bodhisattvas, out of compassion for sentient beings who subsist on vomited food,
repeatedly eat and then vomit up their food and drink to give it away.
This is called the mixed giving of internal and external objects.
As for all other objects that ought to be given by bodhisattvas, apart from those already mentioned:
This is called giving only external objects of gift.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas briefly give their own internal bodies to those who come seeking through two aspects.
First, regarding those who seek the body as a whole, one gives the body to them;
according to their desires, one becomes their subordinate and accords with them.
This is like a person who, for the sake of food and clothing, forcibly makes himself a servant to others.
In this way, the bodhisattva possesses a mind free from attachment;
he acts solely for the sake of swiftly realizing supreme enlightenment and solely for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
However, for the sake of swiftly fulfilling the perfection of generosity,
one gives one's body to them, acting according to their wishes, remaining bound to them, and conforming to them.
Second, regarding those who specifically seek hands, feet, head, eyes, limbs, joints, flesh, blood, sinews, bones, and even marrow:
he bestows everything upon them according to their desires.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas also [act] by means of two characteristics.
One gives external objects of generosity to sentient beings;
for those who seek to enjoy them,
one allows them to use whatever they require, according to their wishes and as they please.
Second, regarding those who seek mastery:
they bestow everything, including their very minds, having severed all attachment.
Furthermore, these bodhisattvas are not without distinctions.
With all kinds of internal and external objects of giving that exist, they bestow them upon all sentient beings;
these bodhisattvas, by means of those various internal and external objects of giving...
Regarding sentient beings, there are those to whom one gives and those to whom one does not give.
What is giving, and what is not giving?
It is said that when bodhisattvas recognize various internal and external objects for giving:
One might cause sentient beings to experience only happiness without providing them with benefit;
or, one might provide neither happiness nor benefit,
and thus simply not give at all.
If one knows that various internal and external objects of giving will certainly bring benefit to those sentient beings, though not necessarily happiness;
or alternatively, if one knows they will certainly bring both benefit and happiness; [one should give].
Although the giving that bodhisattvas should and should not practice has thus been briefly explained, it shall now be analyzed in detail.

That is to say, if there are those who come seeking to become a companion to a bodhisattva with the intent to commit irrational acts, such as coercion, injury, or deception; [the bodhisattva should not give].
In this regard, he does not offer his own body to others;
rather, he acts according to their wishes, remains bound to them, and complies with them.
For Bodhisattvas would rather undergo this a hundred times, a thousand times, or even a hundred thousand times.
They sacrifice their own lives to give to all sentient beings;
they never follow the commands of others to act in ways that please them by inflicting unreasonable oppression, harm, or deception upon sentient beings.
If bodhisattvas possess pure intention regarding the generosity they practice,
and see immeasurable matters for benefiting sentient beings directly present before them,
even if someone should come to request their own limbs and members.
One should not give it away.
Why? It is because that bodhisattva’s intention regarding the gift they are practicing is not impure, nor does their mind become discouraged or weak.
They form this thought:
"This should be given; this should not be given.
This should be bestowed; this should not be bestowed."
In order to purify his resolute intention (*āśaya*),
that bodhisattva must relinquish the immediate task of benefiting sentient beings and give away his own body parts;
this is because his resolute intention has already been purified.
One should not give away one's own body parts while neglecting beneficial activities for sentient beings that are currently present before them.
Furthermore, if the Māra deities harbor intentions to cause disturbance, [the Bodhisattva should remain steadfast].
If someone should appear and beg for one's body, limbs,
or members, one should not give them by breaking the limbs and members apart. Why is this?
This is so that they do not incur superior transgressions or suffer harm,
as was the case with the gods of Māra’s host;
one should know that it is likewise for the sentient beings whom they employ.
If there are sentient beings who, being deluded and deranged with a distracted mind,
come to beg for the limbs and members of the Bodhisattva’s body,
he should likewise not break his limbs and members to give them away.
Why is this? Because he does not abide in a mind of inherent nature,
and because he does not beg for the sake of worldly gain.
Because their minds are deranged and lack self-mastery,
they utter all manner of empty and delusory speech; therefore,
one should not give them a portion of one's body.
Except for those cases already mentioned and their opposites,
if someone comes seeking the limbs and members of a bodhisattva’s body,
one should give that body to them according to their desire.
He acts according to their wishes, remains bound to them,
complies with them,
and even gives away his own limbs and members to them.
It should be understood that these are called the internal objects of a bodhisattva’s giving—
those which may be given and those which should not be given.
Furthermore, regarding the external objects of a bodhisattva’s giving:
If there are sentient beings who come seeking such things as poison, fire, weapons,
or alcohol— whether for their own harm or to harm others—
one should not give them these.
If there are sentient beings who come seeking such things as poison, fire, weapons, or alcohol— whether for their own benefit or for the benefit of others—
a Bodhisattva should indeed grant them.
Furthermore, a Bodhisattva does not practice giving with objects that belong to others or over which they have no consent.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas do not act as matchmakers, nor do they practice giving by means of the wives or concubines of others.
Moreover, bodhisattvas do not bestow gifts such as food or drink that contain living insects.
Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who come seeking various objects for giving that lead to frivolous pleasure or lead to what is meaningless,
a bodhisattva should not grant them.
Why is this? Because when giving to them,
although it may temporarily cause them to feel joy toward the Bodhisattva, [the benefit does not endure].
Furthermore, it causes them to perform various kinds of unbeneficial actions;
that is to say, because of such giving, they engage extensively in arrogance and heedless misconduct,
and after the dissolution of the body, they fall into the evil destinies.
Even if one bestows various implements for play and amusement,
they shall not cause sentient beings to fall into the evil destinies,
nor shall they increase their unwholesome roots.
The bodhisattva, desiring that those sentient beings, by means of these gifts of amusements and enjoyments, may be gathered and benefited,
and that their minds may give rise to pure faith, becoming easy to guide and easy to bring to maturity.
They bestow everything according to whatever is requested.
Regarding these bodhisattvas, if there are those who come seeking various forms of amusement and pleasure,
what should be given and what should not be given?
That is to say, Bodhisattvas never bestow upon others methods such as hunting and the like.
Furthermore, within various impure sacrificial rites,
they employ great skillful means to gather many sentient beings together.
To harm their lives would incur immeasurable sin; therefore,
one should never perform such sacrifices oneself, nor incite others to do so,
nor conduct animal sacrifices by slaughtering sheep within the temples of those deities.
If there are immeasurable sentient beings who come seeking a place of refuge, whether by water or on land,
and if a person intends to kill those beings for their sake,
the Bodhisattva, having understood this, will never grant it.
If there are those who come seeking nets, snares, or traps—
whether for the purpose of harming sentient beings or for the sake of practice—
he shall not give them to anyone.
If an enemy comes seeking retribution for a grievance—
desiring to revile, bind, kill, plunder their wealth, or inflict punishment—
one never grants it to them.
In brief, whatever instruments of play,
sport, and so forth there may be that oppress or harm other sentient beings,
should anyone come seeking them—
None of these bodhisattvas give them away;
nor do they give various elephants, horses,
chariots, clothing, or ornaments.
Exquisite food and drink;
the practice of song and dance and so forth;
as well as musical instruments, ointments, fragrant garlands, and precious playthings.
There were parks, groves, towers, pavilions, and residences;
female attendants trained in various arts and crafts;
and all such implements for play and pleasure.
Desiring to cause them to give rise to pure faith toward the Bodhisattva,
he gives everything away to those who come to ask for it.
Furthermore, if there are bodhisattvas who have fallen ill,
they shall not bestow upon those who come seeking it food or drink that is either excessive or unsuitable.
Likewise, if there are sentient beings who, having already eaten their fill, are by nature excessively gluttonous, [they shall not provide such food].
They repeatedly come to beg for rare and exquisite food and drink,
yet he does not give it to them.
Furthermore, when sentient beings are oppressed by sorrow and anxiety...
If they seek to kill themselves, strike their own bodies,
consume poison, fall from cliffs, cast themselves into abysses, or throw themselves into fire,
one must never grant them their desires.
Furthermore, if there are those who come seeking [the gift of] their parents or teachers,
a bodhisattva must certainly not grant it. Why is this?
Because Bodhisattvas, toward their parents, honored teachers, elders, and even those who have shown them the slightest kindness by nursing and raising them,
constantly contemplate carrying them upon the crown of their heads throughout the long night of saṃsāra without ever becoming weary.
Constantly maintaining the thought that one's own body is subject to and compliant with whatever may be done to it— whether slaughtered, beaten, bound, or sold—
one does not even dare to harbor a secret intention to give,
let alone openly bestow it upon those who come to beg.
Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas become consecrated kings,
exercising sovereign authority over a territory,
they [behave] toward all the officials and commoners within their own realm.
He never seizes the wives or children of others to give them away to someone else;
rather, he gives as alms only villages, towns, settlements, or lands,
whether in their entirety or in part.
And he addressed him, saying:
"Just as my grace and transformation have been,
so should yours likewise be."
Furthermore, if bodhisattvas do not first use correct speech to inform and persuade their own wives, children, slaves, servants,
and kinsmen so as to make them joyful, [they commit an offense].
He never compels those who come seeking gifts to feel distress or anxiety;
rather, he first uses correct speech to instruct and persuade them, causing them to rejoice and give rise to a mind of joyful aspiration.
One does not bestow medicine upon enemies, evil associates, yakṣas, rākṣasas, or those of violent occupation.
Nor does one give one's wife or children—regardless of their appearance or frailty—to those who come seeking them as slaves, even if they belong to noble families.
Furthermore, if there are bodhisattvas who seek the throne of a king— being those who severely afflict sentient beings and take pleasure in practicing various forms of violent and evil deeds—
the bodhisattvas will never grant it to them.
If such a violent and wicked person has previously occupied the royal throne,
a bodhisattva who possesses the power should even depose them,
let alone grant [the throne] to them.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas never encroach upon or seize the property of their parents,
wives, children, slaves, servants,
or kinsmen and relatives.
He uses all his wealth and possessions for the purpose of giving as alms,
and he does not cause distress to his parents, wife, children,
slaves, servants, or laborers.
Relatives and kinsmen give the objects they have been given to those who come seeking them;
furthermore, all bodhisattvas [give] by means of the True Dharma.
One accumulates wealth without violence or abruptness and practices giving;
one does not do so through unrighteous means or by violent means.
Furthermore, they do not practice giving by coercing or harming others.
Moreover, if bodhisattvas have gone forth within the holy teachings of the Buddhas,
they never transgress any of the precepts.
And they practice giving.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice generosity,
they do so toward all classes of sentient beings without exception.
They give gifts while maintaining a mind of equanimity and dwelling in the perception of the field of merit, never making distinctions between enemies, friends, or neutral parties;
between those with virtue and those with faults; between inferior, equal, or superior classes; or between those who experience suffering and those who experience happiness.
Furthermore, as previously stated and as previously promised,
Bodhisattvas never give less than what was requested to those who come seeking;
they give to them either an equal amount, or more, or even more.
Furthermore, Bodhisattvas never first promise superior and excellent wealth and later give something inferior;
rather, if they have first promised inferior wealth, they may subsequently give something superior and excellent if such is available.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas do not practice giving with a distracted mind or with a mind agitated by anger. Moreover,
once they have given, bodhisattvas never praise themselves or repeatedly proclaim their own deeds.
He says, "I have previously bestowed such and such gifts upon you;
I have gathered you in, nurtured you, and rescued you.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice giving toward those who are lowly and humble:
One should not even give without respect or by tossing it carelessly;
how much less so when the recipient possesses virtue?
Furthermore, if a petitioner comes to a bodhisattva...
They remain settled in various forms of transgression, misconduct, agitation, and restlessness,
failing to guard themselves; they are intent on reviling, anger, and reproaching others,
and never for a moment give rise to misconduct toward them, nor do they practice generosity with a mind of weariness or aversion.
He understands that it is precisely because he has been seduced by the afflictions that his original nature has been altered;
thus, dwelling even more deeply in a heart of compassion, he practices giving.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas do not practice giving based on false attachments arising from wrong views;
that is to say, they do not consider the killing of living beings in vast and cruel sacrifices to be a religious dharma.
Furthermore, they do not practice giving by falsely grasping at signs that correspond to auspicious omens or favorable responses.
Moreover, bodhisattvas never falsely calculate that it is only when all aspects are utterly pure that they should practice the bestowal of gifts.
That is to say, it is the mundane and supramundane purity that is free from desire;
one simply discerns and understands that the practice of giving is merely the provision for that purity free from desire.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas do not practice giving with a view toward its results;
rather, they dedicate all acts of giving so as to swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas understand, as it truly is, all varieties of practiced generosity and all varieties of the ripening of the fruits of giving;
they thus give rise to profound faith and understanding.
One practices giving without depending on external conditions and without being led by others, namely:
giving food and drink can induce great strength;
giving various garments can induce excellent complexion.
Giving vehicles brings about the attainment of happiness;
giving lamps brings about the attainment of pure eyes.
One should understand that such categories are explained at length in this manner.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas do not practice giving out of fear of their own poverty;
they practice giving solely through the intentional resolve of compassion for sentient beings.
Furthermore, when seekers come to them, bodhisattvas never bestow upon them items that are inappropriate;
that is to say, they do not give such things to those who have gone forth into the religious life.
Leftover food and drink,
or various excretions, mucus, saliva, vomit, pus, and blood—
anything mixed with or defiled by such impurities.
Furthermore, one does not confess it nor cause others to know of it,
as in the case of the rule for discarding things such as when giving gruel or rice to someone who does not eat onions.
This refers to those who abstain from eating leeks.
To those who do not eat leeks, one gives food and drink mixed with leeks or stained by leeks;
to those who do not eat meat,
one gives food and drink mixed with meat or stained by meat.
To those who do not drink alcohol,
one gives food and drink mixed with or tainted by alcohol;
or else, one practices giving by engaging them in activities that are inconsistent with proper decorum.
A bodhisattva does not perform such types of improper giving. Furthermore,
a bodhisattva does not cause a seeker to come repeatedly, to go back and forth, to become attached, to comply, to remain dependent, or to become weary before finally giving.
He gives immediately upon someone's merely coming to request it.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas do not practice giving based on worldly fame or praise,
nor do they practice giving based on the expectation of receiving a reciprocal repayment of their kindness.
One does not practice giving for the sake of attaining the fruits of Śakra, Māra, a Wheel-Turning King, or Īśvara;
nor does one bestow gifts for the purpose of deceiving or seducing others.
That is to say, one desires to cause other kings,
ministers, cities, towns, villages,
various brahmins, wealthy merchants, and householders to abound in riches and treasures.
"A great and wealthy merchant, a donor and benefactor, gives because he knows that I practice giving;
he surely practices this act of charity because he intends to honor, respect, praise, and make offerings to me."
Furthermore, one practices generosity without narrow-mindedness;
that is, even when wealth is meager, one gives with a broad mind,
let alone when wealth is abundant.
Furthermore, one does not practice giving with the intent to deceive others;
that is to say, one does not first give a small amount to another in order to cause them to develop attachment or to become personally attached to oneself.
Thereafter, it will perish.
Furthermore, one does not practice giving for the sake of alienating others, thinking,
"I shall alienate this village or town by means of my gift."
He causes a portion of the villages to become separated from the kingdom,
and he causes a portion of the kingdom to turn away from their sovereign and come under his own authority.
Furthermore, these bodhisattvas are diligent and free from indolence.
Arousing resolve and being fully endowed with vigor and sharpness, one adorns oneself;
first practicing giving oneself, one subsequently exhorts others to give.
One does not remain indolent oneself while exhorting others to practice giving with diligence.
Furthermore, when immeasurable multitudes gather together to beg for alms,
he understands as they truly are those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them;
according to their seniority and juniority, he has them sit in proper order.
From top to bottom, they circulate and return,
exhausting all their various goods and distributing them to others.
Furthermore, these bodhisattvas currently possess immeasurable and vast wealth and resources.
They never practice limited giving.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas do not give gifts while causing harm or distress to others;
that is to say, they do not revile, strike, threaten, or humiliate them.
They bind, harm, imprison,
cut, pierce, drive away, and banish from here to there. Furthermore,
bodhisattvas experience joy before giving, a pure mind while giving, and no regret after giving.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas do not practice giving with deceit or guile;
that is to say, they never give things that are not genuine, such as counterfeit mani-jewels,
pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, or cowries.
They give precious objects such as jade, pearls,
and coral to those who hope for true jewels;
furthermore, there is no wealth belonging to bodhisattvas— whether small or great— that they do not apply their minds to giving.
First giving to all subsequent supplicants is like taking one's own wealth;
when the Bodhisattva gives, it is as if returning that very object to them.
Furthermore, Bodhisattvas give at the proper time and not at an improper time.
One gives pure offerings from oneself and others, not impure ones;
one gives in accordance with proper conduct, not improper conduct;
and one gives with an undistracted mind, not with a scattered mind.
Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas see those who come to them seeking something, they never mock or deride them;
nor do they cause them to feel shame or embarrassment,
nor do they frown.
With a relaxed countenance and level gaze, he smiles first and speaks before others;
he never delays, bestowing gifts with rapidity.
Furthermore, even when other bodhisattvas do not seek it, they freely offer what is requested.
