Whatever is sought, they give in accordance with that need;
they always cause the joy of those who seek to arise as they take what they desire.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas do not practice giving with impaired wisdom.
One always practices giving with skillful wisdom.
What is the skillful wisdom of a bodhisattva’s giving?
It refers to when bodhisattvas possess various kinds of material wealth suitable for giving.
Even before a petitioner has arrived, one first gives rise to this thought:
"Suppose two petitioners were to come to me at the same time—
one being one who seeks peace and happiness."
The first is not poor and not lowly, having support and protection;
the second is in peril and suffering,
being poor and lowly, without support or protection.
At that time, I should personally evaluate all my wealth;
if it is sufficient to fully satisfy the wishes of both,
I should give to both so that their wishes are fulfilled and they are satisfied.
If his wealth is insufficient to fully satisfy both and fulfill their wishes,
he should employ skillful means to send them away safely and happily, ensuring they are neither poor nor lowly, and that they have support and protection.
Giving away all that one possesses to those who are in peril and suffering— those who are poor, lowly, and without refuge or protector—
one resolves upon this intention and then accomplishes such deeds exactly as they have been conceived.
When those who come seeking happiness and other such things cannot be fully satisfied by one’s power,
one should first employ skillful means to reflect with a sincere mind before declining them and sending them away.
"I have already relinquished and promised these objects of my gift to those in peril and suffering;
therefore, I give them to them now, not because I lack the desire to give to you,
but simply because I no longer have the power."
I only pray, O Noble One,
that you do not harbor resentment toward me or turn your back on me.
Furthermore, these bodhisattvas currently possess various kinds of material wealth fit for giving.
He knows there is a stingy household, an extremely stingy household, which is miserly regarding its wealth and treasures, so rigidly attached that it trembles with fear;
in that house, they have never bestowed anything in charity upon any śramaṇas, brahmins, or others.
The bodhisattva then went to his house,
and with greetings of well-being and through skillful means of respectful compliance,
he said to him, "Come here."
"I shall not allow your storehouses to be depleted;
rather, I will provide you with great benefit in the present.
My household currently possesses vast wealth and treasures, as well as abundant goods for distribution."
"In order to fulfill my perfection of generosity,
if any seeker comes to you, do not let them return empty-handed.
You may go to my house and take as much wealth and treasure as you wish to give away."
"If there should be a seeker who comes to me,
when I practice giving, you should give rise to sympathetic joy toward this gift.
Upon hearing this, they will feel great delight.
Since my treasury has not been diminished at all,
yet I have also fulfilled the wishes of that good son,
you should therefore comply with his request and accomplish what he intends to do.
In this way, the bodhisattva causes them to gradually plant the seeds for the future subduing of stinginess.
Through skillful means preceded by wisdom,
he causes them to gradually practice the relinquishing of their own small amounts of wealth.
Based on the lower degree of non-attachment, one advances to attain the middle degree;
based on the middle degree of non-attachment, one advances to attain the superior degree.
Furthermore, regarding the preceptors and instructors of all bodhisattvas:
Co-resident disciples and fellow practitioners of the holy life who are by nature stingy and greedy,
or who belong to the class of those who are stingy and greedy;
or even those whose nature is not of the class of stinginess and greed.
Yet, lacking the necessary resources and being destitute of what they desire,
when a bodhisattva wishes to plant and cultivate the meritorious karma of giving within the fields of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha,
he gives away the objects intended for donation to those [poor people] and has them perform the act, while he himself does not do so.
Through such skillful wisdom and expedient means,
the bodhisattva’s own generated merit becomes even more vast and abundant;
furthermore, he causes a class of fellow practitioners of the holy life to subdue all afflictions of stinginess and greed.
Furthermore, it causes the aspirations of those who delight in wholesome dharmas to be fulfilled;
it gathers in sentient beings and brings them to maturity.
Moreover, bodhisattvas currently possess abundant material wealth that may be given as gifts.
Seeing those who came with signs of longing,
he understood their minds and bestowed upon them everything according to their desires.
Furthermore, there was a merchant of a deceitful nature who wished to practice fraud.
Having understood this, the bodhisattva still conceals their own faults so as not to let others know them,
much less provoke them;
he fulfills their wishes so that they may be free from shame.
Leaping for joy and free from fear, they departed with great delight.
Furthermore, there were others who practiced deceit and fraud;
the Bodhisattva did not perceive them at first, but became aware of them later.
Even though he is aware of it, he does not bring this matter to the person's attention,
nor does he reprimand him; rather,
he merely brings it to his mind out of compassion.
"He committed such an act of taking what was not given against me through error;
I now rejoice in this so that he may be free from guilt.
Such are the types of [expressions].
It should be known that this is called a bodhisattva who, possessing material wealth available for giving, practices skillful wisdom in bestowing it.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva currently possesses no material wealth available for giving...
The mental attention toward those various worldly crafts and occupations with which he was previously familiar becomes manifest;
with little exertion of effort, he accumulates great wealth and bestows it upon all sentient beings.
These bodhisattvas, moreover, for the sake of others, proclaim the true Dharma using various kinds of exquisite and skillful speech,
causing even those who are impoverished and suffering to take pleasure in practicing generosity.
How much more so for those who possess wealth and pleasure;
they can still practice giving even when they are prone to stinginess and greed.
How much more so for those who have habituated themselves to generosity?
Or there may be a family with pure faith and abundant wealth that constantly delights in giving;
one repeatedly instructs beggars to go there to solicit alms so that they may practice generosity.
Or, when that family bestows gifts and cultivates meritorious deeds, [one encourages them].
He went in person to that place with diligent effort and without indolence;
endowed with the exertion of a resolute mind and filled with deep joy,
he assisted with both body and speech according to his strength and ability.
He causes those who seek gifts to obtain wholesome satisfaction;
for at the time of giving, they may lack sufficient resources or provide poor-quality offerings.
Either falling into factionalism,
or lacking respect,
or losing mindfulness.
Due to the assistance of virtue,
none of these faults exist.
Thus, although the bodhisattva appears to lack material wealth, [he is not truly destitute].
They practice generosity through skillful means and wisdom.
This description applies until they have realized the superiorly pure intention (*adhyāśaya*).
If bodhisattvas have already realized the superiorly pure intention, [they act otherwise].
Just as they have already attained transcendence over all evil destinies,
so too in every birth they will certainly obtain inexhaustible wealth and treasures.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas never orally transmit teachings that seek out the faults of non-Buddhists.
One should not bestow any of the True Dharma upon them.
Furthermore, one should not give it to those who, having written out the scriptures, are known to be of a greedy nature, seeking after gain, and intent on trafficking in scriptural volumes.
Knowing that [the recipient] harbors secret attachments, one does not bestow [the teaching].
Not seeking superior wisdom, one likewise does not bestow it;
rather, one must seek superior wisdom.
If one has personally realized that the meaning [of the teaching] regarding such things as the scriptural volumes has already been explained,
one should then bestow them accordingly, as desired.
If he realizes for himself that the meaning of a scripture or similar text has not yet been discerned,
he constantly examines it himself in order to discern that meaning.
Likewise, if a bodhisattva sees another person who possesses a scripture or similar text...
One should immediately employ skillful means to seek out and give it,
or else transcribe it further and bestow it.
This applies even if no other copies of the sūtra or similar texts are found.
Furthermore, if one lacks the power or ability to transcribe it,
one should carefully and thoroughly examine one's own mind:
"Is it not that the stain of stinginess regarding the Dharma has entangled my mind, such that I am unable to give?"
"Is it that I am hindered by some ulterior motive regarding the Dharma and thus do not wish to give?
Or is it that I have something superior required for the sake of the Dharma and therefore should not give?
Having thus scrutinized his mind with careful observation.
If one recognizes for oneself that one has not given because of being slightly fettered by stinginess regarding this Dharma or being hindered by a private intention,
one should immediately form this thought:
"I must now resolutely practice the gift of the Dharma."
Even if, by virtue of practicing this Dharma-giving,
I were to become deluded and mute in this present life,
I should still practice Dharma-giving, for I cannot endure the afflictions.
How much more so when one lacks the provisions for sublime wisdom?
Furthermore, having observed this,
if one knows for oneself that one is not bound by even the slightest stinginess regarding this Dharma.
There is no other intention here;
it is simply that one should not give to those who would not accomplish what is most necessary.
At such a time, the bodhisattva should reflect further.
When I bestow this Dharma upon others,
is it for the sake of harming my own afflictions,
or is it for the sake of fulfilling the equipment of wisdom?
"Is it for the sake of loving and cherishing all sentient beings?
Having reflected thus, he correctly understood: "I do not perceive any afflictions of my own."
One does not give away such things as these scriptures to others;
rather, my own accumulation of wisdom for the present and future lives increases and becomes ever more excellent.
It is not by giving to another that one establishes this merit.
However, in the future, there will be meager benefit from the Dharma and no abundance of awakened wisdom;
if one does not give to them, one will be unable to cultivate and accumulate the skillful means and wisdom that bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
This constitutes loving-kindness toward this one sentient being as well as all others;
whereas if one were to give only to that [one], it would constitute loving-kindness toward this one sentient being alone, and not toward all others.
When a bodhisattva has thus known things as they truly are, if he does not give to that person,
he incurs no fault and feels no remorse;
furthermore, he does not transgress the pure precepts of a bodhisattva.
What is a bodhisattva’s skillful means of not giving?
It refers to when bodhisattvas cannot bear to dismiss a petitioner with blunt words,
saying, "I am unable to bestow anything upon you."
One must employ skillful means and provide instruction to exhort and dispatch them.
What is meant by employing skillful means?
It refers to when bodhisattvas first regard all their accumulated requisites and all items for giving.
In order to purify [the gift], one should relinquish it with a pure intention to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions,
just as a bhikṣu relinquishes his own robes for the sake of purification.
He gives them away to his preceptors, instructors,
and others. Thus, through the causes and conditions of such pure giving,
although the bodhisattva may store various kinds of excellent implements and all manner of objects for giving, [he remains free from attachment].
One may still be said to dwell securely in the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
Because one constantly contemplates this merit,
immeasurable merit arises and increases at all times, following along with one.
One should always regard all things given as pure gifts,
maintaining them with the same care as if they were entrusted to a Buddha or a Bodhisattva;
upon seeing a seeker come, one should immediately examine [the situation].
When one gives away things that have been purified as a gift according to one's desire,
one should act in accordance with correct principle by forming this thought:
"There is not the slightest thing that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not give to sentient beings."
Having understood this, one accepts pure offerings and fulfills the wishes of those who come seeking them; yet,
if at the time of giving, one observes that it does not accord with the correct principle.
One should immediately recall the previously performed rite of pure giving (*śuddha-dāna*) and say:
"O noble one, such items as these belong to another and have not been permitted for you to give."
He should comfort them with gentle words and skillful means to send them away,
or provide other items,
giving them with double or triple the respect.
Then, having dismissed them,
cause them to understand that it is not because the Bodhisattva is stingy or greedy that he does not wish to give these to me;
rather, he will certainly [bestow] these Dharma scrolls and so forth.
Because they lack self-mastery, they do not bestow [gifts] upon me;
one should know that this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful wisdom in practicing the gift of Dharma.
Furthermore, regarding all forms of giving by bodhisattvas:
That is to say, the gift of Dharma, the gift of material wealth, and the gift of fearlessness;
whether by way of different categories or by way of their essential characteristics.
Whether it be the etymological definition or the distinctions between cause and effect,
one practices giving after understanding these things as they truly are.
One should know that this is also called a bodhisattva practicing generosity with skillful wisdom.
Furthermore, when encountering those who harbor enmity toward them,
bodhisattvas practice giving with a disposition of loving-kindness.
One practices generosity toward those who suffer with a compassionate intention,
and toward those who possess virtue...
One practices giving with a joyful intention;
toward those who have been kind, one's kin, and those with whom one shares common interests,
one practices giving with an equanimous intention.
It should be known that this is also called the bodhisattva’s skillful wisdom in practicing generosity.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas understand, as they truly are, the obstacles to generosity and their respective remedies.
In this regard, there are briefly four kinds of obstacles to giving:
first, lack of prior habituation;
second, scarcity of objects to be given.
Third, they are attached to excellent and pleasing material wealth;
fourth, they deeply rejoice upon seeing the future fruition of abundant wealth.
If bodhisattvas currently possess various kinds of material goods fit for giving...
Even though a petitioner appears directly before them,
the Bodhisattva’s mind does not incline toward giving;
at that time, the Bodhisattva employs right wisdom.
The swift realization that "this is a fault resulting from my lack of prior habituation to giving" is further penetrated by sublime wisdom as follows:
"I certainly lacked habituation to giving in previous lives."
Consequently, although there are currently various kinds of material goods available for giving in this present life,
and even when seekers are seen standing directly before one,
the mind does not incline toward the act of generosity.
If one does not practice giving with diligent reflection in this present life,
one will certainly come to detest and turn away from what ought to be given in future lives.
Having correctly understood this, the bodhisattva—
Relying on this antidote to the obstacles to giving,
one practices generosity with diligent reflection and discernment; thus,
one is able to avoid following after the faults committed through prior lack of cultivation.
They act with sovereign ease.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva sees a seeker appearing before them,
yet possesses only a meager supply of material goods;
When the mind does not incline toward such giving,
the bodhisattva then swiftly penetrates this state with right wisdom,
[recognizing] these causes and conditions for the obstruction of giving due to deprivation.
Enduring the manifold sufferings caused by deprivation,
one should exert effort in discernment, give rise to a mind of compassion,
and practice wise giving, reflecting as follows:
Whether due to the faults of past karma or due to being bound to others in the present,
it causes me to fully experience many intense sufferings such as hunger and thirst.
I am unable to benefit all sentient beings.
Even if I were now to benefit others through the practice of giving,
I would undergo various sufferings in this present life, even unto death.
Practicing generosity in this manner is already most excellent;
it is not merely to send away those who come seeking empty-handed,
let alone when there are further things such as vegetable leaves available to sustain one's life.
In this way, the bodhisattva endures the various sufferings caused by deprivation while practicing generosity.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva sees a petitioner appearing before them, [he acts accordingly].
Because the objects to be given are extremely pleasing and most excellent,
the bodhisattva’s mind does not incline toward practicing generosity;
at that time, the bodhisattva employs right wisdom.
To swiftly penetrate [this truth] is the fault of my own attachment.
I have now given rise to the perversion of conceiving suffering as false pleasure;
from this, the manifold sufferings of the future are produced.
Because he has thoroughly understood these inversions,
he exerts effort and applies discernment in order to abandon them,
and thus gives gifts with these material goods.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas have practiced giving,
they perceive the superior merit in the vast wealth and benefits that will result from such giving,
and they develop a profound sense of joy and delight.
Not seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
the bodhisattva at that time, by means of right wisdom,
swiftly and thoroughly penetrates the faults committed through this view of false results.
One observes according to reality that all conditioned phenomena are entirely unstable,
and that all conditioned phenomena perish moment by moment.
The fruits one enjoys quickly perish and quickly disperse.
When one contemplates in this way, one is able to sever and extinguish the views that give rise to delight in such false fruits.
All acts of giving are dedicated toward unsurpassed enlightenment.
Thus, regarding these four kinds of obstacles to a bodhisattva’s giving,
one should know that four kinds of remedial wisdom serve as their antidotes.
First is awakening;
second is enduring all sufferings;
third is thoroughly knowing perversion.
Fourth, they perceive that the nature of all conditioned phenomena is not solid.
By means of these three types of counteractive wisdom,
these bodhisattvas are definitively capable of correctly practicing generosity.
By means of the latter kind of counteractive wisdom,
one is able to correctly appropriate the superior fruit of the merit of giving;
it should be understood that this is also called a bodhisattva practicing generosity with skillful wisdom.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas dwell in inner seclusion,
through their pure intention, profound sincerity, pure faith, and analytical resolve,

they repeatedly bring to mind various kinds of sublime and immeasurable wealth and treasures; by the power of their resolute conviction, they delight in practicing generosity toward all sentient beings.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, these bodhisattvas generate immeasurable merit with little effort;
it should be understood that this is also called the bodhisattva’s skillful wisdom in practicing generosity.
Such is the practice of giving by the Bodhisattvas of Sublime Wisdom and Great Wisdom through skillful means.
To summarize the essential meaning:
it is comprised of the gift of material wealth and the gift of non-material wealth.
Thus, by means of the gift of Dharma,
by means of the gift of unimpeded analytical knowledge,
and by means of the gift of superior intention.
Because it is the gift of wisdom that serves as the antidote to obstacles to giving,
and because it is the gift of superior intention and resolute conviction, it should be understood that this is called the unique practice of giving belonging exclusively to Bodhisattvas.
Having thus explained at length the various characteristics of all forms of giving practiced by bodhisattvas regarding internal and external objects,
from this point forward, within those very same various characteristics of giving:
One should understand that all other distinctions, such as difficult-to-practice giving and so forth,
are also categorized therein.
What is the bodhisattva’s difficult-to-practice giving?
It should be known that this giving is, in brief, of three kinds.
That is to say, when a bodhisattva’s material wealth is meager,
they endure their own poverty and suffering to bestow gifts upon others.
This is called the bodhisattva’s first difficult practice of giving:
when a bodhisattva possesses objects that are dear to them,
or to which they are deeply attached by nature.
Whether through long-term habitual practice,
or because of a superior degree of gratitude, or due to an intense attachment to a most excellent object that one can only resolve to part with, giving it away to another—
this is called the bodhisattva’s second type of difficult-to-practice generosity.
If a bodhisattva bestows upon others wealth and goods acquired through extreme hardship,
this is called the third difficult practice of giving for a bodhisattva.
What is the bodhisattva’s giving through all doors?
It should be understood that this generosity briefly has four characteristics:
namely, when bodhisattvas [give] either their own wealth and goods,
or wealth and goods obtained by exhorting and transforming others.
Or they give to relatives, parents, wives,
children, slaves, laborers, good friends,
ministers, kinsmen, and attendants.
Or again, giving to others who come seeking;
these four characteristics are called the bodhisattva’s giving through all doors.
What is the giving of a noble person (*satpuruṣa*) practiced by a bodhisattva that is called the "giving of a noble person"?
It should be known that this giving briefly has five characteristics:
namely, that bodhisattvas give with pure faith.
One gives with reverence;
one gives with one's own hand;
one gives at the appropriate time.
One practices giving without harming or vexing others.
These five characteristics are called the "giving of a noble person" (satpuruṣadāna), which is the conduct of a bodhisattva as a noble person.
What is the bodhisattva’s giving in all its aspects?
It should be known that this giving has thirteen characteristics.
The first is giving without dependence.
Second, extensive giving;
third, joyful giving; fourth, repeated giving;
fifth, giving to a worthy field.
Sixth, giving to those who are not worthy recipients;
seventh, giving all things;
eighth, giving in all places.
Ninth is giving at all times;
tenth is blameless giving;
eleventh is giving material things to sentient beings.
The gift of the products of the twelve directions;
the gift of wealth and grain— these thirteen kinds of characteristics should be known as the bodhisattva’s giving in all its forms.
What is the bodhisattva’s giving that accords with the seeker's request?
It should be known that this giving has eight aspects.
Namely, when there are seekers who lack food and drink and come to beg for them...
They give food and drink to those who beg for them;
they give vehicles to those who lack vehicles and beg for them;
and they give clothing to those who lack clothing and beg for it.
To those who beg for clothing, he gives clothing; to those who beg for ornaments because they lack them, he gives ornaments;
to those who beg for various necessities and utensils of life because they lack them, he gives those things.
To those who beg for various necessities of life and lack various ointments, perfumes, and garlands,
he gives various ointments, perfumes, and garlands.
To those who lack dwellings and beg for them,
he gives dwellings;
to those who lack light and beg for it, [he gives light].
Bestowing light—
these eight characteristics are called the bodhisattva’s giving that fulfills requests.
What is the bodhisattva’s giving for the happiness of this world and the next?
It should be known that this generosity consists briefly of nine aspects:
namely, the gift of material wealth, the gift of fearlessness, and the gift of the Dharma.
Taken together, these are called the "generosity that enables sentient beings to attain happiness in this life and future lives."
The gift of material wealth refers to practicing generosity with excellent, pure, and lawful goods;
it is practicing generosity while subduing the defilement of stinginess.
One practices giving by subduing the defilement of hoarding.
Subduing the defilement of stinginess means relinquishing attachment to material wealth.
To subdue the defilement of hoarding is to relinquish attachment to possessions;
fearlessness-giving is as follows:
That is to say: rescuing one from the fears of lions, tigers, wolves, ghosts, and demons;
rescuing one from the fears of kings and bandits;
and rescuing one from the fears of water and fire.
The gift of Dharma refers to teaching the Dharma without error, teaching the Dharma in accordance with reason, and exhorting others to train in the points of discipline;
all such instances are collectively described as having nine aspects.
This is called the bodhisattva’s gift that brings happiness to sentient beings in this life and in future lives.
Among these, the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*) and the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*), along with their specific varieties,
can bring peace and happiness to sentient beings in this life.
The Dharma-gift and its distinctions can bring peace and happiness to sentient beings in future lives.
What is the pure gift of a bodhisattva?
It should be known that this giving has ten characteristics:
first, giving without lingering attachment;
second, giving without grasping.
Third, giving without accumulation;
fourth, giving without arrogance;
fifth, giving without dependence.
Sixth, the gift that is not weak;
seventh, the gift that is not inferior;
eighth, the gift that is not turned away.
Ninth, giving without expectation of a reward;
tenth, giving without hope for karmic maturation.
What is giving without delay?
This means that when Bodhisattvas see a petitioner appearing before them,
they bestow gifts with rapidity and without delay;
it is not that the petitioner is in haste to obtain wealth.
Just as bodhisattvas swiftly aspire to generosity,
how is it that they do not grasp at giving?
It means that bodhisattvas do not grasp at giving through false views.
Some maintain that this giving is empty and has no fruit;
some maintain that practicing generosity through killing is the true Dharma;
and some maintain that only giving which is utterly pure and perfect constitutes ultimate purity, both worldly and transcendent.
What is giving without accumulation?
It means that bodhisattvas do not gradually accumulate a vast amount of wealth over a long period of time and then give it all at once. Why is this?
It is not the case that a bodhisattva, while currently possessing objects for giving,
would be able to refrain from giving when a petitioner appears directly before them.
Not seeing [the need for] non-giving is what is called the correct principle.
Why then would one accumulate wealth and not give it away quickly?
Furthermore, bodhisattvas do not see the accumulation of wealth.
To provide [offerings] all at once afterwards is a gateway for generating much merit.
Furthermore, it is the correct contemplation to observe whether the seekers are individuals or a collective.
When the objects given are similar, whether given gradually or all at once, and the material wealth is equal,
for what reason do you maintain that there is a difference in merit?
Furthermore, bodhisattvas perceive that giving from a hoarded accumulation is a faulty act.
Seeing [a recipient] and giving as soon as one obtains the gift is blameless.
Why is this? Because if one were to first accumulate [the goods] and only then give them all at once, [it would be improper].
This means that previously, when there were those who came seeking [gifts],
their number may have been as many as a hundred, yet he did not give to them,
causing them to give rise to resentment, intolerance, and lack of faith.
Later, there is a class of people who, perhaps without aspiration,
forcibly and suddenly bestow their accumulated precious wealth.
For this reason, a bodhisattva does not practice accumulation in giving.
What is giving without arrogance?
It refers to when bodhisattvas give with a humble mind to those who come seeking.
Nor does one give while competing for victory with others, nor does one give and then give rise to arrogance, thinking:
"I am able to give; I am a donor, whereas others are not."
What is giving without dependence?
It refers to when bodhisattvas do not give based on reputation, praise, or verses of eulogy,
for they fundamentally realize that worldly reputation, praise, and verses are false conceptual constructions.
That which arises from written characters is merely empty sound,
bound to illusory resonance;
it is like a heap of chaff and leaves in the world.
What is the generosity that is free from weakness?
It refers to when bodhisattvas feel joy in their minds before giving, maintain purity of mind while giving, and feel no regret after having given;
and when they hear of the vast, foremost, and most excellent generosity of other bodhisattvas.
Not disparaging oneself, nor being terrified or discouraged.
What is non-inferior giving?
It refers to how bodhisattvas, regarding all objects of giving...
Diligently and repeatedly discerning the most excellent and sublime things— such as food, drink, vehicles, and clothing—
and holding them to offer as gifts:
what is meant by "giving without turning one's back"?
This means that the minds of bodhisattvas are impartial and do not follow partisan factions;
they bestow compassion equally upon both enemies and kin.
How is it that they bestow gifts without expecting a reward?
This means that when bodhisattvas practice giving with a heart of compassion and sympathy,
they never hope for a reciprocal reward from others; rather,
they simply observe those who seek happiness yet are consumed by the fire of craving.
To those sentient beings who lack power and whose nature is suffering,
he practices giving with a heart of profound compassion.
What is giving that does not hope for maturation?
It refers to when bodhisattvas practice generosity,
never hoping for the maturation of the fruit of giving— namely, the perfection of wealth or the perfection of one's own person— in a future life.
One contemplates that the nature of all conditioned phenomena is deceptive and illusory,
and one contemplates the supreme merits of great enlightenment.
Through these ten aspects, the bodhisattva’s practice of giving becomes pure and utterly purified.
In this way, when a bodhisattva, relying on the practice of generosity through these nine aspects,
has perfected the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā),
they are able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 39;
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 40;
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.

In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth part of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the first section on the *Yogasthāna*, the tenth chapter on Ethics (*Śīla*), Part One: What is the Bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*)?
The summary verse says:
Intrinsic nature, all [difficulties], All gateways, noble beings, all modes,
fulfillment of requests, Happiness in both worlds, and purity.
These nine kinds of characteristics are called the brief exposition of the precepts;
that is to say, the precepts characterized by these nine aspects are termed the Bodhisattva-śīla-pāramitā.
The first is the precept of essential nature (svabhāva-śīla).
Second, the morality of all things;
third, the morality of difficult practices;
fourth, the morality of all doors.
1. The morality of a virtuous person;
2. The morality of all aspects;
3. The morality that fulfills aspirations.
8. The precept of happiness in this world and other worlds;
9. The pure precept.
What is the bodhisattva’s natural precept (*svabhāva-śīla*)?
Briefly stated, it should be understood that what possesses four qualities is called the bodhisattva’s natural morality (*svabhāva-śīla*).
What are these four?
First, receiving it correctly from another;
second, having a thoroughly pure intention;
third, restoring purity after an offense has been committed.
Fourth, they maintain deep respect and focused mindfulness, remaining free from transgressions;
for since these bodhisattvas have formally received the precepts from others,
should there be any violation of the training rules, [they feel remorse].
He immediately observes others and feels deep shame;
because the bodhisattvas possess such thoroughly pure intentions,
should they commit any transgression regarding the precepts they have undertaken, [they feel remorse].
He immediately looked within himself and felt a profound sense of shame;
because Bodhisattvas purify themselves after transgressing any of the precepts,
they maintain deep reverence and focused mindfulness, never committing a violation from the very beginning.
Due to these two causes and conditions,
he is free from all remorse.
Thus, the bodhisattva correctly receives [the precepts] from another with a thoroughly pure intention.
Based on this reliance, one gives rise to a sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*);
through shame and dread of blame, one is able to properly guard the ethical discipline (*śīla*) one has undertaken;
and by properly guarding the precepts one has undertaken, one becomes free from all remorse (*kaukṛtya*).
Furthermore, within this context,
one receives it correctly from another with a thoroughly pure intention.
These two are dharmas that,
once violated, can be restored to purity;
through profound reverence and focused mindfulness, one remains free from transgression.
These two are induced by the first two dharmas.
Furthermore, within this context,
one correctly receives them from another.
With a thoroughly pure intention,
profound respect, and single-minded mindfulness, one remains free from transgression;
by means of these three qualities, it should be understood that one is able to prevent the violation of the pure precepts received by a bodhisattva.
Having committed an offense, one returns to purity;
by means of this single factor, it should be understood that one is able to emerge from having committed an offense.
Thus, a bodhisattva possesses the morality of essential nature endowed with four qualities.
One should know that this is precisely the sublime and pure ethical discipline;
by correctly receiving and training in accordance with it,
one is able to benefit both oneself and others.
For the sake of bringing benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings;
out of compassion for the world’s devas and humans,
so that they may attain meaningful goals, benefit, peace, and happiness.
One should know that this is the pure ethical discipline of immeasurable extent,
because it encompasses the immeasurable trainings of bodhisattvas.
One should know that this is the pure ethical discipline that benefits all sentient beings.
Because it is able to manifest and bring about the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings,
one should know that this is the pure ethical discipline that attains great fruits and supreme benefits;
for it encompasses and bestows the fruit of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
This is called the bodhisattva’s natural morality (*svabhāva-śīla*).
What is the bodhisattva’s all-inclusive morality?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of bodhisattva morality.
First, the precepts pertaining to the household life;
second, the precepts pertaining to the life of renunciation—these are called all the precepts.
Furthermore, it is precisely based on these two categories of pure precepts for householders and renunciants that [the classification is established].
Briefly stated, there are three types:
first, the morality of restraint;
second, the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas.
Third is the precept of benefiting sentient beings.
Regarding the precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*),
it refers to the sevenfold Pratimokṣa restraints received by Bodhisattvas.
That is to say: the bhikṣu precepts,
the bhikṣuṇī precepts,
and the śikṣamāṇā precepts.
The śrāmaṇera precepts for males,
the śrāmaṇerī precepts for females,
and the upāsaka precepts for males.
The upāsikā precepts.
Thus, these seven types rely upon both the lay and monastic divisions.
It should be understood accordingly.
This is called the bodhisattva’s morality of restraint (saṃvara-śīla).
As for the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas (kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla):
This refers to all the roots of virtue accumulated through body, speech, and mind for the sake of great enlightenment by bodhisattvas after they have received the vows of restraint.
Taken collectively, these are called the precepts for gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
Furthermore, what are they?
They refer to all bodhisattvas who rely upon the precepts and abide in the precepts.
Regarding hearing, reflection, and cultivation— both śamatha and vipaśyanā— and delighting in dwelling in solitude,
he applies himself with diligence to study;
likewise, from time to time, toward his elders and superiors.
He diligently cultivates the practice of joining his palms, rising to welcome, inquiring after others' well-being, prostrating, and showing reverence;
he zealously attends to and serves his elders and superiors,
and with profound compassion and earnestness, he looks after, serves, and provides for those who are ill.
One should express approval with "Excellent! for all sublime teachings,
and one should offer sincere praise to individuals who possess virtuous qualities.
With a superior intention and pure faith, one expresses sympathetic joy through speech for all the meritorious deeds of all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
and regarding all transgressions committed by others, one exercises discernment and practices patience.
They dedicate all roots of virtue— whether already performed or yet to be performed by way of body,
speech, and mind— toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. From time to time,
they give rise to various correct aspirations and offer to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha every kind of supreme and exquisite offering.
One should constantly and vigorously cultivate all categories of wholesome qualities;
remain heedful regarding body, speech, and mind;
and practice the trainings with right mindfulness, clear comprehension, and correct conduct.
He guards the doors of the sensory faculties with secrecy,
observes moderation in eating,
and constantly practices wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night.
One draws near to virtuous persons and relies upon spiritual friends.
One thoroughly and accurately recognizes one's own transgressions and perceives them as deep faults.
Having thus thoroughly recognized and perceived them as deep faults, [one proceeds].
Those who have not yet committed offenses shall maintain them with single-minded devotion;
those who have already committed offenses shall, in the presence of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or fellow practitioners of the Dharma,
confess with a sincere heart and repent according to the Dharma.
All such categories of precepts that attract, sustain,
and increase all wholesome dharmas are called the bodhisattva’s precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
What is the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings?
It should be known that this discipline briefly has eleven aspects.
What are these eleven?
That is to say, bodhisattvas act as companions to sentient beings in various undertakings that lead to their welfare and benefit;
and regarding the sufferings such as illnesses that arise for sentient beings, [they provide assistance].
Attending to the sick and so forth also constitutes acting as a companion.
Furthermore, based on various mundane and supramundane benefits,
bodhisattvas are able to expound the essential points of the Dharma for sentient beings.
First, they employ skillful means and speak in accordance with reason;
subsequently, they cause others to obtain their respective benefits and purposes.
Furthermore, regarding sentient beings who have previously shown them kindness, bodhisattvas maintain a firm sense of gratitude.
They provide immediate recompense according to what is appropriate.

Furthermore, regarding sentient beings who have fallen into various fears—such as those of lions, tigers, wolves, malevolent spirits, kings, thieves, water, or fire—the bodhisattvas [act accordingly].
They are able to rescue and protect all,
causing them to leave behind such places of fear and dread.
Furthermore, regarding those sentient beings who have suffered the loss of wealth, treasures, or kinsmen, the bodhisattvas [act on their behalf].
He skillfully provides explanations and consolation to cause them to be free from sorrow and anxiety.
Furthermore, regarding those sentient beings who lack the various necessities of life,
the bodhisattvas bestow all such requisites upon them.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas accord with reason by correctly relying upon and guiding the community in accordance with the Dharma;
moreover, bodhisattvas accord with the world.
Engaging in administrative affairs and speech,
summoning others, coming and going,
conversing, and offering greetings of comfort and consolation.
He goes at the appropriate time and receives food,
drink, and other necessities from others;
in short, this is how it is.
He remains far removed from all conduct that leads to what is meaningless or disagreeable,
and his mind follows along with all other matters.
Furthermore, whether in private or in public, the bodhisattva...
It reveals all true virtues,
causing sentient beings to rejoice and advance in their learning.
Furthermore, regarding those who have faults, the bodhisattvas...
With an internal disposition of intimacy, benefit, and happiness, and with a superior intention, he disciplines, reprimands, punishes, and expels them,
desiring to lead them out of unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states.
Furthermore, by means of their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*),
bodhisattvas skillfully manifest the appearances of various realms of existence, such as the hells (*naraka*),
causing sentient beings to feel weary of and renounce unwholesome states.
By means of skillful means, they are led to enter the Buddha’s holy teaching, where they develop joy, faith, and delight, giving rise to a sense of wonder and diligently practicing correct conduct.
How does a bodhisattva abide in the morality of restraint?
Abiding in the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas,
abiding in the morality of benefiting sentient beings,
and well-guarding the morality of restraint.
They skillfully cultivate the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas and the precept of benefiting sentient beings in every way;
that is to say, when bodhisattvas abide in the ethical discipline of the prātimokṣa vows.
Having renounced the status of a wheel-turning monarch and gone forth into homelessness,
he disregarded the royal throne as if discarding grass or filth,
just as a commoner, for the sake of sustaining his life, [disregards wealth].
Having renounced inferior desires and gone forth, one does not look back at those inferior desires;

yet this is not like a bodhisattva who, with pure intention, renounces the status of a wheel-turning monarch and goes forth, thereafter disregarding even the position of a wheel-turning monarch, the most excellent among all men.

Furthermore, bodhisattvas dwelling in the morality of restraint do not give rise to delight or pleasure toward the exquisite sensual desires found within the palaces of the celestial Māras in future ages.
Nor do they seek those various sublime desires while practicing the holy life;
rather, they contemplate those sublime desires as they truly are,
as if entering a vast and dense forest of manifold terrors.
How much more so for other desires?
Furthermore, once bodhisattvas have gone forth,
regarding the various superior and exquisite gains and honors from noble sentient beings in the present life—
When one examines with right wisdom,
even that which is like vomited food is not tasted or relished;
how much less so the inferior gains and honors belonging to other lowly sentient beings?
Furthermore, whether in a solitary, quiet place or amidst a multitude, bodhisattvas always delight in remaining far removed from distraction,
dwelling at all times with a mind exclusively focused on seclusion and tranquility.
Not being content merely with this ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*),
he dwells in the precepts and relies upon them, diligently cultivating the immeasurable bodhisattva samādhis in order to bring forth and attain mastery.
Furthermore, although bodhisattvas may dwell among a diverse assembly,
they do not take pleasure in even the slightest improper discourse; rather,
they abide in seclusion.
They do not give rise to even the slightest unwholesome thoughts;
should they at times lose mindfulness and allow such thoughts to manifest for a brief moment,
they immediately give rise to intense regret and shame.
Deeply perceiving their faults, he repeatedly feels remorse and shame.
Because he deeply perceives these faults, even if improper speech or various evil thoughts should momentarily arise,
he is able to swiftly establish himself in right mindfulness.
Having attained therein the resolve not to act again,
one is thereby able to exercise restraint.
Through the practice of restraint, one gradually becomes as one was before.
One feels deep joy and pleasure in their manifestation;
now, as they do not manifest, one likewise feels joy and pleasure in that non-manifestation.
Furthermore, they are able to counteract [unwholesome states] so that they do not manifest.
Moreover, regarding all the training precepts of bodhisattvas,
as well as the vast, immeasurable, inconceivable, and long-term most difficult-to-practice training precepts of bodhisattvas who have already entered the great stages (mahābhūmi) upon hearing them—
His mind was free from alarm or fear, nor was it timid or inferior;
he thought only this:
"Since they are human beings..."
Gradually training in all the bodhisattva precepts— vast, immeasurable, and inconceivable— including the ethical discipline of the pure body, speech, and so forth,
they achieve complete perfection.
I, too, am a human being.
By practicing and training gradually,
I shall certainly and without doubt attain the complete perfection of those various vows of restraint for body and speech, such as the pure discipline.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas dwelling in the morality of restraint constantly examine their own faults and do not look for the transgressions of others;
toward all sentient beings who are violent or violate the precepts, they remain impartial.
With a mind free from malice and a mind free from ill will,
the bodhisattva, by virtue of harboring the supreme great compassion for the Dharma toward them,
manifests a heart of profound pity and a desire to benefit them.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas abide in the morality of restraint (saṃvara-śīla),
even if they encounter harm inflicted by others through the contact of hands, feet, clods of earth, stones, swords, or clubs,
they harbor not even the slightest thought of malice or resentment toward them.
How much less would they wish to utter harsh words or inflict harm upon them;
how much less would they speak words of disparagement, insult,
or reproach, causing harm by means of even slight suffering?
Furthermore, bodhisattvas dwelling in the morality of restraint fully accomplish five factors subsumed under heedful practice:
first, heedful practice associated with the past limit.
Second, the practice of heedfulness concurrent with the future limit;
third, the practice of heedfulness concurrent with the middle limit;
fourth, the practice of heedfulness performed at an earlier time.
Fifth is the practice of non-negligence that accompanies [the preceding practices] at all times;
this refers to when bodhisattvas are correctly training in the bodhisattva precepts,
they duly repent and eliminate any transgressions previously committed in the past.
This is called the bodhisattva’s practice of heedfulness associated with the past.
If one rectifies and eliminates future transgressions in accordance with the Dharma,
this is called the bodhisattva’s practice of heedfulness associated with the future.
If one rectifies and eliminates according to the Dharma those transgressions currently being committed in the present,
this is called the bodhisattva’s practice of heedfulness concurrent with the middle limit. If a bodhisattva,

regarding those transgressions that will be committed at a later time, generates a fierce and intense resolve and aspiration for self-vow, [this is called the practice of heedfulness concurrent with the future limit].
That is to say: "I shall certainly act in whatever manner is appropriate for action;
I shall abide in whatever manner is appropriate for abiding;
in such and such a way I shall act."
Abiding in this way and that way,
one ensures that no transgressions are committed;
this is called the bodhisattva’s practice of heedfulness prior to [the occurrence of a fault].
If bodhisattvas rely upon such previously practiced heedfulness as their basis,
then in whatever manner they ought to act and in whatever manner they ought to abide, [they do so].
Acting in such a manner and abiding in such a manner,
one does not give rise to transgressions.
This is called the bodhisattva’s practice of heedfulness that proceeds simultaneously [with other virtues].
Furthermore, bodhisattvas dwelling in the morality of restraint conceal their own good deeds and disclose their own faults.
He has few desires and is content; he is able to endure all forms of suffering.
By nature, he is free from sorrow and grief, neither restless nor agitated, and his deportment is tranquil.
He is devoid of all factors that give rise to wrong livelihood, such as hypocrisy and the like.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten factors,
they are said to abide in the morality of restraint and to be well-guarded in the morality of restraint;
that is to say, they do not look back with longing toward past sensual desires.
Furthermore, he does not long for future desires,
nor does he become attached to present desires; moreover,
he delights in seclusion and does not give rise to complacency.
Furthermore, one is able to sweep away improper speech and all evil discursive thoughts;
one is also able to avoid self-contempt;
and one is by nature gentle and flexible.
Furthermore, he is able to endure;
moreover, he is not negligent;
and furthermore, he is fully endowed with proper conduct and pure livelihood.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas have already been able to abide securely in the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas,
they do not even tolerate the slightest attachment to their bodies or possessions.
How much more so when they occur frequently?
Furthermore, regarding all causes and conditions for violating the precepts— whether they arise from root afflictions, secondary afflictions, or anger and resentment—
he does not tolerate them.
Furthermore, one does not tolerate the arising of thoughts of malice, harm,
or resentment toward others;
nor does one tolerate the arising of indolence and laziness.
Nor does he tolerate them.
Furthermore, regarding the attachment to the flavor of the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that have arisen, as well as the afflictions associated with those attainments,
he likewise does not tolerate them.
Furthermore, one understands five points as they truly are:
namely, one understands as they truly are the excellence of the results of wholesome actions,
and one is also able to understand as they truly are the causes of wholesome actions.
Furthermore, they are able to know, as it truly is, the inversion and non-inversion regarding the causes and effects of the wholesome.
Moreover, they know, as it truly is, the obstacles to the gathering of wholesome dharmas.
These bodhisattvas are able to perceive great benefits in the fruits of the wholesome and seek out their wholesome causes.
In order to gather wholesome qualities, he understands inversion and non-inversion as they truly are.
By means of this, the bodhisattva attains wholesome fruits and does not falsely perceive the impermanent as permanent.
One does not falsely perceive suffering as pleasure;
one does not falsely perceive the impure as pure;
and one does not falsely perceive the non-self as self.
By understanding, as they truly are, the obstacles to the gathering of wholesome dharmas,
and by swiftly abandoning them for the sake of gathering those wholesome dharmas,
the bodhisattva— by means of these ten aspects— [proceeds].
This is called abiding in the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas;
it is able to swiftly gather all aspects of the wholesome,
namely, the gradual sequence of giving.
Whether it be the gradual sequence of ethical discipline,
the gradual sequence of patience,
the gradual sequence of diligence, the gradual sequence of meditative concentration, or the fivefold wisdom.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas are said to abide in the morality that benefits sentient beings in every way by virtue of eleven aspects.
Within each of these aspects, they accomplish every kind of benefit; that is to say, regarding the various activities of sentient beings, bodhisattvas [apply themselves accordingly].
All serve as companions;
that is to say, they can act as companions for whatever tasks are performed through deliberation and whatever tasks are performed through effort, whether on the road while going or returning.
Whether it be in the application of unerring activities,
or in the protection of all one's wealth and possessions,
or in the reconciliation of those who have become estranged from one another.
Whether at assemblies for the Dharma or in the cultivation of merit,
they act as companions; likewise,
in all efforts to rescue others from suffering, they also act as companions.
That is to say, when encountering sentient beings afflicted by pestilence,
one attends to and provides for them;
and for those who are blind, one acts as their guide.
For the deaf, he gestures the meaning;
for those who speak with their hands, he clarifies through mental imagery;
for those who have lost their way, he shows them the path they encounter.
To those whose limbs were incomplete, he granted the gift of the vehicle to carry them;
to those who were foolish and deluded, he instructed them in supreme wisdom;
and for sentient beings suffering from the entanglements of craving and desire, [he provided relief].
He provides an explanation so as to cause them to be free from the suffering of being entangled by sensual desire;
likewise, if they are afflicted by ill will, lethargy,
torpor, or restlessness.
For sentient beings who are suffering from the fetters of regret and doubt,
he provides liberation and causes them to be free from the suffering of those fetters and the like.

Sentient beings who are afflicted by the fetter of discursive thought concerning sensual desire are enlightened and liberated so that they may be freed from the suffering of discursive thought concerning sensual desire; as it is with discursive thought concerning sensual desire, so it is with the others.
One should know that all discursive thoughts associated with malice toward one's kin or country, associated with the fear of death, or associated with contempt for one's lineage, are likewise so.
This applies to sentient beings who suffer from being despised by others or surpassed by others.
He provides instruction and guidance to liberate those suffering from the misery of being despised.
For sentient beings afflicted by the exhaustion of traveling on the road,
he gives seats and places to rest, and provides physical massage to relieve their fatigue.
He causes them to cease their weariness and manifold sufferings.
Furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings, the bodhisattvas teach them correctly;
that is, regarding those sentient beings who delight in practicing unwholesome deeds.
In order to cause the severance of all unwholesome conduct,
he employs corresponding phrases as companions that are harmonious,
clear, functional, appropriate, and compliant.
He teaches the Dharma by means of the constant and diligent accumulation of provisions,
or else he teaches through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*),
just as he does for sentient beings who delight in unwholesome conduct, in order to cause them to abandon all such unwholesome deeds.
Regarding sentient beings who practice stinginess,
in order to cause them to abandon such behavior,
[the Buddha] provides for those who seek wealth and treasures in the present life.
It is for the sake of causing those who harbor hatred and jealousy toward the Buddha’s holy teaching to gather abundant wealth with little effort and to guard it without loss;
and it is for the sake of causing them to attain pure faith and realize pure vision.
It should be understood that it likewise transcends all evil destinies, exhausts all fetters,
and overcomes all suffering.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas encounter sentient beings who have been kind to them,
they are deeply aware of that kindness and constantly contemplate repaying it;
even upon a brief meeting, they express their respect by greeting them with the words, "Welcome."
With a cheerful countenance and joyful consolation, he spoke candidly with them in conversation and jest. He prepared seats and a formal banquet for them to sit upon;
whether their status was equal or superior, he provided them with material wealth and offerings, responding to them personally.
One should not consider them inferior;
even if they do not request assistance for their tasks,
one should still provide support and aid.
How much more so regarding that which has a fixed destiny?
As it is with regard to undertakings,
so it is with regard to suffering.
In speaking according to reality,
in speaking with skillful means,
and in rescuing others from fear.
He provides consolation and relief from grief and anxiety in times of decline and distress;
he bestows material requisites and grants support.
He causes them to feel deep joy by manifesting their actual virtues in accordance with their inclinations;
he tames them through skillful means by inspiring affection;
and he draws them in by manifesting supernatural powers to inspire wonder and awe.
It should be understood that this is to be explained in detail accordingly.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas are able to provide protection for sentient beings who encounter fear,
such as from various birds and beasts, water, or fire.
Kings, thieves, enemies,
householders, masters, officials,
lack of livelihood, and ill repute.
The majestic power of the great assembly can protect all from fear of non-humans, risen corpses,
and malevolent spirits, enabling them to attain peace and security.
Furthermore, when sentient beings encounter decline and affliction,
Bodhisattvas are able to skillfully provide them with consolation and cause them to be free from sorrow and anxiety;
or, regarding the loss of relatives— namely parents, brothers, and so forth— they provide such solace.
Wife and children,
slaves and servants, clan elders,
friends, and both internal and external kinsmen.
When one's preceptors,
instructors, or other venerable elders have passed away.
One skillfully provides consolation so that they may be freed from sorrow and affliction;
or [it concerns] the loss of wealth and treasures,
such as being plundered by kings or thieves.
Some are burned by fire or drowned by water;
some are deceived and enticed by the crafty and fraudulent;
or they suffer loss due to lack of method in their undertakings.
Or they may be unjustly and forcibly seized by wicked relatives;
or they may be consumed by the fires born within the household.
Regarding such losses of wealth and treasure, [one should remain undisturbed].
He skillfully provides explanation and resolution so that they may be freed from sorrow and affliction.
By means of these causes and conditions, for all classes of sentient beings who experience the three grades of grief— mild, medium,
and intense— the Bodhisattva is able to correctly provide explanation and resolution.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas possess the necessities of life,
they bestow them all immediately upon whoever comes to seek them;
that is to say, to sentient beings who seek food, they give food, and to those who seek drink, they give drink.
Seeking a vehicle, they give a vehicle; seeking clothing, they give clothing;
seeking ornaments, they give ornaments;
seeking various household utensils, they give those utensils.
Seeking garlands and unguents,
they give garlands and unguents;
seeking places of rest, they give places of rest.
To those who seek light, they bestow light.
Furthermore, by their very nature, bodhisattvas are inclined to gather and sustain all classes of sentient beings;
they lead the assembly in accordance with the Dharma and benefit them through skillful means.
With a mind free from attachment, he first grants them formal reliance;
with a heart of compassion, he manifests beneficial action;
and thereafter, he bestows upon them robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and other articles for sustaining the body, all in accordance with the Dharma.
If one does not possess these oneself, one should seek them from faithful householders, lay devotees, or brahmins and accept what they give.
Regarding the robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, medicinal requisites for illness, and other personal articles obtained by oneself through lawful means in accordance with the Dharma:
He uses things in common with the community and incurs no private expenses.
From time to time, he correctly instructs them by means of the eight kinds of instruction and correctly exhorts them by means of the five kinds of exhortation.
The instructions and admonitions explained herein should be understood as having been already analyzed in detail in the previous "Chapter on the Lineage of Powers.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas naturally accord with the mental dispositions of sentient beings.
When acting in accordance with the mind, one first knows the essence and nature of sentient beings;
having known their essence and nature,
one dwells together with those sentient beings as is appropriate for them.
One should dwell together with them in this very manner;
according to the conduct that various sentient beings ought to practice,
one should likewise practice that same conduct together with them.
If bodhisattvas wish to act in accordance with the minds of those beings they seek to transform,
they should carefully examine whether,
in relation to such and such phenomena, they are engaging in physical or verbal conduct.
This gives rise to grief and suffering in others.
If such grief and suffering do not cause them to emerge from unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states,
then at that time the bodhisattva engages in such actions of body and speech.
In order to protect that mind, one employs skillful means through discernment and exerts effort to restrain it,
so that it does not manifest.
Thus, if such sorrow and suffering can cause one to emerge from unwholesome states and establish one in wholesome states, [they are to be accepted].
At that time, regarding such matters, the bodhisattva manifests through body and speech while abiding in a mind of compassion;
he does not follow the inclinations of such sentient beings,
but rather applies skillful means, deliberates, and exerts effort to ensure that [the virtuous practice] is actually carried out.
He further examines with scrutiny:
if, in relation to such matters concerning other sentient beings, he engages in physical or verbal conduct that causes other sentient beings to experience sorrow and suffering.
If such sorrow and suffering do not cause others or other sentient beings, or both, to emerge from unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states,
then at that time the Bodhisattva engages in such actions of body and speech.
In order to protect other states of mind, one employs skillful means and deliberation to exert effort in restraining them so that they do not manifest.
Thus, if sorrow or suffering can cause another person, or other sentient beings, or both, to emerge from an unwholesome state and establish them in a wholesome state, [it should be maintained].
At that time, the bodhisattva engages in such actions of body and speech while abiding in a mind of compassion,
and does not allow himself to be swayed by the minds of such sentient beings.
Through skillful means, he deliberates and exerts effort to bring [the bodhisattva’s conduct] into manifestation;
furthermore, he carefully examines whether the physical or verbal actions performed by the bodhisattva in his own affairs would give rise to sorrow or suffering in others.
Such manifest actions of body and speech are not subsumed within the training precepts of bodhisattvas,
nor do they accord with the accumulations of merit and wisdom.
In such cases, although this sorrow and suffering cannot cause others to emerge from unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states,
at that time the bodhisattva manifests such conduct through body and speech regarding these matters.
In order to protect the minds of others, one should skillfully deliberate and exert effort to restrain [unwholesome conduct] so that it does not manifest.
One should understand that the manifestation of bodily and vocal actions contrary to this is as previously described.
Just as it is with the arising of sorrow and suffering,
so too should it be understood in detail for the arising of joy and bliss, each according to its appropriate application.
Furthermore, this applies to a bodhisattva who acts in accordance with the minds of others.
Knowing that another sentient being is currently entangled by the fetter of anger and that this entanglement is difficult to relinquish,
one does not even praise them,
let alone revile them.
At that time, he likewise does not offer admonition or instruction.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva who acts in accordance with the minds of others does not wait for others to come and engage him in conversation or offer greetings of comfort.
One should still go in person to converse with them and offer greetings of joy;
how much more so when they have come to one and one fails to respond?
Furthermore, this applies to a bodhisattva who acts in accordance with the minds of others.
He never intentionally vexes or offends others,
except when reprimanding those who have committed transgressions; rather,
he gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, with his sense faculties serene and tranquil.
He should reprimand them as appropriate to bring them under control.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva who acts in accordance with the minds of others never mocks or derides another to cause them shame or embarrassment.
He does not dwell in insecurity,
nor does he cause the other's mind to give rise to sorrow or regret;
although he is able to subdue and triumph over them, [he does so without malice].
Yet he does not reveal his own lapses into positions of defeat.
Although he possesses pure faith,
he gives rise to humility and never manifests signs of self-exaltation.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva who acts in accordance with the minds of others does not fail to associate with sentient beings, yet does not associate excessively;
nor does he associate with them at inappropriate times.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva who acts in accordance with the minds of others never manifests before them to disparage what they hold dear,
nor does he manifest before them to praise what they find unlovely.
One who does not engage in sexual intercourse with non-sentient beings should not speak untruths or fail to express sincerity.
One should not repeatedly harbor expectations, but rather receive things according to one's capacity.
If one has previously promised another food, drink, or other such items, [one should fulfill that commitment].
He never makes excuses or fails to attend prior requests;
by nature he is humble and provides instruction in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, the nature of all bodhisattvas is to praise genuine virtues, thereby causing others to rejoice.
In the presence of those endowed with the merit of faith,
one praises the virtue of faith to cause them joy.
In the presence of those endowed with the merit of ethical discipline...
One should praise their virtue of ethical discipline to bring them joy;
before those who are endowed with the merit of learning,
one should praise the virtue of learning to bring them joy.
In the presence of one who is fully endowed with the virtue of equanimity,
one praises the virtue of equanimity to bring them joy.
In the presence of one who is fully endowed with the virtue of wisdom...
He praises their wisdom and virtue to bring them joy.
Furthermore, because the nature of bodhisattvas is compassionate,
they tame sentient beings through the methods of taming.
If sentient beings have minor faults or minor transgressions,
and one harbors feelings of affection within while being free from any intent to harm or vex them,
one should reprimand them with gentle censure.
If there are sentient beings who possess moderate faults and moderate transgressions,
and whom he reproves with moderate censure, while inwardly harboring affection and a mind free from malice toward them.
If there are sentient beings who have committed grave or extremely grave transgressions,
and one, harboring inner affection and a mind free from malice,
rebukes them with severe reproach.
As with the method of reprimand,
so too is the application of disciplinary punishment.
If sentient beings commit transgressions or offenses of minor or medium degree that warrant expulsion, [they should be expelled].
At that time, in order to instruct and admonish him and other sentient beings, the bodhisattva,
out of a heart of compassion and a heart of benefit,
temporarily expels him and later receives him back.
If there are sentient beings who possess grave faults and transgressions for which they ought to be expelled,
the bodhisattva shall expel them for as long as life lasts,
not dwelling with them nor sharing any resources with them.
Out of compassion for them, he does not take them back into his care,
lest those individuals accumulate much demerit within the Buddha’s holy teaching;
furthermore, it is for the sake of instructing and benefiting other sentient beings.
Furthermore, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings,
bodhisattvas manifest supernormal powers,
or do so to cause them fear.
Or for the purpose of attracting and gathering them;

"Out of compassion, please bestow upon me the pure bodhisattva precepts.
Having made this request,
one should focus the mind single-pointedly on a single object.
He nurtures a pure mind, thinking:
"Before long, I shall attain the inexhaustible, immeasurable, and unsurpassed treasury of great merit.

He remained silent.
At that time, a wise and powerful bodhisattva [addressed] that bodhisattva who was practicing right conduct.

Are you able to receive [this teaching]?
The recipient replied, "I am able to receive it.

Having prostrated at his feet, he withdrew with reverence.
Such is the code of discipline (vinaya-śīla) undertaken by a bodhisattva;
compared to all other codes of discipline undertaken, [it is the most supreme].
It is followed by a most excellent, unsurpassed, immeasurable, and boundless treasury of great merit,
and is originated by the foremost and supreme intention of a virtuous mind.
It is universally able to counteract all types of misconduct among all sentient beings;
and compared to all the vows of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*),
this bodhisattva vow of ethical discipline [is superior].
A hundredth part does not equal it;
a thousandth part does not equal it;
even a numerical fraction does not equal it.

First, one should repeatedly and with focused attention reflect for oneself:

Furthermore, Bodhisattvas do not [rely] upon everything.
