those lacking pure faith should not receive them from such a person,
that is, regarding these pure precepts thus received.
From the beginning, they lack faith and understanding and are unable to enter [the path]; they engage in unwholesome reflection;
they are possessive and greedy, corrupted by stinginess and greed;
they have great desires and lack contentment.
One should not receive [the precepts] from one who has violated the pure precepts,
nor from one who lacks reverence for the various points of training (śikṣāpada).
One should not receive [the precepts] from someone who is negligent or lax regarding the restraint of the ethical code,
nor from one who harbors anger and resentment.
One who has little patience— that is,
one who is unable to endure the transgressions of others—
should not receive [the precepts] from such a person.
There are those who are indolent;
there are those who are lax;

for the most part, they are addicted to the pleasure of sleeping day and night, the pleasure of reclining, the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of associating with companions, and the delight in idle talk.
One should not receive [the precepts] from such a person.
One whose mind is distracted— even to the extent that they cannot maintain a single-pointed cultivation of a virtuous mind for as long as it takes to milk a cow—
should not be followed for receiving them.
There are those who are obscured by darkness,
those of a deluded nature,
and those whose minds are extremely inferior.
One should not receive [the precepts] from one who slanders the Bodhisattva Sūtra-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva Piṭaka-mātṛkā.
Furthermore, regarding the method for receiving the bodhisattva vow of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), all bodhisattvas...
Although he has already fully mastered and maintained [the teachings] to their ultimate conclusion,
he never hastily reveals or awakens those sentient beings who lack faith and disparage the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Why is this? Because, having heard it, they are unable to believe or understand it; being shrouded by the obstruction of great ignorance, they immediately give rise to slander.
Because of such slander,
one who abides in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline accomplishes an immeasurable treasury of great merit.
That slanderer is also pursued by a vast storehouse of immeasurable sinful karma,
including all evil speech, evil views, and evil thoughts.
As long as one has not permanently abandoned them, one will ultimately not escape separation from them. Furthermore,
when Bodhisattvas wish to confer the Bodhisattva precepts upon another Bodhisattva,
they should first explain for them the Bodhisattva-piṭaka-mātṛkā, the training rules (śikṣāpada) of the Bodhisattvas, and the characteristics of the points of transgression.
He causes them to listen and receive [the teaching],
and through the observation of their own inclinations with wisdom,
they become capable of discerning and undertaking the bodhisattva precepts.
One who does not merely act upon the exhortation of others nor for the sake of surpassing others should be known as a firm bodhisattva,
capable of receiving the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline.
Having received the precepts through the appropriate and correct method of conferral,
a bodhisattva thus abides in the ethical discipline of restraint.
Regarding this, there are four types of defeats (*pārājika*).
What are the four?
If bodhisattvas, out of a desire to seek gain and honor,
praise themselves and disparage others.
This is called the first *pārājika* offense.
If a bodhisattva, while possessing wealth, is by nature stingy with material goods,
and a person who is suffering, impoverished, without refuge, and without protection comes before him seeking wealth;
Without giving rise to compassion, they practice the relinquishment of generosity.
When those who correctly seek the Dharma appear before them,
because they are by nature stingy regarding the Dharma, they do not bestow it as gifts even though the Dharma is currently present.
This is called the second *pārājika* offense.
If a bodhisattva nurtures such a form of the obsession with anger,
and by reason of this cause does not merely initiate harsh speech and then cease, [but continues further].
Obscured by anger, they strike, injure, and afflict sentient beings with their hands, feet, clods of earth, stones, swords, or clubs;
inwardly harboring an intense disposition of resentment and malice.
If one commits an offense and, when another comes to offer counsel and apologize, refuses to accept it, fails to endure it, and does not relinquish the knot of resentment,
this is called the third *parājika* dharma. Furthermore,
if a bodhisattva slanders the Bodhisattva-piṭaka...
To delight in proclaiming, revealing, establishing,
and [adhering to] a counterfeit of the true Dharma— whether through personal conviction or by following others—
is called the fourth *pārājika* offense.
These are called the four types of defeats for a bodhisattva.
Regarding these four defeats, if a bodhisattva commits even one,
let alone all of them, [he is defeated].
They are no longer capable of increasing and gathering the vast provisions for enlightenment of a bodhisattva within this present life;
they are no longer capable of purifying their intention within this present life.
Such a person is called a counterfeit bodhisattva and not a true bodhisattva,
provided that the bodhisattva employs only the weak or medium grades of entanglement.
Having committed a transgression of any of the four *pārājika* dharmas through intense fetters (*adhimātra-paryavasthāna*),
yet not relinquishing the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*).
This is precisely what is called "abandonment.
If a bodhisattva violates the four types of defeats (pārājika-dharmas) and repeatedly engages in them without any sense of shame or dread of blame, [they have abandoned their vows].
If one develops deep attachment and delight while perceiving these as merits,
it should be known that this is called an offense committed through superior entanglement (*adhimātra-paryavasthāna*).
It is not [an offense] for all bodhisattvas.
If one momentarily manifests an act constituting a defeat (pārājika),
one immediately abandons the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline,
just as bhikṣus who commit an act of defeat immediately relinquish the prātimokṣa vows.
If a bodhisattva, through such a transgression,
abandons the bodhisattva vow of pure ethical discipline,
they are capable of receiving it again in this present life; they are not incapable.
Just as a bhikṣu who, while abiding in the prātimokṣa vows,
commits a pārājika offense is no longer fit to receive them again in this present life, so too,
briefly stated, there are two conditions by which one relinquishes the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline.
First, the abandonment of the great vow for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
second, the commission of an offense involving the defeat-stages through the manifestation of superior-grade fetters.
Even if these bodhisattvas were to take rebirth throughout the worlds of the ten directions in every place of birth, [they would still be considered to have fallen].
He does not abandon the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*).
Because of this, the bodhisattva does not forsake his great vow for unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*),
nor does he manifest the commission of a defeat (*pārājika*) through the operation of intense fetters (*adhimātra-paryavasthāna*).
If bodhisattvas, having taken rebirth elsewhere, forget their original resolve,
they encounter virtuous friends who,
desiring to awaken their mindfulness of the bodhisattva precepts, [provide instruction].
Although it is experienced repeatedly,
it is not a new experience, nor is it newly acquired.

In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth part of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the first section on Yoga, the tenth chapter on Ethics (Śīla), part two: Thus does a bodhisattva abide in the ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) of a bodhisattva.

Day after day, whether toward the Tathāgata or for the sake of a stūpa built for the Tathāgata,

If one does not make offerings with various articles of worship— whether few or many—

There is no offense in cases where the mind is deranged.

For a bodhisattva who has attained pure intention,

It is not committed out of arrogance, nor with a mind free from resentment or ill will;
rather, it arises solely from laziness, indolence, forgetfulness, and a neutral state of mind.

There is no violation in the following case:

or having a deranged mind,

If a bodhisattva dwells in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline,
as the Bhagavān [has taught]:

Why is this? Because the śrāvakas regard self-benefit as supreme and disregard the benefit of others.
To dwell with few activities, few tasks, and few expectations while engaged in the welfare of others may be called "excellent";
however, for bodhisattvas, the welfare of others is paramount.

It is not considered excellent for them to disregard their own welfare and dwell with few activities, few tasks, and few expectations while engaged in the welfare of others; such would not be the case for a bodhisattva acting for the sake of others.
From non-relatives— such as elders, householders, brahmins, and those who give freely—
one should seek hundreds or thousands of various kinds of robes,
while observing whether those sentient beings have the means or lack the means [to provide them].
He accepts whatever is given as appropriate.
As it is said regarding the seeking of robes, so it is for the seeking of alms bowls; as it is for the seeking of robes and bowls, so it is for all else.
In this way, having personally sought various threads and fibers, one causes those who are not relatives to weave them into robes;
for the sake of benefiting others, one should keep various *kauśeya* garments and various sitting and lying implements.
Each of these matters reaches up to one hundred.
The produced colors that can be dyed reach hundreds of thousands of koṭis;
beyond this number as well, one should likewise take them as accumulated.
Among such matters as these, regarding those offenses that involve minor affairs, minor activities, and minor expectations— which are prohibited and forbidden—
a bodhisattva does not train together with the śrāvakas.
A bodhisattva who abides in the code of pure ethical discipline [should understand this].
If, in the midst of benefiting others, one harbors a mind of resentment or a mind of malice,
and dwells with few activities, few duties, and few aspirations,
this is called an offense and a transgression.
This is a defiled transgression.
However, if it occurs due to laziness, indolence, forgetfulness, or a neutral state of mind,
such as dwelling with few activities, few duties, and few expectations, it is not a transgression.
This is called an offense and a transgression;
it is a non-afflicted violation.
If a bodhisattva dwells in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline...
For the sake of benefiting others through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), one may occasionally engage in certain natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
By virtue of this cause and condition, there is no violation of the bodhisattva precepts; rather, much merit is generated.
That is to say, for example, when a bodhisattva sees robbers and thieves who, out of greed for wealth, intend to kill many beings,
or who intend to harm great śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas.
Or again, desiring to commit many deeds of immediate retribution,
one sees this matter and reflects with the thought:
"If I were to take the life of that evil person, I would fall into hell."
If I do not sever it,
the karma of immediate retribution will be completed and I shall undergo great suffering;
I would rather kill him and fall into hell.
He never causes them to undergo the suffering of the Avīci hell.
Thus does the bodhisattva reflect with such an intention;
toward those sentient beings, he may act with either a virtuous mind or a neutral mind.
Having understood this matter, one should give rise to profound shame and remorse for the sake of the future;
then, with a heart of compassion, one may take that life.
By reason of these causes and conditions, there is no transgression of the bodhisattva precepts, and much merit is generated.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva sees high-ranking officials who are exceedingly violent and cruel toward sentient beings, lacking any compassion and intent solely on inflicting harm,
the bodhisattva, upon seeing this, gives rise to a heart of pity.
One should cultivate the intention to bring about benefit and happiness.
To the extent of one's ability, if one dismisses or deposes those in superior positions,
by reason of this, there is no transgression of the bodhisattva precepts and much merit is generated.
Furthermore, it is as when a bodhisattva sees a robber or thief who has seized the property of others—
whether it be the goods of the Saṃgha or the goods of a stūpa—
and having taken a great quantity of these items, claims them as his own and enjoys them according to his pleasure.
Having seen this, the bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of compassion;
he conceives an intention for the benefit and happiness of those sentient beings and,
to the extent of his power and ability, forcibly takes [the object] away from them.
Lest they enjoy such wealth,
they would undergo long nights of meaninglessness and disadvantage;
for this reason, the treasures and wealth have been seized from them.
If it is property belonging to the Saṃgha, restore it to the Saṃgha;
if it is property belonging to a stūpa, restore it to the stūpa;
if it is property belonging to sentient beings, restore it to sentient beings.

Furthermore, seeing a leader of a community or a leader of a grove who takes property belonging to the Saṃgha or property belonging to a stūpa, claiming it as his own and enjoying it according to his whim,
the bodhisattva, having seen this, reflects upon that evil and gives rise to a mind of compassion.
One should not, on account of such improper enjoyment, undergo harm and disadvantage for a long night;
rather, one should relinquish what one controls to the best of one's ability.
In this way, although the bodhisattva takes what is not given, [it is not a transgression].
Yet, there is no transgression, and much merit is generated.

Furthermore, suppose a bodhisattva living as a householder sees a woman who is currently unattached [to others] and practices the ways of sexual desire, and she directs her mind toward that bodhisattva seeking non-celibate conduct.
Having seen this, the bodhisattva reflects with focused attention:
"Let me not allow my mind to become resentful, which would produce much demerit;
if I comply with their wishes, they will attain mastery."
By means of skillful methods, they establish them so that they may plant roots of goodness and cause them to abandon unwholesome karma; yet,
while dwelling in a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, they engage in non-celibate conduct.
Although they practice such defiled and tainted dharmas,
they commit no transgressions and generate much merit;
for the renunciant bodhisattva acts to protect the instructions of the śrāvaka āryas so that they do not perish.
One should never engage in unchaste conduct.

Furthermore, for the sake of liberating many sentient beings from life-threatening dangers, imprisonment, or hardships such as having their hands or feet cut off, their noses sliced off, their ears slit, or their eyes gouged out, a bodhisattva [may act].
Although bodhisattvas do not knowingly utter false speech even at the risk of their own lives,
they may nevertheless speak falsely after deliberate reflection for the sake of rescuing and liberating those sentient beings.
In brief, a bodhisattva contemplates only what is beneficial for sentient beings and not what is harmful;
being free from defiled thoughts, he acts solely for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
If one intentionally speaks words contrary to the truth while being fully aware of it,
yet at the time of speaking those words does not transgress the bodhisattva precepts and instead generates much merit—
just as in the case of a bodhisattva.
Seeing sentient beings who are possessed by evil friends and, out of affection for them, do not abandon them,
the Bodhisattva, having seen this, gives rise to a heart of compassion and generates the intention to bring them benefit and happiness.
According to one's ability and strength,
one should utter divisive speech to cause [beings] to distance themselves from evil friends and abandon their mutual affection,
so that sentient beings do not suffer long nights of meaninglessness and disadvantage due to their proximity to evil friends.
In this way, when a bodhisattva speaks words that cause division with a mind intent on benefiting others,
there is no transgression in alienating those who are attached to one another, and much merit is generated.
Furthermore, it is as when a bodhisattva sees sentient beings whose conduct has strayed from the path and who act unrighteously.
Uttering harsh words and sternly rebuking them,
he employs skillful means to lead them out of unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states.
In this way, the bodhisattva acts with a mind intent on benefiting others.
When speaking harsh words to sentient beings,
there is no transgression and much merit is generated.
Furthermore, it is as when a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who take pleasure in performing arts, chanting, and singing.
There may be those who take pleasure in talk concerning kings, thieves, food and drink, sexual indulgence, or the senseless chatter of the streets;
the Bodhisattva is skillful in all such matters and gives rise to a heart of compassion for those sentient beings.
With the intention of producing benefit and happiness,
one engages in idle chatter, manifesting various performances,
recitations, songs, and satirical verses, as well as discourses concerning kings, thieves, food and drink, the brothels, and so forth.
He causes those sentient beings to rejoice,
draws them in, brings them under his influence,
and through skillful means guides them out of unwholesome states and establishes them in wholesome states.
In this way, when a bodhisattva engages in frivolous speech,
there is no transgression and much merit is generated.
This is so for a bodhisattva who dwells securely in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline.
They give rise to deceitful talk and false appearances;
they employ various means to seek profit through profit;
they relish the dharma of wrong livelihood without shame, persisting in it without relinquishing it.
This is called an offense and a transgression;
it is a defiled violation.
There is no violation in the following case:
If, in order to eliminate [these afflictions], one generates the desire and exerts diligent effort,
yet the afflictions still blaze up and suppress the mind, manifesting from time to time—
this is the case for those bodhisattvas who abide in the bodhisattva’s code of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*).
Agitated by restlessness, their minds are not tranquil and they do not delight in tranquility;
they engage in loud play and clamorous chatter,
acting with frivolity and leaping about, seeking to provoke laughter in others.
Such conditions are called an offense, a transgression,
and a defiled violation.
If it arises through forgetfulness,
it is a non-afflicted transgression.
There is no transgression in the following cases:
If one generates the desire to dispel [these states],
it is explained at length as before.
If one wishes to employ skillful means to resolve the resentment produced in others so that it may cease:
If one wishes to dispel the sorrow and affliction produced in others, or if others naturally delight in the aforementioned matters,
one should employ skillful means to gather them in, treat them with reverence and care,
and act in accordance with their inclinations.
If other sentient beings harbor suspicion and obstruction toward a bodhisattva,
inwardly concealing resentment, malicious schemes,
and hostility while outwardly manifesting a joyful countenance to represent inner purity;
In all such cases, there is no transgression.
If a bodhisattva, dwelling in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline,
should give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine:
A bodhisattva should not rejoice in nirvāṇa;
rather, they should cultivate a sense of aversion toward nirvāṇa itself,
as well as toward all primary afflictions and secondary afflictions.
One should not seek their total cessation out of fear,
nor should one give rise to a mind of exclusive revulsion;
for Bodhisattvas undergo the cycle of birth and death throughout three incalculable eons in pursuit of great enlightenment.
If one makes such a statement,
it is called an offense, a transgression;
it is a defiled violation.
Why is this? It is because,
just as the śrāvakas delight in and draw near to their own nirvāṇa,
they feel a profound sense of weary detachment toward all afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
In this way, the bodhisattva delights in and draws near to great parinirvāṇa,
while feeling deep-seated revulsion toward all afflictions and secondary afflictions;
[this latter] exceeds the former by hundreds of thousands of koṭis.
Because the śrāvakas apply themselves to the correct practice solely for the sake of attaining their own individual welfare,
whereas the bodhisattvas do so universally for the sake of all sentient beings attaining their welfare.
One diligently cultivates correct practice;
therefore, a bodhisattva should diligently cultivate and gather an undefiled mind,
acting in accordance with contaminated phenomena.
They achieve the unsurpassed, uncontaminated dharmas that transcend all arhats.
If bodhisattvas abide in the bodhisattva’s code of ethical discipline,
they will inspire even those who previously held no faith or respect for them.
Regarding so-called evil reputation, ill repute, and bad fame:
if one neither guards against nor clears them away— remaining indifferent even when the matter is true—
this is called an offense and a transgression.
This is a defiled offense.
If the matter is not true and one does not clear oneself of the charge,
this is called an offense and a transgression.
This is not a defiled offense.
There is no offense if it is another non-Buddhist,
another who is hateful and envious, or if one has gone forth oneself.
If one is engaged in the practice of begging for alms or cultivating virtuous conduct, and slanderous rumors circulate;
or if one is obscured by anger or possesses a perverted mind, and slanderous rumors circulate—
in all such cases, there is no transgression.
If bodhisattvas, dwelling securely in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline,
see sentient beings who could achieve their welfare through various harsh applications or intense applications, they protect those beings from distress and do not manifest such actions themselves.
This is called an offense and a transgression;
it is a non-afflicted violation.
There is no offense in the following case:
Observing that by reason of this, one gains little benefit in the present life and gives rise to much distress and affliction—
if a bodhisattva abides in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline...
If he reviles in response to reviling, responds with anger to anger,
strikes in response to striking, or plays tricks in response to being tricked,
this is called an offense and a transgression.
This is a transgression of defilement.
If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline,
commits an offense against another sentient being.
Or, although one has not personally committed an offense that might provoke suspicion of an invasion [of their rights],
due to a mind of resentment and envy, or being gripped by pride,
one fails to apologize in accordance with reason and instead treats them with contemptuous indifference.
This is called an offense, a transgression;
it is an afflicted violation,
occurring if one acts out of indolence, laziness, or heedlessness.
To abandon [the practice] lightly without expressing regret is called an offense and a transgression;
it is a non-afflicted violation.
There is no transgression if one intends to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue them, leading them out of unwholesome states and establishing them in wholesome states;
or if they are followers of external paths.
If that person expects that an apology must be preceded by the commission of an unrighteous and culpable act,
or if that sentient being is by nature prone to strife and becomes even more enraged at the time of receiving an apology; [then one should not apologize].
Furthermore, if one knows that the other person is by nature patient and free from resentment;
or if one definitely understands that the other person feels deep shame because of having committed an offense and has already apologized;
yet one still does not apologize in return.
In all such cases, there is no transgression.
If a bodhisattva, dwelling securely in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline,
is subjected to aggression by others...
If that person returns to offer a formal and impartial apology,
yet one harbors a mind of resentment and seeks to harm or vex them by refusing to accept the apology,
this is called an offense and a transgression.
This is a transgression of passion.
Although one harbors no resentment toward the other and has no desire to cause them harm,
because of an innate disposition that lacks forbearance, one does not accept their apology.
This is also called "having an offense" or "having transgressed," yet it is not a defiled transgression.
There is no transgression in the following cases:
If one wishes to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue them,
all details should be understood as previously explained at length. If, however,
the apology is not made according to the Dharma or is not equitable, [the matter remains unresolved].
There is no offense if one does not accept their apology.

However, if a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, harbors anger toward another, maintains it continuously, and having given rise to it, does not relinquish it; [this constitutes an offense].
This is called an offense and a transgression;
it is a defiled violation.
There is no violation in the following case:
In order to abandon those [faults], he generates the desire to do so;
the details are as previously explained.
If bodhisattvas abide in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline...
Due to the predominant power of attachment to service and offerings,
one manages the assembly with a mind of craving and defilement;
this is called an offense and a transgression.
This is a transgression involving defilement.
There is no transgression when one manages a community of followers without greed for service and without a mind of passionate attachment.
If bodhisattvas, while abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline,
are indolent and lazy, becoming addicted to sleep, pleasure in reclining, pleasure in lying down, and pleasure in leaning,
at improper times and in excessive measure.
This is called an offense, a transgression;
it is an afflicted violation.
There is no violation in the following case:
If one encounters illness, or lacks the strength to travel, or becomes utterly exhausted on the road,
one should generate the desire to abandon those [obstacles].
All details should be understood as previously explained at length.
If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline,
spends time in vain by engaging in worldly talk with a mind of attachment,
this is called an offense and a transgression.
This is a transgression involving defilement.
If one wastes time through forgetfulness,
this is called an offense and a violation.
This is not a defiled offense.
There is no offense when one observes others engaged in conversation and acts to protect their feelings.
Abiding in right mindfulness, listen for even a brief moment.
There is no offense if the matter is extraordinary, or if one briefly asks another a question or answers another's question.
If bodhisattvas, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline,
desire to settle the mind and stabilize it,
yet their minds are possessed by resentment and pride;
If one does not go to the teacher’s presence to request instruction,
this is called an offense, a transgression;
it is an afflicted violation.
If one fails to request [instruction] due to indolence or laziness,
it is an unafflicted transgression.
There is no transgression in the following cases:
If one encounters illness, or lacks physical strength;
or if one knows that the teacher teaches erroneously;
or if one is oneself well-learned and possesses the intellectual power capable of stabilizing the mind.
If one has already received the necessary instruction but does not request further guidance,
there is no transgression.
This applies when a bodhisattva abides in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*).
If one gives rise to the hindrance of sensual desire and endures it without relinquishing it,
this is called an offense, a transgression;
it is an afflicted violation.
There is no transgression if,
while one has generated the desire to abandon them and exerts diligent effort,
the afflictions are so intense that they overwhelm the mind and thus manifest from time to time.
Just as it is with the hindrance of sensual desire,
so too should one understand the hindrances of ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt to be exactly the same.
If bodhisattvas, while abiding in the bodhisattva code of ethical discipline,
relish meditative absorption and perceive such relishing as a merit,
this is called an offense and a transgression.
This is a stained transgression.
There is no transgression if one generates the desire to abandon that [transgression].
The detailed explanation is as before.
If bodhisattvas, while dwelling in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline,
give rise to such views and establish such doctrines:
A bodhisattva should not listen to the teachings associated with the Śrāvaka vehicle;
they should not uphold them, nor should they train in them.
Why should a bodhisattva listen to, uphold, or diligently train in the teachings associated with the Śrāvaka vehicle?
This is called an offense and a transgression;
it is a defiled violation. Why is this so?
A bodhisattva should apply themselves with diligent study even to the treatises of non-Buddhist paths,
let alone to the words of the Buddha;
in doing so, there is no transgression.
In order to cause those who are exclusively devoted to the lesser Dharma to relinquish that desire, it is said:
"If bodhisattvas abide in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline..."
Without having thoroughly investigated the Bodhisattva-piṭaka,
they completely abandon the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and devote themselves exclusively to the study of the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
This is called an offense and a transgression;
it is not a defiled transgression.
If a bodhisattva dwells securely in the ethical discipline of the bodhisattva vows...
If one currently possesses the Buddhist teachings yet fails to study them with thorough diligence,
while instead applying oneself assiduously to the treatises of heterodox paths and various non-Buddhist doctrines,
this is called an offense and a transgression.
This is a defiled offense.
There is no offense if [the person] is exceptionally intelligent or capable of receiving [the teaching] quickly.
If one is able not to forget it over a long period of time;
if one is able to contemplate and penetrate its meaning;
and if one examines the Buddha’s teachings according to reason.
One who has achieved the unshakable awakening that proceeds in tandem [with practice] should,
throughout each day, constantly devote two parts of their time to training in the Buddha’s word and one part to external study.
In such cases, there is no transgression.
If a bodhisattva, while dwelling securely in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline,
violates the bodhisattva dharma...
They seek mastery in the treatises of heterodox paths and various non-Buddhist doctrines;
they cherish, delight in, and become attached to them with a profound mind,
treating them not as if they were bitter medicine, but rather as something to be habitually pursued.
This is called an offense and a transgression;
it is a defiled violation.
If a bodhisattva abides in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline...
Upon hearing the Bodhisattva-piṭaka,
they do not give rise to faith or understanding regarding its most profound and supreme depths— the true meaning of the Dharma and the inconceivable spiritual power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—
but instead feel aversion, turn their backs on it, and slander it.
That which does not lead to the meaning, does not lead to the Dharma, and was not spoken by the Tathāgata,
and which cannot benefit or bring happiness to sentient beings—
this is called an offense, a transgression.
This is a defiled transgression.
Such slander may arise either from one's own internal improper mental attention or by following the lead of others in making such a statement.
If bodhisattvas, while dwelling in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline,
hear of a point that is profound or most profound and their minds do not believe or understand it,
those bodhisattvas should at that time exert themselves to believe and accept it.
One should train thus, free from deceit and crookedness:
"I am unwholesome, blind, and devoid of the eye of wisdom;
regarding that which has been proclaimed by the Tathāgata’s own eye, I have produced slander toward the intentional language of the Tathāgatas."

In this way, the bodhisattva, regarding himself as lacking knowledge, looks up to and defers to the Tathāgata, who possesses unobstructed knowledge regarding all Buddha-dharmas and perceives them with equal and thorough insight;
thus practicing correctly, he commits no transgression.
Although they lack faith and understanding, they do not disparage [the teaching].
If bodhisattvas abide in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline,
regarding others...
If one possesses a mind of attachment and craving, or a mind of anger and hatred,
and praises oneself while disparaging others,
this is called an offense and a transgression.
This is a defiled offense.
There is no offense if it is for the purpose of subduing various evil non-Buddhists.
Whether for the purpose of upholding the holy teachings of the Tathāgata,
or desiring to employ skillful means to discipline and subdue others—
as was explained in detail previously— [one may act accordingly].
Or, wishing to cause those who have not yet developed pure faith to do so,
and to cause those who already possess pure faith to increase it further—
this is the case when bodhisattvas abide in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline.
When one hears that there is a discourse on the sublime Dharma for discussion and definitive resolution, yet,
being constrained by pride and harboring a mind of resentment or a mind of malice, does not go to listen to it—
this is called an offense and a transgression.
This is a transgression of an afflicted nature.
If one fails to go and listen because of being obscured by indolence or laziness,
it is a transgression of a non-afflicted nature.
There is no transgression if one does not perceive it,
or if one is afflicted by illness.
If one lacks the strength;
if one knows it would be explained erroneously;
or if one does so to protect the mind of the speaker of the Dharma.
If one correctly understands the meaning of what was spoken—
that which has been repeatedly heard, retained, and comprehended—
if one has already heard much and is fully endowed with hearing and retention, such that the accumulation of what has been heard is complete.
If one wishes to dwell the mind uninterruptedly upon an object,
or if one strives to induce the superior meditative concentrations of a bodhisattva,
or if one recognizes for oneself that one’s own dullness is of the highest degree and that one’s wisdom is dull and turbid.

There is no transgression if one does not go to listen to the Dharma when it is difficult to receive, difficult to retain, or difficult to collect the mind upon the object of focus to bring it into meditative concentration.
If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline,
intentionally disparages a Dharma teacher,
fails to show deep respect, and mocks or ridicules them.
If one relies solely on the letter and does not rely on the meaning,
this is called an offense, a transgression;
it is a defiled violation.
If bodhisattvas, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline,
harbor a mind of resentment or a mind of malice toward sentient beings regarding tasks that ought to be performed for them, and thus fail to act as their companions.
That is to say, regarding the performance of tasks that ought to be done,
or while traveling on a road whether going or returning,
or during the application of effort toward the correct explanation of an undertaking.
Whether it be regarding the protection of all one's wealth and treasures,
or regarding reconciling those who are estranged and settling disputes,
or regarding auspicious gatherings or meritorious deeds, they do not act as companions.
This is called an offense, a transgression;
it is an afflicted violation.
It occurs if one fails to act as an assistant because of being shrouded by indolence and laziness.
This is not a defiled offense.
There is no offense if one has a physical ailment or lacks physical strength.
If one knows that the person can accomplish it themselves;
if one knows that the seeker already has their own support;
or if one knows that what is being done would lead to what is unbeneficial or to what is contrary to the Dharma.
If one wishes to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue them,
it is explained at length as before.
If one has previously consented to act as an assistant to another, [one may do so].
If one requests another who is powerful to provide assistance;
if one is diligently practicing wholesome qualities and does not wish to abandon them even for a moment;
or if one is by nature dull-witted and finds it difficult to receive and retain the teachings heard.
As explained extensively before:
if it is for the sake of protecting the minds of many sentient beings,
or if one does not act as a companion in order to uphold the regulations of the Saṃgha.
In all such cases, there is no transgression.
If a bodhisattva, dwelling securely in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline,
sees sentient beings afflicted by a severe illness.
If, harboring a mind of resentment or a mind of malice, one does not go to serve and attend upon them,
this is called an offense, a transgression;
it is an afflicted violation.
If one fails to go and provide service because of being shrouded by indolence or laziness,
it is a non-afflicted transgression.
There is no transgression in the following cases:
If one is personally ill or lacks physical strength,
one should request another who is capable and compliant to go and provide service; or,
if one knows that the patient has someone to rely upon and someone to protect them.
If one knows that the patient possesses the strength to attend to their own needs;
if one understands that the patient, though afflicted by a chronic illness, is capable of supporting themselves;
or if it is for the sake of diligently cultivating vast, unsurpassed, and sublime wholesome qualities.
If one wishes to protect and maintain the wholesome qualities one has cultivated so that they remain uninterrupted,
yet realizes for oneself that one is of superior dullness and that one's wisdom is clouded and turbid, making it difficult to receive and retain the teachings one hears;
It is difficult to collect the mind upon the object of focus and bring it to concentration;
however, if one first permits others to perform services for them,
such as for a sick person, [it becomes easier].
One should act as a companion to those who suffer;
it should be understood that one likewise desires to remove their suffering.
This is how a bodhisattva abides in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*).
Seeing that sentient beings engage extensively in unrighteous conduct for the sake of achieving goals in this life and future lives,
he harbors a mind of resentment and a mind of malice,
and thus fails to proclaim to them the correct principles as they truly are.
This is called an offense and a transgression;
it is an afflicted violation.
If one fails to explain [the teaching] because of being shrouded by indolence and laziness, it is likewise an offense.
This is not a defiled offense.
There is no offense if one lacks knowledge or lacks the physical strength [to act].
If one requests another who possesses the power [to explain] to speak;
or if that person themselves possesses the power of wisdom;
or if they are sustained by other virtuous friends.
If one wishes to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue them—
as explained in detail previously—

and knows that if one were to speak the correct principle as it truly is, they would give rise to a mind of resentment, utter malicious words, misunderstand it perversely, or lack affection and respect.
Furthermore, if one knows that the other person is of a base and stubborn nature,
there is no offense in not preaching the Dharma to them.
If bodhisattvas, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline,
fail to recognize or acknowledge the kindness shown by sentient beings who have previously rendered them assistance.
To harbor a mind of resentment and thus fail to respond appropriately in person constitutes an offense and a transgression;
it is an afflicted violation.
If one fails to manifest a response because of being obscured by indolence or laziness, it is not a defiled transgression.
There is no transgression in the following cases: [omitted].
Even if one exerts diligent effort, being without power or ability, one will not obtain the reward.
If one wishes to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue them,
it is explained at length as before.
If one wishes to repay a kindness but the other does not accept it,
there is no transgression in either case.
If a bodhisattva dwells securely in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline...
Seeing sentient beings fallen into states of misfortune— having lost their wealth, treasures, kinsmen, and positions of honor—
and being born into much sorrow and affliction,
one harbors a mind of resentment and fails to go and offer consolation.
This is called an offense and a transgression;
it is a defiled violation.
If one fails to go and provide explanation and resolution because of being shrouded by indolence and laziness, [it is likewise a violation].
This is not a defiled offense.
Regarding those who are without offense,
it should be understood as previously explained.
If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, possesses various requisites for livelihood such as food and drink,
yet does not act as an assistant in the affairs of others...
If one sees a seeker arrive who is specifically seeking food, drink, or other such things,
yet out of a mind of resentment or a mind of malice fails to give them,
this is called an offense and a transgression.
This is a transgression committed through defilement.
If one fails to give due to indolence, laziness, or negligence,
it is a transgression not committed through defilement.
There is no transgression if one currently possesses no material goods to give;
or if the other person seeks that which is not in accordance with the Dharma or is unsuitable.
If one wishes to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue them,
it should be explained at length as previously stated.
If there are those who come seeking [something], and it is not appropriate for the king, one should protect the king’s intentions.
If one refrains from giving out of respect for the monastic regulations, there is no transgression.
However, if a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline,
accepts disciples with a mind of resentment, [it is a transgression].
Yet, failing to provide timely, unerring instruction and unerring admonition,
and knowing the community’s lack of resources,
he does not seek [provisions] from those faithful laymen, householders, and brahmins for their sake.

If one fails to provide at the appropriate times clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicinal requisites for illness— all items necessary for sustaining the body— pursuing them in accordance with the Dharma,
this is called an offense and a transgression.
This is a defiled transgression if one fails to go and provide instruction due to laziness, indolence, or negligence.
If one does not go to provide instruction and admonition,
nor seeks out requisites in accordance with the Dharma,
it is a non-afflicted transgression.
There is no transgression if one desires to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue them,
as explained in detail previously.
If one is observing the monastic regulations, or if one is afflicted by illness,
or if one lacks the physical strength to engage in the practice,
or if one has requested another who possesses such strength to take one's place.
If one knows that the assembly is widely recognized by the world as possessing great merit,
such that each member has the capacity to seek out their own requisites for the body, such as clothing and other necessities; then,
one should provide them with instruction and admonition according to what is appropriate for each.
All have already been provided with unerring instruction and admonition. However,
if one knows that within the assembly there is a former outsider who has entered among the group for the sake of stealing the Dharma, and who is incapable and cannot be tamed;
In all such cases, there is no transgression.
However, if a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline,
harbors a mind of resentment and does not comply with the wishes of other sentient beings, [it constitutes a fault].
This is called an offense and a transgression;
it is a defiled violation.
If, due to indolence, laziness, or negligence, one does not comply with it, [it is likewise a violation].
This is not an afflicted transgression.
There is no transgression if that which is desired by the other is not suitable for them.
If one has an illness, or lacks the physical strength to engage in the practice;
or if it is prohibited by the monastic regulations;
or if it is something the person holds dear, even though it may be suitable for them.
Yet, this would be neither appropriate nor pleasing to the great assembly. However,
if it were for the sake of subduing various evil non-Buddhists,
or if one wished to employ skillful means to discipline and overcome them, [it would be permissible].
As explained extensively above, there is no transgression in cases where [the mind] does not follow the movement of the mind.
If a bodhisattva dwells securely in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline...
With a mind harboring resentment,
one does not wish to proclaim the actual virtues of others,
nor does one wish to praise their actual reputation.
If he does not praise a truly excellent teaching by saying "well said," it is called an offense, a transgression;
it is an afflicted violation.
If [the failure to proclaim] is due to laziness, indolence, or negligence,
it is a non-afflicted transgression;
there is no transgression in such cases.
If one knows that a person’s nature is inclined toward few desires,
one should protect their feelings;
likewise, if they are ill or lack physical strength.
If one wishes to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue them,
as explained in detail previously;
or if one is observing the regulations of the Sangha.
If one knows that through such causes as manifesting [the faults], those afflictions, arrogance, and agitation arise, which are meaningless; then,
in order to prevent this fault,
one should know that although those qualities appear to be virtues, they are not actual virtues.
If one knows that although their praise appears to be good praise, it is not actually good praise;
or if one knows that although their speech appears to be sublime speech, it is not actually sublime;
or if it is for the purpose of subduing various evil non-Buddhists.
If one acts out of a desire to wait for the completion of another's discourse,
or because of not wishing to proclaim it oneself,
there is no transgression in any such case.
If bodhisattvas, dwelling securely in the bodhisattva code of ethical discipline,
see sentient beings who ought to be rebuked,
ought to be punished, or ought to be expelled.
They harbor defiled minds and do not reprove them;
or, although they reprove them, they do not discipline or instruct them in accordance with the Dharma;
or, although they discipline and instruct them in accordance with the Dharma...
If one does not expel or banish them,
this is called an offense, a transgression;
it is an afflicted violation.
If, due to indolence, laziness, or negligence,
one fails to reprimand [the offender] or even expel them,
this constitutes a non-afflicted transgression.
There is no transgression if one knows that the person is incurable and cannot be spoken to.
One who delights in harsh speech generates much resentment;
therefore, it should be abandoned. However, if one considers the appropriate timing, [it may be permitted].
If one observes that because of this there will be strife, litigation, contention, and rivalry;
or if one observes that because of this the Saṅgha will become noisy and distracted and the Saṅgha will be split;
yet one knows that those sentient beings do not harbor deceit or crookedness, but have accomplished superior and intense shame and remorse.
If they quickly restore their purity and do not reprimand or even expel them,
there is no transgression. This applies when bodhisattvas abide in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline.
Fully endowed with the power of various supernatural transformations and manifestations,
he is able to terrify those among sentient beings who should be terrified,
and is able to attract and gather in those who should be attracted.
If, for the sake of avoiding offerings made out of faith, one does not manifest supernormal powers to inspire awe and attract others,
this is called an offense and a transgression;
it is a non-afflicted violation.
There is no transgression if one knows that the sentient beings therein are mostly attached to perverse dogmas and are wicked non-Buddhists who slander the noble ones.
If one has established wrong views,
there is no offense in not manifesting supernormal powers to terrify or attract others.
Furthermore, there is no transgression in any case if the mind is severely deranged by insanity,
or if one is oppressed by intense physical suffering.
If one has never previously received the pure vows and ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*),
it should be known that there is no transgression whatsoever.
Furthermore, regarding these various matters arising from the bodhisattva training precepts:
The Buddha taught these matters scattered throughout various sūtras according to the capacities of his listeners—

namely, the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the morality of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*).
Now, they are compiled and explained here in this *mātṛkā* of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Within this regard, a bodhisattva should give rise to respect, abide in extreme reverence, and practice with dedicated diligence.
Once these bodhisattvas have correctly received the code of discipline from another, they should proceed as follows.
Through the perfectly pure intention of seeking learning, the intention for enlightenment, and the intention to benefit all sentient beings,
he gives rise to the utmost reverence and respect.
From the very beginning, one should apply oneself with single-minded diligence and not commit any transgression.
Should a transgression occur, one must immediately repent and eliminate it according to the Dharma so as to restore purity.
Furthermore, regarding all such transgressions of this bodhisattva:
One should know that these are all subsumed under *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
One should confess them before a person of the Śrāvaka or Mahāyāna vehicles who is capable, able to understand the meaning of verbal expression, and able to accept it.

If a bodhisattva violates the aforementioned rules of defeat through an intense degree of entanglement, they lose the ethical discipline of the vows. This is rectified by confessing and repenting. If they commit such an offense with an intense degree of entanglement, they forfeit the vow of ethical discipline.
One should undergo re-ordination.
If one commits an offense against the aforementioned rules of defeat (*pārājika*) due to middling-grade fetters (*madhyama-paryavasthāna*),
one should do so before three persons (*pudgala*).
If the number exceeds this,
one should proceed according to the ritual for the disclosure and removal of evil deeds (*pratikarman*):
first, one must state the name of the offense committed.
One should speak thus:
"Venerable One" (āyuṣmat), or with focused intent,
or address them as "Virtuous One" (bhadanta).
I, [name], have transgressed the Bodhisattva Vinaya rules.
For the matter as described, I have committed a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The remainder is according to the method for confessing and extinguishing *duṣkṛta* offenses as practiced by *bhikṣus*.
It should be stated thus:
if one commits an offense through a minor degree of entanglement (*paryavasthāna*),
it is as in the case of the *parājika* rules and other offenses mentioned above.
One should confess and repent before a single *pudgala*;
the method for this should be understood as previously described.
If there is no suitable *pudgala* available to whom one may confess and eliminate the offense committed, [one should proceed as follows].
At that time, the Bodhisattva, with a pure intention, gives rise to a self-vow:
"I shall certainly guard against future [transgressions] so as never to commit them again.
In this way, one emerges from and purifies oneself regarding the transgression.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva wishes to receive the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*),
if they do not encounter an individual (*pudgala*) endowed with all the necessary qualities,
they should at that time personally receive the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline before an image of the Tathāgata.
One should receive it in this manner:
baring the right shoulder, placing the right knee on the ground,
or squatting or kneeling, one should speak as follows.
I, who am named [so-and-so],
respectfully address all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the assembly of Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages.
I now wish, before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in the worlds of the ten directions, to...
I vow to undertake all the training precepts of the bodhisattvas;
I vow to undertake all the pure ethical discipline of the bodhisattvas, namely:
the morality of restraint, the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas, and the morality of benefiting sentient beings.
Such training rules and such pure precepts have been fully possessed by all bodhisattvas of the past,
and shall be fully possessed by all bodhisattvas of the future.
All present bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions now fully possess these training rules and these pure precepts;
all past bodhisattvas have already trained in them.
All bodhisattvas of the future shall study this;
all bodhisattvas currently existing throughout the ten directions are studying it now.
The second and third [sections] are also spoken in the same manner.
Having finished speaking, one should rise.
All else should be understood as before.
Furthermore, regarding the path of transgressing the precepts for a bodhisattva:
There is no offense that is without remainder.
As the Blessed One has said,
these bodhisattvas mostly commit offenses arising from anger.
It does not arise from greed.
One should understand that the intended meaning (saṃdhi) spoken here is this:
namely, that bodhisattvas cherish all sentient beings.
By the sovereign power of compassion for all sentient beings,
whatever they do is entirely the work of a bodhisattva; it is not that which is not the work of a bodhisattva.
It is not through mere action or non-action that an offense can be established.
If a bodhisattva harbors hatred toward sentient beings or feels envy toward them,
they will be unable to practice the conduct that benefits both themselves and others.
To perform what is not to be done by bodhisattvas constitutes an offense when such improper action is carried out.
Furthermore, there are soft, medium, and superior grades of offenses for bodhisattvas.
This should be understood as it is set forth in the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*.
In this way, the bodhisattva, relying upon his own entire vinaya,
diligently trains in what is to be learned.
One then attains the accomplishment of three kinds of perfect states and dwells in peace and happiness:
first, the accomplishment of the perfection of application;
second, the accomplishment of the perfection of intention.
Third is the perfection of the accomplishment of past causes.
What is meant by the perfection of application?
It refers to bodhisattvas practicing within the pure precepts without any deficiency or transgression.
To practice purity of body, speech, and mind,
and to repeatedly confess one's own transgressions without further violation—
this is called the perfection of application.
What is called the perfection of intention?
It means that bodhisattvas go forth into homelessness for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of livelihood;
they seek great enlightenment, not for the sake of not seeking it.
One seeks for the sake of the state of a śramaṇa and for the sake of nirvāṇa, not without seeking.
One who seeks in this manner does not abide in indolence or inferior diligence;
they do not become mixed with the many evil and unwholesome dharmas that defile future existence, nor with the various blazing ripenings of suffering.
All future birth, aging, sickness, and death—
this is called the perfection of intention (*āśaya*).
What is called the perfection of past causes (*pūrvahetu*)?
This means that because bodhisattvas cultivated merit and performed wholesome deeds in their previous lives,
they now possess various kinds of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and personal articles for physical sustenance.
Being personally free from lack,
one is further able to practice extensive acts of giving toward others;
this is called the perfection of past causes.
When a bodhisattva thus trains diligently in the trainings according to the Vinaya,
they dwell in the accomplishment of these three kinds of perfection and happiness.
It should be understood that, conversely, they dwell in the accomplishment of three kinds of decline and suffering.
Having thus briefly and extensively explained all the precepts for bodhisattvas, whether in the category of householders or the category of those who have gone forth,
from this point onward, regarding all such precepts:
One should understand the distinctions among the remaining difficult practices,
such as ethical discipline (*śīla*),
and so forth. *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 41.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Forty-two.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.

In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth section of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, within the first *yogasthāna* on the "Foundation," in the tenth chapter on "Ethical Discipline" (*śīla*), part three: What is the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline that is difficult to practice?
It should be known that this discipline is, in brief, of three kinds.
It refers to those bodhisattvas who, currently possessing great wealth, great lineage, sovereignty, and supremacy,
renounce such great wealth, great lineage, sovereignty, and supremacy.
To undertake and maintain the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline is called the first difficult-to-practice morality of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, after the bodhisattvas have received the pure ethical discipline, [they...]
Even when encountering urgent calamities or facing the loss of one's life,
one would not allow even the slightest deficiency in the precepts one has received,
let alone commit a full violation.
This is called the second difficult-to-practice morality of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, in this way and that way, throughout all activities, postures, and mental attentions,
a bodhisattva constantly abides in right mindfulness and is always free from negligence.
Until the end of their lives, they shall have no errors or transgressions regarding the precepts they have received;
they shall not even commit a minor offense,
let alone a grave one.
This is called the third difficult-to-practice ethical discipline of a bodhisattva.
What is the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline of all doors?
It should be known that this ethical discipline consists briefly of four types.
First is the morality of formal undertaking;
second is the morality of natural disposition;
third is the morality of habitual practice.
Fourth is the morality associated with skillful means.
Regarding the formal undertaking of the precepts:
this refers to the bodhisattvas' acceptance of the three types of bodhisattva pure ethical discipline previously received.
These are the morality of restraint, the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas, and the morality of benefiting sentient beings.
As for natural morality,
it refers to those bodhisattvas who abide in the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Those who are naturally virtuous and noble have body and speech karma that constantly proceed with purity within their mental continuum.
Regarding those who are habituated to ethical discipline:
this refers to those bodhisattvas who, in previous lives, have repeatedly practiced the three types of pure ethical discipline as previously described.
Sustained by the power of past causes,
one does not delight in the manifestation of any unwholesome dharmas in the present life; rather,
with a mind of deep revulsion toward all unwholesome dharmas, one delights in cultivating virtuous conduct.
Regarding the precepts associated with skillful means,
it refers to those bodhisattvas who, relying upon the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), deeply aspire to virtuous conduct with a sincere mind.
Regarding the constant and continuous engagement in wholesome physical and verbal actions toward all sentient beings:
what is the bodhisattva’s morality of a true spiritual being (*satpuruṣa-śīla*)?
It should be known that this morality consists briefly of five types.
That is to say, bodhisattvas themselves possess ethical discipline (*śīla*),
encourage others to receive the precepts,
and praise the merits of ethical discipline.
Seeing those who share the same Dharma, one rejoices with a profound heart.
Should there be any transgressions, one rectifies them through repentance in accordance with the Dharma.
What is the bodhisattva’s morality in all its aspects?
It should be understood that, to state it briefly,
these precepts consist of six kinds and seven kinds,
totaling thirteen kinds.
Regarding the six kinds:
first is the precept of dedication,
because it is dedicated toward great enlightenment.
Second, the extensive precepts,
because they comprehensively encompass all points of training.
Third, the precepts that are faultless and a source of joy.
Fourth is the constant precept, because one does not abandon the points of training even for the duration of one's entire life,
thereby remaining far removed from the two extremes of indulgence in sensual pleasures and self-mortification.
Fifth, the firm precepts,
which cannot be overcome or stripped away by any gain, honor, heterodox doctrines, or root and secondary afflictions.
Sixth, the precepts associated with the ornaments of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Because it is fully endowed with the adornment of all ethical discipline (*śīla*).
The characteristics of this adornment of ethical discipline should be understood as they are described in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
As for the "seven kinds":
First, the precept of cessation,
because it involves distancing oneself from all acts such as killing;
second, the precept of engagement.
Because it encompasses all virtues and benefits sentient beings,
it is the third: the morality of restraint,
which consists of guarding, ceasing, and transforming [unwholesome conduct].
1. The morality that is the maturation of the four great beings;
2. The morality that is the maturation of the five higher mental states;
3. The morality that is the maturation of desirable realms of rebirth.
Seventh is the ethical discipline that is the maturation of benefiting sentient beings.
What is the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline for fulfilling requests?
It should be known that this ethical discipline consists briefly of eight types.
It means that bodhisattvas reflect for themselves:
"Just as I desire that they not take my life or take what is not given to me,
so too [should I act toward others]."
Defiled desire,
misconduct,
and falsehood.
Slander, harsh speech,
and frivolous talk.
"Having sought this out, [I realize that] hands,
clods of earth, staffs, and so forth— various unpleasant contacts—
inflict harm upon me."
If he were to act in opposition to this,
my desires would not be fulfilled and my mind would be displeased; as I seek this, so too does he.
"May I not, having been entreated by him, act contrary to his request by carrying out the taking of life,
and so forth, up to inflicting harmful contact."
His request was not granted, and his mind was displeased.
If my actions cause others' requests to fail and their minds to be displeased,
what purpose would there be in manifesting such conduct?
Having reflected thus with careful deliberation,
even for the sake of his life, the bodhisattva does not manifest before others the eight kinds of unpleasant matters that arise when one's desires are frustrated.
These eight types are called the bodhisattva’s morality of fulfilling one's aspirations.
It should be known that this morality consists briefly of nine kinds.
This means that for the sake of sentient beings,
bodhisattvas correctly prohibit what should be prohibited and correctly permit what should be permitted.
Those sentient beings who should be gathered, he correctly gathers;
those who should be disciplined, he correctly disciplines.
Within this, the Bodhisattva’s two activities of body and speech proceed with constant purity.
These are called the four kinds of pure ethical discipline.
Furthermore, there is the pure ethical discipline that is practiced in conjunction with the remaining perfections: generosity, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
These constitute five types;
collectively, they are called the nine kinds of pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Such is the pure ethical discipline possessed by a bodhisattva.
Because it enables both oneself and others to attain peace and happiness in both the present life and future lives,
it is called the bodhisattva’s morality that brings happiness in this world and the next.
What is the bodhisattva’s pure morality?
It should be known that this morality briefly comprises ten kinds.
The first is the initial excellent undertaking of the precepts,
undertaken solely for the sake of the threefold perfect enlightenment of a śramaṇa.
It is not for the sake of life.
Second, it is not excessively lax discipline,
because when a transgression occurs, one avoids being faint-hearted and instead gives rise to remorse and shame.
And fourth, the precept of not being overly agitated,
because it involves remaining far removed from giving rise to regret and shame in inappropriate circumstances.
Third, the precept of being free from indolence.
Because one does not indulge in the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, or the pleasure of lying down;
and because one diligently cultivates all categories of wholesome qualities day and night—
this is the fourth type of ethical discipline, which is comprised by freedom from all negligence.
One should cultivate this as previously described;
because of the five factors of heedfulness,
the fifth is the precept of right aspiration.
Because they are far removed from craving for gain and honor;
because they do not aspire to rebirth in the heavens but instead undertake the practice of the holy life (brahmacarya) through their own vow;
sixth, the morality encompassed by the perfection of conduct (ācāra).
It is the morality comprised by the perfection of pure livelihood, because one’s various activities and virtuous applications within all modes of conduct are excellent, complete,
and perfectly realized through the correct manifestation of body and speech in accordance with the Dharma.
Seventh is the morality comprised by the perfection of pure livelihood.
It is because it is free from all faults of wrong livelihood, such as hypocrisy and the like.
Eighth is the precept of avoiding the two extremes,
because it is far removed from the two extremes of indulgence in sensual pleasures and self-mortification.
Ninth is the precept of eternal renunciation,
because it is far removed from all views of non-Buddhists.
Tenth is the precept of no loss regarding what was previously received.
Because the pure bodhisattva precepts previously received are without deficiency and without breach.
These ten kinds are called the pure precepts of a bodhisattva;
such is the great treasury of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*) of a bodhisattva.
It is capable of giving rise to the fruit of great enlightenment in the future;
that is to say, by relying upon this, once a bodhisattva has brought the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) to fulfillment,
they realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Until one attains unsurpassed bodhi,
by diligently practicing this immeasurable treasury of bodhisattva precepts,
one will constantly obtain five kinds of benefits.
First, they are constantly protected and remembered by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Second, when they are about to relinquish their lives, they abide in great joy.
Third, after the destruction of the body, wherever they are born, [they are always in favorable circumstances].
They constantly associate with a multitude of bodhisattvas whose pure precepts are equal to or superior to their own,
acting as their companions, fellow practitioners of the Dharma, and spiritual friends.
Fourth, they accomplish an immeasurable treasury of great merit.
One is able to fulfill the perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Fifth, in both the present life and future lives, one constantly achieves the nature of pure ethical discipline;
ethical discipline becomes one's very nature.
It should be understood that all the nine types of ethical discipline (*śīla*), such as the naturally pure ethical discipline and so forth that have been explained,
are subsumed within three kinds of pure ethical discipline:

namely, the ethical discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*).
In brief, these three kinds of bodhisattva pure ethical discipline are capable of accomplishing the three tasks of a bodhisattva.
That is to say, the morality of restraint enables one to settle the mind;
the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas enables one to bring one’s own Buddha-qualities to maturity;
and the morality of benefiting sentient beings enables one to bring sentient beings to maturity.
In this way, all that should be done by a bodhisattva is summarized:
namely, causing the mind to dwell in abiding in happiness in the present life;
and, with body and mind free from weariness, bringing the Buddha-dharmas to maturity and bringing sentient beings to maturity.
In this way, for a bodhisattva, there is only this much bodhisattva pure ethical discipline;
there is only this much benefit of pure ethical discipline;
and there is only this much that is accomplished through pure ethical discipline.
Beyond this, there is nothing superior or more extensive.
Bodhisattvas of the past who sought great enlightenment studied within it;
bodhisattvas of the future who seek great enlightenment shall likewise study within it.
Throughout all the boundless and limitless worlds of the ten directions, present bodhisattvas who seek great enlightenment are currently training therein.

In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth section of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, within the "Chapter on Endurance" (*Kṣānti-paṭala*) of the first *yogasthāna*, the eleventh chapter, it is asked: What is the bodhisattva’s perfection of endurance (*kṣānti-pāramitā*)?
The summary verse says:
Intrinsic nature, all, difficult, All doors, noble person, all modes,
fulfillment of requests, Happiness in both worlds, and purity.
These nine kinds of aspects are called, in brief, patience;
that is to say, patience characterized by these nine aspects is termed the bodhisattva’s perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
First, patience of intrinsic nature;
second, all-encompassing patience;
third, patience in difficult practice.
Fourth, patience in all aspects;
fifth, the patience of a true person;
sixth, patience in every respect.
Seventh is the patience of seeking [the goal];
eighth is the patience of happiness in this world and other worlds;
ninth is pure patience.
What is the intrinsic nature of a bodhisattva’s patience?
It refers to when bodhisattvas, either relying on the power of analytical discernment or by virtue of their own innate capacity,
are able to endure harm and injury.
One is able to endure everything universally;
one is able to endure all things everywhere.
It is by virtue of an undefiled mind and pure compassion that one is capable of such endurance.
One should know that this is a brief explanation of the essential nature of a bodhisattva’s patience.
What is a bodhisattva’s all-encompassing patience?
One should know that this patience is, in brief, of two kinds.
First is patience based on the category of householders;
second is patience based on the category of those who have gone forth.
It should be understood that for each of these two categories of patience, there are three types.
First, the patience of enduring harm from others;
second, the patience of calmly accepting various sufferings;
third, the patience of superior resolve through reflection on the Dharma.
What is the bodhisattva’s patience in enduring the harm and enmity of others?
It refers to when various forms of suffering arising from the harm and enmity of others— intense, continuous, diverse, and long-lasting— manifest before the bodhisattvas.
One should train oneself in this way:
"This is merely the fault of my own karma;
it is because I myself created various impure karmas in previous lives."
Now I am experiencing such various fruits of suffering;
if I do not endure this meaningless suffering now,
it will become the cause for even greater suffering in the future.
If I were to conform to and follow this dharma that is the cause of great suffering,
I would be doing what is unwholesome to myself;
I would be bringing about my own bondage.
This brings about enmity and harm for oneself, not for others;
furthermore, it concerns all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) belonging to one's own body and that of others.
All [beings] take the nature of suffering as their essence;
because they lack knowledge,
they further increase their suffering upon the essence of suffering within my own body.
Since I possess such knowledge, how could it be appropriate to further inflict suffering upon those whose very nature is one of suffering?
Moreover, most śrāvakas cultivate practices that serve primarily their own benefit.
One should not even give rise to intolerance that produces various sufferings for oneself and others;
how much less so should I now give rise to intolerance while I am precisely striving to practice deeds for the benefit of others?
Having thus correctly investigated and analyzed, the bodhisattva diligently cultivates the five perceptions toward all sentient beings—whether enemies, friends, or neutral parties;
whether inferior, equal, or superior; and whether they possess happiness or suffering, or are endowed with virtues or faults.
One is able to endure all suffering caused by enmity and harm.
What are the five perceptions?
First, the perception of former kinship and friendship.
Second, the perception of conformity to phenomena alone;
third, the perception of impermanence;
fourth, the perception of suffering.
Fifth is the perception of embracing.
How does a bodhisattva cultivate the perception of former-life intimacy toward those sentient beings who have caused harm?
It means that Bodhisattvas should train themselves in this way:
it is not easy to find even a small number of sentient beings who, throughout the long course of time,
have not in some previous life been one's father, mother, brother, sister, preceptor, teacher, or someone resembling a venerable teacher.
By thus reflecting correctly and in accordance with reality,
one abandons thoughts of enmity toward those sentient beings who cause harm and dwells instead in thoughts of loving-kindness.
Relying on the perception of loving-kindness, one is able to endure all forms of enmity and harm.
How does a bodhisattva cultivate the perception that accords with the mere nature of phenomena (*dharmamātra*) toward those sentient beings who harbor enmity and cause harm?
It means that all bodhisattvas should train in this way:
relying upon and depending on various conditions, there is only activity and only phenomena;
herein, there is absolutely no self, sentient being, life-principle, or living being.
This refers to being able to revile, to be angry, to strike, to mock, or to scold;
or being reviled, being made angry, being struck, being mocked, or being scolded.
It is by means of such correct and systematic reflection that one understands this.
Toward those sentient beings who harbor malice and harm,
one abandons the perception of a sentient being and dwells with the perception of mere phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*).
Relying on this perception of mere phenomena, one is able to endure all forms of malice and harm.
How does a bodhisattva cultivate the perception of impermanence toward those sentient beings who harbor enmity and cause harm?
It is said that all bodhisattvas should train themselves in this way:
Whatever sentient beings there may be, whether born or growing,
all are impermanent and subject to death;
the ultimate repayment of enmity is said to be the taking of their life.
The lives of these sentient beings are severed moment by moment.
For what reason would a wise person wish to further sever such a nature of birth and death that is inherently impermanent?
