first, beneficial conduct that exhorts others toward benefits in the present life;
second, beneficial conduct that exhorts others toward benefits in future lives.
Third, there is the beneficial conduct of exhorting others toward benefits in both the present life and future lives.
Regarding the beneficial conduct of exhorting others toward benefits in the present life,
it refers to correctly exhorting them by means of the Dharma.
One gathers [wealth] through the virtue of karma,
and protects and increases one's station and resources;
know that this is called the beneficial conduct of exhortation regarding benefits in the present life.
By this, one is able to obtain extensive renown from others and happiness in the present life;
through the enjoyment of material requisites, one dwells in comfort,
and one encourages practitioners toward the benefits of future lives.
That is to say, it refers to correctly exhorting [others] to renounce wealth and status,
to go forth into the pure life, and to sustain themselves by the practice of begging for alms;
this should be known as the beneficial conduct of exhortation regarding the benefits of future lives.
By this means, one is certain to obtain happiness in future lives,
though not necessarily happiness in the present life; thus,
one encourages and benefits the practitioner regarding the welfare of both the present and future lives.
That is to say, correctly exhorting householders or those who have gone forth to practice gradually and progress toward the departure from desire;
one should know that this is called the beneficial conduct of exhortation regarding benefits in both the present life and future lives.
By means of this, one is able to attain physical pliancy and mental pliancy within the present life,
and to dwell in ease and happiness.
In future lives, they may be reborn among the pure devas,
or they may attain parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder.
What is the bodhisattva’s difficult practice of beneficial conduct?
It should be understood that this practice consists briefly of three types.
First, there is the performance of beneficial conduct toward sentient beings by bodhisattvas who have not yet previously cultivated the causes of superior roots of virtue.
This is called the first difficult practice of beneficial conduct. Why is this?
Because those sentient beings are difficult to exhort and guide.
If bodhisattvas are able to practice beneficial conduct toward those sentient beings who possess virtuous causes and manifest attachment to vast wealth, status,
and the perfection of all necessary requisites.
This is called the second difficult practice of beneficial conduct. Why is that?
Because they [engage] in vast tracks of extreme negligence and places of extreme negligence.
Because they transform through attachment,
if Bodhisattvas are able to practice beneficial conduct toward those sentient beings who are attached to their own original heterodox paths,
holding wrong views and engaging in wrong practices.
This is called the third difficult practice of beneficial conduct. Why is this?
Because they are deludedly attached to their own tenets.
Because they harbor hatred toward and reject the true Dharma and Vinaya,
how does a bodhisattva practice beneficial conduct through all doors?
It should be known that this conduct consists briefly of four kinds.
This refers to when bodhisattvas diligently exhort, and even establish, sentient beings who lack faith so that they may become perfected in faith;
and [likewise] those sentient beings who have transgressed the precepts.
He diligently exhorts and establishes sentient beings in the perfection of ethical discipline,
and likewise diligently exhorts and establishes those with impaired wisdom in the perfection of wisdom.
For sentient beings who are stingy,
they diligently exhort them toward the perfection of relinquishment, even establishing them therein.
This is the seed.
That is to say, bodhisattvas exhort sentient beings toward the meaning of reality;
they exhort sentient beings at the appropriate time;
and they exhort sentient beings toward the attainment of supreme and sublime benefit.
Gently exhorting all sentient beings;
exhorting all sentient beings with a mind of loving-kindness.
What is the bodhisattva’s beneficial conduct in all its aspects?
It should be known that this practice consists of six types and seven types,
totaling thirteen types.
What are the six types?
That is to say, if there are sentient beings who should be gathered, the bodhisattvas gather them correctly;
if there are sentient beings who should be disciplined, they discipline them correctly.
If there are sentient beings who hate and turn their backs on the holy teaching, one should remove their anger and affliction;
if there are sentient beings who dwell in the middle [neither hating nor favoring], one should cause them to enter the holy teaching;
and if there are sentient beings who have already entered the holy teaching...
He brings them to maturity within the three vehicles,
and causes those sentient beings who have already matured to attain liberation.
What are the seven types?
This refers to how bodhisattvas establish a portion of the sentient beings they seek to convert in the protection and cultivation of the accumulations for virtue,
namely, by relying on the renunciation of the Lesser Vehicle.
Alternatively, it may be based on renunciation through the Mahāyāna;
just as one causes those to be trained to guard and nurture their wholesome provisions,
so too [does one cause them to do so] regarding seclusion.
Either regarding one-pointedness of mind,
or regarding the purification of hindrances,
or regarding the cultivation of mental attention.
He establishes them correctly therein.
If they possess the lineage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha,
he establishes them correctly within the vehicle of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
If there are sentient beings belonging to the lineage of the Tathāgatas who are correctly established in the Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment of the Supreme Vehicle,
how does a bodhisattva subsequently carry out beneficial conduct for them?
It should be known that this practice consists briefly of eight kinds.
That is to say, when bodhisattvas see sentient beings who,
in situations requiring a sense of shame, are entangled by the fetter of shamelessness.
One employs skillful means to explain and resolve [the situation] so as to cause them to be free from those obsessions (*paryavasthāna*).
Just as with the obsession of shamelessness (*āhrīkya*),
one perceives that there are those who, in situations where they ought to feel shame, are instead ensnared by the obsession of lack of shame (*anapatrāpya*).
If one is entangled by the fetter of lethargy, the fetter of drowsiness,
the fetter of restlessness, the fetter of regret, the fetter of envy, or the fetter of avarice,
one employs skillful means to unravel and release them from those fetters.
What is the bodhisattva’s practice of beneficial conduct that brings happiness in this world and the next?
It should be known that this practice consists briefly of nine types;
namely, regarding other sentient beings, the bodhisattvas [perform these acts].
Relying on pure physical action,
he exhorts others to abstain from all killing and exhorts them to abstain from taking what is not given.
They exhorted them to distance themselves from all sensual misconduct and to abstain from all *surā*, *maireya*, and *madhya*— the intoxicants that are the basis for negligence.
Relying on pure verbal karma,
they exhort others to distance themselves from all false speech, exhort them to distance themselves from all divisive speech,
and exhort them to distance themselves from all harsh speech.
They exhort them to distance themselves from all frivolous speech.
Relying on pure mental action,
they exhort them to distance themselves from all covetousness, ill will, and wrong views.
Regarding the bodhisattva’s pure beneficial conduct,
it should be known that this conduct consists briefly of ten types;
namely, those which bodhisattvas [direct] toward all sentient beings.
There are five types of beneficial conduct based on external purity,
and five types of beneficial conduct based on internal purity.
What are the five types of beneficial conduct that a bodhisattva practices toward sentient beings based on external purity?
First, beneficial conduct that is faultless;
second, beneficial conduct that is irreversible;
third, beneficial conduct that is gradual.
Fourth, beneficial conduct that is universal;
fifth, beneficial conduct as appropriate.
This refers to how bodhisattvas [deal] with sentient beings who engage in various forms of misconduct.
Those who previously engaged in unwholesome conduct,
those who engage in transgressive conduct,
and those who engage in defiled conduct.
To be able to correctly establish oneself within all virtues is called the bodhisattva’s faultless beneficial conduct toward sentient beings.
Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings, the bodhisattvas...

Regarding those who seek what is not true liberation or what is not the purity of meditative concentration within states that are neither liberation nor the purity of concentration, he is able to correctly exhort and guide them therein.
This is called the bodhisattva’s unswerving beneficial conduct toward sentient beings.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas first carefully examine sentient beings and,
knowing those of inferior intelligence, teach them shallow teachings.
For those of coarse and superficial wisdom, he provides instruction and admonition that corresponds to their level;
for those of middling wisdom, he explains the middle Dharma and provides instruction and admonition corresponding to the middle way;
for those of extensive wisdom, he explains the profound Dharma and provides instruction and admonition corresponding to its subtle and hidden depths.
Causing them to gradually cultivate and accumulate the categories of wholesome qualities—
this is called the bodhisattva’s gradual beneficial conduct toward sentient beings.
Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings, from those of the four castes up to gods and humans, the bodhisattvas...
To act for the benefit of others according to one's strength and capacity,
and to exhort those who seek profit and happiness to do likewise within their respective categories—
this is called a bodhisattva’s practice of beneficial conduct toward all sentient beings.
Furthermore, regarding sentient beings, bodhisattvas [act] according to the distinctions in their capacities—
whether inferior, middling, or superior— with respect to the categories of wholesome dharmas that pertain to their own welfare.
Those who can be exhorted,
as well as those who can be exhorted through the differentiation of the power of skillful means.
According to what is appropriate for each case,
he skillfully exhorts and guides them in such a manner;
this is called the bodhisattva’s beneficial conduct toward sentient beings as it should be.
This is called the bodhisattva’s five kinds of beneficial conduct based on external purity toward all sentient beings.
What are the bodhisattva’s five kinds of beneficial conduct based on internal purity toward all sentient beings?
That is to say, bodhisattvas give rise to a vast and expansive intention of compassion toward all sentient beings and engage in beneficial conduct in their presence.
Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings, bodhisattvas...
Regarding the beneficial purposes he accomplishes,
although he undergoes all manner of great suffering and toil,
his mind never tires and he gives rise to profound joy.
They practice beneficial conduct for the sake of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, although these bodhisattvas manifest as dwelling in the most excellent, foremost, and perfect station of wealth and status,
they remain humble, like slaves or servants.
Furthermore, like a filial son who is the son of a caṇḍāla,
his mind is humble and submissive, free from pride, free from arrogance, and free from self-clinging;
thus he performs beneficial actions for all sentient beings.
Furthermore, toward all sentient beings,
bodhisattvas act with a mind free from attachment and devoid of hypocrisy,
performing beneficial deeds out of genuine compassion.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas perform beneficial conduct by generating a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings that is ultimately irreversible.
This is called the bodhisattva’s five kinds of beneficial conduct based on internal purity regarding all sentient beings.
Thus, there are five kinds each of beneficial conduct based on internal and external purity.
In total there are ten kinds;
these are called the bodhisattva’s pure beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*).
What is the bodhisattva’s commonality of purpose (*samānārthatā*)?
That is to say, when Bodhisattvas exhort others to accept and train in a certain meaning or a certain root of goodness,
they themselves personally accept and train in that same meaning or that same root of goodness,
either equally or with greater intensity.
In this way, the bodhisattva acts in common with others;
therefore, it is called "common purpose" (samānārthatā).
The sentient beings being transformed recognize that this bodhisattva practices such common purpose.
They will then firmly resolve upon the roots of goodness they have received and studied within themselves,
never regressing. Why is this?
He thinks to himself:
"The Bodhisattva who exhorts me to undertake these trainings will certainly bring me benefit and happiness."
Because that which was bestowed upon me by this Bodhisattva is precisely what he himself practices therein;
there is no one who knows how to practice for their own benefit, welfare, and happiness without practicing it themselves.
It is not the case that when bodhisattvas thus engage in commonality to exhort sentient beings,
others may challenge them by saying, "You yourself are unable to train in virtue," while they repeatedly exhort, instruct, and admonish others.
You should earnestly seek instruction and admonition from others.
There are bodhisattvas who share the same purpose as you,
yet they do not manifest themselves as sharing that same purpose with you.
There are bodhisattvas who, though not actually sharing the same activities as others,
manifest themselves as sharing those same activities;
there are also bodhisattvas who are indeed sharing the same activities as others.
Furthermore, some manifest themselves as sharing the same activities with others;
some bodhisattvas do not share the same activities with others,
nor do they manifest themselves as sharing the same activities with others.
Regarding the first phrase:
it refers to a bodhisattva whose merit and power are entirely equal to those of other bodhisattvas,
and who considers himself a teacher to them regarding the bodhisattva path, his merit and power being equal to theirs.
Because Bodhisattvas conceal their own virtues, they do not manifest their own meritorious power and majesty.
As for the second phrase:

it refers to when Bodhisattvas see sentient beings of inferior disposition who give rise to fear in their hearts toward the profound depths; they then correctly deliberate and act out of a desire to skillfully guide and transform them.
He manifests his own body as being of the same class as them—
namely, from those of the lowest outcaste (caṇḍāla) class down to the class of dogs—
in order to bring them benefit, to eliminate their calamities and afflictions, and to discipline and transform them.
Therefore, they intentionally take birth among the same class as the caṇḍālas or dogs.
As for the third case,
it refers to those bodhisattvas who see that the roots of virtue of those to be converted are still susceptible to being shaken.
In order to cause others to abide firmly, one engages in the same activities as them,
whether they are equal or superior. As for the fourth case,
it refers to those bodhisattvas who themselves act with negligence and abandon the welfare of others.
Thus have been explained the various types of generosity and ethical discipline,
extensively described up to and including the final [means],
*samānārthatā* (common purpose); within these, all the *pāramitās* are included.
It is able to bring all Buddha-dharmas to full maturity within oneself;
and through all the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*),
it is able to bring all sentient beings to maturity.
It should be understood that this briefly explains the activities of all the wholesome dharmas of a bodhisattva,
up to and including the final "sameness of purpose" (*samānārthatā*).
In this way, there are these many immeasurable wholesome dharmas that assist the factors conducive to enlightenment.
One should understand their manifestation through three causes and conditions;
one should understand their preeminence through two causes and conditions;
and one should understand their purification through three causes and conditions.
It should be understood that these various wholesome dharmas manifest through the three causal conditions of body, speech,
and mind; they are so because they are vast and free from defilement.
It should be known as most excellent;
it is also called unsurpassed and also called unshared.
It should be understood that herein, this is due to the lack of distinction among sentient beings.
Because there is no distinction in phenomena and no distinction in time,
it is called "vast.
Regarding "no distinction in sentient beings":
That is to say, bodhisattvas universally, in relation to all sentient beings as their locus and for the sake of all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm,
practice such roots of goodness as giving and the rest.
It is not for one's own sake alone.
Regarding the fact that there is no distinction among these matters:
it refers to how all bodhisattvas universally [apply] all types of roots of goodness, such as generosity and so forth, toward all beings.
They apply themselves with diligence in study;
at such times, there is no distinction between them,
meaning that all bodhisattvas are constant and uninterrupted, never departing from application and never relinquishing the yoke of virtue.
Whether by day or by night, in this life or in future lives,
one constantly practices roots of virtue such as giving without interruption, precisely because of these causes;
it should be understood that herein, through four aspects, there is the accomplishment of non-defilement.
This means that when bodhisattvas cultivate various wholesome dharmas with a joyful mind,
by virtue of these causes and conditions, they are free from suffering, free from sorrow, and free from all forms of regret. Furthermore,
these bodhisattvas do not harm or afflict others, do not adhere to dogmatic views, and do not engage in unwholesome conduct.
They cultivate immeasurable roots of goodness, such as generosity and the like;
furthermore, these bodhisattvas apply themselves with earnestness and total dedication toward those immeasurable wholesome dharmas, such as generosity and the like.
Seeing only merit, seeing only reality, and seeing only tranquility,
one becomes thoroughly resolved, does not rely on others, is not led astray by anything else, and correctly undertakes the training.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas do not, on account of the wholesome dharmas they practice— such as generosity—
aspire for the ripening fruits of becoming a universal monarch, Śakra, Māra, or Brahmā.
Nor does one seek any recompense from others;
being without dependence,
one does not rely on any gain, honor, or worldly reputation.
Even to the point of not relying on the maintenance of one's own body and life,
through such characteristics as pure joy accompanied by equanimity,
one practices generosity and the other perfections with earnestness and without dependence.
To speak at length, this extends even to "acting in concert" (samānārthatā);
for the sake of immeasurable wholesome dharmas hereafter,
it is called "untainted" (asaṃkliṣṭa).
It should be understood as pure because it is blazing, because it is immovable,
and because it is thoroughly purified.
This applies to those bodhisattvas who have already entered the stage of pure intention (*śuddhāśayabhūmi*).
All roots of goodness blaze forth and are unshakable.
As for "blazing forth," it means that this bodhisattva’s intentionality (āśaya) is pure.
All wholesome dharmas manifest with intensity not through deliberate deliberation;
they are called "unshakable" because this bodhisattva’s intentionality is pure.
Whatever wholesome dharmas they have attained and whatever they have accumulated, none shall ever regress;
in future lives, they shall never diminish.
In this way, as the Bodhisattva passes through various days and nights,
and as he traverses various stages of his own life,
all his wholesome qualities increase and never diminish, like the moon during the bright fortnight.
If bodhisattvas dwell in the stage of ultimate consummation,
or are bound to their final existence with only one more birth remaining,
all their wholesome dharmas—
It is called "thoroughly pure," because above this there are no further stages of a bodhisattva that encompass superior, purified dharmas.
Such are generosity and the others, including cooperation.
One should understand its manifestation through three causes and conditions for the sake of immeasurable wholesome dharmas hereafter;
one should understand its preeminence through two causes and conditions.
One should understand that it is pure by virtue of three causes and conditions.
Herein, all giving, all ethical discipline, and so forth,
up to all collaborative action— [are purified].
If these are extensively cultivated, well purified, and fully perfected,
they can bring about the fruit of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, a vajra-like adamantine body, and the long endurance of the True Dharma.
Among these, all the difficult practices of generosity, the difficult practices of ethical discipline,
and so forth, up to the difficult practice of collaborative conduct—
if they are extensively cultivated, well-purified, and fully perfected.
It is capable of bringing about the fruit of the Tathāgata’s accomplishment of incomparable and marvelous qualities.
Within this, there is giving through all doors, ethical discipline through all doors,
and so forth, up to and including working for the common welfare through all doors.
If it is extensively cultivated, well-purified, and fully perfected,
it can bring about the fruit of being honored by all the most excellent sentient beings, gods, and humans, as is the case with the Tathāgata.
In this regard, there is the generosity of a true person toward a true person, the ethical discipline of a true person toward a true person,
and so forth, up to the communal activities of a true person toward a true person—
whether practiced extensively, well-purified, or fully perfected.
It is capable of bringing about the Tathāgata’s [manifestation] among all sentient beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed;
whether with form or formless; whether with perception, without perception, or in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Among all classes of sentient beings, this is the most supreme fruit.
Within it are included every kind of giving, every kind of ethical discipline,
and so forth, extensively up to every kind of collaborative service.
If it is extensively cultivated, well-purified, and fully perfected,
it can bring about the fruit of the Tathāgata’s body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs, which are encompassed by immeasurable and preeminent merit.
Whatever therein consists of giving according to request, ethical discipline according to request,
and so forth, up to working together according to request—
if these are extensively practiced, well purified, and fully perfected.
It brings about the fruit of being able to sit upon the seat of enlightenment such that all demonic adversaries cannot afflict or disturb one, nor can they cause one to waver;
herein lie the giving of happiness in this world and the next, and the morality that bestows happiness in this world and the next.
To speak at length, up to the point of sharing in the happiness of this world and other worlds;
if one practices this extensively, purifies it well, and brings it to full perfection,
it can bring about the fruit of the Tathāgata’s most supreme joy of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), concentration (*samādhi*), and attainment (*samāpatti*).
Whatever pure generosity, pure ethical discipline,
and so forth, up to pure communal activities there may be herein—
if they are extensively practiced, well-purified, and fully perfected.
It can bring about the fruit of the Tathāgata’s four kinds of purity in all aspects—
namely, purity of the basis, purity of the object, purity of mind, and purity of wisdom—
and it also brings about the Tathāgata’s three ways in which there is nothing to guard against, the ten powers, and the four fearlessnesses.
The three foundations of mindfulness are the fruit of the utter purity of all the unshared Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
In this way, the bodhisattva’s wholesome dharmas,
such as generosity and the rest, can bring about the unsurpassed, ultimate fruit.

It should be understood that one also experiences the remaining immeasurable and boundless desirable and blameless superior fruits that accord with the bodhisattva practice within the cycle of birth and death.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 43; *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 44.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

The *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the Fifteenth Section of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, Part One: The Stage of Yoga (*Yogasthāna*). Chapter Sixteen: Offerings, Attending, and the Immeasurables (*Pūjāsevāpramāṇapaṭala*). Section 16: Chapter Sixteen on Offerings, Attending, and the Immeasurables. Subsection 1: Enumeration of the Three Gates. What are the bodhisattvas’ offerings, attendings, and cultivation of the immeasurables?
The summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
Making offerings to the Three Jewels, Associating with spiritual friends, And cultivating the immeasurables— These are the final two items.
Regarding the first item, "making offerings," how does a bodhisattva make offerings to the Tathāgata?
It should be known that there are briefly ten kinds of offerings:
first, offering to the śarīra;
second, offering to the caitya.
Third, making offerings in one's presence;
fourth, making offerings in one's absence;
fifth, making offerings by oneself.
Sixth, making offerings by instructing others;
seventh, making offerings with material wealth and respect;
eighth, making vast and extensive offerings.
Ninth is the undefiled offering;
tenth is the offering of correct practice.
If bodhisattvas personally and directly make offerings to the physical body (rūpakāya) of a Tathāgata...
This is called making offerings to the śarīra.
If bodhisattvas [make offerings] to all the stūpas, niches, or terraces constructed for the Tathāgata.
Whatever offerings have been presented to ancient shrines or newly constructed shrines.
This is called making offerings to a caitya.
If bodhisattvas make offerings before the body of a Tathāgata or at a caitya,
facing it directly and beholding it with their own eyes.
This is called "present offering.
When bodhisattvas provide offering materials in the presence of a Tathāgata or at a shrine (caitya),
it is [an offering made] before their eyes.
Arousing a mind endowed with superior intention and a mind endowed with pure faith,
one reflects thus:
"If the dharma-nature of even a single Tathāgata..."
This is the dharmatā of all Tathāgatas of the past, future,
and present. The dharmatā of the stūpa of a single Tathāgata is the dharmatā of all the stūpas of all Tathāgatas throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions.
Therefore, making offerings now to the Tathāgata present here is equivalent to making offerings to all other Tathāgatas of the three periods of time;
it is making offerings to the present Caitya.
This is equivalent to making offerings to all the stūpas,
niches, terraces, ancient caityas,
and new caityas throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the other ten directions.
One should know that this is called the bodhisattva’s simultaneous making of offerings to all Tathāgatas and their shrines (caityas), both those present before them and those not present before them.
If there are bodhisattvas who [make offerings] to all Tathāgatas who are not present before them...
And regarding the reliquaries (caityas),
one should conceive of them as the Tathāgata;
[one should do this] universally for all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time and for all reliquaries of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
One should know that this is called a bodhisattva’s offering solely to Buddhas who are not present and to their reliquaries (caityas). This applies when bodhisattvas,
after the parinirvāṇa of a Buddha, [make offerings].
For the sake of the Tathāgata, they construct images, stūpas, niches, or platforms,
according to their strength and ability— whether one, two, or many.
Even up to hundreds of thousands of koṭis in number,
such a bodhisattva, even if not personally present before the Tathāgata,
performs vast and extensive offerings.
One shall obtain the fruit of immeasurable great merit and gather the vast and immeasurable merit of Brahma; by this,
a bodhisattva is able to avoid falling into the evil realms throughout immeasurable kalpas and great kalpas.
For this reason, his accumulation of the requisites for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is not incomplete;
herein, the bodhisattva makes offerings solely to the Buddhas present before him and to their shrines (caityas).
One should know that one obtains the fruit of vast merit.
If one makes offerings solely to Buddhas who are not present or to reliquaries (*caitya*),
one should know that one obtains the fruit of even greater merit.
If one makes offerings to both manifest Buddhas and their shrines (caityas),
it should be known that one obtains the greatest fruit of merit,
which is unsurpassed.
If bodhisattvas wish to present offerings to the Tathāgata or to a shrine (caitya),
they should perform the task with their own hands alone.
One does not employ servants, laborers, friends, colleagues, commoners, or relatives to perform the service;
rather, one provides offerings without relying on indolence or any state of negligence.
This is called a bodhisattva’s personal offering.
If bodhisattvas wish to make offerings to the Tathāgata or to a shrine (caitya),
they do not do so by themselves alone.
He also exhorts his parents, wife, children, slaves, servants, friends, colleagues, commoners, relatives, as well as other kings, princes, ministers, elders,
householders, brahmins, and wealthy merchants from cities, towns, villages, and settlements.

Down to all men and women, great and small, the destitute and those afflicted by suffering and misfortune, the caṇḍālas and others, as well as one’s preceptors, instructors, and all disciples living together or nearby.
May fellow practitioners of the holy life, renunciants,
and those of other paths perform various offerings, according to their strength and ability, before the Tathāgata or at his shrines (caityas).
One should know that this is called the Bodhisattva’s offering made by both oneself and others together.
If a Bodhisattva possesses even a small amount of material wealth fit for offering,
they should give rise to a mind of compassion.
Therefore, one should intentionally give to sentient beings who are poor, suffering, of little merit,
and powerless, so that they may take it and use it as an offering to the Tathāgata or at a shrine (caitya).
May they receive abundant peace and happiness in the future.
May they obtain these items to make offerings to the Tathāgata and the caityas;
as for the Bodhisattva, he himself has no need for such offerings.
It should be understood that this is called the bodhisattva’s exclusive teaching of others to perform offerings.
In this regard, it should be known that if a bodhisattva performs offerings only for themselves to the Buddhas and caityas,
they will obtain a vast fruit of merit.
If one merely instructs others [to make offerings],
it should be known that one obtains a very great fruit of merit;
if one is able to make offerings both oneself and together with others, [the merit is even greater].
One should know that the attainment of the fruit of supreme merit is unsurpassed,
whether for bodhisattvas in the presence of a Tathāgata or at a shrine (caitya).
With various garments, food, drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and personal articles;
with respectful inquiries, prostrations, welcoming salutations, and joined palms;
and with various types of incense and powdered perfumes.
Incense, unguents,
flower garlands, music, banners,
parasols, flags, and lamps.
They offer praise and eulogy;
they prostrate with the five limbs, circumambulate to the right, and thus perform offerings.
Alternatively, they present inexhaustible material offerings.
Or again, they may offer such treasures as mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, musaragalva, agate, amber, gold,
silver, red pearls, and right-turning conch shells.
Or again, they may offer various ornaments such as mani-jewels, bracelets, bangles, and seals;
even offering various kinds of jeweled bells;
or scattering rare and wondrous treasures, or wrapping them with precious threads as an act of worship.
This is called a bodhisattva’s material and reverential offering to the Tathāgata or to a shrine (caitya). Furthermore,
when bodhisattvas [make offerings] to the Tathāgata or to a shrine...
Provisioning for a long duration refers to the aforementioned offerings of material wealth and respect,
whether consisting of many articles of worship or excellent articles of worship.
Whether it is present before one or not present before one;
whether performed by oneself or caused to be performed by others;
or if one makes offerings with a pure mind and the manifestation of intense, superior resolve.
One dedicates these very roots of goodness thus planted toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
such are the seven kinds.
This is called the bodhisattva’s vast offering.
If a bodhisattva, in the presence of a Tathāgata or at a shrine (caitya),
makes offerings with their own hands without harboring any sense of contempt or disdain.
One causes others to make offerings.
One does not offer while dwelling in negligence, laziness, or disrespect;
nor does one treat the offering with contempt or discard it.
One should perform this offering with a mind free from distraction and pride, and with a mind untainted by defilements;
one should not do so in the presence of kings, ministers, or other noble and eminent persons who have faith in the Buddha.
For the sake of wealth and honor, one falsely provides various kinds of offerings;
one does not smear with yellow orpiment, nor bathe with clarified butter,
nor use various *kuruṇṭaka* incenses, *arkapuṣpa*, or other impure substances.
Thus, these six kinds are called the bodhisattva’s undefiled offerings.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas perform vast and undefiled offerings of wealth and honor to the Tathāgatas and their shrines (caityas),
they may do so with wealth and treasures gathered through the strength of their own arms.
Having performed such various kinds of offerings— whether by obtaining wealth and treasures sought from others, or by attaining the wealth of mastery over all requisites— [he proceeds].
He attains mastery over all requisites.
The Bodhisattva manifests emanated bodies,
whether one, two, or many.
Even numbering up to hundreds of thousands of koṭis,
all these bodies pay respectful homage and prostrate before the Tathāgata and the stūpas.
Furthermore, from each of these individual transformation bodies, many hands were manifested—
whether a hundred, a thousand, or exceeding that number.
All these hands held immeasurable, exquisite flowers, incense, and various kinds of precious jewels, surpassing those of all the heavens and most sublime, lovely, and excellent.
They were offered as scattered gifts to the Tathāgatas and the caityas.
Furthermore, from all such emanated bodies,
they produced immeasurable, supreme, and wondrous sounds.
They sang praises of the Tathāgata’s vast,
profound, and true merits. Furthermore, from all these emanation bodies,
they manifested immeasurable, most supreme, and most exquisite ornaments such as bracelets, bangles, rings, and seals.
Having made offerings to the Tathāgatas and their shrines (caityas) with various ritual implements such as banners, parasols, pennants, and lamps,
one attains mastery over all requisites.
All offerings presented by a bodhisattva pertain solely to their own mind.
Thus, such a bodhisattva no longer aspires for the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world. Why is this?
By this, the bodhisattva has already attained entry into the stage of non-retrogression,
because they encounter no obstacles in traveling to and from all buddha-fields to make offerings.
Furthermore, if bodhisattvas did not possess the wealth and treasures accumulated through their own power...
Nor can he obtain wealth and treasures from others,
nor are there any articles of offering consisting of the sovereign wealth and provisions acquired by bodhisattvas;
yet, whatever exists within Jambudvīpa—
Whether it be the four great continents,
or a thousand-world system, or a two-thousand-world system,
or even a three-thousandfold great thousand-world system.
Furthermore, regarding all the articles of offering— whether inferior, middling, or superior— used to worship the Tathāgatas throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions,
the bodhisattva, with a mind accompanied by pure faith and accompanied by resolute conviction, [dedicates them].
Reflecting universally upon all [merits], he rejoices in them.
In this way, the bodhisattva, with little exertion of effort, performs boundless and vast offerings and gathers the vast provisions for enlightenment.
A bodhisattva should constantly and uninterruptedly give rise to a truly wholesome mind and a joyful mind,
and should diligently train therein;
even for brief moments, for short intervals, and for fleeting instants.
At the very least, for as long as it takes to milk a cow,
one should cultivate a mind imbued with loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward all sentient beings who move about.
One cultivates the perception of impermanence regarding all conditioned phenomena, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent,
and the perception of non-self in what is suffering. One cultivates the perception of excellence regarding nirvāṇa,
and one practices the recollections of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the pāramitās.
From moment to moment and for brief intervals,
they give rise to a small portion of inferior patience, wisdom, and resolute belief regarding all phenomena;
they abide in a non-conceptual, signless mind directed toward the ineffable nature of reality, suchness.
How much more so if they exceed or augment this;
thus guarding the ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) undertaken by a bodhisattva,
they should diligently train in *śamatha*, *vipaśyanā*, and the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
Furthermore, they diligently train in all the perfections and the means of attraction;
this is called a bodhisattva’s correct practice of making offerings to the Tathāgata.
Such an offering is the foremost, the highest, the most excellent, the most sublime, and the unsurpassed.
Such an offering surpasses all the previously described forms of material and reverential offerings in every respect.
A hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold;
by these ten aspects,
one should know that this is called making offerings to the Tathāgata in every respect.
Just as with making offerings to the Buddha,
so too should one understand that making offerings to the Dharma or the Saṅgha is likewise appropriate according to the circumstances.
In this way, when a bodhisattva offers worship to the Three Jewels by means of ten kinds of signs,
they should give rise to six types of resolute intention directed toward the Tathāgata.
First, the superior intention regarding the unsurpassed field of great merit;
second, the superior intention regarding the unsurpassed and great quality of kindness;
third, the superior intention regarding being the most honored among all sentient beings—whether legless, two-legged, or many-legged.
Fourth, the superior intention that is as difficult to encounter as the exquisite udumbara flower;
fifth, the superior intention of appearing alone within a trichiliocosm.
Sixth, the superior intention that is the basis for all goals and the perfection of all mundane and supramundane merits.
By means of these six types of superior intention, [one directs them] toward the Tathāgata, or toward the Dharma of the Tathāgata, or toward the Saṃgha.
If one performs an offering with even a small degree of contemplation,
one still obtains the fruit of immeasurable great merit;
how much more so when it is done extensively!
Furthermore, by how many characteristics is a bodhisattva endowed to be able to act as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)?
By how many kinds of characteristics is a spiritual friend not in vain?
And by being endowed with how many characteristics does the nature of a spiritual friend become a ground for trust?
Furthermore, how many kinds of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) are there who perform the work of a spiritual friend for those beings they seek to convert?
In how many ways does a bodhisattva attend upon a spiritual friend?
And by means of how many kinds of mental orientations (*saṃjñā*) does one listen to the sublime Dharma from a spiritual friend?
When listening to the Dharma from a spiritual friend,

one should know that a bodhisattva who does not harbor divergent thoughts toward the teacher of the Dharma accomplishes eight factors that constitute the perfection of all the characteristics of a spiritual friend.
First, abiding in ethical discipline:
within the bodhisattva’s vows of restraint,
one dwells excellently and well, without deficiency or breach.
Second, extensive learning;
third, the accomplishment of awakened wisdom; and fourth, the possession of realization.
One attains any one of the superior virtues produced through cultivation,
achieves śamatha and vipaśyanā,
and fourthly, possesses compassion.
Fifth is fearlessness: being inwardly endowed with compassion, one is able to relinquish one's own abiding in happiness in the present life,
and through diligent and tireless effort,
one brings benefit to others.
When proclaiming the teachings of the True Dharma for others,
one does not lose mindfulness or eloquence due to fear;
sixth, there is forbearance.
One is able to endure all manner of unpleasant speech, insults, mockery, derisive remarks,
and acts of defiance from others, as well as various other unwholesome behaviors.
Seventh is tirelessness:
his strength is full and robust, enabling him to engage in extensive reflection and discernment when he dwells among the fourfold assembly and teaches the true Dharma.
His speech is free from stammering and his mind is never weary;
eighth, he possesses excellent eloquence,
for his speech is perfect, does not violate the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), and his words are clear and discerning.
If bodhisattvas possess five characteristics,
they will be endowed with manifold virtues and be able to fulfill the functions of a spiritual friend without fail.
First, they first desire to bring about the benefit and happiness of others.
Second, one possesses non-erroneous awareness that understands their benefit and well-being as it truly is.
Third, regarding the skillful means and appropriate methods for teaching the Dharma and taming sentient beings according to their capacity to receive it:
First, possessing capability and power;
second, having a mind that benefits others without weariness;
third, being endowed with impartial great compassion.
Regarding all sentient beings— whether inferior, middling, or superior— their mind is free from partiality.
If bodhisattvas accomplish five characteristics,
they cause their nature as a virtuous friend to become a basis for trust.
It causes others to hear of it from afar and give rise to supreme pure faith,
let alone those who behold it in person.
First, it is sublime and wondrous.
His deportment is perfect, his deportment is tranquil, and his deportment is complete;
all his limbs are free from agitation.
Second, he is grave and dignified.
The three types of action manifest without agitation or disturbance.
Third, there is no hypocrisy:
one does not intentionally feign a dignified and orderly demeanor for the sake of deceiving others.
Fourth is freedom from envy:
one never gives rise to intolerance regarding the gains, offerings, or respect obtained by others through their preaching of the Dharma;
rather, one constantly exerts oneself to invite others to preach the Dharma.
Furthermore, he constantly encourages others to extensively offer material support and respect to them with a mind free from flattery or hypocrisy;
moreover, his mind toward others is always purely virtuous.
Upon seeing others preach the Dharma and receive wealth and honor, they feel profound sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
Just as they would feel joy in their own hearts upon obtaining gain and veneration,
so too do they rejoice in their hearts when seeing others obtain gain and veneration.
It exceeds even this.
Fifth is frugality:
possessing few stored vessels and discarding them as soon as they are obtained.
The Bodhisattva Good Friend performs the function of a good friend toward those beings to be converted through five modes:
first, he is able to admonish and censure them.
Second, it enables one to remember;
third, it enables one to instruct;
fourth, it enables one to admonish.
Fifth, he is able to teach the Dharma.
These various points should be understood through extensive analysis as they appear in the *Śrāvakabhūmi* regarding instruction and admonition;
they are explained in detail as previously set forth in the "Chapter on the Lineage of Powers" (*Balagotra-paṭala*).
It should be known that a bodhisattva attains the perfection of attending upon a spiritual friend through four aspects:
first, by serving the spiritual friend at all times, whether they are ill or healthy.
First, they constantly give rise to love, respect, and pure faith.
Second, they timely pay their respects, prostrate, welcome, and join their palms in greeting to spiritual friends;
they diligently cultivate acts of harmony and reverence as an offering.

Third, one should provide at the appropriate times offerings to spiritual friends consisting of robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine for the treatment of illness, and other requisites for sustaining the body in accordance with the Dharma.
Fourth, regarding spiritual friends upon whom one correctly relies, one should [discern] whether they are in accord with or separated from the meaning of the Dharma.
Acting in accordance with their will without wavering,
they manifest their intent to follow instructions as it truly is;
at the appropriate times, they approach them, respectfully serve them, inquire, and listen to their teachings.
When bodhisattvas wish to listen to the Dharma, they should listen to the sublime Dharma from a spiritual friend while maintaining five types of perceptions.
First, they should form the perception of it as a jewel.
Second, one should form the perception of it as eyes;
this enables one to attain vast, innate, and sublime wisdom.
Because of the meaning of the causal nature,
one forms the perception of light in three ways;
having thereby attained the vast, co-emergent eye of wisdom.
Fourth, one should form the perception of great fruit and supreme merit because it illuminates equally all aspects of that which is to be known as it truly is.
One is able to attain nirvāṇa and the unsurpassed, wondrous state of perfect enlightenment (sambodhi),
by virtue of the meaning of its being the causal nature.
Fifth, one forms the perception of great, faultless joy.
In this present life, one has not yet attained nirvāṇa or perfect awakening (sambodhi);
rather, it is because it serves as the causal nature for the faultless great bliss of śamatha and vipaśyanā that arises from the thorough discernment of phenomena as they truly are.
When bodhisattvas wish to hear the Dharma from a virtuous friend,
they should listen with a pure mind and attentive ears, without harboring divergent thoughts regarding the teacher of the Dharma in five respects.
First, one does not harbor divergent thoughts regarding the destruction of ethical discipline;
that is, one does not think: "This person has broken the precepts and does not abide in the code of restraint;
I should not listen to the Dharma from them."
Second, one does not harbor a prejudiced attitude toward those of low birth;
that is, one does not think, "This person is of inferior lineage;
I should not listen to the Dharma from them."
Third, one does not form a contrary attitude toward the discolored appearance;
that is, one does not think, "This person is ugly;
I should not listen to the Dharma from them."
Fourth, one does not harbor a contrary attitude toward the corruption of the text;
that is, one does not think, "This [teacher] is not skilled in literary embellishment;
I should not listen to the Dharma from him."
One should rely solely on the meaning and not on the literal expression.
Fifth, one does not harbor a contrary attitude toward what is unattractive;
that is, one does not think, "These words are coarse and full of malice, spoken with much anger rather than with pleasant speech," when the various dharmas are being taught.
"I should not listen to the Dharma from him.
Thus, when a bodhisattva wishes to listen to the Dharma,
he should not direct his attention toward these five points.
One should simply revere and uphold the True Dharma,
never finding fault with the teacher who expounds it.
If there are bodhisattvas whose wisdom is slight, [they should likewise act].
If one conceives feelings of disdain and contempt for the Dharma teacher and does not wish to listen to the sublime Dharma from them,
you should know that such conduct seeks no self-benefit and leads to the loss of superior wisdom.
How does a bodhisattva cultivate the four immeasurables—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity?
Briefly stated, there are three ways in which bodhisattvas cultivate the four immeasurables.
The first is the immeasurable with sentient beings as its object.
Second is the immeasurable with a dharma-object;
third is the objectless immeasurable.
If bodhisattvas establish all sentient beings within these three categories, [they cultivate these immeasurables].
Regarding that which is neither suffering nor pleasure, but rather suffering and pleasure:
for one who initially seeks pleasure,
they give rise to a superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) directed toward pleasure.
Universally taking as its object the resolute confidence (*adhimukti*) of sentient beings who abide securely and unerringly throughout the ten directions,
one cultivates a mind accompanied by loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
It should be known that this is called "loving-kindness directed toward sentient beings" (*sattvālambanā maitrī*).
If bodhisattvas abide in the superior intention of the perception of phenomena alone,
correctly observing that it is only phenomena that are conventionally designated as "sentient beings," they cultivate a mind accompanied by loving-kindness.
One should know that this is precisely what is called "compassion conditioned by phenomena" (*dharmālambanā maitrī*).
Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas cultivate a mind associated with compassion while remaining free from conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena.
One should know that this is precisely what is called "objectless compassion" (*anālambana-maitrī*).

Just as there are these three distinctions among the three types of compassion— those directed toward sentient beings (*sattvālambana*), those directed toward phenomena (*dharmālambana*), and those without an object (*anālambana*)—
one should know that the same applies to the three [immeasurables] of pity (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
If bodhisattvas, toward those who suffer,
give rise to the superior intention to eliminate suffering and cultivate a mind imbued with compassion by universally taking the ten directions as their object.
This is called compassion.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas give rise to a superior intention of sympathetic joy toward those who possess happiness.
Universally taking the ten directions as one's object, one cultivates a mind associated with sympathetic joy;
this is called joy (*muditā*).
If bodhisattvas, regarding these three kinds of sentient beings—those who are without suffering or pleasure, those who have suffering, and those who have pleasure—[cultivate such a mind...]
Following that sequence, one generates the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) of distancing oneself from the delusions of ignorance, hatred, and attachment;
universally taking the ten directions as an object, one cultivates a mind associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*).
This is called equanimity.
Among these, it should be understood that the bodhisattva’s immeasurables, such as loving-kindness, which take sentient beings as their object,
share the same characteristics as those of the non-Buddhists;
however, those which take phenomena as their object—
One should know that its characteristics are shared with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
but not shared with non-Buddhists;
this applies if there is no objective referent.
One should know that its characteristics are not shared with any of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the three kinds of immeasurables of bodhisattvas are subsumed within the intention for the welfare and happiness [of others].
It should be understood that the three immeasurables— loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy— are subsumed under the intention to benefit;
this is what is called equanimity.
In this way, all the immeasurable qualities of a bodhisattva are called "compassion" (*anukampā*), because bodhisattvas have accomplished these.
He is called one who possesses compassion.
In this regard, the bodhisattva perceives one hundred and ten kinds of suffering within the realm of sentient beings.
One cultivates the immeasurable state of compassion toward all sentient beings.
What are the one hundred and ten types of suffering? They are as follows:
there is one type of suffering.
Based on the suffering of undifferentiated saṃsāra,
for there is not a single sentient being who does not fall into the suffering of saṃsāra.
Furthermore, there are two other types of suffering.
First is the suffering rooted in desire,
which refers to the suffering produced when desirable objects undergo change or destruction.
Second is the suffering born from the maturation of delusion (*moha-vipāka-ja-duḥkha*).
That is to say, when one is touched by a sensation that is intense in its nature,
one grasps at one's own body as "I" and "mine," and through the confusion of ignorance,
gives rise to extreme resentment and lamentation.
Due to these causes and conditions, one experiences the sensation of two arrows:
namely, the bodily arrow-sensation and the mental arrow-sensation.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of suffering.
First, the suffering of suffering; second, the suffering of conditioned formations;
third, the suffering of change.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of suffering.
First is the suffering of separation,
which refers to the suffering born from being separated from those one loves.
Second is the suffering of disintegration,
which refers to the suffering produced by death through the relinquishing of the homogeneous life-stream (nikāya-sabhāga).
Third is the suffering of continuity.
This refers to the suffering produced by the continuous succession of repeated deaths and births thereafter.
Fourth is ultimate suffering,
which refers to those classes of sentient beings who definitively lack the nature for parinirvāṇa.
The suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
Furthermore, there are five types of suffering:
first, the suffering conditioned by the entanglement of sensual desire.
2. Suffering conditioned by the obsession of ill will;
3. Suffering conditioned by the obsession of lethargy and drowsiness;
4. Suffering conditioned by the obsession of restlessness and remorse.
The fifth is the suffering conditioned by the fetter of doubt.
Furthermore, there are six kinds of suffering:
first, the suffering of causes.
Because one practices the causes for the miserable destinies,
there is the suffering of the fruit,
as one is born into various miserable destinies.
Third, the suffering of seeking wealth and status;
fourth, the suffering of diligently guarding them;
fifth, the suffering of lack of contentment.
Sixth is the suffering of change.
These six types are collectively termed "suffering.
Furthermore, there are seven kinds of suffering.
First, the suffering of birth;
second, the suffering of old age;
third, the suffering of illness.
Fourth is the suffering of death;
fifth is the suffering of association with the disliked;
sixth is the suffering of separation from the beloved.
Seventh is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks despite yearning for it.
Furthermore, there are eight sufferings;
the first is the suffering of cold.
Second, the suffering of heat;
third, the suffering of hunger;
fourth, the suffering of thirst.
Fifth is the suffering of lack of mastery;
sixth is the suffering of self-inflicted affliction,
which refers to those such as the various non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas) who are not bound [by the Buddhist precepts].
Seventh is the suffering of being afflicted by others,
which refers to encountering contact with others' hands or clods of earth, or contact with mosquitoes, gadflies, and the like.
Eighth is the suffering of remaining for a long time in a single posture.
Furthermore, there are nine kinds of suffering:
first, the suffering of one's own decline;
second, the suffering of another's decline.
Third is the suffering of the decline of relatives;
fourth is the suffering of the decline of wealth and status;
fifth is the suffering of the decline of health.
Sixth, the suffering of the decline of precepts;
seventh, the suffering of the decline of views;
eighth, the suffering of the present life.
Ninth is the suffering of subsequent dharmas.
Furthermore, there are ten types of suffering:
first, the suffering of being destitute of food and requisites.
Second, the suffering of lacking the requisites for drink;
third, the suffering of lacking the requisites for mounts;
fourth, the suffering of lacking the requisites for clothing.
Fifth, the suffering of lacking the requisites for ornaments;
sixth, the suffering of lacking the requisites for utensils and implements;
seventh, the suffering of lacking the requisites for perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
8. The suffering of lacking the requisites for song, dance, and music;
9. The suffering of lacking the requisites for illumination;
10. The suffering of lacking the requisites for male and female attendants.
It should be known that there are further nine kinds of suffering:
first, all-encompassing suffering;
second, vast suffering.
Third, the suffering of all doors;
fourth, the suffering of wrong conduct;
fifth, the suffering of saṃsāra.
Sixth, the suffering of not obtaining what one desires;
seventh, the suffering of adversity and harm;
eighth, the suffering of persistence.
Ninth, the suffering of all modes.
Within all suffering, there are further two types of suffering:
first, suffering produced by past causes.
Second, suffering produced by present conditions.
Within these extensive sufferings, there are further four types of suffering:
first, long-term suffering.
Second, intense suffering;
third, diverse suffering;
fourth, uninterrupted suffering.
Within all the gates of suffering, there are likewise four types of suffering:
first, the suffering of the hells (narakas);
second, the suffering of animals (tiryag-yonis).
Third is the suffering of the realm of ghosts;
fourth is the suffering subsumed under the happy destinies.
Within the suffering of misconduct, there are furthermore five types of suffering.
First, there is the suffering arising from contact with others in the present life that is not beneficial to them;
second, there is the suffering arising from the imbalance of the elements due to the consumption of various kinds of unwholesome food.
Third, suffering that is naturally produced and initiated by being oppressed by the sufferings of the present life;
fourth, various sufferings arising from the entanglements of afflictions and secondary afflictions experienced through dwelling frequently in improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
Fifth, there is the suffering of the various evil destinies to be experienced in the future due to the manifold unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind initiated by many [afflictions].
Furthermore, within the suffering of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), there are six kinds of suffering regarding the indeterminate birth within the cycle of birth and death.
First, one's own body is uncertain;
second, one's parents are uncertain;
third, one's wife and children are uncertain.
Fourth, slaves, servants, and laborers are impermanent;
fifth, friends, officials, and relatives are impermanent;
sixth, wealth and status are impermanent.
Regarding the uncertainty of one's own status:
it means that one may first be a king and later become a servant.
Regarding the uncertainty of parents and so forth: [it means they may likewise change their status].
This refers to those who were previously one's parents or even close relatives,
but later, through the cycle of rebirth, turn instead into enemies, harmers, or evil associates.
Regarding the instability of wealth and status:
This refers to those who were previously very wealthy and noble but later become extremely poor and lowly.
Within the suffering of not obtaining what one desires, there are further seven types of suffering.
First, the suffering of being born with a short lifespan when one desires a long life, despite not obtaining it as desired.
Second, the suffering of being born ugly when one desires to be handsome;
third, the suffering of being born into a low family when one desires to be born into a noble family;
fourth, the suffering of being born into poverty when one seeks great wealth.
Fifth, seeking great power through the five desires, one experiences the suffering of weakness and inferiority when it does not arise as desired.
Sixth, seeking to fully understand the objects of knowledge through the six desires,
one experiences the suffering of the manifestation of delusion and lack of wisdom when it does not arise as desired.
Seventh, when seeking to surpass others, one does not achieve one's desires but is instead defeated by them, giving rise to great suffering.
Within the category of suffering caused by adversity and harm, there are further eight types of suffering.
First, for householders, the loss of their wives, children, and other possessions gives rise to suffering.
Second, the suffering arising from the increase of afflictions such as greed among those who have gone forth;
third, the suffering produced by the oppression of famine;
and fourth, the suffering produced by the oppression of enemies.
Fifth, the suffering arising from being oppressed and afflicted by the perils and narrowness of the wilderness;
sixth, the suffering arising from being subject to another;
seventh, the suffering arising from the impairment and affliction of incomplete limbs and joints.
There are eight kinds of suffering arising from killing, binding, cutting, slicing, beating, driving away, banishing, and afflicting; furthermore,
within the category of following suffering, there are nine types of suffering,
consisting of eight kinds of suffering based on the eight worldly dharmas.
First, the suffering when things subject to disintegration disintegrate;
second, the suffering when things subject to exhaustion are exhausted;
third, the suffering when things subject to aging age.
Fourth is the suffering of illness when one is subject to illness;
fifth is the suffering of death when one is subject to death;
sixth is the suffering of not obtaining what is beneficial.
Seventh is the suffering of ill repute;
eighth is the suffering of being censured.
These are called the eight sufferings.
Ninth is the suffering of longing.
These, taken together, are called the suffering of persistence.
Furthermore, among all types of suffering, there are ten kinds of suffering.
As previously stated,
there are five kinds of suffering that are the opposites of the five pleasures.
The first is the suffering of causes.
Second, the experience of suffering;
third, the experience of nothing but suffering without pleasure;
fourth, the experience of uninterrupted suffering.

The five types of suffering that are the opposites of the bliss of renunciation, seclusion, tranquility, and awakening— namely, domestic life, the fetters of the desire realm, discursive thought, and the suffering of ordinary beings—
are called the five sufferings. Furthermore,
there are another five sufferings.
First, the suffering of oppression;
second, the suffering of the lack of necessities;
third, the suffering of the inequality of the elements.
Fourth is the suffering of the transformation and decay of what is cherished;
fifth is the suffering of the coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the afflictive categories within the three realms.
These are called the five sufferings.
The five preceding [categories] and these five together constitute ten types of suffering;
one should know that this is called "suffering in all its aspects.
The five preceding [sets of] fifty-five and these current fifty-five [make one hundred and ten].
In total, there are one hundred and ten kinds of suffering.
These are the objective spheres for a bodhisattva’s compassion.
It is by taking these objects as its focus that [compassion arises].
The compassion of all bodhisattvas arises, increases, is cultivated, and reaches fulfillment.
Furthermore, regarding the great mass of suffering,
all bodhisattvas give rise to great compassion by taking nineteen types of suffering as their object.
What are the nineteen kinds of suffering?
First, the suffering that is the maturation of delusion;
second, the suffering subsumed under the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).
Third, the suffering of ultimate exhaustion;
fourth, the suffering of causes;
fifth, the suffering of birth.
Sixth, the suffering of self-inflicted affliction;
seventh, the suffering of the decline of ethical discipline;
eighth, the suffering of the decline of views.
Ninth, the suffering of the intermediate states;
tenth, vast suffering;
eleventh, the suffering of the hells (*naraka*).
12. Suffering subsumed under the twelve happy destinies;
13. Suffering produced by all forms of misconduct;
14. Suffering of all cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Fifteenth is the suffering of ignorance;
sixteenth is the suffering of increase;
seventeenth is the suffering of pursuit.
Eighteen: the suffering of experiencing [the fruits of] karma;
nineteen: the suffering of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Compassion is termed "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*) by virtue of four conditions.
First, because it arises taking as its object the suffering of sentient beings, which is profound, subtle,
and difficult to comprehend; second, because it is accomplished through long-term cultivation,
meaning that Bodhisattvas accomplish it by practicing over immeasurable hundreds of thousands of great eons.
Third, it is because it is initiated through intense attention directed toward the object of focus;
that is to say, by means of this attention, bodhisattvas are sustained by compassion in order to pacify the causes and conditions of the manifold sufferings of sentient beings.
If one is still able to relinquish hundreds of thousands of lives,
how much more so a single life and material wealth,
even in the face of all forms of punitive suffering?
They are able to endure all things for the sake of all sentient beings because they possess four kinds of supreme purity;
that is to say, these bodhisattvas have already reached the ultimate purity of a bodhisattva.
When the Tathāgatas have already reached the stage of Buddhahood and attained the purity of a Tathāgata,
and when Bodhisattvas cultivate compassion toward sentient beings by means of the one hundred and ten types of suffering previously described;
Thus, one cultivates all the compassion possessed by bodhisattvas;
furthermore, one is able to swiftly realize the purity of the compassionate intention and enter the bodhisattva stage of pure intention.
Toward all sentient beings,
they attain the bodhisattva’s mind of extreme intimacy and the mind of extreme affection.
One should wish to cultivate a heart of gratitude,
a heart free from weariness,
and a heart that takes upon itself the suffering of others.
With a mind that is pliant, masterful, and capable,
the noble śrāvakas have already attained realization and entered [the path];
they have reached the ultimate consummation of the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of the Truth of Suffering.
Their mental continuum proceeds accompanied by a profound and far-reaching aversion toward suffering;

it is not so for a bodhisattva, whose mind is preceded by compassion for all sentient beings and who correctly contemplates how they have fallen into the one hundred and ten kinds of extremely great aggregates of suffering.
Because the bodhisattva has thus cultivated the mind through the practice of compassion,
there is not the slightest internal or external thing that they cannot relinquish,
nor is there any ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) that they do not train in.
There is no hostile harm that he cannot endure;
there is no diligence that he cannot arouse;
there is no meditative concentration that he cannot realize.
There is no sublime wisdom that he cannot penetrate.
Therefore, if anyone asks the Tathāgata by what the bodhi of a bodhisattva is established, he always answers correctly: "The bodhi of a bodhisattva is established by compassion."
As previously stated,
each and every one of these immeasurables possesses immeasurability;
the bodhisattva’s perfect qualities of mastery function accordingly.
All are able to encompass immeasurable fruits of affection;
all proceed in an exclusively sublime, virtuous, and blameless manner in their infinite varieties.
It should be known that the bodhisattva diligently cultivates such immeasurables.
One is able to attain four kinds of meritorious benefits;
that is to say, by practicing these immeasurables,
one first attains the most excellent dwelling in happiness in the present life.
They gather and increase immeasurable, most excellent provisions of merit;
their resolve for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment becomes firm,
as they desire to bring benefit to all sentient beings.
Within the cycle of birth and death, they are capable of enduring all great sufferings.

From the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth section of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, within the "Chapter on the Factors Conducive to Enlightenment" (*Bodhipakṣyapada*), the first part of the seventeenth chapter, "The Chapter on the Factors Conducive to Enlightenment": What are the factors conducive to enlightenment for a bodhisattva?
The summary verse says:
Shame, modesty, firm strength, and upholding; Insatiability, treatises, worldly knowledge, and the four correct supports;
The analytical knowledges, the provisions, and the factors of enlightenment.
The nature of śamatha and vipaśyanā is skillful means;

there are three types of dhāraṇī, right aspirations, and samādhi. Regarding the fourth summary of the Dharma (dharmoddāna), what is meant by the bodhisattva’s sense of shame (hrī) and dread of blame (apatrāpya)?
One should know that shame and modesty are briefly of two kinds: first, their essential nature (*svabhāva*);
second, their basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Regarding the essential nature:
That is to say, when bodhisattvas engage in an unwholesome act,
they are able to correctly recognize it as contrary to the Dharma and feel a sense of shame within themselves.
This is called *hrī* (moral shame).
It is the ability to correctly awaken to this within oneself,
and the sense of shame that arises externally through reverence for others.
This is called "moral dread" (apatrāpya).
The bodhisattva’s sense of shame is by nature intense and sharp.
Furthermore, the cultivation of such [qualities] should be known as the essential nature of a bodhisattva’s sense of shame and dread of blame.
As for the basis:
Briefly, there are four kinds.
If bodhisattvas feel shame regarding the failure to establish themselves in what ought to be done,
you should know that this is called the first basis.
If bodhisattvas feel shame regarding the establishment of what should not be done,
this should be known as the second basis.
If bodhisattvas feel shame regarding the concealment of their own evil deeds, [this is the third basis].
One should know that this is called the third basis.
If bodhisattvas experience shame regarding the remorse they have produced, which persists and follows them without being abandoned, [this is the third basis].
One should know that this is called the fourth basis.
In this way, one should understand what are known as the bases for a bodhisattva’s sense of shame and dread of blame.
Briefly, their nature is of two kinds.
First is intrinsic nature;
second is the basis.
Regarding "intrinsic nature":
That is to say: the nature of being able to restrain the mind from defilement;
the nature of not acting under the sway of the afflictions;
and the nature of being capable of enduring suffering.
Even when various and manifold intense fears manifest before him,
his correct application remains unshakable;
endowed with natural courage, he is able to engage in correct discernment.
Therefore, one achieves the nature of firm power and endurance.
This is called the essential nature of the nature of firm power and endurance.
Briefly stated, it should be understood that there are five bases for this firm power and endurance of a bodhisattva.
First, encountering sentient beings who are to be converted by means of the various wrong practices resulting from the manifold great sufferings of the cycle of birth and death;
second, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
Third, they vow to undergo the long-term cycle of birth and death;
and third, to encounter the disputes, rivalries, and difficult interrogations of those belonging to opposing factions,
as well as to proclaim the meaning of the Dharma before great assemblies.
Fourth, the vow to undertake all the training precepts that bodhisattvas should observe;
fifth, hearing the vast, profound, and inconceivable Dharma.
These are called the bases for the nature of firm power and maintenance.
How is it that a bodhisattva’s mind is free from weariness?
It should be known that, by virtue of five causes and conditions, a bodhisattva’s mind is free from weariness throughout all correct applications.
First, because the Bodhisattva’s nature is inherently powerful, there is no weariness or fatigue.
Second, because the Bodhisattva repeatedly cultivates and familiarizes themselves with such a mind free from weariness,
there is no weariness or fatigue.
Third, the bodhisattva’s skillful means of gathering [beings] through courageous and fierce diligence allows for correct contemplation;
because what is attained later is progressively more excellent than what was attained before, there is no weariness.
Fourth, the bodhisattva achieves fierce, superior, and sublime wisdom;
by the power of correct discernment, they are free from weariness.
Fifth, regarding all sentient beings, the bodhisattva...
Because intense compassion and a heart of supreme pity are constantly present before him, he never grows weary.
How does a bodhisattva skillfully know all treatises?
That is to say, regarding those phenomena associated with the collections of names, phrases, and syllables within the five fields of knowledge,
bodhisattvas properly receive them from others and thoroughly master them through verbal recitation;
they then [apply themselves] to the sublime meaning of these very phenomena.
Whether by listening well and resolving [the meaning] well from others,
or by personally applying oneself with diligence to discern and contemplate well—
such a bodhisattva knows the Dharma and knows its meaning.
One does not forget the Dharma or its meaning,
remaining constantly diligent and never relinquishing application;
furthermore, one acts for the sake of understanding the ever-new and successive distinctions between the superior qualities of the Dharma and its meaning.
Although they have reached the ultimate through hearing and reflection,
it is by means of this that they gradually mature in the meaning of these teachings and attain pure faith.
From these characteristics, it should be known that the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the treatises is immeasurable, perfected, and free from error.
Regarding the world,
this refers to how bodhisattvas universally [engage] with the entire world of sentient beings.
He understands it as it truly is:
that this world is extremely perilous and profoundly ignorant,
in that there is birth, aging, and death, and the repeated cycle of dying and being born.
Furthermore, sentient beings do not know, as it truly is, the transcendence and emergence from old age, death, and so forth.
Moreover, Bodhisattvas understand, as it truly is, that in the world of sentient beings there are various corruptions when the turbid age increases.
There is no time of decline characterized by various defilements and turbidity;
that is to say, based on the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
The first is the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*).
Second is the turbidity of sentient beings;
third is the turbidity of afflictions;
fourth is the turbidity of views.
Fifth is the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
As in the present time, human life spans are short;
even those with the longest lifespans do not exceed one hundred years.
In former times it was not so;
this is called the defilement of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).
For example, nowadays sentient beings for the most part do not recognize their parents.

They do not recognize śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, nor those who are venerable householders who act for their own welfare and perform what ought to be done; they see no fear in the offenses of this life or those of future lives.
They do not practice giving nor perform meritorious deeds;
they do not observe the fast-day precepts nor receive the pure precepts.
This was not the case in the past.
This is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).
For example, at the present time, sentient beings for the most part practice unrighteous greed and unequal greed;
they brandish swords and carry weapons, engaging in strife, litigation, and contention.
