They frequently practice flattery, deception, fraud, falsehood, and the utterance of lies, and they embrace false teachings.
There are now immeasurable kinds of evil and unwholesome dharmas that can be clearly perceived,
which did not exist in former times.
This is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
For example, in the present age, sentient beings for the most part destroy the True Dharma and seek its extinction by establishing numerous counterfeit versions of the True Dharma.
Because they prioritize false investigations into erroneous teachings and erroneous meanings,
whereas it was not so in former times;
this is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).
Just as at this present time we are gradually entering the intermediate kalpa of famine,
where many instances of famine are currently observable,
so too are we gradually entering the intermediate kalpa of pestilence.
Numerous epidemics are currently prevalent;
the intermediate kalpa of weapons is gradually approaching.
Numerous instances of mutual slaughter with weapons are currently prevalent.
In former times it was not so;
this is called the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
This is called a bodhisattva’s thorough and accurate understanding of the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).
Furthermore, bodhisattvas understand, as it truly is, the destruction and formation of the receptacle world;
they know it according to the distinctions of how the receptacle world is destroyed and formed.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas [have thorough knowledge] regarding the world,
the origin of the world, the cessation of the world,
and the practice that leads to the origin of the world.
Regarding the practice that leads to the cessation of the world,
he knows, as they truly are, the gratification, the danger, and the escape from that world.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas understand as it truly is that from the eye up to the mind,
the formless aggregates and the material forms derived from the four great elements constitute the human body;
there is only this much that is designated by the conventional name "person."
Regarding all perceptions therein—
whether of a self or of a sentient being—
these are merely perceptions.
Regarding all the conventional designations used therein,
such as "I see forms with my eye," and so forth, up to "I cognize phenomena with my mind"—
these too are merely conventional designations.
Regarding all worldly conventions therein, it is said:
"This venerable one has such a name, such a category, and such a clan."
Thus one partakes of food and drink; thus one experiences suffering or pleasure;
thus one lives long and endures for a long time.
In this way, they exhaust the limits of their lifespan;
yet even this is merely a conventional expression.
The bodhisattva knows all of this as it truly is.
Because bodhisattvas understand, as they truly are, the distinctions in the流转 (pravṛtti) of the world of sentient beings,
the distinctions in the流转 of the vessel-world (bhājana-loka),
the meaning of observing the world through eight aspects, and the ultimate reality (paramārtha) of all worlds.
For this reason, he is said to be "skilled in knowing the world.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva sees one who is superior in both age and virtue,
he is able to properly welcome them, prepare a seat, and invite them to sit.
One should respectfully inquire after others, prostrate, and join one's palms with earnest devotion to cultivate the practice of harmony and respect.
If one encounters those whose age and virtue are similar to one's own,
one should properly exchange greetings.
He responded with joy and comfort,
engaging in conversation with gentle and elegant words,
without relying on pride or arrogance to measure himself against others.
If one sees someone who is inferior in both years and virtue,
one should encourage them to cultivate superior qualities and manifest the truth according to one's strength and ability;
one must never expose their few virtues, conceal their reality, or publicize their many faults so as to cause them shame and embarrassment.
Nor does he treat others with contempt or cause their minds to sink in despondency.
Aware that they have aspirations for either material wealth or the Dharma,
he never turns his back on them nor frowns upon them.
They do not mock errors or mistakes, nor do they despise those who have fallen from honor;
toward all sentient beings— whether inferior, equal, or superior—
they first offer words of greeting and praise, saying "Welcome," whenever they see them.
He establishes others in the non-erroneous state and is able to correctly gather them according to their capacity through both material wealth and the Dharma.
Although he dwells in a position of high honor, he never acts in opposition to sentient beings;
he does not prize himself as extraordinary, nor is he arrogant.
Even if the sentient beings under their care possess all necessary provisions,
[the bodhisattva] never abandons them, whether they are ill or healthy;
in both physical and verbal actions, they act with complete compliance toward them.
Whether recognized or unrecognized, they treat all with an equal mind;
acting as friends and companions, they harbor neither resentment nor enmity toward any sentient beings who lack a protector.
According to one's strength and capacity, one acts as a support and a refuge;
one does not resort to other means to provoke grief or suffering in others, causing them to dwell for even a moment in a state of unease.
If there is a specific cause or condition that necessitates it, one may engage in jesting.
One should speak in accordance with principle and not that which is contrary to principle.
Even when meeting those with whom one has an intimate personal relationship, who are of similar age, and with whom there is no estrangement,
one must still not engage in conversation concerning anything other than benevolent discourse.
He never harbors resentment toward others for long;
even if it should arise briefly, he does not expose their hidden faults.
Furthermore, he does not disparage or insult others through body or speech.
Either through skillful discernment,
or by relying on the true Dharma,
or by reflecting upon one's own faults and thereby attaining self-understanding.
They do not reproach others;
their minds are peaceful and calm rather than frivolous or restless.
Their actions of body, speech, and mind are always undertaken with careful deliberation.
They are universally able to distance themselves from the fourteen defiled karmas,
conceal the six directions,
stay far away from the four evil friends, and embrace the four virtuous friends.
All such matters should be understood as they are fully explained in the Śikhālakasūtra;
or rather, they may pertain to matters of benefit in the present life, such as wealth, status, and rank.
He is endowed with diligence, endowed with protection, and maintains his livelihood with equanimity.
He is skilled in all worldly arts and crafts;
he is free from flattery and deceit, and by nature does not deceive others.
They feel deep shame regarding the commission of transgressions;
they are fully endowed with right conduct, honoring and guarding that right conduct;
and they are deeply trustworthy when entrusted with responsibilities.
He harbors no designs upon the wealth and property of others;
when borrowing from others, he never defaults on his obligations.
This is his portion.
Sharing wealth with equality and without hypocrisy;
knowing true treasures together,
such that even a seller who does not recognize them calls them treasures when paying their price.
Without erring by even a hair’s breadth,
he established models for proper conduct regarding worldly affairs;
for the benefit of the world, he was eloquent and swift in discerning what is correct.
In whatever various tasks ought to be done,
whenever others come to seek his assistance, he acts as their companion;
being sincere and steadfast, he does not make excuses by relying on other circumstances.
Skillfully managing one's affairs is not unwholesome.
If one acts as a sovereign, one should govern the world according to the Dharma,
not employing unlawful means or taking pleasure in punitive retribution.
If one leads a great assembly, one should exhort them to abandon unwholesome precepts and cultivate wholesome precepts,
thereby accomplishing the eight kinds of noble speech. That is to say,
when asked about what one has seen, one answers, "I have seen it."
Regarding what has been heard, perceived, and known, he answers that he knows it;
regarding what has not been seen, he answers that he has not seen it;
regarding what has not been heard, nor perceived, nor known, he [answers accordingly].
Answer: It is not known.
A bodhisattva accomplishes such dharmas as are correctly to be known by the world.
Just as the world rightly functions,
he knows all of that exactly as it is; therefore,
he is called one who "skillfully knows the world."
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 44;
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 45;
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.

In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth section of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the first *Yogasthāna*, the seventeenth chapter, "The Factors Conducive to Enlightenment" (Part Two): How does a bodhisattva practice the four correct reliances?
This means that bodhisattvas listen to the Dharma from others for the sake of seeking the meaning,
not for the sake of seeking worldly ornamental phrasing.
Bodhisattvas seek the meaning, not the words.
Furthermore, when listening to the Dharma, even if one encounters the preaching of the Dharma through ordinary speech and sounds,
one should listen and receive it with reverence, relying solely on its meaning. Moreover,
bodhisattvas understand as they truly are both cryptic teachings and grand proclamations.
Having known it as it truly is,
one relies upon reason rather than accepting it simply because it was spoken by the Buddha or the Saṅgha, or by an elderly person who is well-known among the community.
Therefore, one does not rely on the person (*pudgala*).
In this way, the bodhisattva relies upon reasoning,
for the person is not a basis of reliance.
Their minds are unshakable regarding the true meaning,
and within the sublime Dharma, they cannot be diverted by external conditions.
Furthermore, regarding the Tathāgata, the bodhisattvas—
They have deeply planted right faith and deeply planted purity;
they are single-mindedly clear and pure, relying solely upon the Tathāgata’s sūtras of definitive meaning (nītārtha) and not those of non-definitive meaning (neyārtha).
Because they rely upon the sūtras of definitive meaning,
they cannot be led astray regarding the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma and Vinaya. Why is this?
Because one relies on the various approaches of the Buddha’s discourses of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) to discern the meaning of the fundamental nature,
one has not yet reached certainty and still gives rise to doubt;
this is because they are not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
If bodhisattvas are not certain regarding the sūtras of definitive meaning,
they may still be led astray from the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Buddha.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas regard the wisdom of direct realization as the ultimate reality.
It is not through hearing or reflection;
rather, it is the knowledge of the meaning of the Dharma that is not yet true realized wisdom.
It is that which Bodhisattvas understand according to reality as that which is to be known by the wisdom born of cultivation.
This cannot be fully comprehended by the consciousnesses produced merely through hearing and reflection;
rather, having known it as it truly is, one hears the most profound dharmas and meanings taught by the Tathāgata.
One never slanders or disparages them;
this is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the four correct reliances.
Relying upon the four correct reliances, one practices them well.
Therefore, the four means of valid cognition are briefly elucidated:
namely, the object to be expressed and correct reasoning.
The Great Master’s wisdom born of cultivation and his knowledge of true realization;
furthermore, all bodhisattvas rely upon the four reliances as their basis.
Because he diligently initiates correct application,
he clearly elucidates the path to liberation without any confusion.
What are the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) cultivated by a bodhisattva?
This refers to the bodhisattvas’ unimpeded and non-regressive wisdom regarding all phenomena and all their various aspects,
in terms of both their full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and their mode of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*),
which is based on that which is produced through cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
This is called the bodhisattva’s unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, regarding all phenomena and all their diverse characteristics,
[the bodhisattva understands] their full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and their mode of being (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
Based on the unimpeded and non-regressive wisdom produced through cultivation,
this is called the bodhisattva’s analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, regarding all phenomena and all etymological explanations, the bodhisattvas—

The knowledge that is unimpeded and non-regressive, based on the wisdom produced through cultivation regarding the nature of all that exists (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*),
is called a bodhisattva’s analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, regarding all phenomena and all their various categories, bodhisattvas possess,
based on the wisdom produced through cultivation, an unimpeded and non-regressive knowledge of the full extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and the mode of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
This is called the Bodhisattva’s unimpeded analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
It should be understood that if Bodhisattvas rely upon these four unimpeded analytical knowledges,
they will attain immeasurable and most excellent skillfulness in five areas.
First, skillfulness regarding the aggregates;
second, skillfulness regarding the elements;
third, skillfulness regarding the sense bases.
Fourth, skill in dependent origination;
fifth, skill in what is possible and what is impossible.
By means of these four modes of practice, the bodhisattva [proceeds].
One is able to personally and excellently realize perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena,
and is also skilled in unerringly revealing them to others;
beyond this, there is nothing superior that one can personally and excellently realize as perfect enlightenment.
How much more so for one who skillfully provides others with unerring instruction.
Regarding the provisions,
it should be known that these provisions for enlightenment are, in brief, of two kinds.
First is the accumulation of merit;
second is the accumulation of wisdom.
These two accumulations are explained in detail according to their meaning.
The characteristics of these should be understood as previously explained in the chapter on the welfare of oneself and others.
Furthermore, regarding this accumulation of merit and wisdom:
That which was practiced by the Bodhisattva during the first incalculable great eon should be known as "inferior.
That which was practiced during the second incalculable great eon—
It should be known as "middling" if it is that which has been cultivated during the third asaṃkhyeya mahākalpa; it should be known as "superior" if it is that which has been cultivated thereafter.
How does a bodhisattva diligently cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment?
It is by relying upon the four types of unimpeded analytical knowledge (pratisaṃvid) of the bodhisattvas.
By means of sublime wisdom encompassed by skillful means,
one understands the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as they truly are,
yet does not realize them [as a final cessation].
These bodhisattvas universally and correctly know all thirty-seven factors of enlightenment within the principles of all two vehicles;
that is to say, regarding the principles of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Furthermore, they know as they truly are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment within the principles of the Mahāyāna,
as well as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment within the principles of the Śrāvaka-yāna.
One should understand this as it truly is,
exactly as all was previously explained in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
How does a bodhisattva [apply] the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment according to the principles of the Mahāyāna?
They understand it as it truly is:
namely, that bodhisattvas are able to abide in the contemplation of the body within the body,
without conceptualizing the body as having an inherent nature.
Furthermore, one does not conceptually differentiate that all types of phenomena are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature;
moreover, regarding one's own body, one understands as it truly is the dharma-nature that is free from the intrinsic nature of verbal expression.
It should be known that by relying on the principle of the ultimate truth, one dwells in the contemplation of the body within the body and cultivates the foundations of mindfulness;
this is so for all bodhisattvas who accord with the immeasurable.
When one proceeds by means of the sublime wisdom that establishes the correct principles,
it should be known that this is based on the conventional principle for abiding in the contemplation of the body within the body as a practice of mindfulness.
Just as one dwells in the application of mindfulness by practicing the contemplation of the body within the body,
so too should it be understood for all remaining applications of mindfulness and all remaining factors conducive to enlightenment.
In this way, the bodhisattva does not conceptually differentiate suffering regarding phenomena such as the body,
nor does he differentiate its origin,
nor does he differentiate the cessation of what is to be done.
One does not conceptually differentiate this as the path that causes the cessation [of suffering].
Furthermore, regarding this very nature of phenomena (dharmatā) which is free from verbal expression—
whether it be the nature of suffering or the nature of origination.
If one understands, as they truly are, the nature of cessation and the nature of the path,
it should be known that this is the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment based on the ultimate mode of reality, relying upon the truths as the objective condition.
If bodhisattvas proceed in accordance with immeasurable principles by means of the sublime wisdom that establishes those principles,
it should be known that they are practicing the truths based on the conventional principle.
In this context, that a bodhisattva does not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding any phenomena should be known as *śamatha*. If,
regarding the ultimate mode of reality of all phenomena, there is the wisdom of suchness as it truly is—
Furthermore, one should know that the sublime wisdom regarding the conventional mode of infinite established principles is called "contemplation. In this regard,
there are briefly four modes of conduct for a bodhisattva.
One should know that this is called "stopping" (śamatha):
first, it is the precursor to both ultimate and conventional wisdom;
second, it is the fruit of both ultimate and conventional wisdom.
Third, one proceeds effortlessly amidst all conceptual proliferations regarding mental constructions.
Fourth, with respect to such ineffable reality alone,
one is without conceptual differentiation because of the absence of signs.
Their minds are tranquil, tending toward the equality of all phenomena and their single-flavored true nature.
By means of these four modes of practice,
the path of śamatha of these bodhisattvas proceeds.
Gradually, they are even able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
with wisdom and vision brought to perfection.
In this regard, there are briefly four practices of a bodhisattva.
One should know that this is called "contemplation.
It refers to the preliminary stage of the path of cessation consisting of the four modes of practice,
which remains free from the extreme of improper adherence through superimposition regarding all phenomena.
It is far removed from the extreme of the incorrect attachment of denial,
and it establishes the principles of sublime contemplation in accordance with the distinctions of immeasurable phenomena.
By means of these four modes of practice,
the paths of these bodhisattvas proceed,
gradually leading them even to the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The perfection of wisdom and vision—
this is called, in brief, the śamatha and vipaśyanā of a bodhisattva.
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means (upāyakauśalya)?
It should be known that, briefly stated, there are twelve kinds.
Regarding the internal cultivation and realization of all Buddha-dharmas,
there are six kinds.
Relying on external means to mature all sentient beings also consists of six kinds.
What are the six kinds of skillful means for relying on internal cultivation to realize all Buddha-dharmas?
First, the bodhisattva acts toward all sentient beings with a mind accompanied by compassion,
cherishing them and not abandoning them.
Second, the bodhisattva [acts] toward all conditioned phenomena.
They understand things as they truly are.
Third, the bodhisattva constantly and with deep resolve delights in all the sublime wisdom pertaining to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Fourth, because the bodhisattva relies on compassion for sentient beings,
he does not abandon saṃsāra.
Fifth, regarding all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra)...
Because they rely on thorough knowledge of reality as it is,
their minds remain unstained even while transmigrating through birth and death.
Sixth, because Bodhisattvas rely on their joyful aspiration for the Buddha’s wisdom.
With blazing diligence,
one should know that these are called the six kinds of skillful means by which a bodhisattva relies on internal cultivation to realize all Buddha-dharmas.
What are the six kinds of skillful means by which one relies on external factors to mature all sentient beings?
First, a bodhisattva’s skillful means is able to cause sentient beings to experience immeasurable fruits from even a small root of virtue.
Second, a bodhisattva’s skillful means...
It enables sentient beings to attract and gather vast and immeasurable roots of virtue with little exertion of effort.
Third, it is the bodhisattva’s skill in means (upāyakauśalya) to eliminate the resentment and affliction of sentient beings who harbor hatred toward the Buddha’s holy teaching.
Fourth, the bodhisattva’s skillful means consists in causing sentient beings to enter into the sphere of the Buddha’s holy teaching.
Fifth, the bodhisattva’s skillful means...
Sixth is the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), which brings to maturity those who have already entered the Buddha’s holy teaching,
and brings to liberation those who have already been matured in the Buddha’s holy teaching.
How does a bodhisattva’s skillful means cause sentient beings to experience immeasurable results from even a small root of virtue?
It is through the bodhisattva’s skillful means.
He exhorts all sentient beings to relinquish even minor or inferior objects, down to a single, most humble ball of flour,
and to give them to even the lowliest fields of merit, down to the class of wriggling animals.
Having performed such giving, one dedicates it toward seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Thus,
although the roots of goodness and the objects or fields may be inferior,
through the power of dedication, they bring about immeasurable fruit.
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means (upāyakauśalya) by which sentient beings are led to gather vast and immeasurable roots of virtue with little effort?
It is as follows: the bodhisattva’s skillful means.
If there are sentient beings who, out of faith and understanding, observe false fasts and precepts— such as not eating for even a single month— and so forth,
he teaches them the Dharma of the Eightfold Noble Fast Precepts.
They cause them to abandon the most extreme hardships of observing false precepts, which result in undesirable fruits;
they exhort them to practice and study the observance of true precepts, which involve no extreme hardship and result in great desirable fruits.
If there are sentient beings who practice self-mortification with diligent and tireless effort,
yet employ wrong means in their desire to seek liberation,
[the Buddha] preaches the Middle Way for them to cause them to abandon the two extremes and enter [the path].
If there are sentient beings who, seeking rebirth in the heavens, employ perverse means—
such as throwing themselves from cliffs, leaping into fire, or abstaining from food and drink—
for them he proclaims the unerring meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
This causes them to attain a state of dwelling in happiness in the present life,
and to reach the superior fruit of rebirth among the gods in the future, which is free from all hardships and accompanied by joy and bliss.
This applies to those sentient beings who have faith in the Brahminic *vaidika* mantras and their false conceptualizations.
They apply themselves with diligence to receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting [the teachings] until they reach their ultimate conclusion.
With pure skillful means, they encourage others to receive, uphold, read, recite, and contemplate the meaning of the Buddha’s holy teachings.
Furthermore, they correctly proclaim and reveal for others, in such and such a manner, the sublime Dharma corresponding to the profound emptiness taught by the Tathāgata.
This causes them to give rise to courageous resolve, intense renunciation, and sharp, pure faith;
it is by means of such a virtuous mind, conjoined with renunciation and pure faith for even a single moment, that this occurs.
They are still able to gather and sustain incalculably vast roots of goodness;
how much more so their continuous succession!
Furthermore, there are all the various kinds of exquisite, precious jewels, fragrant garlands, and articles of worship found in the world for bodhisattvas.
Arousing pure faith and a superior intention,
one practices resolute conviction and makes offerings to the Buddha, Dharma,
and Saṅgha, and likewise exhorts others to practice such resolute conviction and offerings.
Furthermore, regarding all places throughout the worlds of the ten directions where offerings are made to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, one should,
with such a superior intention accompanied by pure faith, [make offerings].
They universally extend their attention in all directions and give rise to deep sympathetic joy;
they also exhort others to do likewise.
Furthermore, these bodhisattvas constantly practice the recollection of the Buddha, the recollection of the Dharma, and so forth, up to the recollection of the devas.
Furthermore, they exhort others to practice the six recollections.
Moreover, through the mental verbalization of paying homage to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha,
these bodhisattvas ensure that their lives are not spent in vain until the moment of death.
Furthermore, they exhort others to practice this meritorious deed.
Moreover, all bodhisattvas universally rejoice in all the meritorious deeds of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
Furthermore, they also exhort others to practice such sympathetic joy.
Moreover, all bodhisattvas universally enter into a state of superior intention characterized by vast compassion toward all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
I vow to take upon myself all the sorrows and sufferings of others in their entirety.
I also exhort others to give rise to this compassionate vow.
Furthermore, regarding all past and present errors and transgressions of all bodhisattvas—
With a mind that is pure, disciplined,
and joyful, one conforms to the training precepts.
Facing the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions,
one should with utmost sincerity confess and repent for past deeds and cultivate oneself for the future;
furthermore, one should exhort others to practice these same matters.
By thus repeatedly confessing their transgressions,
they shall all be liberated from their karmic obstructions with little effort.
Furthermore, these bodhisattvas have already perfected their supernormal powers and attained mastery over the mind.
Throughout the ten directions, at the abodes of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, as well as among sentient beings,
they manifest numerous and diverse emanations,
thereby gathering an immeasurable mass of great merit.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas constantly cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity,
and they also exhort others to practice them.
In this way, through minimal effort, these bodhisattvas attract and gather vast, immeasurable roots of goodness and their most excellent, sublime fruits.
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means regarding sentient beings who harbor hatred and hostility toward the Buddha’s holy teaching?
It is the removal of their resentment and affliction.
Those who abide in the middle state are caused to enter;
those who have already entered are caused to reach maturity;
and those who have already reached maturity are caused to attain liberation.
It should be understood that for Bodhisattvas who wish to accomplish these four kinds of benefit for sentient beings,
there are, in brief, six further types of skillful means.
First, skillful means that accord with and harmonize;
second, skillful means of establishing mutual agreements;
third, skillful means of diverse dispositions.
Fourth is the skillful means arising from oppression;
fifth is the skillful means of bestowing favors and repaying kindness;
sixth is the skillful means of ultimate purity.
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means of conformity and integration?
It refers to when bodhisattvas are about to teach the Dharma to sentient beings,
they first employ skillful means to conform to them.
They manifest gentle and beautiful conduct of body and speech,
and they also practice giving and compliance in order to remove the anger and resentment that others may feel toward them.
Once their malice and affliction have been removed, they give rise to love and respect;
having given rise to love and respect, they develop delight in the Dharma;
thereafter, one proclaims the True Dharma for them.
The True Dharma thus taught is appropriate to the needs of beings, easy to enter, and easy to understand;
it is timely, gradual, and free from inversion;
it leads to meaningful benefit and is capable of withstanding challenges.
Regarding those sentient beings, in the work of their discipline, he achieves a supreme resolve for their benefit and compassion;
for their sake, he manifests supernormal powers and reads their minds, clearly expounding the True Dharma according to reality.
Or they may exhort others;
or they may manifest various and manifold extraordinary miraculous feats to bring all those sentient beings to complete subdual.
If it serves to draw out the meaning and benefit,
even the most concise treatises can provide extensive exposition;
if it serves to draw out the meaning and benefit...
He is able to provide concise explanations of the most extensive treatises,
causing them to receive and uphold them, providing reminders for them, and answering their questions.
Once they have been able to receive and uphold the Dharma, [he further assists them].
Furthermore, he proceeds to extensively expound the correct principles for them.
Moreover, regarding the entry into the samādhi doors that universally take all things as their object,
he is able to provide corresponding instructions and admonitions.
He gathers and benefits sentient beings by causing them to practice beneficial conduct.
If there are sentient beings who do not understand the Tathāgata’s intentional meaning regarding the profound sūtras on emptiness taught by the Buddha, [he guides them].
In this sutra it is taught that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, devoid of substantiality, and neither arise nor cease;
it is taught that all phenomena are equal to space and like illusions and dreams.
Having heard this, they were unable to comprehend its meaning and purpose;
their hearts were filled with alarm and fear,
and they slandered all such sutras, claiming that they were not the words of the Buddha.
For the sake of those sentient beings,
the bodhisattva employs skillful means to correctly interpret and reconcile the profound intended meaning of the Tathāgata within such sūtras.
He brings those sentient beings together with him in accordance with reality.
When the bodhisattva thus correctly reconciles them,
he says to them:
This sutra does not state that all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely non-existent;
it merely states that the expressed intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is entirely non-existent.
Therefore, it is said that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.
Although there are all things that are expressed through speech,
and it is in dependence upon them that various verbal expressions proceed,
nevertheless, the expressible intrinsic nature of those things so described [is as follows].
According to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they do not possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, it is said that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are without any substantiality (*avastuka*).
Since the principle regarding the so-called intrinsic nature of all phenomena is thus, [it follows that they are empty].
Since beginningless time, nothing has ever existed at all.
What, then, could arise? What could cease?
Therefore, it is said that all phenomena are without arising and without cessation.
For example, within space there are many forms and form-actions that can accommodate all forms and form-actions;
that is to say, within the void of space, various activities such as going, coming, staying, rising, falling, bending, and stretching are actually present.
If at that time all forms and form-activities are entirely dispelled,
then at that very moment, the nature of formlessness alone—
the pure, empty space— manifests its characteristic.
Thus, with respect to that which resembles space— a reality beyond verbal expression—
there arise various false conceptualizations and discriminations produced by speech, which follow after and adhere to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
They appear as the activity of form;
furthermore, all such verbal expressions, false conceptualizations, discriminations, and attachments to conceptual proliferation appear as the activity of various forms—
all of which are accommodated by that which is like space and transcends verbal expression.
When a bodhisattva, by means of sublime noble wisdom,
eliminates all false conceptualizations and discriminations arising from verbal expression that follow after attachment to conceptual proliferation—
at that time, the bodhisattva is a most excellent noble one.
By means of sublime noble wisdom, one realizes that all phenomena are beyond verbal expression;
they are manifested solely by the nature of all speech,
which is itself the absence of intrinsic nature.
For example, it is like the appearance of the pure characteristic of space;
beyond this, there is no further intrinsic nature to be sought.
Therefore, it is proclaimed that all phenomena are equal to space.
Furthermore, just as illusions and dreams do not exist in reality as they appear,
yet it is not the case that all illusory and dreamlike forms are entirely non-existent,
so too these phenomena do not exist in reality as they appear through the force of the habitual tendencies of the conventional expressions of foolish beings.
Nor is it the case that the ultimate nature of all phenomena, which is beyond verbal expression, is entirely non-existent.
By means of this expedient, one realizes the principle that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent.
Just as illusions and dreams are non-dual in their nature,
so it is taught that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams.
In this way, the bodhisattva universally [perceives] all phenomena within the dharmadhātu.
Without grasping at even a small portion and without discarding even a small portion;
without diminishing and without augmenting;
there is nothing that is lost or destroyed.
If a phenomenon truly exists, he knows it as truly existing;
if a phenomenon truly does not exist, he knows it as truly non-existent.
He reveals things exactly as they have been known.
One should know that this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means of conformity, integration, and penetration.
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means of establishing a mutual covenant?
It refers to when bodhisattvas see sentient beings seeking the ten types of physical requisites, such as food and drink.
Even if one were to establish a formal covenant with them, saying:
"If you are able to recognize the kindness of your parents and respectfully provide for them,
as well as for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas," [you would still not escape].
The detailed explanation is as before.
Up to: "If you are able to uphold the pure precepts, I shall provide you with food, drink, and all other requisites for the body according to your wishes."
If he were unable to do so, he would not give it to them.
In this way, when a bodhisattva sees sentient beings coming to request various matters concerning fields,
houses, or marketplaces, [he gives them].
Matters of state, matters of territory,
matters of wealth, and matters of grain;
or there may be those who come seeking instruction in various fields of craft and various branches of knowledge.
Some come seeking to become friends;
some come seeking to enter into marriage alliances;
and some come seeking to establish communal assemblies.
Or there may be those who come seeking assistance for their worldly undertakings;
the Bodhisattva makes a formal agreement with them, saying:
"If you are able to recognize the kindness of your parents and honor them with respectful offerings," [then I shall help you].
As previously explained in detail:
"In this way, I shall give you fields and houses," and so forth, up to "I shall assist you in your undertakings.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas see sentient beings who have committed transgressions or have been accused and prosecuted, [they act accordingly].
Or they may perform various harmful acts and be seized by others,
facing execution, binding, mutilation,
beating, and humiliation.
When they are coerced, driven away, or exiled;
or when they are seized by others with the intent to beat, bind, or sell them—
the Bodhisattva, at that time, according to his ability and strength, establishes a solemn pledge, saying:
If you are able to recognize the kindness of your parents and honor and provide for them,
as extensively explained before,
then I shall employ skillful means to rescue you and cause you to escape this calamity.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas see sentient beings encountering various fears— such as those arising from kings,
thieves, water, fire, humans, non-humans, lack of livelihood, or ill repute— [they act accordingly].
At that time, the Bodhisattva established a solemn covenant, saying:
"If you all can recognize the kindness of your parents and respectfully make offerings to them,
as previously explained at length..."
"In this way, I shall employ skillful means to rescue you and cause you to escape this fear.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who desire union with what they love and seek separation from what they do not love,"
At that time, the Bodhisattva established a solemn covenant, saying:
"If you are able to recognize the kindness of your parents and respectfully make offerings to them,
as previously explained at length..."
"In this way, I shall fulfill your wish,
causing you to be united with those you love and separated from those you do not love.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva sees sentient beings suffering from illness,"
He established a solemn covenant, saying:
"If you are able to recognize the kindness of your parents and honor and provide for them as extensively described before..."
"In this way, I shall rescue you from the suffering of illness and bring you peace and happiness.
Once those sentient beings have been thus bound by the Bodhisattva to this solemn vow,
they will swiftly undertake the training in all categories of wholesome qualities.
They swiftly eliminate all unwholesome qualities;
thus, Bodhisattvas are able to fulfill all their aspirations.
It should be known that this is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful means of establishing a mutual covenant.
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means regarding the intention of a different category?
It refers to when bodhisattvas have established a formal agreement with sentient beings,
and those sentient beings, regarding the various matters previously described, [fail to fulfill their part].
He does not practice as swiftly as he desires.
At that time, regarding the matters sought as described above,
the bodhisattva does not grant them at all.
It is solely for the sake of benefiting those sentient beings,
and not out of any other intention, that he does not bestow [gifts] upon them;
such is his conduct even in the midst of various calamities and hardships.
Sentient beings who are afflicted by the suffering of illness and who, in various states of fear, desire the meeting with what is beloved and seek the separation from what is unloved.
They may temporarily relinquish [the practice],
solely for the sake of benefiting those sentient beings;
it is not that they relinquish it with a different underlying intention.
It is not that he lacks the altruistic intention to rescue them;
rather, it is when such a bodhisattva,
through skillful means, manifests harsh actions toward sentient beings.
With the sole intention of benefiting others and no other motive,
he gradually causes them, at another time, to sever all evils as they desire and to train themselves in all virtues.
Therefore, as a skillful means for the time being, he relinquishes them.
Even if sentient beings have no requests of the bodhisattva and encounter no hardships, [the bodhisattva still acts].
To speak at length, up to the point that they are free from all suffering of illness;
and having previously been close friends with the bodhisattva,
the bodhisattva exhorts them as appropriate to their circumstances.
They abandon all unwholesome dharmas and cultivate all wholesome dharmas.
That is to say, they cause others to recognize the kindness of their parents and to honor and make offerings to them;
this is explained in detail up to their conforming to and training in pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).
If those sentient beings, despite being thus exhorted by the bodhisattva,
remain willfully negligent and arrogant, failing to practice accordingly,
the bodhisattva then manifests indignation and reproach toward them.
His intention is solely to benefit others and not out of malice; thus,
although he appears to act in opposition to all that is done,
his intention is solely to benefit them and not to oppose them.
Or, toward a certain class of beings, he may manifest actions that appear to be unbeneficial to the world,
yet his intention is solely for their benefit and not for their harm;
such is the external conduct manifested by a bodhisattva toward sentient beings.
Because their internal dispositions are of a different nature from his own,
he employs skillful means to establish them therein,
causing those sentient beings to gradually abandon all evils and gradually cultivate all virtues.
Therefore, this skillful means by which a bodhisattva thus disciplines sentient beings is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means of distinct intention (*āśaya*).
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means arising from coercion?
This refers to bodhisattvas who, whether as heads of households or as kings, having attained superior power,
are able to provide correct instruction to their own relatives or to their subjects.
He should speak accordingly, saying:
"All my kinsmen, all my ministers and subjects,
if you do not recognize or repay the kindness of your parents..."
To speak at length, even up to those who violate the precepts,
I shall cut off their regular provision of clothing and food,
or I shall subject them to corporal punishment.
Thinking, "Either my kinsmen will be separated from me,
or my subjects will be permanently banished," he appointed a man who was skillful and quick-witted.
He constantly supervises those affairs;
for this reason,
those sentient beings stand in fear of punishment.
One should diligently abandon all evils and diligently cultivate all virtues.
Even if they lack the desire to cultivate virtue,
one should by these means compel them to practice it.
Therefore, this is called the skillful means arising from being pressed by circumstances.
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means regarding bestowing favors and repaying kindness?
It refers to when bodhisattvas first [act] toward sentient beings.
According to the extent of one's capacity, one should bestow favors:
either by giving what is needed, or by relieving distress,
or by removing fear, or by bringing together those who are beloved.
Or they may free them from what is unpleasant,
or treat their suffering from illness so that they attain peace and happiness;
those sentient beings, deeply perceiving this kindness, desire to repay its virtue.
At that time, the Bodhisattva exhorted them to cultivate wholesome deeds in order to repay his kindness, saying:
"It is not by means of other worldly wealth that you come to recompense me; this is what constitutes the great repayment of my kindness."
If you are able to recognize the kindness of your parents and respectfully provide for them—
with the full details extending even to the observance of the pure precepts—
this is what is called the great repayment of their debt of gratitude.
In this way, when a bodhisattva first bestows kindness upon sentient beings and exhorts them toward the cultivation of virtue,
it is called "great gratitude.
By means of this skillful method, he causes others to diligently apply themselves to the study and practice of virtue.
Therefore, this is called the skillful means of bestowing kindness and repaying kindness.
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means of ultimate purity?
It refers to those bodhisattvas who abide in the bodhisattva stage of reaching the ultimate.
Having already thoroughly purified the bodhisattva path,
he first manifests rebirth within the common lot of the Tuṣita heaven,
where immeasurable sentient beings think to themselves: [He has been born here.]
A bodhisattva named [Name] has now been born among the class of beings in Tuṣita Heaven;
before long, he shall descend to Jambudvīpa and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
May we be able to encounter him and not fail to do so;
wherever this bodhisattva is born,
may we also be reborn there.
Thus, it is for the sake of causing immeasurable sentient beings to give rise to right aspiration,
and for the sake of their extensive cultivation of this aspiration;
furthermore, it is because this Bodhisattva has descended from among the hosts of Tuṣita Heaven to come down to the human world.
Born into a noble or prestigious family—
such as a royal family or the family of a state preceptor—
he renounces the exquisite sensual pleasures of the world without lingering attachment and goes forth into the pure life of homelessness.
This is in order to cause all sentient beings to give rise to reverence;
furthermore, it is to manifest the undertaking of difficult and arduous ascetic practices so that those sentient beings who take pleasure in such austerities may abandon what they cherish.
Furthermore, having realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
one causes other sentient beings to aspire toward the excellence of the enlightenment and liberation that they share in common.
Moreover, once one has realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening...
He did not preach the True Dharma to sentient beings immediately,
but waited for Brahmā, King of Devas, to come in person to request it,
so that all sentient beings might develop reverence for the True Dharma.
He formed this thought:
"Since the Dharma that is about to be taught must certainly be sublime,
the Brahmā King now looks forward to it with longing."
Because the Blessed One has spoken this Dharma, he has come in person to request it.
Furthermore, with his Buddha-eye,
he observes the world so that sentient beings do not engage in such slander.
It was solely because the Brahmā King came in person to request it that,
out of respect for the Brahmā King, I proclaimed the True Dharma;
it was not that I gave rise to compassion for sentient beings on my own account.
This was indeed prompted by others;
it was not that he himself could discern whether the capacities and circumstances were appropriate or not.
He acted out of a desire to destroy such false attachments held by a certain class of sentient beings.
First, he observed the world with the Buddha-eye;
thereafter, he turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma,
which has never before been turned by anyone in any world.
In this way, he further proclaims the true Dharma and establishes the rules of training;
this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means of ultimate purity.
By means of these explained skillful means, [the bodhisattva acts].
There is no other skillful means superior to or more excellent than this;
therefore, it is called ultimate purity.
Such are the six kinds of skillful means taught by the bodhisattva, whether in brief or in detail.
It can eliminate the anger and afflictions of sentient beings who revile and turn their backs on the holy teachings;
it causes those who remain in the middle to enter [the path];
and it brings to maturity those who have already entered.
Those who have already been matured, he causes to attain liberation.
Beyond this, there is nothing superior or more extensive.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*).
Dhāraṇīs are briefly of four kinds:
first, the dhāraṇī of the Dharma;
second, the dhāraṇī of the meaning.
Third is the dhāraṇī of incantations;
fourth is the dhāraṇī for attaining the bodhisattva’s patience.
What is the bodhisattva’s dharma-dhāraṇī?
This refers to bodhisattvas who have attained such support from the power of mindfulness and wisdom;
by virtue of this support, they hear words never heard before that they have not yet rehearsed and have not yet mastered.
They organize and compile the collections of names, phrases, and syllables in their proper sequence and systematic arrangement;
they collect immeasurable sūtras in due order and are able to maintain them without forgetting for immeasurable periods of time.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s dharma-dhāraṇī.
What is the Bodhisattva’s meaning-dhāraṇī?
It is as previously described.
This distinction refers to the fact that regarding the immeasurable meanings and intentions of those very dharmas,
the mind has not yet become warmed by familiarity nor has it attained thorough mastery.
To be able to maintain [the teachings] without forgetting them for immeasurable periods of time—
this is called the Bodhisattva’s *arthadhāraṇī*.
What is the Bodhisattva’s *mantradhāraṇī*?
This refers to bodhisattvas who have attained such mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
through the empowerment of this mastery,
they are able to eliminate the calamities and afflictions of sentient beings.
All these mantra phrases shall be entirely efficacious;
they are supremely efficacious and never fail to produce their intended results.
It is able to eliminate various kinds of calamities and afflictions;
this is called the Bodhisattva’s mantra-dhāraṇī.
How does a bodhisattva attain the bodhisattva’s patience-dhāraṇī?
This refers to those bodhisattvas who have accomplished the naturally firm causal practice,
are endowed with sublime wisdom,
and dwell alone in secluded solitude, free from speech.
Never having seen any being travel along a path,
he eats with moderation, avoids impure food, and eats only of a single kind.
He remains constantly in profound meditative concentration, sleeping little and staying awake much during the night.
Regarding the mantra phrases for attaining bodhisattva-patience as taught by the Buddha,
one should contemplate them with careful attention.
The words of the mantra are as follows:
*Eṭi miṭi giṭi vīrya-pāṇite svāhā.* Regarding the meaning of these mantra verses:
He reflects with careful discernment, deliberates,
and observes; he thus correctly practices the meaning of these mantra verses.
Without hearing it from another, one naturally attains realization.
One understands that these mantra syllables and phrases are entirely devoid of meaning; they are the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), being nothing but meaningless.
One understands the meaning of these words as they truly are—
namely, that they have no meaning—
and therefore, beyond this, one does not seek any further meaning.
This is called being skillfully and excellently proficient in the meaning of the mantra phrases.
Having thus correctly mastered the meaning of these mantra phrases,
he immediately follows that meaning without hearing it from another.
One personally and correctly penetrates the meaning of all phenomena;
that is, one penetrates this meaning as follows:
the meanings of the intrinsic natures of all phenomena expressed by all verbal designations are not established as real.
There is only the ineffable intrinsic nature (*nirabhilāpya-svabhāva*) of all phenomena;
this is the meaning of "intrinsic nature. Once one has correctly realized this meaning of intrinsic nature regarding all phenomena, there is no further meaning to be sought beyond it.
Because they have thoroughly mastered this meaning,
they attain supreme and vast joy;
by means of this, the bodhisattva acquires dhāraṇī.
It should be said that they have already attained the superior patience established by these dhāraṇī verses.
Because they have attained this patience,

these bodhisattvas will, before long, attain the pure and superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya*) and proceed by means of the superior patience belonging to the stage of practice through superior conviction (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) of the highest degree.
It should be known that this is called the bodhisattva’s dhāraṇī for attaining bodhisattva patience.
Within this, there are the bodhisattva’s dhāraṇī of phenomena (dharma-dhāraṇī) and the dhāraṇī of meaning (artha-dhāraṇī).
If, after passing beyond the first incalculable great eon,
one has already entered the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*),
that which is attained is certain, firm, and vast.
From this point onward, whether by the power of aspiration or by relying on meditative concentration,
although there may be attainment, it is not certain,
nor is it stable, nor is it extensive.
Just as with the two dhāraṇīs of the Dharma and its meaning,
it should be known that the same applies to the dhāraṇī of mantras;
one is able to attain the bodhisattva’s dhāraṇī of patience.
As explained previously,
it is attained in this very way:
if bodhisattvas possess these four qualities.
Only then does one obtain these various dhāraṇīs;
it is not the case that even one of them may be missing.
What are the names of these four kinds of merit?
First, one is without attachment or craving for any sensual desires.
Second, one does not give rise to resentment or envy toward the superior achievements of others, nor does one begrudge their prosperity.
Third, one gives equally whatever is requested without regret.
Fourth, they develop a profound sense of joy and delight toward the True Dharma.
One who delights in the Dharma feels deep-seated love and affection for the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka-mātṛkā.
What is the correct aspirational prayer cultivated by a bodhisattva?
It should be known that this prayer is briefly of five kinds.
The first is the aspiration for the arousal of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda-praṇidhāna*).
Second is the vow regarding rebirth;
third is the vow regarding practice;
fourth is the correct vow.
Fifth is the great vow.
If bodhisattvas first give rise to the mind directed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
this is called the vow of the arousal of the mind.
If bodhisattvas vow to be reborn in the future in favorable realms that accord with and benefit sentient beings,
this is called the vow for taking birth.
If bodhisattvas vow to be able to correctly discern all phenomena through investigation, [this is called the vow for correct discernment].
The aspiration to cultivate immeasurable and other such sublime virtuous dharmas within the objective sphere is called the "aspiration regarding conduct. Furthermore,
when bodhisattvas aspire to embrace all the virtuous dharmas of bodhisattvas in the future, [this is also an aspiration regarding conduct].
To embrace all existing merits,
whether in their entirety or in detail, and all correct aspirations—
this is called "correct aspiration."
It should be known that the great vows of a bodhisattva arise from right aspiration;
these are further of ten kinds.
If a bodhisattva makes a vow regarding the future:
One should know that making offerings to immeasurable and boundless Tathāgatas with all kinds of supreme and exquisite ritual implements is called the first great vow.
If bodhisattvas aspire that, in the future,
they shall uphold and protect all the true Dharma of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
and maintain the eye of the Dharma so that it remains unbroken and undestroyed.
One should know that this is called the second right vow.
It is when bodhisattvas make a vow for the future,
from descending from the Tuṣita heaven as previously described, up until entering great parinirvāṇa.
It should be known that this is called the third great vow.
If bodhisattvas vow that in the future they will practice every kind of correct bodhisattva conduct.
One should know that this is called the fourth great vow:
that if bodhisattvas should aspire in the future to be able to universally bring all sentient beings to maturity.
One should know that this is called the fifth great vow.
If all bodhisattvas make the vow that in the future they will be able to manifest themselves in all worlds.
One should know that this is called the sixth great vow.
It is the vow of all bodhisattvas that in the future they may universally and purely cultivate all buddha-fields.
One should know that this is called the seventh great vow.
It is the vow of all bodhisattvas that in the future,
all bodhisattvas shall enter the Great Vehicle with a single, identical intention and application.
One should know that this is called the eighth great vow.
It is the vow of all bodhisattvas that, in the future,
all their unerring applications shall never be in vain.
One should know that this is called the ninth great vow:
if bodhisattvas aspire that in the future they may swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
One should know that this is called the tenth great vow.
What is the bodhisattva’s emptiness samādhi?
It means that all bodhisattvas contemplate all things as being devoid of any intrinsic nature of verbal expression, such that there are only phenomena possessing an ineffable intrinsic nature.
The mind is correctly and peacefully established;
this is called the bodhisattva’s samādhi of emptiness.
What is the bodhisattva’s samādhi of wishlessness?
It refers to how bodhisattvas correctly contemplate all phenomena as having an ineffable intrinsic nature,
yet being grasped by afflictions and various sufferings arising from false conceptualization.
All are defiled by immeasurable faults;
one does not wish for them to be foremost in future lives, but dwells with a mind correctly settled.
This is called the bodhisattva’s samādhi of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
What is the bodhisattva’s signless samādhi?
It refers to when bodhisattvas, through correct reflection, [abandon] all conceptualizations and the various signs of proliferation regarding all things that possess an ineffable intrinsic nature.
He understands as it truly is that which is eternally extinguished and tranquil;
his mind abides correctly therein.
This is called the bodhisattva’s signless samādhi.
Question: For what reason are exactly three samādhis established—neither more nor less?
Answer: There are two kinds of phenomena (dharma), namely existence and non-existence.
Conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are designated as existence.
"I" and "mine" are termed non-existent.
Because within conditioned phenomena there is the absence of aspiration and because they are to be reviled and rejected,
one should know that the wishless samādhi is established based upon this.
Because one aspires for nirvāṇa within the unconditioned and because it is correctly embraced by delight,
one should know that the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*) is established based upon this.
Regarding the bodhisattva who does not engage with existing things, there is neither aspiration nor non-aspiration.
However, regarding that which does not exist, the bodhisattva perceives it as non-existent just as it truly is.
Based on this perception, one should understand that the samādhi of emptiness is established.
Thus, within these three types of samādhi, the bodhisattva...
Diligently practicing and studying,
one thereby establishes a thorough understanding of reality as it is,
regarding the other modes of the three samādhis.
One enters into realization as it truly is.
One establishes the underlying principles.
One enters into realization as it truly is.
One practices the principles of cultivation as they truly are;
that is to say, within this [teaching],
the assembly of śrāvakas diligently trains and attains full realization.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 45;
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 46;
Spoken by Bodhisattva Maitreya.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.

In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth section of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the first *Yogasthāna*, the seventeenth chapter, "The Factors Conducive to Enlightenment," part three: Furthermore, there are four types of *dharmoddānas*.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas teach this because they wish to bring sentient beings to purity.
What are these four? All conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
This is called the first summary of the Dharma:
all conditioned phenomena are suffering.
This is called the second summary of the Dharma.
All phenomena are devoid of self;
this is called the third summary of the Dharma.
Nirvāṇa is peace.
This is called the fourth summary of the Dharma (*dharmoddāna*).
Buddhas and bodhisattvas frequently proclaim such meanings corresponding to the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings;
therefore, it is called a summary of the Dharma.
Furthermore, from time immemorial, the Munis whose minds are tranquil have successively proclaimed this at all times;
therefore, it is called an *uddāna*.
Furthermore, this course of practice leads to great rebirth and also leads to emergence from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*);
therefore, it is called an *uddāna*.
How does a bodhisattva equally and thoroughly observe that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent?
It means that a bodhisattva observes that the verbal nature (*abhilāpa-svabhāva*) of all conditioned phenomena is at all times eternally non-existent.
Thus, these conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are eternally unapprehendable;
therefore, they are called impermanent.
Furthermore, one contemplates those very things as being beyond verbal expression.
Because one does not understand their true reality,
arising and ceasing are perceived with ignorance as their cause;
thus, these conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), which possess a nature beyond words, have both arising and ceasing.
Therefore, they are called impermanent.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas contemplate past formations that have already arisen and already ceased,
they find that those formations have no obtainable cause and possess no intrinsic nature.
Therefore, one observes that the causal nature and intrinsic nature of those [formations] are entirely non-existent.
One observes present formations as already arisen but not yet ceased;
for their causes cannot be found, since they have already yielded their results.
Because its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is still obtainable and has not yet ceased.
Therefore, one contemplates that while that intrinsic nature exists, it lacks a cause;
and one contemplates future formations (saṃskāra) as neither yet arisen nor yet ceased.
Because those conditioned phenomena have causes that can be apprehended yet have not yet yielded their results,
and because they lack intrinsic nature as they have not yet arisen;
therefore, one observes that they possess only the nature of causality and no intrinsic nature.
Having thus seen the continuous succession of the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) within the three periods of time,
the bodhisattva observes each and every moment of those conditioned phenomena with equal and thorough insight.
All conditioned phenomena possess three characteristics of the conditioned;
following the moment [of arising], there is a fourth characteristic of the conditioned,
namely, the destruction of the intrinsic nature of the preceding moment within this very process.
One correctly contemplates that the arising of the intrinsic nature of the moments of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is not preceded by an interval;
once these conditioned phenomena have arisen, they do not perish immediately.
Correct contemplation constitutes abiding.
These already-arisen formations, when compared with the previously ceased formations,
differ in their momentary intrinsic natures.
To contemplate correctly [this] as aging:
immediately after the moment in which these conditioned phenomena arise,
this very moment of those arisen conditioned phenomena undergoes destruction by its own nature.
One correctly contemplates them as cessation.

Having contemplated this, the Bodhisattva perceives that the intrinsic nature of these arisen momentary conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is itself the intrinsic nature of arising, abiding, and aging.
One does not perceive that arising and so forth possess a separate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Rather, one observes them as they truly are: immediately after the moment of arising, these very conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of arising and so forth perish by their own intrinsic nature, having no other nature apart from this.
These four characteristics of the conditioned encompass all conditioned phenomena;
to state it briefly:
It is manifested by two aspects:
first, that which is manifested by having parts;
second, that which is manifested by being partless.
In this context, the Blessed One established one characteristic of the conditioned based on the "constituent part" (bhavanga),
and he established the second characteristic of the conditioned based on the "non-constituent part" (abhavanga).
Both arising and change are manifested by the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) themselves;
thus, the third characteristic of the conditioned is established.
In this regard, the bodhisattva contemplates that at all times there are only conditioned factors, and apart from these, there is no arising, abiding, aging, or cessation.
There is always a real entity established by way of its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva). Why is this?
Because when conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) arise, only these very same conditioned phenomena are perceived.
There is no other separate entity of birth, duration, aging,
or cessation. Thus, when these conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) undergo duration, aging, and cessation,
it is only these very same conditioned phenomena that are perceived.
There is no other distinct entity for birth, abiding, aging, or cessation.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas investigate through reasoning for a real substance such as birth and so forth,
it is likewise not to be found.
Regarding the fact that such [a thing] cannot be found through investigation:
this means that if there were a dharma of arising distinct from those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) such as form (*rūpa*),
it would necessarily have an intrinsic nature of arising just like the intrinsic natures of those conditioned phenomena such as form.
In this way, this birth must also have a birth;
thus, there would be two kinds of birth:
first, the birth of formations (*saṃskāra*).
Second, there is the "arising of arising.
In this way, is this "arising of arising" identical to or different from that [primary] "arising"?
If one says they are identical, then the calculation that birth truly exists becomes futile;
yet to say that there is a distinct birth [is likewise untenable].
It is not logical that this exists as a substantial entity.
If you say it is different [from the formations],
then it would follow that the arising of formations does not arise.
It is unreasonable for this activity to produce production.
As was said regarding the characteristic of production (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*),
so it should be explained in detail regarding duration (*sthiti*).
One should know that the same applies to the cessation of aging:
if the dharma of cessation possessed a separate intrinsic nature established as a reality,
then this very cessation would itself have arising and cessation.
If [the seeds] were to perish at the same time as birth, then all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) would necessarily perish together.

In that case, one would require little effort, as all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) would perish entirely, just as they do upon entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
If cessation were itself subject to cessation, then even though all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have already ceased,
they would necessarily arise once again,
because that cessation would be non-existent.
Therefore, to say that there is cessation and that there is arising and cessation is not reasonable.
Furthermore, son of good family, whether it be a son of good family or a daughter of good family...
At all times, there is always a real entity whose intrinsic nature is established;
yet, by viewing it as conventionally existent,
one is able to cultivate revulsion, detachment, and liberation.
This is not reasonable;
the opposite of this is reasonable.
By means of this mode of apprehension, bodhisattvas correctly understand that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas contemplate the continuous progression of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
they see that these serve as the basis for three kinds of suffering.
The first is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Second is the suffering of change;
third is the suffering of suffering.

In this way, bodhisattvas correctly understand that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely suffering. Furthermore, bodhisattvas correctly understand the nature of the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*) regarding all phenomena, both conditioned and unconditioned.
First is the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*),
and second is the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
Regarding these, the selflessness of persons among all phenomena is as follows:
This means that the person (*pudgala*) is not truly existent as being identical to the phenomena (*dharmas*),
nor is there a truly existent person existing separately from the phenomena;
rather, it is the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) within all phenomena.
That is to say, regarding all matters of verbal expression,
the intrinsic nature of all dharmas expressed therein is entirely non-existent.
In this way, the bodhisattva understands, in accordance with reality, that all dharmas are devoid of a self.
Furthermore, all bodhisattvas contemplate that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) have their prior causes eternally severed and subsequently extinguished without remainder;
the rest will ultimately never arise or be born again.
It is called "nirvāṇa.
One should know that the essence of nirvāṇa is quiescent,
because all suffering has been utterly stilled.
Because all afflictions have been ultimately extinguished.
Thus, such a bodhisattva who has not yet attained the pure superior intention (adhyāśaya) has not yet seen the noble truths.
Although those of the Śrāvaka vehicle conceive a resolute conviction toward nirvāṇa and speak thus, saying,
"Nirvāṇa is peaceful," they have not yet understood nirvāṇa as it truly is.
They have not yet turned toward the transformation of knowledge and vision in accordance with reality;
nevertheless, they do possess appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*),
just like the son of a prince or the son of a householder.
Since his birth, he had not yet left the royal palace or the inner chambers of the elder’s house;
for the sake of the young child, both the king and the elder fashioned various playthings, such as deer-carts, ox-carts, horse-carts, and elephant-carts.
And he bestowed them upon him.
At that time, the prince and the son of the elder used them for play, amusement, and recreation.
Regarding such artificially constructed deer, oxen, horses, and elephants,
he gave rise to the perception of them as real deer, oxen, horses, and elephants.
Later, at one time, the king and the elder...
Knowing that their sons had gradually grown up and their faculties were matured,
they praised and spoke of the real deer, oxen, horses, and elephants.
At that time, the prince and the son of the elder—
Hearing his father’s praise, he thought to himself:
"Could it be that my father the king and my father the elder are praising the four kinds of vehicles we possess— deer, oxen, horses, and elephants?"
Later, when the king and the elder knew that their son had grown older,
they led him out from the inner palace to travel abroad and showed him actual deer, oxen, horses, and elephants.
Upon seeing this, he gave rise within himself to a realization of reality through wisdom:
"This is the true meaning; these are the deer-carts, ox-carts, horse-carts, and elephant-carts that our father has always described to us throughout the long night."
However, it is only because we lack wisdom that we conceive a conviction of reality regarding those mere resemblances and mere images,
such as deer and the like, which are not as they truly are.
By reason of these causes and conditions, one subsequently gives rise to shame regarding one's former resolute convictions.
In this way, the palace is a metaphor for saṃsāra.
The various young children he has fathered and raised are like bodhisattvas who have not yet realized the pure superior intention (*adhyāśaya*),
as well as śrāvakas of the vehicle who have not yet seen the truths (*satya*).
The father represents the Buddhas and those Bodhisattvas who have already entered the Great Stages (*mahābhūmi*).
His initial construction of vehicles such as deer- and ox-carts symbolizes his preaching of the characteristics of *nirvāṇa* as a deer.
Next, he spoke in praise of the true deer and so forth as metaphors for how Buddhas and Bodhisattvas personally realize and perceive true nirvāṇa,
and then describe what they have seen before those bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
They praise and speak of the true merits of nirvāṇa.
Having heard this, others merely employ a cognition that conforms to the sound of the voice to develop resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the virtues of nirvāṇa throughout the long night.
If at this time the provisions have matured,
they gradually increase and develop into a pure superior intention (*adhyāśaya*);
thus the bodhisattva perceives the truths (*satyadarśin*).
The śrāvaka gives rise to the wisdom of direct realization regarding true nirvāṇa;
at that very moment, there arises within him an internal, accurate understanding and insight into such nirvāṇa.
That which has been realized by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
and which was previously praised and taught by the Buddhas and bodhisattvas—
this we formerly [perceived] with the cognitive wisdom of fools.
Regarding that which is not as it truly is— merely resembling it and being merely its reflection—
one gives rise to a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that it is the true *nirvāṇa*.
By reason of this, one subsequently feels shame for one's previous resolute conviction.
Relying upon subsequent resolve as it truly is,
it is like a patient who goes to a great physician;
for the sake of curing the illness, they seek out and obtain a suitable medicine and take it constantly.
He develops profound conviction and deep affection for that medicine, perceiving it alone as the reality.
Due to these causes and conditions, his previous illness is cured;
however, another illness subsequently arises, requiring him to take a different medicine.
At that time, the great physician, knowing that the previous illness had been cured but a subsequent illness had arisen again,
understood that further medicine was required;
he therefore advised [the patient] to discontinue the former medicine and take the other medicine.
At that time, that patient, being ignorant and lacking discernment,
develops a deep conviction regarding what he had previously taken;
conceiving it to be appropriate, he is unwilling to discard it.

At that time, the great physician explained to him the natures of the medicines for both the preceding and subsequent stages of the illness, stating that for the current ailment, the preceding medicine was unsuitable while the subsequent medicine was superior.
Although the patient heard these words, he did not develop a resolute conviction in them.
Just as that patient did not yet have deep faith in what the skilled physician said,
so too are all ordinary beings, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas possessed by the disease of the afflictions.
The great physician is a metaphor for the Tathāgatas;
the excellent medicines and so forth are metaphors for the teaching of that which is superior, most superior, and supreme.
Whether it be the profound, the superior, and the most profound;
whether it be inferior, superior,
or the most excellent teaching of the Dharma and the correct instruction.
Although they have heard the instructions and admonitions, they are unable to gain realization or produce resolute conviction;
they are unable to practice the "Dharma in accordance with the Dharma" (dharmānudharmapratipatti), even though they possess pure faith.
Bodhisattvas and śrāvakas do not give rise to doubt or confusion regarding what the Buddha has taught;
they ride upon the vehicle of the Buddha’s teaching as if it were a magnificent, well-adorned chariot complete with all its parts and equipment.
The unsurpassed Dharma-vehicle is like a skilled charioteer;
according to the ground traversed and the destination to be reached,
it advances swiftly and without delay.

Chapter 18: The Qualities of a Bodhisattva. In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth part of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the first section on the "Yogic Stations," this is Chapter Eighteen: The Qualities of a Bodhisattva. What are the qualities possessed by a bodhisattva?
The summary verse says: Rare and not rare;
