Benefiting with an impartial mind, repaying kindness, and rejoicing in praise; The nature of non-futile application.
It should be known that when bodhisattvas diligently train in the vehicle of unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment, there are five most marvelous qualities. What are these five?
First, they feel affection for all sentient beings even in the absence of any causal conditions;
second, they act solely for the purpose of benefiting all sentient beings.
First, they constantly abide within birth and death, enduring immeasurable suffering.
Second, they are well able to understand and apply the skillful means for taming sentient beings who are beset by manifold afflictions and difficulties. Third, [they possess] these qualities.
Fourth, they are able to penetrate and realize the true meaning and principles that are extremely difficult to understand.
Fifth, they possess inconceivable and great majestic spiritual power.
These five kinds of most marvelous qualities possessed by bodhisattvas are not shared with any other sentient beings.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas accomplish five kinds of non-extraordinary qualities,
yet they are said to have accomplished most extraordinary qualities.
What are these five?
This means that for bodhisattvas, the suffering caused by benefiting others is itself their own happiness; therefore,
bodhisattvas constantly and universally undergo and practice the suffering that serves as the cause for benefiting others.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the first non-marvelous quality,
yet it is called the accomplishment of a most marvelous quality.
Furthermore, although Bodhisattvas thoroughly understand the faults of saṃsāra and the merits of nirvāṇa, they...
Yet, to delight in universally purifying sentient beings is itself his own delight; therefore,
for the sake of the sovereign power to purify sentient beings, the bodhisattva vows to undergo birth and death.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the second non-marvelous quality,
yet it is termed the accomplishment of a most marvelous quality.
Furthermore, although Bodhisattvas thoroughly understand the flavor of the joy of silence, they delight in bringing all sentient beings to purity.
This is itself his own happiness.
Therefore, through the predominant power of purifying sentient beings,
the bodhisattva constantly and diligently employs skillful means to preach the true Dharma for them.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the third non-marvelous quality, yet it is called the accomplishment of an exceedingly marvelous quality.
Furthermore, although Bodhisattvas accumulate all the roots of virtue belonging to the six perfections, they delight in causing all sentient beings to become pure.
This is itself their own happiness.
Therefore, for the sake of the predominant influence of purifying sentient beings,
the Bodhisattva gives to all sentient beings with a pure intention.
Yet, they do not seek the ripening of the fruit of giving;
this is called a bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the fourth non-marvelous quality, which is nonetheless called an accomplishment of a most marvelous quality.
Furthermore, for bodhisattvas, the welfare of others constitutes their own self-interest;
therefore, bodhisattvas constantly manifest the practice of all activities that benefit sentient beings.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the fifth non-marvelous quality, which is nonetheless termed the accomplishment of a most marvelous quality.
One should know that through five aspects,
their mind is universally impartial toward all sentient beings.
What are these five?
First, the Bodhisattva initially generates the aspiration for great enlightenment (mahābodhi) for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
First, they give rise to a mind of equanimity.
Second, regarding all sentient beings,
bodhisattvas abide in a mind of equanimity accompanied by compassion.
Third, the bodhisattva develops, with a profound mind, a heart of equality toward all sentient beings, accompanied by the love one has for an only child.
Fourth, the bodhisattva [regards] all conditioned phenomena that have arisen from various causes and conditions.
Having understood that these are merely imagined entities of sentient beings,
one knows that the dharma-nature of a single sentient being is the very dharma-nature of all sentient beings.
With a mind that proceeds with the equality of dharmas, [one acts].
He abides in a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
Fifth, just as a bodhisattva performs beneficial actions for a single sentient being,
he likewise performs beneficial actions for all sentient beings.
With a mind characterized by benefit for all sentient beings,
they abide in a state of equanimity toward them.
By these five aspects, the minds of these bodhisattvas are equal toward all sentient beings.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas are able to perform all manner of beneficial deeds for sentient beings through five aspects.
What are these five?
First, he provides instruction on right livelihood for the sake of benefit.
Second, regarding those activities that do not accord with what leads to meaningful goals,
he provides instruction on what does accord with them for the sake of benefit.
Third, for those who are without support or protection, suffering, and impoverished,
he is skillfully able to act as their support and protection, thereby providing them with benefit. Fourth,
he provides benefit by teaching and bestowing the path that leads to the happy realms.
Fifth, he teaches and bestows the three vehicles for their benefit.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas repay the kindness of sentient beings who have shown them favor by means of five modes of manifestation.
What are the five?
First, establishing sentient beings so that they may train in one's own virtues;
second, employing skillful means to establish them so that they may train in the virtues of others.
Third, for those who are without support or protection, suffering, and impoverished,
one acts as their support and protection according to one's strength and ability.
Fourth, one encourages them to make offerings to all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Fifth, they cause others to receive, uphold, recite, copy, and make offerings to the true Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas should always rejoice in and praise five kinds of matters.
What are the five?
First, to encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world and always be able to serve him.
Second, to constantly hear the Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, including the six perfections, in the presence of all Buddhas.
Third, they possess constant power to bring sentient beings to maturity in every respect.
Fourth, they are capable of swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Fifth, once they have realized awakening, their assembly of disciples is always harmonious and free from strife.
Furthermore, by means of five causes and conditions, bodhisattvas are able to perform effective and non-futile practices for the benefit of sentient beings.
What are these five? They are as follows:
first, bodhisattvas desire to bring about the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings;
second, they understand the benefit and happiness of sentient beings as it truly is, possessing non-erroneous awakening.
All these points should be understood according to their characteristics as previously explained in the "Chapter on Immeasurable Offerings and Approaches.
Furthermore, the summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
Non-perverted application, the actual merit resembling both decline and progress,
and the skillful training of sentient beings—
these are the five applications of all bodhisattvas.
One should know that this universally encompasses all the unerring applications of a bodhisattva.
What are the five?
First, the application of protective cultivation.
Second, the application of faultless conduct;
third, the application of the power of discernment;
fourth, the application of the superior intention of purity.
Regarding the five types of application that lead to certainty:
what is the bodhisattva’s application of protective cultivation?
It should be known that this, in brief, consists of five kinds.
First, guarding against the loss of intelligence,
which means swiftly grasping the teachings by means of innate wisdom;
second, guarding against the loss of right mindfulness.
That is to say, by means of this right mindfulness, one retains the dharmas as they are grasped so that they are not forgotten.
Third is the guarding of right awareness;
that is to say, by means of this right awareness, one skillfully examines the meaning of the dharmas thus retained.
Because one penetrates with right wisdom and remains far removed from the causes and conditions conducive to the decline of sagacity, right mindfulness, and awakening-intelligence;
and because one cultivates and draws near to the causes and conditions conducive to the state of abiding and the state of excellence.
Fourth, one protects one's own mind by being able to skillfully guard the doors of the sense faculties.
Fifth, one protects the minds of others.
Because they are able to correctly conform to the minds of others.
What is the faultless application of a bodhisattva?
It refers to the various bodhisattvas regarding all wholesome dharmas.
They dedicate [their merit] toward enlightenment in a manner that is unerring, fervent, immeasurable, and uninterrupted.
What is the bodhisattva’s application through the power of discernment?
It refers to all these [practices] while the bodhisattvas are still on the stage of conduct through aspiration (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
One should know its characteristics.
What is the bodhisattva’s application of the purified superior intention (*adhyāśaya*)?
It refers to all those bodhisattvas who abide in this very stage of the pure superior intention and the stage of practicing correct conduct.
One should know its characteristics.
What is the bodhisattva’s falling into the application of certainty?
It refers to those bodhisattvas who, within these very stages—the stage of certainty, the stage of certain practice, and the stage of reaching the ultimate—[enter therein].
One should understand their characteristics.
These five types of bodhisattva application comprehensively encompass all unerring applications.
Furthermore, it should be known that there are five factors conducive to decline for bodhisattvas. What are these five?
First, they do not respect the true Dharma or the teachers of the Dharma.
Second, negligence and indolence;
third, intimacy with and attachment to various afflictions;
fourth, intimacy with and attachment to various unwholesome actions.
Fifth, there is the arising of overweening pride by comparing oneself with other bodhisattvas to determine superiority or inferiority,
as well as the arising of overweening pride through misconceptions regarding the Dharma.
Furthermore, it should be known that there are five factors conducive to excellence for bodhisattvas.
What are these five?
They should be understood as being respectively the opposites of the aforementioned five factors belonging to the dark category.
Furthermore, there are briefly five kinds of counterfeit virtues of bodhisattvas which should be understood as being,
in reality, bodhisattva faults.
What are these five?
First, they cause harm to those sentient beings who are violent, wicked, and have violated their pure precepts;
second, they falsely manifest various forms of perfect dignified conduct.
Third, among the worldly expressions, incantations, and treatises of the non-Buddhists that correspond to conventional dharmas,
he is counted among the wise and the intelligent.
Fourth, he practices virtuous deeds such as giving that involve worldly faults.
Fifth, they proclaim and establish counterfeit true Dharma,
causing it to spread widely.
Furthermore, Bodhisattvas briefly possess five kinds of genuine merit.
What are the five? First,
toward those sentient beings who are violent and transgress pure ethical discipline,
one gives rise to a superior mind of compassion by reason of this very circumstance.
Second, they are naturally accomplished and fully endowed with dignified deportment.
Third, regarding the pure, sublime, and true teachings and realizations spoken by the Buddha,
they are counted among the ranks of the wise and the sagacious.
Fourth, they practice virtuous deeds such as blameless giving.
Fifth, they reveal the true Dharma to suppress and eliminate all counterfeit dharmas.
Furthermore, in brief, bodhisattvas [act] in ten spheres.
He skillfully and unerringly tames those sentient beings to be converted.
What are the ten points?
First, the point of distancing oneself from misconduct.
Second, the state of being far removed from all sensual desires;
third, the state of single-minded diligence in non-transgression and the ability to emerge from transgression once it has occurred;
fourth, the state of closely guarding all the doors of the sense faculties.
Fifth, dwelling with clear comprehension;
sixth, staying away from places of clamor and bustle;
seventh, staying in a secluded place and remaining free from all unwholesome discursive thoughts.
Eighth, the state of being far removed from obstructive conditions.
Ninth, the state of being far removed from all entanglements of affliction (*kleśa*).
Tenth, the state of being far removed from all forms of heavy dysfunction (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to the category of afflictions.
Furthermore, the summary verse (udāna) says:
The prediction of the bodhisattvas, Falling into the state of certainty,
That which must certainly be done and that which should be done, The most excellent, and finally, the ultimate.
It is said that bodhisattvas, briefly by way of six aspects,
receive from the Tathāgatas the prophecy of their unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
What are these six?
First, the stage of abiding in the spiritual lineage before the arousal of the thought of enlightenment;
second, the stage of having already aroused that thought;
third, the stage of its being present before one.
Fourth is the stage of non-manifestation;
fifth is the presence of a definite time limit,
meaning that after such a period of time, one shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Sixth is the absence of a fixed time limit;
that is, bestowing a prophecy without declaring a specific temporal limit.
Furthermore, there are briefly three ways in which bodhisattvas fall into certainty.
What are the three?
First, abiding securely in the spiritual lineage (gotra) and falling into certainty;
second, generating the bodhicitta and falling into certainty.
Third, those who practice without falsehood fall into certainty;
those who dwell securely in their spiritual lineage fall into certainty.
This refers to bodhisattvas abiding in the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
He is then called a bodhisattva who has entered the state of certainty. Why is this?
Because, by virtue of this, if such a bodhisattva encounters superior conditions, he is certainly capable of realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Regarding those who have generated the bodhicitta and entered the state of certainty:
this refers to a certain class of bodhisattvas who have already generated the mind of certainty toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
From this point until they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
they shall never again regress;
their practice will not be in vain, and they will enter the state of certainty.
This means that bodhisattvas who have already attained mastery never fail in their intended practice throughout all activities for the benefit of sentient beings,
acting exactly as they desire and according to what they undertake.
Among these three types of entry into certainty,
it is based on the final stage of entry into certainty that the Buddhas,
the Tathāgatas, bestow upon bodhisattvas the prediction of their entry into certainty.
Furthermore, there are briefly five points that all bodhisattvas must certainly perform;
if they fail to do so, they will ultimately be incapable of realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
What are the five?
First, generating the bodhicitta;
second, giving rise to profound compassion for all sentient beings.
Third, ardent diligence;
fourth, skillful cultivation in all fields of knowledge;
fifth, freedom from weariness.
It consists of five [aspects]:
first, that which should always be practiced with heedfulness;
second, [the practice] toward those sentient beings who are without support or refuge, and who are suffering and impoverished.
One should constantly act as a refuge and so forth for them.
Third, one should always make offerings to all Tathāgatas.
Fourth, one should always thoroughly understand what is faulty and what is faultless.
Fifth, in all activities— whether walking or staying— among all mental engagements,
the great bodhicitta must always serve as the guiding leader.
These five kinds of practices are what all bodhisattvas should constantly perform.
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas of the bodhisattvas that all bodhisattvas acknowledge as most excellent and preeminent,
established within the supreme dharma.
What are the ten?
First is the bodhisattva lineage,
which is the most preeminent among all lineages.
Second, the initial generation of the mind of awakening is the most excellent among all right aspirations.
Third, diligence and wisdom.
It is the most excellent among all the pāramitās.
Fourth is the means of attraction through kind speech;
it is the most excellent among all the means of attraction.
Fifth, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One,
is the most preeminent among all sentient beings.
Sixth, he has compassion for sentient beings.
It is the most excellent among all the immeasurables.
Seventh, the fourth dhyāna is the most excellent among all the dhyānas.
Eighth is the emptiness samādhi,
which is the most excellent among the three types of meditative concentration.
Ninth is the attainment of cessation.
It is the most excellent among all meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Tenth, it is the most excellent among all skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), encompassing all the pure skillful means as previously described.
Furthermore, the summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
The establishment of all designations, The investigation of all phenomena and the thorough knowledge of them as they truly are— Such are these immeasurables.
The fruits and benefits of teaching the Dharma, the nature of the Mahāyāna, and the inclusion of the bodhisattvas—these ten should be known. Regarding the establishment of various names:
in brief, there are four types of designations established for bodhisattvas.
Only the Tathāgata and the various bodhisattvas are able to correctly designate and correctly establish this;
it is not so for any others— whether devas, humans, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas.
Except for having heard it.
What are the four? First is the establishment of the designation of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti-vyavasthāna*).
Second is the establishment through the designation of truths;
third is the establishment through the designation of principles;
fourth is the establishment through the designation of vehicles.
What is meant by the establishment through the designation of the Dharma?
It refers to the twelvefold teaching, such as the Sūtras and so forth, spoken by the Buddha,
which were compiled in sequence, arranged in sequence, and established in sequence.
This is called the establishment of the designation of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti-vyavasthāna*).
What is called the establishment of the designation of truths (*satya-prajñapti-vyavasthāna*)?
It is of immeasurable kinds.
Alternatively, one truth is established,
meaning that which is non-false;
for there is only this one truth, and no second.
Alternatively, two truths are established:
first, the conventional truth;
second, the ultimate truth.
Alternatively, three truths may be established:
first, the truth of characteristics;
second, the truth of language.
The three truths of function,
or alternatively, the four truths:
first, the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Second, the truth of the origin;
third, the truth of cessation;
fourth, the truth of the path.
Alternatively, five truths may be established:
first, the truth of cause;
second, the truth of result.
Third, the truth of knowledge;
fourth, the truth of objects;
fifth, the supreme truth.
Alternatively, six truths may be established:
first, the truth of truth;
second, the truth of falsehood.
Third, the truths that should be fully known;
fourth, the truths that should be permanently abandoned;
fifth, the truths that should be realized.
There are six truths to be cultivated,
or alternatively, seven truths may be established:
first, the truth of the gratification of craving (*āsvāda-satya*).
Second, the truth of affliction;
third, the truth of renunciation;
fourth, the truth of the nature of phenomena.
5. The truths of resolute conviction;
6. The noble truths;
7. The non-noble truths.
Alternatively, eight truths may be established:
first, the truth of the nature of suffering as conditioned existence;
second, the truth of the nature of suffering as change.
3. The truth of the nature of suffering as suffering;
4. The truth of cyclic existence (saṃsāra);
5. The truth of cessation.
Sixth, the truth of affliction;
seventh, the truth of purification;
eighth, the truth of correct application.
Alternatively, nine truths are established:
first, the truth of impermanence;
second, the truth of suffering.
Third, the truth of emptiness;
fourth, the truth of non-self;
fifth, the truth of craving for existence.
Sixth, the truth of the absence of craving for existence;
seventh, the truth of the means for its abandonment;
eighth, the truth of nirvana with remainder.
The ninth is the truth of nirvāṇa without remainder.
Alternatively, ten truths may be established:
first, the truth of the suffering of oppression.
Second, the truth of suffering consisting in the deprivation of wealth and status;
third, the truth of suffering consisting in the lack of harmony within the three realms;
fourth, the truth of suffering consisting in the transformation and decay of what is beloved.
5. The truth of the suffering of coarse heaviness;
6. The truth of karma;
7. The truth of afflictions.
8. The truth of hearing the sublime Dharma and attending to it correctly;
9. The truth of right view regarding the truths;
10. The truth of right view regarding the fruit.
Such categories as these are called the establishment of the conventional designation of the truths of a bodhisattva.
One should know that if they were analyzed in detail, they would be immeasurable.
What is meant by the establishment of the conventional designation of principles?
This refers to the four principles;
their detailed analysis should be understood as previously explained.
What is meant by the "establishment of the designation of vehicles"?
That is to say: the Śrāvaka-yāna, the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, and the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.
Each of these three is established and designated by means of seven distinct modes of practice.
This is called the designation and establishment of the vehicles.
Regarding the seven aspects of the first, the Śrāvakayāna:
first is non-perverted wisdom with respect to the four noble truths.
Second, the basis of this wisdom;
third, the object of this wisdom;
fourth, the concomitants of this wisdom.
5. This is the activity of wisdom.
6. This is the equipment for wisdom.
7. This is the attainment of the fruit of wisdom.
It should be understood that by means of these seven modes of designation and establishment,
nothing is lacking in the Śrāvakayāna.
Just as the Śrāvakayāna is established through these seven modes of designation, so too [is the Bodhisattvayāna].
It should be understood that the same applies to the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas.
Regarding the seven aspects of the unsurpassed Mahāyāna:
first, there is the wisdom of renunciation, which is non-conceptual and equal toward the suchness found within all phenomena—the reality that transcends verbal expression.
Second, the basis upon which this wisdom relies;
third, the object of focus for this wisdom;
fourth, the accompanying factors of this wisdom.
5. This is the activity of wisdom;
6. this is the equipment for wisdom;
7. this is the attainment of the fruit of wisdom.
It should be known that by means of these seven modes of designation and establishment,
the unsurpassed Mahāyāna is fully complete.
This applies to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Furthermore, all the unerring designations and establishments made by the bodhisattvas—
whether those already performed, those yet to be performed, or those being performed now—
all arise from these four matters.
Beyond this, there is nothing superior or additional.
Furthermore, in order to attain the four kinds of thorough knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūtaparijñā*),
bodhisattvas engage in the four investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*) regarding all phenomena.
What are the four? First, the thorough investigation of names;
second, the thorough investigation of things.
The investigation into the designation of the three natures,
and the investigation into the designation of their distinctions—
these four types, when analyzed in detail, should be understood as they were previously explained in the "Chapter on the True Meaning."
Furthermore, there are briefly four kinds of thorough knowledge of all phenomena as they truly are for bodhisattvas.
The first is the thorough knowledge of reality induced by the investigation of names.
2. Thorough knowledge as it truly is, induced by the investigation of things;
3. Thorough knowledge as it truly is, induced by the investigation of the designation of intrinsic nature;
4. Thorough knowledge as it truly is, induced by the investigation of the designation of distinctions.
If these four types are to be analyzed in detail,
they should be understood as previously explained in the "Chapter on the Meaning of Reality.
Furthermore, regarding the five immeasurables, the bodhisattvas—
It is capable of initiating all skillful activities.
What are these five?
First, the realm of sentient beings is immeasurable.
Second, the immeasurability of worlds;
third, the immeasurability of the dharma-realm;
fourth, the immeasurability of the realm of those to be disciplined.
The realms of the immeasurable means of subduing are fivefold.
What is the immeasurability of the realm of sentient beings?
It refers to the sixty-four classes of sentient beings, which are called the realm of sentient beings.
As has already been set forth in detail in the preceding section on the mental ground (*manobhūmi*),
if [worlds] are differentiated according to their individual continuities (*saṃtāna*), they are infinite;
how then can it be said that worlds are immeasurable?
This refers to the fact that in the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, there are immeasurable names, each distinct from the others.
For instance, this world is named Sahā,
and the Brahmā king of this realm is named Sahāpati.
All of this should be fully understood.
How is the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) immeasurable?
It refers to all phenomena that are wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
One should know that such categories of distinctions are immeasurable.
In what way is the realm of those to be disciplined immeasurable?
That is to say, there may be one kind of realm of those to be disciplined,
because all sentient beings who are capable of being disciplined belong to a single category;
or there may be two kinds of realms of those to be disciplined.
First, those bound by all fetters;
second, those not bound by all fetters.
Alternatively, there are three kinds of realms of those to be disciplined.
First, those of dull faculties;
second, those of middling faculties;
third, those of sharp faculties.
There are four types of realms of those to be disciplined:
first, kṣatriyas;
second, brāhmaṇas.
Third, the vaiśyas;
fourth, the śūdras.
Or, there may be five kinds of realms to be disciplined.
1. Those of greedy temperament;
2. those of hateful temperament;
3. those of deluded temperament.
Fourth, those of conduct characterized by pride;
fifth, those of conduct characterized by discursive investigation.
Alternatively, there may be six kinds of realms to be disciplined.
First, householders;
second, those who have left the household life;
third, those who are not yet matured.
Fourth, those already matured;
fifth, those not yet liberated;
sixth, those already liberated.
Alternatively, there are seven kinds of realms of those to be disciplined:
first, the disparaging;
second, the mediocre.
Third, the wisdom that extensively reveals;
fourth, the wisdom that briefly opens up;
fifth, that which manifests what is to be tamed.
Sixth, that which is to be disciplined;
seventh, discipline induced by conditions, meaning that upon encountering such and such conditions,
one undergoes such and such transformations.
Alternatively, there are eight kinds of realms to be disciplined,
namely the eight classes of beings,
from the kṣatriyas up to the Brahmā-kāyikas.
There are nine kinds of realms of those to be disciplined:
first, those transformed by a Tathāgata;
second, those transformed by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Third, those transformed by bodhisattvas;
fourth, those difficult to subdue;
fifth, those easy to subdue.
Sixth, subduing through gentle speech;
seventh, subduing through censure and banishment;
eighth, subduing from afar.
Ninth is the sphere of those who are tamed through proximity.
Alternatively, there are ten spheres of those to be tamed:
first, the hell-beings (*naraka*).
Second, the animals;
third, the world of Yama;
fourth, the devas and humans of the desire realm.
Fifth, those in the intermediate state;
sixth, those with form;
seventh, those without form.
8. Having perception;
9. Without perception;
10. Neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
It is not the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Thus, in brief, there are fifty-five varieties of distinctions.
If one follows the principle of distinctions based on continuity, [there are further subdivisions].
One should know that they are immeasurable.
It is asked: The realm of sentient beings is immeasurable;
the realm of those to be disciplined is immeasurable.
What is the distinction?
Answer: There is no distinction between all sentient beings, whether they abide in the lineage (gotra) or do not abide in the lineage.
Collectively, these are called the "immeasurable realm of sentient beings.
When those who abide in the spiritual lineage (gotra) progress through their respective stages,
this is termed the "immeasurable realm of those to be disciplined" (vineya-dhātu).
What is the immeasurability of the realm of skillful means for subduing?
It is as previously explained;
one should know that within this, there are also immeasurable varieties of distinctions.
Question: For what reason are these five immeasurables taught in this specific order?
Answer: Because Bodhisattvas apply themselves with single-minded diligence to benefiting sentient beings, for this reason the immeasurable realm of sentient beings is taught first.
These sentient beings can be transformed by relying upon specific locations;
therefore, the second [immeasurability] is taught as the immeasurability of worlds.
These sentient beings exist within various realms through diverse dharmas.
Because distinctions between the defiled and the pure can be perceived,
the third teaching states that the dharma-realm is immeasurable; that is,
one contemplates it within this realm of sentient beings as being thus.
There are sentient beings who possess the capacity and great power to be able to ultimately liberate themselves from all suffering;
for this reason, the fourth [section] speaks of the immeasurable realm of those to be disciplined.
It is by means of such skillful methods that all sentient beings are brought to ultimate liberation; therefore,
the fifth [immeasurable] is said to be the immeasurable realm of the means of discipline (*vinaya-upāya-dhātu*).
Therefore, it is said that a bodhisattva is able to initiate all skillful activities through these five kinds of immeasurables.
The Buddhas and bodhisattvas proclaim the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
One should know that there are five kinds of great fruits and benefits. What are these five?
First, when a certain class of sentient beings hears the Buddha or a bodhisattva preaching the true Dharma...
Distant from dust and free from defilement,
the Dharma-eye arises regarding all phenomena.
Second, when a certain class of sentient beings hears the Buddha or Bodhisattvas expound the True Dharma...
Third, there is a class of sentient beings who, upon hearing the Buddha or Bodhisattvas preach the sublime Dharma,
immediately give rise to the mind of right aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Fourth, there is a class of sentient beings who, upon hearing the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas teach the true Dharma,
realize the most supreme Dharma-patience of a Bodhisattva.
Fifth, there is a class of sentient beings who, having heard the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas teach the true Dharma...
To uphold, recite, study, and practice correctly;
and to employ successive skillful means so that the eye of the True Dharma may long endure without perishing—
these are the five kinds.
One should know that this is called the great fruit and benefit of the true Dharma taught by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
because it is associated with these, it is called the Mahāyāna. What are the seven?
First is the greatness of the Dharma.
This refers to the Bodhisattva-piṭaka within the twelvefold division of the teachings,
which encompasses the Vaipulya scriptures.
Second is the greatness of the generation of the mind,
which refers to a certain class of individuals who generate the mind of right aspiration for unsurpassed,
perfect enlightenment. Third is the greatness of resolute conviction.
This refers to a certain class of individuals who give rise to superior faith and understanding regarding the greatness of the Dharma.
Fourth is the greatness of the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*):
this refers to a certain class of individuals who have already transcended the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*).
One enters the stage of pure superior intention.
Fifth is the greatness of the accumulations,
namely, the accumulation of merit and the accumulation of wisdom.
Through the perfection of cultivation, one is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Sixth is the greatness of time,
which refers to the passage of three great incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
One then realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Seventh is the perfect realization of the nature of greatness,
which refers precisely to that realized unsurpassed enlightenment.
Because of this, the very essence of the realization of enlightenment is such that it has no equal, even when compared to the essence of other realized virtues.
How much more so could there be anything that surpasses or exceeds it?
One should know that herein lies the greatness of the dharmas, the greatness of the generation of the mind of awakening,
the greatness of resolute conviction, and the greatness of the superior intention.
Whether it be the greatness of the provisions or the greatness of the time—
these six kinds are all causes for the greatness of perfect realization.
The perfect realization of the great nature is the fruit of the six aforementioned types of great nature.
There are eight factors that can fully encompass all of the Mahāyāna.
First is the teaching of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
second is the teaching that reveals the true meaning of all phenomena within this very Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

Third, within this very Bodhisattva-piṭaka, there are teachings that reveal the inconceivable, most supreme, and vast power of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; fourth, listening to what has been explained above in accordance with the truth.
Fifth, preceded by reflection in accordance with reality,
one proceeds toward a superior intention.
Sixth, preceded by proceeding toward a superior intention...
Entering the characteristics of practice.
Seventh, entering the characteristics of practice as a prerequisite for the fulfillment of the fruits of cultivation.
Eighth, through the very fulfillment of such fruits of cultivation, there is ultimate transcendence.
When a bodhisattva has thus diligently practiced and studied,
they are able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. What kind of bodhisattva,
having diligently practiced and studied, is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
It should be known that there are, in brief, ten types of bodhisattvas:
first, those abiding in the lineage;
second, those who have already entered.
Third, those with unpurified intention;
fourth, those with purified intention;
fifth, those who are immature.
Sixth, those already matured;
seventh, those not yet fallen into certainty;
eighth, those already fallen into certainty.
Ninth, those bound by one more birth;
tenth, those in their final existence while abiding [in the stages].
Herein, it refers to bodhisattvas abiding in the spiritual lineage who resolve their minds and engage in cultivation and study.
It is called "having already entered";
that is, having already entered,
up until one has not yet entered the stage of pure intention (*śuddhāśayabhūmi*).
It is called "impure intention" (*aśuddhāśaya*);
if one has already entered [the stage], it is called "pure intention" (*viśuddhāśaya*),
which is to say, pure intention itself.
Up until one has entered the ultimate stage,
it is called "unmatured";
once one has already entered it, it is called "matured."
From the stage of immaturity up until one has not yet attained entry into the stage of certainty (*niyama*) or the stage of certain practice (*niyata-caryā*),
it is called "uncertain" (*aniyata*).
If one has already attained entry, it is called "certain" (*niyata*).
Within those who have already reached maturity, there are again two types.
The first is those bound by only one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*),
meaning that immediately after this life, they shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Second, abiding in the final existence,
which means abiding in this very life and being able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This is the lineage (*gotra*).
To speak at length, up until the point of being able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—
these ten types of bodhisattvas are able to correctly train in the bodhisattva training;
beyond these, there is nothing further that can be correctly trained in.
If one trains in this way, or trains thus,
one is not like those bodhisattvas who,
above [this level], are able to correctly train in the bodhisattva training.
Regarding what has been thus explained,
all bodhisattvas should know that there are further such categories, which are designated by provisional names according to their qualities without distinction;
namely, they are called *bodhisattva* and *mahāsattva*.
He is the one who has accomplished awakened wisdom, the supreme illumination, the most excellent true son, the supreme sustainer, and the universal conqueror;
he is the most excellent sprout, also named the Valiant and the Most Holy.
He is also called the Caravan Leader, and he is also called the One of Great Renown.
He is also called Compassionate, and he is also called the One of Great Merit.
He is also called Sovereign, and he is also called the Dharma Master.
Thus, one should know that within the boundless and limitless worlds of the ten directions,
there are boundless bodhisattvas who possess internal virtues and each have distinct,
immeasurable, and boundless provisional names and designations.
If there are bodhisattvas who publicly declare themselves to be bodhisattvas,
yet practice incorrectly regarding the bodhisattva training,
you should know that they are called "semblance bodhisattvas."
They are not true bodhisattvas.
If there are bodhisattvas who, being present before others, declare of themselves,
"I am a bodhisattva," and are able to correctly practice the training of a bodhisattva, one should know that they are called true bodhisattvas.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 46;
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 47;
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Order.

In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth part of the *Maulībhūmi*, within the second section on the Yoga of Following the Dharma (*Anudharmayogasthāna*), the first chapter: "Characteristics of Bodhisattvas. What are the true characteristics of bodhisattvas?
The summary verse says:
One should know that for the true Bodhisattvas, there are five aspects:
Their essential nature, their basis, and their fruit; These are sequentially subsumed within the five transformations.
It is said that there are five marks of a true bodhisattva;
one who accomplishes these is counted among the ranks of bodhisattvas.
What are these five?
First is compassion;
second is kind speech;
third is valor.
Fourth, giving with an outstretched hand;
fifth, being able to explain profound meanings and esoteric intentions.
These are the five qualities.
It should be known that each one has five aspects:
first, its intrinsic nature;
second, its basis.
Third is the benefit of the fruit;
fourth is the sequential order;
fifth is the mutual inclusion.
Joy. Second, it resides in right practice.
Regarding that which resides in the mental disposition (*āśaya*):
That is to say, when bodhisattvas possess the intention to benefit and the intention to bring happiness toward all sentient beings,
this is called compassion (*anukampā*).
Regarding correct practice:
it refers to bodhisattvas providing benefit to sentient beings through body and speech,
according to their aspirations and to the extent of their strength and ability.
This is called compassion;
its essential nature is kind speech,
as previously described.
Whether it be words of consolation, words of rejoicing, or words of supreme benefit,
one should know that their essential nature is as previously explained in the "Chapter on the Means of Attraction" (Saṃgrahavastu-paṭala).
This is the essential nature of valor.
This refers to bodhisattvas who are resolute and firm,
free from cowardice or inferiority, and possessed of great power;
it refers to those bodhisattvas whose nature is vast generosity and whose nature is untainted generosity.
This is called the essential nature of open-handed generosity.
It consists of the bodhisattvas’ four kinds of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*),
as well as the wisdom of correct application that is undistortedly induced therein.
This is called the nature of the secret intent regarding the profound meaning and principles.
It should be known that there are, in brief, five bases for a bodhisattva’s compassion. What are these five?
First, sentient beings who suffer;
second, sentient beings who engage in misconduct;
third, sentient beings who are heedless.
Fourth, sentient beings who engage in wrong conduct;
fifth, sentient beings with underlying tendencies of affliction;
and all sentient beings such as those in the hells.
All are subject to painful sensations that arise in continuous succession, pressing and oppressing them;
such beings are called "beings with suffering.
Alternatively, there are beings who, though not necessarily experiencing suffering, [are nonetheless afflicted].
Furthermore, they frequently engage in various misdeeds of body, misdeeds of speech, and misdeeds of mind,
taking pleasure and finding stability in such evils; namely,
those belonging to the classes of non-virtuous practitioners who raise sheep, pigs, chickens, and so forth.
These are called sentient beings of evil conduct.
Alternatively, there are sentient beings who, though not necessarily experiencing suffering nor engaging in evil conduct,
nevertheless remain constantly attached to and enjoy various sensual desires, dwelling therein with pleasure.
They entertain themselves with various performances, songs, dances, laughter, and amorous glances;
such are those who indulge in the objects of sensual desire.
These are called heedless sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, though not necessarily practicing painful asceticism, committing evil, or being heedless,
nevertheless practice various forms of ascetic conduct for the sake of liberation based on false views,
such as renouncing all sensual desires.
Those who have gone forth within a poorly taught Dharma and Vinaya are called beings of wrong conduct. Alternatively, there are beings who,
though not necessarily suffering, and so forth as previously described, do not practice wrong conduct.
Furthermore, there are those who are either fully bound or not fully bound,
being under the latent influence of various afflictions— namely,
ordinary persons who are practicing correctly and virtuously, as well as those in training (*śaikṣa*).
These are called sentient beings with the latent tendencies of afflictions;
these are called the five bases of a bodhisattva’s compassion.
It is by means of these bases and these objects of focus that compassion is set in motion.
Beyond this, there is nothing further or more extensive.
It should be known that the bases for a bodhisattva’s pleasant speech are also fivefold. What are these five?
First, speech that is correct discourse;
second, speech that is correct rejoicing;
third, speech that is correct consolation.
Fourth, speech that is correct, extensive, and unrestrained;
fifth, speech that accords with reality.
Such detailed distinctions should be understood as previously explained in the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*.
These are called the five bases upon which a bodhisattva’s pleasant speech relies.
It is by means of these bases and these objects of focus that pleasant speech proceeds;
beyond these, there is nothing further and nothing more.
It should be understood that there are likewise five bases for a bodhisattva’s valor. What are these five?
They are precisely the five bases for a bodhisattva’s nature of firm strength and endurance, as previously explained in the "Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment" (Bodhipakṣa).
It should be known that these are the five bases of a bodhisattva’s vigor.
It is by means of these bases and these objects of focus that vigor proceeds;
beyond these, there is nothing further and nothing more.
It should be known that the bodhisattva’s open-handed generosity also has five bases. What are the five?
First, giving repeatedly.
Second, giving with joy;
third, giving with earnestness;
fourth, giving without attachment.
The five kinds of supportless giving (*anāśrita-dāna*).
These five types have been explained in detail as previously set forth in the Chapter on Giving (*Dānapaṭala*).
It should be understood that by means of this basis and this object of focus,
the bodhisattva practices the giving of open-handed generosity;
beyond this, there is nothing superior or additional.
It should be known that there are five bases for a bodhisattva’s ability to understand the profound meaning and the underlying intent (saṃdhāya-bhāṣita) [of the teachings].
What are these five? They are as follows:
regarding the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata...
It conforms to the profound and appears as profoundly profound;
it is associated with emptiness and consists of dependent origination.
This should be known as the first basis.
Skillfulness regarding transgressions in the Vinaya and skillfulness regarding restoration to purity should be known as the second basis.
One should know that the establishment and formulation of the characteristics of phenomena without error within the Mātṛkā is called the third basis.
One should know that the fourth basis is that which correctly reveals and removes the meanings of the characteristics of those dharmas whose underlying intentions are difficult to understand;
it concerns the distinctions among the categories of etymological explanations for the dharma and its meaning regarding all phenomena.
It should be known that this is called the fifth basis;
by means of this basis and this object of focus, a bodhisattva is able to understand the profound meanings and intentions and proceed accordingly.
Beyond this, there is nothing superior or additional.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings,
the bodhisattva is first able to sever enmity, harm, and resentment.
Out of compassion, the bodhisattva is able to perform all activities that benefit sentient beings without any timidity or inferiority of mind;
in these applications, they never experience weariness or fatigue.
Dwelling frequently in compassion, one is able to encompass that which is blameless:
the blissful abiding in the present life and the benefit of others;
furthermore, it is as the Blessed One has described regarding the benefits obtained from cultivating loving-kindness.
This refers to such things as not being harmed by poisons, weapons, or staves in one's present body;
all such instances of a bodhisattva’s compassion should be understood in this way.
This is called the fruit and benefit of a bodhisattva’s compassion.
Through a bodhisattva’s pleasant speech,
they eliminate the four faults of speech in the present life.
That is to say: false speech,
divisive speech,
and harsh speech.
And [avoiding] frivolous speech.
By means of this pleasant speech,
one is able to sustain oneself and sustain others in the present life.
It proceeds with peace and security.
Through the bodhisattva’s pleasant speech,
his words will be earnest and solemn in future lives, and his speech will certainly be trusted and accepted.
This is called the fruit and benefit of a bodhisattva’s pleasant speech.
A bodhisattva who is courageous is able,
in this present life, to remain free from all sloth and indolence of mind.
Always joyful, they are able to receive the bodhisattva’s pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*).
Having received it, they never again violate it or succumb to despondency;
they are able to correctly endure and embrace both themselves and others.
Regarding all the activities undertaken by Bodhisattvas in future ages,
his nature is steadfast;
whatever he undertakes to cultivate, he never falters or retreats until it is fully accomplished.
This is called the fruit and benefit of a bodhisattva’s valor.

It should be understood that this is the fruit and benefit obtained by a bodhisattva who, through the generosity of outstretched hands, is able to resolve the profound meanings and secret intentions [of the teachings].
Just as there are distinctions between the power of generosity and the power of wisdom in the "Chapter on Power," one should know that this is called the Bodhisattva’s open-handed generosity,
which is capable of elucidating the profound meanings and esoteric intentions.
There are two kinds of fruits and benefits.
These are called the fivefold fruits and benefits of a bodhisattva.
What is the sequence of these five aspects?
This means that bodhisattvas first cultivate compassion to gather and sustain sentient beings,
regarding them with concern and desiring to bring them benefit;
subsequently, they cultivate kind speech.
For the sake of those sentient beings, one establishes them in wholesome states by leading them out of unwholesome states,
proclaiming the correct principles and providing instruction through guidance;
thereafter, one cultivates heroic diligence.
Regarding those sentient beings who have already entered [the path],
he is able to endure whatever various afflictions and transformations arise from the wrong conduct of those sentient beings.
In order not to abandon those sentient beings who abide in various forms of right or wrong conduct,
these bodhisattvas, having cultivated valor,
bring certain classes of sentient beings to maturity by means of gathering them through material gifts.
Some classes of sentient beings can be brought to maturity through the gathering of them by means of the Dharma;
some classes of sentient beings can be brought to maturity through the gathering of them by means of both material goods and the Dharma.
Therefore, the bodhisattva subsequently practices open-handed generosity and is able to understand the profound meanings and secret intentions [of the teachings].
One should know that these are called the five characteristics of the bodhisattva in their sequential order.
Question: Regarding the five marks and six perfections (pāramitās) of a bodhisattva, by which perfection are they subsumed?
What are these marks?

Answer: It should be understood that a bodhisattva’s compassion is subsumed under the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), and a bodhisattva’s pleasant speech [is subsumed under the perfection of ethical discipline].
Śīla and Prajñā are subsumed under the perfection (pāramitā) of [ethical discipline].
The bodhisattva’s vigor,
progress, and patience are subsumed under the perfection of Prajñā.
Whatever hand-outstretched generosity a bodhisattva possesses should be understood as being subsumed within the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Whatever capacity a bodhisattva possesses for understanding profound meanings and esoteric intentions [should be understood as being subsumed within the perfection of wisdom].
These are subsumed within dhyāna and prajñā-pāramitā.
Thus, one should know that each of these five characteristics of a true bodhisattva has five further aspects.
That is to say: intrinsic nature, basis,
and fruit-benefit.
The sequence and the mutual inclusion [of these factors] have already been analyzed in detail; they should be understood as they truly are.

Chapter Two: The Section on the Classification of the Two Types of Bodhisattvas—Lay and Ordained—within the Second Yoga Station of "Holding and Following the Dharma" in the Fifteenth "Bodhisattva Stage" of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, Part Two.
There are several dharmas which, when correctly practiced and studied, lead to the swift realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. The summary verse (*udāna*) says:
The two categories of bodhisattvas First, the excellent cultivation of their activities.
Skillfulness in benefiting others, and dedication as the final one—
these are briefly the four dharmas that distinguish the various modes of engagement for bodhisattvas, whether belonging to the class of householders or the class of renunciants.
It should be known that these four things cause both the lay and ordained bodhisattvas, who practice with right diligence, to swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
What are the four?
First, the excellent cultivation of one's undertakings;
second, skill in means;
third, benefiting others.
Fourth is non-erroneous dedication.
How does a bodhisattva skillfully cultivate their activities?
It refers to how bodhisattvas [apply themselves] to the six pāramitās.
Resolute cultivation, thorough cultivation,
constant cultivation, and faultless cultivation.
How does a bodhisattva engage in the resolute cultivation of the perfection of generosity?
This refers to when bodhisattvas possess various material goods and teachings suitable for giving,
and toward all supplicants who are currently present before them— whether they have been kind or unkind, or whether they possess virtue or faults— they make no distinction whatsoever.
One must certainly give it away,
whether to humans or non-humans, to śramaṇas or brahmins,
or to anyone else in the world who acts in accordance with the Dharma.
It can cause the mind of generosity to waver.
How does a bodhisattva practice the perfection of generosity with thorough and detailed application?
It means that bodhisattvas currently possess various kinds of material wealth and dharmas that can be given as gifts.
When those who beg and seek are present before him,
he gives everything away; there is not the slightest thing that he cannot relinquish to sentient beings,
even his own internal body and life.
How much more so regarding external objects?
How does a bodhisattva constantly practice the perfection of generosity?
It is said that regarding the cultivation of giving, bodhisattvas...
Without weariness,
at all times and continuously,
he bestows whatever he obtains as soon as it is acquired, without any stinginess.
How does a bodhisattva engage in the faultless practice of the perfection of giving?
It means that bodhisattvas distance themselves from all defiled forms of giving as previously described in the chapter on giving.
The remaining practice is giving that is free from affliction;
in this way, the bodhisattva is able to skillfully cultivate the perfection of giving.
Just as one is able to practice the perfection of generosity well,
so too should it be understood that this applies accordingly to the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
This is called the bodhisattva’s definitive practice, thorough practice,
constant practice, and faultless practice regarding the six perfections by means of these four modes of conduct.
What is the bodhisattva’s skill in means?
It should be known that such skill in means is, in brief, of ten kinds. What are these ten?
First, skillful means for removing the anger and afflictions of sentient beings who hate and turn their backs on the holy teachings;
second, skillful means for causing sentient beings dwelling in the intermediate state to enter [the path].
Third, skillful means for bringing to maturity those who have already entered [the path].
Fourth, skillful means for enabling those who have reached maturity to attain liberation.
Fifth, skillful means regarding all various heterodox doctrines in the world;
sixth, skillful means regarding the correct observation of the acceptance and violation of the bodhisattva’s code of ethical discipline.
Seventh, skill in means regarding all correct aspirations;
eighth, skill in means regarding the Śrāvaka vehicle;
ninth, skill in means regarding the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
Tenth is skill in means regarding the Great Vehicle.
All such skills in means have already been extensively analyzed in their respective places within this very *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, as previously described.
It should be understood accordingly.
In this way, these ten kinds of skillful means possessed by bodhisattvas are able to perform five tasks;
that is to say, by means of the first four kinds of skillful means.
It enables all bodhisattvas to correctly establish those beings they seek to convert in their own welfare,
through skillful means regarding all the various worldly doctrines.
It enables all bodhisattvas to skillfully refute all heterodox arguments;
through the correct observation of skillful means regarding the acceptance and violation of the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline.
He causes all bodhisattvas not to transgress what should not be transgressed;
having transgressed, they swiftly repent and eliminate it according to the Dharma,
regarding the pure ethical discipline of the vows received by well-purified bodhisattvas.
One is able to skillfully polish and refine [the mind] through the skillful means of right aspiration,
enabling all bodhisattvas to realize the fulfillment of all desired aims and purposes in the future.
By means of skillful means regarding the three vehicles,

[the Buddha] causes bodhisattvas to teach the Dharma to sentient beings in accordance with their respective lineages, faculties, and superior dispositions, and to speak in conformity with correct reasoning.
These are called the ten kinds of skillful means that enable bodhisattvas to perform five tasks. By means of these five tasks,
bodhisattvas are able to bring all matters and purposes pertaining to both the present life and future lives to ultimate fulfillment.
How does a bodhisattva benefit others?
It is by relying on the four means of attraction—
namely, generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.
It is able to provide benefit for a portion of sentient beings;
it is able to provide happiness for a portion of sentient beings;
and it is able to provide both benefit and happiness for a portion of the sentient beings to be converted.
This is a brief explanation of all the ways in which a bodhisattva benefits others;
the detailed explanation is as previously stated in the chapter on the Benefit of Self and Others,
where its characteristics should be understood.
What is the non-erroneous dedication of a bodhisattva?
It refers to all the roots of virtue accumulated by bodhisattvas through the three gates,
which constitute the well-cultivated performance of deeds.
Through skillful means, they benefit others,
gathering all beings of the past, future, and present; with a single, pure,
and wondrously serene faith, they embrace them all.
They dedicate [these roots] toward seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
they never use these accumulated roots of goodness to seek any other worldly fruits or maturations,
except for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Whatever dharmas for training have been taught by the Blessed One for bodhisattvas, whether belonging to the class of householders or the class of those who have gone forth,
one should know that they are all subsumed within these four.
That is to say: skillfully cultivating one's activities;
benefiting others through skillful means;
and dedicating [merit] without error.
Therefore, those bodhisattvas who thus skillfully cultivate their activities and employ skillful means to benefit others, and who correctly dedicate [their merit],
draw near to and approach unsurpassed enlightenment, which is difficult to attain and difficult to realize.
It should be known that all bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present—
whether belonging to the class of householders or the class of those who have gone forth—
who have diligently practiced and studied, and who have realized, will realize, or are currently realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
All [these qualities] arise from these four dharmas;
beyond these, there is nothing superior or additional.
Furthermore, whether Bodhisattvas belong to the class of householders or the class of those who have gone forth, [they rely on these].
Although they may equally apply themselves with right effort to train in these four dharmas,
the one who has gone forth is vastly different from and vastly superior to the one who remains at home.
Why is this so? It should be known that all bodhisattvas who have left the household life have attained liberation from the faults of being bound by their parents, wives, children, and relatives.
A householder bodhisattva is not like this.
Furthermore, all monastic bodhisattvas,
regarding the gathering together of parents and relatives...
Those who engage in farming, commerce, trade, service to the king, and other such various arduous tasks and urgent affairs of distress shall all attain liberation;
for a bodhisattva living at home, it is not thus.
Furthermore, all ordained bodhisattvas are consistently able to practice the "linked chain" brahmacarya,
whereas lay bodhisattvas are not so.
Furthermore, all bodhisattvas who have gone forth quickly realize supernormal wisdom regarding all factors conducive to enlightenment,
in accordance with whichever various wholesome dharmas they practice and cultivate.
All are able to reach the ultimate goal with great swiftness;
a lay bodhisattva is not like this.
Furthermore, all bodhisattvas who have gone forth...
Abiding in the definitive and pure discipline,
whatever words they utter are faithfully accepted by all;
a bodhisattva living at home is not like this.
One should know that all such immeasurable categories of wholesome dharmas make the renunciant bodhisattva vastly superior and far more exalted than the householder.

Chapter 3: Higher Resolve (Adhyāśaya), from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth part of the *Yogācārabhūmi*. Second Section: The Stage of Yoga Concerning the Adherence to the Dharma (*Anudharmayogasthāna*). Chapter Three: Higher Resolve. What is the higher resolve (*adhyāśaya*) of a bodhisattva?
The summary verse says:
The wise one has seven aspects of compassion for sentient beings, fifteen superior intentions, and performs ten deeds; this should be known.
This means that bodhisattvas give rise to compassion toward all sentient beings through seven aspects within their profound resolve;
it is because bodhisattvas are endowed with such compassion.
It is called "good intention" and "excellent intention.
What are the seven aspects of compassion?
First is fearlessness compassion.
Second is compassion that accords with reality;
third is tireless compassion;
fourth is compassion free from seeking.
Fifth is undefiled compassion;
sixth is vast compassion;
seventh is impartial compassion.
That is to say, bodhisattvas, out of compassion for sentient beings and not out of fear,
engage in physical, verbal, and mental actions that are compliant with their needs,
which are appropriate to their minds and bring them benefit and happiness.
This is called the fearless compassion of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, the compassion that bodhisattvas extend toward sentient beings does not proceed in an irrational manner.
That is to say, one never encourages sentient beings by means of what is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya,
contrary to the conduct of the virtuous, or through improper means;
this is called the bodhisattva’s compassion that accords with reason.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas, out of such compassion for all sentient beings,
initiate all manner of beneficial activities as appropriate to their needs, never becoming weary or disheartened.
This is called the tireless compassion of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings,
bodhisattvas give rise to compassion spontaneously and act for their benefit without waiting for a request.
This is called the bodhisattva’s compassion that is free from seeking.
Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings,
the bodhisattvas give rise to compassion with a mind free from attachment.
This refers to benefiting others without seeking gratitude or recompense,
nor hoping for the ripening of desirable fruits in the future;
this is called the bodhisattva’s undefiled compassion.
This is also called the bodhisattva’s objectless compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*).
Furthermore, it is the compassion that bodhisattvas arouse toward all sentient beings.
It is exclusively vast and not narrow.
To say it is "vast" means that,
with respect to all sentient beings, it is...
Even when encountering all manner of harmful circumstances, they do not abandon [their resolve];
rather than causing harm through evil desires, the bodhisattva would sooner suffer what is unpleasant themselves.
This is called the vast compassion of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, the compassion of bodhisattvas, which is endowed with such characteristics and such qualities,
is entirely equal and impartial toward all classes of sentient beings.
It is without limitation within the realm of sentient beings;
this is called the bodhisattva’s impartial compassion.
The bodhisattva is endowed with these seven aspects of compassionate concern.
It is called "good intention" and "excellent intention.
It should be understood that herein, it is the resolute conviction regarding all the Buddha-dharmas, preceded by pure faith and preceded by the discernment of phenomena (dharmapravicaya).
This seal is established;
this is called the bodhisattva’s resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*).
Such is the bodhisattva’s resolute intention.
It should be known that, briefly stated, there are fifteen kinds.
What are these fifteen?
First, the supreme intention (*adhyāśaya*).
Second, the intention of restraint;
third, the intention of the perfections;
fourth, the intention of the ultimate meaning.
Fifth, the intention of power;
sixth, the intention of benefit;
seventh, the intention of happiness.
8. The intention of liberation;
9. The firm intention;
10. The non-deceptive intention.
11. Impure intention; 12. Pure intention;
13. Thoroughly pure intention.
Fourteenth is the intention of subduing;
fifteenth is the simultaneous intention,
which refers to how bodhisattvas regard the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha as the most supreme and true.
To give rise to a superior intention—
this is called the supreme intention of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, regarding the pure ethical discipline that bodhisattvas have undertaken and maintain:
To give rise to a superior intention—
this is called the bodhisattva’s intention of restraint.
Furthermore, regarding the generosity, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom that bodhisattvas cultivate and realize:
The arousal of the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) is called the bodhisattva’s intention regarding the perfections (*pāramitā*). Furthermore,

regarding the profound ultimate reality— the true suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena— which consists in the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), the bodhisattvas...
To give rise to a superior intention—
this is called the bodhisattva’s intention regarding the ultimate meaning.
Furthermore, regarding the inconceivable power of supernatural transformations or innate power belonging to Buddhas and bodhisattvas, [the bodhisattva gives rise to a superior intention].
To give rise to a superior intention—
this is called the bodhisattva’s intention of majestic power.
Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings, the bodhisattvas...
Desiring to bestow upon them the wholesome dharmas—
this is called the bodhisattva’s altruistic intention (*hitāśaya*).
Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings, the bodhisattvas...
Desiring to benefit them, he bestows [these things] upon them;
this is called the bodhisattva’s intention of providing happiness (*sukhāśaya*).
Furthermore, regarding such sentient beings, the bodhisattvas possess a mind free from attachment.
Furthermore, his mind is unattached to the desirable maturation in the future;
this is called the bodhisattva’s intention of liberation (*vimokṣāśaya*).
Moreover, regarding unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, the bodhisattvas—
Their mind is focused and remains entirely unchanging;
this is called the bodhisattva’s firm intention (*āśaya*).
Furthermore, it refers to the bodhisattvas’ skillful means for benefiting all sentient beings.
The resolute belief that accompanies non-erroneous wisdom regarding the means for realizing great enlightenment is called the bodhisattva’s intention free from falsehood.
Furthermore, it includes all superior intentions belonging to the bodhisattva stage of conduct through resolute belief.
This is called the impure intention of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, all the superior intentions (adhyāśaya) of bodhisattvas from the stage of pure superior intention up to the stage of certain conduct.
This is called the bodhisattva’s pure intention (*śuddhāśaya*).
Furthermore, all the superior intentions (*adhyāśaya*) of bodhisattvas who have reached the ultimate stage.
This is called the bodhisattva’s well-purified intention.
Furthermore, that which is the bodhisattva’s unpurified intention is termed the intention that should be disciplined.
Because this intentionality should be investigated through reflection,
and because the pure intentionality and the thoroughly purified intentionality of all bodhisattvas are what is termed "simultaneous intentionality."
Because this nature of intentionality is accomplished and because it is well-established within its basis,
such are the fifteen sublime and virtuous superior intentions (*adhyāśaya*) of a bodhisattva.
It follows all stages;
in brief, it is able to perform ten functions.
What are these ten?
They are the supreme aspirations of bodhisattvas,
which enable them to perform every kind of most excellent worship toward the Three Jewels.
It is the foremost among all the accumulations for enlightenment.
Furthermore, it is the bodhisattvas' intention of restraint that enables them to maintain the pure ethical discipline they have undertaken.
Even when faced with life-threatening circumstances, they do not intentionally commit any transgression;
should they happen to commit one, they swiftly repent and eliminate it.
Furthermore, this is the bodhisattva’s resolute intention regarding the pāramitās.
They are able to constantly and diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas, abiding in heedfulness,
and always dwelling in the most excellent state of heedfulness.
Furthermore, this is the bodhisattvas’ intentionality regarding the true meaning.
They are able to circulate through birth and death for the sake of sentient beings with an undefiled mind,
yet they do not abandon their superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) for nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, this is the bodhisattvas’ intention of power (*prabhāva-adhyāśaya*).
One is able to experience the pure, sublime flavor of the Dharma within the Noble Teaching;
furthermore, one is able to give rise to firm resolve regarding cultivation, taking delight in dwelling in it frequently,
rather than being satisfied merely with hearing and reflection.
Furthermore, there are the bodhisattvas’ intention to benefit,
the intention for happiness,
and the intention for liberation.
They are able to diligently cultivate all activities that benefit sentient beings;
though they constantly practice them, they never grow weary.
Furthermore, this is the firm resolve of the bodhisattvas.
They are able to initiate and abide in various forms of blazing diligence and vast diligence,
characterized by unslackening application and uninterrupted application;
furthermore, these bodhisattvas possess an intention free from falsehood.
One is able to swiftly realize the supernormal knowledges regarding those various wholesome dharmas that have been induced,
and does not give rise to complacency upon attaining a minor, inferior, or feeble distinction.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas should cultivate the intention of discipline (*vinayāśaya*),
which can induce the co-emergent intention (*sahajāśaya*).
Moreover, bodhisattvas possess this co-emergent intention.
They will be able to swiftly attain and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and they will be able to bring about all manner of benefit, welfare, and happiness for gods and humans.
The intention that should be disciplined is the impure intention and the co-emergent intention.
This refers to the pure intention (*śuddhāśaya*).
Because it is a thoroughly purified intention (*suviśuddhāśaya*), it is not mentioned separately.
It is that which belongs to all bodhisattvas, O Bhagavat.
One should know that whatever various superior intentions (adhyāśaya) are proclaimed, established, and revealed in those various places,
they are all subsumed within these fifteen types of intention.
Therefore, those bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present who possess sublime and noble intentions have realized,
will realize, and are currently realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
All [these] arise from these fifteen types of intentionality as they have been described;
beyond these, there is nothing further and nothing more.
Such are the fifteen intentions of a bodhisattva.
One is able to attain the benefit of the fruit of supreme enlightenment.
Therefore, by relying on this intentionality (*āśaya*), a bodhisattva swiftly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

[The *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth part of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in the section on the "Abodes" (*vihāra*) within the second "Yoga Station of Following the Dharma" (*anudharmayogasthāna*): The Fourth Chapter on Abiding, Part One. Thus begins, starting from the endowment with the spiritual lineage (*gotrasampad*).
To speak at length, up to and including the training of a bodhisattva as it has been described,
they apply themselves with right diligence to train therein,
and regarding the various characteristics of a bodhisattva as they have been described.
They appear correctly and equally;
they apply themselves with right diligence to the training in the various stages of the bodhisattva path.
Regarding the bodhisattva’s intentionality as it has been described,
the assembly of bodhisattvas who are able to purify and cultivate it briefly consists of twelve kinds of bodhisattva abodes.
By means of these twelve abodes of a bodhisattva,
all the abodes of all bodhisattvas are universally subsumed,
and all the practices of all bodhisattvas are universally subsumed.
Furthermore, there is the thirteenth dwelling of the Tathāgata.
Because of this dwelling, one manifests the vast awakening of great bodhi;
it is called the Unsurpassed Dwelling.
What are the twelve stages (*vihāra*) of a bodhisattva?
The summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
Lineage (*gotra*), practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā*), supreme joy (*pramuditā*), and superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*).
The three types of wisdom of the higher mind,
the signless with effort and the signless without effort,
as well as the unimpeded analytical knowledges and the supreme Bodhisattva dwelling, and the most ultimate Tathāgata dwelling.
That is to say: the bodhisattva's stage of the lineage,
the stage of practice through resolute belief,
and the stage of supreme joy.
The stage of superior morality,
the stage of superior mind,
and the stage of superior wisdom.
Furthermore, there are three kinds:
first, the dwelling of superior wisdom associated with the factors of enlightenment;
second, the dwelling of superior wisdom associated with the truths.
The third is the dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the cessation of the flow of dependent origination.
This refers to how bodhisattvas, as they truly understand, realize both the reality that observes and the reality that is observed.
Furthermore, among all sentient beings who abide in reality,
it is through the absence of wisdom that they undergo the circulation of manifold sufferings,
and it is through the presence of wisdom that these manifold sufferings are brought to cessation.
Thus, because the bodhisattva observes by means of wisdom through these three gateways,
there are three types of abidings in superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā-vihāra*):

the signless abiding that proceeds via a path involving application and effort (*sābhisaṃskāra-sābhyāsa-avicchinna-mārga-pravṛtti-nimitta*) and the signless abiding that proceeds via a path free from application and effort (*anabhisaṃskāra-anabhyāsa-avicchinna-mārga-pravṛtti-nimitta*), as well as the abiding in the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid-vihāra*) and the supreme, perfected bodhisattva abiding (*parama-pariniṣpanna-bodhisattva-vihāra*).
These are called the twelve kinds of bodhisattva abodes.
In this way, these twelve kinds of bodhisattva abodes universally encompass all the abodes of bodhisattvas.
It universally encompasses all bodhisattva practices.
As for the "Tathāgata-abiding," it refers to that which transcends all bodhisattva abidings.
One dwells in the manifest, perfect awakening to great enlightenment (*abhisambodhi-mahābodhi*). Among these,
the final Tathāgata-dwelling is established in the final chapter on the establishment [of the stages] within the subsequent section on ultimate yoga (*paryanta-yoga-sthāna*).
I shall now fully expound them.
