I will now explain the twelve stages of a bodhisattva exactly as they have been established.
The bodhisattva abides in the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotrastha*).
This means that when all bodhisattvas abide in the stage of the spiritual lineage,
their very nature is inherently virtuous and noble.
The bodhisattva’s qualities naturally perfected by nature and the manifold wholesome dharmas appropriate for a bodhisattva are also manifest in their active engagement;
through the impelling power of their innate benevolence and virtue, they are led toward the practice of the wholesome.
It is not through deliberation that there is restraint or protection; rather,
when bodhisattvas abide in the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-vihāra*),
they maintain the seeds of all Buddha-dharmas.
Within their own being and within their basis,
they already possess in full all the seeds of all the Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, these bodhisattvas abide in the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotrastha*).
By nature, they are free from coarse defilements and are unable to manifest the higher fetters of affliction;
it is due to these fetters that [such states arise].
They may commit an act of immediate retribution or sever their roots of goodness;
these various characteristics of abiding in the lineage,
as explained in the "Chapter on Lineage," apply here within this stage of the bodhisattva’s abiding in the lineage.
This should also be explained in detail and understood as it truly is;
this is called the bodhisattva’s dwelling in the spiritual lineage (*gotra-vihāra*).
What is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*)?

It should be understood that all bodhisattva practices undertaken by bodhisattvas from the first generation of the mind of awakening until they have not yet attained pure intention are termed the stage of practice through resolute belief.
Furthermore, while in the stage of the lineage (*gotra-vihāra*),
for the remaining eleven bodhisattva stages and the stage of the Tathāgata,
there is only the operation of the cause.
One embraces those causes,
yet regarding all other bodhisattva dwellings,
one has not yet set out toward them, nor attained them, nor purified them.
How much more so for the Tathāgata’s dwelling!
If a bodhisattva in the dwelling of practice through resolute belief [is compared] to all other bodhisattva dwellings and the Tathāgata’s dwelling...
All are termed "those who have set out," yet they have not yet attained or purified [the path]; that is,
while abiding in this very stage of practice through resolute belief.
It is also called "setting forth," and it is also called "attainment. One practices correct conduct in order to bring about purification.
Once the stage of dwelling in conduct through resolute belief has been purified, [one proceeds further].
Having previously set out in the stage of Extreme Joy,
one now attains it and practices correctly to purify it;
once the stage of Extreme Joy has been purified, [one proceeds further].
Having previously set out toward the stage of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-vihāra*),
one now attains it and practices correctly to purify it;
thus it is explained in detail, progressing successively until the supreme and perfected bodhisattva stage.
Once this supreme fulfillment of the bodhisattva stage has been purified,
one should know that immediately thereafter, the Tathāgata stage— which was previously set out for—
will now be attained and purified all at once.
This is the dwelling of the Tathāgata.
One should know that within the dwellings of a bodhisattva, there are such distinctions as these.
What is the bodhisattva’s dwelling of extreme joy?
This refers to the bodhisattvas’ dwelling in the purified superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).
What is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*)?
It is that which has the bodhisattvas’ purified superior intention as its condition.
He dwells in accordance with the nature-precepts he has attained.
What is the bodhisattva’s dwelling of the higher mind?
It is that which takes as its condition the purification of the bodhisattva’s dwelling of the higher ethical discipline.
Regarding the dwelling in the worldly meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), absorptions (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*) that have been attained:
what is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the factors of enlightenment?
It refers to those bodhisattvas who rely upon a meditative absorption that serves as the basis for pure worldly knowledge.
For the sake of awakening to the truths, he dwells in the sublime discernment of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, such as the foundations of mindfulness.
What is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the truths?
This refers to how bodhisattvas, relying upon the discernment of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*),
abide in the realization of the truths exactly as they are.
What is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in superior wisdom associated with the cessation of the forward progression of dependent origination?
This means that by the superior power of the bodhisattvas’ ability to awaken to the truths,
they analytically discern and reveal how suffering and its cause arise due to ignorance,
and they analytically discern and reveal how suffering and its cause cease and abide due to wisdom.
What is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in the signless with application and effort?
It refers to the fact that, by the superior power of those very three dwellings in higher wisdom, the bodhisattvas [abide therein].
With application and effort, without deficiency or interruption,
one dwells in the cultivation of non-conceptual wisdom regarding the suchness of all phenomena.
What is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in signlessness that is without application and without effort?
It refers to the dwelling in which the bodhisattvas, having extensively cultivated the aforementioned dwelling in signlessness,
spontaneously and naturally proceed with a path that functions without deficiency or interruption.
What is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)?
It refers to the bodhisattvas taking as their basis the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of well-purified and immovable wisdom.
Having attained vast wisdom, he teaches the Dharma to others;
relying on the unsurpassed, he abides in sublime discernment regarding the various gateways, meanings, intentions, and etymological distinctions of all phenomena.
What is the bodhisattva’s supreme fulfillment of the bodhisattva dwelling?
It refers to those bodhisattvas who, by abiding in this,
have reached the ultimate consummation of the bodhisattva path.
They have already received the great Dharma consecration regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
they are either bound to only one more birth or reside in their final existence.
Immediately following this stage, at that very moment, one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and is able to perform all the deeds of a Buddha.
Furthermore, regarding the stage of the bodhisattva’s practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*):
Regarding the cultivation of a bodhisattva,
their practice is narrow,
their practice is deficient, and their practice is unstable.
There is regression from what has been attained;
the stage of extreme joy involves vast cultivation of the bodhisattva's practices.
His actions are flawless and his actions are resolute;
whatever he attains, he never regresses from,
just as in the Stage of Utmost Joy.
It should be understood that the same applies even up to the three types of abidings in higher wisdom.
From the initial abiding in the signless up to the supreme, perfected bodhisattva abiding.
Regarding the cultivation of a bodhisattva,
what is performed is immeasurable, what is performed is flawless, and what is performed is definitive;
according to what is attained, there is ultimately no regression.
Furthermore, it should be known that when Bodhisattvas dwelling in the stage of practice through resolute belief engage in the signless cultivation of a Bodhisattva,
they are setting out for the stage of extreme joy.
The stage of superior ethical discipline,
the stage of superior mind,
and the stage of superior wisdom.
Regarding the bodhisattva’s cultivation of signlessness,
one should know that the first stage of signlessness is attained through this cultivation of signlessness by the bodhisattva.
One should know that this is the perfect realization of the second stage, the signless abiding;
regarding the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the signless,
one should know it as the pure and unimpeded abiding of analytical knowledge.
One should know that the bodhisattva dwelling in the supreme fulfillment receives the fruit of the bodhisattva’s practice of signlessness.
Question: When a bodhisattva abiding in the stage of practice through resolute belief (adhimukti-caryā-vihāra) proceeds, what conduct, what marks, and what signs should be known?
Answer: When a bodhisattva abiding in the stage of practice through resolute belief proceeds, [the following should be known].
The power of analytical reflection is superior;
regarding the various applications performed by bodhisattvas,
one must repeatedly analyze them with discerning wisdom before being able to cultivate and carry them out.
He has not yet been able to accomplish his tasks according to his own will;
he has not yet attained the firm, continuous, and non-regressive superior cultivation of a bodhisattva as it truly is;

nor has he attained the various unimpeded superior resolves, supernormal powers, liberations, meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that are the fruits of such superior cultivation.
Nor has he yet attained it;
he has not yet transcended the five kinds of fear,
namely, the fear of being unable to make a living.
Fear of ill repute,
fear of death,
and fear of the miserable realms.
Feeling timid and fearful when among the multitude,
one must exert oneself through diligent reflection before being able to perform the beneficial activities for sentient beings that ought to be done.
Unable to act with spontaneous compassion and affection,
they may at times engage in unwholesome conduct toward sentient beings through body, speech, or mind.
At times, one gives rise to craving and attachment toward various objects;
at other times, one manifests stinginess regarding the necessities of life.
They practice by placing faith in other Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
yet have not yet attained internal realization of the truth for themselves;
that is, regarding the Tathāgata, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha.
Whether it be the ultimate reality, the affairs of sentient beings,
the supernatural power and majesty of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
or cause and effect.
Either one should attain the meaning,
or attain the skillful means,
or in all that one practices, follow the faith of others.
One achieves a limited wisdom derived from hearing and a limited wisdom derived from reflection, rather than an immeasurable one;
furthermore, one may occasionally forget even this,
possessing the quality of forgetfulness and achieving the bodhisattva’s practice of painful progress with sluggish superknowledge.
They lack intense aspiration for great enlightenment,
they lack fervent diligence,
and they lack profound, firm, and pure faith.
In those three instances, there is a loss of mindfulness:
first, regarding objects— whether they be agreeable or disagreeable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena—
at times his mind becomes inverted and he loses right mindfulness.
Second, having been born into various successive bodies,
one forgets one's previous lives once reborn;
third, regarding the various dharmas received and upheld, which were performed long ago or spoken long ago.
At times, there may be forgetfulness;
thus, there is loss of mindfulness regarding these three points.
At other times, one is fully endowed with intelligence.
They are able to receive and uphold those various teachings,
and they are capable of penetrating their underlying principles;
yet at other times, it may not be so.
At times he possesses full mindfulness,
while at other times he becomes subject to forgetfulness; thus,
regarding sentient beings, he is unable to understand the skillful means for taming them as they truly are.
Furthermore, regarding their own Buddha-dharma, they have not yet attained mastery in the skillful means for realizing it as it truly is;
nevertheless, they proceed to teach, instruct, admonish, and exhort others by preaching the Dharma to them.
Exerting oneself in what has become habitual leads to a lack of knowledge as it truly is;
sometimes it is spent in vain, and sometimes it is not spent in vain,
like shooting arrows in the dark— sometimes hitting the mark and sometimes missing it.
Because they act according to their whims:
at one time, although they have already generated the mind directed toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), they subsequently regress and abandon it;
or at another time, they discard the pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) previously undertaken by a bodhisattva and are unable to train in it.
At times, although they diligently cultivate activities for the benefit of sentient beings,
because weariness arises in the interim,
they once again abandon those activities for the benefit of sentient beings.
By way of intention, one desires one's own happiness;
by way of discernment, one desires the happiness of others.
Regarding all transgressions committed by bodhisattvas:
For the most part, there is thorough knowledge but not complete enumeration-knowledge;
there is no remainder-free, permanent abandonment,
because of the frequent recurrence of transgressions.
At times, they may have their [entrustment] in the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and the Dharma-vinaya seized by others;
or at times, upon hearing the teaching of the profound and vast Dharma, they may give rise to fear and trepidation.
His mind is wavering, hesitant, and full of doubt;
he remains far removed from the actualization of great compassion toward all sentient beings,
and he provides only a minimal measure of benefit and happiness to them.
It is not yet vast, nor is it immeasurable.
Regarding all the perfections of the bodhisattva training as described above,
one has not yet studied them universally.
He has not yet fully accomplished all the aforementioned marks of a bodhisattva in their entirety,
nor has he yet manifested equally all the aforementioned two-fold correct applications of a bodhisattva in their entirety.
Regarding the bodhisattva’s intention as described above,
it is still not yet purified;
consequently, he considers himself far removed from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
They have not yet established a firm and deep resolute intention toward nirvāṇa,
as they have toward the long-term wandering in saṃsāra;
nor [have they established it] toward the blazing, immovable, and sublime factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
They have not yet attained accomplishment.

Such categories as these should be understood as the characteristics and signs of the conduct of a bodhisattva when abiding in the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*).
This refers to the time when those bodhisattvas are abiding in the stage of practice through resolute belief and are operating within the lower degree of patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*).
Regarding the various modes and characteristics of the formations as described above,
one should know that when the superior degree of medium patience (*madhyādhimātra-kṣānti*) proceeds,
these same modes and characteristics of the formations as described above [apply].
It should be understood that when the medium-grade superior patience (*madhyamā-adhimātrā-kṣānti*) arises,
it is as previously described;
it should be understood that its nature is subtle and slight in the case of the inferior grade (*mṛdu*).
As one progresses through this stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*),
one is able to gradually bring about the permanent and complete eradication, without remainder, of all the aforementioned modes, characteristics, and signs of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Immediately following this, one should know that the bodhisattva enters the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*).
Within this Stage of Extreme Joy, through the attainment of skillful means,
all those dharmas described in the Stage of Practice through Devotion (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*) are found to be non-existent.
All dharmas of the white class that are the opposite of those [defilements] become fully manifest.
Because bodhisattvas accomplish this,
they further receive the name "pure superior intention" (*śuddhāśaya*).
When a bodhisattva abiding in the stage of practice through resolute belief undergoes this transformation,
although there exists a small portion of progressively purified resolute belief consisting of weak, medium, and superior grades of skillful means,
it is not yet called "pure resolute intention" (*śuddhāśaya*).
Why is this? Because by means of this resolute conviction,
it proceeds while being defiled by those various secondary afflictions.
When a bodhisattva dwells in the stage of "Utmost Joy," all forms of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) are present,
and all secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are forever severed;
free from secondary afflictions, pure resolute conviction proceeds.
Question: When a bodhisattva transitions into the stage of "Supreme Joy," what conduct, what marks, and what signs should be known?
Answer: When bodhisattvas enter the stage of Supreme Joy from the stage of practice through resolute belief, [the following should be known].
Previously, regarding unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,
the bodhisattva’s great vow had not yet fully mastered the intrinsic nature of enlightenment.
Not having yet fully mastered the skillful means of enlightenment,
they mostly proceed in accordance with external conditions;
because they have not definitively resolved to abandon those [conditions], they give rise to six aspects.
The nature of internal realization through the firm determination for new goodness;
the great vows of the bodhisattva that transcend all other pure and white vows;
and the incomparable, unique fruit.
This world transcends the sphere of all worldly realms because it accords with the salvation of all sentient beings from suffering; thus,
it is not shared by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Although this vow is generated in a single moment,
the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is such that it can spontaneously yield the immeasurable, desirable fruits of a bodhisattva’s pure qualities (*śukladharma*).
Furthermore, once this great vow has been attained, its intrinsic nature is unchanging and inexhaustible.
There is no other cause or condition by which their regression, transformation, or alteration could be found;
furthermore, this supreme portion falls within the final limit of great enlightenment.
Such is the well-determined vow of the bodhisattva.
It is also called "arousing the mind.
Furthermore, this very arousal of the mind by a bodhisattva should be understood briefly through four aspects.
What are these four?
First, what are the characteristics of the bodhisattva who generates the resolve;
second, what is the object of focus for that generated resolve?
Third, what are the manifestations, what are the characteristics,
and from what intrinsic nature does the arousal of the mind arise?
Fourth, what are the benefits of generating the mind?
Through these four aspects, one should understand the generation of the mind by Bodhisattvas;
that is to say, the dwelling of Bodhisattvas in the stage of practice through resolute belief.
Having already well accumulated all roots of goodness and having correctly transcended the bodhisattva practices,
this is a brief description of the characteristics of the bodhisattva’s production of the thought of enlightenment.
Furthermore, all bodhisattvas take as their object the future, unerring, and rapid fulfillment of all the accumulations for enlightenment,
as well as the fulfillment of all bodhisattva activities for the benefit of sentient beings.
The complete perfection of all aspects of all Buddha-dharmas of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
the complete perfection of all the activities performed by the Buddhas—
in brief, such is the object of focus for generating this resolve.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas unerringly and swiftly initiate all the accumulations for enlightenment,
acting in accordance with everything that a bodhisattva does for the sake of sentient beings.
One accordingly attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
as well as the untaught, spontaneous,
and sublime wisdom that accords with the performance of all types of Buddha-activities in every respect.
They accord with a vast and expansive aspirational mind.
Furthermore, once these bodhisattvas have generated this mind,
they transcend the stage of ordinary beings among bodhisattvas.
They enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth;
they are born into the family of the Tathāgatas as true sons of the Buddha;
and they are destined to proceed toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
They will certainly succeed to the noble lineage of the Tathāgata;
furthermore, they will correctly attain the profound joy of verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) as it truly is,
and toward other sentient beings, they will remain largely free from anger, malice, and contention.
Regarding all modes of bodhisattva activities for benefiting sentient beings,
regarding the fulfillment of all modes of the accumulations for enlightenment,
and regarding all aspects of unsurpassed enlightenment and all buddha-dharmas.
Regarding all types of Buddha-activities,
one enters by means of pure resolute intention,
taking them as an object through resolute conviction.
Thereupon, they swiftly and perfectly realize all phenomena;
observing their own bodies, they are able to correctly accord with this understanding and comprehend it,
feeling extreme joy.
Furthermore, one personally observes that it is sublime and virtuous,
vast, capable of inducing renunciation, untainted, peerless, encompassing, and beneficial; thus,
body and mind are filled with joy.
In this regard, they fully accomplish these immeasurable and blazing wholesome dharmas;
furthermore, they personally realize that they have now drawn near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Regarding great enlightenment, my superior intention has already attained purity;
I am now free from all fear,
and for this reason, I experience extreme joy.
Because these bodhisattvas have already been able to give rise to a mind of firm resolve,
they have completely severed all five fears by means of their well-cultivated,
sublime wisdom of selflessness.
Even the conceptualization of a self no longer arises,
let alone the conceptualization of attachment to a self or attachment to the necessities of life.
For this reason, there is no fear of being unable to subsist.
Because he has no expectations whatsoever,
he constantly generates this aspiration:
"I shall bring benefit to all sentient beings."
He does not seek anything from sentient beings;
for this reason, he has no fear of ill repute.
Because he is free from the view of a self, the notion of the self’s destruction does not arise in him.
Therefore, there is no fear of death.
Knowing for oneself that after death one will certainly encounter the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in future lives,
one is thereby certain to have no fear of the evil realms.
From the perspective of his intention, he perceives that throughout the entire world there is not even one who is his equal,
let alone anyone superior.
Therefore, there is no timidity or fear when among a multitude.
In this way, the bodhisattva remains far removed from all five kinds of fear and far removed from all alarm and terror upon hearing the profound true Dharma being taught.
He remains far removed from all forms of arrogance and haughtiness;
he remains far removed from all anger arising from various harmful and wrongful actions committed by others;
and he remains far removed from all craving for and delight in worldly wealth.
Because it is undefiled, there is no aversion;
because it is blazing, there is no mundane inclination;
and it is able to fully realize all wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, in the present life, one can give rise to all the diligence of a bodhisattva,
because it is preceded by the dominant power of faith;
and in future lives, there are the ten kinds of great vows regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), as previously described.
Now, within this very stage of Utmost Joy,
one is able to fully bring them forth by virtue of attaining a pure and superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).
Desiring to make offerings to the Supreme Being, the true field of merit, the Great Teacher,
and the Lord of Dharma, they thus bring forth the first great vow;
desiring to uphold the unsurpassed True Dharma proclaimed by him.
For this reason, he brings forth the second great vow.
Desiring to exhort [the Buddhas] to turn the unprecedented, wondrous wheel of the sublime Dharma,
he therefore brings forth the third great vow.
In order to accord with those [beings] and practice the conduct of a bodhisattva,
he brings forth the fourth great vow;
and in order to bring those sentient beings who are suitable vessels to maturity.
For this reason, one brings forth the fifth great vow,
desiring to travel to the lands of all Buddhas to pay homage to and behold the Tathāgatas.
By attending upon and making offerings to [the Buddhas] and hearing the true Dharma,
one thereby brings forth the sixth great vow:
to purify and cultivate one’s own Buddha-field.
Therefore, one should bring forth the seventh great vow:
that in all places of birth, one may never be separated from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
and that one may always share the same flavor of intention and application as those Bodhisattvas.
Therefore, he brings forth the eighth great vow:
that he shall always benefit all sentient beings without ever failing to do so.
Therefore, he brings forth the ninth great vow.
In order to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and perform the various deeds of a Buddha,
one thus brings forth the tenth great vow,
making this aspiration:
Just as the realm of sentient beings continues in succession without ever being exhausted,
and just as the worldly path continues in succession without ever being exhausted,
so too shall this great vow of mine continue from birth to birth until the ultimate limit of enlightenment.
"May I never be separated from them; may I never forget them; may I never be alienated from them.
Thus one makes a vow to oneself and generates a right aspiration.
It should be understood that herein, the former refers to generating the aspiration with respect to the objects that ought to be aspired for.
Thereafter, one immediately accords with those vows to give rise to further vows.
In this way, with these ten kinds of great vows as the foremost,
a bodhisattva is able to produce countless hundreds of thousands of correct vows.
In this way, the bodhisattva possesses all great vows in future lives and exerts great diligence in the present life.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of dharmas for purifying the stages of abiding.
By means of this, one can cause the dwelling in extreme joy to quickly attain purification.
First, one generates profound pure faith in all Buddha-dharmas;
second, one contemplates the principle of dependent origination regarding all sentient beings.
Realizing that there is nothing but a mere mass of great suffering,
he gives rise to great compassion;
thirdly, having observed them thus, he makes this vow to himself:
I shall cause those sentient beings to be liberated from such a mass of pure great suffering and attain supreme bliss;
thus I arouse great loving-kindness.
Fourth, desiring to rescue all from sorrow and suffering, I am without self-regard.
Because they are free from attachment,
they are able to relinquish all internal and external bodies and wealth,
practicing generosity toward all sentient beings.
Fifth, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings,
they diligently seek mundane and supramundane dharmas from others without ever becoming weary.
Sixth, because of being free from weariness,
one realizes the purity of knowledge regarding all treatises and becomes skilled in knowing all treatises.
Seventh, because of being skilled in discourse,
one practices correct conduct in accordance with what is appropriate and suitable toward all sentient beings— whether inferior, middling, or superior.
Being well-versed in the world;
eighth, within such correct application,
practicing correctly according to the appropriate time, measure, and so forth.
And they cultivate a sense of shame and dread of blame.
Ninth, within such correct application, they attain non-retrogression and a nature of firm, powerful endurance.
Tenth, one honors the Tathāgata with all manner of excellent offerings, respect, and correct practice.
These are called the ten dharmas for purifying and cultivating the stages of abiding.
By means of this, one can cause the stage of extreme joy to be swiftly purified;
that is to say: pure faith, loving-kindness, compassion, and generous relinquishment.
He is free from weariness;
he is well-versed in all treatises and thoroughly understands the ways of the world.
Cultivate a sense of shame and remorse;
maintain a nature of firm strength and resolve;
and make offerings to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, after these bodhisattvas have studied, followed, and extensively practiced these ten dharmas,
they further [apply themselves] to the other nine bodhisattva abodes, such as the higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*) and so forth.
From the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he single-mindedly and diligently seeks all paths of every kind, their merits and faults, as well as their supernormal powers;
delighting in the path that is free from ruin, he skillfully grasps their practices and attains the characteristics of their natural outflow.
Spontaneously advancing through all stages of abiding,
he realizes great bodhi and becomes a Great Teacher,
leading the caravan of all sentient beings.
One transcends the perilous path through the wilderness of birth and death.
It should be known that herein, the various formations (*saṃskāra*) that are able to enter [this state] are called "practice" (*caryā*);
when one enters correctly, it is called "attainment" (*prāpti*).
Having entered [this stage], the accomplishment and perfect realization of its fruits and benefits is called "concordant flow" (*niṣyanda*).
Furthermore, while dwelling in this abode,
bodhisattvas directly perceive the Buddhas through two causes and conditions.
Either by hearing the teachings of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka,
or by generating resolute conviction within their own minds,
they believe that in the various worlds of the ten directions with their diverse names, there are Buddhas, Tathāgatas with their diverse names.
By means of a mind accompanied by coarse, pure faith, one seeks to see [the Buddha] face-to-face;
having sought thus, it is fulfilled exactly as requested.
One should know that this is called the first causal condition.
Furthermore, one should give rise to such a right vow in the mind:
"In whichever various worlds Buddhas appear,
may I be reborn there."
When such a vow has been made and is fulfilled exactly as intended,
one should know that this is called the second causal condition.
In this way, through coarse pure faith, the bodhisattva perceives the Buddhas directly before their eyes.
By the power of right aspiration, one directly beholds all Buddhas;
having seen them, one performs every kind of respectful service and offering according to one's strength and ability,
presenting various excellent and sublime articles of enjoyment.
Furthermore, they respectfully make offerings to the Saṅgha,
listen to the true Dharma from the Tathāgata,
correctly receive and uphold it, and practice with diligence according to the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
One brings sentient beings to maturity through the four means of attraction and dedicates all roots of virtue toward unsurpassed enlightenment;
by these three causes and conditions of purity, [one attains purification].
Those roots of goodness become even more brilliant and pure,
because they have made offerings to and embraced the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha,
and because they have brought sentient beings to maturity through the four means of attraction.
Because they dedicate all roots of goodness toward awakening;
thus, even for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great eons,
it is like a skillful craftsman in the world.
Just as gold in its ore form, when placed in fire and repeatedly smelted and refined,
becomes increasingly bright and pure,
so too do all the roots of virtue belonging to a bodhisattva whose superior intention is thus purified.
By means of these three causes and conditions for purification, one should know that they become even more luminous and pure;
furthermore, dwelling therein, one frequently becomes a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) in whatever place of birth one takes.
The King attained great sovereignty over Jambudvīpa;
he was far removed from all stains of avarice,
and his majestic power subdued the stinginess of sentient beings.
In all activities performed through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*),
one never departs from the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha,
and realizes the awakening of all aspects (*sarvākārabodhi*).
One should constantly bring this to mind and make the vow:
"I shall become the most honored among all sentient beings and the locus of reliance for the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings.
If one delights in initiating such diligence, [one will attain it].
Having renounced all family, wealth, and status,
he went forth with pure faith into the Buddha’s holy teaching;
in a single kṣaṇa, a muhūrta, or an instant, he was able to realize one hundred bodhisattva samādhis.
With the pure divine eye, one is able to see a hundred Tathāgatas in various Buddha-fields;
furthermore, one likewise perceives within them the manifestations, the sustenances, and the abodes of Bodhisattvas.
They are all able to understand and comprehend this.
By means of their supernormal powers, they can shake a hundred worlds;
their bodies can also travel there, emitting great radiance that shines everywhere in all directions.
He causes others to see him universally manifest as a hundredfold variety of forms to ripen a hundredfold variety of sentient beings to be converted.
If he wishes to prolong his life, he can remain for a hundred eons.
He possesses knowledge and vision regarding the events of a hundred eons each in both the past and the future limits.
They are able to enter into various dharma-gates such as the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases;
within a hundred dharma-gates, they are able to correctly discern and emanate a hundred bodies,
and each body is able to manifest a hundred bodhisattvas.
Surrounded by their retinues,
from this point forward, it should be known that these bodhisattvas, by virtue of the power of their vows,
will manifest immeasurable majestic powers and miraculous transformations.
For the assembly of bodhisattvas dwelling in this stage of Utmost Joy,
their power of aspiration is predominant, enabling them to draw forth immeasurable and sublime right aspirations;
such are the miraculous transformations resulting from these right aspirations.
Even for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great eons, it would not be easy to enumerate them.
It should be known that this is called a brief explanation of the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*),
because of its perfect determination.
Because of the arousal of the four marks;
because of initiating diligence and eliciting right aspirations;
and because of purely cultivating the dharmas of abiding.
Because of awakening others who dwell [in other stages],
because of cultivating and purifying the roots of goodness,
and because of taking birth.
By virtue of its majestic power.
If explained in detail, it is as taught in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* regarding the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Those ten stages of the bodhisattva are extensively proclaimed in that *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
This refers to the ten bodhisattva stages briefly proclaimed in the *mātṛkā* included within the Bodhisattvapiṭaka,
which follow their proper sequence from the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*) up to the Stage of the Most Perfectly Accomplished Bodhisattva (*parama-pariniṣpanna-bodhisattva-vihāra*).
It should be understood that herein, it is called a "ground" (bhūmi) in the sense that it can sustain a bodhisattva,
and in the sense that it serves as a dwelling place for enjoyment.
This is called "abiding.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 47;
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 48.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.

In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth section of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the second *Anudharmayogasthāna*, the fourth chapter, "The Abidings," part two: Inquiry concerning the transformation of a bodhisattva dwelling in the stage of *adhiśīla* (higher ethical discipline).
One should know what the practice, characteristics, and signs are.
Answer: If bodhisattvas, having previously dwelt in the Stage of Extreme Joy, [proceed] by means of ten kinds of mental dispositions.
Having already attained purity of intention,
what are the ten? First,
one does not practice deception toward any teacher, object of veneration, or field of merit.
Second is the aspiration for patience, gentleness, and ease of communal dwelling with fellow bodhisattvas who practice the same Dharma.
Third is the aspiration for the mind to function with mastery, having completely subdued all afflictions, secondary afflictions, and the activities of Māra.
Fourth, the intentionality that deeply perceives the faults in all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Fifth, the intentionality that deeply perceives the benefits in great *nirvāṇa*.
Sixth, the intentionality that constantly and diligently cultivates all the sublime and virtuous factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
Seventh, the intention to delight in seclusion because it is conducive to that very cultivation;
eighth, the intention to have no attachment or longing for worldly positions of authority, gain, or honor that involve defilement.
Ninth is the intention to remain far removed from the Lesser Vehicle and to proceed toward the realization of the Mahāyāna.
Tenth is the intention to bring about every benefit and welfare for all sentient beings.
These ten kinds of unerring intentions function in dependence upon the mind.
Therefore, it is called the purity of intention (*āśaya-viśuddhi*).
It is by means of these ten types of intention that [the practice] becomes superior and perfectly complete.
These bodhisattvas enter and realize the second stage, the Stage of Higher Ethical Discipline (*adhiśīla-vihāra*).
In this stage, they are endowed with natural ethical discipline (*prakṛti-śīla*),
such that there is extremely little evil conduct comprised within the paths of unwholesome action or transgressions of the precepts.
They do not even manifest at all,
let alone at a medium or superior degree.
Furthermore, regarding the ten types of perfected paths of action:
Manifesting by its own nature,
the bodhisattva is thus fully endowed with natural morality (*dharmatā-śīla*) and,
through sublime wisdom, [discerns] between the defiled and undefiled, and between the evil destinies and the happy destinies.
Furthermore, one understands as they truly are the manifestation of various karmas within the various vehicles,
as well as their establishment through cause and effect and the realization of their cultivation.
Regarding these various karmas that result in ripened effects (*vipākaphala*) and concordant effects (*niṣyandaphala*),
he understands them as they truly are;
thus, he is able to personally and completely sever all unwholesome karma.
He himself is able to personally undertake all wholesome karma;
therein, he delights in exhorting others and is truly capable of exhorting them.
Regarding the realm of sentient beings defiled by the faults of engaging in various forms of unwholesome karma, [he acts].
Whether in prosperity or in decline, there is no distinction;
all fall into the ultimate suffering and abide in hardship.
Pressed by various forms of distress, they are truly to be pitied.
Therein, they attain vast compassion and contemplate reality as it is.
These bodhisattvas, dwelling in this stage of superior ethical discipline,
extensively behold the Buddhas and purify their roots of goodness.
This should be understood as previously explained.
The distinction here is as follows:
it is like a skilled worldly craftsman.
Just as refined gold placed in a crucible within a fire becomes increasingly bright and pure through repeated smelting,
so too should one understand that the purification of a bodhisattva’s roots of goodness is likewise.
Within this dwelling, the pure mental disposition reaches fulfillment;
he enters into successive births where he frequently becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) ruling over the four continents,
and by his sovereign power, causes many sentient beings to cease from the unwholesome paths of action consisting of transgressing the precepts.
One should know that exhorting others to undertake and practice the various paths of wholesome action possesses a power ten times greater than the former;
this is known as a brief explanation of the Bodhisattva’s stage of superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-vihāra*).
This means: because of the purity of his intention;
because he is fully endowed with natural morality (*prakṛti-śīla*); because he is free from all forms of the defilement of violating the precepts;
and because he has thoroughly understood and mastered all paths of action (*karmapatha*) and all causes and effects.
Because they are able to personally undertake and practice all pure deeds,
and also delight in exhorting others to undertake and practice them,
they attain great compassion for the manifold sufferings and hardships born of karma within the realm of sentient beings.
Because of observing things as they truly are;
because of the purification of the roots of goodness;
because of taking birth; and because of majestic power.
If explained in detail, as it is taught in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* regarding the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*):
because it is far removed from all stains of transgressing the precepts,
it is called the Stainless Ground.
Because it is free from all stains of transgressing the precepts,
this very stage is called the "Abiding in Higher Ethics.
It should be understood that the "Stainless Stage" (*vimalā-bhūmi*) is precisely this Abiding in Higher Ethics.
Question: When a bodhisattva transitions into the stage of superior mind (*adhi-citta-vihāra*), by what conduct, what marks, and what signs should they be known?
Answer: If a bodhisattva has previously dwelt in the stage of superior ethical discipline (*adhi-śīla-vihāra*).
Having already attained the ten kinds of pure intentionality,
one attends to them with mental attention, understands them, and penetrates them;
furthermore, one attends to them with mental attention by means of another ten kinds of pure mental intentionality.
Because it has been brought to the highest degree and because it is utterly perfected,
one transcends the stage of higher ethical discipline and enters the stage of higher mind.
What are the ten?
First, one reflects with focused attention:
"I have attained purification regarding the ten kinds of pure mental dispositions.
Second, one reflects with focused attention:
Because I have already purified the ten kinds of pure mental dispositions,
I am able to avoid falling back;
third, the mental attention of reflection.
My mind does not enter into any outflows or phenomena associated with outflows;
it dwells correctly within their opposition.
Fourth is mental attention through reflection.
I am able to know that my consciousness is correctly settled within those cultivated antidotes.
Fifth is mental attention:
I am able to ensure that I do not again fall away from those cultivated antidotes.
Sixth is the mental attention of reflection:
"By means of such firm antidotes, I shall not be overcome by any outflows (*āsrava*),
any phenomena associated with outflows (*sāsrava-dharma*), or any of the hosts of Māra."
Seventh is mental attention:
"I am now able to engage with all the Buddha-dharmas with a mind free from timidity or inferiority."
Eighth, one attends to the thought:
"I am now able to face all ascetic practices without any cowardice.
Ninth, one attends to the thought: [as follows].
My mind is single-mindedly devoted to the Mahāyāna, giving rise to deep faith and understanding;
I shall never take pleasure in other inferior vehicles.
This is the tenth reflection.
I deeply cherish and delight in all matters that benefit sentient beings.
By means of these ten kinds of pure mental intentions (*cittāśaya*), through such mental attention (*manasikāra*),
one is able to enter the Bodhisattva’s stage of Superior Resolve (*adhyāśaya-vihāra*).
When a bodhisattva dwells securely in the stage of superior mind (*adhyāśaya-vihāra*),
they are able to destroy all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) through various aspects of their defects and afflictions,
and develop a profound sense of weary detachment toward those formations.
Regarding the Buddha’s sublime wisdom, one is able to perceive its great benefits through various modes of excellence;
furthermore, within that [wisdom], one is able to maintain a single, pure flavor of aspiration and delight.
Deeply conceiving a sense of longing and affection,
he is able to contemplate the realm of sentient beings as being characterized by suffering through various forms of affliction,
and thus gives rise to a heart of compassion and attachment toward all sentient beings.
Abiding in the mind that takes meaning as its object, one is never indolent regarding any form of conduct;
for the sake of great enlightenment,
one applies oneself with fervent diligence and is able to give rise to a vast intention of compassion toward all sentient beings.
He contemplates that the ultimate means for liberating all sentient beings from their manifold sufferings is precisely the unobstructed wisdom regarding all afflictions and entanglements;
he contemplates those who are able to perfectly realize such liberation.
Only through non-conceptual wisdom, which serves as the antidote to the arising of all conceptualizations and active defilements within the dharmadhātu,
does one perceive that the light of that wisdom is accomplished solely by means of the supreme samādhi that is free from error.
One observes that all the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), absorptions (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*) thus induced belong to the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
they are preceded by hearing and have the correct Dharma as their causal condition.
Having observed this, he exerted great diligence to seek out extensive learning;
for the sake of hearing the true Dharma, he did not spare his body or life,
and there was no wealth or cherished object, whether internal or external, that he could not relinquish.
There is no teacher whom he does not vow to serve;
there is no venerable instruction which he does not vow to practice;
there is no physical suffering that he does not vow to undergo.
If one hears even a single four-line verse of the Buddha’s Dharma,
the joy and exultation one feels surpasses that of obtaining a great mass of precious jewels filling the entire trichiliocosm.
To hear even a single phrase of the Dharma spoken by the Buddha—
which can lead to perfect enlightenment and purify the bodhisattva conduct—
is more joyful and exultant than attaining all the most exalted positions, such as those of Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, or the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin).
Suppose someone were to say:
"Good son, listen!
I have a single verse of the Dharma taught by the Buddha."
"It can lead one to perfect enlightenment and purify the bodhisattva practices.
Would you wish to hear it?
If you are now able to cast yourself into a great pit of fire and undergo great suffering, [I shall teach it to you]."
"I shall explain it for you.
Upon hearing this, the bodhisattva was filled with joy and leaped for gladness,
replying, "I am capable of it."
If I were to hear even a single phrase of the Dharma meaning as previously described,
then even if a fire pit equal in size to the trichiliocosm were filled with blazing flames, [I would enter it].
I would even cast myself down from the Brahma Heaven,
let alone into a small fire pit;
to seek the Buddha-dharma, one should even endure great suffering for a long time in the great hells.
How much more so regarding other minor sufferings that one ought not to undergo.
Having initiated such diligence to seek the true Dharma,
the bodhisattva is further able to reflect upon it according to reality and according to principle.
One must practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma through correct cultivation;
only then can one be said to be in accord with the Buddha's teachings.
It is not merely by hearing the sounds of words and letters that one attains purity.
Having understood this, one relies upon the characteristics of phenomena as they were heard and correctly contemplates them;
thereby, one distances oneself from all desires and unwholesome, evil states, and so on,
up to attaining the four mundane dhyānas and the four formless attainments.
He fully dwells in the four immeasurables and the five supernormal powers;
having dwelled in them extensively, he subsequently relinquishes the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*).
By the power of mastery over aspirations, he returns to the desire realm to observe various places,
so that he may act for the benefit of sentient beings and bring the factors of enlightenment to fulfillment.
Even when taking rebirth,
it is not merely by their own power that they are born in those places;
thus, because these bodhisattvas have abandoned sensual desire, they are said to have severed the bonds of desire.
Because they abandon dhyāna, samādhi, and samāpatti, they are said to sever the bonds of existence.

This is because the bodhisattva has previously cultivated resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the suchness (*tathatā*) of phenomena while on the stage of practice through conviction (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*).
Having severed the fetters of views,
false greed, hatred, and delusion never again arise;
having extensively beheld the Buddhas, their roots of goodness become purified.
It should be understood as previously described.
The distinction here is as follows:
it is like the pure gold in the hands of a skilled worldly smith, which, having been previously smelted and refined so that all impurities are exhausted, remains constant when weighed.
In this way, it should be understood that the purity of a bodhisattva’s roots of virtue is likewise.
For the most part, they take birth as Śakra, Lord of the Devas,
skillfully transforming sentient beings and causing them to abandon desire and greed.
All the powers [previously] mentioned in the preceding abodes were numbered in the thousands;
it should be known that here they are numbered in the hundreds of thousands.
It should be known that this is called a brief explanation of the Bodhisattva’s Abode of Superior Mind.
This means that because one enters into fulfillment through the mental engagement of the mind’s intention,
one is able to correctly penetrate all conditioned phenomena, the realm of sentient beings, and great enlightenment.
Because they are able to correctly investigate the means for liberating all sentient beings from suffering,
and because they seek the sublime Dharma with great reverence and without weariness.
They are able to correctly practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma;
because they are able to induce and abide in worldly meditative absorptions (dhyāna), concentrations (samādhi), attainments (samāpatti),
and immeasurable supernormal powers (abhijñā).
Because they have relinquished that [birth], and because they take birth according to their will through the power of mastery over aspirations,
and because their roots of goodness are purified,
and because of their taking birth.
By virtue of supernatural power,
if it were to be explained in detail, it would be as described in the "Luminous Ground" (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*) of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
This is due to the cultivation of the practice of hearing.
It is manifested by the light of the samādhi of the illumination of the True Dharma;
therefore, this stage is named the Ground of Radiant Light (Prabhākarī),
for through the purity of the inner mind, it is able to emit radiance.
Therefore, it is called the "Abiding in Higher Resolve" (*adhicittavihāra*).
For this reason, it is named the "Radiant Stage" (*prabhākari-bhūmi*);
one should know that for this very same reason, it is also called the "Abiding in Higher Resolve."
What is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the factors of enlightenment?
It refers to those bodhisattvas who, having previously dwelled in the dwelling of higher mind,
[proceed] by means of the superior power of seeking extensive learning.
Having attained the ten entries into the light of the Dharma,
by virtue of these ten entries into the light of the Dharma being of the highest grade and being utterly perfected, [one attains the stage of the Path of Seeing].
Having transcended the stage of higher mind (*adhicitta-vihāra*), one enters the first stage of higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-vihāra*).
These ten entries into the light of the Dharma (*dharmāloka-praveśa*) are as set forth in the sūtras.
One should know its characteristics:
namely, that which is designated,
and that within which it is designated.
If, by virtue of this designation,
it becomes defiled or purified through affliction or purification, whether in terms of conventional reality or ultimate truth.
Whether it be defiled by the fetters of afflictions or purified by unsurpassed purity,
one should know that this is called the summarized meaning of the "Entrance into the Illumination of the Ten Dharmas."
These bodhisattvas, dwelling in this state,
have an unshakable intention (*āśaya*) as their primary characteristic, as stated in the sūtras.
He has fully accomplished all ten kinds of wisdom that bring about maturation,
as well as the dharmas that mature wisdom.
Having entered the family of the Tathāgata and attained its essential nature,
one contemplates all aspects of the bodhisattva through superior power,
taking the four foundations of mindfulness as the foremost practice.
Regarding the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment,
as stated in the sūtras:
because one skillfully embraces and diligently cultivates these dharmas.
The most subtle view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which clings to all aggregates, elements, and bases, and all such disturbances,
is entirely brought to a state where it never again manifests and is utterly severed.
Because those [defilements] have been severed, all actions censured by all Tathāgatas no longer manifest,
while all actions praised by all Tathāgatas are followed in accordance with reality.
Once this has occurred, his mind becomes further moistened, gentle, and pliable;
his mind becomes further purified in all its various aspects.

Furthermore, they are well-versed in gratitude and the repayment of kindness; they fully accomplish various pure dharmas (*śukladharma*) that accord with their resolute intentions (*āśaya*), and they seek the practices capable of cultivating the higher stages.
Having aroused great diligence, they attain stable abiding.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, all their intentions (*āśaya*), superior intentions (*adhyāśaya*), resolute convictions (*adhimukti*), and fundamental dispositions (*dharmatā*) become fully perfected.
By these causes and conditions, all various demonic armies of the non-Buddhists and enemies of the holy teaching cannot eclipse or displace them;
they extensively behold the Buddhas, and their roots of goodness become pure.
The details of its characteristics should be understood as previously explained.
The distinction here is as follows:
it is like a skillful worldly craftsman who fashions ornaments from refined gold.
Just as gold that has not yet been fashioned into ornaments cannot be outshone by other [ordinary] gold,
so too the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva herein cannot be outshone by the roots of goodness of any other bodhisattvas who abide in the stage of ordinary beings.
Just as the light emitted by a mani jewel cannot be eclipsed by any other gemstone,
and cannot be extinguished by any wind, water, or rain in the entire world.
Such is the radiance of light that is emitted.
Among these, the radiance of wisdom possessed by a bodhisattva cannot be eclipsed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
No demonic adversaries can sever or extinguish it.
Upon taking birth, he frequently becomes the King of Suyāma Heaven,
skillfully transforming sentient beings and causing them to eliminate the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
All the powers [previously] described in the preceding stage as numbering in the hundreds of thousands should be understood here as numbering in the millions (*koṭi*).
It should be known that this is called, in brief, the Bodhisattva’s dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the factors of enlightenment;
that is to say, because of the attainment of entry into the perfection of the illumination of the Dharma,
and because of the accomplishment of knowledge.
Because of cultivating the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*);
because of severing all attachments and disturbances such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
and because of restraining unwholesome actions, engaging in wholesome ones, and distancing oneself from what should be avoided.
Because the mind has become pliant through these causes and conditions;
because all concordant virtues flourish and increase;
and because one exerts great diligence based on the cultivation of the stages of practice as sought after.

By these causes and conditions, because his intentions, superior intentions, resolute convictions, and fundamental nature have been thoroughly purified, he cannot be eclipsed or shaken by any adversaries of the holy teachings.
By these causes and conditions, all enemies of the holy teachings are unable to overpower or disturb him.
Because of the purity of the roots of goodness,
because of the manner of taking birth,
and because of spiritual power.
If explained in detail, it is as described in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* regarding the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).
In this stage, the flames of the wisdom that knows the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) as they truly are [blaze forth].
Because it is able to bring about the illumination of wisdom through the teachings of the True Dharma,
this stage is called the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, that very stage is here designated as the "Abiding in Higher Wisdom Corresponding to the Factors of Enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣya-pratisaṃyukto 'dhiprajñā-vihāraḥ*).
What is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the truths?
It refers to the bodhisattvas who, having previously dwelled in the higher wisdom associated with the factors of enlightenment,
have already attained ten kinds of pure intentions that are equal.
Because that equal and pure intention has become superior and perfectly complete,
one transcends the first stage of higher wisdom and enters the second stage of higher wisdom.
The textual expressions for the ten kinds of equal and pure intention should be understood according to their characteristics as taught in the sūtras.
That is to say, the peerless awakening is equal to all awakenings;
it transcends the entire realm of sentient beings and all phenomena.
One should know that such equality is what is briefly described as the meaning of the ten kinds of pure intentions.
In this way, while dwelling in this stage,
the bodhisattva for the most part seeks the excellence of wisdom regarding the four noble truths by means of ten aspects.
One should understand the characteristics of all literary expressions as they truly are,
as explained in the sūtras.
That is to say, it is called "this teaching" because it relies on the basis of awakening others, the basis of one's own internal wisdom, and the basis of both together;
and because it relies upon the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās.
The name is thus explained:
it refers to the intrinsic nature of present suffering,
and to the nature of arising as the cause of future suffering.
It is said that [the nature of] their exhaustion and non-arising based on the exhaustion of causes,
and [the nature of] the means for their abandonment based on cultivation,
are described in this way.
One should know that this is the brief meaning of the knowledge of the four noble truths in its ten aspects.
Thus, a bodhisattva who is skilled in the truths correctly deconstructs all conditioned formations through wisdom.

He increases his compassionate intention toward the realm of sentient beings and is able to correctly comprehend the misconduct of those sentient beings who are deluded regarding the past and future limits of existence.
In order to bring about their liberation,
he gathers the vast provisions of merit and wisdom, forms right aspirations, and—
centered upon those very intentions— gathers right mindfulness, wisdom, and conduct as his primary guides.
All manifold and supreme qualities increase and flourish;
all other forms of mental attention are completely abandoned;
and by means of various skillful methods of maturation, he brings sentient beings to maturity.
As stated in the sūtras:
"All various worldly fields of knowledge— such as scripts, treatises, seals, arithmetic, and so forth— that are capable of benefiting sentient beings,
he is able to bring all of these forth for the sake of generating deep compassion for all sentient beings."
Gradually, up until the point of skillfully establishing sublime enlightenment;
for the sake of conforming to worldly conventional discourse;
and because of the desire to skillfully eliminate poverty.
It is for the purpose of extinguishing all calamities arising from the disturbances of the various realms of the world, whether caused by humans or non-humans;
and it is for the purpose of bestowing blameless means of amusement and sport, thereby eliminating those forms of play that are contrary to the Dharma.
For those who seek various dwellings and the requisites for life,
he is able to bestow all kinds of dwellings and requisites with little effort.
It is for the purpose of rescuing kings, bandits, and others from the afflictions of their oppressions;
for the purpose of opening up and restraining the various applications regarding what is possible and what is impossible;

From the great clouds of the Dharma of all Tathāgatas,
they are capable of receiving the most vast and subtle rain of Dharma, which is difficult for all other classes of sentient beings to receive.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva is like a great cloud that has not yet manifested the realization of unsurpassed enlightenment; yet,
once it does manifest the realization of unsurpassed enlightenment,
it is able to act for the sake of immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.
They rain down the incomparable, subtle rain of the Dharma,
extinguishing all the dust of afflictions and enabling the various crops of roots of goodness to grow and reach maturity.
For this reason, this stage is named the Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).
From this very meaning, it should be understood that it is also called the "Supreme and Perfectly Accomplished Bodhisattva Abode.
Such are the qualities of the constituent parts within each successive abode as they have been described.
It is not that those preceding stages are entirely non-existent;
however, because they are of inferior grade, they do not fall within that [current] enumeration.
One should know that these very same stages, through successive cultivation, become middling and superior grades.
It is only upon attaining fulfillment in the subsequent stages that these are established.
Furthermore, within each of these individual abodes:
It is only after passing through many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of great kalpas,
or even exceeding that number, that one attains and fulfills [the stages].
Nevertheless, all the abodes collectively require two incalculable great kalpas to be fully realized.
That is to say, after the first incalculable great eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*),
one finally transcends the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) and successively realizes the stage of supreme joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
This refers to one who is constantly courageous and diligent in their effort,
not to one who lacks such courage and diligence;
furthermore, they pass through a second incalculable great eon.
Only then does one transcend the Stage of Extreme Joy,
up to the Stage of Signlessness with Application and Effort,
and successively realize the Stage of Signlessness without Application or Effort.
This means that this bodhisattva has attained pure intention and is resolutely courageous and diligent; thus,
they further pass through a third incalculable great eon.
Only then does one transcend the stages of non-application, effortlessness, signlessness, and the unhindered analytical knowledges,
and realize the supreme, perfected bodhisattva stage.
It should be understood that within this process, there are briefly two kinds of incalculable great eons (*asaṃkhyeya-mahākalpa*).
First, because the calculation of days, nights, months, fortnights,
and so forth involves an immeasurable duration of time,
it is also called an "incalculable great kalpa" (asaṃkhyeya-mahākalpa).
Second is the method of calculating great kalpas,
which exceeds all measurable quantities of calculation;
it is also called "innumerable great kalpas."
If one follows the previous explanation regarding incalculable great eons (*asaṃkhyeya-mahākalpa*),
it requires immeasurable and incalculable great eons before one realizes unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
If one follows the latter explanation regarding incalculable great eons (*asaṃkhyeya-mahākalpa*),
one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment after passing through merely three incalculable great eons.
However, if one practices correctly with the most supreme and intense diligence,
it may be possible to turn back many intermediate kalpas.
Some may even transform many great eons;
however, it should be known that there is certainly no one who can transform incalculable great eons.
Furthermore, this is by virtue of the twelve bodhisattva abodes as thus described.
Throughout the duration of three incalculable great eons,
one is able to sever all the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) belonging to the category of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
as well as all the heavy residues belonging to the category of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Within the three stages, one should know that the heavy burdens (*dausthulya*) belonging to the category of afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are abandoned.
Specifically, within the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*),
all heavy burdens belonging to the category of afflictions pertaining to the evil destinies are forever severed.
All categories of afflictions, whether superior or middling, no longer manifest.
Within this state of dwelling in the signless, which is effortless and without application,
all heavy residues (*dausthulya*) of the categories of affliction that obstruct the entirely pure patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) are forever severed.
All afflictions do not manifest.
Within the supreme and perfected Bodhisattva abode,
one should know that all obstacles consisting of the habitual tendencies and latent dispositions of the afflictions are forever severed, and one enters the Tathāgata abode.
It should be known that all the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) belonging to the category of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are likewise of three kinds:
first, those residing in the outer skin;
second, those residing in the inner skin.
Third is the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) within the flesh;
one should know that herein, the heaviness within the skin is entirely severed in the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*).
The heaviness of the skin has been entirely severed;
the state of dwelling in signlessness, which is without application and without effort, has been fully attained.
As for the heaviness of the flesh:
In the state of the Tathāgata, all [afflictions] have been completely severed,
and he has attained the utterly pure wisdom that is free from all obscurations;
within these three states of abiding, the two obstacles— those of affliction and those to the known— are forever eliminated.
The remaining stages, in their respective order,
constitute the equipment for abandonment;
that is, within these thirteen stages.
It should be known that there are briefly eleven kinds of purity.
That is to say, within the first stage, the Dwelling of the Spiritual Lineage (*gotra-vihāra*),
there is the purity of the spiritual lineage.
In the second stage, the stage of practice through resolute belief,
the purity of faith and resolute belief is attained.
In the third stage, the stage of extreme joy, [the purity of superior intention is attained].
The purity of superior intention pertains to the fourth stage, the stage of higher ethical discipline;
therein lies the purity of higher ethical discipline.
In the fifth stage, the Abiding in Higher Mind,
the higher mind is purified;
in the sixth, seventh, and eighth stages, the Abidings in Higher Wisdom.
The initiation of non-erroneous wisdom is purified;
in that ninth stage, the stage of signlessness with application and effort,
the perfection of application and practice is purified.
In the tenth stage, the dwelling of signlessness without application or effort,
true knowledge and supernormal powers are brought forth and purified;
in the eleventh, the dwelling of unimpeded analytical knowledge.
He possesses the purity of unimpeded analytical knowledge in correctly proclaiming the meaning of the Dharma to others.
Within the twelfth and supreme stage of fulfillment for bodhisattvas,
he enters the purity of the sublime wisdom that encompasses all aspects of all that is knowable.

Within the thirteenth stage, the Tathāgata-abode, all afflictive obstructions, cognitive obstructions, along with their habitual tendencies, are ultimately purified. As previously stated in the "Chapter on Bodhisattva Qualities," the Mahāyāna is subsumed by eight factors.
It should be understood that these are subsumed within these thirteen dwellings (*vihāra*).
Specifically, within the first and second dwellings,
one generates faith and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, and engages in hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*).
In the third dwelling,
one attains the characteristic of superior intentionality, proceeding forward with superior practice;
this continues through all other stages, up to and including the signless dwelling that involves application and effort.
One attains vast cultivation.
Within these three types of pure conduct,
the bodhisattva abides and brings the cultivation of the fruit to completion.
One should know that while abiding therein, the Tathāgata attains ultimate liberation.
One should know that the twelve stages of the bodhisattva correspond in their sequence to the stages of the śrāvaka.
Just as the śrāvakas abide in their own spiritual lineage (*gotra*),
it should be known that the bodhisattvas' first stage (*bhūmi*) is likewise.
Just as the śrāvakas abide in the preparatory application for entering the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma-praveśa-prayoga*).
It should be known that the second dwelling of a bodhisattva is likewise.
Just as the śrāvakas who have already entered the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) abide,
it should be known that the third dwelling of a bodhisattva is likewise.

Just as the śrāvakas who have already attained the purity of conviction (avetyaprasāda) dwell in the training in higher ethics (adhiśīla-śikṣā), which is the flavor beloved by the noble ones for the sake of exhausting the outflows of the higher realms,
it should be known that the fourth dwelling of the bodhisattva is likewise.
Just as the śrāvakas, relying on the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*), give rise to and abide in the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*),
so too should it be understood for the fifth stage of the bodhisattva.
Just as the śrāvakas abide in the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*) through the knowledge of the noble truths (*āryasatya*) as they have attained it.
It should be understood that the sixth, seventh, and eighth dwellings of a bodhisattva are likewise;
they are like the dwelling in the preparatory application for the signless samādhi through the thorough investigation of the objects of knowledge by the śrāvakas.
It should be known that the ninth dwelling of a bodhisattva is likewise.
Just as the śrāvakas achieve the fulfillment of the signless dwelling,
it should be known that the tenth dwelling of a bodhisattva is likewise.
Just as the śrāvakas, having emerged from this, enter and abide in the state of liberation,
so too should one know the eleventh dwelling of the bodhisattva.
Just as the śrāvakas abide in the state of an arhat endowed with all marks.
It should be known that the twelfth dwelling of a bodhisattva is likewise.

[End of] the Fifteenth Chapter, the Bodhisattvabhūmi, within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Section on the Main Stages (*Maulī Bhūmi*), Sub-section on the Ultimate Yoga Station (*Niṣṭhā-yogasthāna*). First: The Chapter on Birth (*Janma-varga*). Briefly stated, there are five kinds of births for bodhisattvas that encompass all forms of birth.
In all abodes, all bodhisattvas undergo blameless births and bring benefit,
welfare, and happiness to all sentient beings.
What are these five?
First, birth that eliminates calamities;
second, birth according to species;
third, birth of great power.
Fourth is the birth of superior excellence;
fifth is the final birth.
What is the bodhisattva’s birth for the removal of calamities?
This refers to when Bodhisattvas, through either the power of their great vows or their sovereign mastery,
act during times when famines, calamities, and wildernesses are actually present,
so that sentient beings may sustain their lives with minimal effort.
They are born among the species of great fish and the like;
their physical forms are vast, and wherever they are born,
they provide the flesh of their own bodies to all hungry sentient beings.
They cause all to be fully satisfied.
When numerous epidemics manifest among sentient beings,
they attain the power of mastery through the power of their great vows.
Possessing the power of the efficacious vidyā-mantras, he assumes the form of a vast and excellent king of medicines to pacify all epidemics among sentient beings.
When sentient beings are currently being oppressed by mutual strife and conflict with neighboring kingdoms, [he acts].
By the power of great vows, he attains the power of mastery;
as a sovereign lord of the great earth,
he possesses great influence and governs with righteousness through skillful means.
They pacify the afflictions of war and strife in neighboring kingdoms;
when sentient beings are currently engaged in mutual conflict and contention,
they attain mastery through the power of their great vows.
They utter words of sincerity and faith, coming and going to establish harmony and remove the bonds of resentment.
When sentient beings encounter evil kings who unjustly bind, arrest, punish, and oppress them, causing their bodies and minds to be disturbed and turmoil to manifest before them; [at such times...]
By the power of his great vows, he attained the power of mastery;
he was born into that royal family and became a king who acts in accordance with the Dharma,
out of compassion for sentient beings, bringing to rest all forms of oppression and suffering.
If there are sentient beings who give rise to various wrong views and commit various evil deeds,
yet develop deep faith and understanding toward a particular celestial realm,
[the Bodhisattva], out of compassion for them, by means of the power of great vows and the power of mastery, [manifests there].
Having been born in that celestial realm, they employ skillful means to sever wrong views and unwholesome conduct;
this is called, in brief, the bodhisattva’s birth for the removal of calamities.
If explained in detail:
Through the power of great vows, having attained the power of mastery and preceded by compassion,
one should know that the various births he undergoes in various places are immeasurable.
How does a bodhisattva take birth in accordance with the species [of beings]?
This refers to how bodhisattvas, through the power of their great vows and the attainment of mastery,
are born among various classes of beings within the animal realm— such as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and asuras— who are characterized by mutual plotting, harm, and conflict.
Or they are born among Brahmins who hold wrong views;
or they are born among those who delight in practicing evil deeds;
or they are born among those who take pleasure in wrong livelihoods.
Alternatively, among those classes of sentient beings who have developed an extreme attachment to and an inclination toward sensual desires,
he is born into that same category of beings as their leader, in order to eliminate those faults.
Having become their leader, he employs skillful means to transform and guide them away from the evil they practice;
though the bodhisattva does not personally engage in what they do not practice,
he manifests such conduct in order to cause them to manifest the practice of virtue.
He teaches the true Dharma for them;
because the Bodhisattva’s current conduct differs from theirs and because he teaches the true Dharma,
he employs skillful means to eliminate all the faults of those sentient beings.
This is called a brief explanation of the bodhisattva’s taking birth in accordance with various types of beings;
a detailed explanation is as previously stated and should be understood as immeasurable.
What is the birth of great power of a bodhisattva?
It refers to the lifespan, physical form, lineage, sovereignty, wealth, and so forth, which are experienced by all bodhisattvas at the time of their natural birth.
All these ripened fruits (*vipākaphala*) are the most preeminent in all the world;
such is the activity performed by these ripened fruits.
The Chapter on the Benefit of Self and Others has already been extensively explained.
