This is called the brief explanation of the birth of the Bodhisattva’s great power;
if it were to be explained extensively:
It should be understood that within each respective class of beings, there are immeasurable births of great power.
What is the superior birth of a bodhisattva?
It refers to all bodhisattvas beginning from the first dwelling, the Dwelling of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*).
Up to the tenth and most supreme fulfillment stage of the bodhisattva dwellings,
there is the aforementioned differentiated taking of birth;
in this context, it is termed "superior birth" (*abhyudaya*).
This refers to the initial dwelling as a wheel-turning king who rules over Jambudvīpa with great sovereignty,
up to and including the tenth dwelling, which is the most supreme and perfected state of all bodhisattvas.
It exercises great sovereignty;
surpassing all places of birth up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, it is the most preeminent.
Only those bodhisattvas who have attained the supreme, perfected state of dwelling as mahāsattvas are able to be born therein.
Those bodhisattvas are induced by the predominant influence of these very karmas;
this is called, in brief, the superior birth of a bodhisattva.
If explained in detail, one should know it to be immeasurable.
In this life, the bodhisattva has already brought the provisions for enlightenment to complete perfection;
he is either born into the family of a great brahmin state preceptor.
Or they may be born into the royal families of great kṣatriya nations,
where they are able to manifest the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and extensively perform all the deeds of a Buddha.
This is called a brief explanation of the final birth of a bodhisattva;
if it were to be explained in detail,
one should know that it is immeasurable.
If all bodhisattvas, regarding their births in the past, future, and present that are pure, noble, and excellent, have ever been, will be,
or are currently being born, they are all entirely subsumed within these five types of birth.
Apart from this, there is nothing superior or additional.
This is with the sole exception of the births taken by bodhisattvas on the level of ordinary beings. Why is this?
In this context, the intention is to take the various births assumed by wise bodhisattvas as the five types of birth;
such births serve as the basis for the fruit of great enlightenment.
Causing all bodhisattvas to swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Chapter Two: Embracing, from the Fifteenth Bodhisattva Stage within the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the Section on the Main Grounds; specifically, the second chapter, "Embracing," within the third section, the "Ultimate Yoga Station. Regarding all the practices of a bodhisattva throughout every stage of abiding:
It should be known that there are, in brief, six ways in which a bodhisattva correctly embraces sentient beings.
What are these six?
First, instantaneous and universal reception;
second, superior reception;
third, inclusive reception.
Fourth is long-term inclusion;
fifth is short-term inclusion;
sixth is final inclusion.
How does a bodhisattva suddenly and universally embrace all sentient beings?
It means that when a bodhisattva first generates the mind of enlightenment,
they embrace the entire realm of sentient beings as their own retinue.
He reflects thus:
"I shall perform every kind of beneficial, peaceful, and advantageous deed for them, according to my ability and according to my strength.
Whatever he contemplates, he acts accordingly.
This is called the bodhisattva’s instantaneous and universal embracing of all sentient beings.
What is the bodhisattva’s superior embracing of sentient beings?
It refers to when bodhisattvas, acting as heads of households, embrace their parents, wives, children, slaves, servants, and laborers.
Or, as a king, he may take charge of all the officials and commoners under his jurisdiction.
Having thus generated the superior perception of gathering others,
the Bodhisattva proceeds according to the proper protocols for those he has gathered.
He acts in accordance with the conduct and activities appropriate for a bodhisattva;
if he serves as a head of a household,
he employs various skillful means to encourage his parents to cultivate all manner of virtues.
He made offerings at all times without ever becoming weary or negligent;
he was well aware of their kindness and knew how to repay it,
and he was able to perfectly accord with the hearts of his parents.
He exercises mastery over both the Dharma and its meaning;
and regarding his wife, children, servants, and others,
he freely provides them with clothing and food according to the Dharma as circumstances require.
They never press others with various tasks;
even when there is an offense, they are able to endure it;
and if the other falls ill, they are truly capable of attending to and treating them.
They encourage others to cultivate all virtuous deeds;
they bestow excellent material goods upon them from time to time;
they comfort them with kind words and do not regard them as slaves or servants.
He regards, honors,
and nurtures them as if they were his own self; even when acting as a king,
he does not carry out dismissals or punishments, nor does he employ the sword or the staff.
And he is able to transform others correctly,
benefiting them through both the Dharma and material wealth,
while relying on his own local fields for his personal sustenance.
One does not use violent force to invade or plunder the territories of others.
To the best of one's ability and strength,
one exhorts all sentient beings to cease all evil and teaches them to cultivate all that is wholesome.
He regards all sentient beings as a father regards his son;
since he even delights in giving equally to other sentient beings,
how much more so would he not provide impartial relief to his own kinsmen?
He does not practice deception, and his speech is truthful and sincere.
He remains far removed from all acts such as killing, binding, beating, punishing, coercing, and mutilating.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s superior gathering-in of sentient beings.
How does a bodhisattva gather and sustain sentient beings?
It should be understood that when a bodhisattva correctly guides a retinue,
this is called, in brief, a bodhisattva’s gathering and sustaining of sentient beings.
To explain in detail:
by means of two causes and conditions, one correctly gathers a following;
this is called a bodhisattva’s grasping and embracing of all sentient beings.
What are these two?
First, to properly gather a following with a mind free from attachment;
second, to correctly teach and cultivate oneself for one's own benefit.
He does not entrap or obstruct them through improper application.
Furthermore, regarding all that should be embraced,
his mind remains impartial and does not fall into partiality.
Furthermore, one should not be stingy with the true Dharma toward them,
nor act as a teacher who keeps things hidden;
nor should one harbor expectations of being served, honored, or provided with offerings by them.
Because he delights in what is wholesome, he does not prevent others from seeking to perform such deeds for themselves,
desiring instead that their provisions of merit may increase;
furthermore, at other times, he also serves and makes offerings to them.
For those who have not yet understood its meaning, he brings them to awakening so that they may understand;
for those who already understand, he causes their understanding to become further clarified and purified;
and whatever doubts arise, he eliminates them accordingly.
If remorse arises, one skillfully provides resolution;
one penetrates profound meanings and phrases with wisdom and,
from time to time, correctly elucidates them.
He shares equally in their suffering and their joy;
for the sake of wealth and profit,
he accomplishes superior management and urgent affairs on behalf of others even more than for his own.
Whenever others commit transgressions, he correctly points them out to bring about their awakening;
at the appropriate time and in accordance with reason, he reprimands or expels them.
Yet, even if they suffer from illness or are overcome by grief, he never abandons them.
Through skillful means and expedient methods, they heal afflictions and diseases and dispel sorrow and anxiety;
regarding all those who are inferior in physical form,
they maintain mindfulness, diligence, wisdom, and so forth.
He never treats them with contempt or arrogance;
from time to time, he accords with their weariness and,
as is appropriate, preaches the True Dharma for them.
From time to time, in order to cause mindfulness to be fixed,
he provides correct instruction regarding the object of focus and remains patient with difficult questions without giving rise to resentment.
In those virtuous practices, they are either equal or superior, never declining or inferior;
nor do they seek gain, offerings, or honor;
they are endowed with compassion and free from agitation or instability.
He was perfected in ethical discipline, views, conduct, and right livelihood.
With a relaxed countenance and a steady gaze, he was free from frowning.
His speech was gentle and beautiful; he was the first to speak, greeting others with a smile.
They constantly cultivate all categories of wholesome qualities,
refrain from negligence, and remain free from indolence;
they instruct and train their followers precisely in these matters.
He also causes his own practice to progress further and become more excellent.
A bodhisattva should not, at all times, gather a following;
nor should he fail to gather one, nor should he act with partiality.
This is called a bodhisattva’s gathering and embracing of sentient beings.
How does a bodhisattva embrace sentient beings for a long duration?
It refers to a bodhisattva’s embracing and benefiting those sentient beings who abide in a state of inferior maturation.
One should know that this is called "long-term embrace," because it is only after a long period of time that [the beings] become fit for purification.
What is the bodhisattva’s short-term embrace of sentient beings?
It should be understood that when bodhisattvas provide assistance and benefit to sentient beings who abide in a state of middling maturation,
this is called "short-term inclusion," because they do not become fit for purification until after a long period of time has passed.
What is the final gathering-in of sentient beings by bodhisattvas?
It refers to the gathering-in and benefiting of those sentient beings who abide in the highest degree of maturity.
One should know that this is called "final inclusion," because it is capable of purification within this very life. Thus,
there are briefly six kinds of unerring inclusion of sentient beings by a bodhisattva.
By virtue of this inclusion,
past, future, and present bodhisattvas have correctly included,
will correctly include, and are currently correctly including all sentient beings.
Beyond this, there is nothing superior or additional.
When a bodhisattva thus engages in the six kinds of gathering sentient beings in an unerring manner,
it should be known that they encounter, in brief, twelve kinds of difficult circumstances.
The wise bodhisattva should correctly awaken to those twelve difficult matters.
What are the twelve?
First, regarding sentient beings who frequently abide in transgressions.
Whether it be punishment or abandonment,
these are called the hardships encountered by a bodhisattva;
second, for the sake of subduing malevolent sentient beings.
To employ skillful means and engage in arduous practices in order to prevent afflictions from arising within one's own mental disposition is called a bodhisattva encountering difficult circumstances.
Third, the objects currently available for giving are extremely scarce,
while those who come seeking them are exceedingly numerous;
this is called a bodhisattva encountering a difficult situation.
Fourth, there is only a single body,
yet the various activities of many sentient beings all manifest before it;
they come simultaneously to request that one act as their companion.
This is called a bodhisattva encountering difficult circumstances.
Fifth is dwelling in a state of negligence;
that is, if one abides in worldly, lovely, and sublime meditative concentrations.
If one is born in a heavenly realm of blissful worlds and causes the mind to become disciplined and virtuous,
this is called a bodhisattva encountering a difficult circumstance.
Sixth, constantly seeking to perform all manner of deeds for the benefit of sentient beings,
yet being without the strength or capability to do so—
this is called a bodhisattva encountering a difficult and distressing situation.
Seventh, when one either preaches the Dharma to or abandons sentient beings who are ignorant, deceitful, and stubborn,
this is called a bodhisattva encountering a difficult situation.
Eighth, constantly perceiving the great faults within birth and death,
yet not abandoning sentient beings for the sake of delivering them—
this is called a bodhisattva encountering difficult and perilous matters.
Ninth, when one has not yet realized the pure superior intention (*adhyāśaya*),
there is frequent apprehension that one might die with a distracted mind;
this is called a bodhisattva encountering a difficult circumstance.
Tenth, when one has not yet realized the pure superior intention (*adhyāśaya*),
and another comes to beg for the foremost and most excellent object of affection,
this is called a hardship encountered by a bodhisattva.
Eleventh, when bodhisattvas must either provide individual instruction or collectively abandon sentient beings who possess various differing views and various inclinations,
this is called a bodhisattva encountering a difficult situation.
Twelfth, while constantly practicing the most extreme form of heedfulness,
one should not sever all afflictions;
this is called a bodhisattva encountering a difficult situation.
In some cases, one should contemplate the relative gravity [of the offense] and apply skillful means as appropriate;
in other cases, one should carefully examine and discern the *pudgala*.
Or, within that state, one may take it as an object of focus;
through vigorous application and grasping, it proceeds as a cause,
provided that a correct aspiration is formed.
Or, within that state, one restrains the mind so that it does not wander;
or, one causes the mind to abide therein,
applying intense discernment without becoming weary, and thus maintains patient endurance.
In some cases, one practices relinquishment therein;
in others, one arouses diligent effort that is fervent and untiring;
and in yet others, one correctly practices through skillful means.
In this way, through skillful means in direct antidotes,
although a bodhisattva encounters all manner of hardships appearing before them,
they remain free from cowardice and are able to liberate themselves.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 48 and Fascicle 49,
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.

In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifteenth part of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, within the third section, the *Yogasthāna*, Chapter Three: "The Stages. Regarding the thirteen stages (*vihāra*) as previously described:
It should be understood that, according to that establishment, the first six of the seven stages are exclusively Bodhisattva stages,
while the seventh stage is both Bodhisattva and Tathāgata.
These are established collectively as stages.
What are the seven? First is the stage of the nature of the lineage (*gotrabhūmi*).
2. The stage of conduct through resolute belief;
3. The stage of purified superior intention; 4. The stage of practicing correct conduct;
5. The stage of certainty.
The sixth is the stage of definitive practice;
the seventh is the stage of reaching the ultimate.
Within these seven kinds of bodhisattva stages:
The last type is called the "Mixed Ground" (miśrabhūmi).
The first, the Abiding in the Spiritual Lineage (gotrastha), is called the "Ground of the Spiritual Lineage" (gotrabhūmi).
The Abiding in Conduct through Resolute Conviction (adhimukticaryā) is called the "Ground of Conduct through Resolute Conviction" (adhimukticaryābhūmi).
The stage of extreme joy is called the ground of pure superior intention;
it is the stage of higher ethics and the stage of higher mind.
The three types of abidings in superior wisdom—
the abiding in signlessness with application and effort—
are called the stage of practicing correct conduct.
The dwelling in signlessness, which is without application and without effort, is called the stage of certainty (*niyata-bhūmi*).
Because Bodhisattvas on this stage have entered the third certainty,
the dwelling in the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) is called the stage of certain conduct (*niyata-caryā-bhūmi*).
The supreme fulfillment of the bodhisattva stage and the stage of the Tathāgata is called the stage of ultimate attainment.
The stages of the Tathāgata’s dwelling will be explained in detail later in the chapter on the Establishment of the Buddha-dharma.
[This begins] from the stage of practice through resolute belief.
When entering the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*), how does one transcend the evil destinies and so forth?
The answer is: these bodhisattvas rely upon mundane pure meditative concentration (*laukika-śuddha-dhyāna*).
Having already well accumulated the provisions for enlightenment on the stage of conduct through aspiration,
he cultivates compassion toward the aforementioned one hundred and ten types of suffering sentient beings, without any other thought.
By virtue of having cultivated this as a causal condition,
one attains a disposition of compassion and a disposition of pity toward those sentient beings of that same class.
For this reason, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings in the evil destinies,
they vow to dwell in those evil destinies as if in their own homes,
making this solemn declaration:
If I were to dwell only in such a place,
I would be able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and I would also be able to endure it.
For the sake of eliminating the suffering of all sentient beings,
[he] purifies all the karmic actions leading to the evil destinies of all sentient beings through a pure intention.
They make a correct aspiration with their minds, wishing that they themselves might take upon themselves the ripening fruits of suffering for those beings,
so that all evil karma may never again manifest and all virtuous karma may constantly be practiced until the ultimate end.
By virtue of cultivating such worldly, pure meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), compassion, and the power of aspiration,
all the heavy burdens (*dausthulya*) belonging to the category of afflictions within the various evil destinies [are eliminated].
He completely eliminates [the afflictions] based upon his own support.
Because of this abandonment, the bodhisattva will before long attain the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti),
and will ultimately never again commit any unwholesome karma that leads to the evil destinies.
They will certainly not go to any of the evil destinies.
Up to this point, a bodhisattva is said to have "transcended all evil destinies" and is also said to have "transcended the stage of practice through resolute belief."
This is also called "having entered the stage of pure superior intention.
As explained in the previous Chapter on Abiding, it refers to the ten dharmas— such as faith and the rest—
that are able to purify and cultivate all the stages of abiding.
Now, within this context, one should know that it is also capable of purifying and cultivating the stages.
Thus, regarding the establishment of these ten dharmas,
the brief meaning of both the objects to be remedied and the remedies, as well as their sequential order, should all be understood.
Those ten methods for purifying the stages serve as antidotes;
because they counteract those factors to be remedied, they are established. What are these ten?
That is to say: having not yet generated the mind [of awakening] in any respect whatsoever,
and not yet having undertaken the bodhisattva training rules in any respect whatsoever—
this is called the factor that is the antithesis of faith.
To counteract that, one establishes oneself in faith.
A mind that intends harm toward sentient beings is what is called the state opposed by compassion.
To counteract that, compassion is established toward all sentient beings who possess a mind of malice.
These are called the factors to be countered by loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Loving-kindness is established as the antidote to them;
it is that which is free from attachment to one's body, life, or wealth.
This is called the state opposed to equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Because it is the antidote to that [opposition], one establishes oneself in equanimity;
toward all sentient beings, one seeks their gratitude in return.

Seeing that those who engage in wrong conduct and are attached to gain and honor have many activities, [the Buddha] established non-lassitude as the antidote to that which is characterized by weariness; it is the counteractive factor for such states.
Therefore, non-lassitude is established as the remedy for them.
The absence of skillful application of means is the factor to be counteracted by proficiency in treatises; therefore,
proficiency in treatises is established as its antidote.
His nature is not gentle and harmonious;
he does not act in accordance with the minds of others.
This is called skillfully knowing all the phenomena of the world that are to be counteracted.
To counteract that, one establishes the thorough knowledge of all the world;
laxity and indolence regarding the cultivation of wholesome dharmas are called the factors to be countered by shame and dread.
To counteract that, one establishes a sense of shame and dread of blame;
one develops a profound sense of timidity and weakness toward the various, intense, uninterrupted, and continuous great sufferings of saṃsāra over a long period of time.
One should know that these are the factors to be countered by the nature of firm power and maintenance (*dṛḍhabalapratisthānatā*).
It is for the sake of counteracting them that the nature of firm power and maintenance is established.
[These factors consist of] hesitation and doubt regarding the Great Teacher.
One should know that this is called the dharma to be countered by the offering to the Tathāgata.

Because it serves as the antidote to that [dharma], the offering to the Tathāgata is established. Thus, for the time being, ten dharmas have been set forth as the objects to be countered and their respective antidotes.
Such is the summary of the meaning:
these ten dharmas briefly manifest two points.
The first is the manifestation of the purity of intention (*āśaya*).
The second demonstrates the purity of application (*prayoga*).
It should be understood that the first three demonstrate the purity of the bodhisattva’s intention (*āśaya*),
while the remaining seven demonstrate the purity of the bodhisattva’s application.
First, one possesses profound and pure faith in awakening;
next, one gives rise to compassion for all sentient beings who are suffering;
and when such compassion arises, one makes this vow:
"I should deliver all sentient beings and bring them to peace and happiness," thus he gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
Having given rise to a mind of loving-kindness, he is able to relinquish everything— his body, life, and wealth.
He is without attachment.
Being without attachment, he applies himself with diligent effort toward that goal without weariness.
Being without weariness, he becomes well-versed in all treatises.
Having thoroughly understood the treatises, one understands the world just as it revolves in the world; having thus understood the world,
if one's own afflictions should suddenly manifest, one feels deep shame and remorse.
Having developed a sense of shame and remorse, one no longer acts under the sway of the afflictions and is thus able to attain a nature of firm fortitude.
By attaining this nature of firm fortitude, [one proceeds].
One is able to remain irreversible in correct application;
immeasurable wholesome qualities increase more and more;
and one is able to offer the Tathāgata the supreme offerings of correct practice, as well as material and reverential offerings.
Therefore, making the final offering to the Tathāgata is called the sequential cultivation and realization of the ten dharmas.
One should know that these are the ten kinds of wholesome dharmas.
One is able to purify and cultivate [the path] throughout all stages.

Chapter Four: The Chapter on Conduct, within the Fifteenth Stage of the Bodhisattva in the *Maulī Bhūmi*, the Third Section on the Ultimate Yoga Station. From the stage of conduct through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) onwards, the bodhisattva...
Up until the final ultimate stage,
one should know that throughout all these bodhisattva stages,
there are briefly four types of bodhisattva conduct.
What are the four?
First, the practice of the pāramitās;
second, the practice of the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Third is the practice of supernormal powers;
fourth is the practice of maturing sentient beings;
and [the fifth is] the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
And the perfection of skillful means,
the perfection of aspiration,
and the perfection of power.
The perfection of wisdom.
These ten kinds of perfections are collectively termed the practice of the perfections (*pāramitācaryā*).
The skillful means consisting of the twelve aspects previously described should be known as the perfection of skillful means (*upāyakauśalyapāramitā*).
As for the five kinds of great vows previously described:
One should know that the purity of the application of the ten powers is called the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā).
One should know that the purity of the application of the ten powers is called the perfection of power (bala-pāramitā).
The pure, sublime wisdom that establishes all phenomena as they truly are should be known as the perfection of wisdom (*jñānapāramitā*).
Within this context, it is able to apprehend the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The pure, sublime wisdom that functions without conceptual differentiation should be known as the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*);
it is the pure, sublime knowledge that can apprehend the conventional [truth] which functions with conceptual differentiation.
One should know this as the perfection of knowledge (*jñāna-pāramitā*).
These are called the two types of distinctions.
Furthermore, there is another method of exposition.
It refers to immeasurable wisdom;
one should know that this is called the perfection of skillful means (upāyakauśalyapāramitā),
characterized by the pursuit of ever-increasing excellence in subsequent knowledge.
One should know that this is the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā).
That the nature of the path cannot be destroyed by any māras or adversaries,
one should know that this is the perfection of power (bala-pāramitā).
One realizes the nature of the objects of knowledge as they truly are,
abiding in all thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, such as the foundations of mindfulness,
as well as the four modes of thorough investigation and the four kinds of correct cognition.
All are as previously explained;
collectively, these are termed the bodhisattva’s practice of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma). This is the general [classification].
This is called the supernormal power of psychic travel.
First, the realms of those to be disciplined are immeasurable;
second, the realms of the skillful means for disciplining them are immeasurable.
And as explained in the Chapter on Maturation:
all maturation of sentient beings is collectively termed the bodhisattva’s practice of maturing sentient beings.
It should be understood that these four kinds of sublime conduct of bodhisattvas universally encompass all the virtuous practices performed by bodhisattvas;
one should know that within this context, there are ten dharmas, beginning with generosity.
Having practiced for a long duration throughout three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one then realizes it perfectly;
therefore, its essence of natural purity is preeminent.
Therefore, they surpass all other roots of virtue belonging to the world, the śrāvakas, and the pratyekabuddhas,
and thereby embrace the most supreme fruit of awakening;
thus, these ten dharmas can only be fully realized after an extremely long period of time.
Because its intrinsic nature is supremely pure and sublime,
and it is able to attain the supreme fruit of excellent enlightenment,
it is therefore called a *pāramitā*.
It should be understood that these pāramitās are established in their successive order by way of three causes.
What are these three?
First, by way of the antidote;
second, by way of arising;
and third, by way of the ripening fruit.
How are these pāramitās established in their successive order by way of their respective antidotes?
Namely: stinginess, misconduct, resentment and affliction toward sentient beings, laziness, distraction, and dullness and delusion.
These six factors can obstruct awakening.
The six factors beginning with generosity serve as their remedies;
accordingly, the six perfections (pāramitās) are established.
It should be understood that the remaining perfections are subsumed within these;
this is called their establishment in sequence by way of their antidotes.
How, then, are these perfections established in sequence by way of their arising?
This means that bodhisattvas first have no attachment to wealth or status;
they renounce household life and all sensual desires to receive pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Because they revere the precepts, they are able to endure the harm inflicted by others and do not cause harm to others.
Having undertaken and maintained the pure precepts and cultivated patience,
their ethical discipline is pure, unshakable, uninterrupted, and continuous;
they then diligently apply themselves to the practice of all categories of wholesome qualities.
By thus cultivating diligent effort, one becomes free from all negligence and is able to touch upon the sublime state of one-pointedness of mind.
Because the mind has attained concentration, one understands things as they truly are.
One should know that observing all objects of knowledge is termed "established by way of arising. How, then,
are these pāramitās established by way of the sequence of their maturation fruits?
This means that when bodhisattvas diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas such as generosity in the present life,
by virtue of these causes and conditions,
they will in future lives obtain all manner of excellent external wealth and treasures, none of which will fail to be complete.
One should know that the attainment of the five internal perfections of the self-body is produced by the causal power of this perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā);
the others are produced by the causal power of the remaining perfections, such as ethical discipline (śīla) and so forth.
What is the internal perfection of the five aggregates?
It refers to being included within the happy realms, whether as a deva or a human,
possessing a lifespan and other qualities that are superior to those of other sentient beings.
One should know that this is called the first perfection.
If one possesses innate [virtue],
one will never grow weary of constant application to what is wholesome.
Being able to endure the afflictions of others and taking no pleasure in afflicting them—
know that this is called the second perfection.
If these qualities are innate, [they are even more excellent].
One should know that being firm and courageous in all undertakings whatsoever is called the third perfection;
it is that which is innate.
One whose nature is thin in defilement is able to exercise mastery over one's own mind;
with a mind possessed of capability, one swiftly realizes supernormal knowledge regarding all objects.
It should be known that this is called the fourth perfection.
If there is innate wisdom that is vast, keen, and sharp regarding all objects of knowledge,
one should know that this is called the fifth perfection.
It should be understood that this is called the sequential establishment of these six perfections by way of their maturation results (*vipākaphala*),
as well as their equipment (*sambhāra*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), retinue (*parivāra*), and protection (*rakṣā*).
One should know that the training in higher ethics of all bodhisattvas is fulfilled by means of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
One should know that the training in higher mind of all bodhisattvas is fulfilled by means of the same.
By means of this *prajñāpāramitā*,
one should know that the bodhisattvas' training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*) is brought to fulfillment;
beyond these three trainings, no further path of bodhisattva training can be found.
Therefore, these three universally encompass the entire path of training for all bodhisattvas;
it is on this basis that the pāramitās are established as being exactly six in number.
Beyond this, there is nothing further or superior.
Furthermore, there are briefly four kinds of tasks that a bodhisattva ought to perform,
by which all activities are universally subsumed.
What are the four?
First, practicing all virtuous deeds in order to realize bodhi;
second, by means of this as a prerequisite, attaining the true meaning.
Third is the power of perfect realization;
fourth is the maturation of sentient beings.
These are the four types of activities performed by a bodhisattva.
It should be understood that these four modes previously explained are established according to their respective purposes and sequences; therefore,
beyond these, no further modes are established.

Chapter Five, Part One: The Establishment of the Stages, within the Fifteenth Stage of the Bodhisattva in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the Main Section, specifically the Third Station of Ultimate Yoga based on the Abodes of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, based on the Tathāgatas reaching the ultimate stage,
the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess one hundred and forty unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
These refer to the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) possessed by all Tathāgatas.
The eighty minor marks,
the four kinds of purity in all aspects,
and the ten powers.
The four fearlessnesses,
the three foundations of mindfulness,
and the three ways in which he needs no protection.
Great compassion, the quality of non-forgetfulness,
the permanent destruction of habitual tendencies,
and the sublime wisdom of all modes.
Regarding the marks:
first, he possesses the mark of a great man’s feet being well-settled and level with the ground;
this is a mark of a great man among great men.
Second, on the soles of his two feet there appear wheels with a thousand spokes,
whose hubs, rims, and all other characteristics are perfectly complete.
Third, he possesses the mark of a great man’s long and slender fingers.
Fourth, his heels and insteps are long.
Fifth, his hands and feet are slender and soft.
Sixth, his hands and feet have webbed fingers and toes.
Seventh, when standing, his hands reach his knees.
Eighth, his calves are like those of the eneya antelope.
Ninth, his body is not hunched.
Tenth, his male organ is concealed within a sheath.
Eleventh, his physical form is perfectly proportioned like that of the nyagrodha tree.
Twelfth, he possesses a constant radiance extending one fathom.
Thirteenth, the body hairs slant upward.
Fourteenth, from each and every pore of the body grows a single hair,
which is deep blue in color like sapphire and curls to the right in a spiral pattern.
Fifteenth, his body skin is golden in color.
Sixteenth, his body skin is fine and smooth, such that dust and grime do not adhere to it.
Seventeenth, seven parts of his body—the two hands, the two feet, the two shoulders, and the nape of the neck—are all well-filled.
Eighteenth, the upper half of his body is like that of a lion king.
Nineteenth, his shoulders are well-rounded and full.
Twentieth, the area between his shoulder blades is well-filled.
Twenty-first, his body parts are large and straight.
Twenty-second, he possesses forty teeth, all of which are perfectly even.
Twenty-third, there are no gaps between his teeth.
Twenty-fourth, his teeth are bright white.
Twenty-fifth, his jaw is like that of a lion.
Twenty-sixth, his tongue is broad and thin.
Twenty-seventh: that which issues from his mouth covers his entire face, including the perimeter of his hair.
Twenty-eighth: he attains the supreme sense of taste among all flavors.
Twenty-ninth: he attains the great Brahma-voice.
His speech was sorrowful yet elegant, capable of gladdening the minds of the multitude;
it was like the song of the kalaviṅka bird,
and its resonance thundered like a celestial drum.
Twenty-ninth, his eyes are deep blue.
Thirtieth, his eyelashes are like those of a bull king.
Thirty-first, the uṣṇīṣa appears upon the crown of his head.
The thirty-second is the mark between the eyebrows consisting of a tuft of hair, white in color and radiant, with a spiral pattern turning to the right.
This is a mark of a Great Man among great men.
What are the eighty secondary marks of the Tathāgata?
That is to say, the two hands and two feet possess twenty fingers, as well as their joints and nails;
all of these are exceptionally exquisite,
and this is what is called the twenty secondary marks (anuvyañjana).
The eight locations— the two hands, the two feet,
and the four surfaces [of the palms and soles]— are all exceptionally sublime;
these are what are known as the eight secondary marks (aṣṭānuvyañjana).
The six locations—the two ankles, knees, and thighs—are exquisite;
these are called the six secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*).
The six locations—the two upper arms, elbows, and wrists—are likewise exquisite.
These are what are called the six secondary marks (anuvyañjana).
The exquisite seam at the waist is one secondary mark;
the two exquisite testicles are two secondary marks.
The excellence of the male organ concealed within a sheath is one secondary mark (anuvyañjana).
The excellence of the two buttocks is a second secondary mark.
The excellence of the hips, the chest, and the navel—these three—are each a single secondary mark.
The two sides of the torso, the armpits, and the breasts are all exceptionally sublime, constituting six secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*).
The abdomen, chest, neck, and spine each constitute one secondary mark.
Thus it is said.
Excluding those above the neck,
there are sixty secondary marks (anuvyañjana) on the lower part of the body;
the upper and lower rows of teeth, both being exceptionally exquisite, constitute two of these secondary marks.
The palate being exceptionally exquisite constitutes one minor mark;
the two lips and their surrounding areas being all exceptionally exquisite constitute two minor marks;
and the chin being well-rounded constitutes one minor mark.
The two cheeks, being full and well-proportioned, constitute two secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*).
The two eyes and their surrounding features, all being exceptionally exquisite, constitute two secondary marks.
The two eyebrows, being exceptionally exquisite, constitute two secondary marks.
The two nostrils of his nose are both exceptionally exquisite, constituting two secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*).
His forehead is exceptionally exquisite, constituting one secondary mark.
His brow-ridges and both ears are all exceptionally exquisite, constituting four secondary marks.
The excellence of the hair is one secondary mark (*anuvyañjana*).
Thus it is said;
these are the twenty secondary marks from the neck upward.
There are sixty in the front and twenty in the back;
taken together, they are called the eighty secondary marks (anuvyañjana).
Such are these primary marks (lakṣaṇa) and secondary marks.
When bodhisattvas first enter the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*), they have already attained maturation (*vipāka*);
from this point upward, their primary marks and secondary signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) progressively attain ever more sublime purity.
It should be known that one must sit upon the seat of enlightenment before realizing all other uncommon Buddha-qualities, such as the four kinds of perfect purity in every respect.
It is perfectly pure and complete;
even those of inferior capacity have already accomplished it prior to becoming bodhisattvas,
beginning from the stage of the pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*).
All the requisites for enlightenment (bodhipakṣa) are without distinction in their capacity to bring about all the primary marks (lakṣaṇa) and secondary signs (anuvyañjana).
Furthermore, these requisites for enlightenment are, in brief, of two kinds.
This refers to being either distant from or near to enlightenment.
In this context, "distant" refers to the time when one has not yet obtained the maturation fruits of the primary marks and secondary signs.
What is called "proximate" refers to the time when one first attains the maturation fruits of the primary marks and secondary signs,
or the successive attainment of increasingly superior purity beyond that point.
Furthermore, by the power of those to be converted,
the Bhagavat proclaimed to the assembly that the performance of various karmas brings about such fruits as these marks and secondary characteristics. Why is this so?
The sentient beings to be converted take deep delight in the performance of various types of unwholesome karma;
such various performances of unwholesome karma are what is to be counteracted.
The various virtuous karmas associated with the primary marks and secondary signs are their antidotes.
Upon hearing of such various, supreme, great fruits and benefits,
they develop a profound sense of love and delight for these great fruits and benefits.
For this reason, one should abandon all evils and cultivate all virtues. Therefore,
it is taught at length as explained in the *Lakṣaṇa-sūtra*.
It means that because bodhisattvas are well-established in ethical discipline, ascetic observances, patience, and generosity,
they obtain the mark of feet that are well-placed;
and because they have made various offerings to their parents.
By providing various forms of protection from the manifold sufferings and afflictions of all sentient beings through the karma of coming and going and other movements,
one attains the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of the feet.
One should refrain from harming other sentient beings and from taking what is not given.
Toward one's elders and superiors, one should first offer greetings and inquiries,
and practice acts of harmony and respect by paying homage, prostrating, joining the palms, and rising to welcome them.
Because he felt deep affection for others and ensured that they were not deprived of the wealth and status they cherished and loved,
and because he was able to subdue his own pride,
he attained the mark of a Great Man characterized by long, slender fingers.
The aforementioned karma that produces the three marks collectively brings about the length of the heels and the insteps,
because these are the bases upon which those three marks depend.
By gathering all elders and superiors through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*),
one thereby attains hands and feet with webbed fingers and toes;
this results from offering elders and superiors unguents for the body, massage, bathing, and clothing.
Therefore, one attains hands and feet that are delicate and soft.
By practicing various wholesome dharmas without becoming complacent,
one causes all wholesome dharmas to increase progressively.
Therefore, he has attained the physical mark of hands reaching down to his knees;
he personally upholds the True Dharma as it truly is, bringing it to ultimate fulfillment,
extensively teaching it to others, and properly acting as a skillful servant for them.
Therefore, one perceives the *cīnakya* feet;
because the continuous cord revolves, the True Dharma is gradually and equally revealed therein.
They are able to cease all various unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind.
Toward those who are ill, they serve with humility, providing excellent medicines;
when the strength of the sick has failed and they are exhausted, they are able to properly support and uplift them.
Knowing moderation in food and drink, he never succumbed to the various desires;
therefore, he obtained a body that was not hunched.
Toward sentient beings who had been expelled by others and were without refuge...
By means of the Dharma and the Right Path, one gathers others through compassion;
by cultivating a sense of shame and dread of blame, one gives clothing to others.
Therefore, one attains the secret organ concealed within a sheath like a mountain peak.
He is able to restrain himself in body, speech, and mind;
he knows the proper measure regarding his own possessions and all food and drink;
he provides medicine for the sick; and he engages in activities that counteract imbalance.
Furthermore, they do not conform to any unequal or improper enjoyments;
rather, they can bring about harmony among the conflicting elements of the constituents (*dhātu*).
Therefore, they attain a physical form as perfect as that of the *nyagrodha* tree, and by the power of karma, they attain the mark of standing with their hands reaching their knees.
One will thereby be able to obtain the following: the hairs of one's body will all point upward;
one will naturally observe well and draw near to those of clear wisdom to contemplate subtle meanings;
and one will be able to purify, repair, arrange, and bathe the dwelling place of one’s honored teacher.
Because it is the sole abiding, because it relies on a single factor, because it enters into the meaning of subtlety,
because it can eliminate impurities such as grass and leaves,
and because it can further remove adventitious defilements.
He perceived that each hair-pore of his body produced a single hair, deep blue in color like sapphire and curling to the right like a conch shell.
He was able to bestow pleasing and joy-inducing offerings such as food, drink, vehicles, clothing, ornaments, and other articles for the maintenance of the body.
Being free from all anger and resentment,
he thus attained a golden-colored body with a constant radiance extending one fathom.
By virtue of this karma, a single hair grew from each and every pore of his body.
It should be known that this very [merit] can further bring about a body with skin so fine and smooth that dust and grime do not adhere to it,
by means of providing vast quantities of excellent, sublime, and pure food and drink.
By bestowing gifts so as to satisfy the great multitude,
one thereby attains the mark of the seven parts of the body being full;
this arises in accordance with [the merit] produced toward all sentient beings.
Acting in accordance with the Dharma, they serve as leaders and companions;
free from pride and devoid of all harshness,
they are able to restrain sentient beings from what is unbeneficial and establish them in what is beneficial.
By this, he attains an upper body like that of a lion king;
because his nature is courageous and decisive in all matters like a lion,
one should know that through this very karma he further attains well-rounded shoulders and a full space between the shoulder blades.
By this karma, one acquires the mark of long, slender fingers;
furthermore, one attains well-proportioned and upright limbs,
and remains far removed from all speech that causes the destruction of friendships or sows discord.
If there are sentient beings who have become estranged, he is able to bring them into harmony;
by this, he attains forty teeth that are all perfectly even and without any gaps between them.
He cultivated loving-kindness toward the realm of desire and contemplated the meaning of the Dharma;
by this, he attained teeth that were bright white.
If there are sentient beings who have hopes and aspirations, [he fulfills them].
According to their inclinations, he rightly relinquished his precious wealth;
by this, he attained a jaw like that of a lion and came to regard all sentient beings as his own children.
Through cherishing, protecting, pure faith, and compassionate pity,
and by providing medicine that is clear, pure, and free from defilement,
one thereby attains the supreme sense of taste among all flavors.
Because they bestow the flavor of the Dharma and because they taste the flavor of the Dharma,
they are able to purify and cultivate themselves by transforming and abandoning worldly flavors;
thus, they are able to personally undertake and maintain the protection of the five precepts, beginning with the abstention from killing.
Furthermore, because he exhorted others to receive and cultivate a compassionate mind,
and because he was able to practice correctly regarding the reception of the Great Dharma,
he attained as a result the appearance of an *uṣṇīṣa* upon his crown and a tongue that is broad and thin, capable of covering the entire circle of his face.
He constantly cultivates truthful speech, pleasant speech, timely speech, and speech in accordance with the Dharma.

By reason of these causes and conditions, he attains the great Brahma-voice; his words are mournful and elegant, capable of gladdening the minds of the multitude, like the song of the kalaviṅka bird, and his voice resounds like the thundering of celestial drums.
By constantly cultivating a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward all in the world, like a father or a mother,
he attained eyes that are deep blue with eyelashes like those of a bull king.
By truthfully praising and extolling the virtues of those who possess them,
one attains the mark of the ūrṇā-kośa between the eyebrows, which is white in color and spirals to the right like a conch shell.
In this way, all thirty-two marks of a great man are without distinction;
one should know that they are all brought about by taking pure ethical discipline as their cause.
Why is this? If bodhisattvas violate the pure precepts,
they will not even obtain a human body of lowly status.
How much more so for those that can evoke the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa)?
One should know that herein, the uṣṇīṣa appears upon the crown of the head,
as well as the Tathāgata’s mark of the invisible crown.
These are combined to establish a single mark of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*),
for apart from these, nothing else can be found.
Thus, we have briefly explained the various karmic causes that bring about the thirty-two marks which correspond to them.
Having established this extensively,
next, to speak briefly, there are four types of well-cultivated activities belonging to bodhisattvas of both the lay and monastic divisions.
It should be known that these are capable of bringing about all the marks and signs of physical excellence.
That is to say, within this context,
there is a definitive cultivation and practice that can bring about the mark of the soles of the feet being well-settled; through thorough and detailed cultivation and practice,
one can bring about the mark of the thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of the feet.
Standing with his hands reaching his knees;
his hands and feet are webbed;
and his body skin is fine and smooth.
The seven parts of his body are all full;
his shoulders are well-rounded and his upper arms are fleshy and firm;
his limbs are large and straight.
His tongue is broad and thin;
by constantly practicing [this], he attains slender and long fingers,
and his heels and insteps are elongated.
His body is not hunched;
it is perfectly rounded like a nyagrodha tree.
His teeth have no gaps between them.
Faultless cultivation can bring about other marks;
one should know that herein, there is no harmful application toward sentient beings.
By this, one is able to bring about hands and feet that are delicate and soft, and skin that is fine and smooth;
among all wholesome deeds, one applies oneself through successive stages and at the appropriate time.
By this, one attains calves like those of the eneya antelope;
one gives rise to deep joy and practices all virtues with a mind of supreme luminous purity.
By this, one attains a body that constantly emits light for a fathom, skin the color of gold, teeth that are bright white, and a white tuft of hair between the eyebrows.
One cultivates virtue without relying on praise, fame, or verse, and conceals one's own merits;
by this, one is able to bring about the concealment of the male organ within a sheath.
One dedicates the roots of virtue thus cultivated toward enlightenment.

By this, he attains the mark of body hairs curling upward, possesses forty teeth that are all perfectly even, attains the supreme sense of taste among all flavors, and has the *uṣṇīṣa* appear upon his crown.
He practices wholesome deeds with tireless and undaunted application;
by this, he acquires a body whose upper portion is like the jaw of a lion king,
and he gazes upon all sentient beings with an eye of equanimity and a mind intent on their benefit.
His teeth are even and level, his eyes are deep blue, and his eyelashes are like those of a bull king.

Because he does not find satisfaction in inferior virtues but gives rise to superior application, by this cause and condition he attains the voice of Great Brahmā—his speech is mournful and elegant, capable of gladdening the minds of all beings.
It is like the voice of the kalaviṅka bird, its resonance thundering like a celestial drum.
By thus properly cultivating these four kinds of activities,
one can attain the thirty-two marks of a great man, which are exceptionally sublime and pure.
It should be known that these thirty-two marks of a great man and eighty secondary characteristics exist within the bodhisattva while in the stage of the lineage (gotrabhūmi) merely as seeds,
abiding in dependence upon the physical body.
If a bodhisattva is on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*),
they are first able to cultivate the skillful means for attaining that [result].
If a bodhisattva is on the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*), [they have already attained it].
This is what is called "attainment.
If a bodhisattva is in any of the other higher stages,
such marks and signs become increasingly superior and pure.
If one has reached the ultimate stage as a Tathāgata,
it should be known that the marks and signs are perfectly pure and unsurpassed;
since these various marks are material in nature, they consist of inferior, middling, and superior grades.
Because they are easy for all classes of sentient beings to understand,
although all the unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma) could be termed the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa),
these alone are established as the marks of a Great Man.
Furthermore, these thirty-two marks of a great man are so called because they are capable of being sustained by their respective bases,
and because they bring about supreme excellence and physical majesty.
These are called the secondary marks (anuvyañjana).
Furthermore, to state the essential point here:
they are equal in measure to the mass of merit of all sentient beings.
The mass of merit required to produce a single pore of the Tathāgata is equal to the mass of merit that enters into all his pores;
the mass of merit required to produce one of the Tathāgata’s secondary marks (anuvyañjana) is equal to that same measure.
Furthermore, all the accumulations of merit associated with every single secondary mark increase a hundredfold;
such an accumulation of merit can bring about a single major mark of a Tathāgata.
Furthermore, all other marks, with the exception of the *ūrṇā-kośa* and the *uṣṇīṣa*, enter into this accumulation of merit,
increasing it a thousandfold.
The mass of merit from that [act] is capable of producing the white tuft of hair between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows;
furthermore, as the white tuft of hair itself enters into that mass of merit,
it increases by a hundred-thousandfold.
The mass of merit from that [act] is capable of evoking the Tathāgata’s crown-protrusion (uṣṇīṣa) and the mark of the invisible crown,
up to and including the mass of merit that follows into the white tuft of hair (ūrṇā).
When increased a hundred thousand times ten millionfold,
that mass of merit can bring about the mark of the great Dharma-conch, which is not included among the Tathāgata’s primary marks and secondary signs.
By means of this Dharma conch, the Tathāgata, according to his will,
emits a great sound that can universally proclaim [the teaching] to all sentient beings to be converted throughout boundless and limitless worlds.
Thus, having brought to perfection the cultivation and realization of immeasurable accumulations of merit,
one is able to manifest a self-body that is inconceivable, unsurpassed, peerless, and comprised of the most ultimate perfection in every respect, as attained by a Tathāgata.
Furthermore, it should be understood that these immeasurable virtuous karmas which bring about the primary marks and secondary signs are called "immeasurable" for three brief reasons:
namely, because they are practiced throughout three incalculable great eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Because it is fully realized through uninterrupted cultivation,
it is called "immeasurable in time.
It is so named because it is accomplished through the dominant condition of the superior intention to bring about immeasurable benefit and happiness for all sentient beings.
It is called "Infinite Sublime Intention" because it is accumulated from the various categories of infinite virtuous karma; thus,
it is called "infinite in its constituent factors."
Therefore, it is said that the complete realization through the cultivation of immeasurable stores of merit and wisdom gives rise to the primary marks and secondary signs of a Tathāgata;
this is the purification of the basis for all aspects.
Second is the purification of the object of focus in all its aspects;
third is the purification of the mind in all its aspects;
and fourth is the purification of wisdom in all its aspects.
What is the purification of the basis for all aspects?
It refers to the permanent and complete extinction, without remainder, of all heavy impediments belonging to the category of afflictions,
along with their habitual tendencies, within one's own basis.
Furthermore, regarding one's own body, one exercises mastery over its appropriation,
maintenance, and relinquishment according to one's own wishes;
this is called the purification of the basis in all its aspects.
What is the purification of the object of focus in all its aspects?
It refers to exercising mastery over all objects of focus—whether they be emanated, transformed, or manifested—in their various forms.
This is called the purification of the object of focus in all its aspects.
What is the purification of the mind in all its aspects?
It refers to the permanent elimination and separation from all mental coarseness (*dausthulya*), as previously described.
Furthermore, because all types of roots of goodness are accumulated within the mind,
this is called the purity of the mind in every respect.
What is the purity of omniscience in every respect?
This means that, as previously described, because all the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) associated with the category of ignorance have been eternally extinguished and abandoned,
his wisdom functions with unimpeded mastery throughout the entirety of all objects of knowledge.
This is called the purity of the knowledge of all modes.
What are the ten powers of the Tathāgata?
The first is the power of the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible.
Second is the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma;
third is the power of knowledge regarding dhyāna, vimokṣa, samādhi, and samāpatti;
fourth is the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties.
Fifth, the power of knowledge regarding various inclinations;
sixth, the power of knowledge regarding various elements;
seventh, the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere.
Eighth is the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of past abodes.
Ninth is the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth.
Tenth is the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava*).
These ten kinds of Tathāgata’s powers of knowledge should be understood in detail as they are explained in the *Daśabala-sūtra*.
It should be understood that whatever is expressed, spoken, or proclaimed herein [is based upon them].
Because all things are as they truly are and entirely devoid of falsehood, he is called the Tathāgata.
Pure and impure fruits do not arise from causes that are unequal;
rather, they proceed from causes in accordance with reality.
This is called the "basis" (sthāna);
it is also called "establishment" (vyavasthāna), "support" (āśraya), and "arising" (utthāna).
The inequality of causes for pure and impure fruits—
contrary to what has been stated above— is called "impossible.
Knowledge that is free from all overweening pride (adhimāna) is called "suchness" (yathābhūta).
Whether it be omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), unimpeded knowledge (*apratihata-jñāna*), or pure knowledge (*viśuddha-jñāna*),
one should know that these are designated as the knowledge that is free from all overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Such is the case for all these phrases, beginning with "omniscience."
It should be understood as previously explained in the "Chapter on the Most Ultimate Unsurpassed Bodhi.
It is called "first" because it occupies the very beginning of the numerical sequence and is unsurpassed.
Because it is endowed with the capacity to benefit all sentient beings in every way,
and because it possesses great power that ultimately and completely overcomes all Māras and adversaries, it is called a "power" (*bala*).
Because it embraces the causes for the perfect realization of reality as it truly is,
one is able to manifest and act with sovereign mastery according to one's desires;
therefore, it is called the attainment of supreme nirvāṇa.
It is called "Great" because it is unsurpassed;
for it is realized through the Noble Eightfold Path and is free from all calamities and fears.
It is called the exalted station of the Sages because they are able to personally realize what they have themselves attained;
thus it is termed "self-knowledge."
Having personally realized it, one extensively reveals and teaches it to sentient beings out of a heart of compassion;
therefore, it is called "turning the Brahma-wheel. Why is this so?
This refers to the designations of all Tathāgatas:
they are called "Brahmā," they are called "Tranquil," and they are also called "Cool."
At first it is able to turn;
from that point onward, one thing in turn becomes another for yet another.
Thus, through successive transmission, it is impelled and set in motion by Brahmā.
It is called the Brahma-wheel because it revolves among the entire assembly of sentient beings;
it is so named because it manifests itself as being included within the perfection of the Unsurpassed Great Teacher, who is established in the supreme state.
Because it can explain that path as the antidote to all other false paths;
because it is without cowardice when confronted by hostile arguments from adversaries regarding the path;
and because it seeks to overcome and subdue all other doctrines.
Because he proclaims the vast and unsurpassed treatise,
it is called the "Lion’s Roar in the midst of the Great Assembly.
To speak in brief:

It should be understood that herein are revealed, elucidated, designated, and demonstrated the fulfillment of one's own welfare, the fulfillment of the welfare of others, and the unique perfection of both one's own welfare and the welfare of others.
Furthermore, there is another formulation; this is the summary meaning therein.
This refers to the superior means for attaining what ought to be attained.
Regarding these superior means, all members of the assembly, whether gods or humans, may follow whatever they desire; all of them proceed from me.
Having attained this supreme skillful means,
like the healing of a disease,
one should know that this reveals the self-knowledge of having already attained the state of great peace and security.
Just as there are skillful means for curing that disease,
one should know that this reveals the turning of the Brahma-wheel;
it is like warding off all false physicians.
Having thus proclaimed himself,
he is certain to be able to cure all ailments;
one should know that this proclamation constitutes a true lion’s roar in the midst of the great assembly.
If there are various karmas that have already been performed, already accumulated, and already ceased, they are called "past.
If there are various karmas that have not been performed, have not been accumulated, and have not ceased,
and which are neither being performed now nor are yet to be performed, they are called "future."
If there are various karmas that have not yet been performed, accumulated, or extinguished, but are being performed, created, and undertaken, they are termed "present.
Furthermore, these various types of karma are further divided into three categories.
These are the actions of body, speech, and mind.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of conceptualization regarding the reception of dharmas,
as explained in detail previously.
That is to say, there are dharmas that, when undertaken, result in happiness in the present life but have a ripening of suffering in the future;
this is explained at length.
Furthermore, these various karmas differ in their preparatory application regarding whether they are beneficial or non-beneficial in the present life and in the future.
It should be understood accordingly:
if the location upon which an action is performed is designated as the "place" (sthāna);
and if the objective basis (vastu) upon which an action is performed consists of either sentient beings or non-sentient things.
This is called the "phenomenon" (vastu).
If the karma that is produced has unwholesome roots or wholesome roots as its causal conditions,
this is called the "cause" (hetu).
If the various fruits corresponding to desirable, undesirable, faulty, or meritorious results are produced by karma,
these are called maturation (*vipāka*).
This is a brief explanation of all time periods.
All categories,
all stages, all distinctions of application,
and all locations.
All bases, all causes and conditions,
and all faults and afflictions.
And as for their merits,
he knows all these various types and distinctions exactly as they truly are.
This is called the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding his own karma.
Beyond this, there is nothing superior or additional.
There are the four dhyānas and the eight liberations.
By means of such meditative absorptions and liberations,
the mind becomes capable and attains mastery;
thus, whatever one desires can be accomplished.

When one enters meditative absorption by following the specific characteristics of various types of samādhi, it should be understood that this is called "concentration" (samāhita) and "attainment" (samāpatti).
As it is said: "When the Blessed One entered meditative absorption by following the specific characteristics of such-and-such a type of samādhi..."
Just as his concentrated mind radiated a great light that universally illuminated all the Brahma worlds, he preached the Dharma with sublime sounds;
yet, though they heard his voice, they saw nothing at all.
This is explained at length.
In this way, the Tathāgata manifests various matters and meanings according to his will—
whether they pertain to the mundane or the supramundane—
and enters meditative absorption by means of the signs of samādhi corresponding to each such category.
One is able to accomplish it with great swiftness;
it should be understood that herein, by the power of dhyāna and vimokṣa,
the mind attains mastery.
Because of mastery over the mind, one relies upon the mind;
whatever is desired is accomplished accordingly.
Up to this point, it is called all that is to be done by one who cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Beyond this, there is nothing superior or additional.
The Tathāgata knows, exactly as they truly are, all the various types of activities performed within these meditative concentrations.
Therefore, only dhyāna, vimokṣa, samādhi, and samāpatti are taught.
Furthermore, to speak briefly, there are two kinds of defilements regarding these states of dhyāna and so forth:
first, the defilement of obstacles that hinder the attainment of what has not yet been attained.
That is to say: first, the application of lack of skillful means;
and second, the manifestation of any one of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), whereby one acquires the defilements (*saṃkleśa*) of one's own stage (*svabhūmi*) among those that ought to be attained.
This refers to the entanglements of the afflictions (*kleśa-paryavasthāna*) and their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
There are likewise four kinds of purification;
their characteristics should be understood as being the opposite of those mentioned above.
Furthermore, the various designations provisionally established for these meditative concentrations and so forth are appropriately assigned according to their respective categories;
this is called "establishment" (vyavasthāna).
Furthermore, having fully attained these various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and so forth,
one subsequently advances further until their cultivation is perfected;
thus, one attains whatever is desired without difficulty and without obstruction.
This is called purity.
Regarding this, the Tathāgata, as it has not yet been attained and as it has already been attained,
[discerns] whether that which has been attained is inferior or superior.
Whether it be those provisional designations or the ultimate limits of their development—
all such things he knows exactly as they are. Therefore,
it is said that the Tathāgata universally [knows] all meditative absorptions (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), concentrations (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti).
One attains unsurpassed wisdom.
Just as that which has been matured is fully realized through cultivation,
the five faculties— faith and the others— become weak, middling, and superior.
One should know that this is called the superiority or inferiority of the faculties.
It is preceded either by faith in others or by the contemplation of phenomena.
One should know that the attainment of soft, medium, or superior degrees of affectionate understanding and conviction is called "diverse inclinations" (*nānādhimukti*).
If one were to establish the various spiritual lineages (*gotra*) in detail:
Whether it be the spiritual lineage of the śrāvakas,
the spiritual lineage of the pratyekabuddhas,
or the spiritual lineage of the Tathāgatas.
There are various不定 (aniyata) dispositions,
or the principles of differentiation such as those of greed and other temperaments,
up to the eighty thousand types of conduct of sentient beings.
It should be understood that herein these are called the "various realms" (*nānādhātu*).
If one enters these various gates of rebirth in accordance with right practice— such as,
for example, a person of greedy temperament practicing the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*)— [this constitutes the realm].
As has been extensively explained in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*,
it should be understood that these are called the "paths leading everywhere.
Furthermore, there is another formulation.
This refers to the practices that lead to all five destinies;
one should know that these are called "practices leading everywhere.
Furthermore, there is another formulation.
This refers to various factions and categories that,
being mutually contradictory, hold distinct views,
have divergent desires, engage in contentious debate, and oppose one another.
The various types of non-Buddhists— namely, those among the śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who possess all manner of practices,
or any other distinct categories—
that constitute blameless courses of action leading to this world and the next.
One should know that these are called the "paths leading everywhere," as explained at length in the Kālāma Sūtra and other texts.
Regarding the various assemblies of sentient beings:
That is to say, regarding the directions of east,
south, west, and north, there are various names, provisional designations, established categories, and distinctions,
which follow all previous past self-entities.
Within the eight categories of distinctions in verbal expressions,
there are six types of concise practices for recollecting past lives;
these comprise immeasurable varieties of the recollection of former existences (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*).
What are called the eight bases of discourse?
They are: such a name, such a birth-class, such a lineage, and such food and drink.
In this way they experience the distinctions of pleasure and pain;
in this way they possess long life and abide for a long time;
such is the limit of their lifespan.
What are called the phrases that follow conventional expression?
There are six types of abbreviated practices:
first, the provisional designation of summoning.
Second, the distinction of caste classes, such as the kṣatriya and others;
third, the distinction of parents;
fourth, the rules for food and drink.
Fifth, the waxing and waning of prosperity;
sixth, the differentiation of lifespan.
It is by relying upon these eight modes of discourse and six types of concise practices that all worldly beings exist.
Regarding oneself and others, one gives rise to speech and utterances, saying:
"This is my name; that is his name.
I am a kṣatriya; he is a kṣatriya."
"I am a brahmin, a vaiśya, or a śūdra;
he is a brahmin, a vaiśya, or a śūdra.
This is my mother; that is his mother."
As it was said regarding his mother, so it was for his father as well:
"I ate food of such a kind,
namely, curd-milk, soup, rice, gruel, and so forth."
He partakes of such kinds of food and drink,
and so forth, as has been explained at length.
I likewise undergo such kinds of fluctuations in prosperity and decline.
Such are the variations of rise and fall that occur within these classes of forms;
such are the stages of age in which I abide—
namely, whether as a youth, in middle age, or as an elder.
He dwells at such an age and stage of life, and so forth,
as has been explained in detail;
he possesses only such a personal existence as previously existed in the past.
Among the various categories of the eight modes of verbal expression (*vyavahāra-pada*), there are six types of concise practice (*saṃkṣepa-caryā*).
Beyond these, there are no further modes of verbal expression or concise practices;
therefore, [these] exist only within such categories.
There is no further increase in the arousal of mindfulness;
within this very state, there are the modes of activity involved in verbal expression,
as well as the designations and utterances involved in verbal phrases.
Furthermore, one immediately gives rise to mindfulness regarding this;
therefore, it is said that one is able to recollect both the signs and the teachings.
Herein, meditative absorption (dhyāna) is called the "divine abode" (devasthāna) and the "eye."
Because it relies upon that, because it is its fruit,
and because it is sustained by that,
it is called the "divine eye."
Because it is the fruit of meditative concentration that is utterly perfect and thoroughly purified,
it is called "extremely pure.
Among human beings, none of their names are similar to it.
Therefore, it is said that they transcend humans.
Among the devas of the desire realm, there are also those born who attain a name similar to this;
however, such pure divine eyes do not exist even among humans.
When sentient beings are about to pass away, it is called the time of death;
when they abide in the intermediate state (antarābhava), it is called the time of birth.
Those who proceed toward darkness—
It arises from two characteristics;
such a mind-born intermediate state (antarābhava) is like the light of a black sheep or the darkness of a cloudy night.
It is called "unwholesome form.
That which leads toward clarity arises by way of two characteristics.
The mind-born intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of this kind is like a clear,
cloudless night or a most brilliant white garment from Vārāṇasī; therefore,
it is called "of beautiful color."
All unattractive forms are called inferior;
all beautiful forms...
That which is called "sublime" refers to those who are base and inferior;
they are said to go to the evil realms.
Those who are excellent and sublime are said to go to happy destinies.
All instances of impaired morality and that which arises from them are said to constitute the accomplishment of the three types of misconduct of body, speech, and mind.
There are two types of wrong views:
namely, the wrong view established by one who holds nihilistic views,
and the wrong view that consists of slandering all things while abiding in such an intention.
Those who hold wrong views resulting from such divergent categories and who slander the noble ones—
all such as these are called those who slander the noble ones.
Due to wrong view, one clings to false causes and false effects;
with this as a condition, one performs wrong karma.
Because of performing wrong karma, whatever dharmas are experienced may result in the experience of pleasure in the present life.
They will experience the ripening of suffering in future lives;
or they may experience suffering in the present life and experience the ripening of suffering in future lives.
For this reason, it is further stated that they give rise to the causes for experiencing the karmic phenomena of various wrong views.
Although they may have accomplished all other various wholesome dharmas,
they nevertheless go to the evil destinies solely by virtue of this;
therefore it is said that "by reason of this cause and condition."
Because the two factors of name-and-form are mutually separated,
it is called the "destruction of the body.
Among all forms of death, such is the death [of this kind].
Because it is the most extremely base,
it is called "ultimate death.
This is intended to reveal the perception of the hell realms (*naraka*).
Therefore, it is said that they fall into the perilous and evil destinies.
In order to reveal the essential nature and substance [of this],
it must further be explained that one goes to those *naraka* hells by means of unrighteous conduct and unequal conduct.
Therefore, it is called "perilous.
Within this realm of rebirth, one encounters various painful contacts and undergoes manifold,
intense, and uninterrupted suffering for a long duration.
They are called "evil destinies" because they appear equally [to all],
because one falls into their lower parts,
and because they are great, deep pits.
Because they are difficult to rescue and deliver;
because they are most pitiable;
and because they are utterly base and lowly.
Because one constantly harbors grief and resentment through grandiose and deceptive speech,
it is called "falling.
This is because such speech can give rise to a superior degree of weary detachment (*saṃvega*).
Therefore, it is said that one falls into hell;
