one should know that herein, both the arising by means of this [karma] and the experience of various sufferings once born are intended.
If, after having experienced suffering, one further gives rise to various other sufferings produced by one's own karma—
all such things are revealed by these various perceptions.
One should understand that all white factors (śukla-pakṣa), which are the opposites of the aforementioned [black factors], apply accordingly.
This is the distinction.
All realms of existence preceded by virtuous conduct are called "fortunate realms" (*sugati*).
Because they experience supreme bliss, they are called "blissful worlds."
Having permanently and without remainder severed all outflows (āsrava) and all underlying tendencies (anuśaya),
one attains the superior uncontaminated mind (anāsravacitta) and superior uncontaminated wisdom (anāsravaprajñā) that serve as their antidotes;
this is what is subsumed under the most excellent higher training in mind (adhicittam śikṣā) and higher training in wisdom (adhiprajñām śikṣā).
Due to the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava*), it is called the "outflow-free liberation of mind and wisdom" (*anāsravacittajñānavimukti*).
This very twofold liberation of mind and wisdom is termed "internal realization" (*pratyātma-adhigama*) in the context of one's final existence (*caramabhava*).
The sixth supernormal power, because it is realized internally by relying on both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation,
is such that once one has realized it for oneself,
one understands it as it truly is and is able to explain it to others according to their needs.
Therefore, it is said that within this very life, one possesses the direct realization of personal gnosis (*pratyātmajñāna*),
and the various distinctions of phrases such as "I have awakened to the end of birth" and so forth,
as explained at length in the subsequent *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.
One should know its characteristics.

Thus concludes the second part of the fifth chapter, "The Establishment," within the third section, "The Ultimate Yoga Station," of the fifteenth book, the "Bodhisattva Stage," from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva and translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Having thus explained the ten powers of the Buddha individually.
Now, this shall be explained in summary. The uddāna says:
Essential nature and discrimination, The uncommon and the equal.
Function, sequence, and differentiation are the final [topics].
Thus, one should understand the essential nature of the ten powers of the Tathāgata as they have been explained,
and one should understand their various classifications.
All that is unique should be understood;
all that is equal should be understood;
all activities should be understood.
One should understand all their sequences;
one should understand all their distinctions.
By means of these seven aspects, the summarized meaning of the Tathāgata’s ten powers should be understood.
What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the Tathāgata’s ten powers?
It is said that, taken collectively, the five faculties constitute their intrinsic nature.
Because wisdom (*prajñā*) is predominant, they are described as having wisdom as their intrinsic nature.
Therefore, it is only called the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*);
it is not called the power of faith (*śraddhābala*), nor any other power.
It is just as with the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible.
It should be understood that the remaining powers are likewise.
This is called the intrinsic nature of the Tathāgata’s ten powers.
What is the analytical classification of the Tathāgata’s ten powers?
Briefly stated, one should know that conceptualization is immeasurable by virtue of three aspects.
First is conceptualization by way of temporal division;
this refers to all objects of knowledge belonging to the past, future, and present worlds.
First, by way of sequential realization;
second, by way of differentiation according to categories,
which refers to all modes of activity regarding the specific and general characteristics of each and every conditioned phenomenon.
Because of entering into realization accordingly.
Third, by way of the differentiation of continuities:
this refers to all the various distinct continuities and all matters and meanings within the realms of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
Because they enter into realization accordingly,
the ten powers of the Tathāgata are thus distinguished by means of these three types.
One should know that these are immeasurable;
this is called the differentiation of the Tathāgata’s ten powers.
What is the non-commonality of the Tathāgata’s ten powers?
This means that only the Tathāgata possesses these ten powers, which are not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
this is called the "unshared ten powers of the Tathāgata. What is the equality of the Tathāgata’s ten powers?
This means that all Tathāgatas are equally endowed with and have fully accomplished these ten powers;
therefore, they are said to be equal and without distinction.
However, if one considers the many states in which a Tathāgata dwells...
Thus, these ten powers of the Tathāgata differ from one another;
that is to say, other Tathāgatas dwell frequently in some other power,
while yet other Tathāgatas dwell in still other powers.
This is called the equality of the Tathāgata’s ten powers.
What is the activity of the Tathāgata’s ten powers?
It refers to the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*).
Among all causes, he knows causes as they truly are;
among all fruits, he knows fruits as they truly are;
and he is able to subdue all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who engage in various disputes concerning the absence of cause or false causes.
The Tathāgata possesses the power of knowledge regarding his own karma;
he understands, as it truly is, the karma of his own performed actions and the resulting fruits he experiences,
and he is able to subdue all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who engage in various disputes concerning the transference of the merit of giving.
The Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations,
and attainments enables him to manifest three kinds of miraculous transformations and to provide unsurpassed instruction to sentient beings who are to be converted.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties [of beings] is that which is able to subdue all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who abide in various opposing categories,
as well as those who harbor malice and engage in contentious debate.
He understands, as they truly are, the distinctions among the various categories of sentient beings— those of weak, middling, and superior faculties—
and is able to preach the True Dharma to them in a manner that is appropriate and suitable for each.
The Tathāgata possesses the power of knowledge regarding various inclinations;
he knows as they truly are the distinctions among the inferior, middling, and superior inclinations—whether pure or impure—of all sentient beings.
He causes pure resolute conviction to gradually increase and causes impure resolute conviction to be gradually abandoned.
This is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the various elements (*dhātu-jñāna-bala*).
He understands, as they truly are, the distinctions among the inferior, middling, and superior dispositions of sentient beings;
and he acts toward sentient beings according to their faculties, according to their inclinations, and according to their latent tendencies.
Based on each respective gateway of entry,
the unerring instructions are established as appropriate; herein,
the Tathāgata [provides them] for the śrāvakas.
Within each respective gateway of entry, he provides the authentic instructions,
as set forth in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*,
explaining, revealing, clarifying, designating, and demonstrating them exhaustively in every respect and without interruption.

How does the Tathāgata instruct the assembly of bodhisattvas who are beginners and novices— those who have gathered the provisions for meditative concentration (*samādhi*), who are being sustained, and who wish to abide in mental stability—
so that their minds may become settled?

This refers to the initial, unerring instructions provided by the Tathāgatas for those bodhisattvas who are beginning their practice— their first undertaking— of the equipment for meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
characterized by being free from deceit, crookedness, and possessing reverence and affection.
Having spoken thus:
"Come, son of good family!
You should settle yourself in a secluded dwelling, alone and without a second, and contemplate correctly within with inner tranquility."
Reflect in this way: "This is the name given to you by your parents,
or the name given to you by your preceptors or teachers."
Is there now, apart from the six sense bases, a self-nature that is real,
whether internal, external, or in between,
such that within this existence the designation of names, concepts, conventions, and verbal expressions proceed?
Once you have engaged in such correct reflection, you shall find that within these phenomena there is nothing whatsoever to be apprehended;
you should simply understand them as they truly are: that it is merely within adventitious phenomena that adventitious perceptions arise.
"O son of good family,
if at that time you have already produced and attained the notion of 'guest' regarding your own name,"
Furthermore, you should inwardly reflect upon this in accordance with reason:
regarding that which is established as the name "eye" within your own eye,
it is merely a mental conception of "eye" and a conventional designation of "eye."
Reflecting in this way,
one realizes that within this eye there are only two things to be found:
namely, this [physical organ] established as the "eye."
The designation "eye" is a conventional designation for the eye;
it is a name, concept, and designation established upon this mere thing.
Apart from this, there is nothing further and nothing additional.
Regarding this eye, whatever is established as the name "eye," the perception of "eye," and the conventional designation "eye"—
none of these are the eye; there is only the underlying entity (vastumātra).
Within this, the designation "eye" and so forth are conventionally established;
one should know that their intrinsic nature is likewise not the eye. Why is this?

In this context, it is not the case that there is even a slight occurrence of the cognition of "eye" that could function— apart from the established name "eye," the perception of "eye," and the conventional designation of "eye"—
if such a thing were to exist, its substance would be real.
Regarding what is expressed by the designation "eye," one should not have to wait for the name "eye" to arise before such a cognition of an eye occurs;
rather, it should arise solely from its own intrinsic nature, independent of hearing.
It does not arise from conceptual discrimination;
the name established for it merely functions as a visual cognition with respect to this object.
However, no such cognition can be found that functions independently of verbal designations.

Therefore, herein, it is only with respect to adventitious phenomena that there exists the adventitious designation of "eye," the notion of "eye," and the conventional metaphorical attribution of "eye.
Since you have thus reflected correctly upon the internal eye, [you should proceed likewise].
Furthermore, regarding the perception of the eye, one should give rise to and attain only the perception of its being adventitious.
As it is with the eye,
so it is with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and so forth.
To speak at length, this extends even to what has been seen, heard, sensed, and known, or what has already been attained and sought;
or whatever has already been brought to mind through initial and sustained mental application. In short:
Regarding all conceptualizations of phenomena,
only the notion of "guest" should arise and be attained.
In this same way, you should regard all provisional designations within your own body as such.
One should correctly embrace the path of diligent application that completely eliminates [all conceptualizations];
this is explained at length up to: one should correctly embrace the path of diligent application that completely eliminates all conceptual designations regarding all phenomena.
By means of such an awareness that thoroughly examines all that is to be known,
you should give rise to the notion of mere adventitiousness regarding all conceptualizations of phenomena,
and regarding all conceptual proliferations concerning all phenomena.
Repeatedly dispelling [distractions],
one proceeds by means of a non-conceptual and signless mind that apprehends only the meaning;
one dwells extensively in the cultivation of this state.
If you act in this way, you shall,
by relying on the lineage of the Tathāgata’s sublime wisdom and pure meditative concentration,
attain the non-erroneous one-pointedness of mind.
In this way, if you direct your attention to the contemplation of the foul,
do not abandon this mental engagement; likewise,
if you direct it toward loving-kindness.
Whether it be regarding dependent origination by way of conditions,
the differentiation of the elements,
or mindfulness of breathing.
Whether it be the first dhyāna,
or as extensively described up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there are the immeasurable bodhisattva dhyānas, supernormal powers, samādhis, and meditative attainments.
Reflect with mental attention;
do not abandon this mental attention.
If you cultivate this unerring mental attention of a bodhisattva in such a manner, [you will succeed].
Gradually, until one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and ultimate liberation—
this should be known as the "universal practice leading everywhere" of all bodhisattvas.
The Tathāgatas of the past also correctly established such instructions for the bodhisattvas who were beginners;
the Tathāgatas of the future will likewise [establish them] for the bodhisattvas who are beginners.
When such instruction is being correctly imparted,
the Tathāgata of the present likewise imparts such instruction to the assembly of bodhisattvas who are beginners.
When the śrāvakas and others diligently practice this mental attention (*manasikāra*),
they too can swiftly attain superior supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*).
If they can penetrate this mental attention as it truly is, without error, [they will likewise achieve this].
One is then able to attain the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of all phenomena.
Regarding the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñānabala*),
it concerns the path that leads to emergence from all suffering.
He understands, as it truly is, conduct that does not lead to transcendence,
and causes others to abandon such conduct.
He is able to correctly bestow the practice of renunciation;
having repeatedly recollected his past lives and former existences through the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge consisting in the recollection of past abodes, he [teaches].
In order to cause the minds of those sentient beings to be inspired with renunciation and pure faith,
he correctly proclaims [the teaching],
and is able to subdue all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who cling to the doctrine of eternalism.
The Tathāgata possesses the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth;
he is able to correctly declare the past deaths and transitions, as well as the future births, of all his disciples.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows enables him to subdue all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who cling to the doctrine of annihilation; thus,
he is without confusion or doubt concerning his own liberation.
Furthermore, it is the ability to subdue all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who harbor overweening pride regarding their status as arhats;
this is called the activity of the Tathāgata’s ten powers.
What is the sequence of the Tathāgata’s ten powers?
It is said that when the Tathāgatas first realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
they immediately and instantaneously attain all ten powers.
Having been realized all at once, they subsequently manifest in sequence.
That is to say, when the Tathāgatas first attain Buddhahood,
they first give rise to the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*).
Having observed all phenomena and established the entirety of unerring cause and effect,
he next gives rise to the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma (*karmasvakajñānabala*).
If there is a seeker who desires a desirable and excellent matured fruit (*vipākaphala*) within the homogeneous realm (*nikāyasabhāga*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), [he knows it].
He employs skillful means to teach them so that they may distance themselves from all unwholesome actions and cause them to practice all wholesome actions; subsequently,
he gives rise to the power of knowledge regarding dhyāna, vimokṣa, samādhi, and samāpatti.
If there are sentient beings who seek the mundane dharma of freedom from desire,
he provides them with instruction to lead them toward mundane freedom from desire and enables them to attain the path as it truly is.
Next, he gives rise to the remaining seven powers of a Tathāgata.
If there are sentient beings who seek the supramundane dharma of detachment from desire,
he teaches them, as appropriate, the path leading to the supramundane state of detachment from desire.
That is to say, within this context, one first gives rise to the power of knowledge regarding the superiority and inferiority of faculties (*indriya-parāpara-jñānabala*),
observing as it truly is the faculties of those who seek the supramundane and desire renunciation;
subsequently, one gives rise to the power of knowledge regarding various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñānabala*).
First, he observes that intention preceded by those faculties as they truly are;
next, he gives rise to the power of knowledge regarding the various elements (*dhātu-jñānabala*) and observes the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) preceded by that intention as they truly are.
Having thus understood their faculties, intentions, and latent dispositions,
he next gives rise to the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading to all destinations (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñānabala*).
Accordingly, he causes them to enter the gateways for entering the objects of focus as is appropriate.
Next, he gives rise to the power of knowledge consisting in the recollection of past lives and the power of knowledge concerning death and rebirth.
Having stabilized his mind through the preparatory application of entering the gates of objects as appropriate,
and having purified his practice, he [attains these powers].
I teach the Middle Way for them,
so that they may distance themselves from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which is the root of all extremes of eternalism and nihilism,
and so that they may forever sever all afflictions (*kleśa*).
From this point onward, the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows arises.
If one is sustained by the power of śamatha through such correctly cultivated skillful means,
although one has not yet permanently severed all afflictions, [one possesses this power].
Furthermore, for those who give rise to the overweening pride of "non-doing" based on the non-manifestation [of afflictions] they have attained,
this causes them to abandon that overweening pride.
This is called the sequential order of the ten powers according to one method.
Furthermore, there is another method for the sequential order of the ten powers, which is as follows:
when the Tathāgatas first realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
First, he brings to presence the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible with respect to the initial origination [of phenomena],
throughout all dependently arisen dharmas.
One contemplates the wisdom that abides in the most excellent and sublime Dharma;
based upon this wisdom that abides in the sublime Dharma,
one subsequently gives rise to the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma.
Regarding the category of householders:
due to the various distinctions among their respective karmas, there are differences in cultivation,
realization, and attainment based on the past, future, and present states within the category of householders.
Having thus observed the category of householders,
he next gives rise to the power of knowledge regarding dhyāna, vimokṣa, samādhi, and samāpatti,
and observes the category of those who have gone forth.
That is to say, within this category of those who have gone forth,
is there anyone capable of explaining the right path for escaping suffering and transcending suffering,
or is there none?
Having observed thus, he correctly knows that nothing exists at all.
He contemplates how all worlds are without protection and have no refuge.
Out of great compassion, he observes all worlds as they truly are with his Buddha-eye.
Having thus performed contemplation, he next gives rise to the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties of beings;
he clearly realizes that various sentient beings dwelling in the world are born in the world and grow old in the world.
Whether they possess dull faculties, middling faculties, or sharp faculties,
once they have directly known this, their minds enter into the teaching of the Dharma.
Subsequently, as before, all other matters such as the power of knowledge regarding various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*) follow in sequence.
One should know that this is the sequence of the ten powers according to the second method.
Furthermore, there is another method for the sequence of the ten powers, namely:
regarding their unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, all Tathāgatas—
At the time of initial realization,
one first brings forth and manifests the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*).
He contemplates the dharma-realm of all dependently arisen phenomena.
Next, he gives rise to the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma;
that is, within these very dependently arisen phenomena.
He observes the realm of sentient beings— the conventional designations and conceptual notions of "sentient beings"—
and sees that these sentient beings create such types of karma for themselves and subsequently experience such types of results.
Having thus observed the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) as they truly are,
he next gives rise to the power of knowledge regarding meditative absorption, liberation, concentration,
and attainment; this is for the sake of liberating these very classes of sentient beings from suffering.
He instructs them by manifesting three kinds of unerring miraculous transformations.
Having so instructed them, he next exerts further power;
as before, he sequentially discerns their faculties and so forth.
Having caused them to enter that right path,
one then employs skillful means to liberate those sentient beings from all suffering;
this is the third gateway in the sequence of the ten powers.
What is the distinction among the ten powers of the Tathāgata?
It is that these ten powers, when compared with one another,
possess both distinctions and non-distinctions.

What is the difference between the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*) and the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma (*karmasvakatā-jñānabala*)?
It is that [the latter] correctly understands how wholesome and unwholesome karmas can bring about all their respective desirable and undesirable fruits.
It should be understood that this is due to the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*).
If one correctly understands that those who perform wholesome or unwholesome actions are precisely those who will experience the agreeable or disagreeable results, and no others.
It should be known that this is due to the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma (*karmasvakajñānabala*).
If one correctly understands those who are capable of cultivating dhyāna, liberation (*vimokṣa*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), then only they can enter such states as dhyāna and the rest, and no others.
It should be understood that this is due to the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma.

Having correctly understood this, he relies upon such meditative concentrations as the dhyānas to manifest the three miraculous powers and provide unerring instruction to the sentient beings to be converted.
It should be known that this is due to the power of the knowledge of dhyānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
If one correctly perceives the mind arising together with and associated with faith and so forth,
it should be known that this is due to the power of the knowledge of dhyānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
If one correctly discerns the various distinctions among those faculties— whether they be weak, middling, or superior—
it should be known that this is due to the power of the knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of faculties (*indriya-parāpara-jñānabala*).

If one correctly perceives the various inclinations (*adhimukti*) regarding various phenomena that are preceded by those faculties, [it should be known that this is due to the power of the knowledge of the diversity of dispositions].
One should know that this is due to the power of knowledge regarding the superiority and inferiority of the faculties (*indriya*).
If one correctly discerns the various distinctions in those very inclinations (*āśaya*),
one should know that this is due to the power of knowledge regarding the diversity of resolutions (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*).
One should know that those very intentions are briefly distinguished into six types.
The first is the intention lacking renunciation,
which refers to [the aspiration for] individual realms such as those of Maheśvara, Nārāyaṇa, and the Brahma-world.
First is the aspiration of those who have developed faith and understanding;
second is the aspiration of renunciation,
which refers to the aspiration of those who have developed faith and understanding in the three vehicles.
Third is the distant pure intention (*dūrapariśuddhāśaya*),
which refers to the intentions of those who abide in the lower and middle grades of maturation.
Fourth is the proximate pure intention (*āsannapariśuddhāśaya*).
This refers to the intention of those who abide in the highest degree of maturity.
Fifth is the intention of attaining nirvāṇa in this very life;
that is, the intention of those who have conceived faith and understanding in the nirvāṇa attained through the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
Sixth is the aspiration for nirvāṇa in a future life;
that is, the aspiration of one who gives rise to faith and understanding regarding the nirvāṇa attained through the Mahāyāna.
It consists in correctly apprehending the corresponding seeds produced by that resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
It should be understood that this is due to the power of knowledge regarding various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñānabala*);
for when one correctly discerns those very seeds in their distinctions,
one differentiates them into immeasurable categories.
One should know that this is due to the power of the knowledge of the various elements (*nānādhātu-jñānabala*).
Furthermore, one should know that those very elements are briefly divided into four types:
first, the seeds abiding in their original nature (*prakṛtistha-bīja*).
Second, those that have previously been cultivated to produce seeds;
third, those that are capable of being refined—
namely, the seeds possessed by those who have the nature for parinirvāṇa.
Fourth are the seeds that cannot be cultivated or remediated;
these refer to the seeds belonging to those who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa.
If one correctly understands them according to their specific categories, elements, and modes of engagement, [one will not attempt to cultivate them].
It should be understood that this is due to the power of the knowledge of the various elements (*nānādhātu-jñānabala*).
If one correctly discerns all the various categories of those very tracks (*pratipad*),
such tracks are able to bring about freedom from defilement.
Such paths of practice can lead to ultimate purification;
such paths of practice cannot lead to ultimate purification.
One should know that this is due to the power of the knowledge of the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*).
If one knows, as it truly is, that all causes for rebirth in previous states of existence are concomitant with those previous states,
this should be understood as being due to the power of the knowledge of the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*).

If one correctly understands, as previously analyzed, the various types of conformity to the eight conventional expressions and the six kinds of concise practices, [this is likewise due to that power].
It should be known that this is due to the power of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānabala*).
If one correctly understands the death and rebirth of sentient beings based on the prior limit (*pūrvānta*),
it should be known that this is due to the power of the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
If one correctly observes the various deaths and births of sentient beings in the future limit,
it should be known that this is due to the power of the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñānabala*).
If one correctly understands that one’s own purpose has not yet reached its ultimate consummation, [it is likewise due to this power].
One should know that the continuity of rebirth for sentient beings at the future limit is due to the power of the knowledge of death and birth;
and that if one correctly understands this, having attained the ultimate goal of one's own welfare and being well-liberated in mind, one realizes nirvāṇa in the present life.
One should know that this is due to the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*).
One should know that these ten powers of the Tathāgata, when compared with one another, both possess distinctions and lack distinctions.
Regarding the textual passages on the four fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata,
their characteristics should be understood as they are explained in the sūtras;
that is to say, in four matters, all Tathāgatas—
In the midst of the great assembly, he praised himself,
saying: "Because I am forever liberated from the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
regarding all phenomena in all their aspects."
Manifesting perfect enlightenment is the first point not shared with the śrāvakas,
because of the permanent liberation from all afflictive obstructions.
To realize the exhaustion of outflows in common with all śrāvakas is the second point;
for the sake of liberating all sentient beings from their manifold sufferings.
The path of renunciation is the third point;
it constitutes an obstacle to attaining the path that leads out [of saṃsāra].
He taught that one should distance oneself from all obstructing dharmas;
this is the fourth point.
Thus, regarding these four points, the Tathāgata—
Having thus praised himself according to the actual state of affairs,
others subsequently raise criticisms and objections regarding the contradictions between his self-praise and his prior bodily, verbal, and mental actions in those two aforementioned instances.

Furthermore, regarding the two subsequent instances of self-praise, there are contradictions and inconsistencies between earlier and later statements that fall into irrationality; thus, you raise a refutation based on such censure.
Specifically, this concerns those in the world who possess vision and those who do not.
Whether one possesses the knowledge of others' minds or does not possess the knowledge of others' minds,
the Tathāgata, within this sphere of self-praise, sees no sign of a factual cause whatsoever among the various refutations and difficulties that serve as counter-arguments.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, one is able to personally understand these four points;
being composed and fearless, the mind is free from timidity or inferiority,
devoid of doubt or suspicion, and entirely without alarm or dread.
Furthermore, there are only these qualities by which the Great Teacher, the Buddha, should be praised:
namely, that his practice for his own benefit and his practice for the benefit of others are both perfectly fulfilled.
It should be understood that among these, the first two praises refer to the fulfillment of the practice for his own benefit.
The latter two [statements] praise the fulfillment of his altruistic conduct.
In this context, when the Tathāgata praises himself,
he does so because he has attained perfect enlightenment by realizing all phenomena through manifest awakening.
One should know that this is specifically for the sake of those bodhisattvas who are correctly progressing toward the Mahāyāna.
If one were to praise oneself for having exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*),
one should know that this is specifically for the sake of those sentient beings who are correctly progressing toward the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles.
Furthermore, if one praises the path of deliverance as well as the factors that constitute obstacles,
it should be understood that both are for the sake of leading all sentient beings equally toward their respective vehicles.
Such are the scriptural passages spoken by the Tathāgata.
"I have taught the path of deliverance to the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas," and so forth,
as extensively explained by the compilers.
In the Śrāvaka Piṭaka that was compiled,
with the exception of the word "bodhisattva";
and in the Bodhisattva Piṭaka that was compiled.
One should understand its characteristics simply by reciting these words of the Bodhisattva:
namely, that throughout the long night, all Tathāgatas have had such an aspiration.
"How may I cause all classes of sentient beings to dwell in accordance with reality within my well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, practicing them without error?
Thus, when I, as a Master who desires and delights in the Dharma, guide and govern the assembly throughout the long night."
If what is desired is either attained or not attained, no affliction arises,
because this is briefly revealed by means of the three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Furthermore, these three applications of mindfulness are established through the differentiation of the three assemblies.
What are the three assemblies?
If all of them practice exclusively and correctly,
they constitute the first assembly.
If all of them practice exclusively in a wrong manner,
this is the second group;
if within that group some practice correctly while others practice wrongly, [this is the third group].
This is the third assembly.
Regarding the textual passages on the Tathāgata’s three kinds of non-protection (*trirakṣa*),
their characteristics should be understood as they are explained in the sūtras.
In brief, it means that all Tathāgatas have permanently severed the concealment of any base or evil deeds in every respect,
as demonstrated by their three forms of non-protection (*trirakṣa*).
Because of lapses in mindfulness, some Arhats occasionally and briefly engage in neutral, base, or evil actions; however,
the Tathāgata is entirely free from all such things.
All things are utterly non-existent.
Therefore, regarding his disciples, the Tathāgata acts in accordance with the precepts he has established, which are identical to their own intrinsic nature;
he earnestly exhorts them and sternly rebukes them.
Furthermore, he would at times act with sudden impulsiveness and forceful urgency,
showing no restraint or consideration toward his disciples, thinking:
"Let it not be that they dwell together with me for too long."
Knowing that my three karmas were impure,
he felt displeasure in his mind on account of the previous matter;
because of this lack of compliance, our relationship became discordant.
Whether they revile me to my face or speak ill of me behind my back,
one should know that all aspects of the Tathāgata’s great compassion are exactly as previously described in the "Chapter on Immeasurable Offerings and Approaches."
One should know that such great compassion of the Tathāgata is immeasurable and unsurpassed.
What is the Tathāgata’s quality of being free from forgetfulness?
It means that all Tathāgatas possess constant mindfulness and recollection.
Regarding whatever action, in whatever place, in whatever manner, and at whatever time was performed,
the Tathāgata maintains correct mindfulness of that very action, in that very place, in that very manner, and at that very time.
This is called the Tathāgata’s quality of non-forgetfulness;
that is to say, regarding all activities whatsoever and all distinctions of place and direction, the Tathāgata is universally [unfailing].
Regarding all skillful means employed and all distinctions of time,
he maintains mindfulness without forgetfulness, abiding constantly in right mindfulness.
One should know that this is called the quality of non-forgetfulness.
What is the Tathāgata’s permanent eradication of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)?
It refers to how the Tathāgatas, whether in movement or in gazing, [act without error].
Whether in discourse or in repose,
the activities arising from afflictions appear to no longer manifest;
this is called the Tathāgata’s permanent eradication of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Although the Arhats have severed the afflictions,
in their movements, gazes, speech, and even in their states of composure,
there appear various activities that resemble those arising from afflictions.
What is the Tathāgata’s sublime wisdom of all aspects?
In brief, it refers to the Tathāgatas’ manifestly perfect awakening regarding the three categories of phenomena.
What are the three?
First, those phenomena that lead to a collection of meaningful things;
second, those phenomena that lead to a collection of meaningless things.
Third, there are factors that do not lead to a collection of what is meaningful and do not lead to a collection of what is meaningless.
It should be understood that herein, if the Tathāgatas, regarding those factors that lead to a collection of what is meaningless...
Or, regarding both the collection of phenomena that can induce a meaningful existence and the collection of phenomena that cannot induce a meaningless existence—
within all such phenomena taken as a whole—
one possesses non-erroneous knowledge.
This is called the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).
It is the non-erroneous wisdom regarding all phenomena that constitute the collection of things conducive to the welfare of beings.
One should know that this is called the sublime wisdom of the Tathāgata;
herein, both the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the sublime wisdom (*prajñā*) are combined into one.
It is called the "excellent wisdom of all aspects.
All such qualities as these are collectively termed the one hundred and forty unique buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) of the Tathāgata.
Within this very state, all the primary marks and secondary signs have already been realized as utterly pure during the final existence of the bodhisattva stage.
When a bodhisattva sits upon the seat of awakening while dwelling in his final existence,
having perfectly fulfilled the path of a bodhisattva and the provisions for awakening,
he then cultivates the thirty-seven factors of awakening without a teacher.
The attainment of a single moment [of consciousness] is called the *samādhi* of unobstructed wisdom;
this is the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) included within the bodhisattva’s path of training.
Immediately following this, in the second moment:
One suddenly attains the remaining unshared Buddha-dharmas,
beginning with the ten powers of the Tathāgata and ending with the sublime wisdom of all modes.
All are utterly pure and entirely unsurpassed;
by attaining these, one is universally unimpeded and unobstructed regarding all objects of knowledge.
The revolution of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) through the most supremely pure and stainless wisdom;
having momentarily awakened and contemplated, it is perfectly fulfilled like a chariot,
transcending all bodhisattva practices and bodhisattva stages.
Having entered the stage of the Tathāgata, which is the practice of all Tathāgatas,

one attains the supreme transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) because all coarse residues (*dausthulya*) belonging to the category of cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the flesh have been abandoned without remainder.
Such a transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is supreme and unsurpassed.
One should know that all other transformations of the basis, up to and including those of Bodhisattvas dwelling in the most sublime stage of fulfillment (niṣṭhā-gata), are still surpassable.
Question: Regarding the wisdom of all bodhisattvas who abide securely on the ultimate stage and the wisdom of the Tathāgata,
how should one understand the distinction between these two?
Answer: Just as a person with clear vision sees various forms and images through thin silk,
one should know that the sublime wisdom of all Bodhisattvas who abide securely in the ultimate stage is likewise toward all objects.
Just as a person with clear vision perceives various forms and images without any obstruction,
so too should one understand the sublime wisdom of the Tathāgata regarding all objects.
It is like a work of painting where all the colors have been fully applied, yet only the final exquisite hues remain to be refined and perfected.
It should be understood that the sublime wisdom of a bodhisattva who has reached the ultimate stage is likewise so:
it is like a work of painting where all the colors have been fully applied, and which is finally purified and refined by the application of the most exquisite hues.
It should be known that the sublime wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise.
It should be known that the sublime wisdom of a bodhisattva who has reached the ultimate stage is likewise, like a person with clear vision perceiving various forms in dim light.
Just as a person with clear vision perceives all forms when free from all darkness,
so too should the sublime wisdom of the Tathāgata be understood;
just as a person with clear vision perceives various forms from afar.
It should be known that the sublime wisdom of a bodhisattva who has reached the ultimate stage is likewise.
It should be known that the sublime wisdom of a Tathāgata is likewise, like a person with clear vision observing various forms up close.
Just as one with eyes afflicted by a slight film perceives various forms,
it should be known that the sublime wisdom of a Bodhisattva who has reached the ultimate stage is likewise.
Just as one with perfectly pure eyes perceives various forms, so too is the wisdom of a Tathāgata.
One should know that the sublime wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise.
One should know that the bodies of Bodhisattvas who have reached the ultimate stage are likewise, like the body within the womb.
Just as with a body that has emerged from the womb,
one should know that the bodies of all Tathāgatas are likewise;
they are like the mental activities within the dream of an Arhat.
It should be known that the mental activities of a Bodhisattva who has reached the ultimate stage are likewise.
Just as the mental activities of an Arhat during the waking state,
so too should the mental activities of a Tathāgata be known.
Just as the nature of a dim lamp is,
so too should the nature of the wisdom of a Bodhisattva who has reached the ultimate stage be understood;
just as the nature of a bright lamp is.
One should know that the essence of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise so.
Therefore, one should know that all bodhisattvas who dwell securely in the ultimate stage are identical with the sublime wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
There is a great distinction between body and mind.
Thus, once the Tathāgata has realized bodhi,
he pervades all buddha-fields throughout the ten directions.
It is universally capable of performing all buddha-activities.
What are called "all buddha-activities"?
They are the activities of the Tathāgatas, the deeds of the Tathāgatas, and that which is performed by the Tathāgatas.
Briefly, there are ten kinds.
In this way, each and every deed of a Tathāgata, performed by a Tathāgata,
is capable of accomplishing immeasurable benefit for sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is nothing that exceeds or surpasses this.
What are the ten? They are as follows:
first, the Tathāgatas personally manifest the body of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa).
In order to cause sentient beings to give rise to pure faith in their hearts,
the body of a Great Being is the most excellent for inspiring such faith;
this is called the Tathāgata’s first deed.
Such deeds are accomplished through the primary marks and secondary signs.
Furthermore, all Tathāgatas act universally for the sake of all classes of sentient beings.
The arousal of the application of instruction in all its aspects is called the second deed of the Tathāgata.
Such is this deed.
It is accomplished through the four kinds of purity in every respect.
Furthermore, the Tathāgatas are able to perform all deeds for the benefit of sentient beings and are able to sever all doubts that may arise.
This is called the third deed of the Tathāgata.
Such deeds as these can be accomplished by means of the ten powers of the Tathāgata.
Because the ten powers of the Tathāgata, as previously described,
possess the capacity to accomplish every benefit and welfare for all sentient beings.
Furthermore, regarding the questions and challenges raised concerning the ten powers realized by the Tathāgata,
only the Tathāgata can know, see, understand, and comprehend them;
for only the Tathāgata is able to provide the correct answer to those questions and challenges.
Furthermore, all Tathāgatas are universally able to subdue all opposing arguments and universally able to establish all their own doctrines;
this is called the fourth deed of a Tathāgata.
Such deeds are accomplished through the four fearlessnesses.
Furthermore, regarding the sentient beings transformed by the Tathāgatas:
Whether the Buddha’s instructions are correctly established or not correctly established,
the Tathāgata’s mind remains undefiled therein;
this is called the fifth task of the Tathāgata.
Such deeds as these can be accomplished through the three applications of mindfulness.
Furthermore, all Tathāgatas act exactly as they have spoken.
This is called the sixth deed of the Tathāgata.
Such deeds are accomplished through the three kinds of non-protection.
Furthermore, all Tathāgatas constantly observe the world throughout the divisions of day and night with their Buddha-eye.
This is called the seventh deed of a Tathāgata.
Such is this deed.
That which can be accomplished by the great compassion of the Tathāgata,
and wherein all Tathāgatas never retreat or abandon any of their manifold activities at once—
this is called the eighth activity of the Tathāgata.
Such activities are accomplished through the quality of non-forgetfulness.
Furthermore, the Tathāgatas act in accordance with their prescribed conduct exactly as it is,
never overstepping their functional activity.
This is called the ninth deed of the Tathāgata.
Such a deed can be accomplished only by one who has forever eradicated the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Furthermore, the Tathāgatas do not lead toward those dharmas that gather what is meaningless,
nor do they lead toward those dharmas that gather what is meaningful, nor do they lead toward those dharmas that gather what is meaningless.
Having discerned and abandoned [what is unwholesome],
he proclaims, reveals, and elucidates for the assembly those dharmas that lead to a collection of meaningful purposes.
This is called the tenth deed of the Tathāgata.
Such a deed can be accomplished only by means of the excellent wisdom of all modes.
In this way, by means of the one hundred and forty kinds of unique Buddha-qualities previously described,
the Tathāgata is able to perform all the activities and all the Buddha-deeds of a Tathāgata.
If these Buddha-activities were to be analyzed in detail, they would not be easily enumerated;
even if one were to speak for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great eons (*kalpas*), one could not exhaust them.
Such are the dwellings of all Tathāgatas and the stages (*bhūmi*) of all Tathāgatas as herein described.
This is called "establishment.
Why? Because it is by depending upon this and abiding in this that the category of aspiration arises.
The assembly of bodhisattvas is able to correctly train in the bodhisattva training,
and it is by relying on this that they attain realization.
That is to say, by relying on this, one is able to accomplish all aims and benefits for all sentient beings;
therefore, this is called "establishment.
Furthermore, regarding all these aforementioned Buddha-dharmas:
It is most conducive to the work of benefiting others;
all Tathāgatas are manifested through this work of benefiting others,
whereas Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are not so.
Therefore, they are called the "unshared Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, within these Buddha-dharmas,
there are specific Buddha-dharmas that none of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas can ever attain.
That which is called great compassion,
the quality of non-forgetfulness,
and the eternal eradication of habitual tendencies.
The sublime wisdom of all modes possesses its own Buddha-dharmas;
although one may partially attain them in a semblance, they are not complete in every respect.
The Tathāgata has fully realized all of those things;
in every respect, there is nothing that is not perfected.
It is supremely transcendent and supremely exquisite;
therefore, it is all described as "unshared" (āveṇika),
in the sense that it exists uniquely and alone.
This is the meaning of its uniqueness.
Thus, it perfectly reveals the entire path of training for bodhisattvas as well as the fruit of that path of training;
this is called the Bodhisattva-bhūmi.
It fully explains the path of training for all bodhisattvas as well as the fruit of that path of training,
because it is the actual basis for all types of teachings.
Furthermore, this Bodhisattvabhūmi is also called the Bodhisattvapiṭaka-mātṛkā.
It is also called the Compendium of the Mahāyāna;
it is also called the Revelation of the Paths of Destruction and Non-destruction;
and it is also called the Pure Foundation of Unobstructed Wisdom.
Whatever exists in the world of gods and humans—
whether gods or humans,
or śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and so forth.
Regarding this *Bodhisattvabhūmi* as it has been explained herein, one should give rise to firm faith and understanding;
delight in hearing, receiving, and upholding it; apply oneself diligently to its cultivation and study; and extensively explain it to others.
At the very least, one should write it down, preserve it, make offerings to it, honor it, and cherish it with a profound mind.
To summarize the mass of merit thus obtained:
it is like the mass of merit that the Blessed One has proclaimed, elucidated, analyzed,
established, revealed, and praised in all the subtle sūtras included within the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, through such activities as delighting in hearing them and so forth.
They are equal and without difference. Why is this?
Because this Bodhisattva stage encompasses all the categories of brief indications and detailed explanations found throughout the entire Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
In this stage, one can extensively expound the Dharma and Vinaya,
such that many sentient beings to be trained receive,
uphold, read, recite, and practice in accordance with the Dharma within this True Teaching.
Abiding in stability, increasing, expanding, and progressing further,
during that time the counterfeit Dharma shall not flourish and the true Dharma shall not perish;
however, if at that time the counterfeit Dharma were to flourish...
At that very time, all the true teachings (*saddharma*) capable of leading to the realization of ultimate reality shall swiftly perish;
therefore, one should give rise to firm faith and understanding regarding this Bodhisattva stage.
One who delights in hearing, receiving, and upholding this, and so forth, as extensively explained, shall obtain an immeasurable and boundless mass of merit.

Thus concludes the Chapter on Generating the Mind of Perfect Enlightenment within the Fourth Stage of Successive Yoga, in the Fifteenth Ground of the Bodhisattva within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. The meaning of the Bodhisattva Ground has thus been fully expounded.
How should one understand the sequence herein?

It is that bodhisattvas must first abide securely in the bodhisattva lineage before they are able to correctly resolve their minds toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Having already resolved his mind, he practices the conduct that benefits both himself and others in a correct and upright manner.
While correctly practicing for the benefit of self and others,
he attains skillful means free from defilement.
Because it is free from affliction, one attains the skillful means of being free from weariness;
because one is free from weariness, one attains the skillful means of the increase of all roots of goodness.
Having attained the increase of all roots of goodness, [one...]
One is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, regarding such unadulterated skillful means for the application of the welfare of oneself and others,
and tireless skillful means, [one applies them].
Regarding the skillful means for increasing roots of goodness:
when one is about to engage in practice toward the attainment of great enlightenment.
First, one establishes firm conviction in the profound and vast true Dharma;
having established firm conviction, one seeks the true Dharma;
having sought the true Dharma, one explains it extensively for others.
Furthermore, one is able to accomplish right practice by oneself;
at the time of accomplishment, if by means of this, for this purpose, and in this manner one ought to act,
then by that very means, for that very purpose, and in that very manner one acts.
Thus, when practicing this in this manner, one acts exactly as one should act so that merit and wisdom may increase.
Once merit and wisdom have increased,
one is able to correctly practice the skillful means for not abandoning saṃsāra;
and while practicing correctly in this very way:
One is able to practice the conduct of saṃsāra without defilement;
while practicing correctly therein,
one is able to act without attachment toward one's own pleasure.
While practicing correctly within this very state,
one is able to practice correctly without weariness amidst the immeasurable great suffering of birth and death.
Because they never grow weary of birth and death,
they are able to correctly seek out various divergent doctrines and attain fearlessness regarding all treatises.
Having mastered the treatises, he is further able to discern what should be taught, what should be proclaimed, and how it should be spoken.
By means of this wisdom, he thoroughly understands the world.
Thus, once the bodhisattva has become well-versed in all treatises and worldly matters,
they are further able to seek the true Dharma in accordance with reason.
Having sought it, they are capable of effectively severing all doubts and uncertainties of all sentient beings.
In this way, one is capable of severing the doubts of others,
causing one's own merit to increase successively,
and gradually bringing the accumulation of merit to full completion.
One's own wisdom also increases and develops,
and the accumulation of wisdom gradually becomes perfected.
Once both types of accumulations have been perfected, [one attains the fruit].
He diligently practices the factors of enlightenment within the correct cultivation of the aspects of the truths;
he correctly understands the skillful means of cultivation,
and thus maintains that which is cultivated through such right effort.
They dedicate [their merit] toward the fruit of parinirvāṇa in the Mahāyāna,
not seeking the fruit of parinirvāṇa in the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Having thus attained such skillful means, they...
They are able to hear, listen to, and uphold all the speech of bodhisattvas.
By the power of cultivation,
they are able to discern and understand all aspects and characteristics of all dharmas previously unheard.
Having attained perfection in both dhāraṇīs and unimpeded eloquence,
they diligently cultivate the three gates of liberation in order to forever sever all hindrances.
While practicing correctly within this very state,
one diligently cultivates right practice in order to sever all inverted views and overweening pride in oneself and others.
In this way, one is able to bring the correct practice to perfection regarding all aspects and characteristics.
Having thus brought the correct practice to perfection, [one proceeds].
It is superior to all sentient beings, as well as to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
that is to say, it is superior in terms of the merit of correct practice and superior in terms of the merit worthy of praise.
It should be understood that herein, the bodhisattva of superior merit in correct practice diligently cultivates right conduct for the benefit of both self and others,
regarding the welfare of others as their own personal business.
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not like this;
because bodhisattvas take the welfare of others as their own purpose,
they give rise toward all sentient beings to a mind of equality, regarding them as themselves.
Because they give rise to such a mind of equanimity,
they constantly bestow benefits upon all sentient beings without expecting anything in return.
When a bodhisattva practices diligently in this manner,
One constantly gives rise to hope for sentient beings,
desiring that they may obtain benefit and happiness;
it is by virtue of this intention for their benefit and happiness [that one acts].
One should know that being able to constantly initiate unfailing preparatory application is called the excellence of the merit of successively inducing right practice;
one should know that herein, the Bodhisattva is praised for the excellence of this merit.
They receive the prophecy of enlightenment from the Buddhas—
not as śrāvakas nor as pratyekabuddhas—
and having received the prophecy, they are able to abide securely on the stage of non-retrogression.
Abiding therein, one attains a firm state free from forgetfulness regarding all that is definitively to be done and that which is to be done constantly.
Such is the firm and non-forgetful dharma established by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
it is the supreme establishment among all sentient beings.
He is universally incapable of failing in any task that ought to be performed;
he is likewise incapable of failing even in what has not yet been attained.
At no time does he fail, for all wholesome qualities constantly and uninterruptedly increase, like the moon during the bright fortnight.
Because all wholesome dharmas continue to increase,
at that time the bodhisattva is called "genuine" and not "semblance.
By virtue of receiving the name of a genuine bodhisattva, [he is so designated].
He understands, as they truly are, all the skillful means for disciplining all sentient beings in every respect;
because he knows them as they truly are.
One becomes skillful in all established arrangements.
From this one seeks, by means of this one seeks, and through this one seeks;
having sought, one establishes everything correctly through this finality.
This is called being skillful in all established systems.
Because one has attained skillfulness regarding these established systems,
one further attains skillfulness in the instructions.
Because they have attained skill in these instructions,
they are further able to obtain the king of samādhis with immeasurable objects of focus;
having obtained such a samādhi, they are able to ensure it is not in vain.
He proclaims the various aspects of the sublime Dharma.
When the sublime Dharma is taught, there are always supreme fruits,
which enable one to achieve ultimate liberation through the Mahāyāna.
Because it departs [from saṃsāra] by relying on the nature of the Great [Vehicle],
it can encompass the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, due to this, it receives various names according to its respective stages of departure within those various Mahāyāna states.
All bodhisattvas share this together;
it is that which all Buddhas and bodhisattvas of all worlds collectively establish and collectively praise.
One should know that this is called the excellence of the meritorious qualities worthy of praise.
Because one has attained such an eminent name,
it should be known that one has acquired the marks of all bodhisattvas;
the manner in which the marks and the characterized [body] are perfected is as follows.
The correct practice of all aspects is that which can be accomplished by both lay and ordained bodhisattvas.
Having accomplished it within these two divisions,
their correct practice becomes firm regarding all categories of wholesome qualities.
One attains a resolutely superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).
Such an intention is to be embraced either by the class of householders or by the class of those who have gone forth.
Or, they are able to correctly establish [beings] in virtuous qualities,
even up to causing them to abide therein. Beyond this,
they intentionally take on birth in various states of existence.
In those places of birth, they shall always encounter Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
and be able to perform all manner of beneficial deeds for sentient beings;
they shall constantly and uninterruptedly receive the unerring instructions of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
One sustains the categories of wholesome qualities and experiences the stages of superior realization.
By virtue of this experience, one is able to receive and embrace the praiseworthy stages of superior realization.
One is able to dwell correctly therein as if in one’s own home;
having established oneself in this stage, one is able to advance the awakening wisdom through all aspects of the increasingly superior stages that follow.
Progressing gradually until reaching the ultimate goal,
one does not give rise to complacency along the way;
thus advancing upward, one realizes the final consummation.
From this point on, one no longer seeks any higher stages;
because one has reached the ultimate limit, it is called "attaining the unsurpassed.
This is the first [point].
16. The Stage of Having a Remainder (Sopadhiśeṣabhūmi), the Sixteenth Chapter of the Main Section. Thus has the Bodhisattvabhūmi been explained.
What is the Stage of Having a Remainder?
It should be known that this stage has three characteristics:
first, the establishment of the designation of the stage;
second, the establishment of the designation of tranquility.
Third is establishment based on designation,
which refers to the stage with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*),
excluding one portion of five stages.
That is to say: the stage of no-mind,
the stage produced by cultivation, the stage of the śrāvaka,
and the stage of the pratyekabuddha.
The Bodhisattva-bhūmi,
with the exception of one entire bhūmi—
namely, the Nirupadhiśeṣa-bhūmi (the stage of no remaining substrate).
The remaining stages of existence are called the stages with remainder;
this is termed the establishment of the designation of the stages.
What is the establishment of the designation of tranquility?
That is to say, the stage with remainder (sopadhiśeṣa-bhūmi) is designated and established by way of four kinds of tranquility:
first, by way of the tranquility of suffering.
Second, by means of the pacification of afflictions;
third, by means of the pacification of not harming sentient beings;
fourth, by means of the pacification of equanimity.
What is the pacification of suffering?
It refers to a bhikṣu who is an arhat,
whose outflows are forever exhausted.
All future sufferings of renewed existence have been forever severed;
they have attained complete knowledge,
such that they will never manifest again, like a *tāla* tree whose roots and crown have been cut off.
Because one has attained the state of non-arising in the future,
this is called the pacification of suffering.
What is the pacification of afflictions?
That is to say, for an Arhat bhikṣu,
sensual desire is permanently severed;
ill will is permanently severed.
Ignorance is forever severed;
all afflictions are entirely and forever severed,
because one has attained the state of dharmas that are ultimately non-arising.
This is called the tranquility of afflictions.
What is the tranquility of not harming sentient beings?
It refers to an arhat bhikṣu.
Greed is forever exhausted;
hatred is forever exhausted;
delusion is forever exhausted.
All afflictions are forever exhausted;
one refrains from committing any evil and cultivates all that is wholesome.
This is called the tranquility of not harming or vexing sentient beings.
What is the tranquility of relinquishment?
It refers to an arhat bhikṣu whose outflows are forever exhausted.
He frequently and continuously dwells for the most part in the six constant abodes;
that is to say, having seen a form with the eye, he is neither elated nor dejected.
Abiding in equanimity with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension,
so it is after hearing sounds with the ear, smelling odors with the nose, tasting flavors with the tongue, feeling tangibles with the body, and cognizing mental phenomena with the mind.
Neither rejoicing nor grieving, one dwells in sublime equanimity with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension;
this is called the tranquility of equanimity.
It is based on these four kinds of tranquility that the stage of the remainder of substrate (*sopadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*) is taught.
It is supremely tranquil and supremely cool;
this is called the designation and establishment of tranquility.
What is the designation and establishment based upon?
This refers to eight kinds of bases:
first, the basis of designation;
second, the basis of appropriation.
Third, the basis of abiding;
fourth, the basis of transmigration;
fifth, the basis of obstruction.
Sixth, the basis of affliction;
seventh, the basis of gratification;
eighth, the basis of the final limit.
What is the basis for designation?
It refers to the five aggregates of clinging;
by depending upon these, one designates a self, a sentient being, a living being, a creature, a nourisher, and so forth.
The various designations such as "pudgala," "manuja," "mānava," and so forth,
are conventional expressions based on conceptualization;
it is in dependence upon these that they arise.
One designates them with such names,
such classes of birth, such lineages, such food and drink,
and such experiences of pleasure and pain.
"Long-lived," "thus long-abiding," "such a limit to the lifespan," and so forth— these are all designations, conceptualizations,
and conventional verbal expressions employed for the sake of communication.
What is the basis of appropriation?
It refers to the seven objects of appropriation, namely:
oneself, one's parents, wife, and children.
Slaves, laborers, servants,
friends, and kinsmen—
these are the seven objects of acquisition.
As has already been extensively analyzed in the *Manobhūmi*,
it is by means of this that one understands how various classes of sentient beings possess what they have appropriated.
What is the basis for their maintenance?
That is to say, there are four kinds of nutriment:
namely, edible food, contact-nutriment, [volition-nutriment, and consciousness-nutriment].
The nutriment of mental volition and the nutriment of consciousness:
by depending upon these, sentient beings who have already been born abide, remain, and are sustained.
Furthermore, it can sustain and nourish all those who seek existence.
What is the basis for transmigration?
It refers to the four stations of consciousness and the twelve links of dependent origination.
Namely, the station of consciousness in the pursuit of form,
the station of consciousness in the pursuit of feeling,
and the station of consciousness in the pursuit of perception.
The courses of action, the stations of consciousness,
and the conditionality of ignorance for volitional formations, and of volitional formations for consciousness,
explained in detail up to birth as the condition for aging and death.
Because of depending upon this,
all classes of sentient beings flow along in accordance with the cycle of birth and death within the five destinies.
What is the basis for obstruction?
This refers to how the devas and māras go before those who are practicing various wholesome dharmas and create obstacles for them.
What is the basis of suffering and affliction?
That is to say, the entire desire realm is called the basis of suffering and affliction;
because one relies upon it, sentient beings experience mental distress and physical pain.
What is the basis of gratification?
This refers to the bliss of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-samāpatti*) being called the basis of satisfaction;
for it is by depending upon this that sentient beings,
when they actually enter those respective concentrations in the present life, [experience such satisfaction].
If one is born there and experiences throughout the long night the bliss of dhyāna and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*),
what is the "basis for the final limit"?
It refers to the aggregates (*skandha*) within the continuum of an Arhat.
Based on this, it is said that all Arhats sustain their final bodies.
Question: When an Arhat bhikṣu has eternally exhausted all outflows (āsrava) and dwells in the stage of the remaining substrate of existence (sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa), [how is this so?]
With how many kinds of bases (*āśraya*) should it be said to be associated?
Answer: It should be said to be exclusively associated with one kind of base, namely, the final base (*paścima-āśraya*).
It is not associated with the six bases of appropriation (*parigraha-vastu*);
it is entirely and completely dissociated from both the basis of transmigration (*pravṛtty-āśraya*) and the basis of obstruction (*vibandhāśraya*).
It is neither associated nor dissociated with the remaining support;
this is called the establishment of the designation of the support. 17.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, the Stage of No-Remainder Support (*anupadhiśeṣabhūmi*), within the Main Section on the Stages (*mūlabhūmi*) of the Stage of No-Remainder Support. Thus has the Stage with Remainder Support (*sopadhiśeṣabhūmi*) been explained.
What is the stage of the nirvana without remainder?
It should be known that this stage also possesses three characteristics.
The first is the establishment of the designation of the stage.
Second is the establishment through the designation of cessation;
third is the establishment through the synonyms for cessation.
What is the establishment through the designation of the [elements of] earth?
It should be understood that those portions of the five stages previously excluded are subsumed within this stage of no remaining support (*anupadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*), namely,
the stage of no-mind (*acittaka-bhūmi*).
The stage consisting of cultivation,
the stage of the śrāvaka,
and the stage of the pratyekabuddha.
In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
how is the designation and establishment of "quiescence" (śānti) defined?
It is by means of two kinds of quiescence.
The ground of nirvana without remainder is thus designated and established:
first, by virtue of its being tranquil and quiescent;
second, by virtue of its being quiescent through the absence of affliction and harm.
What is tranquil and quiescent?
It refers to first attaining and realizing the four kinds of tranquility on the stage of with-remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*).
Now, within the realm of nirvana without remainder,
there are likewise four most excellent forms of tranquility:
first, the tranquility of enumeration and teaching.
Second, the pacification of all bases;
third, the pacification of suffering based on the bases;
fourth, the pacification of doubt regarding the arising of suffering based on the bases.
As it is said:
"By means of a mind free from inferiority, one is able to endure arduous toil;
that toward which one proceeds is liberation, just as a lamp is extinguished when its oil is exhausted."
What is the tranquility that is free from affliction?
It refers to being dissociated from all bases [of existence] and being contrary to the arising and circulation of all afflictions and sufferings.

The true, untainted realm revealed through the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is as described when it is said that "the monk’s ultimate quiescence is called the dwelling in true peace and bliss," and as it is further said that "there truly exists that which is unborn,
unarisen, uncreated, unconditioned, and without equal origination."
There is also that which has birth, arising, activity, conditioned formation, and equal origination;
if there were no such thing, there would be no birth, no arising, no activity, no conditioned formation, and no equal origination.
I never say that there is birth, arising, activity, conditioned existence, or origination, and yet there is a permanent transcendence [of them].
This is because, in reality, there is no birth, no arising, no activity, no conditioned existence, and no origination.
Therefore, I say that there is birth, arising, activity, the conditioned, and equal origination, as well as the definitive transcendence [of them].
It was with this underlying intention (*saṃdhāya*) that the Blessed One said: "Profound, vast, immeasurable, and incalculable—this is called cessation (*śānti*)."
Because the virtues contained herein are difficult to comprehend, it is called "profound.
Because it is exceedingly vast, it is called "extensive.
Because it is inexhaustible, it is called "immeasurable."
It is called "incalculable" because it cannot be calculated and because there is no dualistic discourse regarding it.
Why is it that it cannot be calculated here?
It is because it is neither existent nor non-existent, and thus cannot be expressed in words.
Because it cannot be said that form is identical to form or distinct from form;
because it cannot be said that sensation is identical to sensation or distinct from sensation;
because it cannot be said that perception is identical to perception or distinct from perception.
Because it is ineffable that movement is separate from movement;
because it is ineffable that consciousness is separate from consciousness. Why is this so?
Revealed by this purified suchness and being exclusively stainless,
it is called the "unafflicted tranquility.
These are the two kinds.
In summary, it is designated and established as a single "tranquility.
What is the designation and establishment of the various synonyms for tranquility?
It should be known that, herein, there are immeasurable kinds of synonyms for tranquility.
That which is called "permanent" is also called "constant," "long-enduring," "unchanging," and "an existent phenomenon."
It is also called a dwelling;
it is also called an island; it is also called protection;
it is also called a refuge; and it is also called the destination.
It is also called peace and security, and it is also called detachment.
It is also called a virtuous matter, and it is also called auspiciousness.
It is also called non-reversion, and it is also called stainlessness.
It is also called "difficult to see" and "ambrosia.
It is also called "free from sorrow" and "free from perishing.
It is also called "without blazing" and "without fever."
It is also called "freedom from illness" and "immovability.
It is also called "nirvāṇa" and "the eternal cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
One should understand that such categories as these are taught as synonyms for "quiescence" (*śānti*).
This is called the designation and establishment of the various synonyms for *śānti* (quiescence).
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 50; the *Maulī Bhūmiḥ* is completed.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 51.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Within the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, this is the first part of the *Manobhūmi* corresponding to the *Pañcavijñānakāyabhūmi*. Thus has the *Maulī Bhūmi* been explained.
Next, the expertise in the discernment of the stages (*bhūmi-viniścaya-kauśalya*) is explained.
Relying upon this expertise in discernment,
one is well able to engage in questions and answers regarding all the stages.
Now, first, the determination (*viniścaya*) of the five consciousness-bodies (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya-bhūmi*) and the mind-ground (*mano-bhūmi*) shall be explained.
Although the *ālaya-vijñāna* has been mentioned,
its causes and conditions for existence and the meaning of its detailed classification have not yet been explained.
Why is it not taught?
For what reason should one know that there is a meaning of extensive differentiation?
How should this be understood?
Answer: This was not stated because it is established as the most profound and secret prophecy of the Buddha, the World-Honored One;
as the World-Honored One said:
The ādāna-vijñāna is profound and subtle; Containing all seeds, it is like a torrential stream.
I do not reveal this to the foolish and the ignorant, Lest they should conceptualize and grasp it as a self.
Furthermore, the summary verse (uddāna) says:
Appropriation, initial clarity, seeds, karma, bodily sensation,
the mindless attainments, and death— these would all be untenable on account of eight reasons.
It is established that the ālayavijñāna definitely exists;
for it is illogical if there were no ālayavijñāna as the basis for the appropriation [of the body],
and it is illogical for the initial arising [of consciousness] to occur.
It would be unreasonable for there to be a nature of clarity;
it would be unreasonable for there to be a nature of seeds;
and it would be unreasonable for there to be distinctions in karmic function.
It would be unreasonable for there to be distinctions between bodily experiences;
it would be unreasonable to abide in the meditative attainment of non-conception;
and it would be unreasonable for consciousness to exist at the time of death.
For what reason is it illogical for there to be no ālayavijñāna as the basis for appropriation?
It is because of five reasons.
What are these five?
That is to say, the ālayavijñāna has the karmic actions performed in previous lives as its cause,
while the evolving consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and others, have the various conditions of the present life as their causes,
as described in relation to the sense faculties and their objects.
