"Due to the power of mental attention (*manasikāra*), the various evolving consciousnesses arise," and so forth at length; this is called the first cause.
Furthermore, the six groups of consciousness are found to possess natures such as wholesome and unwholesome.
This is the second reason.
Furthermore, the category of the six groups of consciousness that is unobscured and neutral, which is comprised within maturation (*vipāka*), cannot be found.
This is the third reason.
Furthermore, the six groups of consciousness each function based on their respective supports;
as each consciousness functions upon its particular support,
that very support ought to be appropriated.
It is not reasonable that the remainder be non-appropriated;
even if one were to concede they are appropriated, it would still be unreasonable,
because consciousness is absent from them.
This is the fourth reason.
Furthermore, the basis [of consciousness] would incur the fault of being repeatedly appropriated. Why is this so?
Because that visual consciousness sometimes arises and sometimes does not arise,
and the same applies to the other consciousnesses;
this is the fifth reason.
Thus, because past karma and present conditions serve as causes,
and because the natures of the wholesome and unwholesome can be apprehended,
while the specific types of maturation cannot be so apprehended.
Because the various consciousnesses would evolve based on their respective individual supports,
and because there would be the fault of repeatedly appropriating those supports, it is not logical.
For what reason is it illogical for initial arising to occur if the ālayavijñāna does not exist? To this,
an objection is raised:
If the ālayavijñāna were definitely to exist,
there would have to be two consciousnesses arising simultaneously;
one should say to them:
You falsely conceive the notion of fault where there is no fault. Why?
Because it is possible for two consciousnesses to arise simultaneously.
Why is this? Suppose, for instance,
there were someone who simultaneously desired to see,
and so on, up to desiring to know.
It is not logical that any single consciousness should arise for the first time,
because at that moment there is no distinction in attention (*manasikāra*),
nor is there any distinction in the sense faculties or their objects.
For what reason do the consciousnesses not arise simultaneously? Why,
if there were no simultaneous arising of the various consciousnesses,
would the mental consciousness that functions together with the visual consciousness and the others [not exist]?
Is it that the essential nature [of consciousness] cannot be apprehended?
That is to say, there may be times when one recollects objects previously experienced in the past;
at such times, the activity of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not clear.
When the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) operates upon a present object, it cannot possess such a characteristic of being unclear;
therefore, one must either admit that all consciousnesses arise simultaneously or admit that the mental consciousness lacks clarity.
Why is it that, if the ālayavijñāna did not exist,
it would be illogical for there to be the nature of seeds?
Because the six groups of consciousness are mutually distinct from one another.
Why is this? Because from an immediate succession of the wholesome,
that which is unwholesome by nature arises.
From the immediately subsequent to the unwholesome, the wholesome nature arises;
from the two [unwholesome and wholesome], the indeterminate nature arises immediately after;
and from the inferior realm, the intermediate realm arises immediately after.
From the intermediate realm, the sublime realm arises without interval;
likewise, from the sublime realm, even down to the inferior realm, it arises without interval.
From the contaminated, the uncontaminated arises without interval.
The outflow-free arises immediately after the outflowing;
the supramundane arises immediately after the mundane;
and the mundane arises immediately after the supramundane.
It is not logically tenable that such characteristics possess the nature of seeds.
Furthermore, since those various consciousnesses are interrupted for long periods of time,
they should not continue to flow in succession over a long duration.
Therefore, this too is not logical.
Why? Because if the various consciousnesses did not arise simultaneously, the differentiation of their functional activities would be illogical.
Briefly stated, there are four kinds of karma:
first, the karma that differentiates the vessel-world;
second, the karma that differentiates the basis.
Third is the activity of discerning the self;
fourth is the activity of discerning objects.
These various discernments are observed to arise simultaneously, moment by moment.
Therefore, it is unreasonable for a single consciousness to possess such diverse functional activities within a single moment. For what reason?
Because if the ālayavijñāna did not exist...
It would be unreasonable for there to be a distinction in bodily experience;
that is to say, as when someone reflects correctly or incorrectly,
or without reflection, or in accordance with vitarka and vicāra.
Whether the mind is in meditative concentration or not in concentration,
at that time, various, numerous, and manifold distinct sensations arise within the body.
That [consciousness] should not exist, yet it is presently perceived;
therefore, the ālayavijñāna must certainly exist.
For what reason? Because if the ālayavijñāna did not exist...
It would be unreasonable for one to abide in the mindless attainments;
that is to say, upon entering the attainment of non-conception or the attainment of cessation,
it would be as if consciousness had departed from the body at the moment of death.
It is not that consciousness is not separated from the body,
for as the Blessed One has said, "At that time, consciousness is not separated from the body.
For what reason would this be so if the ālayavijñāna did not exist?
It would be illogical for consciousness to cease at the time of death;
that is to say, at the moment of passing away, consciousness would gradually depart from the upper parts of the body,
and the sensation of coldness would gradually arise there.
Or [it may be] from the lower parts of the body;
it is not the case that the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) does not sometimes arise there.
Therefore, one knows that only the ālayavijñāna is capable of maintaining the body.
If this is abandoned,
then a sensation of coldness can be perceived in the body parts,
and the body will be devoid of tactile sensation.
The mental consciousness is not like that.
Therefore, it is not logical that the ālayavijñāna should be non-existent.
Furthermore, the summary verse (uddāna) says:
If the objects of perception are associated, they mutually function as conditions;
together with consciousness and so forth, they revolve, and through their defilement and cessation,
the ālayavijñāna is briefly explained.
The process of saṃsāra is established by way of four aspects;
the process of cessation is established by way of one aspect.
What are the four aspects by which saṃsāra is established?
It should be understood that this is established because of the functioning of the objective referent (*ālambana*),
the functioning of association (*samprayoga*),
and the functioning of mutual conditionality (*anyonya-pratyayatā*).
This is because it establishes the simultaneous evolution of consciousness and its associates.
How is the establishment of cessation established as having a single characteristic?
It is by way of establishing the evolution of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
And because of establishing its cessation.
How is the mode of transformation through the object of perception established?
Briefly stated, it refers to the ālayavijñāna.
It evolves with respect to two kinds of objects:
first, by means of discerning internal appropriation;
second, by means of discerning the external, non-conceptual appearance of the vessel-world.
Regarding the discernment of internal appropriation:
this refers to the ability to discern the habitual tendencies of false attachment to the imagined nature,
as well as the various material sense faculties and their physical bases.
This exists within the realm of form; if it is in the formless realm,
there is only the discernment of habitual tendencies and grasping.
Regarding the discernment of the external, non-conceptual appearance of the vessel-world:
this refers to the ability to discern the support [of consciousness],
because the ālayavijñāna takes internal appropriation as its object-condition.

At all times, without interruption, the characteristics of the receptacle world are like the flame of a lamp: when it arises, it internally grasps the oil and the wick while externally emitting light.
In this same way, the ālayavijñāna takes internal appropriation as its object and takes the external receptacle world as its characteristic.
The principle of its arising should be understood in the same way.
Furthermore, because the object-condition of the ālayavijñāna is so subtle,
it is difficult even for those of worldly wisdom to comprehend.
Furthermore, the ālayavijñāna’s engagement with its objects is uninterrupted and unchanging,
from the initial moment of appropriation until the end of life.
Furthermore, because it functions through the discernment of a single flavor, one should know that the ālayavijñāna arises and perishes moment by moment with respect to its objects;
it flows in a continuous succession of moments, being neither unitary nor eternal.
Furthermore, it should be said that the ālayavijñāna,
within the desire realm, takes as its object a limited sphere of appropriation;
within the form realm, it takes as its object an extensive sphere of appropriation.
In the formless realm, one takes as objects the immeasurable appropriated spheres of the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness;
in the sphere of nothingness, one takes as an object the subtle appropriated sphere.
In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it takes extremely subtle apprehended objects as its objective support.
Thus, because it discerns two kinds of objective supports and because it discerns its objective support with extreme subtlety.
Because it is a discernment of similarity;
because it is a discernment of moments;
and because it is a discernment of limited objects of appropriation.
Because it discerns vast objects of appropriation;
because it discerns immeasurable objects of appropriation;
because it discerns subtle objects of appropriation.
Because it discerns extremely subtle objects of appropriation,
one should understand that this establishes the mode of activity regarding the object of the ālayavijñāna.
How is the mode of activity regarding association established?
This refers to the ālayavijñāna,
which is always associated with the five universal mental factors (pañca-sarvatraga-citta-saṃprayukta-dharma),
namely: attention (manasikāra), contact (sparśa), sensation (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and volition (cetanā).
These five dharmas are likewise comprised solely within the maturation (vipāka) and are most extremely subtle; thus,
they are difficult even for those of worldly wisdom to comprehend.
Furthermore, it always functions by taking a single type of object as its condition.
Moreover, the sensation associated with the ālayavijñāna is consistently categorized as neither-painful-nor-pleasant and neutral (avyākṛta).
One should know that the mental aspects of the remaining mental factors (*caitasika*) are likewise.
This is because they are associated with the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*),
and because they are associated with a single category of maturation (*vipāka*).
Because it functions in association with an extremely subtle transformation;
because it functions in association with a constant, uniform engagement with its object;
and because it is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Because it is exclusively associated with the indeterminate (avyākṛta),
one should understand that this establishes the mode of activity associated with the ālayavijñāna.
How is the mode of activity characterized by mutual conditionality established?
That is to say, the ālayavijñāna serves as two kinds of conditions for the evolving consciousnesses:
first, by acting as their seeds.
Second, because it serves as their support.
Regarding its being the seed:
this refers to all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate evolving consciousnesses when they evolve.
Because all things take the ālayavijñāna as their seed,
it serves as the basis;
that is to say, it is by means of the ālayavijñāna that the material sense organs are appropriated.
The five groups of consciousness function in dependence upon it;
they are not without appropriation.
Furthermore, because the ālayavijñāna exists, the manas can exist.
Based on this manas as its support, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) arises,
just as the five groups of sensory consciousness arise based on the five sense organs such as the eye;
it does not occur without the five organs.
Consciousness is likewise not without the faculty of mind (*manas*).
Furthermore, the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) serve as two types of conditions for the ālayavijñāna.
First, because it can nourish those seeds within the present life;
second, within the future life.
In order to bring about their arising and to plant their seeds,
that which nurtures those seeds within the present life refers to how,
based upon the *ālayavijñāna*, the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate *pravṛttivijñānas* (active consciousnesses) evolve.
In this way, within a single basis that arises and ceases simultaneously,
the *ālayavijñāna* is perfumed;
by virtue of these causes and conditions, the subsequent evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) proceed as wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate in nature.
It increases further, becomes more intense, and becomes more distinct as it proceeds.
That which, for the sake of its arising in a future state, gathers and plants its seeds— namely,
that which is of the nature of perfuming (*vāsanā*).
It is able to induce and encompass the future neutral maturation (vipāka),
because the ālayavijñāna serves as its seed and its basis.
Because it nurtures seeds and because it gathers and plants seeds,
one should understand that the establishment of the *ālayavijñāna* and the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) as mutual conditions constitutes their mode of transformation.
How is the simultaneous arising of the ālayavijñāna with the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) established?
It is said that the ālayavijñāna,
at certain times, arises simultaneously with only one type of evolving consciousness.
That which is called manas. Why is this?
Because by means of this manas.
The [notion] of self-view, pride, and so forth are always associated with it;
they have the mode of activity of deliberation and function simultaneously with the ālayavijñāna at all times, whether in states with mental activity or without mental activity.
Taking the ālayavijñāna as its object,
it functions with the mental aspect of conceiving a self and giving rise to pride;
at times, it operates simultaneously with two [other consciousnesses].
This refers to the manas and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
At times, they function simultaneously with three [consciousnesses],
namely, when any one of the five groups of sensory consciousnesses (pañcavijñānakāya) functions.
At times, it functions simultaneously with four [mental factors],
namely when the five groups of sensory consciousness (pañca-vijñāna-kāya) function in accordance with two [of them].
At other times, it may even function simultaneously with seven.
That is to say, when the five groups of consciousness function in conjunction,
and furthermore, when they rely upon the afflicted manas as their support,
as long as that [manas] has not been extinguished, the bondage of the discernment of signs cannot be liberated.
Once the manas has ceased, the bonds of the marks are liberated.
Furthermore, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able to take other objects as its domain as well as its own object.
Regarding that which takes other objects as its domain:
This refers to that which takes as its object the spheres of the five groups of sensory consciousness, whether taking its own objects simultaneously or non-simultaneously;
that is, it takes the sphere of mental phenomena (dharmas) as its object.
Furthermore, this refers to the ālayavijñāna.
At times, it arises simultaneously with painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
this feeling is associated with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and arises in dependence upon them.
This refers to the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that arises spontaneously among humans,
or among certain classes of gods in the desire realm, as well as among certain classes of hungry ghosts and animals,
which is associated with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
Painful, pleasant, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations arise in conjunction and intermingle with one another. However,
in places such as the hells, where they are overwhelmed by others,
neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation coexists with pure suffering.
There is no simultaneous occurrence of unmixed feelings;
one should know that because these feelings are eclipsed, they are difficult to discern,
just as in the hells and similar realms where feeling occurs exclusively as suffering.
In this way, throughout the three lower dhyāna stages,
[the mind] proceeds exclusively in conjunction with pleasant feeling;
from the fourth dhyāna stage up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), it is likewise.
It always functions in conjunction with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Furthermore, the ālayavijñāna may at times function simultaneously with various mental factors— wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral— that are associated with the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna).
In this way, although the ālayavijñāna evolves simultaneously with the evolving consciousnesses,
it also evolves simultaneously with adventitious mental factors— whether adventitiously afflicted, virtuous, non-virtuous, or indeterminate.
However, one should not say that it is associated with that [mind].
Why? Because it does not function by taking the same object as that [mind].
Just as visual consciousness, although it arises simultaneously with the eye faculty, is not associated with it,
so too is this case.
One should understand that here, the analogy is established by relying on a partial similarity in principle.
Furthermore, although all mental factors (caitta) are indistinguishable in their nature as mental factors,
they nevertheless arise simultaneously within a single continuum without mutual contradiction, because their characteristics are distinct.
In this way, the ālayavijñāna and the various evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñānas) evolve simultaneously within a single body;
it should be understood that they do not contradict one another.
Furthermore, it is like a single torrent where many waves arise simultaneously without contradicting one another;
or like a single clear mirror surface where many reflections appear simultaneously without contradicting one another.
In this way, within a single ālayavijñāna,
many evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) may arise simultaneously;
one should know that they do not contradict one another.
Furthermore, for example, at one time, with respect to a single object,
a single visual consciousness apprehends only one type of non-differentiated color-form;
or, at another time, it may simultaneously apprehend many different types of color-forms.
Just as visual consciousness [relates] to various forms,
so too does auditory consciousness [relate] to various sounds,
and olfactory consciousness to various fragrances.
The tongue-consciousness regarding various tastes is likewise.
Furthermore, the body-consciousness may, at one time, apprehend only a single type of non-distinct tactile characteristic within a single objective sphere;
or, at another time, it may simultaneously apprehend many different kinds of tactile characteristics.
In this way, the discriminating mental consciousness,
at one time, may grasp the aspect of a single object,
or it may grasp various aspects of many different objects.
This should be understood as not contradicting reason.
Furthermore, it was previously stated that the manas functions simultaneously with the ālayavijñāna until it is severed;
one should know that it is always associated at one time with the four innate, spontaneous afflictions.
That is to say: the view of a self-identity,
the conceit "I am," and self-love.
Together with ignorance—
these four afflictions,
whether in the state of meditative concentration or in the non-concentrated state.
It should be understood that this ālayavijñāna, which functions constantly and is not incompatible with the wholesome and so forth,
is of a nature that is obscured-neutral (nivṛtāvyākṛta).
Because it evolves simultaneously with the evolving consciousnesses;
because it evolves simultaneously with all feelings;
and because it evolves simultaneously with the wholesome and so forth.
One should understand the establishment of the simultaneous functioning of the ālayavijñāna.
How is the characteristic of the cessation of the defilements of the ālayavijñāna established?
Briefly stated, the ālayavijñāna is the root of all defilements.
Why is this so? Because this consciousness is the root from which the world of sentient beings arises,
as it is capable of producing the sense faculties, the bases upon which those faculties rely, and the evolving consciousnesses.
It is also the fundamental basis for the arising of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*),
because it is capable of bringing about the receptacle world;
it is also the fundamental basis for the mutual arising of sentient beings.
Because all sentient beings, in relation to one another, serve as mutual dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Why is this so?
Because there is no instance where sentient beings do not mutually perceive one another and so forth.
Suffering, pleasure, and so forth do not arise through mutual enjoyment;
by this principle, one should know that the realm of sentient beings serves as a reciprocal dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for one another.
Furthermore, it is precisely this *ālaya-vijñāna* [that functions in this way].
Because it can maintain the seeds of all phenomena,
it constitutes the essence of the truth of suffering in the present world and is also the cause for the arising of the truth of suffering in the future.
Furthermore, it is the cause for the arising of the present truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Thus, it is able to produce the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) and is able to produce the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
Because it is the essence of the Truth of Suffering;
because it can produce the Truth of Suffering in the future;
and because it can produce the Truth of Origination in the present.
One should know that the ālayavijñāna is the root of all defilements.
Furthermore, it contains the seeds of wholesome dharmas such as the factors conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya) and the factors conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya).
This is not the cause of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*),
because the roots of virtue such as the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*) are contrary to the process of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
This refers to all other remaining mundane roots of virtue.
Because they arise from this, they become increasingly bright and flourishing.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, the seeds of their own kind that are grasped by them become increasingly functional and increasingly powerful.
The seeds increase and quickly attain fulfillment.
Furthermore, by virtue of these seeds, those various wholesome dharmas arise with increasing clarity and vigor.
Moreover, they are able to bring about, in the future, various ripened fruits (*vipāka-phala*) that are increasingly enhanced, increasingly superior, desirable, and pleasant.
Furthermore, based on this ālayavijñāna which contains all seeds,
the Bhagavat said:
"There exists the eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-consciousness-element."
This extends even to the existence of the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*),
and the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), because there are various elements (*dhātu*) within the ālayavijñāna.
Furthermore, it is as the sūtra describes by means of the simile of the cluster of akṣa fruits.
Because the ālayavijñāna contains many realms,
furthermore, this ālayavijñāna, which is the root of all affliction,
can only be transformed and extinguished through the cultivation of wholesome dharmas.
Regarding this cultivation of wholesome dharmas,
if ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) dwell with their minds through the skillful means of mental attention directed toward the evolving consciousnesses as objects,
they are able to enter the initial clear realization (abhisamaya) of the Noble Truths.
One who has not yet seen the truths and has not yet attained the Dharma-eye among those truths cannot penetrate the ālayavijñāna that contains all seeds.
Having cultivated such practices, those who have not yet seen the truths may either enter the state of rightness and departure from birth of a śrāvaka,
or enter the state of rightness and departure from birth of a bodhisattva.
Having realized the true dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) of all phenomena,
one is also able to penetrate the ālayavijñāna;
at that time, one is able to comprehensively observe all internal defilements.
Furthermore, one is able to understand that for oneself, externally one is bound by the bondage of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*),
and internally one is bound by the bondage of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*).
Moreover, the practitioner who cultivates insight (*vipaśyanā*)...
Because the ālayavijñāna is the realm of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) subsumed under all conceptual proliferations (prapañca),
those conditioned phenomena are briefly condensed within the ālayavijñāna into a single mass, a single accumulation, and a single heap.
Having become a single mass, through the cultivation and repeated practice of the knowledge that takes *tathatā* as its object, one attains the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
Immediately upon this transformation of the basis, it should be said that the *ālayavijñāna* has been severed.
Because of this abandonment, it should be said that all defilements have been abandoned.
It should be understood that the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), by virtue of its opposition,
is able to serve as the perpetual antidote to the ālayavijñāna.
Furthermore, the substance of the ālayavijñāna is impermanent and possesses the nature of grasping;
the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), however, is permanent.
It is devoid of the nature of grasping and receiving,
because it is only through the Noble Path taking True Suchness (tathatā) as its object that the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) can occur.
Furthermore, regarding the ālayavijñāna:
It is constantly accompanied by all forms of *dausthulya* (dysfunction).
Upon the ultimate transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), it is forever separated from all *dausthulya*.
Furthermore, regarding the *ālayavijñāna*:
This is the cause for the transformation of afflictions;
it is not the cause for the transformation of the noble path.
The transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is the cause for the non-transformation of afflictions.
One should understand that the cause for the turning of the noble path is solely a cause of establishment (*vyavasthāna-hetu*),
not a cause of production (*janana-hetu*).
Furthermore, the ālayavijñāna prevents one from attaining mastery over wholesome, pure, and indeterminate phenomena;
through the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), it enables one to attain great mastery over all wholesome, pure, and indeterminate phenomena.
Furthermore, regarding the characteristic of the cessation of the ālayavijñāna:
it means that because this consciousness is correctly severed and ceases, one abandons the two kinds of grasping;
although the body remains, it is like a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya).
Why is this? Because the causes for future existence have been severed,
one thereby abandons the grasping for future existence.
Because all causes of affliction have been permanently severed within this present life,
one abandons the grasping that serves as the basis for all defilements in this present life;
because all coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) has been permanently relinquished.
Only conditioned by life does it abide for a brief time.
Because this exists, the Sūtra states:
"At that time, one experiences only the feeling of the limit of the body and the feeling of the limit of life."
To speak at length, it continues until all that is experienced in this very life is ultimately extinguished.
Thus, because it establishes the root of affliction, and because it involves the entry into,
the thorough penetration of, and the cultivation of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Because it establishes the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*),
one should know that it establishes the characteristics of the cessation of the defilements (*saṃkleśa*) of the ālayavijñāna.
Thus, having already relied upon the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-yukti*).
One establishes the distinctions in the definitions and meanings of mind (*citta*), mentation (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). By means of this principle,
one understands the principles of all defilement and purification regarding the mind, mentation, and consciousness within the three realms and so forth.
One should understand this accordingly.
The principles of mind, mentation, and consciousness revealed in other passages are merely presented in accordance with the differences among the sentient beings to be converted.
This is taught through the transformation of the wisdom of an infant;
it is a provisional teaching of skillful means intended to facilitate their easy entry [into the Dharma].
Question: If one accomplishes the *ālayavijñāna*, does one also accomplish the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*)?
If one accomplishes the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), does one also accomplish the ālayavijñāna?
It should be answered by means of four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There may be cases where one accomplishes the ālayavijñāna but not the evolving consciousnesses.
This refers to those who are mindless while asleep or mindless while in a state of fainting;
those who have entered the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); those born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñi-deva*);
or those who possess the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) but not the ālayavijñāna.
This refers to Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas,
and Tathāgatas who abide in the state of possessing mind;
some among them possess both [the two types of cessation].
This refers to other sentient beings who abide in the state of possessing mind;
or there are those for whom neither is accomplished, namely:
Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas.
Entering the sphere of nirvana without remainder from the state of the meditative attainment of cessation.

Question: Since internal and external phenomena each have distinct intrinsic natures and abide in their own specific characteristics, for what reason are only the six consciousness-elements established as having intrinsic nature among the eighteen elements?
Are the remaining elements established as their basis, object, and accompaniment?
Answer: Because the six consciousness-elements undergo rapid transformation from moment to moment, instant to instant, and throughout periods such as days and nights.
Depending on various respective conditions, such as the sense faculties of the eye and so forth, and taking objects such as visible forms and so forth as their objective supports,
they arise in manifold ways— neither singular nor merely numerous— by employing the various mental factors as their companions.
Because they arise based on various respective supports, they receive various respective names;
just as fire, by depending on various respective conditions, burns, and at that time receives various respective designations.
Because grass, wood, cow dung, husks, chaff, and so forth serve as conditions,
fire is able to burn;
at that time, it is accordingly designated as "grass-fire" up to "chaff-fire."
In this way, because the eye and visible forms serve as conditions, visual consciousness arises; it is thus designated by the name "visual consciousness.
This continues in the same manner up to what is designated by the name "mental consciousness.
The full explanation should be understood accordingly.
As for the remaining elements such as the eye-element and so forth, once they have arisen from their initial origination with a particular intrinsic nature,
they arise in a manner similar to that very intrinsic nature,
continuing in a successive stream until the very end.
Furthermore, a particular category of consciousness arises with a diverse self-nature depending upon various respective conditions;
therefore, the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*) is established by way of its self-nature.
The remaining elements are established as its basis (*āśraya*), its object (*ālambana*), and its companions (*sahāya*).
Furthermore, the thorough knowledge of the aggregate of consciousness shall now be analyzed.
Question: By how many modes does a bhikṣu practicing for the purification of the mind thoroughly know his own mind?
Answer: Briefly stated, it is by way of three aspects:
first, the aspect of attachment to affliction;
second, the aspect of the defects of affliction.
The third is the characteristic of skillful means for the cessation of the three types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
How does a bhikṣu practicing mental purification fully understand the characteristics of the affliction and attachment of his own mind?
It is when the bhikṣu practicing mental purification forms this thought:
Now, this mind of mine has long cherished various defilements throughout the night of saṃsāra;
having recognized its own attachment to these defilements,
it now emerges from the nature of craving.
He settles his mind upon the state of freedom from desire;
yet at that time, his mind is unable to abide in that state of freedom from desire, nor does it find delight therein.
Without any other object of focus, there is only the rapid returning and entering into a state of flowing, scattering, and racing within a nature characterized by craving;
just as it is from a nature characterized by craving,
so too does one emerge from a nature characterized by aversion, delusion, inferiority, agitation, lack of tranquility, and distraction.
To speak at length, this continues until he emerges from dwelling in the nature of heedless attachment and establishes his mind in the constant and diligent cultivation of all wholesome dharmas.
At that time, his mind [is fixed] upon the constant and diligent cultivation of all wholesome dharmas.
Unable to abide therein and finding no delight, they have no other object of focus;
there is only the swift return to enter into, disperse toward, and race after the nature of heedlessness and sensual attachment.
This is called the bhikṣu of pure mental conduct thoroughly knowing the characteristics of the defilements and attachments of his own mind.
Having known the characteristics of the defilements and attachments of his own mind, he...
This bhikṣu of pure conduct further thoroughly understands the characteristics of the defilements and faults within his own mind,
thinking as follows:

Now, this mind of mine possessed by greed can bring harm to myself, harm to others, and harm to both; it can give rise to offenses in the present life, offenses in future lives, and offenses in both the present and future lives.
Furthermore, it can serve as a condition for producing the mental and physical suffering of grief that arises from it;
just as it is with the nature of having craving,
so it is up to the nature of delighting in negligence.
One should know that it is likewise so.
Furthermore, one forms this thought:
"This is a mind possessed by greed, up to and including a mind that delights in negligence."
Because there are faults and afflictions, there are epidemics, untimely deaths, calamities, and distress.
Having understood the characteristics of the faults of mental defilement,
one is further able to thoroughly know the skillful means for the complete cessation of the defilements of one's own mind.
I should not now allow myself to follow along with my own defilements, which possess various faults, epidemics, calamities, and afflictions,
such that my mind functions according to their power; rather,
I must certainly cause my own mind to function freely according to my own mastery.
Having understood this, he thinks:
"I should no longer allow my mind to follow its own impulses;
rather, I shall cause my mind to follow me."
Having repeatedly investigated and analyzed,
one causes the mind that possesses craving to abandon its nature of craving,
and to dwell with delight in the state of non-craving.
Furthermore, one perceives superior qualities therein;
in this way, one comes to abandon heedlessness and delight in the nature of abiding,
until finally one dwells in delight within the constant and diligent cultivation of all wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, having seen those superior qualities therein, he dwells in them extensively.
Having practiced in this way, at that time his mind— without relying on deliberate deliberation—
naturally abides in and delights in the constant and diligent cultivation of all wholesome dharmas.
He develops a profound sense of revulsion and reproach toward that previously mentioned nature of afflicted attachment.
By means of this cause and condition, the bhikṣu who practices mental purification understands his own mind’s afflicted attachment as it truly is.
It possesses a nature of rapid reversal that is beyond analogy;
furthermore, it is well able to know the defects inherent in such an afflicted mind,
and it is also well able to know the skillful means for the cessation of such an afflicted mind.
By means of such purity of mind, a bhikṣu who practices mental purification will swiftly realize the unsurpassed state of mental purification,
namely, the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava).
Regarding skill in distinctions and skill in the transformation of the mind:
one should understand that skill in the distinctions of the mind is based upon the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Based on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
one should understand that the transformation of the mind involves skillful distinctions.
Furthermore, one who is skillfully able to cultivate the mind will attain two benefits.
First, at the time of the fruit, one realizes and experiences peace and bliss;
second, at the time of the cause, one proceeds with mastery. Furthermore, there are three faults regarding the turbidity of the mind:
first, the fault of improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
Second, the fault of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
third, the fault of the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
One should simply apply oneself with profound skill, vigor, and correct reasoning to observe [the mind] thoroughly.
It is stated in the *Smṛtyupasthāna* [Sūtra]:
"One must dwell observing the body as the body, and so on, up to dwelling observing phenomena as phenomena.
What is the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) of this?
Answer: It is in order to demonstrate that the four foundations of mindfulness consist solely in the observation of the mind.
That is to say: observing the mind as grasping, observing the mind as experiencing, observing the mind as cognizing, and observing the mind as defiled or purified.

It is solely for the purpose of observing what the mind grasps, what the mind experiences, what the mind discerns as objects, and the defilement or purity of the mind that the four foundations of mindfulness are taught.
Furthermore, there are certain bhikṣus.
Abiding in the three modes of abiding and practicing the six correct practices,
one performs much within the Teacher’s instruction;
that is to say, one abides in the abiding of liberation.
He dwells in the doors of liberation and dwells in the dharmas that lead to the doors of liberation;
he practices uninterrupted application.
The practice of reflecting on the cultivation of merit;
the practice of generating roots of goodness induced by cultivation;
and the practice of discerning the truths while remaining detached from all worldly relish.
In practicing, one does not engage in conduct characterized by overweening pride;
rather, one practices the conduct of pure and correct enjoyment.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of relinquishment and giving.
First, the recipient gives;
second, the donor gives.
There are likewise two kinds of fruits of giving.
First, one attains great wealth;
second, one attains the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) in the enjoyment that flows from such [wealth].
Furthermore, the reasoning that establishes this shall now be explained.
Question: By what principle should it be understood that the arising of formations (*saṃskāra*) is taught to occur solely from the future, which is neither real nor existent?
Answer: If the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of future dharmas were real and yet could arise, [then there would be no distinction between past, present, and future].
Is this dharma spoken of as being produced through transition?
That is to say, does it mean transitioning from the state of the future world to the state of the present world?
Or is it birth and death?
That is to say, does death and birth in a future life arise by taking that [future state] as a condition in the present life?
It means that while future phenomena abide without changing their function, other phenomena arise in the present life by taking them as conditions.
Is "arising" (jāti) spoken of in terms of having functional activity?
That is to say, does it mean that what was originally without functional activity in the future comes to possess functional activity upon reaching the present world?
Or is "arising" spoken of in terms of the fulfillment of characteristics?
That is to say, while the characteristics of the future are not yet complete, they become complete upon reaching the present world.
Is it then by way of different characteristics that "arising" is spoken of?
It means that in the future there exists a portion of the future and a portion of the cause.
Because these two types differ in their characteristics:
that which has arrived in the present possesses both a present portion and a fruit portion;
because these two types differ in their characteristics.
Thus, the arising of these six kinds of phenomena is in every way illogical.
Why is this? Because there can be no such thing as that which is without direction and without location.
Phenomena possess the characteristic of migrating from one location to another;
furthermore, there is no such thing as death for a phenomenon that has not yet arisen or has not already been produced.
If it were to arise by taking that [death] as a condition, [then it would follow that it had already existed].
Thus, a distinct phenomenon arises rather than something arising from the future;
this would then be non-existent in the future.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), all phenomena lack functional activity.
The functional activity is not found to be distinct from its characteristics;
it is merely provisionally established upon those very characteristics.
Were there any difference, [it would be untenable].
It is logically untenable to claim that while the future and the present share the same characteristic of real existence, only the present possesses functional activity.
Furthermore, this karmic activity would then have to arise de novo where it previously did not exist;
moreover, it would contradict the subtle and profound teachings of the World-Honored One.
As it is said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are neither eternal nor permanent, you demonstrate that the activity (*karma*) of conditioned phenomena is impermanent.
By this reasoning, conditioned phenomena would have to be eternal, and they would likewise be identical to a single characteristic.
If the distinct part of the characteristic were to exist,
why would the characteristic itself not exist?
Furthermore, the distinct part of the characteristic is non-existent originally and comes into existence now.
Why do the distinct parts of the characteristics not establish that what was originally non-existent now exists?
Furthermore, apart from all conditioned phenomena such as form and so forth,
no other future part can ever be found.
Furthermore, it should be that the characteristic of the fruit does not exist in the future, but rather arises in the present when the fruit-characteristic exists.
Having thus established the reasoning for proof,
one should understand [the matter] based on this principle.
He proclaims that all aspects of future phenomena are neither real nor existent, being originally non-existent and now existent.
As it is with the future,
so it is with the past, as appropriate.
By this principle, one should know that what is taught is neither real nor existent.
Furthermore, what is past action?
This means that when characteristics have already ceased and vanished and its intrinsic nature has already been relinquished,
what is the present activity?
It is the momentary abiding at the time of arising, before characteristics have ceased and vanished and before the intrinsic nature has been relinquished.
What are future formations?
They are those formations which, though presently existing as self-characteristics, have not yet arisen and have not yet attained their own nature.
Question: If those formations were originally non-existent in the future and yet come into being, [how is this so?]
Why do things such as flowers in the sky, the horns of a rabbit, or the son of a barren woman not arise?
Answer: Because flowers in the sky and the like lack the causes for arising;
all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), being distinct from one another, necessarily possess their own specific causes for arising.
Question: If all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) each have their own distinct causes for arising, by what cause and condition do they not arise all at once simultaneously?
Answer: Although conditioned phenomena each have their own distinct causes for arising, [they do not arise simultaneously].
Nevertheless, they must depend upon conditions to arise.
When the conditions for the arising of this or that formation are present,
the causes for that specific formation give rise to it.
Therefore, although conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) appear to have causes,
there is no fault of their arising simultaneously and instantaneously.
Furthermore, in this context, what is meant by the "cause" of conditioned phenomena?
What is meant by "condition" (pratyaya)?
The Blessed One has said:
"In brief, there are four kinds of conditions for the arising of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra)."
1. The causal condition (hetu-pratyaya).
2. The immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya).
3. The object condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
There are four predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Among them, the single type known as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is both a cause and a condition;
the remaining three types are only conditions and not causes.
What is the causal condition (*nidāna*)?
It refers to the material sense faculties, their bases, and consciousness;
these two [categories] are explained in brief.
It is capable of sustaining the seeds of all phenomena;

following along with the material sense-faculties, it contains the seeds of those material sense-faculties, as well as the seeds of all other material phenomena and the seeds of all minds and mental factors.
If one follows the consciousness, there are the seeds of all consciousnesses, as well as the seeds of other formless dharmas, the seeds of the material sense-faculties,
and the seeds of the remaining material dharmas.
It should be understood that the intrinsic nature of all remaining material phenomena is followed solely by their own seeds,
with the exception of the materiality of the great elements.
Because it is followed by two kinds of seeds of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*);
that is to say, the seeds of the primary elements and the seeds of derived matter.
It is precisely this established continuity of seeds, distinguished by their respective followings, [that constitutes the basis].
That which corresponds to its respective object in relation to the phenomena to be produced is called the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, it refers to the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and their own primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
If it were not that which is followed by the seeds of the mind and mental factors,
then for one who has entered the attainment of cessation, the attainment of non-conception, or is born in the heaven of non-conception,
consciousness and the other [mental factors] should not arise again at a later time.
Nevertheless, they must arise again.
Therefore, one should know that the seeds of the mind and mental factors follow along with the material sense faculties;
taking these as conditions, those [faculties] are able to arise again.
Furthermore, if the various consciousnesses were not pursued by the seeds of form,
then when ordinary beings born in the formless realm pass away after their lifespan and karma are exhausted, and they descend again to be born below, [the seeds of form would not exist].
If form had no seeds, it would not arise again;
yet it necessarily arises again.
Therefore, one should know that the seeds of all forms follow along with consciousness.

With this as a condition, material phenomena arise once more. Furthermore, if ordinary beings enter the first dhyāna by means of the worldly path and are born there, at that time, all defiled phenomena of the desire realm—
As well as the seeds of all other phenomena belonging to the desire realm,
which are merely suppressed and not permanently destroyed. Why is this?
Because, due to this, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) falls away from that meditative absorption and the defiled phenomena of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) manifest once again;
and because, after passing away from the first dhyāna,
they are reborn once more in the desire realm.
Furthermore, there are briefly three types of subduing through impairment:
first, subduing through distancing;
second, subduing through revulsion.
Third, suppression by means of śamatha.
What is suppression through distancing?
It refers to the case where someone abandons the household life and goes forth into homelessness.
He distances himself from various requisites for enjoyment and undertakes the observance of precepts;
regarding those precepts he has undertaken, he remains distant from their violation.
Through approaching, practicing, and frequently cultivating [this],
because of the continuity of such approaching, practicing, and frequent cultivation,
the mind does not incline toward the various objects of desire.
The mind does not flow outward;
the mind does not abide in peace;
the mind finds no delight.
Nor does one give rise to the afflictions that are produced by the dominant power of those [afflictions] and take them as their objective domain.
This is called "distant removal through subduing.
What is "removal through aversion"?
That is to say, there is someone who, either by means of the perception of defects,
or by means of the perception of impurity,
or by means of the perception of bluish discoloration and so forth, [contemplates the body].
Alternatively, by means of a certain appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*),
one becomes increasingly weary of all sensual desires;
although one has not yet abandoned desire, because one cultivates a sense of revulsion toward those desires, [the hindrance is suppressed].
"The mind does not enter [into it]," and so forth, as explained at length.
This is called subduing through weariness and repulsion.
What is subduing through *śamatha*?
That is to say, there is someone who, by means of the mundane path,
has attained detachment from the desires of the desire realm or detachment from the desires of the form realm;
because they maintain the continuity of the mind through *śamatha*.
The mind does not enter into the realms of desire or form,
and so forth, as explained at length.
This is called the subduing [of the mind] through śamatha.
If a noble disciple, by means of the supramundane path, becomes free from desire for the realm of desire,
and so on until they fully attain freedom from desire for all three realms,
at that time the seeds of all defiled phenomena of the three realms are forever destroyed.
Why is this? Because a noble disciple,
in the present life, is no longer capable of falling back from detachment to give rise again to the afflictions of a lower stage,
nor can they be reborn in a higher stage.
Nor are they capable of passing away from that state and being reborn in a lower realm,
just as external seeds such as rice or barley placed in open space or in a dry vessel [do not sprout].
Although a sprout does not arise, it is not the case that the seed is not present;
however, if the seed is damaged by fire, at that time it will never again become a seed.
The principle regarding internal dharmas—wherein seeds are damaged, suppressed, or permanently destroyed—is likewise the same.
When a noble disciple is about to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder,
all seeds of every wholesome and indeterminate dharma are damaged.
Because the seeds of defiled phenomena have been extinguished,
they can no longer bring about future ripened fruits (*vipākaphala*),
nor can they again produce fruits of their own kind.
It should be known that this is called the fourth subduing by destruction,
namely, the subduing by destruction through the permanent eradication of its associates.
Furthermore, regarding all thoughts that arise in one who is bound by all fetters:
Whether accompanied by pleasure, or accompanied by pain,
or accompanied by neither-pain-nor-pleasure—
all such minds.
All are pursued by the seeds of pleasure,
the seeds of suffering,
and the seeds of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Whether a wholesome mind, an afflicted mind, or a neutral mind arises,
all such minds are pursued by wholesome seeds, afflicted seeds, and neutral seeds respectively.
Furthermore, whatever minds arise in those trainees who are not fully bound—
whether they be mundane wholesome minds, supramundane minds,
defiled minds, or neutral minds— [are all included].
All these minds are pursued by the seeds of all afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation;
because they have not yet been abandoned, [the afflictions] may arise at times.
Furthermore, it is also pursued by the seeds of all other dharmas.
Moreover, it refers to the arising of the mind belonging to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) who have eternally severed all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Whether it be a mundane wholesome mind,
a supramundane mind,
or an indeterminate mind.
All these minds have forever abandoned the seeds of defiled dharmas;
they arise merely as a continuous succession accompanied by the seeds of all wholesome and indeterminate dharmas.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this principle of establishing seeds is explained based on the scriptural teachings that have not yet established the ālayavijñāna; however,
once the ālayavijñāna has been established, [the principle is as follows].
It should be understood that, in brief,
the seeds of all phenomena depend entirely upon the ālayavijñāna;
furthermore, as long as those phenomena have not been permanently severed.
If it is not that which is to be abandoned, one should understand that its corresponding seeds persist accordingly.
Question: As the Blessed One said:
I say that an Arhat bhikṣu may fall away from one or another of the four states of higher mind that provide dwelling in happiness in the present life,
even though all seeds of defilement have been permanently destroyed.
How, then, can afflictions of the lower stages arise again?
If they do not arise again, how can there be regression?
Answer: There are two kinds of regression.
The first is falling away from abandonment;
the second is falling away from abiding.
That which is called falling away from abandonment pertains exclusively to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding those who abide in decline:
these include both noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
If, through a mundane path (*laukikamārga*), they have severed the various afflictions (*kleśa*), yet these afflictions arise and manifest once again.
It should be understood that at that time, because one has severed [the defilements] and yet regresses,
this is also a regression from abiding.
This occurs when, after severing the afflictions through the supramundane path, the mind engages in worldly affairs.
Because they do not single-mindedly cultivate appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*),

they are unable to repeatedly bring forth the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukhavihāra*) during that interval, as they did previously, nor can they do so again later in the same way.
However, since the afflictions of the lower stages have already been abandoned and do not manifest again,
this is called "retrogression by way of abiding," and not "retrogression by way of abandonment."
Furthermore, if one has already severed all afflictions and attained the fruit of arhatship,
yet the seeds of all those defiled phenomena have not been permanently destroyed,
how can one be said to have attained the "well-liberated mind" of an arhat, with all outflows (āsrava) forever exhausted?
If [the seeds] have already been permanently destroyed,
such that there are forever no seeds of any defiled phenomena within the continuum,
one should not even give rise to improper mental attention.
How much more so for the various afflictions.
Therefore, one should know that those who abandon the afflictions by means of the supramundane path will certainly never fall back.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Scroll 51;
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Scroll 52;
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Within the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, in the section on the *Pañcavijñānakāyasamprayuktā Bhūmiḥ* and the *Manobhūmi*, Part Two: Furthermore, what is the immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
That is to say, when these various minds and mental factors arise immediately after those various minds and mental factors,
the former are said to be the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the latter.
If these six consciousnesses serve as the equal-and-immediate condition for those [subsequent] six consciousnesses,
they are then designated as the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*),
and are also called the mental base (*mana-āyatana*) and the mental element (*mano-dhātu*).
What is the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya)?
It refers to the five groups of consciousness taking the five objects,
such as form and so forth, as their respective object-conditions in their proper order.
If the mental consciousness takes all twelve internal and external bases as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
what is its dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)?
It refers to the bases such as the eye acting as the co-arising dominant condition for the visual consciousness and so forth.
If attention is directed toward an object,
it serves as the dominant condition for the arising of the various consciousnesses,
as do all mental states and mental factors.
They function as simultaneous and mutual dominant conditions (*sahabhū-adhipati-pratyaya*) for one another. Furthermore,
pure or impure karma serves as the prior performed dominant condition for subsequent desirable or undesirable results, as well as for their maturation results (*vipāka-phala*).
If things such as fields, manure,
and water serve as the predominant conditions for the growth and completion of various crops,
or if it is the knowledge of various crafts and skills [that serves as such].
It serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the various worldly crafts and occupations.
Furthermore, among these four conditions,
the single condition of the cause (*hetu-pratyaya*) acts as the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*) with respect to the phenomena that arise from it.
It should be understood that the remaining three types of conditions, in relation to the phenomena they produce,
serve merely as contributory causes (*upāya-hetu*); therefore,
those various conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) arise.
When the conditions for skillful means (upāya) manifest,
the seeds of various formations (saṃskāra) are able to give rise to those respective formations. Therefore,
there is no principle whereby various formations arise simultaneously and all at once.
It should be understood that the ten causes are established based upon these four conditions, as has already been explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* and other texts.
Question: As the Blessed One said:
Conditioned by past formations, consciousness arises;
conditioned by future formations, consciousness arises.
Yet, past and future formations do not exist.
For what reason did the Blessed One declare that mental consciousness arises with those [five] as its conditions?
If mental consciousness can also arise by taking non-existent objects as its conditions,
how is this not in contradiction with the subtle teaching?
As the Blessed One has said:
"Consciousness arises by means of two conditions. What are these two?"
It refers to the eye and visible forms;
thus it is explained in detail up to the mind and mental phenomena.
The answer is: because it can maintain the objects that are not accessible to the five groups of consciousness.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, provisionally designates "dharmas" as names.
Therefore, it is said that mental consciousness arises conditioned by the mind and dharmas.
Question: For what reason and by what evidence do we know that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses this underlying intention (*abhiprāya*)?
Answer: Because that mental consciousness also takes past and future consciousness as its object, as is evident in worldly experience;
yet those objects and the consciousness [of them] are not subsumed under the *dharmāyatana*.
Furthermore, "possessing a nature" (*sabhāva*) means being established as having existence and being capable of maintaining existence.
If there were no intrinsic nature, then that which establishes non-existent objects and sustains non-existent objects would not exist;
therefore, all are called *dharmas*.
This is because that mental consciousness [operates] with respect to objects that possess intrinsic nature.
If one establishes [a thing] by means of this meaning,
then one gives rise to consciousness that cognizes it by means of this very same meaning; yet, in the sense of being devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva), [it is not so].
If consciousness is established by means of a certain object,
it arises as the discernment of that very object. If, regarding two types of objects,
it were to arise as discernment without being based on those two objects, [it would be illogical].
One should not say that the mind takes all objects as its conditions and grasps all objects;
if one were to say so,
it would contradict one's own siddhānta.
Furthermore, one should not say that as something exists, so too does its non-existence;
this is the teaching according to the principle of reality (*yathābhūta*).
Therefore, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has no truly existent characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), just like past and future phenomena.
Taking that as its object,
one thereby knows that the mental consciousness also takes what is non-existent as its object.
Furthermore, there is the principle of the extensive discourse.
From this it is proven that there is consciousness without an object;
that is to say, as the Sublime One has taught in his subtle discourse:
whether internally, externally, or in between the two, there is absolutely no self.
This self-lack-of-nature is neither included within the conditioned nor the unconditioned;
yet, consciousness that contemplates common characteristics does not arise without taking that object as its basis.
This is called the first principle of discourse.
Furthermore, based upon the arising and transformation of form, odor, taste, and tangibility in such and such ways,
one designates various things such as food, drink, vehicles, clothing, ornaments, dwellings, armies, and forests.
These foods and drinks, being devoid of color, fragrance, and so forth, do not exist at all.
This absence of intrinsic nature is neither subsumed under the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Although consciousness observes their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), it does not fail to arise by taking those objects as its conditions.
This is called the second principle of discourse.
Furthermore, there is the false view that denies everything, asserting that nothing exists at all;
namely, that there is no giving, no affection, and no sacrificial offerings.
As explained at length previously:
if the naturelessness of things such as the sacrifice for loved ones were itself existent,
then such a view would not be a false view.
Why is this? Because he sees things as they truly are and speaks of them as they truly are;
if this were non-existent, [he could not do so].
For those with false views, consciousness would not arise in relation to this object;
this is called the third principle of discourse.
Furthermore, among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), there is no permanence, no constancy, and no immutability.
Within these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), there is a nature that is permanent, eternal, and unchanging;
it is neither included within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The consciousness that contemplates their common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) does not fail to arise by taking this object as its cognitive domain.
If consciousness does not arise taking this object as its condition, one will be unable to observe,
through wisdom as it truly is, that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāras) are devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva), being eternal and unchanging.
If one does not contemplate, aversion will not arise;
if aversion does not arise, one will not become free from desire;
and if one is not free from desire, there will be no liberation.
If there were no liberation, there would be no ultimate exhaustion that is final nirvana.
If such a principle were to exist,
all sentient beings would eternally follow after afflictions and there would be no time of emergence from them.
This is called the fourth principle of discourse.
Furthermore, since future formations have not yet arisen,
how much less could they cease?
However, the noble disciple does not dwell without contemplating the arising and passing away of future formations.
This is called the fifth principle of discourse.
By this, it is proven that there is consciousness which takes non-existence as its object.
Furthermore, there are other such types of discourse and reasoning that establish the definite existence of consciousness that takes non-existence as its object;
these should be understood accordingly.
Question: As the Blessed One has said, "There is past karma.
If the substance of past karma were non-existent, [how could this be so?].
At this time, there should not be one who experiences a painful sensation,
nor should there be one who experiences a non-painful sensation.
What is the underlying intention here?
Answer: In past lives, pure and impure karma that has already arisen and already ceased is capable of producing future desirable and undesirable fruits;
this karma is comprised of seeds that have been grasped and perfumed.
Because the continuity of formations proceeds in succession without interruption,
the Blessed One, in order to manifest such a continuity,
said: "There is past karma."
Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke thus for two reasons: first,
to refute the views of those who propound unequal causes, and second,
to reveal this principle.

That is to say, they falsely view that all sentient beings' experiences of the pure and the impure proceed from Maheśvara, Śakra, Brahmā, the Self-Nature (svabhāva), the Person (puruṣa), and other such causes.
Second, in order to refute the views of all proponents of causelessness,
this principle is revealed:
namely, that their false view— that all sentient beings' transitions into purity or impurity occur entirely without cause— is utterly baseless.
Question: As the Blessed One has said:
"There are past formations;
regarding those formations, my well-heard noble disciple dwells without attachment."
There are future formations;
regarding those formations, my well-heard noble disciple dwells without expectation.
What is the underlying intention here?
Answer: Past formations exist because they have already yielded their fruit;
future formations exist because they encompass their causes. Why is this so?
Present conditioned phenomena are manifested by three characteristics:
first, because they are of the nature of past effects;
second, because they are of the nature of future causes.
Third, because their own characteristics continue in an uninterrupted succession.
To reveal this principle, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke these words.
Furthermore, he made this statement by contemplating two meanings.
First, in order to refute and sever the attachment to the real existence of past and future phenomena,
this principle is revealed:
that is to say, if the nature and characteristics of past and future conditioned formations were substantially existent, [then...]
One should not say that [phenomena] exist by virtue of their nature of coming and going;
rather, this principle is revealed in order to refute the attachment to nihilism.
This refers to their false conceptualization that just as the past and future do not exist, the present likewise is entirely non-existent.
Question: As the Blessed One has said, "There is a past element, there is a future element, and there is a present element."
What is the underlying intention here?
Answer: If the continuity of seeds has already yielded its fruit, it is termed the "past element" (atīta-dhātu).
If seeds that have not yet yielded their fruit continue in succession,
they are called the future realm (*anāgata-dhātu*).
If seeds that have not yet yielded their fruit continue in succession in the present, [they are called the present realm].
This is called the "present realm.
One should understand that within this, there is such an underlying intention (*abhiprāya*):
if monks and others attain skillfulness regarding such a continuity of seeds (*bīja-saṃtāna*).
This refers to attaining skill in the various elements (*dhātu*) of immeasurable and manifold intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) within each and every phenomenon.
Furthermore, how should one understand that birth, aging, duration, and impermanence do not exist as distinct, substantial entities apart from the aggregates (*skandha*) such as form?
This means that since the real existence of future conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) has already been refuted,
one should know that the real existence of arising (*utpāda*) is likewise refuted. Why is this so?
Since that which arises in the future world is itself non-existent,
how could it produce the remaining formations?
Nor can an arising in the present produce formations in the present.
From this characteristic of arising, there is a designation of distinction,
namely: that conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) arise, originate,
or possess a present nature.
Apart from this distinction, a different characteristic of arising cannot be found at all.
Therefore, wise persons should not say that it is by means of the present itself that those conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) become present in nature.
Why is this? If one were to say that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise from arising.
It should be understood that the meaning revealed here is that the very nature of the present is capable of producing the present.
Furthermore, since all phenomena each possess their own distinct seeds as causes,
what need is there to postulate a separate "birth" (jāti) capable of producing them?
Furthermore, is this characteristic of arising identical to the arising of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) themselves,
or is it the cause for the arising of those conditioned phenomena?
If it were identical to the arising of the conditioned phenomena themselves, [then...]

It is not logical that the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) can produce the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), for it is by virtue of [the phenomenon] already being born that the conditioned phenomena arise.
If this were the cause of the arising of those conditioned phenomena, [it would be untenable].
When conditioned phenomena arise, it would follow that for each individual phenomenon there are two types of arising:
namely, the arising itself and the arising of the arising;
this is not logically tenable.
Just as it is with birth,
so too should aging, duration, and impermanence be understood according to this principle.
Therefore, it is known that birth and the others are merely conventional designations applied to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Because they exist by virtue of existence and causes, the fact that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) do not arise from their own original characteristics is called "birth" (*jāti*).
The subsequent arising of conditioned phenomena with a distinction from the preceding state is called "aging" (*jarā*).
The state in which those conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) momentarily abide at the time of their arising is called "staying" (sthiti).
After the moment of arising, the exhaustion of the characteristics of those phenomena is called "cessation" (nirodha),
and it is also termed "impermanence" (anityatā).
Question: If conditioned phenomena are fully endowed with the four characteristics of the conditioned— arising, aging, abiding, and cessation—
why did the Blessed One speak of only three?
1. Arising; 2. Cessation;
3. Abiding and change of state.
Answer: Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are manifested by the three periods of time, they arise from the future where they previously did not exist.
Therefore, the Blessed One, with respect to the future period, [speaks] regarding conditioned phenomena.
It is taught that conditioned phenomena possess the characteristic of arising.
Once they have arisen, they fall away into the past;
therefore, the Blessed One, by means of the past, [perceives] conditioned phenomena.
The cessation of conditioned characteristics is explained as being manifested by two characteristics in the present state of phenomena:
namely, duration and change.
Why is this so? Because it is only in the present that abiding can be apprehended;
likewise, change—both preceding and succeeding—is also found only in the present.

Therefore, the Blessed One, with respect to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) in the present time, has taught "abiding and change" (*sthity-anyathātva*) collectively as a single characteristic of the conditioned.
Question: Should the noble disciples of the Buddha contemplate conditioned phenomena as being complete with all three characteristics?
Why is it that only the noble disciples are said to dwell contemplating the arising and passing away within the aggregates, and not the contemplating of their abiding and changing nature?
The answer is: arising, as well as abiding and changing, are manifested simultaneously with birth.
Therefore, these two characteristics are combined into one part to establish the category of arising;
this is explained as observing the characteristic of the abiding of a single birth.
In the second part, the category of cessation is established.
He then speaks of abiding in the contemplation of the single characteristic of cessation.
Furthermore, if one gives rise to the contemplation of revulsion by means of this characteristic,
it is precisely this characteristic that is spoken of here.
That is to say, by contemplating the characteristic of impermanence within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
one is able to give rise to revulsion, detachment, and liberation; therefore,
one contemplates only the nature and characteristics of impermanence.
The characteristic of impermanence is that what was originally non-existent now exists;
having existed, it returns to non-existence— this is what is revealed by "originally non-existent, now existing."
This is called arising.
That which, having existed, returns to non-existence is called cessation.
Furthermore, there are many varieties of the distinctions of arising.
That is to say: arising moment by moment,
arising as a continuity,
and arising through growth.
Mental differentiation arises:
the unlovely arises,
and the lovely arises.
Birth in an inferior state,
birth in a middling state,
and birth in a superior and sublime state.
There is superior arising and unsurpassed arising.
Within this, all conditioned phenomena arise anew at every single moment.
This is called "arising in an instant.
Whether possessing all fetters or not possessing them,
one passes away from this or that group of sentient beings and goes to that or that group of sentient beings.
The continuous arising of the aggregates is called "successive arising" (*prabandhaja*).
From the stages of infancy and childhood up until the transition to old age and so forth,
it is called "growth arising" (*upacayaja*).
If, with respect to various objects,
in various days and nights, and in various moments (*kṣaṇa*), units of time (*lava*),
and hours (*muhūrta*), numerous, manifold, and diverse states of mind arise repeatedly as they successively pass away.
It is associated either with pleasure,
or with pain, or with neither-pain-nor-pleasure;
it is either a mind possessed of greed or a mind free from greed.
To speak at length, it extends even to a mind that is well-liberated or a mind that is not well-liberated;
such is called the arising of mental differentiation.
This includes those born in the miserable realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
This is called birth that is not desirable.
If one is born among the happy destinies of humans or devas,
it is called desirable birth.
If one is born in the inferior realm of the desire world (kāmadhātu),
it is called an inferior birth;
if one is born in the intermediate realm of the form world (rūpadhātu), it is called an intermediate birth.
