Birth in the Form Realm is called "birth in the intermediate state.
If one is born in the sublime and exquisite Formless Realm,
it is called "sublime and exquisite birth."
Furthermore, there is another distinction:
namely, one who first enters the womb is termed an inferior birth.
Regarding those who enter the womb in the middle two [lifetimes],
they are called "born from a place.
Regarding those who enter the womb last:
It is called "the arising of the excellent and sublime.
Furthermore, there is a distinction:
namely, the arising of defiled phenomena and the fruits of defilement.
The arising of inferior dharmas is called an inferior birth;
the arising of all wholesome dharmas and their wholesome fruits is called a sublime birth.
Excluding the wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant indeterminate dharmas,
the remaining indeterminate dharmas that arise are called "arising within the locus.
This is stated with reference to arising within the realms of existence (*dhātu*).
Birth beginning from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness is called "birth with something superior.
Birth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is [called "the highest birth"].
It is called "supreme birth.
If one speaks according to the continuous succession of moments at the point of falling into and taking rebirth,
this excludes the final terminal state of Arhats and others.
The arising of all formations belonging to all other states within the various aggregates is called "arising with something superior. However,
the arising of all formations belonging to the final state of termination for Arhats and others [is otherwise].
It is called "unsurpassed birth.
Furthermore, one should know that there are many varieties of the distinctions of aging, namely:
aging of the body, aging of the mind, aging of the lifespan, aging as transformation and decay, and aging as the transformation of the personal entity (*ātman*).
In this context, from "decline and transformation" up to "the breaking up of the body," as explained at length in the Sūtra,
this is called the aging of the body.
If the mind associated with pleasant feeling transforms,
it turns into a mind associated with painful feeling,
or it transforms into a wholesome mind.
The defiled mind evolves;
or else, regarding desirable objects, the mind transforms through longing,
and when that longing is not fulfilled, the mind evolves [into distress].
This is called the aging of the mind.
It refers to the repeated transition and passing away, and the gradual diminution of the lifespan, throughout various days and nights,
moments (kṣaṇa), instants (lava), and hours (muhūrta).
Gradually diminishing until it is completely exhausted—
this is called the aging of life.
It is also the decline and loss of all wealth, nobility, and prosperity.
The transformation of health, physical vigor,
and a joyful appearance is called "aging as deterioration.
This occurs when one's personal existence has already perished from a flourishing aggregate within a happy realm of rebirth.
The arising of one's own physical existence within the inferior aggregates of the miserable realms is called aging as the transformation of the physical basis.
Furthermore, there is another form of aging that serves as a condition capable of producing all the types of aging described above;
namely, the aging characterized by the moment-to-moment transformation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that there are also many kinds of distinctions regarding abiding:
namely, momentary abiding and continuous abiding.
Abiding through the continuity of conditions;
abiding without distraction;
abiding established in the proper conduct of a preceptor.
If conditioned phenomena that have already arisen remain for a brief moment at the time of their arising,
this is called "momentary abiding" (*kṣaṇasthiti*).
If sentient beings, in various places and with various individual existences...
By depending upon various types of food,
life persists for as long as it may last; likewise,
the external receptacle world persists for the duration of a great eon (*mahākalpa*).
It is called "abiding as a continuity" (saṃtati-sthiti).
This refers to whether one experiences pleasant feeling, painful feeling, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
or whether it concerns wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate dharmas.
It remains for as long as each respective object of focus manifests before it;
this is called "abiding by way of a continuous stream of objects.
If the various concentrated states of mind arise and manifest correctly through samādhi, [they abide in that manner].
This is called abiding without distraction.
Whether in various directions or regions, or in kingdoms,
cities, villages, or hamlets.
In royal capitals, royal palaces,
or among assemblies of logicians, merchants, townspeople, and others,
one should follow the established traditions and precedents set by the masters of old.
This is called abiding in the established rules of conduct.
Furthermore, one should know that there are also many varieties of the differentiation of impermanence,
namely, the impermanence of disintegration and destruction.
The impermanence of arising,
the impermanence of transformation,
and the impermanence of disintegration.
There must be impermanence;
it is manifest that one falls into impermanence,
for all conditioned phenomena perish as soon as they arise.
That which is called "impermanence as destruction" refers to the fact that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) did not previously exist but now exist.
That which is called "impermanence as arising" refers to this same process of coming into being.
If conditioned phenomena that are desirable arise with altered characteristics,
this is called the impermanence of transformation.
If desirable requisites and superior states undergo disintegration and decline without being physically destroyed, this is [the impermanence of] dissolution.
It is called the impermanence of disintegration;
that is, the four types of impermanence in their future state are called the impermanence of what-is-to-be.
That which exists in the present moment, manifesting right now,
is called "presently falling into impermanence.
This applies to one who indulges in sensual desires and is largely heedless.
Although they are able to contemplate the impermanence of transformation, the impermanence of disintegration, and the manifest impermanence of falling away,
and thus give rise extensively to lamentation, distress, and dejection,
they are nonetheless unable to cultivate weary detachment toward all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
If those of other paths reflect extensively upon such impermanence itself,
yet are only slightly able to employ skillful means for weariness with and detachment from desire.
However, by merely becoming weary of and detached from a portion of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one cannot reach the ultimate end.
If a noble disciple (*ārya-śrāvaka*) fully contemplates the nature of impermanence (*anityatā*) in all conditioned phenomena,
they will ultimately become weary of them and even attain liberation.
Furthermore, how is attainment achieved?
To state it briefly:
that which is called "attainment" refers to the cause of the flourishing of the conditions for birth through their gathering together.
By this reasoning, one should know that "attainment" (prāpti) is a conventional existence (prajñaptisat).
If it were said that attainment is a substantial existence (dravyasat),
would it then be the cause for the arising of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra)?
It serves as the cause for the non-dispersion of these phenomena.
If it were the cause for the arising of these conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*),
then one who had not previously obtained these phenomena would [now] obtain them.
Since this lacks the acquisition of a cause for its arising,
it should never arise;
by this logic, it should also ultimately remain unattainable.
If these phenomena were not subject to causes of separation,
then since the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of all wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral phenomena would exist simultaneously,
those [phenomena] that are mutually contradictory would necessarily manifest all at once.
Therefore, both [theories] are unreasonable.
Furthermore, the cause of arising refers to the respective seeds of phenomena as they are grasped by their individual conditions.
Regarding the cause of non-dissipation:
it refers to the dissipation of other conditions due to the presence of other conditions.
If, within the context of the projecting conditions, there is mastery over their power, this is conventionally designated as "attainment" (*prāpti*).
By relying on this sovereignty, all persons and individuals,
although those various phenomena have already arisen and already ceased, [perceive them as such].
If one desires that [the attainment] should again manifest before one,
one can swiftly induce the various conditions to arise;
for this reason, it is also called "attainment" (*prāpti*).
It should be known that this attainment is briefly of three kinds:
first, the accomplishment of the seed;
second, the accomplishment of mastery.
Third is the accomplishment through manifest activity.
This refers to all defiled phenomena, those neutral phenomena acquired at birth,
and wholesome phenomena that manifest spontaneously without effort.
If those seeds have not been suppressed by śamatha,
have not been permanently destroyed by the noble path,
and have not been suppressed by wrong views such that one's roots of goodness are severed;
This is called the accomplishment of the seed.
Why is this? Because as long as this seed has not been impaired or suppressed.
It has not been permanently destroyed.
At that time, those defiled and other such phenomena—
whether currently manifesting or not manifesting— are all said to be "possessed" (prāpti).
Therefore, the seeds that serve as the causes for the flourishing of wholesome dharmas produced through preparatory effort (*prayoga*),
as well as a portion of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas, when they are embraced by the conditions for their arising,
are termed "attainment of mastery" (*vaśitā-samanvāgama*).
If the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of present phenomena manifest and function before one,
this is called the accomplishment of active manifestation (*samudācāra-samanvāgama*).
Furthermore, what is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
It refers to the measure of the duration of the physical existence produced in various places by prior karma;
this force is called "life-force" (*āyus*) and the "life-faculty" (*jīvitendriya*).
Furthermore, there are many varieties of distinctions, namely:
determinate and indeterminate;
conforming and non-conforming.
Whether few or many;
whether with limits or without limits;
whether they proceed by their own power or do not proceed by their own power.
Excluding the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa,
the lifespans in all other places of birth are fixed;
however, the lifespan in this Jambudvīpa is at times vast and immeasurable.
At times it is short; the lifespan is indefinite.
The lifespan of the people of Uttarakuru varies accordingly, yet it functions as if it were a fixed measure that functions invariably.
Because there is no premature death [there],
all other places are called "non-conforming.
When the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa is ten years, it is called a short lifespan.
A portion of animals is also said to have short lifespans. Why is this?
Because for some animals, a lifespan of only a single day and night can be found.
There are some beings born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception whose lifespan can last for one, two, or three [eons], up to a maximum of ten days and ten nights.
They are called "long-lived" because they pass through eighty thousand great kalpas.
Arhats and others are said to have a finite lifespan.
If those in training (śaikṣa) attain parinirvāṇa with certainty in the present life,
and if ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) abide in their final existence,
they are also said to have a lifespan that has reached its limit.
It should be known that the remainder of their lifespan is boundless.
This refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of Arhats, Tathāgatas, and Bodhisattvas,
who possess mastery over the prolongation or contraction of the formations of life (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*).
It is called "functioning by its own power.
One should know that all others are called "not functioning by their own power.
Furthermore, what is the "homogeneity of a group" (nikāyasabhāga)?
To speak briefly,
it refers to those sentient beings who, having taken birth in various places,
share the same realm, the same destiny, the same mode of birth, the same category, the same stage, the same nature, and the same form.
The mutual similarity among various parts [of sentient beings] is called "homogeneity" (*nikāya-sabhāga*);
it is also termed "homogeneity of sentient beings" (*sattva-sabhāga*).
In this context, some sentient beings are said to be "of the same class" (*sabhāga*) by virtue of their similarity in realm (*dhātu-sabhāgatā*),
meaning they are born together in the same realm;
or some sentient beings are said to be "of the same class" by virtue of their similarity in destiny (*gati-sabhāgatā*).
This refers to being born together in the same realm of existence (*gati*).
Alternatively, there are sentient beings who are called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) by virtue of their shared homogeneous birth-class (*nikāya-sabhāga*),
meaning they are born together in one and the same birth.
There are sentient beings who are called "homogeneous" (sabhāga) by virtue of their commonality of genus,
meaning they belong to the same species.
There are also sentient beings who are called "homogeneous" by virtue of their commonality of state, essential nature, complexion, shape, voice, clothing, and means of sustenance.
Alternatively, there are sentient beings who, by virtue of sharing the same category of faults or virtues, are said to be "of the same class" (sabhāga).
This refers, for example, to a killer in relation to another killer, and so on,
up to those with wrong views in relation to others with wrong views.
One who has abstained from taking life compared to one who has abstained from taking life,
and so on up to one with right view compared to one with right view;
or a stream-enterer up to an arhat or pratyekabuddha compared to a stream-enterer and so forth.
A bodhisattva in relation to a bodhisattva,
and a Tathāgata in relation to a Tathāgata—
thus, these are mutually called "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā).
Furthermore, what is the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
It refers to the seeds of the factors of the three realms that are to be abandoned through seeing;
the mere state of not having yet permanently destroyed these is designated as the nature of being an ordinary person.
This, in brief, consists of four types:
first, that which is comprised within the lineage of those who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa;
second, that which is followed by the śrāvaka lineage.
Third, it is followed by the lineage of the pratyekabuddhas;
fourth, it is followed by the lineage of the tathāgatas—
due to various conditions.
Taken collectively as one, it is called "conjunction" (saṃnipāta).
This is also termed the "cause of common purpose" (samānārtha-hetu).
Furthermore, regarding its specific distinctions:
There is also the experience of conjunction, namely:
contact conditioned by the six sense bases;
or [contact] conditioned by visible forms and so forth; or [contact] conditioned by attention and so forth.
Or there is contact as the condition for feeling;
or there is that which draws forth the conjunction with future existence,
namely, ignorance as the condition for volitional formations, and so forth.
With feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, grasping arises.
This is explained in detail up to: with birth as condition, aging and death arise.
Or, there may be the dwelling in the six sense bases through their coming together.
This refers to the four nutriments and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Alternatively, it refers to the accomplishment and integration of the bases of craftsmanship (*śilpasthāna*), namely:
skill in craftsmanship, the tools associated therewith, and the human effort involved.
There may be pure and harmonious assemblies,
namely twelve kinds of unmixed gatherings,
such as those consisting of the perfection of oneself and others, and so forth.
Furthermore, there is mundane concord,
which refers to sentient beings who, through the predominant power of their mutual intentions, do not oppose one another,
are without contention or dispute, and likewise do not become estranged.
Furthermore, what is meant by "name-body" (*nāmakāya*)?
It refers to the designation of intrinsic nature and the designation of specific characteristics based upon all phenomena;
through pervasive conceptualization, it is merely the establishment of mental images (*saṃjñā*) for the sake of verbal expression.
This is called the "name-body" (nāmakāya).
What is the "phrase-body" (padakāya)?
It refers to the designation of the various distinctions among all phenomena based upon those very [names] as their specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa).
The conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) concerning the establishment of merit, faults, defilement (*saṃkleśa*), and purification;
this is called the "phrase-body" (*padakāya*).
What is the "syllable-body" (*vyañjanakāya*)?

That which constitutes the collection of phonemes (vyañjana-kāya) is the collection of syllables (akṣara-kāya) that serves as the basis for the collections of names (nāma-kāya) and phrases (pada-kāya).
Furthermore, regarding all objects of knowledge and all things expressed [by language]:
The most abbreviated characteristic is a syllable (*vyañjana*);
the intermediate is a name (*nāman*);
and the extensive is a phrase (*pada*).
If one relies solely on the words, one can only comprehend the phonetics,
but cannot comprehend all the referents and meanings;
this is if one relies upon names (*nāman*).
One is then able to thoroughly comprehend the intrinsic nature and specific characteristics of each respective phenomenon,
and is also able to thoroughly comprehend all phonetic sounds;
yet one cannot thoroughly comprehend the profound and extensive distinctions among the phenomena that have been analyzed.
If one relies upon these phrases,
it should be known that all can be thoroughly understood.
Furthermore, regarding these bodies of names, phrases, and syllables:
It should be understood that this is established through a classification based on the five fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*),
namely: inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*) and logic (*hetu-vidyā*).
The science of grammar,
the science of medicine,
and the science of worldly arts and crafts.
Furthermore, what is meant by "cyclic progression" (*pravṛtti*)?
It refers to the nature of the uninterrupted continuity of the causes and effects of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
This is called cyclic progression.
Furthermore, these varieties of cyclic existence (saṃsāra) are manifold.
There is, for instance, the cyclic existence of seeds,
which refers to those phenomena that possess seeds but do not manifest.
There is that which flows through the power of sovereignty,
namely, those phenomena consisting of the manifestation of impaired seeds;
and there is that which flows as the fruition of seeds.
This refers to those dharmas that exist as seeds and whose manifestation is not impaired;
or it refers to the flow of what is called "name," namely the four non-material aggregates (skandhas).
There is the flow and circulation of materiality,
which refers to the ten internal and external bases of materiality as well as all forms subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Furthermore, there is the flow and circulation of the desire realm.
This refers to the formations associated with the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, there is the flow and transmigration of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*),
which refers to the formations associated with the realm of form.
Furthermore, there is the flow and circulation of the formless realm,
namely the formations associated with the fetters of the formless realm.
Moreover, there is the flow and circulation of pleasure.
This refers to pleasant feeling and its basis;
one should know that the flow of suffering and the flow of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling proceed in the same manner.
Furthermore, there is the flow of the wholesome which proceeds.
This refers to all wholesome courses of action.
Furthermore, there is the flow and wandering of the unwholesome,
which refers to all unwholesome courses of action.
Furthermore, there is the flow of the indeterminate,
which refers to all indeterminate formations;
there is also the flow that conforms to the stream.
This refers to that which accords with dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Furthermore, there is a flow that moves against the current,
which refers to the reversal of dependent origination.
Furthermore, what is meant by "determinate differentiation"?
It refers to the nature of the various causes and effects that have existed since beginningless time as being definitively distinct and non-confused,
whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear.
It is the natural law of all phenomena (*dharmāṇāṃ dharmatā*).
Furthermore, this fixed distinction is manifold;
there is, for instance, the fixed distinction between the process of transmigration and its cessation.
This refers to the dependent origination in forward and reverse order.
Alternatively, there is a fixed distinction among all phenomena:
that is, all phenomena are subsumed within the twelve bases (āyatana), neither more nor less.
There may be a fixed distinction in experience,
meaning that all experiences are subsumed within the three types of sensation— neither more nor less than these.
Or there may be a fixed distinction in abiding.
This refers to all internal components, up to and including the life span,
as well as all external components that endure for a great kalpa;
or those whose dimensions and quantities are fixed and distinct.
This refers to the determination of the size and shape of the bodies of sentient beings born in various places where form exists,
as well as the determination of the size and shape of external factors such as the four great continents.
Furthermore, what is association (*samyoga*)?
It refers to those various phenomena that serve as equal designations, equal establishments, and equal explanations through superior skillful means;
this is called association.
Furthermore, there are four principles for the analytical differentiation of these associated [factors]:
namely, the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*), the principle of function (*kāritra-yukti*), and so forth.
The principle of logical proof and the principle of the nature of phenomena—
these principles should be understood as having been extensively analyzed in the *Śrāvakabhūmi* and other such texts.
Furthermore, what is rapidity?
It refers to the nature of the swift movement associated with the arising and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
this is called rapidity.
Furthermore, this rapidity of momentum is of many kinds. There is,
for instance, the rapidity of the flow of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
which refers to the nature of the arising and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena.
There are sentient beings that move on land who possess lightness, agility, and great speed,
such as humans, elephants, and horses;
there are also sentient beings that move through the air who possess great speed.
This refers to the various birds, the sky-faring yakṣas, and the devas,
some of whose vocal expressions are swift in their momentum—
that is, whose diction and rhythm are rapid and sharp.
Some possess the rapidity of flowing moisture,
such as the swift currents of rivers and the like;
others possess the rapidity of burning combustion.
This refers to the blazing of fire with fierce flames and whirling winds;
or it refers to that which is induced by momentum and velocity,
such as the flight of an arrow or the rolling of a ball.
There is the swiftness of the power of wisdom,
which refers to the nature of the swift discernment of objects of knowledge by one who practices contemplation.
There is also the swiftness of the power of supernormal faculties.
This refers to the supernormal powers of those possessing great supernatural faculties, such as the swiftness of bodily movement and mental influence.
Furthermore, what is their sequence?
It refers to [the occurrence] within the respective continuities of individual formations.
The successive progression of each [factor] one after another is called "sequence.
Furthermore, there are many varieties of this sequence.
There is also a sequence of transmigration,
namely: ignorance conditions volitional formations,
and so on, as explained at length, up to birth conditions aging and death.
Or there is the sequence of cessation, namely:
because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease;
and so on, up to: because birth ceases, old age and death cease.
There is a sequence for the conduct and dwelling of both householders and those who have left the home life:
namely, rising at dawn, washing and adorning the body,
putting on clothes and ornaments, and attending to one's affairs.
Having bathed, anointed oneself, and adorned with perfumes and garlands,
one partakes of food and drink before finally retiring to rest;
such is the sequence of activities for a householder.
If, for the sake of begging for alms, one adjusts one's robes and enters a village or similar place, proceeding in regular order;
having received food in accordance with the Dharma, returns and sits down peacefully;
and after finishing the meal, washes the hands, rinses the bowl, and washes the feet.
Entering a secluded chamber, he recited and chanted the sūtras and reflected upon them according to the principle.
During the day, he sat in meditative seclusion and practiced walking meditation,
purifying his mind and severing all hindrances.
At the middle watch of the night, one should rest for a short while;
at the final watch of the night, one should quickly rise again,
adjust one's robes, compose oneself, and return to the practice one has undertaken.
This is the sequence of conduct for those who have gone forth:
whether entering the midst of the Saṃgha, they observe the practice of harmony and respect according to seniority;
they arrange the beds and seats, and receive voting sticks in order to distribute the bedding.
Regarding dwellings, gains, and undertakings of business,
there may be a sequence of growth;
that is to say, the eight stages beginning with the infant and the young child arise in successive order.
There is the sequence of clear realization,
which refers to the sequential clear realization of the four noble truths, such as suffering and so forth;
and there is the sequence of entering meditative absorption.
That is to say, entering the nine successive attainments in their proper order.
Or, there is the sequential training,
which refers to relying upon the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*).
Next, the training in higher mind arises;
based upon the training in higher mind,
the training in higher wisdom subsequently arises.
Furthermore, what is meant by "time"?
It refers to the establishment and manifestation of the distinctions between temporal seasons through the predominant power of the rising and setting of the solar disk.
Furthermore, by the predominant power of the arising and ceasing of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
the distinctions of temporal stages are established and manifested;
these are collectively designated as "time" (*kāla*).
The distinctions of time are further manifold, namely:
the divisions of years, months, fortnights, days and nights, kṣaṇas, lava-s, and muhūrta-s;
as well as the past, future, and present.
Furthermore, what is enumeration?
It refers to the establishment and manifestation of individual entities and the calculation of their numerical distinctions.
This is called counting.
These distinctions in counting are further of many kinds, namely:
single counting and double counting.
From this point onward, all are designated as "numerous" (*bahusamkhyā*).
Furthermore, the limit of number is called *asaṃkhyeya*;
from this point onward, it can no longer be processed by any calculation.
Therefore, the limit of number is called "incalculable.
Furthermore, as for the seed: why is it that there is no separate, substantial entity apart from the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) that is called a "seed"?
Nor is it found elsewhere. Rather,
it is precisely these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)— their such-and-such nature, their such-and-such arising, and their such-and-such arrangement—
that are called the "seed" and are also called the "fruit."
It should be understood that herein the fruit and the seed are not confused.
Why is this? Because, with respect to past formations, these very [formations] are called the fruit.
If one considers future conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), these are precisely what is called "seeds.
Thus, at whatever time something is designated as a seed in relation to those [phenomena],
it is not at that very time designated as a fruit.
When something is designated as a "fruit" in relation to that [cause],
it is not at that same time designated as a "seed.
Therefore, one should know that the seed and the fruit are not conflated.
For example, when one grinds, crushes, and analyzes the seeds, sprouts, stalks, leaves,
and so forth of substances such as grain or barley, one can never find a distinct seed within those things.
Nor does it exist elsewhere; rather,
the primary elements (mahābhūta) possess such a nature,
arise in such a manner, and are arranged in such a configuration.
Just as grains, wheat, and other such things are called "seeds" because they can act as conditions for those [plants] to arise,
one should know that the principle here is likewise.
Question: It was previously stated that the seeds of defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) are impaired and suppressed.
How are the seeds of wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) impaired and suppressed?
Answer: If one constantly and earnestly practices what is wholesome.
Various defiled phenomena that are contrary [to the path] are first suppressed;
if one clings to false views and frequently practices such views, as do the various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
This is the second form of impairment and subjugation:
if one extensively cultivates wrong views and slander,
such as one who has severed their roots of goodness.
This is the third subduing by impairment.
If one can permanently destroy the seeds of defiled phenomena,
it is as previously explained.
This is the fourth suppression.
Furthermore, to speak briefly, one should know that all seeds are of nine kinds.
First, that which has already given its fruit;
second, that which has not yet given its fruit;
third, that whose fruit is currently manifesting.
Fourth, the fruits do not manifest before one.
Fifth, the soft grade.
Sixth, the medium grade.
Seventh, the superior grade;
eighth, being suppressed and subdued;
ninth, not being suppressed or subdued.
If it has already given its fruit,
this is called the fruit being present before one.
If the fruit is present before one, [it is so].
This is called having already given its fruit;
if it has not yet given its fruit,
this is called the fruit not being present.
If the fruit does not manifest,
this is called "not yet having given its fruit.
If it abides in its original nature, [it is likewise].

That which is called "weak grade" refers to when wholesome or unwholesome dharmas have been cultivated or refined but have not yet reached their ultimate consummation. That which is called "middling grade" refers to the same state when they have reached a further stage of development.
If cultivation or refinement has reached its ultimate limit,
it is called "superior.
Whether there is impairment or no impairment should be understood as previously explained.
Furthermore, I shall briefly explain the establishment of seeds.
What is the brief explanation of the establishment of seeds?
It refers to [their presence] within the ālayavijñāna.
The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the false attachment to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of all phenomena are called "established seeds" (*vyavasthāpita-bīja*). Furthermore,
these habitual tendencies exist as substantial entities (*dravyasat*).
This exists conventionally;
with respect to those phenomena, its characteristic cannot be definitively described as either different or not different from them,
just like true suchness (tathatā).
This is also called the omnipresent heavy burden (*sarvatraga-dausthulya*).
It encompasses all seeds;
furthermore, it is called the omnipresent heavy burden because—
From what seed do all supramundane phenomena arise?
If one says they arise from seeds whose nature is that of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*),
it is not logical.
Answer: All supramundane phenomena arise from seeds that have true suchness (*tathatā*) as their objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*);
they do not arise from seeds accumulated through habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Question: If they do not arise from seeds accumulated through habitual tendencies, [how can they exist]?
For what reason are the distinctions among individuals (pudgala) belonging to the three types of lineages (gotra) who attain parinirvāṇa established,
as well as the establishment of individuals belonging to the lineage of those who do not attain parinirvāṇa?
Why is this so? Because all things possess the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) of true suchness (tathatā).
Answer: It is due to the distinction between the presence and absence of obstructions.
If, within the objective condition for the realization of suchness,
there exists the seed of an ultimate obstruction,
one establishes that person as belonging to the lineage of those who do not possess the nature for parinirvāṇa.
If it were not so, one would establish them as individuals belonging to the lineage of those destined for parinirvāṇa; yet,
if there were seeds of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that are ultimately present within their basis (*āśraya*).
Those who do not possess the seeds of the afflictive hindrances are established as individuals of the śrāvaka lineage in one portion,
and established as individuals of the pratyekabuddha lineage in another portion.
If it were not so, one would have to establish a person (pudgala) belonging to the lineage of the Tathāgata;
therefore, there is no fault.
If supramundane dharmas have arisen and immediately follow along [with the transformation],
it should be known that this is sustained by the power of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
However, this transformation of the basis is mutually contradictory with the *ālayavijñāna*.
The antidote to the ālayavijñāna is called the untainted realm (anāsravadhātu), which is free from all conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca).
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 52.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Fifty-three.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
In the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, within the section on the *Pañcavijñānakāyasaṃprayuktā Bhūmiḥ* and the *Manobhūmi*, part three: Furthermore, what is informative action (*vijñapti-karman*)?
Briefly, there are three kinds:
first, that which is defiled (*kliṣṭa*).
Two are wholesome;
three are indeterminate.
[This applies] regarding the ten unwholesome courses of action of body, speech, and mind.
Because they do not depart from the dominant force of active manifestation,
all bodily and vocal informative actions are termed defiled informative actions.
If, at that very moment, one undertakes the vow of abstention,
all bodily and vocal informative actions (vijñapti-karma) are termed wholesome informative actions (kuśala-vijñapti-karma).

If the bodily and vocal informative actions belonging to a portion of the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) are called neutral informative action (*avyākṛta-vijñapti-karma*),
provided that they do not intend to communicate anything to another.
When one merely gives rise to a thought within and performs internal mental deliberation without speaking words,
but instead initiates the manifestation of wholesome, afflicted, or neutral dharmas through the mind,
this is called mental manifest action (*manovijñapti-karma*).
In this context, that which consists solely of the body— whether it arises in another location after ceasing in one, or arises as a mere transformation in that very same location—
is called bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti*).
That which consists solely of vocal sound is called vocal informative action (*vāgvijñapti*).
Only the volition (*cetanā*) that initiates the mind and performs an action is called mental informative action (*manas-karman*). Why is this?
Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
It is not reasonable that [a thing] should migrate from one location to another. Furthermore,
apart from the mere arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), there is no other real activity perceived by the eye or the ear.
The mind cannot be apprehended in any way.
Therefore, one should know that all manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*) is conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*).
When a person of proper conduct has a discernment and personally generates a formal resolve, [it constitutes manifest action].
That is to say, one thinks, "I shall maintain my life by means of this livelihood," and furthermore,
one repeatedly gives rise to a mind that desires, delights in, and approves of this livelihood;
at that time, one is called a person of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
Because it is comprised within non-restraint,
and because it is comprised within extremely heavy improper mental attention that harms the mind.
They merely bring about vast roots of unwholesomeness,
yet they have not yet accomplished the unwholesome karma produced by the act of killing or other unwholesome paths of action.
This continues until the intended activity has been carried out;
subsequently, whether it is performed to a small or great extent, it proceeds according to what is appropriate.
Furthermore, they accomplish various unwholesome karmas,
just as those born into families of non-restraint do;
this applies to whoever such a person may be.
It should be understood that this is explained in detail according to whatever matter gives rise to a resolute and fierce mind;
this applies to such a person for as long as they have not yet abandoned the volition of non-restraint.
They are always designated as "those lacking restraint" because,
throughout each division of the day, they extensively accumulate unwholesome volitions and their unwholesome karma frequently manifests.
One should know that non-merit increases incrementally.
Furthermore, this volition of wrong aspiration always functions in conjunction with lack of faith, laziness, forgetfulness, distraction, and impaired wisdom.
One who is capable of undertaking those actions and capable of initiating those actions—
from that point onward, by virtue of both the seeds and the actual manifestation—
while they are currently active within the continuity of the stream of existence, is called one who possesses non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
This continues until, due to the causes and conditions of relinquishment, it has not yet been relinquished or abandoned. In this regard,
if one does not have a lack of affection for the unpleasant results of evil karma,
nor lacks faith and understanding, nor enters into them accordingly, [then that karma is not accumulated].
This is called lack of faith.
If one follows one's desires and proceeds with delight toward those evil deeds,
one is unable to exert diligence to extinguish such karma.
This is called laziness.
If it is associated with faults,
one is unable to clearly and accurately recognize, as they truly are, those dharmas that are blameworthy as being blameworthy.
This is called forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*).
If the continuum of the mind is unstable due to distraction and defilement,
this is called distraction (*vikṣepa*).
If the continuum of the mind proceeds in a state of perversion,
such that one perceives faults as superior virtues,
this is called "unwholesome wisdom" (kuprajñā).
Due to the predominant influence of unwholesome ethical discipline (*duḥśīla*),
when unwholesome factors such as lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) that accompany unwholesome volition (*cetanā*) are currently active,
they are termed "unwholesome discipline."
If it is contrary to this,
one should understand that restraint (saṃvara) is obtained as appropriate.
As for the distinctions in its subsequent application:
That is to say, one who is capable of receiving the vows may then receive them.
In this regard, some receive the vows through another or by themselves,
while others receive them solely on their own initiative.
Excluding the bhikṣu vows. Why?
Because not everyone is capable of receiving the bhikṣu vows.
If the bhikṣu-vinaya were not necessarily received from another,
it would apply whether one is fit for ordination or unfit for ordination.
If those who merely wish to leave the household life were to do so spontaneously according to their every desire,
then the holy teaching would cease to exist.
There is also no teacher;
yet the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya can be understood.
Therefore, for a bhikṣu, there is no sense of receiving the discipline spontaneously.
Question: If, apart from the bhikṣu vows,
there are other vows that are naturally acquired (*svarasapravṛtta*),
for what reason must they nevertheless be received from another?
Answer: It is due to two kinds of factors that distance one from immoral conduct and support its restraint:
namely, shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*). These consist of feeling profound shame when committing a transgression, whether in the presence of others or within oneself.
In this way, one is able to fully undertake the observance of the precepts for abstaining from immoral conduct; therefore,
one receives them from another.
If shame (*hrī*) is present before one, there is necessarily also a sense of dread of blame (*apatrāpya*);
however, one who possesses a sense of dread of blame does not necessarily possess shame.
Therefore, the dharma of shame is the most powerful and preeminent.
If one deeply protects and upholds [the teachings] exactly as they have been received,
you should know that the merit produced is equal and without distinction.
Furthermore, if one gives rise to the thought of going to the teacher’s presence and earnestly requests [instruction], [the merit is likewise].
One skillfully initiates acts such as prostration and so forth;
remaining before the teacher with correct deportment,
one further expresses through speech the superior purpose one intends to accomplish.
These are called bodily informative action and vocal informative action.
As for mental informative action,
it refers to the two that precede [the actual action].
If it is acquired naturally, there is only mental manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*).
If it is acquired through the abandonment of volition (*cetanā*), it is contrary to non-restraint (*asaṃvara*);
because it is predominant through the power of abandonment, it is said to be "restraint" (*saṃvara*) when it functions together with the five faculties.
Furthermore, it should be understood that one undertakes the restraint through its inclusion of a hundred modes of conduct;
that is to say, by partially abstaining from the ten unwholesome paths of action,
ranging from partial abstinence from killing up to partial abstinence from wrong view.
These are called the first ten practices.
If one largely abstains from taking life,
and so on, up to largely abstaining from wrong views.
This is called the twentieth practice:
if one completely abstains from taking life,
up to and including completely abstaining from wrong views.
This is called the thirtieth practice.
It consists of abstaining from killing, up to and including abstaining from wrong views, for even a short time—
such as for one day and one night.
Whether for half a month, one month,
or up to one year—
this is called the fortieth practice.
If one abstains from killing and so forth, up to abstaining from wrong views, for a long period—
meaning for more than a year until the end of one's life—
this is called the fiftieth practice.
If one abstains from taking life up to and including abstaining from wrong view for as long as life lasts,
this is called the sixtieth practice.
If one personally abstains from taking life up to and including abstaining from wrong view...
This is called the seventieth practice.
If one encourages others toward this matter,
it is called the eightieth practice.
If one then praises and extols those very individuals through immeasurable gateways,
this is called the ninety-first practice.
If one sees those who have abstained from taking life, up to those who have abstained from wrong views.
With a profound mind, he rejoices and gives rise to great joy;
this is called the tenth of the ten practices.
These ten sets of ten practices are collectively described as one hundred practices.
One should know that the measure of merit produced is likewise so.
Furthermore, it should be known that there are briefly eight types of restraint (*saṃvara*):
first, the restraint that initiates [virtuous conduct].
Second, the discipline of embracing;
third, the discipline of protection;
fourth, the discipline of re-integration.
1. Inferior-grade restraint;
2. Intermediate-grade restraint;
3. Superior-grade restraint.
The eightfold pure restraint:
if one has not yet formally undertaken it, one first forms the thought, "I shall certainly undertake this," and thus practices such abstinence.
This is called the arousal of restraint;
when one correctly undertakes the precepts of abstinence,
it is called the undertaking of restraint.
From this point onward, because of the predominant power of the five faculties that sustain this state of detachment from thought,
it constantly functions together with those seeds,
and from time to time, it also functions together with their active manifestations.
By means of wholesome volition encompassed by the five faculties,
one proceeds with the restraint of the vows as previously undertaken; yet,
due to this volition, one may, for instance, associate with evil friends.
Or, if afflictions increase and one feels a desire for the manifestation of whatever evil arises,
one immediately feels shame and is able to abandon it quickly.
"May I not, through violating what I have undertaken, fall into the evil destinies"—
this is called the restraint of guarding. When, due to a lapse of mindfulness,
various evils manifest, [one applies oneself to their abandonment].
Even if one quickly causes mindfulness to abide,
one should personally entreat and reproach oneself, confessing what was transgressed to eliminate regret;
thereafter, one should firmly guard the vows one has received.
This is called the "reinstatement of restraint.
It refers to the partial and temporary distancing from various unwholesome courses of action, such as killing and so forth.
They merely distance themselves from [unwholesome conduct] without encouraging others to do so;
they do not praise or extol it through immeasurable doors,
nor do they see those fellow practitioners of the Dharma as being deeply joyful or filled with great delight.
This is called the inferior grade of restraint (*avara-saṃvara*).
If one largely abstains from various evils for a long duration, though not until the end of life, and both personally abstains and encourages others to do so; this is the inferior grade.
However, if one does not praise and extol seclusion through immeasurable doors,
and does not experience deep-seated rejoicing or great joy upon seeing fellow practitioners of the Dharma,
this is called the medium-grade discipline.
If one is personally able to distance oneself from all aspects of all evils at all times, and likewise encourages others to do so;
if one extols and praises [this practice] through immeasurable means;
and if, upon seeing those who share the same Dharma, one feels profound joy in one's heart and gives rise to great delight.
This is called the superior grade of restraint (*saṃvara*). If,
based on this very restraint one has undertaken, one is able to remain without deficiency or transgression, and thereby cultivates freedom from remorse and so forth,
until one fully enters the first dhyāna.
Through the power of śamatha to suppress and subdue,
all seeds of transgressing the precepts are suppressed and subdued;
this is called the restraint of meditative concentration (dhyāna-saṃvara).
As it is with the first dhyāna,
so it should be understood for the second, third, and fourth dhyānas as well.
The distinction here is as follows:
As the path of śamatha, subsumed under the antidote of distancing, becomes increasingly profound,
it suppresses the seeds of immoral conduct;
one should know that this is called the pure restraint induced by the first power of purification.
If one remains without any deficiency or transgression regarding this very restraint of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*),
and furthermore, by relying upon the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*),
enters into the direct realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) and attains the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
At that time, all seeds of unwholesome discipline are forever destroyed.
If one realizes the first fruit by relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*),
at that time all seeds of unwholesome discipline capable of leading to rebirth in the evil destinies are forever destroyed.
This is precisely what is called "the precepts beloved by the noble ones.
It should be understood that this is named the second pure restraint induced by the power of purity;
it is also termed the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*).
When this untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) is attained upon reaching the fruit of arhatship,
it is superior solely by virtue of the excellence of its antidote (pratipakṣa), which is pure,
and not by virtue of the excellence of the abandonment of that which is to be countered (vipakṣa).
These eight types are collectively established as three:
first, receiving the vows;
second, maintaining the vows.
The three types of pure discipline (*tri-śīla-viśuddhi*):
the first two are "undertaking" (*samādāna*),
while the protection that subsequently induces [the restraint] is "maintaining" (*dhāraṇa*).
The three grades—lower, middle, and upper—are each received and maintained in two ways.
Those belonging to meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and those that are untainted (*anāsrava*) are comprised within the pure category.
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One establish the three types of restraint: the bhikṣu, the upāsaka, and the upavāsa?
Answer: It is due to three causes.
That is to say, there are three types of those emanated by the Buddha:
some are capable of practicing the conduct of abandoning unwholesome deeds and the conduct of abandoning desire.
There are those who are able to practice the conduct of abandoning unwholesome actions but not the conduct of abandoning desire;
there are also those who are unable to practice either the conduct of abandoning unwholesome actions or the conduct of abandoning desire.
Based on the first type of person to be converted, the bhikṣu-prātimokṣa discipline is established.
The lay practitioner's vow (upāsaka-saṃvara) is established based on the second class of those to be trained.
Why is this? Because it is not for those who are constrained by the domestic life and currently dwell amidst the secular world.
And because one is able to continuously and perfectly maintain all the rules of training in an unswerving manner,
the *upavāsa* restraint is established based on the third category of those to be trained. Why is this so?
Because of this, they are unable to practice the path that completely abandons both [extremes].
One should instead encourage and support them through two causes,
lest they consider themselves weighed down by a heavy burden.
That is to say, the first three branches cultivate the abandonment of unwholesome conduct,
while the latter four branches cultivate the abandonment of sensual conduct;
the abandonment of non-celibacy cultivates both types.
Question: One should know by how many factors each of the bhikṣu, upāsaka, and upavāsa vows is comprised.
Answer: The bhikṣu vow is comprised of four factors.
What are the four?
First, the branch of receiving full ordination;
second, the branch of receiving the training rules that accord with the Dharma.
Third, the branch of protecting the minds of others;
fourth, the branch of protecting the training rules as they have been received.
If one performs the formal announcement and the fourth *karmavācanā*, [the ordination is complete].
And the brief summary:
following the coarse rules of training (śikṣāpada) is called the limb of receiving full ordination (upasaṃpadā-aṅga).
By virtue of possessing these factors,
he is called a "first bhikṣu" endowed with the bhikṣu precepts.
From this point onward, all the bhikṣu śīla that accord with the Prātimokṣa within the Vinaya [are to be observed].
If one guards and practices all those numerous rules of training that have been prescribed,
by this one is called a "guardian of the prātimokṣa restraint."
This is called the branch of training in accordance with the Dharma through acceptance.
For one who accomplishes these two branches, there is the fulfillment of proper conduct and the fulfillment of practice;
this is called the branch of guarding the minds of others.
He is complete in his conduct and complete in his observance of the rules,
as already explained in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
He perceives even the slightest transgressions with deep dread.
Regarding the various training rules one has undertaken, one is able to refrain from violating them;
and should a violation occur, one is able to emerge from it—
namely, by virtue of a profound perception of fear and through wisdom.
This is called the branch of guarding in accordance with the precepts as they have been received.
The lay devotee’s discipline (upāsaka-saṃvara) is comprised of three branches.
What are these three?
First, the branch of undertaking the excellence of abstaining from actions that most severely harm others;
second, the branch of intensive cultivation when transgressing what has been undertaken;
third, the branch of not transgressing what has been undertaken.
If one forever abstains from harming another's life, damaging another's property, or violating another's wife or concubines,
this is called the first branch; the second branch is the complete abstention from false speech.
Abstaining from all intoxicants and sources of heedlessness is the third limb.
This is a brief explanation of the one-day precept (upavāsa-saṃvara).
It is comprised of five branches.
What are these five?
First, the branch of undertaking the avoidance of harming others.
Second, the branch of avoiding harm to oneself and others through undertaking restraint;
third, the branch of the intensive cultivation of what has been undertaken when it is transgressed;
fourth, the branch of the abiding in right mindfulness so as not to transgress what has been undertaken.
The fifth is the factor of unimpaired right mindfulness.
If one can remain far removed from harming the lives of others or destroying the property of others,
this is called the first factor.
Abstaining from unchaste conduct is the second limb. Why is this so?
By being free from this, one does not harm oneself because one does not become habituated to one's own wife or concubines;
nor does one harm others because one does not become habituated to the wives or concubines of others.
Abstinence from false speech is the third limb.
Abstaining from all intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence, and abstaining from the other three [unwholesome] bases—
this is the fourth limb. Why is this so?
Having been habituated to singing, dancing, music, anointing with unguents, wearing crowns, garlands, and perfumes, ascending high beds, and eating at improper times,
if one distances oneself from these and repeatedly recalls them [with aversion], [one attains the first dhyāna].
I now abide securely in the definitive observance of the precepts.
At all times, I firmly maintain right mindfulness and remain far removed from all intoxicants and sources of heedlessness.
This is the fifth limb.
Why is this? Because although he dwells securely in the limb of right mindfulness, [he does not yet possess the others].
That is to say: "I now abide in the definitive observance of the fast.
If I were to become intoxicated by various liquors, I would fall into madness and lose my self-control.
Therefore, within this context, [I shall observe] the bhikṣuṇī discipline."
If one is correctly training in the vows of a śrāmaṇera or a śrāmaṇerikā,
since these are all subsumed within the category of the renunciant,
it should be understood that they are included within the bhikṣu-vinaya.
Since the female lay practitioner’s (upāsikā) discipline belongs to the category of householders and is manifested by a corresponding training,
it should be understood as being subsumed under the lay practitioner’s discipline.
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One establish the two groups of the bhikṣu and śrāmaṇera vows within the bhikṣu discipline,
yet establish the three groups of the bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, and śrāmaṇerī vows within the bhikṣuṇī discipline?
Answer: Because those women are subject to many afflictions, they are led to gradually undertake the training in the bhikṣuṇī discipline;
if they develop a deep inclination toward even a small portion of the śrāmaṇerikā precepts, [they may proceed further].
Next, one should confer upon them all the training rules (śikṣāpada) for female trainees (śikṣamāṇā).
If they have developed a deep affinity for the majority of the training rules for female trainees,
one should not hastily confer full ordination (upasampadā) upon them.
He must dwell and train for another two years;
only after he has developed a deep affection for it should the full ordination be conferred upon him.
Thus, having accumulated and cultivated training over a long period in the few rules of training, [he is ordained].
Only after this does one have the capacity to receive the extensive multitude of training rules (*śikṣāpada*), and subsequently, one is able to fully practice and study the bhikṣuṇī discipline.
Question: For what reason is the abstention from gold and silver added within the śrāmaṇera discipline?
Is it not [the case] regarding the one-day precept (upavāsa-saṃvara)?
Answer: Because that śrāmaṇera is included among the ordained community;
and for one who has gone forth, there are two situations that are utterly impure and improper.
First, falling into the extreme of sensual pleasure:
one indulges in play, adorns the body, and in all actions and experiences, follows whatever is pleasurable.
Second, amassing wealth and treasures.
To eliminate the first unwholesome and non-sublime condition,
one establishes the practice of abstaining from singing, dancing, music, and even eating at improper times;
this is for the purpose of abandoning the second unwholesome and non-sublime condition.
He establishes the renunciation of accepting gold and silver,
because gold and silver are the root of all wealth and treasures,
and because they are the most excellent.
Question: For what reason, among the śrāmaṇera vows,
are the two factors of abstaining from singing, dancing, and music, as well as from anointing the body and wearing garlands and perfumes,
established as separate precepts?
Is it combined into a single branch within the *upavāsa* restraint?
Answer: For householders, there is nothing improper regarding this matter;
for those who have gone forth, however, it is extremely improper.
Therefore, for those living at home, these minor regulations are combined into a single training rule.
This is so that if they should momentarily transgress, they will immediately reproach themselves and confess both together as one, rather than by means of two separate acts.
For those who have gone forth, these two points are established as separate precepts within this single section.
This is so that if they should commit a transgression, they may both reproach themselves and confess the two types of offenses, rather than relying on only one.
Question: Why is it not permitted for *śaṇḍhaka*s and *paṇḍaka*s to go forth and receive full ordination?
Answer: Because if these two types of persons are placed within the community of bhikṣus, they will incur the faults associated with women.
If one were placed among the community of bhikṣuṇīs, they would incur the fault of associating with men due to physical contact and the like;
because it is improper for them to dwell together with the two communities,
such individuals are not permitted to go forth or receive full ordination.
Furthermore, because these two afflictions are so prevalent and because the innate afflictive obstructions are extremely pervasive,
one is unable to initiate such analytical discernment.
He is not even able to exercise discernment so as to cause his aggregate of ethical discipline to manifest in purity,
let alone realize the superhuman states that transcend others.
For this reason, such persons are not permitted to go forth or receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Furthermore, it is difficult to find good people within such groups, and they are likewise difficult to examine.
Question: Why is it that these two types of persons, although they have received refuge, are also able to subsequently receive all the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) of a lay follower (*upāsaka*)?
"And why is one not called an upāsaka?
The answer is: "An upāsaka is one who is able to draw near to and serve the community of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs."
Although he is able to guard the vows he has received,
he should not frequently associate with or serve the community of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs;
nor should the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs associate with or accept him by rubbing or touching him.
Furthermore, such persons should not maintain close intimacy with laymen (*upāsaka*).
For this reason, they cannot be called laymen;
nevertheless, they do receive the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) that constitute protection.
One should know that merit and so forth are without distinction;
this does not apply to non-restraint.
That is to say, with the exception of the karma of restraint and non-restraint as previously described.
One should know that all wholesome and unwholesome actions of body, speech,
and mind are entirely subsumed under karma that is neither discipline nor non-discipline.
This is what is received.
Whether received from another,
or received from another and then naturally undertaken—
such is the merit obtained from the restraint thus received.
Is there a distinction of superiority or inferiority?
Answer: If one receives [the precepts] with an impartial mind and likewise maintains them, you should know that there is no distinction.
Question: By how many causes and conditions should the bhikṣu-prātimokṣa discipline not be conferred, even if one desires to receive it?
Answer: Briefly, the bhikṣu-prātimokṣa discipline is [refused] due to six causes.
First, impairment of intention;
second, impairment of the basis;
third, impairment of the male organ.
Fourth, it harms the four white dharmas; fifth, it belongs to others; sixth, it is for the sake of protecting others.
This applies if one is coerced and detained by a king, or coerced and detained by violent bandits.
Either being oppressed by creditors,
or oppressed by fear, or fearing the inability to subsist.
He thought to himself: "It is difficult for me to survive while living at home;
these bhikṣus find it very easy to make a living.
I should now go among the community of bhikṣus."
He falsely presents himself as being of the same dharma as them in order to easily maintain his livelihood.
Having thus gone forth with such a deceitful intention,
although he harbors fear, he guards and practices even a single precept.
"May no bhikṣus dwell together with me;
once they know that I have committed an offense against the precepts, they shall expel me.
However, because his underlying intention was thus harmed, [the Buddha spoke].
This is not called "leaving the household life and receiving full ordination.
Such is what is meant by the impairment of one's intention (*āśaya*).
Furthermore, suppose there is someone who thinks as follows:
"It is difficult to sustain my life while remaining at home;
I must certainly go forth into homelessness to easily provide for myself.
Just as the bhikṣus practice the holy life, so shall I do."
"Even until the end of life, one should practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Such a renunciant is not said to have impaired their intention (*āśaya*).
Although they are not entirely pure, it is nonetheless said that they have gone forth and received full ordination."
If one has physical ailments such as abscesses or swellings,
with symptoms as described in the section on prohibitions,
this is called impairment of the physical basis.
Because their physical basis has been impaired,
although they have gone forth, they lack the capacity to serve their teachers;
due to such incapacity, they...
The karma of serving one's teachers and fellow practitioners of the holy life,
as well as receiving pure objects of faith— such as clothing, food, drink, and other offerings—
from donors of pure faith; these two kinds of gifts bestowed through pure faith.
That which is extremely difficult to digest should not be consumed,
as it causes the decline of all wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*).
Therefore, one relies upon that which has been impaired.
One should not go forth or receive full ordination if one is a *śaṇḍha* or a *pandaka*,
as these are termed "damage to male form."
One should not go forth or receive full ordination.
The causes and conditions for this should be understood as previously explained.
Furthermore, there are briefly three types of paṇḍaka.
1. The paṇḍaka who is deficient in his entirety;
2. the paṇḍaka who is deficient in one part;
3. the paṇḍaka who is impaired.
If one is born and does not develop a male organ at all,
this is called a "complete" paṇḍaka (eunuch).
If one possesses male potency for half of the month, [this is called a "half" paṇḍaka].
There are some who commit an offense against themselves by another,
or whose male potency arises only when they see another practicing unchaste conduct;
these are called *ekadeśa-paṇḍaka* (partial paṇḍakas).
If one is harmed by weapons and the like,
or afflicted by diseases, medicines, fire, mantras, and so forth,
such that the male organ previously obtained is now severed or destroyed.
Once it has been severed and destroyed, the male faculty no longer functions;
this is called the *paṇḍaka* who is impaired.
The first type of *paṇḍaka* is named both *paṇḍaka* and *śaṇḍha*.
The second [category] consists only of paṇḍakas and not śaṇḍhas;
the third, provided they have not been made an object of reproach by others,
consists only of śaṇḍhas and not paṇḍakas.
If one has committed an offense against oneself by another,
they are called a paṇḍaka or a śaṇḍhaka;
likewise for one who commits an ānantarya crime or defiles a bhikṣuṇī.
If one is an outsider, a thief-dweller, one who dwells separately, or one who does not dwell together [with the Sangha],
this is called the impairment of the white dharmas;
such a person should not be granted full ordination.
Why is this? Because, due to those extremely defiled states of lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*),
all wholesome states (*śukladharma*) such as shame and dread of blame are rendered exceedingly weak and diminished.
Whether they be ministers of kings whom the king dislikes,
or those who have committed acts unfavorable to the king,
or those who are seized and held by creditors;
If one is another’s servant, or another’s slave, or has been acquired by another, or is involved in a legal dispute,
or has not been granted permission by one’s parents—
this is called being subject to another.
One should not confer full ordination upon them.
If they are transformation bodies, one likewise should not confer full ordination upon them for the sake of protecting others. Why is this?
There may be nāgas and others who, for the sake of receiving the Dharma, transform their own bodies into the likeness of bhikṣus and seek to receive full ordination.
If one were to confer full ordination upon them, [it would be improper].
When he falls asleep, he returns to his original form;
once awakened from sleep, he manifests as a bhikṣu, or as a mentally visualized bhikṣu,
or as a park-keeper, or as a lay follower (upāsaka).
Having impulsively approached and seen that his body had thus transformed,
he conceived a sense of hatred toward all true bhikṣus,
thinking, "None of these bhikṣus are human beings."
Who can respectfully serve others by providing them with food and clothing,
so that no one else may fall into such an evil view? Therefore,
this is done for the sake of protecting others.
One should not confer full ordination upon them.
For these six reasons, one should not bestow the bhikṣu vows upon them;
furthermore, this excludes cases where the necessary quorum for performing the *karmavācanā* is deficient.
The Ācārya Upādhyāya, residing with a community of monks who dwell in pure and perfect ethical discipline, asked:
"By how many causes and conditions should the upāsaka vow not be conferred upon someone?"
Answer: Briefly stated, it is due to two causes:
first, because of the impairment of the intention;
second, because of the impairment of the male organ.
If there is damage to the mental disposition,
one should know that in all such cases it is not to be accepted;
if there is damage to the male organ, [it is likewise not to be accepted].
There may be those who undertake the precepts for the sake of receiving [the benefits], yet they cannot be called upāsakas;
the reasons for this have already been fully explained above.
If it concerns the one-day precept (upavāsa-saṃvara),
one should know that it must not be undertaken if it would be undermined by one's underlying intention. Why is this?
Some follow others; some,
for the sake of obtaining wealth, profit, or honor, falsely claim that they wish to receive the upavāsa precepts.
However, since he actually lacks the intention to seek and receive [the gift],
it should be understood that this is called "corruption of intention.
If there is no such cause or condition for receiving as has been described, [it is likewise corrupted].
One should know that one must receive all the vows as previously described.
Question: How many causes and conditions are there by which a bhikṣu’s vow, once received, is relinquished?
Answer: It may be due to abandoning the training rules.
Either due to committing a root offense,
or due to the disappearance of one's gender and the emergence of both genders,
or due to the severance of the roots of goodness.
Or, due to the abandonment of the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous life-stream),
one who has received the bhikṣu vows may relinquish them;
this occurs when the True Dharma is destroyed or the True Dharma disappears.
Although there is no new reception of the bhikṣu vows,
it should be understood that what was previously received is not relinquished. Why is this so?
Because at that time the degenerate age (kaliyuga) was just beginning,
there was not a single sentient being whose intention was not impaired who could receive full ordination,
much less anyone who could realize the fruits of the śramaṇa.
It should be understood that for a lay male practitioner (upāsaka),
[the discipline is lost] due to the arising of a dissimilar state of mind and due to the severance of the roots of goodness.
Because one abandons the homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga),
what has been acquired is relinquished when the True Dharma disappears.
Just as it is with the principle of the bhikṣu vows,
so too should it be understood for the upāsaka vows.
As for the upavāsa vows:
It should be understood that this occurs either after sunrise,
or by the arousal of a dissimilar state of mind,
or by relinquishing the homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga) in the interim.
Even though it has already been attained, it will inevitably be relinquished again.
Furthermore, what is the attainment of non-perception?
It refers to one who is already free from craving for the Realm of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*), but not yet free from craving for the realms above.
Because it is preceded by the mental attention of the perception of renunciation,
all minds and mental factors merely cease and become tranquil, and do not function at all;
this is called the attainment of non-perception.
This is a conventional existence and not a substantial existence.
One should know that its distinctions are briefly of three kinds:
first, inferior cultivation.
Second is middling cultivation;
third is superior cultivation.
If one practices with inferior cultivation:
If one falls away from it in the present life, one cannot quickly bring it back into manifestation;
this is also the case for the physical basis obtained among the non-conceptualizing beings (asaṃjñisattva) in the heavens.
They are not very pure;
their majestic radiance is brilliant and their forms are vast, like those of other celestial hosts,
yet they are certain to meet with an untimely death.
If one practices with middling intensity,
although there may be regression in the present life,
one is nonetheless able to swiftly bring it back into manifestation.
If one is born among the non-conceptualizing beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) in the heavens,
the physical basis (*āśraya-deha*) experienced therein,
though extremely pure, radiant, brilliant, and vast in form and color, [is still subject to transformation].
However, it is not ultimately and most extremely pure;
although there may be premature death, it is not certain.
This is for one who practices at the superior level.
There will certainly be no regression.
If one is born among the non-conceptualizing beings (asaṃjñisattva) in the heavens,
the physical basis (āśraya) experienced therein—
They are exceedingly pure, with a majestic radiance that blazes forth and a physical form that is vast and expansive.
Furthermore, they reach the ultimate state of supreme purity and will certainly not suffer an untimely death;
only after exhausting their full lifespan will they finally pass away.
Furthermore, when all minds and mental factors acquired at birth are extinguished by virtue of this cause and this condition,
it is called "non-conception" (asaṃjñā).
Furthermore, what is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)?
It refers to one who has already abandoned craving for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) but has not yet abandoned craving for the higher [spheres],
or alternatively, one who has already abandoned [craving for those spheres] by means of mental attention preceded by the perception of cessation (*nirodhasaṃjñā-manasikāra*).
The state in which all minds and mental factors are solely extinguished and stilled, and solely non-functioning,
is called the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
This attainment is capable only of extinguishing and stilling the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
It cannot extinguish or quiet the ālayavijñāna;
one should know that this meditative absorption is also nominally existent (prajñaptisat) and not substantially existent (dravyasat).
There are, briefly, three varieties of this absorption.
The cultivation of the inferior grade is as previously explained.
One who cultivates at the inferior grade may regress in this present life and will not be able to swiftly re-induce it to manifest.
One who practices with middling intensity may regress in the present life,
yet is able to swiftly bring [the attainment] back into manifestation;
one who practices with superior intensity never regresses at all.
Noble learners (*śaikṣa*) who are body-witnesses (*kāyasākṣin*) non-returners (*anāgāmin*) are able to enter this meditative absorption;
noble adepts (*aśaikṣa*) are likewise able to enter it.
This refers to those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
The aforementioned state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) is neither entered by those in training (*śaikṣa*) nor by those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Why is this?
Because within this state there is no manifestation of wisdom;
because above this there exist superior states of peaceful abiding and rebirth;
and furthermore, because this meditative concentration cannot realize those supreme wholesome dharmas not yet realized.
Because it is a place of lingering, deception, and illusion.
Furthermore, what is space?
It is that which is manifested solely by the absence of matter.
This is called space.
Why is that? Because in whatever location one may travel, nothing at all can be apprehended.
In this context, the perception of space arises;
therefore, one should know that this exists only as a designation and not as a substantial entity.
Furthermore, what is cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?
That is to say, when the conditions for the arising of other phenomena are present,
because those other phenomena arise, [the intended phenomenon] cannot arise;
this state of mere cessation and mere stillness is called non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Whatever phenomena are due to arise at this particular time will never again arise at that time once they have passed beyond their moment of arising; therefore,
this cessation is also nominally existent, not substantially existent.
Why is this so? Because there is nothing else here whose own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) can be apprehended;
and because this category of phenomena is not dissociated [from its nature].
Furthermore, at other times, it may arise due to conditions;
therefore, analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is not invariably determined.
This is the case for those in training who have seen the tracks [of the path].
Regarding those born from eggs or moisture, those in Uttarakuru, those in the Heaven of Non-conception,
and those born as females, *śaṇḍhas*, *paṇḍakas*, the formless, or those with both sexual organs, [they do not possess it].

Furthermore, regarding future existence, one should know that the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) obtained through craving or aspiration is invariably determined by the traces of training (śaikṣa-darśana).

One does not, at any time thereafter, give rise to the fetter of aspiration for renewed existence that produces renewed existence, except when the seeds of craving have not yet been completely and irrevocably destroyed.
Question: For what reason is it called "dissociated from mind" (*cittaviprayukta*)?
Answer: This is a conceptual construct.
It is employed for the purpose of verbal expression regarding various phenomena;
