it is neither of the two types, such as "possessing form" and so forth.
Regarding existence, views, and so forth, both of these are to be understood as neither [existent nor non-existent].
One should know all such principles of formal establishment as they are explained at length.
Thus, the six types of expertise have been explained.
This refers to skill in the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*) up to skill in the faculties (*indriya-kauśalya*).
How should one understand the extensive establishment of the meaning of these skills?
Furthermore, the summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
The distinctions in meaning regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), their sequential inclusion, and their basis.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature of form (*rūpa*)?
Answer: Briefly stated, there are eleven.
This refers to the ten material bases (rūpāyatana) beginning with the eye, as well as the matter included within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
Furthermore, there are generally two types:
the four great elements (mahābhūta) and derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
All such things possess the characteristic of transformation and resistance.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature of sensation?
Answer: Briefly stated, there are six kinds.
This refers to that which arises based on the six types of contact, such as that of the eye and so forth.
This, in turn, is of two kinds:
if it has form (*rūpa*) as its basis, it is called bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*).
That which relies on the formless is called mental feeling. Why is this?
Because the first five faculties are all of the nature of form.

Question: If the first five faculties are all of the nature of matter (*rūpa-dharma*), and are designated as "bodily feeling" (*kāyikī-vedanā*) based on the eye and so forth, why are the eye and the others not considered to be merely the body?
Answer: Because their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are distinct.
Why is this so? Because the five faculties, such as the eye and so forth, are mutually distinct from one another.
Question: If the characteristics of the faculties such as the eye are distinct, they do not all share the characteristic of the body.
Based on those various feelings, for these reasons and conditions, they should not be considered bodily feelings.
Answer: Because the other material sense-faculties are not separate from the body, they are designated by way of that [body].
What fault is there in this?
Question: If there is no fault because [feeling] does not exist apart from the body, then the mental faculty (*manas*) is likewise active without being separate from the body;
therefore, feeling based on the mental faculty should be called "bodily feeling" (*kāyikī vedanā*).
Does this mean that all [feeling] is bodily feeling and there is no mental feeling?
Answer: All material sense-faculties are necessarily not separated from the body, whereas the mind is not so; therefore, there is no fault.
Why is this so? Because for sentient beings born in the formless realm, the mental faculty (manas) functions independently of the body.
Therefore, all sensations produced by the five [physical] faculties are collectively termed "bodily sensation" (kāyikī vedanā).
That which relies solely on the mind is uniquely termed mental feeling;
therefore, they are collectively described as two:
namely, bodily and mental feelings.
Furthermore, all feelings (vedanā) have the characteristic of experiencing.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of perception (saṃjñā)?
Answer: This also consists of six kinds.
This should be understood as before.
Furthermore, there are six types of perception:
first, the perception of signs (*nimittasaṃjñā*).
Second, the perception of signlessness;
third, the perception of narrowness;
fourth, the perception of vastness.
The five perceptions of the immeasurables;
the perception of nothingness.
Furthermore, there are briefly two types.
First, the perception of the world;
second, the supramundane perception.
Regarding the narrow and limited perception:
The perception of the desire realm is called "limited perception";
the perception of the form realm is called "vast perception."
The perception of the immeasurable refers to the worldly perception of the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness.
The perception of nothingness refers to...
This refers to the perception of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
All of these are called perceptions with signs (*sanimittasaṃjñā*).
As for perceptions without signs (*animittasaṃjñā*):
This refers to the perception of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as well as all perceptions of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) who have transcended the world.
Furthermore, all perceptions are characterized by the nature of being fully cognized.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of formations (*saṃskāra*)?
Answer: This also consists of six kinds, as should be understood from what preceded.
Furthermore, these modes of activity cause the mind to engage in formation through five types.
First, there is the yielding of objects;
second, there is their conjunction;
and third, there is their separation.
Fourth, it can give rise to afflicted karma;
fifth, it causes the mind to function with mastery.
Furthermore, these modes of activity are, in brief, of three kinds.
First, wholesome conduct;
second, unwholesome conduct;
third, indeterminate conduct.
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) possess the characteristic of being produced through volitional effort.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of consciousness?
Answer: Briefly stated, there are six kinds.
That which is called visual consciousness up to mental consciousness is the differentiation of the intrinsic nature of consciousness.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of consciousness.
First, the distinction of reception;
second, the distinction of apprehending objects;
third, the distinction of stages.
There are three distinctions in reception;
six distinctions in the apprehension of objects;
and three distinctions in states.
Thus, the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) has eighteen distinct natures in total;
one should know that these are called the natures of the aggregates.
Furthermore, what is the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha)?
For what purpose are the aggregates established?
It is to reveal that all form—whether past, future, or present, and whether distant or near—is so defined;
and as it is for form, so it is for the other aggregates up to consciousness.
Thus, in brief, all aggregates (skandha) are subsumed.
The meaning of "aggregate" is the sense of a "collection.
Furthermore, the aggregates consist solely of various conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) characterized by their nominal nature.
It should be understood that the aggregates (skandhas) are established in order to reveal the meaning of selflessness (anātmatā).
Furthermore, how many classifications of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) are there?
Briefly, there are six kinds.
First, by way of the object;
second, by way of the characteristic;
third, by way of whether consciousness grasps it or not.
Fourth, by virtue of consciousness being empty or non-empty;
fifth, by virtue of the range of perception;
sixth, by virtue of the limit.
"Phenomenon" (vastu) refers to all forms, which are the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements.
"Characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) refers to...
Briefly, there are three kinds:
first, pure form;
second, form that is the object of pure [perception].
Third, there is matter apprehended by the mind.
Furthermore, the characteristic of transformation and resistance is the common characteristic of matter.
Regarding whether consciousness grasps it or not:
If consciousness relies upon and grasps [something], that is called "appropriated matter" (*upātta-rūpa*). What, then, is this?
It refers to that which consciousness relies upon, with which it shares a common destiny in terms of security and peril, and with which it is integrated, growing together.
Furthermore, this serves as the basis for the arising of various sensations;
it is the opposite of non-appropriated matter.
Regarding consciousness, whether it is empty or not empty:
If consciousness is not empty, it is called "congruent matter" (*sabhāga-rūpa*),
because it functions in a manner equivalent to that consciousness.
If consciousness is empty, it is called "non-congruent matter" (*tatsabhāga-rūpa*).
Because it proceeds in accordance with what appears to be its own continuum.
Regarding "the sphere of perception," there are,
in brief, three types of perception that take form as their object.
First, the perception of form;
second, the perception of resistance;
third, the perception of diversity.
The perception of form is also threefold:
first, the sign of light and shadow;
second, the sign of spatial location.
Third is the characteristic of abiding through accumulation.
These three characteristics follow their respective order:
the range of the three perceptions consists of grasping the characteristics of blue and so forth.
That which is called the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) is so named because it can apprehend physical obstruction.
That which can apprehend the distinct conventional designations of male, female, house, field, and so forth is called the perception of difference (*nānātva-saṃjñā*).
This is called the differentiation of the range of ideation.
As for the "limit," there are briefly two kinds of limits regarding form (*rūpa*).
First, falling into the lower realm,
namely the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
second, falling into the middle realm.
This refers to the form of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
It should be understood that, within this context, it is said that there is no form in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) with respect to the various forms produced through the predominance of karma.
This is not said with reference to the matter that is mastered through superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Why?
Because that superior concentration brings about the manifestation of the preparatory applications (*prayoga*) of all concentrations, thereby attaining mastery over all forms of matter.
It should be understood that this form is called "form produced by the extremely subtle meditative concentration.
Furthermore, how are the distinctions within the aggregate of feeling categorized?
Briefly, they are fivefold.
First, by way of the object;
second, by way of the characteristic;
third, by way of arising.
Fourth, by way of observation;
fifth, by way of renunciation.
As for the "matter":
This refers to the phenomena of experiencing and that which is conducive to experiencing.
As for their characteristics,
these refer to specific characteristics and general characteristics.
There are three specific characteristics:
the sensation of pleasure, the sensation of suffering, and the sensation of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
The sensation of pleasure is suffering because it is subject to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
Painful feeling is suffering because it is the suffering of suffering.
Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling...
Because it is suffering by virtue of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*), all feelings whatsoever are said to be suffering due to this cause and condition.
This is called the common characteristic of feeling (*vedanā-sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
"Born" refers to all feelings produced by the sixteen types of contact.
What are the sixteen?
They are: eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, and tongue-contact.
Contact of the body, contact of the mind;
contact of resistance and contact of designation;
and contact conducive to pleasant feeling.
Contact conducive to painful feeling;
contact conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
and the contact of craving.
Contact of aversion,
contact of clarity,
and contact of ignorance.
Contact that is neither luminous nor non-luminous is established as the six types of contact and as contact with resistance, by virtue of its basis and its apprehended object.
Contact of designation (*adhivacana-sparśa*) is established by way of the conceptualization of objects;
contact conducive to pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanīya-sparśa*) and so forth is established by way of the experiencing of objects;

and contact of craving (*tṛṣṇā-sparśa*), aversion (*pratigha-sparśa*), clarity (*vidyā-sparśa*), ignorance (*avidyā-sparśa*), and neither-clarity-nor-ignorance (*naiva-vidyā-na-avidyā-sparśa*) is established by way of defilement and purification.
This is called the distinction of birth.
As for the distinction of observation:
all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas appear in the world.
In all cases, one gives rise to eight types of contemplation regarding sensations (*vedanā*):
namely, how many kinds of sensation are there,
and what is the origin of sensation?
Who is it that experiences the cessation of feeling?
Who is it that proceeds toward the origination of feeling?
Who is it that proceeds toward the cessation of feeling?
Who experiences the gratification of feeling?
Who experiences the danger of feeling?
Who experiences the escape from feeling?
When observing in this way, one understands as it truly is that there are three kinds of feeling.
Because of the accumulation of contact, there is the accumulation of feeling;
this should be understood as explained in detail according to the Sūtra.
One should know that these eight ways of observing feelings briefly reveal their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*):
observing the causes for the operation of phenomena in the present life, and observing their cessation.
One contemplates the subsequent dharma as the cause for its transformation, and contemplates its cessation;
one contemplates those two as the causes for their transformation,
and contemplates the cessation of those two transformations.
The causal contemplation and the pure contemplation—
these are called the distinctions of observation.
As for renunciation:
That is to say: the first dhyāna transcends the faculty of grief;
the second dhyāna transcends the faculty of suffering;
the third dhyāna transcends the faculty of joy.
The faculty of pleasure is the renunciation of the fourth dhyāna;
the faculty of equanimity is the renunciation of the realm of non-perception.
This is called the distinction of renunciation.
Furthermore, what are the distinctions within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*)?
Briefly, they are fivefold.
First, by way of object (*vastu*).
Second, by way of characteristics;
third, by way of inversion;
and fourth, by way of non-inversion.
Fifth, by way of conceptual differentiation.
"Entity" (vastu) refers to the grasping of the characteristics of the object of perception (*ālambana*) and the phenomena that accord with them. "Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to...
There are six kinds of specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa),
which should be understood as previously explained.
The characteristic of general cognition (samānyalakṣaṇa) is the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
This is called the differentiation of characteristics.
As for the differentiation of inversions,
it refers to the fact that all foolish commoners lack understanding.
Following upon ignorance, improper mental attention arises;
with respect to its object, it proceeds by conceiving the impermanent as permanent and grasping at its signs.
This is called the perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*).
Just as one conceives of the impermanent as permanent,
so too is it a perversion of perception to conceive of suffering as pleasure, the impure as pure, and the non-self as self.
Those who are householders are able to give rise to perversions of mind;
a portion of those who have left the home life are able to give rise to perversions of view.
This is called the distinction between perversions.
This perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) further has distinctions.
That is to say, erroneously grasping the characteristics (*nimitta*) regarding four matters is called the perversion of perception.
If, by means of such conceptualization of characteristics, one becomes attached to an object, [it is the perversion of mind].
This is called the inversion of the mind. If,
by means of such characteristics of equality and so forth, there is attachment, one will firmly adhere to,
accept, demonstrate, and establish that which is an inverted matter.
This is called the inversion of view.
Regarding the absence of such inversions,
it refers to those who are wise and possess clear understanding.
Following the light of wisdom, one gives rise to appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*),
perceiving impermanence as impermanent and suffering as suffering within the objects of focus.
Knowing the impure as impure,
and knowing the selfless as selfless,
one turns by correctly grasping the characteristics.
This is called non-perversion of perception,
non-perversion of mind,
and non-perversion of view.
This is called the distinction of non-perversion.
As for the distinction of conceptualization,
there are briefly five kinds of characteristics of conceptualization through perception (*saṃjñā-vikalpa*).
First, discrimination of objects;
second, discrimination of experience;
third, discrimination of designation.
Fourth is the discrimination of false imaginings;
fifth is the discrimination of real meaning.
If one grasps at the signs of flavor within an object, [it is the former].
The discrimination of objects is called "discrimination of the objective sphere.
The various feelings produced by the grasping of objects are called "discrimination of experience."
If one grasps at various conventional verbal designations regarding oneself and others— such as their names, categories, clans, and so forth—
this is called "conceptualization of imputation.
It consists of grasping at inverted characteristics with respect to all objects.

That which is called "false conceptualization" (abhūtaparikalpa) is the grasping of non-erroneous characteristics regarding various objects; that which is called "conceptualization of real meaning" (tattvārthaparikalpa) is [the grasping of such characteristics].
Such is the general designation for the detailed classification of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Furthermore, how is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) classified?
It is also by way of five aspects.
First, by way of the object;
second, by way of the state;
third, by way of the affliction.
Fourth, by way of purification;
fifth, by way of performance.
Regarding "by way of the object":
This means that within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), six groups of volition (*ṣaṭ-cetanā-kāya*) are established.

As for establishment by way of states (*avasthā*), this refers to the establishment of the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth; for those [factors] such as birth are manifested solely through their particular states.
By way of affliction (*saṃkleśa*),
it means establishing the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) within afflicted formations (*saṃskāra*).
By way of purification (*vyavadāna*), [it means...]
This refers to establishing faith and so forth regarding pure formations (*saṃskāra*).
As for "by way of the agent," this means taking as objects the five characteristics of agency as previously described, such as "conforming" (*anuvartana*) and so forth.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 53;
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 54;
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Within the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, in the section on the Stage Corresponding to the Five Collections of Consciousness and the Stage of the Mind (4): Furthermore, what are the distinctions within the aggregate of consciousness?
This, too, should be understood as fivefold:
first, by way of abiding;
second, by way of affliction.
Third, by way of the basis;
fourth, by way of abiding;
fifth, by way of distinct characteristics.
What is abiding?
It refers to those who indulge in desire; their various consciousnesses of the desire realm grasp external objects of form, which is called abiding in name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
If the consciousnesses of the pure form realm (*rūpadhātu*) grasp internal name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*),
they abide together with both [name and form].
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), consciousness grasps only internal name.
It is called "abiding in names.
This is what is meant by the differentiation of the abiding of consciousness.
What is the differentiation of defilement?
It means that the consciousness of all foolish commoners is defiled by way of two doors:
first, in this present life, by way of the enjoyment of sense objects;
and second, in future lives, by way of birth, aging, and so forth.
This is called the differentiation of the defilement of consciousness.
What is the differentiation of the basis?
It refers to the six bases upon which the various consciousnesses evolve accordingly.
This refers to the six groups of consciousness arising in dependence upon the six sense bases,
such as the eye and so forth, just as fire in the world arises in dependence upon chaff, cow dung, firewood, and wood shavings.
This is called the differentiation of the supports of consciousness.
What is the differentiation of abiding?
It refers to the four stations of consciousness,
as stated in the Sūtra:
There are four reliances upon which consciousness depends as its objects of focus to remain established.
That is to say, consciousness dwells in accordance with form, taking form as its objective sphere.
This is explained in detail as in the Sūtra.
I do not say at all that this consciousness goes to the east, nor even to the four intermediate directions.
Rather, I say only that within this very life it is necessarily free from the shadow of desire, extinguished, stilled, cooled, and purified.
Thus, having already clarified the characteristics of the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) as taught by the Tathāgata in the sūtras,
I shall hereafter proclaim the distinctions among these characteristics;
that is to say, this sūtra briefly reveals the characteristics of the stations of consciousness and their causal conditions.

One should know that herein, regarding the two types of limits of the causal conditions for the stationing of consciousness and the two types of tranquility of the causal conditions for the stationing of consciousness,
these refer to all matters of the afflictions.
If they belong to those afflictions,
they are called "based on grasping" (*upādāniya*);
it should be understood that these two are also termed "objects of cognition" (*ālambana*).
Because they are objects of cognition and because they possess objects of cognition,
those cravings and attachments serve as the conditions for afflictions; thus,
they are called "objects of engagement" and "clung-to entities."
Due to the four kinds of bodily fetters, such as sensual desire and the rest,
they are called "conditions" (*pratyaya*) because they serve as the conditions for the arousal of karma;
this is because the objects of those [fetters] are pursued by their two corresponding latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
This is called the establishment of the matter.
If various ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) have not yet attained the antidote of weary detachment toward the craving for pleasure.
The consciousness that is moistened by this [karma] is able to grasp and fulfill a future internal body;
through this process of successive grasping and fulfillment,
it is unable to abandon the state of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Because it is able to grasp and fulfill the internal body,
its continuity is determined within the process of saṃsāra;
this is called "abiding."
The remaining conditions for abiding should be understood as previously explained.
This is called a brief explanation of the characteristics of abiding and its conditions.
In the realm of form, consciousness comes and goes.
The consciousness of the formless realm undergoes both death and birth;
furthermore, these two abide until the end of their lifespan;
moreover, these two involve the meanings of growth, increase, and expansion.
This should be understood as before.
This is defined as the limit of the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) and the limit of the causes and conditions for their abiding.
If one were to designate anything other than this, [it would be incorrect].
One should know that there is only a distinction of words and not a distinction of meaning,
because no other objective referent for the meaning exists.
If one is correctly challenged by another, one does not know how to answer.
Furthermore, because the object does not exist according to other meanings,
or because one might later naturally observe it as it truly is,
one becomes confused and bewildered, thinking, "I am foolish to have made such a statement."
If a wise person can permanently sever and abandon the fetters of craving comprised within the craving for form up to the craving for formations,
they will also permanently sever the fetters of the four bodily ties that give rise to karma, which are comprised within the category of afflictions.
Why is this so? Because the householders,
relying upon the two fetters of sensual desire and ill will,
initiate various karmas that take the appropriation of sense objects as their cause.
Because it has the harming of sentient beings as its cause,
if members of the ordained community rely on the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*),
they give rise to various karmas through the two fetters of this [clinging] and the clinging to [views as] real (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Because the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is like craving for rebirth in heaven,

and this clinging to [false] reality (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is like hatred that slanders *nirvāṇa*, one should know that the four fetters of the body (*kāyagrantha*) arise solely from the conceptualization of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
From this point forward, through the repeated cultivation of superior antidotes,
one is further able to permanently sever the two types of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the fetter of craving for the body (*kāyagredhāsaṃyojana*).
Because these are severed, the objects of the afflictions— such as form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and so forth— no longer continue in succession.
Because of ultimate dissociation from fetters and because the objects of focus no longer continue,
consciousness accompanied by latent dispositions (anuśaya) attains ultimate cessation.
One no longer dwells within the stations of consciousness, such as form and sensation,
because the counteractive consciousness is eternally purified;
this is called the cessation of the causal conditions for the stations of consciousness.
Furthermore, because future causes and conditions are extinguished,
one does not grasp at or become incomplete regarding internal constituent parts;
there is definitively no continuity of transmigration.
This is called the dwelling of consciousness in tranquility.
Furthermore, the pure consciousness that is subsumed under the antidote is called "dwelling nowhere.
Due to those causes and conditions, it is said to be "non-arising."
Because of having well cultivated the liberation door of emptiness,
it is called "having nothing to be done.
Because of having well cultivated the liberation door of wishlessness...
It is called "contentment.
Because of having skillfully cultivated the signless door of liberation,
it is called "abiding securely."
Because it does not grow in this way, and so forth,
up to because it is firmly established,
it is called "ultimate liberation."
Furthermore, one does not cling at all to a self or what belongs to a self regarding the formations and so forth.
For this reason, when form and the other aggregates disintegrate, one is not terrified.
By this characteristic, it is shown that his very essence has already attained purity.
Furthermore, because that consciousness is eternally purified,
it enters into quiescent extinction spontaneously and naturally without depending on other causes;
for the continuity of this consciousness has been ultimately severed.
Because one no longer transmigrates within the worlds of the ten directions and because one does not long for life or death,
it is called "permanently free from desire."
Furthermore, all sensations are the shadows of the tree of consciousness;
since those no longer exist at that time,
it is called "permanently free from shadow."
Because all contaminated consciousnesses are ultimately extinguished within this very life,
they are called "quiescent.
All uncontaminated consciousnesses, in their respective order, constitute the liberation of those in training.
It is called "quiescence.
The liberation of one beyond training is termed "coolness."
Because the remaining support is eternally extinguished,
it is called "purified.
Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of all consciousnesses is not defiled.
Because the Blessed One has taught that the nature of all minds is fundamentally pure.
Why is this? It is not the case that the intrinsic nature of the mind is ultimately impure and thus capable of producing faults.
Just as all afflictions such as craving do not function as causes and conditions for affliction independently, like form, sensation, and so forth; why is this?
Because it is absolutely impossible for defiled attachment to arise toward the nature of consciousness alone, as it does toward form and the like.
Therefore, consciousness alone does not establish a station for consciousness;
this is called the differentiation of the aggregate of consciousness by way of its stations.
What is the differentiation of its distinct characteristics?
That is to say, there is a mind with greed and a mind free from greed, a mind with hatred and a mind free from hatred, and so forth, as explained at length in the sutras,
up to an unliberated mind and an utterly liberated mind.
This is called the differentiation of distinct characteristics according to a single gate.
Furthermore, there is the differentiation of distinct characteristics based on the realms (*dhātu*).
That is to say, there are four types of mind in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Wholesome mind, unwholesome mind,
obscured-neutral mind,
and unobscured-neutral mind.
In the form realm there are three types of consciousness,
excluding the unwholesome.
In the formless realm there are three types of consciousness.
It also excludes the unwholesome.
There are two types of untainted minds:
those of the learner (śaikṣa) and those of the non-learner (aśaikṣa).
Furthermore, wholesome minds of the desire realm are of two types:
those acquired through application (*prayoga*) and those acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika*).
Unobscured-neutral minds are of four types, including the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
The mind of deportment,
the mind of craftsmanship,
and the mind of transformation.
This is exclusively acquired by birth;
that is to say, [it exists] among devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and so forth, yet they lack minds resulting from cultivation.
Within the form realm (rūpadhātu), there is no mind of craftsmanship (śailpasthānika-citta).
The same applies to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
It should be understood that wholesome minds are likewise in both the lower and upper [stages],
existing in all places.
Furthermore, there is a distinction based on the different characteristics of the categories [of mind],
namely that there are five types of minds in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*):
first, the mind to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
2. Minds abandoned through the vision of the origin;
3. Minds abandoned through the vision of cessation;
4. Minds abandoned through the vision of the path.
Regarding the five types of minds abandoned through the path of cultivation:
just as there are five minds in the desire realm,
so too there are five minds each in the form and formless realms, together with the untainted mind.
In total there are sixteen;
first, regarding the meaning of the distinctions among minds with differing characteristics,
I shall now analyze them.
All sentient beings, in brief, comprise three categories:
first, those who have not yet set out toward meditative concentration;
second, those who, although they have already set out, have not yet attained meditative concentration.
The third is the category of those who have already attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This, moreover, is of two kinds:
first, that which is impure;...
Second, regarding extreme purity:
within the first category, one may at times give rise to a defiled mind,
because that mind is ensnared by the fetters of greed and so forth.
At times, one gives rise to wholesome or neutral states of mind because one is temporarily free from the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) such as greed;
in the second stage, at times, one causes the mind to rest in tranquility within.
At times, through loss of mindfulness, his mind becomes distracted by the five types of sensual pleasure;
at other times, due to excessive tranquility,
his mind becomes shrouded and overwhelmed by lethargy and drowsiness.
At times, in order to sever that [distraction],
one settles the mind upon a pure and sublime object;
at other times, when the mind is not properly settled upon that [object], it becomes agitated.
If one settles [the mind] correctly, it does not become agitated;
yet, because the hindrances of dullness and agitation have not been abandoned,
the mind remains unpacified in both of those states.
Through abandonment, the mind attains tranquility;
if, through appropriate mental attention,
one has already attained the fundamental dhyānas.
It is called a concentrated mind;
if it has not yet been attained, it is called an unconcentrated mind,
because the path has not reached its culmination.
It is called the well-cultivated mind because it has severed [defilements] to their ultimate end;
it is called the utterly liberated mind.
The opposite of this is called the poorly cultivated mind and the unliberated mind;
from the state of the concentrated mind onwards, it should be known as the third category.
This is called the differentiation of the specific characteristics of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Furthermore, how are the aggregates ordered?
It should be understood that there are five ways of explaining this differentiation.
First, that which is produced by origination;
second, that which is produced by counteraction;
third, that which is produced by transmigration.
The four acts of abiding,
the five acts of establishment,
and the act of origination.
That is to say, with the eye and visible forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises;
and so on, up to: with the mind and mental phenomena as conditions, mind-consciousness arises.
Within this context, the aggregate of form is explained first, followed by the aggregate of consciousness.
This, then, is the basis for all mental factors (*caitta*).
Because mental factors such as sensation (*vedanā*) arise by depending upon it, the Sūtra subsequently states:
"From the coming together of the three, contact (*sparśa*) arises."
With contact as condition, feeling arises, and so forth;
this is called the sequential teaching on the functioning of the arising of the aggregates.
As for the functioning of the antidote:
The four foundations of mindfulness are taught as an antidote to the four perversions:
namely, the perversion of conceiving the impure to be pure,
and the perversion of conceiving suffering to be pleasure.
The inversion of conceiving a self where there is no self,
and the inversion of conceiving permanence where there is impermanence;
herein, the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is explained first.
Next, the aggregate of feeling is explained;
next, the aggregate of consciousness is explained;
and finally, the two aggregates of perception and formations are explained.
This is called the sequence of the teaching on what is to be accomplished through remedies.
As for what is to be accomplished regarding the process of transmigration:
it is because the faculties and their objects serve as the basis.
In this present life, defilement arises through two types of aggregates regarding the enjoyment of objects:
namely, the aggregate of experiencing objects and the aggregate of adorning objects.
Through one type of aggregate, all wholesome and unwholesome karma is performed.
Within subsequent states of existence, all defilements such as birth, aging, and so forth arise.
Because it is that which is defiled, it is explained last.
As for "abiding" and "activity":
It is taught according to the sequence of the four stations of consciousness and consciousness itself;
this is called the function of the stations.
As for the establishment of their functions:
That is to say, when people in the world see one another, they first perceive their form;
therefore, the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is established first.
Subsequently, by means of the aggregate of sensation (vedanāskandha), one knows their advancement or decline, and whether they experience suffering or pleasure.
Therefore, the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) is established next.
Subsequently, by means of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha), one recognizes that [the object] has such a name, belongs to such a class, and possesses such a nature;
therefore, the aggregate of perception is established next.
Next, by means of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one knows that such a person is thus deluded and such a person is thus wise;
for this reason, the aggregate of formations is established next.
Finally, by means of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), the internal self is established.
This refers to the establishment within the aggregates of what is understood as suffering and pleasure,
followed by the arising of conventional expressions and the distinction between the ignorant and the wise;
this is called the sequential exposition on the functions of establishing the aggregates.
Furthermore, the sequential order in which the aggregates are taught should be understood as being based on the objects of my requisites and the objects of myself;
that is to say, the self, depending upon the body, experiences pleasure and pain with respect to various sense objects.
Regarding oneself and others, one gives rise to verbal expressions such as "having such a name," "belonging to such a class," or "possessing such a nature.
These two types [of expressions] can only be accumulated based on what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.
In this way, one should understand the matters pertaining to my own requisites.
One should know that the final aggregate (skandha) is the matter pertaining to the self.

Furthermore, how many aggregates, how many elements (dhātu), how many bases (āyatana), how many factors of existence (bhavāṅga), how many instances of possibility and impossibility (sthānāsthāna), and how many faculties (indriya) are subsumed within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha)?
As it is with the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), so it is for all others up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
That is to say, the aggregate of form comprises one entire aggregate,
ten entire elements (*dhātu*), and ten entire bases (*āyatana*).
A portion of one realm and one base;
a portion of six members of existence;
and a portion of the possible and the impossible.
The seven faculties in their entirety;
the aggregate of feeling subsumes one aggregate in its entirety and a portion of one element and one base.
The entirety of one link of existence (bhavāṅga),
a portion of three links of existence,
and a portion of the appropriate and inappropriate (sthānāsthāna).
The five faculties in their entirety and three faculties in part;
the aggregate of perception encompasses one aggregate in its entirety.
A portion of one realm and one base;
a portion of three links of dependent origination;
and a portion of what is possible and what is impossible.
Non-restraint of the sense faculties is comprised of one aggregate in its entirety,
and a portion of one element and one base.
The four members of existence in their entirety;
a portion of the fifth member of existence;
and a portion of the appropriate and inappropriate.
The six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are complete;
three sense bases are partially included.
The aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) comprises one entire aggregate.
The seven elements in their entirety,
one base in its entirety,
and one link of existence in its entirety.
A portion of the four members of existence (*bhavāṅga*),
a portion of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna*),
and one faculty (*indriya*) in its entirety.
A small portion of the three faculties.
Thus, there are six kinds of inclusion,
namely, inclusion by aggregates up to inclusion by faculties.
By means of this principle of mutual inclusion, one should understand how they include one another in turn as appropriate.
Furthermore, there are ten other types of inclusion that should be understood: first, inclusion by way of the realms (*dhātu*).
This means that the aggregates and so forth are subsumed by their respective seeds.
Second is subsumption by characteristics,
meaning that the aggregates and so forth are subsumed by their specific and general characteristics.
There are three types of inclusion:
namely, the aggregates and so forth are included within their own respective categories;
and there is inclusion by way of the four stages.
This refers to the inclusion of the aggregates and so forth within states conducive to pleasant feeling and the like.
Fifth is inseparable inclusion,
which means that each individual phenomenon among the aggregates and so forth, together with its attendants, includes all the aggregates and so forth.
Sixth is inclusion by time (*kāla-saṃgraha*).
This refers to the fact that the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth include their own respective characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) across the past, future, and present.
Seventh is inclusion by direction (*deśa-saṃgraha*).
This means that when the aggregates and so forth function in this location or arise based upon this [basis], they are subsumed by this very location.
The eighth is "complete subsumption," meaning that the aggregates and so forth are subsumed by the five [categories] and so on.
Ninth is inclusion by way of a partial portion,
which means being included by the respective distinct partial portions of the aggregates and so forth.
Tenth is inclusion by way of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
That is to say, there are sixteen categories in total for the comprehensive inclusion of all such aggregates (*skandha*) as those subsumed under the characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness).
As it is with the aggregates, so it is likewise for everything up to the faculties (*indriya*).
Furthermore, all phenomena are subsumed by three factors:
namely, the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), the element of mental objects (dharmadhātu), and the sphere of mind (manāyatana).
Next, upon how many spheres does the aggregate of form depend for its occurrence?
In dependence upon how many bases do the four aggregates, as comprised by the name, function?
They function in dependence upon the six bases; that is to say, the aggregate of form functions in dependence upon one established base.
Second, the locus of concealment;
third, the locus of requisites;
fourth, the locus of the faculties.
The five faculties are their locus;
the six are the sphere of activity for meditative concentration possessing majestic power;
and the seven loci are the basis upon which the four aggregates, as subsumed by names, proceed.
First, desire;
second, aspiration;
third, the objective sphere.
Fourth, investigation and analysis;
fifth, clear comprehension;
sixth, the means of purification.
The seven purifications.
Those who enjoy sensual pleasures rely upon four bases.
One who abides in the vows and practices with diligence,
relying on a single location,
has already attained the preparatory concentration (*sāmantaka-samādhi*).
One who dwells in the fundamental concentration by relying on a single location relies upon a single location.
Thus, it should be understood that these seven points comprise, in brief, four stages.
Furthermore, I shall first explain the individual meanings of each constituent of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*),
and thereafter explain the meanings of the remaining four aggregates.
How is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) analyzed?
The summary verse (uddāna) says:
Substance, atoms, arising, establishment, continuity, and function.
The unique range of a single moment; the others are mixed. Regarding the final question:
within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), how many entities are subsumed under the eye?
Answer: If categorized according to their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is subsumed by only one entity.
It refers to the translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) that serves as the basis for visual consciousness.
If categorized according to their inseparable inclusion, there are seven substances:
namely, this eye itself, as well as the body, earth, visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
If all are categorized according to their constituent elements (*dhātu*), there are ten substances:
namely, these seven substances and the elements of water, fire, and wind.
As it is with the eye, so it should be understood for the ear, nose, and tongue as well.
The distinction here is as follows:
it refers to the translucent matter that serves as the basis for the ear and the ear-consciousness,
and the translucent matter that serves as the basis for the nose and the nose-consciousness.
The tongue is the pure matter that serves as the basis for tongue-consciousness;
the rest is as previously explained.
If it concerns the body, one should exclude the four [senses] beginning with the eye.
Why is this? Because it is perceived exclusively as being distinct from that [body].
This characteristic refers to the pure matter (*rūpa*) which serves as the basis for body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*).
Regarding external forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles, as well as their respective modes of activity,
one should understand that everything except for the sense faculties is as previously described.
This is because sound and the sound-element do not exist at all times.
Now it shall be explained separately:
if there is sound in a particular place,
one should know that this place has increased by one.
It should be understood that the sound-element increases in all places.
Furthermore, the objective spheres of form and so forth have been analyzed in detail in the *Maulī Bhūmi*.
Regarding the derived matter from the smooth to the vigorous mentioned within the sphere of the tangible,
it should be understood that these are merely provisionally designated upon the states of the primary elements.
That is to say, the quality of smoothness is provisionally established upon the clarity of the primary elements.
Heaviness is conventionally designated upon the solid nature of the primary elements;
roughness and lightness are conventionally designated upon the impure and non-solid nature of the primary elements;
and softness is conventionally designated upon the impure and lax nature of the primary elements.
Cold is conventionally designated because it arises from the conjunction of water and wind;
hunger, thirst, and weakness are conventionally designated due to the deficiency of sustenance and its imbalance;
and strength and satiety are conventionally designated due to the absence of deficiency and the absence of imbalance.
Illness is conventionally established due to the disharmony of transformation and the confusion of disharmony;
old age is conventionally established due to the disharmony of transformation over time;
and death is conventionally established due to the disharmony of transformation of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Itchiness is metaphorically established due to the presence of defects and imbalances in the blood;
fainting is metaphorically established due to the presence of imbalances from unwholesome food and drink;
and stickiness is metaphorically established due to the production resulting from the conjunction of earth and water.
Exhaustion is metaphorically established due to the inequality caused by the fatigue of coming and going;
rest is metaphorically established when one is free from that through equanimity;
and vigor is metaphorically established through the removal of impurities and the like, which brings about freedom from dejection.
Thus, it is said that all the primary elements (mahābhūtas) collectively comprise six states:
namely, the pure and impure states,
and the firm and non-firm states.
The stage of laxity,
the stage of integration,
and the stage of inequality.
The state of equality.
Thus, these six stages are further divided into eight;
whether eight or six, they are perfectly equal.
Furthermore, all forms up to tactile objects are each cognized by two types of consciousness:
namely, that which is cognized by its own respective consciousness and that which is cognized by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Whether gradual or sudden,
the five faculties such as the eye are cognized by a single mental consciousness.
Furthermore, within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), although odors and tastes do not manifest, that realm does exist.
Why is this? Because both of these are subsumed under edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*);
due to the absence of these two, the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses likewise do not exist.
This is stated with reference to active manifestation (*samudācāra*), not with reference to the realm (*dhātu*).
Thus, among all forms subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*),
nine types exist as substantial entities (*dravyasat*).
Among those included within the tangible, the four great elements (mahābhūta) exist as substantial entities (dravyasat);
one should know that the remainder exists only as designations (prajñaptisat).
Form belonging to the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana-rūpa) is likewise of two kinds.
This refers to substantial existence (*dravyasat*) and conceptual existence (*prajñaptisat*).
If there is a domain of activity for meditative concentration possessing majestic power, such as a transformation (*nirmāṇa*),
then its fruit, its object, and the objects of the consciousnesses associated with them are substantially existent entities (*dravyasat*).
If both the matter of restraint (*saṃvara-rūpa*) and the matter of non-restraint (*asaṃvara-rūpa*) are conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*),
then the matter that is the object of meditative concentration (*samādhi-gocara-rūpa*), if it belongs to a particular realm of concentration,
is likewise derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) belonging to that same realm.
Furthermore, this meditative form (dhyāna-rūpa) is merely mundane, being either tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted (*anāsrava*), as it arises from meditative concentration;
it is not supramundane (*lokottara*), because this meditative form involves discursive proliferation (*prapañca*) and has meditative concentration as its cause.
Furthermore, not all states of meditative concentration possess the functional capacity to produce this form;
only a specific type has such power, namely that which arises without deliberate reflection.
It should be understood that this meditative concentration alone—
induced by prior mental attention, free from all obscurity,
and appearing with extreme purity and clarity— is capable of producing form.
If one sees it through the power of resolute conviction by means of intense concentration and repeated reflection,
one should know that such form cannot actually be produced.
Furthermore, although this form is not within the range of supramundane meditative concentration,
it can nevertheless be manifested through the predominant power of that concentration;
one should know that this matter is inconceivable.
Question: What is the distinction between the substantial forms (*rūpa-dravya*) in the two realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and form (*rūpadhātu*)?
Answer: The forms in the realm of form are pure and most excellent, capable of emitting light.
Furthermore, they are extremely subtle and thus inaccessible to the sense faculties of the lower realms; moreover, they are devoid of suffering.
Because painful feelings do not arise based on those various forms,
whereas it is not so in the desire realm;
this is called the distinction.
Furthermore, the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) should be understood briefly by way of six aspects:
first, its specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa);
second, its general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
Third, the characteristic of the relationship between the support and that which is supported;
fourth, the characteristic of enjoyment;
fifth, the characteristic of activity.
Sixth is the subtle characteristic.
Regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*):
it refers to earth and the other elements having solidity and so forth as their characteristics.
The eye and the other [faculties] have their respective pure matter as their characteristic.
Their common characteristic is that all matter has the characteristic of being subject to transformation and resistance.
Regarding the characteristics of the supported and the support:
as for the characteristic of belonging,
the primary elements (mahābhūta) serve as the support.
Derived matter is that which is supported.
As for the characteristic of being experienced,
it is because internal bases of matter possess the dominant power of being experienced.
External forms arise as distinct objective spheres;
there may be material aggregates that arise with solidity alone,
or with moisture alone, or with heat alone.
It is either merely movement or produced through combination.
This is for the purpose of conforming to the various distinctions in the enjoyment of the internal sense-bases of form (*rūpāyatana*).
As for the characteristic of karma:
This refers to the primary elements such as earth and so forth,
which have the characteristics of supporting, maintaining, maturing, and increasing.
Furthermore, there are other functions of karma that shall be explained in detail later.
Regarding the subtle characteristic,
it refers to the characteristic of the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*).
Furthermore, there are briefly three kinds of subtlety.
First, the subtlety of diminution;
second, the subtlety of category;
third, the subtlety of the mind’s sovereign transformation.
Regarding the reduction of subtlety:
when all forms are analyzed down to their most minute state,
it is termed an "atom" (paramāṇu).
The subtlety of type refers to the form of wind and so forth,
as well as the form of the intermediate state.
The subtlety of the mind’s sovereign transformation refers to...
This refers to all forms within the two realms of form and formlessness,
as stated in the Sūtra:
"There are gods who possess equanimity of mind."
Having previously, among human beings, thus and thus refined, polished, and clarified their minds through cultivation,
they abide within a space the size of a single hair-tip, each occupying a ground-measure equal to the void,
yet moving back and forth without obstructing one another.
Those of such a kind should contemplate and examine the distinctions among the categories of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Question: By how many kinds of characteristics should it be understood that the atoms of form (*paramāṇurūpa*) are established?
Answer: Briefly stated, it is by way of five aspects;
if established in detail, it is as in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
What are these five?
First, by way of conceptualization;
second, by way of differentiation;
third, by way of independence.
Fourth, by way of companions;
fifth, by way of being partless.
As for their analytical establishment:
This means that by means of analytical discerning wisdom,
one analyzes all forms until reaching their ultimate limit, thereby establishing the atom;
it does not exist as a substantial entity.
Therefore, atoms are neither produced nor destroyed,
nor are they formed by the aggregation of atoms.
As for the establishment of their distinctions:
Briefly stated, there are fifteen types of atoms (paramāṇu).
That is to say, the five sense organs, such as the eye, consist of five types of atoms;
likewise, the five objects, such as visible form, also consist of five types of atoms.
Furthermore, there are four types of atoms (paramāṇu) such as earth and so forth.
Among them, there is one type of atom that is a real entity (dravya) included within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana),
which possesses form and is established as independent.
This means that the self-characteristic is established by way of the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) as a substantial entity.
As for the establishment of the accompaniment,
it refers to the accumulated ultimate atoms.
Why is this? Because within the space occupied by a single atom of the earth element,
all other atoms are gathered together in the same location, remaining inseparable from one another.
Therefore, based on this, the atom (*paramāṇu*) as a collection is established.

Question: For what reason do all obstructive phenomena (*sapratigha-dharma*) occupy the same location together without being separated from one another, yet they are not said to possess the nature of being non-obstructive (*apratighatva*)?
Answer: Because they arise in accordance with one another;
that is, by means of their mutual conformity in arising, they do not obstruct each other.
Furthermore, they arise in such a manner due to the predominant influence of karma of this specific kind.
Why is this? Because all material aggregates and all material faculties are experienced in common.
If it were otherwise, [the following would occur].
Within any aggregate, there is not a single instance where all material elements such as earth and so forth are not mutually inseparable.
If that were the case, then the objects of the visual consciousness and the other sensory consciousnesses would not pervade the entirety of every aggregate.
In this way, there would be no pervasive enjoyment [of space].
Therefore, one should know that there must certainly be various forms occupying the same location without being separated from one another.
Furthermore, there are various forms.
In some cases, they mutually obstruct one another; in other cases,
they do not mutually obstruct one another, as in the case of those with form in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and so forth.
Furthermore, those various forms are not non-obstructive;
one should know that the principle here is likewise.
Regarding the establishment of atoms as being partless:
This means that those atoms have no further parts;
for they do not possess the nature of an aggregate.
It is only aggregates that can have subtle divisions.
If the location of an atom is precisely that location alone,
such that no further subtle parts can be analyzed,
one might ask: regarding these five characteristics of the atom thus described, there are furthermore five kinds of eyes.
These are the so-called flesh eye,
the divine eye,
and the noble wisdom eye.
Regarding the Dharma-eye and the Buddha-eye,
one should say how many eyes they are and how many atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitute their objective sphere (*gocara*).
Answer: It should be said that, with the exception of the fleshly eye and the divine eye, all other functions of the eye take all atoms as their objective range. Why is this?
Because those divine eyes perceive only the surface, top, bottom, front, back, and two sides within a collection of matter, whether it be light or dark.
One certainly cannot apprehend the location of an atom, because the substance of an atom is established through analytical discernment by means of wisdom. Question:
For what reason is it said that atoms are neither produced nor extinguished?
Answer: When a collection of matter first arises, it arises as a whole;
when it finally ceases, it does not reach the state of infinitesimal atoms (paramāṇu).
In the interim, its total destruction is like that of a drop of water.
Furthermore, one should know that there are five modes by which the improper conceptualization of atoms (*paramāṇu*) is understood.
Namely, [the notion] that within a mass of matter (*rūpa-kalāpa*) there exist atoms abiding as intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*)—
this should be known as the first improper conceptualization of atoms.
Some claim that atoms undergo arising and ceasing;
some claim that atoms either conjoin with or disperse from other atoms;
and some claim that various forms abide as an accumulation within the measure of atoms.
Some claim that atoms can produce various and numerous aggregates of form;
one should know that such subsequent conceptualization of atoms is not in accordance with correct principle.
Therefore, one should employ skillful means to contemplate atoms through reflection that accords with reality.
One should abandon these five kinds of irrational speculation.
Furthermore, it should be understood that there are five benefits in establishing the atom (*paramāṇu*):
namely, the application of the method for analyzing a composite mass of matter (*saṃghātarūpa*).
One is then able to purify and extensively cultivate the object of focus;
this is the first benefit.
Furthermore, one can gradually abandon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
This is the second benefit:
just as one can gradually abandon the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
so too can one gradually abandon conceit (*māna*).
This is the third benefit.
Furthermore, one is able to gradually subdue the various entanglements of the afflictions;
this is the fourth benefit.
Furthermore, being able to swiftly dispel all signs is the fifth benefit.
Such categories as these should be reflected upon according to reason. Next, to briefly explain the arising of material objects (*rūpa*), it should be known that there are five kinds.
What are the five?
First, arising based on a support;
second, arising from seeds.
Third, birth induced by momentum;
fourth, birth through appropriation;
fifth, birth through diminution.
What is arising by way of dependence?
It refers to the arising of other derived matter within the location of the primary elements that serve as its basis.
Therefore, it is said that the four great elements (mahābhūta) create the derived matter (upādāyarūpa), which is held together within the same location.
Furthermore, regarding this accumulation of matter:
If the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of those primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) can be apprehended,
one should know that those phenomena exist therein; however,
if the specific characteristics of those phenomena cannot be apprehended at all in a given place, [they do not exist there].
One should know that in this place, those phenomena do not exist;
this is called the general establishment of the characteristics of existence and non-existence.
If someone were to say that although the intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) of those phenomena cannot be apprehended in this location, they nonetheless must exist:
Now one should question them:
Are that which is unobtainable and that which is obtainable identical or different?
Regarding "if the things were equal":
since the things are equal and yet cannot be apprehended,
this is not logically tenable.
If they are not equal,
is it because these very measures are said to have unequal substances,
or is it based on their functional power that they are said to be unequal?
If it were said that these very measures are unequal,
then even a partial intrinsic characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) could not be apprehended;
this would be unreasonable.
If it were argued that they are unequal on account of their power,
this would be unreasonable, because apart from their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa),
no other power can be found.
Such categories as these should be known as arising based on a support (*āśraya*).
What is arising from seeds (*bīja*)?
It refers to all forms (*rūpa*) that arise each from their own respective seeds, such as a mass of solidity.
At times, encountering conditions, it becomes moist;
encountering further conditions, that moisture becomes solid and hard.
That which was not warm becomes warm, and that warmth again becomes cold.
The immovable gives rise to the movable, and the movable gives rise to the immovable;
in this way, one should understand the distinctions such as beautiful and ugly forms.
Although these lack intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), they nonetheless possess their respective elements (*dhātu*).
It arises from the differentiation of various material phenomena (rūpa-dharma) within this or that collection.
Such categories as these should be known as arising from seeds.
What is meant by "arising through the drawing forth of momentum" (vega-ākṣepa)?
This means that by the predominant power of the internal material sense faculties,
external differentiated continuities arise,
such as the receptacle world and so forth.
Furthermore, due to being drawn forth by the force of prior karma,
the various internal sense bases of form arise in their distinct forms.
Moreover, the gods experience either manifest desires or non-manifest desires.
Furthermore, regarding all the requisites of Uttarakuru,
one should know that for the most part they arise through the power of projection and function with differentiation;
among humans, those born in a continuous succession possess only the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
Such categories as these should be known as "arising through the power of attraction.
What is "arising through appropriation"?
It refers to encountering various conditions for appropriation.
Various material phenomena arise through mutual reinforcement and progressive intensification,
just as water and other elements nourish sprouts and the like;
such categories are termed "appropriative arising."
That which is contrary to this should be known as the arising through diminution (*apacaya*).
Furthermore, when the various aggregates of form arise,
they do so like various substances ground into powder with water, which are blended together and produced as a mass.
It is not like a heap of mustard seeds, wheat, or beans. Why?
Because it follows the predominant power of its own causes of arising.
They arise in this way because they serve a purpose.
Question: If all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are produced from their own seeds, for what reason is it said that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) create the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)?
Answer: Because they undergo transformation through the transformation of those [great elements], and because they are established and sustained by them.
Due to these three causal conditions, the transformation of the great elements causes the derived matter to transform and proceed accordingly.
First, because of the activity of a single person;
second, because of the performance of karma;
and third, by means of superior meditative concentration.
The "agent" (purusa) refers to that which,
by virtue of being struck and touched by the earth element,
constitutes the differentiation of the vessel.
Due to differences in the field (*kṣetra*),
the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) can be observed to undergo transformation;
this occurs either through being moistened by water, ripened by fire, or dried by wind.
One should know that when derived matter is observed to undergo transformation,
this is called the arising of derived matter through the transformative power of those primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Regarding that which is produced by karma:
first, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) arise according to the power of karma;
subsequently, the transformation of matter (*rūpa*) arises following that power.
This is called "produced by karma.
Regarding "by superior meditative concentration":
due to the power of superior concentration, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) arise first.
Thereafter, derived matter arises through transformation.
It should be understood that this is called the transformation of the primary elements due to superior meditative concentration, by which derived matter arises through transformation.
Furthermore, briefly stated, there are five conditions by which all primary elements (mahābhūta) cause their respective effects to transform into different effects.
What are these five?
First, by the power of the primary elements themselves.
Second, by the power of human effort;
third, by the power of mantras and incantations;
fourth, by the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*).
Due to the power of the five types of karmic actions.
Question: Having passed away from here, by what cause and by what condition [does one arise]?
Can a material aggregate arise as a continuity within the intermediate state?
Answer: It should be understood that this material form takes its own seeds as the cause and the karma that brings about birth as the condition.
Question: By what cause is it known that there is an intermediate state (antarābhava)?
Answer: Because once one has passed away from here, if there were no basis for the various mind and mental factors, [they could not exist].
Because there is no principle by which it could move to another location;
because it should not be like an echo, for that would be mere delusion;
and because it should not be like a shadow, for that [shadow] does not cease when the object ceases.
Nor should it be said that [the mind] takes an object in the manner of grasping,
for it does not proceed by way of movement; such are the analogies set forth.
This is not logical. Therefore, one should know that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) definitely exists.
One should further reflect on such matters as: when the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) arises, what serves as its precursor, and what constitutes its locus?
Do other derived forms arise based on this location?
It should be understood that the primary elements first occupy the location,
and subsequently, the other derived forms arise depending upon this location.
It should be understood that it is only the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that manifest in this location,
obstructing the remaining derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) so that its own characteristics are pervasively filled;
by their power, they maintain [the location] such that there is a basis for obstruction.
Furthermore, it should be understood that among the four great elements, such as earth and so forth,
they are progressively coarser and more manifest;
namely, the earth element and its fruit.
It is capable of sustaining the functions of flowing, moistening, burning, and moving— such as those of water, fire, and wind—
and it is by depending upon it that [the world] is able to circulate.
Furthermore, as soon as sounds are uttered, they immediately cease;
therefore, within a collection of matter (*rūpa-skandha*), they do not persist in a continuous succession.
Moreover, when these sounds arise in dependence upon a physical basis (*upādāna*),...
The internal and external objects are both simultaneously apprehended;
in whatever place they are heard,
they arise instantaneously and pervasively throughout that location, like the light of a flame.
It does not arise gradually nor proceed by successive transition.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of wind:
that which is constantly continuous and that which is not constantly continuous.
The winds that circulate through the wheels are called "constantly continuous.
Those that move through space are called "not constantly continuous.
Those that move within material objects are called "constantly sustaining."
Furthermore, one should know that the movement of the wind-mechanism is called "constant continuity.
One should know that all else is not constant continuity.
Question: What is called the space element (*ākāśadhātu*)?
Answer: The derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) comprised of light and darkness is called the space element (ākāśa-dhātu).
This also has two types: first, that which is constantly continuous; [second, that which is occasional].
Second, they do not continue in a constant succession.
If the dwelling places where sentient beings reside are always dark or always light, they are said to be in constant succession;
other places are not so, and thus are not in constant succession.
It should be understood that this also depends upon the aggregation of matter (*rūpa-kalāpa*).
Furthermore, that which is comprised of light within the space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu*) is called "pure," while that which is comprised of apertures and cavities is called "impure."
Question: Regarding the shapes described as long, short, and so forth, should they be said to exist substantially or exist nominally?
Answer: They should be said to exist nominally.
Why is this? Because it exists as an accumulation, it is called "shape" (saṃsthāna).
Only the accumulation of various colors can be apprehended.
Because other forms and characteristics cannot be apprehended.
Furthermore, they necessarily depend upon one another;
if a phenomenon that depends upon others were to possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), [it would be a contradiction].
Those dharmas would then incur the fault of being disordered,
just like a chariot and so forth,
because those cognitions are subject to destruction.
Furthermore, among the forms that are the results of superior meditative concentration (samādhi) subsumed within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana),
one should know that there are only the characteristics of visible color (varṇa) and so forth. Why is this?
Because the causes for the production of those odors and so forth are lacking there,
and because they would serve no purpose;
likewise, it is so with respect to the wind moving through space.
There are no odors and so forth that are co-nascent;
there are only those produced by artificial combination.
Furthermore, apart from the wheel, there is light emitted externally.
The remaining primary elements (mahābhūta), as well as odors and so forth, are all unapprehendable.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the form which is the fruit of superior meditative concentration (samādhi) subsumed within the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) depends solely upon superior concentration and does not depend upon the primary elements.
However, because it arises from a meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that has as its object an image (*pratibimba*) of that same category,
it is also said to be "derived from those primary elements" (*bhautika*).
It is not called "derived" in the sense of being produced based upon them.
Question: Within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), how many dharmas abide by virtue of being visible and resistant (sanidarśana-sapratigha)?
How many abide by virtue of being invisible but resistant (anidarśana-sapratigha)?
And how many abide by virtue of being both invisible and non-resistant (anidarśana-apratigha)?
Answer: One [element] arises from two kinds;
namely, that which is traversed by the eye, while the others possess only resistance.
Excluding the matter included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*),
it should be understood that this matter is invisible and non-obstructive.
In such ways, one should contemplate the establishment of the aggregate of matter (*rūpaskandha*).
Furthermore, by how many kinds of flows does the aggregate of form continue to evolve?
It is by three kinds:
first, the flow of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-niṣyanda*).
Second is the stream born of maturation;
third is the stream of nourishment.
Furthermore, the first, the stream of outflow, is of four kinds.
1. The flow of maturation and outflow;
2. The flow of nourishment and outflow;
3. The flow of transformation and outflow.
Regarding the four types of natural outflows,
the flow of maturation (vipāka-srotas) further consists of two kinds.
The first is the initial [moment],
and the second is the continuous [series],
namely, the maturation produced by karma and that which is produced from maturation.
That is to say, regarding those which evolve at a later time, being drawn forth by the maturation (vipāka) of that very karmic force,
the "streams of nourishment" (puṣṭi-srotas) are likewise of two kinds.
First, the stream of nourishment that is extensive and pervasive in one location;
second, the stream of nourishment in which the characteristics increase and flourish.
Regarding the first, the stream of nourishment, it consists solely of the nourishment of matter (*rūpa*).
It should be understood that bodily form is nourished by food, sleep, the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*);
it should be understood that other modes of nourishment likewise proceed from food,
because it is their support.
Because of cultivating superior mental attention and because of long-term, thorough maturation,
it attains nourishment and growth.
All material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are nourished by two types of nourishment (*āhāra*).
All immaterial phenomena (*arūpadharma*) are designated as "nourished" solely in the sense that their characteristics increase and flourish.
Furthermore, matter in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is nourished by all four types of nutriment as well as by all other causes and conditions for nourishment.
The various forms in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) are not nourished by solid food, sleep, or the holy life (brahmacarya).
Furthermore, it should be understood that the various sense-faculties (indriya) proceed through two kinds of streams.

Because the material sense-faculties (rūpīndriya) are distinct from the continuity of maturation (vipāka) and nourishment (puṣṭi), there is no separate outflow (niṣyanda) apart from these two streams.
Question: Is it not the case that within the continuity of maturation, there are times when growth and expansion are observed?
Why is it that what is comprised by maturation (*vipāka*) is not itself the same as what is nurtured (*aupacayika*)?
Answer: Because there exists separately a continuous process of nurturing that is capable of encompassing and maintaining the flow of maturation and outflow (*niṣyanda*).
It should be understood that material forms currently existing that are not included among the sense faculties—
such as those that increase and so forth— possess three types of flow:
the flow of outflow (niṣyanda), the flow of maturation (vipākaja), and secondly, the flow of growth (aupacayika) which is nourished by growth.

Regarding the matter included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it is not born of maturation (*avipākaja*); its continuity and other characteristics should be understood as being like those of the mind and mental factors.
Furthermore, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all internal and external forms are fully present and undergo maturation.
Within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is an absence of odor and taste.
Furthermore, while the various material faculties (*rūpīndriya*) in the desire realm may be matured, complete, or incomplete,
in the form realm they are necessarily complete.
Furthermore, within the sphere of sound (*śabdadhātu*), there are also those that are results of maturation (*vipāka*) yet are not sound.
One should contemplate the meaning of the flow of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) through such categories.
