Next, how many functions can the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*), which is subsumed under the aggregate of form, perform?
Up to the wind element, how many functions can it perform?
It should be known that all of them perform five functions.
That is to say, the earth element performs the functions of striking, touching, and transformation.
The karma of establishment,
the karma of reliance,
and the karma of contradiction and impairment.
The water element performs the function of cohesion and the function of moistening and maintaining.
The karma of irrigation,
the karma of violation and destruction,
and the karma of gathering and sustaining.
The fire element performs the functions of illumination,
maturation, and combustion.
The wind element performs the function of obstructing and damaging,
as well as the function of gathering and supporting; it performs the functions of initiating and following along.
The karma that eliminates aridity,
the karma that causes harm through opposition,
and the karma that brings about gathering and support.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the primary elements perform five functions with respect to the derived matter they produce;
namely, the function of production.
The function of serving as a basis,
the function of establishing,
and the function of sustaining.
It increases karma,
because it acts as the precursor when that transformation arises;
and once the transformation has arisen, it serves as its locus, remaining inseparable from it and acting as its support.
It is "grasping" because it can establish them by taking on their welfare, harm, and common security;
it is "sustaining" because it maintains their original measure so that it does not diminish;
and it is "augmenting" because it causes them to accumulate, progress, and expand.

Question: Regarding the wholesome and unwholesome forms that are the objects of the eye and ear, by what causes and conditions do they possess the nature of being wholesome and so forth, rather than other forms?
Answer: Briefly stated, it is due to the distinctions among the three grades of volition—weak, medium, and intense.
First, the volition of preliminary application;
second, the volition of determination;
third, the volition of actualization.
From this, one is able to initiate wholesome or unwholesome informative actions (*vijñapti-karma*) of body and speech;
it should be understood that because they rely upon superior volition (*cetanā*), they are able to give rise to wholesome or unwholesome karma.
Question: Motion exists in dependence upon the aggregation of matter (*rūpa*).
Should it be said that this is different from that or not different?
Answer: It should be said that it is not different. Why is this so?
Because in that location, whether [the entity] arises or does not arise, or ceases or does not cease, motion would entail faults in every case.
Question: What are these faults?
Answer: If one says that it arises and possesses motion, this contradicts the characteristic of momentariness (*kṣaṇa*).
If one says it does not arise, then there should be no motion.
If one says it ceases, it would be the same as other [entities].
If one says that [motion] does not perish, it would contradict the characteristics of its activity.
Furthermore, the causal conditions for its arising in a different location can be clearly perceived.
Therefore, one should know that no distinct, substantial entity of motion can be found.
In this manner, one should contemplate the functions of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Furthermore, it should be said that the entire aggregate of form is of a nature that perishes moment by moment (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). Why is this?
All conditioned phenomena perish as soon as they arise,
for this is perceptible in the present.
Furthermore, one should not maintain that the cause which produces them is itself the cause of their destruction.
Because their characteristics are distinct,
and because no other cause for the continued abiding of phenomena after they have arisen can be found,
one should therefore know that all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) perish spontaneously.
By this reasoning, the meaning of momentariness is established.
If it is claimed that fire and so forth are the causes of destruction,
that is not tenable.
Why is this? Because it is observed that fire and so forth arise and perish simultaneously with those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
thus, they can only be said to have a functional activity as the conditions for the arising of transformation within them.
Furthermore, to claim that destruction is the cause of destruction is not reasonable. Why is this so?
Because it is illogical for [the entity] to arise simultaneously with that [destruction].
If it were to perish at the very moment of its arising,
it would entail the fault of the continuity being severed and destroyed.
Furthermore, it is only the destruction of intrinsic nature that is called "cessation.
To say, therefore, that [a cause] can act as a cause for cessation is not logical.
If one claims that there exists a distinct nature of destruction separate from those phenomena, or that there exists a characteristic of cessation apart from them,
this is untenable because such a thing can never be found.
Therefore, it does not accord with reason.
If it is claimed that fire and so forth must act as auxiliary conditions for cessation in order for things to perish,
this cannot be maintained, for such conditions are not observed in the case of lamps, lightning, and the spontaneous cessation of mind and mental factors.
This is not logical.
If it is claimed that there are distinct and separate capacities for producing those [results],
such a distinction cannot be apprehended.
This is not logical.
If it is claimed that both types possess the capacity for cessation within a single location,
then there would be the fault that both types must either simultaneously possess the capacity for cessation in both parts or lack the capacity in both parts.
This is not logical.
One should reflect in this manner upon the meaning of the momentary destruction of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*),
namely, by virtue of its cause for spontaneous disintegration.
It is to refute the reckoning that fire and so forth are the cause of cessation;
to refute the reckoning that the characteristic of cessation is the cause of cessation;
and to refute the reckoning that both together are the cause of cessation.
All such categories as these should be fully understood.
Furthermore, because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are the fruits of the mind,
one should know that, like the mind itself, they all perish moment by moment (*kṣaṇika*).
Furthermore, regarding derived matter in relation to the primary elements,
should it be said that they have different characteristics,
or should it be said that they do not have different characteristics?
It means that there are distinct characteristics. Why is this?
Because distinct characteristics can be apprehended.
In this context, "distinct characteristics" refers to the fact that they are the respective objects of different sense faculties. Why is this so?
Because other material sense faculties can apprehend the primary elements (*mahābhūta*),
and because other faculties can apprehend derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*);
furthermore, [matter] may be mobile or immobile.
Because it is perceptible in the world.
That is to say, it is observed in the world that the fragrance from various flowers can be transported and placed within sesame seeds;
however, their solidity and other such qualities cannot be so transported.
Furthermore, because both change and non-change are perceptible in manifestation;
that is to say, in substances such as clarified butter (*sarpis*), one perceives specific changes in color, taste, and so forth,
but not in their solidity and other such qualities.
Therefore, one should know that the primary elements (mahābhūta) and the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) differ in their characteristics.
If one were to insist on their unity despite these differing characteristics,
would it not follow that the same should apply to the primary elements themselves?
Since the characteristics of the primary elements (mahābhūta) differ from one another in their mutual relations,
if you were to grant this [that they are distinct],
it would follow that there should be only a single primary element.
Therefore, one should know that all derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) necessarily possesses distinct characteristics when compared to those primary elements (mahābhūta).
One should reflect upon such categories as the characteristics of the primary elements being both singular and non-singular.
Furthermore, among all phenomena subsumed under form (*rūpa*),
how many are of the nature of faculties (*indriya*) and how many are of the nature of objects of activity (*gocara*)?
That is to say, five are of the nature of faculties (indriya), and six are of the nature of objects of activity (gocara).
Question: What are the objects of activity?
Is this the range of the faculties?
Answer: It is as has been explained in detail in the *Maulī Bhūmi*, such as "if the faculties are unimpaired," and so forth.
That is to say, by way of the basis,
or by way of the characteristic,
or by way of the direction.
Either by way of time,
or by way of clarity or lack of clarity,
or by way of the whole object or a part of the object.
Question: By how many causes and conditions are the faculties said to be impaired or unimpaired?
Answer: By two causes and conditions:
first, by way of being weakened and damaged.
Second, by way of complete destruction;
one should know that what is contrary to this is non-destruction.
Furthermore, briefly stated, the transformation of the sense faculties occurs due to four conditions.
First, that which arises from external conditions:
namely, by means of the enjoyment of, or the impairment and destruction of, external objects;
or by means of the harm or benefit inflicted by others.
Second, it arises from internal conditions; that is,
by means of the various enveloping afflictions such as desire, which arise from individual improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*),
or by means of the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and so forth, which arise from proper mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
Third, it arises from the condition of karma;
that is, because one obtains such states as being handsome or ugly through the dominant power of prior karma.
Fourth, it arises from the transformation of the physical body itself.
This refers to the distinct characteristics of those respective faculties.
Question: By how many causes and conditions is the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) destroyed?
Answer: By four causes and conditions.
First, it is due to the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*);
that is, the mind is obscured by any one of the five hindrances.
Second, it is due to distraction (*vikṣepa*).
That is to say, first, because their minds are disturbed by malevolent spirits;
and third, because of what has not yet been realized,
meaning that within their own minds they have not yet attained the superior qualities of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) or the formless realms (*ārūpya*).
Nevertheless, within that state, one forcibly generates mental attention.
Fourth, due to not having understood what is to be done,
namely regarding matters such as extensive learning and technical skills.
When the mind is not yet mature, one forcibly applies skillful means.

How is it that objects such as visible forms are said to be "present" in relation to their respective faculties? It is when a visible form is neither in contact with the eye, nor in darkness, nor is it extremely subtle or distant.
Furthermore, the presence of an obstruction does not constitute "being present" (pratyakṣa).
It is only when there is vision, light, and no obstruction, and the object is within the range of action, that it is called "present.
Moreover, even when an object is obscured by darkness, it is still said to be present to a single eye.
Sound, with respect to the auditory faculty, is also necessarily neither conjoined nor extremely subtle or distant to be termed "present.
Whether obstructed or unobstructed, whether in light or in darkness, as long as it is within the range of possibility, it is all termed "present."
As for the three objects— odor, flavor, and tangibility— the nose, tongue,
and body can apprehend them only through contact; they are said to be "present" only when they exist within the range of their respective faculties.
Regarding the sphere of their activity:
if the various divine eyes illuminate only that which is visible, whether obstructed or unobstructed,
whether bright or dark, whether near or far.
All are termed "manifest.
However, this applies to places where one may act, not to places where one may not.
If it is the eye of noble wisdom, then all types of forms are its sphere of activity.
Question: As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there are six types of objective spheres (*gocara*).
What is the distinction between them?
Answer: Regarding the first type of objective sphere...
This refers to form included within the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) and form included within the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
The second is the nature of the sphere of activity,
which is characterized by the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Due to the distinction of intrinsic nature,
the distinction of characteristics,
and the distinction of function.
Due to the distinction of states.
Regarding the distinction of color-forms (*varṇa*),
this refers to blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth, as explained at length.
As for the distinction of function,
it refers to the manifest and the unmanifest,
as well as restraint and non-restraint.
The activity comprised by neither restraint nor non-restraint is distinguished by its various states,
namely: agreeable forms, disagreeable forms, and forms that are conducive to equanimity.
Regarding the distinctions among the characteristics of sound:
they are those caused by appropriated primary elements (*upātta-mahābhūta-hetu*) and those caused by non-appropriated primary elements (*anupātta-mahābhūta-hetu*).
It has appropriated and non-appropriated primary elements as its cause.
As for the distinction in its function,
it refers to vocal informative action (*vāgvijñapti-karman*).
Regarding the distinctions of states,
they should be understood as previously explained.
Regarding the distinctions of the characteristics of fragrance:
This refers to the roots, stems, bark, pith, flowers, leaves, fruits, and fragrances.
Regarding the distinctions in their functions:
it means that fragrance, flavor, and tangibility possess no functional differentiation in terms of their specific states.
It should be understood as previously stated.
Regarding the distinctions among the characteristics of taste:
these refer to sweet, bitter, and so forth, as already explained above.
The distinctions of the characteristics of contact should also be understood as being of many kinds, as previously explained.
Third is the nature of the sphere of activity,
which refers to the distinctions of the directions and intermediate points, such as east, south, west, north, and so forth.
One should know that the nature of the fourth sphere of activity consists of the distinctions between the past, future, and present;
this is how the nature of the fifth sphere of activity should be understood.
It should be understood that this refers to the distinction between grasping at what is real and what is unreal.
Regarding the nature of the object of the sixth [consciousness],
it should be understood as the distinction between grasping at a partial object or a pervasive object.
Such categories as these should be understood as the distinctions in the manifestation of the various objective spheres of form (*rūpa*).
What is meant by "the attention that gives rise [to cognition]"?
It refers to the fact that the basis (*āśraya*) remains unimpaired.
Because the objective sphere is present before one,
the mental factors that arise and are able to induce [cognition]—
such as these types of things— one should contemplate as the characteristics of the range of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Furthermore, for one dwelling in the desire realm who relies upon a body of the desire realm,
the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm arise and become manifest.
How does it coexist with the matter of the lower realm?
Is it in a different location or not a different location?
It should be said that it is like water and sand; it does not abide in a different location.
In this manner, one should contemplate how the various categories [of the form aggregate] abide in mutual intermixture.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Scroll 54; *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Scroll 55.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Within the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, this is the fifth section on the *Manobhūmi* corresponding to the *Pañcavijñānakāyabhūmi*. Thus has the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) been investigated.
I shall next explain the four formless aggregates (ārūpya-skandha) as they are subsumed under names,
establishing their characteristics as appropriate;
just as a single mental state was established in the *Maulī Bhūmi*.
Now, first, it shall be demonstrated.
As the Blessed One said:
"If there are sentient beings who, in the presence of the Tathāgata..."
If one simply gives rise to a single thought and utters the words "Sugata, Great Teacher, Sugata,
Great Teacher," by giving rise to such a thought,
I would say that person has accomplished much regarding all wholesome dharmas.
How much more so when one follows and practices with body and speech in accordance with the measure of that mind?

Furthermore, regarding such statements as "by a single pure mind one shall go to a happy rebirth," it should be understood that these refer here to a single-minded continuity subsumed within the transformation [of the basis].
By means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), it is said that one arouses a single thought;
furthermore, based on the principle of mundane continuity (*saṃtati*),
it is said that one arouses a single utterance and bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
Question: Should it be said that the conceptual mind and the non-conceptual mind take the same present object as their cognitive support,
or are they different?
Answer: It should be said that they have the same object, namely the present sphere.
Why? Because of three reasons.
That is to say: because of extreme clarity;
because of mental attention directed toward that [object];
and because of the two supports of nourishment.
Question: When a defiled mind arises,
should it be said that it is defiled by virtue of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
or by virtue of its association (*saṃprayoga*)?
Regarding the question of whether they are latent dispositions (anuśaya),
the answer is: they should be said to be [latent dispositions] by way of association and by way of being latent dispositions,
but not by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
If its intrinsic nature were defiled,
it would be ultimately impure, just like greed and so forth;
if that were the case, there would be a great error.
Because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is undefiled, it is said that when the mind arises, its intrinsic nature is pure.
Question: Among the two types of causes for defilement that afflict the mind, which one should be said to apply here?
Answer: It should be said that they are associated (*saṃprayukta*).
Question: What herein is designated as the latent tendency (*anuśaya*)?
Answer: It is the state of heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and lack of peace within the category of all afflictions (*kleśapakṣya*).
Furthermore, they maintain that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) possess the nature of suffering.
Therefore, the Noble Ones, by virtue of the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā),
realize them as suffering through direct insight (abhisamaya) and abide in the contemplation of suffering regarding all conditioned phenomena.
How is it observed?
It is like a poisonous, inflamed boil, and so forth, as explained at length;
it should be observed in this way according to the stage characterized by applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, there are three kinds of factors that defile and afflict the mind;
one should know that these encompass all forms of defilement and affliction.
Namely: the defilement of karma, the defilement of sensation, and the defilement of afflictions.
The first two types of affliction are bound exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while the final type of affliction pertains to all three realms (*traidhātuka*).
Question: What is meant by the "bondage of mental afflictions" (*citta-kleśa-bandhana*)?
Answer: All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Question: What is called the "bondage of karma" (*karmabandhana*)?
Answer: Attachment to worldly activities and occupations is called the bondage of karma.
Furthermore, karma that acts as an obstacle in three respects is also called "karmic bondage":
namely, with respect to the mind of renunciation,
and with respect to the joy and bliss derived from renunciation.
Furthermore, karma that obstructs the attainment of the noble path is also called "karmic bondage.
Additionally, karma characterized by wrong aspirations is also called "karmic bondage."
Thus, these four types of specific distinctions, when combined with the six general ones, constitute four [categories].
Question: When the various consciousnesses arise, with how many universal mental factors (*citta-dharma*) do they co-arise?
Answer: Five.
First, attention;
second, contact.
3. Feelings;
4. perceptions;
5. volitions.
Question: With how many non-universal mental factors (*citta-dharma*) do they arise simultaneously?
Answer: There are many types of non-universal factors;
however, the predominant ones are only five.
First, desire;
second, resolve;
third, mindfulness.
What are the four samādhis,
the five wisdoms,
and the mental attentions?
What is contact (*sparśa*), which is able to induce mental factors?
It is the apprehension of an object resulting from the conjunction of the three.
What is feeling (*vedanā*)?
This means that because of the conjunction of the three, one is able to experience an object.
What is perception (*saṃjñā*)?
It means that because of the conjunction of the three, one designates a focal object and grasps it as a conceptual construct.
This, moreover, is of two kinds:
first, the perception that follows discursive thought;
second, the perception that follows latent tendencies of verbal expression.
"Conformity with the perception of verbal expression" refers to the perceptions of "human," "deva," and so forth, which are verbal expressions.
"Perception that conforms to latent tendencies" refers to...
This refers to unwholesome speech and the perceptions of infants and so forth, up to those of birds and beasts.
What is volition (*cetanā*)?
It is that which causes the mind to act through the conjunction of the three [faculties].
Regarding the objects of perception, what is desire that accords with experiencing them as either agreeable or disagreeable?
It refers to the inclination toward and longing for various respective objects.
What is resolve (*adhimokṣa*)?
It is the assent and confirmation directed toward various respective objects.
What is mindfulness (*smṛti*)?
This refers to the clear recollection that follows after various objects.
What is samādhi?
It refers to the compliant inclination toward various objects.
What is wisdom that serves as the basis for deliberation and one-pointedness of mind?
It refers to the discernment of phenomena in accordance with their respective objects, following after and inclining toward them.
Either observing in accordance with reality,
or observing not in accordance with reality,
or observing neither in accordance with nor not in accordance with reality.
Furthermore, what is the function of attention (*manasikāra*)?
Its function is to direct the mind toward its object.
What is the function of contact (*sparśa*)?
Its function is to serve as the basis for feeling, perception, and volition.
What is the function of feeling?
Its function is to serve as the condition upon which craving depends for its arising.
What is the function of perception (*saṃjñā*)?
Its function is to paint the mind with verbal designations regarding its objects.
What is the function of volition (*cetanā*)?
Its function is to initiate the activities of vitarka and vicāra, as well as bodily and vocal karma.
What is its purpose? Its purpose is to give rise to exertion.
What is the function of resolve (*adhimokṣa*)?
Its function is to maintain a firm conviction regarding the qualities, the defects, or the neutrality of the object of focus.
What is the function of mindfulness (*smṛti*)?
Its function is the recollection of what was long ago thought, done, or said.
What is the function of samādhi?
Its function is to serve as the basis for wisdom.
What is the function of wisdom (*prajñā*)?
Its function is to examine, in accordance with what is defiled or purified, that which proceeds within the domain of discourse.
Question: Is this not one of the five mental factors that are omnipresent (*sarvatraga*)?
In what distinct objects do they arise?

Answer: They arise, respectively, with respect to four types of objects—those that are beloved, those that are determinate, those that are familiar through habituation, and those that are investigated;
while samādhi and wisdom arise with respect to the last object.
The others follow in sequence regarding the three preceding objects.
Question: Should those remaining aggregates associated with the mind, which are subsumed under the category of "names" (nāman), be said to arise suddenly?
Is it sought or is it determined?
Answer: If it relies upon a particular type of mind, it should be said to be of that very same type.
Question: As it is said in the Sūtra:
"These four formless aggregates should be described as being in combination, not as being non-combined;
it cannot be said that these dharmas can be divided or analyzed so as to make them distinct."
Why is it that while those phenomena possess distinct characteristics, they are described as being in a state of harmonious integration (saṃnipāta) without differentiation?
The answer is: because it is only when a multitude are integrated that the experience and comprehension of the object of perception (ālambana-viṣaya) become fully perfected.
If it were not so, then with the absence of even one [of these factors], the intended purpose would not be fulfilled.
Now, regarding the various minds and mental factors:
How many different names are there?
Answer: There are many names, namely:
"that which has an object" (sālambana).
It is associated,
possesses mental formations,
has a basis, and so forth, with immeasurable distinctions.
Question: Why is it that although the eye and other [faculties] also have objects (*viṣaya*),
only they [the consciousnesses] are said to possess an object-of-attention (*sālambana*), and not the eye and others?
Answer: Because those [faculties] such as the eye can arise even when separated from their respective objects of apprehension;
the mind and mental factors, however, are not like this.
Question: For what reason are they called "associated" (*saṃprayukta*)?
Answer: Because they are equal in terms of the object,
equal in terms of the location,
and equal in terms of the time.
Because their activities are equal.
Question: Why is it called "with activity" (*sābhisaṃskāra*)?
Answer: Because it proceeds with immeasurable varieties of differentiated modes of activity (*ākāra*) toward a single object of focus (*ālambana*).
Question: For what reason is it called "having a basis"?
Answer: Because a single category evolves by depending on various distinct bases;
thus, although there is no conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*) that lacks a basis.
However, this is not the meaning of "basis" as explained in this context;
rather, it refers to that which serves as the constant basis for these [feelings] as their measure.
Question: Why is pleasant feeling compared to painful feeling, and painful feeling compared to pleasant feeling?
If pleasure and pain are said to be mutually opposed by contrast with that which is neither-pain-nor-pleasure,
the answer is: because they are mutually opposed by virtue of belonging to different categories within their own respective classes.
Question: Why is it that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is said to be mutually opposed to ignorance?
Answer: Because it acts as an associate for all afflictions in relation to all feelings.
Because they are mutually opposed.
Question: Why are clarity (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) said to be mutually opposed?
Answer: Because that which acts as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) and that which is to be remedied (*vipakṣa*) are mutually opposed.
Question: For what reason are clarity (*vidyā*) and nirvāṇa said to be mutually opposed?
Answer: Because they are mutually opposed as cause and effect are related.
How are the four formless aggregates (*ārūpyaskandha*) established?
Are they of a virtuous, non-virtuous, or indeterminate nature?
It is said that all are without distinction.
The summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
Based on their locus, intrinsic nature, association, conventional reality, and so forth,
as well as distinctions such as being weak and so on, and the categories of qualities, faults, the remedial and the remediable,
and the inquiry into wholesome phenomena— how many kinds of loci for wholesome phenomena are there?
Answer: Briefly stated, there are six.
First, the time of determination;
second, the time of cessation.
Third, the time of performing activities;
fourth, the time of mundane purification;
fifth, the time of supramundane purification.
Sixth, regarding the time of gathering sentient beings:
Question: What is its intrinsic nature?
Answer: It is faith, shame, and dread of blame.
Non-attachment, non-hatred,
non-delusion, diligence,
pliancy, and heedfulness.
Abandoning non-harming—these dharmas are called "virtuous by nature" (*svabhāva-kuśala*).
Question: How should the meaning of the mutual association (*samprayoga*) of these dharmas be understood?
Answer: At the time of making a firm resolve, there is faith;
at the time of pacifying afflictions, there is shame and dread of blame, as one regards oneself and others;
and at the time of engaging in wholesome activities, there is non-attachment, non-hatred, non-delusion, and diligence.
When one becomes free from desire through the mundane path, there is pliancy;
when one becomes free from desire through the supramundane path, there is heedfulness;
and when one embraces sentient beings with equanimity, there is non-harming.
This is because it is embraced by compassion.
Question: Among these various wholesome dharmas, how many exist conventionally and how many exist as substantial entities?
Answer: Three exist conventionally.
This refers to heedfulness, equanimity, and non-harming. Why is this so?
Because heedfulness and equanimity are components of non-attachment, non-hatred, non-delusion, and diligence.
Thus, the meaning of being free from defilement is established as equanimity (*upekṣā*);
the meaning of counteracting defilement is established as heedfulness (*apramāda*).
Since non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) is a constituent part of non-aversion (*adveṣa*), it has no separate substantial entity.
Question: What are called the weak roots of goodness?

Answer: They are all roots of goodness belonging to the non-concentrated stages (*asamāhita-bhūmi*), or those in the concentrated stages (*samāhita-bhūmi*) that are capable of counteracting superior-grade afflictions (*kleśa*).
Question: What is called "middling-grade wholesome roots"?
Answer: They are mundane wholesome roots belonging to the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*), or those capable of counteracting middling-grade afflictions (*kleśa*).
Question: What is called "superior-grade wholesome roots"?
Answer: It refers to all supramundane wholesome roots, or those capable of counteracting inferior-grade afflictions.
Furthermore, various wholesome dharmas arise either through the power of application (*prayoga*),
or through the power of habitual practice (*abhyāsa*),
or through the power of their own nature (*svabhāva*).
Whether by the power of the field or the person,
or by the power of purity,
one should know that it becomes superior.
Question: Upon how many kinds of bases do the roots of goodness arise when they are produced?
Answer: Briefly stated, they arise based on eight kinds of bases.
First, the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving (*dāna-maya-puṇyakriyāvastu*).
Second, the meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline;
third, the meritorious action consisting of cultivation;
fourth, the meritorious action consisting of hearing.
Fifth, matters accomplished through reflection;
sixth, matters accomplished through other forms of cultivation;
seventh, matters accomplished through discernment.
The eighth is the accomplishment of the welfare of sentient beings through gathering them in.
It should be understood that, as appropriate in each case, based on the matters already explained,
this occurs either in the present life or in future lives.
Whichever one of the three— greed, hatred, or wrong view— arises within the mental continuum,
it first becomes defiled;
once it has been so defiled, [the mind remains stained].
Because that antidote causes [the afflictions] to no longer be associated with this state.
Question: What are the distinctions among wholesome dharmas?
Answer: There may be one kind, up to ten kinds.
As has been extensively explained in the *Maulī Bhūmi*,
furthermore, among the various wholesome dharmas, some serve as antidotes to affliction (*saṃkleśa*),
while others serve to bring about the cessation of affliction.
Some do so for the sake of securing desirable fruits;
some for the sake of purifying the continuum;
and some for the sake of making offerings at shrines.
There are also those that involve the gathering of sentient beings;
such distinctions among wholesome dharmas should be understood.
Furthermore, what are the merits of wholesome dharmas, given that they are free from faults?
The virtues of wholesome dharmas are of immeasurable kinds;
that is to say, they are able to purify the mind so that it is freed from the entanglements and latent tendencies of afflictions,
and they cause one to be free from error regarding the objects of cognition.
It enables one’s roots of goodness to become firm and non-retrogressive,
causing them to flow equally and continue in succession,
so that one is neither harmed by oneself nor harmed by others.
One does not bring about harm to both;
one does not give rise to offenses in the present life,
nor does one give rise to offenses in future lives.
It prevents the arising of offenses pertaining to this life and future lives;
it enables one to experience the joy and bliss born thereof; it brings to an end all sufferings headed by birth;
and it further increases one’s resolute conviction toward nirvāṇa.
One is able to draw near to them;
one’s wealth and status will not decline or be lost;
and when among the multitude, one is courageous, fearless, and without dread.
His vast renown shall spread throughout the ten directions,
he shall be praised by all the sages and worthies,
and at the time of his death, he shall feel no sorrow or regret.
After the dissolution of the body, one will be reborn in the various happy realms;
one will not fall away from any wholesome dharmas,
and will be able to swiftly realize the goals sought for oneself.
Such categories of wholesome merits are boundless and immeasurable;
one should come to know them all completely.
How are the various wholesome antidotes established? By way of fifteen kinds.
That is to say: by way of the antidote of revulsion,
the antidote of abandonment,
and the antidote of maintenance.
Because it is an antidote that distances [the defilements],
because it is an antidote to the fetters of the desired realm,
and because it is not an antidote to the fetters of the undesired realm.
Because it is the antidote to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*);
because it is the antidote to weak-grade afflictions (*kleśa*);
and because it is the antidote to medium-grade afflictions.
Because it is the antidote to superior-grade afflictions,
the antidote to distraction,
and the antidote to remorseful reproach.
Because it is the antidote to weakness,
the antidote that subdues,
and the antidote that brings about dissociation.
Furthermore, all defiled phenomena are manifested by two characteristics:
first, the root afflictions;
second, the secondary afflictions.
Now, first the fundamental afflictions (mūlakleśa) shall be explained;
later, the secondary afflictions (upakleśa) shall be analyzed.
Question: How many bases (āśraya) do the fundamental afflictions have?
Answer: There are six.
First, agreeable defiled objects associated with ignorance;
second, disagreeable defiled objects associated with ignorance.
Third, that which is associated with improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) and has defiled objects as its domain;

fourth, that which is associated with ignorance (*avidyā*), consisting in the perverted attainment and non-attainment of the five appropriated aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*)—which are distinct for each sentient being according to whether they are inferior, equal, or superior—as well as perverted qualities.
Fifth, hearing incorrect teachings together with ignorance and improper mental attention;
sixth, becoming indolent regarding the hearing of the correct Dharma together with ignorance and improper mental attention.
It should be understood that the first is the basis for delighting in union;
the second is the basis for delighting in separation;
and the third is the basis for perversion regarding objects.
The fourth is the basis for contemptuous arrogance;
the fifth is the basis for practicing with adherence to false views;
the sixth is the basis for not cultivating correct practice and for failing to achieve cessation.
Question: How many kinds are there in the intrinsic nature of the afflictions?
Answer: There are six kinds.
First, attachment.
2. Hatred; 3. Ignorance; 4. Pride.
The five views and the six doubts.
Question: Which afflictions are associated with which afflictions?
Answer: Ignorance and all forms of doubt are entirely absent [in this state].
Greed and hatred are mutually absent from one another.
This [state] may also be associated with pride and views.
That is to say, at the time of passionate attachment, there is either elation or seeking;
as it is with passionate attachment, so it is with hatred and aversion.
Furthermore, these may be associated with pride and views.
That is to say, at the time of arrogance, one further engages in false conceptualization.
Question: Among these afflictions, how many exist as conventional designations (*saṃvṛti-sat*) and how many exist as substantial entities (*dravya-sat*)?
Answer: Those that are views exist as conventional designations, because they are a division of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Other real entities possess the distinct nature of mental factors (*caitasika*).
Question: How are these afflictions established as weak, medium, or superior grades?
Answer: Those abandoned last are designated as the weak grade.
Those abandoned in the middle are called medium-grade;
those abandoned at the beginning are called superior-grade.
Furthermore, afflictions become superior-grade by virtue of six causes.
First, those afflictions arising from sensual desire are for the most part of a superior grade;
second, those afflictions arising from habitual practice are for the most part of a superior grade;
third, the afflictions pertaining to the state of abiding.
This means that those whose faculties are mature possess, for the most part,
the four types of incurable afflictions in their superior degree;
that is, those who lack the nature for nirvana possess, for the most part, [these afflictions] in their superior degree.
Fifth, the afflictions of improper application,
which are by nature predominantly of the highest degree toward those who are venerable, fields of merit,
and so forth. Sixth, the afflictions associated with karma.
This refers to one whose nature for undertaking right action is predominantly of a superior grade.
Question: When afflictions arise, by how many types of afflictive matters do they arise?
Answer: Greed arises from ten matters.
First, the aggregate of grasping;
second, various views;
third, objects not yet attained.
Fourth, objects already attained;
fifth, past objects already experienced and utilized;
sixth, unwholesome conduct.
Seventh, sons and daughters;
eighth, friends and relatives;
ninth, requisites.
Regarding the ten [types of] existence and non-existence:
Question—In what objects does which craving arise?
Answer—In accordance with their respective order, the ten types of craving arise in relation to the ten objects.
What are the ten? They are:
attachment to things, attachment to views, attachment to craving, and attachment to stinginess.
Namely: craving for misconduct,
craving for children, craving for relatives,
craving for requisites, and craving for existence and non-existence.
There are also ten types of objects for anger:
first, oneself;
second, beloved sentient beings.
Third, sentient beings who are not beloved;
fourth, past enemies and kin;
fifth, future enemies and kin.
Sixth, present enemies and kin;
seventh, objects of an undesirable nature;
eighth, envy.
Ninth, habitual practice;
tenth, the views of others.
Hatred also has ten [factors].
They arise in succession based upon those [objects].
Based on the preceding six matters, nine grounds for resentment are established.
All hatred that takes these as its object is termed "hatred toward sentient beings."
The remainder is called aversion toward objects (*viṣaya-dveṣa*).
There is also aversion toward sentient beings (*sattva-dveṣa*) when preceded by intolerance.
Furthermore, there is aversion arising from past habituation (*pūrva-śīlita*) and aversion arising from perception (*dṛṣṭi*).
These ten types of hatred, in brief, are of three kinds:
first, hatred toward sentient beings;
second, hatred toward objects.
Third, the view of ill-will (*dveṣa-dṛṣṭi*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) arises based on seven things:
first, worldly affairs (*loka-vastu*).
1) The establishment of the two worlds;
2) the activity of cyclic existence; 3) the activity of transmigration;
and 4) the supreme reality.
5. The reality of the five true objects;
6. The reality of affliction and purification;
7. The reality of overweening pride.
Based on these seven matters, seven types of ignorance arise;
alternatively, it should be understood that there are nineteen. Regarding the first matter, doubt arises through three doors.
Regarding the second matter, there arise views concerning the six internal bases—whether external, both together, or as a combination—such as "self" and "mine," or "enemy" and "friend."
Regarding the third matter, there is the view that the maturation of karma and the co-arising agent and experiencer are without cause or have bad causes;
regarding the fourth matter, there is the denial of the Three Jewels.
Regarding the fifth matter, they slander the truths;
regarding the sixth matter, they give rise to false understanding and practice;
regarding the seventh matter, relying on their attainment of their own aims, they give rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Pride arises based on six objects:
first, inferior sentient beings;
second, equal sentient beings.
Third, superior sentient beings;
fourth, the internal appropriated aggregates;
fifth, the inversion regarding what has been attained and what has not yet been attained.
Regarding the six inversions of merit,
based on these six matters, seven types of pride arise,
namely: pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), and so forth.
It should be understood that the two types of pride arise based on the matter of superior sentient beings;
the others each arise based on a single matter;
and the [five] views arise based on two matters.
First, the matter of superimposition;
second, the matter of denial.
There are four types of the matter of superimposition.
First, the superimposition of the nature of a self;
second, the superimposition of the nature of permanence or impermanence;
third, the superimposition of the means for higher rebirth.
There are four ways to increase the skillful means for the four liberations,
and there are likewise four matters concerning decrease:
first, slandering the cause.
Second, slandering the fruit;
third, slandering functional activity;
fourth, slandering wholesome phenomena.
It should be understood that herein, the denial of giving, up to the denial of wholesome and unwholesome conduct,
is called the denial of causes.
The denial of the ripening of the results of wholesome and unwholesome actions is called the denial of effects.
This is called slandering the fruit;
that is, to say that this world does not exist, up to and including the denial that there are beings born by transformation—
this is called slandering activity.
Why is this so? It is because the term "agent" (puruṣakāra) here carries the sense of "activity.
Furthermore, this activity of the agent is of four kinds.
First, the function of coming and going;
second, the function of maintaining the womb-treasury;
third, the function of placing the seeds.
Fourth is the function of karma that leads to future existence.
To claim that there are no arhats and so forth in the world is called slandering wholesome phenomena.
Based on these eight matters in detail and two matters in brief,
the five views arise;
namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The view of extremes,
the grasping at views,
and the grasping at precepts and observances.
Regarding wrong view:
furthermore, based on the sixty-two matters, there arise views of extreme attachment (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*),
namely, the reckoning of matters pertaining to the past limit and the reckoning of matters pertaining to the future limit.
As explained at length in the Sūtra,
based on this matter, there are sixty-two views;
doubt arises based on six matters.
First, hearing the incorrect Dharma;
second, seeing the teacher’s wrong conduct;
third, seeing differences in the views held by those one trusts; and fourth, being naturally dull-witted and ignorant.
Fifth, the profound nature of phenomena;
sixth, the vast teaching of the Dharma.
Question: What are called the distinctions among the afflictions?
Answer: Briefly, there are fifteen types of distinctions.
First, afflictions of the internal door;
second, afflictions of the external door.
1. Afflictions to be abandoned through seeing;
2. Afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation;
3. Afflictions comprised within the fetters of desirable realms.
Sixth, afflictions comprised within the entanglements of undesirable realms;
seventh, afflictions comprised within the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
eighth, afflictions of weak degree.
9. afflictions of medium intensity;
10. afflictions of superior intensity;
11. afflictions in the state of distraction.
12. Afflictions at the stage of admonition and repentance;
13. Afflictions at the stage of weakness;
14. Afflictions at the stage of subjugation.
Fifteenth, regarding the state of dissociation from afflictions: furthermore, afflictions possess no merit and have many faults;
that is to say, in the state of active outburst (*paryavasthāna*), they defile the mental continuum.
A detailed explanation is as found in the *Savitarkā Savicārā Bhūmiḥ*.
Furthermore, afflictions are not antidotes.
Although the Sūtras state that one relies on craving to abandon craving and relies on pride to abandon pride,
these [antidotes] are not themselves afflictions.
However, because the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of a wholesome mind— which seeks out and practices lofty conduct— resembles that [state],
it is metaphorically designated as "craving" and "pride.
Furthermore, as previously stated, there are fifteen distinct types of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) for the mind.
It should be known that the afflictions which are their opposites are likewise fifteenfold.
Furthermore, it should be known that there are briefly nine bases for the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*):
first, dwelling together in mutual interaction.
Second, mutual promotion;
third, gain and offerings;
fourth, wrong livelihood.
Fifth, disrespecting one's venerable teacher;
sixth, intolerance;
seventh, disparaging the higher training in ethical discipline.
Eighth, it destroys the higher mind (*adhicitta*);
ninth, it destroys the higher wisdom (*adhijñāna*).
Furthermore, what is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)?
Namely: anger, enmity, concealment, vexation, envy,
parsimony, deceit, guile,
arrogance, harmfulness, and lack of shame.
Lack of shame, lethargy,
restlessness, lack of faith,
laziness, and heedlessness.
Forgetfulness and distraction;
lack of clear comprehension and regret;
sleep, vitarka, and vicāra.
As has been extensively explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi*,
such categories as these are termed the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Among these, the first two arise based on the first foundational locus (*āśraya*).
The third and fourth depend on the second;
the fifth and sixth depend on the third;
the seventh and eighth depend on the fourth.
The ninth relies on the fifth;
the tenth relies on the sixth;
the eleventh and twelfth rely on the seventh.
The remaining twelve arise based on the latter two bases.
It should be understood that herein, the disparagement of the higher mind (*adhicitta*) and the disparagement of the higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) proceed by way of three doors.
First, by way of the door of disparaging the characteristics of calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Second, by way of the door of the characteristic of disparaging and censuring;
third, by way of the door of the characteristic of disparaging and abandoning.
Dullness and drowsiness arise from the first basis.
Excitement (*auddhatya*) and remorse (*kaukṛtya*) arise from the second basis;
lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) up to applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) arise from the third basis.
Furthermore, how do the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) correspond with one another?
One should know that lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) are associated with all unwholesome states.

Lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), heedlessness (*pramāda*), forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), and faulty wisdom (*duṣprajñā*) are associated with all defiled minds.
Sleep and remorse are associated with all wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral states; it should be understood that the remaining [secondary afflictions] are mutually dissociated from one another.
Furthermore, among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), how many exist as conventional entities (*prajñaptisat*) and how many exist as substantial entities (*dravyasat*)?
That is to say, anger, enmity, vexation, envy, and harmfulness are all conventionally existent because they are branches of hatred (*dveṣa*).
Avarice, pride, and restlessness are all conventionally existent because they are branches of greed (*lobha*).
Concealment, deceit, guile, lethargy, sleep, and regret are all conventionally existent because they are branches of delusion (*moha*).
Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), and laziness (*kausīdya*) exist as substantial entities (*dravyasat*).
Heedlessness (*pramāda*) exists as a conventional designation (*prajñaptisat*),
as previously explained.
Forgetfulness, distraction, and impaired wisdom are all conventionally existent, as they are subdivisions of delusion (*moha*).
The two types, vitarka and vicāra, are both provisionally existent, as they are subdivisions of the mental application that initiates speech and are also subdivisions of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, how do the secondary afflictions (upakleśa) become weak, medium, or superior?
It should be understood that they are explained in the same manner as the primary afflictions (kleśa).
Thus, regarding these secondary afflictions, one should understand their objective basis, their distinctions, their faults, and their antidotes.

It should be understood that all [factors] are to be treated according to their respective cases, just as with the afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, it should be known that there are, in brief, four kinds of bases for neutral phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*):
namely, those produced by the projection of karma (*karmākṣepaja*).
Once born, whether it be walking or staying,
maintaining life,
or the distinctions of meditative concentration (samādhi).
Furthermore, what is its intrinsic nature?
It refers to the aggregates born of maturation; those comprised within the intermediate application of effort, namely the modes of deportment and the spheres of craftsmanship;
and those comprised within the application of effort for play, namely emanations.
Question: How do they correspond with one another?
Answer: The modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) may, at certain times, correspond with one another as described.
For instance, there are activities that are easier to perform while walking than while standing, sitting, or lying down.
Even so, there may be certain activities— whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down— that are all easily performed,
as explained at length in the sūtra.
As for the remainder, there is no mutual correspondence between them.
Question: Among these indeterminate (avyākṛta) phenomena, how many exist as substantial entities (dravyasat) and how many exist as designations (prajñaptisat)?
Answer: They are designated based upon the aggregates (skandha) comprised within maturation (vipāka), as well as upon the distinctions in mental application (cittaprayoga).
One should know that all these exist conventionally (*saṃvṛti-sat*).
How do they become weak, medium, or superior?
It is said that those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and those belonging to the sphere of deportment (*airyāpathika*) are both of the weak grade, because they are not intense.
Because the nature of the various fields of craftsmanship (*śilpasthāna*) is sharp and acute, they are said to be of medium grade.
It should be understood that because the nature of emanation (*nirmāṇa*) is extremely sharp and acute, it is of superior grade.
Furthermore, each of these four types has its own distinctions.
That is to say, the maturation of the formless realm is of weak grade;
the maturation of the form realm is of middling grade;
and the maturation of the desire realm is of superior grade.
Sitting or lying down is the inferior;
abiding in the postures is the intermediate;
and practicing the postures is the superior.
Regarding deportment (*īryāpatha*): for a beginner practitioner, it is inferior craftsmanship;
for one who has already become proficient, it is intermediate craftsmanship;
and for one capable of acting as a teacher, it is superior craftsmanship.
That which is obtained through the cultivation of inferior samādhi is an inferior transformation;
that which is obtained through the cultivation of middling samādhi is a middling transformation;
and that which is obtained through the cultivation of superior samādhi is a superior transformation.
One should understand that there are such distinctions as weak, medium, and superior among these types.
Question: Upon what objects do all these neutral states arise?
Answer: It should be known that, briefly stated, they arise based on twelve objects.
As has already been explained in the *Śrutamayībhūmi*,
what are the various distinctions among the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) states?
They are distinguished by the five destinies (*gati*) of rebirth born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
There are five types of distinctions.
If distinguished by way of deportment (*airyāpathika*), there are four types of distinctions.
If distinguished by way of the sphere of arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*), there are twelve types of distinctions due to the twelve matters.
One should know that there are eight types of distinctions regarding emanations: the distinction between ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas;
and the distinction between emanations of body and speech for the purpose of sport or for the benefit of others.
Because these distinctions already encompass other matters, they are not mentioned separately.
Furthermore, that which arises from maturation (*vipākaja*) is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
the [other] two types may be found, while one type possesses both kinds.
If one initiates deportment based on music and performance with a defiled mind,
it is of a defiled nature;
if based on tranquility, it is of a virtuous nature.
If craftsmanship is initiated based on defiled attachment, it is of a defiled nature;
if it is produced through wholesome application,
it is of a wholesome nature.
One should know that when a transformation is produced for the sake of guiding others or for the benefit of sentient beings, it is wholesome and free from defilement.
Furthermore, among these five aggregates, how many are subsumed under the [Four] Truths?
Furthermore, regarding how many aggregates these truths are subsumed under:
it should be understood that the three truths are mutually subsumed by the five aggregates,
whereas the truth of cessation is not mutually subsumed by the aggregates.
Because the nature of the truth of cessation is manifested by that very tranquility.
Question: As has already been explained in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*, there are sixteen aspects of contemplation (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) regarding the four truths;
why, then, are there only four aspects of contemplation for the truth of suffering?
Answer: It is for the purpose of counteracting the four inversions (*viparyāsa*).
That is to say, the first line counteracts the first inversion;
the next line counteracts the subsequent two inversions.
The latter two aspects counteract the latter type of inversion.
Question: For what reason is there contemplation of the Truth of Origination through four aspects?
Answer: Because craving is of four kinds.
These four types of craving should be understood as being established through their distinctions of craving for permanence, pleasure, purity, and self.
With the first craving as a condition, the craving for future existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*) is established.
The second and third [types of craving] are established with craving as their condition: craving accompanied by joy and greed, and craving for various specific objects.
The final [type of craving] is established with craving alone as its condition.
One should know that this craving follows after the self-entity.
Furthermore, what is craving?
It is the intimacy with, and the concealment and protection of, the self-entity.
What is craving for future existence?
It is the seeking of a distinct self-identity in the future.
What is craving accompanied by joy and greed?
This refers to the arising of attachment and craving toward pleasant forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects, whether they are currently present or have already been acquired.
What is the craving for various expectations?
This refers to the arising of longing and craving toward other pleasant forms and so forth that remain to be obtained.
Question: For what reason is the contemplation of the four aspects applied to the truth of cessation?
Answer: Because it is manifested by the cessation of the four kinds of craving.
Question: For what reason is the contemplation of the four aspects applied to the truth of the path?
Answer: Because one is able to realize the cessation of those four types of craving.
Furthermore, as the ten modes of practice, such as "destruction" and so forth, have already been explained in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, what is meant here by "non-apprehension"?
That is to say: there are only the faculties, there are only the objects,
there are only the feelings produced by them,
and there are only the minds produced by them.
There is only the reckoning of a self and the perception of a self;
there is only the view of a self and the conceit of a self; there is only the verbal proliferation of "I" and "mine."
Apart from these seven, no other characteristic of a real self can be apprehended.
How is it that [the self] lacks autonomy?
It means that it is comprised within the characteristics of impermanence and suffering, being produced by a multitude of conditions.
Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are devoid of the characteristic of a self (*ātman*).
Question: By which of these ten characteristics is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*) subsumed?
Answer: It is subsumed by the characteristic of bondage (*bandhana*) and by the distress (*daurmanasya*) arising from the predominance of transformation (*vipariṇāma-adhipati*).
One should know that this is the nature of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*);
it is not merely the fact of transformation,
for even one who is already free from sorrow is not harmed when encountering such [change].
Question: By what aspect is the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā) subsumed?
Answer: By the aspect of being undesirable.
Question: By what aspect is the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā) subsumed?
Answer: Because it has the aspect of being non-quiescent.
Furthermore, as the Sūtra says:
"Birth is suffering," and so forth, up to "in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering."
Among these various characteristics of suffering, how many are subsumed under the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*)?
That is to say, the first five.
How many are subsumed under the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*)?
That is to say, two of the middle [categories] are subsumed under the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā).
That is to say, the last one is [so subsumed].
Furthermore, the first seven [types of suffering] are subsumed under the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);
the pure and sublime afflictions that are their opposites are subsumed under the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
The last line subsumes suffering.
This is because the Blessed One stated that one enters into a mind subject to transformation and decay;
furthermore, he said that due to the obscurations and entanglements, one experiences the mental distress and suffering arising therefrom.
Therefore, one knows that afflictions are the suffering of change;
thus, the principle of suffering is established.
Furthermore, as the Sūtra says, there are four kinds of suffering.
First is the suffering of birth;
second is suffering conditioned by internal factors;
third is suffering conditioned by external factors.
Fourth is the suffering of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Question: Among these, which practices subsume which sufferings, and which sufferings subsume which practices?
Answer: The first practice and the first suffering mutually subsume one another.
Next, there are three lines that are mutually inclusive with the second suffering.
Next, there are three lines.
It is mutually inclusive with the third suffering;
the final line is mutually inclusive with the final suffering.
The four modes of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), established through the distinctions of the intrinsic nature of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as previously explained, [are as follows]:
It should be understood that this is for the sake of producing the four kinds of suffering that differentiate the present fruit.
Furthermore, among these sixteen aspects, how many are the aspect of emptiness?
It is two.
These are the last two aspects of the Truth of Suffering.
How many are the aspects of wishlessness?
They are six.
That is to say, the first two lines of the Truth of Suffering and the entirety of the Truth of Origination.
How many are the modes of signlessness?
They are the entirety of the Truth of Cessation.
How many are the practices manifested by the causes of purification?
They are all those belonging to the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Question: Is it necessary that one abides in the notion of non-self (*anātmasaṃjñā*) by means of the notion of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*)?
Why is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) taught first in this context?

The answer is: this is because once the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*) has arisen, the contemplation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) is established by means of the contemplation of impermanence (*anitya*).
This is because these two contemplations mutually cultivate and refine one another in successive alternation.
Furthermore, regarding the sequence in which the Four Noble Truths are taught:
it is because of this that suffering exists, and this is stated first;
it is because of this that suffering exists, and this is stated second.
These two encompass the culmination of the dark category (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
Because of this, delighting in this [state] is the third;
because of such [delight], this is the fourth.
These two encompass the culmination of the white category (*śuklapakṣa*).
For example, there are distinctions among the causes of a serious illness, the illness itself, its recovery, and the excellent medicine—
just as there is a sequence of suffering encountered in the world.
One should know that this establishes the sequence of the Noble Truths. Why is this?
Because it is just as suffering has been experienced by all those in the world.
In this very place, one first directs the attention;
next, toward the causes of encountering suffering;
and next, toward liberation from suffering.
Subsequently, one gives rise to mental attention regarding the means of liberation.
If it is asked, "What is the meaning of the truths?
the answer is: "It is the sense of not abandoning the characteristics as they have been described."
Because one reaches the ultimate meaning of purity by contemplating this, it is the meaning of truth (*satya*).
Question: What is the meaning of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*)?
Answer: It refers to the meaning of formations (*saṃskāra*) produced by afflictions (*kleśa*).
Question: What is the meaning of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*)?
Answer: It refers to the meaning of that which can produce the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Question: What is the meaning of the truth of cessation?
Answer: It is the meaning of the simultaneous quiescence of both [suffering and its origin].
Question: What is the meaning of the truth of the path?
Answer: It is able to establish the meaning of the three truths.
Question: Are these four noble truths subsumed under conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) or ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)?
Answer: It is subsumed under ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). Why?
Because within all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) that accord with suffering, pleasure, or neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, [it is so].
The conventional truth is established by way of the distinctions among their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
It should be understood that the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is established by way of their common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), which is the single flavor of suffering (*duḥkha*).
Question: For what reason is it said that one must thoroughly know (*parijñā*) the truth of suffering?
He permanently severs the truth of origination,
realizes the truth of cessation,
and cultivates the truth of the path.
Answer: Because that truth of suffering is the basis for the four perversions, one fully understands suffering in order to eliminate those perversions.
Once suffering is fully understood, the origin is also fully understood.
Because the truth of origination is subsumed within the truth of suffering,
even though one has fully understood suffering, one remains pursued by the truth of origination; therefore,
it is necessary to further explain the permanent abandonment of the truth of origination.
"Touching and realizing" means direct perception;
because one perceives the truth of cessation directly before oneself, one does not give rise to fear, but instead feels joy and embraces it.
Therefore, it is next explained that one realizes the truth of cessation.
If one diligently cultivates the path, one can accomplish the three meanings previously described;
for this reason, the truth of the path is explained last.
Question: How many kinds of the clear realization of the truths (satyābhisamaya) are there?
Furthermore, what are their characteristics?
Answer: The meaning of "clear realization" (abhisamaya) is the sense of "ascertainment" (niścaya).
This has as its essence the definitive wisdom regarding the various truths, along with their causes, their associated factors, and their co-existent factors.
This is called the characteristic of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that there are six types of this, as explained in the *Savitarkā-savicārā-bhūmi*.
In this context, what is called the first clear observation (*abhisamaya*)?
It refers to the definitive contemplation of the truths.
What is called the second clear observation?
It refers to the three kinds of pure faith directed toward the Three Jewels,
because one has reached certainty regarding the meaning of the Jewels,
as well as the definitive wisdom consisting of that which is heard and realized.
What is called the third clear realization?
It is the morality cherished by the noble ones,
because one has attained the restraint of definitely not performing actions that lead to the miserable realms.
What is called the fourth clear realization?
It refers to the fact that within the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), one has previously gathered the accumulations to complete perfection,
and furthermore, because the mind has been polished through skillful means (*upāya*).
Immediately following the ultimate roots of goodness belonging to the mundane aids to penetration (*laukikāgradharmas*),
there arises for the first time a mind that internally dispels the conceptualization of sentient beings and takes phenomena as its object.
It can eliminate the coarse residues (*dausthulya*) of the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of seeing that are of weak grade.
Immediately following this, a second internal mind arises that takes as its object the conventional designations of phenomena;
it can eliminate the coarse residues of the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of seeing that are of medium grade.
Immediately following this, in the third stage, there arises a mind that takes as its object all phenomena of sentient beings as mere designations;
it is capable of eliminating the coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of all afflictions to be abandoned through the path of seeing.
Furthermore, this clear realization (*abhisamaya*) is precisely the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
and it is also called the path of union (*yuganaddhamārga*).
Within this, although there are three moments of mind belonging to the category of insight (*vipaśyanā*) and three moments of mind belonging to the category of calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Nevertheless, three minds are established by combining them through their union,
because both calm abiding and insight are simultaneously attainable within a single moment.
It should be understood that these minds take as their object only the non-conceptually-constructed truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*).
Furthermore, the first two moments of mind are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna),
while the third moment of mind is associated with subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
Moreover, it is precisely by the power of these moments of mind that [the result is attained].
Within the established truths such as suffering,
there arises a second stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) characterized by pure and unimpeded knowledge of suffering and so forth.
It should be understood that it is based on this knowledge that the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path are established.
That is to say, the aforementioned three minds, together with the category of śamatha and vipaśyanā, are able to realize the cessation of afflictions abandoned through seeing,
and are able to attain the permanent extinction of all afflictions along with their underlying bases.
The supramundane path is called the clear realization of the knowledge of the truths (*abhisamaya-jñāna-satya-abhisamaya*).
What is called the clear realization of the knowledge at the conclusion of the clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-jñāna-satya-abhisamaya*)?
This refers to the subsequently attained wisdom following this clear realization;
it is called "wisdom at the limit of clear realization" (*abhisamayāntika-jñāna*).
It should be understood that this wisdom arises immediately after the third moment of mind, manifesting only after one has emerged from the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Based on the wisdom previously cultivated through observation of the two levels—lower and upper—as well as the two types of established truths (*vyavasthāpita-satya*) and the two superior truths (*adhipati-satya*), this resembles both dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*);
it is subsumed under conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and encompasses both mundane and supramundane realms.
This is the subsequently attained wisdom following supramundane wisdom.
In accordance with their respective order, two kinds of wisdom arise for each of the truths:
namely, the wisdom of acceptance and aspiration, and the wisdom of realization and certainty.
Thus, having arisen based on the aforementioned clear realization (*abhisamaya*),
two cognitions arise for each of the lower and upper truths;
this is called the "clear realization of the truths through cognition at the conclusion of clear realization" (*abhisamayāntika-jñāna-satya-abhisamaya*).
Among these, the former wisdom is non-conceptual because it eliminates the objective conditions of conventional phenomena;
the latter wisdom is conceptual because it follows after the objective conditions of conventional phenomena.
Furthermore, the former wisdom is able to sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of afflictions to be abandoned through seeing within their respective bases.
Because subsequent knowledge (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) contemplates its object, that which was abandoned by it will not arise again.
Furthermore, prior knowledge can progress toward the supramundane path of abandonment within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
The second wisdom is that which can advance toward the mundane and supramundane paths of abandonment.
No purely mundane path is capable of permanently destroying the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*),
because the mundane path is something already familiar through prior practice.
Because it is induced by the grasping at signs;
just as it is induced by the grasping at signs,
so too it cannot subdue or eliminate all signs.
Just as one cannot obliterate or subdue all signs,
so too one cannot permanently destroy the coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Therefore, that path lacks the capacity to permanently destroy the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
What is called "ultimate realization" (*atyantābhisamaya*)?

It refers to the arising of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), resulting from the permanent abandonment of what is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
It is either exclusively supramundane or common to both the mundane and the supramundane,
because within this present life there is the certainty of the permanent abandonment of all afflictions.
Because it is certain that all bases for future existence will be eternally extinguished,
it is called ultimate realization (*niṣṭhā-abhisamaya*).
What is meant by "supramundane knowledge of exhaustion" (*lokottara-kṣayajñāna*)?
That is to say, if wisdom is non-conceptual regarding cessation,
what is called mundane and supramundane knowledge of cessation?
That is to say, if wisdom is conceptual regarding cessation.
What is called supramundane knowledge of non-arising?
It refers to the non-conceptual knowledge regarding the non-arising of future bases of existence,
based on the fact that those very bases have already ceased their causes.
What is called mundane and supramundane knowledge of non-arising?
It refers to all conceptual knowledge regarding the non-arising of phenomena in the future, based upon their objective bases.
Furthermore, there are brahmins of noble lineage who establish three bases as real and true; yet,
because those brahmins of noble lineage abide in these three bases, they defile their minds with three faults.
From the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they all fall into the category of those who are not true brahmins (*abrahmaṇya*).
What are these three points?
First, for the sake of sustaining their livelihood.
The second is for the cultivation of merit;
the third is for the establishment of the fruit,
serving as the means for sustaining one's life.
This refers to those brahmins of that lineage who, for the sake of their livelihood,
perform either blessings, praises, or introductory recitations before a donor.
Regarding "blessings," this refers to those brahmins of that lineage.
Seeking any one of the necessities of life,
he approaches the king, or a royal minister, or a brahmin, a householder, a lay devotee, a merchant leader, or others of their kind.
He feigned the recitation of benedictions:

"I pray that all your enemies may be utterly extinguished, and that all calamities, misfortunes, oppressions, and imprisonments you have encountered may be crushed; furthermore, I pray that all your auspiciousness shall remain forever unshakable and inviolate."
As for flattery:
out of desire, one goes to that person's presence and artfully utters words of praise,
saying, "You are brave, resourceful, and skilled at destroying your enemies."
Furthermore, regarding those who harm their enemies, one may feign praise and say:
"It is truly rare that you all eliminate your enemies in such and such a manner;
people like you are difficult to find in this world."
Furthermore, regarding those whose wealth and status have long been flourishing, he falsely offers praise, saying:
"Among all people in the world, it is extremely rare to find one as auspicious, accomplished, and unshakable as you."
Regarding "making a formal introduction":
this refers to going to another person out of a desire for gain and falsely making a formal introduction by saying,
"You possess the marks of a virtuous man."
Before long, all enemies shall surely be utterly extinguished, and those who have met with calamity and misfortune or are being crushed and bound shall be liberated.
Furthermore, if one achieves such marks as these:
It shall certainly be auspicious and free from regression.
Furthermore, in the homes of your kinsmen and friends, or in the homes of donors,
there shall never again be any other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who receive offerings therein and claim them as their own.
"I alone am constantly honored with offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding, and so forth.
Because of such means, he develops a deep attachment to the gains and offerings he receives.
