It is impossible for light and darkness to coexist at the same time;
it is possible for there to be a place where one exists and a second does not arise.
There is no such location or state.
It is impossible and there is no occasion for coarse portions of water and fire to come together simultaneously;
it is possible only when one or the other is present.
There is no place and no state where this could occur.
It is impossible for two coarse material aggregates to occupy the same location;
it is possible only for a single atom. There is no place, nor any occasion, where this could otherwise occur.
It is impossible for two minds or mental factors of the same kind to meet and coexist simultaneously;
it is possible for them to arise one by one.
There is no place and no occasion [where otherwise occurs].
Of the same kind:
whether wholesome or unwholesome;
or whether wholesome-indeterminate or unwholesome-indeterminate.
It is impossible for suffering and pleasure to coincide at the same time;
it is only possible that one or the other occurs.
There is no place and no occasion where both exist simultaneously.
It is impossible that the results of the agreeable and the disagreeable should coincide at the same time;
it is possible only if either one of them occurs.
One should thus observe the characteristics of the distinctions between the second category of the "possible" (*sthāna*) and the "impossible" (*asthāna*).
What is the third distinction regarding the gate of the possible and the impossible?
It means that there is no possibility and no occasion for a barren woman to give birth to a child; such a thing is impossible. However, if she is not a barren woman, then it is possible.
There is no possibility, there is no occasion, for a paṇḍaka to be born as a male or female;
such a thing is impossible. If they were males, then it would be possible.
There is no such possibility, nor any such occasion:
that one who is blind should see forms, or one who is deaf should hear sounds;
or that one whose nose or tongue is impaired should smell fragrances or taste flavors—such things cannot exist.
That one whose faculties are unimpaired could [attain this] is possible;
there is no place or occasion where one who has not yet completed the accumulations could realize the ultimate liberation of the state of training or beyond-training within the present life.
That is impossible.
It is possible for one who has already completed the accumulations.
There is no place and no occasion [where this could otherwise occur].
It is impossible that one who has not yet attained the noble path could realize nirvāṇa,
or realize the enlightenment of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha,
or realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
It is possible for one who has already attained the Noble Path;
there is no place or occasion where a being of the human realm could satisfy their seasonal festivals by using the grass and other fodder of the animal realm as food and drink.
If the hosts of devas were to eat human food,
it would be impossible for those in the form and formless realms to consume edible food;
the opposite of this is possible.
There is no place or possibility that one could obtain a human body without relinquishing the physical form of a hell-being;
likewise, there is no such possibility of obtaining any other body without relinquishing the remaining physical forms.
Only after relinquishing [the former] does one obtain this; such is the case.
In this manner, one should observe the characteristics of the distinctions within the third door of possibility and impossibility (*sthānāsthāna*).
What are the distinctions within the fourth door of possibility and impossibility?
That is to say: there is no possibility and no occasion where the earth element, having abandoned its own characteristic, could become the characteristic of another element;
it is impossible. That it does not abandon its own characteristic—this is possible.
As it is with the earth element, so should the other primary elements be understood accordingly.
There is no place or occasion where one born in the desire realm who has not attained the divine eye could see the forms of the gods; such a thing is impossible.
It is possible for one to see the forms of human beings;
in this same way, it should be understood that the same applies to the other sense faculties as appropriate.
There is no place or occasion [where this would not be so].
Those who possess craving are shrouded by craving;
it is impossible for one whose craving has not been severed to have a mind free from attachment toward wealth and gain.
The same should be understood accordingly for hatred and delusion.
It is impossible and out of place that one should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness while not severing any of the afflictions, secondary afflictions,
or entanglements such as greed. It cannot be.
The opposite of this is possible.
Just as it is with the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness,
so too should it be understood for the remaining factors of enlightenment.
There is no place, there is no possibility,
that one who has not abandoned contentious views, contentious desires,
and contentious thoughts toward the Tathāgata could face him directly; such a thing cannot be.
Whether one rejects it or grants it, this is possible;
there is no place or occasion where an All-Knowing One, an All-Seeing One, could fail to know an object within the scope of their cognition.
Furthermore, it is impossible and there is no occasion for one who has lost mindfulness to perform what is not done by an Omniscient One;
the opposite of this is possible and such a case exists. There is no place and no state [where the former could occur].
For Bodhisattvas who have already entered the great stages, it is impossible that they would give rise to a harmful mind toward sentient beings,
or that their bodhicitta would ever regress.
The opposite of this is possible.
One should observe such categories as the distinctions between the fourth door of what is possible (*sthāna*) and what is impossible (*asthāna*).
Furthermore, there are briefly four possibilities and four impossibilities.
Based on the previously explained principle of dependence,
the principle of function,
and the principle of logical proof.
One should correctly examine this through the principle of natural law (*dharmatā-yukti*).
If one does not contradict the principles thus explained, [one has correctly understood].
To manifest and proclaim [this] is called the "basis.
If one manifests and proclaims that which is contrary to this, [it is not the basis].
This is called the impossible.
These four points, together with those previously mentioned,
constitute the eightfold skill in the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).
Question: What is the distinction between skill in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*) and skill in the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*)?
Answer: Only the clear realization of correct knowledge regarding the principle of the arising of cause and effect is termed skill in dependent origination.
If one correctly understands the principle of non-perversion regarding all things through right knowledge,
this is called skill in the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).
The remaining textual analysis concerning skill in the possible and the impossible is not presented here again.
Thus has been explained skillfulness regarding the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).
Now I shall explain skillfulness regarding the faculties (*indriya-kauśalya*) through four topical gateways.
The summary verse (uddāna) says:
First, the establishment of the meaning and intent; followed by the detailed analysis.
What, then, is the meaning of "faculty" (indriya)?
Answer: The meaning of "predominance" (adhipati) is the meaning of "faculty" (indriya).
Question: To clarify what meaning?
Answer: To clarify the sense of being most excellent (parama) with respect to various matters and various phenomena.
How are the twenty-two faculties established?
They are established as six faculties in the sense of predominance over the apprehension of objects;
they are established as two faculties in the sense of predominance over the uninterrupted continuity of the lineage.
One faculty is established for the purpose of predominance over the means of sustaining life;
five faculties are established for the purpose of predominance over the enjoyment of the fruits of karma.
The five faculties are established on the basis of their predominance regarding mundane purification;
the three faculties are established on the basis of their predominance regarding supramundane purification.
Furthermore, the six faculties are established on the basis of their predominance regarding the experience of manifest objects.
The two faculties are established on the basis of their predominance in the experience of concealed objects;
the one faculty is established on the basis of its predominance in the temporal limit of the experience of objects.
The five faculties are established on the basis of their predominance in producing affliction regarding the objects of experience;
the eight faculties are established on the basis of their predominance in establishing purification.
Furthermore, the six faculties are established to demonstrate their predominant role in the internal engagement with objects;
the two faculties are established to demonstrate their predominant role in the external engagement with objects.
One faculty is established on the basis of its predominance in the experience of one's own internal body;

five faculties are established on the basis of their predominance in the experience of external objects and in the production of affliction (saṃkleśa) regarding both external objects and the internal body.
The eight faculties are established on the basis of the predominant meaning of counteracting affliction and establishing purification.
Furthermore, the five faculties are established on the basis of the predominant meaning of physical excellence and beauty.
One faculty is established on the basis of the sense of predominance in causing the basis to function according to its mastery;
another faculty is established on the basis of the sense of predominance in causing the basis to abide securely.
The two faculties are established based on the predominant sense of origination;
the five faculties are established based on the predominant sense of benefit and harm;
and the eight faculties are established based on the predominant sense of liberation.
Furthermore, the six faculties are established on the basis of their predominance over the manifestation of sentient beings;
the two faculties are established on the basis of their predominance over the production of sentient beings;
and one faculty is established on the basis of its predominance over the maintenance or the dissolution of sentient beings.
The five faculties are established to demonstrate the predominant significance of sentient beings' enjoyment of their objective spheres;
the five faculties are established to demonstrate the predominant significance of the means for the superior rebirth of sentient beings.
The three faculties are established to manifest the sense of being the sovereign over the definitive and superior means for all sentient beings.
Furthermore, the six faculties are established to manifest the sense of being the sovereign over the affairs of sentient beings.
Two faculties are established to clarify the predominant meaning of the increase of sentient beings;

one faculty is established to clarify the predominant meaning of the gradual decrease of the lifespan of sentient beings; and five faculties are established to clarify the predominant meaning of the flourishing and decline of sentient beings.
The eight faculties are established in order to clarify the predominant meanings of the virtues and faults of sentient beings.
Furthermore, the six faculties are established based on such names;
the two faculties are established based on such lineages and such clans.
Based on such food and such experience of pleasure and pain, the five faculties are established.
Based on such longevity, such endurance, and such limits of lifespan, one faculty is established.
It should be understood that these faculties are established and designated based on the category of householders,
relying upon such faith, such diligence, and so forth,
up to such wisdom, such orientation, and such fruition.
The eight faculties are established;
it should be understood that these faculties are designated and established based on the category of those who have gone forth.
Furthermore, the six faculties are established based on the sense of the practitioner’s superior mastery in guarding the doors of the sensory faculties.
The two faculties are established on the basis of their predominance in being capable of renouncing the household life and realizing the fruits of śrāmaṇya;
the one faculty is established on the basis of its predominance in accumulating the collection of wholesome qualities.
The five faculties are established on the basis of their predominance in conduct characterized by clear comprehension;
they are established on the basis of their predominance in the various paths of skillful means for realizing the fruits of śrāmaṇya.
The three faculties are established for the purpose of the superior meaning of realizing the fruits of śrāmaṇya.
The intermediate summary verse says:
"Turning according to the object, and so forth; by way of manifestation and the internal door."
Adorning the two types of sentient beings and provisionally establishing [the categories of] protection and so forth.
Question: What is the function of the eye faculty?
Answer: Its function is that which has seen, is seeing, or will see various visual objects.
In this manner, the functions of the ear faculty up to the mental faculty should be understood as they appropriately apply.
Question: What is the function of the male faculty and the female faculty?
Answer: Their function is the mutual support of parents, wives, children, relatives, and kinsmen, thereby manifesting their roles.
Question: What is the function of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
Answer: Its function is to cause sentient beings to fall within the category of those who are alive, sustained, and maintained.
Question: What is the function of the faculties comprised within feeling (*vedanā*)?
Answer: Its function is to cause sentient beings to experience all forms of prosperity and decline.
Question: What is the function of the faculties such as faith?
Answer: Their function is to bring about rebirth in the happy realms and to perfect the provisions for nirvāṇa.
Question: What is the function of the final three faculties?
Answer: Their function is to lead to the realization of nirvāṇa in the present life.
Question: Among these faculties, how many are substantially existent and how many are not substantially existent?
Answer: Sixteen are substantially existent;
the remainder are not substantially existent.
Question: How many are comprised within the category of matter?
Answer: Seven. Question:
How many are subsumed under the mind? Answer: One and a small portion of three.
Question: How many are subsumed under mental factors (caitta)?
Answer: A portion of thirteen.
Question: How many are subsumed under the formations dissociated from mind?
Answer: One.
Question: How many are comprised within the conditioned?
Answer: All are conditioned;
there is no faculty that is unconditioned.
Question: To which faculty do the two faculties of male and female belong?
Answer: They are parts of the body faculty (*kāyendriya*).
Question: To which faculty do the final three faculties belong?
Answer: It consists of nine faculties, namely:
the faculty of mind, the five faculties beginning with faith, and the faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity.
Question: Of which faculties does the life-faculty consist?
Answer: This has no specific category to which it belongs.
Because it is established based on the determination of the duration of time projected by prior karma, it is said to exist only as a designation (*prajñapti-sat*).
Question: How many are wholesome?
Answer: Either eight, or five, or a portion of six.
Question: How many are unwholesome?
Answer: A portion of six.
Question: How many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
Answer: Eight and a portion of five.
Question: How many have maturation (*savipāka*)?
Answer: Eleven and a portion of one.
Question: How many are without maturation?
Answer: Eleven and a portion of one.
Question: How many have maturation as their concomitants?
Answer: The final three can assist those dharmas that have desirable maturation to cause them to become more brilliant and flourishing;
they are capable of inducing the definite maturation of humans and devas.
Question: How many are maturation (*vipāka*)?
Answer: One [aggregate] and a portion of nine.
Question: How many possess seeds of maturation?
Answer: All possess them.
Question: How many are not maturation?
Answer: Twelve and a small portion of nine.
Question: How many are born of maturation (*vipākaja*)?
Answer: All [of them], because they are produced from maturation and are comprised within all seeds.
Question: How many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
Answer: A portion of forty-five.
Question: How many are bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu)?
Answer: A portion of fifteen.
Question: How many are bound to the formless realm?
Answer: Eight partial portions.
Question: How many are unbound?
Answer: A portion of three and nine.
Question: How many are obtainable in the stage of the threshold (anāgamya)?
Answer: Eleven.
Question: If the faculty of joy exists in the stage of the Not-Yet-Arrived (anāgamya), why is joy not established there in the same way as it is in the stage of the First Dhyāna?
Answer: Because the joy in that stage is subject to fluctuation.
Question: What teaching serves as proof for this joy?
Answer: As the Blessed One said:
"In this way, bhikṣus, the rapture and bliss born of seclusion moisten their bodies."
It thoroughly moistens, pervades, and gladdens everywhere;
there is not even the slightest part that is not filled or saturated.
This is called the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
Among these, the first gate describes the stage of the threshold (anāgamya), while the latter gate describes the fundamental stage (maula).
Question: How many faculties (indriya) are obtainable in the level of the first dhyāna?
Answer: Eighteen.
It is the same for the stage of the second dhyāna.
Question: How many faculties (indriya) are obtainable in the stage of the third dhyāna?
Answer: Seventeen.
Question: How many faculties (indriya) can be found in the stage of the fourth dhyāna?
Answer: Sixteen.
Question: How many faculties (indriya) can be found in the stage of the sphere of infinite space?
Answer: Eleven.
As it is with the stage of the sphere of infinite space, so it is with the others.
It should be understood that the same applies to the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of nothingness.
Question: How many faculties (indriya) are obtainable in the stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
Answer: Eight.
Question: Should the various faculties subsumed under the stage of the first dhyāna be said to be with-outflows (sāsrava)?
It should be said that they are untainted (*anāsrava*).
Answer: It should be said that they are of two kinds, such as the various faculties (*indriya*) subsumed under the first dhyāna.
It should be understood that the same applies to the faculties included within the stage of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
As for the faculties included within the stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*),
they should be said to be with outflows (*sāsrava*).
This is according to their categories.
If considered according to their continuity, they should be said to be of two kinds.
Furthermore, it is because of liberation from the afflictions.
It causes those faculties to become untainted (*anāsrava*).
Just as with the tainted and the untainted,
so it is with what should be abandoned and what should not be abandoned, and with the mundane and the supramundane.
One should know that it is likewise so.
Question: If one is born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), how many faculties (indriya) should be said to be possessed?
Answer: It is possible for all of them to be present.
Question: When one is born in the hells (*naraka*), how many faculties (*indriya*) does one possess?
Answer: Eight.
Both those that are manifest and those that exist as seeds are possessed.
Excluding those three, the remainder are either possessed or not possessed. Regarding these three,
they are not possessed in terms of their active manifestation (*samudācāra*),
but they may be possessed in terms of their seeds (*bīja*).
That is to say, those possessing the nature for parinirvāṇa; or they are not accomplished,
meaning those lacking the nature for parinirvāṇa.
The other three are not accomplished by way of active manifestation,
but are accomplished by way of seeds,
just as when one is born into the destiny of the hells, it is exclusively so.
It should be known that the same applies to the suffering realms of animals and hungry ghosts.
In the realm where suffering and pleasure are mixed,
the latter three types [of contact] are also present and accomplished.
Question: If one is born in the human realm, how many faculties (indriya) does one possess?
Answer: It is possible to possess all of them;
as it is for those born among humans, so it is for those born in the heavens.
Question: How many faculties do those with deficient faculties possess?
Answer: With the exception of five, they may possess the remainder.
Question: How many faculties do those with complete faculties possess?
Answer: It is possible for all [faculties] to be present.
Question: How many faculties do various types of *paṇḍaka* (eunuchs) possess?
Answer: Excluding five, there may be others.
Question: How many faculties does a woman possess?
Answer: There may be twenty-one.
Question: How many faculties does a male possess?
Answer: He may also possess twenty-one.
Question: How many faculties do those with both sexual organs (ubhayavyañjana) possess?
Answer: There may be nineteen.
Question: How many faculties does one who has severed the roots of goodness possess?
Answer: Excluding eight, there may be the remainder.
Question: How many faculties does one who has not severed the roots of goodness possess?
Answer: It is possible for them to possess all of them.
Question: How many faculties do ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) possess?
Answer: Nineteen, excluding the last three.
Question: How many faculties do those who have realized the truths (satyadṛṣṭi) possess?
Answer: It is possible for them to possess all of them.
Question: How many faculties does one in training (śaikṣa) possess?
Answer: There may be twenty-one.
Question: How many faculties does one beyond training (aśaikṣa) possess?
Answer: There may be nineteen.
Question: How many faculties does one heading toward the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala-pratipannaka) possess?
Answer: There may be twenty.
Question: How many faculties (indriya) does one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna-phala) possess?
Answer: It is also possible for there to be twenty, just as in the case of one who is a candidate for the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-phala-pratipannaka).
It should be understood that the same applies to those who are candidates for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of non-returning.
Question: How many faculties does one who has attained the fruit of non-returning possess?
Answer: There may be nineteen.
As it is for the fruit of non-returning, so it is for the candidate for arhatship.
Question: How many faculties (indriya) does one who has attained the fruit of arhatship possess?
Answer: There may be nineteen.
Question: If one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), how many faculties (*indriya*) does one possess?
Answer: It is possible to possess eighteen.
Question: If one is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), how many faculties does one possess?
Answer: There may be eleven.
Question: When one passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the desire realm, how many faculties should it be said that one abandons, and how many faculties does one acquire?
Answer: For the time being, this is explained in terms of what is possible regarding the physical sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*).
Either one relinquishes deficient sense faculties and acquires deficient sense faculties, or one relinquishes deficient sense faculties and acquires complete sense faculties.
Either one abandons complete faculties and acquires complete faculties;
or one abandons complete faculties and acquires deficient faculties;
or one abandons inferior faculties and acquires inferior faculties.
Either one abandons inferior faculties and acquires superior faculties;
or one abandons superior faculties and acquires inferior faculties;
or one abandons superior faculties and acquires superior faculties.
It should be understood that the same applies to the acquisition and relinquishment of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) and the life-faculty (*jīvita-indriya*),
whether they are superior or inferior. Furthermore, regarding the acquisition and relinquishment of the various faculties of sensation (*vedanā-indriya*),
it is likewise according to their respective circumstances.
This distinction is made with respect to the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
As for the roots of goodness with respect to the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*),
one abandons each preceding inferior state and attains each subsequent superior state.
It is not by virtue of birth that one abandons the superior and acquires the inferior;
such a principle applies only later through improper means (*mithyā-prayoga*).
As for the final three faculties, they are in contradiction with birth at all stages.
Therefore, it is not mentioned.
Question: When one passes away from the desire realm and is born into the form realm, how many faculties are abandoned and how many are acquired?
Answer: It is possible to relinquish everything belonging to the lower stage and to acquire everything belonging to the higher stage,
as when one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the form realm.
It should be understood that the same applies when one passes away from the desire realm to be born in the formless realm,
and when one passes away from the form realm to be born in the formless realm.
The final three faculties are acquired through the means of realizing the fruits of śrāmaṇya, not by passing away and being reborn;
for they are sustained by the power of prior cultivation,
and subsequently arise as increasingly intense outflow-results (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Furthermore, it can act as a condition to cause the fruition of maturation (*vipākaphala*) to arise with increased clarity and intensity.
The intermediate summary verse (*uddāna*) states:
"Karma is truly possessed of form and so forth; It is wholesome and so forth, and its fruition is likewise."
Regarding the question of how many faculties (indriya) possess an object (*sālambana*) by way of their objective sphere (*viṣaya*),
and how many do not— whether in terms of the realms (*dhātu*), the stages (*bhūmi*), or in relation to death, birth, acquisition,
and relinquishment— the answer is: twenty-one possess an object.
First, it is not.
Question: How many function as the meaning of non-material accompaniments?
Answer: The seven material sense faculties.
Question: How many material phenomena have non-material phenomena as their companions?
Answer: The remaining sense-faculties that possess meaning.
Question: In what sense are the five material sense-faculties [so called]?
Answer: The five [faculties], such as form and so forth, each have distinct objects.
Question: What is the meaning of the sixth faculty?
Answer: All phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
Question: What is the meaning of the male and female faculties?
Answer: They are associated with desire and are subsumed under contact (*sparśa*).
Question: What is the meaning of the five feeling faculties (*vedanendriya*)?
Answer: They correspond to the bases of suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity;
this is precisely the meaning of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
Question: What is the meaning of the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*)?
It is that which accords with what should be abandoned regarding all objective spheres.
Question: What is the meaning of the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*)?
Answer: It is the absence of any hesitation regarding both the attainment and the abandonment of these two types of objects.
Question: What is the meaning of the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*)?
Answer: It is the non-forgetting of what has been heard, reflected upon, and cultivated through meditation.
Question: What is the meaning of the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*)?
Answer: Śamatha and vipaśyanā. Question: What is the meaning of the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya)?
Answer: The true reality of that which is to be known.
Question: What is the meaning of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"?

Answer: For one who practices the clear realization of the truths, from the stage of desire for wholesome dharmas onwards, throughout all paths of preparation, it refers to the meaning of those very five faculties.
One should know that this is the meaning.
Question: What is the meaning of the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātendriya*)?
Answer: It refers to the stage from the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
One should understand that the meaning of those five faculties is the same as this meaning.
Question: What is the meaning of the faculty of one who has attained final knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*)?
Answer: From the initial path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) up to the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣanirvāṇadhātu*).
One should know that the meaning of those five faculties is the same as the meaning of this [term].
Question: How many have form, and how many have form as their object?
Answer: Seven.
Question: How many are formless?
What is the meaning of "form" and "formless"?
Answer: All except for the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
Question: How many are neither material nor immaterial?
"Neither material nor immaterial" is the meaning [of the question].
Answer: It is precisely this life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), because it is a conventional (*prajñapti*) phenomenon.
Question: How many are with visibility?
What is the referent of "with visibility"?
Answer: None of them are with visibility.
First, that which possesses form has "being visible" as its meaning;
this includes the remainder of what is not possessed of form and one portion thereof. Question: How many have "being resistant" as their meaning?
[Answer: Those that are resistant.
Answer: Seven [elements] are material, and the remainder are immaterial and non-resistant; these constitute one portion.
Question: How many are with-outflows (*sāsrava*)?
That which has outflows as its referent.
Answer: Only seven.
Excluding the last two and the faculties of suffering and mental grief, the remaining ones—whether tainted or untainted—have "tainted" and "untainted" as their respective referents.
One should know that the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) has both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*); its meaning is the contaminated.

The faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*) has both the contaminated and the uncontaminated as its meaning. The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*)... [is] the uncontaminated.
If it is remote from the fruits of śramaṇaship and comprised within mundane practice, it is with outflows (sāsrava);
if it is proximate to the fruits of śramaṇaship and comprised within supramundane practice, it is without outflows (anāsrava).
Question: How many are conditioned (saṃskṛta)?
"Conditioned" is the meaning.
Answer: All [dharmas] are conditioned.
Eight [of them] have "conditioned" as their meaning.
The remaining [dharmas] are conditioned;
their meaning is unconditioned.
Question: How many are subject to contention?
"Having contention as its meaning.
Answer: As it was said regarding "with outflows," one should know that this is also the same.
As it was said regarding "with contention," one should know that the same applies to "having a relish for," "relying on indulgence," and "worldly and supramundane.
Question: How many are past?
"Past" means having an object.
Answer: With the exception of the material faculties and the faculty of suffering, it refers to one portion of the remaining [faculties] that possess an object.
If there are material faculties (*rūpindriya*) and the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) that exist in the past, they do not have the past as their referent.
Question: How many have both the past and the present as their referents?
Answer: It is as has been stated regarding one portion;
it should be understood that this very [portion], when existing in the past, takes the future as its object.
Furthermore, this very [present] takes the past and future as its object.
Question: How many [factors] have the present as their object? Answer: The present.
Answer: All material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), along with a portion of what was previously mentioned;
furthermore, this portion exists in the future.
It takes the past, future, and present as its referent.
If the various material faculties (rūpīndriya) exist in the future,
they do not take the future as their referent.
The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is likewise.
Question: How many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
"Bound to the desire realm" is the intended meaning.
Answer: Four.
Two are bound to the desire and form realms;
their referent is that which is bound to the desire realm.
Three are bound to the desire and form realms;
their meaning is being bound to the desire and form realms.
Two are bound to the desire and form realms as well as being unbound.
The meaning refers to those bound to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, as well as those that are unbound.
The same applies to the seven [categories] bound to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, as well as those that are unbound.
One [category] is bound to the realm of form, as well as those that are unbound.
The meaning is that all are bound and unbound. The second [category] has the meaning that those which are unbound are bound by all [factors].
The meaning is that they are unbound.
Question: How many are wholesome?
What is the meaning of "wholesome"?
Answer: Eight are exclusively wholesome.
It has the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate as its meaning.
The five [factors] are wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate;
they have the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate as their meaning.
First, wholesome and unwholesome;
these have the meaning of being wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
Fifth, the indeterminate.
It has the indeterminate as its meaning.
It has both the two types of indeterminate and the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate as its meaning.
Question: How many trainings (śikṣā) are there?
"Training" is the meaning [of the term]. Such are the questions.
Answer: There are nine categories—those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
These are taken as the three meanings.
Seven are categorized as neither in training nor beyond training.
This is precisely what constitutes its meaning:
it applies generally to all three types,
having the sense of being neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
First, that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner,
taking the three types as its meaning;
second, the learner.
It has three meanings:
first, the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa);
it has three meanings.
Question: How many are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?
That which is abandoned by insight is the referent (*artha*). And so forth.
Answer: Fourteen are partially abandoned by insight and partially abandoned by cultivation;
twelve are partially abandoned by cultivation.
One part is not to be abandoned (*aheya*).
That is to say, among the fourteen [faculties], six and the remaining six, as well as the other two, are not to be abandoned.
Herein, the meaning is that the material faculties are to be abandoned by both seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*).
The formless faculties have three types of objects as their referents:
namely, those abandoned by seeing, those abandoned by cultivation, and those not to be abandoned.
Question: How many faculties are characterized by the relinquishing of defilement regarding these objects?
Answer: With the exception of the various roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
This is because the various roots of goodness are manifested by the relinquishing (*tyāga*) that is pure in its meaning.
Question: How many faculties (*indriya*) have a perverted meaning?
Answer: Excluding all wholesome roots, what is the meaning of the six faculties?
Question: How many faculties serve as the basis for perversion?
Answer: Seven material faculties.
Question: How many faculties have an inverted intrinsic nature?
Answer: A portion of six.
Question: How many faculties serve as antidotes to perversions?
Answer: Eight entities.
Question: How many faculties contemplate the faults of objects?
Answer: Either eight, five, or one.
Question: If those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are also found to be associated with the four virtues, why does one contemplate them only as defects?
What are the four virtues?
First is the virtue of firm abiding;
this means, for example, that a single aggregate remains for a hundred years.
If there is anyone who is about to be governed or who has transgressed,
there are two powers and virtues:
namely, the ability to produce happiness and to manifest purity.
Third is the quality of transformation,
which refers to the sovereign transformation of projecting, purifying, enjoying, and relinquishing.
Fourth is the quality of being delightful.
This means that because various attachments arise based on those states, these are called the four characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Answer: Although there are those in the world who grasp at those phenomena as being meritorious qualities.
However, all of those are pursued by various faults.
Question: What are these "various faults"?
Answer: Although they may endure for a short time, they are not ultimate.
Because the impermanence of transformation in affection is perceptible,
and because the impermanence of death and passing away is perceptible,
one should contemplate that all conditioned phenomena are devoid of their initial qualities.
Furthermore, because various forms of suffering and affliction can be perceived in the present,
and various forms of impurity can be perceived in the present,
one should contemplate all conditioned phenomena as being devoid of a second quality.
Furthermore, because aging, sickness, death, and so forth are observed to manifest regardless of one's wishes,
one should contemplate that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are devoid of the third excellence.
Moreover, because dung-worms, pigs, dogs, and the like are also observed to be intensely attached to the impurities of excrement, [conditioned phenomena lack this excellence].
One should contemplate all conditioned phenomena as being devoid of the fourth quality;
since those conditioned phenomena are devoid of all virtues,
they are therefore associated with every fault.
Therefore, one should contemplate that [the eye] is possessed of various faults.
Question: What is the locus of the eye-faculty?
Answer: It is the locus for the seeing of forms.
Question: Up to and including the faculty of mind (*manas*), what is their respective basis?
Answer: Each takes its own objective sphere as its respective basis.
Question: What is the basis for the two faculties of male and female?
Answer: It is the basis for the cultivation of desire.
Question: What is the basis for the life-faculty?
Answer: It is the basis for the prior existence (pūrvakālabhava) up until the moment of death-existence (maraṇabhava).
Question: Upon what do the various feeling-faculties (*vedanendriya*) depend?
Answer: They depend upon objects that are agreeable or disagreeable, and they are the basis for attachment, aversion, and so forth.
Question: What is the basis for the faculty of faith?
Answer: It is the basis for entering into wholesome phenomena (*kuśaladharma*).
Question: What is the basis for the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*)?
Answer: It is the basis for having entered the wholesome dharmas and for their constant cultivation.
Question: What is the basis of the faculty of mindfulness?
Answer: It is the basis for acting with clear comprehension.
Question: Upon what does the faculty of concentration rely?
Answer: It relies upon the purification of knowledge and vision.
Question: Upon what does the faculty of wisdom rely?
Answer: It is the basis for the permanent abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Question: Of what is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) the basis?
Answer: It is the basis for realizing the first, second, and third fruits of śramaṇaship (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
Question: What is the basis for the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*)?
Answer: It is the basis for the realization of the fruit of arhatship (*aśaikṣa-śrāmaṇyaphala*), up to and including the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
Question: What is the basis for the faculty of one who possesses complete knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*)?

Answer: It is the basis for the eternal cessation of the support upon which the realization of the permanent severance of immediate afflictions and the dwelling in happiness in the present life depend.
Question: Based on which faculty did the Blessed One speak these words?
This body is material, composed of coarse dregs;
it is fashioned from the four great elements and produced from the union of the impurities of father and mother.
It is nurtured by various kinds of food and drink;
it constantly relies on clothing for covering, bathing, massage, and grooming.
It is subject to being cut and severed.
Regarding the teaching on the dharma of destruction and dissolution:
it should be understood that this statement is made in reliance upon the seven material faculties (*rūpīndriya*),
wherein the various material faculties of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are explained in brief.
The first phrase explains its common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*);
the second phrase explains its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
and the following three phrases explain its causal characteristic (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*).
This refers to the cause upon which it depends, the cause by which it arises, and the cause by which, having arisen, it increases.
Next, there are three phrases that describe its mode of transformation:
namely, those caused by cold, those caused by heat, and those caused by fatigue.
The subsequent four phrases describe the characteristics of its transformation and disintegration:
the first two phrases refer to what is produced by affliction during the state of life,
while the latter two phrases refer to what occurs after death.
Because it is other-dependent and because it is naturally subject to transformation and decay, this should be understood.
Question: Based on which faculty did the Blessed One speak these words:
"Wandering far and wandering turbidly, bodiless, one lies within the cave"?
Answer: It is based on the sense base of the mental faculty (*manas*),
because it has no beginning in the past and because it universally takes all knowable objects as its cognitive range.
It is called "Far-Reaching" because each moment of the mental continuum proceeds one after another,
and because it lacks a sovereign master.
It is called "solitary" because it is formless,
invisible, and without resistance;
it is called "bodiless."
Because it relies upon form (*rūpa*), it is said to "sleep in a cave.
Question: With reference to which faculty (*indriya*) is this statement spoken?
Men are bound by women through eight bases:
namely, dancing, singing, laughing, glancing, beautiful countenances, exquisite touch, respectful service, and formal courtesy.
Answer: This is based upon the two faculties of male and female.
At the time of play, one is bound by four points;
at the time of enjoyment, likewise by four points.
At the time of play:
With body, speech, and countenance relaxed and joyful, her eyes bright and pleasant,
she served the youth with a beautiful appearance, soft and supple touch, and respectful devotion during their enjoyment.
Question: Based on which faculty (indriya) is it said that "sentient beings survive, abide, and dwell in security"?
Answer: It is said based on the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
Because they possess the breaths of life, they are called sentient beings (*sattva*).
Because they are associated with volitional thought (*cetanā*), they are said to be alive.
Because they abide in equilibrium with others, they are said to "dwell" (*sthiti*).
Because it functions with predominance, it is called "sustaining" (*dhṛti*).
Because it is free from the affliction of illness, it is called "secure" (*kṣema*).
Question: With reference to which faculty (*indriya*) is such a statement made?
It is said that "equanimity is comprised within feeling.

The answer is: this is stated in reference to the faculties of joy and pleasure, because [feeling] is manifested by its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), its common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and its basis (*āśrayalakṣaṇa*) in relation to the remaining feelings.
Just as with "evenness" and so forth,
one should understand that "unevenness," "neither even nor uneven," and so forth are to be understood accordingly.
Question: World-Honored One, based on which faculty did you speak these words:
"In the Tathāgata, pure faith has taken root deeply and firmly, established as a foundation;
[this applies] to all those in the world, whether they be śramaṇas..."?
Whether it be a brahmin,
a deva, a Māra, or a Brahmā,
there is none who can lead one toward liberation in accordance with the Dharma.
Answer: This is explained in reliance upon the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
It reveals the sense that one's conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding hearing, reflection, and cultivation is firm.
Furthermore, this firmness is demonstrated through the skillful means (*upāya*) corresponding to what one has come to believe and resolve.
This means that even those who are lords of wisdom, pure, and most excellent cannot move it,
let alone ordinary beings.
Furthermore, there is another distinction regarding the meaning of "firmness."
This means that his faith is profound and firm;
for mundane well-determined resolute conviction serves as the foundation for supramundane resolute conviction,
and it is also established by means of supramundane pure resolute conviction.
It should be understood that the first is the declarative statement (*uddāna*), while the latter two are the explanatory statements.
Question: Upon which faculty (*indriya*) does the Blessed One rely?
He spoke these words:
"Abiding with power and diligence, possessing valor, fortitude,
and steadfastness, one should never cast off the yoke of wholesome qualities."
Answer: This is explained in reliance upon the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).
Briefly stated, there are five distinctions in its characteristics:
namely, the diligence of donning the armor (*saṃnāha-vīrya*).
Exertion through skillful means, undaunted exertion,
and unshakable exertion.
Regarding the diligence of non-contentment, he asked the World-Honored One:
"Based on which faculty did you speak these words:
'mindfulness, constant mindfulness, recollection, specific mindfulness, and non-forgetfulness'?"
The mind clearly remembers without loss; it is the state of non-forgetfulness and non-loss.
This explanation of its specific meaning should be understood according to the *Smṛtīndriya* (faculty of mindfulness) as set forth in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.
Question: World-Honored One, based on which faculty (indriya) did you speak these words:
"causing the mind to abide, to abide evenly, to abide securely, and to abide closely"?
Tranquility, serenity, and calm abiding; one-pointedness and the nature of meditative concentration—
these distinctions regarding the faculty of concentration (samādhīndriya) should be understood as explained in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*.
Question: Venerable Sir, based on which faculty did you speak these words:
"Discerning phenomena, thoroughly discerning them, searching everywhere, and examining everywhere"?
Answer: This distinction of meaning is explained in reliance upon the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*);
it should be understood as being the same as in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
As for the remaining wholesome faculties, they are subsumed within faith (*śraddhā*) and the others.
No further distinction in meaning can be found.
Question: In how many faculties (indriya) is the application of mindfulness to the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna) established?
Answer: Seven.
Question: In how many faculties (*indriya*) is the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*) established?
Answer: Five.
Question: In how many faculties is the application of mindfulness to the mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*) established?
Answer: One. Question:
In how many faculties (indriya) is the application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) established?
Answer: In the last eight and the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
Question: How many faculties are the most preeminent bases for the truth of suffering?
Answer: Nine.
Question: How many faculties are the most preeminent bases for the truth of origination?
Answer: Five.
Question: How many faculties have the truth of cessation as their basis? Answer: All.
Question: How many faculties (indriya) have the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya) as their basis?
Answer: The last eight.
Question: Based on how many faculties does one contemplate what is to be contemplated through right reflection (samyakcintā)?
Answer: Nine.
Question: Based on how many faculties (indriya) are the well-spoken teachings explained?
Answer: Ten.
Question: Based on how many faculties does one perform what is wholesome?
Answer: Sixteen.
Likewise for what is unwholesome, which is thought upon.
One should understand accordingly that what is spoken is ill-spoken and what is done is ill-done;
this refers to the question of how many faculties serve as the basis for the most predominant afflictions and karmas.
Answer: Nine.
Question: Based on how many faculties do afflictions and karma arise?
Answer: Five.
Question: Based on how many faculties (*indriya*) are afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma severed?
Answer: The final eight.
Question: By means of how many faculties does one experience all the auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) of both the mundane and supramundane realms?
Answer: Excluding two.
Question: By means of how many faculties does one experience all auspiciousness and ruin?
Answer: Eleven.
Question: How many faculties are able to bring about all forms of auspiciousness?
Answer: The final eight.
Furthermore, as the Blessed One said:
Briefly stated, there are five kinds of methods for performing auspicious rites for those who indulge in sensual pleasures:
namely, patience and gentleness.
Observing others, one should practice virtuous conduct and heedfulness.
What is patience?
It should be understood through three types of practice:
first, the absence of anger.
Second, not retaliating for grievances;
third, not harboring malice.
If distinguished individually, there are ten types.
First, patience toward harm already received;
second, patience toward manifest harm;
third, patience toward anticipated harm.
Fourth, patience toward those who cause harm to enemies and those one dislikes;
fifth, patience toward those who cause harm to friends and relatives;
sixth, patience toward all forms of enmity and injury.
Seventh is patience toward harm from all causes;
eighth is patience toward harm while receiving instruction;
ninth is patience toward harm through the power of discernment.
Tenth is the patience regarding natural hostility and harm.
All such instances are collectively termed "patience toward adversity and injury.
What is gentleness?
That is to say, being naturally virtuous and gentle,
one protects others through body, speech, and mind so as to prevent them from suffering harm;
furthermore, one causes blameless joy and happiness that have not yet arisen in others to arise.
Once they have arisen, he protects them accordingly.
Regarding sinful states accompanied by anxiety and suffering: if they have not yet arisen, he prevents them from arising;
if they have already arisen, he employs skillful means to bring about their cessation.
In this context, patience (*kṣānti*) consists of enduring the harms inflicted by others and being gentle toward them without causing injury;
such are the two distinctions.
One should know that there are two temporal distinctions in observing persons:
first, the time of gathering them in;
second, the time of establishing them.
When receiving [a person] into the community, one should observe that individual through five characteristics before accepting them:
first, by means of their sincere devotion;
second, by means of their skillful ability.
Third, by means of wisdom;
fourth, by means of the path of practice;
fifth, by means of frugality.
When assigning them to positions, one should also observe the individual through five aspects before assigning them.
First, those capable of performing manual labor are assigned to manual labor.
Second, those capable of performing mental labor are assigned to mental labor.
Third, those actions suitable for the category of harmonizing activities are placed among harmonizing activities.
Fourth, those actions suitable for the category of protecting one’s person and wealth are placed among the actions of protecting one’s person and wealth.
Fifth, those actions suitable for the category of Dharma are placed among the actions of Dharma.
Renunciation is briefly of five kinds:
first, renunciation of land;
second, renunciation of wealth and goods.
Third, relinquishment as appropriate;
fourth, relinquishment of food and drink;
fifth, supreme relinquishment.
In this context, equanimity (*upekṣā*) refers to both the characteristic of equanimity and the means for its cultivation.
One who practices with excellence is by nature free from any transgression or offense toward others.
There is no deception and no breach of obligation.
Furthermore, there are five kinds:
first, no breach of obligation through inversion.
Second, there is no breach of entrusted confidence;
third, there is no breach of service;
fourth, there is no breach of contract.
The fifth is the absence of failure due to other means.
Regarding heedfulness (*apramāda*):
it refers to the cultivation of all wholesome dharmas.
One guards the unwholesome mind.
Because cause and effect are interconnected, both should be understood as its characteristics.
Furthermore, this should be known to have five types.
First, diligence in seeking wealth;
second, diligence in guarding wealth;
third, diligence in protecting the body.
The four protections are called non-laxity (*apramāda*).
The five practices of the Dharma are also non-laxity.
Thus, all together there are five powers capable of producing auspiciousness.
First, the power of virtuous ethical discipline;
second, the power of virtuous friends;
third, the power of being free from malice and stinginess.
Fourth is the power of being trustworthy;
fifth is the power of the Dharma.
It should be known that auspiciousness likewise possesses five kinds.
First, one is beloved by the multitude;
second, one possesses wealth, honor, and sovereignty;
third, enemies are repelled and subdued.
Fourth, the basis for benefiting others;
fifth, proceeding to the various happy realms.
These first four types of power are collectively able to give rise to the four kinds of auspiciousness.
The fifth single power is able to produce the fifth.
Question: How many faculties are first acquired through the retribution of afflictions and karma?
Answer: Eight.
Question: How many faculties have form as their condition?
Answer: One.
Question: How many faculties have contact as their condition?
Answer: Five.
Question: How many faculties have exertion as their condition?
Answer: Eight.
Question: How many faculties (*indriya*) should be guarded?
Answer: Eight.
Question: How many faculties should be tamed and stilled?
Answer: One.
Question: How many faculties (*indriya*) should be stilled?
Answer: Five.
Question: How many faculties are by nature disciplined, tranquil, and stilled, and are furthermore capable of disciplining, tranquilizing, and stilling?
Answer: Eight.
What is the relinquishing of the faculties?
It refers to the cessation of the faculties belonging to a particular homogeneous class, realm, and level, and the arising of others.
What is the discarding of the faculties?
It refers to the cessation of the faculties belonging to a different sphere or level and the arising of others.
How are the faculties severed?
It refers to severing all afflictions that bind them.
What is the decline of the faculties?
It refers to the loss and ruin of worldly prosperity, whether in meditative concentration or in rebirth.
Question: What are the differences between the faculties of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas?
Answer: It should be known that, in brief, there are five kinds of distinctions:
first, the distinction of categories;
second, the distinction of support.
Third, the distinction of the snares;
fourth, the distinction of correct practice;
fifth, the distinction of realization.
Regarding the distinction of categories:
the faculties of all bodhisattvas are of the superior grade,
whereas the faculties of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are of the inferior or middling grades.
Regarding the distinction of maintenance:
the faculties of all bodhisattvas maintain skillfulness in all fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*),
whereas the faculties of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas maintain skillfulness in only a portion of the fields of knowledge.
Regarding the distinctions of the noose (*pāśa*):
the faculties of the Bodhisattvas are ensnared by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*),
whereas the faculties of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are not so.
Regarding the distinction of correct practice:
the faculties of all bodhisattvas manifest as the correct practice of benefiting both oneself and others;
the faculties of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas manifest as the correct practice of benefiting only themselves.
Regarding the distinction of realization:
the faculties of all bodhisattvas realize the fruit of unsurpassed great enlightenment;
the faculties of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas realize the two fruits of inferior and middling enlightenment.
Question: If a person, relying on the *anāgamya* concentration, cultivates the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*),
when they attain the fruit, does the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) of the first dhyāna arise before them, or does it not?
Answer: There is one that can arise and one that does not arise.
If there are many roots of goodness that provide assistance for those of sharp faculties.
It is he who can manifest it, and no one else.
Question: How many faculties enter the first dhyāna?
Answer: Eight [factors].
The latter three are partially capable of entering and partially incapable.
As it is with the first dhyāna, so it is with the second;
and there are likewise eight in the third.
However, these are not identical to those of the fourth dhyāna or the formless attainments.
Seven faculties are able to enter;
among the final three, one is able to enter and one is not.
Question: How many faculties (indriya) are required to attain the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala)?
Answer: Either one, eight, two, or nine [faculties] are required to attain the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-phala).
Although the faculty of mental grief (daurmanasyendriya) serves as a basis for the Path, it is not subsumed within the Path itself.
These are not included herein.
Because the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is not stable, it is likewise not included;
if it were universally included, their number would increase.
Question: Through how many faculties is the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) attained?
Answer: Either eleven or two; the principle regarding the faculty of mental grief (daurmanasyendriya) should be understood as previously explained.
Question: Through how many faculties is the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala) attained?
Answer: Either one or ten.
As the Sūtra says:
"One feels grief and distress due to longing for higher liberations."
What is longing?
It refers to the practitioner forming this thought:
"In this place, the noble ones are able to dwell in full perfection."
What is seeking?
It refers to the practitioner forming this thought:
"In this state, I shall dwell in full accomplishment."
What is dejection (*daurmanasya*)?
It is the lack of contentment with what is inferior.
What is sorrow (*śoka*)?
This refers to the longing for the unsurpassed mind.
In this regard, because the stream-enterer and once-returner are complete in every respect,
the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is established.
Although the fruit of non-returning possesses the first two [roots], because the other two are absent,
the faculty of sorrow is not established;
it consists solely of the desire for wholesome dharmas.
Question: Is there any case where, by relying on the faculty of joy (*prīti-indriya*), one can abandon the faculties of joy, sorrow (*daurmanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)?
Answer: There is; namely, by relying upon the faculty of joy that is based on renunciation (*naiṣkramya*).
The relinquishing [of the afflictions] depends upon the three roots of non-attachment.
Question: Is there a case where one relies upon the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) to relinquish the faculty of sorrow?
Answer: There is.
This means that by relying on renunciation as a support, one abandons reliance on worldly attachment.
Question: Is there any case where, by relying on the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), one abandons the faculty of equanimity itself?
Answer: Yes.
This is because one relies upon the relinquishment of a single nature as a basis;
that relinquishment, in turn, relies upon the relinquishment of various natures.
Because it takes non-reliance as its basis,
equanimity relies on the singleness of equanimity;
at the time of attaining the fruit of stream-entry, this is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
It is both extinguished and relinquished;
it is neither produced and then discarded, nor severed, nor regressed.
At the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship, one understands the principle of the faculty of "already-known" (ājñātendriya).
It should be understood that it is likewise so.
Question: How many types of *pudgalas* undergo the refinement of their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*)?

Answer: All those of the *śaikṣa* and *aśaikṣa* stages who possess the lineages of those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), those of reflection (*cetana-dharman*), those of protection (*anurakṣaṇā-dharman*), those of stability (*sthitākampya-dharman*), and those capable of penetration (*prativedhanādharman*).
Neither the Pratyekabuddhas nor the Bodhisattvas [possess this], because their faculties are naturally sharp.
Question: When a Stream-enterer cultivates the refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃvara), [what occurs]?
"Once one has attained the refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃskāra), does one also realize the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin)?
Answer: Yes. Question: Does one also realize the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmin)?"
Answer: It is not realized because its antidote is difficult to obtain and because the meaning that is to be attained is exceedingly vast.
Question: When a non-returner cultivates the refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃskāra), does he both refine the faculties and further progress toward the abandonment of desire?
Answer: He does progress.
Question: Does he also realize the fruit of arhatship?
Answer: He does not realize it, due to the aforementioned cause.
After the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), all [attainments] are realized.
Question: For what reason does one transform the faculties?
Answer: Because one does not give rise to complacency regarding slight progress.
It is for the purpose of planting the power of inducing superior concentration;
for the purpose of planting the power of extensive learning;
and for the purpose of planting the power of analytical discussion and discernment.
In order to plant the power of the patience that observes the profound Dharma, he asks:
How are the three faculties—the faculty of "those who wish to know what they do not yet know," and so forth—established for bodhisattvas?
He answers: The first faculty is established on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
The second faculty is established in the stage of the superior intention of purity (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*) and so forth;
the third faculty is established in the stage of the Tathāgata.
Question: By how many kinds of fulfillment is "fulfillment of training" (*śikṣā-sampad*) defined?
Answer: By way of three kinds of fulfillment:
first, the fulfillment of the faculties, which refers to having sharp faculties.
Second is the fulfillment of meditative concentration, namely the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa).
Third is the fulfillment of the fruits [of the spiritual path].
This refers to the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
If those who are beyond training (aśaikṣa) possess two fulfillments:
first, the fulfillment of the faculties (indriya).
This refers to the immovable dharma (akopyadharman).
The fulfillment of the two concentrations should be understood as previously explained.
All those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are said to be "perfected" because their fruits are perfected.
Question: As it is said that the faculties are not tamed, not guarded, not protected, not restrained, and not cultivated; [how is this so?]
What is the meaning of these specific designations?
The answer is: briefly stated, the faculties are called "undisciplined" due to four causes and conditions.
This means that by relying on the power of discernment,
regarding those objects of experience for which one should not allow the sense faculties to run wild,
one initiates application so as not to become heedless.
If it is appropriate to relax [the faculties], one initiates the application of effort to relax those faculties,
guarding against the afflictions so that they do not manifest,
by relying on the power of the antidote that abandons them.
Regarding the objects previously described,
his nature is one of non-attachment and his afflictions no longer manifest.
If these four means of disciplining the sense faculties were absent, [the practitioner would not succeed].
One should know that those faculties are called "undisciplined" because they are not restrained,
not guarded, not prevented, and not cultivated.
If there are those who discipline their faculties through these four [methods], [they are called disciplined].
One should know that the opposites of those four are termed "discipline" up to and including "cultivation.
Why does a lack of discipline lead to manifold suffering?
This refers to the fact that it gives rise to six kinds of suffering:
first, the suffering arising from dwelling in agitation and affliction;
second, the suffering of being expelled or rejected by others.
Third, the suffering of being reviled and disparaged by others;
fourth, the suffering arising from remorse;
fifth, the suffering of rebirth in the miserable realms.
Regarding the six types of suffering, such as birth and so forth:
it should be known that for those whose faculties are well-disciplined,
the opposite occurs— these six kinds of suffering are severed and various forms of happiness are brought forth.
Question: Regarding the fourteen types of faculties and the sentient beings of the three aggregates,
do the fourteen subsume the three,
or do the three subsume the fourteen?
Answer: The three encompass the fourteen, but the fourteen do not encompass the three.
What is it that is not encompassed?
This refers to a portion of the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
As for the three groups of sentient beings,
they are those of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Question: Regarding the five faculties and the three feelings,
do the five subsume the three,
or do the three subsume the five?
Answer: They mutually encompass one another.
Question: Regarding the five faculties and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, do the five encompass the thirty-seven?
Question: Do the thirty-seven factors subsume the five, or do the five subsume the thirty-seven?
Answer: The thirty-seven subsume the five;
it is not that the five subsume the thirty-seven.
What is not included?
That is to say, vocal action, livelihood, joy, tranquility,
equanimity— these six, or in some cases four, are not included therein.
Question: Regarding the five faculties and the three faculties,
do the five subsume the three,
or do the three subsume the five?
Answer: The three encompass the five;
the five do not encompass the three.
What is not encompassed?
That is to say, regarding the question of how many faculties (indriya) encompass the nine thorough knowledges (parijñā)— namely, the faculties of mind, pleasure, joy, and equanimity—
the answer is that because these nine thorough knowledges are subsumed under the thorough knowledge of abandonment (prahāṇa-parijñā),
they are not themselves subsumed under the [ten] faculties.
What are the nine? They are:
the abandonment of the suffering and origin associated with the desire realm that is to be abandoned through the vision [of the truths];
this is the first thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
The abandonment through the vision of suffering and origin pertaining to the form and formless realms is the second thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
The abandonment through the vision of cessation pertaining to the desire realm [is the third].
The third thorough knowledge is the abandonment of that which is to be abandoned by insight, pertaining to the cessation of the realms of form and formlessness.
The fourth thorough knowledge is...
The abandonment of those factors bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of the path is the fifth thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
The abandonment of those factors bound to the form and formless realms that are to be abandoned by the vision of the path [is the sixth].
The sixth thorough knowledge is the abandonment of the lower fetters.
The seventh thorough knowledge is...
The eighth thorough knowledge is the exhaustion of craving for the realm of form;
the ninth thorough knowledge is the exhaustion of craving for the formless realm.
It should be understood that thorough knowledge is established briefly by way of two conditions.
First, because of the abandonment through the thorough penetration of the truths;
second, because of the abandonment through the permanent transcendence of the realms,
due to the similarity and dissimilarity of the realms as well as their homogeneity.

Two types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) are established based on their distinct characteristics and distinct spheres (*dhātu*). Four types of thorough knowledge are established based on their distinct characteristics, distinct spheres, and shared spheres.
One type of thorough knowledge is established because it brings about the permanent transcendence of the inferior sphere.
One thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) is established because of the permanent transcendence of the intermediate realm;
one thorough knowledge is established because of the permanent transcendence of the sublime realm.

Question: By how many faculties (*indriya*) are the marks (*lakṣaṇa*), secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and other unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) subsumed?
Answer: The primary marks and secondary signs are subsumed under the tongue faculty and the bases of the four faculties.
What are these four?
That is to say: the body faculty,
the male faculty,
and the eye faculty.
The faculty of the tongue and the ten powers of the Buddhas are subsumed within the faculty of wisdom within the body of the Tathāgata.
The faculty of one who has already attained full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) and the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) are subsumed under the five faculties;
furthermore, they are this very same [faculty].
As it is with the fearlessnesses, so it is with the forms of non-protection.
The three applications of mindfulness are not included among the faculties;
nevertheless, they are induced by the six faculties and are comprised within non-attachment and non-hatred.
Great compassion is likewise induced by that [wisdom] and is subsumed under non-hatred and non-delusion;
it is not subsumed under the faculties.
The quality of non-forgetfulness should be understood as being like the powers.
The Buddha’s omniscient wisdom is likewise:
it eternally severs the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and is not subsumed under the faculties;
yet it is realized by the six faculties and is subsumed within the eternal severance of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Question: Regarding the heaviness (*dausthulya*) belonging to all categories of afflictions,
which has been eternally severed without remainder by Arhats and others—
what further category of heaviness remains?
That which has not yet been abandoned even by Arhats and others—by abandoning this, the Tathāgata is said to have "permanently severed the habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*).
Answer: It is the heaviness (*dausthulya*) belonging to the category of maturation (*vipāka*).
That which the Arhats and others have not yet been able to sever, only the Tathāgata is said to have severed completely.
Question: As the Sūtra says:
There are four kinds of nutriment that are all capable of nourishing the sense faculties and the great elements.
What are the four nutriments?
How do they nourish the sense faculties and the great elements?
Answer: It is edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), contact-food (*sparśa-āhāra*), volition-food (*manaḥsaṃcetanā-āhāra*), and consciousness-food (*vijñāna-āhāra*).

By means of these four types of food, the five material sense-faculties, the mental faculty (*manas*), and all the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which those faculties depend are nourished and maintained.
Question: What is edible food?
Answer: Whatever is eaten or consumed that is capable of nourishing the sense faculties and the primary elements.
That which is contrary to this should be known as non-nutriment (*anāhāra*).
Just as with edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), it should be understood that other foods and non-foods are likewise.
Question: How does edible food function as nutriment?
This applies even to the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*).

Answer: If various types of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) can sustain and benefit consciousness, making it vigorous, then by means of this, they also nourish the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the great elements (*mahābhūta*), making them vigorous as well.
Contact can appropriate a portion of joy, pleasure, or equanimity;
by means of this, it further benefits the various consciousnesses.
Because it provides benefit, it is further able to nourish the sense faculties and the primary elements.
The mental faculty (*manas*) functions to realize desirable objective aspects;
relying on correct means, it gives rise to defiled or undefiled aspiration and the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*),
taking future objects as its condition to benefit the consciousness.
By means of this, the sense faculties and the primary elements are nourished;
thus, these three types of nutriment sustain and benefit consciousness by causing its substance to increase and flourish,
and by serving as the conditions for its arising in the present and future.
Because consciousness further nourishes the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the great elements (*mahābhūta*), the four nutriments (*āhāra*) are established.
Question: How does consciousness serve as nutriment for the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*)?
Answer: Because it is sustained by three kinds of support.
It serves as the cause for subsequent states to increase and flourish, thereby enabling them to arise.
Question: For what reason are sleep, dreams, the holy life (brahmacarya), and meditative attainments (samāpatti) mentioned?
All [nutriments] are able to nourish the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the great elements (*mahābhūta*), yet they do not establish [them as] food.
The answer is that there are two kinds of nourishment:
first, nourishment in the sense of specific appropriation (*parigraha*).
The second is that which nourishes without causing harm.
Although phenomena such as sleep and dreams can indeed nourish at a later stage,
they do not do so at the initial stage.
Therefore, it is not established [as a nutriment].
Question: Why is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) able to sustain the body yet not established as a nutriment?
Answer: Because if one were separated from food, the body could ultimately never be nourished and maintained.
Question: What kind of edible food is called coarse?
Answer: That which is not consumed by the devas.
Question: What is called subtle?
Answer: Regarding the food consumed by the various devas, it is digested within their bodies immediately after consumption rather than through a gradual process.
Question: What kind of contact, mental volition, and consciousness-food is termed "coarse"?
Answer: If it pertains to the desire realm.
Question: What is called "subtle"?
Answer: If it pertains to the form and formless realms.
Question: What is meant by "sentient beings who have already been born"?
Answer: Those who have already been born and are currently increasing [in their development] within the present life.
Question: What is meant by "sentient beings who seek existence"?
Answer: If there is a seeking after future existences (*bhava*).
Question: What is called "abiding" (*sthiti*)?
Answer: If there is neither harm nor nourishment.
Question: What is meant by "sustenance" (*yāpanā*)?
Answer: It refers to gathering and nurturing.
Question: How do sentient beings who have already been born maintain their existence through nutriment?
Answer: It should be understood according to the principles previously explained.
Question: How do sentient beings seeking existence (bhavābhinandin) come to be sustained by nutriment?
Answer: Because two kinds of afflictions (saṃkleśa) increase by way of three doors.
That is to say, the two types of defilement—karma and afflictions—exist dependent upon consciousness;
for it is through these three gateways that the defilements nourish and increase consciousness.
