That is to say, there is someone who, for the sake of harming living beings, repeatedly pursues and reflects upon such thoughts throughout the long night;
by reason of this, they eventually increase those evil and unwholesome states induced by the taking of life.
However, there is no karma of killing that both constitutes action and increases.
As for that which both constitutes action and increases,
this refers to cases other than those previously mentioned where it constitutes action but does not increase, or where it increases but does not constitute action.
All other characteristics of the karmic action of killing that are neither performed nor accumulated refer to those cases excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
In the same way, the remaining [unwholesome courses of action], from taking what is not given up to frivolous speech,
should be understood according to their respective applications as being like killing.
This also applies to covetousness, malice, and wrong view.
There is no second mode of increase that does not involve the performance of the act.
Within the first mode, there is no performing without intention or being compelled by another to perform it.
The remainder is as previously explained.
Furthermore, if one is habituated to killing, practices it repeatedly, and performs it extensively,
one is born in the hells;
this is called the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of killing.
If, after passing away from that state, one is reborn here among the human class with a short lifespan,
this is called the outflowing fruit (niṣyanda-phala) of killing.
Within the external world of the vessel-realm that has been acquired,
food, drink, fruits, and medicinal herbs all lack luster and potency;
their karmic maturation and majestic power are both exceedingly feeble.
The transformation and elimination of imbalance gives rise to diseases.
Due to these causes and conditions, immeasurable sentient beings do not complete their natural lifespan but die prematurely.
This is called the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) of killing.
Regarding the remaining paths of action,
the distinctions between their two fruits— maturation and outflow—
should be understood as they appear in the sūtras.
The dominant fruit (adhipatiphala) shall now be explained.
If the receptacle world has few fruits,
the fruits do not flourish and many become rotten.
The fruits are not firm or substantial, and there is often a lack of rain;
all fruits wither and dry up, or there may be no fruit at all.
All such cases are called the dominant result (*adhipatiphala*) of taking what is not given.
If the vessel-world (bhājanaloka) abounds in excrement, filth, mud, and impurities;
if it is a foul-smelling, cramped place where many unclean and stinking things arise;
and if everything therein is utterly unpleasant—[then one should cultivate renunciation].
All such things are called the dominant results (*adhipatiphala*) of sexual misconduct.
Furthermore, the agricultural, maritime,
and worldly occupations of the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*) will not flourish significantly.
There is very little that is favorable, and for the most part things do not harmonize;
there are many causes and conditions for fear and dread—
all such things are the dominant results of lying.
If the location of the vessel-world consists of ground that is uneven with mounds and pits,
separated by intervals and obstructed by difficult terrain,
abounding in many causes for terror and fear.
All such things are the dominant results (*adhipatiphala*) of divisive speech (*paiśunya*).
As for the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*),
its terrain and locations abound with stumps, thorns, poisonous spikes, shards, stones, gravel, and parched, withered ground.
There is no moisture; the ponds, lakes, rivers, and springs have all dried up.
The soil is saline and barren, and the landscape is filled with hills, mounds, and treacherous ravines, abounding in causes for various terrors and fears.
All such things are the dominant results (*adhipatiphala*) of harsh speech (*pāruṣya*).
As for the fruit trees in the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), their fruits are not properly formed;
they bear fruit out of season, fail to bear fruit at the proper time, and grow appearing as if ripe.
The faculties are not firm and their power does not endure for long;
the gardens, groves, and ponds are for the most part unpleasant,
abounding in many causes and conditions for fear and terror.
All such things are the dominant results (*adhipatiphala*) of frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*).
As for the material world (*bhājanaloka*), all its prosperities—years, seasons, days, nights, months, and fortnights—gradually decline and fade away.
All odors only diminish and do not increase;
all such things are the dominant results (*adhipatiphala*) of sensual desire.
Furthermore, the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) will be plagued by many epidemics, calamities, disturbances, and enemies.
They are terrified by lions, tigers, and wolves;
by various malevolent birds and beasts;
and by pythons, vipers, scorpions, and centipedes.
Centipede-like *mātaras*, *piśācas*, *yakṣas*, and various evil bandits—
all such beings as these are the predominant results of hatred (*dveṣa*).
Furthermore, all the most excellent and sublime flowers and fruits within the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) will completely vanish.
All impure things appear momentarily as pure;
all things of suffering and affliction appear momentarily as blissful;
they are not places of dwelling, not places of refuge, and not places of reliance.
All such things are the dominant results (*adhipatiphala*) of wrong view.
Furthermore, as the Blessed One said:
"There are three kinds of killing."
This refers to that which arises from greed, hatred, and delusion;
this applies likewise even to wrong views.
How should this distinction be understood?
If one kills sentient beings for the sake of their flesh, blood,
and so forth, or forms the intention:
"Having killed them, I shall seize their wealth and property."
Whether hired by others, or out of gratitude;
whether constrained by friendship, or desiring to become a friend;
or for the sake of food and clothing, carrying out acts of killing in obedience to the instructions of their master.
Some may kill thinking that the victim can cause them harm;
some may kill thinking that the victim can obstruct their wealth and profit.
This applies accordingly to gain and loss, defamation and praise, fame and insignificance, and suffering and pleasure.
One should know that it is likewise so.
All such cases are called the path of action of killing born of greed.
Furthermore, if one were to say that he commits the act of killing because it serves no purpose for his own pleasure;
Either one thinks that the other has previously done one harm;
or one fears that the other will do one harm in the future;
or one sees that the other is currently doing one harm, and thus carries out the act of killing.
To speak at length, one should understand all nine grounds for resentment in this same way.
All such instances are called the karmic path of killing born of hatred.
Furthermore, there is the case where one commits an act of killing while considering it to be for the sake of the Dharma.
Thinking, "I am a good friend to other sentient beings;
because of me, they will, upon the destruction of the body at the end of life, be reborn in the heavens"—
such killing arises from delusion.
Or one might have this thought:
"For the sake of my elders and superiors, it is according to the Dharma that I should kill.
Or one might have this thought: [and so forth].
Those who revile the gods, Brahmā, and the Lord of the World,
and who abuse brahmins,
deserve to be executed according to the law.
Such a mind that kills arises from delusion;
it either calculates that the act of killing and its accumulation bear no ripened fruit,
or it expounds this to others and exhorts them to engage in the act of killing.
When that person carries out the act of killing because of such instigation,
the offense of killing incurred by the instigator arises from delusion (*moha*).
This refers to the subsequent explanation of the karmic action of killing arising from delusion.
The same principle applies to all other courses of action, up to and including wrong view; it should be understood that they are likewise.
There may be those who falsely imagine that by casting their parents, loved ones, or kinsmen into fire [they will achieve some merit].
Fasting, throwing oneself from cliffs, and abandoning oneself in the wilderness—
these are the true Dharma.
All such acts are called paths of karmic killing born of delusion.
Furthermore, if one greedily seizes the wealth or food of others,
this taking what is not given arises from covetousness; or,
if one commits robbery while being hired by another for that purpose.
They commit robbery and theft either out of gratitude, or in hope of future favors,
or to provide food and clothing by carrying out their master’s commands,
or for the sake of reputation, or for the sake of personal comfort.
All such acts of taking what is not given are born of greed.
Furthermore, one might think:
"He intends to act harmfully toward me."
To speak at length, up to and including the fact that it is through the predominant influence of the nine causes of malice that one commits robbery and theft;
it is not necessarily out of attachment to the wealth belonging to another, nor is it necessarily out of a desire for other material goods.
This taking of what is not given arises from hatred;
for instance, when one burns down villages, houses, wealth, treasures, and utensils out of malice toward others,
it should be known that such contact arises from hatred.
A transgression similar to theft;
or, out of increased intensity or malice toward others,
one causes them to plunder and disperse another's wealth.
When he carries out the task according to the instructions he has received,
the instructor incurs the offense of taking what is not given arising from hatred.
Furthermore, if he forms this thought:
To commit robbery and theft for the sake of one's elders and superiors is considered the True Dharma;
this is called the offense of taking what is not given born of delusion.
Or, one might form such a thought:
If one slanders, reviles, or abuses the gods, Brahmā, the Lord of the World, or a brāhmaṇa,
it is the natural law that all their wealth shall be seized;
this taking of what is not given also arises from delusion.
Or one might think:
"If it is for the sake of a sacrifice, for the components of a sacrifice, or for the requisites of a sacrifice,
it is lawful to commit theft."
This taking of what is not given also arises from delusion.
Furthermore, if one sees or hears of an act that should not be performed,
one then engages in improper conceptualization and grasps at its signs.
Thus, being bound and fettered by the entanglement of craving, one commits unrighteous acts;
this is called the offense of sexual misconduct born of craving.
Alternatively, it refers to acting as a matchmaker for others upon receiving payment.
By means of this stratagem, he engages in what is not to be practiced;
he thereby incurs the offense of sexual misconduct born of lust,
or seeks to win over friends and acquaintances.
Whether for the sake of clothing and food they obey the commands of their teachers,
or for the sake of survival they engage in unwholesome conduct in hopes of acquiring wealth, grain, gold, silver,
and precious jewels— all such cases are termed the offense of sexual misconduct arising from greed.
Furthermore, if one thinks:
"He practices what is unbeneficial toward me," and so on at length, up to:
"he acts with perverse conduct based upon the nine grounds of malice."
It is not that he was previously bound by the fetters of desire;
rather, regarding matters that are contrary and improper to perform,
he exerts himself in order to take revenge.
This is termed the offense of sexual misconduct arising from hatred; or,
out of malice toward another, one causes that person’s wife or concubine to be defiled by another,
provided that the other accepts the instruction and commits the act of sexual misconduct.
One then incurs a transgression of sexual misconduct that is similar to what arises from anger,
or perhaps even more grave;
such is the case for all transgressions of sexual misconduct.
It is called "born of hatred.
Furthermore, it is when one forms the intention to take the life of one's mother,
father, or another woman for the sake of an illicit act.
If one does not practice it, one incurs great transgression;
if one practices it, one obtains great merit.
To regard what is non-Dharma as Dharma and to engage in such perverse conduct is [an error].
This is called the offense of sexual misconduct arising from delusion.
Furthermore, it includes speaking falsehoods for the sake of gain and profit,
or out of fear that others will damage one's own property.
Whether for the sake of praise or for the sake of comfort, one speaks false speech;
all such instances are called the path of action of false speech born of greed.
Furthermore, if one speaks false speech based on the nine grounds of malice and harm, [it is likewise].
This is called the path of action of lying born of hatred. If one forms the thought:
"For the sake of my elders, or for the sake of an ox, or for the sake of sacrificial implements, it is according to the dharma that I should lie."
Such false speech arises from delusion.
If one forms this thought:
"Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas there may be..."
Contrary to the various devas, contrary to the Lord of the Brahma-world, and contrary to the brahmins,
one falsely claims that such lies accord with the True Dharma.
Such lying is called the path of karmic action for lying born of delusion.
If one forms such a conception,
perceiving phenomena as phenomena and the Vinaya as the Vinaya.
There is no unrighteousness in breaking the Sangha through a deliberate lie with the intent to conceal;
such a lie likewise arises from delusion,
just as in the case of the path of action consisting of lying.
The two paths of vocal action— slander and harsh speech—
should be understood to be likewise according to their respective circumstances.
Furthermore, if one engages in frivolous speech for the sake of amusement, [it constitutes a path of action].
Or, one may engage in frivolous speech (sambhinna-pralāpa) in order to manifest oneself as being wise;
or, one may engage in frivolous speech for the sake of wealth, profit, fame, or pleasure.
This is called the path of action of frivolous speech born of greed.
If one utters frivolous speech based on the nine occasions of malice, it is called the karmic path of frivolous speech born of hatred;
if, within that [frivolous speech], one seeks what is true or seeks what is firm, [it is otherwise].
To engage in frivolous speech for the sake of seeking liberation or for the sake of seeking the Dharma is called the course of action of frivolous speech born of delusion.
Furthermore, if one, with respect to the wealth and material possessions of another sentient being who is not an enemy,
first grasps their characteristics and, through the dominant power of hope and pursuit, gives rise to such a thought:
Whatever vows they may have shall belong to me.
Furthermore, that which arises from craving and gives rise to craving is called the karmic path of covetousness born of greed.
If one does not regard another's wealth as desirable,
yet gives rise to such a thought solely through the predominant power of the nine grounds for resentment, thinking:
"Whatever belongs to that person shall all belong to me."
Furthermore, when greed arises from hatred,
it is called the karmic path of desire born of hatred.
If one holds such a view:
All those who wish to seek Rudra,
Viṣṇu, Śakra, or Brahmā, the Lord of the World;
In the World of Many Wonders,
one who fixes the mind and dwells there frequently will obtain great merit and blessings.
One should form this intention and fix the mind, dwelling there frequently.
It is called the path of action of sensual desire born of delusion when, for the sake of wealth, profit, reputation, or pleasure,
one gives rise to a harmful intent toward other sentient beings,
rather than merely conceiving feelings of enmity or aversion toward them.
That is to say, they have been our enemies throughout the long night.
Furthermore, when hatred arises from craving,
it is called the path of action of hatred born of greed.
Furthermore, if, due to the predominant power of the nine grounds for resentment,
one gives rise to a harmful mind toward an adversary,
this is called the path of action of hatred born from hatred. This applies whether one abides in these [Buddhist] teachings or in the teachings of non-Buddhists.
Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas there may be who loathe the views of others,
[they do so] toward those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold those views and who are associated with them.
To give rise to a harmful mind is called the path of action of hatred born of delusion.
Furthermore, if one forms such a thought:
Regarding those who hold the view that negates giving and so forth—
as explained at length—
they nevertheless receive great offerings, clothing, and other requisites from kings and others.
By the dominant power of this very principle, one gives rise to such a view;
this is called the path of action of wrong view born of greed.
If one forms such a thought:
"There is giving, there is love," and so forth, as explained at length.
One who holds such a view contradicts and harms me.
I should not now hold the same view as my enemy.
It is due to his hatred and malice that he gives rise to such a view,
[claiming] "there is no giving, there is no love," and so forth, as explained at length.
This is called the path of action consisting of wrong view born of hatred.
If one reflects upon, deliberates over, and examines phenomena in an improper manner,
through this means, the vitarka and vicāra that are induced give rise to wrong view.
This is called the path of action consisting of wrong view born of delusion.
Furthermore, regarding the path of action of killing:
three [factors] constitute the preliminary effort, while it is brought to completion through hatred.
As it is with the path of action of killing,
so it is with the paths of action of harsh speech and malice;
the same applies to the path of action of taking what is not given.
Third, there are those whose preparation is by means of greed and whose completion is also by means of greed,
such as the paths of action of taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and covetousness; it is the same for these as well.
Excluding the path of action consisting of wrong view,
the remaining paths of action have three as their preliminary means and are completed by three;
the path of action of wrong view has three as its preliminary means and is completed by delusion.
Furthermore, there are killing, sexual misconduct,
lying, divisive speech,
harsh speech, and malice.
These six courses of action arise among sentient beings.
The course of action of taking what is not given arises with respect to material possessions;
the course of action of frivolous speech arises with respect to names and bodies.
The paths of action of wrong view arise from various courses of conduct.
Furthermore, through three causes and conditions,
unwholesome paths of action become fully perfected in their nature as evil and unwholesome.
What are the three?
First, because of the fault of intrinsic nature;
second, because of the fault of causes and conditions.
Because they are defiled by the faults of the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*),
herein [are included] the volition (*cetanā*) induced by killing,
up to and including the volition associated with it that is induced by wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
All such [actions] are called "evil" because they are defiled by nature and unwholesome by nature;
they are so designated due to their intrinsic fault when they are instigated by the entanglements of intense greed, hatred, and delusion.
This is also called "the fault of causes and conditions.
It constitutes a grave and evil nature, a supreme unwholesome state,
capable of inducing superior and undesirable results.
If it reaches its ultimate limit, this too is called "due to the fault of defilement";
it constitutes an extremely grave evil and a supreme unwholesome state,
capable of inducing superior and undesirable results.
Why is this? Because if one employs a defiled mind,
one can bring about for others suffering that is undesirable and devoid of joy.
Due to the power of that person’s mental state of suffering,
they are able to give rise to the thought of a suffering *pudgala*,
whereby they immediately incur a vast transgression.
Therefore, this is called the fault of defilement.
Even though they do not give rise to such a conceptual mind,
[they still harm] those who bring about suffering for me.
One will certainly encounter a great offense;
indeed, by the very nature of things, one encounters a great offense,
just as a magnet, though it does not form an intention, [attracts iron].
All iron that comes into proximity with me adheres to me;
for such is the natural law that whatever is near iron adheres to the magnet without the exertion of effort.
The principle herein should be understood to be likewise.
The analogies of the sun and the jewel should also be understood in this way.
Furthermore, there is no distinct entity existing apart from volition (cetanā).
The mutual dependence between that [volition] and its power from birth onwards is called "staining" (*vāsanā*);
one should know that this is merely a transformation of this very volition.
It is originated by the power of that [cause],
just as the various qualities of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion are produced by the power of the karma and majesty of the four great elements.
It is not that there exist such various natures separately outside of the primary elements (mahābhūta);
rather, it is precisely these primary elements that undergo such transformation through the power of karma.
Just as they transform through the force of the power of karma, so too do they transform through the conditions [of other factors].
It should be understood that the transformation through the power of conditions for the application of the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda-prayoga*) is likewise so.

Furthermore, it was as when the Māra-king deluded and seduced the minds of immeasurable Śāleyyakas, brahmins, and householders, causing them to perceive the World-Honored One as having become perverse and violent.
It is not that some distinct dharma is added to those minds and called "delusive enchantment" (māyā); rather,
it is solely through the application and majestic power of Māra that those various minds are produced and transformed into something extremely violent and evil.
The principle herein should be understood to be likewise.
Furthermore, regarding the karma of performance and accumulation as previously described,
if it is by means of the five causes and conditions as previously stated:
When extremely heavy karma is accomplished,
it is called "karma of certain retribution.
That which is contrary to this is called "karma of uncertain retribution."
Furthermore, there are four types of karma:
first, that which is determinate regarding its maturation;
second, that which is determinate regarding its timing.
In three cases both are determinate;
in four cases both are indeterminate.
This applies to all unwholesome states belonging to the arhats.
Karma that is certain to be experienced was either performed in a previous life or performed during this very life while one was still in the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*).
When one is afflicted by even slight and minor suffering,
it is said that the karmic retribution has already ripened;
this is so if one has already undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
Because the seeds of karmic retribution have been forever severed, nothing whatsoever is experienced.
Why is this? It is because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, based himself upon a continuum that is not yet liberated.
This is because it establishes the karma that is definitely experienced.
Question: If at one and the same time one both drags and seizes a sentient being to steal them and then cuts off their life, should this be called one karma or two karmas?
Answer: It should be said that there are two types of karma, because they proceed rapidly.
Regarding these two types of karma, [the distinction arises] through overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
This is called "one.
If one thinks, "I shall draw that [object] toward me," this is the first volition (*cetanā*).
At the very moment of stealing, he further thinks, "I shall seize and kill him.
This is the second volition.
However, at the time he drags him away, he does not seize him.
When one squeezes [the object], at that moment there is no pulling;
because it rotates so rapidly, one gives rise to the conceit of superiority (adhimāna), thinking it occurs all at once.
Therefore, in this case, it should be said that there are two actions.
Furthermore, briefly stated, there are three causes and conditions by which karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karma*) is established.
What are these three?
First, because the field (*kṣetra*) is vast.
Second, because the volition is vast;
third, because the continuity is pure.
The field becomes vast by way of five aspects.
First, there is that which arises from abiding in the superior intention for the primary benefit and happiness of all sentient beings;
this refers to the meditative attainment of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samāpatti*).
Second, it arises from the foremost dwelling that protects the minds of all sentient beings,
namely, the meditative concentration of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*). Third,
it arises from the foremost noble dwelling that resembles the bliss of the tranquility of nirvana, namely, the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Fourth, having already attained the restraint of non-action regarding all unwholesome states;
that is, the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
Fifth, the ultimate culmination of the extremely pure continuum.
This refers to the great community of bhikṣus, headed by Arhats and Buddhas;
such is called the vastness of the field.
If, in this regard, one possesses profound, earnest, and pure faith, [one attains great fruit].
To relinquish pure wealth is called the nature of vast intentionality. If,
in a previous life, one [gave] clothing or other items bestowed by others...
Because body, speech, and mind do not constitute obstacles,
nor does one contemplate giving rise to a defiled mind; thus,
there being no obstruction, it does not hinder that continuum.
One should know that this is called the purity of continuity.
If one possesses all three of these causal conditions,
one should know that such karma is certain to be experienced in the present life.
It may be experienced either in this life or in a future life.
If one performs unwholesome karma through three types of causes and conditions that are the opposite of these,
it should be known that it likewise becomes fixed as to be experienced in the present life.
There may be a certain momentary action that, once produced, is to be experienced solely in the present life;
or there may be a certain momentary action that, once produced, is both to be experienced in the present life and to be experienced upon rebirth.
There are cases where karma produced in a single moment is experienced throughout all three periods of time.
For example, a single thread, though minute in measure, can support a flower;
yet once it has bound the flower, its strength is exhausted and it can no longer hold it.
Furthermore, there is one thread that can support two flowers;
once it has tied them again, its strength is exhausted.
There is also another thread that can support many flowers.
Once many flowers have been bound together, their power is exhausted.
It is like flowing water: its nature is slight, and its force is spent after flowing for a single step.
There is a second kind of water whose nature is somewhat greater, and its force is spent only after flowing for two steps.
There is a third kind of water whose nature is vast; it flows for many paces before its power is exhausted.
It is like a drop of vinegar, whose nature is weak and thin: it can only sour that single drop of water and cannot sour much more.
There is a second drop whose nature is somewhat more pungent and sour;
these two drops cannot sour many [other drops].
There is another sour drop whose nature is even more pungent, such that it can sour a great many drops of water.
The principles regarding the distinctions among these various karmas should be understood in the same way.
Furthermore, the ten unwholesome courses of action are bound exclusively to the desire realm and can only induce maturation within the desire realm.
Beings are many in the evil realms and few in the good realms;
furthermore, all karma leading to the evil realms has already been completely eliminated at the stage of the fruit of stream-entry.
If ordinary worldlings have become free from desire in this world or are born in a higher realm,
they have all suppressed [the defilements] but have not yet permanently severed them.
As for those who have attained the fruit of non-returner, whether their bodies still abide here or they are born in a higher realm, [they have likewise suppressed them].
And for Arhats,
all unwholesome karmas are utterly severed.
This is also the case for those who have already entered the stage of pure superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).
A bodhisattva completely and utterly severs all unwholesome karma solely by means of being sustained by the power of non-forgetfulness;
it is not because they have attained dissociation from the afflictions.
Furthermore, volition (cetanā) is karma but not a path of action (karmapatha).
Killing and so forth, up to frivolous speech, are both karma and paths of action.
Covetousness, malice, and wrong view are paths of action but not karma.
The remaining analytical texts concerning these paths of action will not appear again hereafter.
The subsequent summary verse says:
Nature, characteristics, extensive and concise [explanations], The preparatory stages, and lightness and heaviness.
"Increase and decrease, as well as yoga, The drawing forth of results, and the determination of arising—
Thus has the determination of the paths of action been explained.
Now I shall explain the determination of the defilement of birth."
Regarding the meaning of birth as a form of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) as previously explained,
it should be understood that this birth is, in brief, of eleven types.
The first is birth solely in the realms of pleasure.
That is to say: first, a portion of the gods;
second, those born in states of constant suffering, namely, the various hell-beings (nāraka).
Third, birth mixed with pleasure and pain;
this refers to a portion of gods, humans, ghosts, and animals.
Fourth, birth that is neither painful nor pleasant.
This refers to a portion of the devas: first,
those born in a state that is entirely impure,
namely, the ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Sixth is birth that is entirely pure,
which refers to Bodhisattvas who have already attained mastery.
Seventh is birth that is both pure and impure.
This refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the form and formless realms;
and those born in the eight states that are impure yet conducive to purification,
namely, those in the desire realm who possess the nature for parinirvāṇa and are born in a state of leisure (*kṣaṇa*).
Ninth, birth in a pure yet impure place;
that is, birth as an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) in the form or formless realms.
Tenth, birth in an impure and impure place.
This refers to an ordinary person born in the desire realm who lacks the nature for parinirvāṇa;
or one who, even if possessing the nature for parinirvāṇa, is born in a state lacking leisure;
or one born in any of the eleven states of complete impurity.
This refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have been born in the form or formless realms and are not ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"For a long night, you have increased the *kaṭasi* and constantly received drops of blood."
What is called *kaṭhalla*?
It refers to craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The term "craving" and the name "*kaṭhalla*" are synonymous.
This statement indicates the inclusion of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
"Constantly receiving drops of blood" indicates the inclusion of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
The Blessed One, referring to the defilement of death, spoke these words:
"There are five who, though not insane, act as if they were insane. What are these five?"
First, those who dismember limbs refers to those who,
having other means of livelihood,
yet delight in analyzing their own limbs and members in order to sustain themselves.
This is called the first instance of acting like one who is insane, though not actually insane.
Second, the stingy and greedy person refers to one who is obscured by stinginess and greed.
Due to the causes and conditions of stinginess and greed, one neither consumes nor gives away the wealth and treasures acquired;
yet at the end of life, these great treasuries are suddenly and pointlessly squandered.
This is called the second instance of acting like a madman without being mad.
Third, regarding those who take pleasure in being born in the heavens:
although there are other means for birth in the heavens consisting of various sublime practices of body, speech, and mind,
they instead delight in the false attachment of throwing themselves into fire, drowning in water, or leaping from high cliffs.
To take one's own life in order to create the cause for rebirth in heaven is called the third instance of acting like a madman without being mad.
Fourth is the one who delights in liberation.
That is to say, there are yet other means for liberation consisting of the eightfold noble path,
yet they delight in falsely clinging to various ascetic practices that only oppress and afflict themselves as the cause of liberation.
This is called the fourth instance of acting like one who is insane though not actually insane.
Fifth is the lamentation for the deceased;
that is, [acting] based on the conditions of grieving for those who have passed away.
They wail various lamentations, lacerating and clawing their own bodies,
smearing themselves with ashes, plucking out their hair, and abstaining from food,
thus destroying themselves in their desire to cause the deceased to return to life as before.
This is called the fifth instance of acting like one who is insane, though not actually insane.
Furthermore, a verse is spoken:
"In the world there is no certainty; Through inversion, one conceives of a self."
Parents and wives, brothers and friends;
a stepmother becomes one's wife, and a wife again becomes a daughter-in-law;
a daughter-in-law turns into a servant, or else becomes the wife of an enemy.
A father once becomes a son; a son again becomes an enemy, and an enemy again becomes a slave. Or one becomes a servant and the like;
a former king becomes a minister, and a minister again becomes destitute.
Or those born in villages as lowly persons, despised and held in contempt by the world;
having once been Brahmins, they have passed through various stages to become members of the three [lower] castes,
or even Caṇḍālas, Pukkasas, and the like.
Throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of lifetimes,
acting as father and son, as well as enemy and so forth,
he manifests various forms and types among the multitudes like a phantom being.
Ordinary beings wander through the realms of existence; likewise, they manifest many bodies.
With afflictions and karma as their causal conditions, various formations are repeatedly accumulated, arising like magical illusions.
Though encountering these manifold illusions, they are shrouded by ignorance;
constantly amidst all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), they take pleasure and attachment therein without ever wearying of them.
Having already deluded themselves, they smear themselves with ashes and wail in lamentation.
Where there is no cause for grief or sorrow, you have needlessly given rise to various afflictions;
having abandoned your kinsmen who are but conventional designations, you indulge in manifold personal lamentations,
casting aside the practice of the True Dharma as you raise your hands and wail in tears.
Confused and distracted by pride and arrogance, they repeatedly practice various forms of heedlessness;
such categories as these should be understood in detail and in their entirety.
Furthermore, during the kalpa of strife, there are four faults.
That is to say: the decline of lifespan,
the decline of well-being,
and the decline of merit.
All the prosperities of the world decline.
Furthermore, during the kalpa of strife,
sentient beings briefly cease to take account of one another in eight respects.
First, do not count upon the True Dharma;
second, do not count upon fame and reputation;
third, do not count upon one's clan and lineage.
Fourth, one does not count those who are worthy of compassion;
fifth, one does not count virtuous friends;
sixth, one does not count those possessed of merit.
Seventh, one does not enumerate those who have been kind.
Eighth, one does not enumerate friends and relatives.
[The links] proceed from volitional formations up to birth as the condition for aging and death.
How should the distinct meanings of these twelve links, beginning with ignorance, be understood?
Answer: Briefly, by way of five aspects.
First, by way of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Second, by way of intrinsic nature;
third, by way of karma;
fourth, by way of phenomena.
Fifth, by way of cause and effect.
Question: What is the characteristic of ignorance?
Answer: The characteristics of greed, hatred, and pride are the characteristics of ignorance.
The characteristic of calculating "I" and "mine," the characteristic of lack of shame and lack of dread,
and the characteristic of excessive heedlessness.
The characteristic of being naturally weak and dull;
the characteristic of being prone to sleep;
the characteristic of having a sorrowful and dejected mind.
The manifestation of various types of unwholesome karma and so forth are the characteristics of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of ignorance?
Answer: The general characteristics of their intrinsic nature have already been explained previously.
There is ignorance accompanied by latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and there is also awakened ignorance.
There is ignorance that functions in conjunction with the afflictions,
there is ignorance that functions independently and alone,
and there is ignorance that obscures and suppresses the nature of the mind.
There is ignorance that initiates karma;
there is non-afflicted ignorance;
and there is shameless ignorance.
There is also a firm ignorance, namely the ignorance possessed by those who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa.
Question: What is the function of ignorance?
Answer: To give rise to delusion regarding objects that are not directly perceived is the function of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Likewise, [this applies] to objects that are directly perceived, regarding inferior objects as superior objects.
The meaning of benefit,
the meaning of non-benefit,
and the meaning of reality.
The meaning of the perverse,
the meaning of the cause,
and the meaning of the fruit.
Thus, delusion arises;
this is the karma of ignorance.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of ignorant sentient beings.
It encompasses all classes of ignorant sentient beings:
first, those with deficient ignorance;
second, those with deranged ignorance.
Third, the delusion of distraction;
fourth, the delusion of intrinsic nature;
fifth, the delusion of attachment.
Sixth is the delusion of confusion;
seventh is the delusion of firmness;
eighth is the delusion of supremacy.
Ninth is the delusion of non-apprehension;
tenth is the delusion of direct perception.
Regarding the delusion of deficiency:
That is to say, there may be someone who lacks either the eye or the ear,
[and thus cannot perceive] the forms cognizable by the eye or the sounds cognizable by the ear.
Because they do not comprehend or understand any objects of experience whatsoever,
they are thus deluded.
Regarding those who are deranged and deluded:
it refers to a certain person who, having encountered oppression, or great suffering,
or a severe illness, or being tormented by pain.
Or again, epilepsy may cause the mind to become deranged;
because of this, one does not discern what is well done and what is ill done,
and is therefore deluded.
One who is distracted and deluded refers to someone whose mind is scattered toward various objects and is thus unable to discern what else is well-done or ill-done.
Therefore, there is delusion.
Regarding the nature of delusion:
it refers to a certain individual who, within the cycle of birth and death, has been so since beginningless time.
By their very nature, they do not understand suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they do not realize that sentient beings lack a self,
nor that phenomena lack a self.
Therefore, there is delusion.
One who clings to delusion refers to someone who has fallen among the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika).
For him, the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is the root;
he is unable to comprehend the various inclinations toward views,
and for this reason he is deluded.
Regarding those who are deluded and ignorant:
this refers to cases where a person experiences confusion regarding name and concept, or confusion regarding shape and dimension,
or confusion regarding color and appearance, or confusion regarding activity and function.
One cannot understand or comprehend phenomena in a state of confusion;
therefore, one is deluded. One who is firmly established in delusion is called "one of steadfast ignorance."
That is to say, there is someone who ultimately lacks the nature for parinirvāṇa;
their delusion is so firm by its very nature that even all the Buddhas cannot uproot it.
Regarding those with predominant delusion:
it refers to someone who constantly and uninterruptedly practices various wrong conducts,
and is further tormented by the manifold sufferings produced by the causes of such wrong conduct.
Although they know and see [the truth], they nevertheless rush toward it, becoming attached to and delighting in play;
moreover, those who practice with greed and so forth are also characterized by predominant delusion.
One who lacks understanding is a deluded person.
That is to say, there is someone who, because they have not heard, reflected upon,
or cultivated [the teachings], is unable to understand the Dharma or its meaning;
therefore, they are deluded.
To "directly perceive a fool" means,
for example, there is someone who directly perceives that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely impermanent, yet gives rise to the notion of permanence;
or who directly perceives that they are entirely suffering, yet gives rise to the notion of pleasure.
One perceives impurity directly yet gives rise to the notion of purity;
one perceives non-self directly yet gives rise to the notion of self;
one perceives directly the nature of sickness, the nature of old age, and the nature of death, yet gives rise to the notion of security and the notion of being free from affliction.
Furthermore, this ignorance acts as an obstacle in five respects:
first, it obstructs the joy of true knowledge;
second, it obstructs the attainment of the cessation of afflictions.
Third, they can obstruct the fulfillment of the noble path;
fourth, they can obstruct progress toward the happy realms;
fifth, they can obstruct all auspicious matters pertaining to the present life in the world.
Question: What is called the phenomenon of ignorance (*avidyā*)?
Answer: There are those who, due to ignorance, fall into the destiny of ignorance;
they are described as being deluded, yet not afflicted by delusion, not defiled by delusion, and not enticed by delusion.
This refers to abiding in latent ignorance (*anuśaya-avidyā*).
Alternatively, there is delusion that is afflicted by folly, yet is neither defiled by folly nor seduced by folly; this refers to ignorance comprised within the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
There may be one who is foolish, afflicted by delusion, defiled by delusion, yet not infatuated by delusion; that is to say,
due to the ignorance that initiates karma,
having initiated an evil deed, he feels shame for this unwholesome conduct.
There may be some who are foolish, afflicted by delusion, defiled by delusion, and enticed by delusion;
that is to say, due to ignorance, they give rise to various kinds of evil and unwholesome karma.
In this regard, they feel no shame for their misconduct. Herein,
due to the first three types [of afflictions], they are said to be "deluded" and have "fallen into the realm of ignorance," yet they are not called "fools."
By the latter type, one is called a foolish person.
Alternatively, there is the obscuration of phenomena known as ignorance (*avidyā*),
which exists within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
There is the ignorance that obscures the Dharma,
which exists in the form realm;
there is also the ignorance that clouds the Dharma.
This refers to those in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Question: What are called the causes and effects of ignorance (*avidyā*)?
Answer: The causes are as already explained in the *Maulī Bhūmi*.
The result refers to all the subsequent links of dependent origination (*paunarbhavika-aṅga*).
Furthermore, one is unable to comprehend *tathatā* and the meaning of the truths,
or else remains in doubt regarding them.
Or one may form a false certainty regarding this very life,
by means of inverted attachment to the principles of the truths— either exaggerating or diminishing them— due to [misconceptions of] impermanence and so forth,
or due to overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Or perhaps, due to self-contempt,
the remaining texts of the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* have not been further presented here.
Furthermore, as the Blessed One said:
With the eye as cause and visible forms as condition, visual consciousness arises;
and so on, up to: with the body as cause and tangibles as condition, tactile consciousness arises.
Furthermore, it is said:
Contact is the condition for feeling.
Furthermore, it is said that the attention capable of producing [consciousness] acts as the cause for the arising of the consciousness produced.
In this context, the eye and so forth are not the causes for the arising of visual consciousness and so forth;
nor is contact the cause for the arising of feeling;
nor is the generative attention the cause for the arising of the consciousness that is produced.
Since those various phenomena arise with their own respective seeds as their generative causes (*janakahetu*),
why is it stated here that the eye and so forth are the causes of visual consciousness and so forth?
It should be understood that this is explained based on the *sahabhū-āśraya* (simultaneous support) as a cause of induction (*ākṣepakahetu*).
It is not a cause of arising. Why is this?
Because it has the coexistent sense organs, such as the eye, as its basis.
The various consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, do not arise without a basis when they engage their respective objects;
likewise, feelings arise by depending upon the simultaneously occurring contact (sahabhū-sparśa).
Because the consciousness that arises depends upon the attention (manasikāra) capable of producing it simultaneously,
the arising consciousness does not lack a basis. Therefore,
in these various instances, the Blessed One [taught as follows].
This is stated in reference to the inducing cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) as subsumed under the co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*),
and not in reference to the producing cause (*janana-hetu*); or it is stated in reference to the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-hetu*).
Why is this? An eye that has already ceased cannot serve as the support for an eye-consciousness that has already arisen;
the same applies to the ear and the other faculties.
A contact that has already ceased cannot serve as the basis for a feeling that has already arisen;
nor can an attention that has already ceased and produced [its effect] serve as the basis for a consciousness that has already arisen from it.
Furthermore, there are briefly four types of sequential order in dependent origination:
first, the sequence of attraction;
second, the sequence of production.
Third, the sequence of the enjoyment of objects;
fourth, the sequence of the experience of suffering:
ignorance conditions volitional formations, and volitional formations condition consciousness.
This is the sequence of attraction:
consciousness conditions name-and-form, and name-and-form conditions the six sense bases.
This is the sequence of arising.
With the six sense bases as condition, there is contact; with contact as condition, there is feeling.
This is the sequence of the enjoyment of objects once [birth] has arisen.

With feeling as condition, there is craving; with craving as condition, there is clinging; with clinging as condition, there is becoming; with becoming as condition, there is birth; and with birth as condition, there is aging and death.
This concludes the sequence of the suffering of experience (*upabhoga-duḥkha*).
No further explanatory texts regarding this section appear hereafter.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle Sixty.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 61.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
In the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, regarding the four sections on the three stages beginning with "with vitarka and vicāra," it is as stated in the sūtra spoken by the Blessed One to King Udayana:
at one time, that king went to where the Buddha was.
Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he said to the World-Honored One:
"World-Honored One, there is a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa who comes to my place."
Because of these untruthful faults,
he confronted me with reproaches and admonitions;
yet at that time, my mind gave rise to no regret, vexation, or sorrow.
Why is this? Because when one examines these faults,
they are not seen at all within one's own person.
Furthermore, there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who come to me and [speak] of non-authentic merits.
Although they were present before me and praised and exhorted me,
at that time my mind did not give rise to joy or exultation. Why was this?
Having observed these merits,
I did not perceive them within my own person at all; thus,
those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, having failed [to find them], withdrew and returned.
I then dwelt alone in a secluded and quiet chamber,
giving rise to this thought and engaging in deliberation and investigation:
"How shall I come to know the true faults and true virtues of kings?"
If I were to know them, I would abandon their faults and cultivate their virtues.
But which śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa is able to discern the true faults and true virtues of kings?
"Furthermore, he is able to provide me with a broad exposition.
Having thus investigated and reflected, he then thought:
"Only my World-Honored One is the All-Knowing One and the All-Seeing One."
"I shall certainly come to understand the true faults and true virtues of all kings.
I shall now go to the presence of the Blessed Buddha to inquire about this matter."
Therefore, I have now come to the presence of the Buddha to request a definitive resolution of this matter.
I only pray that the Tathāgata will reveal it for me:
O World-Honored One, what are the true faults of kings?
"What are the true merits of kings?
Having made this request,
at that time the World-Honored One—
He addressed King Priyadarśin, saying:
"Great King, Great King!
Now you ought to clearly understand both the faults of a king and the virtues of a king."
The doors of a king’s decline, the doors of a king’s skillful means,
the qualities that are dear to a king, and those qualities that can bring about what is dear to a king—
what are called the faults of a king?
Great King, you should know that there are,
in brief, ten kinds of faults of a king.
If a king is possessed of such faults,
then even though he possesses great treasuries, great ministers, and a great army,
he is not to be relied upon or taken as a refuge.
What are the ten?
First, one's lineage is not noble;
second, one does not attain mastery.
Third, their nature is violent and evil;
fourth, their outbursts of anger are fierce and intense;
fifth, they are extremely stingy with favors.
Sixth, accepting the words of the wicked and sycophantic;
seventh, acting without reflection and contrary to established rules;
eighth, disregarding wholesome dharmas.
Ninth, he is ignorant of distinctions and forgets the kindness he has received.
Eleventh, he is self-indulgent and habitually practices negligence.
What is meant by a king whose lineage is not noble?
This refers to a king who is born into a lower class of royal family rather than one of long-standing nobility;
or, though born into such a royal family,
he is the son of a low-born woman and thus not a legitimate heir.
Or he may be the son of a great minister, a state counselor, a royal preceptor, or one of the various officials;
such is called a king of low lineage.
What is meant by a king who lacks sovereignty?
This refers to a king who, being constrained by his ministers, chief counselors, state preceptors, and various officials,
does not act according to his own will in performing his duties or bestowing gifts upon his subordinates.
Even regarding the five excellent sensual pleasures, he does not enjoy them with the delight and playfulness he desires;
this is called a king who lacks self-mastery.
What is meant by a king whose nature is violent and cruel?
This refers to a king, his various ministers, or other persons who,
when even a minor disagreeable incident occurs in some respect,
immediately dismisses them to their faces and utters harsh and abusive words.
Roaring with rage and resentment, he remains with a frowning face.
At times, giving vent to his indignation, even when not face-to-face,
he turns away from that person toward others and performs acts such as excluding or insulting them in their absence.
Even if one does not face them directly, nor turn one's back toward others while acting before them, yet performs acts such as reviling and scolding; nevertheless,
one harbors internal resentment and indignation,
maintaining a mind of malice and harm, and a mind of enmity and hatred.
Yet, they do not maintain a state of anger for a long duration in a continuous succession that is not abandoned;
furthermore, there is internal resentment and dejection,
harboring a mind of malice and harm, and a mind of enmity and hatred.
Furthermore, for a long period of time, they maintain a state of resentment in a continuous succession without relinquishing it;
by means of such states, they are violent and cruel both face-to-face and behind one's back.
Malice and cruelty;
temporary malice and cruelty;
long-term malice and cruelty.
This is what is meant by a king being inherently violent and cruel.
Great King, you should know that long-term violence and cruelty result in great transgression.
It is not others. What is meant by a king who is prone to violent outbursts of anger?
It refers to a king who...
Whenever the various ministers committed even minor transgressions or slight violations,
their fiefs and stipends were immediately confiscated and their wives and concubines seized;
or else they were punished with severe penalties.
This is called a king who is prone to fierce outbursts of anger.
What is meant by a king whose favors and kindness are meager?
It refers to a king who...
Although the various ministers served and attended upon him with the utmost purity and in a manner that accorded perfectly with his mind,
they comforted and exhorted him only with faint, feeble, and gentle words.
In bestowing ranks and emoluments as rewards for meritorious services,
they were neither complete nor in accordance with established custom;
some were diminished, while others were delayed.
Or having first delayed or shown resentment, he only then bestows [the gift].
This is called a king whose favors are meager. What is meant by a king who listens to the words of the wicked and sycophantic?
If there is a king whose ministers and officials are actually not wise, yet possess the pride of wisdom; who are greedy,
corrupt, and partisan, and are unacquainted with the laws and regulations.
With a disposition intent on rebellion and failing to cultivate virtuous governance,
he listens to and places his trust in the advice and counsel offered by such individuals as these.
Due to these causes and conditions, the king’s affairs, wealth, reputation, and virtuous administration all decline and perish.
This is what is meant by a king who accepts the words of the wicked and sycophantic.
What is meant by a king whose actions are unreflective and contrary to established rules?
It refers to a king who...
They are unable to investigate thoroughly,
they do not examine with care; they are unable to discern wisely,
they do not deliberate with care, regarding those various matters of state and confidential affairs.
He appoints those who are unfit for the commission,
yet does not appoint those who are fit for the commission;
he fails to employ those who are fit for service.
Those unfit for service were driven into labor;
those deserving of rewards were punished;
and those deserving of punishment were rewarded.
Furthermore, the ministers failed to properly observe the protocols established by the former kings;
consequently, when they were present at great assemblies,
their discourse was interrupted even before it had concluded.
Without respect or trepidation, they raise remonstrances and disputes;
they do not follow the instructions as intended, yet claim to practice them well;
they do not dwell correctly within the king’s commands.
This is called a king performing actions that are unreflective and contrary to established rules.
What is meant by a king who disregards wholesome qualities?
It refers to a king who—
They do not believe in future lives, nor do they understand them.
Because they neither believe in nor understand future lives,
they [lack conviction] regarding the pleasant and unpleasant fruits of wholesome and unwholesome actions in the future.
They are unable to have faith and understanding.
Because they lack faith and understanding, they are devoid of shame and remorse,
and thus commit three kinds of unwholesome actions— of body, speech, and mind— in accordance with their own whims.
When a king is unable to practice giving from time to time, cultivate merit, observe the fasts, and train in the precepts,
he is said to be one who disregards wholesome dharmas.
What is meant by a king who lacks discernment and forgets the kindness he has received?
It refers to a king who,
regarding his various ministers, counselors, state preceptors, and officials,
possesses a perverted mind and lacks the skillful discernment to distinguish between their loyalty, integrity, artistic talents, and wisdom.
Because of ignorance, one conceives the notion of faithfulness and trustworthiness toward that which is not faithful and trustworthy;
one conceives the notion of lack of faithfulness and trustworthiness toward that which is faithful and trustworthy;
and one conceives the notion of skill toward that which lacks skill.
One perceives skill where there is no skill;
one perceives wholesome wisdom in the presence of unwholesome wisdom,
and perceives unwholesome wisdom in the presence of wholesome wisdom.
Due to such a perversion of mind, he honors, respects,
cherishes, and supports ministers who are unfaithful, lacking in skill,
and possessed of evil wisdom.
Those ministers who were loyal, trustworthy, skilled in the arts,
and possessed of wisdom were instead treated with contempt;
furthermore, many of the ministers had reached an advanced age and were in decline.
Having served and attended upon them for a long night,
one comes to realize they possess no power, no strength, and no courage;
consequently, one ceases to respect or love them.
If he does not confer rank or emolument, nor reward their merits;
or if they are treated with contempt and left unheeded—
such a king is said to be ignorant of distinctions and to forget the favors he has bestowed.
What is meant by a king who is consistently self-indulgent and exclusively given to negligence?
It refers to a king who is completely immersed in the five excellent sensual pleasures.
Devoted to amusements and delighting in their pursuit,
he is unable from time to time to exert himself through skillful means to perform his duties or to provide for his ministers;
this is called a king who is entirely self-indulgent and exclusively given over to negligence.
If there is a king who possesses these ten kinds of faults,
although he may have great treasuries, great ministers, and a great army, [he shall not succeed].
And it cannot be relied upon or looked up to.
Great King, you should know that these are the ten faults.
The first is the fault of the royal lineage;
the remaining nine are the faults of the king's own nature.
What are called the virtues of a king?
Great King, you should know that the virtues of a king are,
in brief, of ten kinds.
If a king accomplishes such virtues,
although he lacks great treasuries, lacks great ministers, and lacks a great army,
he is still worthy of being looked up to and relied upon.
What are the ten? First, noble lineage;
second, the attainment of great sovereignty.
Third, their nature is not violent or malicious;
fourth, their outbursts of anger are slight;
fifth, their beneficence is intense and profound.
Sixth, receiving words with integrity;
seventh, reflecting deeply on one's actions and acting in accordance with proper decorum;
eighth, cherishing and longing for wholesome dharmas.
Ninth, he possesses excellent knowledge of distinctions and recognizes the kindness shown to him.
Tenth, he does not indulge himself and does not act with negligence.
What is meant by a king whose lineage is noble?
It refers to a king who is born into a royal family of similar status and was noble in his previous lives.
He is a son who resembles [his father].
This is what is meant by a king whose lineage is noble and exalted.
What is meant by a king who has attained great sovereignty?
That is to say, there is a king who,
according to his own desires, performs his proper duties, rewards his ministers,
and enjoys himself with delight and play amidst the five exquisite sensual pleasures.
Regarding all the ministers, counselors, state preceptors, and various officials,
his issuance of commands and proclamations is unimpeded;
such is called a king who has attained great sovereignty.
What is meant by a king who is not violent or cruel by nature?
It refers to a king whose various ministers and officials, wherever they may be, [act accordingly].
Even when performing superior deeds that result in undesirable consequences,
he is naturally able to endure them; he does not manifest expulsion or rejection,
nor does he utter coarse words or display outbursts of rage.
To speak at length, up to and including not giving rise to resentment;
nor turning one's back to perform such acts;
nor harboring within one's mind the entanglement of concealed anger.
Nor does he harbor a mind of resentment for a long night, continuing it without relinquishing;
he does not manifest violence and cruelty, nor turn his back on violence and cruelty,
nor conceal violence and cruelty, nor persist in violence and cruelty.
This is called a king who is not violent or cruel by nature.
What is meant by a king whose outbursts of anger are slight?
It refers to a king who...
Although his various ministers may have committed great transgressions or grave violations,
he does not entirely strip them of their fiefs and emoluments or seize their wives and concubines;
nor does he punish them with severe penalties.
He inflicts punishment according to the gravity of the offense.
This is called a king whose indignation is mild. What is meant by a king whose favor is intense?
It refers to a king who...
The various ministers and officials attend upon him with upright sincerity, serving and protecting him;
their minds are pure and their dispositions are harmonious.
From time to time, they console and encourage him with words that are correct, perfect, and gentle.
He fully bestows ranks, emoluments, and rewards for meritorious service,
ensuring that those who labor do not suffer depletion, delay, exhaustion, or resentment;
thus they can provide offerings with ease and serve without difficulty.
This is called the king’s intense and powerful benevolence.
What is meant by the king receiving upright speech?
It refers to a king who...
The various ministers are truly wise and free from pride regarding their wisdom;
they are untainted and impartial, well-versed in the legal codes,
and with hearts free from rebellion, they delight in cultivating wholesome dharmas.
By listening to, accepting, and placing trust in the words and counsel offered by such persons as these,
for this reason, the affairs of state, wealth and treasures, reputation, and wholesome dharmas will all flourish and increase.
This is called a king who accepts upright counsel.
What is meant by a king who acts with careful reflection and in accordance with proper rules?
It refers to a king who...
He is capable of investigating and is able to investigate thoroughly;
he is capable of deliberating and is able to deliberate thoroughly regarding various affairs and secret matters concerning his ministers and officials.
Those unfit for appointment were not appointed;
those fit for appointment were appointed.
Those unfit for labor were not driven into service.
Those fit for labor were made to labor;
those deserving of reward were duly rewarded;
and those deserving of punishment were duly punished.
In all that he does, he deliberates and discriminates with care before acting,
never acting with haste or violence; furthermore,
he is able to skillfully maintain the ancestral protocols of the former kings among his ministers.
Consequently, although these ministers were present at banquets,
they never spoke to interrupt the ongoing discourse; rather, they waited until the speaker had finished,
and then, out of reverence and awe, they would offer their counsel and remonstrance.

One who skillfully practices according to the king’s instructions and is able to dwell correctly in accordance with the king’s commands is said to be one whose actions are well-considered and who properly conforms to the established rules.
What is meant by a king who looks back with affection upon the wholesome Dharma?
It refers to a king who has faith and knowledge of the world beyond.
Through knowing by means of faith, one is able to correctly believe and understand that pure and impure actions will result in pleasant and unpleasant fruits in the future.
Through such belief and understanding, one becomes fully endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame.
Furthermore, he does not indulge his passions by committing the three types of misconduct of body, speech, and mind;
rather, from time to time, he reflects upon and practices generosity, cultivates merit, observes the fast-day vows, and trains in the precepts.
This is what is meant by a king who is mindful of and devoted to wholesome dharmas.
What is meant by a king who well understands distinctions and recognizes the kindness of those he has benefited?
It refers to a king who,
toward his various ministers, counselors, state preceptors, and officials—
With a mind free from inversion, he is able to skillfully discern the differences among ministers in terms of their loyalty, skill, and wisdom.
As for those ministers who possess loyalty, skill, and wisdom—
Whether something exists or does not exist, one knows it as it truly is;
regarding that which is non-existent, one treats it with indifference and distance,
while regarding that which is existent, one honors and loves it.
And he correctly accepts them.
Furthermore, there are various ministers who are aged and decrepit,
having served and attended him throughout the long night.
Although he knows that [the recipient] possesses no power, no strength,
and no valor, he nevertheless recalls past kindness and feels increasing respect and affection rather than contempt;
thus, ranks, emoluments, and rewards for meritorious service are distributed without fail.
This is called a king who well understands distinctions and recognizes the kindness he has received.
What is meant by a king who does not indulge himself and does not act with negligence?
It refers to a king who...
He does not sink into, become attached to, or indulge in play, love, or enjoyment regarding the five excellent sensual pleasures;
rather, from time to time, he exerts himself through skillful means to perform his duties and provide for his ministers.
This is called a king who does not act according to his own whims and does not practice heedlessness.
If a king is endowed with such qualities,
even though he lacks great treasuries, lacks great ministers, and lacks a large army, [he will still be successful].
And thus they may be taken as objects of refuge and veneration.
Great King, you should know that such are the ten kinds of royal virtues.
The first is called the quality of the lineage (*gotra-guṇa*);
the remaining nine are called the qualities of the essential nature (*svabhāva-guṇa*).
What is meant by the "gateways to the king's decline"?
"Great King, you should know that there are briefly five ways in which a king undergoes decline.
The first is to gather ministers without careful examination."
Second, although he observes carefully, he lacks gracious and wondrous conduct toward his ministers, even if such conduct exists at other times.
Third, he is exclusively given to negligence and does not attend to state affairs.
Fourth, he is exclusively given to negligence and does not guard the treasuries.
Fifth, they are exclusively devoted to negligence and do not practice the Dharma.
These five types are all called the gates of a king’s decline.
What is meant by a king who governs his ministers without proper discernment?
It refers to a king who is unable to investigate or thoroughly examine his ministers and officials,
and is unable to exercise discernment regarding them.
Without carefully examining the distinctions among their loyalty, trustworthiness, skills, and wisdom,
he took them as personal attendants, bestowed affection upon them,
granted them high ranks and emoluments, and conferred heavy rewards for their services.
They were entrusted with the most secret matters and repeatedly consoled with gentle words; yet,
much of the wealth and treasures committed to these ministers was squandered.
If they encounter an enemy, a wicked friend, or a military array, they will be the first to retreat and flee;
struck by fear and scattered, they will be defeated by others,
lingering behind the ranks and fleeing in flight without any sense of loyalty.
He practices deceitful conduct and employs evil stratagems to agitate the king’s administration.
This is called a king who fails to examine carefully when appointing his ministers.
What is meant by a king who, although he examines carefully when appointing his ministers, lacks gracious and wondrous conduct, such that even if it exists, it is untimely?
It refers to a king who,
although he is naturally capable of investigating and thoroughly examining his ministers,
and naturally capable of discerning and thoroughly discerning their distinctions in terms of loyalty, skill, and wisdom, nevertheless gathers them as his personal attendants.
He did not show them special favor,
nor did he bestow upon them titles and emoluments in accordance with their merit;
even the most confidential matters were not entrusted to them.
He did not frequently speak gentle words or manifest signs of consolation;
later, on one occasion, the king encountered an enemy or a hostile army,
and so forth, until a great state of terror arose and a threat to his life presented itself.
At that time, the king was bestowing special favor upon the minister;
as it is said at length, he even repeatedly comforted and exhorted him with gentle words.
Then the assembly of ministers said to one another:
"Knowing that the King, due to his current state of peril and urgency,
is only practicing this sublime conduct toward us for the time being and not with a long-term intention."
Although there may be those who possess loyalty, integrity, skill, and wisdom, these remain hidden and unmanifest.
This is called a king who, despite being skilled in observation, fails to provide kindness or sublime conduct to his ministers, even when they are present at the proper time.
What is meant by a king who exclusively practices negligence and fails to attend to his administrative duties?
It refers to a king who,
regarding those matters of state that ought to be conducted through conciliation and those tasks that must be accomplished, [neglects them].
Yet they do not, from time to time, dwell alone in seclusion,
nor do they engage in correct reflection, weighing,
and examining harmonious skillful means together with wise persons.
Likewise, regarding the affairs and duties to be performed and accomplished that involve estrangement;
the affairs and duties to be performed and accomplished that involve the giving of gifts;
and the affairs and duties to be performed and accomplished that involve military arrays.
Regarding the affairs and tasks to be accomplished by a powerful faction that ought to be supported,
he does not, from time to time, dwell alone in seclusion,
nor does he engage in correct reflection and deliberation together with wise persons.
From the method of observing discord and estrangement up to the method of gathering strong factions—
this is called a king who exclusively practices negligence and does not attend to his administrative duties.
What is meant by a king who exclusively practices negligence and fails to guard his treasuries?
It refers to a king who is negligent in his affairs, unskilled in conducting affairs,
who does not maintain his affairs, and does not inspect his affairs.
They do not restrict access to the royal gates, nor the palace gates, nor the treasuries.
They may frequent places of actors, musicians, jesters, and the like who engage in frivolous and dissolute behavior;
or they may indulge in the pleasures of gambling, board games, and other such diversions.
He squanders all his wealth and treasures without measure;
this is called a king who practices exclusively in negligence and fails to guard his treasuries.
What is meant by a king who practices exclusively in negligence and does not cultivate the practice of Dharma?
It refers to a king who is known throughout the world for being gentle, honest,
wise, and eloquent.
Having attained liberation through skillful means,
they delight in harmlessness and the dharma of harmlessness;
this applies to all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
I am unable to go frequently to pay my respects and inquire: what is wholesome and what is unwholesome;
what is blameworthy and what is blameless;
and what kind of actions lead to auspiciousness and bring one far away from all evils?
Even if he has heard [the teachings], he does not exert himself to practice according to what was taught;
he is unable to practice giving from time to time, plant roots of merit, observe the fast, or train in the precepts.
This is called a king who practices only negligence and does not cultivate the practice of the Dharma.
If there is a king who possesses these five doors of decline,
it should be known that this king will fall away from the benefits and purposes of both the present life and future lives.
This means that by means of the first four gates, one falls away from the benefits of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*),
and by means of the final gate, one falls away from the benefits of future lives (*sāmparāyika*).
What is called the "gate of royal skillful means" (*rājopāyamukha*)?
Great King, you should know that there are briefly five kinds of gates of royal skillful means. What are these five?
First, he carefully examines and receives his ministers;
second, he is able to bestow gracious and wondrous deeds upon them at the proper time;
third, he is free from negligence and focuses exclusively on state affairs.
Fourth, being heedful, he guards his treasury well.
Fifth, being heedful, he is single-mindedly devoted to the practice of the Dharma.
What is meant by a king who is able to observe and properly receive his ministers?
It refers to a king who,
regarding his ministers and others, is naturally capable of investigation and capable of thorough investigation;
naturally capable of discernment and capable of thorough discernment.
Distinguishing them by their loyalty, integrity, skill, and wisdom,
he appoints them as his personal attendants;
this is called a king who is able to skillfully examine and gather his ministers.
What is meant by a king who is able to skillfully perform the sublime practice of bestowing favors at the proper time?
It refers to a king who,
having carefully examined his various ministers, [bestows favors upon them].
He took him into his personal service and bestowed upon him special favor;
according to his capacity, he generously conferred ranks and emoluments, and granted him heavy rewards for his meritorious services.
He entrusted him with matters of the highest confidentiality and repeatedly consoled and encouraged him with gentle words.
At one time, he...
When the king encounters enemies, hostile friends, military arrays, or great terrors, and when the threat to his life is imminent,
he immediately exhausts all his resources to manifest his loyalty, faith, skill, and wisdom.
This is called a king who is able to skillfully perform acts of grace at the proper time.
What is meant by a king who is free from negligence and is single-mindedly attentive to his administrative duties?
It refers to a king who...
Regarding the affairs and duties to be performed for the sake of reconciliation and harmony,
he is able from time to time to dwell alone in seclusion,
or to engage in correct reflection and deliberation together with wise persons.
He observes the skillful means for reconciliation;
likewise, regarding the affairs and duties to be performed concerning those with whom he should sever ties,
and the affairs and duties to be performed concerning those to whom he should give gifts.
Regarding the affairs and tasks to be performed and accomplished concerning military arrays,
and regarding the affairs and tasks to be performed and accomplished concerning the recruitment and maintenance of powerful factions.
They are all able from time to time to dwell alone in seclusion,
or to engage in correct reflection, weighing and examining [the teachings] together with the wise—
ranging from the methods for severing [unwholesome states] to the methods for gathering a strong following.
This is called a king who is not negligent and is exclusively attentive to his administrative duties.
