What is meant by a king who is not negligent and skillfully guards his treasuries?
It refers to a king who...
He extensively undertakes enterprises and skillfully manages his affairs;
he maintains his undertakings well and examines them with care;
he strictly secures the royal gates, the palace doors, and the state treasuries.
Furthermore, regarding actors, musicians, jesters, and those who indulge in frivolous amusements,
he does not squander wealth and treasures through improper means,
nor does he become addicted to gambling, games, and the like.
This is called a king who is free from negligence and properly guards his treasuries.
What is meant by a king who is free from negligence and is exclusively devoted to the practice of the Dharma?
It refers to a king who...
He is known in the world for his gentleness and sincerity,
his intelligence and eloquence,
and his skillful means in attaining understanding and liberation.
It is harmless and brings happiness;
it is a Dharma that all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas should frequently visit and pay homage to.
He inquired: "What is wholesome and what is unwholesome?
What is with fault and what is without fault?
By performing what kind of karma can one bring about auspiciousness and remain far removed from all evils?"
Having heard this, he is well able to exert himself and practice according to the teaching;
furthermore, he is able from time to time to give gifts, plant roots of merit, observe the fast, and train in the precepts.
This is called a king who is free from negligence and is single-mindedly devoted to the practice of the Dharma.
If a king accomplishes these five doors of skillful means,
it should be known that this king does not fall away from the benefits of both the present life and future lives;
that is to say, by means of the first four doors, he does not fall away from the benefits pertaining to the present life.
Regarding the benefits of the final gateway, the Dharma of Non-retrogression:
Great King, you should know what is called the "Dharma beloved by kings.
Great King, you should understand this.
Briefly, there are five kinds of things that are desirable, delightful, pleasing, and agreeable to kings.
What are these five?
First, being respected and loved by the world;
second, possessing sovereign supremacy;
third, being able to crush enemies.
Fourth, one properly nurtures and maintains the body;
fifth, one is able to go to the happy realms.
These are the five kinds.
This is a dharma that is lovely, delightful, pleasing, and agreeable to the king.
How does it lead to the dharma that is lovely to the king?
Great King, you should know this.
Briefly stated, there are five kinds of qualities that can attract the affection of kings.
What are these five?
First, nurturing the world with kindness.
Second, being endowed with heroic vigor;
third, possessing skillful means;
fourth, correctly experiencing the objective sphere.
Fifth, the diligent practice of the Dharma.
What is meant by a king who nurtures the world?
It refers to a king who...
By nature, one is fundamentally content regarding wealth and treasures;
by nature, one is prudent and free from perverse greed or attachment.
One accumulates wealth and treasures as is appropriate, rather than seeking them through extensive or expansive endeavors.
Furthermore, there was a king whose nature was free from greed and stinginess,
who had accomplished the pure dharma of non-attachment.
With the treasures and wealth from his own treasury,
he bestowed gifts upon all who were poor, destitute, and without shelter, according to his strength and ability.
Furthermore, there was a king.
Gentle and patient, he frequently instructs the realm with mild words.
From time to time, he distributes ranks and emoluments according to what is appropriate.
He never assigns ministers tasks that exceed their capabilities, nor does he employ them in evil or excessively heavy labors.
Regarding all offenses that may be excused,
he immediately grants pardon;
regarding all offenses that cannot be excused, [he does not].
He governs and punishes according to reality, at the proper time, and in accordance with reason.
This is called a king nourishing the world through the grace of the Dharma of righteous governance.
Because the king receives and practices such a method of nourishing the world, [he brings about its welfare].
Consequently, he becomes an object of respect and affection for the world.
What is meant by a king being "endowed with heroism"?
It refers to a king who...
His strategic planning is tireless and his military tactics are perfected;
he subdues those not yet subdued and protects those already subdued.
He extensively carries out his affairs as previously described, up to and including not being excessively addicted to gambling, games, and the like.

Furthermore, he skillfully examines what ought and what ought not to be granted; regarding the officials and commoners who deserve punishment, he diligently and justly inflicts the appropriate penalties.
Those who ought to be nurtured, he properly nurtures.
This is called a king being fully endowed with valor.
Because the king practices such a dharma of being fully endowed with valor, [he attains this state].
Thus he is able to evoke sovereign supremacy.
What is meant by a king’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*)?
It refers to a king who...
Regarding the affairs and duties to be performed and accomplished in matters such as making peace and reconciliation,
and so forth, up to the affairs and duties to be performed and accomplished in matters such as securing the alliance of a powerful faction, as previously described.
He is able to correctly understand the methods for conciliation and reconciliation, up to the methods for winning over powerful factions.
This is called the king’s skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
Because the king practices such dharmas of skillful means, [he attains his goals].
Thus he is able to subdue all enemies.
What is meant by a king who correctly experiences his domain?
It refers to a king who...
He is skillfully able to calculate the increase and decrease of the treasury;
he dwells in equanimity, being neither extravagant nor parsimonious,
and makes use of various requisites— whether pure, impure, or sublime— with integrity.
They should be enjoyed according to what is appropriate for the season;
they should be enjoyed together with ministers,
assistants, and relatives, in an excellent location.
One enjoys various musical performances as a source of enjoyment;
one enjoys them without fault.
"Without fault" refers to times when one is afflicted by illness or distress.
One should eat what is suitable and avoid what is unsuitable.
When one is in good health, one should eat only after the previous meal has been digested;
if food has not yet been digested, or if one suffers from diarrhea after eating, one should not eat.
None of these should be eaten.
When those with whom one ought to eat are present,
one should not eat alone of exquisite and superior flavors.
He excludes all others.
This is called the king’s correct reception of his domain.
Because the king practices this dharma of correctly receiving his domain, [he attains such results].
Thus, he is able to skillfully sustain his own person.
What is meant by a king who diligently practices the Dharma?
It refers to a king who...
He is fully endowed with pure faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and wisdom.
In what way is a king said to be fully endowed with pure faith?
It refers to a king who...
He has conviction in future worlds;
he has conviction in the pure and impure actions of the future, as well as their pleasant and unpleasant fruits and maturations.
This is called a king who is endowed with pure faith.
What is meant by a king being endowed with pure ethical discipline?
It refers to a king who stays far removed from taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, lying, drinking intoxicants, and all other bases for negligence.
In this way, a king is said to be endowed with pure ethical discipline.
What is meant by a king being endowed with pure learning?
It refers to a king who...
Regarding the meaning of the present life, the meaning of future lives,
and the meanings of both the present and future lives,
they listen well, receive well, study, recite, and master these various sublime Dharma gates.
He applies his mind single-mindedly to study until he attains excellence and thorough mastery.
This is called a king being endowed with pure learning.
What is meant by a king being endowed with pure relinquishment?
It refers to a king who,
although surrounded by a multitude enshrouded in the defilement of stinginess,
maintains a mind that is constantly pure and free from the defilement of stinginess.
While dwelling in the household life, he constantly practices relinquishment, extends his hand in joyful giving,
delights in performing meritorious sacrifices, and is perfected in the virtue of generosity.
When practicing giving, he always delights in impartiality.
This is called a king who is endowed with pure relinquishment. What is meant by a king who is endowed with pure wisdom?

It refers to a king who understands, as they truly are, wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, those that are blameworthy and those that are blameless, those that should be cultivated and those that should not, and those that are superior or inferior, black or white.
He also knows, as they truly are, the various phenomena that arise through conditions in their extensive differentiation.
Even if, through a lapse of mindfulness, he should give rise to unwholesome greed, malice, anger, resentment, concealment,
vexation, stinginess, envy, deceit, guile, or crookedness.
When he lacks shame and dread of blame, possesses evil desires and wrong views,
yet his mind remains awakened and does not persist in them,
such a king is said to be endowed with pure wisdom.
This is called the king’s diligent practice of the Dharma;
by the king’s undertaking and practicing this Dharma,
he is able to go to the happy realms.
These five kinds [of qualities] are able to bring about the king’s desirable dharmas and can induce all benefits for kings in both the present life and future lives;
that is to say, the first four are able to bring about the king’s benefits in the present life.
The last type can bring about the benefit of the king's subsequent dharma.
Furthermore, Great King,
you should know that I have briefly explained the faults of a king.
The virtues of a king;
the gateways of a king’s decline;
and the gateways of a king’s skillful means.
These are the qualities dear to a king,
as well as those that can bring about such qualities;
therefore, Great King, you should practice and train in them.
The king’s faults should be avoided;
the king’s virtues should be cultivated;
and the king’s doors of decline should be shunned.
The king should cultivate and study the gateways of skillful means;
he should aspire to the qualities dear to a king;
and he should practice those methods capable of bringing about those qualities dear to a king.
Great King, if you can train yourself in this way,
you shall obtain all benefit and happiness.
Furthermore, as it has been said regarding the suffering of birth:
...up to the brief statement that the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
What is the suffering of birth?
It should be understood that this suffering consists of five aspects.
That is to say: because it is accompanied by manifold sufferings;
because it is accompanied by coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*);
and because it is the basis for manifold sufferings.
Because it is the basis for the afflictions (*kleśa*),
and because one cannot separate from its phenomena as one desires;
how is it suffering because it is accompanied by manifold sufferings?
This refers to those born in the hells and those in the realm of hungry ghosts who experience constant suffering;
as well as those born from a womb or from an egg,
who are pursued by various forms of grief and pain at the time of birth.
It is called "suffering" because it is accompanied by manifold sufferings.
How is it suffering because it is accompanied by *dauṣṭhulya* (coarseness)?
This means that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) within the three realms are accompanied by the *dauṣṭhulya* belonging to the category of afflictions (*kleśapakṣya*).
Because its nature is not pliant and it does not function with mastery,
it arises following the formations (*saṃskāra*) of sentient beings within the three realms; therefore,
it is called "suffering due to being accompanied by coarse heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulya*).
In what sense is it suffering because it is the basis for various forms of suffering?
It means that it is the basis for the various distinctions of suffering, such as aging and so forth.
In what sense is it suffering because it is the basis for the afflictions?
That is to say, having already taken birth,
one feels attachment toward objects of attachment, aversion toward objects of aversion,
and delusion toward objects of delusion.
Because of these causes and conditions, one dwells in a state of non-quiescence, with a body and mind that are agitated and lacking stability, which is suffering;
therefore, it is called "suffering because it is the basis for the afflictions.
What is "suffering because of being separated from things according to one's wishes"?
That is to say, all sentient beings who are born must die; birth is inevitably followed by death.
Whatever lifespan they possess has death as its limit and death as its ultimate end.
Such matters are not what they desire.
Due to these causes and conditions, one experiences only manifold suffering.
Therefore, because it is a phenomenon that separates one from what is desired, birth is said to be suffering. What is the suffering of old age?
It should be understood that this also occurs by way of five aspects.
It refers to suffering due to decline in five areas:
first, the decline of physical beauty;
second, the decline of vital energy and strength.
Third, because the faculties decline;
fourth, because the enjoyment of objects declines;
fifth, because the lifespan declines. What is the suffering of illness?
One should know that the suffering of illness also arises through five aspects:
first, because the nature of the body undergoes transformation and decay;
second, because one dwells extensively in the increase of sorrow and pain.
Third, because one does not joyfully enjoy desirable objects;
fourth, because one forcibly enjoys undesirable objects against one's will;
and fifth, because it causes the life-faculty to quickly depart and perish.
What is the suffering of death?
It should be known that this suffering also arises through five aspects:
first, because of being separated from beloved and abundant wealth and treasures.
Second, because of separation from beloved and flourishing friends;
third, because of separation from beloved and flourishing kinsmen;
fourth, because of separation from one's own beloved and flourishing self.
Fifth, because at the time of death one undergoes all manner of extremely heavy sorrows and sufferings.
What is the suffering of association with the disliked?
One should know that this suffering also arises through five aspects.
First, because encountering them gives rise to sorrow and suffering;
second, because they are the basis for the fear of punishment;
and third, because they are the basis for the fear of ill repute.
Fourth, because it is the basis for the fear of death when oppressed by the four sufferings;
fifth, because it is the basis for the fear of the evil destinies when transgressing the true Dharma. What is the suffering of separation from the beloved?
It should be understood that this suffering also consists of five aspects:
namely, because not meeting with them gives rise to sorrow and affliction;
and because, due to these causes and conditions, lamentation arises.
Due to these causes and conditions, the body is agitated and distressed;
due to the causes and conditions of mindfulness of those various virtues and longing for them, the mind is feverishly afflicted;
and because there are deficiencies in what should be utilized and enjoyed.
Just as with the suffering of separation from the beloved,
one should know that the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks is likewise.
What is the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging?
It should be understood that this suffering also consists of five aspects:
namely, because it is the instrument of the suffering of birth,
and because it is the basis for the instrument of the suffering of birth.
Because it is the vessel for the suffering of suffering,
because it is the vessel for the suffering of change,
and because it is the nature of the suffering of conditioned formations.
Furthermore, three types of persons are established based on the distinctions in their conduct:
namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
[The inferior person] possesses neither conduct for their own benefit nor conduct for the benefit of others.
These are called persons of inferior capacity.
There are those who possess conduct for their own benefit but lack conduct for the benefit of others;
and there are those who possess conduct for the benefit of others but lack conduct for their own benefit.
One who possesses conduct for their own benefit is called a person of middle capacity; one who possesses conduct for the benefit of others is called a person of superior capacity.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of persons (*pudgala*):
some practice evil but do not delight in evil;
others delight in evil but do not practice it.
Some commit evil deeds and also delight in evil;
others neither commit evil deeds nor delight in evil,
because they believe that all evils will bring about undesirable retributive fruits in the future.
Due to loss of mindfulness,
or due to negligence,
or due to associating with evil friends.
One performs unwholesome deeds;
this is called practicing evil rather than delighting in evil.
It is because one has habituated oneself to evil from previous lives.
Delighting in various evils and led astray by evil desires,
they, through associating with virtuous persons and hearing the true Dharma, [are transformed].
Relying upon proper mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*),
one perceives that all unwholesome actions bring about undesirable retributive results in the future,
and thus exerts oneself and strives to remain far removed from all evils.
This is called delighting in evil without practicing it.
If one’s nature delights in evil and one does not distance oneself from it,
this is called both practicing evil and delighting in evil.
If one possesses a conditioned nature that does not delight in various evils and is also able to distance oneself from them,
this is called neither practicing evil nor delighting in evil.
Among these, those who practice evil and also delight in evil—
This is called the inferior person.
There may be one who commits evil but does not delight in evil,
or there may be one who delights in evil but does not commit it.
This is called the person of middle capacity.
If one neither practices evil nor delights in evil,
this is called the person of superior capacity.
Furthermore, there are three types of persons:
first, those who prioritize the enjoyment of sensual desires;
second, those who prioritize worldly affairs.
Regarding the threefold sublime Dharma:
the first is designated as the person of inferior capacity,
and the next as the person of middling capacity.
The latter is called a superior person (*uttamapuruṣa*).
Furthermore, there are three types of persons (*pudgala*):
first, those who take what is not their own task as their own task.
Second, taking one's own affairs as one's own affairs;
third, taking the affairs of others as one's own affairs—
such as engaging in unwholesome conduct in order to sustain oneself.
To regard what is not one’s own task as one’s own task is called "regarding non-task as one’s own task.
To fear unwholesome conduct and practice wholesome conduct is called "regarding one’s own task as one’s own task."
If bodhisattvas regard the affairs of others as their own affairs and so forth,
the former are called inferior persons,
and the latter are called middling persons.
Such a person is later called a superior person (*uttamapuruṣa*).

Furthermore, kings possess three perfections, namely: the perfection of karmic fruition (*vipāka-sampad*), the perfection of wealth (*bhoga-sampad*), and the perfection of retinue (*parivāra-sampad*).
The perfection of human effort and the perfection of merit;
this applies to those kings who are born into wealthy and noble families.
Long-lived, with few ailments, and possessing a great lineage,
he is endowed with innate, sharp intelligence;
such a king is said to have "perfection of karmic fruition."
If kings are sustained by skillful means and expedient methods,
they will constantly achieve perfect valor;
such a king is said to possess the perfection of human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
If kings uphold the True Dharma, they are called Dharma-kings;
if they abide securely in the True Dharma, they are called Great Kings.
Together with their inner palace, princes, ministers, heroes, nobles, and the people of the land, they practice the giving of alms.
Planting roots of merit, observing the fast, and firmly upholding the precepts—
this king is named Puṇyaparipūrṇa (Perfected in Merit).
As for "perfected in karmic fruition":
The perfection of human effort consists in enjoying the karmic fruit of pure deeds from previous lives,
while the enjoyment of desirable fruits in the present life constitutes the perfection of human effort.
Those whose merit is perfected shall also,
in the future, enjoy the full fruition of the results of pure karma.
If there should be a king...
One who lacks all three types of perfection is called an inferior person (*hīnapuruṣa*).
If one possesses either the perfection of maturation (*vipāka-sampad*) or the perfection of human effort (*puruṣakāra-sampad*), [one is a middling person].
If all three are complete,
one is called a person of middling capacity.
If these three are fully present and nothing is lacking, [one is a person of superior capacity].
He is called a superior person.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of ministers:
first, one who possesses loyalty and integrity but lacks skill and wisdom.
Second, those who possess loyalty, trustworthiness, and skillful ability but lack wisdom;
third, those who are endowed with loyalty, trustworthiness, skillful ability, and wisdom.
The first is designated as an inferior person.
Next is called the middling person;
last is called the superior person.
If one is neither loyal nor trustworthy, possesses no skillful arts, and lacks wisdom, you should know that such a minister is the lowest of the low.
Furthermore, there are four types of speech:
first, that which is unpleasant yet appears pleasant;
second, that which is pleasant yet appears unpleasant.
Third, that which is unpleasant yet resembles the pleasant;
fourth, that which is pleasant yet resembles the pleasant.
These are various utterances and phrases that are well-composed and harmonious, yet inappropriate to the occasion.
This is called the first kind of speech.
Alternatively, there may be speech whose words and phrases are contrary [to convention] yet appropriate to the occasion;
this is the second kind of speech.
There may be speech whose words and phrases are abrupt and contrary, and thus inappropriate;
this is the third type of speech.
There may also be speech whose words and phrases are skillful and compliant, and thus appropriate.
This is the fourth type of speech.
If one utters speech that is unpleasant, or appears unpleasant, or is unpleasant while appearing pleasant,
such a person is a person of inferior character.
If there is one who proclaims speech that appears pleasant but is actually unpleasant,
they are a person of middling capacity.
If there is one who proclaims speech that is both pleasant and truly pleasant, [they are a person of superior capacity].
This is the superior person.
Furthermore, there are three types of those who experience various desires.
Some experience desire through unrighteousness, recklessly accumulating wealth and treasures.
They are unable to dwell in peace and properly nourish themselves, their wives, and their children;
to speak at length, they do not even cultivate the field of merit among śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
There are those who, whether by lawful or unlawful means, or through reckless or non-accumulative ways,
enjoy sensual pleasures and are able to provide for the well-being and proper sustenance of themselves, their wives, children, retinue, and friends.
He does not cultivate the field of merit among śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas;
or he may enjoy desires exclusively through the Dharma,
and he accumulates wealth without recklessness.
One who is able to properly nourish one's own body with peace and happiness—
and, as explained at length, even one who is able to cultivate fields of merit among śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—
is designated as an inferior person (*hīnapuruṣa*) among these three types.
Next is called the person of middling capacity;
last is called the person of superior capacity.
Furthermore, there are three types of persons.
First, there are those who eat with greedy attachment;
they are covetous and gluttonous, even to the point of being addicted,
failing to see the faults and disadvantages [of such eating] and not knowing how to transcend them.
Second, there are those who eat with discernment;
they are neither stained nor attached,
nor do they greedily devour, gulp down, become deluded, remain stubbornly addicted, or indulge in craving.
Third, there is one who, having deeply perceived the faults [of food] and well understood renunciation,
has not yet abandoned or fully realized [the transcendence of] this eating.
Fourth, there is one who eats with discernment.
He does not give rise to lustful attachment.
To speak at length, he even thoroughly perceives the faults [of food] and well understands renunciation.
Furthermore, regarding this food, he has already abandoned it and fully known it.
The first is called the inferior person;
the next is called the middling person;
and the last is called the superior person.
Furthermore, based on the objects given as gifts, three types of persons are described. First,
there is the person whose gift possesses only exquisite fragrance, but lacks exquisite flavor and texture.
Second, there are those who give objects that possess excellent fragrance and flavor but lack excellent tactile quality.
Third, there are those who give objects...
Possessing excellent fragrance, flavor, and tactile qualities:
the former is called the inferior person;
the latter is called the middling person.
The latter is called a superior person (*uttamapuruṣa*).
Furthermore, based on the field of giving (*dānakkhetta*), three types of persons are taught.
First, there is the person who practices generosity toward those they love and those who have been kind to them.
Second, there are those who practice giving toward the field of the poor and suffering.
Third, there are those who practice giving toward the most excellent field of merit, which is endowed with virtuous qualities.
The first is called the inferior person;
the next is called the middling person;
and the last is called the superior person.
Furthermore, there is a distinction:
giving to those one loves is called the practice of an inferior person;
giving to those who have been kind is called the practice of a middling person.
One who gives to the poor and suffering, who possess virtue, and who are superior fields of merit is called a superior person (*uttamapuruṣa*).
Furthermore, based on the mind of giving, three types of persons are taught.
First, there is the person who feels joy in their heart before they are about to bestow a gift.
First, when actually giving, the mind is not pure,
and after having given, one immediately regrets it.
Second, there are those who first feel joy in their hearts.
First, there is one whose mind is pure at the time of giving,
yet feels regret after having given. Third, there is one whose mind was joyful beforehand,
whose mind is pure at the time of giving, and who feels no regret after having given.
The first is called the inferior person;
the next is called the middling person;
and the last is called the superior person.
Furthermore, regarding the meritorious activity of upholding the precepts,
three types of persons are established.
The first is a person who has abandoned only a single portion.
One is not able to remain constantly and always free from [unwholesome states];
one merely refrains oneself without encouraging others to refrain, nor does one praise such abstention;
and upon seeing fellow practitioners of the Dharma, one’s heart feels no joy.
This is called the inferior person.
Second, there are those who are separated from all parts at all times;
they only distance themselves personally, neither encouraging others nor praising [the practice].
One who does not feel joy upon seeing fellow practitioners of the Dharma is called a person of middling capacity.
Third, there is a person for whom all [these qualities] manifest together.
These are called superior persons.
Furthermore, regarding the sphere of upholding the prohibitive precepts,
three types of persons are established.
First, there are those who abide within a poorly taught Dharma and Vinaya,
yet observe the prohibitive precepts.
Second, there are those who abide within a well-taught Dharma and Vinaya.
First, there is one who observes the prohibitive precepts but with omissions and flaws.
Second, there is one who, while abiding in this very state, observes the prohibitive precepts without omissions or flaws.
The first is designated as an inferior person (*hīna-puruṣa*).
Next is called the person of middling capacity;
the latter is called the person of superior capacity.
Furthermore, regarding the mind that upholds the precepts:
Three types of persons are established.
First, there are those who observe the prohibitive precepts for the sake of livelihood.
Second, there are those who observe the prohibitive precepts for the sake of rebirth in heaven.
Third, there are those who observe the prohibitive precepts for the sake of nirvāṇa.
The former is called an inferior person;
the latter is called a middling person.
The latter is called the superior person (*uttamapudgala*).
Furthermore, regarding the observance of the *prātimokṣa* vows,
it is said that there are three types of persons.
First, there are those who are able to undertake only the *upavāsa* (fasting) vows;
second, there are those who are also able to undertake the *upāsaka* (lay disciple) vows;
third, there are those who are also able to undertake the *bhikṣu* (monastic) vows.
The first is called the inferior person;
the next is called the middling person;
and the last is called the superior person.
Furthermore, regarding the observance of the bhikṣu vows,
it is said that there are three types of persons.
First, there is the person who is able to accomplish only the factor of full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*).
There is no branch consisting of training rules that follow the Dharma without acceptance;
nor is there a branch consisting of guarding the minds of others;
nor is there a branch consisting of guarding the training rules as they were previously received.
Second, there are those who accomplish the first three branches but lack the final one;
third, there are those who fully accomplish all four branches.
The first is called the inferior person;
the next is called the middling person;
and the last is called the superior person.
Furthermore, there are three types of persons:
first, those who possess only the prātimokṣa restraint;
second, those who possess both the prātimokṣa and dhyāna restraints.
Third, there are those who achieve the three types of restraint—the prātimokṣa, dhyāna, and untainted (anāsrava) restraints.
The first is called an inferior person;
the second is called a middling person.
The latter is called a superior person (uttamapudgala).
Furthermore, there are three types of persons:

first, there is one who is able to accomplish only that which is comprised by the restraint of undertaken precepts (samādāna-śīla-saṃvara), which is neither non-restraint (asaṃvara) nor formal discipline (saṃvara).
Second, there are those who are also able to accomplish the ethical discipline (śīla-saṃvara) received in association with the Śrāvakas and others;
third, there are those who are also able to accomplish the ethical discipline received by Bodhisattvas.
The first is called the inferior person;
the next is called the middling person;
and the last is called the superior person.
Furthermore, based on the skillful means of cultivation and reflection,
three types of persons are established.
The first is one who attains only the reflection that functions through strenuous effort.
Second, there are those whose [mental] activity proceeds intermittently;
even if they attain continuity, they must exert effort for it to proceed.
Third, there are those who have already attained accomplishment and engage in spontaneous reflection.
The first is called the inferior person;
the next is called the middling person;
and the last is called the superior person.
Furthermore, based on the distinctions in the cultivation of what has already been attained,
three types of persons are established.
First, there is the person who has already attained internal *śamatha* concentration.
First, there are those who have not yet attained the dharma of higher wisdom,
vipaśyanā; second, there are those who have already attained the dharma of higher wisdom, vipaśyanā,
but have not yet attained internal mental śamatha concentration.
Third, there are those who attain both types;
the former is called an inferior person (*hīnapuruṣa*),
and the latter is called a middling person (*madhyamapuruṣa*).
The latter is called a superior person (uttama-pudgala).
Furthermore, there are three types of persons:
first, there is one who has already attained the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra.
Second, there are those who have already attained the samādhi of no vitarka and only vicāra;
third, there are those who have already attained the samādhi of neither vitarka nor vicāra.
The first is designated as an inferior person (hīna-puruṣa).
Next is called the person of middling capacity;
last is called the person of superior capacity.
Furthermore, these are distinguished according to their respective abidings and practices.
Three types of persons are established:
first, there is the person who dwells in defiled meditative absorption;
second, there is the person who dwells in mundane pure meditative absorption.
Third, there are those who abide in untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-dhyāna*).
The first is called an inferior person;
the next is called a middling person.
These are subsequently called "superior persons.
Furthermore, there are ten classes of sentient beings who take delight in and rejoice in ten kinds of phenomena.
What are the ten dharmas?
First, life-span;
second, physical form.
The three riches,
the four friends,
and the five precepts.
Sixth, hearing;
seventh, holy conduct;
eighth, wisdom.
Nine dharmas.
Ten ways of being born in the heavens.
What are called the ten classes of sentient beings? First, animals (*tiryag-yoni*).
Second, the mother’s community;
third, those who enjoy sensual pleasures;
fourth, those who seek what is to be done.
Fifth, those who have gone forth;
sixth, those for whom much learning is their life;
seventh, those who have entered into realization.
Eighth, those who seek through investigation;
ninth, those who exert themselves with diligence;
tenth, those who cast off the body.
Furthermore, for one who listens to the true Dharma,
there are briefly six kinds of afflictive faults,
namely: the fault of pride.
The fault of non-desire,
the fault of lack of faith,
and the fault of physical and mental affliction.
The fault of distraction and the fault of delusion;
by means of such faults as these.
One is unable to listen to the Dharma with reverence and earnestness,
as explained at length in the sutra.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of faults regarding the affliction of distraction.
That is to say: distraction while speaking,
distraction after having spoken,
and confusion.
That is to say, perversion.
Furthermore, there are briefly three ways in which afflictions give rise to karma:
first, arising through association.
Second, arising from the parents;
third, arising from the predominant [condition],
because it is initiated by drawing forth other afflictions.
Furthermore, there are briefly six kinds of unloved phenomena:
first, enemies;
second, illness.
Third, unpleasant objects;
fourth, the various sufferings such as birth;
and fifth, bitter and pungent medicinal herbs.
Six are non-habitual virtues;
the former four should be abandoned, while the latter two should be cultivated. Furthermore, there are briefly five ways of enjoying sensual pleasures.
First, the enjoyment of experiencing;
second, the enjoyment of gathering joy;
third, the enjoyment of investigation.
Fourth, craving for their enjoyment;
fifth, craving for one's own enjoyment.
Furthermore, there are briefly eight aspects of the faults of sensual desires.
First, the characteristic of having little flavor, much suffering, and many disadvantages;
second, the characteristic of being a causal condition for suffering through oppression by others;
third, the characteristic of being a superior causal condition for the enjoyment of defilement.
Fourth, the characteristic of the causal conditions for falling into the various miserable realms;
fifth, the characteristic of the causal conditions for the disturbance of discursive thought;
sixth, the characteristic of the causal conditions for the exhaustion of what has been enjoyed.
Seventh, the characteristic of the superior causes and conditions for the destruction and dissolution of the body.
Eighth, the characteristic of the superior causes and conditions that can obstruct wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, there are briefly six kinds of transformation and decay regarding the causes and conditions of all desires.
First, transformation through being oppressed by others;
second, transformation through the mutual conflict of the elements;
third, transformation through the death of beloved sentient beings.
Fourth, the transformation and disintegration of the body;
fifth, the transformation and disintegration of the mind;
sixth, the transformation and disintegration of impermanence.
Furthermore, it should be understood that all sensual desires receive the name "dense forest" (*gahana*) due to five kinds of analogous qualities:
first, by virtue of their numerous analogous qualities;
second, by virtue of their defiled analogous qualities.
Third, by way of the similarity to the act of nurturing sentient beings;
fourth, by way of the similarity to a place of concealment;
and fifth, by way of the similarity to a perilous difficulty.
Regarding the *Viniścaya*:
in various places herein, further explanatory passages from the *Viniścaya* do not appear again.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 61;
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 62;
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.

This concludes the first part of the *Samāhitā-bhūmi* within the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, concerning the determination of the three stages beginning with "with vitarka and vicāra. Thus has been explained the determination of the three stages, including those with vitarka and vicāra.
I shall now explain the determination of the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhitabhūmi*).
When the mental continuum is defiled,
one is unable to correctly realize one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
What are called the many secondary afflictions?
They are those such as guile,
deception, and hypocrisy.
Lack of shame and lack of remorse;
lack of faith and laziness;
forgetfulness and lack of concentration.
With corrupted wisdom, arrogance, and laxity,
they proceed forward amidst vulgar and chaotic entanglements,
abandoning the yoke of seclusion.
They lack profound reverence for the precepts they have undertaken;
disregarding their status as śramaṇas,
they seek only to sustain their livelihood.
One does not go forth seeking liberation for the sake of *nirvāṇa*.
How, then, can there be deceit?
It means that one has faults yet is unable to disclose them truthfully before the Great Teacher, the wise, and fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*).
What is deception (*śāṭhya*)?
It is the false manifestation of one's own virtues.

Although one lacks such virtues in reality, one desires that other wise fellow-practitioners (*sabrahmacārin*) should likewise perceive one as possessing them. What is hypocrisy (*mada*)? It is the violation of the moral precepts (*śīla*) regarding superior ethical discipline.
Or, when one has violated the rules of conduct regarding a preceptor and is censured by others on account of what was seen, heard, or suspected,
one then resorts to other matters as a pretext for those other matters.
Or they may employ external words to entice and lead one astray,
as explained at length in the sutras;
that is to say, through the predominant power of flattery and deception.
What is hypocrisy? It is that which arises from the fear of others,
or from having some expectation regarding them.
Although they have committed a grave offense, they neither confess it nor engage in its practice.
Lacking genuine intention, they feign affection,
respect, and gentle physical and verbal actions toward wise fellow practitioners of the holy life.
What is lack of shame and lack of dread?
It refers to the absence of any sense of shame or embarrassment when considering oneself or others,
and thus intentionally violating the precepts.
Having committed an offense, one is unable to emerge from it in accordance with the Dharma;
one delights in various forms of quarreling, strife, and contention.
What is lack of faith?
It refers to having a mind that is not pure toward the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha,
and giving rise to a lack of compliant understanding regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation,
and the path. What is indolence?
This refers to clinging to sleep and reclining as pleasure,
and thus wasting day and night by abandoning all categories of wholesome qualities.
What is forgetfulness?
That is to say, regarding what was done and said long ago,
one is unable to recollect it or bring it to mind; furthermore,
one does not guard the sense faculties and dwells without clear comprehension.
What is indeterminate?
It refers to that which cannot be attained even through the application of attention (*manasikāra*) at the level of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
What is poor wisdom (*duṣprajñā*)?
This refers to abiding in the grasping of one's own views, clinging to an unequal discourse that is difficult to relinquish.
What is meant by "sluggishness" (mandatā)? It means being neither swift nor clear.
Not exerting oneself, one is incapable of doing anything;
one cannot serve and attend to wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life.
How is this a state of vulgar confusion?
That is to say, one delights in dwelling in close association with householders and those who have gone forth,
and further delights in the pursuit of various evil and unwholesome thoughts, such as thoughts of sensual desire, up to thoughts concerning family influence.
He frequently engages in vitarka and frequently engages in vicāra.
How does he proceed forward?
This refers to receiving all manner of gains and offerings, such as robes from the Saṃgha or from individual persons.
Whether one invites the Saṃgha as a whole or an individual,
both are termed "approaching.
If the bhikṣus are the first to proceed in such matters, [they are said to have approached].
Therefore, it is called "proceeding toward the goal.
What is the abandonment of the yoke of seclusion?
It refers to dwelling in a secluded lodging at the edge of solitude—a place frequented by those who have abandoned evil persons, which resembles a chamber of tranquility.
One utterly abandons them and does not give rise to desire for them.
How could one not show great reverence for the precepts?
This means that even when encountering calamity or distress, one would rather abandon the precepts than forsake one's body or life.
Seeking only bodily pleasure and longevity, they are unable to follow and protect any of the trainings.
How can one be said to disregard the state of a śramaṇa? It means that having abandoned the trainings, one delights in falling back from them.
Or they may violate the precepts and practice various evil dharmas, rotting within;
as explained at length, they are not actually practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) yet claim to be so—
how much less could they hope to attain the fruits of the śramaṇa?
One realizes the Noble Eightfold Path.
How is it that one seeks to go forth into homelessness merely out of a desire for livelihood and not for the sake of nirvāṇa?
It refers to those who seek to go forth because they have been oppressed by a king.
Or they may be oppressed by hostile bandits;
or they may be pressed by creditors;
or they may be pressed by terrors.
Some go forth into homelessness because they are constantly deprived of wealth and treasures, fearing they will be unable to survive;
they do not go forth for the sake of self-discipline, self-pacification, or their own parinirvāṇa.
It should be understood that among these, there are transgressions committed in relation to dwelling together with fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*),
which give rise to the first four secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*);
and there are transgressions committed in relation to superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*).
One should know that shamelessness and lack of dread give rise [to further afflictions].
Based on the higher mind (*adhicitta*) and the higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*),
one should know that they give rise to all secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), ranging from lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) up to corrupted wisdom (*duṣprajñā*).
In this context, lack of faith and laziness arise based on transgressions against both [the higher training in ethics and the higher training in concentration];
forgetfulness and distraction arise based on transgressions against the higher training in concentration;
and faulty wisdom arises based on transgressions against the higher training in wisdom. This occurs through the predominant force of lack of faith and laziness.
One should know that they give rise to indolence and mental confusion,
proceeding forward while abandoning the yoke of seclusion.
One should know that due to the predominant influence of forgetfulness, a distracted mind,
and impaired wisdom, one fails to show proper reverence for the various training rules and disregards the state of a śramaṇa.
They seek to go forth from the household life solely for the sake of maintaining their livelihood, not for the sake of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, there are three types of persons who,
based on three bases, give rise to various secondary afflictions (upakleśa).
What are the three types of persons?
First, those who have gone forth in reliance upon the true Dharma;
second, those who remain in the household life and enjoy sensual desires.
Third, regarding those who have gone forth outside the True Dharma,
there are three points that give rise to secondary afflictions;
namely, first, the individual (pudgala).
Based on the locus of negligence, secondary afflictions are induced;
these are further of two kinds:
namely, either relying on internal falsehood to manifest one's own virtues, or...
For the sake of gain, honor, robes, and other requisites,
one either claims for oneself that one has attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*),
or relies upon others who are wise and fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*).
By means of bodily and verbal actions, they oppress, harm, afflict, and humiliate others; thus,
based on the pursuit of sensual desires, they give rise to secondary afflictions.
Due to the causes and conditions of being addicted to various sensual desires,
they indulge in those desires and engage in the three types of unwholesome conduct through body, speech, and mind.
These are the three types of persons.
Based on the spheres of wrong conduct, secondary afflictions are induced;
briefly, there are three kinds, namely:
those that follow along with, and those that distance themselves from [the primary affliction].
How does one give rise to secondary afflictions by following after worldly clamor? How does one give rise to secondary afflictions by following after the training rules?
And how does one give rise to secondary afflictions by following after seclusion?
This refers to those non-Buddhists who, though following a secluded dwelling,
have their minds shrouded by the five hindrances;
or because they abide in suffering, experiencing various physical and mental afflictions.
Alternatively, they are far removed from the remedies for the afflictions because they lack the five faculties, such as faith;
thus, they abide in a state of defilement.
Because one dwells in suffering and affliction,
and because there is no antidote capable of removing that dwelling in defiled suffering and affliction,
this is called "following after" while remaining far removed from all secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

What is the secondary affliction that arises following from social clamor? It refers to the mutual adherence to differing views and differing desires, engaging in contradictory discourse, and establishing distinctions between one's own faction and that of others.
Extensively giving rise to anger and resentment, up to and including deception and guile—
these are called the secondary afflictions that follow after worldly clamor.
What are the secondary afflictions that arise following the precepts?
This refers to observing the various transgressions committed by oneself and others,
yet lacking a sense of shame and failing to maintain or violating the precepts;
these are called the secondary afflictions that follow along with the training in higher ethical discipline.
If one relies upon worldly meditative attainments (*samāpatti*),
one may conceive oneself as superior to that which is inferior,
or conceive oneself as superior to that which is merely similar.
The mind becomes uplifted;
this is called a secondary affliction that pursues the training in the higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*).
If one has heard little, one will be unable to examine any wholesome dharmas.
These are called the secondary afflictions that follow upon the training in higher wisdom.
All such things, in brief, are termed unrighteous conduct and unequal conduct.
That which has the sense of being unwholesome is called "unrighteous conduct" (*adharma-caryā*);
that which has the sense of having undesirable results is called "uneven conduct" (*viṣama-caryā*).
Furthermore, if a practitioner...
The cultivation of the ten universal bases (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*) can accomplish five things. What are these five?
They are [accomplished] by virtue of cultivating the universal base of earth (*pṛthivī-kṛtsnāyatana*), and so forth, up to the universal base of white (*avadāta-kṛtsnāyatana*).
One is then able to induce the noble supernormal powers that manifest transformations and miraculous feats.
Furthermore, by cultivating the universal sphere of the base of infinite space,
one is able to induce the noble supernormal powers of unimpeded coming and going.
Furthermore, by cultivating the universal sphere of the station of infinite consciousness,

one is able to bring forth various supreme qualities, such as the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), and the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, by means of this very mastery of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-kṛtsnāyatana*),

one is able to accomplish the liberation of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-vimokṣa*) as well as the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-vimokṣa*).
Furthermore, by means of this very cause of fulfillment,
one is able to realize and enter the most excellent dwelling comprised within the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling;
moreover, this is due to the sphere of infinite consciousness.
They proceed by way of infinite, immeasurable, and all-pervasive activity.
For this reason, the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) and the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) are not established above these;
the spheres of totality constitute the path of purification for the various liberations (vimokṣa).
Furthermore, all liberations are characterized by liberation from the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
It is by means of this that the minds of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas,
and others are liberated from the cognitive obstructions.
Furthermore, briefly stated, there are three aspects to the cultivation of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
The first is the attainment characterized by relishing (*āsvādana*),
which refers to regarding an attainment as pure after having emerged from it.
It is delightful, joyful, lovely, and agreeable; it is relished through recollection,
whether it has not yet been attained or has already been attained,
by the predominant power of future relish.
Seeking after joy, one gives rise to relishing;
or, having attained it, one reckons it as pure.
From "delightful and pleasurable" up to the full exposition, one manifests this relishing.
If one emerges from meditative concentration, one may give rise to relish;
while actually in concentration, there is no relish.
As for what is called "relish":
That is to say, within these [states], one gives rise to pervasive attachment.
Furthermore, as for the dharmas of the lower stages,
if they arise in a higher stage, they do not manifest.
When dharmas of a higher stage arise in a lower stage,
those who have attained detachment from desire may bring them into manifestation; or,
having been born in a lower stage, they may give rise to craving for the higher stages.
For one who has not yet attained a mind free from desire and whose mind is not fixed,
it should be said that this craving is bound to the desire realm;
it should be known that this craving is either afflicted or non-afflicted.
What is defilement?
It is when one gives rise to this thought:
"How might I now realize such an attainment accompanied by vast and great joy?"
If I should attain realization,
I shall experience such and such a relish;
furthermore, how may I come to be born in the higher realms, eternal and unchanging?
One should know that this craving is defiled craving.
If one gives rise to a mind that single-mindedly seeks to transcend desire and delights in realizing entry into the tranquility of a higher stage,
one should know that this craving is undefiled.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of cessation of phenomena:
namely, cessation through antidotes and cessation through non-manifestation.
Abandoning and severing that which is manifested by the various phenomena of the afflictions—
this is the first severance.
That which is manifested by the arising and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is the second cessation.
This occurs when one is born into a higher realm or enters the realm of nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
The third abandonment is that which is manifested by the relinquishing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the lower stages as well as all conditioned phenomena whatsoever.
Furthermore, there are three types of retrogression.
First, falling away from dharmas not yet attained;
second, falling away from dharmas already attained;
third, falling away from the practice of dharmas.
Furthermore, based on the various mundane preparatory concentrations (*sāmantaka-samādhi*),
whether they be the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) or the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
If one cultivates the path of liberation either for the purpose of abandoning or for the purpose of realizing [the fruit],
one contemplates either the defects or the tranquility of that object.
One contemplates the faults of the lower [realms] and the tranquility of the higher [realms].
If it is the path of superior progress,
one should know that it has either a pervasive object or an untainted object as its focal point.
Furthermore, the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) comprise six types of mental application (*manasikāra*), namely:
the mental application of discerning characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*) up to the mental application of the culmination of the preparation (*prayoganiṣṭha*).
Among these, there is the mental application of discerning characteristics through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika*).
It is subsumed under the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
excluding the attention of the culmination of application (*prayoga-niṣṭha-manasikāra*).
It is subsumed under the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
The mental application of "gathering through delight" is subsumed under four types of paths;
the mental application of "investigation."
It is subsumed within the path of supreme progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*).

Question: For what reason is it said that the objective domain (*gocara*) of one who cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is inconceivable? Answer: Because one who cultivates meditative concentration has already thoroughly cultivated, refined, and polished their mind.
Possessing such marks, majestic power, and efficacy,
they are able to accomplish whatever they desire;
this is not because of an unfavorable nature of phenomena (dharmatā), but rather because it is so.
Therefore, it is said that they are inconceivable by means of the path of discursive thought.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of practitioners of dhyāna who,
regarding a single object, both manifest the supernormal power of transformation through resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) and attain mastery over them.
These two supernormal powers (abhijñā) mutually obstruct one another;
however, when neither of these two powers is particularly predominant, they do not eclipse or supplant each other.
Immediately thereafter, regarding this particular matter, one [power] functions without impediment.
Whatever one desires, one is able to transform;
however, the second supernormal power (ṛddhi) then becomes obstructed.
How should the causes and conditions herein be understood?
Due to the equal power and majesty of those two individuals, they simultaneously manifested supernatural transformations;
however, their respective deeds were not similar to one another.
Because the matters intended by those supernormal powers were incompatible,
these two types of supernormal powers mutually obstructed one another in this single matter. At that time, there was one who thought as follows:
"For what reason do these supernormal powers of mine now encounter an obstruction?
Could it be that my meditative concentration is about to decline?
This is surely a state of fixed concentration."
Regarding this very object, another mind arises;
as for the second absorption,
it is the repeated focusing of the mind upon this same object without distraction.
The supernormal powers they manifest are unimpeded;
according to the power of these supernormal faculties, they transform things at will.
If the majestic power of two such supernormal powers is unequal, [the weaker one is overcome].
Success is achieved according to whichever [power] is superior.
If two supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are equal in their majestic power (*vīrya*),
that which was first brought to mind is accomplished, and no other.
Furthermore, there are four types of those who cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*):
first, those who cultivate meditative concentration based on the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*);
second, those who cultivate meditative concentration based on defiled concentration (*kliṣṭa-samādhi*).
Third, those who cultivate dhyāna based on mundane concentration;
fourth, those who cultivate dhyāna based on supramundane concentration.
Regarding these, there are six modes of mental attention (*manasikāra*).

It should be understood that this refers to the initial stage when one practices meditative concentration through the mental orientations ranging from the "mental orientation of discerning characteristics" up to the "mental orientation of the culmination of application.
This includes everything from attachment to dhyāna, as explained at length, up to doubt regarding dhyāna.
One should know that the second [case] is when one abides in other wholesome mundane meditative concentrations;
one should know that the third is as follows.
This refers to the ability to bring forth immeasurable mental orientations (*manasikāra*) for dwelling in happiness in the present life and worldly merits;

furthermore, it brings forth the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) manifested by the gates of liberation—emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness—which are comprised within the supernormal powers of playful mastery and the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
It should be known that, furthermore, the fourth [attainment],
the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), should be described as exclusively impure (*sāsrava*);
the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) should be described as pure (*anāsrava*).
Because it is dissociated from the afflictions,
because it is not associated with them,
and because it lacks an object of perception.
Because it is not produced by any of the afflictions,
and because it cannot be practiced by any ordinary worldlings of the mundane realm,
except for those bodhisattvas who have already entered the distant stages.
Although a bodhisattva is able to give rise to supramundane dharmas so that they manifest before them,
by the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they do not abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, these attainments (*samāpatti*) should be said to be comprised within neither the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) nor the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Because it is not within the sphere of activity [of the mind] and because it resembles nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati) shall now be explained.
The Sūtra says:
A bhikṣu whose mind is pure in conduct has four types of secondary afflictions:
first, the violation of prohibitive precepts;
second, distracted discursive thought.
Third, attachment to the internal body;
fourth, attachment to external objects.
These refer to those who violate the prohibitions and precepts.
Through the gateway of remorse and regret,
one is able to create obstacles to samādhi;
for those with distracted discursive thought, it acts as an obstacle through three gateways.
First, by way of distraction through recollecting past objects;

second, by way of distraction consisting solely in the delight in hearing, reflecting, and so forth, based on restlessness, proliferation, wrong views, improper learning, evil speech, and evil conduct.
Third, there is the gate of distraction sustained by the force of prior habituation;
and for those who cling to the internal body,
there is the gate of having no weariness toward saṃsāra.
Those who cling to external objects are afflicted by future objects through the gateway of longing and delight.
One cultivates a single type of attention,
namely, the attention of correct awareness (*saṃprajanya-manasikāra*),
in order to counteract the second secondary affliction.
One cultivates three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*):
namely, mental attention that accords with and conforms to that object of focus;
mental attention that discerns its characteristics and serves as the antidote to discursive thought (*vitarka*); and [mental attention that]... [the text continues].
To counteract the third secondary affliction, one should cultivate the mental attention that analyzes the composite through the mental attention that trains the mind which serves as its basis.
In order to counteract the fourth secondary affliction,
one should practice the mental attention of impurity;
furthermore, this is because of having practiced and cultivated that initial mental attention extensively.
Through the second mental application (*manasikāra*), by means of cultivation and repeated practice,
one is able to sever forgetfulness and sever the two kinds of craving— attachment to one's own body and attachment to external objects.
Through the repeated cultivation and intensive practice of the third mental attention,
one is able to sever all distractions such as wrong views.
Through the repeated cultivation and intensive practice of the fourth mental attention...

By means of the fifth mental application (*manasikāra*), through its repeated cultivation and intensive practice, one is able to sever all distractions sustained by the force of previous habitual tendencies,
and is able to sever the notion of purity regarding the body and the notion of sentient beings.
Through the sixth mental engagement, by means of repeated cultivation and intensive practice,
one is able to sever the four types of craving:
namely, craving for form, craving for contact, craving for shape, and craving for service.
Relying on such mental attention and cultivation as a basis,
one abandons the secondary afflictions, brings the mind into contact with right concentration,
and realizes the superior attainments of both the preparatory and fundamental stages.
Furthermore, one is able to realize the pure bliss that is accompanied by joy and free from joy.
Moreover, by relying on such a mind of right concentration,
one understands, in accordance with reality, the impermanence of sentient beings in the higher realms.
And regarding the impermanent nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*):
how does one thoroughly understand the impermanent nature of sentient beings?
It is by attaining the pure divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), which transcends that of humans, and seeing all sentient beings.
...and so on, as extensively explained.
How does one thoroughly understand the impermanent nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)?
It is by means of the wisdom that enters into accordance with the fact that mental attention (*manasikāra*) arises dependently in the future, past, and present.
This mindfulness of the body relies upon three bases,
namely: the training in higher mind and the training in higher wisdom.
The cultivation of the stage of action,
based on the training in higher mind and based on the training in higher wisdom.
It serves as the basis for cultivating all the factors conducive to enlightenment, such as the foundations of mindfulness, in order to sever the remaining fetters;
and by virtue of three causes and conditions, it is not shared with any of the non-Buddhist śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
This means that because the provisions for the stage of purifying karma have been perfected,
there is no relish for the collection of *śamatha*,
and the mind is accompanied by a longing for and delight in parinirvāṇa.
Because it is not a place produced by the fire of afflictions,
and because it relies upon the perfection of the provisions for the cultivation of mindfulness,
the four fruits are purified.
That is to say: one is not defiled by the afflictions arising from dwelling in a village;
one is not defiled by the afflictions arising from dwelling in a forest hermitage or a secluded place;
and one is not defiled by the afflictions arising from dwelling in either a forest hermitage or a village.
In these two locations, one is unable to endure the suffering of leaks and the like, yet remains undefiled by afflictions;
because one relies on the meditative absorption (*śamatha*) aggregate that is free from craving, the five fruits are purified.
That is to say: the four kinds of pure dhyānas,
as well as peaceful liberations,
and a mind that follows with a longing for parinirvāṇa.
Because it takes as its basis that which is not produced by the fire of afflictions,
the nine fruits are purified;
namely, the first three fruits and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
This mindfulness of the body should be understood as being comprised of five kinds of purity:
namely, purity of the non-concentrated state and purity of the concentrated state.
Because of the purity of inclusion,
because of the purity of the unshared,
and because of the purity of the unshared fruit.
Furthermore, because it follows and accompanies the body and is sustained by it,
it is called "mindfulness of the body."
Furthermore, regarding the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, there are two types of liberation:
first, liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*);
second, liberation through the mind (*citta-vimukti*).
That which is practiced should be understood as the establishment of unwholesome conduct, wholesome conduct, and their respective causes and conditions.
As for its essential nature:
One should know that this is precisely the knowledge of unwholesome and wholesome conduct,
as well as their causes and conditions— the distinctions in the essential natures of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and so forth—
possessed by suchness and right wisdom.
Furthermore, regarding liberation of the mind,
that which serves as the basis for the defilement and purification of the mind should be understood as the objective spheres of form and so forth.
One should know that the wisdom which is able to apprehend and discern that world,
and the fruit of the liberation of the mind,
arise from emerging from those corresponding, associated, and inferior categories of affliction.

That which is the domain of supramundane wisdom by virtue of the predominant power of liberation through wisdom should be understood as being due to the predominant power of mundane wisdom and liberation of mind.
To know all objects as they truly are is the fruit of the liberation of the mind through supramundane wisdom;
it should be understood that this is because it emerges from all types of affliction.
In this context, both mundane wisdom and supramundane wisdom are collectively condensed into one and termed right view.
This is the causal condition for right view.
One should know that this is precisely the appearance of a Buddha in the world, the hearing of the true Dharma, and its unerring contemplation;
furthermore, it is the mark of the fruit of supramundane right view.
One should know that this is because it is eternal throughout the past and future, and because it is without any counterpart.
If a phenomenon has that which it opposes, or if, having arisen, it has that which opposes its non-extinction,
or if, being non-extinct, it has arising—
such a phenomenon is said to have a counterpart.
If a phenomenon is that which is to be remedied—
whether it exists or does not exist,
whether it arises or does not arise.
It exists at all times;
that dharma is called "without an opposite.
Furthermore, this very fruit arises through the predominant power of the mind's liberation.
One who attains purity regarding their own conduct and its basis should be known as one who,
through the predominant power of a purified mind,
does not give rise to defilement within the spheres of activity of the material sense faculties.
Furthermore, because it causes the various faculties to accord with purity;
moreover, that which is called the "liberated mind" should be known as being identical to life-force and warmth.
They exist in a state of mutual dependence and connection.
Furthermore, regarding the distinction between the two kinds of fruits of liberation— the mundane and the supramundane—
it should be understood that these reside within all feelings and within their causal conditions.
For one who possesses ignorance and craving, future existence will arise;
for one who lacks ignorance and craving, future existence will not arise.
Furthermore, this is because they are mutually intermingled and associated.
One should know that when those dependent mental factors are purified,
they are no longer defiled by present conditions because one experiences them as such.
This is precisely the distinction between the two types of liberation and their respective abidings.
It should be understood that this is because of the six types of tranquility;
it is due to the submergence of purified consciousness into equality,
and not due to the equality of its support.
Because one enters into tranquility at the time of entering meditative absorption without relying on preparatory effort;
because one emerges from tranquility at the time of emerging from meditative absorption without relying on preparatory effort;
and because one emerges sequentially.
Because during the time of meditative concentration, the three types of activity cease and tranquility is attained;
and because upon emerging from seclusion, the mind is tranquil—
referring to these three times.
First, dwelling in a forest hermitage (āraṇya) in close association with fellow practitioners of the holy life;
second, dwelling within a village in close association with householders;
third, manifesting the conduct of both these places.
Because the mind becomes tranquil upon emerging from proximity [to meditative concentration];
that is, at three times:
first, upon emerging from the superior concentration within the world of form (*rūpadhātu*).
Second, because one emerges from the superior meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of the formless world (*ārūpya-loka*);
third, because one emerges from the meditative concentrations with mind (*sacittaka-samādhi*) that transcend the world (*lokottara*).
Furthermore, these various concentrations are not attained only after emerging from the cessation concentration (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Furthermore, those previously attained now arise and become manifest.
Among these, the first two, by virtue of being successive meditative concentrations,
mutually attain the purity of superior concentration.
The latter one does not arise from successive meditative absorptions;
rather, by means of penetrating the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*),
one successively attains the purity of superior concentration.
Furthermore, regarding the concentration with signs (*sanimitta-samādhi*), one enters, abides in, and emerges from it by means of the mental application with signs (*sanimitta-manasikāra*).
Regarding the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*), one enters and abides in it by means of the mental application without signs (*animitta-manasikāra*);
it should be understood that one emerges from it by means of the mental application with signs.
Furthermore, I shall now explain the *Dharmapratyaya-sūtra*.
This refers to a bhikṣu or upāsaka who is skilled in the Abhidharma and the Abhivinaya.
Those who wish to inquire based on understanding should raise their questions according to eight aspects.
What are these eight aspects?
That is to say: understanding the phenomena,
understanding that which is to be remedied,
and understanding the fruit.
Understanding self-nature;
understanding the distinctions among fruits;
and understanding the basis.
The realization of merit;
the realization of attainment;
and the objective entity.
This means being able to comprehend the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*).
As for "comprehending that which is to be countered," it refers to the defilement of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃkleśa*) and the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃkleśa*).
Due to the defilement of craving, one does not take delight in the cessation of future existence;
due to the defilement of views, although one may take delight in it, one is unable to realize it.
This refers to the one who understands the fruit.
This refers to the permanent abandonment of these three types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
As for "understanding its intrinsic nature," this refers to the Noble Eightfold Path.
Furthermore, this is distinguished by various differences;
because it proclaims the remedies for the various false paths of the non-Buddhists,
it is called the Eightfold Noble Path.
The three aggregates are established in order to counteract the three types of affliction:
namely, to counteract the affliction of misconduct,
and to counteract the affliction of sensual desires.
Because it serves as the antidote to the defilements of various views,
it is supramundane and subsumed under the category of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Regarding the differentiation of its results:
This refers to all forms of cessation,
which are comprised within supramundane unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
As for "that which is understood as the basis":
This refers to samādhi.
Furthermore, it should be understood as being of four kinds:
first, by way of lineage (gotra).
This means that all meditative concentrations (samādhi) arise from the lineage of dhyāna;
one is able to comprehend all the factors of dhyāna (dhyānāṅga) as they are taught.
Second, it is by way of their characteristics (lakṣaṇa).
Third, by way of the characteristic of the arising of the object;
fourth, by way of the characteristic of the accomplishment of causes and conditions.
As for the understanding of qualities:
It refers to the cessation attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the foremost dwelling,
which is called the "merit of thorough understanding.
One should know that this characteristic further consists of five kinds.
This is because it involves the cessation of phenomena,
because it is a quiescent semblance-image,
and because it is the causal condition for entering meditative concentration.
Regarding the causes and conditions for emerging from meditative absorption,
the merits of emerging from meditative absorption,
and the realization through thorough understanding:
That is to say, one observes feelings within the five aggregates of clinging by means of eight aspects:
namely, observing their intrinsic nature and observing the causes and conditions for their manifestation in the present life.
He contemplates the causes and conditions for the cessation of present phenomena;
he contemplates the causes and conditions for future arising;
and he contemplates the causes and conditions for the cessation of both.
One contemplates the causal conditions of the turning of dependent origination,
contemplates the causal conditions of the reversal of dependent origination,
and contemplates that reversal itself.
Among these, the antidote associated with pleasure refers to the most excellent fundamental dhyānas;
the antidote associated with suffering—
This refers to the attainment of the preliminary stage (sāmantaka) which is accompanied by detachment from desire and accompanied by neither-pain-nor-pleasure, serving as the antidote;
that is, within the fundamental dhyāna itself.
In order to demonstrate the cessation of the causal conditions for transformation,
it is stated that all feelings are indeed suffering;
this is because those three types of feeling are, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), entirely suffering.
Regarding "relative":
it means that because this exists, that is established;
this is called "relative."
Among these, all feelings are mutually related because they are all subsumed under suffering;
furthermore, this is due to the existence of this ultimate suffering (*paramārtha-duḥkha*).
Ignorance is designated;
because this exists, the supramundane wisdom that remedies it is designated;
and because this exists, its fruit—quiescent nirvāṇa—is designated.
