Furthermore, it is due to the permanent severance of causes so that [phenomena] do not arise in the future,
and because the causes from previous lives have been exhausted through experience.
The spontaneous cessation of all present conditioned phenomena is the truth of cessation established by way of predomiance over nirvana without remainder.
Furthermore, it is the right view that can realize and understand the ultimate truth.
Furthermore, all noble paths preceded by right view are called the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).
Moreover, it is intended that one should fully comprehend suffering and permanently abandon its origin.
Because one realizes cessation and cultivates the path,
the characteristics of the noble truths are established here in brief;
if they were to be established in detail, one should know that their characteristics are immeasurable and boundless.
Furthermore, by causing one to understand the coarse characteristics of the truth of suffering as a basis,
one is gradually able to enter into the subtle characteristics of the truths;
therefore, the various sufferings such as birth and so forth are first established.
Subsequently, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging is revealed.
Furthermore, the distinctions among the phenomena that constitute the basis of sustenance are established by way of five aspects. What are these five?
First, the food of edible morsels;
second, the food of contact;
third, the food of mental volition.
The four nutriments of consciousness and the fifth, the life-faculty— or, in the case of coarse edible food—
are all currently obtainable within the five destinies of the desire realm.
This refers to certain individual hells (*pratyekanaraka*),
not the great hells (*mahānaraka*);
it concerns other food and life-sustenance.
These are all manifest and obtainable throughout the three realms.
Since "sentient beings" are conventionally designated based upon the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
the Blessed One has said that these dharmas sustain sentient beings, causing them to abide without destruction.
Question: There are seven causes and conditions that sustain all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), causing them to abide without disintegration.
For what reason did the Blessed One say only that sentient beings abide by means of nutriment?
What are these seven?
Birth is the cause for the abiding of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
It is only through the arising of conditioned phenomena that their abiding can occur;
there is no such thing as abiding without arising.
Second, the life-faculty;
third, the nutriments;
fourth, the supernormal power of mastery over the mind.
By the power of that [merit], the formations of life are increased,
such that one may abide for an eon or for the remainder of an eon;
this occurs through the conjunction of five causes and conditions.
These are the causes for the persistence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
namely: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas,
as long as their causal conditions have not yet disintegrated.
During that time, they persist in a continuous succession without interruption.
Sixth, through the instigation of wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral mental orientations (*manasikāra*), prior karma is activated,
which is able to draw forth the various formations (*saṃskāra*) and cause them to abide without cessation.
What is called the arising through external factors produced by common and uncommon karma consists of seven types of non-obstruction;
these are the causes for the persistence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
By this, it enables the various formations (*saṃskāra*) to arise without obstructing causes and conditions;
once arisen, the formations persist as a continuous succession of similar states,
remaining far removed from causes and conditions that lead to contradiction or destruction.
If it were not so, they would perish and disintegrate.

Answer: Although conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) abide by means of these seven kinds of causes and conditions, these four nutriments (āhāra) are the predominant causes and conditions for the subsistence of conditioned phenomena.
Through various means, they enable the continuity of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to persist;
furthermore, these foods enable the continuity of sentient beings to persist,
being easy to grasp and easy to enter.
Even those such as fools and infants can perceive them accordingly,
whereas they cannot perceive other phenomena.
Furthermore, these various foods enable the emaciated sense faculties and great elements to all attain increase and nourishment.
Furthermore, it causes diseases to be cured and healed,
which other dharmas cannot do;
moreover, there are sentient beings who possess long lifespans.
If one does not obtain food, one will meet an untimely death;
furthermore, these various foods facilitate entry into the Path and enable the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness, such as mindfulness of the body.
This means that all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment.
Therefore, for these five reasons,
the Blessed One has taught that all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment.
For what reason, then, is it further said that conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) abide by depending upon the life-faculty (jīvitendriya)?
It is because there is such a case where one has never lacked food or drink,
nor does one encounter any difficulty in seeking them.
In those locations, beings abide solely by the power of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*),
remaining for as long as the lifespan they have experienced.
Therefore, the Blessed One, with reference to those locations, stated that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) endure by means of the life-faculty for all sentient beings.
Furthermore, among these, edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) should be said to be comprised within the spheres of odor, taste, and tangibility. Why is this?
Because it is through the proper digestion and transformation of odor, taste, and tangibility that [the body] is nourished and sustained.
Improper digestion and transformation constitute diminution;
however, other phenomena such as form (rūpa) do not undergo such nourishment, diminution, or transformation.
Therefore, it is said that they do not possess the nature of edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra).
If various material objects, at the time of being swallowed,
cause the mind to rejoice and the sense faculties to be gladdened,
they should not, at that very moment, be designated as "edible food."
It is merely called the nutriment of contact;
once it has been consumed, it is digested and transformed with ease,
increasing joy and happiness.
It is only at the time of digestion and transformation that it is called "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
If there is digestion and transformation that cannot nourish the sense faculties or bring about well-being,
then although it undergoes digestion and transformation, it is not called edible food.
If various substantial objects, at the time of swallowing,
do not give rise to joy nor cause the sense faculties to be gratified,
then at that time they are not called "food" at all.
If, at a later time, it becomes peaceful, undergoes digestion, increases, and brings about well-being,
only then is it called "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
If it does not undergo digestion, increase, or bring about well-being, [it is not so called].
Although that [nutriment] undergoes transformation through digestion, it is not called "food.
Question: Is whatever is a substantial entity (kavaḍīkāra) also food?
And if something is food, is it also a substantial entity?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions as appropriate.
There may be edible substances that are not food, namely those edible substances that cannot nourish the sense faculties and the primary elements.
There may be that which is food but not a physical morsel;
namely, contact, mental volition, and consciousness,
which are able to nourish and develop the sense faculties and the primary elements.
There may be that which is both food and a material substance,
namely those material substances capable of nourishing the sense faculties and the primary elements;
or there may be that which is neither a material substance nor food.
That is to say, if there is contact, mental volition,
and consciousness that cannot nourish the sense faculties and the primary elements—
such is the case for all remaining instances of contact up to consciousness.
In each case as appropriate, one should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Furthermore, regarding those dharmas that are results of maturation (*vipāka-dharma*) and those that are the process of maturation itself (*vipāka*):
If they are phenomena born of maturation,
all should be understood as such;
briefly stated, there are phenomena that possess maturation.
This refers to the outflows (*āsrava*) and that which is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
One should know that those which possess power, are not impaired, and have not yet been fully experienced through enjoyment are termed "dharmas with maturation" (*savipāka*).
Among the outflows (*āsrava*), those that are unwholesome (*akuśala*) are said to be powerful;
those that are obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) are said to be powerless.
Among the tainted (*sāsrava*) states, those that are wholesome or unwholesome are said to be powerful.
The remainder are termed "powerless.
If outflows (āsrava) or things associated with outflows (sāsrava) are abandoned by the mundane or supramundane paths of detachment from desire,
they are termed "damaged."
That which is contrary to this is called "non-harming.
If, in the past, its ripening fruit has already matured,
it is said to be "already exhausted through enjoyment."
Since that ripened fruit has already passed, it no longer exists;
as for that which would yield a ripened fruit in the future,
or that whose ripened fruit is currently manifesting in the present, [it likewise does not exist].
It is called "enjoyment not yet exhausted.
Based on these distinctions, outflows (*āsrava*) and that which is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) apply as appropriate.
If wholesome or unwholesome states have not been treated or abandoned, [they are so designated].
Its maturation fruit has not yet matured previously;
it is in this way that they are called "dharmas with maturation.
This applies to all those that are untainted (anāsrava), indeterminate (avyākṛta), or tainted (sāsrava).
If wholesome or unwholesome tainted dharmas have already been abandoned,
or if their ripened fruit has already matured,
all such cases are termed "dharmas without ripening."
Furthermore, at the time of death, the final moment of consciousness is a resultant phenomenon (*vipāka*).
If the mind that immediately follows in the linking of rebirth (*pratisandhi*) is also a resultant phenomenon,
then all subsequent moments of consciousness that abide in their own nature are likewise resultants.
Excluding the virtuous, the defiled,
and the preparatory neutral states of mind,
all remaining states are termed "abiding by nature."
If the mind, though free from desire, still continues to function,
one should know that this mind— excluding the wholesome states of the lower stages and the unwholesome-neutral minds resulting from application—
is also a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
Furthermore, this maturation (vipāka) in all instances should be said to be exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta),
provided it arises from the maturation of all seeds.
Excluding those phenomena that have already been abandoned or not yet attained,
the remainder are produced with their own seeds as the cause;
they may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
All such [phenomena] should be known as being born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Furthermore, this includes the final dying-consciousness in all states,
as well as the subsequent minds that follow in the first and second moments of the continuum.
Within the three realms, one should know that there is only the sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure,
with the exception of the initial moment of the mental continuum;
it should be understood that this sensation is comprised of maturation (*vipāka*) in all instances.
It should be understood that all other feelings of suffering and pleasure are produced from maturation (*vipāka*).
Just as their seeds are comprised within maturation,
so too do they function as causes and conditions by virtue of those specific causes and conditions.
For those classes of sentient beings born into the hells from a state of maturation (*vipākaja*),
there is a state of maturation immediately following that maturation;
the continuity of suffering and mental distress is just as it is for those born in the hells.
If one is born among a portion of the hungry ghosts or animals,
it should be known that it is likewise so.
If one is born among the classes of sentient beings in the human realm or the heavens of the desire realm, [it is also so].
There is no fixed maturation;
it may be either suffering or mental grief at one time,
or pleasure or joy at another.
At times, there arises only a continuous succession of neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations.
If the maturation of the first or second dhyāna arises,
immediately thereafter there arises only a continuous succession of joyful sensations born of maturation.
If one is born in the third dhyāna,
there is only the continuity of pleasure-feeling born of maturation;
if one is born in the fourth dhyāna or above.
There is only the ripening (vipāka) sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant;
therefore, one should know that this very sensation is designated as "born of ripening" because it is embraced by vast joy and bliss.
When those various wholesome karmas manifest as neither-painful-nor-pleasant states,
they are also called "desirable maturation.
Contrary to this, it should be known that [karmas] resulting in the opposite are "undesirable maturations."
Furthermore, the result of maturation that is neither-obscured-nor-defined (anivṛtāvyākṛta), obtained from white karma with white maturation,
is exclusively a desirable experience,
because it is sustained by seeds.
One should know that [this] is exclusively desirable and exclusively agreeable;
one should know that karma with black-black ripening is the opposite of this;
and [one should know] karma with both black and white ripening.
Because they are followed by two kinds of seeds,
it should be known that the resulting ripened fruits also consist of two kinds of feelings born of ripening (*vipākaja*).
Furthermore, black and white karma are established according to the distinctions of their types of birth.
This means that in cases where both black and white [karma] are present,
karma in that very place is established as being "black-and-white" in its entirety.
Furthermore, it is established based on the distinction of the specific action (*vastu*).
That is to say, there is someone who, with respect to a certain object and at a certain time, gives rise to a mind of benefit which manifests;
yet, with respect to that very same object and at another time, a mind of non-benefit likewise manifests.
Or one may take the property of others and practice giving it away;
thus, it should be understood that these are established through the distinction of their objective basis (*vastu-viśeṣa*).
Furthermore, such black-and-white mixed karma is established by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
That is to say, there is someone who, having performed a beneficial act for another person,
subsequently performs a harmful act toward that same person by means of some other matter;
for example, as when one acts toward a person who is extremely violent and evil.
When a thought concomitant with aversion arises and one takes no pleasure in that evil,
it should be understood that this thought is concomitant with aversion.
It falls within the dark portion because one does not delight in those things associated with evil;
it falls within the white portion.
Therefore, this karma is called "black-and-white.
The same applies to the remaining types as well.
This is because the seeds of all phenomena have not yet been impaired.
All those phenomena are called "conditioned phenomena" because they arise from causes that produce them.
Furthermore, there are the various karmas and afflictions previously committed.
Within the three realms, the fruit of maturation (vipāka-phala) ripens;
because this fruit of maturation is induced by karma and afflictions as its causal factors,
it is called a "dharma with causes."
Furthermore, because it is induced by the three bases being correctly present before one,
it arises within the womb;
one should know that this too is called a "dharma with causes."
Because of the combination with moisture, one is born among those born from moisture;
because of being enclosed within an eggshell, one is born from an eggshell.
One should know that it is likewise in these cases.
Furthermore, the six groups of consciousness are called "conditioned phenomena" (sahetudharma) because they have the eye and visible forms, up to the mind and mental objects,
as their dominant conditions (adhipatipratyaya) and their co-existent causes (sahabhūhetu).
Furthermore, there are co-emergent minds and mental factors which,
because they act as mutual, reciprocal causes for one another in performing the same function,
are termed "conditioned phenomena" (sahetudharma).

Furthermore, unwholesome phenomena are called "conditioned phenomena" because they are induced by causes, namely: proximity to evil friends, hearing what is not the true Dharma, and improper reflection.
One should know that, by contrast with these, all wholesome dharmas are called "dharmas with causes" because they possess three kinds of productive causes.
Furthermore, when one dwells in affliction, wrong diligence arises.
Abiding in fruitless toil gives rise to sorrow and suffering;
because it is produced by an inducing cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*), it is called a "conditioned phenomenon" (*sa-hetuka-dharma*).
Furthermore, abiding in non-defilement gives rise to right diligence (*samyag-vīrya*).
There is a state of abiding in joy born of the exertion for the sake of fruit;
because it is produced by an inducing cause, it is called a "dharma with a cause.
Furthermore, the mundane path leads toward the departure from desire.
Furthermore, they are able to induce the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
Because they are induced by such causes, these are called "conditioned phenomena" (*sahetuka-dharma*).
Moreover, within the present life, they rely upon the meditative attainments of the *dhyānas* and *ārūpyas*.
They are reborn in higher stages as appropriate.
Because they are produced by a productive cause (*ākṣepahetu*), these are called "conditioned phenomena" (*sahetudharma*).
Furthermore, mundane phenomena produce supramundane phenomena.
Because they arise from an inducing cause (*ākṣepahetu*), these are called "conditioned phenomena" (*sahetudharma*).
Furthermore, supramundane phenomena, which are subsumed under the Noble Path, are able to realize nirvāṇa;
that realization of nirvāṇa occurs by virtue of an inducing cause.
These are called "conditioned phenomena" (*sa-hetuka-dharma*).
One should understand that conditioned phenomena are established by means of the various characteristics thus described.

Furthermore, among these, the factors that give rise to the "arising of arising" (jāti-jāti) are called "factors possessing fruit" because they each have their own respective outflow-fruit (niṣyanda-phala).
If there are karmas and afflictions pertaining to future existence,
they are called "dharmas with fruit" because each has its own distinct ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).
If any of these three conditions are present—
namely, the presence of moisture and its combination,
or the presence of an eggshell or womb.
Whether it be the eye and visible forms,
or the various minds and mental factors arising simultaneously with them,
or proximity to evil friends and the like.
Whether it be associating with virtuous friends and so forth,
all such pairs of three dharmas are likewise due to their respective dominant fruits (*adhipatiphala*).
These are called phenomena that possess fruit.
If, within this present life, one dwells in defilement and gives rise to wrong diligence,
one will experience the dwelling of sorrow and suffering born from fruitless toil.
If, in the present life, one dwells without defilement and generates right effort,
there arises the dwelling in joy and bliss through fruitful exertion;
all such cases are due to their respective results of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
These are called dharmas that possess a fruit.
If one enters the path leading to birth in a world free from desire,
it is because of the predominance of the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).
It is called a phenomenon that possesses fruit;
furthermore, it can lead forth the supramundane path and enable the realization of nirvana and the supramundane noble path.
Because it is the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) resulting from dissociation (*visamyoga*),
it is called a "dharma with fruit";
that is to say, by virtue of the ultimate fruit of dissociation (*niṣṭhā-visamyogaphala*).

It is called a "dharma with fruit" because it possesses the fruit of ultimate dissociation; even if it is a mundane path, it is called a "dharma with fruit" by virtue of that fruit of ultimate dissociation.
One should know that this is called the distinction between the two paths.
By means of such characteristics as those described,
one should understand the established distinctions among all phenomena that possess results.
That is to say, according to what is appropriate,
one establishes either a result of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*) or a ripened result (*vipākaphala*).
Whether it be the dominant fruit,
the fruit of human effort,
or the fruit of dissociation.
One should understand that the establishment of dharmas that lack causes and dharmas that lack results is the opposite of this.
Furthermore, dharmas that arise through conditions are those that are without a master and without an agent.
This has already been analyzed in detail in the preceding "Analysis of Skill in Dependent Origination" within the *Manobhūmi*.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the distinctions among internal phenomena are established briefly by way of five causes.
For this reason, it is called "internal.
What are the five? They are so called by way of conventional designation.
Because of false attachment,
because of predominance,
and because of the appropriation of seeds.
It is a designation.
In whatever context such a category is conceptually established—
namely, as being posited as a "self" or as being posited as a "sentient being"— it is merely a designation.
"He has such a name and such a class of birth;
[the details] are explained at length up to such a lifespan.
This is what is called an 'internal phenomenon' (ādhyātmika-dharma) by way of conventional designation."
If, in this regard, one falsely gives rise to such types of attachment—
namely, reckoning [it] as a self or giving rise to the conceit "I am"—
this is called being designated as an internal phenomenon due to false attachment.
If, through the predominant power of these phenomena,
external objects such as forms and sounds arise in their various distinctions as things to be experienced,
they are thus called "internal phenomena" by virtue of that predominance.
If it can grasp the seeds of all phenomena— whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—
it is called "internal" because it grasps these seeds.
This refers to the five kinds of pure form, as well as mind, thought, and consciousness.
In this way, it is called "internal phenomena" by virtue of its objective basis (*vastu*).
Furthermore, other phenomena may be established as internal through conventional designation (*prajñapti*). Why is this so?
Because that which is obtainable internally is also categorized as an external sense base (*bāhyāyatana*) and is thus called "internal.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are subsumed under "form" (*rūpa*). Why is this so?
Because it can be observed to increase in various locations,
and because it undergoes transformation and decay through contact with hands, clods of earth,
and so forth, the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is therefore called "form" (rūpa).
The remaining four aggregates, by virtue of the power of various designations and by depending upon those various designations,
for the most part flow toward and move toward their respective objects of focus.
Therefore, these four formless aggregates (arūpaskandha) are called "name" (nāman).
Furthermore, briefly, the distinctions among the appropriated dharmas (upātta-dharma) are established by way of five aspects.
What are these five?
This means that initially, only matter (rūpa) is said to be "appropriated" (upātta).
One should know that this statement excludes the mind (citta), mental factors (caitta),
and so forth, because they are not appropriated.
Furthermore, among all forms, those internal faculties and that which the faculties depend upon are called "appropriated" (*upātta*).
It should be understood that this term excludes external forms that do not belong to the faculties.
Because that is not appropriated (*anupātta*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that "appropriation" (*upādāna*) refers to the mind and mental factors maintaining and not relinquishing [the body];
this term excludes [the appropriation of] things such as the sense organs, hair, body hair, nails, and so forth.
Furthermore, it excludes all internal bodies that exist after death,
because they are not appropriated;
moreover, appropriated matter undergoes transformation due to four causes and conditions.
It is called "appropriation. What are the four?
First, due to being pressed and touched by external forms.
Second, because it is induced by the internal elements' mutual opposition and equilibrium;
third, because afflictions such as greed and hatred frequently manifest as entanglements;
and fourth, because it involves the thorough investigation of the objects of perception.
That is to say, when external forms that are capable of causing harm and affliction manifest and oppress the appropriated body,
suffering, grief, and vexation immediately arise.
If there is an external form that is beneficial,
and one encounters it directly through a tangible object possessing appropriation,
then pleasure, peace, and benefit immediately arise.
If there are internal elements that mutually conflict,
they give rise to suffering and affliction;
if they are equal, they are embraced by peace and happiness.
Furthermore, when one is afflicted by afflictions such as craving,
suffering immediately arises, becoming intense and burning;
moreover, this occurs because of improper deliberation regarding the objects of perception.
Alternatively, because one is correctly examining the object of focus,
one gives rise to the reception of pliancy, joy, and bliss;
furthermore, one acts either to cause harm or to bring benefit.
Therefore, it is called "transformation.
Thus, whether it be form, the internal [faculties], or the mind and mental factors, if they maintain [the object] without relinquishing it,
and if such conditions cause it to become transformed, [it is so termed].
This is called the differentiation of appropriated dharmas.
One should know that those contrary to this are called non-appropriated dharmas.
Furthermore, [this includes] the four great elements and their derivatives.
One should know that only these are called "material phenomena" (rūpadharma).
Question: Just as the four great elements arise from their own seeds, so too do derived matter (bhautika-rūpa).
Why is it said that all derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)?
Answer: Because within the sense organs and the mind, the seeds of the various primary elements are present and follow along.
There is, moreover, the seed of derived matter that follows along.
When the seeds of the primary elements are capable of producing their fruit,
at that time, the seeds of derived matter that follow them must also necessarily produce their own fruit.
Therefore, it is said that derived matter is produced from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Those seeds of the primary elements that follow along with the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*) are called "having a location" (*sapradeśa*);
those seeds of the primary elements that follow along with the non-material sense faculties (*arūpīndriya*) are called "without a location" (*apradeśa*).
Furthermore, the primary elements (mahābhūta) are briefly of two kinds:
first, those comprised solely within the realm (dhātu);
second, those capable of performing their own functions.
That which is comprised solely within the elements refers to the seeds of the primary elements that are capable of performing their own functions.
This refers to the primary elements (mahābhūta) produced from their own seeds;
furthermore, these primary elements and the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) exist simultaneously and are mutually inseparable.
Because it is produced from causes of that same nature,
it is like a single mass of flavor that mutually interpenetrates and pervades all places;
it is not like a heap of parched grain, rice, or mani-jewels.
Furthermore, within a mass of matter that is exclusively solid,
only the earth element (pṛthivī-dhātu) is capable of performing its functional activity;
however, within the desire realm (kāmadhātu), the elements of visible form, odor, and taste also perform their functional activities.
Within the form realm (rūpadhātu), only the element of form (rūpadhātu) possesses the functional capacity to perform an action;
the remaining elements of water, fire, wind,
and sound exist there merely as seeds that follow along.
It must wait for other conditions before it can perform its function.
Likewise, within the conceptual clusters designated as water, fire, and wind,
the sequence is similarly applied according to what is appropriate.
Within the internal aggregate of matter, the activities of all the elements such as earth and so forth are fully present and can be perceived;
that is to say, there are various distinctions such as hair and body hair,
as explained at length in the sūtras.
One should know that externally there exist various aggregates, such as the earth element and so forth;
when these encounter such and such specific conditions,
they are able to act as the causes for the arising of such and such resultant phenomena.
For example, it is like when a skilled person drills dry wood and fire is immediately produced;
or like when white tin, lead, pewter, gold, silver, and other such substances are melted and flow.

Furthermore, it is as described in the *Pañcavijñānakāyasaṃprayuktā Bhūmi* regarding the nature of roughness, smoothness, and so forth, which are subsumed within the sense-field of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
One should know that these are all distinctions among the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
According to the various categories and states of these great elements,
they correspond accordingly to the four great elements.
The natures of roughness, smoothness, and so forth are merely designated by conventional names;
therefore, one should know that they all exist only as designations (*prajñapti*).

Question: As the Blessed One said, "Contact refers to the external sense base (*bāhyāyatana*), which consists of either the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) or that which is derived from the four great elements, being material, invisible, and resistant."
What is the underlying intention?
The answer is: it should be understood that these primary elements (mahābhūta) are capable of producing two kinds of derived matter (upādāyarūpa):
first, distinctions within their own class; [and second, distinctions among different classes].
Second, the distinction of different categories.
Regarding derived matter distinguished by its own category:
this refers to the various great elements producing qualities such as roughness, smoothness, and so forth.
Due to such causes and such conditions,
these primary elements arise through their respective distinctions and transformations;
it is with respect to them that various distinctions, such as roughness, smoothness, and so forth, are metaphorically designated.
Derived matter distinguished by its different categories refers to four of the five internal material bases— namely, the eye, ear, nose, and tongue—
and the external material base, as well as a portion of the mental-object base (*dharmāyatana*).
With the sole exception of the sense-field of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*).
It is because the Blessed One spoke these words in reference to derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) that is distinguished according to its own respective categories.
If it is derived from the four great elements,
one asks: regarding the form that the Blessed One described as "invisible and non-obstructive," by which great elements should it be said to be derived?
Answer: If one in a state of meditative concentration contemplates the various material phenomena of the desire realm,
and an image arises,
it should be said to be produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) of the desire realm.
If one with a concentrated mind contemplates the various material phenomena of the form realm,
and an image arises,
it should be said to be derived from the primary elements (mahābhūta) of the form realm.
Regarding these derived material phenomena produced from the great elements,
no further analytical texts appear elsewhere.
Furthermore, what is a "phenomenon that exists"?
That is to say, all mundane phenomena (*laukika-dharma*) are termed "existent phenomena" (*saddharma*).
Question: The mundane wholesome phenomena of Arhats and others, being mundane, are therefore included within this category.
By what causes and conditions is it called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: It is called "included within existence" because it falls within the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*).
Because it is eternally liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), it is called "outflow-free."
Question: As the Blessed One has said, "What are the phenomena with outflows?
They are the mind, worldly phenomena, and the worldly mental consciousness.
What is the underlying intent of this?

Answer: The Blessed One, with reference to those worldly mental phenomena (*manodharma*) and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) which are not to be abandoned yet should be abandoned, spoke these words.
In this context, the Blessed One speaks of various kinds of existence (*bhava*).
These refer to existence in the desire realm, existence in the form realm, and existence in the formless realm.
Their detailed establishment is as found in the "Stage of Wisdom Derived from Hearing" (*śrutamayī-prajñā-bhūmi*) within the sections of the Buddha’s teaching that are to be known;
all other phenomena are subsumed therein.
One should know that nirvana is the unsurpassed dharma by virtue of five causes and conditions.
What are these five?
First, because it is the cessation of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Second, because it is the cessation of the truth of suffering;
third, because it is the great security that is free from fear, calamities, and epidemics;
fourth, because it is the objective support for the unsurpassed dwelling in happiness in the present life.
This is because it abides in signlessness;
and fifth, because it is eternally abiding, ultimately peaceful, meaningful, blissful, and non-deceptive.
These five causes cannot be found collectively in any other place.
Only in nirvāṇa can everything be obtained;
therefore, nirvāṇa is called the unsurpassed dharma.
Furthermore, what is the dharma that should be cultivated?
This refers to all conditioned wholesome dharmas.
Within this context, it should be understood that there are briefly four types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*):
first, the cultivation of acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*).
Second, the cultivation of practice;
third, the cultivation of removal;
fourth, the cultivation of the antidote.
In this context, the intentional cultivation of unarisen wholesome dharmas for the purpose of their arising is called "cultivation by acquisition" (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*).
The intentional cultivation of already arisen wholesome dharmas so that they remain present and are not forgotten, and so forth, as explained at length, is [called "cultivation by practice"].
This is called cultivation by practice (*āsevana-bhāvanā*).
Cultivation through intentional application for the purpose of abandoning unwholesome states that have already arisen is called cultivation by removal (*vinirdhāvana-bhāvanā*).
The cultivation of mental attention through various doors of antidotes, such as revulsion and so forth, for the purpose of preventing unwholesome states that have not yet arisen from arising,
is called "cultivation by way of antidote" (pratipakṣabhāvanā).
It should be understood that herein, from the mental attention of discerning characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) up to the mental attention of conviction (*adhimokṣika manaskāra*),
it is called the cultivation of the antidote of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇāpratipakṣabhāvanā*).

From the mental attention of withdrawal (*prāvivekya manaskāra*) up to the mental attention of the culmination of skillful means (*prayoganiṣṭha manaskāra*), [it is called the cultivation of the antidote of abandonment].

The cultivation of the antidote of abandonment is called the mental attention to the fruit of the culmination of skillful means; the cultivation of the antidote of maintenance is called the mental attention to the fruit of the culmination of skillful means.
From this point upward, all these seven types of mental attention are included within the superior stages and the higher stages;
it should be understood that all of them are termed "cultivation as the antidote of distancing."
These four types of cultivation are, in brief, summarized as two kinds of cultivation:
namely, the cultivation of guarding and upholding,
and the cultivation of mental attention and reflection.
In this context, the cultivation of the body is called the cultivation of protection;
the cultivation of ethical discipline is called the cultivation of undertaking;
and if it pertains to the stage of meditative concentration, it is the cultivation of mental attention.
If one practices through mental attention on the stage of the knowledge of reality,
this is collectively termed "cultivation by means of mental attention and reflection.
Among these, the initial cultivation by means of mental attention is called "cultivation of the mind."
The second cultivation of attention is called the cultivation of wisdom.
Furthermore, what are past phenomena?
They are those whose causes have already been exhausted.
Once its intrinsic nature has ceased,
it serves as an immediate condition for the arising of subsequent dharmas,
with the exception of the final mind and mental factors of an Arhat and their associated perfumed continuities.
Even though they have already ceased after hundreds of thousands of kalpas,
they are still able to cause the maturation of pleasant and unpleasant fruits to ripen for that being,
just like the various past events one has experienced.
Some are capable of giving rise to recollection alone,
while others do not give rise to recollection;
they are manifested merely by their cessation and are devoid of all functional activity.
This is called the differentiation of past phenomena.
It should be understood that these past phenomena are established in their specific distinctions briefly by way of five aspects.
What are these five?
It refers to those phenomena that have passed away in a single moment;
that is, among all conditioned formations within a moment,
it refers to all formations subsequent to that moment.
Furthermore, there are phenomena that have died away and passed into the past;
that is to say, when various sentient beings pass away from their respective homogeneous classes of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*),
and so forth, up to the time of death and the moment of passing.
Furthermore, there are certain phenomena that have passed away through the destruction of the eon (*saṃvartakalpa*),
namely those comprised within the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) which have been ruined by calamities such as fire.
Furthermore, there are certain phenomena that involve the loss of what was past;
that is to say, there may be someone who, regarding the various wholesome merits and states of abiding in bliss previously attained,
subsequently falls away from them in accordance with their respective types.
Furthermore, there are phenomena that have been completely extinguished in the past;
this refers to all that has been extinguished within the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder and the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
Next, what are future phenomena?
This refers to that which, because its intrinsic nature has not yet been experienced,
awaits conditions for its future arising; it is about to arise, is on the verge of manifesting,
and is either proximate to arising or distant from arising.
It is also established through five aspects as distinctions:
namely, the future of a single moment (*kṣaṇa*),
and the future of a single lifetime (*janman*).
The kalpa of formation is future;
active manifestation is future;
that which is to be attained is future.
Furthermore, what is a present phenomenon?
It refers to that which has already been experienced due to its causes, whose intrinsic nature of experience is not yet exhausted,
and which is characterized by the certain destruction occurring after the moment [of its arising], being manifested by all defilements.
It is manifested by a portion of purity and is established through five aspects as being momentary and present.
The present of a lifetime;
the present of the kalpa of formation;
the present of active manifestation.
The final present refers to the final moments of mind and mental factors of an arhat.
Furthermore, what are the phenomena associated with the desire realm?
That is to say, one who is born in the desire realm or has grown up therein,
and has not yet abandoned the desires of the desire realm,
with a mind that is not in meditative concentration.
Within this state, all phenomena that have been practiced,
are being practiced, or will be practiced, whether through innate acquisition or through mental attention.
These are called the phenomena associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*).
Furthermore, what are the phenomena associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*)?
They are those which one, having been born in the desire realm, is able to realize through direct experience.
Having become detached from the desires of the desire realm through one meditative absorption (dhyāna),
but not yet having become detached from the desires of the form realm,
and not yet having initiated the higher preparatory application.
Or, upon emerging from that meditative absorption,
all those worldly dharmas belonging to the mental level—
which have been practiced, are being practiced, or will be practiced through the application of attention— [arise].
These are called the phenomena bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma).
Alternatively, they refer to those born in the form realm who have not yet abandoned desire for it and have not yet initiated superior application (prayoga).
Whether acquired by birth or through mental attention,
all mundane phenomena that have been practiced, are being practiced,
or will be practiced are likewise called phenomena associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*).
As it is with phenomena associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*),
so should it be understood for phenomena associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*) according to their respective natures.
Furthermore, what are wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*)?
To speak briefly,
all wholesome phenomena are called "wholesome" for two reasons:
namely, their intrinsic nature is non-erroneous.
Furthermore, it can counteract inverted states and provides security. Why is this so?
All wholesome dharmas function with respect to their objects without inversion by nature;
furthermore, they can counteract the defiled dharmas that function with inversion toward their objects,
leading one to the happy realms and the realization of nirvana.
Therefore, it is called "peaceful and secure.
One should know that the opposite of this, due to two causes and conditions, is "unwholesome":
namely, because its intrinsic nature is inverted and because it is not peaceful and secure.
The nature of all indeterminate dharmas is not inverted,
nor can they remedy inverted dharmas;
their nature is neither secure nor insecure.
Furthermore, one should understand that the distinctions among wholesome dharmas are established by way of five characteristics:
first, because they bring about desirable fruits in the future;
second, because they serve as antidotes to affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
This refers to the impurities and so forth which serve as antidotes to greed and so forth,
up to the Eightfold Noble Path, which serves as the antidote to all defiled phenomena;
for it is manifested by the cessation of the three types of defilement.
What is called nirvāṇa is that which is manifested by the four abodes of purity; that is to say,
those who have already abandoned desire abide in the noble and sublime dwelling in the bliss of the Dharma.
Fifth, because it is manifested by the benefiting of sentient beings;
that is to say, one who has already abandoned desire performs various kinds of altruistic virtuous deeds out of compassion for others— namely, for śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas.
Furthermore, the distinctions among unwholesome phenomena are established by way of five characteristics;
their characteristics should be understood as being the opposite of those mentioned above, namely:
because they bring about undesirable results in the future.
Because it is that which is counteracted by the remedies for affliction;
because it is manifested by the non-peace of defilement;
and because it is manifested by the abiding of various afflictions and disturbances.
Because it is manifested by the ability to harm others.
There are five causes and conditions by which wholesome dharmas become powerful. What are these five?
First, due to application;
second, due to past habituation;
and third, due to the embracing of superior qualities.
Fourth, because of the field, the object,
and the location; fifth, because of its intrinsic nature—
namely, that which is produced through uninterrupted application and earnest application regarding all wholesome dharmas.
If it is performed through the differentiation of immeasurable categories—
namely, either performing it oneself or exhorting others to perform it in that regard.
One should know that by means of immeasurable methods of consolation, encouragement, and praise,
and by feeling deep joy in the heart upon seeing fellow practitioners of the Dharma,
this is called the flourishing of wholesome qualities through application.
Furthermore, regarding all wholesome dharmas that were previously cultivated, practiced, or frequently practiced in other lifetimes,
by reason of these causes and conditions,
his mind in this present life is naturally inclined toward entering into those wholesome dharmas.
One dwells in opposition to all unwholesome states;
it should be known that this is called the power of wholesome dharmas due to past habituation.
Furthermore, these wholesome dharmas are comprised within the lower stages.
By means of those who have attained worldly detachment and those who have seen the noble path,
they deeply dedicate their minds toward liberation or unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
turning away from all speculative views.
It should be known that this is called the flourishing of wholesome qualities due to the gathering of supreme merits.
Furthermore, these wholesome qualities arise from giving excellent and sublime things to the great field of merit, to those who are worthy of respect.
One should know that these are called "wholesome dharmas that are powerful" because of their field, object,
and basis. Furthermore, among all wholesome dharmas,
those accomplished through giving are inferior in their intrinsic nature compared to those of morality and meditative cultivation.
If it is accomplished through ethical discipline,
its intrinsic nature is superior to that which is accomplished through generosity,
but inferior to that which is accomplished through cultivation.
If all wholesome dharmas produced through cultivation are superior in their very nature to [wholesome dharmas] regarding generosity and ethical discipline,
one should know that these are called "powerful wholesome dharmas" by virtue of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
By virtue of five causes and conditions that are the opposite of these,
one should know that they are called "unwholesome and powerful.
Furthermore, the distinctions among indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena are established by way of five characteristics.
What are the five?
First, the neutral state born of maturation;
second, the neutral state of deportment.
Third, the indeterminate [states] pertaining to the arts and crafts;
fourth, the indeterminate [states] of transformation;
fifth, the indeterminate [states] by their very nature.
Among these, that which is neutral by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*) refers to the material sense-faculties,
those which are nurtured (*aupacayika*), and the external material bases (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth that are not comprised within [the categories of] maturation (*vipāka*) and the like.
Excluding wholesome and defiled forms and sounds.
Furthermore, what are the dharmas of training?
They are those persons in training who are stream-enterers, once-returners, or non-returners.
Whether they be supramundane conditioned phenomena or mundane wholesome phenomena,
these are called the dharmas of training.
Why is this? Because by relying on these dharmas, one diligently trains from time to time in the higher training in ethical discipline,
the higher training in mind, and the higher training in wisdom.
What are the dharmas of one beyond training?
They are the supramundane conditioned dharmas of an arhat whose outflows are exhausted.
If they are mundane wholesome dharmas, these are called the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*).
What are the dharmas that are neither of training nor beyond training? They are defined as excluding the previously mentioned dharmas of training and those beyond training.
The remaining dharmas, from those of a stream-enterer up to an arhat,
whether they fall within the continuum of any ordinary person (pṛthagjana) or are the various dharmas that have them as their dominant influence.
One should know that these are called the dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Furthermore, what are the dharmas to be abandoned by the path of vision?
They are the five views, such as the view of a self-entity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and so forth.
And those [afflictions] that arise based on various views— namely, greed, hatred,
and pride— as well as associated ignorance and the non-associated ignorance regarding the truths.
Doubt regarding the Truths and so forth,
as well as the karma leading to all evil destinies and so forth—
these are called the dharmas abandoned by the Path of Seeing.
What are the phenomena to be abandoned through the cultivation of the path?
They are all wholesome contaminated phenomena and all unobscured-neutral phenomena.
Excluding the previously mentioned defiled phenomena,
all other defiled phenomena are called the phenomena to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.
What are the dharmas not to be abandoned?
They are all supramundane dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa),
and all dharmas present within the continuum of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
In this context, supramundane phenomena are not to be abandoned because their intrinsic nature is pure at all times;
other mundane phenomena are not to be abandoned because they have already been abandoned.
Furthermore, what is the dharma that is profound and difficult to see?
It refers to all dharmas;
one should know that they are all profound and difficult to see.
Why is this? Because the foremost,
most profound, and difficult-to-perceive Dharma is that which,
by its very nature, transcends all conceptual proliferation and lies beyond the path of language.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena transcends all conceptual proliferation and lies beyond the path of language;
nevertheless, by relying upon verbal expression,
they can then be apprehended, observed, and realized.
Therefore, one should know that all phenomena are profoundly deep and difficult to see;
they are phenomena that cannot be seen,
whether they are phenomena with resistance or without resistance.
Dharmas with outflows and dharmas without outflows;
dharmas with contention and dharmas without contention;
dharmas with defilement and dharmas without defilement.
The dharmas based on attachment and those based on renunciation;
mundane and supramundane dharmas; dharmas that lead to falling away and those that do not;
and conditioned and unconditioned dharmas.
The phenomena that are objects of knowledge, objects of cognition, and objects of focus;
the phenomena that sustain existence;
and the phenomena that have maturation and those that do not have maturation.
Phenomena with causes and phenomena without causes;
phenomena with fruits and phenomena without fruits;
dependently arisen phenomena and internal phenomena.
Phenomena subsumed under name-and-form;
phenomena that are appropriated and those that are not appropriated;
phenomena derived from the primary elements and those not derived from the primary elements.
There are phenomena that exist and do not exist;
phenomena that should be cultivated;
and phenomena that are surpassable and unsurpassable.
Phenomena of the past, future, and present;
phenomena associated with the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm;
and wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena.
The dharmas of those in training, those beyond training, and those who are neither;
the dharmas abandoned through the path of seeing, those abandoned through the path of cultivation, and those not to be abandoned;
and the dharmas that are profound and difficult to see.
If there are things that ought to be reflected upon by means of skillful reflection,
one should diligently apply skillful means to reflect upon and discern such phenomena in accordance with the principle of reality (*yoniśas*).
The remaining text on definitive analysis (*viniścaya*) follows.
It does not appear again.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle Sixty-six;
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle Sixty-seven.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya spoke;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.
Thus has been explained the analysis of the stage of wisdom consisting of reflection within the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*. Now follows the stage of wisdom consisting of cultivation.
I shall now explain the determination (*viniścaya*) regarding the stage of wisdom consisting in cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā-bhūmi*).
It should be known that there are, in brief, sixteen kinds of cultivation:
cultivation through mental engagement associated with the vehicle (*yāna-saṃprayukta-manasikāra-bhāvanā*), and so forth.
The cultivation of mental attention associated with the Mahāyāna,
the cultivation of images,
and the cultivation of the limits of phenomena.
The cultivation of accomplishing what is to be done,
the cultivation of attainment, and the cultivation of practice.
The cultivation of removal,
the cultivation of antidotes,
and partial cultivation.
Universal cultivation,
shifting cultivation,
and cultivation with applied effort.
It is the cultivation of that which has already been accomplished,
not the cultivation of factors produced by cultivation,
but the cultivation of factors produced by cultivation.
What is the cultivation of attention associated with the Śrāvaka vehicle?
It refers to a certain individual who is a śrāvaka abiding in the nature of a śrāvaka,
or who has not yet entered into the state of rightness and departure from birth.
Or, having already entered the state of rightness and freedom from birth,
they do not consider the welfare of others,
but consider only their own welfare.
By means of the mental application (*manasikāra*) on the established truths,
one internally contemplates suchness (*tathatā*),
taking finite and conceptual phenomena as its object.
In order to exhaust craving and attachment,
one cultivates mental attention through the aspects of disenchantment, detachment from desire, and liberation;
this is called the cultivation of mental attention associated with the Śrāvaka vehicle.
What is the cultivation of mental attention associated with the Mahāyāna?
It refers, for example, to one who is a bodhisattva abiding in the *dharmatā* of a bodhisattva,
yet has not yet entered into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-nyāma*).
Or, having already entered into the state of right determination and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma-avakrānti*),

they contemplate their own and others' various beneficial activities through the gateway of mental attention directed toward both the established and non-established truths (*vyavasthāpita-avyavasthāpita-satya-manasikāra*).
Internally contemplating suchness,
they take as their object the immeasurable and non-conceptual dharmas,
through the predominant power of great compassion.
In order to exhaust all craving belonging to oneself and others,
by means of the modes of practice that embrace the various beneficial activities for sentient beings,
and by means of the causes and conditions for proceeding toward the unsurpassed state.
The mental engagement of cultivating the aspects of practice is called the cultivation of mental engagement associated with the Mahāyāna.
What is the cultivation of images?
That is to say, because one attends to the mental image— the object of samādhi belonging to the category of conceptualized vipaśyanā—
as being concordant with the known thing (*jñeyavastu-sabhāga*).
Alternatively, because one attends to the mental image— which shares the same characteristics as the object of knowledge—
within the meditative concentration that belongs to the category of non-conceptual *śamatha*,
all such cultivation is called "cultivation of the image."
What is the cultivation of the limit of phenomena?
It refers to the mental attention and contemplation of phenomena—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; sublime or base; near or distant.
Or one attends to and contemplates true suchness (tathatā) in this way:
either by way of its exhaustiveness (yāvadbhāvikatā) or by way of its mode of being (yathāvadbhāvikatā).
All cultivation whatsoever is called "cultivation reaching the limit of names and things.
What is "cultivation that accomplishes what is to be done"?
It refers to having already entered the fundamental dhyānas or various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Whether it be mundane concentration or supramundane concentration,
all cultivation is termed "cultivation that accomplishes what is to be done.
What is "cultivation of attainment"?
That is to say, there is someone who, relying on the first dhyāna,
cultivates the perception of impermanence,
or even cultivates the perception of death.
Whatever other perceptions he possesses that are not manifest are either comprised within his own level or comprised within a lower level.
Furthermore, regarding all other virtues induced by that—
whether mundane or supramundane—
one is able to cultivate them so that they increase, become purified, lead to rebirth therein, and result in the attainment of mastery and accomplishment.
This is called cultivation through attainment (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*). What is cultivation through practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*)?
It refers to when someone directs their attention and reflects upon various wholesome perceptions, such as impermanence and so forth, with respect to each respective object.
Or, regarding wholesome dharmas, because of practicing through cultivation, one practices them all in the present;
this is called the cultivation of practice (*āsevanā-bhāvanā*).
What is the cultivation of removal (*vibhāvanā-bhāvanā*)?
That is to say, there is one who, by means of mental attention to the signs of the images that are the objects of samādhi,
removes them through the skillful means of using a wedge to extract a wedge,
thereby discarding all signs of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, just as one might use a fine wedge to drive out a coarse wedge,
so too does the practitioner remove the coarse and heavy body by means of the pliant body.
The rest is as previously explained.
This is called cultivation by removal,
which is either the counteractive of abandonment or the counteractive of maintenance.
Alternatively, the cultivation consisting of all mental attention directed toward the antidotes that act as distant counteragents is called "cultivation as an antidote."
Among these, the antidote of revulsion refers to all mundane wholesome paths,
with the exception of the immeasurables and those mental orientations induced by the playful supernormal powers of other practitioners.
The antidote of abandonment refers to mental attention that takes suchness as its object.
The antidote of maintenance refers to...
This refers to the subsequent mundane and supramundane paths, or the path of liberation;
as for the "distant counteractive" (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*),
it means that once the afflictions have been abandoned, one further cultivates the path of counteraction.
Alternatively, there is another distinction: the paths of hearing, reflection,
and cultivation are called the "antidotes of revulsion."
The supramundane path is called the antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*).
Its fruit, the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), is called the antidote of maintenance (*ādhāra-pratipakṣa*).
The mundane path of cultivation is called the antidote of distancing (*dūribhāva-pratipakṣa*).
What is partial cultivation?
It refers to any single wholesome dharma, such as the perception of impermanence and so forth.
The cultivation of whatever [practices] one attends to with mental attention is called "partial cultivation.
What is "universal cultivation"?
It refers to all cultivation consisting of mental attention directed toward the single-flavored *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena;
this is called universal cultivation (*sarvatraga-bhāvanā*).
What is cultivation with fluctuation?
It refers to cultivating by means of the application of signless cultivation at times when it is intermittently interrupted by signs.
This is called the cultivation of transformation.
What is the cultivation with application?
It refers to that very time when one is practicing through skillful means.
Cultivation that is practiced with intervals separated by application is called "cultivation with application";
this refers, for example, to the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Whether it be the vehicle of the solitary realizers or the Great Vehicle,
they have already attained the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) in its entirety.
And the attainment of mastery over all dharmas—
all such cultivation is called the cultivation of accomplishment;
it refers to the cultivation of all wholesome dharmas, such as ethical discipline and so forth.
There is cultivation that is not a dharma accomplished through cultivation, and there is cultivation that is a dharma accomplished through cultivation;
the latter refers to the cultivation of all wholesome dharmas belonging to the stages of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*).
This is called the cultivation of the dharmas accomplished through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*).
Within this stage, no further texts of definitive analysis (*viniścaya*) appear.
Thus concludes the first part of the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi* within the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, concerning the definitive analysis of the stage of wisdom accomplished through cultivation.
I shall now explain the *viniścaya* (determination) regarding the stage of the śrāvaka.
This is called "one who ultimately lacks the nature for parinirvāṇa."
In this regard, some may give rise to doubt, asking:
"How can there be those who possess the nature of never attaining parinirvāṇa?
One should instruct them as follows:
What do you intend?
That the various dispositions and the immeasurable dispositions of all sentient beings [are known by the Tathāgata]?
Do the natures of the inferior realm and the sublime realm exist, or do they not?
If one were to say that such a person exists,
it would be unreasonable to claim that there is no individual (pudgala) who lacks the quality of attaining parinirvāṇa.
If one were to say that [the self] does not exist,
it would be unreasonable for the Sūtra to state that "sentient beings possess various natures (dhātu),
up to and including the most excellent and sublime nature."
Having instructed them in this way,
someone raised an objection, saying: "Just as there are various types of sentient beings, ranging from those with diverse dispositions up to those with supremely sublime dispositions,
yet there are no sentient beings who lack sense faculties."
If this is so, why is it that those who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa do not likewise [possess roots]?
Or one should grant that there are beings without faculties;
such a person should be questioned as follows:
What is your position?
Are those who lack sense-faculties sentient beings or non-sentient beings?
If they are sentient beings, [then...]
External objects that lack sense faculties would then have to be sentient beings;
however, this is not logical.
If they are not sentient beings, [then...]
To ask why it is not permitted that there are sentient beings without roots is unreasonable.
Having thus been questioned:
A kṣatriya may at times also become a brāhmaṇa,
a vaiśya, or a śūdra.
In this way, having even become a śūdra, one may at times even become a kṣatriya;
and having even been born in the hells, one may at times even become a deva.
If one becomes a deva and at another time even becomes a hell-being (*naraka*),
why is it that one who is of the nature not to attain parinirvāṇa does not, at another time, become one who is of the nature to attain parinirvāṇa?
One should question him as follows:
"What is your position regarding the kṣatriyas, and so on, down to the śūdras?"
Including the hells (*naraka*) up to the various heavens (*deva*),
is there a totality of realms (*dhātu*),
or is there only a single realm?
If there were all realms,
the analogy would be dissimilar and thus illogical;
if there were only a single realm, [the same would follow].
Previously a kṣatriya,
he may at some time even become a śūdra; previously a denizen of hell,
he [may likewise become so again].
Or at some time, [the claim] that they even become gods is not reasonable.
Having thus been interrogated:
It is difficult to explain how, for example, while kṣatriyas and others possess all elements (*dhātu*),
those who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa do not likewise possess the element of parinirvāṇa.
One should question him as follows:
"What is your position?
Do you maintain that there exists a realm of sentient beings who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa?"
Regarding the element of those subject to parinirvāṇa and the element of those not subject to parinirvāṇa:
are these two elements mutually contradictory,
or are they not contradictory?

If they are mutually contradictory, it is illogical to say that while there are those who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa, there is no such thing as the dharma-realm of those who possess the nature for parinirvāṇa.
Conversely, if they are not contradictory, then this very same *pudgala* would both lack the nature for parinirvāṇa and possess the nature for parinirvāṇa.
This is not logical.
Having been thus interrogated,
[it is shown that] at one time and in a single location, there is no gold-seed-nature.
At one time there may be the nature of gold,
while at another time there may be no nature of mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli,
and so forth; or at one time there may be that nature.
At one time there is no salt-element nature;
at another time there is that element nature.
At one time there is no nature of the various-characteristic realm.
Or suppose that at one time there were that lineage;
since such a person was previously of a lineage lacking the quality of parinirvāṇa,
why would they not at some time become of a lineage possessing the quality of parinirvāṇa?
One should question him as follows:
"What is your position?
Is it that in a certain region this lineage did not previously exist?"
There may be this lineage later,
or there may have been this lineage earlier,
and later it may no longer exist.
Thus, there may be those who previously possessed the fixed lineage of the śrāvaka,
but later lack that lineage; and so on,
up to those who previously possessed the fixed lineage of the Mahāyāna.
Is it that one who previously lacked this lineage later comes to possess a definite lineage?
Or is it that one who previously lacked a definite lineage later comes to possess a definite lineage?
If one says this,
then the roots of goodness conducive to liberation would be empty and fruitless.
Furthermore, if that were the case:
It is not logical to establish fixed spiritual lineages.
Otherwise, your statement that there are those who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa would be untenable.
Having previously resided in the state of lacking the spiritual lineage, one later resides in the state of possessing the spiritual lineage;
it is like a certain location where there are those who possess the nature for parinirvāṇa.
It is not logical that one who previously resided in the state of possessing the lineage should later reside in the state of lacking the lineage,
just as with a particular location.
Furthermore, one should challenge them:
"What do you maintain?
Is it that those of inferior disposition who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa [are such]?"
Abiding thus within this inferior realm,
will they attain the state of parinirvāṇa in this very life,
or in a future birth?
If you say that it arises in this very life,
what do you think?
Once they have encountered the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha...
In this present life, is it possible to give rise to the roots of goodness conducive to liberation, or is it not?
If you say it is possible:
Having encountered the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha,
they are able to give rise to the roots of goodness conducive to liberation within this present life;
yet, it is said that they lack the nature for parinirvāṇa.
This is not logical.
If you say they are incapable,
then having already encountered the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, [how could this be so?]
It is unreasonable to claim that one becomes destined for parinirvāṇa while being unable to produce the roots of goodness conducive to liberation within this present life.
If you say that one only becomes a candidate for parinirvāṇa in a subsequent birth,
what do you think?
Is it because they have previously accumulated roots of goodness that they encounter the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha in that subsequent birth?
Can one give rise to the roots of goodness conducive to liberation?
Or is it that one has not previously accumulated roots of goodness?
If you say that one has previously accumulated roots of goodness:
If one encounters the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha within this very life and is able to give rise to roots of goodness,
yet it is said that one will only achieve the dharma of parinirvāṇa in a future life, [how can this be so?]
This is not logical.
Furthermore, in that case, the cause would be empty and without fruit.
If it is argued that one has not previously accumulated roots of goodness, [the response follows].
In this case, the preceding and succeeding states are similar;
both have likewise failed to accumulate roots of goodness.
To say that one becomes a candidate for parinirvāṇa only in a future life and not in this very life [is untenable].
This is not logical.
Furthermore, there are briefly ten kinds of śrāvakas.
What are these ten?
That is to say: the śrāvaka of the pure realm,
the śrāvaka who has already encountered conditions,
and the śrāvaka born of the defiled realm.
Śrāvakas are born in the pure realm;
śrāvakas are born in the age of the decline of the Dharma;
śrāvakas are born in the age of the virtuous and good.
The śrāvaka who has not yet attained the eye;
the śrāvaka who has already attained the eye;
the śrāvaka with the pure eye.
The Śrāvaka of Utmost Pure Vision:
if one abides in the lineage of a Śrāvaka,
this is the first type of Śrāvaka.
Those who have already entered the Dharma are called the second [category].
If there is a world-system where Śrāvakas are born, [they are included therein].
Within it, many forms of suffering are to be found,
and the five corruptions (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*) may exist—
namely, from the corruption of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*) up to the corruption of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).
This is called a śrāvaka born from the realm of affliction (*saṃkleśadhātu*).
One should know that the opposite of this is a śrāvaka born from the realm of purity (*vyavadānadhātu*).
How can the characteristics of those śrāvakas born during the age of the final dharma (*paścimadharma*) be known?
That is to say, there will be śrāvakas born in a future age during the final period of the Dharma who,
for the most part, will cherish gain and honor,
thereby turning their backs on the sublime Dharma.
All forms of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as unwholesome dharmas, flourish and increase.
Their minds are entangled and disturbed by various secondary afflictions such as stinginess and envy;
they dwell in stinginess.
Miserliness regarding one's home,
miserliness regarding gain,
and miserliness regarding honor.
There is no lack of perfection regarding stinginess with praise and stinginess with the Dharma.
Flattery, deception, and hypocrisy are constantly present before them.
To speak at length, they have gone forth into homelessness for the sake of making a living rather than for the sake of nirvāṇa;
they are full of restlessness.
Arrogant and flighty,
harsh-mouthed and boastful, indolent and forgetful,
his mind is not settled in meditative concentration and is beset by much confusion.
Their faculties and natures are dull and inferior, and they possess many afflictions.
These afflictions manifest continuously without interruption;
though they experience much sorrow and suffering, they do not give rise to weariness or revulsion.
Delighting in large assemblies,
they abandon secluded lodgings in the forest retreats and enter among the crowds,
frequenting the vicinity of villages.
They find delight in all bedding and requisites;
likewise, they even find delight in frivolous talk and delight in noisy crowds.
Delighting in vulgar and mixed company,
they are self-exalting and heedless,
unable to properly cultivate their body, precepts, mind, and wisdom.

They completely reject all the sūtras spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, which are profound, accord with emptiness, and conform to dependent nature, dependent origination, and dependent arising.
Regarding the compositions and recitations of the world’s wise ones—
those with flowery rhetoric and brilliant literary embellishments—
they follow worldly treatises, respectfully uphold them, and give rise to deep joy.
They falsely conceive the notion of "Dharma" regarding that which resembles the True Dharma but is not the True Dharma,
while conceiving the notion of "non-Dharma" regarding the True Dharma.
Furthermore, they take delight in manifesting, proclaiming, and revealing that very [false teaching].
They slander the True Dharma and the Vinaya;
they conceive thoughts of enmity toward those individuals who teach the True Dharma and the Vinaya;
they frequently violate the precepts and habitually practice various unwholesome dharmas.
Internally rotten while appearing virtuous on the outside;
to speak at length, even down to those who are not actually practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) yet claim to be so.
They still intentionally commit and manifest the two categories of grave offenses—those with no remainder and those with remainder—and thus violate their precepts.
How much more so for those that are middling or light?
Having already committed such violations, they frequently fail to confess and apply remedies in accordance with the Dharma,
or they confess only when their transgressions have been discovered by others.
Because it is not his true intention,
he desires to cultivate friendly relations with the families of his relatives and those who provide him with food;
thus, amidst the various activities performed for householders that lead to meaningless and manifold worldly affairs, [he becomes involved].
He is fond of wholesome undertakings.
Toward those householders who wear white robes,
he frequently gives rise to feelings of affection, respect, reverence, and compassionate regard.
They do not dwell with much joy in the practice of the holy life among those of similar dharma, nor do they give rise to modes of wrong livelihood such as feigning signs and appearances;
rather, they repeatedly engage one another with hearts of scheming and intrigue.
They delight in various forms of strife, litigation, and contention;
they take great pleasure in accumulating household property and requisites,
and they falsely maintain formal rules, regarding such things as superior.
Whenever they ordained people or administered the precepts,
they did so entirely for the sake of providing services with defiled minds,
yet they spoke as follows:
Now, solely out of compassion, I have caused him to go forth and receive full ordination; furthermore, I have [caused] his disciples—
those who dwell with him and those who dwell near him— to do the same.
Regarding those who constantly serve and attend to one’s every wish:
although they may be slow or negligent, they are deeply affectionate and accept one with a pleasing disposition; others are not so.
Although he is not indolent,
he does not harbor affection or take delight in receiving others; yet,
if he sees a bhikṣu who has many relatives and extensively attracts gains such as robes and other requisites, [he feels envy].
They will then respect, revere, and make offerings to them.
Even if they see a bhikṣu who lacks relatives,
provided that he is fully endowed with qualities such as few desires and so forth.
They nevertheless give rise to contempt and refuse to accept [the teachings],
consuming the property of the *saṃghika* and individuals without any sense of regret or shame.
They take pleasure in gathering those who violate the precepts and delight in forming cliques;
their sense of remorse is either feeble or excessive.
All that they hear and receive is for the sake of reputation and the causes and conditions of recitation;
or else it is mostly for the sake of gain and honor.
It is never for the purpose of disciplining their own body and mind.
