All such various defiled phenomena as these are fully accomplished.
As for the "time of the dharma's end," it refers to the period after the Great Master has entered parinirvāṇa and the holy teaching has vanished.
At that time, such śrāvaka disciples,
upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, mostly fall into evil destinies and are born in the hells;
however, those who possess qualities contrary to these and are undefiled [by them] are otherwise.
One should know that these are called the śrāvakas born at an auspicious time;
they appear when the Tathāgata has first appeared in the world, before the growth of the tumor [of the Dharma], while the Great Teacher is present before them.
There may be a certain class of beings who, after attaining parinirvāṇa,
through such manifold manifestations, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, again attain a favorable rebirth,
being born in the heavenly realms within worlds of bliss.
If ordinary persons and śrāvakas are said to have not yet attained the eye,
those such as stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners are said to have already attained the eye,
and the arhat liberated by wisdom is said to possess the pure eye.
If one possesses the three types of clear knowledge (*traividyā*) and is liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), they are called one with the utterly pure eye.
Furthermore, there may be a śrāvaka who,
though exerting themselves with vigor and diligence as is appropriate, [does not yet possess these qualities].
In this present life, they are unable to realize the superhuman states that transcend ordinary persons; however,
there are some śrāvakas who,
in this present life, possess the power to attain those superhuman states.
The fruits of the ascetic life cannot be realized due to negligence.

Furthermore, I shall now explain the distinctions between the various phrases—such as "endowed with virtue," "endowed with qualities," and "gentle in wholesome dharmas"—found in the *Candropama-sūtra*.
It refers to four kinds of pure and sublime dharmas among the śrāvakas,
by which sentient beings, upon seeing them, generate immeasurable merit through body, speech, and mind.
What are the four? They are:
dwelling in the perfection of ethical discipline;
maintaining the restraint of the Prātimokṣa.
The detailed exposition is as in the sutra.
This is called the first dharma.
Furthermore, there is the praise of being content with few desires, ranging from the detailed exposition up to the realization of the permanent exhaustion of all outflows.
This is the second quality.
Furthermore, there is gentleness and ease of association,
not troubling wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life.
Causing the bhikṣus to dwell together in joy and happiness,
and further accomplishing the four kinds of verified confidence (avetyaprasāda)—
this is the third dharma.
Furthermore, there are those who do not crave gain and offerings,
who do not cling to honor,
and who have compassion for others.
One conceals one's own virtues and discloses one's own faults;
although one truly possesses various merits, one does not desire that others should know they exist.
That is to say, wishing to cause others to know that one has accomplished such meritorious qualities—
this is the fourth dharma.
Furthermore, if there is a śrāvaka who wishes to go to another's household, [he should reflect:]...
One should first sever three secondary afflictions before proceeding.
What are these three?
First, the secondary affliction of forming intimate ties with the families of friends.
Second, the secondary affliction of stinginess regarding the two [requisites];
third, the secondary affliction of practicing the gift of Dharma with a mind that is defiled by attachment.
In this regard, the śrāvaka [acts] by means of six aspects.
One should go to another's house only after having severed the fetters and the secondary afflictions associated with the families of friends;
that is, one should go from time to time and not go too frequently.
Regarding pleasant things, one should not act improperly.
Upon grasping at their characteristics, they may momentarily give rise to craving, yet they immediately feel shame;
they do not employ violence, harsh speech, arrogance, or perverse conduct to pursue clothing and other such items.
He should well protect himself and well cover his body;
he should not touch with his body what should not be touched,
nor sit upon what should not be sat upon.
One shall never eat what should not be eaten,
nor ever drink what should not be drunk,
nor accept what should not be accepted.
Furthermore, with a mind that accords with seclusion,
a mind that inclines toward seclusion, and a mind that is on the verge of seclusion,
he reflects upon all virtues as being like mountain peaks— places difficult to approach.
They cause those who lack pure faith to attain it;
like ancient, well-trodden springs and pools,
they cause those with pure faith to increase all the more.
Having abandoned the secondary affliction of stinginess regarding families, one then approaches other families; that is,
when approaching other families, one is neither defiled nor attached to matters concerning sentient beings,
just as one is not with respect to those very sentient beings.
One should know that it is likewise with regard to matters of gain and matters of honor.
Furthermore, one does not give rise to sorrow or suffering regarding what is disadvantageous;
as it is with what is disadvantageous,
so it should be understood for lack of respect as well.
Furthermore, his mind remains equanimous amidst all gains and honors, whether for himself or others.
Regarding the gains and honors he himself receives, he does not praise himself;
regarding the gains and honors received by others, he never disparages them.
Having bestowed gifts and removed the secondary afflictions, he then proceeds to other households;
that is, he does not expect others to have pure faith in him,
and he understands the dharma of renunciation as it truly is.
Furthermore, one should cultivate three kinds of purely benevolent intention toward others.
What are these three? They are:
for the sake of bringing about happiness, for the sake of dispelling suffering, and [for the sake of establishing them in the Dharma].
Because one who respectfully listens to and receives the Dharma and practices in accordance with the Dharma attains great benefit;
and because it causes those afflicted by the sufferings of birth and so forth to be liberated from suffering;
and for those who have already been liberated.
Taking as an object the excellent and sublime nature of all phenomena, which is comprised within the *sūtras*, *vinaya*, and *mātṛkās* of the conventional true Dharma,
he acts so that the true Dharma may be upheld, recited, and long endure.
Therefore, it is proclaimed:
one should know that because the initial secondary afflictions have been abandoned,
dwelling without vulgar confusion constitutes the ultimate goal.
Because the second secondary affliction is abandoned,
the ultimate goal is the correct enjoyment of wealth.
Because the third secondary affliction is abandoned...
One should take the correct enjoyment of the Dharma as the ultimate goal.
Furthermore, I shall now explain the Vāthaka Sūtra:
if there is a śrāvaka who wishes to be skillful in the means regarding defilement and purification...
It should be thoroughly understood in brief across three points:
namely, with respect to the basis of affliction and purification by way of being the basis of affliction and purification;
and with respect to affliction by way of being affliction itself.
Regarding purity, it is pure by virtue of being pure.
What is the basis for both affliction and purity?
It is precisely this body, which possesses materiality and coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*).
As explained at length in the sutra:
this is the basis for the defilement of the foolish who lack wisdom and proceed toward ignorance;
it is also the basis for the purification of the wise who possess great wisdom and proceed toward clarity.
What is defilement?
It refers to when foolish worldlings, desiring to perform pure or impure actions,
first engage in mental investigation and subsequently perform all pure or impure actions with body and speech.
Due to these causes and conditions, within the cycle of birth and death across the five destinies,
one brings about the arising of a personal existence that is either desirable or undesirable, and either afflicted or unafflicted.
How is it purified?
This refers to the foremost and most excellent practitioner among those training in the category of purification,
who is able to perform their activities by relying upon the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*).
The second type of practitioner is one who has attained dissociation from all afflictions.
Furthermore, this purity is briefly demonstrated by five causes.
There are five:
first, the correct teacher;
second, the correct practitioner.
3. Right practice;
4. the abandonment of secondary afflictions that are the objects to be remedied by the training in higher mind;
5. the abandonment of secondary afflictions that are the objects to be remedied by the training in higher wisdom.
In this context, the Tathāgata is the one who correctly teaches;
the śrāvaka whose faculties are mature is the one who correctly practices,
and is also called the wise one.
That which is encompassed by the knowledge of the truths is called "right practice," because it functions as the unsurpassed antidote in the sense that it is capable of severing the afflictions.
Briefly stated, there are five factors that are the secondary afflictions to be remedied by the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*):
first, all hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) belonging to one who dwells in seclusion;
second, all anger and resentment toward those who are unable to endure instruction and admonition.
Third, the stinginess and envy of those who are deeply attached to gain and honor;
fourth, the arising of wrong thoughts regarding objects previously used or experienced;
fifth, the conceptual craving that conforms to the renunciation of what has been studied.
Briefly, there are three factors that are called secondary afflictions (upakleśa) to be remedied by superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
The first is the ignorance (*avidyā*) belonging to one who does not understand the meaning of phenomena through the gateway of conventional reasoning.
Next, there is the doubt and uncertainty regarding the truths that remains unsevered in ordinary worldlings who have already understood the meaning of the Dharma;

and subsequently, there is the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*) which is the object countered by the wisdom included within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) of those trainees (*śaikṣa*) who have already seen the track of the truths.
Because these secondary afflictions have been permanently abandoned and extinguished,
it should be known that one has realized the most excellent purification of the training in higher mind and the training in higher wisdom, as well as the fruit of arhatship.
It should be known that this Arhat is called "supremely pure.
Regarding these śrāvakas who are the basis for both defilement and purification,
they should be thoroughly understood in brief by way of three characteristics.
First, by way of intrinsic nature;
second, by way of causes and conditions;
third, by way of defects.
Regarding its nature (*svabhāva*):
the nature inherent in this human body is revealed by three characteristics.
Because it possesses form (*rūpin*), it reveals the common characteristic shared by all other bodies.
By means of their coarseness (*dauṣṭhulya*), they manifest the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of each individual body;
by means of their impurity, they manifest the characteristic of being dissimilar to the bodies of devas.
Briefly, there are three kinds.
This refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which are the common causal conditions for all bodies;
furthermore, there are two kinds of causal conditions for the individual, specific characteristics of the human body.
First is the causal condition for causing that which has not yet arisen to arise,
namely, the union of the impurities of the father and mother.
Second is the causal condition for causing that which has already arisen to abide.
That is to say, it is nurtured by such things as gruel and rice.
Its nature refers to the quality of impermanence and the quality of suffering.
If, during cold weather, one seeks out clothing and coverings as an antidote to treat the suffering of cold; or if,
during hot weather, one seeks them to treat the suffering of heat.
One pursues bathing as an antidote.
For those who experience fatigue from traveling on roads or performing labor,
one seeks massage and the like as an antidote to treat that exhaustion and suffering.
One should know that such things are of the nature of suffering,
because they are subject to destruction when encountered by hands, clods of earth, sticks, and the like,
and because they are subject to severance and ruin when encountered by swords.
Because once they have finally perished, they are either buried in the earth,
or consumed by fire,
or devoured by various kinds of animals and insects.
Alternatively, because they are withered and dried by the winds and sun right there,
all such things are of a nature subject to dispersal, destruction, and extinction;
one should know that this category is characterized by impermanence.
That which was once assembled but is now separated is called "dispersion.
Once dispersed, it undergoes transformation and decay until finally it is completely exhausted; this is called "annihilation.
Furthermore, it is due to the object of thought.
As it is said: "The name pervades all things without exception; by means of this name, all phenomena proceed according to its mastery.
What is the meaning of these words? To state it briefly:
Because of observing the cause of purity;
because of observing specific characteristics;
and because of observing the cause of affliction.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
If one thoroughly understands the four formless aggregates (*arūpa-skandha*) as being devoid of a person-self, [one realizes these two forms of selflessness].
To be able to sever all appearances of one's own objective spheres is called "outshining all.

This occurs when one thoroughly understands that the imputed nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of phenomena— which consists of conventional names and designations— is devoid of self-nature (*dharmanairātmya*).
That which can eliminate all those signs upon which [the self] depends is called "surpassing all.
If one transcends the four formless aggregates, no objective basis for the characteristics of a self can ever be found.
If one does not find even the phenomena that constitute the signs of the thoroughly imagined nature beyond worldly designations and names,
and if one lacks understanding regarding both of these types,
then one will give rise to the defilement of all objective appearances that follows along with them, as well as all the defilements inherent in those objective appearances.
It is because there is nothing that does not arise through the power of this predominance (*adhipati-bala*).
With this underlying intention (*saṃdhi*), the Blessed One said:
"Because of clinging to the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharma-svabhāva*), one proceeds by clinging to the nature of a self (*ātma-svabhāva*)."
By awakening to this, one awakens to that; through awakening, there is cessation.
Furthermore, there are the Four Noble Truths, which the Blessed One has taught for his disciples as the objects of focus for purifying the afflictions.
This refers to the Truth of Suffering and so forth, as previously explained.
Question: If the characteristic of truth is the state of being real and non-erroneous, [then...]
The various heterodox teachers perceive various false convictions and false doctrines that are neither true nor real, but are entirely inverted; how, then,
could these be subsumed within the Truths?
If it were not included [among the causes],
it would not bring about future existence (punarbhava),
and it would not be a cause of suffering.
Answer: Although it is neither true nor correct, it is nevertheless subsumed under the two truths of suffering and its origin. Why is this so?
Although all these are subsumed under the nature of falsity,
yet the very characteristics of this falsity are true,
real, and entirely non-erroneous.
Because it is of the nature of suffering and because it is the cause of suffering.
Furthermore, the meaning of impermanence is revealed by way of two characteristics:
first, the characteristic according to the principles of the Mahāyāna.
Second is the characteristic according to the principles of the Śrāvaka-yāna,
which refers to the meaning of non-existence and the meaning of the destruction of its characteristics;
it demonstrates the meaning of suffering through these two aspects.
This refers to the meaning of the heavy burden (*dausthulya*) of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of grasping at what does not exist,
and the meaning of the manifestation of the eight aspects of suffering, such as those arising in accordance with the three types of sensation.
The meaning of emptiness is revealed by means of these two characteristics.
This refers to the meaning of the characteristic of the intrinsic isolation of the person (*pudgala*) and the meaning of the characteristic of the intrinsic isolation of all phenomena (*dharma*);
through these two aspects, the meaning of selflessness (*anātman*) is revealed.
That is to say: the meaning of the characteristic of selflessness regarding the nature of the person according to the principles of the Mahāyāna and the Śrāvaka-yāna;
and the meaning of the characteristic of selflessness regarding the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Furthermore, there are two teachings:
namely, the teaching of impermanence and the teaching of beginninglessness.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of thorough penetration:
namely, the thorough penetration of the conditioned realm and the thorough penetration of the unconditioned realm.
Furthermore, for five reasons,
that which is impermanent is suffering.
First, by way of appropriation.
That is to say, first, because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that are impermanent are grasped by heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Second, by way of their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*),
because they are the intrinsic nature of suffering, such as birth and so forth.
Third, by way of persistence,
meaning that those three types of suffering constantly persist.
Fourth, by way of cause.
That is to say, it is because they are the causes for the increase of formations;
fifth, by way of attachment,
meaning they are the objects of erroneous inversion.
Furthermore, by five causes and conditions,
that which is suffering is without self:
first, because a self cannot be found apart from the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) that are suffering.
Second, those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering because they depend upon manifold conditions;
third, because they lack any autonomous agency;
and fourth, because they arise momentarily and persist in constant flux.
Fifth, because they are mutually dependent.
Question: If that which is subsumed under the truth of suffering is all that is unlovely, unpleasant, and painful, [then how is this so?]
Is that which is injurious and harmful also disagreeable and unpleasant?
And is that which is disagreeable and unpleasant,
being injurious and harmful, all subsumed under the Truth of Suffering?
Answer: If something is undesirable and unpleasant, it is suffering;
it is harmful and antagonistic.
One should know that all such things are subsumed within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
"Or there may be that which is subsumed under the Truth of Suffering but is not unlovely," and so forth at length; that is to say,
excluding those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) subsumed under the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
The remaining [forms of suffering], namely the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) and those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) subsumed under the suffering of formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).
Question: Just as the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, has analyzed the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) by way of eight aspects, [how does he analyze it here?]
That which is called the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age,
and so forth, up to the brief summary of the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*):
among these, how many characteristics manifest the nature of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*)?
How many aspects manifest the nature of suffering due to change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*), and how many aspects manifest the nature of suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*)?
Answer: The first five aspects manifest the nature of suffering as pain (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*).
The middle two [sufferings] manifest the nature of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*):
the suffering of separation from the beloved,
because that which has been obtained as beloved undergoes transformation and decay.
The suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
the suffering of change due to the transformation of what is beloved and not yet obtained;
and finally, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging as a general summary.
This reveals the nature of suffering inherent in conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Question:
Is that which is impermanent suffering? Or is that which is suffering impermanent?
Answer: All forms of suffering are impermanent;
however, there are things that are impermanent yet not suffering, namely, the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya).

Why is this so? Because the Path is not subsumed under painful sensations (*duḥkhā-vedanā*) and the like, it is not suffering as suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); since the Path does not undergo transformation, how could there be a time of transformation that would give rise to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*)?
Furthermore, because the Path is able to liberate one from all the heavy impediments (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to the category of all defilements (*saṃkleśa*).
Because it can oppose all forms of the continuity of birth, it is therefore also not subsumed under the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Question: Are that which is impermanent, that which is suffering, and that which is empty all without self (*anātman*)?
If one asks: "Are all things that are empty and selfless necessarily impermanent and suffering?
The answer is: All things that are impermanent and suffering are empty and selfless;
however, there are things that are empty and selfless which are not impermanent and suffering.
That is to say, herein the truths of suffering and its origin each possess four aspects;
the truth of the path possesses three;
and the truth of cessation possesses two.
It is neither impermanent nor suffering.
Question: If that which is impermanent is suffering because all impermanent things are suffering, then is it so?
Answer: Either because they are impermanent, or because of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
That is to say, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering because they are the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*);
they are suffering because they are impermanent (*anitya*). Furthermore, those that are suffering by their very nature (*duḥkha-duḥkha*) are also suffering.
It is suffering because it is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*); it is suffering because that is its intrinsic nature;
and it is suffering because it is of the nature of affliction and harm.
Because it is afflicted by suffering.
Question: Is that which is the Truth of Suffering also the Truth of Origination?
And is that which is the Truth of Origination also the Truth of Suffering?
Answer: All that constitutes the truth of origination (samudaya-satya) is also the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya).
However, there may be things that are the truth of suffering but are not the truth of origination;
namely, all that is wholesome or indeterminate within the purified continuum of an Arhat.
All dharmas comprised within the maturation of results existing within the bodies of all ordinary beings throughout all worlds;
and all present suffering or pleasure produced by human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
If there are formations associated with neither-pain-nor-pleasure that are indeterminate, one should know that they are subsumed solely within the Truth of Suffering.
Question: If one is weary of future existence...
How can that which is capable of leading away from worldly phenomena toward the supramundane path be subsumed under the truth of the origin (*samudaya-satya*)? By what cause and condition is this so?
Answer: Although they personally feel aversion toward future existence, they are nonetheless able to conform to the sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind that leads to future existence;
therefore, they are also subsumed within the Truth of Origination.

Question: If all karma and afflictions pertaining to future existence are subsumed under the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya) by virtue of their characteristics, for what reason did the Blessed One designate only craving (tṛṣṇā)?
Answer: Because this craving is able to give rise to grasping (upādāna).
Because it can incite karma and pervades all activities;
for when this craving arises, it is universally capable of inciting fifteen kinds of disadvantageous things.
Regarding "pervading all objects":
craving such as this is called "craving for future existence" (*punarbhavābhinandana*).
Craving that accompanies joy and greed, or craving for various specific pleasures, is called "pervading all objects."
One should know that it is likewise so.
Furthermore, craving for future existence is of two kinds:
first, that which takes the realm of future existence as its object.
The second is the cause for future existence (*punarbhava-hetu*).
Craving accompanied by delight and lust refers to [craving] directed toward objects that have already been obtained and are agreeable.
Or, regarding the affection for that which is inseparable from what is currently being enjoyed and which persists for a long time,
as well as the affection for various forms of joy and pleasure—
this refers to the affection for objects of pursuit that have not yet been obtained.
Either for the sake of union,
or for the sake of non-separation,
or for the sake of increasing all that is cherished.
Question: If it is craving (*tṛṣṇā*), is it also that which is accompanied by joy and greed regarding future existence, and consists of various delights?
Answer: One should provide a fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There may be that which is craving (*tṛṣṇā*) but not conducive to future existence, not accompanied by delight and greed, and not the pleasure derived from this or that;
namely, the aspiration and desire to realize the higher liberations.
Or there may be that which is conducive to future existence, accompanied by delight and greed, and consisting of the pleasure derived from this or that, yet is not craving.
This refers to the craving for various forms of pleasure and delight that accompanies the joy and greed associated with future existence,
as well as all the feeling, perception, volition, ignorance, and other mental factors associated with those remaining afflictions.
These three types of craving constitute the third phrase.
Excluding the aforementioned characteristics constitutes the fourth phrase.
Question: Is craving for future existence (punarbhava-tṛṣṇā) necessarily craving accompanied by joy and attachment?
If craving accompanied by joy and lust is also craving for future existence,
the answer is: all craving accompanied by joy and lust is also craving for future existence.
There may be craving for future existence that is not accompanied by joy and greed;
namely, craving associated with afflicted grief,
or craving for separation, or craving for non-union.
Question: Is craving for future existence also craving for specific delights?
And is craving for specific delights also craving for future existence?
Answer: Craving for specific delights is indeed craving for future existence.
There may be craving for future existence that is not craving for specific delights;
this refers to craving conditioned by the object of future existence,
as well as craving accompanied by joy and greed.

Question: If craving accompanied by joy and greed is "craving for this and that with delight and pleasure," is it also the case that "craving for this and that with delight and pleasure" is necessarily "craving accompanied by joy and greed"?
Answer: One should provide a fourfold logical alternative (catuṣkoṭi).
This means that craving for an already acquired desirable object, or for one currently being experienced, constitutes the first category.
Craving for a desirable object that is yet to be acquired in the future and remains uncertain constitutes the second category.
The craving that exists within this very state of certainty is the third clause.
Excluding the aforementioned characteristics,
it is the fourth clause.
Question: If one accomplishes feeling bound to the desire realm, does one also accomplish feeling bound to the form realm?
Conversely, if one accomplishes feeling bound to the form realm, does one also accomplish feeling bound to the desire realm?
It should be answered with four alternatives.
Or, it may be accomplished as being bound to the desire realm but not bound to the form realm;
that is, one who is born in the desire realm and has not yet attained the antidote to the form realm.
Either one accomplishes that which is bound to the form realm but not bound to the desire realm—
namely, those born in the form realm—
or one accomplishes both that which is bound to the desire realm and that which is bound to the form realm.
This refers to those born in the desire realm who have not yet attained the antidote belonging to the form realm,
or those who possess neither;
it also refers to those born in the formless realm.
Furthermore, having been born within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm,
they have accomplished what was to be done and abide in the supramundane path and the meditative attainment of cessation.
Just as there are four permutations when comparing what is bound to the desire realm with what is bound to the form realm,
so it is when comparing what is bound to the desire realm with what is bound to the formless realm,
and when comparing what is bound to the desire realm with what is unbound.
The relation of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*);
the relation of the form realm to that which is unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*);
and the relation of the formless realm to that which is unconditioned.
In each case as appropriate, one should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Question: Are all exquisite desires (*kāmaguṇa*) also desires associated with faults and defects?
Conversely, are all desires associated with faults and defects also exquisite desires?
It can be expressed in four propositions.
There may be a desire for exquisite objects that is not associated with the faults of being a source of affliction;
that is to say, when forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles are able to manifest without defilement.
If one does not exert effort toward those [objects],
one dwells blamelessly and at ease,
and is able to uphold the holy life (brahmacarya).
There may be sensual desires that are associated with faults and defects and are not sublime desires;
that is to say, those forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles which are entirely unlovely, unpleasant, unwelcome, and disagreeable to the mind.
And there are sensual desires that are afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, there may be excellent sensual desires (*maudgalya-kāma*) that are nevertheless associated with faults and defects;
that is to say, those forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles which cannot fail to manifest as defilements.
They are exclusively lovely, even up to being pleasing to the mind.
Or there may be desires that are neither excellent nor associated with faults or defects;
these refer to all the afflictions and their objective bases pertaining to the form and formless realms.
Based on these sublime desires and on desires associated with the faults and disadvantages [of sensual pleasure],
the Blessed One spoke these words:
"Discriminative craving is the desire of a person."
Furthermore, this craving is briefly of two kinds:
the first is craving for existence,
and the latter is craving for enjoyment.
This, moreover, is of two kinds:
namely, due to the distinction between objects of enjoyment already obtained and those not yet obtained;
and furthermore, due to the distinction within the realm of craving itself.
Furthermore, there are three kinds:
namely, craving for the realm of desire (*kāmarāga*), craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*), and craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*).
If one is born in the realm of desire and seeks further existence within the realm of desire, [this constitutes the first].
Delight in things already acquired for one's enjoyment and longing for things not yet acquired for one's enjoyment—
all such craving is called sensual desire (*kāmatṛṣṇā*).
Whether born in the desire realm or born in the form realm,
having already become free from desire for the desire realm.
One who desires and seeks rebirth in the form realm takes delight in the form-sphere attainments already obtained and rejoices in the superior attainments not yet obtained.
Whatever craving there is,
that is called craving for form.
As it is with craving for form, so it is [with the others].
The craving for the formless realm should be understood in the same way, as appropriate.
This very craving for future existence (punarbhava-tṛṣṇā) has the view of eternalism and the view of nihilism as its basis.
It establishes the craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*) and the craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*). Therefore, this craving is said to pervade all objects.
How does this craving, when it arises, universally give rise to fifteen kinds of meaninglessness?
First, it causes the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to become firm;
second, by means of the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), it defiles and afflicts all mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*);
third, it causes the continuity of the mind to revolve in a distorted manner toward its objects of perception.
Fourth, it comprises the remaining afflictions that are grasped by the impulse of appropriation;
fifth, it is able to establish its own continuity;
sixth, it is able to accord with and give rise to unarisen evil and unwholesome states.
Seventh, it is able to cause already arisen evil and unwholesome states to increase and expand.
Eighth, it is able to obstruct unarisen wholesome states so that they do not arise.
Ninth, it is able to obstruct already arisen wholesome states so that they do not remain, are not remembered, and do not increase, grow, and become vast.
Tenth, because it causes one to engage in unwholesome conduct, it compiles all the sufferings of the various miserable realms.
Eleventh, because it yearns for future existence, it compiles the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth.
Twelfth, they cause sentient beings to fear nirvāṇa.
Thirteenth, they cause sentient beings to delight in saṃsāra and to falsely grasp at its perceived merits and benefits.
14. As it is with respect to birth and death, so it is with respect to sense objects.
15. It causes sentient beings to think of harming themselves or of harming others;
as explained at length in the sūtra.
...up to the mental sorrows and sufferings arising from sensation and craving.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle sixty-seven;
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle sixty-eight.
Maitreya Bodhisattva spoke;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.
From the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, the second part of the *Śrāvakabhūmi*: Question: Is the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*)?
If it is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) stilled?
Answer: That which is the truth of cessation is also the stilling of all conditioned phenomena;
however, there may be the stilling of all conditioned phenomena that is not the truth of cessation.
It means that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are stilled through impermanent cessation and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Question: Through the cessation of which phenomena is it called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*)?
The answer is briefly twofold:
first, because afflictions are extinguished;
second, because the basis is extinguished.
Because afflictions are extinguished, there is the extinction-truth with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirodhasatya*);
because that remainder is extinguished, there is the extinction-truth without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirodhasatya*).
Question: If this extinction-truth did not previously exist but comes into being later, [how can it be considered unconditioned?]
How could it be permanent?
If it existed at all times,
why do not all sentient beings attain parinirvāṇa at all times?
Answer: The characteristic of non-transmigration and the characteristic of non-manifestation are the characteristics of the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
How can this truth be said to exist later when it did not exist before?
Furthermore, the characteristic of non-arising and the characteristic of non-ceasing are the characteristic of permanence;
the Truth of Cessation is likewise so.
For this reason, it is called "permanent.
If there is one who realizes the eternal cessation of all coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*),
that person attains parinirvāṇa.
If one has not yet realized it,
one does not attain parinirvāṇa,
because the truth of cessation exists.
Since there are sentient beings who have realized it,
nirvana is manifested through realization,
not manifested through birth.
Furthermore, if one explains the Truth of Cessation while remaining free from four kinds of faults,
this is called the correct explanation.
What are these four kinds of faults?
1. The fault of superimposition;
2. The fault of erroneous discrimination regarding specific characteristics; 3.
The fault of confusion of characteristics.
Fourth is the fault of diminution.
If one says that there is something distinct from the total cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
this is the fault of superimposition (*samāropa*).
To say that there is no difference is the fault of conceptualizing intrinsic characteristics;
to say that there is both difference and no difference is the fault of confusion and contradiction.
To say that they are neither different nor non-different is a fault of negation (*apavāda*). Question:
If all five supramundane aggregates of non-clinging (*anupādānaskandha*) are subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), [what then?]
For what reason is it said that the Noble Eightfold Path, preceded by right view alone, constitutes the Truth of the Path?

The answer is: it is so stated because of the three trainings. This is because a learner (śaikṣa), from time to time, undertakes training based on the training in higher morality (adhiśīla-śikṣā), and from time to time, undertakes training based on the training in higher mind (adhicitta-śikṣā).
From time to time, one undertakes training based on the higher training in wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).
Furthermore, these eight factors of the noble path are subsumed within three aggregates;
therefore, only this is designated as the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).
Question: For what reasons are right speech, right action, and right livelihood designated as the aggregate of morality (śīlaskandha)?
Answer: For two reasons:
first, because they depend upon the correct enjoyment of the Dharma.
Second, regarding the proper enjoyment of wealth:
that is to say, with right speech and right action as the root and the precepts as the basis,
one is then able to properly enjoy all the true dharmas.
Therefore, it is called the "reliance on the enjoyment of the Dharma.
By means of right livelihood, one does not rely on hypocrisy or other factors that give rise to wrong livelihood when seeking robes and so forth;
this constitutes the root and the basis.
It is the actual enjoyment of wealth;
therefore, it is called "based on the wealth of enjoyment.
Furthermore, in this context, the Blessed One described it as the nature of the manifestation of a supremely pure mind.
In this context, based upon greed and so forth, there arises the volition to commit transgressions against the precepts;
based upon hypocrisy and so forth,
there arises the volition to improperly seek after robes and other requisites.
If one is free from these matters, it should be understood that this is called the nature of the manifestation of the supremely pure mind.
Question: For what reason are right view, right thought, and right effort said to constitute the aggregate of wisdom?
Answer: Because this aggregate of wisdom briefly has three kinds of activity, it is by means of these three factors that one attains culmination.
That is to say, penetrating the true meaning of all phenomena is its first activity.
Having thoroughly realized the true meaning of all phenomena,
he then proclaims, designates, establishes, analyzes, and elucidates that very true meaning for others so that it may be easily understood;
this is the second activity.
The practice in accordance with the Dharma for the purpose of severing the remaining fetters is the third activity.
These three activities arise from right view, right intention, and right effort.
They attain the ultimate state in their respective order.
Question: For what reasons are right mindfulness and right concentration designated as the aggregate of concentration?
Answer: For two reasons.
First, by way of intrinsic nature;
second, by way of the basis.
Regarding that which is by way of intrinsic nature:
This refers to samādhi.
It is [established] by way of its basis through four causal conditions.
Mindfulness can serve as the basis for this concentration because it binds the object of focus; that is,
one binds and gathers the mind within the four foundations of mindfulness.
Second, because it is conducive to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
That is to say, by means of this mindfulness,
one dwells in clear comprehension (*saṃprajānan*) while guarding the doors of the sense faculties, within a mental orientation (*manasikāra*) consisting of recollection that is conducive to joy.
It is able to conform to meditative concentration because it is able to abandon the hindrances;
that is to say, within the various mental attentions (*manasikāra*) that serve as antidotes to the hindrances, such as the individual contemplations on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
One is able to sever all hindrances because of the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that consists in the cultivation of the signs of the four [factors]:
namely, that one who has attained detachment extensively cultivates the signs of calm (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) through continuous and earnest application.
Therefore, this mindfulness serves as the basis for concentration.
Furthermore, there are briefly eleven distinctions of right view, namely:
viewing [the aggregates] as a disease.
From the view of a boil,
up to the view of non-self,
and the fetter-view.
The view of dissociation is the view capable of abandoning the fetters.
Regarding the four types of conduct, there are four corresponding views in their respective order.
That is to say, regarding those formations associated with the active outbursts of the afflictions (*paryavasthāna*),
those associated with the latent tendencies of the afflictions (*anuśaya*),
and those associated with the relish for them (*āsvāda*).
Within the course of conduct accompanied by faults,
one views it successively as being like a disease, like an ulcer, like an arrow, and like an obstruction;
furthermore, if one views all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as arising and ceasing.
To view [the self] as impermanent is called the "view of impermanence.
To view it as being pursued by the three types of suffering is called the "view of suffering."
To contemplate that [self] as being devoid of other selves and what belongs to a self is called the "view of emptiness.
To contemplate that the intrinsic nature of those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) lacks the characteristics of being a self or belonging to a self.
This is called the view of non-self.
These eight types constitute right view that takes the truth of suffering as its object.
If one contemplates the Truth of Origination as its cause, its accumulation, and its condition for arising,
it is called the "view of fetters" (*saṃyojana-dṛṣṭi*),
because that Truth of Origination gives rise to defiled fetters within the Truth of Suffering.
If one contemplates the truth of cessation as cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation,
it is called the vision of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-darśana*),
because that truth of cessation is manifested by the dissociation from all afflictions and their bases.
If, regarding the truth of the path, one contemplates it as the path, the practice, and the departure,
this is called the vision capable of abandoning the fetters;
for that truth of the path is manifested by its ultimate capacity to abandon the bonds of the fetters.
Question: If one first gives rise to the views of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self,
and only subsequently gives rise to the views of being like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow, and like an obstruction,
for what reason are the views of being like a disease and so forth explained first in this context?
Answer: Here, it is said that they are "prior" with reference to a person (*pudgala*) who has already attained the Path.
Why is this? Because for those trainees (*śaikṣa*) who have already attained the Noble Path...
By means of the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*),
one contemplates the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*) as being like a disease, and so forth, up to like an obstacle.
Having observed in this way, in order to sever the remaining fetters,
one further gives rise to the superior levels of pure views of impermanence up to the view of non-self.
It should be understood that within this context, there are briefly two types of views of impermanence and so forth.
First is the view [of things] as being like a disease and so forth,
and the view that the basis is impure;
taking these as primary and using them as a guide.
First, it is for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained;
second, it is the vision of things as being like a disease and so forth,
which serves as the basis for pure vision.
Having already attained the vision [of the aggregates] as being like a disease and so forth,
he causes that vision to further increase,
and does so for the sake of attaining the excellent liberation of the mind.
Among these eleven types of right view, the views of emptiness and non-self are called the practice of emptiness;
the other views of practice are called the practice of wishlessness;
and the single view of practice is called the practice of signlessness.
This refers to the vision of the practice of dissociation regarding the truth of cessation.
Furthermore, within the path of cultivation,
all supramundane paths take the four truths as their objects.
One should know that these are all capable of counteracting all afflictions of the three realms.
Why is this? Because those in training who have already seen the path [have realized them].
First, through the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), one gives rise to clear realization regarding all conditioned phenomena,
both manifest and unmanifest. Subsequently, during the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga),
one takes all these conditioned phenomena as a single mass, a single part, and a single collection.
One observes through the successive modes of impermanence and so forth,
yet does not discriminate, thinking,
"This is the mode of desire" or "This is the mode of form."
This is formless activity;
this is directly perceived;
this is not directly perceived.
Therefore, one should know that within the path of cultivation,
the noble paths comprised by the supramundane paths are able to serve as a general antidote for all afflictions of both lower and higher stages.
Furthermore, when those noble ones progress through the path of cultivation by means of the supramundane path,
they for the most part repeatedly bring to mind and contemplate the signless through signless practice.
Why is this? Because by means of this mental attention,
one is most effectively able to induce dwelling in happiness in the present life.
Because it severs the afflictions. Furthermore,
it includes the five supernormal powers, the knowledge of non-contention, the knowledge resulting from vows,
the analytical knowledges, and all the unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma) such as the powers and fearlessnesses of the Tathāgatas.
All these are obtained subsequent to the Path; their nature is pure and they are established by the Path.
For this reason, they are all subsumed within the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Question: Should not all four truths be fully known?
For what reason is it said that only the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) is to be fully known?

Answer: Because the truth of suffering is to be fully known by means of two kinds of characteristics, namely, its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and its general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the remaining truths, one knows only their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*):
that is, one knows the specific characteristic of the truth of origin through the aspect of cause and so forth,
and the specific characteristic of the truth of cessation through the aspect of cessation and so forth.
By means of the practice of the path, one knows the specific characteristic of the truth of suffering.
Therefore, it is said that only the truth of suffering is to be fully known.
Question: The truth of suffering should also be permanently abandoned.
For what reason is it said that only the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) is to be permanently abandoned?
Answer: Because the permanent abandonment of the truth of origination manifests the permanent abandonment of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*);
therefore, it is said that only the truth of origination is to be permanently abandoned.
Furthermore, within the context of the truths (satya), there are briefly two kinds of clear realization (abhisamaya):
first, the clear realization of knowledge (jñānābhisamaya);
second, the clear realization of abandonment (prahāṇābhisamaya).
The clear realization of knowledge refers to the arising of specific-characteristic knowledge regarding the truths in their proper sequence.
The clear realization of abandonment refers to...
This means that by relying on the arising of non-erroneous knowledge in its proper sequence,
one realizes the complete abandonment and cessation of all afflictions.
Furthermore, there are briefly five kinds of causes and conditions for initiating right diligence.
First, proclaiming the true Dharma;
second, practicing and dwelling together;
third, examining the faults of indolence and seeing the merits of diligence.
Fourth, the continuity [of the mind] matures through the power of analytical investigation.
Fifth, one knows the distinctions between what has been realized previously and subsequently.
Furthermore, there are briefly two ways of realizing abandonment.
First, the realization of the suppression and abandonment of the seeds;
second, the realization of the permanent abandonment of the seeds.
It should be understood that disjunction (*visamyoga*) likewise has two kinds.
First, dissociation from the various categories of afflictions;
second, dissociation from the objective bases associated with those afflictions.
Question: As the Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣus, do not practice flattery or deceit.
In this regard, the Tathāgata perceives many kinds of faults in crookedness and flattery;
therefore, he admonishes the bhikṣus not to engage in such flattery."
Answer: It is because one who observes those who are deceitful and crooked finds twelve faults.
First, due to the causes and conditions of deceit and crookedness, one cannot realize true wisdom.
Second, one loses one's reputation.
Third, they lose the confidence of others;
fourth, they lose the increase of their meritorious qualities;
fifth, they lose the opportunity to hear the true Dharma, instructions, and teachings from the side of the wise.
Sixth, all evils increase.
Seventh, it causes the mental continuum to remain far removed from all that is wholesome.
Eighth, through deceit and partiality, it harms the mind, causing one to constantly harbor suffering and dwell in a state of insecurity.
9. Contemplating the suffering of future dharmas;
10. The vessel of non-noble dharmas;
11. Regret at the time of death.
After the dissolution of the body at death, one falls into the various evil destinies and is born in hell.
Furthermore, within the desire realm, there are eight types of conduct and seven types of matters regarding guile (*śāṭhya*).
What are the eight types of conduct?
First, the conduct of delusive flattery;
second, the conduct of concealing flattery.
Third, the manifestation of deceitful conduct;
fourth, the scheming of deceitful conduct;
fifth, the compliant behavior of deceitful conduct.
Sixth, the practice of flattery through scheming;
seventh, the practice of flattery through incitement;
eighth, the practice of flattery by feigning compassion.
What are the seven matters?
First, the matter of verbal expression;
second, the matter of interrogation.
Third, matters of conflict and dispute;
fourth, matters of manifesting friendship;
fifth, matters of manifesting trust and confidence.
Sixth, matters of false pretenses;
seventh, matters of hardship.
It is due to the first of these matters that those who are deceitful [arise].
They engage in conventional discourse with the world,
manifesting what is not meaningful as being meaningful,
thereby deluding others by means of signs.
Alternatively, within the context of meaning, one may manifest what is not meaning;
as it is with meaning and non-meaning,
so too should it be understood regarding existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, regarding the various evil deeds arising from the practice of deceitfulness,
if another person interrogates the deceiver,
he then conceals his actual transgressions and displays unreal virtues.
Furthermore, when those engaged in debate intend to investigate the merits and faults [of their opponents],
at that time the sycophants will immediately form various evil factions.
Moreover, when the sycophantic and crooked see that the debaters possess power and are violent and wicked, [they act accordingly].
Feeling fear arise in his mind,
he immediately manifested the appearance of a close friend by means of humble physical and verbal actions in accordance with respect.
Furthermore, one who is deceitful and crooked, upon seeing someone who is mild and upright and whom they can manipulate for their own profit,
treats them internally as if they were someone untrustworthy;
yet externally, they manifest themselves as being utterly trustworthy, accumulating appearances of purity and goodness throughout their conduct and demeanor.
Furthermore, one who is deceitful first feigns being a companion toward those who are kind, well-disposed, and dear friends regarding future extensive undertakings;
however, when the undertaking to be performed actually manifests, [he acts otherwise].
They manifest various deceptive expedients and shift the blame onto others,
claiming it is for the sake of preventing their own exhaustion.
Furthermore, once those who are deceitful have encountered any kind of painful circumstance, they [act in this way].
Regarding the suffering encountered from those enemies,
there is in reality no such heavy sorrow or heavy pain;
yet, one manifests as having heavy sorrow and pain.
This refers to deep resentment, grief, sorrow, suffering, and affliction,
even unto fainting. Furthermore,
a śrāvaka who utters harsh speech should not even receive instruction or admonition regarding the various truths.
How much less could one attain the realization of the ultimate truth (satyābhisamaya) or purification?
Furthermore, there are nine kinds of harsh speech that characterize the harsh speech of a śrāvaka;
if one is possessed of such characteristics, [one cannot attain them].
It should be known that this is called the "coarse speech of a śrāvaka with whom one cannot converse.
What are the nine? They are as follows:
when a person who has raised a charge is being formally interrogated.
One may answer with unrefined speech that is merely contrived;
or one may answer in a way that is inconsistent or incomplete;
or one may answer by resorting to skillful means through reference to other matters.
This is called the first characteristic.
Furthermore, by means of fallacious speech and the provisional formulation of other arguments,
one employs skillful means to deflect and dismiss the matter under investigation.
This is the second characteristic.
Furthermore, being entangled and disturbed by ill will,
one’s own mind becomes dull, confused, and turbid.
This is the third characteristic.
Furthermore, being bound by the fetter of ill-will, one gives rise to resentment, angry speech, and vulgar language;
this is the fourth characteristic.
Furthermore, he gives rise to a haughty mind,
thinking: "Since he speaks of me, why should I not speak of him?"
This is the fifth characteristic.
Furthermore, stubbornly concealing the transgressions one has committed oneself is the sixth characteristic.
Furthermore, the continuity of a resentful mind persists without being relinquished;
this is the seventh sign.
Moreover, one frequently gives rise to the intention of seeking retribution.
This is the eighth characteristic. Furthermore,
when others openly proclaim the various virtues— whether real or unreal— of one who points out faults,
one does not fail to give rise to faith and understanding, nor does one deny, disparage, or revile them.
This is the ninth characteristic.
Within this context, there are briefly two types of persons who raise charges:
first, those who are collectively respected.
Second, they are not mutually respected.
It should be understood that, among these, the first two types of characteristics pertain to the person who initially incites [the dispute].
The remaining seven aspects rely on the second type of person capable of undertaking [the training].
Furthermore, within the *Maulī Bhūmi*, they rely on the aspects corresponding to the *vinaya* regarding the ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*).
Now, this shall be definitively resolved.
The summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
Restraint, the establishment of ethical discipline (*śīla*), non-negligence, obstacles, training, and contemplation.
Based on the inclusion and enjoyment [of the teachings], there are briefly seven points concerning the profound explanations through analogies and matters;
these encompass the Vinaya and the Prātimokṣa.
What are the seven?
First, instruction;
second, permission.
Third, the prohibitions;
fourth, the grounds for transgression;
fifth, the presence of an offense.
Sixth, non-offense;
seventh, expiation of offenses.
What is instruction?
That is to say, when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, commands the bhikṣus within the Vinaya to abandon unwholesome dharmas and increase wholesome dharmas,
one should know that this is called the brief description of the characteristics of all such instructions.
If one were to analyze this extensively, it would be immeasurable and boundless.
How, then, is it permitted?

It refers to that which the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has authorized within the Vinaya: all causes and conditions for the requisites of life that can be utilized in the present without producing defilement.
What is meant by "prohibition"?

It refers to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, prohibiting within the Vinaya all naturally unwholesome acts (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and those acts that contradict the faultless dharma (*anavadya-dharma*).
What is meant by "the locus of transgression"?
Briefly, there are eighteen:
first, the unwholesome;
second, that which opposes the wholesome.
Third, the action of body;
fourth, the action of speech;
fifth, the action of mind.
Sixth, the corruption of precepts;
seventh, the corruption of views;
eighth, the corruption of rules of conduct.
9. Destruction of right livelihood;
10. Following and protecting the minds of others;
11. Protecting others from harm and affliction.
12. Guarding against doubt regarding improper conduct;
13. Sexual misconduct;
14. The alms bowl.
15. Clothing; 16. Food;
17. Bedding and seating.
The eighteen causes of illness, as well as medicines and other requisites,
are unwholesome; that is to say,
they constitute natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
"Contrary to what is wholesome" refers to all prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) regarding the spheres of bodily, vocal, and mental action.
One should understand their characteristics within all five groups of offenses according to what is appropriate.
Likewise, the remaining grounds for offense should also be understood according to what is appropriate within the five groups of offenses.
What constitutes an offense?
Briefly stated, there are five groups of offenses.
For what reason does one commit transgressions within these five groups of offenses?
That is to say, by way of five causes:
first, the cause as condition;
second, the cause as origination.
By way of three matters,
four skillful means,
and five culminations.
This meaning of the analysis shall be explained by me at length in the *Vinayamātṛkā* within the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*.
Furthermore, there are nine kinds of transgressions.
1. An offense committed by a lay male devotee (upāsaka);
2. An offense committed by a lay female devotee (upāsikā);
3. An offense committed by a male novice (śrāmaṇera).
4. Offenses of the śikṣamāṇā;
5. Offenses of the śrāmaṇerī;
6. Offenses of the bhikṣuṇī.
Seven are committed by bhikṣus;
eight are committed by ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana);
nine are committed by those in training (śaikṣa), but none are committed by those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Why is this? Because there is nothing further for him to do;
by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), he attains the cessation of all training rules (*śikṣāpada*), both minor and those following the minor ones.
Furthermore, one who is concentrated cannot commit an afflicted offense.
How is it that there is no offense?
Briefly, there are four kinds.
First, the beginner;
second, the insane;
third, the mentally deranged.
Fourth, being oppressed by painful sensations.
How does one emerge from the offense?
Briefly, it is by means of five aspects.
First, by means of oneself;
second, by means of another;
third, by means of both oneself and another.
Fourth, because of the transformation;
fifth, because of relinquishment.
Regarding "by way of oneself":
This means that one should personally bring [the transgression] to rest.
Regarding "due to others," it refers to the non-afflicted offenses committed by those who have seen the truths (dṛṣṭasatya) when they have transgressed.
"By way of self and others" refers to the defiled and undefiled offenses of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
"Based on transformation" means:
That is to say, when one relinquishes the status of a bhikṣu and acquires the status of a bhikṣuṇī,
or relinquishes the status of a bhikṣuṇī and acquires the status of a bhikṣu,
at that time, each incurs the offenses committed while in their respective statuses.
Either it transforms into another form or it transforms into formlessness.
Regarding "due to relinquishment," this refers to after death.
The establishment of the training rules (śikṣāpada) consists of two purities:
first, purity of principle;
second, purity of fruit.
Third, the purity of gathering;
fourth, external purity;
fifth, internal purity.
Sixth, the purity of complete discernment;
seventh, the purity of affection and respect;
eighth, the purity of cultivation through the application of antidotes.
Ninth is the purity of cultivating the antidote for the abandonment of the nine latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Tenth is the purity of the uninterrupted continuity.
Furthermore, there is another distinction.
That is to say: purity through the establishment of training rules based on causes and conditions;
purity through being far removed from the extreme of indulging in sensual pleasures;
and purity through being far removed from the extreme of inflicting self-mortification.
Purity of superior conduct,
purity of superior livelihood,
and purity of dwelling together with those of the same Dharma.
Purity through the absence of conflict and dispute;
purity through the subduing of afflictions;
and purity through liberation from the bonds of afflictions.
It maintains the purity of the true Dharma.
Furthermore, there are briefly ten kinds of faults regarding ethical discipline (*śīla*):
first, the fault of violating the training.
Second, the fault of lack of joy;
third, the fault of incompatible companions;
fourth, the fault of aspiration.
Fifth, the fault of negligence;
sixth, the fault of overweening pride;
seventh, the fault of the impurity of latent tendencies.
8. The fault of impurity of intention;
9. The fault of lack of renunciation;
10. The fault of wrong observances.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of merit of ethical discipline (*śīla*):
first, concordant ethical discipline;
second, uninterrupted ethical discipline.
Third is the morality of being without enmity;
fourth is the morality of being without harm;
fifth is firm morality.
Sixth, the morality of renunciation;
seventh, the morality that excels its opposites;
eighth, the morality of non-retrogression.
Ninth, the uncommon śīla;
tenth, the unsurpassed śīla.
Furthermore, regarding the bhikṣu who diligently trains in the vinaya:
One should practice non-negligence based on ten occasions.
What are these ten?
First, the occasion of committing an offense.
Second, based on the time of meditative concentration;
third, based on the time of birth;
fourth, based on the time of begging for alms.
Fifth, based on the time of performing activities;
sixth, based on the time of enjoying gains and honor;
seventh, based on the time of seeking extensive learning.
Eighth, based on the time of reflecting upon the sublime Dharma;
ninth, based on the time of seclusion;
tenth, based on the time of ultimate penetration.
How should a bhikṣu who diligently trains in the Vinaya practice heedfulness at the very first moment of an offense?
It is said that there is a bhikṣu who accomplishes the fivefold heedfulness comprised of [the factors] such as that which accompanies the past limit (*pūrvānta-sahagata*).
As explained extensively above,
this is called the practice of heedfulness by a bhikṣu diligently training in the Vinaya during the first stage.
How does a bhikṣu diligently training in the Vinaya practice heedfulness during the second stage, which relies upon meditative concentration?
That is to say, there is a bhikṣu who,
dwelling either in a secluded place or at the foot of a tree,
gives rise to the hindrance of sensual desire, up to and including the hindrance of doubt.
Ultimately unable to endure it,
one then abandons, dispels, and ejects those [hindrances].
Because the five hindrances can defile the mind and even prevent one from attaining nirvāṇa.
In order to abandon [these states], one should at times cultivate the sign of tranquility (śamatha),
at times cultivate the sign of exertion (pragraha),
and at times cultivate the sign of equanimity (upekṣā).
Having become skilled in these signs of tranquility, exertion, and equanimity,
he correctly practices exertion when his mind is depressed and fears depression;
he practices internal tranquility when his mind is agitated and fears agitation.
Having attained equanimity of mind, one then cultivates superior equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Furthermore, within the samādhi already attained,
one does not give rise to attachment to its flavor nor produce any longing for it.
Being free from attachment and dwelling without clinging—
this is called the second stage of a bhikṣu diligently training in the vinaya, wherein he cultivates heedfulness.
How does a bhikṣu who diligently trains in the Vinaya practice heedfulness during the third period of life?
It refers to a bhikṣu whose mind becomes intense at the time of his approaching death.
One should arouse such a mind of correct application, thinking:
"I shall now die with a mind focused on the Buddha, focused on the Dharma, and focused on the Saṅgha, and with right livelihood;
I shall die with a virtuous mind directed toward what is wholesome."
He then gives rise to such and such a well-guarded mind;
right mindfulness becomes manifest,
and he dies with mindfulness directed toward the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, as well as toward various wholesome states and a virtuous mind.
Because he passes away with right mindfulness directed toward the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Saṅgha, and with a virtuous mind directed toward what is wholesome,
he is said to have a "noble death" and a "noble passing."
It is also called the "Expedient and Virtuous Course.
In future lives,
this is termed the third stage of a bhikṣu diligently training in the Vinaya, wherein he practices heedfulness.
How should a bhikṣu who diligently trains in the Vinaya be heedful during the fourth period of the alms-round? It is as follows:
there is a bhikṣu who dwells in dependence upon a village, town, or settlement.
In that very village or town,
he practices as extensively described in the *Piṇḍapāta-pariśuddhi-sūtra*.
This is called the fourth period of diligent practice in which a bhikṣu trains in the Vinaya, cultivating heedfulness.
How should a bhikṣu who is diligently training in the Vinaya be heedful during the fifth period regarding his duties? It is as follows:
there is a bhikṣu engaged in work related to his alms-bowl.
He applies himself to work regarding robes,
to service and attendance toward wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life,
or to whatever other tasks there may be, remaining entirely free from negligence.
Because there is no negligence, one is neither scorched nor burned;
one does not lose [the Dharma] nor is it destroyed,
nor does it fall away or pass beyond.
What he does is not base; what he does is not evil.
What he does is neither too hurried nor too slow.
What he does is neither restless nor defiled.
Acting in accordance with the world and in accordance with all the rules of the Vinaya—
this is called the fifth period of diligent practice for a bhikṣu training in the Vinaya, wherein he cultivates heedfulness.
How should a bhikṣu who diligently trains in the Vinaya be heedful during the sixth period regarding the enjoyment of gains and honors?
It is as follows: there is a bhikṣu.
Whatever gain, offerings, and honor he may obtain,
he remains unstained by and unattached to them;
he does not indulge in them nor become immersed in them.
Without becoming weary or attached,
and without cherishing or indulging them, one experiences them while deeply perceiving their faults and disadvantages.
He understands renunciation well and makes use of things accordingly;
he is able to exercise self-restraint regarding whatever gains and honors he receives,
and his mind does not dwell in arrogance because of those gains and honors.
This is called the practice of heedfulness during the sixth period for a bhikṣu who is diligently training in the Vinaya.
What is the practice of heedfulness during the seventh period for a bhikṣu who is diligently training in the Vinaya, which concerns the pursuit of extensive learning?
That is to say, there is a bhikṣu who has abandoned all worldly recitations, ornate discourses,
and flowery literary compositions.
In accordance with the world, he possesses extensive learning that corresponds to all the profound,
seemingly profound teachings on emptiness, conditionality, and dependent origination spoken by the Buddha.
Whether in accordance with or contrary to all the sūtras,
one should reverently receive and uphold them,
bringing them to ultimate completion.
It is not by observing that there is something to be found or obtained among all phenomena that one is said to have attained the ultimate;
nor is it by observing that one has escaped from debate and censure among all phenomena that one attains such benefit.
This is called attaining the ultimate;
it is not for the sake of gain or honor,
but is undertaken solely for the purpose of attaining self-discipline.
One attains tranquility for oneself;
one attains nirvana for oneself;
and because one attains for oneself the supreme benefit of the goal of a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa.
In this regard, one who listens well to this Dharma, receives it well, recites it, masters it, becomes proficient in it, and reaches its ultimate consummation—
this is called the seventh occasion of practicing heedfulness for a bhikṣu diligently training in the Vinaya.
How should a bhikṣu who diligently trains in the Vinaya practice vigilance during the eighth period for reflecting upon the true Dharma? It is as follows:
there is a bhikṣu who dwells alone in a secluded place.
In accordance with what has been heard, what has been received, and what has been attained,
one contemplates the meaning of all phenomena, weighing and examining them;
one reflects upon that which should be reflected upon and remains free from that which should not be reflected upon.
In some parts he merely gives rise to faith and understanding;
in other parts he examines with wisdom.
Whatever he contemplates, he does so by relying on the meaning and not on the literal expression.
One understands as they truly are the "black" discourse and the "great" discourse,
reflecting with firm resolve, reflecting with thorough discernment,
and reflecting with continuous application.
Whatever one contemplates, one must bring it to ultimate completion;
in the interim, one never retreats or becomes discouraged.
This is called the cultivation of heedfulness by a bhikṣu diligently training in the Vinaya during the eighth period.
How should a bhikṣu who diligently trains in the Vinaya practice non-negligence during the ninth period based on seclusion?
It is as follows: there is a bhikṣu who does not dwell in association with either the householders or those who have gone forth.
They do not share their joys nor their sorrows.
To speak more extensively, even regarding worldly affairs that arise,
they ultimately do not permit themselves to follow after them.
Dwelling in secluded forest retreats,
he remains in lodgings remote from all the distractions of inhabited areas and towns, as well as from the secondary afflictions that obstruct both serenity and insight, such as indolence.
This is called the cultivation of heedfulness during the ninth period for a bhikṣu who is diligently training in the Vinaya.
What is the cultivation of heedfulness for a bhikṣu who is diligently training in the Vinaya during the tenth period, which relies upon the penetration of the ultimate?
That is to say, there is a bhikṣu who,
regarding what exists, knows as it truly is that it exists;
and regarding what does not exist...
One knows as it truly is that which is non-existent;
one knows as it truly is that which is surpassable as surpassable;
and one knows as it truly is that which is unsurpassable as unsurpassable.
Because he knows existence and non-existence, the surpassable and the unsurpassable, as they truly are,
he does not give rise to the notion of attainment regarding what has not been attained,
nor does he give rise to the notion of realization regarding what has not been realized.
Being free from overweening pride and not being possessed by overweening pride,
he declares his own understanding because he is sustained by it.
This is called the practice of heedfulness during the tenth period for a bhikṣu diligently training in the Vinaya.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of obstacles that can hinder one’s renunciation.
That is to say: the obstacle of intention,
the obstacle of the basis,
and the obstacle of karma.
The obstacle of lack of autonomy.
Regarding the obstacle of intention:
it refers, for instance, to seeking to go forth into homelessness because one is coerced by the power of a king.
Such as these. Regarding the obstacles to the basis:
this refers to those who are blind or deaf, or who are *śaṇḍha* or *paṇḍaka*.
Or their bodies may be afflicted by various malignant diseases such as scabies, leprosy, baldness,
lameness, or being crippled;
such are the karmic obstructions.
This refers to grave evil karmas such as killing one's mother and so forth.
Regarding the obstacle of lack of autonomy,
it refers to not being permitted by one's parents and others.
If male or female servants, or royal ministers, are plundered by others;
or if they are captured,
or if they are able to provide a defense.
Those who have gone forth should certainly train in the Vinaya in this manner.
What are the five?
This means one should train in knowing what constitutes an offense and what does not, whether it is grave or light, as well as the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* as briefly explained therein.
What constitutes an offense and what does not has already been explained previously.
An offense becomes grave through six kinds of distinctions.
First, the distinction of formal establishment;
that is, because it is established within a training rule (*śikṣāpada*).
Second is the distinction between types of offenses.
This means that although both are equally *pāyattika* (offenses requiring expiation),
there is a distinction between natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), such as killing, and other prohibited transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).
Third, the distinction of perforations:
that is to say, as there is one who repeatedly commits offenses.
Fourth, the distinction of afflictions.
This refers to a certain person who, because they have committed an offense through the intense entanglements of greed, hatred, and delusion,
possesses five distinct types of wisdom.
That is to say, there is a certain person whose wholesome qualities are slight and whose wisdom is narrow and inferior.
Although they are equal in their establishment of [the precepts], equal in their activities, equal in their transgressions, and equal in the arising of afflictions,
those who commit such offenses incur extremely heavy obstacles;
this is not the case for those who commit offenses that are contrary to these characteristics.
Just as a small stream can topple sparse grass but cannot sweep away or submerge it,
so too a great torrent of water cannot topple even a mass of accumulated grass and wood.
The principle herein should be understood as being likewise.
There are six temporal distinctions;
