second, because it is not agitated or distracted by any signs (*nimitta*).
Third, because one spontaneously and constantly experiences joy within.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of tranquility:
first, physical tranquility.
Second is the tranquility of speech;
third is the tranquility of mind.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of brahmins.
First, the brahmin who is progressing toward [the goal];
second, the brahmin who abides in the fruit;
third, the brahmin who has reached the ultimate consummation.
In this way, there are likewise three kinds of śramaṇas,
and furthermore, three kinds of brāhmaṇas.
The first is the nominal brāhmaṇa.
Second, the brahmins by birth;
third, the brahmins by right conduct.
These causes and conditions lead to the destruction of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Because ethical discipline (*śīla*) has been impaired, all the wholesome qualities that ought to arise based upon ethical discipline fail to arise;
that is to say, because one has committed transgressions regarding even minor offenses,
and because one has failed to repent for and eliminate those offenses regarding which there remains some residue.
Because they do not recollect what has been transgressed;
because they apprehend a transgression where there is none;
and because they apprehend no transgression where one exists.
One is said to be "endowed with ethical discipline" (*śīla-saṃpanna*) by virtue of four causes and conditions;
its characteristics should be understood as being the opposite of those mentioned above.
Furthermore, there are two causes and conditions by which the ethical discipline one has undertaken becomes pure and complete.
First, because of the purity of its associates;
second, because of the purity of its intrinsic nature.
What is meant by the purity of its associates?
That is to say: purity of view, purity of conduct, and purity of livelihood. What is natural purity?
It is reverent emulation and emulation in all its parts.
Furthermore, there is another distinction:
namely, three causes and conditions that cause the precepts one has received to be pure and complete.
First, because the intention is pure.
Second, because of the purity of livelihood;
third, because of the purity of conduct.
What is the purity of intention?
That is to say, one practices the holy life for the sake of liberation, not for the sake of rebirth in heaven.
What is purity of livelihood?
It is sustaining one's life by seeking sustenance in accordance with the Dharma.
What is meant by "seeking in accordance with the Dharma"?
It refers to seeking in the manner that one ought to seek and from those from whom one ought to seek.
What is meant by "in the manner that one ought to seek"?
That is to say: one does not seek by means of hypocrisy;
nor does one seek by means of flowery speech;
nor does one seek by means of hinting at one's needs.
Nor does one coerce others to make a request,
nor does one hope for profit by means of profit.
What is meant by "seeking according to what [the donor] has provided"?
This means that one seeks [liberation] while excluding the five types of improper places for practice.
What is the purity of conduct?
It is to have deep faith that transgressions result in undesirable fruits.
Whether walking or standing, he maintains mindfulness and reflection, never intentionally committing an offense.
Should he happen to commit one, he immediately confesses and purifies it according to the Dharma before others,
vowing to maintain firm protection against such transgressions in the future.
Furthermore, if there is a bhikṣu who wishes to apply himself diligently to the practice of closely guarding the doors of the sensory faculties,
he should understand the faults of distracted mindfulness through four aspects,
and he should understand improper mental attention through four aspects.
What are the four characteristics for understanding the faults of deluded thoughts?
First, the absence of mindfulness;
second, inferior mindfulness.
Third is loss of mindfulness;
fourth is distracted mindfulness.
As for the deficiency of mindfulness:
This refers to one who does not listen to, does not accept, and does not properly understand the method of closely guarding the doors of the sense faculties,
and whose mindfulness is inferior.
That is to say, although one has heard, received, and thoroughly understood those teachings,
one does not constantly practice them, nor does one practice them with full attention, whether it be cultivation, training, or repeated cultivation.
"Losing mindfulness" means that although one has practiced and cultivated extensively,
there are still times when one acts without correct comprehension.
Distracted thought refers to conceiving the notion of non-affliction regarding that which is actually afflictive,
and conceiving the notion of affliction regarding that which is actually non-afflictive.
How is it that one understands improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) through four characteristics?
First, it is the cause for the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*);
second, it is associated with the arising of defilements (*saṃkleśa*).
Third, the destruction of shame;
fourth, the arousal of confused transgressions.
These are the causes for the arising of afflictions.
That is to say, there is someone who grasps at signs and grasps at secondary characteristics;
by reason of this, in that particular situation,
unwholesome and evil states of mind flow forth and run wild along with the mind.
That which is associated with the arising of defilement refers to that which manifests simultaneously with those very evil and unwholesome dharmas,
thereby destroying a sense of shame.
That is to say, there is one who does not feel shame regarding what is shameful;
furthermore, when those evil and unwholesome states manifest before him, he feels no shame.
Regarding the offense of confusion:
it refers to committing an offense due to that very lack of shame,
or thinking to abandon what has been undertaken as training.
Furthermore, regarding one who diligently practices moderation in eating,
it is called being fully endowed with moderation in eating when eight points are abandoned.
What are these eight?
First, attachment to food and drink;
second, attachment to one's own body;
third, the destruction of the life-faculty.
4. Hunger and weakness;
5. heaviness of the body;
6. not being free from illness.
Seventh, one's livelihood is not pure.
Eighth, one engages extensively in worldly activities.
Furthermore, regarding those who constantly and diligently cultivate the yoga of awakening:
One who has severed these eight points is said to be fully endowed with the correct practice of the yoga of awakening through constant and diligent cultivation.
What are the eight?
First, physical exhaustion due to one's deportment.
Second, taking pleasure in reclining and sleeping;
third, following after the signs of affliction;
fourth, failing to diligently cultivate the remedies for affliction.
Fifth, awakening at an improper time;
sixth, awakening after having wasted one's efforts in vain;
seventh, sleeping at an improper time.
The eighth is sleeping while neglecting [one's duties].
This is the stage of renunciation. What are the six?
First, not conforming to renunciation;
second, lacking renunciation;
third, the household renunciation.
Fourth, departure through non-perfection;
fifth, departure from the lower stages;
sixth, departure from the view of a personal identity (*satkāya*).
"Non-conformity" refers to five kinds of reliance: first,
non-conformity regarding the destination.
Second, non-conformity with birth;
third, non-conformity with diligence;
fourth, non-conformity with obstacles.
The fifth, "non-conformity with delight," refers to being deficient in four kinds of conditions.
First, the deficiency of a spiritual friend;
second, the deficiency of hearing [the Dharma];
third, the deficiency of disappearance.
Because both the teaching and the realization have vanished.

first, because one engages in wrong practice regarding the causal conditions for the clear realization of the truths;
second, because one engages in wrong practice regarding the clear realization of the truths themselves.
Furthermore, based on the practice of desire, the practice of merit, and the practice of mutual cohabitation,
there are six kinds of afflictions consisting of craving and aversion, four bases, and five types of remedies.
What are the six kinds of defilements consisting of craving and aversion?
First is craving for objects;
by frequenting them, one is able to obstruct the various desires.
Second is hatred toward those one dislikes,
by which one gives rise to resentment and malice toward hostile sentient beings;
third is craving that conforms to the teachings.

Fourth, there is the predominance of hatred, whereby one extensively inflicts various forms of harassment and oppression upon sentient beings who, having received instructions from others, lack autonomy.
Consequently, regarding those sentient beings who possess superior happiness and superior joy,
one does not wish for them to attain such prosperity; rather,
one desires only for oneself to experience various forms of jealousy, intolerance, agitation, and dissatisfaction.
In the fifth and sixth [stages], there is greed for merit and hatred toward faults;
due to these causes and conditions, the mind is not equanimous.
Thus, although one may practice giving and cultivate various meritorious deeds within the Saṃgha, [the mind remains unbalanced].
Yet they constantly seek out various distinctions—
whether things have been done or not done, or whether something has been done poorly—
and harboring inner grief and suffering, they dwell in a state of unease.
What are the four bases? They are:
first, the objective field as a basis;
and other sentient beings as a basis.
Furthermore, the first two bases each give rise to a portion of affliction (*saṃkleśa*),
while the remaining bases each give rise to a portion of both [affliction and purification].
What are the five kinds of remedies?
First, impurity;
second, loving-kindness;
third, compassion.
The four types of joy and the five types of equanimity.
Furthermore, there is another formulation consisting of six kinds of afflictions involving craving and aversion, along with five kinds of remedies.
What are the six?
First, attachment to objects;
second, aversion toward objects.
3. Affliction consisting of greed, hatred, and delusion;
4. Non-affliction consisting of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion;
5. Non-affliction consisting of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
Regarding the six defilements of greed, hatred, and delusion, what are the five types of remedies? They are:
the meditation on impurity, loving-kindness, and the three kinds of mental attention.
1. Attention that is afflicted yet non-erroneous;
2. Attention that is unafflicted and non-erroneous;
3. Attention that abandons attachment and aversion through a mind that is both afflicted and unafflicted yet non-erroneous.
Furthermore, there are four types of individuals (pudgala).
It should be understood that those who go forth into homelessness obtain five kinds of merit.
What are these four types of individuals?
First, those who rely on themselves;
second, those who rely on others;
third, those who have already matured.
Fourth, regarding those who are not yet mature:
how should one understand that going forth yields five kinds of merit?
That is to say, by virtue of going forth, a person who relies upon themselves [attains these merits].
Having renounced the wealth and treasures shared with kings and others,
one relies upon the uncommon, pure ethical discipline;
this is called attaining the first merit.
By virtue of renouncing the world, a person who was previously dependent upon others abandons the state of being subject to others, acting according to their will, and lacking autonomy;
they instead attain the state of self-reliance, no longer following others, and acting with sovereign mastery.
This is called obtaining the second merit.
Because a person whose faculties are already mature has gone forth,
if they are free from remaining fetters, they immediately attain the end of all suffering.
This is called attaining the third merit.
If there are remaining fetters, one then attains the end of suffering in the evil realms;
this is called attaining the fourth merit.
By means of going forth, an immature person, in this very life,
is liberated from the immeasurable distress and suffering of the confinement of the household life,
and accumulates immeasurable, vast roots of goodness conducive to liberation.
It enables the continuity [of the mind] to reach maturity in the future;
this is called attaining the fifth merit.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of suffering and nine aspects.
One should know that [suffering] follows along with all contaminated formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*).
What are the three types of suffering?
They are the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), up to and including the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
What are the nine aspects?
It means that each individual suffering has three aspects;
because they follow along with all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*), there are nine aspects.
First, because it is bound by that which follows upon death;
second, because it is bound by that which gives rise to the causes for the evil destinies;
and third, because it is bound by birth in the various evil destinies.
Fourth, because all phenomena are impermanent;
fifth, because within impermanence there is the nature of suffering;
sixth, because within suffering there is the nature of non-self.
7. Because it arises and abides in pleasure through the practice that accords with the relish of craving (*āsvādānugata*).
8. Because it is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*).
9. Precisely because of this nature of the suffering of change.
Because all those who possess wisdom take [such things] to be non-transcendent dharmas.
Furthermore, if there is a bhikṣu who accomplishes the four factors and serves as a leader of the community,
he alone is able to instruct, admonish, and guide his followers without error.
One practices the correct conduct that benefits both oneself and others.
What are its four branches?
First, liberation from secondary afflictions.
Second, not being separated from right knowledge;
third, for the sake of causing all already arisen wholesome dharmas to remain firm, not be forgotten, and to be cultivated to perfection, increased, and expanded, one embraces and sustains them.
Fourth, for the sake of causing all unarisen wholesome dharmas to arise, he embraces and sustains them.
How does a bhikṣu become liberated from secondary afflictions?
It means that he is liberated from five kinds of secondary afflictions.
What are the five?
First, longing for the household life;
second, violating the prohibitive precepts.
Third, improper mental attention (ayoniśo-manasikāra) that accompanies the discrimination of what was previously experienced;
fourth, the arousal of craving and grief by becoming attached to all future objects;
and fifth, stinginess regarding the Dharma.
If foolish worldlings do not know, as it truly is, the specific characteristics of the four great elements and the derived matter,
they designate them as their parents, wives, children, and even friends.
When ministers, relatives, brothers, and so forth,
perceive mere forms and colors— such as laughing and the like—
they give rise to a mental attention accompanied by the notion of a sentient being toward the movements of mere body and speech.
Due to these causes and conditions, false discrimination and deluded conceptualization arise,
[imagining] them as one's parents, wife, children, and even friends;
as officials, relatives, and brothers.
Due to this discrimination and false conceptualization of causes and conditions,
various longings for domestic life arise.

All those who possess wisdom clearly understand that there are only the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of material forms (*rūpa*), and thus no perception of a sentient being (*sattva-saṃjñā*).
One is able to liberate oneself from the first secondary affliction. Why is this?
Because for a long time, one has established and arranged various distinct colors and shapes based on visual perception.
At times, he may encounter others in a gathering;
having seen them thus, he thinks, "These are my parents, wife, and children," and so forth, up to:
"These are my friends, officials, and relatives."
Or it may be said that this is for the sake of others;
however, among those sentient beings born in the formless realms, such a thing does not exist.
Furthermore, foolish worldlings do not know, as they truly are, the characteristics of a fool or the characteristics of a wise person.
Due to not knowing things as they truly are,
one thinks what should not be thought, speaks what should not be spoken, and performs what should not be performed;
thus, all physical, verbal, and mental actions that are manifested are impure.
Furthermore, there is no pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) or right livelihood (*ājīva*),
because those who possess wisdom know them as they truly are;
one should know that everything contrary to those [qualities] is likewise absent.
Therefore, one is able to be liberated from the second secondary affliction.
Furthermore, all foolish worldlings are unable to know what is irrational as it truly is irrational,
and they are unable to know what is rational as it truly is rational.
Regarding those previously experienced phenomena that are agreeable to desire and greed and are pleasing to the mind,
one engages in improper mental attention, giving rise to thoughts of sensual desire;
one clings to them firmly, neither relinquishing nor abandoning nor vomiting them out.
One gives rise to thoughts of ill will toward disagreeable phenomena conducive to ill will;
one gives rise to thoughts of cruelty toward disagreeable phenomena conducive to cruelty.
The rest is as previously explained.
All those who possess wisdom can, in accordance with reality, know that which is rational as being rational,
and know that which is irrational as being irrational.
Regarding the various phenomena previously received and as previously described,
whether by not recollecting them, by correctly reflecting upon them, or by not losing mindfulness,
one does not give rise to thoughts of sensual desire up to thoughts of malice with respect to those objects of focus.
Even if they should arise, one does not adhere to them firmly;
as explained in detail previously,
one is thus able to be liberated from the third secondary affliction.
Furthermore, foolish worldlings do not know, as it truly is, the merit of guarding the sense faculties,
nor do they know, as it truly is, the faults of failing to guard them;
consequently, in the present life, they give rise to the defilements of attachment and aversion toward various objects appearing before them.
His mind yearns to see all objects that are pleasing, such as forms;
his mind feels aversion toward objects that are unpleasing, such as forms;
and his mind feels longing for objects that are agreeable.
This is called greed.
When one harbors this greed, if those objects undergo change or destruction, the mind becomes dejected;
this is called sorrow.
It should be understood that all principles for those who possess wisdom are entirely contrary to this;
therefore, they are able to liberate themselves from the fourth secondary affliction.
Furthermore, among the various unwholesome dharmas of sensual desire, foolish worldlings—
They are unable to know its faults and disadvantages as they truly are;
constantly drifting and drowning under the influence of the other four types of stinginess, they further give rise to stinginess regarding the Dharma.
Those who possess wisdom can know those faults and disadvantages as they truly are.
He does not give rise to even the other four types of stinginess;
should they arise, he abandons them immediately and never clings to them firmly,
let alone giving rise to stinginess regarding the Dharma.
Having thus distanced himself from stinginess regarding the Dharma,
whenever he encounters an individual who delights in the Dharma,
he shall proclaim for them the sūtras spoken by the Great Teacher.
He causes them to receive and uphold the sacred teachings associated with the Vinaya and the Mātṛkā.
He extensively analyzes and elucidates [the teachings] for others without ever concealing them;
thus, he is able to liberate himself from the fifth secondary affliction.
This is called the bhikṣu’s accomplishment of the first branch of liberation from secondary afflictions.
How is it that a bhikṣu does not depart from right knowledge?
It is said that there are four types of knowledge. What are these four?
That is to say, based on the initial continuity of freedom from defilement and the thorough realization of the eightfold noble path, the first knowledge is established;
based on the realization and accomplishment of the eightfold noble path, the remaining three knowledges are established.
It refers to a bhikṣu who, while still in the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), reflects as follows:
"Only within the noble Dharma and Vinaya of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, does the Eightfold Noble Path exist."
In the doctrines of the various non-Buddhist heterodox teachers,
such a path does not exist. Wherever there is the Eightfold Noble Path,
there is the fruit of the śramaṇa.
There are śramaṇas and the state of being a śramaṇa, namely nirvāṇa. Now,
in order to realize the fruit of the śramaṇa, the śramaṇa himself, and the state of being a śramaṇa,
I should arouse the Noble Eightfold Path and cultivate it to purity.
The knowledge regarding all [factors] within the eightfold noble path through such practice is called the first wisdom established based on the thorough penetration of the eightfold noble path;
it is precisely by relying upon and being established in this wisdom that [the second wisdom arises].
In order to realize and accomplish the Noble Eightfold Path as it has been thoroughly understood,
one applies courageous diligence to cultivate the remaining three types of knowledge,
namely, the knowledge consisting of hearing.
The wisdom resulting from reflection and the wisdom resulting from cultivation; for these,
one should diligently cultivate the wisdom resulting from hearing.
Furthermore, in order to purify this wisdom, one seeks to hear the True Dharma.
If there is anyone proclaiming the Dharma and Vinaya realized by the Tathāgata,
one immediately goes to them to listen with reverence and attains joy through realization.
It is encompassed by vastness, excellence, and renunciation.
It is called "vast" because its specific characteristics are sublime;
it is called "excellent" because its intrinsic nature is faultless.
It is called "subsumed under renunciation" because it is associated with *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of diligently cultivating the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and causing that wisdom to attain purity.
If one knows that in a certain place there are bhikṣus who uphold the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.
They gather together to weigh and discern the profound and hidden essential meanings within the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma,
and then proceed to inquire about the various truths (*satya*).
He, for their sake, establishes the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of those truths and the means for their realization.
First, they cause those who have not yet awakened to awaken;
and for those who have already awakened, they provide further clarification so that they may understand.
This is done even regarding the distinctions between words and letters concerning a single meaning.
He skillfully exhorts others so that they do not forget or lose [the teachings].
Furthermore, he penetrates with wisdom the profound meanings and phrases that serve as the basis for realizing the truths associated with selflessness.
He extensively revealed the subtle Dharma verses spoken by the Tathāgata that correspond to emptiness;
by this cause and condition, because he had already attained the purity of the wisdom consisting of hearing and reflection, [he understood].
Furthermore, he diligently cultivates the wisdom born of cultivation so as to bring this wisdom to complete purity; thus,
he dwells in contemplation of the body within the internal body.
This should be understood in detail up to the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness.
This is called establishing the three knowledges based on the realization and accomplishment of the eightfold noble path.
This is called the bhikṣu’s accomplishment of the second limb of not being separated from right knowledge.
How does a bhikṣu cause all wholesome states that have already arisen to remain firm, undiminished, and not forgotten?
To speak at length, up to the point of "gathering and maintaining":
this refers to how the bhikṣus, in reliance upon material requisites and food,
[receive them] from various donors of pure faith.
Accepting robes and other items in accordance with the prescribed measure is called "sustenance. Why is this?
Because by means of these causes and conditions, the bodies of the bhikṣus do not become weak or exhausted.
The mind possesses capability and is free from defilement and affliction;
thus, the wholesome dharmas already arisen do not decline but increase.
How does a bhikṣu, for the sake of causing all unarisen wholesome dharmas to arise, embrace and maintain them?
It refers to those bhikṣus who are advanced in years, whose ethical conduct is pure and sublime,
and who fully understand the joy and bliss of nirvāṇa,
which is the foremost among all joys and blisses.
Having well cultivated the noble path, one is free from overweening pride.

If there is a bhikṣu who can pay homage to, serve, and respectfully attend upon such a person, rejoicing in their virtuous words, being free from all guile and crookedness, and having no mind to seek out faults; [he shall attain great merit].
This capacity to produce that [result] is called "sustenance" (*adhāra*). Why?
Because when it thus functions in accordance [with its cause], from time to time, [it produces that result].
From that, one obtains instructions and teachings capable of generating supreme joy,
which cause all the various excellent factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) that have not yet arisen to arise swiftly.
Thus, these four branches are divided into eleven;
the eleven and the four are equal and equivalent.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 70.
The Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Seventy-one.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.
In the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, within the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, there are five further sections; furthermore, there are seven types of meaning:
first, the meaning to be inferred;
second, the meaning to be subsumed.
Third, the meaning of what should be avoided;
fourth, the meaning of what should be drawn forth;
fifth, the meaning of what should be refuted.
Sixth, the meaning of what should be maintained;
seventh, the meaning of what should be generated.
Furthermore, there are seven kinds of joy.
1. Joy induced by hearing;
2. Joy induced by reflection;
3. Joy induced by cultivation.
Fourth, joy induced by the removal of hindrances;
fifth, joy induced by discussion;
sixth, joy induced by recollecting one's own virtues.
Seventh, the joy induced by not being satisfied with inferior things;
second, the practice of the Dharma;
third, the embracing of the Dharma.
Fourth, the dharma of enjoyment;
fifth, the dharma of realization.
Furthermore, one must possess three kinds of qualities to be able to shoot well.
First, by virtue of the excellence of the bow;
second, by virtue of the excellence of the arrow;
third, by virtue of the excellence of hitting the mark.
An archer’s bow possesses two virtues:
first, its nature is firm and resilient;
second, it is excellent at achieving the ultimate goal.
The arrow possesses one virtue:
it is skillful in achieving its ultimate goal.
The hitting of the target possesses three virtues.
First, ultimate craftsmanship;
second, practiced craftsmanship;
third, craftsmanship learned from a teacher.
Furthermore, the teachings of the Tathāgata are of three kinds:
first, the long-term teaching;
second, the uninterrupted teaching.
Third, the teaching is not taught redundantly.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s immeasurable teachings on the Dharma all proceed by way of three principles.
First, the principle of differentiation by meaning;
second, the principle of differentiation by phrasing;
third, the principle of differentiation by difficult explanations.
Furthermore, one who traverses the Path requires five types of antidotes:
first, the antidote for blazing light;
second, the antidote for perilous difficulties.
Third, the antidote to rivers;
fourth, the antidote to desiccation;
fifth, the antidote to physical fatigue.
Furthermore, there are two aspects of ethical discipline (*śīla*) that lead to rebirth in the happy realms:
first, the ethical discipline of gathering [virtue].
Second is unimpaired ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Furthermore, for those who indulge in sensual desires, there are three matters in the present life: first, the pursuit of wealth and treasures; [the second is the pursuit of status;
and the third is the pursuit of pleasure].
Second, guarding wealth and treasures;
third, attachment to enjoyment.
Furthermore, there are two ways in which life-span undergoes transformation and decay.
First, coarse transformation;
second, subtle transformation.
There are also two types of states of transformation.
First, coarse;
second, subtle;
third, the meaning of practice and virtue.
Second is the excellence of intrinsic nature.
Regarding the excellence of the meaning of correct practice,
it refers to swift and correct practice.
Definitive correct practice,
subtle correct practice,
and the virtue of intrinsic nature.
This refers to the stage of meditative concentration from which there is no regression;
it is supramundane, well-cultivated,
and free from all obstructions regarding its own sphere of activity.
It surpasses all other roots of goodness within its own class;
it surpasses all roots of goodness belonging to other classes.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of attachment.
Cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness can serve as their antidote:
first, attachment to companions;
second, attachment to gain and offerings.
Third, because of attachment to future existence,
due to [past] conduct and due to present realization.
Because it is a continuous succession:
the antidote to desire, greed, and ignorance is the preparatory application (*prayoga*);
the direct perception of the established and non-established truths (*vyavasthāpita-avyavasthāpita-satya*) is the clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
This continuum is characterized by whether one has already abandoned desire or has not yet abandoned it;
furthermore, it depends on the stage (*bhūmi*), the category (*prakāra*),
and the fact that meditative concentration has not yet been cultivated.
Because one has already cultivated [the path] but has not yet attained it;
because it is an obstacle to the purification of the basis;
and because it is an obstacle to the purification of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Because it is the antidote to those hindrances.
Furthermore, as it is said, there are six kinds of clear realization (*abhisamaya*),
namely, the clear realization through reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*) up to the ultimate clear realization (*nisthā-abhisamaya*).
Question: What are the characteristics of the clear realization through reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*)?

Answer: If one accomplishes the clear realization through reflection, they are able to definitively ascertain that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and that all conditioned phenomena are suffering.
"All phenomena are selfless; nirvāṇa is peaceful.
While still abiding in the stage of an ordinary being, one has already been able to realize such certainty.
It cannot be rightfully led away or taken away by any śramaṇas, brahmins, gods, Māras, Brahmās, or others. Question:
What are the characteristics of the clear realization of faith (śraddhā-abhisamaya)?
Answer: If there is one who achieves the clear observation of faith, they may be either an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or a non-ordinary person (*apṛthagjana*);
and this occurs either in the present life, or in both the present life and future lives.
One never falsely claims that others are Great Masters,
that their Dharma is well-expounded,
or that their Sangha practices correctly.
Question: What are the characteristics of the clear realization of ethical discipline (*śīla-abhisamaya*)?
Answer: If one has accomplished the clear realization of ethical discipline, they will never again—down to the point of intentional killing—take the life of even an animal.
Taking what is not given;
engaging in sexual misconduct;
and speaking falsehoods knowingly.
Drinking rice-based liquor and other such sources of negligence.
Question: What are the characteristics of the clear realization of wisdom (*abhisamaya-jñāna*) and the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*)?
Answer: If one has achieved the clear realization of knowledge and the clear realization of the truths,
they will never again act based on false views,
nor will they harbor doubt regarding what they have personally realized.
They harbor lustful attachment toward all places of rebirth;
they manifest worldly appearances and conceive of them as pure;
and they slander the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Mahāyāna vehicles, thereby committing karma that leads to the evil realms.
How much less could one commit the immediate karmas (ānantarya-karma), such as harming one's parents?
Furthermore, one cannot even give rise to an eighth existence.
Question: What are the characteristics of the realization of the truths through the knowledge at the conclusion of the clear observation (abhisamaya-antika-jñāna-satya-abhisamaya)?

Answer: If one has attained the realization of the truths through the knowledge at the conclusion of clear observation (*abhisamayāntika-jñāna*), one will never experience fear when confronted with the interrogations of others.
Question: What are the characteristics of ultimate realization (*atyanta-abhisamaya*)?
Answer: If one has attained the ultimate realization (*atyanta-abhisamaya*),
they will never again be able to transgress against the five points,
nor will they ever again intentionally take the life of any living being, even down to those of the animal realm.
Taking what is not given;
engaging in unchaste conduct and the practice of sexual desire; speaking falsehoods knowingly;
and amassing wealth and various excellent objects of sensual pleasure.
One experiences it,
yet neither fears indeterminate matters nor falsely speculates that all suffering and pleasure are self-made or made by another.
It is produced by both self and other,
and it arises with neither self nor other as its cause.
One should know that such categories as these are called the characteristics of the various clear realizations (*abhisamaya*).
What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the clear observation through reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*)?

Answer: Its intrinsic nature is the superior wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*), or alternatively, it has as its intrinsic nature the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) that accompany it.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the clear realization through faith (*śraddhā-abhisamaya*)?
Answer: Its intrinsic nature is the superior mundane and supramundane pure faith that takes the Three Jewels as its object;
alternatively, it is the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) that accompany this [faith].
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the clear realization of ethical discipline (*śīla-abhisamaya*)?

Answer: Its intrinsic nature consists of bodily and vocal actions beloved by the noble ones (*ārya-kānta-kāya-vāk-karman*), or alternatively, it consists of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) that coexist with them.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature of the clear realization of the truths through the wisdom of clear realization?
Answer: Its intrinsic nature is the wisdom that takes as its object the non-conceptually-constructed truth (*avyavasthāpita-satya*).
Alternatively, its intrinsic nature consists of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) that accompany this wisdom.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the clear realization of the truths through the knowledge at the conclusion of the clear realizations (*abhisamayāntika-jñāna-satyābhisamaya*)?
Answer: Its intrinsic nature is the wisdom that takes the established truths (*prajñapti-satya*) as its object;
alternatively, its intrinsic nature consists of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) that accompany it.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of ultimate realization (*niṣṭhā-abhisamaya*)?

Answer: Its intrinsic nature consists of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), or else it consists of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) that accompany them.
Question: Among these six types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and so forth, up to how many are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*)?
Answer: One is exclusively bound to the desire realm;
one part of another type is either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Or it is bound to the formless realm;
that one part and the other three—these four are not bound.
One is both bound and not bound.

Question: Of these six clear realizations (*abhisamaya*), how many can be obtained based on the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*), and how many can be obtained based on everything up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)?
Answer: One is obtained neither based on [a specific stage] nor not based on one.
The remaining bases can all be obtained as bases;
furthermore, the same applies to the arising of one kind or a portion thereof from three bases or five bases.
Question: If the wisdom of clear observation (*abhisamaya-jñāna*) is called non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) because it is free from all signs (*nimitta*), [how is this so]?
How is it that one can attain meditative absorption based on that which is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra?
Answer: It is because one enters into concentration by means of contemplating the suchness (tathatā) of the complete dhyāna, including vitarka, vicāra, and so forth.
Therefore, although these clear realizations can be attained based on dhyāna with vitarka and vicāra,
they are characterized by detachment and are free from conceptual discrimination.
How many take conventional truth as their object?
How many take ultimate truth as their object?
Answer: One takes conventional truth as its object, and one part of another kind [also does so].
First, that which has no object of focus;
second, that which takes as its object the established ultimate truth and one part of one category;
and third, that which takes as its object the non-established ultimate truth and one part of one category.
Question: Among these various clear realizations (*abhisamaya*), how many possess signs (*sanimitta*) and how many are signless (*animitta*)?
Answer: Four possess signs.
One is signless;
one is both with signs and signless.
[The Buddha] asked about these various clear realizations.
How many are with conceptual differentiation and how many are without conceptual differentiation?
Answer: Just as it is with signs and signlessness, one should know that the same applies to that which is with conceptual differentiation and that which is without conceptual differentiation.
How many are associated with joy (*prīti*), how many are associated with pleasure (*sukha*), and how many are associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*)?
Answer: The first is associated exclusively with joy;
the others are associated with joy, pleasure, and equanimity as appropriate.
Question: Among these various clear realizations (*abhisamaya*),
how many are counteractive by way of destruction (*vidūṣaṇa-pratipakṣa*),
and how many are counteractive by way of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*)?
How many are the antidotes of retention (*dhāraṇa-pratipakṣa*), and how many are the antidotes of distancing (*dūribhāva-pratipakṣa*)?
Answer: Two are exclusively the antidotes of destruction (*vidūṣaṇa-pratipakṣa*).
One is the antidote that acts as a distant separation through abandonment;
one is the antidote that acts as a distant separation through maintenance;
and two are non-antidotes.
Question: Among these various clear realizations (*abhisamaya*),
how many serve as the antidote for the suppression of the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
and how many serve as the antidote for the permanent eradication of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)?
Answer: Three are antidotes that subdue the various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*);
one is an antidote that acts simultaneously; and one is neither.

Question: Among these various clear realizations (*abhisamaya*), how many serve as the antidotes for abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the soft, medium, and superior grades within each respective stage (*bhūmi*)?
Answer: One.
The others that accord with this serve as its auxiliaries;
they are not the antidotes of abandonment.
Question: Through the six clear realizations (abhisamaya), one attains the nine thorough knowledges (parijñā).
That is to say, because the afflictions bound to the desire realm that are abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin are eliminated, the first thorough knowledge is established;
because the afflictions bound to the form and formless realms that are abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin are eliminated, the second thorough knowledge is established.
The third thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) is established because of the abandonment of the afflictions associated with the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation.
The fourth thorough knowledge is established because of the abandonment of the afflictions associated with the form and formless realms that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation.

The fifth thorough knowledge is established because of the abandonment of the afflictions associated with the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing; the sixth thorough knowledge is established because of the abandonment of the afflictions associated with the form and formless realms that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing.
The seventh thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) is established because of the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
The eighth thorough knowledge is established because of the abandonment of desire for the form realm (*rūparāga*).
The ninth thorough knowledge is established because of the abandonment of desire for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*).
Regarding these six clear realizations (abhisamaya), who attains how many fruits of full knowledge (parijñā)?
Answer: One attains the fruit of nine full knowledges;
the others do not attain those fruits.
"Has the antidote for abandonment already been produced,
or has it not yet arisen?
He replied, "It has not yet arisen."
Although it is said that [the antidote] has arisen, this does not refer to a subsequent time.
One should know that at the very moment the afflictions are abandoned and the antidote arises, these two are perfectly equal.
It is precisely at that time that, by way of conventional designation, one says that the antidote has arisen and the afflictions have been abandoned.
One attains all four fruits.
First, one attains the complete fruit of a śramaṇa;
at that time, the others are attained as its auxiliary companions and as its preliminary stages.
Answer: With one exception, all of them.
Question: Among these various clear realizations (*abhisamaya*), how many are able to bring forth the sublime qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)?
Answer: With one exception, all of them.
Question: What function should the clear realization of reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*) be said to perform?
... [and so on] ... up to what function should the ultimate clear realization (*nisthā-abhisamaya*) be said to perform?

Answer: It should be said that the clear realization of reflection has as its function the production of wholesome dharmas belonging to the category of purity, which are subsumed under right practice;
it has as its function the production of blameless joy;
and it has as its function the resolution of all doubts.
Its function is to enable entry into the cultivation of merit;
its function is to lead to the remaining forms of clear realization (*abhisamaya*);
and its function is to lead to all happy destinies (*sugati*).
The clear realization of faith, by virtue of its intentionality,
has as its function the production of unwavering resolute conviction toward the Three Jewels,
and as its function the purification of correct practice.
One part has the function of leading to rebirth in the happy realms.
The clear observation of ethical discipline has the function of liberating one from the manifold sufferings of the miserable realms.
This is the clear observation of the truths through the knowledge of clear observation.
Its function is to attain all fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
Its function is to bring forth the purification of all meritorious qualities.
Its function is to lead to the remaining types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Its function is to assist in bringing about pure results and maturation within the happy realms.
The knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-jñāna*) is capable [of discerning] among all established truths (*vyavasthāpana-satya*).
Its function is skillfulness in answering questions;
its function is swift superknowledge;
and its function is to lead to the subsequent clear realizations.
Ultimate clear realization has as its function the induction of the foremost dwelling in happiness in the present life,
and as its function the liberation from all the great suffering of birth and death.
What is the final embodiment as a basis for abiding?
How many types of clear realization (abhisamaya) are there?
Up to how many types of ultimate clear realization are there?
Answer: One should know that the contemplation of reflection is of immeasurable kinds;
namely, the reflection on the sūtras and the reflection on what should be recited.
The reflection on the *vyākaraṇa* (prophecies),
up to the reflection on the *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, and *upadeśa*;
and the reflection on suffering (*duḥkha*).
Contemplation on the aggregates, cessation, and the path;
contemplation on true suchness, the limit of reality, and the dharma-realm;
and contemplation on the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and so forth.
The reflection of the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth,
the reflection of the Mahāyāna,
and other such categories— know that there are immeasurable varieties of reflection.
The clear realization through faith is also of immeasurable kinds;
that is, it consists of correctly recollecting the past immeasurable Tathāgatas, as well as their Dharma and their Saṃgha.
As it is with the past, so it is with the future and the present.

Furthermore, one correctly recollects all the Tathāgatas, their Dharmas, and their Saṅghas existing in this world and in the infinite worlds of the ten directions, to whatever extent they exist through such correct recollection.
There are likewise as many distinct categories and varieties of the substance of the clear realization through faith (*śraddhā-abhisamaya*).
The clear realization through ethical discipline (*śīla-abhisamaya*) is also of immeasurable kinds,

namely, according to the various distinctions among the ten types of unwholesome courses of action (*akusala-karmapatha*) that are natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), which are to be abandoned.
Furthermore, according to their continuity, there are also many types, namely:
the bodies of stream-enterers up to those of arhats,
as well as the infinite distinctions such as the bodies of pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas.
The clear realization through wisdom regarding the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) is also of immeasurable kinds;

that is to say, it consists of the immeasurable distinctions among the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), such as the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the branches of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and the branches of the path (*mārgāṅga*).

Just as it is with the clear realization through the knowledge of the truths (*abhisamaya-jñāna-satya-abhisamaya*), so too should one understand the clear realization at the conclusion of the clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-jñāna-satya-abhisamaya*) and the ultimate clear realization (*nisthā-abhisamaya*).
Question: Regarding these various clear realizations...
Since it is established by such names and such words,
should it be said that this is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
or should it be said that this is not its intrinsic nature?
Answer: According to conventional discourse, it should be said that this is its intrinsic nature;
according to the ultimate sense, it should be said that this is not its intrinsic nature. Why is this so?
Because the nature of all phenomena (dharmatā) is such that their meaning cannot be expressed in words.
Question: What are the causes and fruits of the realization through reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*)?
And so on, up to: what are the causes and fruits of the ultimate realization (*nisthā-abhisamaya*)?
Answer: The clear realization through reflection occurs when, upon the appearance of a Buddha in the world, one approaches virtuous friends,
hears the true Dharma,
and brings one’s mental continuum to maturity.
Taking correct mental attention as the cause and the karma performed as the fruit,
it is like the clear realization of volition.
It should be understood that all realizations (abhisamaya) are likewise so.
The distinction here is that the realization through faith (śraddhābhisamaya) also has the other realizations as its cause.
The same applies to the clear observation of ethical discipline (*śīla-abhisamaya*).

Furthermore, the clear observation of the truths through the wisdom of clear observation (*jñāna-satyābhisamaya*) has both the clear observation of reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*) and the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) as its causes.
It also takes its own lineage as its cause.

The clear realization of the knowledge at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-jñāna-satya-abhisamaya*) likewise takes the clear realization of the knowledge of the truths (*jñāna-satya-abhisamaya*) as its cause;
the ultimate clear realization (*nisthā-abhisamaya*) is also thus.
Question: Regarding the six clear comprehensions (*abhisamaya*) and the seven mental orientations (*manasikāra*), such as "comprehension of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*) and so forth—
do the seven mental orientations subsume the six clear comprehensions?
Are the six clear realizations (abhisamaya) subsumed under the seven mental orientations (manasikāra)?
Answer: Two clear realizations are not subsumed under the mental orientations;
one clear realization is subsumed under the mental orientation of "delight in cultivation" (bhāvanā-ruci-manasikāra).
One is subsumed under the attention of joy in clear realization (*abhisamaya-prāmodya-manasikāra*) and the attention of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*).
One is subsumed under the attention of seclusion (*viveka-manasikāra*).
One is subsumed under the attention of joy (*rati-manasikāra*) and the attention of the culmination of application (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-manasikāra*).
The first is subsumed under the mental application that is the fruit of the culmination of the preparatory stage for clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
It should be understood that the remaining mental applications are subsumed under the outflow of clear realization (*abhisamayānvaya*),
but are not themselves subsumed under clear realization.
That is to say, the attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) and the attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika manaskāra*).
Question: To which clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) do the boundless wisdoms and the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya kuśalamūla*) belong?
Answer: They are not subsumed under any of the clear realizations.
One should know that this is the outflow of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Is it also the clear realization of faith (*śraddhā-abhisamaya*)?
If it is the clear realization of faith, is it also the clear realization of reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*)?
It can be answered by means of four propositions.
There may be the clear realization through reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*) that is not the clear realization through faith (*śraddhā-abhisamaya*),
namely, with the exception of the decisive reflection that takes the Jewels as its object.
Regarding other determinate objects of thought,
there may be a clear realization through faith (*śraddhā-abhisamaya*) that is not a clear realization through reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*);
namely, the faith produced by hearing and cultivation regarding the [Three] Jewels as its object.
There may be both the clear realization of reflection and the clear realization of faith;
this refers to the decisive reflection that takes the Jewels as its object.
Excluding the aforementioned characteristics, [the remaining types of reflection constitute the clear realization of reflection].
This is the fourth alternative.
By this principle, it should be understood that the remaining cases should likewise be formulated as four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Furthermore, there are immeasurable principles such as the single-line [formula], the antecedent-line formula, the subsequent-line formula, and the four-line formula.
One should understand all this according to the principles of the *Śrāvakabhūmi-viniścaya*.
Furthermore, stinginess (*mātsarya*) combined with impurity (*mala*) is termed "stingy-impurity" (*mātsaryamala*).
By means of these eight kinds of impurities, the mental continuum is defiled.
It provides a foothold for that stinginess;
therefore, it is called the "stain of stinginess.
What are the eight?
First, they have not previously habituated themselves to giving and,
in the present life, cherish wealth and food. Second,
they are excessively attached to their own bodies and lives, disregarding the future world.
Third, dwelling constantly with those who are stingy and conforming to them;
fourth, seeing that the field of offerings lacks superior merit and failing to discern the field of merit;
fifth, not having previously cultivated familiarity with compassion.
Furthermore, one does not perceive superior virtues in that state.
Sixth, because various riches and treasures are difficult to accumulate,
by repeatedly cultivating that perception, one gives rise to indolence and laziness.
Seventh, there is grasping at views and the notion that generosity is accompanied by such defilements.
Eighth, there is seeking wealth and jewels while practicing generosity and dedicating [the merit] toward them.
Furthermore, there are five types of conduct called "taming."
First, the practice that brings about wealth;
second, the practice that brings about rebirth in the happy realms;
third, the practice that brings about freedom from suffering.
Fourth, the practice that brings about one's own welfare;
fifth, the practice that brings about the welfare of others.
Regarding the practice that brings about wealth:
That is to say, the meritorious action consisting of giving brings about rebirth in the happy realms;
the meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline brings about the same.
That which results in the practice of no suffering refers to the cultivation of meritorious activities by nature.
That which results in the practice for one's own benefit refers to...
This refers to the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
That which brings about the welfare of others refers to the path of the bodhisattvas.
To attain that, one should cultivate five perceptions:
first, the perception of impurity regarding all sensual desires;
second, the perception of swift extinction regarding one's own body and life.
Third, one cultivates the perception of dread within the desire realm;
fourth, one cultivates the perception of impermanence regarding all conditioned phenomena;
fifth, one cultivates the perception of compassion toward all sentient beings.
The Sūtra says:
How does one thoroughly understand the discourses (sūtra) up to the analytical expositions (upadeśa)?
Briefly, it is by way of five aspects.
First, by understanding conventional designations;
second, by understanding appropriation;
and third, by understanding the sequence.
Fourth, through the thorough knowledge of the sacred teachings;
fifth, through the thorough knowledge of the basis.
How does one thoroughly know conventional designations?
It refers to being able to comprehend the designations, names, and conceptual constructs of the various dharma-gates.
How does one comprehend their inclusion?
It refers to being able to comprehend the sets of names, the sets of phrases, and the sets of phonemes.
By means of this, the distinct dharma-gates are proclaimed.
How is their sequence to be understood?
It refers to being able to understand how one proceeds from this dharma-gate to that dharma-gate.
Regarding the sequence from this passage to that passage,
how does one understand the sacred teaching?
It means being able to understand that such a dharma-gate was spoken by the Tathāgata or by his disciples.
Whether spoken for householders or spoken for those who have gone forth,
how does one understand the basis?
It means being able to understand that such a Dharma-gate is spoken based on self-benefit.
Such a Dharma gate is taught for the benefit of others;
such a Dharma gate is taught even unto the end for the sake of the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
This is called briefly understanding the sūtras up to the upadeśas by way of five aspects.
The meaning is also established by five aspects:
first, through the thorough understanding of dependent origination.
Second, by means of knowing the distinctions between phrases;
third, by means of knowing the sequence;
and fourth, by means of knowing the underlying principles.
Fifth, because of understanding the summarized meaning.
How does one understand dependent origination?
It means being able to understand the meaning that should be manifested for a portion of those to be trained.
Up to the point where even a single portion of those to be trained should be congratulated;
how does one understand the distinctions between phrases?
It means being able to understand the distinctions in categories regarding different methods, different characteristics, and etymological explanations of words.
What is the thorough knowledge of the sequence?
It refers to being able to thoroughly know the sequence of explanation, the sequence of establishment, and the sequence of fulfillment.
What is the thorough knowledge of the principles?
It refers to being able to comprehend four kinds of reasoning:
first, the reasoning of dependence;
second, the reasoning of establishment.
Third, the principle of functional efficacy;
fourth, the principle of natural law.
How is the summarized meaning to be understood?
That is to say, one is able to discern: "This is discourse associated with the aggregates;
this is discourse associated with the elements, the sense bases, dependent origination, the possible and the impossible, and the truths;
this is discourse associated with the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, up to discourse associated with the noble eightfold path."
This is speech associated with karma;
this is speech associated with afflictions;
this is speech associated with the higher trainings, such as the training in ethical discipline.
How does one know the proper time?
It is by means of five aspects:
first, the thorough realization of the manifestation of present defilements.
Second, because it is defiled when the penetration of reality is about to manifest;
third, because it pertains to the stage of non-defilement;
fourth, because it consists of the attention that brings about the antidote.
Fifth, by means of the mental attention of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-manasikāra*).
Furthermore, how is moderation known?
It refers to what is eaten, what is drunk, what is chewed, and so forth, as explained at length.
It should be understood that herein two kinds of conformity to abandonment are briefly explained:
first, the conformity of support;
second, the conformity of diligence.
Regarding the nature of sustaining and conforming:
it refers to knowing the proper measure of what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted.
Regarding the nature of conforming through diligence:
This refers to being well-acquainted with the proper measure regarding walking, standing, and so forth, as explained at length.
In this context, what does it mean to be well-acquainted with the proper measure regarding food and other such matters?
This means being well-acquainted with the proper measure in both receiving and using [things].
Regarding being well-acquainted with the proper measure in receiving:
it means knowing at what time one ought to receive.
From this point one should receive; this is what should be received;
up to this limit one should receive.
When should it be received?
It should be received at the first part of the day, precisely at that time for the purpose of consumption.
From what should it be received?
That is to say, excluding the five kinds of improper objects.
What should be accepted?
It refers to pure things permitted by the Tathāgata.
Excluding alcohol, meat, and other such things that should not be drunk or eaten,
to what extent should one receive [these offerings]?
It means receiving them while knowing the proper measure.
One should not cause harm to oneself or to others.
Regarding moderation in enjoyment,
this means knowing the proper measure such that one may enjoy what has been received during this specific time.
At what time should it be used?
It should be used during the first part of the day, as previously described.
In what place should it be used?
This refers to a favorable location, whether it be a ritual site (*maṇḍala*) or a village.
What should be used there?
It refers to pure substances and so forth, as previously described.
What should one consume?
One should know the proper measure in what is to be consumed,
so as not to cause the affliction of hunger and not to be contrary to the abandonment [of defilements].
Do not allow the elements to become unbalanced.
How does one know the proper measure of diligent exertion?
It means: at this time, in this place, regarding this matter, to this extent.
One should apply oneself with diligent effort.
At what time should one apply oneself with diligent effort?
It is said: when it is the time to walk, one should walk.
One should awaken at the time when one ought to awaken from sleep.
As for the place where one should apply diligent effort,
it is in a secluded forest or at a site of practice (bodhimaṇḍa).
Whether dwelling in the inner courtyard or while walking for meditation, one should cultivate diligence.
In what matters should one cultivate diligence?

That is to say, one should practice with vigor, abide with vigor, and so forth, up to resolving through vigor against sleep, fatigue, and weariness. To what extent should all such diligence be cultivated?
This means practicing diligence while well-knowing the proper measure,
so as not to fall into excessive sinking or excessive excitation because of it.
Furthermore, how does one well-know the assembly of kṣatriyas?
That is to say, one thoroughly understands the kṣatriya assembly: such is their name,
such their lineage, such their clan, such their food, and so on,
up to such being the limit of their lifespan.
In this manner, he even comes to know well the assembly of householders, elders, and lay devotees.
How does he come to know well the assembly of śramaṇas?
It means he is able to know well their names as follows.
"This one is young; this one is middle-aged; this one is old.
This one is a master of the Sūtras, and so on, up to this one who is a master of the Śāstras.
One skillfully recognizes these as practitioners of Yoga and the like."
What is meant by "knowing well that one should go to this place, and so forth, up to remaining silent"?
Briefly stated, it means: for this purpose one should go, and so forth, up to remaining silent.
And as for such things as "one should go" up to "one should remain silent":
for what purpose does one approach the householders' assembly and so forth, up to remaining silent?
It is for the sake of begging for the various requisites for livelihood.
Or again, it may be to inspire faith in those who have not yet believed and to increase the faith of those who already believe;
or to offer consolation to those afflicted by severe illness and enduring manifold sufferings;
or to provide relief and resolution for those burdened by grief and anxiety.
Either to reconcile those who are in mutual enmity and at odds with one another;
or to comply with the affairs undertaken by others;
or again, because of being entreated by others.
Whether it be to attend upon one's preceptor, teacher, or fellow practitioners of the holy life,
or to manage affairs pertaining to the Saṅgha,
for these reasons one should go, or even remain silent.
How is it that one should understand how to proceed in such a manner?
It is as the characteristics have already been explained in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*.
How is it that one should understand how to abide in such a manner?
This means that having arrived, one should not enter immediately;
rather, one should stand by the side of the inner gate with humility and deference,
or, if free from apprehension, enter the house slowly.
Upon reaching the place where they meet, he stands with composed dignity;
first, he offers greetings with a smile and an open countenance,
remaining free from frowns as he extends words of affection.
How is it that one should know how to sit?
It means that the Buddha has permitted one to sit with upright and dignified deportment upon whatever seat is available that is in accordance with the Dharma.
How does one understand that speech should be given in such a manner?
It means to understand well how to speak with timing, according to principle, and in appropriate measure—speech that is tranquil and straightforward.
There are three kinds of timing.
First, there is delight in hearing, not a lack of delight in hearing.
Regarding "a lack of delight in hearing":
it refers to a case where someone is either hungry, thirsty, or physically exhausted.
Or being afflicted by wind, heat, and so forth—
this is called the first period.
Second, abiding in lawful deportment and not in improper deportment.
Furthermore, there may be one who, though desiring to hear [the Dharma], does not maintain proper decorum;
that is, one who stands while the teacher is seated—this is what is meant by "one who abides in improper decorum. One should not teach such a person while they remain standing.
Excepting those with serious illnesses,
as their characteristics are explained at length in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*;
this is the second period.
Third, his mind is free from defilement and affliction;
it is not a defiled or afflicted mind.
A defiled and afflicted mind refers, for example, to one whose mind is hurried and who exerts excessive effort toward various matters.
Whether they be those who are wild or chaotic, or those who are turbid;
whether they be servants or laborers;
or whether they be killers, adversaries, or enemies.
This is the third period.
There are three types of reasoning, namely:
that which involves seeking and requesting.
One should teach the Dharma only after having requested it in accordance with the Dharma and having requested it in appropriate measure.
He speaks with words that possess meaningful benefit;
one should understand this according to its measure through three characteristics:
first, he speaks without confusion or admixture.
Second, he teaches all phenomena with perfectly complete phrasing.
Third, whatever words he speaks are not redundant, meaning they are not repeated;
furthermore, he does not speak even a single word that is useless, meaningless, or devoid of purpose.
How much more so for speaking extensively.
One should know that tranquility is also of three kinds:
first, tranquility of deportment.
Second, the silence of speech;
third, the silence of the mind;
and fourth, the silence of deportment.
This refers to one whose faculties are tranquil and free from agitation, who is not haughty,
and who speaks while the limbs and joints remain unmoving;
such is the one whose speech and sound are tranquil.
That is to say, when speaking, the voice is neither too loud nor too hurried,
and the mind is tranquil.
This means that even when provoked or troubled, one does not give rise to anger when speaking;
how much more so when not provoked?
Furthermore, one speaks without a defiled mind.
Furthermore, straightforward speech is also of three kinds:
namely, speaking at the appropriate time, up to speaking with tranquility;
or speaking according to one's natural disposition through the application of past habituation.
Alternatively, one speaks by means of the mental attention (*manasikāra*) resulting from habitual practice in the present life;
or, through the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*),
one restrains oneself out of a fondness for the precepts (*śikṣāpada*) before speaking.
At all times, they are free from falsehood;
whether in private or in public, their words are consistent.
How, then, can one discern when it is appropriate to remain silent?
This refers to being well-aware that one should remain silent during five occasions:
first, when the speaker is in the midst of delivering their discourse,
if the listener intentionally utters other words to manifest a distraction or disturbance.
At that time, the speaker should remain silent.
Second, while the speaker is correctly delivering the discourse, if the listener dismisses it by saying, "Stop!
I do not wish to hear this," [the speaker should cease].
At that time, the speaker should remain silent.
Third, while the speaker is delivering the discourse correctly,
if the listener conceives a mind seeking out faults in the speaker.
If they utter words of opposition and manifest signs of contrariety,
the speaker should then remain silent.
Fourth, when a donor comes to offer an invitation with food, clothing, and other requisites.
At that time, the recipient should appropriately remain silent and grant their consent.
Fifth, if there should be an opponent who comes to engage in a formal debate,
at that time the debater should appropriately remain silent and listen to their speech.
Furthermore, one should personally understand one's own faith and so forth, up to being a son of good family, by means of three characteristics:
first, by way of its basis;
second, by way of its intrinsic nature.
Third, by way of temporal division.
How does one understand one's own faith by way of its basis?
It means knowing, as it truly is, that which is the basis upon which faith relies.
One should know that when faith arises conditioned by a particular object, that object is definitively the basis upon which one's faith relies.
How does one understand one's own faith by way of its intrinsic nature?
It means knowing, as it truly is, whether one’s own faith is of inferior, middling, or superior grade.
How does one understand one's own faith by way of time?
It means knowing as it truly is: "At such-and-such a time, I have already attained this faith.
Just as one understands faith, so it is with the others.
One should understand that the subsequent factors, such as ethical discipline (*śīla*) and analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*), follow in sequence.
Among these, faith (*śraddhā*) is the factor for entering;
ethical discipline is the factor for *śamatha* once one has entered.
One hears this branch of vipaśyanā;
one abandons these branches of the provisions for śamatha and vipaśyanā;
and one internally contemplates the wisdom realized through reflection as well as the instructions and admonitions that accord with it.
This is able to encompass the factors of śamatha and vipaśyanā;
by relying upon this, one realizes śamatha and vipaśyanā,
and is further able to attain the various fruits of the śramaṇa.
Regarding the profound and subtle meanings realized by oneself,
if there are those who wish to apply themselves [to these teachings] yet give rise to doubt,
one should explain them to them exactly as they were realized by oneself in order to sever that doubt.
Furthermore, one must possess eloquence in order to subdue opposing disputants;
and when the misconduct of others' bodies and speech arises,
one must possess the nature of a son of good family, which is comprised of patience and gentleness.
Furthermore, lack of faith arises due to three causes and conditions:
first, from failing to correctly understand the merits of the Three Jewels;
second, from practicing the views of non-Buddhist paths.
Third, because they have not yet encountered the three kinds of miraculous transformations of the Buddhas and their noble disciples,
and thus cannot be tamed by any one of these;
furthermore, due to three causes and conditions, they are unable to go frequently to peaceful groves and forests.
First, because they are constrained by heedlessness and indolence;
second, because of their many worldly affairs;
third, because they follow those who are credulous.
Furthermore, for three reasons, one by nature does not like to visit others:
first, because of a lack of fear;
second, because of an arrogant disposition.
Third, because of reliance on words and letters.
Due to three causes and conditions, one is by nature disinclined to associate closely with others:
first, because one's nature is not sharp or clever.
Second, because their two natures are not fields of merit;
third, because they lack the desire for supreme bliss.
Due to these three causes and conditions, their nature is such that they do not like to inquire of others.
First, because of being unskilled in the Dharma;
second, because of being unskilled in the meaning;
and third, because of being unskilled in both.
One is unable to listen attentively due to three causes and conditions:
first, because of excessive discursive thought;
second, because of excessive worldly affairs.
Third, because the mind is defiled by numerous hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and fetters (*paryavasthāna*),
it is by virtue of three causes and conditions that its nature is unable to maintain certainty:
first, due to a lack of hearing [the Dharma].
Second, because of improper hearing;
third, because of obscuring wisdom and superior wisdom.
Due to these three causes and conditions, their nature is such that they are unable to investigate all phenomena.
First, because of being attached to frivolous discourse;
second, because of delighting in dwelling amidst clamor and bustle;
third, because of not having achieved the wisdom of analytical investigation.
Due to three causes and conditions, one is of a nature incapable of practicing in accordance with the Dharma:
first, out of attachment to body and life;
second, due to the predominant influence of that very [attachment], one delights in and clings to gain and offerings.
Third, due to attachment to honor and gain,
one does not delight in practicing the conduct that benefits others for three reasons: first,
because one’s nature belongs to an inferior lineage.
Second, because compassion is slight;
third, because it lacks power.
One should understand that the characteristics of the "white category" (śuklapakṣa) are the opposite of those mentioned above.
Furthermore, it is observed that the noble disciples engage in many various kinds of excursions and contemplations;
namely, excursions by the riverbanks and excursions in mountain valleys.
One may observe the various kinds of wanderings and observations within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). Question:
For what causes and conditions do the great śrāvakas, having already attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), [engage in such wanderings]?
He then went to the realm of hungry ghosts to interrogate them regarding their own karmic retributions from previous lives;
this was both to eliminate his own doubts and to bring benefit to sentient beings.
If it were for the purpose of removing his own doubts,
it would not be logical for him to have already attained supernormal powers;
if it were for the purpose of benefiting sentient beings...
When it is asked how one benefits sentient beings, the answer is: for the sake of benefiting sentient beings;
that is to say, wishing to benefit these hungry ghosts and other sentient beings.
Why is this? By means of their supernormal powers, they cause the hungry ghosts to remember their past lives,
so that they themselves recount the evil karma committed in their previous existences and give rise to profound weariness and remorse.
Because they can attain realization through the teaching of the Dharma,
they will swiftly depart from the realm of hungry ghosts by means of these causes and conditions.
Thus, this is called benefiting all hungry ghosts.
The great śrāvakas who had already attained supernormal powers,
having heard what he said regarding the various unpleasant fruits of his past evil karma,
returned to the human world and proclaimed it from one to another.
Having heard this, he gives rise to a sense of weary detachment (*nirvid*), abandons evil, and cultivates the wholesome.
Such an explanation is called "benefiting other sentient beings.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the forms (*rūpa*) associated with the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) are termed "coarse" (*audārika*) by virtue of six characteristics.
How is it that those are called "coarse" by way of six characteristics?
First, they are coarse because they are manifold;
second, they are coarse because they are heavy.
Third, it is coarse because of impurity;
fourth, it is coarse because of its solidity;
fifth, it is coarse because of its susceptibility to transformation and decay.
Furthermore, because they do not function in accordance with the mind, they are coarse;
moreover, the texts concerning the various determinations (*viniścaya*) regarding the stage of the Pratyekabuddhas no longer appear here.
14 (The Stage of the Pratyekabuddha is missing) *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 71;
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 72;
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Within the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, this is the first part of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*. Thus has been explained the determination (*viniścaya*) of the *Śrāvakabhūmi* and the others.
