and it is unreasonable that their nature— being untamed— is capable of taming others.
Because the Tathāgata is forever free from all outflows (āsrava) and because his nature is disciplined and virtuous,
he is able to discipline and guide all sentient beings.
In what way are the gods not a refuge due to their own karma?
It is because those gods take as their activity the enjoyment of various sensual pleasures and remaining therein.
The harmful karmic actions of sentient beings can be found;
the Tathāgata’s activity consists in abiding in vast, stainless meditative concentration,
and his activity consists in being able to bring benefit to sentient beings.
Why is it that the various devas, by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*),
are not objects of refuge?
It is because all worldly and supramundane auspicious and magnificent accomplishments depend entirely upon one's own power and effort.
If one is devoid of personal effort,
even if one extends the utmost reverence and service toward the devas,
one will still not attain it.
Although they do not serve with reverence,
because they must certainly obtain [the results] through their own exertion,
how is it that the various devas [attain their status] by way of cause and effect?
They are not objects of refuge;
that is to say, the bodies of the various devas are obtained through karma that evokes rebirth as a deva,
and they are not obtained by means of making offerings to the devas.
It would be obtained without cause;
if it were obtained through karma capable of inducing rebirth as a deva,
one should simply take refuge in the actions one has performed oneself.
It is not those devas;
if it were obtained without cause,
one should instead take refuge in the absence of cause.
One should not take refuge in the devas;
for it is by virtue of making offerings to the various devas that one obtains these bodies of the devas.
Is it that the act of making offerings alone serves as the cause for becoming a deva? Or is it both [the offering and the recipient]?

If it were only through making offerings to a deva that one becomes a deva, then such offerings would be in vain; rather, one should attain a celestial body in accordance with the object to which the offering was made.
If it were solely through the offerings of devas that [the result] were established,
then even without making offerings, the devas should cause those [beings] to obtain a celestial body. If, however,
you say it depends on both, [then...]
This means that by means of making offerings, one gathers and subdues the various devas, causing all their thoughts and wishes to be fulfilled.
If that were so, then because the fulfillment of these seven kinds of thoughts would not be certain, [the practice would be ineffective].
This is not logical;
that is to say, those who possess faith and resolve rely upon the objects they have accepted as supports for their offerings,
while those with faith and resolve rely upon the objects of their faith and resolve.
Regarding the objects of faith and understanding,
regarding the ability to proceed toward the most excellent celestial bodies,
and regarding the ability to achieve the most excellent wealth and happiness.
Regarding the ability to destroy all enemies such as the asuras and others,
as well as their displacement;
furthermore, there are four purities.
First is purity of name;
second is purity of speech;
third is purity of intrinsic nature.
Fourth is the purity of form.
Furthermore, this form possesses great majestic power and severs all nets of doubt.
He is able to provide excellent explanations;
he can transform those who are difficult to transform;
he is the refuge for devas and humans, and is skillfully able to instruct and guide them.
Having realized the nature of renunciation, one restrains the various non-Buddhist paths.
Furthermore, how should one understand the objective referents of designations such as "form"?
Designations such as "form" exist as conceptual constructs (prajñapti-sat) and do not exist as substantial entities (dravya-sat).
This refers to the consciousness established by the conceptualization of the habitual tendencies of various linguistic designations.
Taking the objects of conceptualization such as form as its objective support, it imputes them to be the intrinsic nature of form and so forth.
This nature does not exist as a substantial entity.
They do not exist in the ultimate sense.
Therefore, these mental constructions of form and so forth do not truly exist;
they are merely of the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva).
One should know that these exist as mere designations.
If one eliminates the conceptualizations established by the habitual tendencies of names and words, consciousness will no longer take those objects of perception—
such as form and so forth— as its conditions.
Regarding this nature that is beyond verbal expression,
one should know that this nature exists as a substantial entity and exists as the ultimate reality.
The reasoning and discourse for this point are established as they should be understood in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
This refers to the consciousness established by the conceptualizations of the habitual tendencies of linguistic designations (*nāma-vyavahāra-vāsanā*).
Taking the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) as its object,
it is said that this nature is neither internal nor external,
nor can even the slightest thing be found between the two.
It is not already arisen,
not yet to arise,
and not currently arising.
It is not already extinguished,
not yet to be extinguished,
and not currently being extinguished.
It is primordially quiescent and by nature in a state of nirvāṇa. Why is this?
Because it exists only as a conventional designation and not as an ultimate reality.
If one were to depart from the intrinsic nature of all phenomena as expressed by names and conventions,
it should be understood that this nature arises through the conditions of the false attachments produced by ordinary beings;
it has arisen, will arise, and is currently arising, and it has ceased, will cease, and is currently ceasing.
If they have not been permanently severed and fully understood, one remains defiled;
if they have been permanently severed and fully understood,
one becomes purified.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that enable a bodhisattva to correctly embrace extensive learning:
namely, retaining what has been heard extensively and realizing what has been heard extensively.
The fruit of much learning,
the purity of much learning,
and the aspiration for enlightenment, respectively.
Associating with virtuous friends;
the power of discernment;
dwelling in seclusion.
One should know its characteristics.
Question: What is the realm of the bodhisattvas’ intention?
Answer: It is manifested by the faith and understanding that all buddha-dharmas possess an inherent nature.
Question: What is the sphere of the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) of bodhisattvas?
Answer: It is that which is manifested by faith and understanding in the virtues of all Buddha-dharmas.
Question: What is the sphere of the resolute belief (*adhimukti*) of bodhisattvas?
Answer: Because it is manifested by the obtainment of faith and understanding in all the Buddha-dharmas.
Question: What is the compassion of the bodhisattvas?
Answer: It is the arising of sympathetic sorrow toward all sentient beings who are confronted with suffering.
Question: What is the compassion (*karuṇā*) of the bodhisattvas?
Answer: It is the arising of sorrowful pity toward all sentient beings for whom the causes of suffering are manifest.
Question: What is the wisdom (*prajñā*) of the bodhisattvas?
Answer: Because they penetrate the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāvatā*) regarding the objects of knowledge.
Question: What is the wisdom of the bodhisattvas like?
Answer: Because they penetrate the nature of things in their full extent (*yāvadbhāvatā*) regarding the objects of knowledge.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of contemplation on faults:
namely, incomplete contemplation and inappropriate contemplation.
This is inverted reflection.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the practice of generosity as performed by bodhisattvas attains purity through seven aspects.
That is to say: purity of the object given,
purity of ethical discipline,
and purity of view.
Purity of mind,
purity of speech,
and purity of wisdom.
Regarding the purity of the defilements:
it should be understood that all such purities possess ten characteristics.
What are the ten characteristics of the purity of the object given?
First, the vast giving,
which refers to its manifold variety;
second, the impartial giving.
That is to say, because it is without increase or decrease.
Third is giving at the proper time,
meaning that it accords with what the recipient desires.
Fourth is the sublime and excellent gift,
which means it is endowed with [excellent] form and so forth.
Fifth is the pure gift.
That is to say, it is because it is not defiled by being mixed with impure things.
Sixth is giving in accordance with the Dharma,
which means it is associated with what is blameless.
Seventh is giving according to preference,
which means giving in accordance with what the requester loves and desires.
Eighth is beneficial giving.
This means giving according to what is appropriate for them;
the nine types of giving are either immediate or gradual,
meaning they are given by observing the needs of those who seek them.
The ten aspects of uninterrupted giving,
which means it is without interruption.
What are the ten characteristics of pure ethical discipline?
First, one gives away the wealth and goods acquired through the exertion of diligent effort;
second, one gives away the wealth and goods produced by the strength of one's own arms;
third, one gives away things that are free from defilement and impurity.
Fourth, giving in accordance with the Dharma;
fifth, giving as a gift what has been acquired in accordance with the Dharma;
sixth, practicing giving while pacifying and eliminating all evils.
Seventh, one practices giving while subduing the sense faculties.
Eighth, one practices giving with earnestness and reverence.
Ninth, one gives with one's own hands.
Tenth, one first provides for and nurtures one’s own servants and attendants,
and only thereafter bestows gifts upon others who come seeking them.
What are the ten signs of pure vision?
First, one does not conceive the thought, "I am able to practice giving," or "Giving is mine," while practicing generosity.
Second, one does not compare oneself with others,
thinking, "I am superior," "I am equal," or "I am inferior," while practicing generosity.
Third, one practices giving without observing that there will be a reciprocal reward.
Fourth, one practices giving without observing that there will be future superior, sublime, wealth, or happiness.
Fifth, they practice giving without observing that there is no fruit at all in giving.
Sixth, they practice giving without observing that the fruit of giving is dissimilar [to the gift].
Seventh, they practice giving without observing that the fruit of giving is perverted.
Eighth, he practices giving without regarding the slaughter of beings as a companion.
Ninth, he practices giving without regarding signs of portents or auspicious omens.
Tenth, he practices giving not for the sake of worldly fame or praise.
What are the ten aspects of mental purity?
First, practicing generosity with a compassionate mind;
that is, acting toward all sentient beings according to one's own nature.
Second, they practice giving with a mind of preciousness;
that is, regarding the object of giving.
Third, they practice giving with a mind of equanimity.
This refers to practicing generosity toward enemies, friends,
and neutral persons by subduing four types of defiled minds:
namely, the defilement of stinginess and the defilement of hoarding.
One should know that not giving to others is called the stain of stinginess;
not enjoying it oneself is called the stain of hoarding.
One practices generosity with a mind of joyful aspiration.
That is to say, by way of seven aspects:
first, because one generates a mind of joy and delight toward those who seek [refuge] in the future;
second, because one immediately gives rise to pure faith upon first seeing those who have already come seeking it.
Third, because one gives rise to a mind of joy at the time of right giving;
fourth, because one gives rise to a mind of tranquil concentration;
fifth, because one gives rise to a mind of insatiability.
Sixth, because they give with a mind that does not intend to harm or afflict living beings;
seventh, because they have no sense of regret after having given;
sixth, they practice giving with a mind of patience.
That is to say, because one is able to endure the forceful obstruction of those who seek [gifts],
and because one is free from weariness;
seventh, one practices giving with a mind of loving-kindness.
That is to say, one practices giving with a mind of compassion toward those who cause harm;
and toward those who are suffering.
Ninth, one practices giving with a mind of joy,
specifically toward those who possess virtuous qualities;
tenth, one practices giving with a mind of equanimity.
That is to say, regarding one's friends and relatives:
what are the ten aspects of verbal purity?
First, one freely allows the solicitor to choose from among the items to be given.
Second, when they arrive, one should welcome them, saying "Welcome. Third,
one should avoid frowning, maintain a level countenance, and look upon them with a relaxed face and a smile,
being the first to speak and inquire after their well-being.
Fourth, he engages in conversation with gentle words to comfort the beggars.
Fifth, immediately thereafter, he says, "I shall give you desirable wealth," rejoicing in this act of giving.
Sixth, he correctly utters words of giving,
saying, "I now bestow this upon you.
Seventh, if the recipient should object, he distributes it calmly and without using harsh words.
Eighth, whether facing or turning away from those who beg, one does not disparage or revile them, nor does one engage in idle talk.
Ninth, if there is no object to give, one expresses a sincere apology and promises to give according to one's means.
Tenth, toward those who beg,
he never rebukes them face-to-face, drives them away, or mocks and teases them;
nor does he cause them to change their expression or feel ashamed.
What are the ten aspects of the purity of wisdom?
First, the purity of wisdom through giving;
second, the purity of wisdom regarding the seeker.
Third, by the purification of the wisdom regarding the objects given;
fourth, by the purification of the wisdom regarding the application of giving;
fifth, by the purification of the wisdom regarding maturing sentient beings through giving.
Sixth, by means of the purification through the wisdom of skillful means;
seventh, by means of the purification through the wisdom regarding the faults and afflictions of desires;
eighth, by means of the purification through the wisdom that removes defilements.
Ninth, by means of the purity of knowledge regarding being sustained through seclusion from [unwholesome] friends;
tenth, by means of the purity of knowledge regarding the concealment of the six directions.
First, by means of the purity of knowledge regarding generosity:
That is to say: regarding the synonyms for giving,
the essential characteristics of giving,
and the etymological definitions of giving.
Regarding the distinctions of giving,
one practices generosity by knowing them all as they truly are.
Second, regarding the purity of the wisdom of the seeker.
This means that one practices giving by maintaining the realization that all sentient beings are fields of merit;
and because one is able to clearly discern the various distinctions among those who come seeking— whether they be superior or inferior, those with gain or loss,
or those who have been enemies or benefactors— one bestows gifts according to their specific inclinations.
Furthermore, one first renounces all material goods to be given with a resolute intention directed toward the entire class of sentient beings;
when seekers take what they need of their own accord, one feels sympathetic joy in all instances.
Third, regarding the purity of wisdom concerning the objects given:
this refers to being skillful in wisdom regarding all fields of arts and crafts,
whereby one is able to quickly amass all necessary material wealth and bestow it as a gift.
Or it may be due to being sustained by roots of goodness;
that is, giving away wealth acquired through the results of past lives or the present life;
or giving away wealth produced through the manifestation of supernormal powers or through the attainment of the Dharma.
Or one may use all the wealth accumulated by others for the purpose of giving.
This is as when one exhorts others or attends to their affairs.
Fourth, regarding purification through the application of wisdom (*prajñā*).
This means that one is skillfully aware of how to apply the practice of giving,
ensuring that the seeker’s body and mind do not become weary,
and bestowing gifts with a mind free from defilement.
He is skillfully able to distribute gifts to those who come seeking them;
he gives to the poor and destitute,
and he gives to those who have no refuge.
Giving to those who practice evil,
giving to those who practice what is sublime,
and giving to one's own servants and attendants.
That is to say, whether one possesses little wealth or great wealth, one practices giving according to the proper method as appropriate,
and not improperly.
Fifth, the purification of the wisdom that matures sentient beings through giving.
That is to say, having thoroughly understood giving,
one practices generosity after having brought sentient beings to maturity;
one practices giving by sharing the objects of gift universally with the great assembly.
Furthermore, he causes the great assembly to generate immeasurable merit.
Moreover, toward those who are impoverished yet delight in practicing generosity,
he distributes his own wealth and possessions among them, enabling them to practice giving.
There may be those who are not poor yet harbor stinginess within;
although they wish to practice giving, they are unable to use their own wealth to make offerings.
One should therefore give them wealth and property, enabling them to practice generosity.
Or, when one wishes to perform some act for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha field of merit,
one discards wealth and property to give it to them, instructing them to carry out the work.
By this cause and condition, immeasurable merit is generated through these two gateways.
Sixth, regarding purification through the wisdom of skillful means:
this refers to causing one to practice generosity either by means of instruction or by forceful compulsion.
Either by acknowledging that kindness and practicing generosity,
or by virtue of being born [in a certain state] and practicing generosity,
or through supernatural power, one practices generosity.
Seventh, regarding purification through the knowledge of the faults of sensual desires:
this refers to practicing generosity after having understood, as they truly are, all the faults inherent in sensual desires.
This means that within the aggregate of suffering, one at times understands two kinds of disadvantages:
first, those pertaining to the present life;
second, those pertaining to future lives.
At times, one thoroughly understands five kinds of faults,
as described in the *Sūtra on the Five Kinds of Faults*;
at other times, one thoroughly understands six kinds of faults.
That is to say, these various sensual desires are synonyms for "fear," and so forth;
as explained at length in the sūtra.
Alternatively, one may at times understand the seven kinds of disadvantages.
That is to say, one knows that all desires are impermanent, hollow, false, deceptive, and subject to loss— like magical illusions that delude the foolish—
or at times, one thoroughly understands their eight kinds of faults.
That is to say, knowing all desires to be like rotting bones and skeletons,
as explained at length in the sūtras,
up to: "they are like ripe fruit at the top of a tree."
Eighth, regarding purification through the knowledge that removes stains:
this refers to practicing generosity after having understood, as it truly is, the fourteen types of stained actions that are to be eliminated.
This is as stated in the *Śikhālakasūtra* regarding the nine causes for the purification of wisdom through the avoidance of evil friends and the embracing of virtuous friends:
that is, one who is able to skillfully know how to avoid the four kinds of evil friends and embrace the four kinds of virtuous friends while practicing generosity.
This is also as stated in the *Śikhālakasūtra*.
Regarding "purity through the concealment of the wisdom of the six directions":
this refers to practicing generosity while concealing the fact that one is giving to the six directions.
This is also as stated in the *Śīkṣāsamuccaya-sūtra*.
What are the ten aspects of defilement and purification?
First, practicing generosity while remaining far removed from the defilement of laziness.
That is to say, whether internal or external, near or far,
or whether the body is fatigued or not fatigued.
Whether one's body is weak or not weak,
one constantly practices giving;
second, one practices giving while remaining far removed from the defilement of greed.
That is to say, regarding material goods,
one practices giving while remaining free from the stain of ill will toward those who seek it.
Fourth, one practices giving while remaining free from the defilement of delusion regarding cause and effect.
Fifth, one practices giving while remaining free from the defilement of hindrances.
Regarding the term "obscuring defilements," it refers to four kinds of obscurations.
The first is lack of familiarization.
Second, deprivation;
third, indulgence;
fourth, observing the fruit.
Sixth, one practices giving by distributing [wealth] virtuously;
this is the distancing from the stain of irrationality,
namely, [the failure of] those who are destitute toward their own servants and attendants.
If one possesses moderate wealth, [one should give] to that person and to those who are in poverty and suffering;
if one possesses great wealth,
one should give to that person as well as to others who come seeking.
Seventh, one practices giving through fulfillment;
this is the removal of the stains of deficiency,
namely, the fulfillment of the object (*vastu*).
The perfection of intention and the perfection of the objective have seven further aspects.
First, the matter of giving material assets;
second, the matter of giving a kingdom;
third, the matter of giving sentient beings.
Fourth, the matter of the adornment of giving;
fifth, the matter of giving dwellings;
sixth, the matter of giving residences.
Seventh is the matter of giving one's own body.
Regarding the perfection of the intention:
this refers to [the attitude toward] both one's own body and external wealth and treasures.
One attains the intention of non-attachment to intrinsic nature.
Eighth, one practices generosity through purification;
this is the removal of the stains of impurity.
That is to say, by means of ten kinds of purity—
namely, non-attachment, non-grasping, and so forth— as explained at length in the *Yogācārabhūmi*;
and ninth, practicing generosity after thorough investigation.
This is precisely the distancing from the defilement of unwholesome wisdom;
that is to say, it consists of observing the gift and observing the intention.
Observing the field and observing the gift means observing that its enjoyment is superior to its mere accumulation.
One should contemplate that giving is superior to enjoyment. Why is this?
Because if one merely accumulates wealth, it cannot benefit oneself.
It cannot benefit others;
it is neither a benefit for the present life nor a benefit for future lives.
If bodhisattvas only enjoy [the fruits] themselves, it is called benefiting oneself.
That which does not benefit others is called a benefit for the present life,
not a benefit for future lives.
If bodhisattvas are able to practice generosity,
they give rise within themselves to vast joy;
this is called benefiting oneself and benefiting others.
These are called benefits in the present life and benefits in future lives.
Regarding the observation of intention,
it should be known that there are, in brief, four kinds of intention.
First, the intentionality that is unerring regarding causes;
second, the intentionality that is free from attachment regarding results;
third, the intentionality of compassion toward sentient beings.
Fourth, the intention of fulfilling the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*);
it is by means of such intentions as these that one practices generosity.
Regarding the examination of the field,
it should be known that it is briefly characterized by five aspects:
first, that alms can be obtained in this place.
Second, in this situation, those who already beg for alms further become destitute;
third, in this situation, those who are already destitute furthermore lack a protector;
fourth, in this situation, those who already lack a protector furthermore engage in unwholesome conduct.
This is called a field.
Although these [qualities] may not be present in this place,
one can still find the cultivation of wholesome conduct there.
One should understand that there are seven types of persons who are not worthy fields [of merit]:
first, a petitioner who is extremely violent and cruel, who has previously committed acts of enmity and harm,
and who now seeks something while taking refuge in that very enmity and harm.
Second, though exhorted to perform wholesome deeds, one is ultimately unable to achieve them.
Third, harboring defilement in the mind, one makes requests for the sake of defiled matters.
Fourth, one makes requests for the sake of causing harm and affliction.
Fifth, those who beg may be māras themselves or possessed by māras, begging in improper places.
Sixth, they beg from their parents,
or otherwise seek after various things that are not fit objects for giving.
Seventh, it can lead to what is meaningless.
By means of these points, one should understand that this is called observing what is not a [suitable] field.
Tenth, one practices giving while possessing the virtue of skillful means.
This is precisely the removal of the defilement of the fault of lacking skillful means.
In this context, "skillful means" refers to the habitual practice of giving.
Disregarding their own bodies and lives,
they take pity on sentient beings and provide instruction through the supreme resolve for unexcelled bodhi, which is the wisdom of the true meaning.
Through powerful coercion,
by remaining in a position of service to repay kindness,
through birth, and through supernormal powers.
The Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 74 and Fascicle 75,
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Within the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, this is the fourth section of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*. Furthermore, it should be known that the Bodhisattva-vinaya consists briefly of three aggregates.
First, regarding the collection of the Vinaya of the vows of restraint:

one should know that this very collection of the Vinaya is as briefly explained by the Blessed One for the sake of those sentient beings to be trained who are śrāvakas, concerning the characteristics of the Vinaya.
What is the collection of the Vinaya rules for the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas?
It refers to the fact that when bodhisattvas diligently practice the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas,
they should briefly and skillfully observe six types of mind.
What are the six?
First, a mind of contempt;
second, a mind accompanied by indolence.
Third, the mind that is obscured;
fourth, the mind that is weary from exertion;
fifth, the mind accompanied by illness.
The sixth is the mind that follows along with obstacles.
If a bodhisattva, regarding wholesome dharmas,
possesses a mind of slightness, a lack of resolute conviction, and a mind of contempt, this is called a "contemptuous mind."
If the mind is entangled by indolence, pride, intoxication, or negligence,
it is called a mind accompanied by laziness.
If any one of the hindrances, such as sensual desire, is present, [it is likewise so designated].
A mind that is entangled by various afflictions and secondary afflictions is called a "concealed" mind;
if one abides in courageous and superior diligence, [it is not so].
When physical exhaustion and mental fatigue obscure the mind,
it is called "the mind weary from toil.
If various illnesses afflict and distress the mind, it is likewise so named.
The state of being unable to practice due to a lack of strength is called the "mind that follows along with illness.
If there are obstacles such as a fondness for talk and so forth, [this is likewise].
That which follows and pursues that mind is called the "obstructing concomitant mind.
Regarding these six kinds of minds, the bodhisattva...
One should correctly observe:
"Among these six kinds of minds,
is any one of them currently manifesting?"
Or is it that they do not exist?
Regarding these three preceding states of mind,
a bodhisattva should never give rise to them at all.
If [an affliction] has already arisen, one should not tolerate it;
if one tolerates it, one must not abandon it—
this applies universally to all cases.
All these are termed "guilty.
When a mind of weariness due to diligent exertion manifests,
one abandons skillful means because of that mind.
If one practices many wholesome dharmas for the sake of briefly resting the fatigue and afflictions of body and mind,
it should be known that there is no fault.
If one were to completely renounce everything,
thinking, "What use is it for me to diligently cultivate such wholesome dharmas,
which cause me to abide in this suffering in the present?"
If it is thus, one should know that there is an offense;
for when a mind associated with illness manifests,
the bodhisattva has no mastery over it.
One does not engage in the application of wholesome practice according to one's desire;
although one endures it,
there is no fault when the obstructing concomitant mind manifests before one.
If one does not fall into it through desire,
or if one perceives that there is great benefit and purpose therein,
then even though one endures it, there is no fault.
If one enters therein because it accords with one's desires;
or if one perceives that there is no benefit therein;
or if one endures it despite there being only slight benefit.
One should know that these involve transgression.
Thus, regarding these six states of mind, if one endures them after the first three have arisen,
it is invariably a transgression.
If the mind follows along with the illness,
even though one endures it,
there is invariably no fault.
If the other two types of mind arise and are subsequently tolerated,
they may be either with fault or without fault.
This occurs when bodhisattvas are diligently training in the precepts for benefiting sentient beings.
One should correctly observe the conduct subsumed within the six sense bases,
namely: oneself and others,
and the decline of wealth.
Wealth flourishes while the Dharma declines; the Dharma flourishes while wealth declines.
This is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Regarding the decline of wealth:
it refers to not obtaining clothing, food, and so forth that have not yet been obtained, or their loss and destruction after they have already been obtained.
One should know that the opposite of this constitutes the flourishing of material wealth.
As for the decline of the Dharma,
it refers to transgressing what has been studied.
Regarding those sublime phrases of the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata, which are subsumed within the ultimate truth and which one has not heard before,
one does not obtain to hear them;
just as one does not hear what was not previously heard.
Thus, regarding that which was previously not contemplated, one is unable to contemplate it;
there is an obstacle to hearing and an obstacle to contemplation.
Even if one succeeds in hearing and contemplating, one subsequently forgets it.
Regarding the wholesome states consisting of cultivation that have not yet been realized,
one has not yet realized them; even if they were realized,
one would fall away from them again.
One should know that the opposite of this constitutes the flourishing of the Dharma.
In this regard, a bodhisattva brings about the decline of their own Dharma while causing the flourishing of others' wealth.
This should not be done. Just as it is with the flourishing of wealth,
so it is with the flourishing of the Dharma.
The meaning herein refers to that which is subsumed under transgression of the trainings,
that which is conducive to such transgression,
or that which is subsumed under falling away from the realization of the Dharma.
One should know that this is the decline of the Dharma.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas cause their own wealth to decline so as to make the wealth of others flourish,
if that flourishing of wealth does not lead to the decline of the Dharma, [it is not a fault].
This should be done; if it would lead to the decline of the Dharma, this should not be done.
As it is with the flourishing of wealth, so it is with the flourishing of the Dharma.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas bring about the flourishing of their own wealth and cause the flourishing of the wealth of others.
This is what ought to be done;
just as it is so that material wealth may flourish,
so too should the Dharma flourish.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas should act in such a way that they increase their own Dharma and cause others to increase their wealth;
this is what ought to be done.
Just as it is when wealth flourishes,
so too is it when the Dharma flourishes;
if one does not practice in such matters, it is called being guilty of an offense.
If one practices correctly, this is called being blameless.
Thus has been briefly explained the threefold discipline undertaken by bodhisattvas, which constitutes their concise vinaya.
Within this, a bodhisattva should constantly apply their attention, reflect, and train.
If, among these three types of bodhisattva precepts received,
there is any deficiency, one should know that it is not a protection;
one should say that the bodhisattva restraint is not being observed.
One should not say that these three types of precepts are protected separately;
rather, they are brought into harmony by being sustained by the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*).
If one can diligently guard them in this way, [they will be maintained].
One is likewise able to diligently guard the other two;
if one cannot guard this one,
one will also be unable to guard the other two.
Therefore, if one violates the ethical discipline of the vows,
it is called violating all the bodhisattva vows.
This is so that others may clearly understand [the transgression].
Because he complies with others, he receives the bodhisattva precepts through the exhortation of others,
rather than from a superior resolve arising within himself;
he merely observes and examines accordingly.
Having naturally given rise to pure faith,
they abide in a mind of compassion toward all sentient beings,
delighting in wholesome dharmas and receiving the bodhisattva precepts.
It should be said that this is not genuine protection,
nor is it the perfect cultivation of wholesome qualities.
Furthermore, one cannot obtain the excellence of its fruit.
It should be understood that the opposite of this is called "genuine protection," and through it, one can indeed obtain the excellence of its fruit.
Furthermore, it should be known that if one does not abandon such discipline, it will continue to follow one into future lives; this is not the case for those who do abandon it.
Moreover, there are briefly four types of causes for abandonment.
First, one definitely arouses a mind that is discordant with the mind of undertaking [the precepts].
Second, one intentionally utters words of renunciation in the presence of a great person who possesses discernment.
Third, the total or partial violation of the four kinds of qualities surpassed by others;
fourth, the total or partial violation of the four kinds of qualities surpassed by others through the influence of an intense degree of obsession (*paryavasthāna*).
From these causes and conditions, it should be known that one has abandoned the bodhisattva vows.
If one subsequently attains a pure mind of commitment,
one should receive them once again.
Furthermore, if there is an ordained bodhisattva,
whatever surplus possessions they have beyond the three robes—
which are permitted by the Buddha to be kept and used for the body so as to abide in comfort— [are to be treated as follows].
If one intentionally deliberates before giving to a petitioner,
it should be known that there is no fault.
If one does not give because of regard for wholesome qualities, rather than being hindered by stinginess or greed, [there is likewise no fault].
Nor is there any fault.
Suppose there is a leaf manuscript upon which the True Dharma has already been written,
and a sentient being with the intellect of a child comes to beg for it.
If one gives [something] oneself, one should know that it is a transgression;
if one encourages another to give, that is also called a transgression—except when one has formed this thought:
[“I shall cause them to abandon their attachment”].
I now bestow this upon him in order to test whether that person is capable of receiving and upholding the profound Dharma,
and whether they are able to have faith and understanding;
thus, there is no fault.
If one writes what resembles the True Dharma or non-Buddhist treatises on leaf paper,
or if one has already written them and placed them in the hands of sentient beings who possess faith and understanding,
or if one encourages others to give them, one should know that this constitutes an offense.
A bodhisattva should only encourage them to abandon the heterodox arguments in their hands,
or have them transcribe the holy teachings of the Buddhas; otherwise,
if they wish to know for themselves that those [teachings] are not firm and substantial, they should not reveal them.
If there are leaf-manuscripts that have not yet been written upon,
and someone comes to beg for them, the Bodhisattva at that time should ask that person:
"What use do you have for such an object?"
If one answers them, "I wish to sell this for food," then if the leaves and paper are intended for writing the True Dharma (saddharma), they should not be given away; rather,
one who possesses wealth should provide the equivalent value as payment.
If there is no price and neither party gives anything,
there is no offense.
If he should reply, "I seek this object for the purpose of copying the True Dharma," [then it is permissible].
One should immediately provide them with leaf-paper and tell them, "Use it as you please.
If they wish to transcribe inferior texts, [one should grant it].
One does not incur a fault [by writing] that which is not [the Dharma].
This is likewise true for writing inferior texts and the like.
However, if one wishes to transcribe the most excellent scriptures, [one must observe the following].
One should know that there is fault in not giving.
If Bodhisattvas, toward sentient beings who have been kind to them,
give rise to a continuous intention of friendship in accordance with the perception of their kindness;
If one, with a defiled mind, employs skillful means to take [others] under one's influence and seeks to form a faction,
you should know that this is an offense.
Or, toward sentient beings who are hostile,
one follows a continuous stream of thoughts of enmity and gives rise to an attitude of hostility.
One should know that a defiled and turbid mind is sinful;
or, one may develop a neutral state of mind toward sentient beings who are neither benefactors nor enemies, within the continuity of one's own being.
One should know that the intention of renunciation with a mind of attachment is blameworthy,
even if there is one currently seeking to go forth.
When observing in accordance with reality,
if there is a fault yet one does not go forth out of compassion for that person, it should be known that there is no offense,
provided one dwells in a mind of loving-kindness toward them.
Even though one has gone forth and been ordained, there is no offense.
As it is said: "Having gone forth and received full ordination, one provides [another] with a formal reliance (*niśraya*)."
One should know that it is likewise when gathering a retinue of disciples.
By means of all such modes of conduct,
one should know that the bodhisattva’s three aggregates of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) are all brought to perfection.
Furthermore, although giving and the other perfections have already been explained in detail,
they shall now be briefly described.
That is to say, regarding all the giving of the bodhisattvas:
Briefly stated, it corresponds with five kinds of merit to be reckoned as having reached the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
What are these five?
First, non-attachment.
Second is freedom from attachment;
third is freedom from fault;
fourth is freedom from conceptual discrimination.
Fifth is dedication;
one should know that it is the same for giving, ethical discipline, and so forth.
Regarding "non-attachment":
This means that regarding all types of obstructive factors to generosity and the other perfections,
one is without hindrance and without attachment.
This means that regarding both defiled states and their fruits,
the mind is without attachment;
it is "blameless."
This means being free from all types of secondary afflictions associated with giving and so forth.
"Non-conceptual" refers to not observing the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) within giving and the like.
Dedication refers to the aspiration to attain the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of all practices, such as giving and the rest.
In this way, by means of these five virtues,
a bodhisattva’s engagement with all the perfections— from what is called "bodhisattva generosity" up to "bodhisattva wisdom"— is fully embraced.
It is called "the gift of all," and so on,
up to being called "all-encompassing wisdom.
It is called "the gift of hardship."
Up to what is called "arduous wisdom," he extensively explains all the uddāna verses,
fully resolving and understanding them all.
All of these are as explained in the *Maulī Bhūmi*.
Furthermore, regarding the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*),
there are ten secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) arising from both internal and external factors.
In order to counteract those [obstacles], one attains the tenfold purity of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*),
as already explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
This occurs through the progressive increase of each successive stage.
Based on the external door, there are five secondary afflictions:
first, the nature of pervasive defilement and distress;
second, the nature of relinquishment.
Third, the state of not possessing what is delightful;
fourth, the state of unfulfilled aspirations;
fifth, the state of immaturity.
Based on the internal door, there are five secondary afflictions:
first, the nature of non-renunciation;
second, the nature of defiled distress.
Third, the nature of being non-inferior and non-thin;
fourth, the nature of manifesting as falling away;
fifth, the nature of being subject to exhaustion and cessation.
Furthermore, it has already been explained in the preceding Chapter on Ethics that there are ten kinds of purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
It should be understood that the first one is purity of intention (*āśaya*),
while the remaining nine are purity of application (*prayoga*).
Within the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), there are furthermore five kinds:
first, uninterrupted preparatory application;
second, thoroughly cultivated preparatory application.
Third, the application of dedication;
fourth, the application of companionship;
fifth, the application of protection.
The second and third [stages] constitute the first preparatory application;
the fourth constitutes the second preparatory application;
and the fifth constitutes the third preparatory application.
The sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth constitute the fourth preparatory stage (*prayoga*);
the tenth constitutes the fifth preparatory stage.
Furthermore, regarding the ten purities within the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*):
It should be understood that, in brief, there are two kinds of purification:
the first nine are called purification through the power of analytical reflection (*cintā-bala-viśuddhi*),
while the tenth is called purification through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala-viśuddhi*).
The purification through the power of discernment is further fourfold:
first, purification by distancing oneself from the arising of transgressions;
second, purification by their non-manifestation.
Third is the purity of birth free from fault;
fourth is the purity of being far removed from its causes and conditions.
These four types—first, second, third, and fourth—correspond respectively to the first, second, third, and third [categories].
There are further three kinds of conditions for non-endurance:
first, lack of shame;
second, lack of remorse.
Third is the nature of lacking compassion.
Furthermore, the perfection of diligence has ten purities.
The first is the purity of establishing [beings] in [wholesome states].
Second, purity through full maturation;
third, purity through incitement;
fourth, purity through skillful means.
Fifth, purity of abiding at a time that is not in vain;
sixth, purity of abiding without hardship;
seventh, purity of renunciation.
8. Purity of the gathering of companions;
9. Purity of swift supernormal powers;
10. Purity of inexhaustible nature.
Furthermore, the perfection of meditative concentration has ten purities:
first, purity through purification;
second, purity through being untainted (*anāsrava*).
Third, the purity of the fundamental skillful means;
fourth, the purity of the realization of the fundamental;
fifth, the purity of the skillful means of mastery.
Sixth is the purity of mastery over the stages;
seventh is the purity of mastery in the elicitation of supernormal powers;
eighth is the purity of mastery in the maturation of sentient beings.
Ninth is the purity of mastery in subduing non-Buddhists;
tenth is the purity of supreme detachment.
Furthermore, the perfection of wisdom possesses five purities.
First, thorough penetration of the purity of all signs;
second, thorough penetration of the purity of dependent origination;
third, thorough penetration of the purity of instruction.
The four penetrations are purity through application;
the five penetrations are purity through realization.
Furthermore, how does a bodhisattva abide in the contemplation of the body as the body?
This means that one contemplates the body of suchness by revolving through the body of signs;
as it is with the body,
so it should be understood accordingly for sensation, mind, and phenomena.
How does a bodhisattva generate the desire so that unarisen evil and unwholesome states do not arise?
This is explained at length as follows:
it means binding the mind to the object of suchness and causing it to abide therein.
In order that all signs (*nimitta*) and coarse residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) which have not yet manifested may not arise internally,
and that those which have not yet arisen may not come into being, one generates the desire [to practice];
and so forth, as explained at length.
Just as it is so that what has not yet arisen may not arise, likewise,
for that which has already arisen and been attained, manifesting within, it is for the purpose of its abandonment.
Regarding all wholesome dharmas that serve as antidotes,
he causes those not yet arisen to arise,
and those already arisen to remain.
...and so on, as explained at length.
It should be understood that herein, during the stage of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one first binds the mind to the object of observation,
and subsequently causes the mind to abide steadily upon that object.
One diligently cultivates the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).

Having subsequently attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one then diligently applies oneself to the practices of the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) in order to bring this concentration to full perfection.
Once concentration is perfected, in order to achieve dissociation from all signs (*nimitta*) and coarse heaviness (*dauṣthulya*),
one practices the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) based on the faculties such as faith.
Within the path of preparation, these faculties are of inferior grade.
Power is the highest grade.
Having thus correctly cultivated the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
one subsequently attains the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and penetrates the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Having reached the limit of reality, one next cultivates the factors of the path,
gradually proceeding until the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
attaining liberation from all obstacles.
Furthermore, it should be known that there are fourteen distinct types of bondage through the coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*):
first, bondage by the faculties;
second, bondage by objects.
Third, the mutual bond of affection among sentient beings.
Fourth, the bond of establishment;
that is to say, because all the faculties within the receptacle world function in dependence upon it, it is called "establishment."
Fifth, the bond of ignorance regarding the objects of knowledge;
sixth, the bond of ignorance regarding the knowing consciousness;
seventh, the bond of craving for future existence.
8. The bondage of the craving for non-existence;
9. The bondage of clinging to unequal causes and causelessness;
10. The bondage of the overweening pride of realization.
Eleventh, the bondage of attachment to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Twelfth, the bondage of attachment to the nature of the person (*pudgala*).
Thirteenth, the bondage of overweening pride (*abhimāna*) regarding the full knowledge of the person.
The fourteen dharmas are the bonds of overweening pride regarding thorough knowledge.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva who diligently cultivates the foundations of mindfulness based on emptiness [is freed] from,
in brief, six kinds of conceptualization bonds.
One should cause the mind to swiftly attain liberation.
What are called the six kinds of conceptual fetters?
They are the internal perceptions arising toward the body, and so forth, up to phenomena (*dharma*).
This is the first bond of perception.
Within this very state, one gives rise to external perceptions;
this is the second bond of perception.
One then gives rise to the perception of internal and external within this very state;
this is the third bond of perception.

If, regarding the infinite and immeasurable realms of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, one vows to bring them to liberation and practices the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), [this is the fourth bond].
Among these, the various perceptions are the fourth bond of perception.
Those perceptions by which one dwells contemplating the body and so forth as objects are the fifth bond of perception.
Regarding "dwelling while contemplating in accordance with the body and so forth": herein,
these various perceptions constitute the sixth bond of perception (*saṃjñā-bandhana*),
because one contemplates by circling within this very [body].
Furthermore, there are eleven successive fetters of perception.
What are the eleven successive fetters of perception?
They refer to one who dwells observing the body and so forth in relation to the body and so forth.
The conception of ultimate reality regarding the truths of both affliction and purification is called the first bond; specifically,
it is the conception of volitional activity regarding the ultimate reality of affliction.
This is the second bond.
Furthermore, the conception of non-activity that arises regarding the pure ultimate truth is the third bond.
The notion of permanence arising with respect to the unconditioned ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is the fourth bond.
The notion of cyclic flow (*pravṛtti*) arising with respect to conditioned affliction (*saṃkleśa*) is [the fifth].
This is the fifth bond.
Furthermore, the notion of immutability regarding that which is permanent is the sixth bond.
The perception of the nature of suffering that arises within the process of saṃsāra due to its being characterized by suffering and transformation is the seventh bond;
this occurs therein by virtue of the specific characteristics of arising, ceasing, abiding, and changing.
The conceptualization of those intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) that arises because intrinsic characteristics themselves undergo transformation is the eighth bond;
it arises with respect to both the non-transforming and the transforming ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
The conceptualization that grasps all phenomena as being either defiled or pure is the ninth bond;
it occurs precisely regarding all phenomena within the context of both affliction and purification.
To have the notion that "I" am neither defiled nor pure is the tenth bond;
this pertains precisely to all phenomena that are either defiled or pure.
The perception of the characteristic of selflessness in that which arises is the eleventh bondage.
This is because bodhisattvas correctly observe the objects of knowledge through these successive conceptualizations of formations (*saṃskāra*) regarding their bonds.
One is able to rely upon emptiness to skillfully cultivate the foundations of mindfulness,
thereby liberating the mind;
for by means of this, one attains liberation from the fetters of conceptualization.
All bonds of conceptualization are thereby liberated.
Furthermore, within the Mahāyāna, there is a certain class of people who, due to their misapprehension of emptiness,
speak as follows:
"According to the conventional truth, all things exist;
according to the ultimate truth, all things are non-existent.
One should say this to them.
"Venerable sir, what is the conventional?
What is the ultimate?
Having been asked thus, if he were to answer: "If all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, this is called the ultimate."
If, within all phenomena that lack intrinsic nature, an intrinsic nature could be apprehended,
this would be called the conventional. Why is this so?
Because one establishes conventional designations and linguistic expressions within the state of non-existence and thereby gives rise to discourse, you should be asked:
"What do you intend?
Do these conventional designations and linguistic expressions possess an intrinsic nature that can be apprehended as arising from causes?"
It exists only as a conventional designation.
If this conventional designation were to exist by way of causes,
then that which arises from causes would be a conventional designation, rather than [ultimately] existent.
This is not logical.
If it exists merely as a conventional designation,
then it would exist as a conventional designation without an underlying objective basis.
This is not logical.
Furthermore, one should say to them:
"Venerable sir, for what reason is it that all things which are perceivable lack intrinsic nature in this way?"
If, having been questioned thus, he answers that it is because of inverted phenomena, you should further say to him:
"What do you intend? Does this inverted phenomenon exist or does it not exist?"
If one says that they exist,
then to claim that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature by way of the ultimate truth would be unreasonable.
If one says they do not exist,
it is because they are inverted phenomena;
those things which can be apprehended lack intrinsic nature.
This is not reasonable.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the causes and conditions for the arising of the Mahāyāna sūtras are explained by way of five aspects.
That is to say, the first explanation is given in order to engender reverence for the speaker.
The second teaching was given for the sake of gathering the assembly;
the third teaching was given for the sake of engendering respect for the True Dharma;
and the fourth teaching was given for the sake of recounting the events.
The fifth exposition is undertaken for the purpose of proclaiming the true meaning and because it accomplishes much;
furthermore, it is based on the contemplation of the specific and general characteristics of the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
There are ten kinds of non-erroneous paths that can realize all the unshared Buddha-dharmas. It should be known that,
among these, six involve the contemplation of specific characteristics.
The fourfold contemplation of common characteristics refers to the thorough comprehension of the fact that within the nominal designations of the twelve sense bases— such as the eye and so forth—
there exist only the characteristics of mere designation.
This is called the first non-perverted path that can realize all the unshared Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, it is the thorough knowledge of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) as being comprised of the various characteristics of arising produced by false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
This is called the second non-erroneous path capable of realizing all the unshared Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, it is the thorough knowledge of the characteristics of the arising based on causes within the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
This is called the third non-erroneous path capable of realizing all the unshared Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, it is the thorough knowledge of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) as characterized by the transformation of the destruction of marks.
This is called the fourth non-erroneous path that can realize all the unshared Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, it is the thorough knowledge of the characteristics of the pure transformation within the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
This is called the fifth non-erroneous path capable of realizing all the unshared Buddha-dharmas.
It should be understood that herein, based on two kinds of activity, there are two types of purity.
First, purity of origination;
second, purity of cessation.
Furthermore, one thoroughly understands the characteristics of the basis upon which all conventional designations rest within the twelve sense bases (*āyatana*).
This is called the sixth non-erroneous path capable of realizing all the unshared Buddha-dharmas.
Thus one observes these six kinds of specific characteristics.
Furthermore, regarding these twelve bases (*āyatana*):
To be able to thoroughly understand the nature of common characteristics is called the seventh non-erroneous path, which can realize all the unshared Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, it is to be able to thoroughly understand, within these very twelve bases (*āyatana*), the characteristic of the object of non-conceptual activity regarding common characteristics.
This is called the eighth non-erroneous path capable of realizing all the unshared Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, within these very twelve bases (*āyatana*), one thoroughly understands the characteristics of the supramundane dharmas that possess common characteristics as objects of experience.
This is called the ninth non-erroneous path that can realize all the unshared Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, within these twelve bases (*āyatana*),
one is able to thoroughly and completely know the characteristics of the cause for the purification of common characteristics.
This is called the tenth non-erroneous path capable of realizing all the unshared Buddha-dharmas.
Thus are the four kinds of observations regarding common characteristics.
Furthermore, it should be known that by means of eight excellences, each subsequent stage of abiding becomes increasingly superior.
First, the excellence of intention;
second, the excellence of mental purity;
third, the excellence of compassion.
Fourth, the excellence of the perfections;
fifth, the excellence of maturing sentient beings;
sixth, the excellence of seeing all Buddhas, approaching them, serving them, and making offerings to them.
Seventh, the excellence of birth;
eighth, the excellence of supernormal powers.
Furthermore, there are five aspects of ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
First, the characteristic of being free from names and expressions;
second, the characteristic of non-duality;
third, the characteristic of transcending the sphere of discursive thought.
Fourth, it transcends the characteristics of identity and difference regarding all phenomena.
Fifth, it is the characteristic of a single flavor throughout everything.
This ultimate truth is free from the characteristics of names and expressions.
And regarding the absence of dual characteristics,
one should know that it is as stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*,
where the Bodhisattva Yathāruta-paripṛcchaka asks the Bodhisattva Gambhīrārthasamdhinirmocana:
O Son of the Supreme Victor,
when it is said that "all phenomena are non-dual" and "all phenomena are non-dual," what are these "all phenomena"?
"What is non-duality?
The Bodhisattva Gambhīrārthasamdhinirmocana replied to the Bodhisattva Yoniśaḥparipṛcchaka, saying:
Good son, all phenomena are briefly of two kinds: first, the conditioned;
second, the unconditioned.
The second is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Within this, the conditioned is neither conditioned nor unconditioned;
the unconditioned is likewise neither unconditioned nor conditioned.
O Son of the Supreme Victor,
how is it that the conditioned is neither conditioned nor unconditioned,
and the unconditioned is likewise neither unconditioned nor conditioned?
"Good son, that which is called 'conditioned' is merely a provisional designation established by our Original Teacher."
If it is a provisionally established phrase by the Teacher,
it is that which is expressed by words accumulated through pervasive conceptualization.
If it is that which is expressed by words accumulated through pervasive conceptualization, [it is so].
That is to say, because it is ultimately not established as real by the various conceptual verbal expressions,
it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Good son, that which is called "unconditioned" likewise falls within the realm of verbal expression.
Even if one were to set aside the conditioned and the unconditioned,
whatever little might be said would have the same characteristic; yet,
it is not the case that there is something said without a basis in reality.
What is the objective referent?
It is that which the noble ones, by means of noble wisdom and noble vision, realize as perfectly awakened, because it is free from verbal expression.
Regarding this very ineffable nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*),
one establishes provisional names and concepts for the purpose of causing others to realize perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*).
This is called the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Son of good family,
as for what is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*):
This is also a term provisionally established by the Original Teacher.
If it is a term provisionally established by the Original Teacher,
it is that which is expressed through words gathered from pervasive conceptualization.
If it is that which is expressed by words accumulated through pervasive conceptualization,
then it is ultimately expressed by various pervasive conceptualizations;
because it is not established as real, it is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Good son, that which is called "conditioned" also falls within the realm of verbal expression.
Even if one were to set aside the unconditioned and the conditioned,
whatever little is spoken would likewise have such a characteristic; yet,
it is not the case that there is something spoken without a basis in reality.
What is the objective referent?
It is that which the noble ones, by means of noble wisdom and noble vision, realize as perfectly awakened, because it is free from verbal expression.
Regarding this very ineffable nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*),
one provisionally establishes names and concepts for the purpose of causing others to realize perfect awakening.
It is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
O Son of the Most Victorious One,
how is it that these various noble ones [perceive] this matter?
Because it is free from names and expressions through noble wisdom and noble vision,
one realizes perfect awakening; that is,
with respect to this very ineffable nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
