it is just as those aggregates have mutually distinct characteristics.

If the various aspects of dependent origination, the nutriments, the truths, the elements, the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the branches of the path were mutually distinct in their characteristics, and if the suchness, the ultimate reality,
and the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) of all dharmas were likewise distinct in their characteristics, [then...]
If this were so, then true suchness, the ultimate reality,
and the nature of the selflessness of phenomena would also have causes and would likewise be produced from causes.
If it arises from causes,
it must be conditioned; if it is conditioned,
[it must be subject to cessation].
It would not then be the ultimate truth;
if it were not the ultimate truth,
one would have to seek another ultimate truth beyond it.
Subhūti, because of this suchness, the ultimate truth, and the selflessness of phenomena,
it is not said to have a cause.
It is not produced by causes,
nor is it conditioned;
it is the ultimate truth, and having attained this ultimate truth, one no longer seeks another ultimate truth.
Only at all times, and at every single moment,
does a Tathāgata appear in the world.
Even if he does not appear in the world,
the dharma-nature of all phenomena remains established,
and the dharma-realm remains abiding.
Therefore, Subhūti, by this principle,
you should know that the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) has the characteristic of being of one single flavor throughout all things, Subhūti.
For example, within various and manifold forms of diverse characteristics,
space is without characteristic and without conceptual differentiation.
It is without alteration,
a single flavor throughout all things;
such is the ultimate truth within all phenomena that possess diverse natures and diverse characteristics.
It should be known that the characteristic of being of one single taste throughout all things is likewise so. At that time,
the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, [spoke as follows].
And he spoke in verse:
"This pervasive, single-taste characteristic— The ultimate truth, which all Buddhas declare to be without distinction;
If one were to make conceptual distinctions regarding it, That person is certainly deluded and relies on overweening pride."
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 75.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 76.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.

Within the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, this is the fifth [section] of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*. Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of mind (*citta*), mentation (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), they should be understood as they are presented in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*.
The Bodhisattva Viśālamati questioned the Buddha, saying:
"As the Blessed One has spoken of a bodhisattva who is skilled in the secrets of mind, thought, and consciousness—
what is meant by 'a bodhisattva who is skilled in the secrets of mind, thought, and consciousness'?"
To what extent is one called a bodhisattva skilled in the secrets of mind, mentation, and consciousness?
To what extent does the Tathāgata designate one as a bodhisattva skilled in the secrets of mind, mentation, and consciousness?
Having spoken these words,
at that time the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vighuṣṭamati, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent, Vighuṣṭamati!
You are now able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such a profound meaning.
You now desire to bring benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings;
out of compassion for the world, including the devas, humans, asuras, and others,
you act so that they may attain meaningful profit and well-being.
Having raised this question,
you should listen attentively.
I shall explain for you the secret meaning of mind, thought, and consciousness.
Bhadramati, you should know that within the cycle of birth and death in the six realms of existence,
various sentient beings fall among the various classes of sentient beings.
Some are born from eggs,
some are born from wombs,
and some are born from moisture.
Or, in the case of miraculous birth,
the body parts arise; therein,
at the very beginning, the mind-consciousness containing all seeds matures.
Successively combining and uniting,
they increase and expand,
based upon the two types of appropriation.
First, the appropriation of the material sense-faculties and their bases;
second, the appropriation of the habitual tendencies of conceptual proliferation consisting of signs, names, discriminations, and verbal expressions.
Within the realm of form, both types of appropriation are present.
In the formless realm, these two types are not present.
Furthermore, O Vipaśyanā-mati,
this consciousness is also called the ādāna-vijñāna.
Why is this? Because this consciousness follows and sustains the body,
it is also called the ālayavijñāna.
Why is this? Because this consciousness appropriates, stores, and conceals itself within the body, sharing its welfare and peril;
for this reason, it is also called "mind" (citta).
Why is this? Because by means of this consciousness, form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and so forth are accumulated and nourished.
Furthermore, O Vast Wisdom (Bhadramati):
Based upon and established by the ādāna-vijñāna,
the six groups of consciousness arise.
This refers to eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-,
and mind-consciousness. Among these,
consciousness arises with the eye and visible forms as conditions to produce eye-consciousness.
There arises a conceptualizing mental consciousness that operates simultaneously with, in conjunction with, and at the same time as and regarding the same object as the visual consciousness.
There is also consciousness;
namely, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses arise conditioned by the ear, nose, tongue, and body, as well as by sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
Broad Wisdom, there arises a conceptualizing mental consciousness that operates simultaneously with, in accordance with, at the same time as, and regarding the same object as the ear-,
nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses. Broad Wisdom, if at that time a single visual consciousness arises...
At that very time, there is only a single conceptual mental consciousness (manovijñāna) that functions with the same object as the visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna).
If, at that time, two, three, four, or five groups of consciousnesses (vijñānakāya) function, [the same applies].
At that very time, O Broad Wisdom, there is only a single conceptual mental consciousness that functions with the same objective range as the five groups of sensory consciousnesses.
It is like a great torrent of water:
if the conditions for the arising of a single wave appear,
only that one wave arises.
If the conditions for the arising of two or many waves manifest,
then many waves will turn;
yet this turbulent water flows as its own kind constantly, without interruption or exhaustion.
Furthermore, it is like the surface of a well-polished mirror:
if the conditions for the arising of a single reflection appear before it,
only that one reflection arises.
If the conditions for the arising of two or many reflections are present,
many reflections will appear;
yet it is not the case that this mirror surface undergoes transformation to become those reflections.
Furthermore, no exhaustion of its appropriation can be found.
Thus, O Vast Intelligence,
by relying upon the ādāna-vijñāna, which is like a violent torrent—
For the sake of establishment:
if at that time the conditions for the arising of a single visual consciousness are present,
then at that very moment, a single visual consciousness arises.
Vipula-mati, if at that time the conditions for the arising of even the five groups of consciousness are present,
then at that very moment the five groups of consciousness proceed.
In this way, although the bodhisattva relies upon the knowledge of the abiding of phenomena (dharmasthitijñāna) for its establishment,
they are skillful regarding the secrets of mind, thought, and consciousness (cittamanovijñāna).
However, the Tathāgatas do not establish this [definition] uniformly.
For the sake of Bodhisattvas who are skillful regarding all the secrets of mind, mentation, and consciousness, O Broad Wisdom (Vipula-mati),
[they teach as follows].
If bodhisattvas, within themselves individually, do not see the *ādāna* as it truly is,
do not see the *ādānavijñāna*,
and do not see the *ālaya*.
One does not perceive the ālayavijñāna;
one does not perceive the accumulation [of seeds];
one does not perceive the mind.
One does not perceive the eye, forms, or eye-consciousness;
one does not perceive the ear, sounds, or ear-consciousness;
one does not perceive the nose, odors, or nose-consciousness.
One does not perceive the tongue, tastes, or tongue-consciousness;
one does not perceive the body, tangibles, or body-consciousness;
one does not perceive the mind, mental objects, or mind-consciousness.
This is called a bodhisattva skilled in the ultimate;
the Tathāgata designates such a person as a bodhisattva skilled in the ultimate,
O Viśālamati.
To this extent, one is called a bodhisattva skilled in all the secrets of mind, mentation, and consciousness.
It is to this extent that the Tathāgata designates one as a bodhisattva skilled in all the secrets of mind, mentation, and consciousness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The ādāna-vijñāna is profound and subtle; Containing all seeds like a turbulent stream, I do not reveal it to the foolish and ignorant, Fearing they would conceptually grasp it as a self."
Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of all phenomena,
one should know them as they are explained in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*,
where the Bodhisattva Guṇākara questioned the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavān, as the Bhagavān has spoken of a bodhisattva who is skilled in the characteristics of all phenomena—
what is meant by a 'bodhisattva who is skilled in the characteristics of all phenomena'?"
To what extent is one called a bodhisattva skilled in the characteristics of all phenomena?
To what extent does the Tathāgata designate one as a bodhisattva skilled in the characteristics of all phenomena?
When he had spoken these words,
the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Guṇākara, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent, Guṇamati!
That you are now able to question the Tathāgata regarding such a profound meaning.
You now desire to bring benefit, welfare, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings;
out of compassion for the world, including the devas, humans, and asuras,
you act so that they may attain meaningful benefit and peace.
Having raised this question,
you should listen attentively;
I shall explain the characteristics of all phenomena for you.
The characteristics of all phenomena are, in brief, of three kinds.
What are these three?
First, the characteristic of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Second is the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*);
third is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*).
What is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena?
This refers to the provisional designation of names for all phenomena, including their essential natures and specific distinctions,
even to the extent of enabling the arising of conventional discourse. What,
then, is the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena?
That is to say, all phenomena have a nature of dependent origination:
because this exists, that exists;
because this arises, that arises.
That is to say: ignorance conditions volitional formations, and so on, until the gathering of this entire great mass of suffering.
What is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena?
It refers to the true suchness (*tathatā*) that is equal in all phenomena.
It is because of the courageous diligence of the assembly of bodhisattvas toward this true suchness that it serves as the causal condition.
Because of the causal conditions of appropriate mental attention and non-erroneous reflection.
One is then able to achieve thorough penetration;
through this penetration, one gradually cultivates and accumulates [merit and wisdom] until,
at the stage of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, one realizes full perfection.
Furthermore, Guṇamati,
just as the defect of cataracts exists within the eyes of a person with blurred vision,
you should know that the characteristic of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is likewise.
It is like a person with cataracts who perceives various manifestations of the cataract,
such as hair-tufts, circles, bees, flies, or sesame seeds,
or else the distinct appearances of blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth, which manifest before them.
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) should be understood in the same way:
just as a person with clear vision, being free from the affliction of cataracts in the eyes,
perceives the unconfused objects that are the natural range of those clear eyes.
It should be understood that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is likewise.
Furthermore, Guṇākara,
it is like a pure crystal gem.
If it is combined with blue dye,
it resembles the image of an indranīla or mahānīla mani-jewel;
this is due to the erroneous grasping of it as an indranīla or mahānīla mani-jewel.
It deludes sentient beings;
if it comes into contact with red dye,
it appears like an agate mani-jewel.
Due to their false grasping at the amber maṇi jewel,
they delude sentient beings;
if it comes into contact with green dye, [it appears as such].
It is like the image of a *māṇikya* jewel from Murala;
because of the false grasping of it as a *māṇikya* jewel from Murala,
it deludes sentient beings.
If it is combined with a yellow dye,
it resembles a golden image,
because one falsely apprehends it as being a genuine golden image.
They delude sentient beings.
Thus, O Guṇamūla,
it is like the appearance of colors upon a pure crystal that correspond to those very colors.
It should be understood that the linguistic habit-energies of the imagined nature upon the dependent nature are likewise so;
they are like the indranīla and mahānīla [gems] appearing upon a pure crystal.
One should know that the false attachments to amber, Māṇikya, gold, and so forth,
as well as the attachment to the imagined nature upon the dependent nature,
are likewise to be understood in this same way.
Just as that pure crystal gem,
so too should the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) be understood.
Just as the characteristics of sapphire, deep blue gem,
amber, musāragalva, and pure gold [are seen] upon that pure crystal at all times.
At all times and in every way,
there is no reality; it is the nature of being without intrinsic nature.
That is to say, upon the dependent nature (paratantra-lakṣaṇa),
by means of the imagined nature (parikalpita-lakṣaṇa), at all times and for all eternity.
There is no reality; there is no nature of intrinsic existence.
One should know that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is likewise.
Furthermore, Guṇamati,
because the association of characteristics and names serves as a condition,
the thoroughly imagined nature can be cognized.
Because the dependent nature is apprehended by taking the grasping at the imagined nature upon the dependent nature as its condition,
the dependent nature can be cognized;
because [the dependent nature] is apprehended by taking the absence of grasping at the imagined nature upon the dependent nature as its condition.
The perfected nature can be understood.
Furthermore, Guṇākara,
if bodhisattvas, with respect to the dependent nature of all phenomena...
By knowing the thoroughly imagined nature as it truly is,
one is able to know all signless phenomena as they truly are.
If bodhisattvas know the dependent nature as it truly is...
One is then able to understand, as they truly are, all phenomena characterized by affliction.
If bodhisattvas understand, as it truly is, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*),
they are then able to understand, as they truly are, all phenomena characterized by purification.
Furthermore, Guṇamati,
if bodhisattvas are able to understand, as it truly is, the dharma of signlessness upon the other-dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), [they will realize suchness].
One is then able to eliminate phenomena characterized by affliction;
if one can eliminate phenomena characterized by affliction,
one is then able to realize phenomena characterized by purity.
In this way, Guṇamati,
by means of the bodhisattvas’ accurate understanding of the thoroughly imagined nature and the dependent nature, [they realize the perfected nature].
Because it is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*),
one understands, as they truly are, all signless phenomena (*animitta-dharma*) and phenomena characterized by affliction (*saṃkleśa-lakṣaṇa-dharma*).
Because one understands phenomena characterized by purity as they truly are— namely, as being signless—
one eradicates all phenomena characterized by defilement.
Because they have severed all phenomena characterized by defilement,
they realize all phenomena characterized by purity;
up to this point, one is called a bodhisattva skilled in the characteristics of all phenomena.
To this extent, the Tathāgata designates one as a bodhisattva who is skillful regarding the characteristics of all phenomena.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke in verse:
If one does not understand the dharma of signlessness, one cannot sever the dharmas characterized by affliction;
because one does not sever the dharmas characterized by affliction, one fails to realize the dharma of subtle and pure signs.
Failing to contemplate the manifold faults of conditioned formations, the fault of negligence harms sentient beings.
Those who dwell in indolence amidst phenomena that are subject to movement are pitiable, for they suffer ruin and destruction.
Furthermore, one should know that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
as explained in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*.
The Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,"
Once, while staying alone in seclusion,
such a reflection arose in my mind:
"The Blessed One has previously taught the specific characteristics of all the aggregates through immeasurable approaches."
The characteristic of arising,
the characteristic of cessation,
and their permanent abandonment.
Full comprehension.
As it was taught regarding the aggregates,
so it is with the sense bases, dependent origination, and the nutriments.
Through immeasurable gateways, he has previously taught the specific characteristics of all truths,
as well as their thorough knowledge and permanent abandonment.
Having realized and cultivated them,
he has previously explained the specific characteristics of all the elements through immeasurable gateways.
The various natures of the elements (*dhātu*) are not of a single nature; they are to be permanently abandoned through thorough knowledge.
By means of immeasurable gateways, the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) have been previously taught.
It consists of the remedies and that which is to be remedied;
and through cultivation, it causes what has not yet arisen to arise,
and once arisen, it causes it to remain firm, to be not forgotten, and to be further cultivated, increased, and expanded.
As it was taught regarding the foundations of mindfulness,
the right efforts, the bases of psychic power,
the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment.
It is likewise so.
Through immeasurable gateways, he has previously explained the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the Noble Eightfold Path,
as well as that which is to be remedied and its remedy.
Furthermore, through cultivation, that which has not yet arisen is brought into being;
once arisen, it is made firm, maintained without forgetfulness, and repeatedly practiced so as to increase, expand, and become vast.
Yet, World-Honored One, you have further taught that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.
Without arising and without ceasing,
originally quiescent,
and by nature in nirvāṇa.
I do not yet understand,
Blessed One, by what underlying intention you have spoken thus:
that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.
Without arising and without ceasing,
originally quiescent,
and by nature in nirvana.
I now inquire of the Tathāgata regarding this meaning.
I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion,
will explain and clarify how all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.
The profound intent regarding all phenomena being without arising or ceasing,
primordially quiescent, and by nature in a state of nirvāṇa.
When he had spoken these words,
the World-Honored One then addressed the Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Paramārthasamudgata,
what you have investigated is most consistent with reason.
Excellent, excellent!
"Good son,
you are now able to question the Tathāgata regarding such a profound meaning.
You do so now because you desire to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings."
Out of compassion for the world, including the devas, humans, asuras, and others,
and for the sake of enabling them to attain benefit, welfare, and happiness,
he has posed this question.
Listen attentively;
I shall explain for you that all phenomena as they have been taught are devoid of intrinsic nature, neither arising nor ceasing,
and are primordially quiescent.
Regarding the underlying intention behind the statement that all things are by nature in nirvāṇa,
Paramārthasaṃudgata,
you should know that I have based this upon the three kinds of lack of intrinsic nature.
With intentional meaning,
it is said that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; that is to say,
they possess the nature of being without intrinsic nature in terms of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
The nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in arising,
and the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in the ultimate truth,
son of good family.
What is the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in the characteristics of all phenomena?
It refers to the imagined characteristic of all phenomena. Why is this so?
This is established as a characteristic by way of conventional designation,
not established as a characteristic by way of its own-characteristic;
therefore, it is called the naturelessness of characteristics.
What is the nature of the lack of self-nature in the arising of all phenomena?
It refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena. Why is this so?
This exists by virtue of the power of other-dependent conditions and does not exist spontaneously; therefore,
it is called the "naturelessness of arising."
What is the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena?
It refers to the fact that all phenomena are said to have a lack of intrinsic nature by virtue of their lack of intrinsic nature in terms of production.
Furthermore, dependently originated phenomena are also called the "ultimate nature of lack of intrinsic existence. Why is this?
Because among all phenomena, these are the objects of focus for purification.
I demonstrate that as the nature of ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Because the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) is not the objective domain of purification,
it is therefore also called the nature of ultimate lack of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, there are dharmas that possess the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*),
which is also called the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*). Why is this?
The dharma-nature of selflessness in all phenomena is called the ultimate truth;
it is also termed the nature of lack of intrinsic existence (*niḥsvabhāvatā*),
because these phenomena constitute the ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*).
Because it is revealed by the nature of the absence of intrinsic nature,
for this reason it is called the ultimate nature of the absence of intrinsic nature.
Son of good family.
One should know that the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in characteristics is likewise like a flower in the sky.
It is like a magical illusion.
One should know that the nature of the lack of self-nature in arising is likewise so;
one should know that the partial ultimate nature of the lack of self-nature is likewise so.
Just as space is manifested solely by the absence of intrinsic nature in all forms and pervades all places,
so too should one understand the single aspect of the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature.
Because it is manifested by the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and because it pervades all things,
O son of noble family.
"Paramārthasamudgata, it is based on these three kinds of naturelessness that I have spoken with intentional meaning (saṃdhyābhāṣya) that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature."
You should know that it is based on the nature of the lack of self-nature in characteristics (*lakṣaṇaniḥsvabhāvatā*) that I,
with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*), have declared that all phenomena are without arising and without cessation,
and are quiescent from the very beginning.
Nirvana by its very nature. Why is this?
If a phenomenon lacks any self-characteristic whatsoever, then it has no arising.
If there is no arising, then there is no ceasing.
If there is neither arising nor ceasing, then it is primordially quiescent.
If it is primordially quiescent, then it is by nature in nirvāṇa.
Because within that [middle way] there is not even the slightest thing that could further be brought to parinirvāṇa,

I have therefore spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*), based on the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*), that all phenomena are neither produced nor extinguished.
"O son of good family, [the mind] is originally quiescent and by nature in nirvāṇa. I,
too, teach according to the nature of selflessness as it is manifested through the Dharma."
With reference to the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature, it was intended that all phenomena are unarisen and unceasing,
primordially quiescent,
and by nature in a state of nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature is revealed by the selflessness of phenomena.
At all times, at all seasons,
the dharma-nature of all phenomena.
Abiding in the unconditioned,
because it is dissociated from all defilements, at all times.
Because the dharma-nature of all phenomena abides at all times, it is unconditioned;
because it is unconditioned, [it is eternal].
It is without arising and without cessation,
for it is dissociated from all defilements;
it is quiescent from the very beginning.
Because it is by nature in a state of nirvāṇa, I have spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhyābhāṣya*) regarding the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*),
which is revealed through the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), saying that all dharmas are neither produced nor extinguished.
"Originally quiescent and by nature in nirvana.
Furthermore, Paramārthasamudgata,"
It is not because the various classes of sentient beings within the realm of sentient beings perceive the thoroughly imagined nature as being their own intrinsic nature.

Nor is it because I establish the three kinds of naturelessness by viewing the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) as having distinct natures of their own.

However, it is because sentient beings superimpose the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) upon the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) and the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
I establish three kinds of naturelessness:
by way of the characteristic of the imagined nature,
those sentient beings [perceive] the dependent nature.
And within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*),
conventional expressions arise accordingly;
just as they arise accordingly, so do those conventional expressions.
In this way, and by this very process, it is due to the mind being permeated by verbal expression,
or due to the subsequent conceptualization of verbal expression,
or due to the latent tendencies of verbal expression.
Within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*),
one clings to the characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
In whatever way one clings,
in that very same way [one clings] to the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) and the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
By clinging to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*),
one gives rise to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) in future lives through these causes and conditions.
Due to these causes and conditions,
one is either defiled by the defilement of afflictions or defiled by the defilement of karma.
Or, being defiled by the defilements of birth,
they gallop for a long time and wander for a long time within saṃsāra.
Without rest, they may be in the hells or among the animals.
Some are among the hungry ghosts;
some are in the heavens;
some are among the asuras.
Or they may be among human beings,
undergoing various sufferings and afflictions.
Furthermore, Paramārthasamudgata:
If sentient beings, from the very beginning,
have not planted roots of virtue, have not purified their obscurations,
and have not matured their mental continuums.
They have not extensively cultivated resolute conviction,
nor have they been able to accumulate the two types of provisions— merit and wisdom.
For their sake, I [act].
Based on the nature of the lack of intrinsic existence in terms of arising,
he teaches all phenomena; having heard this,
they are able [to understand] regarding all conditioned phenomena that arise dependently.
Having partially understood that all things are impermanent, non-eternal,
unstable, and subject to change and decay,
one develops a sense of dread toward all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
They give rise to profound weariness and aversion;
their minds become fearful.
Having developed deep weariness and aversion, they restrain all evil.
One is able to refrain from committing unwholesome dharmas and is able to diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas;
this is because one practices the causes of virtue.
Those who have not yet planted roots of goodness can plant them;
those whose obscurations have not yet been purified can be made pure;
and those whose mental continuums have not yet matured can be brought to maturity.
By virtue of these causes and conditions,
one extensively cultivates resolute conviction and also extensively accumulates the two kinds of provisions: merit and wisdom.
Although they thus plant various roots of goodness and even accumulate the two kinds of provisions— merit and wisdom—
they [remain] within the nature of non-substantiality in arising.

the Bodhisattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One..."
Upon what do Bodhisattvas rely and abide when they cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā within the Mahāyāna?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying:
"Good son, you should know that for a bodhisattva,
the provisional designation of dharmas and the non-abandonment of the vow for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment serve as the basis and the support."
Within the Mahāyāna, one cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā.
As the Blessed One has taught, there are four kinds of objective referents (*ālambana-vastu*):
first, the objective referent that is a conceptualized image (*savikalpa-pratibimba*).
Second, the objective referent that is the non-conceptual image;
third, the objective referent that is the limit of phenomena;
fourth, the objective referent that is the accomplishment of what was to be done.
Among these four, how many are objects of focus for śamatha?
How many are objects of focus for vipaśyanā?
And how many are objects of focus for both?
Good son, the first is the objective referent of śamatha,
namely, the non-conceptual image.
First is the object-base of vipaśyanā,
namely, the conceptual image.
Second is the object-base common to both [śamatha and vipaśyanā].
That is to say, the limit of phenomena and the accomplishment of what is to be done,
World-Honored One.
How does a bodhisattva, relying on these four kinds of objects for śamatha and vipaśyanā,
seek śamatha and become skilled in vipaśyanā?
"Good son, just as I have provisionally established the teachings for all bodhisattvas—
namely, the sūtras and the geyas."
Prophecies, chanted verses,
self-explanations of causes and conditions,
parables, and past events.
Regarding the Jātaka, Vaipulya,
Adbhutadharma, and Upadeśa,
the bodhisattva listens well and receives them well.
Having well mastered [the teachings], having well investigated with the mind, and having well penetrated through insight,
one dwells alone in a secluded place regarding those dharmas as they have been well reflected upon.
He attends to it with mental engagement;
furthermore, he attends with mental engagement to the very mind that is performing this contemplation,
within the internal continuity of the mind.
Because one dwells extensively in such right practice,
there arises physical pliancy and mental pliancy;
this is called śamatha.
In this way, the bodhisattva is able to seek śamatha.
By relying on the physical and mental pliancy (praśrabdhi) thus attained,
he [perceives] the internal images that are the objects of samādhi regarding those dharmas as they have been well-considered.
Observing the mental aspect of resolve and relinquishment,
one is able to correctly discern and thoroughly investigate the objects of knowledge within the images of such samādhi.
When one thoroughly investigates and thoroughly examines with patience, delight, wisdom, vision,
and contemplation, this is called vipaśyanā.
"In this way, World-Honored One, a bodhisattva is skilled in vipaśyanā.
If a bodhisattva takes the mind as an object and internally contemplates the mind,"
Up until one has attained physical and mental pliancy, what should all such acts of attention be called?
Good son, [they are called "mundane"].
This is not the mental engagement of śamatha;
rather, it is the mental engagement associated with the resolute conviction that accords with śamatha.
Blessed One, as long as bodhisattvas have not yet attained physical and mental pliancy...
When one attends to the mental image that is the object of internal samādhi regarding all those phenomena as they have been contemplated,
what should this form of attention be called?
"Good son, it is not the mental engagement of vipaśyanā itself; rather,
it is the mental engagement associated with the resolute conviction that accords with vipaśyanā."
"Bhagavān,
should it be said that the path of śamatha and the path of vipaśyanā are different?"
One should say they are not different.
Son of good family,
one should say they are neither different nor non-different.
Why is it not different?
Because it takes as its object the mind that is the focal object of vipaśyanā.
Why is it not non-different?
"Because the image with conceptual differentiation is not the object of focus,
O Bhagavan.
These are the images that are the domain of the samādhis of all vipaśyanā."
Should one say that it is different from this mind,
or should one say it is not different?
Son of good family, one should say it is not different.
Why is this? Because those images are nothing but consciousness. Noble son!
"I say that the object of consciousness is manifested solely by consciousness itself.
World-Honored One,
if that image which is the object of activity..."
If it were not different from this mind,
how could this mind see this very mind?
Good son, [it is as follows:]...
In this, there is not even the slightest dharma that can see another dharma;
rather, when this very mind arises in such a manner,
an image corresponding to it appears.
Good son, it is like relying on the surface of a well-polished, pure mirror: with the object as a condition, one sees the original object itself,
yet thinks, "I am now seeing a reflection."
Furthermore, it is asserted that when this mind arises, there appears a reflected image that seems to exist as something distinct from its objective basis.
In this way, although it is similar [to the object],
it appears to be different.
The image that appears as the object of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Blessed One,
if sentient beings, abiding in their own nature, have images that are the objects of the mind directed toward forms and so forth;
"Is that [nature] not also non-different from this mind?
Good son, it is indeed non-different."
However, O Blessed One, due to their inverted cognition, foolish worldlings are unable to know images as they truly are— namely, that they are mere consciousness—
and thus they form inverted understandings.
"In what sense should it be said that a bodhisattva practices vipaśyanā exclusively?
Son of good family,
it is when they apply continuous attention and contemplate only the characteristics of the mind."
“World-Honored One,
to what extent may it be said that a bodhisattva practices śamatha exclusively?
“Good son,” [the Buddha replied].
If one applies attention continuously,
venerable sir, one contemplates only the immediately preceding mind.
In what sense, then, should one say that a bodhisattva’s śamatha and vipaśyanā are conjoined and proceed together?
Son of good family,
it is when one correctly contemplates one-pointedness of mind.
“World-Honored One,
what is the characteristic of the mind?
“Good son,” [the Buddha replied].
It refers, Blessed One, to the conceptual image that is the object of samādhi and the focal point of vipaśyanā.
What is the immediate mind? Noble son,
it refers to the mind that takes that image as its object.
Regarding the object of śamatha,
Blessed One,
what is one-pointedness of mind?
Noble son, it means that one penetrates the understanding that the images which are the objects of meditative concentration (samādhi) are nothing but consciousness;
or, having already penetrated this.
Furthermore, reflecting on the nature of things, [he asked]:
"World-Honored One,
how many kinds of vipaśyanā are there?"
Good son, there are briefly three kinds:
first, vipaśyanā with signs.
Second is the vipaśyanā of seeking;
third is the vipaśyanā of investigation.
What is the vipaśyanā with signs?
It refers to vipaśyanā that consists of conceptual images which are the objects of samādhi through exclusive reflection.
What is vipaśyanā of investigation?
It is by means of wisdom.
Regarding all those various phenomena that have not yet been thoroughly understood,
one engages in the mental application of insight (*vipaśyanā*) for the sake of thorough understanding.
What is investigative insight?
That is to say, by means of wisdom,
within all those various phenomena that have already been thoroughly understood,
one engages in the mental attention of vipaśyanā for the sake of skillfully realizing ultimate liberation.
"Bhagavān,
how many kinds of śamatha are there?
Good son," [the Buddha replied].
One should know that, by virtue of following those immediate states of mind,
there are likewise three kinds within this context.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds,
namely the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
because each has its own type of śamatha.
Furthermore, there are four kinds;
that is to say, because within each of the four immeasurables— loving-kindness, compassion,
sympathetic joy, and equanimity— there exists a specific type of śamatha.
World-Honored One,
you have spoken of śamatha and vipaśyanā based on the Dharma,
and you have also spoken of śamatha and vipaśyanā not based on the Dharma.
What is meant by "relying on the Dharma," and what is meant by "not relying on the Dharma"?
Good son, listen.
If, in accordance with the characteristics of the teachings as received and contemplated,
one attains śamatha and vipaśyanā regarding their meaning,
this is called "relying on the Dharma."
If, without depending on the characteristics of any phenomena that have been received or contemplated,
one relies solely upon the instructions and guidance of others and thereby attains śamatha and vipaśyanā regarding their meaning.
That is to say, it refers to contemplating the bluish discoloration and the putrefaction [of corpses],
or that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent,
or that all conditioned phenomena are suffering.
Alternatively, all phenomena are entirely without self;
or again, nirvāṇa is ultimately quiescent.
Such categories as these are termed śamatha and vipaśyanā that do not rely on phenomena.
Because they attain śamatha and vipaśyanā by relying on the Dharma,
I designate those bodhisattvas who practice in accordance with the Dharma as being of sharp faculties.
Because they attain śamatha and vipaśyanā without relying on the Dharma...
“World-Honored One, I designate the bodhisattva who follows by faith as one of dull faculties.”
As it has been taught regarding śamatha and vipaśyanā that take individual phenomena as their object,
it has also been taught regarding śamatha and vipaśyanā that take comprehensive phenomena as their object.
What is meant by śamatha and vipaśyanā that take individual phenomena as their object?
What, furthermore, is called śamatha and vipaśyanā that take general dharmas as their object?
Noble son, it is when bodhisattvas take individual dharmas, such as the sūtras and so forth, as their objects.
To cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā with respect to the dharmas as they have been received and reflected upon is called śamatha and vipaśyanā based on individual dharmas.
If bodhisattvas take all dharmas, such as the various sūtras, and,
having gathered them into a single mass, a single accumulation, a single portion, and a single collection,
direct their attention toward and contemplate them.
All these phenomena accord with suchness,
tend toward suchness,
and lead into suchness.
It accords with enlightenment,
accords with nirvana,
and accords with the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti).
And those who are tending toward it,
or those who are about to enter it—
in all these cases, these dharmas are proclaimed as immeasurable and innumerable wholesome dharmas.
Reflecting in this way, one cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā;
this is called śamatha and vipaśyanā that take general dharmas as their object,
World-Honored One.
As it is said, there is śamatha and vipaśyanā that take minor general dharmas as their object;
furthermore, there is śamatha and vipaśyanā that take major general dharmas as their object;
and again, there is śamatha and vipaśyanā that take immeasurable general dharmas as their object.
What is called śamatha and vipaśyanā that take the minor general dharma as their object?
What is called śamatha and vipaśyanā that take the major general dharma as their object?
What, furthermore, is called śamatha and vipaśyanā that take as their object the total dharmas of the immeasurable?
Son of good family,
it is when one takes as objects the individual sūtras, up to the individual treatises on the meaning [of the Dharma].
One should know that when one attends to [the object] as a single mass and so forth,
this is called śamatha and vipaśyanā based on small, composite dharmas.
If one takes as an object the dharmas such as the sūtras— up to those that have been received and reflected upon—
and attends to them by way of forming them into a single mass and so forth.
It is not by way of distinct objects;
one should know that this is called śamatha and vipaśyanā directed toward the great universal dharma.
If it takes as its object the immeasurable teachings of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, [it is likewise so called].
The immeasurable phrases and syllables of the Dharma are illuminated and realized by successive stages of immeasurable wisdom,
forming a single mass and so forth.
One attends to and contemplates [this],
not taking as an object even that which is experienced or contemplated;
it should be known that this is called śamatha and vipaśyanā based on immeasurable total dharmas.
“World-Honored One,
to what extent is a bodhisattva said to have attained śamatha and vipaśyanā regarding the universal dharmas as objects?
“Good son,” [the Buddha replied].
It should be known that attainment occurs by virtue of five conditions. First,
at the time of contemplation, one moment by moment dissolves all bases of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*).
Second, being free from various conceptualizations, one experiences the joy of the Dharma;
third, one understands the immeasurable light of the Dharma, which is characterized by non-differentiation throughout the ten directions;
fourth, that which is to be accomplished is brought to fulfillment.
The fifth is the manifestation of the aspect of non-conceptualization associated with the pure portion,
for the sake of bringing the dharmakāya to full completion.
It embraces the causes for progressively attaining ever more excellent and sublime states.
World-Honored One,
this refers to śamatha and vipaśyanā based on the general dharma.
One should know from what this is called "thorough penetration" and from what it is called "attainment. Good son:
From the first stage, the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), it is called "thorough penetration";
from the third stage, the Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), it is called "attainment.
O son of good family!
A bodhisattva who is a beginner should also train in this by following these mental orientations (*manasikāra*);
although they may not yet be praiseworthy,
they must not become lax or negligent.
World-Honored One,
regarding these śamatha and vipaśyanā, what is called the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra?
What is called the samādhi without vitarka and with only vicāra?
What is called the concentration without applied thought and sustained thought?
Noble son, it is [the state] regarding the characteristics of the phenomena of applied and sustained thought as they have been grasped.
If there is a coarse and manifest experiencing and observation of all śamatha and vipaśyanā,
this is called the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra. If,
regarding those signs, there is no coarse and manifest experiencing and observation, [this is the samādhi without vitarka but with vicāra].
When there is a subtle mindfulness of that light, which experiences and examines all śamatha and vipaśyanā,
this is called the samādhi with no vitarka and only vicāra.
If, with respect to those very characteristics of all phenomena,
one entirely lacks mental engagement (*manasikāra*) while experiencing and observing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*,
this is called the concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitarko 'vicāraḥ samādhiḥ*).
Furthermore, son of good family,
if there is seeking through śamatha and vipaśyanā,
this is called the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra.
If there is śamatha and vipaśyanā involving investigation (vicāra),
this is called the samādhi with no vitarka and only vicāra.
If there is śamatha and vipaśyanā taking the total dharma as its object...
This is called the concentration without applied thought and sustained thought.
World-Honored One,
what is the sign of tranquility?
What is the characteristic of uplifting?
What is the characteristic of relinquishing?
Good son, [listen].
When the mind is agitated or when there is fear of agitation,
one should attend to phenomena that are loathsome and attend to the mind immediately following them.
This is called the sign of calming (*śamatha-nimitta*).
When the mind has sunk or when there is fear that it might sink,
one should direct the attention toward objects that are inspiring.
And the mental attention to that mental state is called the sign of uplifting.
If one is in a path of exclusively calm abiding (śamatha), [this is applied].
Whether during a path of exclusive observation or a path of combined application,
when one is defiled by these two secondary afflictions.
All mental engagements that are effortless,
as well as those mental engagements occurring within the spontaneous functioning of the mind,
are called the characteristic of equanimity (*upekṣā-nimitta*).
"Bhagavān,
regarding the bodhisattvas who cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā, they know the phenomena (dharma) and know the meaning (artha).
In what way do they know the phenomena?"
How does one know the meaning?
Noble son, those bodhisattvas understand phenomena through five aspects.
First, knowledge of names;
second, knowledge of phrases;
third, knowledge of syllables.
Fourth is knowing the particular;
fifth is knowing the general.
What is meant by "name"?
This refers to the conventional designation of the conceptualized intrinsic nature established among all phenomena, whether defiled or purified.
What is a "phrase" (*pada*)?
It refers to that which, within the very collection of names,
is able to conformingly proclaim the meanings of both defilement and purification,
serving as their support and establishment.
What is the phoneme (*vyañjana*)?
It refers to the syllables (*akṣara*) upon which those two depend.
How does one discern each of them individually?
That is to say, by means of attention directed toward individual objects of focus,
how does one come to understand them collectively?
It is by means of attention directed toward a collective object of focus.
All these taken together as one are called "knowledge of phenomena.
This is what is meant by a bodhisattva’s knowledge of phenomena.
Good son, those bodhisattvas understand the meaning through ten aspects.
First, knowing the nature of all that exists;
second, knowing the nature of things as they are;
third, knowing the object of the grasper.
Fourth is knowing the meaning of that which is apprehended;
fifth is knowing the meaning of establishment;
sixth is knowing the meaning of enjoyment.
Seventh, knowing the meaning of inversion;
eighth, knowing the meaning of non-inversion;
ninth, knowing the meaning of affliction.
Tenth is knowing the meaning of purity.
Son of good family,
as for the nature of the extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*):
The totality of all distinct categories and limits within all phenomena of affliction and purification is called "the nature of the full extent" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) therein;
for example, the five aggregates (*skandha*).
There are six internal bases and six external bases;
such is the case for all of them.
The nature as it is (*yathāvad-bhāvikatā*) refers to the suchness (*tathatā*) that exists within all phenomena, both defiled and purified;
this is what is meant here by "the nature as it is."
This further consists of seven kinds.
First is the *tathatā* of transmigration (*pravṛtti-tathatā*),
which refers to the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as being without priority or posteriority.
The second is the suchness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇatathatā*).
This refers to the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) regarding all dharmas.
Third is the suchness of discernment,
which means that all conditioned phenomena are of the nature of consciousness alone.
Fourth is the suchness of establishment.
That is to say, the noble truth of suffering which I have taught.
Fifth is the suchness of wrong practice;
that is to say, the noble truth of origination which I have taught.
Sixth is the suchness of purity,
which refers to the noble truth of cessation that I have taught.
Seventh is the suchness of correct practice.
That is to say, regarding the noble truths of the path which I have taught,
it should be understood that herein they are established by means of the suchness of cyclic existence and the suchness of the state of peace.
Because of the suchness of misconduct,
all sentient beings are equal and equal.
This is due to the suchness of characteristics and the suchness of discernment.
All phenomena are perfectly equal,
by virtue of the purity of suchness.
All śrāvaka enlightenment...
The enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha and unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment are equal and identical.
Due to the suchness of correct practice,
there is a wisdom that is perfectly equal and equanimous, which is embraced by śamatha and vipaśyanā and takes the totality of objects as its condition through hearing the true Dharma.
The object of the grasper refers to the five internal bases of form,
as well as the mind, mentation, consciousness, and all mental factors.
The object of apprehension refers to the six external bases;
furthermore, the subject of apprehension is also the object of apprehension.
The meaning of "establishment" refers to the vessel world (bhājanaloka),
within which all realms of sentient beings can be established.
That is to say, a single village district,
or a hundred village districts,
or a thousand village districts.
Whether it be a hundred or a thousand villages and fields,
or even the entire great earth extending to the limits of the ocean—
these hundreds, these thousands.
Whether these be hundreds or thousands,
or even a single Jambudvīpa,
or hundreds and thousands of such [worlds].
Whether these be hundreds or thousands,
or a single four-continent world system,
or hundreds and thousands of such systems.
Whether it be these hundreds of thousands,
or a single small thousand-world system,
or these hundreds and thousands [of such systems].
Whether it be these hundreds of thousands,
or a single medium chiliocosm,
or these hundreds and these thousands.
Whether these be hundreds of thousands,
or a single trichiliocosm, or hundreds and thousands of such worlds.
Whether it be these hundreds of thousands,
or these ten million (*koṭi*),
or these hundreds of ten millions.
These thousands of koṭis,
these hundreds of thousands of koṭis,
or these innumerable [koṭis].
This is countless hundreds;
this is countless thousands;
this is countless hundreds of thousands.
Or as many as the countless hundreds of thousands of atoms in a trichiliocosm,
throughout the immeasurable and innumerable world-systems in the ten directions.
The meaning of "enjoyment" refers to the fact that,
as I have taught, all classes of sentient beings exist for the sake of enjoyment.
The meaning of the perversion regarding the appropriation of requisites refers to the perversions of perception, mind,
and view that consist in conceiving the impermanent as permanent with respect to those very objects, such as the subject (the grāhaka) and so forth.
To reckon suffering as pleasure,
the impure as pure,
and the non-self as self constitutes a perversion of mind, a perversion of thought, and a perversion of view.
Regarding the meaning of non-erroneousness:
its characteristics should be understood as being the opposite of the aforementioned [erroneous states] and as their antidote.
Regarding the meaning of affliction:
This refers to the three kinds of defilements within the three realms:
first, the defilement of afflictions;
second, the defilement of karma.
Third is the defilement of birth.
Regarding the meaning of purification:
it refers to those factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) that constitute the dissociation from these three types of defilement.
Good son, you should know that these ten kinds [of meanings] universally encompass all meanings.
Furthermore, son of good family, those bodhisattvas,
by virtue of being able to understand five kinds of meanings...
This is called "knowing the meaning.
What are the five meanings?
First, the thorough knowledge of phenomena.
Second is the meaning of thorough knowledge;
third is thorough knowledge itself;
fourth is the attainment of the fruit of thorough knowledge.
Fifth, one awakens to this.
Good son, as for the matter of universal knowledge:
One should know that this refers to all that is to be known;
namely, either the aggregates (skandhas) or the internal sense bases (āyatanas).
Or the various external bases;
such is the meaning of thorough knowledge in all these cases.
Up to all categories of objects to be known through their various distinctions,
whether from the perspective of the conventional or the ultimate.
Either due to merit,
or due to fault,
or due to conditions.
Because they are subject to worldly conditions; because they possess the characteristics of arising, abiding, or decaying;
or because they are like a disease and so forth.
Either because of suffering, its origin, and so forth;
or because of true suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and so forth;
or because of expansion and abbreviation.
Either by way of categorical response,
or by way of analytical response,
or by way of response through counter-questioning.
Either because it is set aside as indeterminate,
or because it is cryptic,
or because it is explicit.
One should know that all such categories as these signify the meaning of "thorough knowledge" (parijñā).
As for the term "thorough knowledge":
It should be understood that this refers to the two preceding categories of factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*),
namely the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) or the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*),
which result in the attainment of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
This refers to the Vinaya that severs greed, hatred, and delusion;
the fruits of the ascetic life (śrāmaṇyaphala) through the eternal severance of all greed, hatred, and delusion;
and the śrāvakas and Tathāgatas whom I have taught.
One realizes all mundane and supramundane merits,
whether shared or unshared.
"One who realizes this" refers to one who,
regarding these very dharmas that have been realized,
extensively explains, proclaims, and reveals the wisdom of liberation to others.
"Good son,
you should know that these five meanings universally encompass all meanings.
Furthermore, good son..."
Those bodhisattvas are said to "know the meaning" because they are able to comprehend four kinds of meanings.
What are these four meanings?
First is the sense of mental appropriation;
second is the sense of experiencing;
third is the sense of discerning.
Fourth is the meaning of affliction and purification.
Son of good family, you should know that these four meanings universally encompass all meanings. Furthermore, son of good family:
Those bodhisattvas are said to "know the meaning" because they are able to comprehend three kinds of meanings.
What are these three meanings?
First, the meaning of the words;
second, the meaning of the meaning;
third, the meaning of the elements.
"Noble son, regarding the 'words and meanings,' the 'meanings' refer to the categories such as the group of names (nāmakāya) and so forth;
it should be understood that there are ten kinds of these meanings."
First is the characteristic of reality;
second is the characteristic of thorough knowledge;
third is the characteristic of permanent abandonment.
Fourth is the characteristic of realization;
fifth is the characteristic of cultivation;
sixth is the characteristic of the differentiation of categories, such as the characteristic of that very reality.
Seventh, the characteristic of the relationship between the supported and the supporter;
eighth, the characteristic of those factors that obstruct thorough knowledge and so forth;
ninth, the characteristic of those factors that are conducive to them.
Tenth is the characteristic of the faults and virtues of non-pervasive knowledge and pervasive knowledge, etc.
Regarding the meaning of "elements" (*dhātu*),
it refers to the five kinds of elements.
First, the realm of the vessel-world;
second, the realm of sentient beings;
third, the realm of phenomena.
Fourth is the realm of those to be disciplined;
fifth is the realm of the application for disciplining. Good son.
One should know that these five meanings universally encompass all meanings.
World-Honored One,
as for the wisdom consisting of what is heard...
One understands its meaning through the wisdom derived from reflection;
one understands its meaning through the wisdom derived from the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
What is the distinction between these? Noble son,
the wisdom consisting of hearing relies upon the written word.
However, as it is said, the underlying intention has not yet been well understood;
it has not yet become manifest and accordant with liberation;
nor has one been able to fully realize the meaning of attaining liberation.
The wisdom arisen from reflection also relies upon the literal text;
it does not yet fully accord with the intended meaning as it is explained,
nor has it been brought into direct presence.
It turns toward liberation,
yet it is not yet capable of receiving the realization that constitutes the meaning of liberation.
This refers to the wisdom derived from cultivation possessed by bodhisattvas.
One relies on the letter and yet does not rely on the letter;
one follows the literal expression and yet does not follow the literal expression,
being able to correctly understand the underlying intent.
When the image that is the object of the meditative concentration (samādhi) which shares the same objective sphere as the knowable thing appears before one,
and is extremely conducive to liberation,
one is then able to experience the realization of the meaning of liberation.
"Noble son, these are called the three distinctions in the knowledge of meaning.
World-Honored One."

The sublime wisdom that arises from cultivating śamatha and vipaśyanā by taking specific phenomena as its object is called wisdom (*prajñā*).

First, one skillfully knows the arising of the mind;

What is meant by skill in knowing the arising of the mind?
It refers to knowing, as it truly is, the distinctions in the arising of the mind through its sixteen modes of activity.
This is called "skillfully knowing the arising of the mind.
Regarding the distinctions in the arising of the sixteen modes of mental activity (*ṣoḍaśākāra-cittotpāda-viśeṣa*):
the first is the arising of the receptacle-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is stable and abides in a manner that cannot be perceived.
The first is the ādāna-vijñāna (appropriating consciousness).

this refers to the consciousness of the first and second dhyānas.

What is meant by "skillfully knowing the emergence of the mind"?
