How do the eleven types of divisions encompass all the stages?
It is because Bodhisattvas, first in the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*),
rely upon ten types of dharma-practice to thoroughly cultivate the patience of resolute belief (*adhimukti-kṣānti*).
Having transcended that stage, they enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from corruption (*samyaktvaniyāma*).
By virtue of these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas have fulfilled this portion;
yet, they are not yet able to abide in clear comprehension while subtle transgressions and errors manifest in their conduct.
Due to these causes and conditions, one has not yet perfected this portion;
however, by practicing with diligent effort in order to bring this portion to perfection, one is able to realize it.
By these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas achieve perfection in this portion,
yet they have not yet attained worldly perfection in meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and attainments (*samāpatti*), nor perfection in the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining.
Due to these causes and conditions, this factor remains as yet incomplete;
in order to bring this factor to completion,
one practices with diligent effort and is thus able to realize it.
By means of these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas fulfill this portion;
however, they are not yet able to cause the mind to dwell extensively in the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) as they have attained them.
Because he has not yet abandoned attachment to the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and attachment to the Dharma,
for this reason he is still not perfected in this factor.
In order to bring this factor to perfection, [he exerts himself].
Through diligent cultivation, they are able to realize it;
by this cause and condition, those bodhisattvas fulfill this portion,
yet they are not yet able to observe the principles of the truths as they truly are.
Furthermore, one has not yet been able to abandon the mental attention that is either exclusively oriented toward saṃsāra or exclusively oriented toward nirvāṇa;
nor has one yet been able to cultivate the factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣadharma) as embraced by skillful means.
Due to these causes and conditions, this factor remains as yet incomplete;
in order to bring this factor to completion,
one practices with diligent effort and is thereby able to realize it.
By means of these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas achieve perfection in this stage;
yet they are still unable to observe the flow of saṃsāra as it truly is,
and because they have developed a great degree of weariness toward it.
Because one has not yet been able to dwell extensively in the mental attention of signlessness (*animitta-manasikāra*),
for this reason, one is still not perfected in this particular factor.
In order to bring this factor to perfection:
Through diligent cultivation, they are able to realize it;
by this cause and condition, those bodhisattvas fulfill this portion,
yet they are not yet able to dwell in the cultivation of signless mental attention (animitta-manasikāra) without deficiency or interruption.
For this reason,
this factor remains as yet incomplete;
in order to bring this factor to completion, [one should practice].
Through diligent cultivation, they are able to realize it.
By this cause and condition, those bodhisattvas bring this stage to completion;
yet, they have not yet been able to relinquish effort within the dwelling of signlessness.
Furthermore, because they have not yet attained mastery over signs (*nimitta*),
for this reason they are still not perfected in this portion.
In order to bring this portion to perfection, [they must continue to practice].
By practicing with diligence, they are able to realize it.
Through these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas bring this portion to fulfillment;
yet, they have not yet attained great mastery in teaching the Dharma across all its categories, including its various synonyms, characteristics, etymologies, and distinctions.
For this reason, this factor remains incomplete;
in order to bring this factor to fulfillment,
one practices with diligent effort and is thus able to realize it.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas have fulfilled this portion;
yet they have not yet attained the full realization and direct experience of the perfected dharmakāya.
For this reason, they remain incomplete within this particular aspect.
In order to bring this factor to fulfillment,
they practice with diligent effort and are thus able to realize it;
by these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas bring this factor to perfection.
Yet, they have not yet attained the sublime knowledge and sublime vision that are unattached and unimpeded with respect to all objects of knowledge;
for this reason, they are still not fully perfected in this respect.
In order to bring this factor to fulfillment, one practices with diligence and is thus able to realize it.
By reason of this, this factor becomes fulfilled; because this factor is fulfilled, [the path proceeds].
They attain perfection in all these factors. Good son,
you should know that these eleven kinds of factors universally encompass all the stages (bhūmi).
"Bhagavān,
for what reason is the first called the Stage of Supreme Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi),
and so on, up to for what reason it is called the Stage of Buddhahood (buddha-bhūmi)?"
"Noble son,
because one accomplishes the great purpose and attains what has never been attained before, giving rise to a supramundane mind and experiencing great joy,
it is therefore called the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) at the outset."
Because one is far removed from all subtle transgressions of the precepts,
this second stage is called the "Stainless Stage" (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, because the samādhis and the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining [the teachings] attained therein serve as the basis for immeasurable light of wisdom.
For this reason, it is called the third stage, the Radiant (Prabhākārī).
Because the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) attained therein burn away all afflictions, its wisdom is like a flame.
Therefore, the fourth is named the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).
This is because one attains mastery over those very factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) only after practicing them with skillful means through extreme hardship.
For this reason, the fifth stage is named "The Extremely Difficult to Conquer" (*Sudurjayā*).
One directly observes the flow and turning of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
and by frequently cultivating mental attention (*manasikāra*) regarding the signless (*animitta*), it then manifests before one.
Therefore, the sixth is named the Ground of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*),
because it is able to far-reachingly realize and enter into mental attention that is signless (*animitta*), uninterrupted, and unceasing,
and because it is directly contiguous with the ground of complete purity.
Therefore, the seventh is called the Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā bhūmi*).
Because one attains effortlessness regarding the signless,
one is no longer moved by the active afflictions amidst various signs.
Therefore, the eighth stage is named the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).
Therein, one attains mastery in teaching the Dharma in all its aspects and acquires immeasurable, vast, and great wisdom.
Therefore, the ninth stage is named the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*).
The body of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) is as vast as space, while the *dharmakāya* is perfected,
like a great cloud capable of covering everything.
Therefore, the tenth is named the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).
Because it permanently severs the most subtle afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is characterized by non-attachment and non-obstruction;
and because it manifests perfect awakening (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) regarding all aspects of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-viṣaya*).
"The eleventh is called the Buddha-ground.
World-Honored One,
how many types of delusion are there within these grounds?"
"How many types of *dauṣṭhulya* (coarse heaviness) are there that serve as the objects of counteraction?
Good son," [he asked].
Within these stages, there are twenty-two kinds of delusion and eleven kinds of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) which serve as their respective counteragents.
That is to say, in the first stage (bhūmi) there are two types of delusion:
first, the delusion of clinging to persons and phenomena;
second, the delusion of the afflictions of the miserable realms.
And with those coarse residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) as their respective objects of counteraction,
there are two types of delusion in the second stage:
first, the delusion regarding subtle transgressions.
Second, there is delusion regarding the various courses of karma and its corresponding heavy residues (*dausthulya*), which are the objects to be remedied;
these constitute the two types of delusion in the third stage (*bhūmi*).
First is the delusion of sensual desire;
second is the delusion regarding the perfection of the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining,
along with their respective coarse residues (*dausthulya*), which serve as the objects to be remedied.
In the fourth stage, there are two types of delusion:
first, the delusion of attachment to meditative attainments (*samāpatti*),
and second, the delusion of attachment to phenomena (*dharma*).
And with those coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) as their respective objects of antidote,
there are two types of delusion in the fifth stage: first,
the delusion of exclusively directing one's attention toward the rejection and turning away from birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Second, there is the delusion of one-pointed mental attention directed toward nirvāṇa,
and the corresponding coarse dysfunction (*dauṣṭhulya*) which serves as its counteragent;
these two delusions exist in the sixth stage.
First is the delusion of observing the forward flow of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as they manifest before one;
second is the delusion of the frequent manifestation of signs (*nimitta*),
along with their corresponding coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*), which are the objects to be remedied.
In the seventh stage, there are two types of delusion:
first, the delusion of the subtle manifestation of signs;
second, the delusion regarding the skillful means of mental attention directed exclusively toward the signless.
Furthermore, regarding the coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) that serves as its counteractive object,
there are two types of delusion in the eighth stage:
first, the delusion of applying effort toward the signless (*animitta*).
Second, there is delusion regarding mastery over signs,
and its corresponding coarse dysfunction (*dausthulya*), which are the objects to be remedied;
these two delusions exist in the ninth stage.
First, there is the delusion regarding mastery over the dhāraṇī of wisdom and eloquence concerning immeasurable teachings,
immeasurable phrases of the Dharma,
and immeasurable syllables, as they unfold in successive stages.
Second is the delusion regarding mastery of eloquence,
and its corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*), which are the objects to be remedied;
these two delusions exist in the tenth stage.
First is the delusion regarding great supernormal powers;
second is the delusion regarding the realization of subtle secrets,
along with their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) as the objects to be remedied.
In the stage of the Tathāgata, there are two types of ignorance:
first, the ignorance of extremely subtle attachment toward all objects of knowledge;
second, the ignorance of extremely subtle obstruction.
And their corresponding coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) constitutes what is to be counteracted. Noble son,
it is by virtue of these twenty-two kinds of delusion that [these afflictions arise].
Furthermore, by means of the eleven kinds of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*),
the various stages (*bhūmi*) are established,
and one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Free from those fetters!
World-Honored One,
this unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is most marvelous and rare."
...until they achieve great benefit and great fruit,
enabling all bodhisattvas to shatter such a vast net of delusion and to transcend such a dense forest of coarse heaviness.
One directly realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
World-Honored One,
in how many kinds of excellences are these stages established?
"Good son, there are briefly eight kinds.
The first is the purity of the superior intention."
Second is the purity of mind;
third is the purity of compassion;
fourth is the purity of reaching the other shore.
Fifth is the purity of seeing, making offerings to, and serving the Buddha;
sixth is the purity of maturing sentient beings;
seventh is the purity of birth.
Eighth is the purity of majestic power.
Son of good family,
within the first stage, there is the purity of the superior intention, up to and including the purity of majestic power.

One should know that all the purities— from the purity of the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) up to the purity of majestic power (*anubhāva*)— belonging to each successive stage up to the Buddha-stage,
become increasingly more excellent as they progress.
Only at the stage of Buddhahood is there the purity of birth;
furthermore, all the virtues present in the first stage are equally possessed in all the higher stages.
One should know that the merits of one's own stage are preeminent;
the merits of all ten stages of the bodhisattvas are still surpassable,
whereas the merits of the Buddha-stage should be known as unsurpassable.
“World-Honored One,
for what reason do you say that the birth of a bodhisattva among all births is the most excellent?
“Good son,” [the Buddha replied].
Due to four causes and conditions:
first, because it arises from the accumulation of extremely pure roots of goodness;
second, because it is grasped by the power of intentional deliberation.
Third, because of compassionately pitying and delivering all sentient beings;
fourth, because one is personally free from defilement and can remove the defilements of others.
World-Honored One!
For what reason is it said that all bodhisattvas practice vast vows, sublime vows,
and supreme vows? Good son,
it is for four reasons.
This refers to those bodhisattvas who are able to thoroughly understand the blissful dwelling of nirvana and are capable of swiftly realizing it,
yet nevertheless relinquish that swift realization and its blissful dwelling.
Without conditions or dependencies, they give rise to the mind of great aspiration;
for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings,
they remain amidst manifold, diverse, and long-lasting great sufferings.
Therefore, I say that those bodhisattvas practice vast vows, wondrous vows, and supreme vows.
World-Honored One,
how many kinds of matters are there for these bodhisattvas to study?
Good son, there are briefly six kinds of training for a bodhisattva,
namely: giving and observing the precepts.
The perfections of patience, diligence,
meditative concentration, and wisdom,
O Blessed One.
Regarding these six matters that should be studied,
how many are subsumed under the training in higher ethics (adhiśīla-śikṣā),
and how many are subsumed under the training in higher mind (adhicitta-śikṣā)?
"How many are subsumed under the training in higher wisdom?
Son of good family,
you should know that the first three are subsumed only under the training in higher ethical discipline."
The single category of meditative concentration (dhyāna) is subsumed under the training in higher mind (adhicittam-śikṣā);
wisdom (prajñā) is subsumed under the training in higher wisdom (adhiprajñām-śikṣā).
I say that diligence (vīrya) pervades all of them.
"Bhagavān,
among these six matters that should be studied,
how many are subsumed within the accumulation of merit?"
"How much is comprised within the provisions for wisdom?
Noble son, that which is comprised within the training in higher ethics."
This is what is included within the accumulation of merit.
If it is included within the training in higher wisdom,
this is what is included within the accumulation of wisdom.
"I say that the two types— diligence and meditative concentration— pervade all of them,
World-Honored One.
Regarding these six matters of training,"
"How should a bodhisattva train?
Son of good family,
they should train by means of five aspects."
First, one possesses intense faith and understanding toward the subtle and sublime teachings of the Dharma associated with the perfections within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
Second, one subsequently possesses the sublime wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and meditation regarding the ten modes of Dharma practice.
Third, practicing with diligence;
fourth, drawing near to true spiritual friends.
Fifth, one should diligently cultivate the categories of wholesome qualities without interruption.
Blessed One,
for what cause and condition are such matters of training established?
There are only six numbers.
Good son, it is due to two causes and conditions.
First, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings;
second, for the sake of counteracting all afflictions.
It should be understood that the first three benefit sentient beings.
The latter three serve as antidotes to all afflictions,
while the former three benefit all sentient beings;
that is to say, by means of generosity, the bodhisattvas [benefit others].
One benefits sentient beings by providing them with the necessities of life;
because of maintaining ethical discipline,
one does not harm, oppress, or disturb sentient beings while seeking to benefit them.
By means of patience,
one is able to endure harm, oppression,
and affliction for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Regarding the latter three [perfections] as antidotes to the various afflictions:
it means that although bodhisattvas, by virtue of their diligence,
have not yet permanently subdued all afflictions nor permanently destroyed all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
They are able to courageously cultivate all categories of wholesome qualities;
because of their meditative concentration, those afflictions cannot shake their application toward these wholesome qualities.
One forever subdues the afflictions by means of prajñā;
one forever eradicates the latent tendencies (anuśaya) by means of prajñā.
"Bhagavān,
for what reason are the remaining pāramitās established as being only four in number?
Son of good family, [listen:]..."
Because it acts as an auxiliary companion to the preceding six perfections (pāramitās).
That is to say, regarding the sentient beings encompassed by the first three perfections, the bodhisattvas—
By means of the skillful means of the articles of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*),
one gathers [beings] and establishes them in the wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*).
Therefore, I say that the perfection of skillful means (*upāyakauśalyapāramitā*) acts as an auxiliary companion to the preceding three.
If bodhisattvas, because their afflictions are numerous in this present life,
lack the capacity for uninterrupted cultivation due to their feeble intention and their inclination toward lower realms.
They lack the capacity to abide within their own minds because they have not heard the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and have failed to cultivate it well as an object of focus.
Since none of those meditative absorptions can induce supramundane wisdom,
they instead appropriate a limited and inferior accumulation of merit,
merely for the sake of having slight afflictions in future lives.
One gives rise to a correct aspiration;
this is called the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).
By virtue of this aspiration, [the following occurs].
Because afflictions are subtle and slight, one is able to cultivate diligence;
therefore, I say that the perfection of aspiration is the companion to the perfection of diligence.
If bodhisattvas associate with virtuous persons,
listen to the sublime Dharma, and attend to it correctly according to the principle.
By means of these causes and conditions,
an inferior disposition is transformed into a superior disposition,
and one is also able to attain resolute conviction regarding the higher realms.
This is called the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*).
By means of this power, one possesses the capability for the mind to abide within itself.
Therefore, I say that the perfection of power acts as an auxiliary companion to the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
If bodhisattvas, having already been able to hear and thoroughly cultivate the conditions within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, are thus able to give rise to meditative concentration (dhyāna),
this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
By means of this knowledge,
one is capable of eliciting supramundane wisdom; therefore,
I say that the perfection of knowledge (jñāna-pāramitā) acts as an auxiliary companion to the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
“World-Honored One,
for what reason do you proclaim the six perfections in this specific order?
“Good son,” [the Buddha replied].
Because it serves as the basis for successive inductions;
that is to say, if bodhisattvas have no regard or parsimony toward their bodies or wealth,
they are then able to undertake and maintain pure prohibitive precepts.
To protect the prohibitive precepts, one cultivates patience;
having cultivated patience, one is able to arouse diligence;
having aroused diligence, one is able to accomplish meditative concentration.
Having fully attained meditative concentration, one is then able to obtain supramundane wisdom.
Therefore, O Bhagavān, I have explained the pāramitās in this sequential order.
"Good son, how many distinct categories of types are there for each of these six perfections? Good son,
there are three kinds for each."
There are three kinds of giving:
first, the gift of Dharma;
second, the gift of material wealth.
Third is the gift of fearlessness.
Regarding the three types of ethical discipline (*śīla*):
the first is the discipline of abandoning unwholesome states.
Second, the generation of the morality of superior discipline;
third, the generation of the morality of benefiting sentient beings.
As for the three types of patience:
First, the patience of enduring enmity and harm;
second, the patience of calmly accepting suffering;
third, the patience of discerning the Dharma.
Regarding the three types of diligence:
first, the diligence of donning the armor;
second, the diligence of application that gives rise to wholesome dharmas.
Third is the diligence of application for the benefit of sentient beings.
Regarding the three types of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*):

first is the meditative concentration that dwells in happiness by counteracting the afflictions and manifold sufferings through non-conceptualization, tranquility, supreme tranquility, and faultlessness.
Second is the meditative concentration that induces merit;
third is the meditative concentration that induces the benefit of sentient beings.
As for the three types of wisdom:
First, wisdom that takes conventional truth as its object;
second, wisdom that takes ultimate truth as its object;
third, wisdom that takes the benefit of sentient beings as its object.
"Bhagavān,
for what reason are the pāramitās called 'pāramitās'?"
Good son, there are five causes and conditions:
first, because of being free from attachment and clinging.
Second, because it is free from attachment;
third, because it is free from fault;
fourth, because it is free from conceptual discrimination.
Fifth, because of correct dedication.
"Being without attachment" means not being attached to any factors that are contrary to the perfections (*pāramitā*).
"Being without attachment" means that one's mind is not bound by any of the fruits, maturations, or requitals of the various *pāramitās*.
"Being without fault" means...
That is to say, regarding these pāramitās,
they are uninterrupted by defiled phenomena and free from unskillful practice.
Non-conceptuality refers to not adhering to the intrinsic characteristics of these perfections as they are expressed by words.
Right dedication refers to dedicating the perfections thus performed and accumulated toward the fruit of unsurpassed, great bodhi.
"Bhagavān,
what are called the factors that are contrary to the pāramitās?
Good son," [the Buddha replied].
It should be known that this matter consists briefly of six types.
First, one deeply perceives the merits and advantages within the pleasures of joy, delight, wealth, and mastery over various sensual desires.
Second, regarding the engagement in whatever one pleases through the unrestrained activity of body,
speech, and mind, one deeply perceives its merits and advantages.
Third, regarding the inability to endure the contempt of others.
Fourth, one deeply perceives the merits and benefits in the failure to apply oneself to practice and instead being attached to sensual pleasures.
Fifth, regarding places of clamor and the worldly conduct of distraction,
one deeply perceives their merits and advantages.
Sixth, regarding the conceptual proliferation of speech based on what is seen, heard, sensed, and known.
One deeply perceives its merits and benefits.
Blessed One,
what is the fruit and the maturation of all these perfections?
Good son, you should know that this also briefly comprises six kinds.
The first is the attainment of great wealth.
Second, rebirth in the happy realms;
third, being without enmity or conflict and possessing abundant joy and happiness;
and fourth, becoming a lord of sentient beings.
Fifth, his body is free from affliction and harm.
Sixth, he possesses a great lineage and retinue.
World-Honored One!
"What are the defiled dharmas that are interspersed with the pāramitās?
Son of good family,
you should know that, briefly, they arise from four kinds of application."
First, because of the absence of compassionate application;
second, because of improper application;
third, because of inconsistent application.
Fourth, because of a lack of earnest application;
"irrational application" refers to when one practices the other perfections.
Blessed One, [the bodhisattva] remains far removed from the loss and ruin of the other perfections.
"What is meant by 'non-expedient practice'?
Good son, it is when bodhisattvas, while benefiting sentient beings through the pāramitās,"
If one merely provides benefit to sentient beings by bestowing material wealth,
and is content with that alone without leading them out of unwholesome states and establishing them in wholesome states,
this is called non-expedient practice.
Why is this? Good son,
it is not by merely performing these actions toward sentient beings that one is said to provide true benefit.
For example, whether feces and filth are abundant or meager, there is ultimately no way to make them fragrant and clean.
In the same way, because of the suffering inherent in conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), the nature of sentient beings is suffering.
There is no skillful means by which one can bring about happiness through the mere temporary benefit of material wealth;
only by establishing others within the sublime and virtuous Dharma can it be called the supreme benefit.
"Bhagavān,
how many purifications are there for all these pāramitās?"
"Good son,
I never say that there is any other purification of the pāramitās apart from these five aspects.
Rather, it is precisely by relying upon these matters that [purification occurs]."
The general and specific characteristics of the purity of the *pāramitās* shall now be explained.
Regarding the general explanation of the characteristics of the purity of all *pāramitās*,
one should know that there are seven kinds.
What are the seven?
First, the bodhisattva does not seek for others to know these dharmas.
Second, having seen these dharmas, they do not give rise to attachment.
Third, one does not give rise to doubt or uncertainty regarding these very dharmas,
wondering whether or not they can lead to the attainment of great enlightenment.
Fourth, one never praises oneself or disparages others with any sense of contempt.
Fifth, he never becomes arrogant or heedless.
Sixth, he never gives rise to contentment with having attained only a small measure of realization.
Seventh, he never, on account of these dharmas, gives rise to envy or stinginess toward others.
To speak specifically of the characteristics of the purity of all *pāramitās*,
there are likewise seven kinds. What are these seven?
It means that bodhisattvas practice in accordance with the seven characteristics of the purity of giving as I have explained them.
First, by the purity of the gift itself.
First, they practice pure giving by virtue of the purity of their conduct.
Second, they practice pure giving by virtue of the purity of their ethical discipline.
Third, by means of purity of view,
one practices pure giving.
Fourth, by means of purity of mind.
One practices pure giving through five ways;
fifth, by means of purity of speech,
one practices pure giving.
Sixth, one practices pure giving through the purity of wisdom.
Seventh, through the purity of defilements.
They practice pure giving;
these are called the seven characteristics of the purity of giving.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas are able to thoroughly understand all the training rules established for the observance of discipline.

They are able to thoroughly understand renunciation regarding transgressions, possessing constant ethical discipline (*śīla*), firm ethical discipline, ever-practicing ethical discipline, and ever-advancing ethical discipline,
and they undertake training in all the precepts (*śikṣāpada*).
These are called the seven characteristics of the purity of ethical discipline.
If bodhisattvas develop deep reliance and faith regarding the ripening of the karmic results of their own actions, [they possess this purity].
When any harmful circumstances manifest before them,
they do not give rise to anger,
nor do they respond with verbal abuse.
They do not become angry or strike others;
they do not intimidate or mock them;
nor do they inflict harm upon others by means of various disadvantageous actions.
They harbor no resentment;
when being exhorted or instructed, they do not become angry or distressed,
nor do they wait for others to come and offer them exhortation or instruction.
One practices patience not out of fear,
nor out of attachment or craving,
nor because of a desire for gratitude, but simply through relinquishment.
This is called the characteristic of the purification of the seven kinds of patience.
If bodhisattvas penetrate the nature of equality in diligence,
they do not rely on fierce and strenuous exertion.
Exalting oneself and disparaging others,
possessing great power and great diligence,
and being capable of all things.
Firm and courageous,
one never abandons the yoke regarding all wholesome dharmas;
these are called the seven characteristics of the purification of diligence.
If bodhisattvas possess the meditative concentration and dhyāna that thoroughly penetrates characteristics,
the meditative concentration and dhyāna that is perfected,
and the meditative concentration and dhyāna that pertains to both parts.
There is the meditative concentration of the revolving samādhi;
there is the meditative concentration of the non-reliant samādhi;
and there is the meditative concentration of the well-cultivated samādhi.
There is the cultivation of immeasurable samādhis and dhyānas through hearing and reflecting upon the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
these are called the seven signs of the purification of dhyāna.
If bodhisattvas remain far removed from the two extremes of superimposition and denial,
and practice the Middle Way,
this is called wisdom.
By means of this wisdom, one understands and realizes the meaning of the gates of liberation as they truly are—
namely, the three gates of liberation: emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness.
To understand, as they truly are, the meanings of intrinsic nature,
namely: the thoroughly imagined and the dependent-arising.
If one correctly understands the meaning of the lack of intrinsic nature regarding the three natures of the perfected reality— namely,

This is called the characteristic of being obtainable as something of a different category.
Son of good family, if,
within these remaining characteristics of being obtainable as something of the same category and within the analogies, [one should understand it likewise].
That which possesses various heterogeneous characteristics is,
for these reasons, not determinate with respect to what is to be established;
this is called the non-perfectly-established characteristic (*aparinispanna-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, regarding the dissimilar instances and examples that may be found elsewhere,
since they possess all the characteristics of similar instances,
for this reason, [the probans] is not determinative with respect to the property to be established (*sādhya*).
It is also called the non-perfectly-established characteristic.
Because it is not perfectly established,
it is not a well-examined principle of purity.
Because it is impure,
it should not be cultivated.
This refers to the characteristics induced by analogies of a different class.
If it is not a characteristic of a well-purified verbal teaching,
one should know that its essential nature is entirely impure.
As for the principle of the nature of things (*dharmatā-yukti*):
That is to say, whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear in the world,
the nature of phenomena remains established;
the dharma abides in the dharmadhātu.
This is called the principle of natural law (*dharmatā-yukti*).
Regarding the general and the specific:
it means that after first stating a single sentence of the Dharma in general, [it is then explained in detail].

The ultimate clarification of the distinctions among the subsequent phrases regarding the characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) refers to those factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) which I have described as having activity (*sapravṛtti*), having an object (*sālambana*), and being capable of grasping (*grāhaka*).
That is to say, the foundations of mindfulness and so forth.
This is called their characteristic of essential nature.
As for their characteristic of result:
This refers to the abandonment of all mundane and supramundane afflictions,
as well as the various fruits and virtues induced thereby, both mundane and supramundane.
This is called the characteristic of attaining that fruit.
As for the characteristic of experiencing and demonstrating it,
it refers to experiencing it by means of the wisdom of liberation within that very state.
And extensively proclaiming and explaining them to others—
this is called the characteristic of their reception and exposition.
As for the characteristic of those obstructive factors:
That is to say, regarding the very cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma),
those defiled phenomena that are able to act as obstacles are called the characteristics of obstructing phenomena.
Regarding the characteristic of conformity to those phenomena:
it refers to those very phenomena that are most frequently practiced;
this is called the characteristic of conformity to those phenomena.
Regarding the characteristic of those disadvantages:
one should know that it refers to all the faults inherent in those very obstructive phenomena;
this is called the characteristic of their disadvantages.
Regarding the characteristic of its benefits:
one should know that it consists of all the virtues inherent in those various conformable dharmas;
this is called the characteristic of its benefits.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One [will explain this]."
I shall briefly explain for the sake of the bodhisattvas the meaning of the dhāraṇī of the sūtras, the vinaya, and the mātṛkās that is not shared with non-Buddhists.
By means of this unique dhāraṇī-meaning, [it is so].
To cause all bodhisattvas to enter into the profound and secret intent of the various dharmas taught by the Tathāgata,
the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Good son,"
Listen attentively now.
I shall briefly explain for you the meaning of the uncommon dhāraṇī,
so that all bodhisattvas may skillfully penetrate the intentional terminology spoken by me.
"Noble son, whether they be defiled phenomena or purified phenomena,
I declare that all of them are devoid of functional activity."
Furthermore, there is no person (pudgala) whatsoever,
because it is in every respect free from any purposeful activity;
nor do the phenomena of affliction (saṃkleśa-dharma) first become defiled and subsequently purified.
Impure phenomena are not pure later and defiled earlier;
rather, ordinary worldlings cling to the intrinsic nature and specific distinctions of phenomena and persons within this body of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*).
With the latent tendencies of false views as their condition,
they conceive of a self and what belongs to a self;
based on this, they falsely claim, "I see" and "I hear."
"I smell, I taste, I touch, I cognize;
I eat, I act; I am defiled, I am purified."
When such types of perverse applications of effort arise,
if one knows them as they truly are, one is able to forever sever the body of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and attain the state in which all afflictions no longer abide.
It is supremely pure, free from all conceptual proliferation,
the support for the unconditioned,
and devoid of effortful application.
"Good son, you should know that this is called a brief explanation of the meaning of the uncommon dhāraṇī.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, [spoke as follows].
And he spoke in verse:
"All phenomena of affliction and purification Are devoid of activity; the person (pudgala) does not exist.
I have taught that they are free from purposeful action; Affliction and purification do not occur sequentially."
Latent tendencies toward views reside within the coarse body; taking this as a condition, one conceives of "I" and "mine.
From this, one falsely claims to have views such as "self," or thinks, "I eat," "I act," or "I am defiled and purified.
One who knows this as it truly is can forever sever the coarse body.
Attaining that which is unstained and pure, free from conceptual proliferation, unconditioned, the support, and without effortful application.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One..."
"How should one understand the characteristics of the arising of the minds of all Tathāgatas?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Good son,"
Now, the Tathāgata is not manifested by the arising of mind, intellect, or consciousness;
nevertheless, there is the arising of mental factors involving the Tathāgatas' application of effort (*prayoga*).
"Venerable Lord, you should know that this matter is like a magical transformation.
If it is the dharma-body of all Tathāgatas..."
It is far removed from all application.
Since there is no application,
how could mental phenomena arise?
"Good son, due to the power of the preparatory practices of skillful means and prajñā previously cultivated,
a state of mind arises."
Good son, it is like one who has fallen into a mindless sleep;
they do not apply effort toward awakening.
One awakens again through the force of previously performed preparatory application,
just as when one is currently in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
One does not apply effort toward emerging from meditative absorption; rather,
one emerges from the absorption through the force of the prior application of effort,
just as the mind arises again after sleep or the attainment of cessation.
Thus, World-Honored One, you should know that by the power of the preparatory practice of skillful means and wisdom cultivated previously,
there further arises a mental dharma of the Tathāgata.
"Should it be said that the transformation body of the Tathāgata possesses a mind,
or is it without a mind?
Good son," [the Buddha replied].
It is neither with mind nor without mind. Why is this?
Because there is no mind that relies on itself,
and because there is a mind that relies on others,
O Blessed One.
"What is the difference between these two: the conduct of the Tathāgata and the realm of the Tathāgata?
Son of good family, as for the conduct of the Tathāgata..."
It refers to the pure buddha-field, adorned by a multitude of inconceivable and immeasurable merits common to all Tathāgatas in every respect;
it is the domain of the Tathāgata.
This refers to the differentiation of the five realms in all their aspects.
What are these five?
The first is the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*).
Second is the world-realm;
third is the dharma-realm;
fourth is the realm of discipline.
Fifth is the realm of the skillful means of subduing.
Thus, World-Honored One, these are called the two kinds of distinctions.
The Tathāgata attained equal and perfect enlightenment,
turned the wheel of the true Dharma,
and entered great parinirvāṇa.
Regarding these three kinds,
you should know what their characteristics are,
O son of good family.
One should know that these three are all devoid of dual characteristics;
that is to say, they are neither the attainment of perfect enlightenment nor the non-attainment of perfect enlightenment.
It is not the turning of the wheel of the true Dharma;
it is not the non-turning of the wheel of the true Dharma;
it is not the entry into great parinirvāṇa.
It is not that they do not enter Great Nirvāṇa. Why is this?
Because the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is ultimately pure.
Because the transformation body of the Tathāgata is constantly manifested,
World-Honored One,
all classes of sentient beings produce various merits simply by seeing, hearing of, and serving that transformation body.
For what reason does the Tathāgata [appear] there?
O son of good family,
it is because the Tathāgata is the causal condition for their predominant object of focus (adhipatālambana).
Furthermore, World-Honored One, because that emanation body is sustained by the power of the Tathāgata,
for what reason and by what causal conditions is it equal and without effortful application?
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata radiates the light of great wisdom for all sentient beings and manifests infinite emanation bodies and the liberation-bodies of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
There is no such thing.
Son of good family, it is like this:
for example, from the orbs of the sun and moon, which are devoid of volitional effort (*anabhisamskāra*), two kinds of *sphaṭika* jewels—those of water and those of fire—emit great radiance.
It is not other water or fire;
it is the crystal gem (*sphāṭika-maṇi*), because it is sustained by sentient beings of great majesty and by the predominant power of the karma of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is like the images of seals that emerge from a mani jewel that has been carved and polished by a skilled artisan,
and not from any other uncarved one.
Thus, by means of skillful means and wisdom directed toward the immeasurable realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*),
one thoroughly cultivates, polishes, and perfects them until they integrate into the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
From this, one is able to radiate the great light of supreme knowledge.
Furthermore, various emanated forms and images appear;
it is not only from that body of liberation, Blessed One, that such things occur.
As the World-Honored One has said, through the majestic power and sustaining grace of the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas,
they cause sentient beings to be born into great and wealthy families, such as those of the kṣatriyas and brāhmaṇas, within the desire realm.
There is no human body or wealth that is not fully perfected;
or rather, the bodies and wealth of all those in the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm can be obtained in their full perfection,
O Bhagavān.
What is the underlying intention here? Noble son,
it refers to the majestic power and sustaining presence of the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas, whether in their paths or their practices.
In all places, for those who can cause sentient beings to obtain the perfection of both body and wealth,
one should accordingly proclaim this path and this practice to them.
If there are those who can correctly practice this path and these modes of conduct,
they will attain no lack of perfection in body or wealth in any place.
If there are sentient beings who [practice] this path and these modes of conduct...
Having violated and disparaged [me],
and having given rise to a mind of malice and anger toward me,
after their lives have ended...
In all places, the bodies and resources they obtain are never inferior. Good son,
by these causes and conditions, you should know that this is the majestic power and sustaining presence of the Tathāgatas and the Bodhisattvas.
Not only can it cause the perfection of the body and wealth [of others],
but through the majestic power maintained by Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas,
it can also cause the inferiority of the body and wealth of sentient beings.
"Bhagavān,
among all defiled lands, what things are easy to find and what things are difficult to find?"
Among all the pure lands, what is easy to obtain and what is difficult to obtain?
Son of good family, [listen].
In all impure lands, eight things are easy to obtain and two things are difficult to obtain.
What are the eight things that are easy to obtain?
First, non-Buddhists;
second, sentient beings who suffer;
third, the distinctions between the rise and fall of various lineages and families.
Fourth, engaging in various unwholesome deeds;
fifth, violating the śīla;
sixth, the miserable realms.
Seventh, those of inferior vehicles;
eighth, bodhisattvas whose intention and application are inferior.
What are the two things that are difficult to find?
First, it is where Bodhisattvas who practice with superior intention gather;
second, it is where Tathāgatas appear in the world. Good son!
In all the pure lands, it should be understood that the opposite of the above holds true:
eight things are extremely difficult to obtain, while two things are easy to obtain.
World-Honored One!
Within this Dharma-gate of the *Saṃdhinirmocana*,
what is the name of this teaching?
How should I uphold it?
"Good son, this is called the definitive teaching on the Tathāgata’s fulfillment of his activities.
Regarding this definitive teaching on the Tathāgata’s fulfillment of his activities..."
"You should uphold this.
When these teachings on the definitive meaning of the Tathāgata’s Accomplished Activities were spoken,
there were seventy-five thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the great assembly.
All have attained the perfect realization of the Dharmakāya.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle seventy-eight;
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle seventy-nine.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya spoke;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree.
This concludes the determination of the "Chapter on Merits" within the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Question: As it has been said regarding the five kinds of immeasurables—
namely, the immeasurable realm of sentient beings and so forth—
should all those worlds be described as being equal and equivalent?
There is a distinction.
Answer: One should say there is a distinction.
Furthermore, it is of two kinds.
First is purity;
second is impurity.
Within a pure world-system:
There are no hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts to be found;
nor are there the realms of desire, form, or formlessness;
nor is any sensation of suffering to be found.
Only the assembly of bodhisattvas dwells therein;
therefore, it is called a pure world.
This refers to bodhisattvas who have already entered the third stage.
By the power of mastery over their vows,
they take birth there; among them,
there are no ordinary beings, nor are there any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas who are not ordinary beings.
If ordinary bodhisattvas are born there,
one might ask: if there are no ordinary bodhisattvas,
nor non-ordinary śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas who are born there?
For what reason is it said in the Bodhisattva teachings:
"If a bodhisattva or the like forms a wish for that"?
"All such beings shall be reborn there.
Answer: This was spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) in order to transform those disciples of a lazy disposition who have not yet accumulated roots of virtue.
Why is this? Because when they are thus exhorted and encouraged,
they abandon indolence and diligently apply themselves to the practice of wholesome qualities.
From this point on, one gradually becomes capable of being born there;
one shall attain the *dharmatā*.
It should be understood that this is the intended meaning (*saṃdhi*) within this context.
Furthermore, by relying on four types of abodes, a bodhisattva is able to accomplish four matters:
first, the abode of extreme joy;
second, the abode of superior ethical discipline.
Third is the stage of superior mind;
fourth is the stage of superior wisdom.
What is the stage of extreme joy?
This means that as these bodhisattvas abide accordingly,
having already entered the stage of the pure superior intention (*adhyāśaya*),
they shall remain so until they sit upon the sublime seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
With a pure intention that does not depend on external conditions regarding the Three Jewels—
what is the stage of superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-vihāra*)?
It refers to the bodhisattvas, while remaining in this very stage of extreme joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*).
From this point onward, as they dwell accordingly,
they possess natural ethical discipline (*śīla*),
remaining far removed from all stinginess and transgressions of the precepts.
One dedicates such perfected ethical discipline and renunciation toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
What is the dwelling in the higher mind?
This means that bodhisattvas, relying precisely upon this dwelling in superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-vihāra*),

from this point onward, in accordance with their established state, become free from desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāmadhātu*) and attain the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and the various meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*).
Abiding in compassion,
one practices correctly according to reality, according to one's capacity and strength, toward all sentient beings.
What is the dwelling of higher wisdom?
This means that bodhisattvas, relying precisely upon this dwelling in the superior mind (*adhi-citta-vihāra*),
from this point onward, according to their respective abidings,
gradually attain skillfulness in the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
Skillfulness regarding the truths;
skillfulness regarding dependent origination;
and skillfulness regarding the wisdom that establishes the unique qualities.
It transcends all wisdom realized in common by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
therein, the establishment of wisdom regarding the uncommon dharmas refers to that which is within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
The wisdom of intentional terminology,
the wisdom of the non-established truths,
and the wisdom of the established truths.
Regarding the wisdom attained in common therein:
it refers to the realized wisdom attained by relying on dependent origination.
How is it that, by relying on these four abodes, one can accomplish the four tasks?
This means that from the time bodhisattvas rely upon the first stage until they sit upon the seat of sublime enlightenment,
they never abandon the mind of great enlightenment.
Relying on the second dwelling, up until one sits upon the seat of sublime awakening (bodhimaṇḍa),
one’s own body, wealth, and virtuous qualities will steadily increase.
Relying on the third dwelling...
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings,
they transform their meditative absorptions and,
through the power of great vows, are reborn in the desire realm.
Yet they are not defiled by the afflictions associated with the bonds of desire.
Relying on the fourth dwelling,
they attain skillfulness in the establishment and penetration of all phenomena.
For the sake of delivering sentient beings,
they make a vow to undergo birth and death;
by virtue of this vow, they are able to accumulate vast stores of merit and knowledge.
Then, by virtue of this dwelling being pure as its cause,
one does not depend on other dwellings,
nor does one rely on the instructions or teachings of others.
One will swiftly be able to realize the sublime wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Question: By what should it be said that a bodhisattva experiences suffering?
Answer: The affliction and injury of sentient beings constitute suffering.
Question: One should say that what constitutes the joy of a bodhisattva?
Answer: Benefiting sentient beings is their joy.
Question: One should say that with what mental orientation (*manasikāra*) should a bodhisattva act?
Answer: It is the realization of the limits of the objects of knowledge, and the mental engagement (*manasikāra*) consisting of performing all deeds that benefit sentient beings.
Question: How should it be said that a bodhisattva abides?
The answer is that one abides in non-conceptualization.
Furthermore, there are briefly four superior obstructions for a bodhisattva;
if these are not purified, [the path cannot be realized].
In the end, they are unable to enter the bodhisattva stages or the gradual progression through those stages.
What are the four?
First, they commit defiled transgressions within the *vinaya* of the bodhisattvas.
Second, slandering the sublime Dharma associated with the Mahāyāna;
third, not having accumulated roots of goodness;
fourth, possessing a mind of defiled attachment.
In order to counteract these four obstacles,
there are further four kinds of methods for purifying the obstacles.
What are these four?
First, one should, before all the Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions,
with a profound and earnest mind, confess and reveal one's transgressions.
Second, one should act for the benefit of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
Third, one should universally rejoice in all merits performed by all sentient beings throughout the ten directions,
and exhort all Tathāgatas to preach the Dharma.
Fourth, all roots of goodness that arise are dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
One should fully understand and thoroughly eliminate all secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that are difficult to sever.
Those bodhisattvas should thoroughly understand and correctly eliminate them.
What are the four?
First, attachment to dharmas.
Second, mental attention associated with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
third, attachment to meditative attainments;
fourth, the activities of the māras.
One should know that all instances of the mind moving,
flowing, and scattering amidst various signs are the activities of Māra.
Question: How should one describe the characteristics of a bodhisattva who has entered the first stage?
Answer: One should say that they have transcended all stages of ordinary beings and have entered the bodhisattvas’ state of rightness and freedom from birth.
Because they have already entered [the path],
they are no longer called ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); having transcended all fears and attained the unsurpassed Dharma never before attained, they are so named.
He is always able to dwell securely in the stage of supreme joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*).
Question: What characteristics should it be said that a bodhisattva who has entered the second stage possesses?
Answer: It should be said that, by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) within the Vinaya, he naturally attains the cessation of all training (*śikṣā*) pertaining to the śrāvakas.
Because they are able to practice with purity in the actions of body, speech, and mind,
they are able to remain far removed from the stains of all transgressions of the precepts.
[This concerns] the bodhisattva who has already entered the third stage.
What characteristics should it be said to possess?
Answer: It should be said that one has attained a powerful path of *śamatha* within;
by means of this, one realizes the illumination of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
Question: What characteristics should it be said that a bodhisattva who has entered the fourth stage possesses?
Answer: It should be said that because they have attained a powerful path of *vipaśyanā* within, they establish the flames of wisdom that can incinerate the afflictions.
By means of this, one is able to establish skillfulness regarding all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) exactly as they have been realized.
[This concerns] the bodhisattva who has already entered the fifth stage.
What characteristics should it be said to have?
Answer: It should be said that its characteristic is to transcend all worldly knowledge and to transcend the knowledge of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
One is able to ascend and enter the inconceivable truth and the extremely difficult-to-conquer path.
Question: Having already entered the sixth stage, what characteristics should a bodhisattva be said to possess?
Answer: It should be said that because one has realized and entered into the principle of profound dependent origination,
one conceives a sense of revulsion toward all conditioned formations (saṃskāra) in every state of movement and stillness,
and dwells frequently, inclining toward and attending with mental attention upon the signless realm (animitta-dhātu).
Question: When one asks about a bodhisattva who has already entered the seventh stage, what characteristics should be attributed to them?
Answer: One should say that they possess applied effort (*sābhisaṃskāra*) which is uninterrupted and without flaw.
Through the mental engagement with the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu-manasikāra*), one enters most deeply;
having reached the ultimate limit of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
Question: What characteristics should be attributed to a bodhisattva who has already entered the eighth stage (*bhūmi*)?

Answer: It should be said that it occurs through mental attention directed toward the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*), which is without application (*anabhisamskāra*) and without effort (*anābhoga*);
because it is attained spontaneously, there is no fluctuation.
Because they have attained mastery over all signs, they abide on the stage of purity. Question:

What characteristics should it be said that a bodhisattva who has entered the ninth stage possesses? Answer: It should be said that they have attained mastery over the body of names, the body of phrases, and the body of syllables.
Furthermore, because they have attained faultless, immeasurable, and vast wisdom;
because they have attained vast and unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*);
and because they are able to gladden the minds of all sentient beings.
He is called a Great Dharma Master.
If one asks what the characteristics of a bodhisattva who has already entered the tenth stage should be said to be, the answer is:
it should be said that they have attained the same great empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) as all Tathāgatas.
Because they have already attained the great Dharma-body that is like a cloud,
and because they have already attained all great supernormal powers,
they are also called Tathāgatas.
Question: What characteristics should it be said that a bodhisattva who has entered the stage of a Tathāgata possesses?
Answer: It should be said that it is precisely this attained dharmakāya which has become even more thoroughly purified and perfectly fulfilled.
One attains the permanently free, pure wisdom and vision regarding all types of afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Question: How does one practice these stages?

Answer: If bodhisattvas dwell on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) and cultivate the ten dharma-practices based upon the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one asks: how are these stages attained?
Answer: If bodhisattvas realize entry into the bodhisattva’s state of correctness and freedom from outflows (*samyaktvaniyāma*),
and furthermore attain the pure intention (*śuddhāśaya*),
at that time they suddenly attain all the stages (*bhūmi*).
Question: What is meant by the "outflow" (*niṣyanda*) of the various stages (*bhūmi*)?
Answer: It refers to all the paths of application (*prayoga-mārga*) characterized by spiritual power that follow after the realization [of the stage] within each stage.
Question: How is the fulfillment of these stages accomplished?
Answer: If bodhisattvas, within each of those stages,
pass through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of great eons,
according to the majesty and virtue of each stage as it is extolled.
One can realize this majestic power spontaneously.

Question: As it is said that there are five ways of entering the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), among these, how does a *śrāvaka* enter the state of rightness and departure from birth?
If bodhisattvas enter into the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and equally penetrate the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as it truly is,
how should the distinction between these two be understood?
Answer: Briefly stated, the dharma-dhātu has two kinds of characteristics:
first, the characteristic of differentiation;
second, the characteristic of self-nature.
As for the characteristic of differentiation,
it refers to the characteristic of permanence and the characteristic of quiescence.
The characteristic of permanence refers to the dharmatā that is originally unborn and the dharmatā that is inexhaustible.
The characteristic of tranquility refers to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) that is disjoined from afflictions and suffering.
As for the term "specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa):
This refers to the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya), which is the lack of intrinsic reality in all things— comprised within the true knowledge that discerns signs,
names, and suchness— by virtue of their being of an imagined nature (parikalpitasvabhāva).
In this context, śrāvakas penetrate the dharma-dhātu by means of its differentiated characteristics and thereby enter the state of rightness and departure from birth;
they do not do so by penetrating it through its own-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
By means of the perception of non-perishing and the perception of security,
one attains the perception of tranquility within the dharma-realm;
and toward all conditioned formations, one single-mindedly gives rise to the perception of revulsion.
Furthermore, they are unable to understand, as it truly is, the nature of phenomena comprised within those signs—
that they are not established as real and that they are selfless.
It is precisely within this very meditative concentration on the dharma-realm that the mind proceeds signlessly through the mental attention directed toward the distinctions of the dharma-realm.
It is not by means of mental attention directed toward their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*),
nor because others have proclaimed the specific characteristics of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) for them; rather,
it is those śrāvakas who, having heard [the teaching], partially dedicate [their merit] toward awakening (*bodhi*).
Only after undergoing extreme hardship do they attain realization;
having attained entry, they practice with diligent application.
This refers to those śrāvakas who are exclusively and unilaterally inclined toward quiescence.
It is extremely difficult to gain entry into it,
yet once one has entered, one practices with diligent effort.
If all bodhisattvas were to penetrate the dharma-realm through both modes of appearance, [there would be no distinction].

They enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and having entered that state of certainty, they predominantly abide in mental attention directed toward the specific characteristics of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Why is this?
Because when one frequently applies mental attention to the distinct characteristics of the objects within the dharma-realm, one swiftly proceeds toward nirvāṇa.
Abiding frequently in that state is not the correct means for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
One should know that although they are equal in their penetration of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*),
there are differences due to these causes and conditions.
Question: As it is said that the three times and the three wheels are pure, how are the three times and the three wheels pure?
Answer: By virtue of the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva).
When one correctly observes with wisdom as it truly is that all phenomena of the past, future, and present are equal and identical,
then within those phenomena of the past, future, and present—
To be without longing, hope, or defiled attachment is called the purity of the three wheels throughout the three times.
Question: Regarding the one hundred and forty unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) previously mentioned, [how are they established?]
Other sūtras further speak of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma).
How are such Buddha-qualities established?
By how many categories are they subsumed?
The answer is: it refers to an Arhat bhikṣu whose outflows are forever exhausted,
who enters a village to wander for alms,
and at some time travels along the same road as wicked elephants, wicked horses, wicked oxen, and wicked dogs.
Some enter dense thickets and tread upon thorny enclosures;
some stand on their tiptoes to leap over ditches and moats;
some enter such dwellings that are contrary to the Dharma.
They improperly entice women;
or, while in forest hermitages, they abandon the right path and travel along evil, wrong paths;
or they travel the same roads as thieves, lions, fierce beasts, jackals, wolves, leopards, and the like.
All such errors and lapses possessed by various arhats are forever absent in the Tathāgata. Furthermore,
at times an arhat may wander in a forest of great trees within a wilderness retreat (āraṇya).
They may lose their way or enter an empty house,
raising their voices in loud cries that resound far and wide;
or again, it may be due to the faults of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
With an undefiled mind,
he pursed his lips, bared his teeth, and laughed with a joyful air;
such were the various manifestations of this kind.
Whatever harsh sounds may arise from Arhats,
the Tathāgata is forever free from these.
Furthermore, at times an Arhat may, due to forgetfulness, [act in such a way].
There may be loss regarding the tasks to be accomplished;
however, the Tathāgata possesses none of this forever.
Furthermore, within the realm of saṃsāra characterized by the remainder of the aggregates, the Arhat [is subject to such].
One consistently gives rise to the perception of revulsion,
and within the realm of nirvana without remainder,
one consistently gives rise to the perception of tranquility.
The Tathāgata possesses the perception of non-differentiation regarding nirvāṇa with remainder,
because he dwells in the supreme equanimity of impartiality.
Furthermore, when an arhat enters meditative equipoise, it is termed "concentration."
If one were to emerge from meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), it would no longer be called "concentration" (*samādhi*);
yet the Tathāgata possesses no unconcentrated mind across all states.
Furthermore, an Arhat does not lack skillful discernment (*asuvicita*).
Consequently, they abandon the work of benefiting sentient beings.
Regarding such categories as these,
the Tathāgata does not fail to exercise skillful discernment.
Furthermore, they are abandoned and forever cease to exist. Moreover,
although an Arhat relies on the purification of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
they may still suffer a fall from what has not yet been attained, thereby losing their desire, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
These seven kinds of factors leading to decline are forever absent in the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, at times an Arhat may manifest wholesome bodily action.
At times, indeterminate karma may arise;
as it is with bodily action,
so it should be understood for vocal and mental actions as well.
Because the three types of action of the Tathāgata are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom,
there is no indeterminate (avyākṛta) action.
Because it arises from wisdom, it is called "preceded by wisdom" (*jñāna-pūrvamgama*);
because it proceeds together with wisdom, it is called "concomitant with wisdom" (*jñānānuvartana*).
Furthermore, regarding all objects of knowledge throughout the three periods of time, the Arhat—
One cannot understand through a casual or superficial mental engagement;
therefore, such knowledge and vision are said to be "possessing attachment.
One is unable to achieve a complete and exhaustive correct understanding.
Therefore, wisdom and vision are said to be "unimpeded.
The Tathāgata pervades the objects of the three periods of time;
with a mere momentary act of attention, he is able to correctly comprehend all knowable things and their various distinctions.
Therefore, these eighteen kinds are called the unshared Buddha-dharmas (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
Among them, the first four are comprised within the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*) and the eradication of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-prahāṇa*).
The next one is subsumed by great compassion;
the remainder should be understood as being subsumed by the sublime wisdom of all modes.
Furthermore, regarding the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) spoken of by the Blessed One in other sūtras:
It is displayed for the sake of inspiring pure faith in those to be converted;
however, no defining characteristics are established therein.
The establishment of various characteristics has already been extensively explained in the "Chapter on Establishment."
From these secondary marks (anuvyañjana),
one should know that those various secondary marks are produced; thus,
one should understand them as being of improper conduct (mithyācāra).
One should understand the correct practice of a bodhisattva;
one should understand the benefits of a bodhisattva’s correct practice;

and one should understand how a bodhisattva establishes the practice of the Dharma, the practice of equanimity, the practice of goodness, and the practice of abiding in the Dharma within that correct practice.
One should understand the analogies for how a bodhisattva can generate pure faith;
one should understand how a bodhisattva establishes their training within right practice;
and [one should understand] the training of the śrāvakas and the training of the bodhisattvas.
One should understand the distinctions of excellence.
Among all that bodhisattvas ought to learn,
there is the mundane and supramundane knowledge of well-trained bodhisattvas, as well as their activities for the benefit of others.
One should understand that within the instructions for bodhisattvas, there is also what is to be studied by śrāvakas;
this is how one should understand it.
One should understand that such a person is not a well-trained śramaṇa; rather,
they are a well-trained śramaṇa.
One should understand this.
One who abides in the conventional discipline should understand this.
One who abides in the ultimate discipline should understand the skillful means of the Tathāgatas for taming [sentient beings].
One should understand it;
one should understand the intentional language.
One should understand the benefits of resolute conviction within the instructions of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Thus, all the instructions contained within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka have been briefly set forth.
There are eight characteristics of the subsequent inducement:
first, the wrong practice that causes the loss of the accumulation of wisdom;
second, the wrong practice that causes forgetfulness due to the loss of the accumulation of wisdom.
Third, due to forgetfulness, one is able to destroy pure qualities through wrong conduct.
Fourth, because pure qualities have been destroyed, one is able to manifest wrong conduct through the active operation of malicious intentions that are contrary to the discipline of a bodhisattva.
Fifth, because malicious intentions are actively manifested, it causes conduct that is difficult to subdue;
sixth, because it is difficult to subdue, it causes one to practice on improper paths.
Seventh, because one practices a non-path, it causes one to associate with those who are not virtuous and engage in wrong conduct.
Eighth, because one associates with those who are not virtuous, it causes the bodhisattva’s practice to deviate from its true meaning through wrong conduct.
Furthermore, awakening has wisdom as its essence.
Wisdom is able to bring forth all the remaining perfections;
therefore, when one engages in wrong conduct regarding wisdom, [all other perfections are likewise impaired].
It should be known that a bodhisattva thereby engages in wrong practice regarding both that enlightenment and the dharmas that can bring about enlightenment.
There are four kinds of factors that cause a bodhisattva’s accumulation of wisdom to decline.
What are the four?
First, not listening to [the teaching] oneself;
second, not causing others to hear it.
Third, there is the obstacle to hearing.
Fourth, there is hearing with inverted attachment;
based on these, one causes the accumulation of wisdom to regress.
Due to these four factors,
in either the present life or a future life,
there further arise four kinds of mental states that are contrary to wisdom.
What are the four?
First, the absence of cognitive understanding;
second, the deficiency of various conditions.
Third, it can produce non-merit that induces delusion;
fourth, because one relies on inverted views and does not listen to the teachings oneself,
one lacks understanding regarding the present life.
Because one relies on not allowing others to hear [the Dharma],
there will be a deficiency of conditions for hearing it in future lives;
this serves as the basis for an obstacle to hearing.
It gives rise to non-meritorious karma that results from delusion in future lives;
because one relies upon listening [to the teachings] while holding perverted attachments,
one further increases such perversions within those future lives.
As for those who do not listen:
it is because they hate and reject the Dharma,
and because they hate and reject the person.
Regarding the phrase "because both increase aversion, one does not let others hear it":
this is because one fears that another's wisdom may surpass one's own,
and because of the presence of arrogance.
Because of the fear of being disparaged by others,
it constitutes an obstacle to hearing the Dharma,
as one slanders both the teaching and the person.
Because they are mutually entangled by the signs of misconduct and evasive speech;
because they do not allow for formal requests or permissions;
and because they employ skillful means to disparage those capable of listening.
Those who listen with perverted attachments do so because they grasp at and understand the teaching according to their own faulty realization,
while remaining attached to grasping at and understanding it through a virtuous realization.
Because one relies on others to thoroughly understand, comprehend, and proclaim what is wholesome,
whereas one clings to what is thoroughly understood, comprehended, and proclaimed as unwholesome; herein,
if one does not hear it oneself...
If one does not cause others to hear,
or if one creates obstacles to hearing—
these three factors [constitute such an offense].
For the most part, it causes one to lose the accumulation of wisdom consisting of what is heard;
one listens with inverted attachments.
For the most part, it causes one to lose the accumulations of wisdom consisting of reflection and cultivation.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas that cause a bodhisattva to lose right mindfulness.
What are these four?
This refers to being deluded regarding four types of persons in four respects:
first, regarding the person who reproves one of their faults.
Second, toward individuals who provide instruction;
third, toward individuals who wish to bring benefit;
and fourth, toward individuals who possess virtuous qualities.
That is to say: being confused regarding one's own faults in the presence of fellow practitioners of the holy life;
being confused regarding the training rules in the presence of the training;
and [being confused] regarding those who desire resolute conviction in that Mahāyāna.
Regarding the phrase "one who wishes to practice correctly," this reveals non-differentiation by setting forth and analyzing various faults.
They initiate a practice of deluded resolve,
whereby they misrepresent the hidden intentions of the person who preaches the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas that cause a bodhisattva to destroy pure and white dharmas (*śukladharma*).
That is to say, because of the power of competing with others, one initiates the application of various pure dharmas in an inappropriate manner (*asthāna-prayoga*).
Although one may initiate the preparatory application for the basis of pure dharmas (*śukladharma*),
there are nevertheless three kinds of faults of wrong practice (*mithyāpratipatti*).
The first is the fault of attachment (*saṅga*).
Second is the fault of wrong views;
third is the fault of grasping.
One should understand the fault of defiled attachment through these two causes and conditions.
First, because of improper enjoyment;
second, because of frequenting mixed company.
One should understand the faults of evil views through these two causes and conditions.
First, because they slander and reject the true Dharma and the individuals who uphold it;
second, because they manifest attachment to what is not the true Dharma, claiming it to be the true Dharma.
One should understand that these two causes and conditions constitute the faults of upholding [such teachings].
First, because they uphold only narrow and limited sutras of provisional meaning;
second, because they pre-emptively slander and repudiate those sutras of definitive meaning that they have not yet heard or received.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of un-Bodhisattva-like conduct involving the manifestation of malicious intent.
The first is to give rise to a lack of faith, compliance, and respect toward the Great Master, which is contrary to the marks of training.
First, the manifestation of malicious intent.

Second, the manifestation of malicious intent contrary to the truth when, regarding those who share the holy life—who have accepted one, raised charges against one, or are capable of instructing one—one fails to disclose one's own faults as they truly are.
Third, the manifestation of malice that is contrary to diligence regarding great wisdom, merit, and all wholesome dharmas;
fourth, [the manifestation of malice] regarding vast and profound resolute conviction.
