It should be understood that the manifestation of contrary evil intentions which cause one's own obscurations to be purified occurs through three types of association: namely,
the arising of lack of faith and non-compliance toward the Great Teacher.
This refers to obtaining knowledge regarding those who are substantial and venerable.
One should understand that there are three ways in which one fails to disclose one's own faults as they truly are:
first, with respect to those sentient beings whom one has taken under one's care.
First, because one falsely displays oneself as superior and eminent,
thereby giving rise to a mind of arrogance and haughtiness;
second, toward those sentient beings who are capable of censuring one's faults.
Third, because of concealing one's transgressions;
and third, because of the predominant influence of being expelled by those sentient beings who are capable of providing instruction and admonition.
Because one gives rise to a defiled and turbid mind and causes harm and affliction,
one should understand that there are two types of conditions through which diligence toward all wholesome dharmas is lost:
namely, [acting wrongly] toward sentient beings who possess great wisdom and merit.
Because of attachment to gain, offerings, and honor,
and because of delighting in them;
furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas that make it difficult for a bodhisattva to be disciplined.
This refers to four kinds of obstacles to correct cultivation:
first, regarding what has been heard as being the ultimate;
second, misunderstanding the instructions through erroneous comprehension.
Third, they do not dwell properly in ethical discipline and have many instances of regret;
fourth, they dwell in their own views and cling to those views with dogmatic attachment.
This means that because their minds are not tranquilized by mere hearing,
they cling to hearing as the ultimate goal;
this is due to their inverted conceptualization regarding the instructions.
There is wrongdoing because one has misunderstood the instructions;
because one accepts offerings from the faithful while frequently violating the precepts (śīla);
and because one engages in disputes and rivalries with superior beings.
Regarding those superior beings who dwell predominantly in dogmatic attachment to their own views,
this refers to superiority in the taming of the faculties and superiority in abandonment.
Furthermore, there are four ways in which a bodhisattva acts improperly toward sentient beings.
First, failing to teach those sentient beings who have not yet established pure faith.
Second, not teaching according to what is appropriate for those sentient beings who seek the Great Vehicle while being situated in the Lesser Vehicle;
third, [not teaching according to what is appropriate] for those sentient beings who seek the Lesser Vehicle while being situated in the Great Vehicle.
Fourth, they preach according to their own inclinations rather than following proper ritual decorum;
and fourth, whether abiding by the prohibitive precepts or not abiding by them, they harbor craving for and partiality toward their own factions,
preaching with partiality.
One should know that by means of three characteristics, this is called abiding in the precepts:
first, because one's activities are free from fault;
second, because one’s ethical discipline (*śīla*) is without deficiency.
Third, because they do not revere what they have studied.
One should understand that non-abiding in the prohibitive precepts arises from two types of conditions:
first, because the ethical discipline (*śīla*) is deficient.
Second, because they do not show respect for what they have studied.
Furthermore, due to associating with those who are not virtuous,
a bodhisattva falls away from four matters.
First, the falling away from the vehicle;
second, the falling away from the application of benefiting sentient beings.
Third, the falling away from the noble teaching;
fourth, the falling away from the uninterrupted cultivation of all wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of bodhisattvas who do not accord with their name.
First, upholding the true Dharma;
second, dwelling in an araṇya;
third, diligently cultivating meritorious deeds.
Fourth is governing the great assembly.

This means that although bodhisattvas wish to inspire faith and submission, even their upholding of the true Dharma would not be in accordance with its true meaning [if they failed to govern properly].
It is not as it appears.
If bodhisattvas dwell in forest hermitages merely for the sake of seeking reputation,
[they do not truly abide therein].
It is also not in accordance with reality; it is not as it truly is.
This is because if bodhisattvas fix their minds exclusively upon the fruits of attachment and defilement.
Although one diligently cultivates meritorious deeds,
they are nonetheless not in accordance with the meaning;
they do not accord with the true meaning.
If bodhisattvas fix their minds exclusively on service and reputation,
then even though they govern a great assembly, it is not in accordance with the Dharma; it is not as it should be.
Furthermore, what is right practice?
It refers to that which is contrary to the aforementioned [faults],
being free from those defects and proclaiming their remedies.
One should know that the eight modes of activity induced by each subsequent stage are called "right practice.
This refers to the teaching that through one's own failure to hear [the Dharma], wisdom is caused to decline and be lost.
For what reason?
Because it is manifested by a lack of respect for the true Dharma and for persons [who uphold it].
It is through this that one commits an offense.
Even if one does not commit transgressions, if there is no resolute conviction (*adhimukti*),
one will consequently fall away.
Furthermore, it is said that by not allowing [others] to hear [the Dharma], one causes wisdom to decline.
For what reason?
Because it is manifested by the desire to cause others to have faith and submission;
it is due to this transgression.
If one does not violate [the precepts] but dedicates them toward false teachings,
for this reason one falls away.
Furthermore, it is said that through the hindrance of hearing, wisdom is caused to decline.
For what reason?
Because it is manifested by not wishing to hear, not hearing, and not upholding [the teachings].
It is through this that one commits an offense.
Furthermore, even if one does not commit transgressions,
one may still fall away due to indolence and laziness.
Moreover, it is said that through false attachments, one hears [the teachings] in a way that causes wisdom to decline.
For what reason?
Because it is manifested by the fact that, while practicing, one perceives no actual merit but regards mere verbal expression as the ultimate goal;
it is due to this that one commits an offense.
If one does not refrain from transgressing, wisdom will not become perfected;
therefore, one falls away.
Furthermore, it is said that by being confused by the one who points out the fault, one causes one's own transgressions to cause the loss of mindfulness.
For what reason?
Because one fears loss regarding serious matters,
and fears censure regarding minor matters.
Because it is manifested through the commission of false speech,
one commits an infraction;
and due to this karmic obstruction, there occurs forgetfulness.
Even if one has not committed a transgression, there may still be forgetfulness due to the obstacle of transgression (*āpatti-āvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, it is said that confusion regarding the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) causes the loss of mindfulness.
What is the cause and condition for this?
Because it is manifested by the crookedness of false views that do not accord with intrinsic nature,
one commits transgressions through this;
and due to karmic obstructions, there is forgetfulness.
Even if one does not commit a transgression, there may still be forgetfulness due to the obstacle of transgression.
Furthermore, it is said that confusion regarding the Mahāyāna causes the loss of mindfulness concerning resolute conviction and correct practice.
For what reason?
Because it is manifested by the failure to generate respect for bodhisattvas and by concealing their actual virtues;
it is through this that one commits an offense.
Due to karmic obstructions, there is forgetfulness.
Even if one has not committed a transgression, there is forgetfulness due to the obstruction of transgressions.
Furthermore, it is said that through delusion and confusion, the hidden points are revealed, causing mindfulness to be lost.
For what reason?
Because it is manifested by the fact that one does not give rise to a desire for the Mahāyāna;
it is through this that one commits an offense.
Due to karmic obstructions, there is forgetfulness.
Even if one has not committed a transgression, due to the obstruction of transgression, there is forgetfulness.
Furthermore, it is said that through application in an improper place, the pure and bright dharmas are destroyed.
For what reason?
Because it is characterized by delighting in one’s own narrow self-interest without turning toward others,
and because the mind does not become humble through hearing the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna).
Due to this transgression,
one fails to attain those pure dharmas not yet attained,
because of the resulting slackness in what has been heard and received.
One falls away from what has been attained.
Furthermore, it is said that through the fault of defiled craving, the pure and bright dharmas are destroyed.
What is the cause and condition for this?
Because one does not find contentment with the gains and offerings received at home,
and because deceptive practices and the like are manifested by the presence of expectation,
one thereby commits an offense.
Due to not hearing the Dharma not previously heard,
one becomes distracted by many activities and restlessness,
and is unable to realize samādhi.
Furthermore, it is said that one destroys the pure and bright dharmas (*śukladharma*) through the fault of wrong views.
What is the cause and condition for this?
It is because of harboring malicious intent.
Regarding others,
because his mind is inverted with respect to what is to be studied in both the Śrāvaka and Mahāyāna vehicles,
he thereby commits an offense.
One incurs decline through improper conduct;
one incurs decline through deceiving others.
Furthermore, it is said that by upholding faults, one destroys the pure, bright dharmas.
For what reason?
Because it is manifested by the conceit of omniscience arising within the intentional wisdom of the Tathāgata.
It is due to this transgression.
One incurs ruin by slandering the true Dharma;
one incurs ruin by erroneously evaluating the intentional meaning within the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
It is further stated that because one does not show sufficient reverence for what is to be trained in, malicious intent manifests.
What is the cause and condition for this?
It is because one fails to disclose and confess the transgressions committed.
Because it is manifested by the non-removal of regret (*kaukṛtya*).
Due to this active manifestation,
because there is distraction regarding the object of focus (*ālambana*), the mental activity is not clear.
Furthermore, it is said that malice manifests because one fails to disclose one's own faults as they truly are.
What is the cause and condition for this?
It is due to attachment and longing for one's body and possessions.
Because pleasure is not revealed by the words of truth;
for this reason, when it manifests,
there is distraction regarding the sacred teaching.
One's conduct is not clear.
Furthermore, it is said that due to the conditions of diligence and indolence,
unwholesome intentions manifest.
For what reason?
Because it is manifested by way of intolerance;
it is through this that it becomes active.
Because they cannot endure various sufferings and because their minds are distracted from wholesome dharmas,
their practice is not clear.
Furthermore, it is said that evil intentions manifest due to the causes and conditions of the purification of hindrances.
What are the causes and conditions for this?
Because the Mahāyāna is manifested by means of superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*),
and because one becomes distracted from the vast Mahāyāna through the manifestation of these [opposing states].
Their practice is not clear.
Furthermore, it is said that due to merely hearing [the teachings], the obstacles to ultimate cultivation are difficult to subdue.
What is the reason for this?
Because this is manifested by hearing the discourse on the benefits of liberation from difficulties through mere contemplative observation,
one thereby commits an infraction by deceitfully pretending to be a virtuous friend who upholds the Dharma.
Furthermore, it is said that those who have a distorted understanding of the instructions and whose cultivation is obstructed are difficult to discipline.
For what reason? Because they are incapable of receiving the teachings and stubbornly persist in their transgressions.
Because they fail to show respect for the teacher as revealed [in the scriptures],
they commit such transgressions and hypocritically display themselves as virtuous friends dwelling in forest hermitages (*āraṇyaka*).
Furthermore, it is said that because one does not dwell firmly in ethical discipline (*śīla*), the hindrance of remorseful cultivation is difficult to subdue.
What is the reason for this?
It is because one lacks profound respect for the trainings.
Because they falsely accept the offerings of the faithful,
they commit transgressions and deceitfully display themselves as virtuous friends diligently cultivating meritorious deeds.
Furthermore, it is said that because they abide in their own views and cling to those views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), they are difficult to tame and constitute an obstacle to cultivation. For what reason?
Because [they are opposed] to the bodhisattvas who possess the pure pāramitās.
They do not give rise to reverence; they do not wish to gaze upon [the teacher];
they do not wish to draw near;
and they do not wish to listen.
Because it is manifested by not practicing in accordance with the Dharma,
one commits such transgressions and deceitfully displays oneself as a virtuous friend who guides the community.
Furthermore, it is said that this is due to not proclaiming,
not proclaiming in accordance [with reality],
and not proclaiming in a manner consistent with the meaning.
To speak with partiality is to act upon an unrighteous path.
For what reason?
Because one speaks with a weary and biased mind from beginning to end.
Because they lack knowledge of the skillful means regarding what is taught;
because they possess the resolute conviction of the Lesser Vehicle and a mind stained by attachment;
and because their instruction of disciples is manifested through [merely] preparatory application.
Due to this transgression,
due to the incompleteness of their roots of virtue,
and due to their failure to embrace vast roots of virtue.
Because they abandon vast roots of virtue,
because they produce non-merit,
and because they deceive and delude the various classes of sentient beings who are to be converted.
It is further stated that through four kinds of intimacy with those who are not virtuous, one falls away from four matters.
What is the cause and condition for this?
It is due to stinginess, meager learning, and improper entry into the holy teaching.
Because it is manifested by not hearing the Buddha’s words,
and because one does not cultivate roots of goodness due to this transgression.
Because they fear the suffering of birth and death;
because they are unable to perform deeds for the benefit of others;
and because their roots of virtue are narrow and meager.
Because there is doubt and confusion regarding all phenomena,
there is retrogression and loss.
Furthermore, it is said that this occurs because of four kinds of bodhisattvas who seek to inspire faith and submission.
To seek renown, to seek the fruits of defilement,
and to seek offerings, service, and fame— these are not in accordance with the true meaning for bodhisattvas.
For what reason?
Because, being accompanied by self-love, they perceive no fear in even subtle transgressions;
and because, lacking resolute conviction in selflessness, they disregard the welfare of others.
Because they view the faults of saṃsāra and the merits of nirvāṇa from a one-sided perspective;
because they delight in dwelling in association with others in the present life;
and because they take pleasure in wealth and status in future lives, as manifested by their grasping for material goods and the Dharma.
Due to such transgressions,
one falsely manifests oneself as being able to correctly uphold the Dharma and even lead the community.
Furthermore, what are the benefits of correct practice?
This also has four types,
which should be understood in their successive order.
Such is the bodhisattva who practices correctly.
Because it enables the accumulation of the provisions of merit and wisdom;
because, by relying upon this, obstacles are purified;
and because, by relying upon this, all pure dharmas are integrated through every gateway.
Because by relying on this, one initiates all kinds of applications for the benefit of sentient beings,
and because it can further produce immeasurable merit; furthermore,
there are four dharmas that enable the accumulation of the provisions of merit and wisdom.
First, relying on this correct practice, one makes offerings to and serves all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas;
second, purity of hearing;
third, purity of reflection.
Fourth is the cultivation of purity.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that can cause obstructions to become pure:
first, being naturally unmoving regarding the vehicle.
Second, the cause and condition for remaining far removed from [harming] sentient beings;
third, the cause and condition for remaining far removed from wrong conduct;
fourth, the cause and condition for remaining far removed from incomplete right conduct.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that enable the complete integration of all gateways of pure dharmas (*śukladharma*).
First, the cultivation of what is to be cultivated;
second, the maturation of sentient beings, which is accomplished through that very [cultivation].
Third, being able to endure difficult tasks is what is accomplished thereby.

Fourth, never becoming weary of hearing and reflecting is what is accomplished thereby. Furthermore, there are four other dharmas that enable one to perform every kind of beneficial activity for sentient beings.
That is to say, there are four situations in which one rescues sentient beings:
first, from states of doubt and hesitation;
second, from falling into the utterly defiled and evil realms of existence.
Third, regarding the sphere of faith and understanding in the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*);
fourth, regarding the sphere of the mind of malice that reviles and rejects the holy teaching.
Furthermore, how does a bodhisattva act when currently engaged in correct practice?
One still attains such meritorious benefits as these:
namely, practicing with equanimity within the practice of the Dharma,
and practicing virtuous conduct.
The characteristics of dwelling in the Dharma.
How does a bodhisattva possess the practice of the Dharma?
What are the characteristics of this practice?
It means that whatever practices Bodhisattvas undertake do not transcend the true Dharma;
therefore, this is called being "endowed with the practice of the Dharma.
It should be known that this practice has five aspects.
First, toward those sentient beings who act harmfully and delight in evil conduct,
it is because one desires to lead them into goodness through compassionate gathering;
second, toward those sentient beings who abide in the spiritual lineage but lack external conditions.
First, because they encourage others to generate the bodhicitta;
second, because they themselves understand the excellence of the pāramitās; and third, [because they understand] within the excellence of the pāramitās.
Fourth, because one initiates the application of reverence,
prostration, and homage toward those who are worthy of respect.
Fifth, [because one does so] toward sentient beings who are non-Buddhist outsiders or enemies.
Because they abide securely in the holy teachings without wavering.
How does a bodhisattva possess impartial conduct?
What are the characteristics of this conduct?
This means that bodhisattvas practice with equanimity throughout all activities for the benefit of sentient beings; therefore,
they are said to be "endowed with equal conduct."
It should be known that this practice has eight aspects:
first, because of equal affection for all sentient beings;
second, because of an undefiled and undifferentiated body toward all sentient beings.
There is no differentiation of time;
there is no differentiation of seeking,
because they comfort and console with equal affection.
Third, by abandoning all clamor and bustle, one maintains a relaxed countenance and a pleasant disposition,
because one is able to carry the burden already taken up with equanimity.
Fourth, one is able to take up the burden not yet taken up with equanimity.
Fifth, because of being able to endure all suffering with equanimity;
sixth, because of being able to seek with equanimity the immeasurable skillful means of discipline;
seventh, because of possessing speech that is correct and patient, which is mutually equal toward one another.
Eighth, because all roots of goodness are dedicated equally toward great enlightenment.
How does a bodhisattva possess virtuous conduct?
What are the characteristics of this practice?
This means that bodhisattvas practice virtuous conduct in order to mature the qualities of a buddha within themselves and to mature all sentient beings externally.
Therefore, it is called being "endowed with virtuous conduct.
One should know that this conduct has seven aspects:
first, giving without any basis for dependence.
Second, because one maintains the precepts without relying on anything;
third, because one cultivates patience out of a heart of compassion;
fourth, because one does not practice diligence in a merely limited way.
Fifth, because one cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) for the sake of bringing benefit to all sentient beings;
sixth, because one cultivates sublime wisdom (*prajñā*) through the vision of non-correspondence;
and seventh, because of the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) that bring [beings] to maturity.
How does a bodhisattva possess the abiding in the Dharma?
What is its mode of practice?
It means that bodhisattvas do not regard mere pursuit as the ultimate goal.
It is not merely reciting and chanting that constitutes the ultimate;
it is not merely proclaiming and explaining that constitutes the ultimate;
it is not merely investigating and reflecting that constitutes the ultimate.
And within the superior cultivation of internal śamatha,
he applies diligent means and practices with balanced development.
Therefore, it is called "being endowed with the abiding in the Dharma.
It should be known that this abiding has twelve aspects.
The first is, regarding the instruction on both abiding in the precepts and not abiding in the precepts.
Because it is non-conceptual;
second, because one respectfully receives the instructions by relying upon this.
Third, by relying on this,
one is physically secluded.
Fourth, by relying on this...
Fifth, because the mind is detached,
one relies upon this as a basis to transcend the mental engagement associated with the Śrāvaka vehicle and to cultivate the mental engagement associated with the Mahāyāna.
Sixth, relying upon this,
one does not abandon the yoke of seclusion because one dwells together with all sentient beings.
And because he dwells together with the remainder;
seventh, because by relying on this,
he experiences the fruit of cultivation— the majesty and the great accumulation of merit of pure mundane knowledge.
Eighth, one does not find contentment with mundane knowledge,
because one seeks to cultivate and refine supramundane knowledge.
Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of purity:
One abandons four kinds of faults because of governing the great assembly.
The first is the fault of being unable to endure provocation and disturbance.
Second, the fault of teaching instructions that are not definitive;
third, the fault of acting contrary to what was said;
fourth, the fault of having a mind stained by attachment.
These four types together with the previous eight constitute twelve aspects in total.
Furthermore, what are the similes for how a bodhisattva is able to generate pure faith?
This means that from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment,
bodhisattvas serve as the basis for eliciting roots of virtue in all sentient beings throughout the initial, middle, and final stages; thus,
they act universally toward all, whether they are enemies or benefactors.
The mind is without attachment, just like the great earth;
yet, the bodhisattvas do not function with the same indifference as the earth,
for sentient beings rely upon them to exert their own effort.
Only then can they survive;
yet these bodhisattvas cultivate roots of goodness,
possessing pure faith and joy.
Because it is able to provide nourishment,
it is like a great body of water;
yet, bodhisattvas are not like a great body of water that is incompatible with the ripening of crops.
Nevertheless, because bodhisattvas desire to bring their various roots of goodness to maturity,
they develop a profound sense of wearying revulsion toward phenomena that should be reviled,
for these [phenomena] are capable of burning and refining them.
It is like a great fire;
yet, for the bodhisattvas, this does not contradict their gathering in the buddha-fields.
Rather, these bodhisattvas are able to cause those whose roots of goodness are already matured [to attain realization].
It brings about the attainment of the contact of liberation through the accumulation [of conditions],
because it is able to give rise to correct instruction,
just like a great wind.
Yet, these bodhisattvas are not like a great wind that, having once arisen, ultimately returns to extinction;
rather, because these bodhisattvas cause their own pure dharmas to increase and flourish.
They are like the bright moon;
yet these bodhisattvas are not like the bright moon, which shines with radiant light only during the waxing phase and not during the waning phase.
Nevertheless, all bodhisattvas are equal in their characteristics;
for within all phenomena, whether black or white,
their wisdom shines universally.
They are like the orb of the sun;
yet, unlike the sun which turns back in fear of being seized by Rāhu,
all the bodhisattvas [do not turn back] from any of the realms of existence.
Because they never fear being turned around by the grasping of afflictions,
Bodhisattvas are like lions;
yet, unlike lions, they do not shrink from great burdens.
However, because bodhisattvas are able to bear the great burden of all suffering,
they are like well-tamed dragons;
yet, unlike dragon-elephants, bodhisattvas are not shaken when encountering gain or loss.
Whether speech is gentle or harsh,
whether it concerns pleasure or pain,
it is defiled by attachment and aversion.
However, because all bodhisattvas are not defiled by attachment or aversion toward worldly dharmas,
they are like red lotuses.
Yet, unlike the red lotus which, once its stalk is severed, no longer grows,
the bodhisattvas, although they have subdued their afflictions,
are sustained by the power of their roots of virtue.
Because they continue to grow within the cycle of birth and death,
just as the roots of a great tree remain undamaged;
yet these bodhisattvas are not like the roots of a great tree, which are certain to be destroyed at a later time.
However, because all the roots of goodness possessed by bodhisattvas are dedicated toward nirvana and great enlightenment,
they are like various streams flowing into the great ocean.
Yet, these bodhisattvas are not like those streams that, upon entering the great ocean, immediately become of the nature of the sea.
Nevertheless, because all bodhisattvas sport by relying on the power of the roots of goodness associated with nirvāṇa and great enlightenment,
they are like the gods who dwell upon Mount Sumeru.
Yet these bodhisattvas do not dwell upon Mount Sumeru like the various devas,
who remain exclusively indulgent in their own affairs.
They experience much happiness;
yet, because Bodhisattvas are sustained by skillful means and wisdom,
they accomplish all that is to be done by Buddhas.
For example, there is a great king supported by his ministers;
however, the bodhisattvas are not like a great king supported by his ministers,
for they protect the people of the country for their own benefit.
Nevertheless, these bodhisattvas disregard their own benefit to gather in and protect sentient beings,
just like a great cloud.
Yet these bodhisattvas are not like great clouds that cannot ultimately bring crops to fruition;
rather, these bodhisattvas ultimately cause the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) to grow.
Just as a wheel-turning monarch appears in the world,
yet the bodhisattvas are not like a wheel-turning monarch in that they lack a second assembly of great men;
nevertheless, the liberation of all bodhisattvas is equal.
Those born from roots of goodness mostly appear together,
like a maṇi jewel;
yet bodhisattvas are not like a maṇi jewel, for they are utterly unlike a kāṛṣāpaṇa coin.
However, because all bodhisattvas enter the untainted realm (anāsravadhātu),
their activities are equal,
as they experience identical bliss.
For example, it is like the devas who have entered the Grove of Miscellaneous Trees;
yet these bodhisattvas do not experience an increase in afflictions or a future downfall, as those devas do.
However, because bodhisattvas have subdued their afflictions and do not fall into error,
all their afflictions are like poisons subdued by incantations and the like;
such are the afflictions of bodhisattvas.
It is not like the various poisons subdued by mantras and the like,
which merely do no harm and possess no further virtues;
rather, it is because of their own afflictions that the bodhisattvas [act].
Because they are able to bring about the benefit of all sentient beings,
these afflictions are like heaps of filth within a great city;
such is the nature of all the virtues possessed by a bodhisattva.
Because the coarse [aspects] are things commonly known in the world,
they can serve as analogies;
however, these virtues are so preeminent that [they cannot be fully grasped by such means].
There is no analogy for it;
therefore, one should know that the merit of a bodhisattva cannot be reached by any analogy whatsoever.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 79;
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle 80;
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Within the Section on the Compendium of Determinations (*Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*), the Ninth [Section] of the Bodhisattvabhūmi: Furthermore, how does a bodhisattva establish their training within correct practice?
This refers to those bodhisattvas who are fully established in the Dharma,

regarding those scriptures associated with the Śrāvaka vehicle that are of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) and taught according to the principles of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which they do not rely upon.
Having already established the basis and having already attained skillfulness,
they further transcend that which accords with the Mahāyāna and accords with profound emptiness—
the definitive meaning as explained through the principles of the conventional and ultimate truths.
When one diligently practices and studies in reliance upon the sūtras,
it is called "rightly and correctly practicing with diligence.
When one thus practices with diligence in accordance with reason, [it is called right practice].
This is called the supreme practice of the Middle Way within correct cultivation. Why is this so?
Because this True Dharma penetrates the thirteen practices of the Middle Way.
First, the penetration of the emptiness of the person (pudgala-śūnyatā);
second, the penetration of the selflessness of the person (pudgala-nairātmya);
third, the penetration of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
Fourth is the penetration of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Fifth is the penetration of the extreme of superimposition (*samāropa-anta*).
Sixth is the penetration of the extreme of denial (*apavāda-anta*).
Seventh is the penetration of the realization of the dharma (*dharmābhisamaya*).
Eighth is the dedication of the penetration of the realization of the dharma toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
Ninth is the state in which the mind of such a practitioner is not entangled by the afflictions or the manifold sufferings.
Tenth, the penetration of the distinction in the resolute conviction regarding the two kinds of selflessness;
eleventh, the penetration that the nature of selflessness previously [discussed] is the causal nature for what follows;
twelfth, the penetration of the emptiness that reaches the ultimate limit.
Thirteenth is the penetration of that very majesty.
How does one penetrate the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*)?
It is by means of a single characteristic.
Because it is manifested by way of non-apprehension. In this context,
"non-apprehension" refers to three kinds of things.
First, the matter of sentient beings;
second, the matter of their distinctions;
third, the matter of their enjoyment.
Whether internally, externally, or in between the two,
a self that is conceptually constructed as real by the foolish is entirely unfindable.
How, then, can one penetrate the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*)?
This means that it is because what is to be manifested can be apprehended by means of a single characteristic.
In this context, "apprehended" refers to:
This means that within those very dependently arisen phenomena, which are universally imagined by fools regarding those three things, a permanent and real nature cannot be found;
however, the principle of a self with distinct characteristics as imagined by fools can be found [as a logical negation].
How does one penetrate the emptiness of phenomena?
It is by means of a single characteristic:
because they are revealed as being unapprehendable.
In this context, that which is unapprehendable is the very impermanence of those phenomena,
whether internal, external, or between the two.
The imputed nature of verbal expression, which is conceptually constructed by the foolish, is entirely unfindable.
How, then, does one penetrate the selflessness of phenomena?
It is said: solely by means of a single characteristic.
Because it is that which is revealed by what is attainable. In this context,
"attainable" means that within those very phenomena, the principle is attainable as the domain of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
Furthermore, that which is personally realized within oneself cannot be expressed in words for the sake of others.
By means of six characteristics, the distinct nature of the conceptualized and verbally designated intrinsic nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is perceived by ordinary, ignorant people.
What are the six characteristics?
First, they cannot be investigated by oneself;
second, they cannot be explained to others.
Third, it transcends the domain of the physical sense faculties;
fourth, it transcends all signs;
fifth, it transcends the domain of consciousness.
Sixth is the transcendence of the sphere of activity of the afflictions.
How does one penetrate the extreme of superimposition?
It is by means of two aspects.
First, because it is manifested through the superimposition of distinctions;
second, because it is manifested through the superimposition of intrinsic nature.
What is meant by the superimposition of distinctions?
That is to say, by means of eight successive and mutually related characteristics:
first, the superimposition of permanence upon that very object;
second, the superimposition of impermanence.
Third, taking the superimposition of permanence as a basis;
and fourth, taking the superimposition of self as a basis. Fourth, taking the superimposition of impermanence as a basis.
Fifth, based upon the superimposition of the non-existent self,
there is the superimposition of a truly existent mind.
Sixth is the adherence to the self as a basis for augmentation,
and the adherence to the unreal mind as an augmentation;
this, moreover, is of two kinds.
First is determination;
second is seeking.
As for seeking:
This refers to the basis of pervasive conceptualization and that which is associated with pervasive conceptualization.
Within the afflicted phenomena that are to be countered, there are five faults, namely:
the fault of perversion.
The fault of conceptual proliferation,
the fault of initiating unwholesome conduct,
and the fault of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
The fault of impermanence,
and regarding the pure dharmas that serve as its antidote,
the seventh is the adherence to a truly existent mind, which is superimposed as the basis.
Grasping at the augmentation of the virtuous and so forth,
up to grasping at the augmentation of purity;
eighth, grasping at the augmentation of the unreal mind as its basis.
Grasping at the augmentation of the unwholesome and so forth,
up to grasping at the augmentation of affliction—
this is called the eightfold differentiation of augmentation.
In this regard, the bodhisattva does not at all cling to those superimpositions;
nor does he encourage others to cling to them,
nor does he praise them.
What is called the superimposition of intrinsic nature?
It refers to the superimposition of intrinsic nature through the conceptual proliferation of speech by the ignorant, based upon the superimposition of distinctions.
That is to say, one superimposes existence upon that very object.
How does one penetrate [the truth] by way of negation?
It is by means of a single characteristic.
Because it is manifested by the negation of real entities.
In this context, the negation of real entities refers to the arising of resolute conviction regarding the selflessness of those very same false phenomena.
Since the signs of all phenomena in every respect are entirely non-existent,
how does one penetrate the clear realization of phenomena?
It is said to be by means of three aspects.

First, because it is manifested by the fact that intrinsic nature is unapprehendable within the establishment of the objects to be remedied and their remedies, as well as the conditioned and the unconditioned,
regarding those very phenomena and the phenomena of the fourth birth.
Second, because it is manifested by the fact that their differentiation cannot be apprehended;
third, because it is manifested by the wisdom that penetrates reality as it is, due to the thorough cultivation of that very [wisdom].
In this context, that which is unfindable as intrinsic nature refers to the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) constructed by all foolish worldlings.
In this context, that which is unfindable as specific difference [refers to...].
This means that the two parts—the cessation and the arising of that very intrinsic nature—and their accumulation cannot be apprehended.
Regarding the penetration of wisdom herein:

it refers to the penetration of wisdom realized within oneself through the non-attention, non-contemplation, and non-deliberation regarding the characteristics of that very intrinsic nature, even while engaging in application.
What is the penetration of the realization of the Dharma (dharmābhisamaya) that is dedicated toward the nature of great enlightenment?
It is by means of a single characteristic.
This is because one does not abandon the remedies and the objects to be remedied that have been discerned through investigation.
Among these, the remedy and the object to be remedied refer to the fact that emptiness is the antidote to the afflictions.
The wishless (*apraṇihita*) is the antidote to wishing;
the signless (*animitta*) is the antidote to signs.
All such as these are termed "non-constructive" (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
Furthermore, this is the antidote to karma that leads to future existence;
it is also the antidote to the momentary arising and the arising of the stream of existence.
The practice of extinguishing afflictions is called "having no intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, this takes the cyclic flow of birth and death as its object of counteraction.
If bodhisattvas, by means of this counteraction, [proceed...]
One gives rise to discernment to sever that which is to be countered;
this is because of compassion for all sentient beings and the aspiration for great enlightenment.
How does such a practitioner penetrate [the truth] so that the afflictions and manifold sufferings do not ensnare the mind?
It is by means of a single characteristic.
Although one has not yet permanently severed the factors to be countered,
one is nevertheless able to penetrate them as they truly are.
In this context, "penetrating as they truly are" means:
That is to say, by means of the application of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) regarding those very phenomena,
one contemplates their intrinsic nature as being without defilement and without suffering.
How is this [contemplation] distinguished?
That is to say, by way of four aspects:
first, because it is manifested through the distinction of views;
second, because it is manifested through the distinction of extreme and remote denial of that very [reality].
Third, because it is manifested by the distinction between confusion regarding abandonment;
fourth, because it is manifested by the distinction between confusion regarding the mind.
Among these, "distinction regarding views" refers to:
This refers to those who, abiding in the selflessness of persons and in nirvāṇa,
give rise to the overweening pride of annihilation regarding their future bodies,
and who furthermore engage in the observation of the grasped object.
Because it is utterly devoid of the nature of the verbal expression of the grasper and is not observed as being subsumed within emptiness,
it is called the poorly examined objective domain of the knowable.
Because they cling to all phenomena, [śrāvakas] seek the cessation of afflictions;
however, bodhisattvas do not act in this way.
In this regard, there is an extremely remote distinction in terms of diminution.
This refers to one who dwells in the selflessness of persons,
and who, by means of two causes and conditions, views the self as inferior, more inferior, or even most inferior to others.
That is to say: because one is not liberated from suffering;
because one dwells in suffering;
and because of the loss and ruin caused by the two types of attachment, namely those of the past and the future.
Bodhisattvas, however, are not like this.
Regarding the distinction between the loss and the severance [of delusion] herein,
it refers to abiding in the selflessness of persons (pudgala-nairātmya).
Because they perceive that phenomena are without self and lack intrinsic nature,
they give rise to alarm and fear,
asserting that there is no expressible intrinsic nature and seeking its total annihilation.
The bodhisattvas, however, are not like this.
In this context, the distinction regarding delusion with respect to the mind refers to how such delusion regarding abandonment abides in the personhood-self (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
Within the objects arising from one's own pervasive conceptualization,
one is inverted by such things as the inversion of perception;
however, the bodhisattvas are not like this.
What is the nature of the causal penetration?
It is by way of two characteristics:
first, because it is observed as that which is manifested by the grasper.
Second, because it is manifested through his thorough realization as it truly is.
Herein, the observation of the grasper refers to the observation of this very wisdom of selflessness.
Because it is free from the intrinsic nature of verbal expression;
because it is free from that conceptualization;
and because its signs should be relinquished.
Because there are moments.
In this context, "thoroughly penetrating it as it truly is" refers to observing the two types: the grasped object and the grasping subject.
With correct mental attention as the cause,
there arises an individually realized, definitive wisdom.
How does it penetrate to the limit of emptiness?
This means that by way of a single characteristic,
the wisdom realizing the selflessness of those very phenomena manifests as it truly is.
In this context, "manifesting as it truly is" refers to—
This means that it manifests as being similar in appearance to karma and afflictions,
because it is an ineffable dharma and because its intrinsic nature transcends verbal expression.
Because there is no such attachment and because there is momentariness,
how does one penetrate the majestic power of that very emptiness?
This means that it is manifested by a single characteristic:
as the antidote for the abandonment of karma and afflictions.
In this context, "abandonment" refers to—
That is to say, when that momentary perception of light arises,
it is able to sever all karmas and afflictions accumulated since beginningless time;
what difference is there [between this and other states]?
It is said that there are four kinds of śrāvakas.
One should know that there are thirteen kinds of distinctions between what the śrāvakas train in and what the bodhisattvas train in.
What are called the four kinds of śrāvakas?
First, the transformation śrāvakas;
second, the śrāvakas of overweening pride;
third, the śrāvakas who have turned toward bodhi.
The fourth are the śrāvakas who are exclusively oriented toward tranquility.
As for the emanated śrāvakas, they exist for the purpose of transforming and delivering sentient beings.
For the sake of those sentient beings to be converted,
either bodhisattvas or tathāgatas manifest as śrāvakas,
including those śrāvakas who possess overweening pride.
That is to say, one reckons [these two] as purification solely by means of the knowledge of the selflessness of persons and the knowledge of the selflessness of erroneously grasped phenomena.
Regarding those śrāvakas who turn toward bodhi:
this refers to those whose lineage of compassion has been extremely feeble from the very beginning, yet who,
by virtue of attending upon and dwelling with the Tathāgata, [attain such a state].
Within the vast Buddha-dharma, they conceive the thought of great merit;
thus perfuming and cultivating their mental continuity,
they eventually reach the ultimate state and abide in the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
Having been awakened, introduced, and guided by the skillful means of the Buddhas,
they are able to set out toward vast enlightenment by virtue of this cause;
thus, regarding such vast enlightenment, they...
Although they are able to set out on the path, because they delight in tranquility,
their application of effort is extremely sluggish;
they are not like those who possess the Buddha-lineage and have first resolved to attain enlightenment.
Those śrāvakas who are exclusively oriented toward tranquility are so called because,
from the very beginning, they possess an extremely inferior lineage of compassion and because they are consistently averse to the work of benefiting sentient beings.
Because they are utterly terrified by the suffering of birth and death,
they possess only the aspiration for nirvāṇa and are ultimately unable to proceed toward great enlightenment.
It is like two princes born of similar lineage who equally and identically enjoy royal pleasures;
yet one becomes thoroughly proficient in the arts of governance, poetry, treatises, crafts, and so forth.
The second prince was not like this;
the distinction between those two arose solely from this difference,
and not from their enjoyment of the king's pleasures.
In this way, one should understand the distinction between the assembly of bodhisattvas within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) and the śrāvakas who are exclusively intent upon tranquility.
Furthermore, it should be understood that there is yet another distinction between these two.
That is to say: by way of intention,
by way of the accumulation of pure dharmas,
and by way of the accumulation of wisdom.
By way of category,
by way of lineage,
and by way of maintaining the seed.
By way of application,
by way of majestic power,
and by way of correct practice.
Because it is a field of merit;
because of its distinguished excellence;
and because of cause and effect.
Because they rely on birth,
śrāvakas who are solely intent upon tranquility abandon all conditioned activities and the benefit of sentient beings through the defilements,
and thus remain exclusively settled in a disposition of tranquility.
Although Bodhisattvas possess defilements, they are contrary to those [defilements].
Furthermore, because those Śrāvakas act solely for the sake of their own increase,
their wholesome qualities (*śukladharma*) are narrow and limited.
Because bodhisattvas desire to increase the happiness of all sentient beings,
their pure dharmas (*śukladharma*) are immeasurable.
Furthermore, those śrāvakas, by means of the wisdom of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-jñāna*), [attain their goal].
However, while [the śrāvaka] acts solely to eliminate the afflictions of his own person,
the bodhisattva acts universally for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
Furthermore, although that śrāvaka applies his attention by taking as his object the sphere of the most excellent dharma of liberation, he does so for himself alone.
One who is not a son of the Buddha;
whereas a bodhisattva, although they accumulate mental attention by taking as their object the dharmas and realms of sentient beings whose practices are inferior,
is nonetheless a son of the Buddha.
Furthermore, although those śrāvakas may be diligent and energetic, skillful regarding the truths, and possess well-stabilized minds,
because they do not achieve the characteristics of the Buddha-lineage,
the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are unable to take them under their care.
Bodhisattvas, however, are the opposite of them.
Furthermore, because those śrāvakas have reached the ultimate goal,
although their faculties are matured, they are unable to perform the deeds of a Buddha in future lives.
From the very first moment their initial resolve arises, Bodhisattvas are able to perform [these deeds].
Furthermore, although those Śrāvakas have reached the ultimate goal,
they do not receive the offerings and praises of those gods and humans.
Just as with a bodhisattva who abides in the initial stage of practice,
although these bodhisattvas have not yet reached the ultimate state,
their majestic power and wisdom outshine all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, although the excellent medicine of wisdom that cures the disease of afflictions has been perfected by those śrāvakas,
they are unable to cure the diseases of affliction of all sentient beings.
Bodhisattvas, however, are the opposite of them,
because they are able to practice the ultimate conduct that benefits others.
Furthermore, although those śrāvakas have reached the ultimate state, their intellectual illumination does not shine upon sentient beings.
Neither the gods nor others in the world are true fields of merit in the same way as Bodhisattvas who have not yet exhausted their afflictions;
furthermore, at all times, the Tathāgata is the most supreme among the Śrāvakas.
Among those who are already most excellent, the assembly of bodhisattvas is even more preeminent,
because they have accomplished this [perfection] through its integration.
Furthermore, their excellence should be understood by way of two conditions.
Because they are able to bring sentient beings to maturity and are also able to bring the qualities of a Buddha to maturity,
by these causes and conditions they realize the fruit of enlightenment.
According to the various classes of sentient beings who are to be matured,
he is able to bring them to liberation;
it is like a person who is capable of preparing and cooking food.
The marvelous wisdom of awakening is not for those who merely consume [the teachings] with complacency;
one should know that the principle here is likewise so.
Furthermore, although those śrāvakas single-mindedly receive, study, and practice the causes of pure dharmas, [they do not attain such wisdom].
Furthermore, although they are sustained by immeasurable virtuous friends,
they are unable to lead to the fruit of great enlightenment;
the assembly of bodhisattvas, however, is the opposite of them.
Furthermore, they are able to bring [others] forth;
moreover, all śrāvakas are born from bodhisattvas,
whereas bodhisattvas do not depend upon those śrāvakas.
Furthermore, how is it that through mundane and supramundane wisdom,
one is able to perform deeds for the benefit of others?
This refers to how bodhisattvas, throughout the ten directions, [act in this way].
Either they travel through worlds,
or they travel through lands,
or they travel through births.
Or they may exhort others to become great and excellent physicians,
skillfully able to treat sentient beings possessed by the demons of affliction.
It is unsurpassed.
It proclaims the path of purity through the three trainings.
What is mundane knowledge?
That is to say, regarding the coarse grades of all afflictions,
it serves as the antidote of cessation;
regarding the middling grades, it serves as the antidote of subduing.
What is called the coarse category of affliction?
It refers to the nature of the conduct of greed, hatred, and delusion among householders,
and the nature of reliance on views among those who have gone forth.
And there is the nature of being based upon improper attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) which serves as its support,
and the nature of being based upon the aspiration for future existence (*punarbhava-praṇidhāna*).
This is due to the four inversions (*viparyāsa*), both collectively and individually.
Regarding that which is not liberation, one clings to it as liberation and takes it as a basis.
What is intermediate-grade affliction?
It refers to having already stilled coarse-grade affliction.
By relying on specific antidotes for each [affliction],
one correctly applies mindfulness to the objects of focus, thereby counteracting the underlying tendencies of the entanglements of greed,
hatred, and delusion toward all sensory domains.
It causes those whose minds are unsettled to attain stability;
only by diligently practicing the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) can one truly subdue them.
Because one does not rely on this practice while harboring self-conceit,
one binds the mind to the object of focus, causing it to abide there with courageous diligence.
From this point on, one is able to correctly grasp and maintain abiding;
because of maintaining abiding,
within the accumulation [of merit],...
Because the afflictions that arise from the grasping at a unified whole can be subdued,
and because they are the objects to be countered by supramundane dharmas for the sake of their abandonment.
By relying on the antidote,
one establishes firm abiding; from this,
one is able to subdue ignorance regarding all dependent origination.
Through the delusion regarding the selflessness of persons and the delusion regarding the selflessness of phenomena,
one subsequently attains certainty regarding both the wrong path and the right path.
In this way, one should understand that the knowledge which counteracts, ceases, and subdues the coarse and medium grades of afflictions is called mundane knowledge (*laukika-jñāna*).
What is supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*)?
This means that once one has thus subdued the various defilements consisting of the entanglements of greed, hatred, and delusion,
one is further able to counteract all defilements consisting of subtle latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
This true knowledge is called supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*).
Furthermore, what is this?
It refers to skillfulness regarding the three bases that serve as the antidote for subduing [the afflictions], namely,
skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Skillfulness in the conviction of the selflessness of persons and skillfulness in the conviction of the selflessness of phenomena are for the purpose of transcending the four types of ignorance that constitute the remaining afflictions and their antidotes.
Without waiting for instruction from others,
one diligently observes one's own mind within.
Regarding the four types of ignorance:
First, ignorance regarding common characteristics;
second, ignorance regarding specific characteristics;
third, ignorance regarding the characteristics of affliction.
Fourth, there is ignorance regarding the characteristic of purification.
One should understand the common characteristics of the mind through three aspects:
first, because that which arises dependently does not manifest and lacks functional activity.
Second, with respect to the present, it is because there is no activity for even a single moment.
Third, with respect to greed and so forth, which arise from their own respective conditions, it is because they are not produced by the mind.
Through these three aspects, one should understand the specific characteristic of the mind.
First, because the intrinsic nature as previously described is unapprehendable;
second, because it can be apprehended as it truly is through the six aspects as previously explained;
third, because it is that which is attained by the non-discriminative wisdom of all noble ones.
The characteristics of the defilement of the mind should be understood through three aspects:
first, by way of arising;
second, by way of transformation.
Third, because of its activity:
it is called "defiled arising" because various types of selfhood arise within the various realms of existence (*gati*).
Furthermore, within this very process, that which arises flows on spontaneously from moment to moment.
Because all objects of focus are difficult to subdue and transform,
and because they are governed by the power of craving and attachment,
it is called "transformation as affliction."
If one engages in those activities or engages in them in such a manner,
it is called defiled activity;
that is to say, at one time, one engages in what is wholesome.
At one time they may engage in unwholesome conduct;
at another time, they may engage with sense objects;
and at yet another time, they may engage in the performance of karma.
At times, while practicing amidst afflictions,
one may further practice greed, hatred, and so forth within those afflictions;
there is no fixed practice, nor is it otherwise.
That is, having practiced with attachment toward this very practice, one again practices without attachment;
having practiced without attachment, one again practices with attachment,
and so forth.
Furthermore, among those phenomena conducive to pleasure and so forth,
one attains predominance in their manifestation;
moreover, one gives rise to one's own suffering and brings about the destruction of all forms of happiness.
It is not due to attachment,
but rather due to perversion; by means of this,
one gives rise to manifold sufferings within oneself without ever finding satisfaction.
Or when establishing [the mind] within the wholesome,
one immediately abandons the search for flaws in order to cause the unwholesome to manifest.
Within those vulnerabilities and amidst periods of decline or prosperity,
one is afflicted and distressed by various forms of craving and aversion.
Furthermore, under the influence of heedlessness, all roots of wholesome action that have been performed are caused to be destroyed.
Furthermore, because they are extremely attached to objects such as forms and so forth,
even though they repeatedly contemplate and discern within the nectar-like realm of supreme benefit,
it is difficult for them to establish themselves therein.
Within this context, one should understand that the illustrative analogies established through conventional designation are intended to demonstrate the characteristics of the purity of mind,
which are to be known by means of three types of correspondence.
First, because it is characterized by non-attainment;
second, because it is characterized by the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
third, because it is characterized by the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
If, by practicing diligently according to the principle through some other method,
one seeks the purification of the mind but cannot attain it; yet,
by practicing diligently according to the principle in this very way...
One is then able to realize it;
furthermore, one does not perceive the intrinsic nature of verbal expression,
but perceives the characteristic of suchness.
This should be observed through nine aspects as having the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*):
first, because it does not function within the world;
second, because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be apprehended, unlike that which exists during the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Because the characteristic of suchness can be apprehended,
it is the characteristic of non-duality.
Third, because it is not the characteristic of a birth-body.
Fourth, because it transcends the causal characteristics of the birth-body;
fifth, because it transcends future rebirth;
sixth, because it transcends death and passing away.
Seventh, because it transcends the moment-to-moment succession of instants;
eighth, because it transcends the transition between realms of existence;
ninth, because it transcends the activity of karma and afflictions.
In this context, the characteristic of the lineage (*gotra*) should be understood as the characteristic of the realm of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa-dhātu*).
Within the present life, it transcends five matters.
First, transcending what is produced;
second, transcending what is not produced;
third, transcending the application of effort toward what is produced.
Fourth, it transcends the non-application of what is to be done;
fifth, it transcends the application of what is not to be done.
Within the subsequent dharma, it transcends these six matters.
First, transcending the formations that give rise to future existence;
second, transcending those formations;
third, transcending the arising of their fruit.
Fourth, it transcends dependence on their decline and prosperity.
Fifth, it transcends the period of training, aspiration, and enjoyment within all the neutral fluctuations of those bases.
Sixth, there is the transcendence of the distinctions of the self-nature of that basis.
Furthermore, the characteristics of the lineage (*gotra*) should be understood through four stages and nine aspects.
What are the four stages?
1. The stage of impurity;
2. The stage of purity;
3. The stage of thorough penetration.
The fourth is the stage of culmination.
What are the nine aspects?
They are the impure stage.
Because it conforms to all characteristics equally,
it is like space;
in its state of purity, it is of a single equal flavor and characterized by the detachment of body and mind.
If one proceeds toward the ultimate state during the stage of thorough penetration,
because all afflictions are by nature dissociated and free from defilement,
one transcends the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
And having transcended those various evil views which serve as their root;
and when the state of ultimate consummation is attained,
one transcends the three kinds of transformation and decay.
What are called the three kinds of transformation and decay?
First, transformation and decay such as old age and death;
second, transformation and decay in the state of perversion.
Third is the purification of decline and transformation,
which refers to the *vinaya* regarding all greed and sorrow;
this is the application of the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*).
Because of the mental attention of revulsion,
this is the application of the training in higher mind;
because of the selflessness of persons.
Alternatively, because of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*),
this is the application of the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñāśikṣā*).
In this context, craving and grief are that which give rise to all transgressions.
Furthermore, it is as when one has not yet eliminated [the afflictions],
as when one has already eliminated them,
and as when one is in the process of eliminating them.
Just as they have been dispelled,
one should understand through these four aspects that the desire arising from improper mental attention within one's own mind has been eliminated.
The view of a self-identity and ill-will,
whether by way of their objects, [are abandoned].
Alternatively, if false conceptualization arises due to another [cause],
this is called "not correctly eliminating" it.
If it arises due to the object, [it is likewise].
Or it may be led away and snatched by the harmful actions of others;
this is called "not having eliminated," because it has not been eliminated by any one [of the means].
One should know that when one [factor] is not eliminated,
the other is likewise not eliminated; and by the elimination of one,
one should know that the other is also eliminated.
Furthermore, if one does not eliminate [these faults], even while abiding in the vows,
one is still said to have transgressed the higher training in ethical discipline;
how much more so for one who dwells in non-restraint?
Furthermore, when the training in higher mind (adhicitta-śikṣā) is distracted or erroneous regarding its object of focus,
it acts as an obstacle for one who relies upon the cultivation of higher wisdom (adhiprajñā) based on the selflessness of persons (pudgala-nairātmya).
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is that which obstructs the cultivation of superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) based on the selflessness of phenomena;
the conceptualization and attachment to the distinctions of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa-vikalpa-pratigha*) are those which obstruct these three trainings (*triśikṣā*).
In the correct cultivation of abandonment,
there are eight kinds of factors contrary to training and eight kinds of factors conducive to training. What are these eight?
First is the attachment that is wasted;
second is the bondage resulting from attachment;
third is the obstruction resulting from bondage.
Fourth is the defilement due to obstruction;
fifth is the calamity due to defilement;
sixth is the ulcerous swelling due to calamity.
Seventh, because of the sores and blisters, there is feverish affliction (*paridāha*).
Eighth, because of the feverish affliction, the diseases of the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are difficult to treat.
One should know that the opposites of these are the eight kinds of dharmas conducive to training (*śikṣānulomika-dharma*).
Furthermore, what is meant by a śramaṇa who has not trained well?
It should be understood that there are three types:
first, one who disregards the status of a śramaṇa.
Second, they are concordant in physical form;
third, they are discordant in their observance of rules, right livelihood, application, training in the precepts, views, and intentions.
If one dedicates these requisites, this constitutes superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*).
Similarity in form refers to the higher mind (*adhicitta*) and higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
Similarity in form refers to the dissimilarity in the mental disposition (*āśaya*) regarding those practices.
If it is directed toward reputation, it is a branch of calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Similarity is a branch of vipaśyanā;
similarity is a branch of simultaneous cultivation;
similarity is a branch of simultaneous provisions.
The "homogeneous" (sabhāga) is that which is not homogeneous with one's intention.
Furthermore, how is a śramaṇa well-trained?
It should be understood by way of four characteristics.
First, by way of application;
second, by way of intention;
third, by way of thorough penetration.
Fourth, because it leads to the ultimate goal:
through the application of revulsion in the present life,
and through the application of the maturation of the continuum in previous lives.
One should know that the preparatory application is perfected by means of the resolute intention regarding the selflessness of phenomena; thus,
whatever is to be attained [is achieved].
If one is able to respond appropriately,
it is because one has no attachment to the intrinsic nature of these two modes of expression and correctly seeks the intended meaning.
One should know that the intention is perfected not merely by conforming to words, but because,
regarding the suchness of phenomena, one penetrates its nature as being free from defilement through a wisdom that does not rely on others.
Because, regarding worldly treasures and worldly birth-and-death,
as well as nirvāṇa, liberation,
and bondage, their intrinsic nature is unapprehendable.
It should be known that this constitutes the perfection of thorough penetration,
because one has well cultivated all remedies for the various defilements and because there is no interruption or destruction regarding suchness.
And because they are able to overcome and subdue [the afflictions],
one should know that they are proceeding toward ultimate perfection.
Furthermore, there is the poorly trained śramaṇa.
One should understand that their names do not correspond to their actual nature due to three types of characteristics:
first, the impairment of intention accompanied by the perfection of application;
second, the perfection of intention accompanied by the impairment of application.
Third, there is the decline of intention and the decline of application.
Within this, regarding the decline of intention while being endowed with application,
there are again three types.
First, one is able to listen to this alone as contentment;
second, one is able to speak of this alone as contentment;
third, one is able to realize mundane samādhi and experience its relish, regarding this alone as contentment.
It should be understood that a well-trained śramaṇa possesses both the perfection of intention and the perfection of application by means of a single characteristic.
Furthermore, how does he abide in conventional restraint?
It should be known that there are four aspects:
namely, although one has accomplished the sixfold ethical discipline (*ṣaḍaṅga-śīla*),
it may be impaired by two kinds of harm that damage that ethical discipline.
That is to say, due to being entangled by the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and due to not understanding the renunciation of transgressions,
even though one has distanced oneself from these two kinds of faults.
Yet they have not attained the mundane purification of discipline and are unable to subdue the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Even though they have already attained the mundane purification of discipline...
Having already subdued the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi),
yet not diminishing the fear regarding the nature of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) due to lack of familiarity,
they thereby ruin their ethical discipline (śīla).
Although they have distanced themselves from all other faults,
they still possess a conviction in the non-self of false dharmas and the pride of overestimation.
It is the impairment of the *śīla*.
Furthermore, how does one abide in the ultimate discipline (*paramārtha-saṃvara*)?
It refers to that which is accomplished as supramundane.
It is dissociated from all afflictions and serves as the antidote to the śīla of the three realms.
Furthermore, regarding the four types of abiding in restraint:
Whatever phenomena of conceptual proliferation can be apprehended in the present,
if one can pacify their characteristics,
know that this is called untainted ethical discipline (*anāsrava-śīla*).
What are called the phenomena of conceptual proliferation?
They refer to the apprehension of the notion of "I" and the apprehension of "mine" within the initial stage of ethical discipline.
Whether one commits a transgression, or does not do so,
or performs an intentional preparatory effort.
If it is not that preparatory effort,
if one acts with clear comprehension,
or if one does not act at all.
If one acts with loss of mindfulness,
or if one does not act [properly],
then within the second dwelling of restraint, the grossness associated with the category of the view of a self-entity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) persists.
If name is perceivable,
if form is perceivable,
or if the characteristics of future birth are perceivable.
If at this time there is no manifest sign,
yet the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) are tranquil while the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) remain untranquilized because of them.
If there is no grasping at a person (pudgala-nairātmya),
if the grasping at a person is abandoned,
and if that very nature of being grasped within that absence of grasping at a person [is relinquished].
That which is not of the nature of being grasped;
that by means of which sentient beings conceive of form and so forth;
and that which is designated as a "good grasp."
If one can provisionally assume mental speech and provisionally assume the grasping of praise as good,
then within the third dwelling of restraint,
if one is born into the higher worlds.
If it abandons the lower [levels], it is not mundane;
if it relies upon meditative concentration (samādhi),
or if it relies upon the various desires.
If one relies on one's own ethical discipline (*śīla*) with pride,
or if one looks down upon the ethical discipline of others,
or if one conceives of one's own ethical discipline as pure within the fourth stage of training (*vinaya-vihāra*).
If one discriminates ethical discipline (*śīla*) by way of its intrinsic nature or its specific distinctions,
such conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are entirely stilled within untainted ethical discipline (*anāsrava-śīla*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that the verses spoken in accordance with this very meaning, based upon the three trainings of purification,
are intended to cause the defilements of the equipment of merit to become thin and subtle.
They embrace true persons because they do not suffer ruin;
they gather the equipment of wisdom because they give rise to resolute conviction regarding the profound.
One enters the teaching of the Tathāgata by means of two causes and conditions:
first, through the profound discernment of the knowledge of the abiding of phenomena (*dharmasthitijñāna*);
second, through the thorough determination of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Furthermore, what is the Tathāgata’s skillful means of subduing?
It should be known that there are two kinds:
namely, by virtue of having a commonality of essential nature (*svabhāva-sabhāgatā*).
Furthermore, it is because they share a commonality of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-sabhāgatva*);
and again, because manifesting this commonality causes the mind that receives the teaching to become stabilized;
and because one attains deliverance by relying upon the instructions (*avavāda*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that there are four kinds of instruction for teaching the application of correct purification:

first, instruction on the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) through the apprehension of fear regarding affliction and purification; second, instruction on distancing oneself from the causes and conditions of affliction.
Third, the instruction on distancing oneself from the causes and conditions for fear regarding purity;
fourth, the instruction on the application for dwelling in the supreme happiness of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Within this, there are two kinds of causes and conditions for affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
First, by means of the conceptualization that clings to the nature of defilement through conventional linguistic expression;
second, by means of the conceptualization that clings to the distinctions between those virtues and faults.
One should understand that there are two reasons for the cause of fear regarding the guidance toward purification:
first, because of the conceptualization of defilement within the guidance toward purification at its beginning and end.
Second, because they are free from conceptualization regarding the defilements,
one should understand that there are two causes for fear and terror toward the purity of nirvāṇa:
first, due to the grasping at an intrinsic nature through conventional discourse.
Second, because one forms mental objects within the conceptual designations (*adhivacanasaṃjñā*) regarding nirvāṇa;
and because one thoroughly understands the conceptual designations regarding the mental objects of tranquility.
Because one is completely detached from both of those causes and conditions,
it should be known that this is the instruction on the preparatory application for the first dwelling.
Thus it is said.
It refers to the wisdom of non-dual characteristics, which is capable of penetrating the characteristics of all intentional terminology. What is meant by "non-dual characteristics"?
It refers to the entities that serve as the basis for the establishment of all conventional designations.
Because that intrinsic nature does not exist,
and because it is not an intrinsic nature that exists as the objective domain of conceptualization perfumed by linguistic conventions,
it is said to be non-dual.
If dualistic grasping arises toward this non-duality,
it is called defilement;
if there is no dualistic grasping, it is not.
It is called "pure.
Furthermore, it is not an object that serves as a basis for any conventional designation,
because the nature of the range of mental activity— conditioned by the habitual tendencies of worldly discourse— is non-existent.
Because it is not an intrinsic nature that exists as the object of knowledge perfumed by those [impressions],
it is said to be non-dual.
If one gives rise to dualistic grasping toward this non-duality, [it is an error].
It is called defilement when there is dualistic grasping;
it is called purity when there is no such dualistic grasping.
By means of this non-dual characteristic,
one should understand the entry into all the intentional language (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*) of the Tathāgata.
In this regard, the perfection of the treatise (*śāstra*) is established through five characteristics.
Within these instructions, one should understand that the perfection of the fruit is designated by five aspects,
and the perfection of the excellence of the fruit is likewise designated by five aspects;
both are based on intentional terminology (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*).
In what way is discourse said to be perfected through five aspects?
It refers to that by which it is proclaimed and that which is proclaimed.
That which is proclaimed,
that which is proclaimed in such a manner,
and that which is proclaimed by him.
Thus it is complete.
In what way is it called the completion of the fruit by way of five aspects?
It refers to the realm of nirvana without remainder.
If there is the realm of nirvana with remainder,
if the noble path is perfected,
and if the supreme internal enemy has been conquered.
If it is thus fulfilled by overcoming external enemies,
