how is it that it is called the fulfillment of the excellence of the fruit by way of five aspects?
This means that it is precisely making offerings to the Great Teacher,
repaying the kindness of the faithful laity's almsgiving,
and transcending the suffering of birth and death.
They do not regress from the nature of the field of merit;
born through transformation from the Dharma, they are called sons of the Tathāgata,
relying upon the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, how should one understand the excellence of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) within the instructions of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka?
It should be known by way of five aspects.
First, at the time of establishing the cause, it is able to outshine the dominant causes that bring about great wealth and status.
Second, by means of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti);
third, because one becomes a vessel for the teaching in that very place;
and fourth, because one becomes a vessel for the teacher.
Fifth, because at the time of relinquishing the body one attains the vision of the purity of karma.
One should understand that by means of these five characteristics, the causes for experiencing great wealth and nobility are eclipsed.
This is because this cause can induce finite or infinite results;
because it consists of phenomena that are either exhaustible or inexhaustible;
and because it brings about pleasure that is either not vast or vast.
This is because it is the nature of the wisdom that constitutes the equipment for wisdom,
and because it can induce that [wisdom].
Furthermore, it is due to being free from six kinds of faults.
One should understand the bodily activities.
What are the six kinds of faults?
The first is the fault characterized by sorrow and anxiety.
Second, the fault of not understanding through repeated practice;
third, the fault of deportment due to two kinds of characteristics;
fourth, the fault of the characteristic of fear due to three kinds of characteristics.
Fifth, there is the fault of *āveṣṭaka* (obstructing) due to two aspects.
Sixth, there is the fault of the body being unpliant.
Furthermore, at the time of mutual congratulation and consolation, one should remain free from five kinds of faults.
One should know that there are five kinds of faults regarding verbal conduct.
First is the fault of timidity and fear;
second is the fault of coarseness and harshness.
Third is the fault of abandoning the Buddha’s word and engaging in inconsistent, frivolous conceptual proliferation.
Fourth is the fault of failing to praise the Tathāgata.
Fifth is the fault of failing to offer admonition or instruction to those who share the same Dharma.
Furthermore, when understanding what is expressed in a prophecy, one should know that the activity of speech is free from five kinds of faults.
What are these five kinds of faults?
First, the fault of forgetfulness regarding what has been realized;
second, the fault of contradiction between preceding and succeeding statements;
third, the fault of contradiction with reason.
Fourth, the fault of being rebuked by the devas for lacking reverence and faith in the holy teachings;
fifth, the fault of being rebuked by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, it is due to being free from these five kinds of faults.
One should understand the mental activities (*manas-karma*).
That is to say, based on the meaning of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*), there are the first four types;
based on the meaning of future lives (*paratra-dharma*), there is the fifth type.
What are the five kinds of faults?
First is the fault of intolerance,
because one is unable to endure harmful events occurring in the present or the past.
Second is the fault of concealment.
Because of concealment,
one is tormented by remorse.
Third is the fault of defiled craving:
because of the longing for various sensual desires and their enjoyments,
and because of the longing for the enemy that seeks liberation.
Fourth is the fault of forgetfulness,
because it embraces wrong views and causes confusion regarding the mind of abandonment.
Fifth is the fault of aspiration.
Because they disparage themselves, they distance themselves from the sublime vows for buddha-fields that are empowered by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
and because they give rise to the qualities of a Buddha through a subtle mental disposition.
Because of the arising of pride due to the distinction of worldly prosperity regarding all phenomena,
and because of wishing for that [prosperity],
[this occurs] within the immeasurable definitions and explanations of the benefits of resolute belief in the instructions of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
It should be known that there are immeasurable and innumerable benefits of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
In this section, no further texts of definitive analysis (*viniścaya*) appear. 16–17.

Regarding the sections on definitive analysis contained within the two stages of the stage with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and the stage without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*): the definitive analysis of the Bodhisattva-bhūmi has thus been explained.
The Determination of the Two Stages: With Remainder and Without Remainder. Chapter 2:
The Correct Determination of the Two Stages of With Remainder and Without Remainder. Section 1: Establishing the Chapter Headings. I shall now set forth the summary verse (*uddāna*).
Regarding the distinctions of liberation from the fetters, the life-faculties, the transformation of the basis,
abiding, differentiation, permanence, bliss, excellence, distinct nature, and mastery—
these are now questioned concerning the time when they are currently manifest within the realm of nirvana with remainder.
Should it be said that all afflictions are dissociated, or should it be said that they are not dissociated? Answer:
It should be said that they are dissociated.
Question: Regarding all suffering,
should it be said that one is dissociated from it,
or should it be said that one is not dissociated from it?
Answer: It should be said that it is both dissociated and not dissociated.
Why is this? If one refers to all the various sufferings of future births, they should be said to be dissociated.
If the mental suffering that arises in the present life is also said to be dissociated [from its cause],
then so too would be the suffering of hunger, the suffering of thirst, the suffering of imbalance of the elements, and the suffering of seasonal changes within the present body.
And regarding all other forms of suffering, such as oppression and the like,
one should say that they are not dissociated from it,
because they are currently manifesting.
Because they are not bound by any afflictions.
Question: If all Arhats have attained mastery over the mind, for what reason [is there a distinction]?
He does not abandon the life-force (*āyus-saṃskāra*) to enter parinirvāṇa;
although oppressed by suffering, he remains for a long time. Why?
Because there is a distinction in his functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).
Why is this? There are some Arhats who are able to relinquish the formations of life, while others are not.
There are some arhats who are able to prolong their life-span, while others are not.
Question: If an arhat arises with the six sense-bases exactly as they were previously possessed, [how can this be so?]
Thus abiding, the continuum is not extinguished and remains without change;
what further nature of transformation of the basis could there be?
It does not, however, proceed as a continuity of the six sense bases.
If there were no other transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*),
for what reason [would this occur]?
If the two types of reliance are similar in the former and latter stages, yet at the later time afflictions no longer arise, does the Noble Path then arise?
Answer: All Arhats truly possess the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Furthermore, it cannot be said that this transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is either different from or not different from those six sense bases (ṣad-āyatana). Why is this?
This transformation of the basis is manifested through the purity of suchness;
it is the lineage of suchness and the seed of suchness.
It is the integration of true suchness;
yet, it cannot be said that this true suchness is either different from or non-different from those six sense bases.
The meaning of being "inexpressible" has already been explained above. Therefore,
if one asks whether the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) that is attained is different from or not different from the six sense bases (ṣaḍ-āyatana):
This is not a question posed according to reason.
If this transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) were without substantial reality,
the aforementioned faults would necessarily follow.
This means that for an Arhat, the afflictions should cease to function while the Path should no longer fail to function; therefore,
one should know that there is the nature of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti).
Based on this nature of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), the Blessed One spoke with intentional meaning (*saṃdhi*) as follows:
"Within the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*),
Due to the two types of habitual tendencies— those of grasping and non-grasping— Defilement and purification are established."
This is the realm of outflows; this is the realm without outflows.
This is the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), pure and unsurpassed—like a butcher or his disciple.
Having slaughtered the ox with a butcher’s knife,
he cuts, pierces, hews, and carves it within until the bones, flesh, sinews, and veins are all completely severed;
he then stretches its hide over it to cover it.
One should say that this ox and its hide are neither separate nor joined.
In the same way, once the Arhats have attained the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*),
they have, by means of the sharp blade of wisdom, severed all fetters (*saṃyojana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*).
It should be said that it is neither separate from nor joined to the skin of the six sense bases.
Furthermore, although practitioners who have already undergone the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) perceive various characteristics, [they do so without grasping].
One should know that this differs from what was previously grasped.
This grasped characteristic is like true suchness (tathatā), which is personally realized within;
it cannot be shown to another through verbal expression as "the characteristic I perceive is thus and thus."
Within the realm of nirvāṇa,
what kind of mind does one abide in?
Regarding the realm of parinirvāṇa without remainder:
When entering parinirvāṇa,
he no longer reflects upon any signs;
he reflects only upon the truly signless realm.
Gradually entering the meditative attainment of cessation, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and so forth are extinguished;
subsequently, the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) abandons its basis,
because the retributive consciousness is devoid of grasping (*upādāna*).
The various evolving consciousnesses and so forth no longer arise;
only the pure, unconditioned, and stainless true dharma-realm remains.
Having entered parinirvāṇa within this realm, [one abides].
They will no longer fall among the devas,
nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, or kiṃnaras.
Whether they be asuras or humans,
and so forth— in short.
All sentient beings are merely conceptual designations,
pervading all realms and all destinies throughout the ten directions.
All births; all classes of beings;
all who have obtained a body.
They are born as supreme among all beings;
throughout all stages,
they never again fall back into those [lower] categories.
Why is this? Because this true realm is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*),
being realized only through internal self-realization by those who have accomplished it.
Question: Regarding those Arhats who have already attained parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana with remainder, or within the realm of nirvana without remainder.
What is the distinction?
Answer: He dwells in the state of having a remainder of substrate (sopadhiśeṣa) and remains within the category of the multitude.
Abiding in the nirvana without remainder,
one does not fall into the category of sentient beings;
abiding in the nirvana with remainder, one remains [in the world].
There still remain manifold sufferings;
by abiding in the nirvana without remainder,
one is forever freed from all suffering.
The transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) attained while abiding in the state with remainder (sopadhiśeṣa) is still associated with the six sense bases; however,
while abiding in the state without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa), it is forever dissociated from them.
Question: If, within the realm of nirvana without remainder,
the fundamental transformation (āśraya-parāvṛtti) of one who has attained parinirvāṇa is forever dissociated from the six sense bases (ṣaḍ-āyatana),
then since that [transformation] lacks the basis for the six sense bases, how can it exist?
How does it abide? The answer is:
it is not the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) obtained by an Arhat that takes the six sense bases as its cause;
rather, it takes only the cultivation of the path based on the object of True Suchness (tathatā) as its cause.
Therefore, whether the six sense bases exist or do not exist,
there is still no transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) to constitute a state of change;
how much less so when they perish?
Furthermore, this realm is neither that which is to be fully known nor that which is to be abandoned;
therefore, it cannot be extinguished.
Regarding the attainment of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), should it be said that it exists,
or should it be said that it does not exist?
Answer: It should be said that it exists.
Question: What kind of characteristic should it be said to have?
Answer: The characteristic of being free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
Furthermore, it has the perfectly purified dharma-realm as its characteristic.
Question: For what reason should it be said that this exists?
Answer: Because it exists within both the nirvana-realm with remainder and the nirvana-realm without remainder.
This nature of the transformation of the basis is entirely devoid of any shifting phenomena.
Because it is devoid of shifting phenomena,
it is illogical for that which previously existed to later cease to exist.
Furthermore, this dharmatā is not produced by manifold conditions;
it is without arising and without cessation.
Nevertheless, it is like the nature of water, which is inherently clear and limpid.
It is like the malleable nature of refined gold;
it is like the nature of space, free from clouds and mist.
Therefore, the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) should be said to exist.
Question: Should it be said that this is permanent, or should it be said that it is impermanent?
Answer: It should be said that it is permanent.
Question: For what reason and by what causal conditions should it be said that this is permanent?
Answer: Because it is manifested by pure *tathatā* (suchness) and because it is not produced through dependent origination.
Because it is without arising or ceasing.
Question: Should this be called pleasure, or should it be called non-pleasure?
Answer: It should be said that it is bliss by virtue of ultimate bliss;
it is not called bliss because of the feeling of pleasure.
Why is this? Because one has completely transcended all afflictions and the suffering produced by them.
Question: Regarding the realm of nirvana without remainder...
Regarding those who have attained parinirvāṇa, is there even the slightest distinction or difference in their underlying intent?
Answer: There is none at all.
Why is this? Because within this realm, it is impossible to establish the categories of inferior, middling, or superior;
nor can distinctions of high or low, or excellence or inferiority, be designated.
"This is the Tathāgata; these are the śrāvakas.
Question: For what reason is there no distinction between them? Why is this so?
The various śrāvakas and others possess residual hindrances and attain parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder;
the Buddha, however, possesses no hindrances whatsoever forever.
Answer: Within the realm of nirvana with remainder, it is possible to establish the distinction between being obstructed and being unobstructed;
however, within the realm of nirvana without remainder, this is not the case.
Ultimately, there can be no establishment of distinctions.
Why is this? Because within this realm, all manifold characteristics [are devoid of intrinsic nature].
Furthermore, because all coarse and heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) are forever stilled and forever extinguished. Why is this so?
When the various Arhats abide in the realm of nirvana with remainder,
all manifold signs are not entirely extinguished,
nor is the ripening heaviness (dausthulya) entirely extinguished.
Because it is taught that there are the latencies of afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*),
one establishes the existence of an obstacle in dependence upon those signs (*nimitta*) and the coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*);
[this applies] when abiding in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇadhātu*).
That [distinction] never exists.
Therefore, one should know that within this realm,
there is no distinction between being obstructed and being unobstructed.
Question: If within this realm there is never any obstruction—
just as the Tathāgatas are free from all obstructions,
so too are the Arhats and others— then [what is the distinction]?
For what reason do Arhats differ from Tathāgatas in performing the various deeds of a Buddha?
Answer: Because they lack the fundamental great vows that were cultivated.
Furthermore, because their lineage and spiritual disposition (*gotra*) are such,
Arhats and others definitely lack the intention to arise again;
rather, they enter parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is unable to perform the various deeds of a Buddha.
[Question: Regarding the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu) belonging to those who have entered parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu):
Regarding this and the various forms,
should one say they are different,
or should one say they are not different?
Answer: It should be said that it is neither different nor not different,
just as [it relates] to the various forms (rūpa) and the various feelings (vedanā), and so forth.
One should know that it is likewise with all formations and all elements.
It is likewise with all realms of existence.
Thus it is said.
Regarding phenomena such as form, should it be said that one attains mastery over them, or should it be said that one does not attain mastery?
Answer: It should be said that one attains mastery.
Question: Regarding this attained mastery,
should it be said that it can be brought into manifestation,
or should it be said that it cannot be brought into manifestation?
Answer: One part can be manifested, while one part cannot be manifested;
that is to say, when the Tathāgatas abide within the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Having attained parinirvāṇa, one is able to manifest [this state], whereas the remainder cannot be made to manifest.
Question: If within this realm all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are abandoned...
For this reason, one does not fall into the category of the multitude.
How, then, can [the bodhicitta] arise and manifest before one?
Answer: Because of having previously initiated the correct and great vow.
Furthermore, by the power of cultivating a path that resembles that [state],
it is like one who has correctly entered the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*);
although they have no thought, "I shall emerge from this attainment of cessation," [they nonetheless do so].
Alternatively, having emerged [from concentration], one remains;
however, due to the power of prior preparatory application (*prayoga*),
one emerges again from that meditative absorption.
One should know that the principle here is likewise: [the movement] proceeds based on mental activity.
Question: Do Śrāvakas who have dedicated themselves to Bodhi abide within the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder?
"Can one set out for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, or does one abide in the realm of *nirvāṇa-with-remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*)?
He replied: "Only while abiding within the realm of *nirvāṇa-with-remainder* can this occur."
Why is this? Because within the realm of nirvana without remainder,
all undertakings of activity are utterly transcended.
All functional activities are entirely stilled.
Question: If one abides solely within the realm of nirvana with remainder and is able to set out for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, [how is this possible]?
How is it that one can realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through only a single lifetime? Why is this so?
Because even for those such as Arhats, there would still remain no further lifetimes beyond this one.
How much more so, then, could there be a succession of many births?
Answer: This can only be accomplished by increasing one's life-force (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*).
The Blessed One, for the most part with reference to those śrāvakas who are directed toward enlightenment,
spoke with intentional meaning:
"O noble son of good family, if one has well cultivated the four bases of psychic power..."
"Abiding for one kalpa or more than one kalpa"— here,
the intended meaning is that it exceeds one kalpa.
Although they thus augment their life-force (*āyus-saṃskāra*), [they do not transcend the limit of the kalpa].
They are able to set out toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
yet their practice is extremely slow and dull because they delight in *nirvāṇa*.
This is not equal to a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon the path and begun their practice;
for such a one, having thus increased their lifespan through practice,
leaves behind a body with sense faculties.
He manifests a separate transformation body;
for those who share his Dharma, he first demonstrates the preliminary expedients within the realm of nirvana without remainder.
And having entered parinirvāṇa,
for this reason they all think:
"The Venerable One named so-and-so has attained parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder."
Having already entered parinirvāṇa,
he, by means of his remaining physical body of faculties,
[resided] right here in Jambudvīpa within this world-system.
Dwelling in seclusion according to his pleasure,
even all the devas cannot behold him,
let alone other sentient beings.
Because they take great delight in dwelling in nirvāṇa,
among their travels through various worlds to approach,
serve, and make offerings to Buddhas and bodhisattvas, [they do not seek them out].
Furthermore, while practicing the noble paths that constitute the accumulations for awakening,
whenever they are negligent, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas repeatedly awaken them;
having been thus awakened, [they proceed].
One is able to practice without negligence regarding what is to be cultivated.
Question: If an Arhat can turn toward Bodhi and thereby realize Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, [then...]
For what reason do not all arhats turn toward unsurpassed bodhi?
Answer: Because their spiritual lineages (gotra) differ.
Why is this so? Because it is directly perceived that there are many distinctions among the lineages of the arhats;
that is to say, some arhats are seen to be liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta).
Or again, one may see those who are liberated by wisdom alone (prajñā-vimukta) attaining parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder; therefore,
it should be known that this is due to differences in their spiritual lineages (gotra).
Not all arhats are capable of dedicating [their merit] toward unsurpassed bodhi.
Furthermore, those śrāvakas who dedicate toward bodhi may,
while still in the stage of training (śaikṣa), be able to relinquish their aspiration for the state of a śrāvaka.
Alternatively, they can be relinquished only upon reaching the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*),
due to differences in their faculties (*indriya*) and differences in the various conditions (*pratyaya*) required for their abandonment.
Just as a śrāvaka who has dedicated [their roots of virtue] toward bodhi may, due to encountering certain conditions,
attain parinirvāṇa by mounting the Unsurpassed Vehicle,
so too it is with a bodhisattva, even if they are abandoned by the Tathāgatas and other bodhisattvas.
Because of this abandonment,
if one encounters extremely grave conditions for seeking parinirvāṇa through an inferior vehicle,
one should indeed ride that inferior vehicle and attain parinirvāṇa.
However, there is no place and no possibility for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to be thus negligent or to abandon those beings.
It is absolutely impossible.
Furthermore, regarding a śrāvaka who has dedicated [their merit] toward bodhi:
if they were to subsequently realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), [it would be impossible].
At that time, he entered parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder, just like the Tathāgata.
Question: Regarding those śrāvakas who have turned toward bodhi,
should they be said from the very beginning to belong to the śrāvaka lineage,
or should they be said to belong to the bodhisattva lineage?
Answer: It should be said that they are of indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*).

For example, just as one establishes a group of sentient beings who are of indeterminate nature within the category of those possessing the nature for parinirvāṇa, it should be known that these are of indeterminate lineage.
Furthermore, as he dwells and moves about in this very place,
just as there is no fear of death,
so too is there no fear of old age, sickness, and the like.
The Tathāgata is likewise.
He and all others who have attained parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder—
One should know that throughout the worlds of the ten directions, these are ultimately inconceivable;
they repeatedly manifest and perform all manner of beneficial deeds for sentient beings,
as described in the simile of the illusionist within the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Whether it be the analogy of the merchant leader or the analogy of the boatman,
one should know that the principle here is likewise.
This is called the most ultimate secret of the Tathāgata.
Regarding this and other various distinctions among the secrets of the Tathāgata,
when a bodhisattva practicing on the stage of conduct through resolute belief enters the stage of inferior patience, [he realizes them].
It proceeds according to the distinctions of their respective resolute beliefs (*adhimukti*).
From this progression, they enter the stage of the purity of superior intention (*adhyāśaya-viśuddhi-bhūmi*).
In this manner, it continues up to the ninth stage.
Progressing further and further,
this resolute conviction becomes purified;
in the tenth stage, this resolute conviction is most thoroughly purified.
Regarding those secrets of the Tathāgata,
these bodhisattvas should correctly follow and apply them;
one should know that such are the secrets of the Tathāgata.
It is inconceivable and immeasurable, transcending the entire sphere of measurement.
Question: What is the general meaning of the definitive discernment of phenomena? Answer: [As follows].
Through the differentiation of categories, all phenomena are established;
therein, the resolution of difficulties regarding the single practice and so forth is analyzed.
Thus should the general meaning herein be understood.
In this section, no further texts of definitive analysis (viniścaya) are presented;
one should know that within each and every stage (bhūmi),
there are immeasurable distinctions of definitive analysis.
I shall now briefly reveal a small portion of it.
By means of this direction, this training, and this instruction,
those who possess wisdom should reflect upon the rest by analogy.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Eighty;
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Eighty-one;
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Part One of the Section on Compendium and Explanation. Thus has the compendium of the definitive analysis been explained.
Chapter Two: What is the compendium of the explanation?
The summary verse says:

The essence, the explanation of the meaning of the text, the Dharma; The arising of the meaning, objections, the sequence, the teacher, the assembly, the listening, the praise of the Buddha; And the benefits of learning in brief and in detail.
What is its essence?
The essence of the sūtras consists briefly of two kinds.
First, the letter;
second, the meaning.
The letter is that upon which one relies.
Meaning (*artha*) is that which depends [upon the basis].
These two types together are collectively termed the "entirety of objects of knowledge" (*jñeya-viṣaya*).
How is this explained?
Briefly stated, there are five:
first, the phenomenon (dharma);
second, its origination (samutthāna).
Third is the meaning;
fourth is the resolution of difficulties;
fifth is the sequential order.
What is "letter" (vyañjana)?
It is said to be of six kinds.
The first is the collection of names (nāmakāya).
Second, the body of phrases;
third, the body of syllables;
fourth, speech.
Fifth is the mode of activity;
sixth is the request by capacity.
Regarding "name-body" (nāmakāya):
This refers to the conventional designation commonly known as "name.
Briefly stated, there are twelve types:
first, the provisional name.
Second, names for actual entities;
third, names corresponding to similar categories;
fourth, names corresponding to dissimilar categories.
Fifth is the name according to its qualities;
sixth is the metaphorical name;
seventh is the name commonly understood.
Eighth, names that do not correspond to what is cognized;
ninth, manifest names;
tenth, non-manifest names.
Eleventh is the abbreviated name;
twelfth is the detailed name.
Regarding the provisionally established names:
That is to say, the designation "self," "sentient being," "life-principle," and so forth is applied metaphorically to the internal;
the designation "vase," "robe," and so forth is applied metaphorically to the external.
As for the designation of a real entity:
This refers to the application of names such as "eye" and so forth to the objects of the various faculties,
such as the eye and visible forms;
these are names that correspond to their respective categories.
This refers to names such as "sentient being," "form," "feeling," and "great elements.
As for names consisting of the association of different categories,
these refer to names such as "Buddhadatta," "Guṇamitra," "blue," or "yellow."
Regarding names according to their qualities:
it is called "form" (*rūpa*) because it is subject to transformation and resistance;
it is called "feeling" (*vedanā*) because it experiences.
It is called "the sun" because it emits light;
such names as these are merely conventional designations.
This refers to calling one who is poor "rich," or when other names are established without regard for their actual meaning,
yet are understood as being identical to the name [previously applied].
This refers to a designation that is commonly understood;
its opposite is a name that is not commonly understood.
To illustrate such a name:
That is to say, its meaning is easy to understand.
That which does not manifest its name is such that its meaning is difficult to understand.
Examples include the Dāramiṭa vidyā-mantra and others.
A "abbreviated name" refers to a name consisting of a single syllable.
"Extensive names" refers to names consisting of many syllables.
As for "phrases" (padakāya):
This refers to the perfection of names and phrases.
This, moreover, is of six kinds.
The first is the incomplete phrase.
Second, the phrase of fulfillment;
third, the phrase of that which is accomplished;
fourth, the phrase of that which accomplishes.
Fifth is the indicative phrase;
sixth is the explanatory phrase.
Regarding the incomplete phrase:
This means that the phrasing is not exhaustive and the meaning is not exhaustive;
one should know that it is only by means of the second phrase that [the teaching] becomes complete as described.
Commit no evil; Practice all that is good;
Thoroughly subdue your own mind— This is the sublime teaching of all Buddhas.
If it were merely said, "Commit no evil," [the meaning would be incomplete].
If one speaks thus, the phrasing is not ultimate;
if one speaks of "all evils," the meaning is not ultimate.
Furthermore, it is only by not acting [otherwise] that one attains fulfillment;
this is the "phrase of fulfillment.
As for the "phrase of what is accomplished":
This means that the preceding statement is only established by means of the subsequent statement.
For example:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they have the nature of arising and ceasing, for what is born must necessarily perish."

That tranquility is bliss; however, in order to establish here that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, it is subsequently stated that "there is the nature of arising and passing away.
The former [point] is what is to be established.
That which is established is the thesis;
that which follows is the proof,
which is the argument.
The "indicating phrase" (*padasaṃsūcanā*) is,
for example, saying "the nature of goodness.
The "explaining phrase" (*padanirvacana*) is...
This refers to those who have correctly entered the path of the virtuous person (*satpuruṣa*). Regarding the "body of syllables" (*vyañjana-kāya*):
it refers to the forty-nine syllables that serve as the basis for names and phrases (*nāma-pada*), whether they are ultimate or non-ultimate.
In this context, desire is the primary factor for names;
names are the primary factor for phrases;
and phrases necessarily possess names.
A name must necessarily have a word (akṣara).
If there were only a single word, it would not constitute a sentence.
Furthermore, there may be words that are not subsumed under a name.
There are only syllables, but no names.
Question: For what reason and by what conditions are the three types of bodies, beginning with names, established?
Answer: It is for the purpose of enabling the experience of the sensations produced by contact associated with various designations (*adhivacana*).
Question: What is the meaning of "name" (*nāman*)?
Answer: It is called "name" because it enables various things to be mutually cognized.
Furthermore, it is called "name" (nāman) because it causes the mind to form various mental images;
it is also so called because it is summoned by means of speech.

That which is called "name" (nāman) is so termed because it fully clarifies the meaning of things that are not directly perceived by apprehending various names. That which is called "phrase" (pada) is so termed [for the same reason].
It is called "phrasing" (*vyañjana*) because it manifests names and phrases;
as the Blessed One said: "The designation (*adhivacana*) and the path of designation."
...and so on, as explained at length.
In this context, "designation" (*adhivacana*) refers to all names that correspond to a particular class of beings.
"Path" (*patha*) refers to the fact that, together with that class of beings, one has the desire to give rise to them.
"Terminology" (pada) refers to the speech associated with that [meaning].
Furthermore, it is this very speech which, in various respective instances, either indicates or explains.
That which serves as its basis is called "its path.
As for "provisioning":
That is to say, the individual analysis and designation [of phenomena],
which establishes their respective bases,
is called "their path."
Desire itself is the expression;
there is no desire apart from it.
This is the path of conventional designation through metaphorical nomenclature.

The application of the sense bases (*āyatana-yukti*),

What is the meaning?

This means not abandoning any happiness obtained in accordance with the Dharma,

Relying on the Middle Way, one pursues things in accordance with the Dharma and correctly utilizes requisites such as robes;

Regarding the defilement of afflictions, there are four propositions.
That is, the four inversions.
Regarding the defilement of transmigration, there are two phrases:

those who have gone forth [from the household life]...

Knowledge and liberation exist on the stage of seeing,

Because he had already attained mastery over them,
they then requested of him,
saying: "What should we do now?"
"Please grant us your instruction.
Thereupon, he said to them:
"Regarding such and such matters as these, you [should now act]..."
One should practice correctly;
one should train accordingly.
As for "encouraging and exhorting":
That is to say, if those sentient beings experience despondency regarding what is to be known, what is to be practiced, or what is to be attained,

enabling them to possess the capacity and power for those matters.
"Rejoicing" means that when those sentient beings practice with courageous and correct application in accordance with the Dharma, one should praise and gladden them as they truly deserve.
Furthermore, "manifesting the departure from desire" refers to...
There are cases where one causes another to become free from desire without manifesting [the act] oneself;
for example, when instructing another to become free from desire,
one says to them:
Regarding what [someone] has said that one should not do:
you must certainly not do it again from now on.
Or, fearing their words, [you think]: "If you do this, I will certainly do such and such."
Alternatively, if you seek that [state], and if I am your beloved and virtuous friend,
you must certainly not act [in such a way].
Or, there may be manifestations intended to prevent one from becoming free from desire.
Like one who stands in the middle,
they manifest both virtues and faults,
yet are not yet capable of preventing others from being separated from those faults.
There are also those who cause others to become free from desire and manifest this accordingly,
such as by demonstrating the faults of desire to lead them to detachment;
these are the ones who provide instruction, encouragement, and inspiration.
This means that for those who have not yet undertaken training, one causes them to undertake it;
and for those who have already undertaken training but have not yet ascended to higher progress,
one causes them to ascend.
Regarding "rejoicing":
when one rejoices in that which is worthy of rejoicing,
there are five benefits.
First, it causes those [beings] to become resolute in their minds regarding what they have realized for themselves.
Second, it causes others to develop the aspiration to realize the qualities realized by that person.
Third, it causes the minds of those who slander [the teaching] to become purified.
Fourth, it causes those who are not yet pure to abide with a mind established in the middle way.
Fifth, it causes those who are already pure to increase even further.
If there is a person who rejoices in the virtuous deeds of others, [they shall attain such benefits].
One should know that by performing and increasing such actions,
one can bring about rebirth as a celestial being of pleasing appearance;
and when life comes to an end, [one will be reborn there].
Following each and every birth,
they constantly hear delightful and exquisite sounds;
there is no sensory object whatsoever that is not pleasing to them.
Furthermore, among the practices of desire, some are capable of inducing rebirth in the happy realms,
such as when one performs subsequent wholesome karma for the sake of desire;
others are capable of inducing rebirth in the miserable realms.
Just as when one indulges in sensual desires by means of what is not the Dharma,
if there is a transgression regarding the practice, it can lead to rebirth in the evil destinies;
whereas if one is able to accomplish it correctly, it can lead to rebirth in the happy destinies.
Furthermore, virtuous conduct can bring about rebirth in the happy realms and serve as a provision for attaining nirvāṇa.
Unwholesome conduct can lead to rebirth in the miserable realms, as can ascetic practices,
because one inflicts suffering upon oneself based on wrong views.
Austere asceticism cannot serve as a requisite for nirvāṇa;
rather, it is the factors conducive to decline and the factors conducive to progress that function according to their respective natures.
Retreat, fall, and advancement constitute defiled practices that can induce birth and death;
pure practices can realize nirvana.
The practice for one's own benefit causes only oneself to go to the happy realms and attain the realization of nirvana;
the practice for the benefit of others causes both oneself and others to go to the happy realms.
Up until the attainment of the realization of nirvāṇa through advancement—
within these three matters, there are six fundamental points,
namely, from the initial favorable rebirths up to nirvāṇa as the final one.
There are twelve kinds of skillful means, namely the twelve practices.
There are five kinds of compassionate concern for others.
This refers to the compassionate regard for sentient beings by way of five aspects;
herein, by the predominant power of the fundamental matter,
it relies upon twelve modes of conduct.
Causing others to become free from desire as appropriate,
up to the point of rejoicing;
this refers to the basis of time.
Briefly stated, there are three kinds of verbal objects:

Third is the present verbal activity,

Regarding the basis for the person (*pudgala*):

Because of the matter, the time, and the individual (pudgala),

As for the meaning of "faults" (*ādīnava*),

Regarding the meaning of "excellence" (viśeṣa) in terms of either phenomena (dharma) or persons (pudgala),

To praise that which is worthy of praise—
whether it be a phenomenon (*dharma*) or a person (*pudgala*)—

To state it briefly:
in brief, that which has the sense of being an antidote to all defiled activities.
To state it briefly.

As for the summarized meaning:
it refers to the proclamation that all phenomena correspond according to their respective types.
In its broad sense,
it refers to the proclamation of the various categories of phenomena in their mutual correspondence;
furthermore, it refers to the teaching of the sutras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
Because it is a sūtra of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Second, the summary of meaning.

First is the extensiveness of name;
second is the extensiveness of meaning.
As the Blessed One said: "Śāriputra, the Dharma taught by me..."
Whether concise or extensive,

The detailed explanation is as set forth in the sutras.
It should be understood that herein it is shown that the Blessed One provides extensive text with concise meaning in the sūtras,

In order to encompass ten meanings,

One should understand the meaning of the broad and concise [teachings] regarding the mental engagement with the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*),

Furthermore, having thus briefly explained the tenfold nature of the Buddha’s teaching, [the following is stated]:
Those who preach the Dharma should seek, in accordance with the sacred teachings, whether these ten [aspects] are complete or incomplete;
having sought them for themselves, they should explain them to others.
Thus, the essential meaning of the texts of the various sūtras has been established.
All those who preach the Dharma should explain all the Buddha’s sūtras in accordance with five characteristics.
That is to say: first, they should briefly state the essential meaning of the teaching;
second, they should proclaim the origin [of the discourse].
Next, its meaning should be proclaimed;
next, the objections should be resolved;
and finally, the sequence should be analyzed.
The Dharma,
in brief, consists of twelve types;
namely, the twelvefold teaching beginning with the Sūtras.
The *sūtra* (契經) refers to prose discourses that string together meanings through direct exposition; for the most part,
they encompass the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) and essential nature (*svabhāva*).
"Geya" (Verses) refers to the presentation of gāthās following prose passages;
it also briefly indicates those sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) that have been taught.
"Vyākaraṇa" (prediction) refers to the detailed analysis of the meaning briefly indicated [in a sūtra],

"Verses" (geya) refers to that which is spoken in stanzas;
it may be spoken in two lines, or in three, four, five, or six lines.
"Self-proclaimed" refers to speaking without being requested,
for the purpose of enabling disciples to attain resolute conviction.
In order to cause those sentient beings who are of superior capacity to abide in the sublime principle,

As it is taught regarding the four bodhisattva practices of the seventh stage,

That is to say: by way of the distinctions of the desire realm,

whether a difficulty is raised by oneself or by another, it should all be explained and resolved.
It should be understood that this objection is briefly characterized by five aspects.

For example: "What is the meaning of this passage?"
Second, because there is a contradiction in the words:
for instance, saying, "Why is that which was previously stated by the Blessed One different from what is now being stated?"
Third, because it contradicts reason;
for instance, there are indications of meanings that contradict the four principles of reasoning (*yukti*).
Fourth, because it is not definitively indicated.
As it is said: "For what reason does the Blessed One, regarding a single meaning,

Fifth, because it is ultimately not perceptible to the senses. For instance,

Such categories of objections should be understood as difficult to reconcile.
Regarding these five objections, they should be explained in their respective order;
that is to say, the objection concerning the non-explicit meaning (*neyārtha*) is to be clarified through skillful means (*upāya*).
Just as one demonstrates the underlying intention and provides a coherent interpretation in response to the objection that a statement is contradictory,

Or they may resolve it by means of other teachings;

The second is analytical explanation (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇa*).
This refers to revealing the specific characteristics and natures of various phenomena to those who come to inquire in either a correct or incorrect manner.
Third is the response by counter-question (*paripṛcchā-vyākaraṇa*),

Herein, the Tathāgata speaks in terms of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).

Part II of the *Śāsanasaṃgraha*:
Regarding the Listeners—this refers to when such a speaker of the Dharma preaches the True Dharma.
One should establish others so that they abide in respectful and non-perverted listening.
How does one establish them?
It is by means of either a single cause or even up to ten.
The first cause is listening to the Dharma with reverence,
because it enables one to realize benefit and happiness in the present life.
In this regard, there are four permutations— such as that which is beneficial but not pleasant—
and these have already been explained in the *Dharmasamādāna* section of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
As for the two causes:
This means that all phenomena are well-established.

As for the three causes:
listening to the Dharma with reverence.
Because it enables sentient beings to abandon the evil realms,
attain the good realms,
and swiftly draw forth and encompass the causes of nirvāṇa.
These three matters can only be attained through listening with reverence.
As for the four causes:
First, by listening to the Dharma with reverence,

Second, such is the True Dharma.
It enables sentient beings to abandon all that is unwholesome and to embrace all that is wholesome;

Third, by means of equanimity (*upekṣā*), one abandons the future suffering summoned by unwholesome causes.

The five causes are as follows:
the True Dharma taught by the Buddha, the World-Honored One,

One should praise the Buddha.

Question: What is the meaning of "dwelling in the excellence of training"?
Answer: This designation indicates dwelling in the superior merit of the training in higher morality (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*).
Question: What is the meaning of "having wisdom as the foremost"?
Answer: This metaphorical designation (adhivacana) indicates that among all the faculties, the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya) is supreme.
Question: What is the meaning of "firm liberation" (vimukti-dṛḍha)?
Answer: This metaphorical designation indicates the permanent abandonment of the afflictions (kleśa) to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation (darśana-bhāvanā-heya).
Question: What is the meaning of "having mindfulness as the predominant factor"?
Answer: This designation indicates that one does not give rise to complacency regarding what is meager or inferior.
Question: In other sūtras, the Blessed One has taught the sequence of the three trainings differently.
Why is it that, in this context, higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) is taught after higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*), rather than higher mind (*adhicitta*)?
The answer is: this passage demonstrates the excellence of abiding in training (*śikṣā-viśeṣa*).
By means of these words, it is shown that the wisdom consisting of hearing and so forth (*śrutamayī-prajñā* etc. encompasses freedom from remorse (*avipratisāra*) and other qualities.
Through this, one gradually attains samādhi;
this demonstrates the training in higher mind (adhicitta-śikṣā).
As the Blessed One said, "In these five faculties, one is most capable of mastery."
That which is embraced is the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya).
Because the bhikṣus have accomplished the faculty of wisdom,
they are able to cultivate the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya), and so forth.
In this way, up until the accomplishment of the faculty of concentration,
one should know that all are due to the power of the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
In this sutra, the Blessed One demonstrates that the faculty of wisdom is the cause for inducing samādhi.
Furthermore, the causes for the abandonment of afflictions are taught simultaneously with the training in higher mind and the training in higher wisdom.
Question: In other sūtras, it is said that the cultivation of the three trainings leads to their fulfillment.
Why is it not stated that the training in higher mind is fulfilled through cultivation?
The answer is as previously explained;
one should know that the principle here is likewise.

Answer: One should know that by encouraging the attainment of excellence within the inferior, one also causes the beings to be converted to receive excellence within the sublime.
Furthermore, by gathering them into the Saṃgha, one brings about ten kinds of benefits, such as the Saṃgha’s diligent application and so forth.
It is clear, easy to understand, and easy to enter into realization.
For this reason, only the benefits of abiding in training are explained.
Question: As for that which is liberation, [how is it defined?]
Among all dharmas, it is the most preeminent.
For what reason is it said that wisdom alone is the foremost?
It does not say that one abides in the preeminence of liberation.
The answer is: one should know that this encourages the adoption of preeminence even among inferior qualities.
Furthermore, it causes the sentient beings being transformed to grasp the state of preeminence among the sublime and excellent;
moreover, it demonstrates the unique, distinguished qualities of liberation.
What is called the unique, distinguished merit?
It refers to the fact that, at the limit of unsurpassed wisdom regarding impermanence,
one is liberated from permanence and is thus most firm and stable.
Question: What is called "abiding in the benefits of training"?
Answer: It is to contemplate the ten benefits within the various training rules (śikṣāpada) as they have been prescribed.
Constantly guarding the śīla, firmly upholding the śīla,
always practicing and constantly turning [the wheel of Dharma]—
this is called abiding in the excellence of training.
Question: What is the meaning of the various phrases such as "upholding the Saṃgha"?
Answer: "Upholding the Saṃgha" is the general statement.
"To cause the Saṃgha to be earnest" means to cause them to abandon the extreme of attachment to sensual enjoyments.
"To cause the Saṃgha to be at ease" means...
It causes one to leave behind the extreme of self-inflicted austerity;
it brings about pure faith in those who have not yet attained it.
In order to cause those who have not yet entered the True Dharma to enter it,
and for those who already possess pure faith...
"Causing them to increase" means causing those who have already entered the True Dharma to reach maturity.
To those who are difficult to subdue,

One who purely maintains the precepts is so because they bring about freedom from remorse;

Because it conforms to and subdues the entanglements of the afflictions;

Because it conforms to the permanent abandonment of the afflictions and latent tendencies;
because it causes the holy life of many people to endure for a long time and to further increase and expand;

In order to ensure that the holy teaching continues for a long time without interruption,

What are the three?
First, to cause the Saṃgha to dwell without defilement;
second, to cause the Saṃgha to dwell in peace and happiness.
Third, it causes the Buddha’s holy teaching to endure for a long time.
Herein, by means of seven kinds of protection,

The seven kinds of protection are:
first, protection through respectful service;
second, protection through ascetic self-mortification.
Third, guarding against the deficiency of material resources;
fourth, guarding against mutual physical contact;
fifth, guarding against the mind’s subsequent transformations.

The final phrase demonstrates that the holy teaching continues to function for a long duration.
What is meant by "constantly guarding śīla"?

This means that there are no breaches or holes in the precepts.
How is it that it constantly turns?
It means that after having been pierced and perforated, it returns to purity.
How does one undertake and train in the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*)?
This means that because they fully train in accordance with all the rules of training (śikṣāpada),
such a practitioner constantly guards their ethical discipline (śīla) and firmly maintains their ethical discipline.
Having heard the true Dharma, he dwells alone in a quiet place,

By means of the sublime wisdom born of hearing, reflection, and cultivation,

because this nature of liberation is such that it cannot be lost.
It is called "firm" because it is the fruit of supramundane noble wisdom. Furthermore,

"Do I possess the correct wisdom that thoroughly penetrates all phenomena?
Have I well realized liberation?
Thus, by relying on the power of right mindfulness, one possesses the excellence of training.

In this location,

Because they arise through the transformation of immeasurable kinds of characteristics;

To take a straight plantain pillar means—
This refers to the view of a self as an agent and an experiencer;

This is because that which passes through time lacks any stable abiding;

How much less could any other permanent, eternal, real self—whether as an agent or an experiencer—be perceived?
How is consciousness like a magical illusion?
That which is called a "magical person" corresponds to meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable formations.

The summary verse (uddāna) says:
The storehouse of birth, old age, and death; the afflictions such as those to be rejoiced in;

Because his body is bent forward and he walks leaning on a staff;

"The conditioned phenomena having withered" [means...]

furthermore, "the dead."

Regarding the "receding of life-span" and the "receding of warmth":

while the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) ceases.
Because the lifespan of all beings is completely exhausted;
as for the one who dies,
it is because their consciousness abandons its location in the heart and chest.
Regarding those who have passed away: after death, it may be one week,
or it may pass through two or three weeks.
Furthermore, all foolish ordinary beings, by grasping at a self within the six sense bases, call them "concealments" (*kośa*);
by grasping at what belongs to the self, they call them "protections" (*rakṣā*).
These are rooted in the view of a transitory collection (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The various divergent worldly views and inclinations are called *mrakṣa* (concealment) because they are characterized by the manifestation of self-conceit (*asmimāna*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
This pertains to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) associated with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanīya*).
Because there is sensual desire, it is called "attachment";
regarding the six sense bases associated with painful feelings,
because there is ill will, it is called a "fetter."
Regarding the six sense bases associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,
they are called "conjoined" because of the presence of delusion;
this applies to all six sense bases in the past as well.
Because there is attachment and longing, it is called a latent tendency (*anuśaya*).
Because there is hope for all that exists in future lives,
it is called bondage (*bandhana*).
Regarding the six sense bases existing in the present life,
because there is attachment and defilement toward them, they are called "clinging.
This refers to the six sense bases of one's own appropriated body and those of others.
One clings to these as "mine.
Regarding the inferior, the middling, and the superior, one gives rise to pride based on the six sense bases of other bodies that are not one's own,
through the various types of conceit.
In the non-concentrated stage bound to the desire realm,
one gives rise to successive aspirations;
[likewise] regarding the concentrated stages bound to the form and formless realms.
Accordingly, because it is vast and subtle,
one gives rise to a profound and weighty resolve.
Based on the categories of householders, through the forms, sounds, odors, tastes,
and tangibles, and because they are pursued by the retinue of craving and relishing,
a sense of sweetness arises.
Based on the six bases of the Chapter on Renunciation,
due to the afflictions of indolence and negligence,
one is unable to relinquish them entirely.
Next, regarding that which is "delightful," "joyous," "lovely," and "pleasing," one should know that these four phrases briefly indicate agreeable objects.
These agreeable objects are, in brief, of three kinds.
First, things that are desirable;
second, things that are to be investigated;
third, things that are to be clung to.
Because future desirable things are to be sought after,
they are called "delightful" (*abhinandaniya*).
Because past desirable things are merely to be desired and merely to be enjoyed, [they are not called delightful].
It is called "delightful.
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of presently pleasant things:
first, objective objects; second, internal states.
Second is the object of experience.
Because the objective sphere is desirable and pleasing,
it is called "desirable."
If an object experienced is pleasant and delightful,
it is called "agreeable.
Such are the various agreeable things that have been described.
They differ according to whether they belong to the past, the future,
or the present; or according to whether they are objects or experiences.
It is called an object to be sought after,
or an object to be investigated,
or an object of attachment.
Therefore, all such distinctions among these phrases are proclaimed.
Furthermore, that which is "to be delighted in" refers to the future life,
because it is something to be aspired for.
That which is "pleasurable" refers to the present life,
because what is currently desirable and pleasurable can never bring satisfaction.
"Agreeable" refers to the past;
it is so called because one recollects and recalls that which was agreeable according to one's memory.
"Beloved" refers to its exquisite form and appearance;
it is so called because it is desirable throughout all three periods of time.
Furthermore, "desirable" means that which is pleasing to the mind and brings joy to the memory;
"induced by desire" means...
Because they are bound to the desire realm,
or because they accord with the two kinds of differentiated enjoyment of desires,
they are subject to defilement and attachment.
Because they are the locus of craving,
and furthermore, because they can bring about the conjunction of five kinds of things,
they are called "fetters" (saṃyojana).
The five kinds of matters are:
first, the matter that is bound;
second, the matter that binds.
Third, the matter of transgressions;
fourth, the matter of outflows;
fifth, the matter of orientation.
The objects of the various fetters are called the "bases of bondage.
Why is this? Because craving, aversion, and so forth each conjoin with their respective objects according to their specific characteristics.
Because those various fetters mutually attract one another and coalesce,
they are termed "the things that bind.
Through the causal conditions of these fetters, transgressions and faults are produced within the present life.
...up to the point of experiencing it.
The mental factors of sorrow and suffering arising from that are able to come together by virtue of these causes and conditions.
It is called a "matter of fault" because it serves as the cause for the production of intense greed and so forth in future lives;
it is called a "matter of outflow" because it is a concordant result.
Because it can produce the five destinies and brings about their conjunction within those various destinies,
it is called the "matter of proceeding toward [rebirth].
By reason of this, one personally engages in unwholesome conduct.
It is called "able to harm oneself" because it arises from encountering various kinds of suffering, such as being punished with canes, being bound and imprisoned, being reviled, being driven away,
or being harmed by others. It is [also so called] because,
even if one does not encounter these oneself, one causes others to encounter them.

That which is called "capable of harming others" refers to that by means of which others alone are harmed. That which is called "capable of harming both" refers to that by means of which both oneself and others encounter harm.
That which can produce offenses in the present life refers to the various kinds of suffering and calamities one encounters because of them; however,
it does not necessarily lead to rebirth in the evil destinies.
That which can produce offenses in future lives refers to those [actions] by virtue of which, although they remain unknown to others in the present life,
they nevertheless serve as the cause for rebirth in the evil destinies.
That which gives rise to offenses in both the present life and future lives possesses two characteristics:
it involves being largely possessed by defiled attachment within the present life.
When one's desires are not fulfilled, various mental states of sorrow and suffering arise extensively;
furthermore, one will go to the various evil destinies in the future.
Although the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are immeasurable, speaking of them in terms of their predominance, there are briefly nine fetters.
Furthermore, in terms of the meaning of not being able to act according to one's desires,
it is said that there are three fetters;
namely, greed, hatred, and delusion, because they depend upon the three types of feeling.
Due to those causes and conditions, although one desires to be liberated from them, one cannot be liberated;
therefore, they are called "bonds.
Furthermore, they are pursued by the seeds of the heavy latencies (*dausthulya*) belonging to the category of afflictions.
They are called *anuśaya* (latent tendencies).
This signifies the sense of "binding" and the sense of being "subtle.
Taking their roots, there are only seven types.
Furthermore, because they arise from afflictions,
because one associates with afflictions,
and because they follow and disturb the mind.
They are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*);
they comprise all other defiled mental factors, excluding the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
These are all secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Furthermore, when they manifest and continue in a stream without interruption,
they are designated as "entanglements" (*paryavasthāna*).
There are eight kinds of envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
namely lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and so forth.
Furthermore, they cause [the afflictions] to become intensified and arise as a continuous stream.
Because it renders the body and mind incapable of functioning,
it is called a "stump" (*sthāṇu*).
It is like a saline field that is unfit for plowing or planting.
Furthermore, because their locations differ and because the doubts arising from them differ,
five "stumps of the mind" (cittakīla) are taught.
Because of the distinctions between greed and the others,
they are said to be of three kinds;
furthermore, because they cause one to be impure.
It is called "impurity" (mala).
Furthermore, because it constantly flows through the gates of the various sense bases,
it is called "river" (nirga).
Because they are constantly able to cause harm,
they are also called *niga*.

It is called an arrow because,
like one struck by a poisoned arrow that has not yet been extracted, it is for the most part not tranquil;
furthermore, because it obstructs equanimity and because it constitutes conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
It is called "that which exists.
Furthermore, because unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct manifest before one,
it is termed "misconduct."
Furthermore, because they can give rise to all afflictions and various unwholesome actions,
they are called "roots.
Moreover, because they can produce future births, they are so named.

Furthermore, because they cause one who has already been born to be impoverished by old age, death, and so forth,

Furthermore, because one is tormented by union with the unpleasant, separation from the beloved,
and the craving for gain and offerings,

Furthermore, because it causes lamentation, grief, sorrow, suffering, and affliction,

Moreover, because it causes one to be carried away and submerged by the current, [it is so named].
They are called floods (*ogha*).
Furthermore, because they serve as the primary means for the transmigration of birth and death in the present life based on the past limit (*pūrvānta*),

Furthermore, it is called "grasping" because that which exists in the present serves as the superior means for the future;
moreover, it is so called because it is difficult to understand.
They are called "fetters" (saṃyojana).

Furthermore, in relation to the form and formless realms,

The path of seeing constitutes the lower part;
based on these two distinctions of the lower part,
they are designated as the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni) as appropriate.
These are also called the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīyāḥ saṃyojanāḥ*).
One should know that, as their opposite, there are said to be five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhva-bhāgīyāḥ saṃyojanāḥ*).
Furthermore, regarding what is called a "grove" (*vana*):
It is able to give rise to various aggregates of suffering;
because its essential nature is rooted in affection,
it increases and is therefore called a "dense forest."
Furthermore, it is called "contention" (*raṇa*) because it can give rise to various forms of strife and competition,
