The realm that is accumulated through the habitual practice of false views regarding liberation is like what is said concerning the view of eternalism;
it is likewise so for the view of annihilationism.
The view of nirvana in the present life [arises] from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
the detailed explanation is likewise.

In this regard, the Blessed One, by virtue of the sovereign power of the knowledge of various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñānabala*) and the knowledge of various elements (*nānādhātu-jñānabala*), [acts accordingly].
Seeking out both that prior inclination and that subsequent element,
one primarily employs the fourfold teaching of the Dharma as appropriate to subdue those elements of false inclination.
Or, for the sake of bringing to maturity the wisdom of others whose wisdom is not yet matured;
and for those whose wisdom is already matured, for the sake of liberating them from all afflictions;
[he acts] for the sake of sentient beings who are initially situated in a state of perversion.
It is said that because causes cease, formations cease;
this teaching on impermanence is given through the gateway of the exhaustion of formations in order to subdue those whose realm of inclination is characterized by false resolve.
For the sake of sentient beings who follow the second false realm,
it is said that because causes accumulate, formations accumulate;
and by way of the arising of formations, impermanence is explained.
In order to subdue those whose realm consists of wrong resolve,
and to follow those sentient beings belonging to the third category of wrong realms,
he turns the wheel of the True Dharma teaching by way of the gateway of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
It is for the sake of subduing those whose realm consists of wrong resolve,
and for the sake of following those sentient beings of the fourth wrong realm who,
having departed from all conditioned phenomena, give rise to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
For those who turn toward the teaching of the True Dharma through the gateway of the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
and for those practitioners who give rise to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) regarding those very conditioned phenomena,
the teaching of the True Dharma is turned toward them by means of the gateway of non-self (*anātman*).
In order to discipline those of wrong resolve,
furthermore, the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya is briefly characterized by three unique factors.
It is not shared with non-Buddhists;
it is included among the categories of well-spoken teachings.
First, because it proclaims the reality of ultimate liberation.
Second, because it proclaims those very means;
third, because it proclaims that which is personally realized within.
What is true, ultimate liberation?
This refers to ultimate liberation and all-encompassing liberation;
that is, the fruit of the path of seeing,
as well as the fruits of the mundane and supramundane paths of cultivation attained thereafter.
Among these, the fruit of the path of seeing is designated as "ultimate" (tattva) by virtue of its definitiveness,
yet it is not the final consummation.
Because there is still that which remains to be accomplished regarding all forms of liberation.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of liberation: first, mundane liberation;
[second, supramundane liberation]; and third, ultimate liberation.
Second is the liberation of those in training;
third is the liberation of those beyond training.
Worldly liberation is not the ultimate reality.
Because there is regression,
the liberation of those in training (śaikṣa), though real, is not ultimate,
for there is still that which remains to be done.
It should be understood that the remaining [perfections] possess both types.
What is the skillful means?

It refers to cultivating the perception of impermanence regarding all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) by relying on their mode of existence as it is (yathāvadbhāvatā) and their extent of existence (yāvadbhāvatā).
Based on impermanence, one cultivates the perception of suffering;
based on suffering, one cultivates the perception of emptiness and non-self.
By means of this, when one attains entry into the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), [the path is realized].
By means of correctly observing the objects of knowledge,
one attains right view;
and by relying upon this right view, [one proceeds].
Within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one dwells with a pervasive perception of revulsion toward all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).

While dwelling therein, although the objects of mindfulness and reflection associated with that state do not manifest as clearly present, they appear vividly before the mind through the sensations concomitant with them.
Yet he does not give rise to joy.
By the predominant power of not giving rise to joy,
when he moves about, he does not produce defiled attachment toward those objects of perception that serve as the focal points for his feelings.
Because he attains a state of equanimity toward all objects of pursuit,
he does not even aspire for them, let alone become attached to them.
By means of this, whether remaining still or moving about, he is able to swiftly extinguish the entanglements of joy and greed.
The mind dwells in purity.
Furthermore, it is due to the causal condition of extensively practicing that very path as it has been attained.
By permanently uprooting the heavy latencies (*dausthulya-anuśaya*) of that category,
one attains true and ultimate liberation;
know that this is precisely the "well-liberated mind."
What is that which is personally realized within?
It should be known that there are four aspects when one proceeds toward the liberation of those in training (śaikṣa).
One realizes this through internal wisdom by means of two aspects:

namely, "I have exhausted all conditioned formations arising within the various evil destinies," and "I have exhausted all remaining conditioned formations that would otherwise arise in future lives, except for seven, two, or one more birth."
Furthermore, I already abide in the path that is capable of ultimate exhaustion and is non-retrogressive.
When turning toward the liberation of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
I internally realize it through wisdom by means of these two aspects.
That is to say: "I have already performed what is to be practiced for the abandonment of all remaining afflictions;
even one more birth does not remain for me now, much less two, much less seven."
Furthermore, according to what is desired, one is also able to provide others with accurate explanations and predictions.
This is called that which is personally realized within.
Next, there are two types of preliminary practices for that very liberation.
First is the preliminary practice for the vision;
second is the preliminary practice for the fruit of the path.
Regarding the preliminary practice for the vision, it refers to the superior power of what is personally realized within oneself through liberation and its means.
From the sounds and voices of others, one gives rise to the sublime goodness consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation,
as well as correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*),
before yet entering the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
One is able to enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
attain the supramundane right view that sees things as they truly are,
and [attain] the factors that precede the path and its fruits.
This means that once such right view has been attained,
the remaining factors, such as right thought and so forth,
arise— either simultaneously or at a later time.
The preparatory practices for the Path are for the purpose of severing all remaining afflictions;
furthermore, they are for the purpose of realizing the liberation not yet attained.
One should observe eight matters:
namely, the observation of the gratification, the disadvantage, and the renunciation regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
as well as the observation through the power of hearing, reflection, and discernment, and through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
When observing the gratification within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
one is able to thoroughly penetrate the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of that gratification in conditioned phenomena;
likewise, when observing the danger (*ādīnava*) within conditioned phenomena.
One is able to skillfully understand the common characteristics of the faults within the states of the three types of feeling—
that is, that therein the flavor of gratification is very slight while the faults are many—
and thus understands the common characteristics of the faults associated with attachment to the flavor of gratification.
One should already be able to dispel, suppress, sever,
and abandon the afflictions of desire and greed that arise in relation to all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) that are objects of attachment.
Because sensual desire does not manifest with respect to this, it is said to be "abandoned";
however, it is not called "abandoned" because of permanent separation from desire.
Furthermore, the mind is not yet liberated from those objects.
If one completely transcends the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*),
one becomes eternally free from desire and attains liberation of mind;
this is called the distinction of observation through a single gateway.
Furthermore, when the practitioner correctly contemplates those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
they first understand through the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*)— in accordance with the Āgamas—
that the essence of all conditioned phenomena is impermanent.
Because it is impermanent, it is suffering;
because it is suffering, it is empty and selfless.
He thus gains resolute conviction and thus penetrates this according to the noble teaching.
Having attained such mastery, he further understands that object as it truly is through a subtle mental attention (manasikāra) accomplished by means of analytical reflection.
It is precisely through the dominant power of such mastery and understanding that [he proceeds].
One observes, as they truly are, all the faults pertaining to the present life and the future that arise from the manifestation of the afflictions associated with those [objects],
by relying on the power of analytical investigation.
Even if they should arise again, he does not unrealistically cling to them and is thus able to relinquish them;
this is because he has extensively cultivated such power of thorough penetration, understanding, and analytical discernment.
One is able to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth.
Having entered the state of rightness and departure from birth,
one gradually abandons all desires through the power of the path of cultivation.
By means of the two powers of analytical discernment and the path of vision,
he abandons the various afflictions as appropriate—
that is, by way of their non-manifestation.
And because one portion is severed,
through the power of the path of cultivation, one becomes ultimately free from desire;
thus, by means of these two preceding types, one gradually becomes free from sensual craving.
Through the power of the path of cultivation, the mind attains liberation.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of fruits: the fruit of the abandonment of afflictions and the fruit of the cessation of suffering.
The first is the fruit of what is abandoned through vision.
By virtue of realizing that, one is able to know for oneself: "I have forever exhausted rebirth in the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts;
I have now attained the stage of Stream-enterer, a state from which there is no falling back."
...and so on, as extensively explained.
Second is the fruit of abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-phala*);
it is so called because one realizes it.
He is able to know for himself:
"This is my final body, sustained only for a brief time;
rebirth in a second existence and so forth shall never recur."
Furthermore, there are two kinds of cessation of suffering:
first, the cessation of future suffering caused by present conditions;
second, the cessation of present suffering caused by past conditions.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of cessation of suffering:
first, the cessation of mental suffering;
second, the cessation of physical suffering.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of cessation of suffering:
first, the cessation of the suffering of change and the suffering of suffering;
second, the cessation of the suffering of conditioned formations.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of cessation of suffering:
first, the cessation of suffering that is the result of non-desirable karma;
second, the cessation of suffering that is the result of desirable karma.
Furthermore, there are some noble disciples who have already seen the path of truth;
although they have already transcended the fear of all suffering in the evil destinies,
because they have not yet permanently exhausted all fetters (saṃyojana), [they remain subject to fear].
His mind still possesses the fear of birth, aging, and death shared with other beings in future lives;
in order to sever that,
he is able to give rise to intense aspiration, up to right mindfulness and heedfulness.
Diligently cultivating meditative practice and so forth constitute two [factors].
The first is not knowing, as it truly is, that which ought to be sought.
Second, that which is not to be sought arises instead.
What is called "that which is to be sought"?
It is nirvāṇa, the eternal cessation of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Yet those foolish commoners have no desire whatsoever for the non-arising of future conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra),
but rather for their arising.
There is only delight;
by reason of this, one does not know as it truly is the various sufferings that arise regarding what is to be sought and within all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
What is it that is called "that which should not be sought but instead arises"?
That which is not to be sought refers to old age, sickness, and death.
Encountering what is disliked,
separation from what is loved,
and the suffering of lamentation, grief, and despair due to the lack of what one desires.
Amidst various kinds of burning afflictions,
they give rise to such conditioned phenomena and,
conversely, experience delight in them.
Among all conditioned phenomena, which have birth as their root,
one develops a deep attachment and craving;
regarding all karmic actions that have birth as their root, [one likewise develops such attachment].
Through the accumulation of such formative activities,
by reason of these causes and conditions, one does not attain liberation from the suffering of birth and the various forms of suffering rooted in birth,
such as aging, illness, and death.
This is called that which should not be sought yet arises nonetheless.
Furthermore, within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), there are four certainties:
first, the certainty of impermanence (*anityatā-niścaya*).
Second, the certainty of suffering;
third, the certainty of emptiness;
fourth, the certainty of non-self.
How is it that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are determined to be impermanent?
One should know that by means of three characteristics, even past and future conditioned phenomena are certainly impermanent,
let alone those of the present.
What are the three? They are:
that which was previously non-existent now exists;
and that which was previously existent now no longer exists.
Because they correspond to arising and ceasing:
if future formations were definitely non-existent as something that did not previously exist,
then it would follow that they do not arise from what was previously non-existent.
In this way, it would not be determined as impermanent,
because that which was previously designated as non-existent cannot have non-existence as its antecedent.
They exist only at a later time;
therefore, it is certain that future conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent.
If they were already determined to exist in the present once produced from conditions, [they would not be impermanent].
In that case, it would follow that what previously existed does not cease to exist;
consequently, future conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) would not be definitively impermanent,
and present conditioned phenomena likewise would not be associated with arising and ceasing.
Since present formations, having arisen from conditions, do not exist with fixed certainty,
their non-existence is designated based on their prior existence;
therefore, past formations are definitely impermanent.
In this way, present formations arise from future formations where they previously did not exist,
and they cease from past formations where they previously existed.
Because this designation is associated with arising and ceasing, it is said:
"One should know that the impermanent nature of past and future conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is already certain;
how much more so for those of the present?"
This is called the certainty that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent.
What is the certainty regarding the nature of suffering of all conditioned phenomena?
It means that even past and future conditioned phenomena are dharmas characterized by suffering, such as birth and so forth.
How much more so for the present? Why is this?
Because past formations have already transcended suffering.
Future formations are suffering that has not yet arrived;
present formations are manifest suffering.
This is called the certainty of the nature of suffering in all formations.
What is the certainty of the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)?
It means that even past and future conditioned phenomena are certainly empty in nature,
let alone those of the present.
Why is this? Because future conditioned phenomena have not yet come into being;
for this reason, they are empty.
Past conditioned phenomena have already ceased by their very nature;
for this reason, they are empty.
Present conditioned phenomena, although existing, have not yet ceased and are devoid of the nature of reality and ultimate truth.
Because of this, they are empty;
this is called the determination of the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
What is the determination of the selflessness of all conditioned phenomena?
This means that since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the past and future are certainly without self,
how much more so those of the present? Why is this so?
Future formations do not have the characteristic of self,
because they have not yet manifested.
Past formations do not have the characteristic of self.
Because they have already been transcended;
because present formations lack the characteristic of self,
as they are manifesting right now.
This is called the certainty that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are selfless.
Furthermore, one should know that all conditioned phenomena are certainly impermanent by virtue of two characteristics:
first, because those of the past have already perished and disintegrated.
Secondly, because both the future and the present worlds are phenomena subject to destruction;
furthermore, one should know that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are necessarily suffering by virtue of two aspects:
first, because they are phenomena characterized by suffering such as birth and so forth.
Second, because they possess the nature of the three types of suffering.
These characteristics of suffering should be understood as previously explained.
Furthermore, by means of two characteristics, one should understand that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are definitively empty.
First, because it is the emptiness of ultimate detachment;
second, because it is the emptiness of detachment occurring subsequently.
Regarding "the emptiness of ultimate detachment":
This means that within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the nature of "self" and "what belongs to self" is ultimately empty.
As for the phrase "only subsequently departing from the emptiness of nature," this refers to the liberation of the mind within which all afflictions have already been severed.
Because all afflictions are entirely empty.
Furthermore, one should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are definitively selfless by virtue of two characteristics:
first, because conditioned phenomena possess various external natures.
Second, because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise from various conditions and lack self-mastery.
Furthermore, one should know that the four characteristics of conditioned phenomena are determined by ten aspects,
namely, by way of their disintegration.
It is characterized by transformation and separation,
in accordance with the nature of dharmas.
It is not to be delighted in;
it is a sign of lack of peace and security;
one should distance oneself from it.
Because they are characterized by distinct characteristics.
Such characteristics as these have already been analyzed in detail in the preceding *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
Furthermore, regarding the cultivation of attention based on the supramundane path,
there are five categories of dissociation:
first, the realm of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*).
Second, the realm of desirelessness;
third, the realm of cessation;
fourth, the realm of nirvana with remainder.
Fifth is the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
This refers to the realm of abandonment, so called because all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) to be abandoned through the path of seeing have been abandoned.
Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to be abandoned through the path of cultivation have been severed,
it is called the "desireless realm" (*vītarāga-dhātu*); that is to say,
this state possesses only the remaining basis (*sopadhiśeṣa*).
It is called the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder;
because this basis has been extinguished,
it is called the realm of extinction.
It is also called the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Because all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) therein are eternally stilled,
these five realms are called the cessation of all formations.
Because one is completely detached from attachment to "I" and "mine," from the conceit of "I am," and from all latent tendencies (anuśaya),
it is called "emptiness."
Because all characteristics are completely transcended,
it is called "non-apprehension" within the realm of cessation.
Because all craving for any phenomena associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) has been completely abandoned,
it is called the "exhaustion of craving.
[This also applies to] the desire and greed for the realm of non-desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Because they are all far removed from them,
it is called "desirelessness" (vītarāga).
This applies both within the realm of cessation (nirodhadhātu) and within the realms of nirvana with remainder and without remainder (sopadhiśeṣa- and nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu).
Because they are all eternally extinguished as appropriate,
and because they are all quiescent,
they are designated by the name "cessation" according to their respective order.
It is also called nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, because one diligently practices cultivation with the aim of attaining what has not yet been attained regarding the realm of cessation,
it is called "cultivating revulsion toward all conditioned phenomena."
Because one diligently practices for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained in the realm of non-desire,
it is called the cultivation of detachment from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Because one diligently practices for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained in the realm of cessation (*nirodha*), [it is called the cultivation of cessation].
This is called the cultivation of the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, for one who diligently practices for the liberation of the mind,
there are two successive stages.
First, the gradual sequence of knowledge;
second, the gradual sequence of the fruits of knowledge.
What is the gradual sequence of knowledge?
That is to say, one first gives rise to the knowledge of impermanence regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) by means of discerning the principle of their arising and ceasing;
subsequently, one [gives rise to it] regarding those conditioned phenomena associated with that arising.
One contemplates that phenomena are subject to birth and aging, and even extend to phenomena such as sorrow, suffering, and feverish affliction;
by reason of these causes and conditions, all are suffering.
This is the subsequent knowledge of suffering arising based on the prior knowledge of impermanence.
Furthermore, because those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are by nature subject to birth and so forth, up to being subject to feverish affliction (*paridāha*),
they constitute the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of death and rebirth,
revolving through successive transitions.
Because the principle of the mode of activity [of phenomena] is not subject to independent mastery,
there is no self.
This means that the subsequent wisdom of non-self arises based on the prior wisdom of suffering.
Thus, by observing impermanence, one perceives suffering;
by suffering, one perceives non-self.
This is called the gradual progression of wisdom.
What is the gradual sequence of the fruits of wisdom?
It refers to revulsion, detachment, liberation, and complete liberation.
What is revulsion?
This means that because the antidote has become manifest,
one gives rise to a sense of revulsion so that the various afflictions no longer arise.
What is the abandonment of desire?
This means that by virtue of cultivating a mind of revulsion,
although one does not intentionally direct the mind toward the antidote,
greed does not manifest with respect to any object of defiled attachment.
This occurs by the dominant power of subduing and abandoning [the afflictions].
What is liberation?
It refers precisely to the antidote for that subduing and abandoning.
Through extensive cultivation,
one forever uproots the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
This is called the first distinction of the liberation through revulsion and detachment from desire.
Furthermore, there is a distinction:
because the abandonment of the realm [of desire] is fully perfected during the stage of revulsion,
it is termed "revulsion."
That is to say, based on the reliance upon and the abandonment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
when one attains detachment from the remaining lower stages,
that state is designated as the stage of detachment.
Therefore, it is called "detachment from desire.
When one attains detachment from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
that stage is designated as "liberation."
Therefore, it is called liberation.
This is the second distinction of the liberation through wearying detachment from desire.
What is universal liberation?
This means that through liberation from the defilements of such afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*),
one is also universally liberated from the defilements of birth and other forms of suffering.
This is called universal liberation (*sarvavimukti*).
Thus, by the predominant power of wisdom,
one gives rise to revulsion toward all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
through the cultivation of this revulsion, [one attains liberation].
One attains freedom from desire;
through the practice of freedom from desire,
one attains liberation and complete liberation.
This is called the gradual sequence of the fruits of wisdom.
Within this, there are furthermore four kinds of false attachments. What are these four?
First, the perverted attachment of initial view;
second, the perverted attachment of pride;
third, the perverted attachment of internal selfhood.
Fourth is the false attachment based on the teachings of others.
Regarding the false attachment of views:
this refers to the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Prideful false attachment refers to the arising of the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*) regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
whereby one clings to the aforementioned views as false attachments, thereby obstructing the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*).
Subsequently, the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation—
such as the hindrance of the false attachment of ego-grasping— are severed.
Regarding "internal false attachment," this refers to relying on improper mental discrimination while dwelling alone in seclusion.
Those who cling to a substantially existent self,
or hold wrong views, or harbor pride,
or follow the false teachings of others.
This refers to the arising of false attachments due to the instruction of others,
such as thinking, "This is I" or "This is mine," whereby the conceit of "I" proceeds;
furthermore, it refers to the arising of improper conceptualization within oneself.
To cling to "self" and "what belongs to self" is called internal false attachment;
it is also called false attachment not based on the teachings of others.
The permanent severance of all such false attachments should be known as the fruit of wisdom.
Furthermore, one should understand that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are neither annihilated nor eternal by means of three aspects.
What are the three?
First, because non-abiding practice serves as the cause;
second, because there is no cause for abiding once [the state] has arisen.
Third, because the causal nature of future formations has ceased;
herein, because the causes of formations are impermanent,
and because a cause for their abiding after having arisen cannot be found.
One should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent;
they can give rise to future conditioned phenomena because their nature as present causes has ceased.
One should know that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are not annihilated.
Furthermore, there are four conditions that cause these conditioned phenomena to circulate and flow on from one to another.
What are the four? First, the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya);
second, the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya).
Third, the object-condition;
fourth, the dominant condition.
These four conditions, in brief, comprise two types.
First, causes;
second, conditions.
Causes are exclusively causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The remaining three [conditions] are exclusively object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) refers to the seeds of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) refers to the fact that when the six consciousnesses and their associated mental factors have ceased in immediate succession,
the subsequent six consciousnesses and their associated mental factors arise in immediate succession.
Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
the five groups of sensory consciousnesses take the five specific objects as their objects;
the sixth group of mental consciousness takes all phenomena as its objects.
Regarding the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*):

it refers to the fact that the five consciousnesses and so forth take their respective bases, such as the eye, as their dominant condition, as well as the generative mental attention (*manaskāra*) and so forth as their dominant condition.
The mental consciousness aggregate and so forth take the body composed of the four great elements and the attention that produces them as their dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, previously performed karma serves as the dominant condition for the resulting pleasant or unpleasant fruits.
One should know that this is also a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
Likewise, one should know that the provisions (*sambhāra*) in relation to the path, and the path in relation to the attainment of nirvāṇa,
are also subsumed under the category of the dominant condition.
Furthermore, one should examine defilement and purification through three matters and two types of association.
How does one examine all defilement and purification through these three matters?
First, one observes the causes and conditions of affliction within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
namely, by observing their gratifying flavor as being merely gratifying flavor.
Second, one observes the causes and conditions of purification within all conditioned phenomena.
That is, observing their faults as faults.
Third, observing purification within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
that is, observing their renunciation as renunciation.
All of this, summarized as one,
is called "examining all affliction and purification by means of three factors.
How does one examine all affliction and purification by means of two aspects?
First, by way of the nature of things as they are (yathāvadbhāva);
second, by way of the nature of things in their full extent (yāvadbhāva).
As for the nature of things as they are:
Regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), there is their gratification (*āsvāda*), their disadvantage (*ādīnava*), and their escape (*niḥsaraṇa*).
As for the nature of the full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*):
it refers to the full extent of the gratification found within all conditioned phenomena.
All faults and afflictions are exhausted;
all modes of transcendence are exhausted.
Within this, one observes that conditioned phenomena give rise to happiness and joy.
This is called the relish for that [object].
Furthermore, this relish is extremely limited.
Thus, it is characterized by these two aspects.
One observes the nature of things as they are and their associated gratification;
furthermore, one observes that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent, suffering, and subject to transformation—
this is called [observing] their disadvantage (ādīnava).
Furthermore, these disadvantages are extremely vast.
Thus, one observes the nature of things as they are (yathābhūta) through two aspects, namely, by way of their disadvantages.
Furthermore, he observes within all conditioned phenomena the cessation of sensual desire,
the abandonment of sensual desire,
and the transcendence of sensual desire.
This is called renunciation regarding that [object].
Furthermore, this renunciation is peaceful, unsurpassed, and ultimately secure.

Thus, one observes the nature of things as they are (*yathābhūtatā*) through two aspects: namely, renunciation; and likewise, the gratification (*āsvāda*), the disadvantage (*ādīnava*), and the renunciation of that very [gratification].
Regarding all conditioned phenomena—whether past, future, or present;
whether internal or external;
whether gross or subtle.
Whether inferior or superior,
whether distant or near,
one examines them with thorough discernment.

One should know that this is called the observation of the "nature as it is" (yathābhūtatā) regarding those [three matters], namely: their gratification (āsvāda), their disadvantage (ādīnava), and their renunciation (niḥsaraṇa).
Furthermore, it is for the sake of knowing that the essential nature (svabhāva) of these three matters exists.
One should know that there are three distinct categories of sentient beings:
first, those who are attached to various sensual desires;
second, those who have distanced themselves from various sensual desires.
Third, regarding the multitude of those who are dissociated from all desires,
there are again three kinds of worldly delusion in these three locations;
namely, that of the celestial world.
Whether they be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas,
or all the devas and humans—
these three kinds of beings in the world.
It should be understood that this establishment is based on three causes and conditions:
first, by virtue of attaining mastery over desire and mastery over purity;
that is to say, whether it be the realm of Māra or the Brahma-world.
Second, because they attain those causes through diligent cultivation;
that is to say, if śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas [engage in] the three types of destinies due to the various causes and effects of karma.
That is to say, if various devas and humans,
furthermore, are able to sever and realize [the truth] as appropriate within these three locations,
there are two kinds of paths that abandon the four perverted views.
This refers to those who have already entered the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*) and those who dwell having extensively cultivated the subsequent path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Furthermore, these two types of paths have four characteristics of the fruit of liberation of mind (*citta-vimukti-phala*):
first, the characteristic of liberation from the bonds of greed and hatred.
Second, the characteristic of renunciation through the cessation and abandonment of sensual desire;
third, the characteristic of dissociation from the nine fetters;
fourth, the characteristic of liberation from the various sufferings such as birth.
Among these, the first three characteristics demonstrate liberation from the afflictions at the stage of the cause; the final characteristic demonstrates it at the stage of the fruit.
This demonstrates liberation from all sufferings within the state of fruition.
Regarding this meaning, it is, for example, like a person situated in a prison who is bound by various fetters.
That is to say, one uses either wood, rope, or iron;
furthermore, other persons are stationed there to guard it.
Even if they were to escape from their place of confinement and flee to a distant location, [they would still be restrained].
They will seize them and bring them back;
some will not even allow them to move,
let alone escape.
Or there may be placed various vast, subtle, and lovely objects of desire that bind them;
in these secluded and confining places, they cause those beings to naturally develop a mind of attachment and delight, so that they have no desire to escape.
In this way, that person is bound by all kinds of bonds,
guarded by skillful means as a guard,
and fettered by the most firm shackles.
Furthermore, they will be subjected to harm by enemies according to their desires;
that is to say, they may be beaten or struck, or even dismembered,
or subjected to flogging, or have their lives entirely cut short.
If there are those who can be liberated from these four bonds,
they may truly be called liberated from all bonds.
Thus it is with sentient beings in those three realms of the world, who are bound by various fetters due to their ignorance.
One should know that this is a metaphor for the bonds of greed, hatred,
and delusion; those who observe the prohibitions are metaphors for improper mental application and the fact that the latent tendencies of the afflictions have not yet been permanently uprooted.
Because of improper reflection, one cannot even be moved,
let alone attain freedom from desire and escape to a distance;
for the latent tendencies of the afflictions have not yet been permanently uprooted.
Although one may use worldly paths as skillful means to escape and reach as far as the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra),
one is still seized and brought back;
the lovely and exquisite desires are likened to the nine fetters (nava-saṃyojana).
Due to those fetters, they naturally come to delight in birth and death;
they do not wish for liberation from their own bondage.
Thus, being bound by various ties, they are extremely tightly fettered.
They are tightly bound by the fetters of skillful means;
they are tightly bound by the most firm and secure fetters.
Furthermore, the four Māra-enemies, according to their desires, inflict harm upon them with the sufferings of birth and so forth.
If one is well-liberated from those four kinds of fetters,
one may be called liberated from all bonds.
Furthermore, the summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
The abbreviated teaching and its fruit ultimately fall into enumeration;

the three types of omniscience, the severing of bonds, liberation, views, pride, defilement, purity, and the statement [of these]; being far removed from four [factors], possessing three, and being perfected through three causes and conditions.
There were certain śrāvakas who went to the Great Teacher and requested a brief instruction.
What are these three? They are:
those for whom mere extensive learning is the ultimate goal;
and those who feel aversion toward all other practices.
He conceived this understanding:
"Merely hearing the Dharma in brief is sufficient to achieve one's own purpose;
why rely upon extensive learning as the ultimate goal?"
It is for the purpose of correcting conduct so that it becomes upright and sincere;
furthermore, it is because one abandons the desire for the mere culmination of extensive learning;
and also because there is fear regarding the many things to be done within the gateway of entry.
Because one enters [the path] by means of skillful means that are wholesome,
there may be those who have already listened well to and reflected well upon many teachings,
and they form this thought:
I have already well heard and reflected upon many teachings.
If I were now to rely entirely upon all those teachings I have heard and reflected upon, and were to bind my mind to the state of abiding in the mental object or to the state of liberation; |||
"Lest it cause my attention to become distracted; for if that were so,
I would not even be able to achieve stability of mind,
let alone liberation."
Furthermore, regarding all these phenomena that have been heard and reflected upon,
one does not attain certainty;
upon which of them, then, should one rely to swiftly realize supernormal knowledge?
By relying on what may one swiftly attain deliverance?
By taking what object as a focal point may the mind become established?
By taking what object as a focal point may one attain liberation?
Since he is thus personally uncertain,
if he sees the Great Teacher or a disciple of the Tathāgata well-known to the assembly present before him,
he immediately approaches them and requests a brief instruction.
Furthermore, it should be known that there are four kinds of attainment of the fruit of one's own purpose through correct instruction:
namely, for the sake of which one goes forth, and how one goes forth;
that is, being endowed with the proper physical characteristics.
Perfection of activity,
perfection of intention,
and perfection of the relinquishment and acquisition of the basis.
By means of this, one attains the unsurpassed attainment,
the attainment in the present life,
and the spontaneous attainment.
It is realized through internal realization.
Furthermore, there are six kinds of death, namely: past death.
Dying now; dying unsubdued; dying subdued.
Death with commonality;
death without commonality;
death in the past.
This refers to death as the passing away of past formations,
up to the cessation of the life-faculty;
this is death in the present.
This refers to death as the cessation of present formations,
up to the extinction of the life-faculty;
it is death of one who has not been tamed.
This refers to those who, in past lives, were undisciplined and unsubdued;
their underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and active conduct (carita) followed one another in succession, such that,
according to worldly convention, they are called "persons with underlying tendencies" (pudgala-anuśaya).
And having passed away,
they undergo rebirth and continuity in the present life,
comprised of latent dispositions (anuśaya) and formations (saṃskāra).
They arise from their own nature;
likewise, throughout the present life until the end of one's lifespan,
they remain untamed and unsubdued.
To speak at length, up until:
having passed away,
a future personal existence arises once again.
Furthermore, one can grasp at conduct accompanied by latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
because of grasping at that as a cause,
one becomes bound by the various sufferings such as birth.
They are likewise bound by the great fetters of greed and so forth.
One who has subdued death is one who,
in the present life, has already been disciplined and subdued, such that no latent tendencies remain.
And having passed away,
his future personal existence will no longer arise,
nor will he again take up conditioned formations accompanied by latent tendencies.
Because one does not grasp at those [defilements] as causes,
one is liberated from the various sufferings such as birth,
and is likewise liberated from the great fetters such as craving.
Those who die with a common lot (sabhāga) are those who,
just as in the past they were undisciplined and unsubdued when they relinquished their body and life,
so too in the present world do they relinquish their body and life.
One should know that such is called death by way of commonality,
death by way of similarity,
and death by way of conformity.
If, having previously failed to discipline or subdue oneself and thus relinquished body and life,
one now disciplines and subdues oneself before relinquishing body and life in the present life,
it should be known that this is called death of a different category, dissimilar death, and non-conforming death.
If, in the present, there are latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and activities (*carita*) that mutually reinforce one another,
yet at the time of death it is like dying in the past,
this is called "death of the same class" (*sabhāga-cyuti*) and "conformable death" (*anuloma-cyuti*).
It is not as it was at the time of death in the past,
when one was unable to grasp the future continuity of the homogeneous formations (*saṃskāra*) that were to be reborn.
Furthermore, these six kinds of death should be understood to have two characteristics.
This refers to the characteristics of the faults of the流转 (pravṛtti) of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra),
as well as the characteristics of the benefits of their 还灭 (nivṛtti),
whether in the past or in the present.
Being neither disciplined nor subdued,
they die with their kinsmen and further take up the suffering of birth and so forth in the future,
as well as becoming bound by afflictions such as craving.
This is called the characteristic of the faults of the流转 (pravṛtti) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). If,
in the present, one has already been disciplined and subdued such that death does not occur in a dissimilar state,
and furthermore, if one does not take up manifold sufferings in the future.
That which liberates one from all bonds of affliction is called the characteristic of the excellence of the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, it is [to be understood] by way of eight aspects.
One comes to be included among the conventional designations for persons regarding the arising of those conditioned phenomena,
such that one is said to have "such a name" and "such a kind."
Such is their lineage;
such is their food and drink;
such is their experience.
Whether in suffering or in pleasure,
thus long-lived and thus long-abiding.
Regarding the limits of such lifespans and these various characteristics within the bodhisattva stages of recollecting past lives,
it should be understood that they have already been extensively analyzed as previously described.
Furthermore, one should understand that through three aspects,
there is the thorough knowledge and abandonment of non-self within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
What are these three?
First, thorough knowledge of the internal;
second, thorough knowledge of the external;
third, thorough knowledge of both the internal and external.
Cessation is also like this,
according to what is appropriate;
that is to say, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are entirely devoid of a self.
There is no sense of "mine," nor is there anything else mutually bound to it;
one should know that such is the thorough knowledge and abandonment regarding both the internal and external.
In this context, one attains certainty through the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*).
By thoroughly knowing and repeatedly practicing this,
one abandons all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with it, achieving their ultimate cessation.
It should be understood that herein, for the sake of those who have not yet attained full knowledge (*parijñā*) regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has proclaimed the essential points of the True Dharma. Furthermore,
for those who have already attained full knowledge but have not yet permanently abandoned [those phenomena], [the same applies].
In order to cause them to repeatedly practice that very same previously attained universal knowledge so as to achieve its permanent abandonment,
he further offers this exhortation.
Furthermore, for those who wander through the cycle of birth and death,
there are three kinds of bonds;
because of these bonds, the mind is difficult to liberate.
One should know that it is only through a well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya that one can attain liberation,
not through a poorly expounded one.
What are these three?
First, those tainted phenomena bound by the remaining fetters with the exception of the fetter of craving;
second, those tainted phenomena defiled by the fetter of craving;
third, those formations that can produce future renewed existence.
Regarding these three bonds, the mind is difficult to liberate due to three causes and conditions:
first, because they are manifold;
second, because they are firm.
Because it is lovely and delightful;
the third [reason] is because it is subtle.
Furthermore, regarding those who are bound by the fetters of future existence through five aspects,
it should be known that there are five modes of the manifestation of the conceit "I am," namely, by way of the basis.
By way of the object of focus,
by way of the accompanying factors,
and by way of its intrinsic nature.
Because of cause and effect,
one should know that herein, based upon the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi),
one conceives of the self as either existing or not existing in the future.
That which has both existence and non-existence as its objective referent (ālambana) consists of this:
herein, the objective referent that is non-existent is of only one kind,
while the objective referent that is existent is of five kinds.
That is to say: "I shall have form," "I shall be formless," or "I shall have perception."
"I shall be without perception;
I shall be neither with perception nor without perception.
In this way, all such [states] are collectively subsumed into one.
There are six kinds of objective referents (*ālambana*).
As for "associates" (*sahāya*),
they refer to that which agitates and distracts the mind.
Regarding "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*):
taking up and maintaining its formal characteristics constitutes its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
while the intrinsic nature of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) constitutes its general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Because all afflictions are of the nature of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
As for their causal nature:
it means that they function as the causal nature capable of producing rebirth.
Because the karmic formations one has created are pursued by craving;
furthermore, by means of three characteristics,
one should understand that the mind is well-liberated.
That is to say: because of having fully understood all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
because of having realized the abandonment of the various afflictions (*kleśa*) associated with them;
and because, once the afflictions have been abandoned, one dwells free from craving in all circumstances.
Furthermore, within this context, one thoroughly understands the nature of things as they are—
namely, their impermanence and so forth— by means of four modes of practice regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
By means of eleven modes,
one thoroughly understands the nature of the full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
namely those of the past, future, and so forth.
As explained extensively before,
furthermore, there are two kinds of fivefold defilements along with five kinds of causal characteristics.
These are the two kinds.
Those who are still in training should know them and abandon them;
those who have completed their training have already known them and abandoned them.
What are these two?
This refers to the affliction of views and the affliction of pride.
These two should be understood as having five types of distinctions:
namely, by way of their modes of activity (*carita*), their outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), and their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
What are the five?
First, the conception of a self;
second, the conception of what belongs to a self.
Third is pride;
fourth is attachment;
fifth is latent tendency.
It should be understood that herein, the three types—conceiving of a self, conceiving of what belongs to a self, and the pride of "I am"—serve as the basis.
Regarding the objective referent, one stubbornly clings to and adheres to it, thinking: "Only this is true and real; all else is foolish and false."
It should be understood that herein, by way of the *paryavasthāna* (active outbursts), it is called "clinging";
whereas those very seeds, which persistently bind the continuum,
are called *anuśaya* (latent tendencies).
Furthermore, there are the cognitions of the body, external objects, and so forth;
one should know that these constitute the five kinds of causal characteristics of that [view],
namely, the causal characteristic of imagining a self.
Up to the characteristic of the cause of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
This characteristic of the cause is further of two kinds:
first, the characteristic of the objective cause (*ālambana-hetu-lakṣaṇa*).
Second is the causal characteristic of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The conceit of self and the pride of "I am" take the conscious body as their causal characteristic of the object-condition.
I reckon that what I have mastered takes two kinds as the causal characteristics of the object of focus (*ālambana-nimitta*):
namely, attachment to the hearing of improper teachings (*aśrutadharma*), improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), and their underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
It constitutes the causal characteristic of the cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), through the repeated habituation to the afflictions (*kleśa*) and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) by failing to understand them as they truly are,
constitute the causal characteristic of the cause-condition.
Furthermore, there are four types of assemblies of sentient beings;
one should know that within them, affliction (saṃkleśa) is established.
What are these four?
First, the assembly of sentient beings who are non-Buddhists;
second, the assembly of ordinary sentient beings within this Dharma;
third, the assembly of sentient beings in training (*śaikṣa*).
Fourth is the assembly of sentient beings beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Among the assemblies of sentient beings belonging to non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*),
all [of these] are present.
This dharma is found among the class of ordinary sentient beings in four ways:
as their causal characteristics, along with a portion of the characteristics of grasping.
However, such attachment cannot be found;
among the assembly of sentient beings in training,
there is the dualistic conception of "I" and "mine."
Furthermore, neither the attachment to the characteristics of those causes nor their underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) can be found;
likewise, neither the attachment to the conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*) nor its causal characteristics can be found.
Nevertheless, the underlying tendency of the conceit of "I am" can indeed be found.
Among the assembly of sentient beings who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
none at all can be apprehended.
Furthermore, as for all the practices of the assembly of sentient beings belonging to non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*):
It is not for the sake of severing those [defilements] that ordinary beings among sentient beings practice these various activities; rather,
it is precisely for the sake of severing them that they practice, yet they have not yet succeeded in severing them.
Because they have not yet seen reality as it truly is,
the assembly of sentient beings in training has already abandoned one portion;
they now cultivate correct practice in order to abandon the remaining portions.
Although they see things as they truly are, they do not claim, "I have already seen.
This is because they have not yet attained the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*).
Thus, among the assembly of sentient beings who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), all [defilements] have been completely severed.
Among all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), one claims for oneself: "I see according to reality.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds of phrases of pure exposition.
What are these eight?
This refers to the two types of statements concerning the purification of the mental continuum through transcendence, which are so named because they involve transcending views and conceit;
this occurs by means of severing the causal characteristics thereof.
It is called a phrase for the purity of removing signs because one abandons attachment to them;
it is called a phrase for the purity of tranquility.
Because one has abandoned those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), it is called the "phrase for the purity of excellent liberation.
Furthermore, there are two phrases for the purity of those in training (*śaikṣa*):
namely, regarding all formations (*saṃskāra*) pertaining to future existence.
By way of the principle of non-manifestation,
one is said to have severed craving and abandoned the three fetters;
there are two phrases regarding the purity of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
This is called having reached the end of suffering because one has realized the direct vision that eliminates conceit, and because one has forever uprooted the latent tendencies of craving,
which are the root of all suffering.
All these taken together as one comprise eight types of phrases for pure exposition.
Furthermore, by means of four factors, the perfection of seclusion is called "well-endowed."
What are the four?
First, dwelling without a second;
second, staying in a remote lodging.
Third is physical seclusion;
fourth is mental seclusion.
This means being completely secluded from all signs, discursive thoughts, greed, and hatred that arise in relation to the spheres of domestic life.
Relying on heedfulness, one guards the mind;
furthermore, through five aspects, one exerts diligent effort to swiftly realize supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*).
That is to say, one who possesses power.
One is a person of diligence by virtue of the diligence of donning the armor;
one is a person of diligence by virtue of the diligence of application.
There is the courageous one,
because within the vast Dharma they possess diligence free from cowardice or inferiority;
there is the steadfast and fierce one.
Because their diligence cannot be shaken by cold, heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, and the like,
they do not abandon the yoke of the wholesome;
because their diligence is not satisfied with what is inferior, they do not abandon the yoke of the wholesome.
Furthermore, in order to sever lethargy, drowsiness, restlessness, and remorse—
which are secondary afflictions belonging respectively to the categories of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*—
may right calm abiding and insight never suffer impairment.
Furthermore, within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
there are three perfections.
What are these three?
First, the perfection of conduct;
second, the perfection of the fruit;
third, the perfection of the teacher.
The perfection of practice refers to listening to the true Dharma for the purpose of realizing the realm of cessation through the abandonment of desire.
They expound it for others,
practice correctly themselves,
and act in accordance with the Dharma.
This is called the perfection of practice.
As for the perfection of the fruit,
it refers to the fact that by the predominant power of practicing in accordance with this very Dharma, [the fruit is attained].
The mind is well-liberated,
and one is further able to realize nirvana in the present life;
this is called the perfection of the fruit.
The Teacher’s perfection means that all dharmas that can bring about the holy life take the Blessed One as their root.
This is all because the World-Honored One has turned the wheel of the Dharma-eye;
it is all because they take the World-Honored One as their reliance;
and it is because, through the appearance of the Tathāgata in the world, those teachings can be known.
It is said that the Blessed One is their root;
having appeared in the world, the Buddha, in consideration of those various beings to be trained,
has proclaimed the Eye of the True Dharma.
Because it has been transmitted successively from master to disciple,
it is said that once the World-Honored One had turned the Eye of the True Dharma,
if anyone were to harbor doubts therein—
Because it is only by relying upon the Blessed One that one can reach a definitive understanding,
the Blessed One is said to be the basis of reliance.
Furthermore, there are briefly two kinds of Dharma teachers.
First, by way of teaching;
second, by way of realization.
This is because, having heard the sublime Dharma from another, one subsequently proclaims it.
Because it is taught based on having realized the path of training and the path beyond training.
