The First Part of the Compendium on the Analysis of the Matters in the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Order, as spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva, Part Two. Furthermore, the summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
The practice of the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*) within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) has five aspects:

the aspect of delusion, the aspect of the eye’s excellence, the nine knowledges, the aspect of non-delusion, the aspect of progress, the aspect of the distinction between self and view, and the aspect of the three characteristics. These are explained extensively in the *Dharmasamuccaya* chapter, following the third [section].
Regarding the practice of the perception of impermanence among all conditioned phenomena, there are five types.
That is to say, by virtue of its impermanence,
its lack of constancy,
and its lack of endurance.
It is of an impermanent nature because it is of the nature of transformation and decay;
herein, it perishes moment by moment.
It is impermanent,
because its own nature is bound to a limited duration of life;
it is not eternal.
Regarding external phenomena, because they are determined to have no abiding after an eon,
they do not endure for long;
since their lifespan is not yet exhausted, they may be destroyed by conditions and die prematurely.
It cannot be relied upon;
it remains for only such a duration,
because within that interval, there is no certain peace or happiness.
The phenomena subject to transformation and decay. What are these three?
They refer to how all foolish worldlings regard all conditioned formations as described above.
The five types of impermanence cannot be contemplated;
within that which is not truly superior or inferior,
one discriminates between superiority and inferiority, weighing oneself against others.
To consider oneself superior is called the first mark of a fool;
it is just as when one claims oneself to be superior.
The same applies in detail to those who are equal and those who are inferior.
It should be understood that for the wise person,
there are likewise three types of characteristics of wisdom that are the opposite of these.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the noble ones' eye of wisdom is purified by two kinds of characteristics:
namely, by being free from dust and by being free from defilement.
This is because they have attained dissociation from the fetters of the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing.
It is called "distant from dust" because one has become dissociated from those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
it is called "free from defilement" for that same reason.
Furthermore, at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), a coarse sense of self (*asmimāna*) enters into the mental attention (*manasikāra*), arising continuously and without interval;
yet, if one thoroughly understands the equality of the grasped object (*grāhya*) and the grasping subject (*grāhaka*) as the objective support (*ālambana*).
That is immediately extinguished.
Because it is extinguished,
it is called "distant from dust."
Because all latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the path of vision have been severed,
it is called "stainless" (*vimala*).
Furthermore, it is "distant from dust and free from stain."
When one attains the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena,
it should be known that ten kinds of benefits are simultaneously obtained. What are these ten?
First, because one has already clearly perceived the Four Noble Truths,
it is called "seeing the Dharma.
Second, because one has attained at least one of the fruits of śramaṇaship.
This is called "attaining the Dharma.
Third, regarding what has been realized, one is able to know for oneself: "I have now exhausted all [rebirths as] hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts;
I have realized the stage of stream-entry."
...and so forth, as explained at length. Because of this,
it is called "knowing the Dharma."
Fourth, one attains the four kinds of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*).
Because of knowing the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha as they truly are,
this is called the "thoroughly firm dharma."
Fifth, he is free from doubt regarding his own realization.
Sixth, he is free from uncertainty regarding the realization of others.
Seventh, when proclaiming the teachings associated with the Noble Truths.
Not relying on external conditions;
eighth, not observing the faces of others nor looking at their mouths,
within this True Dharma and Vinaya.
Ninth, he cannot be turned back by any other doctrines.
Tenth, he possesses no fear whatsoever regarding all that has been realized and the liberation [he teaches],
and he enters the holy teaching through two causes and conditions.
This refers to the correct conventional truth and the ultimate truth.
Furthermore, there are nine kinds of knowledge.
One is able to fully know and transcend all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
This refers to the knowledge of the flow of conditioned phenomena and the knowledge of the cessation of conditioned phenomena.
Knowledge of the causes and conditions of affliction;
knowledge of the causes and conditions of purification;
and knowledge of purification.
And the knowledge of suffering,
the knowledge of origination,
and the knowledge of cessation.
Regarding the knowledge of the path:
herein, the knowledge of the流转 (pravṛtti) of all conditioned phenomena arises briefly through the gathering of three kinds of causes and conditions.
All conditioned phenomena are gathered by right knowledge;
that is to say, because of the gathering of delight and because of the gathering of contact.
Due to the arising of name-and-form,
there is accordingly the arising of form, or the arising of feeling and so forth, or the arising of consciousness;
and due to the cessation of these three kinds of causal conditions, [the latter cease].
The cessation of the three types of formations is called the knowledge of the reversal and cessation of all formations.
This refers to the knowledge of the causes and conditions of affliction, the knowledge of the causes and conditions of purification, and the knowledge of purification itself.
That is to say, regarding the gratification, the disadvantage, and the escape [from craving],
it should be understood as previously explained:
the four knowledges of suffering and so forth among the Four Noble Truths.
The characteristics of these should be understood according to the previously analyzed principles of the Noble Truths;
one cultivates the first five knowledges during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
One is able to swiftly realize the knowledge of the latter four noble truths;
by realizing them,
one is able to understand all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as they truly are.
Furthermore, if one lacks any of the aforementioned knowledges,
one will certainly be unable to fully comprehend all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) through the principle of the truths;
it is only upon attaining them that one can achieve such full comprehension.
If one possesses knowledge that comprehensively understands the principles of the truths yet lacks some deficiency in wisdom,
one will certainly be unable to abandon all afflictions through the power of antidotes on the subsequent path of cultivation and thereby transcend all conditioned formations.
That which is contrary to this is able to transcend it;
therefore, it is said that there are nine kinds of wisdom capable of thoroughly knowing and transcending all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, the practitioner of meditation does so by way of three bases.
One dwells without delusion regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
What are these three?
First, one understands, as it truly is, that past conditioned phenomena are impermanent in nature.
Second, one understands, as it truly is, that all conditioned phenomena in the present are of a nature subject to cessation.
Third, one understands, as it truly is, that all conditioned phenomena in the future are of a nature subject to arising and cessation.
By means of this, he is free from delusion regarding the activities of the three times;
with an undefiled mind, he dwells in peace and security,
and is reckoned among those who have attained illumination.
One should know that the opposite of this is the dwelling in delusion,
which falls within the category of ignorance.
Furthermore, there are three other synonymous terms for affliction.
For the most part, these are explained within the category of afflictions (*kleśa*):
first, as synonyms for greed (*lobha*);
second, as synonyms for hatred (*dveṣa*).
These are alternative names for the three types of delusion.
Regarding the alternative names for greed:
it is also called "joy" (nandī).
It is also called greed;
it is also called attachment;
it is also called delight.
It is also called desire;
it is also called intimacy;
it is also called pleasure.
It is also called a "storehouse," it is also called "protection," and it is also called "attachment."
It is also called "rare," it is also called "craving," and it is also called "attachment."
It is also called "affliction" (rajas) and it is also called "thirst" (tṛṣṇā).
As for the synonyms for hatred (dveṣa):
It is also called malice;
it is also called hatred;
it is also called anger.
It is also called anger;
it is also called injury;
it is also called intolerance.
It is also called contrariety;
it is also called violence and wickedness;
it is also called the sting of insects.
It is also called "resistance and opposition," it is also called "cruelty and toxicity," and it is also called "fury and outburst."
It is also called indignation;
it is also called dwelling in resentment;
it is also called the sudden arising of impetuous anger.
Synonyms for delusion (*moha*) include ignorance (*ajñāna*) and lack of vision (*adarśana*).
It is also called non-realization,
it is also called torpor,
and it is also called delusion.
It is also called ignorance (*avidyā*) and also called darkness (*tamas*).
One should know that such names have for the most part already been explained in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.
I shall now explain the distinctions among the types of delight (*nandī*).
That which is the joy arising from the feeling that serves as its basis is called "delight" (*prīti*).
The defiled attachment that arises toward an object of experience produced by dependent origination is called greed (*rāga*).
Furthermore, the state of mind that arises toward an object about to be obtained is called joy (*nandī*).
If desire arises toward an object already obtained, it is called *rāga* (greed).
Furthermore, when one is about to enjoy an object already obtained, it is called *nandī* (delight).
At the very moment of actually enjoying that same object, it is called *rāga*.
Furthermore, the skillful means for attaining an object is called joy (*prīti*);
that which is directed toward the object itself is called greed (*lobha*).
Moreover, that which arises subsequently is also called joy.
Attachment (*rāga*) is defined as [craving] toward present objects.
Furthermore, joy (*nandī*) is defined as delighting in the prosperity and gain of other sentient beings who are beloved,
whereas attachment is defined as delighting in the prosperity and gain obtained by oneself.
Furthermore, for one who practices correctly among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
there are four types of superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*).
Regarding these, the conceptions of superior progress (*viśeṣasaṃjñā*) are, in brief, of three kinds.
First, regarding what has not been attained as attained;
second, regarding what has not been encountered as encountered;
third, regarding what has not been realized as realized.
If it is for the sake of attaining dwelling in happiness in the present life,
this is called the fourth superior progress,
because one is now able for the first time to attain the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala), which was previously unattained.
One should know that this is called "attaining what has not yet been attained.
Because one relies on this very [attainment] to further realize the fruits of higher training,
one should know that this is called "realizing what has not yet been realized."
Taking this very [attainment] as a basis, one is further able to realize the fruit of arhatship,
because one is able to realize the abandonment of all afflictions.
It should be understood that this is called "realizing what has not yet been realized."
If one has already realized the fruit of arhatship,
there is nothing further to be attained that has not yet been attained, nor anything to be realized that has not yet been realized;
therefore, one applies oneself with right effort solely for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life.
Furthermore, when practicing right effort, there are three superior conceptions based on one's own welfare:
namely, the conception of revulsion toward all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
and the conception of their defects (*ādīnava*).
Regarding the perception of reality and the perception of revulsion,
there are further four modes of practice.
This refers to contemplating all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as being like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow, and as afflictive harm.
Regarding "like a disease":
it is as if there were someone who, due to a disorder of the elements (*dhātu*), experiences the suffering born of illness.
One cultivates the perception of revulsion,
as with a boil. This means,
for example, that there is someone who experiences the suffering of a boil produced by past karma.
Regarding the cultivation of the perception of revulsion:
"like an arrow" means,
for example, that there is someone who experiences suffering because they have been struck by an enemy's arrow.
One cultivates the perception of aversion toward those who cause affliction and harm;
this refers to the various sufferings arising from one's own wrong views amidst the deprivation of kin, wealth, and so forth.
One cultivates the perception of revulsion.
This is called the cultivation of the perception of revulsion toward all conditioned phenomena by a practitioner of insight meditation.
As for the perception of danger:
Furthermore, there are two practices:
namely, contemplating all conditioned phenomena as impermanent and contemplating them as suffering.
The perception of the true meaning also has two modes of practice:
namely, contemplating the emptiness and selflessness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
In this context, having first correctly cultivated the perception of defects and the perception of the true meaning,
one is then able to abide in the perception of revulsion;
it should be understood that the result is stated here first.
The cause is explained later.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) which, serving as a basis, can give rise to the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*).
First, the conceptualized view of self.
This refers to the innate view of self arising among all non-Buddhists,
which even extends down to birds, beasts, and other such beings who are capable of giving rise to it.
The third is the view of self based on one's own support,
which arises with respect to each individual internal body.
The fourth is the view of self based on another's support.
This refers to those who, based upon the conceptual view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) arising with respect to the bodies of others, give rise to the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*). That is to say,
by means of this view, they perceive their own and others' bodies as possessing a real self.
Based on these two kinds of view of self,
the conceit "I am" arises;
it is like how, based on the substance and its form reflected upon the surface of a pure, round mirror, a reflected image arises.
Based on the reflection, one generates inferior, middling, or superior perceptions regarding one's own basis;
thus, through such false conceptualization,
one takes the view of self with respect to one's own basis as a condition.
Conditioned by this, the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi) arises based upon it,
just as a reflected image arises based upon a physical object.
Furthermore, conditioned by this, the conceit "I am" (asmimāna) arises.
Regarding those who, comparing themselves to others, perceive themselves as superior, equal, or inferior,
and for whom the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*) arises with the co-emergent view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its condition—
one should know that the analogy differs from the previous one.
Just as a person with clear vision looks into a vessel of pure water and observes their own eyes and ears,
the characteristics of the remaining [factors] should be understood as previously described.
This is the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in all its aspects.
Only by relying on the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya can one permanently sever [the afflictions],
and not through other heterodox teachings;
thus it is known by the Tathāgata and his fellow practitioners of the holy life.
Or, when there are fellow practitioners of the holy life who have been of great kindness and virtue to one's disciples,
it is solely by means of this single causal factor that one is said to truly repay the debt of gratitude toward the Great Teacher, or toward those fellow practitioners after his parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, by means of the second [point]:
that is to say, if there is one who, for the sake of benefiting others, diligently practices the correct conduct based precisely upon these distinct categories of meaning.
This is also called "repaying kindness according to one's capacity," because that which was hoped for has not yet been fulfilled.
Furthermore, it is because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) cease by way of three aspects.
It is called the realm of nirvana without remainder because:
first, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that previously arose have ceased;
and second, all conditioned phenomena have ceased through the destruction of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Third, because one is forever liberated from all afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding "the cessation of those conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) previously arisen," this refers to the actions and afflictions performed in previous lives that were capable of producing future existence (*punarbhava*).
Furthermore, through the seeking and aspiration of former vows,
all currently arising formations are eternally extinguished;
as for the extinction of formations through the destruction of their intrinsic nature, it is as follows:
This refers to the fact that once those [conditioned phenomena] have arisen, they perish according to their own nature;
they do not abide ultimately, but rather all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are eternally extinguished,
and one is forever liberated from all afflictions (*kleśa*).
This refers to the complete and remainderless cessation of all afflictions;
because they are extinguished now, they will not arise again in the future.
Thus, by means of these three characteristics, conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) cease.
Therefore, it is called "quiescence" (śānti),
yet it is not an eternal absence of characteristics,
because its characteristics are distinct [from those of extinction].
If there were no marks whatsoever,
it could not be designated and described as "quiescence" by virtue of its power.
One should know that four summary formulations (dharmoddāna) are established:
namely, the liberation door of emptiness (śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha) and the liberation door of wishlessness (apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha).
Regarding the door of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*):
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
all conditioned phenomena are suffering"—based on the door of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*), these establish the first and second summaries of the Dharma (*dharmanirdeśa*).
"All phenomena are without self" establishes the third summary of the Dharma (dharmoddāna) based on the gate of liberation that is emptiness.
"Nirvana is peace" [establishes the fourth].
Based on the door of liberation that is signless (*animitta*), the fourth summary of the Dharma (*dharmoddāna*) is established.
Furthermore, it should be known that there are two kinds of summaries of the Dharma for those who desire superior practice.
First is desire accompanied by resolute conviction;
second is desire accompanied by intention.
Regarding desire accompanied by resolute conviction:
By means of the summary of four dharmas,
one generates a desire for [the realization of] all conditioned phenomena;
furthermore, one generates a desire for the tranquility of all conditioned phenomena.
Due to his intention, while dwelling alone in seclusion and reflecting with mental attention,
his mind turns back from that tranquility for four reasons.
First, because he does not enter into it due to seeing no benefit therein.
Second, because one lacks faith, there is no pure conviction regarding that [object].
Third, because one does not give rise to joy toward that object of focus, one does not abide in it with stability.
Fourth, because one gives rise to a lack of delight and a lack of resolute conviction toward that [object].
One should know that the opposite of that is desire accompanied by intentionality (*āśaya*).
Furthermore, due to two conditions, there arises a desire based on the conviction of selflessness (*anātman-adhimokṣa*),
which results in fear and dread toward that nirvāṇa.
The mind retreats for two reasons:
first, because one has not practiced this desire with proficiency and has not reached its culmination;
second, because at the time of mental attention, mindfulness is lost due to those causes and conditions.
Furthermore, because this patience and aspiration have not yet been fully cultivated,
at that time, while realizing within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that they are merely phenomena,
his mind becomes dull and he repeatedly thinks, "I, I— at that time, where shall I be?"
Seeking out the subtle, concomitant obstacles that operate within my practice, for this reason, he thinks:
"I shall not exist; I shall cease to be."
He forms this thought: "There are only conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), which will not exist in the future.
Because he thus relies upon and pursues the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), [he falls into nihilism].
A consciousness that arises and evolves through transformation occurs;
due to fear and terror,
the mind retreats from that state of cessation.
Furthermore, in order to sever such fear and anxiety,
there are two things that are of great utility: first,
to reveal oneself as one truly is before wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*).
Second, by means of the desire for wholesome dharmas, one gives rise to a mind of understanding and a pliant mind.
Furthermore, one who gives rise to such a mind of understanding experiences joy through three aspects upon hearing the true Dharma.
First, by way of the predominance of the person;
second, by way of the predominance of the dharma;
third, by way of the predominance of oneself.
Regarding the predominance of the person (*pudgala-adhipati*):
this refers to seeing a Great Teacher who is deeply worthy of admiration, possesses great majesty, and is endowed with physical beauty,
as well as hearing him praised as one who skillfully expounds the Dharma.
Regarding the predominance of the Dharma:
it refers to the taught Dharma being able to bring about deliverance from the suffering of afflictions and karma,
and enabling faith and understanding of the most supreme and profound meaning.
Regarding "superiority by oneself":
it means possessing the power and capacity to fully awaken to and realize the Dharma that has been taught.
Furthermore, it refers to one who has developed such a mind of pliancy and gentleness.
It refers to three types of views:
first, those that function in dependence upon them;
second, those by which they are fully understood.
Third, regarding that which should be induced and which proceeds in dependence upon it:
this refers to those who have not yet attained direct realization (abhisamaya) of the truths.
In order to attain clear realization (*abhisamaya*),
one proceeds by means of a right view that is accompanied by that very resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) and has been thoroughly cultivated through repeated practice;
it is by means of this that one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*).
This refers to the nature of the basis for the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)—
which consists of the grasping at a self regarding three things—
and for the two views of eternalism and nihilism that accompany it, all of which are based upon and conform to right view as it accords with clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
One is able to fully comprehend both these and the fruits attained.
Regarding the "three matters":
First, that which is grasped;
second, that which grasps;
third, the manner in which this is grasped.
What is that which is grasped?
It refers to the five aggregates of grasping (pañca-upādānaskandhāḥ). Who is it that grasps?
It refers to the four graspings.
How does one grasp?
It refers to the four stations of consciousness.
It should be understood according to the sequence as previously explained.
It serves as the basis for the mind of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*),
and it consists precisely of those entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) therein that are induced by what is unreasonable.

One should understand, as previously explained, how the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises with respect to those objects, giving rise to attachment and its underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
How, then, should it be cultivated?
This means that by abiding therein, one is able to permanently sever the threefold attachment to the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) along with its latent tendencies (*anuśaya*),
and regarding the knowledge of the noble truths, one does not rely on external conditions.

Furthermore, when right view—which ought to be fully known—arises in dependence upon that [basis], one gives rise to attachment to a self and latent tendencies regarding those three bases; because of this, one does not correctly understand the arising and passing away of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
If one cannot even enter the middle way regarding the bases,
how much less can one attain liberation?
When one dwells in accordance with the right view of clear realization (abhisamaya), [one attains liberation].
Regarding these three matters, although they are all already dissociated from the grasping of a self,
they are still bound by latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
This is because they are able to thoroughly understand the arising and passing away of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Distant from the two extremes, one enters the middle way;
though not yet having attained liberation, one is capable of attaining it.
If one has already brought about the direct realization of the noble truths, [one is liberated].
By means of right view, one is without attachment to a self regarding the three matters and remains free from latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Having first entered into the middle way,
one subsequently attains liberation by virtue of this.
It should be understood that when these three views arise, there are these distinctions.
Furthermore, the summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
The swift penetration into the intrinsic nature of the sphere of wisdom;
the flow, joy, contentment, practice, following the stream, knowing, severing, characteristics, perception, and establishing the provisions for opposition;
and the teacher’s deeds and so forth—these chapters are extensively set forth in order to realize the unattained true and ultimate liberation.
Briefly, there are three factors that enable one to attain swift super-knowledge (abhijñā):
first, the power of wisdom (jñānabala).
Second is the power of non-negligence;
third is the power of repeated practice.
As for the power of wisdom:
That is to say, if one abides in that state of capability such that the outflows are forever exhausted in the immediate next moment,
it should be known that this is the knowledge and vision of a learner (*śaikṣa*).
As for the power of heedfulness (*apramāda*):
That is to say, having already attained such knowledge and vision,
one relies upon the path thus attained and skillfully and diligently cultivates the guarding of the mind against evil and unwholesome states.
As for the power of repeated practice (*abhyāsa-bala*),
it means that relying precisely upon these skillful means, one practices with diligence, constantly acting and constantly turning,
never thinking, "Have I today attained the exhaustion of all outflows and liberation of mind?"
Thinking, "It will be tomorrow," or "It will be some day later," one's mind becomes weary and disheartened by such wrong reflections.
Being free from weariness, one is then without fear;
being without fear, one does not abandon application and is able to exhaust all outflows.
Question: What is the distinction between knowledge (*jñāna*) and vision (*darśana*)?
Answer: If this wisdom illuminates objects of the past and the future—which are not within the range of direct perception—it is called knowledge;
if it illuminates objects of the present, this wisdom is called vision.
Furthermore, when this wisdom takes the apprehended object as its condition, it is called knowledge (*jñāna*);
when it takes the apprehending subject as its condition, it is called view (*dṛṣṭi*).
Moreover, this wisdom consisting of what is produced through hearing and reflection is called knowledge.
That which is produced through cultivation is called "view" (dṛṣṭi);
furthermore, this wisdom is called "view" because it can sever the afflictions (kleśa).
Once the afflictions have been severed, the wisdom that is able to realize liberation is called "knowledge" (jñāna).
Furthermore, this wisdom that takes objects of specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) as its object is called knowledge (jñāna);
this wisdom that takes objects of general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) as its object is called view (dṛṣṭi).
Moreover, it is so designated by way of conventional designation (prajñapti).
Throughout all various internal and external formations,
one may designate them as a self,
or as sentient beings, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and so forth.
Or one may establish [concepts] such as armies, forests, houses, mountains,
and so forth; by means of such conventional modes of reasoning,
one takes the objects of knowledge as conditions.
This wisdom is called knowledge (*jñāna*).
If it can apprehend both specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), this wisdom is called vision (*darśana*).
Furthermore, when seeking out all phenomena, this wisdom is called knowledge.
Having already sought them out, the wisdom that investigates all phenomena is called "view" (*darśana*).
Furthermore, this wisdom that takes non-conceptual images as its object is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*,
*vidyā*), while the wisdom that takes conceptual images as its object is called "view."
Furthermore, when this wisdom takes the mental image of a form-object (*rūpa-ālambana*) as its condition, it is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*);
when it takes the mental image of a non-form-object (*arūpa-ālambana*) as its condition, it is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
When one practices by relying upon such knowledge or view as a means (*upāya*), [it is called cultivation].
Furthermore, one should diligently cultivate four skillful activities:
first, the activity of observation;
second, the activity of relinquishing and adopting.
Third, the matter of undertaking the practice;
fourth, the matter of skillful means;
and fifth, the matter of observation.
This refers to the four foundations of mindfulness.
They are intended as antidotes to the four inversions,
so that one may thoroughly know all objects of experience as they truly are.
Regarding the matter of abandoning and adopting:
this refers to the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*),
which are for the purpose of eliminating unwholesome states.
Furthermore, regarding the emergence for the sake of cultivating and gathering all wholesome dharmas,
this refers to the "emergence of undertaking activities," namely the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Because one successively transcends [the stages] from the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) up to pleasure (*sukha*) by means of the four dhyānas.
As for the "preparatory matters," these refer to the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
One should know that this is because it is the correct means for severing the afflictions to be abandoned through both seeing and cultivation.
For one who thus diligently practices these skillful activities,
one should know that there are four kinds of meanings regarding the supported and the supporter.
The meaning of the "basis" refers to the practitioner who applies correct diligence in cultivation;
the meaning of the "supported" refers to...
This refers to one who has attained the various untainted (anāsrava) dharmas of training,
yet remains unpurified because they are still enveloped by the remaining shell of ignorance (avidyā-kośa).
Furthermore, those phenomena become purified only after [the practice of] the path of purification;
it should be understood that this path of purification has four distinct varieties.
The first is the cultivation of the sublime Dharma and correct, thorough meditative concentration (*samyak-pravicaya-dhyāna*).
Second, to personally attend upon virtuous friends;
third, to cultivate and refine one's mind through the practice of ethical discipline (*śīla*), the sense-faculties, and qualities such as few desires;
fourth, to dwell alone in secluded and quiet places.
It takes the supreme and correct tranquility and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) as its wings and attendants.
Furthermore, "purification" refers to relying upon that very path of purification.
Through extensive cultivation,
it causes those in training (*śaikṣa*) to break the shell of ignorance and proceed to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*);
furthermore, it serves to attain true and ultimate liberation.
It should be known that there are, in brief, five successive stages:
first, the prior accumulation of the provisions as a basis;
second, relying upon these [provisions].
Third, relying upon this, one cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā and possesses the resolute conviction in the direct realization of the truths and nirvāṇa.
Fourth, relying upon this, one does not give rise to complacency regarding inferior or limited realization, nor does one remain settled therein; rather,
one develops a profound sense of wearying revulsion toward phenomena that should be reviled.
Fifth, relying upon this,
one realizes the final trainee-mind associated with the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
Furthermore, by means of five causes and conditions:
One should know that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) constituting the self are entirely impermanent;
that is to say, the lifespan of every self is limited.
Suppose there were a person who wished to personally verify this for themselves.
"How long can I hold this lump of clay or a lump of cow dung in my hand?
Having made this vow, he takes up that lump;
at that time, the person is able to hold it without letting go, according to his own desire.
Even later, when one wishes to discard it, one can discard it; when one wishes to maintain it, one can maintain it.
This is unlike the body received at birth, which, until the end of its lifespan, cannot fulfill one's own desires for even a single kṣaṇa.
How much more so for that which abides for a long time?
Furthermore, because all self-entities are produced from causes,
those causes act [to produce them].
Because it is impermanent;
and because one can observe that even those with vast and flourishing personal existence ultimately meet with destruction—
namely, those in the form realm and the desire realm, such as the gods, humans, Great Brahmā, Śakra, and universal monarchs (cakravartin).
Furthermore, it is because of the non-erroneous Āgama;
that is to say, the Blessed Buddha, having directly perceived and directly realized the impermanent nature of all personal existences (*ātman*), has proclaimed it.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of distinctions regarding the fulfillment of those who experience sensual desires;
it is due to these causes and conditions that those who experience sensual desires constantly engage in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
What are these three?
First, the perfection of assets;
second, the perfection of the physical body;
third, the perfection of being extensively and excellently honored by sentient beings.
One should know that there are furthermore three kinds of causes and conditions by which such a complete distinction can be attained;
namely, the practice of giving, ethical discipline, and the restraint of the sense faculties together.
As well as the fruits obtained through the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
With loving-kindness as the precursor and loving-kindness as the causal basis,
one refrains from harming any sentient beings.
Because it proceeds with the aspect of tranquility.
Third, regarding the objective domain of knowledge: furthermore, one should know that there are seven kinds of wisdom-activity that correctly penetrate the objects of knowledge as they truly are.
First, knowledge already attained;
second, knowledge not yet attained;
third, non-erroneous knowledge.
Fourth is the knowledge that there is neither existence nor non-existence regarding the four bases.
Fifth is the non-empty knowledge regarding the remaining five bases.
Sixth is the knowledge of suffering and impurity.
Seventh is the wisdom of swift destruction.
Furthermore, by means of fifteen aspects, one clearly comprehends all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and is able to swiftly sever and extinguish all delusion regarding conditioned phenomena.
What are these fifteen? They are:
because it is produced from the water element, it is selfless;
because it manifests as if it were a self, it does not abide.
Because they are produced according to desire,
one realizes that all forms are like a mass of foam;
because they arise from the conjunction of the three [factors] and are thus similar phenomena.
Just as through the skillful means of the conjunction of clouds, earth, and rain,
one realizes that all sensations are like floating bubbles;
for they possess qualities similar to those that can manifest, burn, and cause delusion regarding the objects of knowledge.
One realizes that all perceptions are identical to a mirage,
because the root of the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) has been severed,
and because there are many varieties of self-entities due to their causal distinctions.
Because there is no similar dharma that remains even for a moment after the measure of a kṣaṇa,
one realizes that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are like a plantain trunk;
consciousness accompanied by grasping (sopādāna-vijñāna) relies upon the four stations of consciousness (catvāri vijñānasthiti).
Because they give rise to various types of self-entities and evolve in accordance with similar phenomena,
it is only upon awakening to all consciousnesses that one realizes they are like illusory events.
This detailed analysis should be understood as it appears in the *Paryāyasaṃgrahaṇī*.
Furthermore, there are two types of worlds that encompass all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*):
first, the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*).
The two are the receptacle world and the sentient-being world.
The sentient-being world is called "birth-and-death by way of species," while the receptacle world is called "birth-and-death by way of the vessel."
Because the birth-and-death of categories differs from other dharmas of birth-and-death,
one should know that, in relation to the birth-and-death of the receptacle world, there are briefly five types of dissimilarity.
That is to say, the birth-and-death of the receptacle world is produced by a common cause.
The birth and death of the species (nikāya-saṃsāra) occurs solely through non-commonality;
this is called the first cause of dissimilarity.
Furthermore, the birth and death of the receptacle world (bhājana-saṃsāra) is without beginning or end, severed at its prior and posterior limits.
The birth-and-death of the species (nikāya-saṃsāra) flows on in succession from beginningless time, constantly without interruption;
this is called the second temporal dissimilarity.
Furthermore, the birth-and-death of the receptacle world (bhājana-loka-saṃsāra) may be destroyed by fire, water, or wind.
The birth and death of the various types (*nikāya-saṃsāra*) is not like this;
this is called the third treatment for what is discordant.
Furthermore, the cause of the birth and death of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) is never severed.
The cycle of birth and death by way of species (*nikāya-saṃsāra*) is not like this;
this is called the fourth abandonment of the dissimilar.
Furthermore, the cycle of birth and death as a receptacle world (*bhājana-saṃsāra*) is severed and then continues again.
Once the cycle of birth and death (*jāti-saṃsāra*) has been severed, there is no further continuation;
this is called the fifth "discontinuity of the dissimilar class.
Furthermore, by means of five aspects, all foolish worldlings transmigrate incessantly within birth and death.
First, by way of the cause of craving;
second, by way of the fruit of craving;
third, by way of the intrinsic nature of craving.
Fourth, because causes proceed in succession;
fifth, because these successive causes rely upon a prior limit that is without end.
Herein, ignorance is called the cause of craving.
The various karmas that lead to rebirth in happy realms or miserable realms are called "fruits of craving.
This is because of the karma that leads to rebirth in happy realms.
Bound by the fetter of craving,
the fool naturally delights in going [there],
due to the karma of proceeding toward the evil destinies.
Bound by the fetters of craving,
though the fool does not wish to go, he is forcibly driven away.
Such is the nature of craving.
Briefly, there are three kinds:
first, craving for future existence;
second, craving accompanied by delight and lust.
Third, the craving for various forms of pleasure and joy.
These three types of craving are subsumed into two:
first, craving for existence (*bhavarāga*).
The second is craving for objects.
Craving for future existence is called craving for becoming.
Craving accompanied by joy and greed refers to [craving] directed toward objects that are about to be obtained and present before one,
as well as toward objects already obtained but not yet experienced.
Furthermore, there is craving for objects currently being experienced;
and craving for various forms of delight and pleasure refers to craving for objects desired in the future.
It should be understood that herein, it is called the fetter of craving because of craving accompanied by delight and lust;
and because of craving for future existence and craving for various delights and pleasures.
Therefore, it is called being bound by the fetter of craving.
If one is bound by the fetter of craving toward those objects,
it is called "running about."
If one is bound by the fetters of craving toward those objects, this is called "saṃsāra" (transmigration).
Furthermore, regarding the continuity of formations (*saṃskāra*) that has come down through successive causes over a long period of time,
its prior limit is difficult to know and its end is inexhaustible.
By these five aspects, the foolish should know that cyclic existence proceeds; furthermore, they are bound by another five aspects:
first, being bound to that place;
second, being bound by means of that.
Third, the actual bond itself;
fourth, being bound by virtue of depending upon that [bond];
fifth, there is that which is experienced.
Regarding "bound at that place":
it means that by virtue of karma leading to the happy realms,
one is bound to the pillar of the happy realms.
Alternatively, by means of karma that leads to the miserable destinies,
one is bound to the stakes of those miserable destinies;
furthermore, this occurs through craving accompanied by delight and greed.
They bind themselves to their own tasks by means of craving for various forms of pleasure and craving for future existence;
they bind themselves to their own stakes by means of those very cravings.
Regarding "being bound by that":
it refers to foolish ordinary beings who are bound by ignorance;
this [ignorance] is precisely the binder.
This means that because one's own kindred [beings] share a similar nature in having no weariness toward suffering;
as for "being bound by depending on that," it means being bound by depending on the subsequent aggregates (*skandhas*).
That which is experienced refers to the experience of those various sufferings, such as birth and so forth.
Furthermore, foolish ordinary beings have four forms of delight and contentment regarding contaminated things.
You should know that for the most part these are non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). What are the four?
First, they take pleasure in being content with the human body.
Second, contentment with the bodies of the gods in the desire realm;
third, contentment with birth in the Brahma world;
fourth, contentment with reaching the limit of existence at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Regarding those, for a fool who follows their sequence—
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—
there are furthermore five kinds of paths upon which all fools wander out of attachment.
First, future existence;
second, objects sought in the future;
third, objects about to be attained in the present.
Fourth is all objects already attained;
fifth is objects currently being experienced.
It should be understood that, in their respective order, one should know the distinctions such as "approaching" (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth regarding those [objects].
In this context, there are two kinds of destinations:
first, that which pertains to future existence;
second, that which pertains to the objects sought in the future.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of paths traversed by craving:
first, the mental action of longing for objects;
second, the two actions of body and speech.
Third is acquisition;
fourth is, within what has been acquired, acting according to one's desire by either transforming it or practicing it.
This is the path traversed by craving that initiates karma.
If one seeks objects of experience or further states of existence,
it should be known that within those four types of paths,
there are distinctions such as "treading" and so forth, corresponding respectively to their sequence.

As it has been said regarding "treading" and so forth, there are four distinct categories: the path traversed by delight and contentment toward all other conditioned, outflowing phenomena (sāsrava-dharma) that have been described;
delight; conceptual proliferation (prapañca); and defiled attachment and immersion.
It should be understood that they are likewise in their respective order.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of distinctions in the characteristics of the results of the path of wandering in craving:
first, the distinction of the mind.
Regarding the distinction between the two bodies,
the distinction of the mind further consists of two types.
First, the differentiation of categories;
second, the differentiation of afflictions.
Regarding the differentiation of categories:
That is to say, by way of intrinsic nature,
basis, and object.
Regarding the distinction of affliction by way of its associates:
this refers to all primary afflictions and secondary afflictions, such as greed, hatred, and delusion.
Regarding the differentiation of the body,
there are also two kinds: first,
the differentiation of various types of bodies.
Second, because of the distinction between the two kinds of bodies,
one should know that the various defilements present within the mind serve as the cause for the distinction between these two kinds of bodies.
In order to sever that [affliction], practitioners should diligently cultivate meditative observation by repeatedly applying correct mental attention.
Furthermore, the distinction of the fruit is brought about through four types of causal distinctions.
That is to say: that which constitutes this distinction,
that by which this distinction is made,
and that which is itself this distinction.
If there is such a distinction,
then regarding this distinction,
it refers to all the distinctions between the happy destinies and the miserable destinies.
Regarding this differentiation:
it refers to the differentiation of those [minds] caused by a mind defiled by greed, hatred, and delusion.
This very differentiation is as follows:
This refers to the various distinctions of the body as encompassed by the five types of formations (*saṃskāra*).
These distinctions consist of the causes and conditions for the defiled and purified states within the flow of all formations, as well as the essence of purification itself.
Not knowing things as they truly are,
one gives rise to various distinctions such as the production of delight and so forth, as well as running about and so forth.
Furthermore, one is unable to penetrate the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Based upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
foolish persons proceed with the current;
it should be understood that they are carried away and submerged by the current through five kinds of characteristics.
That is to say: that wherein one is swept away and drowned,
that by which one is swept away and drowned,
and that upon which one relies while being swept away and drowned.
If one is thus drifting and drowning,
whatever signs there may be at the time of such drifting and drowning,
for that person who is drifting and drowning:
This refers to being swept away and submerged in both the happy and miserable realms;
just as one who travels back and forth between two banks is submerged by the current,
so too is it for those who are thus swept away.
This refers to being swept away and drowned by the nature of the ever-flowing river of craving.
One should know that this craving has five characteristics:
first, it wanders through various objects of perception because it tends toward the lower realms.
Second, because it is subtle and its accompanying movements are difficult to discern;
third, because it is difficult to turn back from all objects of experience;
fourth, because it is pursued by all the vast and various formations (*saṃskāra*) up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
The five signs of non-quiescence cause confusion of body and mind.
"Sinking and drifting based on these" means that one is carried away and submerged by the five kinds of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
Regarding the two shores of the happy and miserable realms,
there are five categories of conduct that repeatedly take these as objects and cause one to drift and drown along with the current.
Regarding those who are thus adrift and submerged:
in what way are they adrift and submerged?
It refers to the process of transmigration and so forth within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), as previously described.
Because they do not know [them] as they truly are according to their sequence,
or because they conceive of them as "I" and "mine," [they fail to recognize] the signs present at the time of being swept away and drowning.
That is to say, when one is thus being swept away and submerged,
although one cherishes the body and desires it to endure for a long time,
it cannot be made to remain because of its inherent nature of cessation.
Just as one who is adrift and drowning [is carried with the current],
one should know that the opposite of this is one who flows against the stream.
Furthermore, there are ten characteristics of the wise person.
It should be understood that this fully encompasses all the characteristics of the wise:
namely, because they have achieved innate wisdom (*sahaja-prajñā*),
and furthermore, because they have achieved the wisdoms consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) through skillful means.
Furthermore, because they are accomplished and unwavering,
they think what is well thought, speak what is well spoken, and perform what is well performed; moreover,
they are able to rely upon their own inherent nature.
They have never relied upon others out of a sense of destiny;
furthermore, whatever they seek is always peaceful and joyful,
and whatever they seek they are able to rely upon through right practice.
All things are done according to the Dharma and not contrary to the Dharma.
Furthermore, regarding the assets and various requisites appropriate for oneself,
one is able to guard them correctly so as not to let them be lost or scattered.
Furthermore, one should utilize [medicines] while contemplating their disadvantages.
Moreover, regarding all medicines for the causes of illness,
one should examine and deliberate upon them before consuming them.
Furthermore, one is able to skillfully avoid the conditions for untimely death.
These ten marks of a wise person should be understood as encompassing all the characteristics of wisdom.
Furthermore, regarding those who, within the context of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), know and abandon them by relying on the principle of selflessness (*anātman*),
it should be understood that they are briefly distinguished by three characteristics.
That is to say, they are those who have fully comprehended the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) regarding all conditioned phenomena, yet have not yet abandoned it.
Regarding those conditioned phenomena, they frequently engage in conduct characterized by forgetfulness and only rarely engage in conduct characterized by mindfulness; yet,
their view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) has been permanently severed.
One should know that its characteristics are the opposite of those;
this is called the first distinguishing characteristic.
Furthermore, although one has thoroughly understood the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),...
Yet those who have not yet severed [these fetters] give rise to much joy and pleasure toward vast and desirable things,
and give rise to much sorrow and suffering toward inferior and undesirable objects.
When those two objects appear before them,
even one who is not heedless is unable to bind and maintain right mindfulness,
let alone one who is heedless.
At that time, his mind was entangled by the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
because of this, his mind was unable to comprehend [the truth].
Once the view of a personal identity has been permanently severed, [he is no longer thus bound].
One should know that its characteristics are the opposite of those;
this is called the second distinguishing characteristic.
Furthermore, regarding those who have not yet permanently abandoned the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) with respect to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*):

One who has not yet been able to establish, within all internal formations, the absence of the notion of a sentient being before their mind— just as one does with external objects such as grass, trees, and leaves—
and whose view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) has not yet been permanently abandoned.
One should know that its characteristics are the opposite of those;
this is called the third distinguishing characteristic.
Thus, the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) has been severed.
Regarding these three distinct characteristics,
one should know that there are furthermore three kinds of benefits:
first, the permanent severance of all afflictions that induce further existence.
Second, based on that, one will before long be able to quickly accumulate the path that serves as its antidote.
Third, having accomplished one’s own welfare,
one relies upon that very path to diligently cultivate the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
By this, one attains a state of supreme peace and happiness.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the cultivation of the perception of impermanence and suffering in all aspects is to be practiced through four distinctions.
What are these four?
First, by way of the distinction of results;
second, by way of the distinction of intrinsic nature;
third, by way of the distinction of categories.
Fourth, regarding the distinction of the fruits due to the distinctions in the skillful means:
this refers to the fact that by cultivating this perception, one is able to dispel all sensual desire, desire for form, and desire for the formless, as well as restlessness, pride, and ignorance.
It should be understood that herein three types of abandonment of the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) are revealed,
as well as three types of abandonment of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
The affliction of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) has restlessness (*auddhatya*) as its companion.
The affliction of desire for form has pride as its auxiliary companion;
the delusion of desire for the formless has ignorance as its companion.
Furthermore, there is another distinction.
This refers to the demonstration therein of the lower and higher fetters (*paryavasthāna*) and their exhaustion;
as for the distinction of their intrinsic nature,
it means that herein, through the correct cultivation of the wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
It is called "cultivation through proximity" because,

by means of the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) that has been correctly practiced, one is able to enter into meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). It is called "cultivation through practice" [because of the actual engagement in meditation].
Through the correct cultivation of the wisdom born of meditation,
it is called "extensive cultivation";
furthermore, it is due to the cultivation of the attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-manaskāra*).

This is called "cultivation through proximity," because it arises from the correct cultivation of all other mental orientations (*manasikāra*), with the sole exception of the mental orientation of the culmination of the preparatory stage (*prayoga-niṣṭha-manasikāra*).
Cultivation is called "practice";
the mental attention that brings the application of practice to completion is called "extensive cultivation."
This is called the second set of threefold distinctions.
Furthermore, one should understand that by way of the basis (*āśraya*), the object (*ālambana*), and the mental attention (*manasikāra*),
these are respectively designated as the vehicle (*yāna*), the entity (*vastu*), and the establishment (*vyavasthāna*).
Furthermore, because it has been practiced for a long time,
it is called "perfected"; and because the skillful means have been repeatedly and unerringly cultivated,
it is called "well-received" and "well-initiated."
Regarding the distinction of categories:
it means that when one cultivates such a perception of impermanence,
one is able to swiftly and permanently uproot all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
One abandons all wholesome dharmas of the lower stages and embraces all wholesome dharmas of the higher stages;
regarding all other perceptions of impurity and so forth, one attains their supreme and most expansive nature.
Being able to skillfully maintain [this state],
one universally engages with all things as if observing the objects of apprehension;
in that very same way, one observes the subject of apprehension.
Through that liberation of signs, one attains the perception of the untainted impermanence.
Whether it be tainted perceptions or untainted perceptions,
all such things are well-conducive to, directed toward, and lead into Nirvana.
All of these are able to counteract the great darkness of ignorance and bring about its eternal severance.
Because that [ignorance] is eternally severed, they are pure and bright white.
All perceptions of those beyond training (aśaikṣa-saṃjñā) are attained through the predominance of all untainted perceptions of training (anāsrava-śaikṣa-saṃjñā).
Regarding the distinction of skillful means:
it refers to dwelling alone in a secluded place and repeatedly applying attention without error to observe the impermanent nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
By means of the perception of impermanence, one dwells in the perception of non-self.
Having already dwelled in the untainted perception of non-self during the path of seeing, one then,
through the perception of being a trainee (*śaikṣa*) on the subsequent path of cultivation, permanently destroys the conceit of "I am."
Both types of nirvāṇa are fully possessed upon its attainment.
Furthermore, for one who dwells in nirvāṇa but has not yet accumulated the provisions of merit, there are briefly five kinds of factors that obstruct those provisions:
first, recollecting past events such as laughter, play, amusements, and acts of service.
First, due to the arising of longing accompanied by attention, there occurs sorrow, lamentation,
and so forth. Second, based on those various [conditions],
with respect to the ultimate phenomena that are being experienced.
Frequent forgetfulness prevents one from clearly discerning all phenomena.
Third, the food consumed may be excessive or deficient,
whereby the body becomes heavy and weak.
Fourth, they take no pleasure in practicing the various holy life (brahmacarya);
being fond of sleep and unaccustomed to abandoning it,
they become ensnared by excessive drowsiness.
Fifth, dwelling in association with the vulgar and the profane,
thereby distancing oneself from the application of reflecting upon the sublime Dharma.
These are the five kinds of factors that contravene the provisions for enlightenment.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of factors that accord with those dharmas.
First, although one has become detached from two [types of desire], one is still unable to abandon even one kind of desire;
that is, while practicing the cultivation of wholesome qualities, one remains detached from the various *paryavasthānas* (obsessions) only in a remote sense.
Furthermore, there is the failure to attain the correct antidote for the permanent destruction of latent tendencies and the abandonment of desire;
second, failing to guard the doors of the sensory faculties;
and third, lack of moderation in eating.
Fourth, being unable to diligently practice, exert oneself, and maintain vigilance during the first and last watches of the night;
fifth, being unable to investigate the ultimate nature of wholesome dharmas.
These are the opposites of the aforementioned qualities.
One should know that these are called the dharmas conducive to the provisions (*sambhāra*) and the dharmas that are conducive to those [provisions].
Furthermore, the śrāvakas practice these dharmas conducive to the provisions and their causal conditions.
In the interim while seeking nirvāṇa, the Great Teacher established for them five kinds of instructions on the right path.
The first is: by relying on the investigation of the Dharma as it has been heard.
Pervading all conditioned phenomena are impermanence,
all dharmas are selfless,
and nirvana is tranquility.
Furthermore, one attains freedom from confusion and doubt by means of mundane attention;
second, while remaining [in that state], one does not cling to the three objects nor engage in improper reflection.
What are these three things?
First, the requisites for sustaining life;
second, the signs of harm from others.
Third, either others revile and abuse one,
or some disagreeable conduct occurs,
or there are qualities inconsistent with those of fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*).
Third, preceded by instruction, through relying on the voices of others and applying correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*),
one is able to give rise to right view and sever wrong views;
it should be known that these three are called the teaching of the right path at the time of abiding.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of instructions regarding the right path for when one practices therein:
namely, that when wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin) proclaim to them what is possible and what is impossible, they do not give rise to anger.
Furthermore, the fact that the mind is not tormented by distress, whether one obtains or does not obtain coarse and inferior requisites for sustaining life,
and due to all calamities related to ethical discipline and so forth—
this is called the first [type].
When obtaining gain, offerings, and honor, his mind is not dejected;
this is called the second [point].
By abiding and acting in such a manner, he is able to correctly practice the sublime path to nirvāṇa.
By this means, one shall before long attain nirvāṇa, never to suffer any loss or decline.
Furthermore, the Great Master has, in brief, five kinds of duties toward his śrāvaka disciples.
First, correct subduing;
second, correct acceptance;
third, correct reprimand.
Fourth is the correct exposition of affliction;
fifth is the correct exposition of purification.
Furthermore, for two reasons, one transcends the śrāvakas regarding matters of dispute.
He provides a cryptic prediction regarding the matter of their dispute:
first, because it causes agitation and proliferation;
second, because it is consistent with the Vinaya.
Furthermore, for seven reasons the Great Teacher expelled the assembly of śrāvakas:
first, because he saw that they were all practicing in every respect according to wrong conduct;
second, because he saw that they constituted the majority.
Third, because of the skillful means employed by the leaders of that assembly—the senior monks (sthavira), ācāryas, and upādhyāyas;
fourth, because they were unable to dwell together [in harmony];
and fifth, because they were expelled.
Sixth, to avoid manifest faults;
seventh, to prevent the arising of future faults.
Furthermore, for ten reasons, the Tathāgata enters a village to beg for food.
First, it is for the purpose of manifesting the virtues of the dhūtas;
second, it is because one wishes to lead a certain portion of those beings to enter the practice of begging for food;
third, it is because one wishes to gather a certain portion of those beings through the conduct of "common purpose" (samānārthatā).
Fourth, it is for the sake of acting as a great illumination for sentient beings of the future,
even to the extent of causing them to momentarily give rise to direct contact and realization.
Fifth, it is because one desires to lead those non-Buddhists who possess coarse and inferior inclinations.
Sixth, because those who hear his voice might give rise to slander,
he manifests a wondrous appearance and tranquil deportment,
causing them to be struck with wonder and inspiration so that their hearts turn toward him in devotion.
Seventh, it is for the sake of those beings who dwell in the middle way, so that they may plant great merit with little effort;
eighth, it is to cause those who have violated their faith and are heedless to feel profound shame and remorse.
Because even by performing small meritorious deeds one obtains great blessings;
it is likewise for those who are heedless or indolent.
Ninth, because it causes all manner of calamities for sentient beings who are blind, deaf, insane, or mentally deranged to be completely stilled.
Tenth, it is for the sake of causing the immeasurable, boundless, and vast majesty of devas,
nāgas, yakṣas,
and gandharvas [to arise].
Asuras, garuḍas, and kiṃnaras.
The mahoragas and others followed the Tathāgata to the house where he entered;
they felt deep admiration and veneration, diligently providing him with hospitality and protection.
It is not for the sake of causing affliction or harm.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata enters the tranquil divine abode due to eight causes and conditions.
First, in order to lead those who delight in living in company to enter into seclusion.
Second, it is because he wishes to gather those who dwell in seclusion through the practice of *samānārthatā* (common purpose).
Third, it is for the sake of his own experience of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Fourth, it is in order to manifest the appearance of joining assemblies with the deities of great clans.
Fifth, it is because he observes the worlds of the ten directions with the Buddha-eye,
manifesting great spiritual transformations to perform beneficial deeds according to what is appropriate for each being.
Sixth, it is because he causes the assembly of śrāvakas to give rise to deep longing and yearning upon seeing the Tathāgata.
Seventh, it is to demonstrate that the great śrāvakas are well able to penetrate what has been briefly taught.
Eighth, it is to exhort them to abandon their attachment to the proliferation of conceptual elaborations and the composition of verbal expressions.
Furthermore, the Great Teacher sustains the assembly of disciples by means of five aspects;
first, by means of the Dharma.
Second, because of material wealth;
third, because of providing a basis for support;
fourth, because of initial acceptance.
Fifth, because of being gathered through the act of banishment.
Furthermore, for seven reasons, Śakra, Brahmā, and others go to the presence of the Tathāgata:
first, for the purpose of making offerings to the Tathāgata.
Second, for the sake of hearing the true Dharma;
third, for the sake of resolving doubts that have arisen;
and fourth, for the sake of following others by acting as their attendants.
Fifth, out of compassion for others and the desire to benefit them;
sixth, due to his deep affection and reverence for the holy teaching of the Tathāgata;
seventh, knowing that the Tathāgata had given rise to a conventional mind desiring them to attend the assembly.
Furthermore, one should know that there are five characteristics by which all those who are newly ordained are defined:
first, because they have entered the monastic life late in life.
Second, by virtue of having gone forth while young;
third, by virtue of having gone forth while still a youth;
fourth, by virtue of having gone forth through diligent exertion.
Fifth, because of having received full ordination and gone forth.
Furthermore, remorse arises by way of three aspects.
First, because of the predominance of transgressing what has been studied;
second, because of the predominance of vowing to accept the laws and precepts;
third, because of the predominance of abandoning the household life.
Furthermore, when the Tathāgata intends to proclaim the True Dharma for the sake of the śrāvakas,
he manifests four signs:
first, rising with composed dignity from his very low seat and ascending to sit solemnly upon a very high throne.

First, within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,

"I have no suffering," or rather,

If foolish worldlings, relying upon the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),

In this context, by the predominant power of various forms of grasping,

Nārāyaṇa, and so forth.

it is called the bodily fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*).
Because one practices the holy life based on wrong aspirations,
one gives rise to aversion toward the delightful dharmas shared with fellow practitioners of the holy life.
By these two conditions, one should know that they act as defilements for the training in higher ethics;
furthermore, it is by means of the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) that they act as defilements for the training in higher mind (*adhicittam śikṣā*).
Due to this bond of attachment to a real body,
one becomes defiled regarding the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).
Thus, these four factors function with respect to the engagement in objects and the establishment of activities concerning the physical body and the mental body (*nāmakāya*).
Because they bind the mind, they are called bodily fetters (*kāyayoga*).
Furthermore, because they reside in the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), [they are so designated].
Because of mental discrimination,
because of association with the mind,
and because of latent tendencies within the mind.
Because it is defiled by the *manas*,
it is called "mind-made" (*manomaya*).
Furthermore, as for its cessation:
This means that the various afflictions which take those objects as their conditions are abandoned,
but it is not because those objects themselves are abandoned; rather, it is because one has attained an unerring understanding regarding those very objects.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the consciousness which is the seed of future existence is established upon this basis,
being sustained by the karmas and afflictions of future existence.
Because those do not exist,
the three types [of future states] as previously described will grow,
expand, and increase through their distinct modes of reasoning.
One should know that everything is completely extinguished.
Furthermore, by means of that very consciousness which abides nowhere,
the causal and resultant portions no longer arise.
It is encompassed by all paths and thus attains growth;
furthermore, because it takes the liberation door of emptiness as its basis,

it is called "contentment.
Because it takes the signless gate of liberation as its basis...
This is called "abiding.
Because one repeatedly cultivates delight therein,
one attains wholesome liberation.

the mind is well-liberated;
from this point onward, one attains perpetual abiding.
Although he dwells within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), he is without fear;
having attained the spontaneous cessation of the aggregates (*skandha*),
because the remaining causes have been severed, they will not arise again.
Once that contaminated consciousness has been eternally extinguished,
it no longer proceeds anywhere throughout the ten directions;
there remain only those sensations, which are like shadows, and that tree of the consciousness-aggregate.
One should know that, like a lamp, they all return to extinction;
that is, within the realm of nirvana with remainder,
based on the abandonment of the first fetter.
It is called "tranquility" based on the first abandonment; it is called "coolness" based on the second abandonment.
Based on the third abandonment,
it is termed "silent composure.
Furthermore, due to three conditions, consciousness proceeds toward and dwells in states of consciousness that are entirely non-existent.
