Section 8: Explanation of the Sixth Summary Verse (Uddāna), the Seven Gates beginning with the Factors of Abandonment (Prahāṇa-aṅga). Furthermore, the summary verse states:
The factors of abandonment, reality, manifestation, Practice, conditions, non-existence, and so forth;
The fourfold teaching on the assemblies of sentient beings, And the four paths with five culminations.
Those who practice for abandonment are briefly sustained by five factors;
they are capable of abandoning and can discern all conditioned phenomena as they truly are:
first, through physical seclusion.
Second, by means of mental seclusion;
third, by means of samādhi belonging to the category of śamatha;
and fourth, by means of samādhi belonging to the category of vipaśyanā.
Fifth, it is because of what is performed with constant diligence.
Furthermore, one should know that there are twelve aspects of manifesting reality as it is,
as explained in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.
This refers to: (1) having heard and individually grasped [the teachings] correctly or incorrectly;
(2) the objects of authoritative instruction, direct perception, and inference;
and (3) specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Because of the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāvatā*) and the nature of things in their full extent (*yāvadbhāvatā*),
and because of entering the ultimate stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, there are briefly four kinds of objects of knowledge (*jñeya-vastu*) characterized by the principles that accurately manifest the modes of activity (*ākāra*).
This refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) abiding in internal phenomena who,
due to the power of not knowing things as they truly are, gives rise to feelings within the objects encountered in a sudden, impulsive manner.
Because one knows as it truly is that [ignorance] causes the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) to flow on and become defiled, one is able to bring them to purification.
Furthermore, there are householders who are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Because one does not know, as they truly are, the predominant power within the bases such as delighting in future existence,
it causes the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to flow on and become defiled.
That which is contrary to those [views] is able to bring about purification.
Furthermore, there are various non-Buddhists who engage in false conceptualization regarding what they cherish and delight in.
Because one does not know, as they truly are, the predominant power within the formations that serve as the basis for the joy and pleasure born of meditative concentration,
these formations cause the cycle of existence to flow on in defilement.
That which is contrary to those [defilements] is able to bring about purification.
Furthermore, there are those in training who abide in internal phenomena;
they rely upon all false thoughts regarding the sense faculties and their objects.
Due to the power of not knowing the remaining residual formations as they truly are,
there is the defilement of saṃsāra;
by severing those remaining residues, one attains purification.
It should be understood that within all these categories,
all pure factors abide in internal phenomena;
these are called the four types of objects of focus.
Furthermore, for three reasons,
the teaching spoken by the Tathāgata is peerless:
first, because he proclaims the unshared dharmas (āveṇika-dharma).
Second, because it proclaims the non-erroneous Dharma;
third, because it proclaims the Dharma of self-realization.
This is what is proclaimed herein.
If one proceeds toward the origination of the view of a personal identity,
that is proceeding toward the origination of suffering; if one proceeds toward the cessation of the view of a personal identity, [that is proceeding toward the cessation of suffering].
This is precisely the practice leading to the cessation of suffering;
this is called the teaching that proclaims the unshared dharmas.
Furthermore, if it were said that "this truly exists," [it would be a different matter].
This is called the teaching that proclaims the Dharma without error.
Furthermore, if one says, "I know [this] as it truly is," this is called the teaching that proclaims the Dharma of self-realization.
Furthermore, there are three types of distinctions regarding the流转 (saṃsāra) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*):
first, *satkāya*, because it is the sense of being the locus where sentient beings are stained by attachment and find their footing;
second, *loka*, because it is the sense of being a locus of attachment that is subject to decay and destruction.
Third, because those who possess such defiled attachment are subject to rebirth.
Furthermore, there are briefly four types of such sentient beings.
What are these four?
First, there is the one who exclusively dwells in the fruits of desirable karma,
becoming attached to and indulging in those very fruits;
that is to say, being born in a celestial realm, they practice only heedlessness.
Second, the transformation through one-pointed causes,
which refers to those śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who aspire for that [state];
third, the multitude of sentient beings who delight in parinirvāṇa.
Fourth are the various types of attachment,
which refers to those who, dwelling either in the path or in the fruit,
become addicted to and attached to sensory enjoyments.
Either they delight in securing the desirable fruits of the future,
or they periodically cultivate the provisions for nirvāṇa,
remaining free from all negligence.
Among the three aforementioned classes of sentient beings,
one should understand, as appropriate for each case, the limits of the arising and cessation of that world,
as well as the limits of the arising and cessation of the *satkāya*.
Regarding the fourth group of sentient beings hereafter,
one should know that there are distinctions concerning the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), its origination, its cessation, and the path leading to it.
Furthermore, this is based on two kinds of paths.
One should know that four types of modes of activity are established.
How do they rely upon two kinds of paths?
That is to say, they rely upon the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
How are the four types of aspects established?
First, the aspect of that which should be fully understood;
second, the aspect of that which should be permanently abandoned.
Third, the aspect of what should be realized;
fourth, the aspect of what should be cultivated.
These are the four kinds.
The third relies on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
and the first relies on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
At the time of entering the path of seeing, one is simultaneously able to fully comprehend through the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*).
When one has abandoned a portion of suffering and realized a portion of its origin,
and is able to abandon and realize a portion of cessation,
one does so within the path of cultivation in order to seek the remainderless abandonment and realization.
One should diligently cultivate the path as it has been attained.
By means of cultivating such paths of analytical investigation (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
one permanently abandons the remaining origination (*samudaya*) and realizes the remaining cessation (*nirodha*).
Thus, regarding that which is ultimately perfected,
its perfection should be understood through five aspects.
What are these five? They are:
having realized the exhaustion of suffering and its causes without remainder;
and being capable of fulfilling all one's own purposes as well as the welfare of others.
Because they have realized ultimate abandonment and knowledge;
because they are able to enter the city of final nirvāṇa;
and once having entered it, they are able to dwell securely in that noble abode.
Regarding the first characteristic, there are four types of distinctions, such as the severing of affection,
which should be understood as previously described.
Regarding the second characteristic, there are all the distinctions pertaining to the Arhat who has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), and so forth.
It should be understood as previously explained.
Regarding the third characteristic, there is the ultimate exhaustion of all activities because they are completely severed;
and there is the ultimate stainlessness because all afflictions are completely severed.
There is the ultimate holy life (brahmacarya) as its final limit;
that is to say, because one has already attained its antidote.
Regarding the fourth characteristic, it is, for example, like entering a royal palace in the world when five conditions are fulfilled.
If even one of these is lacking, it is not called "entry.
Thus, because one must possess these five characteristics that resemble those [of the actual city],
it should be known as "entering the palace-city of nirvāṇa."
What are the five worldly characteristics that he possesses?
First, he opens the gates of the palace city.
Second, he leaps over the moats and ditches without falling.
Third, they give rise to profound determination and cross over it.
Fourth, having crossed the moats and ditches, they draw near to the imperial palace.
Fifth, this is not something hoped for by themselves nor by others.
Once the banner of victory had fallen, he slowly entered the inner palace.
Thus, his entry into the palace was free from all obstructions;
his entry into the palace of nirvana is likewise so.
First, one severs the five lower fetters that conduce [to rebirth],
just as one opens a gate;
next, one conceives of nirvana as a deep pit.
Because ignorance and fear have been severed without remainder,
one is like someone who has crossed a moat and trench without falling back;
thus, one is able to reach the further shore of *satkāya*.
Because he is able to maintain his final body,
he decisively transcends it as if reaching the fruit;
he is about to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder like one approaching the royal palace.
Having already severed craving for existence, no further attachment arises toward any objects.
With conceit entirely non-arising toward all things, one enters nirvana,
such that it is not something hoped for by either self or others.
Once the supreme banner has fallen, he gradually enters the inner palace;
one should know that entering the palace of nirvāṇa is likewise according to the five causes and conditions previously described.
Furthermore, having already entered, one dwells in the noble dwelling by means of two aspects:
first, by way of practice;
second, by way of abiding.
Practice should be correctly understood through three characteristics:
first, because it is unique;
second, because it is undefiled.
Because it is the basis for the threefold correct reliance,
because it permanently severs the five lower fetters conducive to the states of existence,
and because it constitutes the ultimate freedom from desire regarding all sensual pleasures.
Because he wanders about in that very state,
it is called "unshared.
Because he constantly maintains the six constant abodes, it is so named.
It is called "untainted," because one discerns and distances oneself from certain categories of phenomena,
namely evil elephants, horses, and so forth.
One reflects upon and cultivates certain categories of phenomena,
namely clothing, food, drink, and so forth;
this is called the basis for right reliance.
Having thus become thoroughly purified in conduct,
one should further understand abiding by means of five aspects;
that is to say, that by which one abides.
If this is the basis; if by this one is disjoined from fetters; if this is the basis.
If one abides by means of this conjunction,
it should be understood that therein one dwells in the immovable liberation of mind,
having discerned and eliminated a portion of phenomena.
This refers to the physical and mental exhaustion resulting from the causes and conditions of wandering about, distraction,
and toil; it is the discernment and endurance regarding certain phenomena,
such as cold, heat, and so forth.
This is called the basis.
It consists in being dissociated from the three kinds of affliction, namely:
the affliction of views, the affliction of craving, and the affliction of discursive thought.
Because one attains liberation from the affliction of views,
the mind is no longer shaken regarding future existence;
because one attains liberation from the affliction of craving.
One is not swept away or submerged by any objects of perception,
because one has attained dissociation from the defilements of discursive thought; thus,
such discursive thoughts are exclusively wholesome and never unwholesome.
This is called being dissociated by means of this;
based on the four dhyānas and the immovable samādhi,
one dwells in the foremost abiding in happiness in the present life.
This is called the basis;
it is because it is associated with the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
which is well-liberated and associated with wisdom that is well-liberated.
Furthermore, because one who is free from craving does not give rise to a second body,
they do not regress from the abode of nirvana.
Because one definitively realizes the unsurpassed, perfect qualities,
it should be understood that through these five aspects, one dwells in perfection within the first stage (*vihāra*).
Furthermore, the summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
The two chapters are summarized as three distinct categories: the nature of the flow [of existence], its cessation, the unwholesome, and the wholesome—both impure and pure.
Through these three points, all dark and bright factors are briefly subsumed, distinguished by such differences as good and bad teachings and their respective teachers.
First, by way of the phenomena to be fully known;
second, by way of full knowledge itself;
and third, by way of the accomplishment of full knowledge.
The phenomena to be fully understood refer to the truth of suffering and the truth of origination;
one should know that these collectively encompass all unwholesome categories.
"Thorough knowledge" refers to the truth of cessation;
it should be understood that this comprises one portion of the white category.
That which constitutes thorough knowledge refers to the person (pudgala) and the truth of the path (mārgasatya).
Although the person is a conventional existence, it is [the object of thorough knowledge].
It should be understood that this is also subsumed within the category of the white side (śuklapakṣa).
This refers to the noble disciples of the Tathāgata,
regarding both conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) and ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
Being thoroughly skillful in all respects,
one contemplates them as they truly are according to the two principles;
both are undeclared.
That is to say: whether the Tathāgata exists after his parinirvāṇa, or does not exist,
or both exists and does not exist.
It is neither existent nor non-existent;
it cannot be grasped and cannot be defined. Why is this so?
Moreover, from the perspective of ultimate truth, he cannot be apprehended;
how much less can he be said to exist or not exist after his passing?
If one relies on conventional truth, the Tathāgata is merely a provisional designation for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Whether with respect to nirvāṇa or with respect to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
after the Tathāgata has passed away, not a single phenomenon can be found that undergoes transmigration.
At that time, where could the designation "Tathāgata" be provisionally established?
Since there is no Tathāgata, how could there be "non-equality" and so forth?
If it concerns nirvāṇa,
nirvāṇa is manifested solely by the absence of conditioned activity.
All conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is severed;
because that which is realized within oneself is beyond conceptual proliferation,
it is unreasonable to designate it as "existent."
Furthermore, one should not posit it as non-existent,
lest one should undermine the positing of the sublime existence of tranquil nirvāṇa;
moreover, this nirvāṇa is extremely difficult to know.
Because it is most subtle,
it is called "profound.
It is manifold and not singular.
It is called "vast" because it is manifested by the severance of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and afflictions (*kleśa*),
and because it cannot be measured by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or valid scriptural authority (*āptāgama*).
It is called "immeasurable.
Furthermore, there is a distinction between internal suffering borne and external suffering borne due to three causes and conditions.
First, that which is to be borne;
second, that which is able to bear it;
third, the time of bearing it.
This refers to that which is externally borne, comprised of a portion of form—
whether it be straw, firewood, or other such kinds— that constitutes what is carried.
Yet the foolish take all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to be what is borne.
Furthermore, while the external burden rests upon the shoulders of the body,
it is these [shoulders] that can carry the load;
yet the fool takes the entire aggregate of craving to be that which carries the load.
Furthermore, while an external porter carries his burden solely by means of his present shoulders,
the fool carries his burden by means of the entire aggregate of craving (*tṛṣṇā-skandha*).
To abandon the burden, one must eliminate the aggregates along with it.
There is no other expedient means by which one can abandon it;
for as long as one has not yet laid down what was being carried, one continues to bear a great and heavy burden,
holding fast to shoulders that are frail, feeble, delicate, soft, and unsteady.
Because they bear their burden for a long duration without interruption,
those within possess three virtues that enable them to undergo such manifold sufferings of bearing the burden;
those without, however, do not.
This is called the distinction between the two kinds of burdens.
Furthermore, there is a distinction between the internal bondage of the foolish and that external bondage by way of five characteristics.
That is to say, just as one is bound by external fetters—
such as being tied with wood, iron, or rope—
so too is the fool bound by the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, while those external bonds and bonds by others bind [others],
the fool is bound by his own bonds. Moreover,
those external bonds are easy to understand, as are their causes and conditions for binding, and the means for their release.
The internal fetters of the fool are difficult for all to know;
furthermore, his external fetters cease to exist after death.
However, the internal fetters of the fool follow the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) after death, coming and going in a cycle without being abandoned.
Furthermore, those renunciants who are bound by external fetters can attain liberation by abandoning all desires;
they cannot be obstructed or restrained by any enemies.
Although foolish people may attain freedom from desire while still bound within,
they are not yet able to escape even up to the Peak of Existence;
how much less so those who merely leave the household life?
It should be understood that herein, when one is in the state of having abandoned desire,
Māra does not obtain mastery over them; however,
when one has not yet abandoned desire, Māra does obtain mastery.
In the stage of renunciation, one has not yet escaped the hands of Māra;
in the stage of household life, one acts according to desire;
and as long as one has not left the state of desire, one is bound by the fetters of Māra.
Although one may have been born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) by means of the mundane path, one has not yet escaped the snare of Māra.
Furthermore, in brief, through four aspects,
one should understand the similarities and differences between a Tathāgata and an Arhat liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*).
They are called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) by virtue of one characteristic,
namely, their similarity in terms of liberation and so forth.
They are called "heterogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*) by virtue of three characteristics.
That is to say: because of manifesting perfect enlightenment;
because of being able to teach the Dharma;
and because of practicing the right practice.
In this regard, the Tathāgata, without a teacher and spontaneously, cultivated the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and attained manifest, perfect awakening;
having attained perfect awakening, he universally relies upon the ultimate truth.
Whether there is capacity or incapacity regarding the present life,
and whether phenomena are directly perceived or not directly perceived—
in every respect, he thoroughly understands them all.
This is called self-arisen, perfectly awakened enlightenment (*svayambhū-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Having thus realized the ultimate dharma,
one becomes well-liberated from those two obstacles.
This refers to being the peerless and unique teacher of liberation for the hosts of devas and the rest of the world,
having [overcome] both the afflictive obscurations along with their habitual tendencies and the cognitive obscurations.
One should know that the thorough realization of these four characteristics is called the self-existent, perfectly awakened enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Because of this, it is not shared with the śrāvakas.
Furthermore, the teaching of the true Dharma through the meanings of dependence, agent,
and action should be understood as unique by virtue of five aspects. What are these five?
First, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, all kinds of paths as paths and all kinds of non-paths as non-paths.
Second, having known them, he teaches, as they truly are, what is the path and what is not the path.
To cause them to proceed toward the path and not toward what is not the path;
third, if there are those who possess the desire and diligence to practice as the path has been taught,
[the Buddha acts] to cause their practice to be embraced by skillful means and the right path induced by correct mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*).
He teaches by means of the gate of instruction.
Fourth, when that person practices according to the holy teachings,
any obstacles or faults regarding serenity and insight are caused to be eliminated.
Fifth, if there are those who accord with that dharma, one causes them all to be embraced.
This is called being able to teach the discordant dharma.
Among these, "discordance in correct practice" refers to:
That is to say, those śrāvakas first rely upon the Tathāgata and subsequently practice the correct conduct.
Now, the Tathāgata has no basis whatsoever.
Furthermore, they who have accomplished the śrāvaka lineage practice this correct conduct.
Furthermore, the Buddha-Tathāgata has perfected his own lineage,
and those śrāvakas have either already matured or will mature; however,
these two types of practice cannot be found within the bodies of bodhisattvas in their final existence.
If they are not yet matured, they will follow the path so as to mature their continuum for the sake of future maturation.
If they are already matured, they become great teachers in this present life.
These two types act exactly in accordance with the holy teaching.
If they follow the path, they shall realize nirvana in a future life;
if they become great teachers in the present life,
they will cause others to rely upon this very body to realize the noble path, the fruits of the path, and nirvana.
This very noble path and the fruit of the noble path are called the "dharmas as they truly are" because they are a bliss free from affliction;
furthermore, they are said to be "wholesome" because of their beneficial nature.
Furthermore, within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), there are briefly two kinds of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding selflessness:
first, that which is predominant through hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*);
second, that which is predominant through cultivation and realization (*bhāvanā-sākṣātkriyā*).
In this context, the superior resolve resulting from hearing and reflection serves as the generative basis for the superior resolve of cultivation and realization.
Noble sons who have gone forth with pure faith [attain this].
Even though one has reached this state of extreme excellence and thoroughness,
one should not be content with it alone; rather,
taking this as a basis, one must proceed further among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Gradually cultivating the perception of impermanence and so forth,
one realizes the superior conviction (*adhimokṣa*) of non-self; then,
in order to cause that realization to become further enhanced, one diligently practices meditative insight.
Furthermore, by means of four aspects,
one should understand that there are two kinds of abandonment regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). What are these four?
First, because the active fetters (*paryavasthāna*) are severed;
second, because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are severed;
third, because the causal nature of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) for future existence is severed.
Fourth, because the defiled formations of the present are abandoned.
These four types should be understood as being summarized into two kinds of abandonment:
namely, the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*) and the abandonment of the objective basis (*vastu-prahāṇa*).
The first two characteristics are called the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*);
the latter two characteristics are explained as the abandonment of the objective basis (*vastu-prahāṇa*).
Furthermore, regarding the initial, middle, and final stages of the流转 (*pravṛtti*, flow) of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) within the desire realm:
It should be known that, in brief, there are three kinds of secret suffering.
First, because at the time of birth one is obstructed and covered by the womb,
there is the suffering of obstruction.
Second, once born, one dwells in the stage of infancy and childhood, where there is much suffering from illness.
Third, in the stage of decline and decrepitude, when the faculties have fully matured, there is the suffering of old age and death.
Furthermore, those conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) arise and flow on through their initial, middle, and final stages of cessation.
It should be understood that this is the cessation of the three kinds of suffering.
Furthermore, there are three types of existence;
in order to sever them, the noble disciples should apply themselves diligently to cultivation.
First, based on the existence of a nature caused by the past,
for this reason and through these conditions, one develops pure faith and leaves the household life for the homeless state,
deeply perceiving faults and becoming weary of all sensual desires.
Second, existence by virtue of future actions that have arisen serving as causes;
third, existence by virtue of present defilements of intention that have not yet been abandoned.
It is for the sake of abandoning these three kinds of existence that [the path is cultivated].
There are three kinds of abandonment:
namely, because of being free from attachment,
and because of not taking delight [in worldly things].
Because it is the accumulation of the abandonment, detachment, cessation, and the realm of integration.
Furthermore, within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), there are briefly two kinds of non-conceited observation of the view of selflessness (*anātman*). What are these two?
First, impurity of the unwholesome;
second, purity of the wholesome.
What is meant by "impurity of the unwholesome"?
That is to say, there is one who dwells in seclusion;
relying on the patience that contemplates the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena,
they give rise to resolute conviction regarding selflessness through mundane knowledge.
Therefore, through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one observes accordingly the forms cognizable by the eye up to the phenomena cognizable by the mind;
because the signs of "I" and "mine" no longer manifest,
this is called "abandonment."
Furthermore, one is able to subdue the three types of greed, hatred, and delusion comprised within the four outer fetters:
namely, all that is comprised by the fetter of covetousness for sensual pleasures,
and all that is comprised by the fetter of ill will.
The remaining two bodily fetters encompass all forms of delusion (*moha*).
It should be understood that in this context, "all" has the sense of being utterly base and defiled.
This refers to the appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) of one who possesses non-conceptual wisdom (*anātma-jñāna*) free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Because it is associated with [mental factors] and because it is comprised within the meditative stages,
one should know that this wisdom is not thoroughly purified due to two causes and conditions.
First, at this very time:
This refers to the stage of entering the roots of virtue conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*),
wherein a coarse form of self-conceit (*asmimāna*) follows along, manifesting as subtle activity that arises continuously and without interruption amidst moments of attention (*manasikāra*).
Due to these causes and conditions, they form this thought:
"I am now able to cultivate and realize emptiness;
emptiness is mine."
Because it is empty, one conceives of the self as superior;
one should know that this is likewise true for being signless and non-existent.
Second, it serves as the causal condition for the manifestation of those phenomena.
This refers to consciousness that is stained by craving for various sensual desires or for the existence of a personal identity (*satkāya*).
It is due to the predominant influence of not fully understanding such consciousness,
which is stained by craving, that [suffering arises].
They are then swept away and submerged by the craving for sensual desires and the attachment to the transitory collection (*satkāya*).
Due to this disposition, they are unable to enter into that nirvāṇa;
their minds turn back.
As previously stated,
one can fully comprehend through eight aspects;
by means of such full comprehension, all faults and afflictions are eliminated.
One should know that this is called the most thoroughly purified,
non-conceptual wisdom of selflessness, which is free from overweening pride;
furthermore, because [the object] has already been destroyed within this state.
Because it is a phenomenon subject to disintegration,
it is called impermanent;
because it is accumulated through various karmas and afflictions, it is so designated.
It is called "conditioned" because it is accumulated through the power of former vows;
it is called "mentally constructed" because it is produced by thought.
Because it is produced from its own seeds through the integration of present external conditions,
it is called "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
Furthermore, because it is subject to the dharma of aging and decay in future lives, it is so designated.
It is called the "dharma of exhaustion" because it is subject to death; it is called the "dharma of passing away" because it is subject to mortality.
Because one is oppressed and afflicted by various calamities such as illness before reaching old age and death,
it is called the "corrupting dharma.
This is because, based on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), one is able to become free from desire and is able to bring about cessation.
It is called "attaining the state of freedom from desire and the state of cessation in the present life.
One should know that herein, setting aside the states of freedom from desire and cessation,
one briefly contemplates all the defects of the three times by means of the remaining characteristics.
One contemplates renunciation by means of the characteristics of what has been eliminated.
If, through such thorough knowledge of the defects and renunciation,
one recognizes that consciousness, it is called "thoroughly knowing that there is no self-nature among all phenomena."
It is called the Seal of All Dharmas.
This Seal of Dharmas was composed by the Dharma King according to the principles of this treatise;
it does not cause affliction or harm to the bodies of the noble ones.
Rejoicing enables one to attain all the noble riches;
by means of this, one naturally and auspiciously transcends the vast, perilous, and long path of birth and death.
For this reason, it is also called the Dharma Seal of the Multitude of Sages.
It should be understood that herein, the former is called "knowledge of penetration" (*prativedha-jñāna*),
while the latter is called "thoroughly purified vision" (*suviśuddha-dṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, it should be known that there are five aspects by which the distinction between superiority and inferiority among internal and external Dharma-teachers and their disciples is established.
First, by way of abiding;
second, by way of governing the assembly;
third, by way of definitive analysis through debate.
Fourth, by way of establishing and elucidating the path;
fifth, by way of practice—
referring to the teachers and disciples of the various non-Buddhist traditions.
The lay disciple constantly dwells in a state of bustle and noise,
whereas the monastic practitioner dwells from time to time in a state of extreme tranquility;
this is called the first distinction of superiority and inferiority.
Furthermore, the teachers of the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika) have a certain number of ordained disciples;
by virtue of these, the various non-Buddhist monastic communities are said to possess a "Sangha.
They likewise have a certain number of lay disciples.

The various groups of non-Buddhists are called the "Assembly" (gaṇa) because they desire that all [beings] collectively accept them as their teachers; thus they are called the "Teachers of the Assembly.
The ignorant classes of sentient beings all claim that these possess virtuous qualities.
Therefore, these are called the "virtuous forms commonly esteemed.
It should be understood that the Tathāgata is the opposite of them;
although he is the unsurpassed Great Teacher for all devas and the world, [he does not possess such forms].
Regarding those [teachings], one honors them as equal yet harbors no expectations [of them].
Furthermore, when non-Buddhist teachers and their own disciples engage in debate to reach a definitive resolution,
whatever is said is understood through mutual interpretation.
Each is distinct and does not accord with one another;
they only increase delusion and do not purify wisdom.
One should know that the internal Dharma is contrary to them.
Furthermore, the teachers of non-Buddhist paths, for the sake of their disciples,
rely upon causelessness and improper causes to establish,
formulate, and reveal their respective doctrines.
Because they have heard such improper teachings,
their minds are harassed and disturbed by great rākṣasas;
furthermore, due to unwholesome reflection associated with irrational mental attention, their minds become distracted and agitated.
Because one harbors a competitive mind toward others, one reproaches them with fault-finding;
if the other person in turn challenges him, he immediately becomes violent and fails to investigate or deliberate with care.
Uttering words lightly,
because one is obscured by self-conceived causes and improper causes,
it is called defilement.
Because of this, since foolish persons do not know the causes and conditions of defilement—
whether regarding themselves or others— as they truly are,
they are called "deluded."
Because it is devoid of purity,
it is called "unclear";
because one is unskilled regarding the causes of purity.
It is called unwholesome.
Furthermore, it extends to speech that ought to be spoken and speech as it is spoken.
In this context, discourse is spoken;
yet, because one does not know all such things as they truly are,
one is said to be "one who lacks measure."
This is because they do not understand the cause.
One should know that internal dharmas are contrary to those [external ones].
Furthermore, although the teachers and disciples of the various non-Buddhists have no differing views [on this matter],...
Because what is spoken is neither deficient nor erroneous;
although it is not diffuse, what is spoken is neither redundant nor superfluous;
and although it is equal, the meaning of what is spoken is consistent.
Although this is a teaching of the Dharma because its words are equal,
and although one may provide predictions concerning the Dharma and that which accords with the Dharma,
one nevertheless forms factions out of a fondness for those who share the same Dharma.
You should know that even those who practice in accordance with the Dharma and have attained realization of their own welfare through heedfulness cannot achieve it;
how much less so those who are heedless?
Because he thus fails to attain his own goal,
he is overcome by the arguments of others;
he is disparaged, and so too are the various evil and false doctrines he has accepted.
One should know that the internal dharmas are the opposite of those;
this is called the fivefold distinction of high and low.
Furthermore, by means of four aspects:
One should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are not necessarily suffering or defiled;
furthermore, by virtue of four characteristics,
they are not necessarily pleasure or purity.
These four characteristics collectively depend upon three matters.
What are these three?
First, they depend upon the place of birth.
Second, by way of sensation;
third, by way of time.
Herein, "pleasure" refers to:
That which is accompanied by pleasure refers to [beings] in the third dhyāna;
that which is accompanied by pleasure refers to [beings] among humans.
There are two kinds of mental ease (*saumanasya*).
That which is pervasive with joy and bliss refers to those in the first and second dhyānas.
"Those who have not yet permanently transcended pleasure" refers to those in the fourth dhyāna and above.
"Suffering therein" [refers to]...
This refers to those among the hungry ghosts and animals who are pursued by suffering;
this refers to those among human beings.
Regarding "pervasive by sorrow and suffering":
this refers to those in the hells who have not yet permanently transcended suffering.
This means that among the hosts of celestial beings above,
they are still followed by suffering;
furthermore, as for what is called "pleasure":
This refers to the state when neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is present.
That which is accompanied by pleasure refers to the state when painful feeling is present.
Regarding "pervasive joy and pleasure," this refers to the state when pleasant feeling is manifest.
Regarding "not being permanently separated from pleasure," [it refers to the same].
This means that in all states, one is accompanied by the causes of pleasure.
One should know that the distinctions of suffering are the opposite of this.
Furthermore, as for what is called "pleasure":
This refers to that which conduces to pleasant experience and that in which pleasure has already ceased;
it refers to that which is accompanied by pleasure,
meaning there is a cause for pleasure that will arise in a future life.
Regarding "pervasive joy and pleasure":
this refers to being in accordance with a state of pleasure in the present,
yet not having permanently transcended that pleasure.
This refers to the other three time periods.
One should understand that there are four such distinctions of suffering,
which are the opposites of these.
The Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Eighty-seven;
The Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Eighty-eight;
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
In the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*, the first part of the *Sūtravastu-kriyā-viniścaya-saṃgraha*, section four. Furthermore, the summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
The two types of wisdom along with their activities, the transformation of the practices such as joy,
and the request or non-request for the preaching of the sutra—
there are two kinds of nirvana and two kinds of wisdom.
First is right knowledge;
second is wrong knowledge.
Among these, right knowledge arises based on an existent object.
It is the same with false wisdom.
Although these two types of wisdom both rely on existent phenomena,
correct wisdom apprehends the phenomenon as it truly is.
When false wisdom and false discrimination no longer apprehend objects as they truly are—
preceded by the authentic teaching and proper mental attention—
correct knowledge arises with respect to the objects of cognition.
Because false teachings and improper mental attention serve as the precursors,
distorted cognition arises with respect to the objects of knowledge;
it is not the case that the arising of correct cognition destroys the objects of knowledge.
However, regarding this object, one abandons false attachments and gives rise to right knowledge;
it is like a form in the darkness:
when a bright lamp appears, it does not destroy that form.
It can only illuminate and discern;
one should know that this principle is likewise so.
Furthermore, because the formations associated with pleasant feeling are conjoined with the characteristic of impermanence.
When one reaches the state of suffering (*duḥkha*), it is then called affliction and oppression;
when one reaches the state of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha*),
it is only then that it is termed the oppression of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
If it did not reach that state,
then it would necessarily and exclusively accord with pleasant feeling and never reach any other state.
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) accompanied by such factors as birth and aging are entirely suffering.
If it reaches the stage of illness,
it is called affliction, distress, and oppression;
if it reaches the stage of the suffering of birth and so forth, [it is likewise].
It is called "the oppression of suffering.
If one does not reach that state,
one is pursued by the causes of suffering, such as birth and so forth, which arise within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
