and it enables them to swiftly attain realization and entry into the Noble Teaching.
That is to say: the marks of a Great Teacher,
or the marks of the Dharma teaching,
or the marks of having already realized the supreme virtue.
His exquisite voice and renown pervade all directions throughout the ten quarters, filling them completely with vast praise;
furthermore, he is able to dispel those who propound theories of no-cause and theories of evil causes.
It encompasses all treatises that explain the correct cause.
Why is this? Because it excludes those treatises that propound the theory of no-cause and the theory of false causes.
This is not even a basis for the resolute confidence (*adhimukti*) of those wise ones who desire to go to the happy realms of humans and gods or seek liberation,
let alone for anyone else;
it is a treatise on the correct causes that one should enter.
One should know that its characteristics are the opposite of those [previously mentioned].
As for the characteristics of the Great Teacher,
they consist in the Blessed One being a true Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, and so forth, up to a World-Honored One.
The detailed explanation is as previously set forth in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.
Regarding the characteristics of the Dharma teaching:
it refers to the teaching of the True Dharma that is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
It should be understood that this is also like the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.
Regarding the realization of the first characteristic of excellence:
That is to say, one spontaneously and thoroughly penetrates all things regarding this world and other worlds,
attaining manifest and perfect enlightenment;
and so forth, as extensively explained.

In this context, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is called "this world," while the form and formless realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*) are called "other worlds," because of the distinction between the two periods of the present and the past.
One should know that this is called the second distinction.
It is termed "self-arisen" (svayambhū) because it is not derived from a teacher,
as the six kinds of supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) are attained through direct realization.
It is called "realization" because it is the most supreme among all sentient beings; thus,
it is said to be "perfect."
Because this primary nature is known naturally,
it is called "manifestation" (uddeśa) because it reveals others.
Furthermore, it is [defined] by two aspects.
The proponents of causelessness (ahetuvādin) maintain that among all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), there is no causal process; that is,
they deny both the causes and conditions for the arising of conditioned phenomena and the causes and conditions for their cessation.
Because of this lack of understanding,
those formations arise through its arising;
because of its cessation, those formations cease.
Being unable to realize these two matters,
and furthermore failing to realize the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
they give rise to such a view.
They establish this doctrine:
that which exists definitely exists;
that which does not exist definitely does not exist.
There is nothing that cannot arise,
and there is nothing that cannot cease.

Yet this proponent [of your view] slanders and opposes the coarse, superficial direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)— commonly understood by all the world— that the arising and ceasing of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) can be directly realized within these three stages.
Why is this? It is because we see directly that when men and women from various families— whether Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, or others— unite through the causes and conditions of sexual union,
they give birth to sons or daughters after eight or nine months have passed.
Once thus born, there may be some who,
at that time, reach the end of their lifespan and die prematurely;
yet there may be others who remain alive, sustained for the duration of their natural life.
Whether it be the states of painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,
all minds and mental factors are ever-new and never old.
Furthermore, there are briefly two kinds of self-praise and disparagement of others.
This refers solely to mere words and the correct practice of teaching the Dharma.
If one uses mere words to praise oneself and disparage others,
it is simply because their mind is entangled by the qualities of those who are not true spiritual beings.
This is called self-destruction;
it is not superior or virtuous.
However, if one practices right conduct by means of teaching the Dharma, [it is otherwise].
Although there is no praising or disparaging, this is in truth self-praise and disparagement of others.
Furthermore, when the Tathāgatas proclaim the True Dharma,
they are able to swiftly destroy two kinds of ignorance.
This refers to the arising of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) and so forth through hearing incorrect teachings;
it is the firm ignorance accumulated over a long period of habituation, as well as the ignorance that arises from not having practiced for a long time.
Furthermore, due to innate [ignorance], one is unable to discern the path leading to the happy realms.
Furthermore, it is because one does not understand the path leading to nirvana in the present life.
Moreover, it should be known that eleven types of characteristics collectively encompass all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), which are established as the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-kāya).
One should know that the meaning of "accumulation" (rāśi) is the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha).
Furthermore, the aggregates of clinging (upādānaskandha) are established by virtue of the predominant influence of causes and conditions that are exclusively defiled.
One should know that the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).
Furthermore, the general aggregates (*skandha*) are established by the two predominant powers of the causes and conditions for both affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*).
It should be understood that these aggregates (skandhas) encompass both the tainted (sāsrava) and the untainted (anāsrava).
Furthermore, afflictions (kleśa) arise among conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) by way of three aspects, namely:
by way of their basis (āśraya).
By way of the object of focus and by way of the accompanying factors.
Furthermore, the summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
The three types of definitive declarations regarding few desires and so forth; the non-declaration regarding the locus of doubt and delusion concerning what resembles the True Dharma;

and the declaration by the Great Teacher regarding transformation and destruction—through these three aspects, such as the three views, the fulfillment [of merit], and the ignorance of outsiders, the Tathāgata’s mind enters and dwells within few desires.
First, because at that time the work of transformation was completed,
and he desired to abide in the blissful dwelling of the present life;
second, because his disciples had become deeply weary of and disparaging toward the gateway of correct practice.
Third, for the sake of transforming and guiding those sentient beings whom he seeks to convert— who constantly delight in busywork and manifold activities—
the Tathāgata enters the celestial abode of tranquility through all causes and conditions, as previously described.
One should know that it is likewise in this case.
Furthermore, there are briefly three types of dispositions among those to be transformed who are to be disciplined:
first, the disposition of delusion and negligence.
Second, the nature of an extremely inferior mind;
third, the nature capable of practicing correct conduct.
Furthermore, by means of four aspects, with respect to four locations.
By abiding in reverence, one swiftly realizes the unsurpassed state:
first, by generating intense aspiration for that which is to be attained;
second, by generating intense affection and delight in the practice of the Dharma according to the Dharma as the means for attainment.
Third, because of generating intense love and reverence toward the Great Teacher;
fourth, because of generating intense pure faith in the Dharma he has taught.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of unsurpassedness.
That is to say: unsurpassed sublime wisdom,
unsurpassed right practice,
and unsurpassed liberation.
"Supreme sublime wisdom" refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
The wisdom of the right view of one beyond training,
which constitutes supreme right practice,
is called the path of pleasant and swift progress.
Regarding "unsurpassed liberation," this refers to the unshakable liberation of mind.
It should be understood that herein, wisdom, abandonment, and dwelling in happiness in the present life are collectively explained.
The sublime wisdom, right practice, and liberation of those in training (śaikṣa) are not called "unsurpassed," because there still remains something superior to them.
It should be known that all practices of the arhats are designated as the "path of swift and easy progress," because all heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) have been eternally extinguished.
Because all that was to be done has been accomplished;
furthermore, because one discriminates among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) based on the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*),
by means of four aspects during two periods.
One who thoroughly knows the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as it truly is realizes the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava-kṣaya) without interval at two times.
What are these two times?
The first is on the stage of ordinary beings;
the second is on the stage of vision.
In what way is this so by means of four aspects?
First, by way of intrinsic nature;
second, by way of location;
third, by way of motivation.
Fourth, by way of the fruit.

Regarding "by way of intrinsic nature," this refers to the intrinsic nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the five types of formations.
They conceive of it as "I" or "mine.
As for "because of the locus," this refers to the objective referent (*ālambana*).
Regarding "by way of origination":
this refers to craving conditioned by feeling born from contact, wherein ignorance is comprised within the grasping at views.
Furthermore, there are five stages of dependent origination:
namely, with the diversity of the elements as condition,
there arises the diversity of contact.
With the diversity of contact as condition, there arises the diversity of feeling;
with the diversity of feeling as condition,
there arises the diversity of craving.
With various kinds of craving as condition,
various kinds of grasping arise.
That which arises through conditions is necessarily impermanent in its nature.
Regarding the point "by way of the result":
it means that the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) acts as an obstacle at three times:
first, at the time of the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) that investigates the dharma of selflessness.
Second, at the time of clear realization;
third, at the time of attaining arhatship.
Among these, at one time, it is due to the predominant influence of those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
There is delusion and doubt; yet,
by virtue of the causal condition of extensively cultivating the patience that investigates the Dharma,
one is able to somewhat dispel that delusion and doubt.
However, at the time of cultivating the clear realization of the truths, due to one's underlying intention, there arises the fear that "I shall no longer exist in nirvāṇa";
this occurs through the predominant influence of the latent tendency of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
Regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), they give rise to false discrimination,
thinking, "I shall cut them off, I shall destroy them, I shall bring them to non-existence. Consequently,
they produce the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) and the view of non-existence (*vibhavadṛṣṭi*) with respect to nirvāṇa.
Due to these causes and conditions,
his mind turns back from parinirvāṇa and does not proceed toward it;
yet at another time, although he has transcended this state, he purifies his mind and further attains the direct realization of the Noble Truths.
However, as for those who think, "I am able to realize the truths and manifest the truths," they have not yet been freed from that conceit because it persists as a latent tendency (*anuśaya*).
Furthermore, from time to time, due to forgetfulness,
one perceives oneself as giving rise to conceit;
because of this, one proceeds through various manifestations of the fetter of conceit.
That is to say: "I am superior," "equal," or "inferior.
Within the first two positions, they can act as obstacles through the power of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
in the third position, they can act as obstacles through the power of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Furthermore, conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) arise and grow by way of three conditions:
first, through the power of karma and afflictions from previous lives;
second, through the power of aspiration.
Third, by the power of present causes and conditions,
because one is able to fully comprehend the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*),
one is able to immediately attain the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*) to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) within the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*).
Because one is able to fully comprehend [the truths] within the stage of seeing,
one subsequently abandons the remaining fetters and attains arhatship,
realizing the permanent exhaustion of all outflows immediately thereafter.
Furthermore, there are five aspects by which one should properly inquire and provide answers regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
What are these five? First, by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Second, because it is the root of both cyclic existence and its cessation;
third, because of cessation;
and fourth, because of cyclic existence.

Regarding "by way of their intrinsic nature": one should know that these are the five intrinsic natures of form and so forth. Regarding "by way of the means for the process of transmigration and its cessation": [this refers to the same].
Regarding the phrase "because it is the root of both saṃsāra and its cessation," this refers to the desire for wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*),
by means of which one can eventually attain the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
Therefore, this desire is called the root of returning and cessation.
If, by means of this desire, one prays: "May I obtain the status of an inferior human being," or even "May I be born among the Brahmakāyika devas and their like," [this is that root].
Because one approaches, cultivates, and practices this mind extensively,
one is born there; therefore,
this desire is called the root of saṃsāra.
Regarding the phrase "because of cessation":
it is because within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), only craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*) are to be abandoned and brought to cessation.
If these very conditioned phenomena were themselves of the nature of grasping, [they could not be ceased].
It should not be subject to cessation,
because the various formations (saṃskāra) still exist and are perceptible even in an Arhat.
If there were a nature of grasping (upādāna) distinct from these formations, [it would follow that it is imperishable].
It must be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because it is unconditioned, it is eternal and cannot be extinguished.
Therefore, the nature of grasping (*upādāna-svabhāva*) is comprised solely within one portion of the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Since this very portion has already been severed and extinguished,
and will never again manifest,
it can be brought to cessation.
Regarding the phrase "because of transmigration," there are further three kinds:
first, because it is the cause for future existence (*punarbhava*).
Second, because of the distinction between the two categories;
third, because they are present causes.
Regarding the cause for future existence:
That is to say, there is someone who aspires to perform various karmas in the future;
they form this thought:
"May I accomplish these practices in a future life."
By this cause and condition, it serves as the productive cause for the arising of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) that lead to future existence,
but it does not produce those of the present,
because it cannot produce them in the present.
The designation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) consists of only two kinds.
As for their classification by category,
there are eleven types of categories of conditioned phenomena.
This should be understood as previously explained. Regarding present causes:
these refer to the four great elements (mahābhūta) which serve as the cause for derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
Mental factors such as sensation have contact as their condition;
all consciousnesses have name-and-form as their condition.
This is the method for the process of transmigration.
That is to say, because the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) serves as the basis,
one gives rise within all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) to the conceit "I am" (asmimāna), as well as various forms of attachment and the views of "I" and "mine.
As for the means of their cessation:
This refers to being free from the conceit of "I" regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
as well as perceiving their defects and the renunciation thereof, [all] being without self or what belongs to a self (*anātman-anātmīya*).
Furthermore, as for the means of cyclic existence (*pravṛtti-upāya*):
This refers to the categories of ignorance and craving;
their characteristics should be understood according to what is appropriate.
As for the means of reversal and cessation:
This refers to their antidote.
Furthermore, for two reasons, unwise śrāvaka disciples overstep the Teacher’s instructions and fall into wrong views.
Or they may give rise to verbal expression.
What are the two conditions?
First, ignorance regarding conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The second delusion concerns the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Due to this delusion, one violates the principles of purely conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as well as the principles of purely ultimate truth.
Regarding the improper mental engagement (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) that flows through the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*):
furthermore, in three matters, only the noble ones (*ārya*), according to their inclination, are able to declare them as they truly are,
whereas ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are not.
Except for what is heard from others—
that is, among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the view of "I" and "mine" is not according to reality;
if one relies upon that, the conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*) arises.
Although that [other defilement] has already been abandoned,
this conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*) has not yet been abandoned in its entirety;
if there were no basis for its arising, [it would not exist].
The conceit of self (asmimāna) continues to manifest as before, unabated.
It should be understood that within this context there are two types of conceit:
first, the manifestation of attachment toward all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra).
Second, it manifests abruptly due to loss of mindfulness; herein,
the manifestation of the conceit of "I am" (asmimāna) is clung to,
which the Noble Ones have already abandoned and no longer manifest.
The second type of pride exists due to the presence of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
thus, although the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) has been permanently severed,
it persists because the Noble Path has not yet been well-cultivated.
They still arise as active manifestations;
however, the view of a self-identity exists only as a latent predisposition that constantly follows one, manifesting at times when mindfulness is lost.
It can serve as the basis for the conceit of "I" (asmimāna),
causing it to manifest even briefly.
For this reason, this conceit is said to be both "not yet abandoned" and "capable of manifesting."
Furthermore, when noble ones contemplate the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
even their conceit (*asmimāna*) no longer manifests; how much more so when they contemplate their common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)?
If one dwells in right mindfulness while reflecting upon and attending to conventional phenomena,
it will also prevent the manifestation of the conceit "I am."
If one attends to and contemplates conventional phenomena without abiding in right mindfulness,
at that time the conceit "I am" temporarily manifests.
Even if ordinary beings contemplate the common characteristics of all conditioned formations, [they still fall into this].
If [the afflictions] still continue to disturb the mind through the conceit of "I am," how much more so when one abides in other states?

Furthermore, within the mental continuum of a noble one (*ārya*), both the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) have already been completely abandoned.
Within the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) persist and have not yet been permanently severed.
If the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of self-conceit (*asmimāna*) and their active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) have both not yet been abandoned,
furthermore, one who conceives of a desire for a self should be known as being subsumed under the active outburst of self-conceit.
Why is this? Because due to the loss of mindfulness,
those who are swept away and submerged by the various flavors of craving regarding desire and meditative concentration [fall].
Based on this gateway of desire, the fetters of various forms of self-conceit (asmimāna) repeatedly manifest.
The statement that they are "not yet abandoned" is due to the presence of their underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
Regarding those who have not yet fully understood:
due to those entanglements,
they are at that time subject to forgetfulness.
Regarding the term "not yet extinguished":
although one may temporarily distance oneself from these fetters,
they soon manifest once again.
Regarding the phrase "before the words have been uttered":
it is because those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) have not yet been permanently uprooted.
Furthermore, there are briefly two kinds of consolation that fellow practitioners of the holy life offer to one another.
First, inquiring about the suffering of illness;
second, inquiring about well-being.
Regarding the inquiry about the suffering of illness:
If one asks them, "Is the ailment you have endured bearable?
it means asking whether their respiration is unobstructed and whether they are able to sustain themselves.
That is to say: "Is it not asked whether painful feeling does not increase?
Is it not uninterrupted?
Is it not touched by an unpleasant contact?"
Is this not contrary to reason?
Is it not a matter of oppressing the body?
Or can those who have been oppressed find release?
Regarding the inquiry after one's well-being:
it is as when someone, in accordance with the question "Are you free from illness?",
asks whether they are not afflicted by any ailment or distress.
"Are you free from affliction? means:
"Are you not being oppressed or assailed by external calamities or misfortunes?
"Is your daily life light and comfortable? means: [the same].
"I ask whether you have slept peacefully during the night,
whether the food and drink you have consumed is easy to digest,
and whether you are free from any distress."
This question asks whether one dwells in blameless contact.
Such various types of expressions are explained in the *Śrāvakabhūmi* within the section on knowing the proper measure regarding food and drink.
It should be understood that this question pertains to four stages:
first, the stage of internal affliction;
second, the stage of external affliction.
Third, abiding during the night;
fourth, abiding during the day.
Furthermore, if it is said that all Arhats, within the present life...
Regarding food, one does not know as it truly is whether the aggregates, elements,
and sense bases are favorable or unfavorable; thus,
it is said that the Arhat is not favorable [to them].
Non-conformity is irrational and false conceptualization;
it is not non-conformity for an Arhat in the present life. Why is this so?
Because those [objects] such as food, the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu),
and bases (āyatana) are directly perceptible, for this reason, the Arhats...
After its cessation,
one does not follow conditioned formations and lacks attachment through non-comprehension;
therefore, the Blessed One said:
That "an arhat is one who does not conform" is certainly an intentional terminology (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*).
One should know that this is a view resembling the true Dharma.
Conditioned by the power of these two types of meanings,
fellow practitioners of the holy life or great śrāvakas desire to eliminate such views that arise resembling the true Dharma.
Exert yourself to the utmost so that such a person does not disclose it themselves or reveal it to others;
by reason of this, they will fall into the most wretched destinies.
Or, out of love and reverence for the holy teaching of the Tathāgata,
one should not allow such views that resemble the true Dharma to cause the Buddha’s holy teaching to perish quickly.
Furthermore, there are two other causes.
There are two factors that give rise to such views that resemble the true Dharma:
first, the failure to permanently eradicate the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) within;
second, relying on this to falsely conceive of a "person" (*pudgala*) who undergoes the process of transmigration and its cessation.
In order to sever these two kinds of causes,
two correct dharmas are taught as their antidotes; that is,
impermanence and selflessness are proclaimed in succession with respect to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
When one investigates for a person who undergoes the process of saṃsāra and its cessation within these four propositions,
such a person is entirely unfindable;
that is, with respect to the conditioned.
Or, based on the unconditioned,
I designate the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddha, the World-Honored One, as "Tathāgata.
It should be understood that this "self" is established in two ways as a conventional designation.
The conditioned is provisionally established within the state with remainder;
the unconditioned is provisionally established within the state without remainder.
However, from the perspective of ultimate truth, it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
It is neither unconditioned nor conditioned.
Because of the teaching of such a true Dharma,
when awakening arises through these six aspects, [it occurs].
It should be understood that one must permanently sever views resembling the true Dharma;
that is to say, an Arhat awakens to impermanence because all phenomena included within the basis [of existence] are subject to disintegration.
In this present life, because it serves as a vessel for various sufferings such as old age and illness,
one awakens to it as suffering;
yet, it ceases spontaneously.
The realm of abandonment,
the realm of detachment,
and the realm of cessation.
Awakening is cessation, tranquility,
coolness,
and final passing away.
If one possesses such right awakening, one is an Arhat;
even the deluded conceptualization associated with overweening pride cannot exist.
How much more so, after his parinirvāṇa, regarding such conceptual proliferation and attachment—whether favorable or unfavorable—to it;
one should know that there are two faults in not having abandoned the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
First, regarding those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that are harmful and associated with suffering,
one clings to them as "I" and "mine.
By reason of this, one is able to bring about the great suffering of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Second, it can obstruct the life-faculty of unsurpassed noble wisdom in the present life.
It is, for example, like a person who knows they lack the power to harm an enemy and thus fears being harmed by them.
When one first associates with another and serves them with agreeable things,
that enemy, knowing they have become close, then takes their life.
Foolish worldlings are just like this.
Fearing that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which is like an enemy, will bring about suffering and harm,
they instead give rise to the bonds of craving and manifest their service through agreeable conduct.
Such is the nature of these deluded worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which is capable of causing harm,
they see only its virtues and do not perceive its faults;
thus, they approach it with earnest devotion.
Once they have become attached,
because they have not yet attained the state beyond falling back,
it is said that they damage the life-faculty of noble wisdom.
In the Vinaya, there are two types of delusion regarding doubt concerning the locus [of existence]. What are these two?
They are the Blessed Buddha’s censure of the view of existence and the view of non-existence.
And after his disciples have passed away,
he records one as having attained birth and another as having attained non-birth.
Furthermore, it is said that the supreme, eternally abiding self is not to be found either in the present life or in the future.
Yet, there are three teachers in the world who claim it can be found in the present:
first, the proponents of eternalism (*śāśvatavādin*).
Second, the proponents of the doctrine of annihilation;
third, the Tathāgatas.
There are two causes for this doubt and delusion.
It should be understood that, as previously stated, the two kinds of teachings on the views resembling the true Dharma are able to sever these causes;
furthermore, this occurs through the two causal conditions as explained before.
This very nature of phenomena (dharmatā) which is selflessness is difficult for those non-Buddhists (tīrthika) to enter and difficult for them to realize,
because this intrinsic nature is difficult to comprehend.
Although these characteristics are easy to discern,
because those characteristics do not correspond [to reality],
one should know that herein there is no sense of deception and no sense of what is personally realized.
Because it is an uncommon meaning,
its intrinsic nature is difficult to penetrate;
this very essence of intrinsic nature is profoundly deep and appears as if it were profound.
Therefore, it is said that its meaning is non-deceptive.
Furthermore, this intrinsic nature is difficult to perceive within oneself and is also difficult to discern through the sounds of others' speech.
Therefore, it is called the meaning realized by oneself.
Furthermore, this intrinsic nature is not that which is sought after by those who engage in discursive thought,
nor is it the objective domain traversed by those who employ logical measurement.
Therefore, it is called the "unshared meaning.
Furthermore, because this very dharma is subtle, profound, and realized within by the wise and intelligent,
it is said to be "difficult to comprehend."
These distinctions should be understood as previously explained in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*:
the knowledge of the meaning of all that is taught by the Tathāgatas is characterized by two aspects.
All should understand this.
What are the two?
First is the wisdom of the teaching.
The second is realized knowledge (*adhigama-jñāna*).

Knowledge based on instruction (*āgama-jñāna*) refers to the wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-maya*, *cintā-maya*, and *bhāvanā-maya* prajñā) belonging to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding "realized wisdom":
this refers to the wisdom of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), as well as all subsequent worldly wisdoms derived therefrom.
Among these, ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) are not able to fully comprehend all the meanings taught by the Buddha.
Nor does one discern pride as pride within that conceit,
nor has it yet been abandoned. Furthermore,
those in training do not lack full comprehension regarding all objects within the view of self.
Furthermore, one may be able to discern pride as pride,
yet fail to abandon it;
whereas those who have attained the state beyond training (aśaikṣa) are capable of accomplishing everything.
And regarding the ultimate truth,
one knows them both as they truly are;
yet, when correctly contemplating those two types of principles, one should not provide a definitive declaration.
Because making a definitive declaration would lead to what is meaningless,
one neither declares nor clings to it—
namely, whether [the Tathāgata] exists after death.
If it does not exist;
if it both exists and does not exist;
if it neither exists nor does not exist.
If the Tathāgata does not provide a prediction based on such wisdom and vision,
one should understand that this reveals his own nature of ignorance, which is accompanied by false views.
Furthermore, it should be understood that there are, in brief, two kinds of transformation and decay.
The first is the transformation and decay of senescence regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
that is to say, for example, there is one who is one hundred and twenty years old, whose physical form has become decrepit.
For these reasons, it is called the aging and illness of the body.
Second, there is the deterioration and transformation of mental anxiety;
for these reasons, it is called the aging and illness of the mind.
First is transformation through decay;
therein both the foolish and the wise do not obtain what they desire.
Second is transformation through destruction.
Among these, the wise can act according to their wishes,
whereas the foolish cannot. Furthermore, when the bodies of foolish commoners grow old or fall ill, [they are unable to do so].
One should know that the mind invariably follows old age and sickness;
however, the wise person,
though their body may be aged and sick, remains master of their own mind and does not follow after old age and sickness.
This is called the distinction between the foolish and the wise herein.
Furthermore, one who properly grasps the Dharma does so through hearing and reflection;
one who reflects well does so through the wisdom of cultivation.
"Thoroughly manifesting" refers to the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāva*);
"thoroughly penetrating" refers to the nature of things in their full extent (*yāvadbhāva*).
These are by way of two aspects.
The noble disciples are able to correctly question the Great Teacher, who provides excellent explanations;
that is, regarding the discourse on the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of all grasping.
What are these two?
First, the discourse on the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of these various graspings;
second, the discourse for the sake of the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of these various graspings.
It should be understood that herein lies the discourse on the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Regarding what is called the Tathāgata:
furthermore, if these various graspings have not been abandoned and one contemplates them,
there are three kinds of defects associated with them.
If one has already abandoned and extinguished [the defilements] while observing them accordingly, there are three kinds of merit:
first, regarding the various forms of grasping that arise amidst all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
If, upon change and decay, sorrow and so forth arise,
one should know that this is called the first affliction;
it is the result produced by the change and decay of conditioned phenomena already acquired.
Second, the various forms of grasping that arise regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*):
when seeking those agreeable conditioned phenomena that have not yet been obtained,
in order to acquire them.
One extensively practices various, manifold, and diverse types of unwholesome deeds;
because one pursues and acts unwholesomely for this reason,
one dwells in four kinds of suffering.
First, that which arises from what is currently present and proximate;
second, that which arises from what is directly manifest and present;
third, that which arises through the predominance of external compulsion.
Fourth, that which arises through the predominance of one's own defilements—
this should be known as the second fault.
Third, it is precisely due to such evil and unwholesome dharmas that craving serves as the cause for habitual practice.
After the dissolution of the body at death, one goes to the various evil destinies;
this should be known as the third disadvantage.
Contrary to this, one should understand the three kinds of meritorious benefits resulting from the contemplation of the abandonment of all grasping.
It should be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, it should be known that, in brief, there are three kinds of noble ones who, through the perfection of three types of vision, are able to transcend the three kinds of suffering.
What are these three kinds of noble ones?
First, being endowed with right view:
this refers to one who, regarding the non-erroneous dharma of selflessness, abides in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Second, having already seen the noble truths.
He has already been able to enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth;
he has already entered into clear realization;
he has already attained the fruit.
Those who dwell in the stage of training (śaikṣa) have already attained the final, ultimate, and foremost fruit of arhatship;
those who dwell in the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa).
What is meant by the perfection of the three views?
First, the perfection of the view—both outflow-free and with-outflows—that accords with that of the initial noble ones.
Second, the perfection of the not-yet-fully-purified outflow-free view.
The three are: purity, the absence of outflows (*anāsrava*), and the perfection of vision.
These three perfections are taught in reference to three types of persons (*pudgala*);
they should be understood according to their sequence as previously explained.
What is meant by "transcending the three kinds of suffering"?
It refers to the first [stage], the perfection of vision,
which is able to transcend the manifold sufferings arising from the conflicting views of a self held by non-Buddhists.
The second vision is perfected;
one is able to transcend all the sufferings of the evil realms.
The third vision is perfected.
One is able to transcend all the sufferings of future existence.
In this context, what are called "the various sufferings arising from the conflicting views of a self held by outsiders"?
This refers to those outside of this True Dharma and Vinaya.
All the various and diverse paths in the world that take the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their root, and all the resulting inverted views and tendencies—
all these collectively are termed the "view of self" (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
This refers to all views associated with the doctrine of a self held by proponents of a self,
or those who maintain that everything is eternal,
or those who maintain that some things are eternal.
Some are proponents of the theory of no cause;
some are proponents of the theory of the finite or the infinite;
some are proponents of the theory of annihilationism.
Or there are those who propound the doctrine of nirvāṇa in this very life, along with all the views associated with that doctrine;
or there are those who propound the doctrine of sentient beings, along with all the views associated with that doctrine.
This refers to all wrong views that deny the existence of beings born by transformation,
slander the next world,
or consist of any doctrinal positions associated with the theories of those who propound a [fixed] life-span.
This refers to those who propound a life-principle (*jīva-vādin*), asserting that the life-principle is either identical to or distinct from the body;
or those who propound auspiciousness (*maṅgala-vādin*), including all such views associated with their treatises,
namely various heterodox doctrines such as astrology, calendrical calculations, and divination.
They falsely imagine that reciting mantras, performing fire sacrifices, and so forth, can obtain desired objects, produce auspiciousness, and sever what is meaningless;
furthermore, they calculate that observing signs constitutes auspiciousness or inauspiciousness.
What, then, are they? They refer to the sixty-two types of erroneous views concerning the past and the future,
which arise based upon the twentyfold view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, they give rise to general denials of all wrong views.
How do these disputes produce manifold sufferings?
It is said that they mutually hold conflicting views and desires.
They engage in mutual disputes,
giving rise to various mental afflictions, distress,
and the suffering of deeply cherished attachments.
The suffering of mutual superiority and inferiority;
the suffering of stubborn attachment.
It should be known that herein, if one is defeated by another, sorrow and affliction arise.
This is called the first suffering.
If one excels others, one then employs skillful means to cause one's own faction to become even more flourishing.
They cause the views of others to gradually become obscured and dim,
while their own view of self remains pure and is not seen by others;
they cling to false views and give rise to deep attachment and concealment.
Due to these causes and conditions, various forms of improper discursive thought arise,
and various states of mental unrest are produced,
which afflict and harm the mind.
This is called the second suffering.
Due to the predominant power of cherishing and concealing false views,
one measures others by means of oneself.
To consider oneself superior, equal, or inferior,
and thereby, out of self-exaltation, to look down upon others—
this is called the third mutual suffering of superiority and inferiority.
Relying upon this, they pursue gain and offerings;
thus, they are touched by suffering in their pursuit.
Whatever they do results only in affliction and agitation.
To refute the arguments of others and to defend one's own treatise against their challenges—
this is called the fourth form of suffering: stubborn attachment.
These four kinds are called the manifold sufferings arising from disputes based on conflicting views.
It should be understood that ordinary beings within this Dharma who abide in a superior resolve regarding selflessness have already severed such sufferings.
Why is this? Because in the future, by virtue of their resolute intention (*āśaya*),
they will be capable of dispelling such erroneous views.

Therefore, if one abides in the perfection of the initial vision, one can transcend the initial suffering; furthermore, by relying upon this very perfection of the initial vision, one draws near to its cultivation and practices it extensively.
With respect to internal formations, one generates dharma-knowledge;
with respect to the unmanifest, one generates subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
These are collectively subsumed as a single aggregate.
One enters into clear realization by means of knowledge that does not take others as its object;
that is, by way of the aspect of impermanence,
or by following any other single aspect.
At that time, he is able to realize the second perfection of vision accordingly,
and is able to transcend the second suffering.
Having established himself therein, he...
By closely approaching, cultivating, and practicing extensively those factors of enlightenment previously attained,
one is able to sever the four kinds of afflictions, such as karma and so forth, as previously described.
One is able to subsequently realize the perfection of vision and transcend the suffering of future existence;
this refers to the first type of person.
There remain two types of suffering,
as well as the remaining suffering of the present physical basis;
this concerns the second type of person (*pudgala*).
Only the suffering of the remaining [afflictions] and the suffering based on the body remain;
as for the third type of person,
all suffering is severed.
It exists for a brief moment based on bodily suffering,
like a magical illusion;
furthermore, twenty propositions are established based on the conceptual view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
It does not depend on that which is co-emergent.
Furthermore, internal phenomena do not possess such activity;
rather, they depend on the meditative concentration of the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
That is to say: "The earth is the self;
the self is the earth," and so forth, as explained at length.
All this should be known.
Furthermore, there are briefly five kinds of characteristics of foolishness among the various non-Buddhist practitioners.
On account of those characteristics, they fall into the category of fools;
that is to say, even those among the non-Buddhists who are by nature intelligent do not escape harboring pride in their intelligence.
How much more so for those who lack wisdom;
this is called the primary characteristic of a fool.
Furthermore, many non-Buddhists, driven by greed for gain and honor, praise themselves and disparage others.
This is called the second characteristic of a fool.
Furthermore, when various non-Buddhists or even noble ones explain the true Dharma, the true teaching, and the true admonition to them,
they immediately oppose, revile, and disparage it.
This is called the third characteristic of a fool.
Furthermore, various non-Buddhists delight in proclaiming their own discourses that resemble the true Dharma,
or they reveal them to others.
This is called the fourth characteristic of a fool.
Furthermore, although various non-Buddhists have been subdued by the Tathāgata and his disciples,
they also recognize that the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata are truly well-expounded.
Knowing that their own doctrine is false and evil teaching,
they nevertheless do not believe or accept it at all due to the overwhelming power of their own conceit.
Furthermore, failing to collect and examine causes and conditions is called the fifth characteristic of a fool.
Moreover, the Tathāgata is endowed with six factors.
He was named the Lion King of the Master of Uninterrupted Debate.
What are the six? They are as follows:
first, he went to the place where the opponents who were non-Buddhist debaters resided.
He even permitted them to inquire freely about all matters;
whatever discourse he initiated was not for the sake of contention,
except out of compassion for all sentient beings.
He causes those who have not yet developed faith to do so,
and he causes those who already possess faith to increase it twofold.
Furthermore, when engaging in debate:
His faculties are tranquil and his physical form remains unchanging;
furthermore, he is not pursued by the habitual tendencies of fear,
nor is he ever overcome by the world of gods or humans.
An unrivaled debater in all the world,
he is able to overcome opponents with a single turn of argument; even when only a single turn is employed,
he is capable of subduing them all.
Furthermore, when those in the world who are most wise and most fearless engage in debate with the Tathāgata, [they are unable to do so].
All their eloquence becomes faltering and stammering;
they are overwhelmed by intense fear that oppresses both body and mind;
and all their deceptive arts and false discourses [cease].
None were able to do so.
Furthermore, among the entire assembly seated together in that same gathering,
everyone conceived a mind of superiority toward the Buddha.
Regarding those non-Buddhist adversaries who harbor thoughts of defeat, the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, possesses speech of majestic authority,
whereas the speech uttered by those adversaries lacks such majesty.
There are two kinds of doctrines. What are the two?
First, the doctrine of a self (ātmavāda).
Regarding the two views on non-self:
the doctrine of non-self is powerful,
while the doctrine of self is powerless.
Proponents of the theory of self are constantly overcome by proponents of non-self,
except when the proponents [of non-self] are weak in strength.
What, then, is meant by "proponents of the theory of self"?
That is to say, there is someone who gives rise to such a view and establishes such a doctrine.
One establishes a self in relation to the formations such as form, thinking:
"I have formations; formations are mine."
Within the formations (*saṃskāra*), I do not flow nor disperse;
I pervade every limb and joint, reaching nowhere unattained.
Therefore, the nature of the self (*ātman*) is identical to that of form (*rūpa*) and all other formations.
Based upon the field of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one generates merit and demerit;
from this, one experiences desirable and undesirable fruits.
It is, for example, like a farmer who, relying on fertile soil, engages in agricultural work and the planting of medicinal herbs and groves.
This is called the doctrine of self.
What is meant by the proponent of non-self?
It is said that there are two kinds.
First, the refutation of the theory of self;
second, the establishment of non-self.
Regarding the refutation of the theory of self:
If one were to conceive of a real self that possesses agency and attains sovereignty over the various karmic results— whether pleasant or unpleasant—
that self would always delight in pleasure and loathe suffering.
Therefore, I should produce only merit and not demerit.
Furthermore, when my activities are constantly present within the internal and external formations,
if they undergo transformation—
One should not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, or grief.
Furthermore, I am eternal, and whatever arises is preceded by awakening.
It should always follow along without change,
yet it cannot be apprehended;
this is called the refutation of the doctrine of a self.
Regarding the establishment of selflessness:
all conditioned phenomena arise from a multitude of causes and conditions;
if they encounter the conditions for merit, merit then arises.
Conversely, non-merit arises;
conditioned by this, one can bring about all desirable and undesirable fruits.
Because they depend upon various conditions, all are impermanent.
It is only with respect to the流转 (pravṛtti) of these conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), which are subsumed within such cause and effect,
that "self" and so forth are conventionally designated; however,
from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha), [they do not exist].
All phenomena are devoid of self;
this is what is called establishing the doctrine of non-self.
Furthermore, by means of five aspects:
There are two distinctions: those of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and those of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).
The wisdom accomplished by all non-learners is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*);
the wisdom accomplished by all learners is called "surpassable" (*sottara*).
Just as wisdom is unsurpassed,
one should know that correct practice and liberation are likewise unsurpassed.
Furthermore, those who are beyond training (aśaikṣas) perceive the Buddha’s Dharma-body with the noble eye of wisdom, which is thoroughly pure and wholesome.
The learners are not so.
Furthermore, all those beyond training serve the Tathāgata with wholesome, perfected, and non-perverted conduct;
the learners are not so.
These are called the five characteristics.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 88;
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 89.
The *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī* within the *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, by Imperial Decree;

Part Two, Section One: The Compendium of the Analysis of the Bases of the Sūtras (*Sūtravastu-viniścaya-saṃgraha*). Thus has been explained the compendium of the analysis of practice (*caryā-viniścaya-saṃgraha*).
I shall now explain the "Compendium of Selections Regarding the Bases.
The summary verse states:
First, the establishment [of the bases], equal wisdom, and so forth; finally, one should know [the sections on] detachment and so forth.
Another summary verse says:
One should know that the establishment [of the categories], their distinctions, the instruction for the ignorant and the non-ignorant,
liberation, the afflictions, and karma are all explained in detail.
One should understand that the distinctions among the various feelings are established by way of five aspects;
first, by way of their intrinsic nature.
Second, by way of their basis;
third, by way of their object;
fourth, by way of their associates.
Regarding "by way of concomitance" and "by way of intrinsic nature":
this refers to the existence of the three feelings.
First, suffering;
second, pleasure;
third, neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Regarding the basis,
there are six kinds: namely, the eye,
ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Regarding "by way of the object":
this refers to the six objective spheres, such as visible form and so forth.
Regarding "by way of the companions": [this refers to...].
This refers to perception, volition, or other mental factors— whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—
that are associated with it and function in accordance with it.
This means that because the mind associated with this [feeling] relies upon it,
the three types of sensation (vedanā) arise in accordance with it;
it serves as the basis for those sensations to arise and perish simultaneously.
Regarding the establishment of the characteristics of all feelings,
one should know that there are further eight types of distinctions.
The first is the distinction of the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).
Second, the differentiation of the external bases;
third, the differentiation of the six groups of consciousness;
fourth, the differentiation of the six groups of contact.
5. The distinction of the six classes of bodies of feeling;
6. The distinction of the six classes of bodies of perception;
7. The distinction of the six classes of bodies of volition.
86. The distinctions regarding attachment to the body (*kāyaprema*).
It should be understood that herein, the first three distinctions are established by way of the meaning of the conjunction of the three;
the fourth distinction is established by way of the meaning of the causal condition for sensation (*vedanā*).
The fifth distinction is established based on the meaning of contact as the fruit arising from the conjunction of the three.
The sixth distinction is established based on the meaning of feeling as it follows conventional expression. Why is this so?
When experiencing various feelings, one forms this perception:
"I am now experiencing this suffering, this pleasure,
or this neither-suffering-nor-pleasure," and likewise gives rise to corresponding verbal expressions for others.
One should understand that the seventh and eighth types of distinctions are established by way of the two meanings of defilement:
karma and afflictions. Why is this so?
Due to that feeling, whether through association or dissociation, volitional formations arise;
in whatever manner those volitional formations are initiated,
in that very same manner do craving and longing arise.
Briefly, there are two kinds of "all":
first, partial all; second, total all.

Regarding the statement that "all are impermanent," one should know that this refers to a limited sense of "all," for it applies only to all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and not to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Regarding the statement that all phenomena are selfless,
one should know that this refers to every single thing.
Furthermore, one should understand that there is delusion by means of three characteristics.
First, by way of intrinsic nature;
second, by way of causes and conditions;
third, by way of results.
Regarding "due to the nature of folly":
this means that due to the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), there is forgetfulness in the present life;
and due to the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), there is the state of being subject to forgetfulness in the future.
Regarding "due to the cause of folly":
this refers to being unable to realize impermanence and so forth within the established presentation of the five aspects of sensation.
Furthermore, because one does not comprehend all the afflictions occurring throughout the initial, middle, and final stages of the entire continuum of the self,
it should be understood that this constitutes a failure to awaken to the dharmatā of birth, aging, sickness, and death.
The initial affliction refers to that which arises from birth;
the intermediate affliction refers to...
This means that due to illness,
there is subsequent affliction;
and due to the two factors of aging and death, there is subsequent affliction.
Regarding "because it is the fruit of delusion":
this refers to the afflictions such as sorrow and the like, and craving and the like;
one knows that [the mind] is not deluded.
1. By way of intrinsic nature;
2. by way of resistance;
3. by way of obstruction.
Non-delusion regarding intrinsic nature refers to being well-able to discern the specific and general characteristics within the fivefold establishment of the apprehended.
By means of this, one is able to sever all afflictions,
realize the Noble Truths,
and attain Nirvana.
Regarding "not being obstructed by delusion":
this is due to the four kinds of māras;
specifically, it refers to the sense that the *skandha-māra* follows one everywhere in all circumstances.
Because that celestial Māra can repeatedly obstruct the meaning of sustaining [the path] from time to time;
and because the affliction-māra serves as the vessel for the manifold sufferings produced by death and birth.
The obscuration of non-delusion refers to the afflictions that take as their object an imperceptible realm,
as well as the envelopments that take as their object a realm that is not imperceptible.
Alternatively, those latent tendencies [are addressed].
Furthermore, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
and the noble disciples of the Buddhas are able to provide correct instruction to the assembly of disciples by means of three aspects.
What are the three?
First, the instruction of guidance;
second, the instruction of settling [the mind] upon the object of focus as appropriate.
Third, the instruction for causing those to be transformed to attain their own welfare.
It should be understood that these instructions, in their respective order,
are precisely the three types of miraculous transformations (*prātihārya*).
Furthermore, one should seek the sublime wisdom that accomplishes liberation through two types of application:
first, wisdom that has long been continuous through hearing and reflection in accordance with reality (*yoniśo-śruta-cintā*); and second, [wisdom arising from] cultivation.
The first is the wisdom of those in training (*śaikṣa*) that has been continuously transmitted over a long period, which is able to accomplish the liberation of one in training.
The second is [the wisdom] that is able to accomplish the liberation of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, there are briefly two kinds of accomplishment of liberation:
first, that of the learner (śaikṣa);
second, that of the non-learner (aśaikṣa).
There is that which belongs to those in training,
which is associated with the vajropama-samādhi;
and that which belongs to those beyond training.
That is what has been stated above.
Furthermore, there are five qualities by which a bhikṣu who practices mental purification accomplishes much.
What are these five?
First, the correct instruction;
second, the factors of śamatha;
third, the factors of vipaśyanā.
Fourth, the application of uninterrupted and earnest effort;
fifth, supramundane wisdom.
These constitute the correct instructions.
That is to say, there are three kinds of true friends who manifest this:
first, the Great Teacher;
second, the preceptor and teacher.
Third, fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*) and wise laypersons who abide in the internal Dharma;
these are called the three kinds of true friends.
Any person of wisdom should seek from them the accumulation of the gates of goodness and the authentic instructions of the true teaching.
Regarding the factors of śamatha:
it refers to someone who dwells endowed with ethical discipline (śīla).
The detailed explanation should be understood as it is in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
Having thus dwelt in the full possession of ethical discipline (*śīla*),
one is then free from remorse.
Because there is no regret, there is joy;
explained at length, up to: because there is pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated.
As for the factors of vipaśyanā:
This refers to attaining three kinds of instructions according to one's inclination:
first, the noble and correct instruction;
second, the instruction on revulsion and detachment.
Third, one commands the mind to leave behind the hindrances and incline toward the teachings of the Noble Ones.
What are the teachings of the Noble Ones?
They refer to all the teachings based upon the five aggregates of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
That is to say, it proclaims that the noble ones have accomplished such morality,
such concentration,
and such wisdom.
Such is liberation; such is the knowledge and vision of liberation.
What is meant by "weariness with and detachment from verbal instruction"?
This refers to the instruction for increasing fewness of desires and contentment based on three types [of factors],
and the instruction for departing from clamor based on delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation.
What is the instruction for causing the mind to depart from hindrances and incline toward the object of affection?
It should be known that this teaching further consists of three gates:
first, the teaching on the departure from all afflictive hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and the inclination toward love;
second, the teaching on the departure from the five hindrances and the inclination toward love.
Third is the instruction on the departure from the veil of ignorance toward the state free from veils through craving.
One should know that, among these, the discourse concerning the attainment of the realm of abandonment, separation,
and cessation constitutes the first instruction.
One should know that the discourse concerning the superior qualities seen in those very [states],
as well as the deep perception of faults and disadvantages regarding the formations within the spheres of the opposing hindrances,
is called the second instruction.
One should know that discourse which accords with such dependent origination through conditions is called the third teaching.
These are the three kinds of teachings.
These are collectively termed the branches of vipaśyanā.
Furthermore, these instructions, when stated briefly, are of three kinds:
first, the instructions that give rise to aspiration.
Second, the instruction that correctly establishes the provisions;
third, the instruction that correctly establishes mental attention (*manasikāra*).
That is to say, the noble and correct instruction is called the instruction that generates the desire for practice (*chanda*).
The instruction on weariness and detachment is called the instruction on the provisions for correct settling;
the instruction that causes the mind to leave behind hindrances and incline toward the sublime is called the instruction on correct settling through mental attention.
The wisdom embraced by this superior śamatha, based on these verbal instructions,
is called vipaśyanā; therefore,
these verbal instructions are taught.
This is called the limb of vipaśyanā.
What is uninterrupted and earnest application?
It refers to that which is performed constantly.
Fully understanding what has been done and abiding in diligent vigor,
one should know that this is precisely the application of meditative insight (*vipaśyanā*) based upon calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Furthermore, one should know that diligent application of effort (vīrya) is of five kinds:
first, the diligence of donning the armor (saṃnāha-vīrya);
second, the diligence of application (prayoga-vīrya).
Third, diligence that does not regress;
fourth, unshakable diligence;
fifth, diligence that is never content with mere partial achievement.
In this regard, one should first understand that one must give rise to an intense aspiration.
Next, in accordance with that aspiration, one must give rise to firm and courageous skillful means.
Finally, for the sake of realizing the various dharmas one has received.
One does not disparage oneself nor feel cowardice;

This is called the fourth type of person (pudgala).

It should be understood that herein,
the first and second bases of resolute belief are the supports for beginners.

one is well able to penetrate such an intention and correctly explain it;
second, the Tathāgata extensively proclaims the holy teaching through immeasurable doors.
He provides various detailed explanations for immeasurable types of individuals;
regarding this teaching of the Dharma, he is able to provide correct predictions without contradicting the nature of reality (dharmatā).
Furthermore, there are two aspects by which newly ordained bhikṣus come to feel deep affection for the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya of the Buddha.
One should correctly understand this:
first, because there is no alteration in the characteristics of the body;
second, because there is no alteration in the characteristics of the mind.
That is to say, because his physical form is of supreme radiance and purity;
because his countenance is serene and exceedingly bright and clean;
and because his body is full and robust, not emaciated or impaired.
Because the sense faculties are pliant and tranquil;
because the body undergoes no transformation as one gives rise to contentment with whatever is obtained;
and because one remains far removed from the greedy enjoyment of accumulating material resources.
Because he has no attachment or longing for his household,
his mind remains unchanging.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of remedies for sensual desire.
It can cause lustful greed that has not yet arisen not to arise, and cause that which has already arisen to be severed immediately.
The first is: contemplating the thought that one should not engage in sexual conduct.
Second, contemplating the perception of extreme impurity;
third, closely guarding all the sense-faculties.
Regarding this, "closely guarding all the sense-faculties" means:
The brief and detailed accounts should be understood as in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*.
That is to say, one who is able to closely guard the doors of the sense faculties does not allow women to touch his body.
He is called "one who well protects the body" because he does not look at, listen to, or dwell upon women.
He is called "one who well guards the sense faculties."
Whether seeing, hearing, or recollecting [these objects],
one is immediately able to maintain right mindfulness for a long duration,
because of having deeply perceived the faults with sharp wisdom.
He is named "Well-Established in Mindfulness.
By means of this, he well guards his body and well protects his sense faculties.
Abiding well in right mindfulness,
one is then able to contemplate the notion of what should not be practiced; by this means,
the afflictions cannot obscure the mind to cause it to momentarily relish [sensual] flavors.
Furthermore, one is able to contemplate the perception of extreme impurity;
by means of this, afflictions cannot obscure the mind, causing it to quickly turn back.

Section Eight: The Second Summary Verse (Uddāna) provides a detailed explanation of the twelve sections beginning with "Exclusively Objectifying" (*kevalālambana*). Furthermore, the summary verse says:
Relying solely on the aspiration for investigation,
one enters the noble teaching through the discipline of all aspects; having fully prepared the excellent provisions,
one abandons the objects of attachment regarding what has been studied, and follows the flow toward the non-virtuous meaning.
The Bodhisattva surpasses other vehicles;
this is established by the treatise as being ultimately due to the sensations induced by previously performed karma, afflictions, and the continuity of one's own seeds.
It merely serves as a condition for the arising of those six bases of contact,
just as the various karmas of grasping and feeling are induced by the functional effort initiated by the mind.
The hand can only act as a contributing condition for grasping;
one should know that the principle here is likewise the same.
This refers to the bedding and requisites at the limit.
Dwelling in seclusion,
if there should arise within the mind any subtle and excellent objective signs that cause discursive thoughts to become agitated and disturbed.
One should know that this is the work of the faction of Māra.
In this regard, a bhikṣu should settle his mind by means of the nine mental abidings,
[thereby withdrawing it] from discursive thoughts associated with various sense objects.
Having gathered the mind and caused it to abide, so that no adventitious discursive thoughts arise again,
if through this basis and this object there is a relishing of flavor regarding that object.
According to what they have attained and according to where they abide,
they are able to distance themselves from those [objects];
at that time, regarding pleasant things, [they remain detached].
They never perform any action while relying upon thoughts of sensual desire,
nor upon thoughts of ill will or thoughts of harm.
They are also able to distance themselves from [defilements], purify their minds,
and attain nirvana in this very life.
Having attained nirvāṇa,
one never remains in contention with others;
that is to say, regarding all forms of contention within the Buddha’s noble Dharma and Vinaya.
It causes extreme ruin.
Such discursive thoughts born of ignorance are not even like those of other non-Buddhists.
In this present life, there are six bases of contact as resultant phenomena that function;
when one is afflicted by the six objects of the senses,
if there is a bhikṣu...
Seeking future existence,
he himself made a vow and practiced the holy life.
At that time, he causes the cause for his seventh and final existence to increase even further,
turning it into a source of affliction and harm,
and being able to obstruct *nirvāṇa* within the present life.
By reason of these causes and conditions, one will obtain leisure in the future;
because it is not yet determined that this will be fulfilled,
there is subsequently the aspiration for existence.
One should know that among those subtle fetters,
this is the most extremely subtle. Why is that?
Just as there is a prison within the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa gods,
wherein gods or asuras are confined and bound,
yet by the very nature of things, they are temporarily released; so it is here.
They dwell sporting with the exquisite desires of the devas until the thought of fleeing arises;
once that thought arises, they lose those exquisite desires.
He again sees himself bound by bonds;
as soon as that thought arises, he is immediately bound by subtle bonds due to the factor of time.
It is called "subtle" because it is difficult to discern, not because it is subtle in the sense of being bound.
This is due to the time of bondage.
One is able to understand for oneself that one currently possesses bonds.
If a bhikṣu’s mind aspires for future existence,
as soon as that thought arises, he is immediately bound.
Once bound, one is unable to discern that one’s own self is bound; therefore, this bondage is most extremely subtle.
It should be understood that both its temporal duration and its difficulty of recognition are likewise subtle.
Therefore, it is called "extremely subtle.
Furthermore, if bhikṣus apply themselves with diligent practice and guard their sense faculties.
One should understand restraint and non-restraint, as well as the weak,
middling, and superior forms of worldly restraint, and the restraint of those in training and those beyond training.
One should understand this.
What is restraint? It is as follows:
suppose there is someone.
Regarding all defiled minds directed toward attractive objects, he does not tolerate them,
does not accept them, does not cling to them, and does not grasp at them;
even if they should momentarily arise, he immediately abandons them.
This is called restraint (*saṃvara*). What is non-restraint?
It refers to a bhikṣu who is like a farmer.
Associating with virtuous persons, hearing the true Dharma,
and applying correct mental attention constitute the excellent field for the proper cultivation of the objects of focus.
He causes the sprouts of their roots of virtue to arise;
however, their disposition is fierce and characterized by intense greed,
and they have never practiced the powerful sense of shame and remorse that serves as the antidote to desire.
Furthermore, it has never happened that when an excellent and sublime object appears before him,
he— due to his naturally intense greed and because he has not practiced the antidotes to greed— [falls under its influence].
Because all sense of shame and dread of blame have become weak and inferior,
one gives rise to the fetter of craving,
clinging to it firmly and refusing to let go.
The mind, failing to guard itself against the fetters of greed,
runs wild; the ox of the mind, associated with improper mental attention,
enters the field of sensory objects and destroys all the sprouts of one's roots of virtue.
For these reasons,
it is called non-restraint.
Furthermore, there is another case:
One is able to quickly direct the attention and withdraw it from all objects; however,
one is not yet able to contemplate their faults and disadvantages so that they do not arise again.
This is called the mild mundane restraint (*laukika-saṃvara*).
Furthermore, there is another who is able to apply attention (*manasikāra*) swiftly.
One should restrain oneself from all sensory objects and be able to contemplate their faults so that they do not arise again.
This is called the intermediate worldly restraint.
Based upon this,
one attains the nine stages of mental abiding comprised of the four types of attention.
It should be understood as previously explained in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*;
by attaining this,
one is called an ordinary person who has become free from sensual desire.
When he previously practiced the preparatory application of meditation, he was like a farmer;
now that he has attained the higher stages, he is like a great king,
[experiencing] the various sublime sensations born from the meditative attainments (samāpatti) previously acquired.
Having correctly understood that this is the basis for great negligence,
he then causes his minister to be protected by vipaśyanā,
which is sustained by the superior śamatha arising from the preeminence of hearing the true Dharma.
He causes him to observe that the nature of the feeling produced therein is dependently originated;
because it is dependently originated, its essence is impermanent.
By means of this, he [understands].
He then attains detachment through mental attention accompanied by the characteristics of the various defects of the mental level (*manobhūmi*).
Having attained detachment,
he further contemplates that the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) differ according to their respective bases.
There are ten types of distinctions based on the differentiation of time,
and many hundreds of distinctions.
Among these, the tenfold distinction based on the difference in the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) refers to:
that with vitarka and vicāra,
and that without vitarka and with only vicāra.
Without applied thought and without sustained thought;
whether accompanied by joy or accompanied by bliss.
If it is accompanied by equanimity,
it belongs to the stage of decline or the stage of maintenance.
If one were to distinguish them by way of time,
there would be many hundreds of variations regarding the factors of progress and the factors conducive to penetration.
That is to say, one should understand that there are hundreds of further distinctions based on the principles of the specific functions performed during the phases of arising, abiding,
and ceasing, as one observes these very characteristics.
Having thus understood that the feelings produced therein are impermanent in nature and possess various distinct modes of flux,
one does so briefly by way of three characteristics.
Furthermore, one carefully contemplates that these are of an impermanent nature,
by way of their being the basis [for arising] and their being manifest activity.
Regarding the cause and the basis:
this refers to the physical body (rūpakāya) extending up to the fourth dhyāna.
Regarding the phrase "it is the basis for feeling because it is active":

this means that from the beginning up until the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*), perception and feeling are for the most part active throughout that interval.
Regarding the phrase "because of the cause":
this refers to the causes for all future experiences,
namely volition, seeking, and aspiration.
He observes that all phenomena, up to and including the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), are impermanent because they are of the nature of dependent origination.
In this manner, he correctly and thoroughly examines the stages of detachment from desire (*vairāgya-bhūmi*).
This is called the superior mundane restraint (*laukika-saṃvara*).
It should be understood that, among these, the first two types of restraint are comprised within the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna-bala*).
The latter is the power of restraint,
which is subsumed under the power of cultivation.
Having thus accomplished such a supreme and wondrous power of heedfulness, he...
Because one penetrates the principle of the Noble Truths as they truly are,
one is able to permanently sever the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self,
which serves as the precursor to all afflictions abandoned through the Path of Seeing.
Furthermore, he is able to attain the discipline of one in training (*śaikṣa-saṃvara*).

He then cultivates that very discipline of one in training and is further able to permanently sever all afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation, preceded by the false grasping of the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*).
He has ultimately realized the restraint of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-saṃvara).
Beyond this, there is no further restraint that is superior or more excellent.
Furthermore, if there are bhikṣus...
Having entered the holy teaching, if one does not guard the sense faculties,
they will then exclusively create manifold sufferings,
namely the suffering of future lives.
Or there is suffering in the present life;
it should be understood that one who does not guard the sense faculties is like a leper entering a thicket of reeds.
Just as leaves are lovely, so too do they shatter their bodies against desirable objects;
yet, failing to realize it, they embrace the subtle, concomitant sufferings of future existence.
This is what is called suffering in future lives;
it is said that by this one creates manifold sufferings.
