Furthermore, one gives rise to defilement and attachment toward these [actions], extensively committing transgressions.
Due to these causes and conditions,
although one dwells in a secluded forest hermitage (āraṇyaka),
one nevertheless experiences the suffering of discursive thoughts (vitarka) arising from present mental remorse.
Like being pricked by the thorns of *kuda* and *māla* grass,
they are unable to approach the assembly of pure seers without fear;
even if they were to force their way into the midst of the pure Saṃgha, [they would remain there].
When fellow practitioners of the holy life who possess wisdom point out his transgression,
because he harbors within him a mind of concealment,
his heart is like a lethal poison.
He gives rise to resentment toward those capable of censuring him and seeks to harm them;
furthermore, his wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life recognize his base inferiority and desire to abandon him as a śramaṇa.
Even if they avoid him from afar and do not dwell with him— whether in villages, towns, or forest hermitages—
they all join in censuring and reviling him, saying,
"This elder has thus committed such a transgression."
Thus they speak wickedly;
thus they act wickedly;
thus they dwell in the defilement of what is contrary to the Dharma.
Those who have already attained pure faith,
cause them to regress;
those who have not yet attained pure faith...
This causes faith not to arise;
therefore, that person experiences such remorse for their actions within this very life.
That which is done out of indignation;
that which is done by way of avoidance from afar;
that which is done through reviling and disparagement.
These various sufferings,
together with the aforementioned sufferings resulting from actions performed in future lives,
are collectively condensed into one.
This is called experiencing manifold suffering.
In this context, what is meant by "non-restraint"?
It refers to [the state] regarding such things in both the present life and future lives.
Possessing manifold faults and afflictions,
one engages with spheres of activity and objects of perception in an irrational manner.
They falsely grasp at various marks and secondary characteristics with perverse conceptions.
Preceded by these perverse conceptions, they give rise to discursive thoughts that accord with and correspond to those [marks] within their dwelling place.
Consequently, they are unable to perceive, as it truly is, all the aforementioned faults.
Although they have observed all such faults,
because they have not yet practiced them repeatedly and extensively,
the heaviness (*dausthulya*) belonging to the category of afflictions remains within their basis (*āśraya*).
They have not yet been eliminated;
the body has not yet attained pliancy—
referring to both form and the mental body.
Because these modes of activity cause the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to remain in conjunction,
they are able to cause one to oppose the two remedial powers of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*);
thus, they are called "non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*).
The opposite of this should be understood as the characteristic of restraint.
Furthermore, this restraint [is established] by way of three causes and conditions.
It enables one to cultivate [the path] so that it is swiftly brought to full completion.
What are these three?
They are as follows: first, within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
Having left the household life out of pure faith, once ordained,
he then employs the wisdom derived from hearing that accords with supernormal power.
Having grasped the six sense faculties that resemble those of insects and beasts,
one then employs the wisdom of attention consisting in correct reflection.
One correctly and minutely examines the faults and disadvantages.
Since the skillful means lie between the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) above and the wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) below,
they are bound in the middle.
Having bound him in the interim,
he then took up a pure sign in order to test and examine whether that person had attained mastery over supernatural powers.
They give rein to their senses amidst various objects;
because they have not yet attained mastery over those supernormal powers,
they scatter in all directions, pursuing each of their respective objects.
Yet they are unable to escape completely,
because they have not skillfully observed those faults and afflictions; consequently,
they leave those insects and beasts unsubdued.
Furthermore, having realized that his supernormal powers (ṛddhi) were no longer under his control,
he again extensively cultivated the wisdom of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā) in accordance with reality.
Causing it to reach its ultimate consummation and transcend all mental application,
he applies himself even more diligently to the cultivation of right mindfulness directed toward the body.
Because they have well cultivated right mindfulness in this regard,
those [senses] are no longer able to scatter and disperse toward various individual objects;
one should know that at that time, they are well-tamed.
They attain mastery over those [powers] through their supernormal powers.
Furthermore, there are bhikṣus who have previously cultivated and accumulated the provisions for sublime wisdom.
Furthermore, one encounters virtuous friends and fully hears of the three kinds of defects of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
namely: the defects pertaining to the present life.
Regarding the disadvantages of future lives and the disadvantages of both the present and future lives,
one should know that among these, all diseases have the mutual conflict of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as their basis.

That which is called the fault of the present life consists of the formations of the miserable realms that constantly follow one and are capable of leading one there. That which is called the fault of future lives consists of those same formations that constantly follow one and are capable of leading one to them.
First, having achieved craving for delight in the present life as a basis,
one is able to bring about old age and death in both the present life and future lives;
this is called the disadvantage of the present life and future lives.
Thus, in brief, there are three kinds of suffering:
first, the suffering of illness;
second, the suffering of the evil realms.
Third is the suffering of death.
This refers to having heard of such faults and calamities based on both the happy realms and the miserable realms.
Through diligent practice and practicing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma,
one is thereby able to enter the clear realization of the Noble Truths.
Next, by means of the perfectly pure wisdom that realizes selflessness,
one directly perceives that both the internal and external six sense bases are empty, just as entering an empty room.
At that time, through wisdom,
he thoroughly penetrates the fact that the various afflictive entangments arising from forgetfulness based upon various objects are capable of causing harm.
Furthermore, there remain residual afflictive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and craving latent tendencies;
moreover, one personally realizes that various afflictions exist within one's own mental continuum.
There are various forms of craving and attachment;
there are various forms of suffering and affliction;
and there are various forms of harm and transgression.
Having realized the nirvāṇa realm with remainder, wherein all afflictions and craving are forever stilled.
Thereafter, he further realizes the realm of parinirvāṇa without remainder.
His previously cultivated wisdom regarding the gateway of the True Dharma— resembling the branches, twigs, stems,
and leaves of grasses and trees— accumulates the Noble Path.
Taking the practice in accordance with the Dharma as one’s raft,
one diligently cultivates it upon the path of meditation,
gradually realizing the complete liberation of the mind.
Abiding in the realm of nirvana with remainder,
one attains liberation from all calamities and afflictions;
having thus abided therein, [one remains].
One should know that they have ultimately transcended all suffering and reached the other shore.
Furthermore, this is due to seven causes and conditions.
Although they have gone forth within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
they subsequently regress and abandon that which they were properly practicing and training in.
What are the seven? They are as follows:
ordinary worldlings who have not yet transcended the stage of an ordinary worldling, [perceive] the five aggregates of clinging as a mass of suffering and affliction.
They are unable to understand the five transitions as they truly are;
or else, ordinary persons are unable to contemplate the faults and dangers of the various exquisite sensual desires to a superior degree.
Furthermore, while walking and while standing,
they are constantly heedless regarding attractive objects,
grasping at all their characteristics in an improper manner.
Because they do not maintain focused mindfulness,
they constantly contemplate virtuous qualities as thorns of evil and engage in irrational discursive thoughts;
furthermore, they lack fearlessness.
If a king or others summon and coerce them for some matter,
they will comply out of fear;
furthermore, there are those who are affectionate and feel attachment toward their kinsmen.
If they are summoned by him out of affection,
they will then follow;
furthermore, regarding sense objects, they may comply with their greed.
Or they may conform to hatred or conform to delusion,
giving rise to fierce and intense entanglements of affliction.
Furthermore, within that very continuum of mind,
there is constant adherence;
moreover, it arises from the possession of inferior resolve.
They lack all vast and superior resolve regarding renunciation, seclusion, and nirvana,
because they have achieved only an inferior resolve.
The mind enters into various objects because it cannot be entirely devoid of attachment toward all things, such as one's parents.
Because they lack resolute conviction in the eightfold noble path,
their minds do not incline toward renunciation;
because they lack resolute conviction in it, their minds do not incline toward seclusion.
Because there is no resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the abandonment of the afflictions that constitute those fruits,
the mind does not enter into *nirvāṇa*. Briefly stated,
all outflows (*āsrava*) are subsumed within two categories.
First, that which is abandoned through seeing;
second, that which is abandoned through cultivation.
It should be understood that among these, it is improper mental attention [that is the cause].
And the objects of focus are called "dharmas conducive to the outflows" (*āsrava-anuloma*).
If those in training (*śaikṣa*) [encounter] the objects of focus for improper attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) which give rise to the outflows to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*):
Although they have not yet permanently severed [the outflows],
because they have correctly and thoroughly penetrated them through sublime wisdom,
it is said that their minds are tranquil regarding these phenomena conducive to the outflows.
Because there still remain the subtle and weak fetters produced through the predominance of lost mindfulness,
it is not yet called "cool" and not yet called "tranquil silence."
However, because all outflows (*āsrava*) arising from it that are to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) have been forever severed,
it is also called "cool" (*śītala*).
Because they will not arise in the future,
they are also called "silent.
Yet, those ordinary beings who possess inferior degrees of resolute conviction—
When the mind is not tranquil with respect to all phenomena conducive to the outflows,
it is not called "cool" and is not called "serene."
It should be understood that by these seven causes and conditions,
one again regresses and abandons what one is correctly practicing and training in; conversely,
by the seven causes and conditions of the white side (śuklapakṣa) which are the opposite of these, [one does not regress].
Having gone forth within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
one shall never regress or abandon that which is rightly being practiced and studied.
Furthermore, if there is a bhikṣu who relies on the four bases of attachment,
it should be known that he practices four kinds of wrong conduct.
What are called the four bases of attachment?
They are as follows: there is a bhikṣu who, because of having craving and affection for the internal and external sense bases, [becomes attached].
Being able to bring about future existence and taking no delight in nirvana within the present life—
this is the first point of attachment.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who,
regarding the external things previously abandoned— such as his parents and other concerns—
still harbors attachment that binds his mind.
This is called the second point of attachment.
Furthermore, there is another who,
in this present life, seeks all forms of gain and honor.
To be attached to and unable to relinquish the gains, offerings, and respect one has obtained—
this is called the third point of attachment.
Furthermore, there is another who is a trainee (śaikṣa) who has already seen the track of the truths,
yet still possesses residual conceit (asmimāna).
Pursued by a degree of craving and attachment,
one dwells in negligence regarding the practice of relinquishment;
this is called the fourth point of attachment.
What are called the four kinds of wrong conduct?
They are as follows: first, a person who delights in future existence does not delight in nirvāṇa in the present life.
If those in training (śaikṣa) act with negligence,
due to the predominant power of this point of attachment,
they delight in dwelling in close association with both householders and those who have gone forth.
This is called the first type of wrong conduct.
Furthermore, it concerns that very same individual who delights in future existence;
because of the predominant power of their delight in future existence, [they engage in such conduct].
To give rise to wrong aspirations while practicing the holy life—
this is called the second type of wrong practice.
Furthermore, if one still feels attachment toward external objects previously relinquished,
through the predominant power of that point of clinging,
it can cause one to regress from what is being correctly practiced and studied.
This is called the third wrong practice.
Furthermore, one seeks gain and honor in the present life;
regarding all such gain and honor that is obtained—
A person who is attached and does not relinquish [their objects] violates the precepts due to the predominant power of that basis of attachment.
To speak at length, even down to those with the voice of a conch and the gait of a dog;
they do so because of their attachment to gain and honor.
They do not relinquish what they have studied;
they do not perceive it as a transgression,
and they openly violate the precepts.
This is called the fourth wrong practice.
Furthermore, there are certain bhikṣus who,
being unskilled in the meaning, hear from others various words and phrases that have but a single meaning.
Consequently, they harbor doubt and do not give rise to joy,
wondering, "Now, among these, which is the truth? Furthermore,
there are four kinds of gateways for inverted-free contemplation that can produce subtle, pure wisdom and vision.
What are the four? They are:
being extremely diligent in the investigation of suffering;
and the sublime knowledge that accords with reality regarding the causes of the arising of sensation.
Furthermore, there is the sublime wisdom that accords with reality regarding the support and its causal basis;
the sublime wisdom that accords with reality regarding the cause of abiding;

and the sublime wisdom that accords with reality regarding the nature, the accompaniments, and the conforming modes of suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure within the conditions of dependence.
Furthermore, for two reasons,
the Tathāgata eliminates the doubts of those individuals who are unskilled regarding the meaning:
first, by demonstrating that various expressions and phrases signify a single meaning.
The phrasing differs,
but the meaning does not differ;
by this, one is able to eliminate doubt.
Second is the revelation of the extensive meaning of the sublime teachings (*āryadeśanā*).
By means of this, one is able to achieve thorough penetration into that meaning.
What is meant by the "extensive meaning of the sublime teachings"?
That is to say, from the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-bhūmi*) up to the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*),
all are designated as the extensive meaning of the Noble Teaching (*ārya-śāsana*). Within this,
one abides in the maturation of the faculties (*indriya-paripāka*) at the ultimate limit.
The Tathāgata’s emanations possess a well-received, firm right view established through hearing and reflection that is consistent with selflessness;
this serves as their basis,
and this serves as their foundation.
Dwelling alone in seclusion,
he contemplates the four stations of consciousness based on the internal and external sense bases,
desiring to utterly eradicate all consciousness associated with grasping at existence.
The cultivation of mindfulness of the body is embraced by superior śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Through the power of this close application and repeated practice,

there arises a realization that accords with reality, which takes the first station of consciousness as its object and is closely contiguous with clear observation (abhisamaya), wherein śamatha and vipaśyanā proceed in tandem.
Immediately thereafter, one is able to enter into the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Noble Truths;
further cultivating them,
one proceeds gradually by means of the path as it has been attained.
One is able to attain the eternal exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
This is like being able to correctly take the first station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) as an object,
up to and including correctly taking the fourth station of consciousness as an object.
One should know that it is likewise so.
Furthermore, as previously stated,
there is the person who does not guard the doors of the sense faculties.
The various entanglements of afflictions manifest and are not relinquished.
There is a deficiency in the two powers of analytical discernment and meditative cultivation, which serve as antidotes for both mundane and supramundane states.
Once afflictions have arisen, their nature is characterized by great stubbornness and attachment.
Once Māra has understood that their nature is firmly attached,
he goes to where they are and entices them with various sensory objects. In this way,
that Māra [acts] toward those individuals (pudgala) whose natures are obsessed by the afflictions (kleśa) and the various fetters (paryavasthāna).
Taking advantage of this opportunity,
they seek to entice and delude [the mind],
establishing an object of focus within its mental continuum.
Furthermore, it is precisely because such a person who fails to guard the sense faculties has a deficient aspiration for parinirvāṇa.
Because they are fond of what is inferior,
it is like a house made of dry, withered reeds and grass;
Māra then piles up the torches of desirable objects and burns them down.
Due to two causes and conditions,
that [object] is constantly obscured and suppressed as its objective sphere:
first, because it causes unarisen fetters to arise.
Second, because it causes the continuity of already arisen fetters (*paryavasthāna*),
one is obscured and overwhelmed by craving for objects; thus,
when extensively searching for various objects, [the fetters arise].
They frequently engage in various kinds of evil and unwholesome conduct;
while practicing such perverse and evil deeds,
they are further overwhelmed and suppressed by various evil and unwholesome states.
As previously stated,
having engaged in wrong conduct,
they proceed by losing their way.
To go downstream with the current is called "flowing with the stream";
that which is contrary to this is [the opposite].
All wholesome factors (śuklapakṣa) should be known as those that do not conform to the stream.
Furthermore, by way of eight aspects:
One should know that this comprehensively encompasses all the correct practices of bodhisattvas in future existences,
as well as the fruits of those paths;
it is superior to the Śrāvaka vehicle and unsurpassed.
What are the eight? They are:
out of compassion, and because of internal fortitude.
Because the nature of the patience that thoroughly examines phenomena (dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti) is manifest;
because it is capable of leading to transcendence;
and because one internally initiates the practice of contemplating the truths.
Because the vast and well-cultivated mundane right view manifests before him;
because he attains purity through the acquisition of the untainted factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma);
and because he has thoroughly purified the cultivation of the factors of awakening.
Together they advance in the cultivation of the unsurpassed, purely pure path of practice.
By relying upon the six bases, they cultivate them to perfection,
thereby attaining the six kinds of most excellent and unsurpassed perfect virtues.
It should be understood that herein, the great bodhisattvas who dwell in their final existence have cultivated their minds through long-term compassion for all sentient beings.
Seeing all foolish beings fallen into the river of craving and swept away by the current,
submerged and tormented by the five types of suffering,
he observes them and gives rise to profound great compassion.
What are the five?
First, seeing that they have fallen into the river of craving and possess improper mental investigations.
First, they are constantly tormented by contact with unlovely water.
Second, they see those six internal and external sense bases as fires of the three poisons, with peacocks dwelling on both banks.
Third, they see them situated within the realm of desire, where numerous sorrows, sufferings, and various calamities—like all manner of evil poisonous thorns—are spread throughout the area below.
Fourth, seeing that [the world] in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) lacks the eye of wisdom, it is as if one were blind and situated therein.
Fifth, seeing that [the world] in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) has already perfected the eye of wisdom.
Because their noble eye of wisdom was deficient,
they were as if dwelling in deep darkness;
having seen in this way the sentient beings fallen into the river of craving and attachment, [they felt compassion].
Being entirely unpeaceful in all respects— whether through contact,
on the shore, or in the depths, middles, and heights of suffering’s oppression—
he gives rise to great compassion.
This is called compassion.
Furthermore, one who has accomplished this compassion will be born either into a royal family or into the family of a royal preceptor.
Although I have not yet left the household life, I have conceived within myself a courageous resolve:
"I shall now certainly attain penetration into the sublime path and return to practice the holy life."
It shall never regress.
This is called internally generating valor.
Furthermore, even while still in the stage prior to going forth [into homelessness],...
Dwelling in the shade of Jambū,
sitting alone in contemplation,
he was able to realize and enter the first dhyāna.
Thereafter, one correctly and thoroughly examines the phenomena of old age, sickness, and death in oneself and others,
and is able to definitively accept them with certainty.
This is called the patience of the thorough investigation of phenomena (dharmavicaya-kṣānti) manifesting within oneself.
Furthermore, it is awakened by all roots of goodness practiced in previous lives and by all virtuous deeds.
Furthermore, through the predominant power of courageous and discerning patience regarding the Dharma,
one is able to renounce vast and sublime sensual desires and,
with pure faith, go forth into homelessness.
Although there is no formal designation,
one who practices the true holy life is able to naturally uphold the prohibitive precepts;
by relying upon these prohibitive precepts as a support, [one attains this state].
Gradually, one is able to realize [the meditative attainments] up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
this is called being able to correctly transcend.
Furthermore, that person, desiring to abandon the worldly path, seeks correct transcendence.
Due to the unsurpassed, ultimate liberation attained by the Perfectly Awakened Ones of former lives,
one gains correct hearing and resolute conviction.
Because their physical continuum has been accumulated through habitual cultivation,
they possess no faith or aspiration whatsoever toward the mundane path.
By means of these causes and conditions, he proceeded to the Bodhi tree;
there, relying upon the path of mental cultivation previously practiced regarding old age, sickness, and death,
he sequentially observed the characteristics of the truths.
He reflected thus:
"These various classes of sentient beings in the world have fallen into manifold perils and manifold sufferings."
There is birth, there is aging, there is illness, and there is death;
yet they are unable to achieve ultimate liberation from aging, illness, and death,
nor do they understand this sequence as it truly is.
He contemplates old age and death;
he contemplates the origin of old age and death;
he contemplates the cessation of old age and death.
One contemplates the practice that leads to the realization of the cessation of old age and death,
by relying on appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) and because of having long since accumulated the great provisions (*mahāsambhāra*).
By means of innate wisdom (*sahaja-prajñā*), one is able to awaken to the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Abiding in the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*) and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*),
this is called the internal initiation of the practice of observing the truths.
Furthermore, desiring to seek the higher exhaustion of outflows,
he applies skillful means to give rise to the knowledge of recollecting past lives and recalls his previous existences.
From the Tathāgatas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones,
he has accumulated the practice of hearing and reflection regarding the path to the exhaustion of outflows;
from this, there arises that which has been accumulated over a long period of time.
Right view pertaining to the world is brought to presence;
however, this right view relies upon the instructor as its basis.
It enables a bodhisattva to remain settled in a single sitting until the ultimate exhaustion of outflows is realized;
this is called the manifestation of vast and well-cultivated right view.
Furthermore, by means of that very right view as instructed, one progressively advances until,
having already abandoned all desires of the lower stages,
one reaches the highest limit of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
When one attains the direct realization (abhisamaya) of the Noble Truths,
one realizes all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma),
beginning with the four applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) that are untainted (anāsrava), up to and including the final eightfold noble path.
By citing the last one,
it should be understood that all preceding stages are also included,
because they are attained through it.
Having attained the fruit of non-returning through the acquisition of the untainted factors conducive to enlightenment,
he is therefore said to have "attained coolness."
Because he has thereby attained ultimate worldly happiness and has attained supramundane,
untainted happiness through the attainment of coolness,
he is said to be "free from burning."
By means of the mundane path,
up to and including having become detached from the afflictions bound to the sphere of nothingness,
as well as having completely abandoned all afflictions to be severed by the path of seeing.
It is called "Free from Feverish Distress" because,
desiring to permanently and completely sever the afflictions bound to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) without remainder,
one further diligently cultivates the purely untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
That which is called the cultivation of the factors of unsurpassed enlightenment is termed the progressive practice of the unsurpassed path of cultivation.
By virtue of this cultivation, [one attains realization].
Within the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣabhūmi*), six kinds of cultivation reach ultimate perfection.
First, the cultivation of noble supernormal powers (*āryābhijñā*) reaches ultimate perfection.
Second, they cultivate the five pure faculties to ultimate perfection.
Third, they realize the complete dissociation from afflictions along with all habitual tendencies, leaving nothing remaining.
Fourth, the complete perfection of attaining the four kinds of happiness-abiding in the present life.
Complete perfection.
Fifth, he realizes the mundane dhyānas, liberations, concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*) to their ultimate perfection.
Sixth, he realizes the mastery of the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-kāya*, *pada-kāya*, *vyañjana-kāya*), obtaining them according to his wish.
One will be able to proclaim the True Dharma without difficulty,
reaching ultimate perfection.
It should be understood that herein, the cultivation of the faculty of pure faith reaches its ultimate fulfillment.
This means that because one's aspiration for nirvāṇa is pure,
one brings the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*) to ultimate fulfillment;
that is, one is able to courageously perform all that is beneficial for sentient beings.
Because it is perfectly pure.
Regarding the ultimate fulfillment of the cultivation of the faculty of mindfulness:
this refers to the three foundations of mindfulness and the quality of non-forgetfulness.
Regarding the phrase "because of being thoroughly purified":
the ultimate fulfillment of the cultivation of the faculty of concentration means that one is thoroughly purified with respect to the noble heavens and the Brahma-abodes.
The ultimate fulfillment of the cultivation of the faculty of wisdom refers to the thorough purification of the ten powers of knowledge (*daśabala*). By means of this,
one is able to abide in the six sense bases through the cause of perfected cultivation.
He becomes a great king,
that is to say, a Dharma King; by means of this, he realizes six kinds of perfection,
namely, through the sovereign power of noble supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).
One attains the perfection of mastery over great wealth and resources.
By virtue of the superior power of the purification of the sense faculties,
one attains the perfection of mastery over a great residence.
By the predominant power of severing all afflictions,
one attains the perfect mastery over comfortable seats and bedding for experiencing peace and happiness;
by the predominant power of dwelling in happiness in the present life.
Dwelling in their homes and amidst their seats and bedding,
they realize the supreme, great abiding in bliss, free from all affliction and harm, characterized by sovereign perfection.
By the sovereign power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*),
one realizes the ability to accomplish all that is for the true benefit of sentient beings,
attaining the perfection of mastery over playful joy (*vikrīḍita-rati*).
Because he possesses the superior power to proclaim the True Dharma without difficulty, he attains mastery over all sets of names, phrases, and syllables according to his desire.
Having become a Dharma King, he is able to obtain [these qualities] from others;
his mastery over the function of impartial distribution is perfected.
This is called the basis for the fulfillment of the six sense bases through cultivation.
One realizes the perfection of the six kinds of mastery.
Furthermore, there are briefly four types of treatises that search for the self;
it is by means of these treatises that [this is established].
For one who has not yet permanently abandoned the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
the discursive investigation seeking a self manifests repeatedly.
What are these four?
First, seeking the self:
by what is my nature constituted?
Second, seeking the self.
Is the self eternal?
Is it impermanent?
Thirdly, one seeks in this way: "What is the self?"
"I am permanent," "I am impermanent"—
these are the four ways of seeking the self.
Regarding all [the notions] of "I" wherever I may dwell,
it should be known that herein there are briefly four kinds of searching for the self.
The first is the search for its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Second, seeking its transformation;
third, seeking its cause;
fourth, seeking its abode.
Within this context, three types [of characteristics] can be established as the distinctions among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, these establishments are not erroneous.
The fourth type, however, exists in every respect.
Ultimately, it is impossible to establish any distinction [between them].

One should know that what is designated as the "intrinsic nature of the self" refers precisely to the six consciousnesses arising from the twelve bases, together with sensation, perception, and volition.
One regards this as the self because no other self can be found beyond it;
furthermore, the very essence of this self is impermanent.
Because of birth, because of old age,
and because of death.

Furthermore, these conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are said to be like magical illusions because they do not constitute a real entity in their various distinctions of arising as diverse self-bodies within the various realms of existence (gati).
Because the nature of perception, mind, and views is delusive and confused,
it is said to be like a mirage;
because they are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing.
It is said that there is increase and decrease;
because it is momentary in nature,
it is called "temporary."
Because it repeatedly perishes and swiftly arises again,
and because it continues in frequent succession,
it is said to have the characteristic of swift manifestation and continuity.
It comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore,
it is said that what was originally non-existent now exists, and having existed, it disperses and ceases.
By such characteristics,
it is briefly stated that the birth-body is successively impermanent,
as is the momentary succession of that which possesses causes.
In this way, these three types of conventional designations— the self-nature of the self as it undergoes transformation or its causes,
and the designated abode belonging to the self—
can ultimately never be found.
Because a real self distinct from the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) cannot be found abiding within those conditioned phenomena,
for this reason:
According to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), even conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are empty and cannot be designated;
how much more so in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, one establishes emptiness solely within emptiness.
In this way, through mental attention that accords with reality,
one understands by means of hearing and comprehends by means of reflection.
Because they have cultivated and fully understood the Truths,
they are described with specific distinctions in their respective order:
"One should rejoice."
One should rejoice equally;
one should rejoice universally.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle Ninety-one.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Ninety-Two.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.
In the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*, the second part of the fourth section on the "Selection of Matters from the Sūtras," there is further a summary verse (*uddāna*) which says:
Higher craving, instruction, and dwelling in suffering; Investigation, production, and unworthiness as an offering;
Clear understanding, liberation, cultivation, and the discourse on non-self; Concentration, phenomena, views, and suffering is the last.
Due to three causes and conditions,
a person exhibits an intense degree of greedy conduct toward their objects of perception.
What are the three?
First, being robust and strong rather than weak and inferior;
second, being handsome and dignified rather than ugly and repulsive.
Third, they practice craving rather than abandoning it;
furthermore, through three kinds of remedies,
they even cause individuals who harbor such intense craving to be brought under their influence.
Within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
he diligently practiced the holy life and disciplined his mind.
It brings about tranquility;
how much more so for those who harbor only mild forms of craving, which are as slight as motes of dust.
What are these three?
First, guarding the doors of the sensory faculties as the basis,
because it is free from the extreme of sensual pleasure;
second, moderation in eating and reducing sleep during the first and last watches of the night as the basis.
Third, because it relies upon supreme right mindfulness and right situational awareness, one practices the path of renunciation via the Middle Way,
thereby remaining far removed from all extremes of self-inflicted suffering.
It should be understood that herein, for one whose mind is well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness,
when an object appears before them while walking,
they do not grasp at its signs or secondary characteristics.
One understands, as they truly are, the arising, abiding, and ceasing of feeling;
if one grasps its signs and secondary characteristics,
one understands, as they truly are, the arising, abiding, and ceasing of perception.
Or, while dwelling [in that state], one understands as it truly is the arising, abiding, and ceasing of those causal discursive thoughts;
by means of such characteristics,
one possesses right mindfulness and right situational awareness.
At all times and in every respect regarding the objects of perception,
one is able to guard the mind according to the correct method.
This is called the most excellent right mindfulness and right situational awareness.
Furthermore, there is another form of the most excellent right mindfulness and right situational awareness:
namely, that of one who has already attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Those who have already attained the attainment of non-perception,
or those who have already attained the state free from vitarka and vicāra,
should be known as relying upon the noble abodes and the divine abodes.
Apart from this supreme abiding through right mindfulness and clear comprehension,
there is nothing else that surpasses it;
or he may abide having arisen from the meditative attainment of cessation.
Or, when about to enter meditative absorption,
he dwells through skillful means,
knowing as they truly are the arising, abiding, and ceasing of feelings.
This is called the most excellent right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
Just as one knows feeling as it truly is by relying on the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*),
so too does one know perception as it truly is by relying on the meditative absorption of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

One should know that the same applies to the meditative absorption free from applied and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra-samādhi*), wherein one understands all applied and sustained thoughts as they truly are.
This is by means of this most excellent right mindfulness and right situational awareness (*samyak-smṛti-saṃprajanya*).
Because they apprehend only phenomena,
they do not give rise to the false discrimination of "I" and "mine" regarding such feeling, perception, applied thought, and sustained thought.
When various foolish persons give rise to the distinctions of feeling, perception, vitarka, and vicāra,
they are unable to initiate the mere notion of "dharmas" regarding these phenomena such as feeling;
rather, they form only this thought:
"I am able to receive it," and so forth,
as explained at length.
By reason of this cause and condition.
He does not even possess right mindfulness and clear comprehension,
let alone the most excellent; herein,
right mindfulness and clear comprehension are explained last.
Whether it be the fruit of non-returning or arhatship,

one should know that what was previously described as right mindfulness and right situational awareness applies from the attainment of mental attention through the state of being heedless— ranging from the stage of an ordinary person up to the fruit of once-returning.
Furthermore, for two reasons,
the Tathāgata himself said:
"I am advanced in years, and my physical strength is exhausted."
He exhorts the śrāvakas to request others to preach the Dharma for the following reasons:
first, to cause those who rely on their youth to practice arrogance exclusively and remain in negligence to become personally fearful and weary of such conduct.
Second, it is to ensure that in future ages,
those bhikṣus who have reached old age and lack physical strength will remain free from doubt and regret.
He exhorted the young bhikṣus to proclaim the True Dharma, saying,
"All you bhikṣus..."
In the prime of their years, fully endowed with vigor and power,
they are far removed from doubt and regret,
and free from all fear.
When preaching the Dharma to others,
one should know that there are, in brief, two ways of proclaiming the sublime Dharma within this context:
first, the definitive exposition (*viniścaya-nirdeśa*).
Second is direct speech.
Regarding decisive speech,
it refers to the employment of methods for interrogation and critical examination.
To speak with correct reasoning so as to eliminate doubt means that the audience remains silent.
To speak directly means that the listeners abide in silence.
Just as a Dharma teacher proclaims the true Dharma,
there are four characteristics by which one is said to be capable of providing conformable instruction and admonition:
first, the ability to analyze the distinctions among the sense bases (*āyatana*).
First, because one attains the purity of the vision of the wisdom of selflessness regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Second, because one attains the purity of the vision of supreme tranquility through the abandonment of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) regarding all feelings (*vedanā*) and their basis.
Third, because it is able to transcend all future sufferings through the purification of vision;
fourth, because it is able to transcend all present sufferings through the purification of vision.
Within this, there is an analysis of the various distinctions among the internal and external bases, consciousness, contact, feeling, perception, volition, craving, and so forth.
It reveals selflessness;
by relying on the principle of the skillful means of dependent origination,
it can lead to the purification of the initial right view.
Just as light depends on a lamp,
and a shadow depends on a tree,
since those do not exist, this also does not exist.
It demonstrates that the various feelings have as their cause the distinctions among the internal and external bases;
because those bases are extinguished without remainder,
these [feelings] also accordingly cease.
Free from overweening pride,
one understands nirvana as it truly is:
the most supreme tranquility.
It can lead to the purification of the second right view;
by means of the sword of wisdom within this present life,
it can forever sever and extinguish all afflictions.
It demonstrates the complete transcendence of all future suffering without remainder,
which leads to the purification of the third right view;
it demonstrates [this] throughout all phenomena that accord with suffering, accord with pleasure, and accord with neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
They do not give rise to desire;
they do not give rise to hatred;
they do not give rise to delusion.
This demonstrates the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
By well-establishing the mind within those foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*),
it demonstrates the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
One cultivates the factors of enlightenment in order to bring about the permanent extinction of all outflows and to transcend the dwelling in the suffering of defilement within this present life.
It can lead to the purification of the fourth right view.
Furthermore, there are certain bhikṣus who do not abide in the guarding of the sense faculties.
Regarding all sensory objects, the mind is largely stained with attachment and largely distracted;
due to these causes and conditions, one experiences two kinds of suffering.
First is the suffering produced by coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*);
second is the suffering produced by doubt regarding all phenomena. Why is this so?
By means of those skillful methods, one should diligently cultivate the body;
having diligently cultivated the body,
one should diligently cultivate the factors of śamatha and ethical discipline.
Because one has not cultivated the branch of śamatha pertaining to the body nor cultivated the branch pertaining to ethical discipline,
the body lacks pliancy.
The mind is not pliant; therefore,
it experiences the suffering produced by coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*),
due to the absence of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
They are unable to touch and realize the supreme samādhi;
for this reason, they should know as it truly is, yet they do not know as it truly is, and thus give rise to much doubt.
Consequently, they experience the suffering produced by doubt regarding all phenomena.
Because one dwells with these two kinds of suffering and affliction,
it is called "dwelling in insecurity due to the various sufferings obtained through the dominant condition of failing to guard the sense faculties.
This is what is meant by the faults of one who does not guard the sense faculties in this present life.
The opposite of this should be understood as the virtues possessed by one who guards the sense faculties.
Furthermore, there are certain bhikṣus.
One diligently cultivates skillful means to become free from sensual desire;
by virtue of correctly practicing the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*),
one subdues all afflictions (*kleśa*).
He reflects thus:
"Do I have sensual desire for these various objects of desire, yet fail to perceive it,
or am I free from it?"
One then attends to and contemplates it with a pure aspect;
only then does one attain certainty regarding what has been abandoned and what remains to be abandoned,
by relying upon the attention of investigation.
One seeks out the locus from which desire arises,
understands it as it truly is,
and recollects it through discernment.
These afflictions are the supreme locus of establishment;
because those afflictions have not been permanently severed,
when the mind is being swept away by them, [it remains there].
Because one understands that [the mind] tends toward inferior states,
one immediately subdues it;
for if one does not subdue it, [it will lead to further decline].
They even fall back and lose the slight degree of samādhi they previously attained,
let alone being able to advance toward superior qualities.
By means of this integration,
one is able to avoid falling back and is also able to advance toward superior qualities.
If one does not investigate, one will again give rise to overweening pride,
and thus there is also retrogression; however,
by means of investigation, this is avoided.
One is able to realize certainty;
if the mind wavers, one correctly understands it and restores its composure,
and for this reason does not regress.
Just as one cultivates skillful means to abandon sensual desire, it should be understood that the same applies accordingly to other higher stages.
This is also the case when one observes with intense insight and careful scrutiny.
They do not arise,
and he thereby attains a resolute conviction:
"I have already been able to overcome [them] in all instances."
That is to say, regarding this object which would otherwise give rise to afflictions,
because I have already overcome it in that regard,
I cause it not to arise.
Having transcended the stage of training,
he is like a great king who can act with sovereign mastery according to his own will,
subduing all the villages of Māra.
He has realized the ultimate knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising;
his holy life is perfected,
yet because the five signs of tranquility are not tranquilized.
One should know that this entails the three kinds of results of suffering:
namely, dwelling in the present life with affliction predominant by way of the faculties,
having unwholesome present conduct as its cause.
Or one may cause another to fall into inferiority;
or be reviled and censured; or be killed.
They experience such various sufferings of the present life;
furthermore, they experience the manifold sufferings of future birth, aging, sickness, and death;
and furthermore, they experience in the future the natural outflows (niṣyanda) induced by their previous habitual practice.
Because of not guarding the sense faculties and due to various defilements,
it is also called suffering.
That which is contrary to this is [happiness].
One should know that through five kinds of signs of tranquility regarding the six sense faculties,
the fruit of the cessation of the three types of suffering is embraced.
Furthermore, there are briefly two kinds of worldly brahmins.
In truth, they are not fields of merit, yet harboring overweening pride,
they claim for themselves the status of a field of merit, declaring, "I am a true field of merit."
One should know that because they have failed to achieve the true nature and characteristics of a field of merit,
they are not worthy of offerings.
First, they exhibit intense attachment toward the gains and honors received from others as they manifest before them.
Their faculties are gluttonous and their nature is restless and agitated;
they falsely manifest before others the conduct of one who has abandoned desire.
Second, they take possession of family estates and live in close proximity with their relatives;
while they are base and impure, they focus exclusively on cultivating themselves.
Whatever practices one performs are neither for one's own benefit nor for the benefit of others;
they are far removed from ethical discipline (*śīla*), the true Dharma, and right practice.
They are far removed from the wholesome conduct that leads to dwelling in the happy realms,
and they are far removed from the sublime conduct that leads to dwelling in nirvāṇa;
it should be known that they are no different from the class of all foolish, ordinary worldlings.
One who dwells in the True Dharma is the opposite of this;
know that such a person is called a brahmin in the ultimate sense.
Furthermore, outside of this True Dharma, there are various śramaṇas, brahmins, and others who,
when preaching the Dharma to their disciples,
for the most part do so primarily to seek the advantage of refutation and censure.
Furthermore, regarding the benefit of seeking to escape the misfortunes of others,
it should be understood that for one who proclaims the Dharma in such a manner,
there is neither purpose nor benefit from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
It is not for one's own benefit,
nor for the benefit of others;
yet the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, proclaim the True Dharma for the sake of their disciples.
It should be understood that those who thus proclaim the true Dharma do so solely for the sake of attaining the two fruits of excellence— clarity and liberation—
and that their great fruit and great benefit, consisting of self-benefit and the benefit of others, are entirely perfected.
One acts throughout the three periods of time without forgetfulness,
because one abides in the supreme meaning and because there is a distinction among the three types of objects of focus.
These are called the three knowledges (vidyā):
liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.
All are termed "liberation," because they are the supreme antidotes to the defilements rooted in craving and ignorance,
and serve to attain the clarity and liberation not yet attained.
It should be known that, in brief, there are four kinds of cultivation of the path:
namely, by cultivating the faculties, one is able to correctly cultivate the body;
and by cultivating the wholesome conduct induced by the cultivation of the body.
One is able to correctly cultivate ethical discipline,
because one cultivates the foundations of mindfulness and the factors of awakening induced by that discipline without error; thus,
one is able to cultivate the mind and wisdom.
Within this context, there are further three types of cultivation of the faculties:
first, mundane cultivation;
second, the cultivation of those in training (śaikṣa).
Third is the cultivation of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
If, based upon the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā-bala*),
one apprehends agreeable or disagreeable objects with an improper aspect (*ayoniśo-nimitta*), [it is still cultivation].
One does not give rise to the afflictions or their entanglements;
even if they should momentarily arise, one immediately dispels them.
This is mundane cultivation.
If one has already attained direct realization of the Noble Truths,
yet due to a lapse of mindfulness, experiences either pleasant, unpleasant,
or both types of mental states.
Yet the mind does not remain firmly bound by these fetters;
it swiftly attains liberation from the defilements.
This is the cultivation of one in training (śaikṣa).
If this very mind remains firm and stable,
as before there will be no constriction within;
it will be well-liberated and well-cultivated.
There is absolutely nothing, down to even a single lapse of mindfulness,
by which they would give rise to the thought of approaching anything agreeable or disagreeable.
One calculates their virtues and directs oneself toward them;
this is called the "thoroughly pure cultivation of the faculties" of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
It should be understood that the three types of cultivation—cultivation of morality (*śīla*), cultivation of mind (*citta*), and cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*)—are likewise so.
Among these, the first is induced by the initial cultivation of the faculties;
the second is induced by the second;
and the third is induced by the third.
It should be understood that the three types of inducements for each of the cultivation of morality, the cultivation of mind, and the cultivation of wisdom are likewise so.
This is because of the distinction between desirable and undesirable objects within these [cultivations].
Because there are distinctions among sentient beings based on those who have been benefactors or those who have been enemies;
because there are distinctions among sentient beings based on those associated with virtues or faults;
and because there are distinctions among sentient beings based on those who are beloved or those who are not beloved.
One should know that there are those that are exclusively agreeable, those that are exclusively disagreeable,
and those that are a mixture of both agreeable and disagreeable; these distinctions arise from the differences between desirable and undesirable objects.
There are objects that are consistently pleasing;
there are objects that are consistently displeasing;
and there are objects whose nature is mixed, being partly pleasing and partly displeasing.
In this way, sentient beings may be exclusively benefactors,
exclusively malevolent,
or a mixture of both benefactors and malevolent ones.
Either there is exclusively attainment,
or there is exclusively loss,
or there is both attainment and loss together.
If one feels affection for a sentient being and that affection further gives rise to more affection,
it should be known that this person is consistently loved by them.
If one feels resentment toward a sentient being and that resentment further gives rise to more resentment, [it should be known that this person is consistently resented].
One should know that these are invariably not what they love:
if, toward a sentient being, love has already arisen and anger subsequently arises;
or if, toward a sentient being, anger has already arisen and love subsequently arises.
It should be understood that these are called "the beloved" and "the unbeloved.
Through such various causes and conditions, there are distinctions among the three types,
beginning with "that which is pleasing to the mind."
Furthermore, one contemplates the faults of unwholesome conduct in the present life and contemplates the faults in future lives;
therefore, one abandons them and cultivates wholesome conduct.
If one is reviled from every quarter regarding the six sense bases,
this is called the disadvantage pertaining to the present life.
For this reason:
They fall into the miserable realms;
this is called the future peril.
In this context, "being reviled by others" refers to this.
This means that non-Buddhists and others in the world who are intelligent,
upon hearing his base and evil reputation and verses of praise,
will all join together in reviling him.
One should know that the rest is as previously described.

Furthermore, regarding the statement here that "one cultivates the foundations of mindfulness," this refers to the initial arousal of the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
In the stage of the ordinary person (pṛthagjana-bhūmi),
it is practiced repeatedly;
in the stage of those in training (śaikṣa-bhūmi), it is cultivated.
One who cultivates the perfection [of the factors of awakening] abides in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣabhūmi),
yet has not yet attained the realm of abandonment while practicing the factors of awakening.
When one correctly aspires toward the realm of abandonment,
it is called "relying on seclusion," though the realm of desirelessness has not yet been attained.
When one correctly aspires toward the realm of non-desire,
it is called "relying on detachment.
When one has not yet attained the realm of cessation but correctly aspires toward that realm of cessation, [it is called "relying on cessation"].
It is called "relying on cessation" because one abandons the inferior cultivation of the factors of enlightenment and redirects oneself toward the sublime cultivation of the factors of enlightenment.
This is called dedication through relinquishment.
Furthermore, because the bhikṣus guard their sense faculties and possess a sense of shame and dread of blame,
by reason of these causes and conditions, [they attain this].
Feeling shame for evil conduct,
one cultivates sublime conduct;
because of cultivating sublime conduct, [one attains excellence].
There is no regret or remorse.
Because there is no regret or remorse, joy arises.
Because this is the prerequisite, the mind attains right concentration;
because the mind is rightly concentrated,
one is able to see things as they truly are.
Because one sees things as they truly are,
both clarity and liberation are fully perfected;
know that this is called the sequence of practice.
Furthermore, there may be a certain ascetic or brahmin who,
being unable to properly cultivate his own sense faculties,
nonetheless improperly instructs others in the method for cultivating the sense faculties.
He perceives that guarding the sense faculties consists merely in turning away from all objective spheres; yet,
he himself develops deep attachment toward his assembly of disciples.
One part gives rise to attachment,
while another part engenders aversion;
this is because the conditions for compliance or opposition toward that teaching constantly manifest as either agreeable or disagreeable.
Regarding this subtle defilement of the self,
they are unable to penetrate it as it truly is with wisdom; yet,
they claim to be well-cultivated in their faculties and thus give rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Those who conform to such a view,
even if they cause their faculties to withdraw from all sensory objects and dwell alone in seclusion, [do not truly transcend them].
Yet, by taking those objects as conditions, they give rise to various defiled discursive thoughts;
however, lacking wisdom, they do not personally awaken to and enter [the truth].
This is also not called the skillful cultivation of the sense faculties.
Furthermore, they do not apply themselves to right practice for the sake of properly cultivating the faculties;
rather, they give rise to false resolve and false pride based solely on the words of others.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas,
for the sake of their disciples, establish the proper method for severing afflictions; therefore,
this is called the "thorough cultivation of the faculties."
It is not that they are unilaterally turned away from all objective spheres;
furthermore, because the Tathāgatas have well-established their minds in the three kinds of unique applications of mindfulness (asamādhāraṇasmṛtyupasthāna).
He is not attached to the assembly of disciples;
he acts with pleasure toward those who practice correctly,
and acts with displeasure toward those who practice incorrectly.
Consequently, the afflictions of sensual desire and the afflictions of malice that would arise from this do not exist at all.
For this reason,
although he has severed the afflictions of his disciples and others,
he is called one who has unsurpassedly cultivated the faculties.
Furthermore, because this cultivation of the faculties (*indriya*) differs according to five types of persons,
it should be understood that there are also five distinct stages of transformation.
That is to say, the Blessed Buddha or some of his disciples may practice exclusively with right conduct and also reach the ultimate end.
There may be disciples who are consistently heedless yet reach the ultimate goal;
there may be disciples who practice the right path but do not reach the ultimate goal;
and there may be disciples who practice wrong paths and do not reach the ultimate goal.
There may be disciples of various types: those who practice with single-minded application,
those who practice with negligence,
and those who practice partially or occasionally with negligence.
Or those who are not heedless;
these are called the fifth category of assembly.
Among them, it is the former whom the Tathāgata finds pleasing.
This refers to how the disciples, within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
practice the correct conduct in order to bring the faculties to perfection through cultivation.
Furthermore, there is another class of beings who are disagreeable,
namely those who practice wrong conduct or do not practice at all;
therefore, the Tathāgata regards these as the foremost among sentient beings.
One arouses a pleasant perception toward the second sentient being,
while perceiving them as unpleasant.
Observing the third type of sentient being,
one gives rise to a pleasant mental state and a displeasing mental state.
Contemplating the fourth class of sentient beings who are displeasing,
one gives rise to a state of being pleased.
Observing the fifth type of sentient being,
one gives rise to a pleasant mind and a displeased mind.
Furthermore, they give rise to both pleasant and unpleasant mental states.
Although the Tathāgata initiates these five distinct variations of pleasant and unpleasant mental states regarding these five aggregates, [he remains equanimous].
Nevertheless, the Tathāgatas are never defiled by the manifestations of craving or aversion,
because they have forever abandoned the fetters of all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies.
Because they have skillfully cultivated the faculties,
the Tathāgata has forever severed all afflictions along with their residual tendencies,
serving as the basis [for this].
Being able to dwell skillfully in mindfulness,
one is free from all defilements among the assembly of disciples;
this is called the unsurpassed cultivation of the faculties through five transformations.
Furthermore, regarding all these five modes of transformation,
one should correctly contemplate the three types of remedies as appropriate to each case.
First, the perception of impermanence;
second, a mind of loving-kindness;
third, the meditative attainment of non-perception.
These three types should be understood according to their respective characteristics. Furthermore,
there are the disciples of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who have accomplished what was to be done and are those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
This is called having cultivated the faculties.
Because they have long cherished the aspiration for nirvāṇa,
even when encountering the appearance of objects— consisting of various sentient beings— as previously described, [they remain undisturbed].
Some are exclusively desirable;
some are exclusively undesirable;
others consist of various mixed types, encompassing both the desirable and the undesirable.
Because of the permanent departure from greed, hatred, and delusion,
and by the predominant power of liberation of mind and liberation through wisdom,
one causes the mind to swiftly relinquish those [objects] by means of the signless (*animitta*).
By virtue of his intention,
he conceives a sense of revulsion toward all sensory objects and perceives the quality of tranquility in nirvāṇa.
In this way, one is quickly able to abide in equanimity.
By virtue of this cause and condition,
even for a single moment, any defiled mind produced through a lapse of mindfulness is [abandoned].
Nor should they arise.
One should know that because one has cultivated them thoroughly up to this point,
it is called "well-cultivated faculties."
If those in training have not yet been able to swiftly abide in equanimity,
it is because other afflictions still permeate their mental continuum, rendering it defiled;
furthermore, this concerns all objects that undergo the three turnings.
Because of his aversion toward the various afflictions that arise,
when he is oppressed by the manifestation of those afflictions,
he is then able to skillfully abide in the perception of repulsion and the perception of danger.
Practicing in this way enables the faculties (*indriya*) that have been cultivated to quickly reach fulfillment.
Therefore, such a person is called one who practices rightly.
Thus should it be understood regarding the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
The Master’s excellent assembly of disciples has attained the realized meaning and is able to practice correctly.
Furthermore, there are briefly three types of correct tasks for a proponent of non-self (anātmavādin).
What are these three? They are:
[the investigation of] the specific and general characteristics of the formations (saṃskāra) subsumed under the truths of suffering and its origin.
One should correctly clarify and establish selflessness;
it should be understood that herein, the individual multiplicity [of phenomena] is revealed,
thereby clarifying their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Because it reveals the similarity between arising and ceasing,
it clarifies the common characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa);
this is called the first correct task to be performed.
Furthermore, regarding the practice of causes alone within selflessness,
one should know that herein, with respect to the three types of feeling as conditions, the various defilements and purifications are revealed exactly as they are.
Three kinds of afflictive latent tendencies (anuśaya) arise,
which have not yet been permanently severed;
among these, the latent tendency of the view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi-anuśaya) pertains to the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
They have not yet eliminated it;
regarding the latent tendency of pride within that path of cultivation,
they have not yet eliminated it.
Regarding the category of views and conceit, the ignorance capable of arising therein has not yet been permanently severed,
nor has the wisdom that serves as its antidote been produced.
Therefore, one is unable to bring an end to suffering.
This is what is called the manifestation of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
That which is contrary to this [is the manifestation of purification].
One should know that this demonstrates purification;
this is called the second correct task.
Furthermore, regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one abandons the superimposition of a self and the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Based on the correct view that the grasper is truly non-existent,
one clearly realizes this view of non-self in accordance with purity.
While in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),
one is able to correctly embrace the clear realization of the Noble Truths (*āryasatyābhisamaya*) and can also attain the various eyes of noble wisdom (*āryaprajñācakṣus*).
In the stage of one in training (śaikṣa),
one is able to attain the subsequent stages, namely the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
In the stage of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), [one attains these].

It can cause all afflictions— whether belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and whether abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) or cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)—
to be permanently severed without remainder.
Therefore, it should be known that this view of selflessness is able to bring about purification.
It should be clearly elucidated;
this is called the third task to be correctly performed.
Furthermore, regarding the accomplishment of mundane right view and extensive learning:
One who does not abide securely in the True Dharma achieves only the mundane right view and much learning;
one who attains secure abiding in the True Dharma [achieves the supramundane].
It should be known that there are, in brief, five kinds of praise for the benefits of the fruit of sublime correct application. What are these five?
They are as follows: first, those who abide in the true Dharma.
First, because his mind has not yet attained concentration,
the ethical discipline that is a factor of śamatha is neither pure nor immaculate.
Furthermore, this second practitioner who abides in the True Dharma has a mind that is pure and bright because it has attained meditative concentration.
One should know that this is called the first praise for the benefits of the fruit of the most excellent right application.
Furthermore, regarding that first type of person whose mind has not yet attained meditative concentration:
Regarding all feelings,
together with their bases and their objects.
Together with its associates and together with its concomitants,
one does not know it as it truly is.
Due to this lack of knowledge,
one is touched by the faults caused by three kinds of ignorance.
What are these three?
First, the faults and afflictions produced by the defilement of experience;
second, the faults and afflictions produced by the defilement of the world;
third, the faults and afflictions produced by the defilement of both the present life and future lives.
It should be understood that herein, the fault committed by the defilement of feeling refers to the bondage of craving for pleasant feeling,
as well as for that which evolves concomitantly with it and that which is defiled in accordance with it, by one who is deluded.
Regarding painful feelings and so forth,
there is the fetter of aversion;
regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings and so forth, [there is the fetter of ignorance].
There are those bound by the fetter of delusion and the fetter of latent tendencies;
because they are accompanied by latent delusion,
there are the faults produced by worldly defilements.
That is to say, the deluded person has the bond of lustful attachment toward the present life,
the bond of longing and attachment toward the past life,
and the bond of mental preoccupation toward the future life.
Regarding the faults resulting from the defilements of both the present life and future lives:
it means that such a person with a defiled mind is subject to defilement in relation to the world and to sensation.
One is then able to grow and produce karma that brings about future existence; by means of this,
one increases the aggregates of future existence,
causing them to arise in the future.
Furthermore, it can increase all forms of craving, namely,
craving for future existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*) and craving for material possessions (*pariṣkāra-tṛṣṇā*).
It is because of craving for future existence that...
Because they crave their own future bodies and material possessions,
at the time of seeking them, they...
One becomes extremely weary and exhausted;
if one encounters sense objects, defilement and affliction arise;
and if one does not obtain what is desired, one's wishes remain unfulfilled.
One then burns oneself.
If one has gained [something] and then lost it, one is harmed by grief and affliction.
This is called the fault and disadvantage pertaining to the present life.
If, precisely by virtue of those [karmas] having been performed and accumulated,
various karmas and afflictions arise through their predominant power, they are able to induce future existence.
It gives rise to the various sufferings of future birth, old age, death,
and so forth; this is called the fault of the subsequent life for a person whose second mind is fixed.
It should be understood that everything is the opposite of what was stated above;
this should be known as the second excellence.
The remainder is as previously explained.
Furthermore, because that first type of person has not yet attained mental stability,
they [experience] the faults and afflictions resulting from their lack of wisdom.
Whether regarding oneself or others, those who do not know things as they truly are—
this second type of person fixed in their mental state—
is able to understand all such things as they truly are.
One should know that this is called the third excellence.
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, regarding that second type of person who has already attained meditative concentration:
Having understood all faults and afflictions as they truly are,
one has entered the stage of cultivation;
that is, the right view associated with selflessness previously attained.
By virtue of this cultivation,
during these two periods,
based upon the realm of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*) and the realm of dispassion (*virāgadhātu*), [he practices] with all those factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*).
All are fully perfected.
This is because an individual who has not yet attained meditative concentration has not yet stabilized the mind.
In all these respects, they are not yet fully perfected;
one should know that this is called the fourth excellence.
The remainder is as previously explained.
Furthermore, for that person who has attained concentration through the second mental state,
all the factors that assist vipaśyanā through extensive learning are able to sustain superior samādhi.
One is able to purify and cultivate vipaśyanā;
by this cause and condition,
the two— śamatha and vipaśyanā— proceed together in equal measure.
It should be understood that for a person who has not yet attained meditative concentration,
both extensive learning and that [concentration] are lacking.
Thus, regarding the attainment of mundane right view, there is extensive learning.
A person who does not abide stably in the true Dharma becomes one who abides stably in the true Dharma by achieving mundane right view and extensive learning.
One should know that there is this fifth benefit of praise resulting from the sublime correct application;
thus, it is by means of having already attained superior śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Relying upon the realm of abandonment,
one is able to correctly and fully comprehend that which should be fully known.
That which should be permanently abandoned,
he is able to correctly and permanently abandon;
that which should be realized...
One is able to correctly realize that which should be realized,
and one is able to correctly cultivate that which should be cultivated.
Relying on the realm of desirelessness, he has fully known, abandoned, realized, and cultivated all of that;
regarding both the physical basis and the mental factors dependent upon it,
he possesses correct knowledge of what has been known.
Having correctly abandoned ignorance, which is the basis, and craving for existence, which depends upon it;
and having [attained] clear knowledge, which is the basis, and liberation, which depends upon it.
Having correctly realized the abandonment of the afflictions, one has realized what was to be realized;
having correctly cultivated the basis of śamatha and the supported vipaśyanā,
one has cultivated what was to be cultivated.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of views regarding phenomena:
first, the view of conditioned phenomena;
second, the view of unconditioned phenomena.
Regarding those who see conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*):
it refers to someone who,
with respect to the basis of the truths (*satyāśraya*) and the intrinsic nature of the truths (*satyasvabhāva*), [perceives them].
All these are known as they truly are.
What is called the "basis for the truths"?
It refers to things categorized as sentient beings, such as name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and humans, devas, and so forth.
What are the truths?
They are the conventional truth and the ultimate truth.
What is the conventional truth?
That is to say, with respect to the very bases of those truths,
one conceptually establishes [the notions of] a self, a sentient being, or even a life-principle and a living being;
furthermore, one makes such claims as, "I see forms with my eye," up to "I cognize phenomena with my mind."
Furthermore, they give rise to verbal expressions,
saying: "It is thus named," and so forth, up to "such is the limit of its lifespan," as explained in detail previously.
One should know that herein there exists only conceptual construction,
only conventional self-designation,
and only conventional verbal expression regarding the distinctions of essential nature, characteristics, and activity.
This is called conventional truth.
What is ultimate truth?
It refers to that very basis upon which those truths depend.
There is the nature of impermanence;
as explained at length, up to:
there is the nature of dependent origination.
As explained extensively above,
it should be understood that this is likewise the case for the nature of suffering, just as it is for the nature of impermanence.
If, regarding this basis of the conventional and ultimate truths,
one understands the conventional truth as it truly is the conventional truth,
and understands the ultimate truth as it truly is the ultimate truth.
This is called the view of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
If a monk possesses this view of conditioned phenomena,
his verbal expression is complete in this regard.
What is called the vision of unconditioned phenomena?
It refers to one who has already attained skill in the two kinds of truths regarding that very basis of the truths.
By the predominant power of this skillfulness,
one perceives profound tranquility in all bases, from the aggregates up to nirvāṇa.
The mind enters therein as extensively explained previously,
up to and including liberation.
