This is called the vision of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
If a bhikṣu is endowed with this vision of unconditioned phenomena,
he is said to be complete in his verbal expression.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this vision of the Dharma is accomplished by three types of individuals (*pudgala*):
first, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who practice in accordance with the Dharma and have already attained a concentrated mind.
First, one who is widely learned and intelligent, capable of observing all phenomena according to correct principle;
second, those in training who have already seen the path of truth;
third, those beyond training whose outflows are forever exhausted.

Furthermore, if there are those who, desiring the prosperity of gods and humans, themselves make vows and practice the holy life (brahmacarya), you should know that they are praising the two kinds of faults inherent in both the human and celestial realms.
What are these two?
First, the manifold sufferings produced by afflictions;
second, the manifold sufferings produced by impermanence.
What are the various sufferings produced by afflictions?
They refer to the dwelling in craving for sense objects among humans and devas,
which, based on the present life, dwells in the pleasure of sense objects.
One dwells with delight regarding objects by depending on the past;
one dwells with joy regarding objects because of the arising of affection and pleasure toward past objects in the present;
and [one dwells with joy] regarding future objects because of the arising of affection and pleasure toward present objects.
If one dwells in defilement regarding such objects of the three times,
it should be known that they will experience the suffering of lacking what they desire,
as well as all the various sufferings of birth, aging, and so forth.
This is called the suffering and calamity produced by the arising of afflictions.
What is the suffering produced by impermanence?
It refers to the fact that even in states conducive to pleasure, there is the occurrence of loss and separation.
The suffering of transformation arises because the conditions conducive to suffering manifest before one;
the suffering of revulsion arises [from that].
Because all self-entities perish and disintegrate at the time of death,
there is the suffering of disintegration.
One should know that these are called the three kinds of suffering produced by impermanence.
In this regard, the Tathāgata has transcended these two kinds of faults and dwells in exclusive bliss;
one should understand this bliss as it truly is, for it is by virtue of this that there is bliss.
Furthermore, one should know the skillful means for happiness as it truly is. What is happiness?
It refers to the supreme peace and security resulting from the eternal exhaustion of all associations with objective conditions.
This is the nirvāṇa-element with remainder.
What is the skillful means?
It is as previously described.
Regarding the five kinds of feeling, he gives rise to the fivefold transformation of suchness-wisdom.
If the śrāvakas were to abandon the sublime bliss that transcends humans and gods, which was realized by the Great Teacher, [they would not attain this].
Those who seek the inferior pleasures of humans and devas should know that they will suffer much humiliation in the presence of the wise.
One also deceives oneself.
Furthermore, the summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
"First, abiding far from nirvāṇa; a brief explanation of what is realized internally."
Discerning the characteristics of omniscience, one abandons the activities of training and so forth,
abiding constantly in accordance with emptiness. The perfection of both teacher and disciple is due to two causes and conditions.
One should know that this is called the second abiding;
that is to say, because of craving for existence (*bhavarāga*),
one desires to bring about a second self-body.
One undergoes and practices its cause.
Because this first entity ceases and the second entity subsequently arises,
how can there be craving?
When objects of perception that are desirable are about to appear before one,
the initial arising of defiled delight is called "having joy" (*sa-nandī*).
From this point onward, until one has attained that [state],
one should dwell frequently in mental attention and contemplation;
even if it has already been attained, one should not yet put it into practice.
In the interim,
by the predominant power of that very delight,
one dwells in a state of stained joy.
It is called "possessing joy" because,
at the time of enjoyment, it gives rise to much craving and attachment; thus,
it is called "possessing craving" (tṛṣṇā) due to its state of being stained by attachment.
Furthermore, because one gives rise to longing for the future and because one experiences the reception [of results] regarding what has already been attained,
it is called "having delight."
Because one recollects [them] in the past,
it is called "having joy";
when they have already been correctly acquired and utilized, [it is called "having satisfaction"].
Because it gives rise to craving and attachment,
it is called "having defiled attachment.
This is termed the second distinction.
How does the second selfhood arise?
It is because delight and so forth serve as the causes of accumulation that,
in a future life, the roots of birth and old age give rise to the manifold sufferings.
The opposite of this should be known as the dwelling that has no second.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of dharmas.
They are mutually contradictory:
first, affliction;
second, nirvana.
Therefore, having become established in the phenomena of affliction (saṃkleśa),
one immediately proceeds in accordance with future existence (punarbhava).
When one proceeds in accordance with future existence, [one is further bound].
It should be known that such a person is said to be far from nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, there are six types of base and fragmented characteristics of a base person (pudgala):
first, one who by nature is prone to much anger and resentment.
Second, one does not reflect upon one's actions.
Third, one delights in afflicting others.
Fourth, when touched by suffering, one immediately utters false and harsh words.
Fifth, one may utter harsh speech that is true yet leads to what is disadvantageous;
sixth, because of this, one successively gives rise to immeasurable varieties of evil speech.
It is not merely by having few words that one gives rise to contentment;
rather, for two reasons,
those who have gone forth exert themselves to practice with diligence.
One can swiftly realize the goals and benefits of the śramaṇa life.
Those who have not yet developed faith shall be inspired with pure faith,
and those who already possess faith shall cause it to increase all the more.
What are these two?
First is patience;
second is gentleness.
What is called patience (*kṣānti*) means never retaliating against the enmity of others.
What is called gentleness (*sauratya*) means...
This means that his mind is free from resentment and he does not afflict others.
Furthermore, to state it briefly,
the Tathāgata relies on two general bases.
The teaching on the realms of non-existence consists of two parts:
first, the teaching on the realm of nirvana with remainder;
second, the teaching on the realm of nirvana without remainder.
If, by virtue of having abandoned such afflictions in this manner,
one is said to have achieved abandonment,
then that person does not possess those afflictions.
In this way, by not abiding in those fruits— the various sufferings of future existence—
one should know that this is called the teaching on the realm of nirvana with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).

If, in this way, one does not abide in the fruits of suffering of future existence arising from the afflictions (*kleśa*), [one should know that this is called the teaching on the realm of nirvana without remainder].
Thus, by means of this process until the end of life, once [the person] has passed away and ceased to exist,
all remaining bases of existence are entirely non-existent,
and they no longer abide in this body.
Not abiding in any other body,
nor abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
one realizes the ultimate limit of all suffering.
One should know that this is called the teaching on the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Briefly, there are three types of causes for the strength of mindfulness:
first, by virtue of being young and in the prime of life.
Second, by way of habitual practice in previous lives;
third, by way of repeated practice in the present life.
Furthermore, by way of five aspects.
One should know that nirvāṇa is a dharma realized within;
that is to say, it is free from faith,
and so forth, up to being free from the acceptance resulting from investigation through views.
This should be understood as previously explained:

that within the present life, one understands as they truly are the existence and non-existence of the various defilements arising from the internal, the individual, and the predominant influence of both the internal and external.
Furthermore, the unsurpassed enlightenment of all Buddhas is revealed through three causes and conditions:
first, because they have realized all objects of knowledge.
Second, because of thoroughly awakening to the reality of existence and non-existence as it truly is;
third, because of thoroughly awakening to all phenomena belonging to the two categories of defilement and purity.
Therefore, regarding these three points, others—
I ask the Blessed One:
furthermore, when all conditioned phenomena arise simultaneously,
they cause the mind to become deluded and distracted.
Because it causes one to engage in false grasping and conceptualization regarding signs,
the Tathāgata has analyzed and revealed [the truth] for the sake of his disciples.
This causes one to decisively awaken to and enter into those characteristics,
for the purpose of thoroughly knowing the true nature and so as not to deceive oneself.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of providing clear and fearless definitive explanations to others.
Moreover, it is because those who have gone forth abandon the predominant influence of their formal training.
One should know that this establishes attachment to sensory objects;
furthermore, for one who has gone forth,
it is due to the predominant force of violating the śīla.
It should be understood that for those who have not yet gone forth, there is the obstruction of the mental stump of turning one's back on and entering [the world],
because they are devoid of shame and dread of blame and are single-mindedly attached to the flavor of worldly pleasures.
If one firmly grasps at the objects of perception,
know that this is called the most extreme attachment to flavor;
by reason of this, [it leads to suffering].
Regarding the cultivation of superior wholesome karmas,
the mind is like a stump or a withered tree;
it is not pliant and lacks functional capacity.
Furthermore, precisely due to this predominant influence,
one engages in various evil deeds,
harboring within oneself the concealment of the manifold evils committed.
It gives rise to concealment.
All such things, when briefly subsumed as one,
are called the "stump of the mind" and the "matter of concealment" consisting of the most extreme relishing of objects.
Furthermore, if one does not practice restraint regarding the sense faculties,
because of the delight in hearing what is not the true Dharma,
there arises a defiled attention produced by contact with ignorance.
Precisely because of the predominant power of this mental attention (*manasikāra*),
one does not know as it truly is all the faults that arise in various states of existence in future lives;
and because one does not know those faults as they truly are, [one remains bound].
Thereupon, aspiration arises;
because of that aspiration,
one performs and increases karma associated with it.
Because one performs and increases corresponding karma,
the six sense bases arise in a future life;
this is called the principle of sequential order.
As for the reverse order:
it means that those six sense bases have karma as their cause,
and karma has craving as its cause.
Craving, in turn, takes that ignorance as its cause;
ignorance, in turn, takes improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) as its cause;
and improper mental attention, in turn, takes contact associated with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*) as its cause.
Furthermore, among these, the karma previously created is the cause for the six sense bases to be experienced in the present life;
this refers to karma created in the present life.
This is the condition for the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) to arise in the subsequent life;
or it is the support by which the six sense bases are experienced later,
according to the respective roles of craving (tṛṣṇā), karma (karman), and so forth.
It should be known that it is likewise.
Furthermore, subsequent arising occurs due to two causes and conditions.
There are two factors: first, karma leading to future existence;
second, craving for future existence.
Yet it is said only that "all classes of sentient beings proceed according to their karma."
It is not said that [craving] follows after craving.
Why is this? Briefly stated, there are three types of craving.
First is craving for sensual desire;
second is craving for form;
third is craving for the formless.
In this context, although sensual craving—
which is unwholesome— has a ripening result,
it does not arise if one does not commit evil and unwholesome karma.
In the end, it cannot [lead to] maturation in the evil destinies.
If there is craving for the desire realm regarding the various feelings produced by contact associated with ignorance—
When seeking arises,
craving is produced toward desirable objects,
and aversion is produced toward undesirable objects.
Delusion arises regarding objects that can cause confusion;
through the predominant power of these three,
one performs unwholesome karma.
It is by virtue of this karma that one is born in the various evil destinies;
it is not merely through being bound by those fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion that one inevitably falls into the evil destinies.
However, this very craving acts as an auxiliary when the maturation of the karma one has performed arises;
furthermore, it does so through the predominant power of the longing for desirable objects.
One practices wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind;
with this as the cause,
one attains rebirth in the happy realms.
Among these, for the various desirable matured fruits (*vipākaphala*),
it is only karma that should serve as the cause of projection (*ākṣepahetu*),
and not defiled craving.
Furthermore, this craving bound to the realms of form and formlessness,
although not unwholesome,
is nevertheless defiled.
None of these possess any ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Furthermore, it is precisely because of this craving for the realms of form and formlessness that they are called "craving for existence" (*bhavarāga*).
Due to the cause of hearing the true Dharma, he contemplates the coarse and base characteristics within that desire realm;
through the realization of clear contact, there arise various sensations associated with worldly correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
Having subdued the greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth of the desire realm,
one performs wholesome, outflow-tainted karma produced through cultivation;
because one performs that karma in this very place.
One will be born there not by virtue of a defiled craving for that place,
but rather through this very craving directed toward the karma one has performed.
When the maturation arises,
it can act as an auxiliary companion;
therefore, it is said that all classes of sentient beings follow their karma.
It is not said that this follows from craving.
Furthermore, regarding external objects,
it is due to the predominant power of worldly conventional designations.
It is also said that there are fruits and there are experiencers;
these may at times appear as empty worlds,
or at other times as non-empty.
If it is so for the experiencer,
one should know that it is likewise for the agent.
This is called the emptiness of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
not the emptiness of ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā).
It refers to the teaching that at all times, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) possess only cause and effect.
There is neither a recipient nor an agent;
know that this is called the emptiness of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya-śūnyatā*).
One should further understand that there are seven kinds of this emptiness.
First, the emptiness of the future limit;
second, the emptiness of the past limit;
third, the emptiness of the middle limit.
Fourth, the emptiness of permanence;
fifth, the emptiness of self;
sixth, the emptiness of the experiencer.
Seventh, the agent is empty.
One should know that herein there are no conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) existing in the future world;
nor is there any collection of conditioned phenomena established by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) from which conditioned phenomena come when they arise.
If such a thing were to exist, it should not arise,
because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) would already be substantially existent in the future;
furthermore, impermanence (*anityatā*) could not be perceived.
Since there is that which can be obtained,
one should therefore know that when all conditioned phenomena arise.
It comes from nowhere;
originally non-existent, it now exists.
This is called the emptiness of the future limit (aparānta-śūnyatā).
Furthermore, there are no conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in the past world;
nor is there any established intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a collection of real entities.
Once arisen and having ceased,
all conditioned phenomena proceed there and abide in accumulation;
if such a thing exists.
One should not posit that conditioned phenomena have cessation,
because the intrinsic nature of the past aggregate of formations remains steadfastly and eternally abiding;
if there were no cessation, [it would be so].
That nature of impermanence would be unknowable;
yet since it is indeed knowable, therefore,
at the very moment conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are ceasing, [impermanence is perceived].
They do not go anywhere to accumulate and abide; once they have arisen,
they disperse and cease without depending on any further cause,
naturally perishing and decaying.
This is called the emptiness of the prior limit (*pūrvānta-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, within the process of momentary arising and ceasing,
there are only the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) that can be apprehended for a brief duration.
Within this, no other formations can be found,
nor is there any separate entity;
this is called the emptiness of the middle limit.
One should know that these, too, are eternally empty and empty of self.
Because there is no self, the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) that constitute the nature of the fruit are empty and have no experiencer.
Because the nature of causes, karma, and conduct is empty and lacks an agent,
this is called the emptiness of both the experiencer and the agent.
This is because neither agent nor experiencer exists.
There are only conditioned phenomena arising and ceasing;
there are only conditioned phenomena.
In subsequent births,
there is absolutely no one who abandons the previous birth and takes up a subsequent birth. Therefore,
it is said that only phenomena arise from various conditions and are able to give rise to further phenomena.
Furthermore, all phenomena are entirely devoid of functional activity;
there is not the slightest phenomenon capable of producing another phenomenon.
Therefore, it is said: "Because this exists, that exists."
"Because this arises, that arises.
This is merely the conventional designation of "activity" within the context of those causal dharmas,
based upon the relative truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
It is taught that this dharma can give rise to that dharma.
Furthermore, by means of five aspects,
regarding the objects of focus that are conducive to joy:
They act in conformity with it and take deep delight in it with their hearts,
yet they do so in a manner that is not in accordance with correct principle.
Grasping at its characteristics,
they give rise to desire and frequently engage in discursive thought.
Seeking through skillful means,
one thereby extensively performs meritorious and non-meritorious actions,
just as one accords with the objects of focus that give rise to joy.
The objects of focus for those associated with sorrow and those associated with equanimity should be understood accordingly as well.
The difference is as follows:
Regarding objects of focus that accord with sorrow,
one acts in conformity with them;
with a deeply loathing mind, one gives rise to hatred.
Regarding objects of focus that accord with equanimity,
one proceeds in accordance with them; thus,
through profound mental delusion, ignorance arises.
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, there are bhikṣus who have realized arhatship,
with all outflows forever exhausted.
Acting in accordance with all objects of perception,
one is constantly unable [to maintain restraint],
even to the point that through loss of mindfulness, various afflictions arise.
Therefore, one constantly dwells in a state free from defilement;
for this reason,
it is called "constant dwelling."
In that regard, within the category of mental concomitants, whether it be joy or sorrow,
or gladness or dejection,
none of these exist at all for Arhats.
Even among wholesome states, such a thing does not exist;
furthermore, because that constant abiding is extremely difficult to practice and is without fault.
They are called "most excellent," for those capable of accomplishing this are extremely rare;
thus they are described as the foremost field of merit in ultimate reality.
"One should invite [them]," and so forth,
as explained at length;
it should be understood as previously detailed in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.
Furthermore, within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
one should understand that both the Great Teacher and his assembly of disciples each possess two characteristics by which their virtues are perfected.
How should one understand that the Great Teacher’s virtues are perfected through these two aspects?
That is to say, with respect to his conduct for the benefit of others,
he intends to lead [beings] to realize that all sensations whatsoever are suffering.
It explains the basis of feeling;
it explains its causes and conditions;
and it explains all the accompanying factors that bring about defilement.
The establishment of the categories of the teacher consists in explaining the objects of counteraction and their respective antidotes.
To explain the ultimate deliverance in all its aspects is called the first perfection of the teacher’s qualities.
Furthermore, based on his practice for self-benefit,
he proclaims the three types of unique applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) that abide without defilement;
this is called the second perfection of the teacher’s qualities.
How should one understand the disciple whose qualities are perfected through the two types of application?
It refers to one who, having been able to comprehend the immeasurable teachings of the Tathāgata,
has not yet reached the further shore of hearing them.
If one is to reach that further shore,
it is essential to practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma and realize liberation.

It is not for the sake of merely receiving and upholding [the teachings], nor for understanding them once they have been understood; rather, one should practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānudharmapratipatti) according to the principle.
It is not that the mere sounds, voices, and words of the teaching constitute the ultimate goal.
This is called the first assembly of disciples whose virtues are perfected.
Thus they practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma,
never becoming complacent through inferiority.
One must surely proceed to the destination reached by the wise and sagacious man;
one will certainly obtain that which is to be obtained.
This is called the second perfection of the virtues of the assembly of disciples.
Furthermore, within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
one should know that the Great Teacher’s qualities are perfected by means of three further characteristics.
Furthermore, one should know that the disciple’s virtues are perfected by means of two characteristics.
How should one know that the Great Master’s virtues are perfected by means of three characteristics?
That is to say, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, for the sake of his disciples,
first established the correct practice of the Middle Way that avoids the two extremes.
This is called the first perfection of the teacher’s qualities.
Furthermore, regarding those who have not yet developed faith in the holy teaching,
or those who have committed transgressions:
By means of correct application, he causes others to enter the noble teaching and remain free from all transgressions;
this is called the second perfection of the teacher’s qualities.
Furthermore, regarding those who have already entered the noble teaching:
He correctly embraces and sustains [his disciples] by means of four dharmas;
this is called the third perfection of a teacher’s qualities.
What are the four dharmas of embracing?
First, regarding secrecy, one instructs them through teachings that are in accordance with the Dharma and characterized by tranquility,
rather than through what is contrary to the Dharma.
Second, regarding transgressions, one employs words that are in accordance with the Dharma and are stern and cutting.
To censure and expel someone in their presence is not contrary to the Dharma;
third, there is the reliance on and attachment to discursive thought.
First, he instructs him to diligently cultivate tranquility within;
fourth, he instructs him to listen to the true Dharma from time to time,
never becoming indolent or negligent.
Furthermore, one should know that causing others to distance themselves from the counterfeit Dharma,
as well as causing them to abandon correct practice through its antithesis,
constitutes [offense] regarding the secret.
One who is capable of providing instruction that is in accordance with the Dharma and conducive to tranquility,
if they correctly perceive a transgression of reality,
must certainly censure and expel [the offender].
Regarding those who are to be disciplined:
one should rebuke and expel them in their presence using words in accordance with the Dharma,
with a mind free from defilement.
For those who engage in discursive investigation,
he employs skillful means to enable them to easily attain certain understanding.
For those who are distracted by the five kinds of exquisite sensual desires, [he employs skillful means].
By demonstrating its faults and disadvantages, one causes [the practitioner] to develop weary detachment.
Through gradual training, they eventually realize and enter the fourth dhyāna.
All discursive thoughts can only achieve ultimate tranquility within by relying upon the abandonment of craving.

One should know that causing oneself to be free from affliction and causing others to embrace [the Dharma] is called listening to the true Dharma from time to time, always without indolence or abandonment.
What are the two characteristics by which the assembly of disciples is perfected in virtue?
They are that the disciples first accept what the Great Master has perceived— namely,
the vision of emptiness and selflessness regarding all phenomena.
By this cause and condition,
one does not superimpose a self upon phenomena to give rise to false attachment,
nor does one subvert conventional reality.
Because of their superior intention, they do not follow after anything;
because they conform to conventional expression, they do not depart from it.
This is called the first assembly of disciples, whose virtues are perfected.
Furthermore, once they have accepted and assented to that vision,
they are able to correctly practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānudharmapratipatti).
At that time, they are sustained by being embraced by the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu).
If those phenomena are suffering and harmful,
one understands them as they truly are and is able to swiftly abandon and extinguish them;
if those phenomena are neither suffering nor harmful, [one understands them as they truly are].
Knowing this as it truly is, one is able to swiftly realize it;
this is called the second perfection of the virtues of the assembly of disciples.
Such is the noble teaching of the Buddhas, which is sustained by both the Great Teacher and his assembly of disciples.
One should know that it is exclusively undefiled and pure,
the destination to which all the wise resort.

In the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*, this is the first part of the third section, the Compendium of Analysis of Dependent Origination, Nutriment, Truths, and Elements. Thus has been explained the compendium of analysis of the bases (*āyatana*).
Now follows the compendium of analysis of dependent origination, nutriment, truths, and elements.
I shall now explain it.
The summary verse (uddāna) says:
"The establishment [of the aggregates], the two truths, and so forth; with contact as a condition, and so forth."
There are the summaries (*udāna*) concerning cessation, the nutriments (*āhāra*), and so forth, and finally those concerning "as it truly is" (*yathābhūta*):
"The establishment of the mass of suffering, the truths, and contemplation; The compendium of the subtle wisdom of the holy teaching."
By means of the investigation of the limit of reflection, and subsequently through the profound [analysis] of overweening pride,
one should know that the distinctions of dependent origination are established by way of three characteristics.
First, arising from the past limit into the middle limit;
second, arising from the middle limit into the future limit;
third, having arisen in the middle limit, continuing to evolve and proceeding toward purification.
In this regard, how is it that from the prior limit the middle limit arises, and having arisen in the middle limit, it continues to evolve? It is as follows:
suppose there is a certain person.
Due to past lack of wisdom, with ignorance as a condition,
one performs and accumulates bodily, verbal, and mental actions— whether sinful, meritorious, or imperturbable. With these as conditions,
[the subsequent states arise].
Following the course of karma, consciousness continues uninterruptedly until the end of life,
serving as the cause for the consciousness that links rebirth in future lives;
thus it proceeds in succession.
There are internal and external cravings which,
at the time when consciousness produces its fruit,
can act as auxiliary companions.
It arises manifestly;
and once life has ended,
by virtue of causes from the prior limit.
In the present life,
one's own body is born; having been born,
it gradually develops within the mother’s womb.
With consciousness as a condition, the resultant consciousness arises in succession and continues without interruption,
maintaining all the stages of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) such as the kalala and so forth,
which become increasingly superior in each subsequent stage.
From the initial stage in the womb until old age and decay,
this very consciousness, at the moment it continues into a new birth,
is capable of bringing about the karma that induces rebirth and its resultant maturation.
The consciousness born of maturation,
moreover, proceeds by depending upon the continuity of name-and-form;
that is to say, it proceeds by depending upon the six bases, such as the eye and so forth.
For this reason, it is said that name-and-form conditions consciousness.
The five sense faculties that arise simultaneously are designated as "form."
That which is designated as "name" refers to the immediately preceding cessation [of mental states] and so forth; as appropriate,
it serves as the basis for the six consciousnesses.
Because consciousness relies upon them,
it continues to follow along repeatedly until the end of life.
Furthermore, the five material sense-faculties rely upon the primary elements as their basis.
The great elements at the sense bases,
the various forms produced by them,
and all other designations.
Because it maintains all the faculties and so forth,
causing them to fall into a continuous stream of transmigration without interruption,
these two together are collectively termed the "concomitant basis" (*anuvartaka-āśraya*).
For this reason, it is said that consciousness conditions name-and-form,
and name-and-form conditions consciousness;
in the present life, they proceed in mutual dependence like a bundle of reeds.
Thus it remains until the end of life;
this is called the dependent origination from the prior limit to the middle limit.
The various formations attain birth;
having been born within that intermediate state, they proceed accordingly.
It should be understood that this sequence of proceeding is explained here with reference to those born from a womb.
With the exception of those born from eggs or moisture while in the mother’s womb,
there are other distinct types of sentient beings with form who undergo apparitional birth within the desire and form realms.
At the time of initial birth, the sense faculties are complete,
distinguishing it from others;
this occurs in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
The consciousness of all sentient beings depends upon the seeds of name-and-form;
the seeds of name-and-form, in turn, evolve in dependence upon consciousness.
Because the seeds of form exist within that consciousness,
although form is interrupted, it shall arise again later;
such is the distinction herein.
By virtue of meritorious karma,
one is born into the two destinies of humans and devas within the desire realm;
by virtue of non-meritorious karma, one is born [into the lower realms].
One is born in the miserable realms due to [unwholesome] karma;
one is born in the form and formless realms due to immovable karma.
What is meant by the arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) through the conditions of the middle limit and the subsequent limit?
What is meant by their non-arising?
By virtue of this non-arising, one realizes purification.
That is to say, in this way, during the intermediate state,
a person (pudgala) is born and experiences the two fruits obtained from previous karma.
First, they experience the internal fruit of maturation;
second, they experience the dominant fruit consisting of sensations arising from objective spheres.
This is because they have heard incorrect teachings.
Alternatively, due to the power of habitual practice from previous lives,
one gives rise to delusion regarding two kinds of results.
This is because one is deluded regarding the internal result of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).
One cannot know, as it truly is, the suffering of future rebirth;
due to the predominant power of ignorance regarding the past and the future,
one performs and accumulates various formations (*saṃskāra*) as before.
Because consciousness is perfumed and transformed by these new karmas,
one proceeds according to those karmas within the present life.
Thus, with ignorance as a condition,
the formative forces arise; with the formative forces as a condition, [consciousness arises].
It causes consciousness to undergo transformation.
One should know that this consciousness, within the present life, possesses only the nature of a cause,
because it appropriates the fruits of all future consciousnesses that are yet to arise.
The six groups of consciousness are designated by way of their entire continuity.
Furthermore, this very consciousness is pursued by the seeds of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) that will exist in the future.
The seed of name-and-form is further followed by the seed of the six sense bases for future renewed existence.
The seed of the six sense bases...
Furthermore, it is followed by the seeds of all future contacts of subsequent existence;
these seeds of contact,
in turn, are followed by the seeds of all future feelings of subsequent existence.
One should know that this is called the cause for projecting future existence within the middle limit (*madhyānta*).
Because it can universally project all individual existences, with consciousness as the precursor and feeling as the final member.
Thus, having first projected a future existence through delusion regarding the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*),
one further [projects it] through the second type of delusion regarding the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) arising from objects.
Conditioned by the experience of objects, craving arises;
due to this craving,
one either seeks after various sensual desires.
Or they seek among the realms of existence;
furthermore, they grasp at the grasping of sensual desire,
or they grasp at the grasping of views, precepts and observances, and the doctrine of self.
Having grasped all that is to be grasped,
the craving and grasping combine to moisten the previously projected causes, causing them to evolve;
this is called "existence" (bhava).
Because this is subsumed under the cause of origination,
once this existence has ended immediately thereafter,
it proceeds exactly as projected by its projecting cause.
Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the first and sensation (*vedanā*) is the last;
they arise either gradually or in succession.
Or else they may arise all at once;
thus it should be understood regarding the present life.
Initially, with the sensation produced by contact associated with ignorance as a condition, craving arises;
with craving as a condition,
grasping subsequently arises.
With grasping as condition,
becoming comes to be;
with becoming as condition...
When birth arises,
because birth serves as the condition,
the various sufferings such as aging, illness, and death manifest in succession.
It should be understood that herein, in some cases the place of birth manifests,
while in other cases the seeds persist;
such is the case with ignorance as the condition for volitional formations during the intermediate state.
With feeling as condition, craving and so forth arise,
which produce the various formations (*saṃskāra*) of dependent origination pertaining to the future limit.
If, within the present life, one hears the Dharma from another...
Alternatively, having already accumulated the provisions in previous lives,
by means of those as causes,
one is able [to engage] with the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that possess the nature of two kinds of results.
One reflects correctly upon its cause, its cessation,
and the practice leading to its cessation.
By attending to that with correct mental attention and reflecting upon it,
right view arises.
Furthermore, they gradually attain the pure knowledge and vision of both the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) regarding the various truths.
By the power of such knowledge and vision,
they are able to completely and utterly sever ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Because those [defilements] have been abandoned,
one does not know, as they truly are,
the feelings produced by contact associated with ignorance that arise from those very objects of perception.
It is likewise abandoned accordingly.
Because of this abandonment,
within the present life...
Through the abandonment of ignorance, one realizes wisdom-liberation;
furthermore, there is the craving-affliction associated with the mind, which is concomitant with all feelings produced by contact with ignorance.
He also attains dissociation from that mind;
through the abandonment of craving,
he realizes the liberation of the mind.
Furthermore, precisely because that ignorance ceases,
when all forms of ignorance have not yet been severed, the formations (*saṃskāra*),
consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth up to sensation (*vedanā*) that would otherwise arise in relation to the future limit (*aparānta*) are all unable to arise.
It becomes a dharma that does not arise; therefore it is said:
"Because ignorance ceases."
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) cease accordingly;
in succession, up until the cessation of all contacts (*sparśa*) born of maturation (*vipāka*),
all feelings (*vedanā*) born of maturation cease accordingly.
Furthermore, in this present life, because ignorance ceases,
contact associated with ignorance ceases;
and because contact associated with ignorance has been eternally extinguished, [the subsequent links cease].
Feeling born of contact with ignorance ceases;
because all feelings born of contact with ignorance are forever extinguished,
craving also accordingly ceases.
Due to the cessation of craving,
as previously explained, all formations— beginning with grasping and ending with affliction—
are extinguished and become dharmas that do not arise.
In this present life, all such conditioned formations no longer circulate.
Because they do not circulate,
one dwells in this present life within the realm of nirvana with remainder.
This is called the realization of nirvana in the present life.
At that time, for him, consciousness conditions name-and-form,
and name-and-form conditions consciousness.
There are others that, though not yet extinguished, can be called pure and bright;
even as long as the conscious body remains and has not been extinguished,
they constantly experience feelings of dissociation.
There is no bondage;
that conscious body remains for as long as the lifespan projected by prior karma.
It abides in constant continuity;
when the lifespan is exhausted,
it is the appropriating consciousness that is able to maintain [the body].
Having relinquished the body they grasped,
they also relinquish the life-faculty;
from this point onward.
All life-faculties are extinguished without remainder and are entirely non-existent.
Furthermore, those various consciousnesses and all sensations,
within this state, [are likewise absent].
They cease spontaneously;
because their prior causes have ceased,
they do not continue further.
Nor is there any further cessation; by this principle,
it is called the realm of parinirvāṇa without remainder.
Because this is the ultimate, quiescent, and eternally abiding sublime track,
for this reason one constantly follows toward nirvāṇa.
Always taking nirvāṇa as its ultimate goal,
one has thoroughly cultivated the holy life under the Blessed One;
this is called the detailed exposition of dependent origination established by way of three characteristics.
That is to say: from the past limit there is the transition into the middle limit;
from that middle limit there is the transition into the future limit;
and furthermore, within the middle limit, there is the purification of the transition.
There are those in the world who lack wisdom;
for them, the new karma created in this present life is like a small tree of suffering.
If those people in the world lack wisdom...
Regarding those bases that are conducive to the outflows (*āsrava*),
one contemplates their gratification (*āsvāda*) based on the present life,
and develops deep attachment based on the past.
Relying on the future life with single-minded attachment,
and having thus remained,
all craving that had not been previously abandoned [arises].
Through repeated practice,
it increases further;
this is not the case for a wise person (pudgala).
Desiring that such a small tree in the future may further flourish and grow, one constantly irrigates it with the water of craving and attachment, so that—
as previously described— it may produce the fruits of grasping to be experienced in the future.
Gradually becoming fully perfected:
if there are learned noble disciples who,
though they have created small trees of contaminated karma that can induce future results, [they do not grow].
However, regarding those formations that accord with the afflictions,
he correctly contemplates their nature of arising and ceasing;
and regarding the cessation of desire and the realm of extinction, [he likewise contemplates them].
One observes this nature of tranquility without error;
by diminishing those karmas, one prevents them from increasing and causes even the waters of craving to completely evaporate.
The wise do not desire that which causes further growth;
they cut off craving at its root.
For craving conditions grasping and leads to ruin.
In this way, even a small tree that has already grown will eventually be made entirely non-existent;
how much more so one that is subsequently allowed to grow further?
Furthermore, there is another kind of person (pudgala).
All previously performed and accumulated karma conducive to experience in a subsequent life belonging to that already-arisen self-body is bound by it within the present life; thus,
both that very self-body and the previously performed karma conducive to experience in a subsequent life [are bound].
Taken together as one,
it is called "subsequent existence" (punarbhava), which is like a great tree of suffering.
This refers to those phenomena that are conducive to the various afflictions (kleśa).
Having remained thus, with the mind focused and attached as previously described,
his previously created karma to be experienced in a future life [arises].
Just as vertical roots cause a tree to grow lush and dense,
so too do those afflictions of craving in the present life act like lateral channels that provide moisture to the tree.
With this as the cause,
it causes the all-seed consciousness— concomitant with afflictions, karma, and formations—
to continue its succession at the time of rebirth in a future life.
Abiding in name-and-form,
the tree of suffering is thus established for a long duration;
one should know that such is the case for this person (pudgala).
This is intended to cause the tree of suffering to flourish and spread further.
Herein, the "white category" (śuklapakṣa) should be understood as previously described.
Furthermore, when the Blessed One was formerly a bodhisattva, he...
Having abandoned all previously acquired mundane paths and worldly teachers,
he sat upon the seat of enlightenment,
taking as his primary motive the desire to compassionately benefit other sentient beings.
Having initiated correct observation regarding the truths,
at that time, desiring to examine the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya) in detail,
[one does so] because the member of old age and death is subsumed within the truth of suffering.
One should understand that, when observing the dependent origination in reverse order,
one examines old age and death correctly by means of three aspects.
First, by observing subtle causes and conditions;
second, by observing coarse causes and conditions;
third, by observing that [the result] is not indeterminate.
The causal conditions for the arising of sensation are also called "arising," and the very essence of that which arises is likewise called "arising."
The preceding birth is subtle,
while the subsequent birth is coarse;
herein, because one observes the existence of the subtle preceding birth, there is old age and death.
One also contemplates that old age and death exist due to the condition of subsequent coarse birth;
future old age and death have subtle birth as their cause,
while present-old-age-and-death have coarse birth as their cause.
What is meant by "not non-determinate"? It refers to the fact that,
apart from those two types of birth-entities included within the specific place of birth,
nothing else is determinately capable of producing the fruit of old age and death.
Just as one contemplates old age and death,
so too should one contemplate birth, existence, grasping,
and craving, each through two kinds of correct observation.
One should know that it is likewise so.
This is called the principle of dependent origination regarding the two truths of suffering and its origin, observed in reverse order starting from old age and death.
It should be understood that herein lies the method for the truth of the origin.
It is like the wick of a lamp;
this very truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) is like the oil,
while the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) is analogous to the lamp.
Those individuals who lack wisdom are like one who pours oil and gathers wicks;
thus the lamp of suffering burns for a long time.
It should be understood that the white category is the opposite of this;
namely, skillful means consisting in the contemplation of the truths of cessation and the path.
Furthermore, there are two types of persons.
What are these two?
First, practicing only that which is not beneficial to oneself;
that is, merely collecting the wick and pouring oil for one's own lamp.
First, one causes a single lamp of suffering to continue and endure for a long time;
second, there is another person who simultaneously practices for the sake of immeasurable multitudes, both themselves and others.
This is not a beneficial practice;
it serves only to ignite the great mass of fire of suffering for oneself and others,
preceded by the grasping and listening to false teachings.
The wrong conduct induced by the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation is, for example,
like a collection of dry firewood, dry grass, and dry cow dung;
by reason of these causes and conditions, [it burns].
It causes the mass of the fire of suffering to blaze for a long time without interruption.
Furthermore, when the World-Honored One was formerly a bodhisattva, he...
Seated upon the bodhi-maṇḍa,
he enters the gateway of dependent origination in reverse order;
first, he correctly contemplates the truth of suffering, from old age and death back as far as craving, with respect to the future limit.
Having thus observed the truth of suffering in the future limit and the truth of the origin of all suffering in the future limit,
he was not yet satisfied;
he then further observed the present manifold sufferings subsumed under the causal conditions of the truth of the origin in the future limit.
That is to say, one contemplates feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, and consciousness in their entirety and in reverse order.
It should be understood that among these,
contemplating future suffering constitutes the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya).
Observing that the cause of their accumulation is itself the truth of accumulation (*samudaya-satya*),
one observes by whom the truth of accumulation of suffering in future lives exists;
one knows it arises with consciousness produced from prior accumulation as its limit.
Since one already knows that the existence of suffering in the present life arises from previous accumulations,
one should not further investigate how it comes to be.
Therefore, when the World-Honored One was formerly a bodhisattva,
he contemplated all future suffering and its accumulation,
contemplating present suffering as well, even down to the mental consciousness associated with attention.
Then, turning back again,
he further gradually contemplates the basis for the truth of origination in the future limit,
which is the locus where the truth of suffering in the future limit depends.
One should know that this is precisely the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) regarding the future limit (*aparānta*).
Thus, up to consciousness, one again proceeds in accordance with the ascending order.
In this way, one correctly contemplates dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)—both in its forward and reverse sequences—as suffering and its origination.
Immediately following this, in order to contemplate the Truth of Cessation,
one enters the sequence in reverse order, beginning from old age and death,
down to ignorance.
Why is this? Because one observes in this way:
how can the present truth of suffering be completely extinguished in its entirety?
This means that because one does not perform new karmic formations conditioned by ignorance, one thus surveys the three noble truths.
Having done so, one next further seeks: "By what path and by what practice can this noble truth of cessation be realized?"
By means of the recollection of past lives as previously described,
one recalls how, in the past, for the sake of seeking the permanent exhaustion of all outflows, one cultivated right view in the world; then,
following the instructions of a teacher, one brings this to mind and reflects in this way.
I have now realized the ancient, original right path traversed by the seers of antiquity;
thus, by means of mundane attention alone,
I have contemplated the Four Noble Truths.
Furthermore, through right view, one enters into the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the truths;
by means of the sequential application of skillful means, one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*),
and through the skillful means of direct vision, one attains the untainted, pure, and excellent knowledge and vision of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
For the sake of this purpose,
throughout three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas,
one practices all the difficult-to-perform deeds.
Now, I have fully realized all these meanings for the sake of benefiting others and out of compassion for the world of humans and devas.
For those who are capable of entering the noble Dharma,
he opens the four noble truths so that they may give rise to perfect awakening.
Furthermore, the teaching of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is subsumed within three points.
What are the three?
First, the excellent establishment that all dependently originated phenomena are devoid of agency;
second, that these serve as the basis for the practice of benefiting others.
Third, because it serves as the basis for practice for one's own benefit:

herein, the well-established teaching that dependently arisen phenomena are devoid of agency refers to the contemplation of the origin of suffering in the prior limit of the present life by way of retrogressive observation from the subsequent limit of suffering.
Name-and-form conditions consciousness,
and consciousness conditions name-and-form;
it is like a bundle of reeds that stand and remain upright by mutually supporting one another.
Among these, all dependently originated phenomena are neither self-made nor made by another.
It is not created by self or by another;
it does not arise without cause.
Thus is it designated.
It is called "well-established" because all dependently arisen phenomena lack functional agency. Why is this?
Because impermanent conditioned formations have no prior limit.
Because there is no future limit,
and because although there is a middle limit, it exists for only a single moment,
there is the movement and transformation of functional activity.
From the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), nothing exists at all;
it is only by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) that things are provisionally designated. Such is the designation.
It is according to reality and without error;
therefore, this is called "well-established.
It is precisely based upon such a well-established nature.
Relying on dependent origination, one proclaims the teaching of the Noble Truths for others;
this is called relying on the practice of benefiting others.
This very [practice] serves as the basis for one’s own ability to enter into the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Noble Truths.
Furthermore, one who practices in accordance with the Dharma can also realize *nirvāṇa* in the present life;
it should be understood that this is called the practice for one's own benefit based upon that [Dharma].
Moreover, there are the assemblies of disciples who have previously accumulated the provisions for wisdom.
Because they have accomplished sharp, innate wisdom,
they are called "intelligent";
because they possess the knowledge of the teachings, they are called "wise."
It is called "clearly understood" because it is endowed with realized wisdom;
it is called "well-tamed" because of this realization.
Because he has personally realized the Dharma without depending on others,
it is called fearlessness;
because he has realized Nirvana as it truly is, it is called fearlessness.
It is called "seeing the nectar" because it takes the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising as its basis,

He is named Śariputra;
he has realized the sublime realm of deathless nectar and dwells therein in full perfection.
Furthermore, there are certain foolish followers of external paths who,

thus, by means of the mundane path, one becomes free from desire for the realm of desire.
Although they have detached from the desires of the form realm up to the Peak of Existence,
one should know that they are still said to be "not yet liberated" with respect to the body. Why is this?
Because within each respective meditative absorption attained,
one polishes that consciousness and grasps it as a self,
remaining therein in a state of affliction.
Furthermore, at a later time, when their lifespan and karma are exhausted,
they fall back and are reborn below because they lack skillfulness regarding dependent origination.
Although the noble disciples have attained skillfulness regarding dependent origination,
they nevertheless contemplate only the subtle impermanence of the body composed of the four great elements.
One does not immediately observe the impermanent nature of consciousness.
Why is this? Because the body composed of the four great elements is observed to persist for a long duration with a characteristic of permanence.
Because its momentary similarity and continuous succession are difficult to perceive,
the impermanent nature of consciousness is perceived as a coarse and manifest characteristic.
From moment to moment, its objects of perception are easily abandoned,
because its characteristics undergo transformations of immeasurable categories and distinctions;
thus, although this very consciousness possesses the characteristic of impermanence.
Although it consists of immeasurable varieties and is coarse, manifest,
and easy to perceive, it is nevertheless called "most extremely subtle," because its nature is difficult to discern.
Because it is difficult to enter.
Why is this? Because it is an object perceived solely by the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
The body composed of the four great elements undergoes increase and decrease, as well as relinquishment and acquisition;
its impermanent nature is already irrational even within the range of the physical eye,
let alone for other eyes that possess skill in the analysis of dependent origination.
Furthermore, when the noble disciples wish to penetrate the most subtle impermanence of consciousness,
they reflect correctly upon dependent origination;
for they are able to discern the distinct states of the various feelings that arise from contact within their own continuum.
He is then able to realize the impermanent nature of consciousness.
Having accomplished such wisdom and vision,
he gradually [turns his attention] toward the body that serves as the basis for feeling.
One is able to cultivate weary detachment toward all contacts that serve as causes,
as well as all other formations subsumed under the category of "name," thereby giving rise to resolute conviction and attaining liberation.
Because they have attained liberation,
they abide securely in the two realms of nirvana— both with remainder and without remainder.
Furthermore, regarding a bhikṣu who is skillful in the dharma of dependent origination:
By means of three aspects,
one is able to correctly contemplate and rightly bring an end to suffering throughout the three periods of time.
What are the three characteristics?
First, the basis of suffering;
second, the causal conditions of suffering.
The three bases that serve as the causes and conditions for suffering are called the three characteristics.
What are the three time periods?
First, the intermediate limit;
second, the past limit;
third, the future limit.
These are called the three time periods.
It should be understood that herein, the internal body is the basis for suffering;
it is the locus where the various distinctions of suffering, such as cold and heat, as well as disease and death, arise in the present life.
For what reason?
Because it is due to the existence of this that they can arise within their supporting bodies.
Maternal relatives, such as maternal grandparents and their kin,
constitute the support for experiencing suffering;
they hold swords and staves to serve as his rear guard.
It is the locus for the various distinctions of suffering, such as sorrow, lamentation, and so forth. Why?
Because it is as previously explained.
These two types of bases, which are grasped through their functioning, have craving as their cause.
Because they arise from craving that resembles the origin [of suffering],
they are called the causal conditions for suffering.
Furthermore, this very craving arises only by depending upon and taking as its basis objects that are pleasant and of exquisite form;
these are called the basis for the causal conditions of suffering.
Furthermore, all present objects of experience,
caused by the heat and affliction of the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion, give rise to parching thirst;
it is because of this that one drinks.
It is like a delicious drink mixed with poison,
which, though its color is exquisite and its flavor sweet,
one cannot bring oneself to abandon.
Thirst increases further;
because of thirst,
there is a basis for future existence.
Because there will be dependence in the future,
there will consequently be manifold sufferings;
thus should it be known.
From the perspective of ultimate truth,
it is called "tending toward death";
that is, by means of such present principles.
One should understand the principle of going and coming;
it should be known that this is called correctly deliberating upon the limits of the past and the future.
Furthermore, this is based upon four kinds of discourse.
One should know that all bases consist of the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The two types of verbal expression—what is seen and what is known—are based on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
the verbal expression of realization is based on inference (*anumāna*).
If one hears the teachings based on the authority of the scriptures,
one should furthermore correctly apply diligent effort to investigate dependent origination through five aspects.
It can exhaust all suffering and bring about the end of suffering.
What are these five?
First, observing the causal conditions for the arising of all dependently originated phenomena.
Second, observing the causes and conditions for that cessation;
third, knowing as it truly is the correct practice that leads to that cessation;
fourth, practicing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
Fifth is being free from overweening pride regarding realization.
This is called the thorough cultivation of investigation and the fulfillment of its fruit,
beginning from future suffering based on causes and conditions.
In reverse order, up to consciousness being conditioned by name-and-form,
one observes, penetrates, and cultivates right practice through four aspects.
That is to say, one examines the future by means of two characteristics:
because the cause exists, the effect exists;
because the cause is absent, the effect is absent.
Having observed thus, one penetrates the non-existence of causes;
having penetrated this through the practice of correct application, one subsequently practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, one correctly observes that within this present life,
because there exist the causal factors of new karma— meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable— conditioned by ignorance,
there likewise exist the results thereof, such as consciousness and so forth, which follow upon meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable karmic formations.
Because that does not exist,
this also does not exist.
Having thus investigated, [one realizes this].
As previously explained regarding thorough penetration and correct practice;
at the time of correct practice:
Because they do not create new karma conditioned by ignorance,
their karma is quickly transformed and cast off upon contact;
thus, within this very life, they realize the noble path as previously directly perceived.
Regarding the fruit of the path, nirvāṇa:
at that time, he is like a potter who raises the fire of the afflictions and the heat of the latent tendencies (anuśaya).
He places those with consciousness— like bodies steaming within a heated cauldron—
upon the shore of Nirvana, which is supremely cool,
so that they may be freed from the steaming heat of all afflictions.
Furthermore, one should cause the body, which is like a clay vessel and is comprised of consciousness, to obtain coolness by relying [on it].
It should be understood that this is as previously described regarding the experience of all feelings pertaining to the limits of the body,
and so forth, in detail.
Until they have relinquished their life, they always abide in a state of constant stability;
they never fall away from the fruit of arhatship,
nor can they produce formations conditioned by ignorance.
How is there freedom from overweening pride regarding realization?
It means that at that time, one has accomplished a sublime, virtuous, and pure knowledge and vision that takes dependent origination as its object,
and reflects as follows:
According to ultimate truth, there is no cyclic existence and no nirvana;
there is only the arising of this or that phenomenon.
Because this or that phenomenon arises, it causes this or that phenomenon to arise;
because this or that phenomenon ceases,
it causes this or that phenomenon to cease.
Furthermore, there are briefly two types of those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*):
first, those with overweening pride regarding those in training (*śaikṣa*);
second, those with overweening pride regarding those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
If there is one who has not yet attained the state of a learner (śaikṣa) but possesses overweening pride (adhimāna), they say to others:
"I have crossed over doubt and have permanently severed the three fetters (saṃyojana)."
Regarding the liberation of one in training that I have realized,
I am free from doubt and have extracted the arrow of poison.
Having already permanently severed all speculative views rooted in the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
if there is one who possesses overweening pride (*abhimāna*) regarding the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*),
he says to others:
I have no superior.
Whatever tasks were to be performed and whatever matters were to be resolved,
I have accomplished them all.
These two types [of teachings] are based either on dependent origination or on nirvana.
Furthermore, when speaking based on the teachings of the Noble Ones,
it refers to explaining matters such as the profound emptiness that transcends the world, the nature of conditions, and the forward and reverse order of dependent origination.
They are unable to comprehend what has been taught and do not follow it through to realization;
for these two kinds of causes and conditions.
They give rise to doubt regarding the awakening to reality as it is,
and they also harbor hesitation regarding the permanent severance of afflictions within their own continuum and the realization of nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because those trainees who possess overweening pride conceive of a self and what belongs to a self.
Constantly pursued and entering along with the mental application (*manasikāra*),
subtle *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") operates continuously,
both intermittently and incessantly, such that it cannot be fully discerned.
Furthermore, śamatha sustains the continuity [of the mind],
preventing coarse afflictions and ensuring that it is not distracted or disordered.
For this reason, regarding that which has not yet been attained,
he conceives the notion that it has already been attained; and regarding that which has not yet been guarded,
[he conceives the notion that it has been guarded].
Having given rise to the perception of protection,
he then informs others;
furthermore, regarding those who possess overweening pride concerning the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
He says to himself:
"I have attained tranquility;
I have attained nirvana."
"I have already abandoned craving; I have already abandoned grasping.
Yet, regarding these subtle manifestations that have not yet been severed, I am unable to fully comprehend my own overweening pride."
Regarding what has not yet been attained, they conceive the thought that it has already been attained;
regarding what has not yet been guarded, they conceive the thought that it has already been guarded,
and then announce this to others.
Furthermore, regarding those who possess overweening pride (*adhimāna*) toward the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*),
it should be known that they have certainly first given rise to overweening pride toward the state of learning (*śaikṣa*);
there is no actual reality [to their claim].
Those who are still in training develop overweening pride toward those beyond training. Why is this so?
It is not that the afflictions manifest within his continuum;
rather, such entanglements remain firmly established in his mind.
For this reason:
Regarding what has not yet been attained, one gives rise to the notion that it has already been attained;
conceiving such overweening pride,
one remains for a long time in firm attachment.
Or they inform others that they have merely experienced a lapse of mindfulness and the manifestation of minor, temporary afflictions.
He then swiftly attains thorough penetration and is able to distance himself from it.
Furthermore, this occurs either because he previously harbored overweening pride (*abhimāna*) regarding the attainment of what had not yet been attained,
or because he now gives rise to doubt concerning what has been attained.
Because hesitation ruins the mind,
one gives rise to sorrow and distress,
and reflects as follows:
If that which I have realized were non-existent,
then that which others have realized would also be non-existent;
thus, one would give rise to the false view of slandering the noble ones.
One undergoes the causes for rebirth in the evil realms and incurs great ruin. How is it that,
as previously stated by the Noble Ones, this is so profound?
That is to say, it is able to reveal and demonstrate profound dependent origination,
ultimate nirvana,
and the distinctions between the essential natures of the conditioned and the unconditioned as they correspond to the three characteristics.
Conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
unconditioned phenomena are eternally abiding.
All conditioned formations are suffering.
Nirvāṇa is tranquility;
all conditioned phenomena are collectively nothing but suffering and nothing but the cause of suffering.
All unconditioned phenomena are simply the total and permanent cessation of all suffering and its causes.
If any bhikṣus...
One who attains nirvana in the present life forever severs the path that is the cause of all suffering in future existence,
ensuring that all resultant suffering in future lives shall ultimately never recur.
When entering parinirvāṇa without remainder,
subsequent suffering does not continue;
as for the present basis of suffering projected by prior causes, it ceases.
They cease spontaneously,
reaching the limit of suffering; herein,
there is absolutely no one who previously transmigrated.
Furthermore, there is no one who attains parinirvāṇa at this present time.
If one can elucidate such meanings and words,
it should be known as the profound holy teaching as previously described.
Furthermore, although the nature of dependent origination is extremely profound,
there is one [teaching] that can reveal it and render it shallow;
this should be known by way of two causes and conditions.
First, because the Great Teacher has skillfully revealed [the path];
second, because this very person possesses a subtle, thorough, sharp, and far-reaching wisdom.
Whether speaking or listening,
these meanings of the phrases should be understood as they were previously presented in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.
It should be understood that, in this context,
the phenomena of dependent origination are most profoundly deep by way of four aspects.
What are these four?
First, because its subtle causes and effects are difficult to comprehend;
second, because selflessness is difficult to comprehend;
and third, because it is difficult to comprehend how sentient beings who are already free from fetters can still be bound.
Fourth, because it is difficult to understand how sentient beings who are bound become liberated from their fetters.
How is the subtle cause and effect difficult to understand?
It refers to the investigation based on the principle of the Noble Truths.
From old age and death back to consciousness, regarding all the links of existence (*bhava-aṅga*) that have name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as their condition:
what is the essential nature of that which has existence as its condition? What is meant by "the essential nature of that which has existence as its condition"?
This means that because the causes and conditions for arising within this [existence] have not been permanently severed,
there is the arising of arising.
Once birth has already occurred,
one can only await subsequent aging and death;
it should be understood that the causal conditions for this birth are also termed "birth."
That which arises through causes and conditions is also called "birth.
Because there is prior birth,
there is subsequent birth.
Because there is future birth,
there is old age and death;
herein, prior birth is the cause of future birth.
It is also the condition for aging and death;
that which arises subsequently is exclusively the condition for aging and death.
Thus, all these are subsumed as one.
Briefly stated, this is called "birth as the condition for aging-and-death.
It should be understood that this is the nature of the first link, aging-and-death, having birth as its condition.
As it was explained regarding the link of birth, so it is here.
It should be understood that the establishment of the members of existence (*bhava-aṅga*) and the members of grasping (*upādāna-aṅga*) is likewise.
As for the distinction regarding grasping:
That is to say, undifferentiated desire and greed are called "clinging" (*upādāna*).
There are four established distinctions of this clinging.

Third, the causes for the abiding of consciousness within the stations of consciousness,

fourth, the causes of defilement in the present life and future lives.
This refers to all outflows (*āsrava*).
The five causes of purification refer to the truths (*satya*) and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
If one truly understands the intrinsic nature of these various causes as being their very nature,
regarding these causal conditions...

and when the causal condition ceases,

To understand, as it truly is, that the path leading to cessation is indeed the true path,

One contemplates dependently arisen phenomena, up to and including ignorance as their limit;
beyond this, there is no further cause for dependent origination.
One contemplates that it is solely by means of this.
The contemplation of one's own welfare is ultimate.
Furthermore, briefly stated, there are three kinds within this present life.
It is true cessation;
until the lifespan has permanently ceased,
it continues to evolve in constant succession as the objective sphere of what is known.
When one is practicing correctly as a learner (śaikṣa),
the state of being a learner is designated;
regarding those who are beyond learning (aśaikṣa), one reflects in this way.
"I have exhausted all things and shall never again be subject to exhaustion.
Because this is the discernment resulting from the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*),
it is called "discernment of dharmas" (*dharmapravicaya*).
What are the three?
First, the six sense bases;
second, contact conditioned by the six sense bases.
Contact conditions feeling.
It should be understood that herein,
all those noble disciples who are well-versed in the teachings [proceed as follows].
Whatever he experiences,
he thoroughly knows that very experience as it truly is;
furthermore, he develops disenchantment toward it.
Desiring to extinguish [suffering], one diligently practices the correct application;
furthermore, one is able to know, as it truly is, that those feelings are produced by contact,

One then applies oneself diligently to the cultivation of right practice in order to become weary of, detached from, and to bring to cessation that contact which is the cause for drawing forth the six sense bases;
furthermore, one does so regarding those feelings, contacts, and six sense bases.
All real entities are briefly subsumed into one:
knowing that all things perish through impermanence is called the "dharma of cessation."
Having already, within this present life,
cultivated revulsion, dispassion, and cessation toward all these three kinds of entities that are impermanent and subject to extinction, as previously practiced.
By means of this correct practice,
one is said to be "constantly and diligently trained";
furthermore, it is by virtue of cultivating this correct practice that [this designation applies].
There is no further effort to be made;
one is ultimately liberated.
Therefore, it is called the constant and diligent discernment of dharmas.
Desiring to realize that which has never before been attained and never before realized,
one practices with uninterrupted and earnest application.
This is called "constant and diligent training," so that one may never fall away from any dwelling in happiness in the present life.
It is practiced without interruption and practiced with earnestness; for this reason,
it is called the "constant and diligent discernment of phenomena" (*dharmapravicaya-sātatyasatkṛtya*).
The collection of names, phrases, and syllables that predominate in the exposition of all phenomena and events is called the *dharmadhātu*,
because those who attain it acquire the unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Because they possess mastery over the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables according to their will,
they are said to have "skillfully penetrated the dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*);
this is due to their thorough penetration of the dharma-realm.
Regarding this very meaning of "true perception," one further explains it through various other names according to one's preference,
distinguishing it in diverse ways.
Furthermore, for as long as seven days and nights, or even exceeding that duration,
their eloquence remains inexhaustible through such various and distinct categories.
He explains it as it truly is:
that is conditioned, produced by volition, and subject to fluctuation;
