...and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this applies to all Arhats who possess full realization.
Briefly, there are six kinds of explanatory formulations regarding what is understood:
first, the explanatory formulation with alternative modes;
second, the explanatory formulation without alternative modes.
Third, the prediction concerning the three types of knowledge;
fourth, the prediction concerning abandonment;
fifth, the general prediction.
Sixth, the specific explanation.
Regarding the "explanation by way of another method":
this refers to when someone else poses a question.
Alternatively, it may have been recorded in this way spontaneously because he wished to cause others to generate great reverence for the Buddha’s holy teaching;
thus he declared:
"At this time, I have not a single doubt."
Regarding the prediction without alternative formulations:
it refers to making this declaration:
"My births have been exhausted."
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding the analytical discernment of knowledge (*jñāna-vyākaraṇa*):
it refers to when someone asks a question, saying:
By what knowledge and by what vision does he,
once birth has been exhausted, declare: "It is so"?
Because the conditions for birth have been exhausted,
that birth has already ceased;
such is its characteristic.
The declaration of one's own knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), which is comprised within the wisdom of excellent liberation,
is called the "declaration of knowledge" (*jñānavyākaraṇa*).
Furthermore, it is precisely regarding this that there is a specific declaration.
That is to say, he specifically explains that those [sufferings] exist due to causes and conditions;
furthermore, he specifically explains the various graspings (*upādāna*) which are the causes and conditions for their arising;
and furthermore, he specifically explains the characteristics of these various graspings.
Because of knowing things as they truly are and seeing them as they truly are,
grasping ceases to exist.
Regarding the summary exposition:
it refers to the realization that all sensations whatsoever within this entire range of what has been explained are suffering.
Having understood this, one causes that birth to be exhausted;
a response given in this manner is called a "comprehensive answer" (saṃkṣipta-vyākaraṇa).
Regarding the analytical explanation of cessation:
it means that precisely because of that internal liberation,
all causes and conditions for craving are completely exhausted.
An answer given in this manner is called a categorical response.
This categorical response—
Just as previously stated regarding specific predictions,
this general prediction should be understood as being comprised, in brief, of three modes of manifestation.
This means: "Regarding all the fetters spoken of by the Bhagavat, I have none of them.
This is called the first general declaration of abandonment.
This means that all fetters have been permanently severed.
Furthermore, I abide in such right mindfulness;
because I abide in this right mindfulness, [I am thus established].
That all greed, sorrow, and evil unwholesome states can be made such that they never again leak into the mind—
this is called the second general summary of abandonment,
namely, because of constant abiding.
Furthermore, within this state, one is personally free from pride;
this is called the third summary statement of abandonment,
meaning that there is no longer any remaining overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Thus, in summary, there are six types of prophetic declarations (*vyākaraṇa*).
Furthermore, there are three kinds of phenomena that are beloved and desired by all the world.
It is explained in terms of the internal: first, power;
second, exquisite form.
Third is lifespan. Furthermore,
there are factors that contradict and harm these three dharmas,
which can induce three corresponding discordant states that are undesirable.
First, illness;
second, old age;
third, premature death.
If one engages in wrong practice regarding the three trainings,
one will be incapable of transcending illness, old age, and untimely death; however,
if one engages in right practice regarding the three trainings, [one will be capable].
One is then able to transcend these three matters.
What are the three trainings?
First, the training in higher ethical discipline (adhiśīla-śikṣā).
Second is the training in higher mind;
third is the training in higher wisdom.
What is meant by engaging in various wrong practices based upon the training in higher ethical discipline?
That is to say, there is someone who,
having committed a transgression among those things that should be avoided during their initial training,
feels no sense of shame whether reflecting upon themselves or others.
Having thus settled into a state devoid of shame,
one fails to exercise restraint regarding all evil and unwholesome states.
Having failed to protect themselves regarding those teachings,
they have likewise failed to arouse reverence for the Buddha,
the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and toward all the trainings, instructions, and admonitions.
They have no sense of reverence or caution.
Due to these causes and conditions,
if others should offer them proper admonition or censure regarding this matter, [they do not accept it].
They are unable to endure what is said by others,
yet they themselves remain silent and do not speak with them; however,
regarding what is appropriate and what is inappropriate, they are able to properly admonish and rebuke individuals.
They detest, reject,
and avoid those who practice unwholesome conduct, yet they draw near to and associate with those whose ways are identical to their own.
They dwell together in harmony; yet,
because they dwell in harmony with evil companions,
they even give rise to aversion toward the noble ones.
How much more so when one actually goes there to personally pay respects and behold him;
even if one were to go there and preach the True Dharma for them,
they would reject it because of their hatred toward the Noble One.
Yet they do not wish to hear it;
even if they momentarily lend an ear, their minds lack respectful compliance.
They harbor only opposition and contention, and do not seek understanding.
Yet, regarding the treatises on wisdom that analyze right practice by distinguishing between what is possible and what is impossible,
they take no pleasure in abiding therein;
this is because they harbor a mind of contention within.
Although they have heard it,
they do not believe or accept it,
nor do they practice in accordance with it.
Furthermore, the noble ones remain silent and do not converse with him,
thinking: "A practitioner such as this is incapable of being spoken to, nor can he be instructed or exhorted."
Since they are naturally devoid of self-restraint and are abandoned by the noble ones,
their inner minds are never tranquil.
They dwell with their bodies, speech, and minds in a state of vulgar confusion;
they are violent, malicious, greedy, garrulous, and arrogant,
and they fail to perceive the faults and transgressions inherent in such behavior.
Having committed many transgressions and failing to repent in accordance with the Dharma,
through the force of habitual practice,
they gradually come to violate all of their ethical discipline (*śīla*).
It should be understood that this is called engaging in various wrong practices based upon the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*). Conversely,
it should be understood that what is contrary to this constitutes engaging in right practice based upon the training in higher ethical discipline.
What is meant by engaging in various wrong practices based on the training in higher mental states (*adhicitta-śikṣā*)?
It refers to acting contrary to correct principle when moving about,
grasping at the signs and secondary characteristics of objects.
Due to these causes and conditions,
deluded thoughts arise;
one consequently fails to perceive the faults and afflictions within them.
Once afflictions have arisen, one clings to them firmly and does not relinquish them;
by reason of this, one dwells in a state of lack of clear comprehension.
Or, while dwelling in a secluded place without a second person,
one may dwell with forgetfulness and lack of clear comprehension as a basis,
causing the mind to wander outwardly.
This is called engaging in various wrong practices based on the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*).
One should know that the opposite of this constitutes the right practice based on the training in higher mind.
What is meant by relying on the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*) to give rise to various wrong practices?
It refers, for example, to someone who stays far away from the noble ones (*ārya*).
Relying on evil friends,
hearing the incorrect Dharma,
and taking resolute conviction as the cause.
It is not as good as investigating all phenomena through correct reasoning,
yet instead taking pleasure in the practice of various evil desires and evil views.
Or, regarding the subtle Dharma attained through the vast training,
one disparages oneself.
This is called engaging in wrong conduct based on the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).
The opposite of this should be understood as the correct practice arising from reliance upon the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).
Among these, there is the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana-pudgala*).
Based on such misconduct arising within these three types of training,
one lacks the capacity to transcend the stage of ordinary beings or to enter correctly into the state of rightness and separation from corruption.
One must permanently sever the three fetters;
because one has not permanently severed these three types of fetters,
one lacks the capacity to rely upon the path of cultivation to attain arhatship.
In this present life, one permanently and completely abandons all afflictions, such as greed, hatred, and delusion, without remainder;
and one transcends future illness, aging, and premature death.
The opposite of this should be understood as the authentic and correct practice of all wholesome factors (*śukla-dharma*) within the three trainings.
To speak at length, up until:
they transcend future illness, aging, and premature death.
Furthermore, if there is a bhikṣu.
Possessing pure ethical discipline (*śīla*),
he abides in the pure restraint of the Prātimokṣa;
this is due to the superior power of the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*).
Relying upon the superior samādhi included within the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna,
and by the predominant power of the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).
One attains the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna) and the knowledge of nirvāṇa (nirvāṇa-jñāna).
Taking these two knowledges as a basis,
one first proceeds by means of four kinds of perfection.
When one turns away from the training of the precepts,
the mind is liberated from all afflictions,
and one attains arhatship.
One achieves liberation through wisdom.
In this context, what is meant by "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*)?
It refers to someone as follows:
Having heard and followed the unerring teaching on dependent origination through conditions,
they abide in the stage of ordinary beings regarding the causal states of dependently arisen formations.
One is then able to reflect upon it correctly through the mental attention (*manasikāra*) consisting of hearing,
reflection, and cultivation;
by means of sublime wisdom, one awakens to and gains conviction that suffering is truly suffering.
Origination is truly origination;
cessation is truly cessation;
the path is truly the path.
All such sublime wisdom as is established within the Dharma according to its causes and effects is called "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*).
Furthermore, what is called "knowledge of nirvāṇa"?
That is to say, it is the very nature of those phenomena that,
regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation,
and the path, one employs sublime wisdom.
When one realizes and enters into the conviction that these are truly the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation,
and the path, one then dwells with a perception of revulsion toward suffering and its origin,
and gives rise to a perception of tranquility toward cessation and nirvana.
That which is called ultimate tranquility and subtlety,
the relinquishing of all bases for birth and death,
and so forth, as extensively explained.
Thus, relying upon that knowledge of abiding in those phenomena,
and based on suffering or the causal conditions of suffering,
one dwells in the perception of revulsion.
One is then able to enter into and gain faith-understanding in nirvāṇa through sublime wisdom for the sake of tranquility and so forth;
such is sublime knowledge.
It is called the wisdom of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
those who are wise and discerning...
When one correctly contemplates these six kinds of perfection,
one is fully capable of manifesting and initiating diligent effort and abiding [in it].
What are called the six kinds of perfection?
First, the perfection of the Great Master;
second, the perfection of the holy teachings;
third, the perfection of the ease with which one enters the holy teachings.
Fourth, the perfection of having realized one’s own supreme goal;
fifth, the perfection of teaching everything in accordance with reality without interruption;
sixth, the perfection of possessing authoritative speech that is about to be completed.
What is meant by the "perfection of the Great Teacher"?
It refers to the Tathāgatas' accomplishment of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth;
this is called the perfection of the Great Teacher.
What is meant by the "perfection of the noble teaching"?
It refers to declaring for oneself:
"I have now attained the exalted position of the Great Sage."
He is able to turn the Brahma-wheel and,
amidst the great assembly, roar the true lion’s roar,
revealing all such matters as dependent origination in its forward and reverse order, as well as cessation and nirvāṇa.
This is called the "perfection of the noble teaching.
What is meant by the "perfection of the noble teaching being easy to enter"?
It refers to all the words and phrases of this noble teaching.
Their nature is luminous and their meaning is profound;
because this sacred teaching is able to correctly elucidate all profound meanings,
it is said that the nature of its words and phrases is luminous and their meaning is profound.
This is called the "easily accessible and perfectly complete holy teaching.
What is meant by "attaining the unsurpassed perfection of one's own goal"?
It means that there is no śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa [who has attained it].
Regarding the Tathāgata,
his supreme attainment consists in the perfect awakening to penetrative wisdom; therefore,
with respect to others who have realized their own welfare and the goals they ought to attain, [he acts as their teacher].
Regarding the meaning that should be realized,
only the Dharma teachings spoken by the Tathāgata are supreme and unsurpassed.
If one transcends this, the path of verbal expression is cut off;
this is called attaining the unsurpassed, perfect fulfillment of one's own purpose.
What is meant by the "perfect fulfillment of teaching everything in accordance with reality without interruption"?
This refers to the Dharma teachings expounded by all Tathāgatas,
which universally reveal the non-erroneous for all humans and devas,
and reveal all phenomena.
Without acting as a teacher who conceals [the truth],
there is no withholding of the opening instruction.
This is called the complete and perfect teaching of everything in accordance with reality without interruption.
What is meant by "possessing the noble speech that is about to be perfected"?
It refers to that which is capable of severing all doubts and giving rise to all roots of virtue.
The great faith that is the basis for all wholesome dharmas,
which can be directly perceived as a place of secure footing where the Great Teacher is present before one—
this is called possessing the authoritative word (*āptavāda*) that is about to become fully complete.
Those who are wise correctly contemplate these six as complete and perfect;
they are presently sufficient to inspire the application of diligent effort and abide therein.
Among the three trainings,
one practices yoga by relying on the training in higher ethics,
and practices heedfulness by relying on the training in higher mind.
Relying on superior wisdom, one practices the yoga of meditation within the Teacher’s instruction;
should there be anyone whose mind dwells in indolence, [they should be exhorted].
One should know that there are two kinds of faults in seeking:
first, seeking that which gives rise to all the afflictions and defilements of present and future lives,
leading to sorrow, suffering, and an unstable dwelling.
Second, there is the longing for the loss of all wholesome dharmas— both those not yet realized and those already realized—
and the loss of the great purpose that leads to and conduces to the happy realms and nirvāṇa.
Conversely, one who exerts diligent effort should be known to seek two kinds of benefits.
This diligence enables one to accomplish one's own welfare,
the welfare of others, and the welfare of both, at the time when one is yet to realize those wholesome dharmas but is capable of realizing them without falling away.
What is meant by "being able to accomplish one's own welfare"?
It refers to having gone forth and,
by means of two characteristics.
It is said that there is a fruit.
First, the attainment of ultimate nirvāṇa through the dissociation from afflictions;
this refers to the fruit of dissociation.
Second, it is able to give rise to superior worldly happiness,
namely, the fruit of maturation consisting of happiness in the happy realms.
How is it called "that which accomplishes the welfare of others"?
That is to say, extensively proclaiming the essential points of the Dharma to others,
enabling them to proceed to the auspicious realms of the world and ultimately attain nirvana.
What is meant by "being able to accomplish both objectives"?
It refers to personally cultivating and purifying the field of merit so that it is capable of receiving and utilizing,
from the side of pure faith, such things as robes and other requisites obtained in accordance with the Dharma.
By means of this, one enjoys and sustains one's own body so that it may accord with all categories of virtue;
furthermore, one enables others to obtain great rewards for the services they have rendered to oneself.
This means that because one will go to the happy realms in the future,
one attains great benefit;
that is, one shall obtain the perfection of both wealth and servants.
One attains great prosperity,
meaning that one shall obtain the self-perfection of longevity, physical form, strength, happiness, eloquence, and so forth;
one attains great cultivation and vastness.
This means that regarding the three aforementioned bases,
one follows them for a long duration without interruption by way of four aspects.

It should be understood that the holy teaching spoken by the Blessed One is called "well-expounded," because it is capable of leading to tranquility and enables the realization of the realm of nirvana with remainder.
Second, it is capable of leading to parinirvāṇa, because it enables the realization of the realm of nirvana without remainder;
third, it is capable of leading to bodhi, because it enables the realization of the śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Because it is the unsurpassed teaching revealed by the Great Teacher, who is manifested through the direct perception of the most ultimate analysis of the Sugata.
Furthermore, being endowed with the four perfections, it is capable of producing birth in a noble realm.
If any one of these is accomplished,
then while practicing correctly within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
[one attains this perfection].
He is called "Welcome" and "Well-Departed.
What are the four kinds of perfection?
First, the perfection of superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).
Second, the perfection of the two faculties;
third, the perfection of wisdom;
fourth, the perfection of encountering a Buddha appearing in the world within a noble realm.
One whose superior intention is perfected is,
for example, someone who [aspires] toward parinirvāṇa.
Only after having thoroughly purified and cultivated the superior intention (adhyāśaya) does one go forth;
it is not out of being oppressed by creditors or various fears.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
It should be understood that one who goes forth in such a manner is said to have gone forth well.
Born in a noble place with complete faculties refers,
for example, to a certain person.
His eyes and ears are unimpaired;
he is not a paṇḍaka;
his limbs are complete.
Because they have thus obtained faculties that are unimpaired,
they are capable of going forth within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya and of preaching the True Dharma.
At that time, one who is capable of listening and receiving [the teaching] and whose wisdom is perfected refers to a certain person as follows:
By nature they are not foolish or dull-witted,
because they lack the hindrance of inferior-grade ignorance; nor are they mute.
Because there is no obstacle of middling delusion,
it is not spoken by means of the hand;
because there is no obstacle of superior delusion, [it is not spoken by means of the hand].
Because they are free from the three kinds of ignorance and delusion regarding knowledge,
they possess the power to understand the meaning of all teachings, whether well-spoken or ill-spoken;
thus, when a Buddha appears in the world within the noble realm, they are able to encounter him in his full perfection.
That is to say, just as at this present time there is the Bhagavān Śākyamuni appearing in the world;
he is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—
and so on, as explained at length.
If explained in detail,
it should be understood as being like the exposition of the True Dharma in the *Saṃgītiparyāya*.
The detailed explanation regarding "tending toward tranquility" and so forth is as previously stated.
It should be understood that because one is born into a noble state therein,
it is called "well-come" (*svāgata*).
He has successfully attained renunciation because his faculties are unimpaired and he is not dull-witted.
Because they are neither mute nor speech-impaired,
and because they do not have to use their hands to communicate,
they are said to have successfully attained a fully endowed human body.
Furthermore, for a practitioner who cultivates contemplation on the flow of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arising through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*),
there are briefly two kinds of factors that give rise to doubt. What are these two?
First, those who follow and practice the doctrine of causelessness;
second, those who follow and practice the doctrine of evil causes.
Regarding these, as for those who follow and practice the doctrine of causelessness:
Observing that all aspects are entirely without cause,
he gave rise to doubt:
"How can all phenomena proceed without a cause?"
Those who follow and study treatises based on faulty causes also give rise to doubt, wondering:
"How can this be due to such dissimilar causes and irrational causes?"
There are dharmas that undergo transformation.
If a learned noble disciple remains far removed from these two kinds of unreal discourse.
By correctly observing that the cycle of existence proceeds through these causes and conditions,
one attains wholesome certainty and is free from doubt.
It is the internal realization of reality. In this regard,
it is said that there are noble disciples who are well-versed in the teachings.
It should be understood that among these, those who are ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) are not included; rather,
this refers only to the noble disciples (ārya-śrāvaka).
It should be understood that this refers to those who have already seen the truths.
Furthermore, within the True Dharma,
there are briefly three types of persons (pudgala).
There still remains suffering, affliction, and lack of abiding in peace.
What are these three? They are as follows:
there is, for example, a certain person.
Within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
they seek nirvāṇa and proceed toward nirvāṇa.
Having abandoned the household life and gone forth into homelessness,
once he has become a renunciant.
One merely upholds all the prohibitive precepts and dwells in contentment with that alone,
rather than transforming them from time to time.
He progresses in the training in higher mind and the training in higher wisdom.
He abandons all the objects of enjoyment belonging to his former household life,
yet he has not yet attained the unsurpassed peace and realized the path to nirvana.
Even while dwelling in the intermediate state,
they still experience suffering and do not abide in peace;
this is called the first type of person (pudgala).
Furthermore, there is another person who,
although not remaining content merely with the precepts they have received,
is nonetheless unable to transcend the stage of ordinary beings.
Because they have not yet transcended the stage of ordinary beings,
they rely upon others for all phenomena; thus,
they constantly look to the faces of others.
He constantly observes the speech of others,
wondering when he might truly know what is to be known and see what is to be seen.
He constantly seeks from others the hearing of the sublime Dharma, instructions, and admonitions;
yet his own mind remains possessed of doubt and confusion,
still burdened by suffering and unable to dwell in peace.
This is called the second type of person.
Furthermore, there is another who is a learner (śaikṣa) who has seen the tracks [of the path].
Dwelling in negligence,
one is incapable of realizing ultimate nirvāṇa in this present life; furthermore,
one possesses the causes for the arising of a second existence.
There is a second dwelling where one still experiences suffering and dwells in insecurity;
this is called the third type of person (pudgala).
Regarding these three types of persons,
there are furthermore three other distinct types of persons who dwell in happiness and perfect peace.
That is to say, the Arhat always dwells in happiness.
Furthermore, the summary verse (uddāna) says:
"Existence, cessation, the śramaṇa, the brāhmaṇa, and the attainment of knowledge."
Regarding the cycle of transmigration and coming and going, the Buddha [taught] the forward and reverse order for those disciples who have seen the path and attained its traces;
though they abide in the cessation of existence, the tranquility of Nirvana.
Not following others,
one relies on the noble eye of wisdom within;
one is able to perceive and see for oneself.
Yet he was still unable to touch and realize it with his own body.
It was like a person driven by heat and thirst who hastens toward a deep well.
Although one sees with the physical eye the water in the well— free from all impurities, cool,
and delicious— along with the water vessel,
one has not yet physically touched or realized this water.
In this way, although a learner (śaikṣa) perceives with the noble eye of wisdom that the subsequent afflictions to be abandoned have been severed and are utterly tranquil,
they have not yet physically realized this cessation.
Furthermore, there are certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who have completely and without remainder abandoned greed, hatred, and delusion;
they possess the true meaning of a śramaṇa and the true meaning of a brāhmaṇa.
Having not yet realized anything at all,
people of the world nevertheless conceive the notion that they are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas,
and they themselves also claim to be true śramaṇas and true brāhmaṇas.
Although the world conceives such a notion regarding them,

in all such cases, one contemplates them as they truly are, as being neither self nor belonging to a self.
That is to say, within this,
there is definitively no self,
nor anything belonging to a self.
Having observed in this way,
at the time one attains the direct realization (abhisamaya) of the Noble Truths,
the roots of all those underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of various views are forever uprooted.
This is called "abandonment.
All other [tendencies] will never again continue.
For this noble disciple, all those factors that lead to dangerous and evil states, which are rooted in those views and inclinations, [are likewise abandoned].
One will certainly be unable to act [virtuously],
and one will certainly be unable to go to dangerous or evil places and the like.
This is called the first gateway of permanently impairing conduct that leads to rebirth in evil destinies.
For this reason, one is able to know within oneself, as it truly is, that one is free from the self and so forth;

furthermore, although other ordinary worldlings may, by means of the worldly path, transcend and depart from unwholesome states and the evil destinies, and attain the four kinds of abidings in happiness in the present life.
Or one may attain the peaceful liberations that transcend all form and formlessness;
yet, one is unable to ultimately eliminate the various evil destinies and the like with which one might later be associated.
Therefore, although those practitioners are able to completely abandon desire for the realm of form and temporarily attain a superior state of blissful abiding,
they will nevertheless again engage in acts such as killing in the future.
"By going to the various evil destinies,
we shall certainly be unable to commit acts such as killing," and so forth,
as explained at length.
"Regarding all unrighteous conduct and unequal conduct,
we shall certainly be able to refrain from committing them.
This is called the gateway of perpetual harm within the Noble Dharma-Vinaya.
This refers to the ability to harmfully obstruct the course of rebirth in evil destinies;
thus, the Buddhas and their disciples truly and universally know all the distinctions regarding the methods for such permanent harm.
Furthermore, these very noble disciples,
desiring to transcend the remaining uneliminated tendencies toward rebirth in the happy realms—
these noble disciples.
Not being satisfied with what has been previously accomplished,
one gives rise to a longing desire for the higher goal of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya) and forms a mind of right aspiration.
Regarding all those mundane paths thus attained,
he carefully contemplates their defects,
namely that they cannot bring about the ultimate cessation of suffering.
This is called the first gate of the aspiration for the resolve to transcend and proceed toward the happy realms.
Having generated this aspiration,
one universally regards all the relishable flavors of future existence within the happy realms as [unsatisfactory].
He deeply contemplates its faults and perils as being like a treacherous and evil path, giving rise to a mind of weary detachment;
he yearns for tranquility and the nirvana of the present life,
and correctly cultivates the skillful means.
By means of this, one proceeds toward nirvana in the same manner as the path previously attained;
this is called the "door of progressive advancement.
Through the cultivation of the path, one gradually becomes free from desire.
Even if one is able to enter the meditative absorption of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
if one indulges in the relish of equanimity (*upekṣā*) and thereby creates the conditions for negligence,
one will not attain parinirvāṇa in this present life.
One who is merely designated as "one who ascends upstream" and has attained the fruit of a non-returner is what is called the subsequent gateway of ascending upstream.
Furthermore, if one then deeply contemplates the faults and perils therein:
Not giving rise to attachment toward that equanimity,
he is able to realize nirvāṇa in this very life,
attaining parinirvāṇa with the remainder of the substrate of existence.
This is called the gateway to parinirvāṇa.
By means of this gateway,
one understands as it truly is that one’s own parinirvāṇa transcends all courses of action leading to the happy realms.
They also possess perfect and complete knowledge regarding the deliverance of others;
namely, the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas.
In this context, the first [of these four] is the door of permanent impairment;
it should be understood as the practice for transcending and avoiding rebirth in the evil destinies.
The latter three—the generation of the aspiration, the advancement toward higher states, and nirvāṇa—are the four doors.
One should know that this is the practice for transcending and proceeding to the happy realms.
Furthermore, it should be understood that for those noble disciples who have seen the path of the truths but have not yet abandoned desire,
there are briefly two kinds of afflictions (*saṃkleśa*).
That is to say, the defilement of desire and the defilement of renewed existence;
regarding these two kinds,
the noble disciples—
One should apply oneself with diligence to purify the mind.
When the noble disciples strive through skillful means to sever the defilement of desire,
they gradually rely upon the three types of conduct.
That is to say: tending toward immovable conduct;
tending toward the sphere of nothingness;
and realizing the meditative absorption of the immovable sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is due to the antidote of abandonment and the antidote of distancing; thereby,
one transcends the defilements of desire.
Or, when one exerts skillful means in order to eliminate the defilements of future existence,
one has already become free from craving for the desire realm.
Not yet free from craving for the realm of form, one thinks: "When shall my possessions no longer exist?
When shall I no longer exist?"
"I shall not exist; what belongs to me shall not exist;
whatever exists now [shall likewise cease to be]."
Whatever I previously possessed—
all such things as these—
I have completely renounced.
Having correctly cultivated the various specific remedial paths capable of severing rebirth in future existence, he becomes free from craving for the form realm,
up to and including the ability to enter the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
If, in this present life,
one generates much relish for that equanimity and does not attain parinirvāṇa,
then in this present life one will not be fully liberated from all the defilements pertaining to future existence.
If one does not give rise to attachment toward that higher equanimity,
one is able to attain parinirvāṇa in this very life and is fully liberated from all defilements pertaining to future existence.
It should be understood that herein, if one cultivates the path of counteraction in order to remedy the defilement of desire,
one gradually proceeds until being able to enter the meditative absorption of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
If, in order to counteract the defilements of future existence,
one cultivates the path of counteraction,
one gradually proceeds until being able to enter the meditative absorption of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
These two types are called "common liberation" (*sādhāraṇa-vimukti*),
because they can both be possessed by noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Therefore, this liberation is not termed "noble liberation" (*ārya-vimukti*).
Having understood, as they truly are, the suffering of the transitory collection (satkāya) from all levels up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra),
one transcends the Peak of Existence and permanently abandons all defilements within this very life.
Such liberation can only be attained by the noble ones (*ārya*);
therefore, this liberation is called "noble liberation" (*ārya-vimokṣa*).
Thus, all these together comprise five locations.
First, the practice of the immovable state of one-pointedness;
second, the practice of the sphere of nothingness;
third, the practice of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Fourth, nirvana in the present life;
fifth, noble liberation.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of faults and disadvantages regarding sensual desires.
First, all sensual desires serve as the causal conditions for the arising of craving toward objects that accord with pleasant feelings.
Second, all sensual desires serve as the causal conditions for the arising of aversion toward objects that accord with painful feelings.
Third, these various desires serve as the conditions for the arousal of ignorance that arises from the objects of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Furthermore, one should contemplate the faults of these various desires in three respects.
First, by way of intrinsic nature;
second, by way of the object of cognition;
third, by way of the accompanying factors.
"By way of intrinsic nature" refers to the craving produced by false discrimination.
"By way of objective referent" refers to...
This refers to the five kinds of objective forms, whether internal or external,
by way of their being concomitants;
as for "by way of association," it refers to inverted perceptions associated with improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
Furthermore, because it is free from superior desire and possesses a mind of supreme skillful means,
it is called "vast. Why is this?
Because those higher stages are progressively superior and more excellent,
the cultivation of that mind is called "vast.
If one is able to cultivate weary detachment toward the world of the lower stages, [that mind is likewise vast].
One should know that through the contemplations of impermanence and so forth, one brings about revulsion and subdues [the mind].
Regarding the states to be attained in the higher stages,
one should know that these are likewise achieved through temporary expedient means.
One should give rise to the perception of tranquility and maintain the mind therein.
Furthermore, I have already attained and fully abide in this state.
Those who give rise to faith and understanding should know that they cultivate pure faith within the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
They produce pure faith toward this very object;
by the predominant power of this pure faith, [they proceed].
By cultivating diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and so forth,
one is able to realize and enter all the immovable meditative absorptions (āniñjya-samādhi), from the first dhyāna up through the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana).
Furthermore, through that wisdom, this resolute conviction arises:
"I am already able to enter such a meditative absorption.
This is precisely what brings about the fruit of birth in the station of immovable consciousness.
If one does not attain parinirvāṇa in the present life,
or does not further seek to proceed to a higher stage,
one will certainly go to this immovable state in the future.
Furthermore, one should know that these stages are established as "unshakable states" (āniñjya-sthāna) by virtue of three conditions.
This means that because external desires and other forms of distraction have been abandoned,
the first dhyāna is established as a state of immovability (*aniñjya*).

Because the movements within the stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)— namely, applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*)— have been abandoned, it is so designated.
The fourth dhyāna is established as the station of the imperturbable (*āneñjya-sthāna*),
because it has severed the movement of various distinct perceptions involving form and resistance.
The sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) are likewise established.
It is the "station of the immovable.
Because all subsequent movements are abandoned within the second and third dhyānas,
it should be understood that these are also called "stations of the immovable."

Because the sphere of infinite consciousness is established as a station of immovability by virtue of its detachment from the outward-moving object-condition of the sphere of infinite space, it should be understood that,
in brief, this is the case.
Because all meditative concentrations (samādhi) are free from agitation,
they are all termed "unshakable" (āneñja).
The limit of these concentrations reaches its ultimate point at the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana).
Therefore, one should know that as far as this point is established as immovable,
so too is all meditative concentration (samādhi) based upon its respective objects.
All these are called "superior" (sopadhika) meditative attainments.
From this point upward, the meditative attainment that takes the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) as its object should be known as the "unsurpassed" (anupadhika) meditative attainment.
From this point upward,
it is further called the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
thus, by means of these three parts, the three modes of practice are proclaimed.
By means of three doors,
the noble disciples cultivate revulsion toward desire and the other [afflictions].
Having thus become weary of and overcome [the lower realms],
one is gradually able to enter, up to and including, the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
For this reason, three types of practice leading to the immovable states are established.
Furthermore, whether it be the perception of form or the perception of immovability,
having thoroughly cultivated revulsion for and the destruction of all lower stages, [one attains this state].
One is able to enter the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness;
this is called the first practice leading toward the sphere of nothingness.
Furthermore, this very stage is the ultimate limit of the cultivation of the untainted path.
This untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) is further of two kinds:
first, that which has a superior;
second, that which is unsurpassed.
If one conceives of a state of existence that has something superior to it,
it is associated with the practice of impermanence;
that which has nothing superior to it is not so.
Accompanied by the practice of non-self,
through the presence of superior practice,
one [abides] in the lower stages.
Having developed a profound sense of wearying revulsion,
one enters this meditative attainment by means of the supreme practice.
Contemplating non-self within all phenomena, both below and above,
one is able to enter the untainted meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness.
This unsurpassed practice should be known as the second course of conduct.
Furthermore, this second course of conduct is distinguished by two further types of practice.
Two kinds are established.
What are the two modes?
They are the distinction between the wisdom of the supported and the supporting.
Among these, the wisdom of selflessness regarding the basis refers to the fact that within all things—
whether the realm of sentient beings or one's own person—
there is absolutely no place belonging to a "mine."
That is to say, the regions and territories belonging to me;
that is to say, all sentient beings.
That which belongs to me refers to such categories as father, mother, companion, or master;
just as these are not objects of belonging for me,
so too am I not an object of belonging for them.
It is not something to which one belongs.
In this same way,
I too am not something to which I belong in that regard.
That which is not a possessor,
that which is not a possessed object—
this is the wisdom of non-self regarding the basis therein.
It means that all worlds are empty and devoid of permanence, a self, or what belongs to a self (*ātmiya*).
Within these, nothing permanent, no self, and no "mine" can be found as real;
there are only phenomena (*dharmas*).
Since this world is thus entirely empty, who could there be,
and where could there be anything to which one belongs?
As for that which belongs to someone:
Since there is a matter to which [the former] belongs,
one should know that the prior wisdom of selflessness is the dependent (āśrayin),
and the subsequent wisdom of selflessness is its basis (āśraya).
In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
there is no untainted path;
it exists solely by means of the repudiation and destruction of the perception of the sphere of nothingness.
One is able to enter this meditative absorption;
within it, there is only this single course of existence.
Furthermore, one thinks: "In this state, when will 'mine' no longer exist?"
That is to say, because of the suffering of birth and so forth, one says, "I have suffering.
As for the thought, "When shall I no longer exist? [it refers to the cessation of that very self].
That is to say, taking suffering such as birth and so forth as the self,
one generates such a mind of aspiration and desire,
and then applies oneself with right diligence and practice.
Having correctly applied the practice,
one attains all the various distinctions between the preceding and succeeding stages;
for this reason:
Furthermore, one attains certainty, thinking: "I shall not exist;
what belongs to me shall not exist."
That which is "presently possessed" refers to all new karma that has been performed and accumulated in this present life;
that which is "formerly possessed" refers to [karma from previous lives].
This refers to all intentional karmas;
he neither desires nor seeks any of their resultant fruits,
because he has relinquished everything without attachment.
Furthermore, the summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
Establishment, limits, and purity; The nature of the obstacles during the cultivation of dependent origination according to reality;
And the explanation of abandonment, arising, and subsequent cultivation.

Among these, thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are established, beginning with the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and ending with the factors of the path (mārgāṅga),
whether presented in brief or in detail.
Its characteristics should be understood as they are described in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*.
Furthermore, one should understand the limits of all objects of knowledge by means of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).
Based on the limit of the objects of knowledge,
one must further understand the limit of the objects of wisdom.
Furthermore, the four foundations of mindfulness arise through desire, diligence, and so forth.
Through the cultivation of the preparatory application (*prayoga*), one attains perfection.
It should be understood that apart from these four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*),
there is no other path of a different category (*asabhāga-mārga*) nor any other object of focus (*ālambana*).
By means of this path and through this object,
one is able to exhaust all outflows and attain nirvana.
Because there is no second path of purification,
it is said that there is exclusively one path leading to the right way;
furthermore, this is the exclusive path leading to the right way.
By two causes and conditions,
one can bring sentient beings to ultimate purification:
first, by the power of analytical discernment.
Second, by the power of cultivation.
In this context, "sorrow" refers to afflicted grief (*daurmanasya*).
That which is called "dissipation" refers to the defiled joy of the desire realm that accompanies restlessness.
Sorrow takes the four worldly conditions as its basis.
With the remaining four worldly dharmas as the basis for his agitation,
he diligently applies himself to the practice of the four foundations of mindfulness;
relying on the power of discernment, he transcends sorrow and agitation.
By virtue of the power of mundane cultivation,
one attains freedom from sensual craving and abandons sorrow and suffering;
by virtue of the power of supramundane cultivation, [one attains the same].
They transcend all suffering of the transitory collection (satkāya) and are also able to realize the true,
sublime Dharma of the Noble Eightfold Path and the fruits of that path.
All sentient beings should know that this is due to the power of both analytical discernment (pratisaṃkhyāna) and cultivation (bhāvanā).
Having attained ultimate purity in all its aspects,
one gives rise to various forms of improper mental attention toward the four types of objects, such as the body and so forth.
Even if one contravenes the four foundations of mindfulness,
by contravening these,
one thereby contravenes appropriate attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
This refers to the noble path, consisting of the factors such as right view, which arises immediately and in accordance with reality for the noble ones;
because it is contrary to this [path],
one thereby becomes contrary to the entire noble path.
Because it contravenes the Path, it likewise contravenes the fruit of the Path: the nectar of ultimate nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, once the yogācāra has understood that the body and so forth arise from causes and conditions, [he realizes their nature].
Furthermore, one dwells in the contemplation of impermanence regarding all phenomena, such as the bodies of the three times;
by dwelling thus in the contemplation of impermanence, [one attains liberation].
Regarding all future existences,
he never dwells relying upon craving for future existence;
furthermore, within this present life...
Regarding all conditioned phenomena, whether internal or external,
one does not grasp at them as "I" or "mine.
Furthermore, it should be understood that in the future, one abides in the contemplation of the arising of phenomena (*samudaya-dharmānupaśyanā*).
Regarding the past, one should know that it abides in the contemplation of the dharma of cessation.
Regarding the present, because it perishes immediately after having arisen,
one should know that it abides in the contemplation of the dharma of the arising and cessation [of suffering].
Because, at the outset, he contemplates the nature of dependent origination regarding phenomena such as the body,
he realizes impermanence;
having thus realized this nature of impermanence, [he proceeds].
He dwells extensively in the cultivation of practice regarding the various points of affliction such as craving and views,
thereby purifying his mind.
When mental attention is cultivated in this way, it becomes fully perfected.
Relying upon this,
one is able to attain, accordingly, the ultimate exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava*).
Furthermore, to summarize all phenomena (dharmas):
they are either wholesome or unwholesome.
Whether it be the category of affliction or the category of purification,
one should know that herein, as for the various categories of affliction:
All [phenomena] of the defiled class have improper mental attention as their origin;
all phenomena of the purified class have proper mental attention as their origin.
All such cases are, in brief,
collectively termed "attention" as the cause of origination.
Furthermore, one cultivates the foundations of mindfulness.
Whether in brief or in detail,
its characteristics should be understood as they are described in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
Furthermore, this is the principle for the cultivation of these foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
It is not only now that the Blessed One has appeared in the world and begun to proclaim this;
rather, the noble disciples have been practicing it from the very beginning since time without beginning in the past.
Regarding the applications of mindfulness,
one practices their continuous flow;
it should be known that this practice will remain inexhaustible throughout future ages.
Furthermore, because they are the basis for the arising of immeasurable wholesome dharmas— both mundane and supramundane— of the past, future, and present,
these four kinds of foundations of mindfulness are taught.
It is called a "heap of the wholesome.
Furthermore, because they can obstruct such a heap of the wholesome,
the five hindrances are said to be a "heap of the unwholesome."
Furthermore, because the four objects of knowledge, such as the body and so forth, are infinite and distinct,
the Tathāgata’s wisdom is unimpeded with respect to them and is likewise without limit.
Because wisdom is boundless,
the unsurpassed Dharma teachings spoken by the Tathāgata are likewise without limit.
Such a teaching of the Dharma is manifested by two conditions:
first, by way of the words;
second, by way of the meaning.
The categories of the distinctions of meaning are immeasurable;
the textual phrases of the Dharma teachings that reveal these categories of meaning are likewise immeasurable.
These phrases are not repeated;
his boundless, successive eloquence is inexhaustible.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has accomplished this rare and unprecedented quality.
He is skillfully able to proclaim all the teachings of the Dharma;
within a single meaning, he can use immeasurable and elegant phrasing to provide expedient explanations without redundant repetition.
Furthermore, because they have successfully accomplished the wisdom that understands the intended meaning of the fundamental tenets of the holy teachings,
they are said to "possess the inclination.
Because they have successfully accomplished the sublime wisdom consisting of innate, heard, and reflected understanding, they are so named.
It is called "possessing intention" because it accomplishes meditative concentration;
it is called "possessing mindfulness."
Because of penetrating the truths,
one is said to possess wisdom.
It should be understood that, herein, the first [phrase] provides a general indication.
The latter three are explained separately.
Furthermore, there are bhikṣus who,
regarding phenomena such as the body, first engage in appropriate mental attention through hearing and reflection.
Abiding in the contemplation of phenomena such as the body alone,
and having realized that all phenomena are selfless,
one does not find mere contentment in this alone through the mental engagement of hearing and reflection.
Seeking only the liberation of a concentrated mind,
he dwells in a secluded place for the sake of attaining concentration.
Taking only the body and so forth as objects,
one establishes the mind through nine modes of mental application.
One causes the mind to be internally tranquil.
Through two causal conditions,
one gives rise to the four foundations of mindfulness.
It is called "well-initiated" for two reasons:
first, by means of the knowledge of reality through appropriate mental attention;
second, by means of the knowledge of reality through meditative concentration.
This wisdom will immediately lead to the attainment of the ultimate through knowledge as it truly is.
Furthermore, there are certain bhikṣus who attain their desired objects regarding the three types of remedies.
One attains freedom from hardship and freedom from obstruction;
this is called the perception of impermanence.
Whether it be the contemplation of loving-kindness or the concentration on the signless,
he does so by means of these three types of remedies.
As appropriate for each case,
as previously explained,
regarding agreeable and other such objects of the body and so forth.
Abiding in the perception of repulsiveness and the perception of non-repulsiveness,
one abandons both of these through equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension;
by virtue of this cause and condition.
One should know that this is called "skillfully cultivating the foundations of mindfulness.
Furthermore, the summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
First, the gratification of the sense faculties; then, there is a distinction between what precedes and what follows.
Grasping at signs and the various fetters— these three roots, which result in great fruit and benefit as their ultimate end,
act as obstacles to all accumulations of virtue within the foundations of mindfulness.
One should know that these are called the collection of unwholesome dharmas.
What are the three?
First, the root of misconduct.
The first causes one to dwell in the suffering of the miserable realms in the future;
the second, the investigation of the faculties,
causes one to dwell in the suffering of unrest in the present life.
Third, as for the "root of roots":
because it serves as the fundamental basis for the roots of unwholesome conduct and the roots of discursive thought,
it is called the "root of roots."
It should be understood that herein,
the three unwholesome roots— greed, hatred, and delusion—
are able to serve as the roots for unwholesome actions of the body and so forth.
The three perceptions of desire and so forth can serve as the roots for the discursive thoughts of desire and so forth;
these are the three realms of desire and so forth.
One should know that it serves as the root for the three roots of greed and so forth, as well as the three roots of sensual perception and so forth.
Furthermore, there are certain bhikṣus who diligently apply themselves to the practice of the four foundations of mindfulness.
By means of the mundane path, one becomes detached from craving for the desire realm;
[this is] explained at length up until:
one fully dwells in the meditative absorption of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
One then develops a strong relish for this very concentration and conceives a sense of complacency regarding it,
failing to exert further effort to attain what has not yet been attained.
Within this noble Dharma and Vinaya,
such a person is not called a "Great Being. Why is that?
Because their minds have not yet attained wholesome liberation,
those who are the opposite of this are designated as "Great Beings" (mahāsattva).
Furthermore, there are certain bhikṣus who,
regarding the body and other objects, diligently abide in the contemplation of the body and so forth,
establishing their minds through nine modes of practice.
One should cause the mind to gather within.
It should be understood that this mind, being subject to the physical and mental lethargy and inferiority that are the objects of remediation in śamatha,
does not attain liberation.
Because it is not liberated,
based on this gathered mind,
there arises within the body the nature of various forms of lethargy.
When inferior qualities arise within the mind,
if one has well-established the mind in the foundations of mindfulness,
one understands, as they truly are, these afflictions that have arisen.
He then withdraws his mind from the internal collection and places it upon external pure and sublime objects—
namely, the conditions of the Buddha’s virtues and deeds—
maintaining the mind so that it remains fixed there.
By taking this as an object, joy arises;
as explained at length, up until:
by means of the sublime exertion (*pragraha*), one brings the mind to concentration upon the focal object.
One attains liberation from the secondary afflictions that are the objects to be countered by śamatha.
From this point onward, one understands them as they truly are;
thus, the mind attains liberation from the secondary afflictions.
For the sake of this purpose, one makes a prayer;
having externally attained this object, one returns once more to gather the mind within as before,
so that it is not disturbed by the various secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Having gathered the mind within, one knows things as they truly are spontaneously and without the need for aspiration;
thus, the mind is liberated from external objects.
Regarding external objects, his mental investigation of their modes of appearance is subject to suppression;
his preparatory application is difficult to set in motion.
They have all attained sovereign liberation;
having renounced ease and comfort, they abide therein,
having already accomplished the supreme śamatha.
Thus, with the mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness,
he is able to correctly discern the distinctions between what precedes and what follows.
Furthermore, one should know this person as follows:
Having previously practiced vipaśyanā,
one relies upon that vipaśyanā as a basis to cultivate the practice of yoga within śamatha.
Furthermore, there are bhikṣus who diligently apply themselves to the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna),
taking vipaśyanā as their basis.
One who delights in the practice of insight (vipaśyanā) within śamatha should,
with respect to the mind subsumed under internal śamatha, take up such a mental image as this:
"What am I contemplating right now?"

What is the reflection that causes the mind, which has been taken up by śamatha, to be troubled and disturbed by physical and mental lethargy and inferiority— the very things to be remedied by śamatha?
Furthermore, what am I contemplating now?
How should I contemplate so that the mind,
sustained by śamatha, is not disturbed or distracted by those phenomena?
If that bhikṣu does not grasp such mental images within his own mind,
but merely recognizes that this mind is defiled by secondary afflictions (upakleśa),
he then grasps pure and excellent signs in external objects.
With this as the cause,
although one may temporarily dispel the currently manifest secondary afflictions,
if at a later time one again withdraws the mind and gathers it within as before, [the same occurs].
Furthermore, one is thus afflicted by these secondary afflictions and fails to attain tranquil concentration,
because one has not previously grasped the characteristics of one's own mind.
For this reason:
They are repeatedly disturbed by secondary afflictions,
fail to attain the goals they seek,
and are further afflicted and distressed by sorrow.
Furthermore, over a long period of time, they are unable to attain inner tranquility (śamatha),
nor are they able to attain the supreme mindfulness and clear comprehension (smṛti-samprajanya) that are purified and preceded by śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Because he has not attained internal tranquility of mind,
he cannot attain the four states of higher mind that dwell in happiness in the present life;
because he has not attained superior and foremost right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
One cannot attain the unsurpassed, secure, and ultimate nirvāṇa not previously attained;
the opposite of this should be understood as all that belongs to the category of the white (wholesome) factors.
...until one attains the unsurpassed peace and ultimate *nirvāṇa* never before attained.
In this context, the cook is a metaphor for yoga;
the master of the household is a metaphor for the mind embraced by internal *śamatha*.
The flavors of the delicacies are a metaphor for the characteristic of grasping;
the exquisite food and clothing are metaphors for internal *śamatha* and so forth.
It should be understood that the "black category" (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) is a metaphor for all that belongs to the foolish.
The "white category" (śuklapakṣa) is a metaphor for the wise.
Furthermore, there are bhikṣus who correctly and diligently cultivate the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
However, this ordinary person may have an excellent, sublime, and desirable object appearing before them,
or they may perceive various signs while dwelling in solitude;
due to a lapse of mindfulness, [the mind becomes distracted].
Not relying on what is contrary to his ideals,
he impulsively gives rise to intense fetters of craving;
he then feels deep-seated revulsion and shame regarding these fetters.
That is to say, just as when one's own body has fallen into a state of calamity or an extremely base and impure place,
one gives rise to an intense resolve for detachment;
by means of such a practice.
Thereupon, his mind becomes liberated from those fetters.
Once liberated, joy arises in his heart,
and from that point forward, he gives rise to intense revulsion.
Following intense revulsion, one attains the perception of impermanence;
like seeing a great plow turn up clods of earth among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
one then practices the correct contemplation of the Noble Truths as they truly are.
Because it relies upon and is dependent on nirvāṇa,
and because it is the attention of observation belonging to those still in training (śaikṣa),
one contemplates the sign of purity regarding the sublime and excellent objects.
Because the latent tendency of attachment has not been permanently severed,
the obsession of attachment suddenly arises and manifests;
yet, one immediately thereafter perceives its faults with deep insight.
Desiring to sever these envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), one enters the concentration of signlessness (*animittasamādhi*).
In this way, one is able to sever other dharmas not yet severed;
having arisen from concentration, one understands with perfect clarity that all have been severed.
One experiences the subtle joy and bliss of liberation;
by seeing oneself as it truly is,
one accomplishes great power of wisdom.
It is called "powerful," for the various classes of Māras are weak and inferior in strength.
Furthermore, it refers to the merit induced by the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness.
It should be understood that it is called "having great fruit" because it can bring about the most excellent, superior, and ultimate fruit.
It should be understood that it can bring about the most excellent, superior, and beneficial happiness.

The Fourth Part of the Compendium on the Selection of Factors Conducive to Enlightenment within the Section on the Matters of Sūtra, as Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Furthermore, the summary verse (*uddāna*) says:

yet achieves only the "grain" [of outward form] for the sake of future existence as a follower of the various non-Buddhist paths.
He establishes himself as a teacher over his assembly of disciples,
seeking exclusively for gain and offerings,
and seeking exclusively for honor and respect.
He sought exclusively his own benefit.
When the conditions converged,
a son of noble family approached him and entered the homeless life.
He then said to him:
"Between you and me, we previously possessed no personal requisites whatsoever that we might share in common.
You ought to go to other places on my behalf to praise my virtues and conceal my faults."
I, too, shall perform such deeds for you.
We two shall mutually support and protect one another,
whether toward kings or those equal to kings.

"Do not hold such a view;

I shall also separately provide protection for others;
since I am unable to protect you,
you likewise need not protect me.

it should be understood that the disciple is one who speaks according to the truth and is one who possesses wisdom.

Because it is present and heavy,
there is furthermore defiled contact that afflicts others;

One gives rise to the two minds of benefit and happiness without a specific object;
one gives rise to the two minds of compassion and loving-kindness without a specific object.

Because of compassion,
one does not afflict others; therefore,
it should be understood that all forms of non-compassion are the opposite of that.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the analogy of the Snowy Mountains represents the Buddha’s well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
Within this, there are briefly three parts to be found:
first, the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣabhūmi*).
Second, the stage of those in training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*);
