the category of residual offenses (saṃghāvaśeṣa) constitutes the middle grade of offense;
and the remaining categories of offenses constitute the lowest grade of offense.
Furthermore, there is a distinction:
those [offenses] other than the superior assembly constitute grave offenses.
Falling away and subsequent regret constitute offenses of the middle grade;
the category of *duṣkṛta* (misdeeds) constitutes offenses of the light grade.
Thus, one should understand that all committed offenses are differentiated into the three grades of lower, middle, and upper by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding transgression:
it occurs due to ignorance and due to negligence.
The multitude of offenses committed due to [the presence of] afflictions are offenses of the lower grade;
the multitude of offenses committed because the afflictions are intense are offenses of the middle grade;
and the multitude of offenses committed due to contempt are offenses of the upper grade.
In this way, it should be understood that through transgression, the various offenses committed are distinguished into three grades: inferior, middling, and superior.
Regarding "by way of intention," this refers to the multitude of offenses committed while being bound by inferior degrees of attachment, aversion, and delusion.
This is a minor offense;
if by means of a middling degree [of intention],
it is a middling offense.
If it is by way of the superior degree,
it is a superior offense;
thus it should be understood.
Due to the underlying intention (*āśaya*),
all committed offenses are distinguished into three grades: inferior, middling, and superior.
"By reason of the object" means that although similar intentions are manifest,
they are not of a single type by virtue of their objects being diverse.
One should know that the offenses committed are distinguished into three grades—lower, middle, and upper.
For example, it is like intentionally killing a sentient being belonging to the animal realm while overcome by the fetter of hatred.
One incurs the sin of causing a living being to fall [into hell].
By means of such an identical entanglement of hatred,
one intentionally kills that person, or a human form, even though they are neither one's father nor one's mother.
One incurs an offense involving defeat (pārājika),
but not an immediate retribution offense (ānantarya).
It is precisely by means of such an affliction of anger (dveṣa-paryavasthāna) that this occurs.
If one intentionally kills one's own father or mother,
one incurs both a defeat (pārājika) offense and an immediate (ānantarya) transgression;
it should be understood in this way.
Due to the distinction of the objective basis (*vastu*), the offenses committed are differentiated into three grades: inferior, middling, and superior.
Due to accumulation (*upacaya*).
That is to say, there is someone who,
having committed a single offense,
is unable to quickly repent and eliminate it in accordance with the Dharma.
It may be two, three, or even up to five;
thus it should be understood that this is due to accumulation.
One incurs a minor offense.
From this point onward,
one may commit ten offenses.
Some commit twenty offenses;
some commit thirty;
and so on, up to committing a number of offenses that can be counted.
One should understand that because [the transgression] has been accumulated, it cannot be swiftly confessed and eliminated in accordance with the Dharma.
One incurs a crime of middling degree.
If the number of transgressions committed is immeasurable and cannot be fully known,
I now confess and repent for such a quantity of offenses.
It should be understood in this way:
through accumulation,
it becomes a grave offense.
How should it be performed?
It means that regarding those [actions], it is by way of non-performance and by way of application.
This constitutes a transgression.
There are, briefly, five kinds of what ought to be done.
First, those tasks that ought to be performed regarding villages and towns;
second, those tasks that ought to be performed regarding places of practice;
third, those tasks that ought to be performed regarding the categories of wholesome qualities.
Furthermore, these tasks to be performed regarding the category of the wholesome are of two kinds:
first, the tasks to be performed regarding the accumulations (saṃbhāra).
Second is the purification of what is to be done.
Such are the tasks pertaining to the provisions (*sambhāra*),
which are explained as being of thirteen kinds in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*.
Such are the duties to be performed for purification,
practiced through the cultivation of attention as explained in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
Furthermore, regarding the duties to be performed within towns and cities:
That is to say, he may enter a village for the sake of his own needs such as clothing;
or again, for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, or for the sake of those practicing the holy life;
or for the sake of causing those who have no faith to develop faith.
He causes those who have already gained faith to increase it twofold.
He enters villages;
[therein] he encounters all obstacles to the five things that ought to be done, which are contrary to this.
It should be understood according to what is appropriate.
Regarding the five kinds of actions that should not be performed,
how is there no offense?
That is to say, there are five causes and conditions that prevent one from committing an offense. What are these five?
They are: dwelling with the sense-gates well-guarded.
Know moderation in eating and drinking;
remain constantly awake during the first and last watches of the night;
and diligently cultivate sublime practices.
He dwells with clear comprehension.
This is called the first causal condition.
Furthermore, he gives rise to a superior degree of diligent effort and longing toward the ascetic life.
Toward their great teacher and toward all wise fellow practitioners of the holy life,
they give rise to supreme affection, delight, and reverence;
and regarding the transgressions they have committed, they develop intense and superior shame and remorse.
This is called the second causal condition.
Furthermore, there are few material possessions,
few concerns, and few activities.
Not being preoccupied with many affairs—
this is called the third cause and condition.
Furthermore, dwelling in contentment.
He was able to clearly discern transgressions from non-transgressions; he did not associate with monastics or laypeople in a dissolute manner,
but exclusively cultivated wholesome qualities without any interval.
This is called the fourth causal condition.
Furthermore, when one who is first practicing the training is afflicted by delusion, insanity, mental distraction, or the oppression of painful afflictions—
this is called the fifth causal condition.
It should be known that by means of these five causes and conditions,
one does not commit an offense from the very beginning.
How, then, is one restored to purity?
That is to say, there is one who,
upon committing whatever offense, immediately gives rise to five kinds of remorse,
relying upon a practice of heedfulness comprised of five factors.
Through five aspects, one eliminates the five kinds of remorse produced by those [transgressions].
How do these five kinds of remorse arise?
First, due to the cause and condition of my own violation of pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).
First, one will certainly feel deep self-reproach and give rise to remorse later on.
Second, due to the cause and condition of my violation of the pure precepts,
I will certainly be rebuked by other devas and give rise to remorse.
Third, due to the cause and condition of my own violation of the pure precepts,
I will certainly be collectively rebuked by the Great Teacher and by my wise fellow-practitioners, and I shall give rise to remorse.
Fourth, due to the cause and condition of my own violation of the pure precepts,
ill repute, bad reputation, evil fame, and negative verses will certainly spread far and wide in every direction, giving rise to remorse.
Fifth, due to the cause and condition of my own violation of the pure precepts, after the dissolution of the body, I will certainly fall into the various evil destinies; thus, remorse arises.
This is the practice of heedfulness comprised of five factors.
Its characteristics should be understood as they are described in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*:
namely, that which accompanies the past limit (*pūrvānta*) and that which accompanies the future limit (*aparānta*).
Co-arising with the middle period:
that which was performed at the initial time,
as well as that which follows along simultaneously.
How does one eliminate those five kinds of remorse through five modes?
First, all the True Dharma taught by the Blessed One possesses causes and conditions,
and it also possesses a way of transcendence.
Therefore, what has been transgressed can be restored to purity;
by this means, the remorse that has arisen is dispelled.
Second, it is due to ignorance, negligence, the intense burning of afflictions, and contempt.
The offenses committed have been eliminated through the cessation of that very ignorance up to and including disrespect for me;
and all correct knowledge up to and including reverence for me has arisen.
By this, the remorse that has arisen is dispelled.
Third, the intention not to commit an offense in the future has already arisen within me;
by this, the remorse that has arisen is dispelled.
Fourth, I have confessed, revealed, and eliminated [these faults] before my wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life;
by this means, the remorse that has arisen is dispelled.
Fifth, having gone forth within the Buddha’s well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, I...
Although it is excellent that one can repent and extinguish [the fault] even after transgressing the training rules,
the Bhagavān has, through immeasurable means, rebuked and condemned the remorse that arises within the mental continuum.
They act as a cover and an obstruction;
because I now dwell much in firm attachment to them, I am unable to dispel them.
This is not at all excellent.
Having understood this,
one thereby eliminates the remorse that has arisen;
this is called the purification of what was transgressed.
Furthermore, it should be known that there are, in brief, five types of dharmas that accompany the Vinaya.
A bhikṣu who trains diligently in accordance with the Vinaya follows these.
What are the five?
First, abiding;
second, dwelling place;
third, basis.
Fourth is enjoyment;
fifth is ritual action (karma).
How does one abide [in these]?
This means that a bhikṣu who diligently trains in the Vinaya should abide in five kinds of mental abidings.
What are these five?
First, when entering a village, one should maintain the perception that one has entered a prison.
Second, while at the site of practice, one should always maintain the perception of oneself as a śramaṇa.
It should be understood that herein, the "notion of a śramaṇa" refers to:
"I have now abandoned the worldly appearance through the distinctness of my physical form;
I have undertaken the wearing of discolored robes and so forth," as explained at length in the sūtra.
One should carefully examine the twenty-two bases.
Third, when eating and drinking, one should always abide in the perception that it is for the purpose of treating an illness.
Fourth, one should dwell in seclusion, away from forms cognizable by the eye, sounds cognizable by the ear, and so forth.
One should dwell with the perception of being blind, deaf, and mute.
Fifth, when sleeping or resting, one should give rise to the perception of being like a startled deer in a vast wilderness or forest, whose life is difficult to preserve.
Thus should a bhikṣu diligently train according to the Vinaya.
One should always abide securely in these five modes of abiding in perception (*saṃjñā-vihāra*).
Having thus become securely established in these modes of abiding in perception,
although one currently enjoys clothing, food and drink, and bedding that are fit for a king, [one remains detached].
And one does not fall into the extreme of practicing for the sake of sensual pleasure.
What is the dwelling place?
It refers to the five dwelling places.
1. A dwelling place for bhikṣus;
2. A dwelling place for bhikṣuṇīs;
3. A dwelling place for non-Buddhists.
The fourth is the dwelling place of the defiled;
the fifth is the dwelling place of the undefiled.
Regarding the dwelling place of a bhikṣu:
This refers to a place where bhikṣus— whether junior, middle, or senior elders—
reside. A residence for bhikṣuṇīs refers to a place where bhikṣuṇīs reside, categorized in the same three ways as mentioned above.
"Abodes of non-Buddhists" refers to those places where various non-Buddhists reside;
that is to say, the Nirgranthas.
The Venerable Pāsupata and others of this kind.
A place of defilement refers to a location where no ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) are established at all,
or where only a portion of the ritual procedures are established.
"An abode free from defilement" refers to a place where all formal monastic procedures (*karmavācanā*) are fully established,
as well as an abode where no defiled monks reside.
One should know that when the assembly is established in a state of orderliness,
it is well-arranged; if there are bhikṣus who are defiled by impurities residing therein,
one should know that the assembly is established in a state of confusion.
Any bhikṣu who delights in what is to be studied should intentionally deliberate upon a dwelling place for bhikṣus that is subject to defilement.
Having renounced gain and honor,
one should not remain [in that place].
Except when one temporarily relies on them due to danger,
or temporarily rests while traveling on a road,
or for the purpose of extracting those bhikṣus from an unwholesome state and establishing them in a wholesome state.
One should not reside in a place where a community of bhikṣuṇīs dwells,
except for the three kinds of causes and conditions previously mentioned.
One should know that the dwellings of non-Buddhists are likewise;
even though one dwells for the remainder of one's life within a monastery of bhikṣus free from defilement through correct discernment,
one should always maintain the perception of being a traveler.
If there is a bhikṣu who,
although dwelling in such various residences,
should conceive thoughts of various anxieties and fears regarding those places.
Although one dwells in such a state free from reproach,
one constantly fears being censured by wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life; what,
then, is the basis for this?
This refers to the five bases. What are the five?
First, the base of the village field.
Second, the basis of the dwelling place;
third, the basis of the person (pudgala);
fourth, the basis of requisites such as clothing and so forth.
Regarding the basis for the five modes of deportment:
if one dwells depending upon a village, a city, or a specific region,
it should be understood that this is called the "basis of villages and fields."
If one dwells by relying on groves, gardens, or walking paths within monasteries and the like,
it should be understood that this is called "reliance on a dwelling place.
If one relies on a donor...
The preceptor, the teacher, those who admonish,
instruct, remind, and provide guidance, and those who preach the sublime Dharma.
And thus one attains stable abiding.
It should be understood that this is called the basis of the *pudgala*.
Whether it be coarse or subtle, it is that which accords with the Path.
One dwells in comfort by obtaining whatever requisites for the body one may acquire—such as clothing, food and drink, and medicinal provisions for the treatment of illness;
it should be understood that this is called the basis for all such requisites as clothing and so forth.
If, by relying on this basis, one dwells in peace and happiness at all times according to one's desire throughout the four modes of conduct,
it should be known that this is called the "basis for deportment."
If one dwells relying upon such a basis,
one will never be led into exhaustion or distress by suffering that is unholy and meaningless, nor will one be harmed in an improper manner by such things that injure oneself.
What is enjoyment?
It refers to five kinds of impure enjoyment and five kinds of pure enjoyment.
What are the five kinds of impure enjoyment?
First, the enjoyment of property belonging to a stūpa,
except in the event of a serious illness.
Even if one encounters a serious illness, there are other remedies;
second, as for the use of the property of the Saṃgha,
that which has not been bestowed by the Saṃgha nor placed within the alms-bowl [is not to be used].
It is not included among those [categories].
Third, it is the enjoyment of another person's distinct property without having obtained it from them.
It is not what they permit;
it is enjoyed according to one's own will.
Fourth, it is not an object entrusted for use.
That is to say: (1) one should not enjoy anything belonging to a person who is not to be fully trusted; (2) one should not enjoy objects defiled by excrement, urine, and so forth;
or (3) through such association, one may diminish wholesome qualities and increase unwholesome qualities.
Or, by associating with them, they cause the world to give rise to censure and reproach;
they cause the world to collectively despise and loathe them;
and they cause those who have not yet developed faith to become even more distrustful.
To cause those who have already developed faith to change their minds—
this is called the five kinds of impure enjoyment.
For a bhikṣu who diligently studies the Vinaya:
One should avoid [the former]. Contrary to this,
one should understand the five kinds of pure enjoyment.
A bhikṣu who diligently trains in the Vinaya should enjoy things in this manner,
remaining far removed from impure enjoyment.
Regarding the bhikṣus who follow in the practice of pure enjoyment,
they are able to properly repay all offerings of faith.
What is the ritual procedure (karmavācanā)?
That is to say, all *karmas* briefly comprise four types:
first, the *jñapti-karman*;
second, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
Third is the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations);
fourth is the *tri-vācika-karman* (the formal act consisting of three utterances).
These four types of formal acts briefly rely upon two matters as their basis.
First, there is that which has sentient things as its basis;
second, there is that which has insentient things as its basis.
Regarding that which has sentient things as its basis:
That is to say: the formal act (karmavācanā) of going forth,
the formal act of receiving full ordination (upasampadā),
or the formal act of consensus regarding a person (pudgala).
Whether it be a formal act for the removal of an offense,
a formal act of censure,
or a formal act of banishment.
If, during the two periods of the rains retreat, one performs any formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for receiving seven, twenty-four, or ten nights,
and so forth— whether for the purpose of gathering sentient beings or for the purpose of subduing sentient beings.
The formal act of designation (*prajñapti-karman*).
This is called a formal act that takes a sentient thing as its basis.
As for that which takes a non-sentient thing as its basis:
That is to say: the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for receiving and maintaining the robe and bowl;
the formal act for maintaining the *kaṭhina* robe and protecting the robes so as not to relinquish them;
and the formal act for establishing the boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*).
If, for instance, there is a formal act (*karma*) regarding pure rice grains performed with the consent [of the assembly],
one should know that all such categories of formal acts are called "formal acts based upon things categorized as insentient."
Furthermore, it should be understood that this *karmavācanā* may be performed by a group of two,
a group of four, or a group of ten.
There may be those performed by a group of twenty,
those performed by a group of forty,
or those performed by the entire assembly.
Regarding that which is performed by two assemblies:
this refers to the formal ritual of confession (*pratideśanā-karman*) where one bhikṣu recites the confession three times before another bhikṣu,
thereby revealing and purifying either a *pārājika* offense, a *duṣkṛta* offense, or other such transgressions.
Regarding "that which is performed by the fourfold assembly":
this refers to a case where someone,
having committed a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), confesses and purifies it before four persons through the ritual of formal act (*jñapti-karman*).
That which is performed by a group of ten refers to the *karmavācanā* for receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).
That which is performed by a group of twenty refers to...
This refers to the *karmavācanā* for the formal act of expiation for a monk remaining after the assembly has departed,
as well as the *karmavācanā* for the full ordination of a bhikṣuṇī;
these are performed by an assembly of forty members.
This refers to the formal act (karman) for the removal of residual offenses from the community of bhikṣuṇīs;
that which is to be performed by the entire assembly is called the *pravāraṇā* (or *vṛddhi*) karman.
Whether it be a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* or any other type of *karman*,
these four types of *karman* become of immeasurable varieties through the differentiation of their underlying matters (*vastu*).
The detailed exposition should be understood as it appears in the Vinaya-mātṛkā.
Thus should one comprehend all formal procedures (karmas).
This concerns a bhikṣu who is diligently training in the Vinaya.
He follows the performance of the *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts);
he is skillful regarding the offenses committed and is also skillful regarding the emergence from those offenses.
One should protect oneself by avoiding [transgressions] so as to attain purity and remain free from all faults.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who diligently trains in the Vinaya should know that there are five ways of contravening the training rules.
One should remain far removed from them.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of dharmas conducive to training that one should accept and uphold.
What are the five dharmas that oppose and contradict the training?
First, obstacles;
second, counterfeit teachings.
Third, having evil friends;
fourth, being foolish and dull-witted with afflictions in full blaze;
fifth, the power of one's provisions from past lives being weak.
What are the hindrances?
There are five hindrances:
first, the hindrance of superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*).
Second, obstacles to the higher mind;
third, obstacles to higher wisdom;
fourth, obstacles to rebirth in the happy realms.
The five obstacles consist of those arising from gain, honor, life, and activities.
What is meant by the obstacle to superior ethical discipline?
It refers to a certain person who...
Or they may be slaves;
or they may be acquired;
or there may be something said.
To explain in detail, all factors that obstruct the life of one who has gone forth (pravrajyā) and are associated with it are called obstacles to higher ethical discipline (adhiśīla).
What are called obstacles to higher mind (adhicitta)?
There are eleven hindrances that should be known as hindrances to the higher mind (*adhicitta*). These are:
first, frequently attending assemblies; and so forth.
The dwelling places are categorized as follows, with the final one being the dwelling place of the ultimate.
What is called the obstacle to superior wisdom?
It refers to failing to give rise to reverence toward the True Dharma and the teachers who expound it.
They despise the True Dharma and the teachers of the Dharma, looking down upon themselves;
they are stingy regarding the Dharma, obstructing others from the True Dharma,
causing them to turn their backs on the True Dharma and leading them to slander it.
One should know that such categories as these are all called obstacles to superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
What is meant by "obstacles to proceeding to a happy rebirth"?
It refers, for example, to someone who...
They abound in evil desires and wrong views, as well as anger and resentment;
this is explained at length.
Such are the types of dharmas that accord with the various evil destinies, which they study and practice.
One should know that this is called the obstacle of the downward paths.
As for the obstacle of gain and honor,
it refers to whatever one pursues accordingly.
This causes those who have not yet gained faith to increase their lack of faith,
and it causes those who already have faith to change their minds and no longer delight in meritorious qualities.
They do not, from time to time, diligently cultivate meritorious deeds consisting of generosity;
they take no pleasure in bringing about the benefit and happiness of others;
such are their characteristics.
Regarding the obstacle to longevity:
it refers to failing to exercise caution and avoid wild elephants,
and so forth, as explained at length, up to...
They do not skillfully distance themselves from evil lands plagued by calamities and epidemics;
nor do they distance themselves from those causes and conditions that, even when the full lifespan has not yet been exhausted, can cause premature death.
Regarding such categories as these,
"obstacles to activities" refers to those things that can obstruct all undertakings, such as the work of preparing robes and alms bowls.
All these taken together should be understood as being collectively termed "obstructions to livelihood, life-force, and activities.
What is meant by "counterfeit Dharma"?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of counterfeit true Dharma:
first, the counterfeit true Dharma of teaching;
second, the counterfeit true Dharma of practice.
If one conceives the notion that what is not the Dharma is the Dharma,
and displays what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma,
causing others to conceive the notion of it being the true Dharma therein.
Because such teachings are real and true,
they are not the True Dharma;
rather, they appear as mere semblances of the True Dharma.
Therefore, this is called the "semblance of the true Dharma that resembles the teaching.
If one extensively proclaims it thus to others,
causing them to receive and study it while also practicing it oneself.
Giving rise to false notions of the Dharma and practicing various deviant conducts,
they are yet conceited and claim, "I am able to cultivate this right practice.
One should know that this is called the semblance of practicing the true Dharma.
In order to extensively proclaim what resembles the true Dharma, he further provides an intermediate summary verse (uddāna), which says:
"First, the five types beginning with the [false] dharma; next, the various views beginning with the faculties."
Regarding improper actions such as remorse and so forth,
they subsequently place forged sūtras within the various scriptures using phrases that merely resemble the Dharma teachings spoken by the Tathāgata, such as the precepts for violent and evil conduct.
To establish counterfeit precepts within the various Vinayas—
this is called a semblance of the True Dharma (saddharma-pratirūpaka).
Furthermore, it arises from views of either exaggeration (samāropa) or depreciation (apavāda).
They exaggerate unreal matters and diminish real ones;
by these means, they extensively proclaim and reveal to others various perspectives on impermanence and so forth, such that both themselves and others practice accordingly.
This is also called a counterfeit of the true Dharma.
Furthermore, regarding those sūtras that teach about the *pudgala*,
they falsely grasp and conceptualize them, asserting that a real *pudgala* exists.
This is also called a counterfeit of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, regarding various phenomena that exist only as designations,
it proclaims and reveals them as having a nature of real existence.
This is also called a counterfeit of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, regarding ultimate nirvāṇa, which is free from all conceptual proliferation,
one discriminates it as either existent or non-existent.
To speak of it as having an intrinsic nature or as lacking an intrinsic nature—
this is also called a counterfeit of the true Dharma.
Furthermore, there is a certain class of persons (*pudgala*).
He spoke thus:
"The Blessed One has proclaimed, revealed, extolled, and praised the guarding of the sense-faculties;
for this reason, it would be better not to look at forms at all."
Even up to the point where one does not direct the mind toward phenomena,
yet remains bound by mental attention while observing various forms, and even up to the point where one directs the mind to contemplate all phenomena—
this is likewise called a semblance of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, having heard the World-Honored One proclaim and praise dwelling in seclusion and tranquility,
he spoke these words:
"It would be better to remain without blame than to judge others."
One does not censure those who deserve censure,
nor does one praise those who deserve praise;
yet, one neither censures nor praises anything at all.
This is also called a counterfeit semblance of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, upon hearing the World-Honored One proclaim and praise gentle and soft speech,
one says this:
To observe the precept of silence and remain entirely without speech is most excellent;
such a practice is also called a semblance of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, one hears the World-Honored One proclaiming and praising moderation in food and clothing.
They then say:
"To remain fasting and to wander about naked is the most excellent and virtuous practice.
This is also called a counterfeit of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, having heard the World-Honored One proclaim and praise dwelling apart from clamor,
and having ceased all speech and worldly activities,
he spoke these words:
Having abandoned bedding and lodgings,
dwelling in solitude and seclusion,
and practicing nothing at all— this is considered most excellent and sublime.
This is also called a counterfeit of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, one hears the Buddha say that the mind leads the world and that the mind constructs everything.
All that arises in accordance with the mind proceeds with complete mastery;
yet, regarding the intended meaning of such sūtras as these, some individuals do not understand it as it truly is.
Or there is another class [of persons].
Based on a mistaken grasp and adherence, they speak thus:
"There is only a single consciousness that flows through birth and death;
it is neither two nor distinct."
This is also called a counterfeit of the true Dharma.
Furthermore, one hears that the Buddha permitted a man or individual who maintains the precepts to receive food of a hundred flavors and hundreds of thousands of garments.
Regarding the sublime desires that obstruct the path:
even when these types of things are being properly enjoyed, they do not constitute an obstruction.
Alternatively, there is a certain class [of persons].
Based on a mistaken grasping, they speak thus:
"Regarding the various desires that the Blessed One said are obstacles to the path,
if one indulges in them, they cannot constitute an obstacle."
This is also called a counterfeit semblance of the True Dharma.

Furthermore, one hears the Buddha say that all Arhats, within this present life, do not abandon nor grasp at the discourse on food, the aggregates, the elements, and the bases, and thus they do not know them as they truly are.
He then spoke thus:
"As I understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha,
for the Saṅgha of Arhats there is no further conscious awareness after death."
This is also called a counterfeit of the true Dharma.
Furthermore, there is another class who do not understand, as they truly are, the principles of the two truths: the conventional and the ultimate.
Contradicting the principle of the two truths,
they speak thus:
"The aggregates are selfless."
"How can it be that there is no self that creates various karmas for me to experience and realize?
One should know that this too is called a counterfeit of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, there is another class [of people].
By nature foolish, they frequently engage in slander and defamation.
They do not know, as it truly is, the ninefold internal abiding of the mind;
nor do they know, as it truly is, the practice of contemplation on the truths or the practice of mindfulness-establishment.
Due to this lack of knowledge,
they explain to others that the mental engagement of mere resolute belief belongs exclusively to the category of śamatha,
and that the mental engagement of mere resolute belief belongs exclusively to the category of vipaśyanā.
Only through the mental engagement of faith and understanding can one attain the ultimate;
yet even practicing it oneself in such a manner—
one should know that this mode of conduct is also called a counterfeit of the true Dharma.
Furthermore, there is another class who do not reflect upon improper remorse;
it should be known that this, too, is called a counterfeit of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, there is another class who possess the capacity for both recitation and contemplative mental engagement,
yet take pleasure in monastic affairs.
Furthermore, if one perceives superior qualities therein and proclaims them to others,
it should be known that this is also called a counterfeit of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, there is another class of persons who are capable in both ethical discipline and cultivation,
yet perceive superior merit in the practice of generosity.
Wandering through various regions,
he frequently violated the prohibitions of his own precepts; yet,
he accumulated various material goods to offer to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.
One should know that this is also called a counterfeit of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, there is another class of people who,
having already gone forth within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, [engage in such practices].
Passing from one to another, they are exclusively devoted to hearing as their ultimate goal;
you should know that this is also called a counterfeit of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, there is another class [of people].
Seeing that various bhikṣus belonging to great clans and possessing great merit were receiving abundant gains such as robes and other offerings,
he abandoned his few desires and went to them to pay respects, offer greetings, and manifest intimacy through instruction and exhortation.
Causing new bhikṣus to act with deviant minds— this,
too, should be known as a semblance of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, there is another class [of people].
They abandon all sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata that correspond to the profound emptiness,
and instead devote themselves exclusively to the study and practice of worldly literature and incantations.
Furthermore, failing to examine oneself while harboring pride in one's own cleverness,
and desiring to make others recognize one’s own intelligence and acuity—
know that this, too, is called a counterfeit of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, there is another class who,
having subdued those who are violent, evil, and transgressors of the precepts,
give rise to malicious intentions with the desire to bring harm to those violent and transgressing individuals.
One should know that this is also called a counterfeit of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, there is a class of people who fabricate and accumulate various kinds of deceptive and hypocritical deportment.
One should know that this is also called a counterfeit of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, there is another class [of people] who,
through their understanding of worldly literature and incantations, [claim to possess the Dharma].
One should know that seeking much and obtaining much gain and offerings is also called a counterfeit of the True Dharma. Furthermore,
there is another class [of people].
One who harms others and accumulates wealth and treasures through unrighteous means, thereby performing meritorious acts that are actually sinful—
this too should be known as a counterfeit of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, this very same thing which leads to what is meaningless is a counterfeit of the True Dharma.
One should know that explaining and establishing [doctrines] by means of various causes and conditions is also called a counterfeit of the True Dharma.
All such things are counterfeit Dharmas.
One should know that these are all contrary to the dharmas of training;
they are the nature and characteristics of evil friends.
A detailed exposition should be understood as it is presented in the *Śrāvakabhūmi* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Furthermore, to speak briefly:
whether it be regarding negligence, or unwholesome conduct,
or inferior virtuous qualities.
And they encourage one another;
you should know that such types are collectively termed "evil friends.
This includes those who are dull-witted, inferior, and of a foolish nature.
All intense and long-lasting afflictions are called "the blazing of deluded and ignorant afflictions.
This occurs because one failed to cultivate wholesome qualities such as faith and so forth in previous lives.
In this present life, their faith and other faculties are weak;
thus, despite being extremely earnest,
they lack the power to attain nirvana in this very life.
One should know that this is called having a deficiency in the provisions from previous lives, such that one’s strength is weak in the present life.
These are called the five kinds of factors that oppose the training.
The opposite of this should be understood as the five kinds of factors conducive to training;
because they achieve those [five], a bhikṣu should diligently train in the Vinaya.

One who is able to correctly cultivate and collect all that is to be learned and has thus accomplished these conforming dharmas possesses five further qualities that can protect the aggregate of ethical discipline: first, right renunciation.
Second, making skillful inquiries;
third, careful observation;
fourth, cultivating remedies.
Fifth is the confidence of being supported:
not being burdened by debts, one seeks to go forth into homelessness,
as explained in detail previously.
Seeking only nirvāṇa and delighting in what is to be learned, one goes forth from the household life;
know that such a person is called one who has gone forth rightly.
Having thus gone forth, regarding what constitutes an offense, what does not constitute an offense, and the restoration of purity—
If there is a bhikṣu who maintains the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma,
and regarding that which he has not yet understood, he personally goes to request a resolution from him and is thereby enlightened,
one should know that such is called "skillful inquiry."
One examines one's own ethical discipline at three times—
either during the first part of the day, the middle part of the day, or the latter part of the day—
and if one sees that there has been no transgression, one gives rise to joy.
Day and night, he dwells in diligent practice and emulation;
should he see any transgression, he immediately and swiftly repents and eliminates it in accordance with the Dharma.
It should be known that this is called "thorough investigation."
From time to time— whether during the first watch of the night, the last watch of the night, or during the daytime—
one should contemplate and cultivate the remedies for all afflictions such as attachment;
one should not be satisfied merely by hearing the teachings on ethical discipline (*śīla*).
One should know that this is called cultivating the antidote:
having deep faith that committing an offense will lead to undesirable results,
and deep faith that not committing an offense will lead to desirable results in the future.
One should know that this is called "maintaining faith.
Furthermore, with right renunciation as the basis, one performs the other four deeds;
through proper inquiry, one never commits a transgression.
One commits an offense through ignorance;
by means of careful examination, one never commits an offense again.
One commits an offense through negligence.
Through the cultivation of remedies, one never commits transgressions;
because afflictions are intensely active, there may be transgressions,
yet through the upholding of faith, one never commits transgressions.
It is an offense committed through negligence.
By relying upon these five kinds of factors, one is able to guard the aggregate of ethical discipline; this is called "skillful protection."
O diligent bhikṣu,
by means of five kinds of dharmas of tranquility,
you are able to extinguish all evils.
What are the five?
First, being gentle and easy to dwell with;
second, renunciation.
Third, the factors for abandonment;
fourth, respectful service;
fifth, the settling of disputes.
What is meant by being gentle and easy to dwell with?
It refers to what is taught in the Sūtras:
briefly, there are six kinds of dharma that are lovely and delightful.
What is abandonment?
It refers to the four wheels possessed by humans and devas.
What are the factors of abandonment?
This refers to the five factors of abandonment.
What is "reverential service"?
It is reverential service toward the Great Master.
The detailed exposition continues up to:
"There is no negligence.
What is the settling of disputes?
This refers to the seven methods for settling disputes.
It should be understood that herein, based on the body and so forth, one manifests what is unlovely toward fellow practitioners of the holy life,
and furthermore, one improperly utilizes the communal property of the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, there are factors that are discordant with the precepts and views;
because one relies upon these, it is difficult to dwell together with others,
and one's nature is not gentle or harmonious.
The mind constantly revolves and constructs [thoughts] in mutual succession;
this is what is called the counteragent to the dharmas that are desirable and pleasant.
That which is contrary to this is [the antidote].
By means of these three causes and conditions of the white side (*śuklapakṣa*),
one should know that six kinds of desirable dharmas are established;
by means of the first [cause], three are established.
Based on the second, the fourth is established;
based on the third, the fifth and sixth are established.
Furthermore, within this context, there is that which causes others to obtain desirable benefit and happiness.
The various karmas of one's own body and so forth in the present life are called "virtuous and kind friends.
If there are things that can be used for the sake of purification, [they too are such friends].
This kind of thing is called "righteous gain.
If a thing is obtained not by means of wrong livelihood or unrighteous methods,
this thing is called "righteously acquired."
If an object has already been placed inside the bowl,
one should know that this object is said to have "fallen into" the bowl;
even if an object has not yet been placed in the bowl but is about to be placed there, it is likewise so designated.
One should know that this object is subsumed under the category of the bowl.
If the food received is neither exclusively exquisite nor excessively abundant, [it is appropriate].
They eat together;
they eat openly and not in secret.
Even when there is only enough food to fill the belly, they distribute it among one another and never intentionally eat in a concealed place.
Nor does one close the door;
when there is food to be eaten, fearing that others might arrive hungry and in need seeking alms but not receiving a share,
one should know that this is called "equal enjoyment."
The detailed classification of the precepts beloved by the Noble Ones should be understood according to their characteristics as presented in the *Saṃgītiparyāya*.
As for the detailed classification of supramundane right view:
Its characteristics should be understood according to the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*.
Furthermore, it constitutes desirability through two aspects:
first, because one honors it as being endowed with those virtues.
Second, because one feels gratitude for their kindness and finds solace in it.
Furthermore, there are two distinctions regarding the nature of being delightful:
first, causing that which has not yet arisen to arise.
Second, once it has arisen, it should be further increased and expanded.
One should know that in this context, "veneration" is predominant;
that is, recognizing their possession of virtuous qualities.
The increase of consolation refers to the two types of gathering— those of material goods and the Dharma.
The increase of these two refers to their being well-harmonized.
The predominance of harmony refers to the mind being free from agitation and affliction.
Being far removed from all agitations and afflictions such as greed is called "non-opposition."
To harmonize through skillful means for the sake of a single purpose is called "non-contention" (araṇā).
To blend together like water and milk is termed "the nature of a single course" (ekāyanatva).
Furthermore, there is the perfection of the basis,
the perfection of instruction,
and the perfection of correct practice.
Based upon the perfection of the accumulations,
one should understand that the four wheels of humans and gods and the five types of excellent dwelling places are established.
This is called the perfection of the basis (*sthāna*).
It should be understood in detail as explained in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*.
[Regarding] the true person (*satpuruṣa*) and the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*):
This is called the perfection of instruction.
It should be understood in detail as explained in the *Śrāvakabhūmi* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
One should personally generate the right aspiration through five aspects.
This is called the perfection of right practice. What are the five?
First, being able to respectfully and compliantly adopt correct instruction.
Second, his conduct is free from contradiction.
Third, he manifests himself as he truly is.
Fourth, his teacher of instruction is content with whatever robes, food and drink, and bedding—whether fine or coarse—he obtains.
There are two types of application— intense and earnest— in which one delights in abandonment and delights in cultivation,
even to the point of practicing the four kinds of remedies for the craving and grasping of a bhikṣu.
Furthermore, due to the predominant power of the roots of virtue from previous lives, this person has performed meritorious deeds in past existences.
One should know that there are five aspects of the excellence of the fruit:
namely, by the predominant power of merit performed in the past,
one dwells in two kinds of desirable retributions.
First, the internal;
second, the external.
Regarding the internal, those with desirable karmic fruition:
That is to say: long-lived and enduring; of exquisite form and dignified appearance;
free from illness and having few afflictions; neither a servant, nor a woman, nor a *paṇḍaka*;
possessing sharp and keen wisdom; commanding a majestic presence when speaking; and endowed with a great retinue.
The external desirable retribution refers to being born into a wealthy and noble family,
as explained at length in the sūtra.
He possesses great wealth, great wings [of power], and a great retinue of attendants.
This is called the first superior fruit and benefit of merit performed in previous lives.
Furthermore, it is due to the predominant power of merit performed in previous lives that...
One attains a state of excellent stability;
neither various malevolent spirits (*piśāca*), yakṣas, non-humans (*amanuṣya*), nor household deities (*gṛhadevatā*) can create obstacles—
meaning they cannot obstruct one’s wealth and status.
Or, one does not encounter obstacles to one's lifespan;
this is called the second superior benefit of the fruit of merit performed in previous lives.
Furthermore, by the predominant power of merit performed in previous lives:
By nature, his mind is able to enter into and cultivate wholesome dharmas without indolence;
this is called the third benefit of the fruit of merit performed in previous lives.
Furthermore, by the predominant power of merit performed in previous lives, [he attains these qualities].
By nature, they feel deep and sincere remorse for their evil deeds;
although they have committed such acts, they repeatedly give rise to a sharp and intense sense of regret,
whereby the consequences of those past evils become attenuated in the present.
One will be able to permanently distance oneself from future evils;
this is called the fourth superior benefit of the fruit of merit performed in past lives.
Furthermore, by the dominant power of merit performed in past lives:
All their undertakings, skillful means, applications,
intentions, and arts flourish ever more;
whatever they perform is done with reverence and compliance.
With little exertion of effort, much is accomplished;
this is called the fifth excellence of the fruit of signs resulting from merit performed in previous lives.
Thus there are four kinds.
Among the devas in the heavens and among humans on earth,
the sublime and wondrous wheels of śamatha and vipaśyanā do not turn if either is lacking.
Furthermore, based on the meaning that ought to be attained, one generates profound faith and understanding.

In the presence of the teacher, one truthfully reveals to them that one possesses physical vigor and mental vigor, and is thus capable of comprehending the meaning of all dharmas, whether well-spoken or ill-spoken.
One should understand that five factors of abandonment are established in their respective order;
if even one factor is lacking, abandonment will not be accomplished.
Furthermore, at the outset, one ought to exert effort and respectfully serve the Great Master.
This refers to being able to proclaim the teachings on the training in higher ethics, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
Next, one should respectfully serve those who have proclaimed these teachings.
Next, when practicing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma,
one should respectfully serve and rely upon the training rules corresponding to the higher training in ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*) and the Vinaya.

Subsequently, one should respectfully serve and rely upon the instructions and exhortations concerning the higher training in concentration (*adhicitta*) and the higher training in wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
From time to time, one should practice material offerings and Dharma offerings.
It should be understood that, in this context,
material and Dharma offerings refer to dwelling together and sharing in common enjoyment.
Next, one cultivates samādhi within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Immediately following this, one penetrates the principles of the truths without craving for their flavor;
thus, all outflows (*āsrava*) are forever exhausted, and there is no negligence.
In this way, the distinctions and sequence of these seven types of reverent service should be understood.
Furthermore, reverent service should be understood by means of three characteristics:
one gives rise to respect because of being able to realize those virtues and their benefits.
According to what they have fully realized, they cultivate reverence through the three types of correct practice— of body, speech, and mind—
and further provide various offerings such as banners, streamers, and canopies.
There are fellow practitioners of the holy life who point out the various offenses committed by another fellow practitioner of the holy life,
doing so face-to-face before their very eyes,
based on what is factual and not unfactual.
...and so on, as extensively explained.
When one who has not yet understood attains correct understanding, there is no further transgression;
because there is no further transgression, these bhikṣus [are purified].
One should not repeatedly raise previously committed offenses based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected;
in this way, the matter of dispute shall be extinguished.
There are bhikṣus who, upon seeing another bhikṣu committing an offense at a certain time, [act accordingly].
At a later time, the one who committed the offense forgot what he had done,
while the one who witnessed the offense remembered it and brought the matter forward, asking:
"Do you remember what you have transgressed?
He replied, "I do not remember anything at all."
Since he does not remember it, he cannot repent of it himself;
yet he falsely claims, "I remember.
It is not through words of regret that one can be freed from remorse (*kaukṛtya*).
Since he has been accused by another,
he should follow that person's lead and request from the Saṃgha the *smṛti-vinaya* (recollection of the rule), the *amūḍha-vinaya* (acknowledgment of past insanity),
and purification. At that time, the Saṃgha shall grant those bhikṣus their purification.
The offender shall be freed from the *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Those monks must not raise again the matter previously committed;
in this way, the dispute shall be extinguished.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu, due to insanity, engages in numerous practices that are unbecoming of a śramaṇa and contrary to the Dharma,
he does not incur an offense on account of those actions.
Furthermore, there is a class of ignorant bhikṣus who claim that another has committed an offense where none exists and raise the issue inappropriately.
Other bhikṣus, in order to prevent such things in the future, provide instruction and reminders.
He causes him to obtain from the community of monks the perception of non-delusion regarding the Vinaya and purity for his own mind;
having heard this, he immediately requests it.
At that time, the Saṃgha should declare that such a person has not committed an offense;
the Saṃgha should remain in harmony and proclaim their purity.
Once the ignorant bhikṣu has heard this, [he should act accordingly].
One shall not again raise the matter of the offense previously committed;
in this way, the dispute shall be extinguished.
Furthermore, there may be a bhikṣu who raises the charge of an offense against another bhikṣu within the community of monks.
The one who brings forth the charge conceives the notion that an offense has been committed,
while the one being charged conceives the notion that no offense has been committed;
because of this notion of non-offense, he declares of himself, "I have committed no offense."
The accuser said, "Venerable sir, did you not perform such and such deeds?
He then spoke truthfully,
"I have never done so."
Regarding the phrase "able to raise [the issue] again," it means that although he has already committed an offense,
even now that it has been raised, he still does not understand it.
Therefore, it is still said that there is no offense.
At that time, the community of monks shall investigate the essential nature of the matter to determine whether it constitutes an offense or not;
once the truth has been established, they shall adjudicate according to the Dharma.
In this way, the matter of dispute was settled.
In another residence, there were many bhikṣus who,
regarding the offenses they had committed, developed mutual doubts and disputes.
Some say there is an offense, while others say there is no offense;
some say it is grave, while others say it is light.
There are also separate residences where the number of the assembly exceeds the previous limit.
Alternatively, if one expects that among the other assembly there are many who possess wisdom and understanding and can receive and uphold the Tripitaka,
they should come to this assembly to request a resolution of their doubts so as to reach a definitive conclusion.
In this way, the matter of dispute will be extinguished.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, having committed an offense,
is stirred by the affliction of remorse and consequently becomes distressed.
Fearing that others might expose him, he then repents in accordance with the Dharma.
By this, all matters of dispute are extinguished.
There were many bhikṣus who mutually accused one another,
each being gripped by arrogance.
Not wishing to confess their transgressions face-to-face,
they were intent solely on causing a schism;
the two groups lived separately, each saying:
Since they are unwilling to come before our assembly to confess and eliminate their transgressions,
why should we unilaterally go before their assembly to do so?
Each of our respective factions should appoint one wise leader to jointly receive the words spoken.
If a person goes together with others to another assembly and is permitted to confess and eliminate their transgression,
such a dispute will then be resolved and extinguished.
Thus, there are briefly four kinds of disputes;
it should be known that their removal and cessation likewise have four kinds.
What are these four kinds of disputes?
First, disputes raised by others;
second, disputes arising from mutual suspicion;
third, disputes raised by oneself.
Fourth, the mutual raising of matters of dispute.
What, furthermore, are called the four kinds of methods for their resolution?
First, resolution through the vow to emerge from what has been transgressed.
Second is elimination through giving;
third is elimination by seeking the true nature;
fourth is elimination through individual confession.
The Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Ninety-nine;
The Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle One hundred;
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
In the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*, within the *Vinayavastu-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, Part Five, Section Two: Furthermore, regarding the bhikṣu who diligently trains in accordance with the *Vinaya*.
One should correctly and fully know five points.
What are these five? First, the full knowledge of phenomena (*vastu-parijñā*).
Second, thorough knowledge of the two types of offenses;
third, thorough knowledge of persons;
fourth, thorough knowledge of the gathering of beneficial aims.
Fifth is the thorough knowledge of affliction.
What is the thorough knowledge of phenomena?
It refers to the five phenomena, such as the aggregates, as already explained in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*.
What is the thorough knowledge of offenses?
It refers to a bhikṣu who diligently trains in the Vinaya,
thoroughly knowing the transgressions through five aspects.
First, thoroughly knowing the causes and conditions of the offense;
second, thoroughly knowing the origination of the offense;
third, thoroughly knowing the matter of the offense committed.
Fourth, the thorough knowledge of the preliminary application of an offense;
fifth, the thorough knowledge of the consummation of an offense.
Regarding the thorough knowledge of the causes and conditions of an offense:
That is to say, either due to the causal condition of greed,
or the causal condition of hatred,
or the causal condition of delusion.
Regarding the thorough knowledge of the origins of transgressions among the various offenses:
it refers to cases where a certain offense originates from the body, but not from speech or mind.
Furthermore, there may be offenses that originate from speech, neither from body nor mind;
or there may be offenses that originate from mind, neither from body nor speech;
or there may be offenses that originate from both body and mind, not from speech.
Furthermore, there are offenses that originate through speech and mind but not through body;
there are offenses that originate through body and speech but not through mind;
and there are offenses that originate through body, speech, and mind.
There are many offenses committed solely through the mind that must be disclosed and eliminated before others;
one should simply be earnest and sincere, guarding oneself deeply from within.
For example, if a bhikṣu gives rise to various unwholesome discursive thoughts, such as thoughts of sensual desire,
he must fully comprehend the nature of the offense committed.
Regarding the matter of the offense, there are briefly two types.
First, things belonging to the category of sentient beings;
second, things belonging to the category of insentient objects.
These are to be fully understood as the applications of the commission of offenses.
It means that the offenses committed involve two types of preparatory application (*prayoga*):
first, the preparatory application of an action that ought not to be performed;
second, the preparatory application of an action that ought to be performed.
Regarding the full comprehension of the culmination of an offense:
it means that where a preliminary effort is established,
therein one attains its culmination.
There is no retrogression in the interim;
for this reason, the offense is considered complete.

Among the various collections of gross offenses—namely, the *pārājika*, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and the preparatory acts—one incurs a downfall (*sthūlātyaya*) or a transgression of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
One attains the culmination within those preparatory efforts and one's own assembly;
furthermore, regarding the preparatory efforts for a downfall offense,
one also commits a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
The four categories of offenses are called "offenses with remainder.
The category of *pārājika* (defeat) offenses is called "an offense without remainder.
If an offense committed is [resolved] through wisdom...
It is not accumulated by name;
nor is it accumulated because it is manifested through others.
The opposite of this is not the case;
it is not that [the merit] has not been accumulated.
If the offense committed has already been confessed according to the Dharma to another and skillfully repented and removed, [then it is not lost].
That which has been explicitly stated is called "already explained";
that which is contrary to this is called "not yet explained."
If one holds onto a transgression committed and intends to repent for it,
this is called "having a fixed aspiration.
That which is contrary to this is [the opposite].
It is called "having no expectation.
If one has committed an offense,
the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, [have prescribed it] within the Pratimokṣa Vinaya.
To establish [an offense] is called "having an established rule.
That which is contrary to this is [the opposite].
It is not established by name;
rather, it refers to the offense committed with respect to a particular category of person.
Alternatively, it may be determined by time without being fixed;
first, a general rule is established without distinction.
One should know that this offense is termed "equal application" (*samāhāra*).
The opposite of this is called non-equal application (*asamavāha*).
What is the thorough knowledge of the person (*pudgala*)?
That is to say, their distinctions should be understood by way of five aspects:
first, by way of the distinction of practice;
second, by way of the distinction of the assembly.
Third, by way of the distinction of increase and decrease;
fourth, by way of the distinction of realization;
and fifth, by way of the distinction of investigation.
Regarding the distinction by way of conduct:
this means that because one can fully comprehend the distinctions in conduct such as greed and so forth,
those [beings] possess such distinctions.
Its characteristics should be understood as they are described in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
Regarding the distinction by way of the assemblies:
this refers to the fact that it possesses distinctions due to the sevenfold classification of the assemblies, such as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and so forth, which one is able to fully comprehend.
Regarding the distinction of increase and decrease:
it refers, for example, to a certain type of person who has gone forth from a noble family.
Some have left the household life from wealthy clans;
some possess handsome and upright features;
others, however, do not share these qualities.
Furthermore, there is another class of persons who are learned and widely knowledgeable,
perfected in speech, possessing great wisdom and great merit,
and who maintain their pure ethical discipline with firm and vigorous protection.
If they commit even minor transgressions, they frequently give rise to remorse;
they are well able to discern both the nature of the transgression and the means of its purification.
Other types of persons are not like this.
If one can fully understand such matters as these,
it should be known that this is called "thorough knowledge" because there are distinctions in increase and decrease,
and because there are distinctions in realization.

This refers to the thorough knowledge of the sevenfold distinctions beginning with those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and ending with those liberated from both parts (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*),
as well as the eightfold distinctions ranging from the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphalapratipannaka*) up to the final fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*).
These various distinctions among types of persons (*pudgala*) have already been explained in their characteristics within the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
Regarding the distinction by way of observation:
That is to say, the person who is able to charge another with an offense should carefully examine the one being charged before charging them and bringing it to their recollection.
This means observing whether the person who has been exhorted feels love and respect toward oneself;
the details of its characteristics should be understood as explained at length in the sūtra.
As for the person who has been exhorted:
One should also carefully examine the one who brings forth the accusation:
whether they are a fool, insane, deluded, or ignorant, and whether they are accusing me unrighteously with the intent to cause me harm.
The details should be understood according to their characteristics as explained in the sūtra.
These are the virtuous qualities (śukla-dharma) belonging to one who is wise, neither insane nor foolish;
the details should be understood according to their characteristics as explained in the sūtra.
Furthermore, regarding a person who is capable of being uplifted,
one should correctly examine whether they should be uplifted;
in this way, one examines the various distinctions among persons.
One should know that this is called the thorough knowledge of the person (*pudgala-parijñā*).
What is the thorough knowledge of the acquisition of beneficial aims?
It refers to the thorough knowledge that there are, in brief, three kinds of acquisition of beneficial aims.
What are these three?
First, the purpose of attracting and securing benefits and gains for oneself;
second, the purpose of attracting and securing the removal of offenses for others.
Third, regarding the gathering of the Saṃgha and the benefit of establishing those who have transgressed the precepts in peace and well-being:
as for the benefit of gathering one's own gains and offerings,
it refers to when the nature of those gains and offerings is pure.
This is called the true reality.
If various gains and offerings are pure in essence and fit for practical use, it is not without purpose;
however, to store them away in great abundance while neglecting the hundreds of basic requisites is merely superfluous.
This is called that which leads to meaningful benefit.
If various gains and offerings do not exceed the proper time and can be maintained and utilized accordingly,
this is called "timely."
If other bhikṣus also manifest an attraction toward those gains and offerings,
this is called "having companions. However,
such having of companions does not constitute leading to a schism in the Saṃgha.
This is called being free from schism in the Saṃgha.
If one is drawn toward and accepts gain and profit while possessing these five factors and abiding in right mindfulness, [one incurs an offense].
One should enjoy [these things] with a mind free from attachment;
thus, the acquisition of gains and benefits in this manner is called "blameless."
Regarding the meaning of drawing others out from their transgressions for the sake of benefit:
this refers to when the transgression committed is actually carried out by them;
this is called "reality."
Furthermore, if one knows for oneself that one can cause another to emerge from an unwholesome state and establish them in a wholesome state,
this is called being able to bring about benefit and profit.
This also applies when another is teaching the Dharma, or when one is respectfully serving elders, honoring them, attending to the sick, and so forth, during the time of correct application.
It is not permissible to raise the charge;
this is called "timely.
If other bhikṣus act as companions in raising that person's offense, [it is likewise timely].
This is called "having a companion.
Such causes and conditions cannot lead to a schism in the Saṃgha;
this is termed the fifth purity.
Regarding the purpose of being drawn out from an offense,
one should abide in right mindfulness with an undefiled mind;
just as a virtuous friend uses gentle words to draw another out from an offense, so too should one draw others toward the purpose of being freed from transgression.
Just as there is the benefit of leading others out of transgressions,
one should know that it is likewise the benefit of leading the Saṃgha to expel those who violate the precepts for the sake of peace and happiness.
As for the distinction: if,
because of the expulsion, the one being expelled does not create an obstacle to the life of the one who expels him.
Or perhaps he does not, because of this, destroy the monastic dwellings and gardens;
nor does he, because of this, damage the caityas,
nor harm other fellow practitioners of the holy life.
This is called that which leads to what is beneficial;
the opposite of this should be understood as being said to lead to what is unbeneficial.
What is the thorough knowledge of affliction?
It refers to five kinds of afflictions in the present life to which ordinary persons resort.
It is the destination of the deluded and that which the wise avoid;
though in truth he is not mad, he acts as if he were mad.
It results in nothing but empty deception and procrastination,
with no increase whatsoever in any meaningful benefit.
What are these five?
This refers to a certain class of people who, grieving over death,
torment themselves through immeasurable means because of their sorrow for those who have perished;
this is called the first affliction in the present life.
Regarding the destinations of ordinary worldlings, and so forth, as explained at length; furthermore,
there is a certain class of people who, despite having other means of easy livelihood available,
[frequent] the main roads, great marketplaces, and public squares.
With his limbs and joints dismembered and his life nearly at its end,
he subjects himself to perverse suffering in order to remain alive.
This is called the second present-life affliction.
Regarding the destinations of ordinary worldlings, and so forth as extensively explained;
furthermore, there is a class of people who are by nature stingy and greedy, obscured by the defilement of avarice,
even though they fortunately possess various resources for sustaining their lives.
Yet they must live by means of great hardship;
this is called the third affliction in the present life.
This applies to the destinations of ordinary persons, and so forth, as explained at length.
What is the stain of stinginess?
It refers to the eight stains of stinginess.
The first is the stain of stinginess consisting in habitual greed for the past and a lack of familiarity with giving.
Second, the stain of stinginess consisting of intense attachment to one’s body and life in this present existence;

third, the stain of stinginess consisting of a weak and unaccustomed lack of compassion toward those sentient beings who dwell together with one as companions of a similar class and follow along with one’s conduct.
Fourth is the stain of stinginess consisting in seeing those of little virtue in the field of merit, violating right conduct, and being defiled by parsimony.
Fifth is the stain of stinginess consisting in conceiving the thought that material goods are difficult to obtain.
Sixth is the stain of stinginess consisting in anxiety and regret at the three times [past, present, and future].
Seventh is the stain of stinginess consisting in seeing only the merits and not the faults of various wealth and treasures.
Eighth is the stain of stinginess consisting in misdirecting one's offerings through wrong dedication.
One should know that these are called the eight kinds of stains of stinginess.
Furthermore, there is another class of people who, out of a fondness for the celestial realms, seek rebirth among the gods;
yet they do not know, as it truly is, the path to rebirth in heaven.
They thus inflict harm upon themselves by fasting, throwing themselves into fire, leaping from high cliffs, and so forth.
This is called the fourth affliction in the present life.
It is the destination of ordinary persons, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, there is another class who delight in purity.
They do not know the path of purification as it truly is; that is,
they believe purification is attained through practices involving self-inflicted suffering,
and thus they subject themselves to harm by means of countless methods.
This is called the fifth affliction in the present life.
It is that toward which ordinary persons proceed, and so forth, as explained at length.
Such are the five kinds of afflictions in the present life.
A bhikṣu who trains diligently in the Vinaya should thoroughly and completely understand [these matters] and swiftly abandon them.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who trains diligently in the Vinaya...
By accomplishing five dharmas,
one causes those who have not yet developed faith to develop it,
and causes those who have already developed faith to increase it manifold.
What are the five?
First, the perfection of ethical discipline;
second, the perfection of right view.
Third, the perfection of the three modes of conduct.
Fourth, the perfection of pure livelihood.
Fifth, the perfection of being free from mutual strife and contention.
The perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*) briefly consists of ten types, as their characteristics have already been explained in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
That is to say: first, it is properly undertaken and maintained, being neither too sunken nor too agitated.
...and so forth, as extensively explained.
Right view is perfected in brief through five aspects:
first, because the increase of the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) have been permanently severed.
Second, because the wrong view of denial, which consists of deprecating and negating [the truth], has been permanently severed;
third, because the grasping at views—namely, all forms of *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* and *śīlavrataparāmarśa*—has been permanently severed.
Fourth, because the false view of conceiving auspicious places has been permanently severed.
Fifth, because the various inverted views that falsely conceive the non-conditioned as conditioned and the conditioned as non-conditioned have been permanently severed.
The perfection of the rules of conduct also has five aspects:
namely, those concerning matters that ought to be performed according to time and circumstance,
or those concerning matters that ought to be performed for the sake of the wholesome qualities.
Alternatively, one should act in accordance with the rules of conduct and the duties to be performed,
following the conventions of the world and the Vinaya;
this should be understood in detail as explained in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
The perfection of pure livelihood also has five aspects;
namely, being able to remain far removed from the five factors that give rise to wrong livelihood, such as hypocrisy and so forth.
Their characteristics should be understood as they are described in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
The perfection of being far removed from mutual strife and contention consists briefly of six kinds.
This is because one is free from the six roots of strife.
Among these, the six roots of strife are as follows:
This refers to anger, resentment, and so forth,
as explained at length in the sūtras.
Furthermore, one should understand that the six roots of contention are established based on the six sense bases.
What are the six bases?
First, the characteristic of non-beneficiality;
second, the conceited persistence in hiding one's own faults.
Third, the manifestation of desire for gain, honor, and sensual pleasure;
fourth, the transgression of the higher training in ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*);
and fifth, the transgression of the higher training in concentration (*adhicitta*).
Sixth is the transgression of the practice of higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
One should know that based on the first point, the first root of contention is established;
and so on, up to the sixth point, where the sixth root of contention is established.
It refers to a certain class of persons who are well-known to the public and receive abundant gains and offerings from others;
by reason of these circumstances, they commit transgressions.
Regarding the offense committed, he desires to conceal it and does not wish for others to know what he has transgressed; yet,
there are bhikṣus who have already become fully aware of it.
Whether confronted by one person, two people, or many regarding the offense committed,
he becomes entirely despondent and his body and mind are consumed by distress;
furthermore, because he is gripped by arrogance, he gives rise to much burning anguish.
"Lest he, in turn, reproach me before others;
thus, that person first conceals what they have transgressed,
which is termed 'concealment' (*paticchādana*)."
Furthermore, they give rise to the affliction of pride.
These two combined are termed "the conceited grasping that delights in concealing one's own faults.
From this, the root of conflict is established.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who manifests reverence for gain and the desire for love;
he sees another person who possesses abundant wealth and treasures, is well-known to all, and is endowed with great merit and blessings.
They will then become intimate with them and serve them with great earnestness—
not out of affection, nor out of respect, nor because they delight in the Dharma,
but solely for the sake of gain and honor.
Reflecting in this way, one should embrace straightforwardness and patience,
taking gentleness as one's reliance.
"Venerable sir,
I have complete freedom of will in that place;
he has performed many services for me there."
Yet I do nothing at all toward them;
thus reflecting, I embrace those of swift wisdom who delight in cultivating merit and practicing the holy life together with me.
Taking them as companions,
he had them perform all monastic affairs and other matters,
while he himself remained solitary and lived in self-contentment.
In this way, there may be those who have violated the prohibitive precepts;
when fellow practitioners of the holy life (sabrahmacārin) formally interrogate them,
they fail to speak clearly and instead resort to pretexts by speaking of other matters.
This is called practicing hypocrisy, deception, and flattery.
By reason of these causes and conditions, quarrels and disputes arise in that place;
the characteristics of other such cases should be understood accordingly as appropriate.
Contrary to these,
there are five kinds of dharmas that cause those who have no faith to further increase their lack of faith.
It causes those who already have faith to undergo transformation immediately.
