Furthermore, a bhikṣu who diligently studies the Vinaya accomplishes five powers regarding all modes of equanimous mental conduct and their respective applications.
What are the five powers?
First, the power of application;
second, the power of intention.
Third, the power of elucidation;
fourth, the power of right knowledge;
fifth, the power of straightforwardness.
If there is one who delights in training in all aspects of the limbs of training and trains therein with perfect excellence;
and who, with the utmost reverence for that which is to be trained, acts for their own self-discipline and for parinirvāṇa.
In this way, one should know the power of application (*prayoga-bala*).
If there is an offense committed, by virtue of one's intention (*āśaya*), one swiftly emerges from it;
in this way, one should know the power of intention.
If, from time to time, one questions those who uphold the Tripiṭaka regarding the points of training,
they will also be able to reveal that which all self-loving sons of good family ought to practice and learn.
In this way, it should be known as the power of clear understanding (*vibhāvanā-bala*).
Having heard from others, one correctly and authentically accepts that which is true and real therein without error;
and one understands as they truly are those false utterances regarding the Vinaya and pseudo-teachings that resemble the True Dharma, which contradict the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Although he did not go there in person to inquire about what he had not yet understood,
because of his great learning, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, neither prohibited nor authorized it.
One is able to reflect for oneself upon the nature of a śramaṇa as being conducive or as being contrary;
having understood this, one is able to practice correctly and distance oneself correctly according to what is appropriate.
In this way, one should know it as the power of correct knowledge and wisdom (*jñānabala*).
If the power of faith and understanding is free from all deceit and flattery,
there will not be even the slightest degree of fraudulent or false discrimination.
One does not engage in practice by superimposing many aspects onto that which is permitted in only a few;
nor does one engage in practice by diminishing a few aspects within that which is permitted in many.
That which they manifest in practice neither increases nor decreases.
Thus, at the outset, they personally experience joy;
subsequently, they cause themselves and others to abide in peace and happiness while practicing the right path.
It is not for the purpose of deceiving others.
In this way, one should understand the power of integrity.
Furthermore, it relies upon the training in the application of the Vinaya.
It should be understood that there are five categories of persons (pudgala).
That is to say, there is a certain class of person who,
within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, [proceeds as follows].
Relying on the dharma of renunciation, one first begins to set out;
yet, although one wishes to set out, one has not yet renounced the world,
and thus afflictions and perverse desires arise as one seeks.
For these reasons, they ultimately do not go forth.
Furthermore, there is another class who, having already gone forth,
contemplate committing offenses because their afflictions are so intense.
Due to these causes and conditions, they experience much regret and remorse;
consequently, afflictions and perverse desires arise, leading them to seek [satisfaction].
Furthermore, there is another class who, having already left the household life, [experience this].
They do not experience joy or delight in the life of renunciation;
they intend to abandon what they have studied and set out [for the world],
and they give rise to sorrow and regret regarding their renunciation.
And he thinks to himself:
"This so-called renunciation that I am practicing is not my own good work.
Due to these two conditions, afflictions and perverse desires arise within him, leading him to seek after them.
Furthermore, there is another class of persons who, having already gone forth,
do not intentionally transgress their training due to life-threatening circumstances;
they remain devoted to the life of a renunciant until the end of their lives, diligently practicing the holy life.
They do not give rise to afflictions or improper desires through these two conditions;
such four types of individuals belong to the class of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, there is another class.
This refers to those in training who have not yet attained liberation;
taking this as their basis,
they subsequently achieve penetration, progress, and advancement through the first moment of mind characterized by wisdom-liberation.
One who understands things as they truly are is called the fifth type of person (pudgala).
This fifth type, when compared to the preceding fourth type of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), [is superior].
Due to the well-tamed, lovely liberation of one in training,
there is a distinction in the subsequent penetration, advancement, and progression toward liberation;
it should be understood that this person has already seen the path of the truths.
Among these, the first three types of persons,
as appropriate, [experience] that which arises from setting out and that which arises from remorse.
Furthermore, one should correctly eliminate all afflictions and perverse desires for seeking that arise together with it;
one should correctly understand the higher liberation.
Regarding the fourth, one should correctly understand it only in relation to the subsequent higher liberations.
If one can do so in all respects, one will attain complete equality.
Within the trainings, one should know that there are, in brief, three types of misconduct.
This refers to a certain class of individuals who,
having first sought nirvāṇa, delight in going forth; yet after they have gone forth,
they become swept away by the attachment to the exquisite sensual pleasures of the devas.
To dedicate the precepts one has undertaken toward a favorable rebirth,
while finding mere protection of the *śīla* (ethical discipline) sufficient for satisfaction—
this is called the first type of wrong practice regarding superior ethical discipline by a person who is externally fettered.
Furthermore, there is another class of individuals who do not merely find satisfaction in guarding their ethical discipline,
but are able to attain and realize one or another of the higher mundane meditative concentrations.

One who becomes deeply attached to this meditative concentration and fails to progress toward the higher realization of the Noble Truths is called an individual with internal fetters who commits the second type of wrong practice regarding the higher mind (*adhicitta*).
Furthermore, there is another class of individuals who are learners (śaikṣa) having already seen the path of the truths; yet,
due to dwelling in negligence, they do not attain parinirvāṇa in this present life.
One should know that this is called the third type of wrong practice regarding superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
This is the *mātṛkā* summary of the essential tenets for training in accordance with the knowledge of the objects of this treatise.
All other matters should be understood by following this same methodological approach.
3. Within the *Mātṛkā-vastu-saṃgrahaṇī*, in the section on the introduction to the *mātṛkā-vastu*: Thus has been explained the *Vinaya-vastu-mātṛkā* and the *Tarka-vastu*.
That is to say, whether it be the Sūtra-mātṛkā or the Vinaya-mātṛkā,
they are collectively and briefly termed one mātṛkā.
Although there is no other separate Mātṛkā,
it is nevertheless included here in brief because it explains,
in a mixed manner, the processes of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, as well as affliction (saṃkleśa) and purification (vyavadāna).
I shall now further explain the Mātṛkā for the differentiation of the characteristics of phenomena.
The summary verse (uddāna) says:
"It is necessary that one thing be explained by another; it is not this very thing that explains itself."
Having briefly introduced the subject matter above, hereafter it shall be analyzed in detail.
If there are various phenomena that ought to be explained to others,
they must first be presented in a general manner by means of other categories.
Furthermore, it will be explained separately later by means of other approaches.
If it were so, it would be called "conforming to correct reasoning" (*yukti-anusārin*);
however, this is not the case for that which was previously presented as a general heading within this very approach.
This very section will be explained separately later.
Just as it was previously stated in general terms—"What is the conditioned?"—it is subsequently explained specifically as "the five aggregates.
If it is done in this manner, it accords with correct reasoning (*yukti*).
It is not that one first states the general heading "What is conditioned? and subsequently provides a detailed explanation by saying "That which is called conditioned.
All such cases should be understood accordingly;
in brief, they are characterized by two aspects.
One should know that the *mātṛkā* for establishing the characteristics of conceptual phenomena consists of two parts:
first, a brief introductory summary of the subject matter;
second, the subsequent detailed analysis based upon that brief summary.

It concerns the phenomena of the category of defilement (*saṃkleśa*) that undergoes cyclic existence, as well as the phenomena of the category of purification (*vyavadāna*) that involves cessation and reversal.
What are the phenomena of the category of defilement that undergoes cyclic existence?
They are the phenomena of the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya*) regarding their intrinsic nature, their basis, their objects, and their accompanying factors.
Whether it be the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases;
the phenomena of the dependent origination of what is possible and what is impossible;
or the phenomena of the three types of feeling.
Whether it concerns matters of the three times,
matters of the four conditions,
or matters of various karmas.
Whether it be the objects of the afflictions,
or the objects of the three realms—
namely, the desire realm and so forth.
If there are ten modes of existence, they are:
namely, the existence of desire (kāmadhātu) and the existence of form (rūpadhātu).
The existence of the formless realm;
the existence of hell-beings;
the existence of animals.
There are ghosts;
there are devas;
there are humans.
There are two types of existence:

karmic existence (*karma-bhava*) and intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), distinguished by their respective roles in detaching from desire and in projecting and leading one toward happy or miserable destinies.
If it concerns the eleven bases of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*),
this refers to the collective exposition of the four bases of consciousness together with the seven bases of consciousness.
If it concerns the nine abodes of sentient beings (*sattvāvāsa*).
As explained at length in the sutras:
whether it concerns the five destinies or the four modes of birth.
Whether it be the four ways of entering the womb,
the four ways of obtaining a physical body,
or the four kinds of nutriment.
Whether it be the objects of the four modes of verbal expression,
the objects of the four types of dharma-acceptance,
or the objects of the four perversions.
Whether it be the matter of the truth of suffering,
or the matter of the truth of origination,
or other such categories.
This is called the brief introduction to the section on the defilement of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
What is the section on the purification of cessation (*nivṛtti*)?
It refers to the reality of the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
Whether it be the matter of the Truth of the Path,
the matter of meditative concentration,
or the matter of various types of knowledge.
Whether it be these various matters of merit thus induced,
or the seven matters of the true Dharma,
or the seven matters of observation through right mental attention.
Whether it be the matter of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment,
the matter of the four paths of practice,
or the matter of the four tracks of the Dharma.
Whether it be the objects of śamatha and vipaśyanā,
the objects of the four meditative cultivations,
or the objects of the three meritorious actions.
Whether it be the matter of the three trainings,
the matter of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya,
or the matter of the four kinds of verified confidence.
Whether it be the matters of the four noble lineages,
the matters of the three vehicles,
or the matters of the four gateways of recollection.
Such categories as these are called a brief introduction to the matters concerning the category of purification through cessation.
These matters are established through extensive exposition.
According to what is appropriate,
one should understand their characteristics as previously explained for each respective stage and its constituent factors.
To summarize all matters,
there are five categories in total.
The first is the category of mental objects.
Second, the category of mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*);
third, the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*);
and fourth, the category of formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Fifth is the unconditioned matter (*asaṃskṛta-vastu*).
How is this very matter, which was briefly introduced above, to be explained in detail?
It is explained in detail by means of four characteristics.
What are the four?
First, by way of the differentiation of synonyms;
second, by way of the differentiation of essential characteristics.
Third, by way of the distinction in the etymological explanations;
fourth, by way of the distinction in categories.
This refers to the distinction in etymological explanations regarding the different gates, entities, and characteristics.
Its characteristics should be understood as they appear in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds of distinctions in its categories:
first, the distinction between the nature of existence and non-existence, and difference and non-difference.
Second, the establishment of the distinctions of realms and stages;
third, the establishment of the distinctions of temporal periods;
fourth, the establishment of the distinctions of spatial locations.
Fifth, the establishment of the distinctions of continuity;
sixth, the establishment of the distinctions of stages;
seventh, the establishment of the distinctions of categories.
Eighth is the differentiation of the principles of establishment.
By means of these eight kinds of differentiations,
[one understands] all things and their various categories.
One should understand this accordingly.
How are the distinctions between existence, non-existence, difference, and non-difference established?
Briefly stated, there are three kinds of existence.
First, substantial existence;
second, nominal existence;
third, ultimate existence.
What is meant by "truly existent"?
It refers to those phenomena expressed through designations for which a name can be apprehended and a referent can be apprehended;
this name functions without obstruction toward its referent.
It does not function at one time and not function at another;
this should be known as a brief explanation of "substantial existence" (dravyasat),
such as in the case of the aggregates of phenomena like form and so forth.
The characteristics of walls, houses, armies, forests, grasses, trees, food, clothing, and so forth are established;
these characteristics function only within this particular collection [of elements] and recede from others.
The various characteristics such as form and so forth follow and operate in all places;
therefore, that which is expressed by these characteristics exists substantially.
One should know that that which is expressed by other characteristics exists nominally.
Furthermore, these provisional existents are briefly of six kinds:
first, provisional existence as an aggregate;
second, provisional existence as a cause.
Third, the provisional existence of the fruits;
fourth, the provisional existence of the objects of engagement;
fifth, the provisional existence of the stages.
Sixth is conventional existence by way of dependence.
Conventional existence by way of aggregation refers to that which is established for the sake of conforming to worldly discourse so that it may be easily understood.
Regarding the general characteristics of the five aggregates and so forth,
one establishes the notions of "self," "sentient being," "individual" (*pudgala*), "living being," and so on;
these notions merely manifest this collection.
Therefore, it is called "provisionally existent as an aggregation.
Regarding "provisionally existent by way of causes," this refers to phenomena that are subject to arising in the future, which exist [only] because they have not yet arisen.
Although it does not exist substantially,
because its causes exist and it is capable of arising,
it is called "provisionally existent by way of cause."
If it is conventionally existent as a fruit—
namely, because analytical cessation is the fruit of the Path—
it cannot be said to be non-existent.
However, it does not exist as a substantial reality;
it is merely a conventional designation established based on the fact that all afflictions have been severed and will never arise again in future lives.
Regarding "conditioned phenomena that exist as mere designations":
this refers to those conditioned phenomena of the past that have already ceased,
which function solely as the objects of present mental attention.
Therefore, it is called "provisionally existent" (prajñaptisat) as an object of engagement;
because it has already ceased and perished,
it is not substantially existent (dravyasat).
Regarding those that exist as designations based on states (*avasthā-prajñapti-sat*):
these refer to the various formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth,
which were previously indicated, analyzed, and explained in the *Manobhūmi*.
Regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), based on their prior existence and subsequent non-existence,
as well as their states within similar and dissimilar successions, one conventionally designates "birth" and so forth.
These [factors] such as birth do not possess a real, intrinsic essence that can be found separately outside of the conditioned phenomena themselves.
Regarding that which exists as a conventional designation through dependence:
this refers to space, non-analytical cessation, and so forth.
Space, an unconditioned phenomenon, is conventionally established in dependence upon the various categories of form.
If, in this context, space is conventionally designated where form does not exist,
it is not that there is some distinct external entity of space to be found apart from form as something manifested.
It is not the case that something is designated as "truly existent" merely because it lacks a manifest basis.
In relation to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), [a dharma] does not arise simultaneously;
thus, among those dharmas that do not arise in the future, [this designation applies].
The non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is established as being manifested by non-arising;
it is conventionally designated as "existent.
However, that which is manifested by non-arising cannot be said to be substantially existent (*dravyasat*).
What is ultimate existence?
It is that in which all conventional designations and all conceptual constructs are forever severed,
and which is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Free from all conceptual discrimination,
he teaches through skillful means that the nature of phenomena is suchness, the limit of reality, emptiness, selflessness, and so forth.

The characteristic of the reality that is the object of knowledge purified of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa-viśuddha-jñāna-gocara-tattva*), as found in the fourth chapter, "The Chapter on the Meaning of Reality," of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
should be understood as being the opposite of the aforementioned [characteristics].
One should know that they do not exist.
Furthermore, one should understand that the establishment of difference and non-difference is due to four kinds of distinctions and non-distinctions.
First, by the distinction or non-distinction of their causes;
second, by the distinction or non-distinction of their bases;
third, by the distinction or non-distinction of their functions.
Fourth, because there is no distinction based on temporal differentiation.
If the various phenomena, such as causes and so forth, were to possess distinct characteristics that could be apprehended,
this difference would be distinct from others.
If no distinct characteristics or differences can be apprehended,
then this prior [state], the subsequent [state], and the present are not different.
This is the analysis of time.
This means that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) abide for only a single moment;
yet, this very essence, when considered in relation to itself,
is said to be non-different.
That which is designated as "alteration" occurs after the passing of a moment;
because it serves as the seed from which this [subsequent state] arises,
it is called the cause.
If it proceeds by depending upon the eye and so forth, as well as the primary elements and so forth,
these are called its "bases" (āśraya).
If it refers to the distinct functions of each of the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), [they are called bases].
This is designated as "activity.
In this way, the distinctions among the categories of existence and non-existence, which are neither different nor non-different, are established.
How, then, are the distinctions between realms (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*) established?
This refers to the distinctions between the three realms: the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
Regarding the "desire realm," it extends from the Avīci Hell below up to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations above, reaching as far as the palace of Māra.
Among these, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are produced by the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Throughout the three periods of time, they serve as the basis for those afflictions;
they are bound and fettered by the heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to that category.
Furthermore, all afflictions within the desire realm have not yet been entirely separated from desire and are not subsumed under the meditative stages (*samāpatti-bhūmi*).
All afflictions of the form and formless realms have, to some extent, been separated from desire.
It is comprised within the stages of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*).
The characteristics of the remaining afflictions should be understood as previously described.
As for the phrase "the realm of form" (*rūpadhātu*):
This refers to the seventeen levels consisting of the four dhyānas along with the intermediate dhyāna.
As for the formless realm,
it refers to the four formless levels, beginning with the sphere of infinite space.
How are the distinctions of temporal periods established?
It is said that within the past, there is that which has ceased immediately without interval,
and there is that which has ceased in close proximity.
There are those that have ceased long ago;
there are those that will arise without interval in the future;
and there are those that are about to arise imminently.
There is that which will arise after a long duration;
in the present world, there is that which is present for a moment and that which is present as a commonality of group (nikāya-sabhāga).
When there is a continuity that has not yet ceased and is present,
how is the distinction of spatial location established?
It is because material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) occupy a specific place.
They possess distinctions of distance, proximity, and location;
however, because formless phenomena lack form,
they have no physical basis or location.
If it arises in dependence upon material phenomena (*rūpadharma*),
then it is said to have a location (*deśa*) therein;
this is due to its characteristic of transformation (*pariṇāmalakṣaṇa*).
Because they do not occupy a fixed location,
material phenomena (rūpa-dharma) possess both [types of causes]. How,
then, is the differentiation of their continuity established?
It should be understood that there are, in brief, four types of continuity (*saṃtati*).
Four types of continuity are established based on the distinctions between one's own and others' faculties and objects.
The first is the continuity of one's own body (*ātma-bhāva-saṃtati*).
Second, the continuity of another's body;
third, the continuity of the sense faculties;
fourth, the continuity of objects.
The second is provisional establishment;
the second is the ultimate meaning.
How are the distinctions of states established?
That is to say: the state of suffering,
the state of pleasure,
and the state of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
That is to say, it refers to all phenomena that accord with the three types of feeling.
How are their categories and distinctions established?
One should know that they are established through the distinction between the two categories of the "antidotes" (*pratipakṣa*) and the "objects to be countered" (*vipakṣa*).
That is to say: defiled and undefiled phenomena;
inferior and superior phenomena;
coarse and subtle phenomena.
Appropriated and non-appropriated phenomena;
material and immaterial phenomena;
visible and invisible phenomena.
Dharmas with resistance and without resistance;
conditioned and unconditioned dharmas;
outflowing and non-outflowing dharmas.
Dharmas with conflict and dharmas without conflict;
dharmas with relish and dharmas without relish;
dharmas based on indulgence and dharmas based on renunciation.
One should know that herein [are contained] mundane and supramundane dharmas,
as well as dharmas that fall within the categories [of grasping] and those that do not.
Defiled phenomena are established by five causes and conditions:
first, because they act as defilements within the three types of sensation according to their respective natures;
second, because they are able to universally encompass the heaviness (*dausthulya*) of all categories of afflictions.
Third, it is because it can universally encompass and bring about undesirable results in both the present life and the future.
Fourth, it is because it can universally link together the continuity of birth.
Fifth, it is because it can universally obstruct all wholesome dharmas as well as the arising of wisdom regarding the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
For this reason, they are called defiled phenomena (*saṃkliṣṭa-dharma*).
One should understand that the characteristics of non-defiled phenomena (*asaṃkliṣṭa-dharma*) are the opposite of these.
These non-defiled phenomena are briefly of two kinds:
namely, wholesome and indeterminate.
This is due to the impurity of putridity and the impurity of afflictions.
It is called "impure" because all sensations within it are entirely suffering; therefore,
it is called "suffering."
Because of its impermanent nature,
it is called "unstable. If,
by such ultimate reasoning, [it is so characterized].
Its nature is impure;
its nature is suffering;
its nature is not solid.
That which is base and impure by nature is called inferior;
one should know that what transcends this is sublime.
Furthermore, the distinction between the two characteristics of the inferior and the sublime exists through mutual dependence.
That is to say, relative to the form realm, the desire realm is inferior;
relative to the formless realm, the form realm is inferior;
and relative to nirvana, all three realms are inferior.
Such categories as these should be understood according to the distinction between the subtle and the manifest,
and the distinction between the pure and the defiled.
One should understand that the establishment of the coarse and subtle aspects of the realms of form (*rūpagati*) is due to differences in their functional efficacy (*śakti-vyāpāra*),
as there are distinctions among their categories such as weak (*mṛdu*) and so forth.
One should understand the establishment of the coarseness and subtlety of all formless phenomena.
Furthermore, because form-possessing and formless phenomena are easy or difficult to comprehend according to the principles of the conventional and ultimate truths, respectively.
One should understand the distinction between the two types, coarse and subtle:
"subtle" refers to an aggregate of atoms,
while "coarse" refers to all other aggregates.
"Purity" refers to the mass of matter belonging to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) or to higher planes;
"impurity" refers to the mass of matter belonging to other existences or to lower planes.
As for the term "dynamic power" (*śakti*):
That is to say, in a place where the power and function of the earth element and so forth are predominant,
although the quantity of the substance may be equal to that of other aggregates,
it is able to surpass the others and be perceived as coarse and manifest.
Regarding the distinction among the categories of weak and so forth:

this refers to the distinctions among the categories of weak, medium, and superior within all phenomena such as the sensations of pleasure and so on, and the mental factors such as feeling and so on. As for "appropriating phenomena":
[it refers to those phenomena which are appropriated].
This means that all material phenomena (rūpa-dharma) are grasped and maintained by the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta).
Because they rely upon those [material phenomena], the mind and mental factors arise; their welfare and peril are identical.
Regarding this identity of welfare and peril:
By the power of the sustaining force of the mind and mental factors,
that matter remains uninterrupted, undestroyed, and uncorrupted;
it is precisely by means of such appropriated matter [that this occurs].
At times there is decline and at times there is benefit;
the mind and its mental factors likewise undergo corresponding decline and benefit.
It is the opposite of this.
It is called "non-appropriated.
As for the term "possessing form," it means that which can be localized in space.
As for the term "formless" (ārūpya),
it means not being dependent on spatial location.
This is established and designated in terms of the objects of perception, the experience [of sensation], and the process of transmigration.
Regarding "that which is visible" (sanidarśana):
it refers to those forms that are capable of being the object of visual consciousness and its basis,
and which are clearly manifest as being here or there.
The opposite of this is called "non-seeing.
As for the term "with resistance" (sapratigha):
That is to say, if various forms can obstruct another's vision or obstruct another's coming and going,
the opposite of this is termed "non-obstructive" (apratigha).
That which is called "conditioned" refers to that which has arising and ceasing and is bound to causes and conditions;
that which is contrary to this is [the unconditioned].
One should know that which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
As for what is called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*),
it refers to those phenomena (*dharma*) that are produced by the various outflows (*āsrava*).
Bound by the heavy burdens of the various outflows,
associated with the various outflows,
and having the various outflows as their object.
It is capable of producing all outflows (*āsrava*) and serves as the basis for outflows in the past, future,
and present; it is the opposite of this.
It should be understood as being untainted (*anāsrava*);
for it serves as the cause of production for the various sufferings of future birth and so forth,
and because it possesses the nature of fault (*sāvadyatva*) within the present life.
That which is called "with contention" is the opposite of this;
that which is the opposite is called "without contention."
Because it follows along with attachment to the self-substance within the internal gate,
it is called "possessing a relishable flavor.
That which is contrary to this is [the opposite].
It is called "lacking relish" because it follows along with attachment to external objects.
It is called "based on indulgence" because of that very attachment.
The opposite of this is called "based on renunciation.
If a phenomenon is with outflows (*sāsrava*), with contention (*saraṇa*), and has a relishable flavor (*āsvādya*), it is based on indulgence (*gardha*).
All such things as these are called "mundane.

Furthermore, the conventional knowledge that arises based on the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) which can counteract these [afflictions], as well as the dharmas induced by it, are also called "mundane."
That which is contrary to this is called supramundane.
If all mundane things are termed "phenomena included within the worldly," [then the supramundane is their opposite].
Because they are included within the world of sentient beings, the vessel-world, and the realms of desire, form, and formlessness;
whereas supramundane phenomena are not included among those that fall [into such categories],
as they do not fall within the aforementioned mundane classifications.
How are the distinctions of reasoning established?
They are the four reasonings:
first, the reasoning of mutual dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*).
2. The principle of logical proof;
3. The principle of functional efficacy;
4. The principle of natural law.
The distinctions among these principles should be understood according to their characteristics as they appear in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
Such are the eightfold categories of distinction.
Furthermore, regarding the alternative formulations, essential characteristics, and distinctions in terminology previously mentioned,
one should understand that they have been correctly and extensively analyzed within all matters as set forth both in detail and in brief.
There is no debate superior to this.
Furthermore, the summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
First, the inclusion of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth; next, the accomplishment and so forth.
Regarding "self-nature, etc., and causes, etc.," the subsequent detailed exposition of the elements (dhātus) and so forth consists of nine groups of phenomena that encompass all dharmas.
What are the nine?
First, the collection of wholesome dharmas;
second, the collection of unwholesome dharmas.
3. The aggregate of indeterminate dharmas;
4. The aggregate of dharmas to be abandoned by vision;
5. The aggregate of dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation.
6. The category of dharmas that are not subject to abandonment;
7. The category of dharmas fixed in wrongness;
8. The category of dharmas fixed in rightness.
The group of nine indeterminate factors and the groups of wholesome and other factors have already had their characteristics fully explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
The aggregate of phenomena to be abandoned by insight refers to all views, as well as greed,
hatred, delusion, and pride that depend upon those views and so forth.
Whether it be karma leading to the miserable realms,
or hesitation and doubt regarding the truths,
or the category of phenomena to be abandoned through cultivation.
This refers to all other dharmas that ought to be abandoned.
As for the aggregate of dharmas that are not to be abandoned,
this refers to untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.
The category of factors fixed in the state of error refers to the immediate karmas and the severance of the roots of goodness.
The category of factors fixed in the state of correctness refers to...
This refers to all dharmas pertaining to those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The category of indeterminate dharmas (aniyata-dharma-rāśi) refers to the remaining dharmas that are neither in training nor beyond training (naiva-śaikṣa-nāśaikṣa).
There is a certain class of persons who do not possess unwholesome states;
namely, those noble ones who have already become free from sensual desire.
Furthermore, with the exception of the seeds of these phenomena,
there may be a certain class of individuals who possess unwholesome and neutral phenomena.
It is not the case that all wholesome dharmas [are absent];
rather, for a person who has severed the roots of virtue, with the exception of the seeds of the dharmas,
there is no possession of either wholesome or unwholesome dharmas.
It is not that non-indeterminate dharmas,
or those that are exclusively unwholesome or exclusively indeterminate, can be obtained. Furthermore,
within this context, one should understand that regarding all dharmas as appropriate, there is either their acquisition or their relinquishment.
That is to say, there is a certain class of persons who,
by virtue of experiencing what is experienced,
or by virtue of relinquishing what is experienced.
Either because of false investigation,
or because of correct investigation,
or because of a transformation of form.
Either by the nature of things,
or through the abandonment of desire,
or by means of preparatory application.
Either due to falling away,
or due to attaining a fruit,
or due to death and rebirth.
Yet there is acquisition and relinquishment,
as in the case of dharmas such as the prātimokṣa restraint;
these are acquired by virtue of undertaking them.
They are abandoned by abandoning those [unwholesome states].
If wholesome dharmas are abandoned due to improper seeking,
they are attained through proper seeking.
Due to the transformation of gender,
one relinquishes either the bhikṣu vows or the bhikṣuṇī vows,
as one or the other is acquired upon the arising of both sexual organs.
Having relinquished everything forever,
by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*),
one is able to enter the meditative absorption obtained through the nature of things at the time of the world's destruction.
Through the abandonment of desire,
one is able to attain all the wholesome dharmas belonging to the higher stages;
this is due to application.
It is able to give rise to those merits induced by that [attainment],
causing them to manifest; however,
this occurs through the process of falling away from it.
One regains the various inferior dharmas of former times; yet,
by virtue of attaining the fruit,
one abandons all worldly dharmas.
One attains supramundane dharmas as well as the subsequently clear and pure mundane wholesome dharmas.
Due to death and birth, at the moment of being born, one acquires the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral dharmas obtained through birth.
When one is born into a higher realm, one acquires only wholesome and neutral dharmas;
whatever [dharmas] were previously abandoned,
these too are accordingly and subsequently realized.
There is no contradiction;
all minds and mental factors are mutually associated and mutually inclusive.
That very momentary formation returns to that same moment;
furthermore, there are no formations of birth and death that can be eternally severed,
nor are there any formations that have never previously arisen which suddenly cause to arise.
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise momentarily;
after the moment of arising, they necessarily do not remain.
All conditioned phenomena undergo a single arising, a single abiding, and a single cessation.
Furthermore, each individual self-nature among all phenomena has no second self-nature that can be found.
Moreover, it is certain that two dharmas of the same kind do not correspond simultaneously.
This is because, according to the second nature, [the self] does not exist;
furthermore, no single dharma possesses two distinct functions characterized by mutual contradiction;
moreover, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) proceed in dependence upon others and do not depend upon themselves.
Furthermore, intrinsic nature does not coexist with intrinsic nature,
nor does it follow after it;
moreover, this very momentary mind does not serve as the object of that same momentary mind.
The intrinsic nature of a single moment serves as its cause;
furthermore, that which arises later does not serve as the cause for what has already arisen,
nor does that which belongs to one category serve as the cause for that which belongs to a different category.
Just as the unwholesome is viewed in relation to the wholesome, and the wholesome in relation to the unwholesome,
so too does the indeterminate function as the cause for the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*).
The summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
First, the various stages and their bases; next, the truths, knowledge, preparatory practices, meditative concentrations, faculties, and paths;
the cultivation of remedial practices consisting of contaminated and uncontaminated dharmas;
and finally, the various fruits and their causal conditions.
Having established the *pudgala*, there are subsequently nine types of ultimate thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
What are these nine?
First, the stage of equipment;
second, the stage of skillful means;
third, the stage of contemplative practice.
4. The stage of seeing;
5. the stage of cultivation;
6. the stage of those in training.
7. The stage of those beyond training (aśaikṣabhūmi).
8. The stage of the noble ones (āryabhūmi).
9. The stage of ordinary beings (pṛthagjanabhūmi).
First, one should accumulate the provisions for transcending the world;
next, one should diligently cultivate skillful means to exhaust the outflows;
and subsequently, when cultivating the levels conducive to penetration, one correctly contemplates the truths.
Next, one is able to realize and enter the state of rightness and freedom from outflows (samyaktva-niyāma).
Thereafter, one gradually realizes the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Among these, the first three belong to the stage of those still in training (śaikṣa-bhūmi).
Its fourth fruit is the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*); having realized the departure from birth, it is the path that gradually ascends through all worldly stages,
termed the "stage of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*),
which comprehensively subsumes the stage of vision (*darśana*).
The stages of those in training and those beyond training are called the stage of the noble ones;
all others besides these are called the stage of ordinary beings,
which refers to those who have not yet cultivated the preparatory application.
For those who have already cultivated the preparatory practices (prayoga) and those who are already free from desire (vītarāga),
all ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) further possess nine bases (niśraya).
One is able to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*).
What are the nine? They are the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*).
Whether it be the first dhyāna,
the intermediate dhyāna,
or the remaining three dhyānas.
And the three formless realms,
excluding the Peak of Existence;
furthermore, there are the four noble truths.
Furthermore, there are ten knowledges that can completely purify the objects of delusion and can awaken one to all objects of knowledge.
That is to say: dharma-knowledge,
subsequent knowledge,
or conventional knowledge.
Whether it be the knowledge of others' minds,
the knowledge of suffering and so forth,
or the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising.
This detailed analysis is as presented in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
Furthermore, there are five types of preparatory application for the yogācāra:
first, that which is intended for the realization of entry into the state of rightness and freedom from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Second, for the sake of attaining the higher fruits;
third, for the sake of progressing toward the abandonment of desire;
fourth, for the sake of transforming the faculties (*indriya*).
The fifth is the inducement of merit.
Furthermore, there are three yogic samādhis:
first, the emptiness samādhi (śūnyatā-samādhi).
Second, the concentration of wishlessness;
third, the concentration of signlessness.
Furthermore, there are three types of faculties for those who are directed toward, abiding in, or have attained the fruit of all practices.
First, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*);
this is the faculty of one who is practicing toward the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala-pratipannaka*).
Second, the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*).
These are the faculties of those from the stage of stream-entry up to those practicing for the fruit of arhatship;
the faculty of one who has perfect knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) is the faculty of one who abides in the fruit of arhatship.
Furthermore, there are nine paths.
What are the nine?
First, the worldly path.
2. The supramundane path;
3. the path of preparation;
4. the uninterrupted path.
Fifth, the path of liberation;
sixth, the path of excellence;
seventh, the inferior path.
The eight paths of medium strength and the nine paths of superior strength constitute the mundane path.
That is to say, by means of this, one is able to realize the abandonment of worldly afflictions,
or fails to realize such abandonment;
and one is able to go to a happy destination or go to an evil destination.
The supramundane path refers to that by which one is able to realize the ultimate abandonment of all afflictions.
The path of preparation refers to...
This means that one diligently cultivates preparatory application (*prayoga*) in order to abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*).
As for the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
it refers to the actual abandonment of the afflictions.
The path of liberation refers to the attainment of liberation through the mind that is immediately subsequent to the abandonment [of defilements].
The path of excellence refers to...
This refers to the initiation of superior application from that point onward.
As for the "inferior path," it refers to that which is able to counteract the superior grade of afflictions.
The medium path refers to that which can counteract medium-grade afflictions;
the superior path refers to...
This refers to that which serves as the antidote to minor afflictions.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of antidotes:
first, the antidote of revulsion and destruction.
Second, the antidote of abandonment;
third, the antidote of support;
fourth, the antidote of distancing.
Furthermore, there are sixteen aspects,
namely contemplating the truths as impermanent and so forth,
as has already been explained previously.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds of cultivation of such remedies with such characteristics;
the manner of this cultivation should be observed as previously described in the *Śrāvakabhūmi* and the *Samāhitabhūmi*.
Furthermore, there are two categories that encompass all phenomena:
first, contaminated phenomena;
second, uncontaminated phenomena.
These two dharmas have already been explained as before;
furthermore, there are five fruits:
first, the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala).
Second, the fruit of outflow;
third, the fruit of disjunction;
fourth, the fruit of human effort.
The fifth is the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Furthermore, there are ten causes:
first, the cause of conventional designation (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*).
2. The dependence cause (apekṣā-hetu);
3. The projecting cause (ākṣepa-hetu);
4. The sustaining cause (parigraha-hetu).
1. The cause of origination;
2. The cause of production;
3. The cause of differentiation.
8. The cause of common purpose;
9. the contradictory cause;
10. the non-contradictory cause.
Furthermore, there are four conditions:
first, the causal condition;
second, the immediately preceding condition.
Third, the object-condition;
fourth, the dominant condition.
Such are all results, causes, and conditions.
As their characteristics have already been explained in such works as the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
there are furthermore seven types of persons (*pudgala*),
namely those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and so forth.
Furthermore, there are six kinds of arhats,
namely those of the nature of falling away (parihāṇadharman) and so forth.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds of persons (pudgala).
This refers to the establishment of those practicing the four paths and those abiding in the four fruits;
it should be understood as described in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*.
Furthermore, there are six kinds of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
First, the thorough knowledge of the truths regarding outflows in the non-concentrated stage;
second, the thorough knowledge of the truths regarding outflows in the concentrated stage;
third, the thorough knowledge of the untainted and unconditioned truths.
Fourth is the thorough knowledge of the untainted conditioned truths;
fifth is the thorough knowledge of the fetters conducive to the lower realms;
sixth is the thorough knowledge of the fetters conducive to the higher realms.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of ultimate attainment:
first, the ultimate attainment of wisdom;
second, the ultimate attainment of abandonment.
The culmination of wisdom refers to the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising.
From this point onward, there is no further need for knowledge in order to abandon the afflictions.
"Ultimate abandonment" refers to the universal and ultimate abandonment of all afflictions;
it is by virtue of that abandonment [that one is so designated].
They have fully and ultimately realized liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.

I humbly observe that as the Sun of the Buddha has set in the west and the Cloud of the True Dharma has faded,
the stream of wisdom has gradually flowed eastward and the teachings of the Elephant Vehicle have just begun to be transmitted.
Thus, rare omens of the age have appeared, and profound meanings have been proclaimed throughout the land of Jambudvīpa.
This most extraordinary treasure, reaching the utmost profundity, ascends to the Dragon Palace;
drawing from its deep source, it crosses the violent river and journeys afar.
Its mysterious interstices emerge from the dilapidated dwelling and gallop onward for eternity.
Dharma Master Xuanzang was a dragon-elephant of the Śramaṇa gate and a crane among the birds of the land of dawn.

Surpassing all in his vigor, he exerted himself in his studies; he brought back Sanskrit texts from afar and, having recently completed this work, it is now being circulated for the benefit of the local realm.
Throughout my life, I have been fortunate enough to hear the True Dharma.
Yet, as one whose cultivation was perhaps insufficient and whose innate nature incomplete,
I now exhaust these meager emoluments to transcribe this profound doctrine.
Every fragment of a word and every single character has been engraved upon my heart and mind;
having personally received the oral instructions, I hope there shall be no further divergence from the truth.
I dedicate this merit to bring blessings to Emperor Taizong Wenhuang.
Thereupon, the Emperor, kings, dukes, ministers, and officials, along with their six types of relatives and kinsmen,
as well as all the common people— whether moving on feet or dwelling in flight or pecking— shall together cultivate and practice this with impartiality.
By relying upon this superior foundation, they shall ascend to Perfect Enlightenment.

On the eighteenth day of the seventh month in the tenth year of Tenchō, the year being *kichi* (癸丑), the donor, the Buddha-teacher Myōkōshō, whose nature is endowed with the characteristics of both form and essence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), and who possesses a mind of joy in awakening and other such states, makes this vow: With distinct discernment regarding form, through the power of reflection, hearing, and the majesty of the Pratyekabuddhas, he [addresses] the worlds, the realms of the gods, the Nirmāṇarati, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin, the Brahmā, and the Akaniṣṭha heavens. For the benefit of himself and others, he is bound to the Dharma; he expounds the treatises on the severing and casting out of worldly objects, the mastery of the precepts, the maturation of the precepts, the benefits of diligence, and the contemplation that takes precedence. He teaches the selflessness of phenomena as the path, possessing wisdom that well understands various royal affairs and worldly duties, and the sharp intelligence that exhorts others. Regarding the fetters of the desire realm, the discursive thoughts of ordinary beings, the suffering of the world, the provisions for the journey, and the application of effort, he universally embraces the station of yoga that dwells in the signless (*animitta*). Thus, the various establishments of the stages of practice and the dharmas of those stages are fully encompassed.
